The commissioners refused to consider the collateral agreement, believing it outside their cognizance, and adjudged liability on the undisputed endorsement. Knowing the commissioners' position, the agent paid the whole £6 into court on all four notes, and Macferlan withdrew it under their order. At the later trial the material facts and Moses's entitlement on the merits were undisputed.
sections.Issue: Could Moses recover the money in the general action for money had and received, although there was no actual agreement to refund and the money had been paid under the judgment of a competent court, or was he confined to a special action on the indemnity agreement?
sections.Holding: The Court of King's Bench, in 1760, in an expressly unanimous opinion delivered by Lord Mansfield, held that the general action was maintainable. The absence of an actual agreement to refund did not defeat it: an obligation arising from natural justice could support a legally implied debt and recovery as though upon a contract. The court allowed Moses to waive the broader indemnity demand and recover the £6, and directed the postea to the plaintiff.
sections.Reasoning:
Macferlan argued that assumpsit required a debt or an actual contract, that no promise to refund could be inferred from an adverse judgment, and that a new action could not correct a competent court's judgment. Mansfield answered that assumpsit was available both where debt would lie and where it would not, and that the obligation here was one imposed by law.

The court described the recoverable categories as including payments by mistake, on a failed consideration, or obtained by imposition, extortion, oppression or undue advantage. It distinguished payments the recipient could in conscience keep despite a legal obstacle to enforcement, such as time-barred debts, infancy debts and money fairly lost at play.

On finality, Mansfield accepted that a competent court's judgment is conclusive on its subject matter until reversed or set aside, and that the King's Bench could not reopen the merits decided by the commissioners. Moses's action accepted the endorsement liability and relied on the separate indemnity, which the commissioners had declined to entertain. The question was whether Macferlan could keep the proceeds consistently with that collateral undertaking.

The general count let the plaintiff prove the special circumstances at trial, while the defendant could raise equitable defenses under the general issue and recovery could not exceed the money received and justly owing. Choosing this route barred another action on the indemnity. The court relied on Dutch v. Warren to show that a special agreement did not exclude money had and received.

CP-062.rule: Under the theory-of-the-pleading approach, a complaint is judged by the cause of action it was designed to state, and a count framed as conversion that omits an element of conversion cannot be saved by treating it as one in contract.

sections.Parties: The plaintiffs, Jones and others, alleged that they had hired Winsor as their attorney and sued him for $1,000 with interest that they said he wrongfully kept. Winsor, the defendant, demurred to the complaint and was the appellant in the South Dakota Supreme Court.
sections.Procedural History: Winsor demurred for failure to state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action. The circuit court overruled the demurrer, and he appealed. The South Dakota Supreme Court reversed the order overruling the demurrer.
sections.Material Facts:
The plaintiffs alleged that they hired Winsor as an attorney to obtain a Sioux Falls city-railway franchise in April 1907. They gave him $2,500 for the required deposit with the city treasurer and a further $130 for efforts to secure the franchise. When the franchise was not granted, the treasurer returned the deposit to Winsor for the plaintiffs' benefit. Winsor furnished an account listing disbursements, charged $1,250 for professional services, and remitted a draft for $1,012.25.

The plaintiffs alleged that reasonable compensation was no more than $250, that $1,000 remained due, and that the excess charge was unjust, unlawful and fraudulent. They repeatedly alleged wrongful conversion and demanded judgment for wrongful conversion of $1,000 with interest from April 17. These were allegations taken on demurrer, not findings.
sections.Issue: Where a single count mixes a contract demand for money had and received with repeated allegations of conversion but omits an allegation needed for conversion, may the court disregard the conversion allegations as surplusage and sustain the complaint as one in contract?
sections.Holding: The South Dakota Supreme Court, in 1908, in an opinion by Justice Corson, held that it could not. Construed as conversion, the complaint lacked the necessary allegation that the plaintiffs owned or possessed the property at the time of the alleged conversion, and the pervasive and deliberate conversion allegations could not be ignored so as to preserve the pleading as money had and received. The court did not determine the reasonable fee, order repayment, or establish tort liability.
sections.Reasoning:
The court agreed with Winsor that a conversion complaint needed an allegation of ownership or possession at the time of the conversion; an earlier description of the deposit as money belonging to the plaintiffs did not supply it.

The complaint also appeared to state a contract demand, and the plaintiffs asked that the references to fraudulent conversion be disregarded. The court refused because the count had been framed with a double aspect: its financial account resembled assumpsit, while its repeated accusations and its prayer for judgment presented conversion. A defendant should be able to identify the legal controversy from the complaint, not wait until trial to learn which of several inconsistent theories the proof would support.

The court relied on the Wisconsin decisions Pierce v. Carey and Supervisors of Kewaunee County v. Decker, which distinguished simplifying the forms of action from leaving the nature of the action uncertain. Abolishing the common-law forms did not allow tort, contract and equity theories to be fused into one uncertain count.

The court also rejected the plaintiffs' reliance on Revised Code of Civil Procedure § 157(2), on arrest in actions involving an attorney's receipt or misuse of money in a fiduciary capacity: there was no allegation of embezzlement or fraudulent misapplication, and the real dispute was over the reasonable value of professional services.

The brief notes that the case illustrates the restrictive theory-of-the-pleading approach under this historical code and does not apply modern federal alternative-pleading rules.

CP-063.rule: Waiving a tort and suing on an implied promise may avoid the shorter tort limitation period, but it does not make an amendment adding new defendants relate back, and it cannot create liability in a successor state agency that has no authority to be sued.

sections.Parties: Garrity, the owner of a farm in Wallace County, Kansas, was the plaintiff and the appellant. He sought the value of a fossil, alleged to be $2,500, that he said had been taken from his land. The original defendant was the state board of administration of educational institutions, which had replaced the University of Kansas board of regents under a 1913 statute. He later added the administration board's members, E. W. Hoch, Ed T. Hackney and Mrs. Cora Lewis, and the former regents' trustees, Frank Strong and Rodney A. Elward.
sections.Procedural History: Garrity filed his original petition on June 9, 1914, naming only the state board of administration. On November 2, 1914, he added the board's members and the former regents' trustees as defendants. The defendants demurred, the demurrer was sustained, and Garrity chose to stand on his petition and appealed. The Kansas Supreme Court affirmed the judgment sustaining the demurrer.
sections.Material Facts:
These are the allegations of the petition, not facts established at a trial. In July 1911 the University of Kansas board of regents, acting through its assistant curator of mammals, entered Garrity's Wallace County farm without his knowledge or permission, removed a valuable fossil, placed it in the university museum for exhibition and scientific use, and paid nothing. Garrity put its value at $2,500. The district judge described the dispute as one over the value of an eighteen-million-year-old lizard.

The board of regents had been a statutory corporation. The 1913 legislation abolished it and transferred management of the educational institutions to a new state agency, the board of administration, which received no corporate powers. Garrity alleged that the new board succeeded to the former board's rights, obligations, debts and contracts. His original petition was filed before three years had passed from the July 1911 taking; the amendment naming the former regents came after the three years had expired.
sections.Issue: Whether the petition could be construed as a claim on an implied promise so as to escape the two-year tort statute of limitations; whether the amendment adding the former regents related back to the original filing so as to avoid the three-year limitation on unwritten contracts; and whether the successor board of administration could be sued for the former board's alleged wrong.
sections.Holding: The Kansas Supreme Court, in 1917, in an opinion by Justice Porter in which all the Justices concurred, affirmed. If the petition stated an actionable claim at all, its allegations were sufficient to permit an implied-contract theory, so the two-year tort statute did not bar the action. The claim against the former regents, who were added after three years, was barred by the three-year limitation on unwritten contracts, because a suit against one defendant does not suspend limitations against another. The board of administration, a state agency given no corporate powers and no express authority permitting suit, could not be sued for the former regents' alleged wrong.
sections.Reasoning:
On the first point, the court relied on decisions directing that the whole petition be considered, especially its leading allegations, and favoring a contract construction where the averments leave the choice doubtful. Garrity could therefore waive the tort and seek the fossil's value on an implied promise to pay. That ruling did not establish that any particular defendant actually owed the implied obligation.

On the second point, Garrity argued that the original implied-contract petition tolled the three-year period and that the amendment related back to commencement. The court rejected this even assuming the facts otherwise disclosed a claim against the former regents. A lawsuit naming one defendant does not suspend limitations against another person simply because its allegations could support liability against that person. Before the amendment no action against the former regents was pending, and by the time they were made defendants the bar had attached. The court applied Kansas law, not the later Federal Rule 15. This discussion comes from the full opinion and is omitted from the assigned excerpt.

On the third point, the new board's authority included managing university property, disbursing appropriations, investing or spending designated funds, and executing trusts or obligations committed to the institutions. The court refused to read that administrative authority as making the board or its members liable for a tort committed by the former regents, and waiving the tort and pleading an implied promise could not create such liability. The university and its managing board were state agencies established for education and administration; without express authority permitting suit, and with no corporate powers conferred on the new board, the action could not be maintained. The court did not find that the removal was lawful or that the fossil lacked value.

CP-064.rule: Under the Federal Rules a complaint need only give a short and plain statement showing entitlement to relief under Rule 8(a); the old formulation requiring facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action is not the governing pleading formula.

sections.Parties: John Dioguardi, representing himself with limited English, was the plaintiff and the appellant. He sought $5,000 plus interest and costs from Harry Durning, individually and as Collector of Customs at the Port of New York, the defendant. The United States Attorney moved to dismiss the complaint. The claim arose from Dioguardi's attempts to import medicinal tonics from Italy.
sections.Procedural History: The district court dismissed the original complaint on the United States Attorney's motion, reasoning that it failed to state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action, but granted leave to amend. Dioguardi amended, repeated his grievances, and challenged the disappearance and sale more emphatically. The district court dismissed again on the same ground and entered a final judgment. Dioguardi appealed to the Second Circuit, which reversed the judgment and remanded the action for further proceedings consistent with its opinion.
sections.Material Facts:
Dioguardi's pleading was difficult to follow, but the court could identify two central grievances: two cases of bottles disappeared before the customs sale, and the remaining merchandise was sold to another bidder at Dioguardi's own bidding price. These were allegations, not findings.

The initial complaint alleged that two cases, each containing nineteen bottles, disappeared three weeks before the October 9, 1940 auction, and that the goods were sold to someone else for $110 despite that person's $120 bid. The amended pleading referred instead to two cases containing thirty-seven bottles and named Springdale Distilling Company as the purchaser. The opinion preserves those uneven statements without resolving the discrepancy. The defendant reportedly explained that the goods had leaked, which Dioguardi disputed because of the way they were bottled.

The court inferred that an earlier dispute with the consignor concerned whether further payment was due, and that the collector held the goods for about a year before selling them as apparently unclaimed merchandise. Dioguardi maintained that he had complied with the revenue laws and had already paid substantial amounts in Italy.
sections.Issue: Did Dioguardi's imperfect allegations disclose a claim sufficient to survive a motion directed solely at the face of the complaint, when the district court had dismissed for failure to state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action?
sections.Holding: The Second Circuit, 1944, in an opinion by Judge Clark for a panel that also included Judges Swan and Augustus N. Hand, held that the allegations were sufficient. Under the Federal Rules the controlling question was whether a short and plain statement showed entitlement to relief under Rule 8(a), and whether a claim upon which relief could be granted had been stated under Rule 12(b). The old formulation requiring facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action was not the governing pleading formula. The judgment was reversed and the action remanded. Dioguardi obtained another opportunity to litigate, not a damages award or a finding that Durning was liable.
sections.Reasoning:
Neither the district court's unexplained conclusion nor the government's assertion that a cursory examination would vindicate it supplied a reason why the discernible claims could not proceed.

Two claims were sufficient. First, the complaint could reasonably be understood to allege that the collector converted or otherwise disposed of two cases of tonics. Second, it alleged a sale inconsistent with the public auction the collector announced and that the customs statute and regulations required. The court added that collectors could be personally responsible for default or negligence in performing their duties, which gave substance to the effort to sue Durning individually.

The auction allegation admitted more than one reading; perhaps the only problem was a failure to collect an additional ten dollars from Springdale. But with reasonable inferences drawn in Dioguardi's favor on a pleading motion, he appeared to claim that he was the first bidder at the actual sale price and should have received the goods.

Durning had chosen a motion confined to the pleading, so the allegations and reasonable inferences had to be accepted. He could instead develop his factual position through a pretrial hearing or a summary-judgment motion supported by affidavits. The decision thus relocated factual testing to a suitable procedure rather than immunizing an unsupported claim.

The court noted further possible grievances about improper cataloguing, a claimed right to buy at a catalogue discount, and interference with an alleged agreement to deliver the goods on payment, and left their substance to the district court. It also strongly advised Dioguardi to obtain competent legal help if he faced summary judgment. No separate opinion is reported.

CP-065.rule: A complaint must contain sufficient factual matter, accepted as true, to make entitlement to relief plausible; for a Sherman Act § 1 conspiracy claim, parallel conduct plus an unsupported assertion of agreement does not suffice.

sections.Parties: William Twombly and Lawrence Marcus sued as representatives of a proposed class of local-telephone and high-speed-internet subscribers. The defendants, petitioners in the Supreme Court, were incumbent regional telephone carriers, including the Bell Atlantic successor Verizon, BellSouth, Qwest, and SBC. The subscribers alleged that an agreement among the carriers kept prices above competitive levels.
sections.Procedural History: The Southern District of New York dismissed under Rule 12(b)(6), concluding that parallel conduct was consistent with independent efforts to preserve each carrier's market position and that the complaint supplied no additional facts suggesting concerted action. The Second Circuit reversed. It understood Conley v. Gibson to permit dismissal only when no possible set of supporting facts could establish that the parallel conduct resulted from agreement. The Court granted certiorari to determine the pleading standard, reversed the Second Circuit, and remanded for proceedings consistent with its opinion. It held that the complaint must be dismissed; it did not adjudicate the truth of the alleged agreement.
sections.Material Facts:
The 1984 breakup of AT&T produced regional local-service monopolies. The Telecommunications Act of 1996 sought to introduce competition by requiring incumbent carriers to share their networks with new competitors and permitting competition in additional markets. Those statutory obligations and the carriers' historically separate territories were the setting for the alleged conspiracy.

The complaint alleged two related forms of parallel behavior: each incumbent impeded new carriers trying to use its network, and the incumbents refrained from entering one another's territories. The plaintiffs also relied on industry contacts and a carrier executive's reported comments about entering another incumbent's territory. From this they inferred a concerted market-allocation arrangement. These were allegations tested on a dismissal motion; there was no trial finding that the carriers had agreed.
sections.Issue: Does a Sherman Act § 1 complaint state a claim under Rule 8(a)(2) when it alleges parallel anticompetitive behavior and a conclusory agreement, without factual context plausibly suggesting that the defendants acted pursuant to an agreement?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States, 2007, in an opinion by Justice Souter for seven Justices. A complaint must contain sufficient factual matter, accepted as true, to make entitlement to relief plausible. Detailed evidentiary pleading is unnecessary, and plausibility does not require showing that liability is more likely than not. For a § 1 conspiracy claim, the pleaded circumstances must suggest agreement and give a reasonable expectation that discovery will reveal evidence of it; parallel conduct plus an unsupported assertion of conspiracy is not enough. This complaint failed because the conduct was naturally explained by each incumbent's independent interests. The Court rejected Conley's no-set-of-facts formula as the minimum pleading threshold.
sections.Reasoning:
First, the cause of action requires concerted conduct. Independent conduct, even knowingly parallel conduct by firms that understand their mutual interests, does not itself establish a § 1 agreement. Because the pleaded behavior could arise from either independent decisions or agreement, the complaint needed a factual setting supporting the latter inference.

Second, Rule 8 requires a showing of entitlement, not labels or a recitation of elements. A court accepts factual allegations even when their truth is doubtful, but need not treat an unsupported legal conclusion as a pleaded fact. Read in context, the complaint derived its allegations of agreement from the parallel behavior it had described.

Third, each carrier already had an incentive to resist competitors and preserve its regional dominance, and the historical monopoly arrangement independently explained staying out of neighbors' territories.

Fourth, the majority weighed the unusually broad and costly discovery threatened by nationwide, multiyear antitrust litigation. It reasoned that summary judgment and case management could not reliably prevent defendants from settling weak claims to avoid those costs, so the plausibility threshold screens claims before discovery.

Finally, Conley's language, read literally, could let a wholly conclusory complaint proceed because unknown evidence might later emerge. The Court kept flexibility in proving an adequately stated claim and declined to impose Rule 9-style particularity on all claims.

Justice Stevens dissented, joined by Justice Ginsburg except as to Part IV. He would have accepted the allegation of agreement as an allegation of conduct, argued that the majority revived unstable distinctions between facts and conclusions, and proposed answers, targeted discovery, case management, and summary judgment instead of dismissal.

CP-066.rule: Under Rule 8, in all civil actions, a court disregards legal conclusions and unsupported recitations of elements and asks whether the remaining factual allegations, taken as true, plausibly support entitlement to relief.

sections.Parties: Javaid Iqbal, a Pakistani Muslim detained after September 11, sued federal officials for damages. The petitioners were former Attorney General John Ashcroft and FBI Director Robert Mueller. Many other officials were defendants below, but only the sufficiency of the claims against these two petitioners was before the Supreme Court.
sections.Procedural History: The Eastern District of New York denied Ashcroft and Mueller's motion to dismiss, which asserted qualified immunity. The Second Circuit affirmed on an interlocutory appeal. The Court accepted review and held that the court of appeals had jurisdiction, because the appeal presented a legal question about whether the pleaded conduct stated a constitutional violation sufficient to overcome qualified immunity. The Court reversed the Second Circuit and remanded, leaving the court of appeals to decide initially whether to remand to the district court so that Iqbal could seek leave to amend.
sections.Material Facts:
Iqbal was arrested in November 2001 on identification-document fraud and conspiracy charges. He was initially held in the general population at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, then placed in its highly restrictive administrative maximum-security unit after officials classified him as a detainee of high interest. He later pleaded guilty, served his sentence, and was removed to Pakistan.

The complaint alleged that FBI officials detained numerous Arab Muslim men, classified some as being of high interest because of protected characteristics rather than evidence of terrorist involvement, and subjected them to harsh confinement. It alleged that Ashcroft and Mueller approved restrictive detention pending FBI clearance and knowingly created or condoned a discriminatory policy. Allegations of abuse by guards concerned other defendants and were not the claims decided here. These were pleadings, not findings established at trial.
sections.Issue: Does Rule 8 require factual allegations plausibly showing that these particular supervisory officials purposefully discriminated, and did Iqbal's allegations satisfy that requirement? Do Rule 9(b)'s provision for alleging intent generally, the non-antitrust setting, or proposed discovery restrictions alter the answer?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States, 2009. Justice Kennedy wrote for the Court, joined by Chief Justice Roberts and Justices Scalia, Thomas, and Alito. A complaint must contain factual matter that, taken as true, plausibly supports entitlement to relief; courts need not accept legal conclusions or unsupported recitations of elements. Plausibility requires more than a sheer possibility of liability but is not a probability requirement, and this reading of Rule 8 applies across civil actions. These officials could not be liable merely because of their supervisory positions; each must be responsible through his own misconduct, and the discrimination theory required purpose, not mere knowledge of a subordinate's discrimination. The complaint did not plausibly allege that Ashcroft and Mueller themselves adopted the classification because of race, religion, or national origin.
sections.Reasoning:
First, the majority classified the assertions that petitioners knowingly and maliciously imposed confinement solely because of protected characteristics as conclusory recitations of discriminatory purpose. It withheld the presumption of truth because they were conclusory, not because it thought them fantastic.

Second, it accepted the allegations that the FBI detained Arab Muslim men and that petitioners approved highly restrictive detention until clearance. It reasoned that a security investigation offered an obvious alternative explanation, and that the pleaded approval did not itself plausibly establish a deliberately discriminatory classification policy.

Third, Twombly was not limited to antitrust, because it interpreted Rule 8, which governs civil pleading generally. Rule 9(b)'s permission to allege mental states generally relaxes the particularity requirement for fraud and mistake; it does not dispense with Rule 8's requirement of factual support.

Fourth, anticipated discovery management did not cure the complaint. The majority stressed qualified immunity's protection against litigation burdens and reasoned that high-level officials might have to participate even in discovery aimed first at lower-level defendants.

The Court assumed without deciding that the particular First Amendment claim could proceed under Bivens.

Justice Souter dissented, joined by Justices Stevens, Ginsburg, and Breyer. He objected that petitioners had conceded liability based on actual knowledge and deliberate indifference and that the majority rejected that concession without full briefing. Reading the complaint as a whole, he found that it described a particular discriminatory policy and linked petitioners to it. Justice Breyer separately dissented, arguing that sequenced discovery and other case-management tools had not been shown inadequate to protect officials.

CP-067.rule: When a plaintiff relies entirely on a unified fraudulent course of conduct, the claim as a whole sounds in fraud and must satisfy Rule 9(b)'s particularity requirement, even if fraud is not an element of the claim.

sections.Parties: William Kearns was the plaintiff in a proposed class action and the appellant. He alleged that Ford Motor Company, the defendant and appellee, and its dealers persuaded consumers to pay a premium for certified pre-owned vehicles by misrepresenting the value of certification. Kearns sought relief under California's Consumers Legal Remedies Act and Unfair Competition Law; Ford maintained that the claims were founded on fraud and lacked the required particulars.
sections.Procedural History: Kearns filed a proposed class action in California state court. Ford removed it under the Class Action Fairness Act's diversity provision, 28 U.S.C. § 1332(d), and Kearns unsuccessfully sought remand under the local controversy exception. An amended complaint was dismissed with leave to amend, and a second amended complaint was dismissed under Rule 9(b). The third amended complaint was again dismissed with leave to amend, and the district court also struck its first footnote. Kearns elected not to amend further, the court dismissed the case, and he appealed. The Ninth Circuit reviewed the Rule 9(b) dismissal de novo and affirmed. It did not reach the challenge to striking the footnote, which dismissal of the entire complaint made moot.
sections.Material Facts:
Ford's certified pre-owned program covered late-model used vehicles. Ford represented that inspection and certification made them safer, more reliable, and more roadworthy than ordinary used vehicles, and sold them at a premium. Ford charged participating dealers an annual fee and a fee for each vehicle, supplied marketing and instructional materials, and advertised nationally; dealers handled sales and service locally.

Kearns alleged that the resulting consumer reassurance cost $1,080 and was worth less than that premium. He disputed the quality of vehicle-history reports, technician training, and inspection, and alleged inadequate disclosure of Ford's limited oversight. These were the complaint's assertions, not findings.

Kearns said national television advertising, dealership sales materials, and dealership personnel led him to buy a certified vehicle. He did not specify the contents or timing of the advertisements and materials, identify those he regarded as material, or explain which sales materials he relied on. He alleged being told that certified vehicles were selected and rigorously inspected and carried a Ford-backed extended warranty, but did not identify the speaker or the time.
sections.Issue: Does Rule 9(b)'s particularity requirement apply in federal court to claims under California's consumer statutes that rest on an alleged fraudulent scheme, including allegations framed as nondisclosure or as an unfair business practice, and did Kearns's complaint satisfy it?
sections.Holding: The Ninth Circuit, 2009, in an opinion by Judge N. Randy Smith for a panel with Judges Pregerson and Hall, affirmed the dismissal. Kearns's complaint rested on a unified fraudulent scheme but did not identify the circumstances of the alleged deception with the particularity Rule 9(b) requires. Calling the scheme an unfair business practice, or describing part of it as nondisclosure, did not remove the defect. Federal law governs how the circumstances of fraud must be pleaded in federal court, even on state-law claims. The decision concerns the adequacy of the allegations, not whether Ford's certification program delivered its advertised benefits.
sections.Reasoning:
The court distinguished Rule 8's short and plain statement from Rule 9(b)'s particularity requirement for circumstances constituting fraud. Fraud need not be an element of a statutory claim for Rule 9(b) to apply. Where a complaint mixes fraudulent and nonfraudulent conduct, only the fraud averments get heightened treatment; deficient ones are stripped out and the rest is assessed under Rule 8. But when a plaintiff relies entirely on a unified fraudulent course of conduct, the whole claim sounds in fraud. Omitting the word fraud does not change the substance.

Particularity means identifying who committed the misconduct, what happened, when and where, and how it was fraudulent. That gives defendants meaningful notice, restrains complaints used to discover unknown wrongs, protects reputations, and prevents substantial litigation costs without an adequate factual basis.

California supplied the elements of fraud, but the Federal Rules governed pleading regardless of the basis of jurisdiction, so state consumer statutes did not import California pleading standards. The court distinguished Swierkiewicz as concerning claims without fraud or mistake.

Applying this, Kearns alleged a coordinated effort to misrepresent certification benefits but gave no particulars of the advertisements, materials, speaker, or time, so Ford could not respond to particular misconduct. The nondisclosure theory, which Kearns rested on Vess, did not save a separate claim: the pleaded omissions were part of an alleged intent to conceal that certified vehicles were essentially ordinary used vehicles, and so were fraudulent in substance. The court did not hold that every omission in a consumer complaint is fraud. Although unfairness is a distinct Unfair Competition Law theory, this complaint relied on one fraudulent course of conduct across its theories, so no separate unfairness analysis was required. No separate writing appears.

CP-068.rule: Under the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act, the inference of scienter must be cogent and at least as compelling as any plausible opposing inference drawn from the alleged facts, considered collectively.

sections.Parties: Purchasers of Tellabs stock, including Makor Issues & Rights, brought a proposed investor class action. Tellabs manufactured equipment for fiber-optic networks; Richard Notebaert was its chief executive officer and president during the relevant period. Tellabs and Notebaert sought Supreme Court review of the ruling allowing the scienter allegations to proceed. Claims against other executives were not before the Court.
sections.Procedural History: The Northern District of Illinois dismissed the initial complaint without prejudice for insufficiently particular pleading. After amendment, it dismissed with prejudice: the alleged misleading statements were adequately specified, but scienter was not sufficiently pleaded. The Seventh Circuit reversed in relevant part, reasoning that the complaint could proceed if a reasonable person could infer the necessary intent from the alleged facts, and it declined to weigh competing innocent inferences. The Court granted review of that standard, vacated the Seventh Circuit's judgment, and remanded for reexamination under the standard it specified. It did not itself decide whether the complaint satisfied that standard.
sections.Material Facts:
The investors alleged that Notebaert misrepresented demand for the existing TITAN 5500 product, the readiness of and demand for the new TITAN 6500, the company's financial results, and its projected revenues. They also alleged that unwanted inventory was pushed onto customers to inflate results. According to the complaint, he knew the favorable public statements did not reflect the company's actual condition. These remained allegations, not findings of fraud.

The proposed class purchased stock between December 11, 2000, and June 19, 2001. After progressively more cautious disclosures, Tellabs sharply reduced its revenue projections and disclosed reduced demand, and its share price fell substantially. The amended complaint relied on 27 confidential sources and added particulars bearing on Notebaert's knowledge. The investors did not allege that Notebaert sold shares during the class period.
sections.Issue: Under the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act's requirement of particular facts supporting a strong inference of the required mental state, must a court compare the inference of scienter with competing nonfraudulent explanations, and how strong must the inference be?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States, 2007. Justice Ginsburg wrote for the Court, joined by Chief Justice Roberts and Justices Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, and Breyer. The inference of scienter must be cogent and at least as compelling as any plausible opposing inference drawn from the alleged facts; a merely reasonable or permissible inference is insufficient. The court accepts the factual allegations as true, considers them collectively with permissible Rule 12(b)(6) materials, and compares the culpable and nonculpable explanations. An equally compelling inference can satisfy the standard, and the inference need not be irrefutable. The Seventh Circuit's standard was too lenient because it omitted the required comparison.
sections.Reasoning:
The statutory word requiring a strong inference would add little if any rational inference of intent were enough. An inference's strength depends on the alternatives supported by the same facts, so a plausible inference of misconduct may still fail when a more compelling innocent explanation emerges from the allegations.

The assessment must also be holistic. Courts consider the entire complaint, incorporated documents, and matters properly subject to judicial notice, rather than demanding that each allegation independently establish scienter. The majority treated this as consistent with both screening weak suits and letting meritorious investor claims proceed.

Motive matters, but its absence is not automatically fatal. Tellabs stressed that the investors did not allege Notebaert sold shares during the class period; the majority refused to make that omission dispositive. Ambiguities and missing particulars can weaken the inference, but their weight is assessed against all the allegations together.

The Court also rejected the Seventh Circuit's jury-trial concern. Congress can define the pleading conditions for a federal statutory claim; once they are met, the jury keeps its role in resolving factual disputes and credibility. The Court did not decide whether or when recklessness suffices as scienter.

Justice Scalia concurred in the judgment but would have required the inference of scienter to be more compelling than the inference of innocence, and criticized reliance on committee reports. Justice Alito concurred in the judgment, agreeing with Scalia's threshold and arguing that only allegations pleaded with particularity should count. Justice Stevens dissented, preferring a probable-cause approach, and would have affirmed.

CP-070.rule: A complaint that shows an intended claim the defendant can reasonably understand survives a motion to dismiss even if imperfectly stated, and a conditional privilege must be raised as an affirmative defense, while an absolute privilege disclosed by the complaint bars the claim.

sections.Parties: Garcia, a citizen and resident of Puerto Rico, was the plaintiff. He sued Hilton Hotels International, a Delaware corporation and his former employer, for defamation. Hilton, the defendant, moved to dismiss for failure to state a claim and, alternatively, to strike paragraphs 5 through 8 of the complaint and to obtain a more definite statement.
sections.Procedural History: Garcia sued in the local District Court of Puerto Rico, and Hilton removed the case to federal court. The complaint contained two causes of action with identical paragraphs pertinent to the motions. Hilton moved to dismiss, to strike, and for a more definite statement, and the parties agreed at the hearing to strike paragraph 9. District Judge Roberts denied the motion to dismiss, granted the motion to strike paragraphs 5 through 8, struck paragraph 9 by agreement, and required a more definite statement concerning paragraph 4. All rulings applied to the second cause of action as well. This was a pleading decision; neither side received a final judgment on the defamation claim.
sections.Material Facts:
Paragraph 4 of the complaint alleged that Hilton discharged Garcia on August 22, 1950, while falsely accusing him of bringing women into hotel rooms for prostitution. It did not expressly say that the alleged slander was published to another person.

Later paragraphs alleged that Garcia sought severance pay and overtime through the Puerto Rico Labor Department, that Hilton repeated the accusation at the department's hearing, and that his compensation claim was later compromised.

Hilton argued that the complaint did not allege publication and that the accusation was conditionally privileged. Puerto Rico's 1902 defamation statute protected communications in legislative or judicial proceedings and other proceedings authorized by law. The Labor Department hearing was authorized by the 1949 labor-enforcement statute, which charged the commissioner with investigating complaints and provided compulsory processes for obtaining evidence.
sections.Issue: Did the defamation complaint state a claim despite not expressly alleging publication and despite a possible conditional privilege? Should the allegations about the repeated accusation at the Labor Department hearing be stricken as privileged, and was paragraph 4 definite enough to require an answer?
sections.Holding: The United States District Court for the District of Puerto Rico, 1951, District Judge Roberts. The court denied dismissal: paragraph 4 showed an intended publication claim that Hilton could reasonably understand, and a conditional privilege did not conclusively defeat the pleading but had to be asserted as an affirmative defense. The court struck paragraphs 5 through 8 as redundant because the accusation at the Labor Department hearing was absolutely privileged. It granted the Rule 12(e) request for a more definite statement because paragraph 4 left unclear the substantial words of the alleged slander and the facts establishing publication.
sections.Reasoning:
The court applied the liberal pleading approach of the time. Rule 8(a) required a short and plain statement showing entitlement to relief, not the former formula demanding facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action. Reading the complaint favorably, the court asked whether evidence within its framework could establish a claim, relying on Dioguardi and other authorities favoring testing the merits after answer and proof.

Paragraph 4 did not expressly allege publication, but its description of a discharge accompanied by a false and slanderous accusation showed an intended publication claim, and Garcia could potentially introduce evidence of publication at trial. The claim was imperfectly stated but need not be dismissed.

On privilege, the court distinguished absolute privilege, which can bar an action when disclosed by the complaint, from conditional privilege, which can be lost through abuse or actual malice. Even assuming a conditional privilege covered the discharge communication, factual questions remained about abuse or malice.

The hearing communication was different. The court understood the Puerto Rico statute's protection for proceedings authorized by law as absolute, and the Labor Department hearing was such a proceeding. Effective labor-law enforcement required participants to supply information freely, and courts elsewhere protected statements to bodies exercising quasi-judicial powers. Alleged malice could not remove that protection. The original discharge accusation was not treated as privileged merely because it was later repeated at the hearing.

Finally, surviving dismissal did not make paragraph 4 definite enough to answer. The words used and the facts of publication mattered to preparing a response asserting conditional privilege, so clarification was required.

CP-071.rule: To satisfy plausibility under Rule 8, a plaintiff must supply enough case-specific detail to tell a coherent story and identify the nature and grounds of the claim; plausibility is not a more-likely-than-not test.

sections.Parties: Gloria Swanson, proceeding without counsel, was the plaintiff and appellant. She alleged that Citibank, appraiser Andre Lanier, and his employer PCI Appraisal Services, the defendants, discriminated against her because she was African-American when she applied for a home-equity loan. She also named her husband Charles Routen as plaintiff and appellant, but she could not represent him without counsel, so the court dismissed him as a party on appeal and addressed only her claims.
sections.Procedural History: Swanson's amended complaint invoked the Fair Housing Act and the Equal Credit Opportunity Act. The district court dismissed the discrimination claims, relying heavily on Latimore v. Citibank, a decision about the evidence needed to survive summary judgment. It initially allowed a liberally construed fraud theory to proceed, then dismissed that as well because the statements were too indefinite and reliance unreasonable. On appeal Swanson pursued only the Fair Housing Act and fraud claims, so the Equal Credit Opportunity Act dismissals were outside the appeal. The Seventh Circuit reversed dismissal of the Fair Housing Act claims against all three defendants and affirmed dismissal of the common-law fraud claims against all three. Each side bore its own appellate costs.
sections.Material Facts:
The court accepted the pleaded events as true without finding discrimination as a fact. In February 2009, encouraged by Citibank's announcement of loans funded through the federal Troubled Assets Relief Program, Swanson applied for a home-equity loan. A bank representative, Skertich, said her husband had to participate because they jointly owned the house; she suspected a discouragement tactic. A manager warned that Citibank used stricter loan criteria than other banks. She disclosed that Washington Mutual had previously denied her a home-equity loan.

When she returned with the application information, Skertich said answering the race question was optional and mentioned that his wife and son were part African-American. Citibank conditionally approved a $50,000 loan, initially using her estimate that the house was worth $270,000. Lanier's appraisal valued it at $170,000, and Citibank denied the loan because the assumed valuation was not met. Two months later, an appraisal Swanson paid Midwest Valuations to perform valued the house at $240,000.

She alleged that the defendants deliberately depressed the appraisal to avoid lending to an African-American applicant. She did not identify an out-of-pocket loss from applying, such as an application fee or an appraisal charge imposed by Citibank.
sections.Issue: After Twombly and Iqbal, did Swanson's allegations of race discrimination in a specific loan and appraisal transaction state a plausible Fair Housing Act claim under Rule 8, and did her fraud allegations satisfy Rule 9(b) and the applicable substantive damages rules?
sections.Holding: The Seventh Circuit, 2010, in an opinion by Judge Wood joined by Chief Judge Easterbrook, with Judge Posner dissenting in part. The panel divided 2 to 1 in holding that the Fair Housing Act claims against Citibank, Lanier, and PCI were sufficiently pleaded: a plaintiff must supply enough case-specific detail to tell a coherent story and identify the nature and grounds of the claim, and Swanson identified the asserted discrimination, the actors, and the early-2009 transaction. All three judges joined in affirming dismissal of the fraud claims, which did not allege actual reliance damages. The housing claims could proceed, but there was no finding of discrimination and no damages award.
sections.Reasoning:
Judge Wood accepted that Twombly had retired the idea that any imaginable set of facts consistent with a pleading sufficed. The question was how to reconcile plausibility with Rule 8's short and plain statement, Erickson's fair-notice reasoning, and the distinction between Rule 8, Rule 9, and specialized statutory pleading rules. The court refused to read the Supreme Court's decisions as silently restoring code fact pleading.

Plausibility did not mean deciding which account was true, applying a more-likely-than-not test, or preferring the plaintiff's inference only if more compelling than the defendant's. Complex allegations could demand more explanation; straightforward discrimination allegations could suffice with less. The majority drew support from Twombly's favorable treatment of Swierkiewicz. Concerns about expensive, asymmetric discovery did not authorize substituting a different regime for Rule 8.

The Fair Housing Act covers racial discrimination in residential real-estate transactions, including secured loans and appraisals. Against Citibank, the specifics identified her case, and her added account of federal funding, the prior denial, and Skertich's family did not plead her out of court. Against Lanier and PCI, she alleged deliberate race-based undervaluation in a specific appraisal by appraisers who knew her race. The majority warned that merely showing different appraisal values would not be enough at summary judgment; the district court's reliance on Latimore confused an evidentiary requirement with a pleading requirement.

The fraud claims failed because she alleged no out-of-pocket loss from applying and no adequate reliance on the appraisal.

Judge Posner would also have affirmed dismissal of the housing claim. He read Iqbal to apply to uncomplicated discrimination cases and to require attention to obvious innocent explanations. Swanson already owed $146,000 on the house, so the loan would have been undersecured at the $170,000 appraisal, and appraisal error and tightened credit were ready nondiscriminatory explanations.

CP-072.rule: Under Rule 8(b) an answer must admit or deny each portion of every allegation or state a genuine lack of knowledge after reasonable inquiry, and it may not decline to respond because an allegation states a legal conclusion.

sections.Parties: Dr. Susan Kegerise, formerly superintendent of Susquehanna Township School District, was the plaintiff. She sued the district and school-board members Carol Karl, Jesse Rawls, Sr., and Mark Sussman, the defendants, mainly challenging her alleged discharge as violating federal and state law. On this motion she sought judgment on the pleadings on six counts; the defendants resisted, arguing among other things that allegations stating legal conclusions required no response.
sections.Procedural History: The case was before the Middle District of Pennsylvania on the defendants' responses to Kegerise's third amended complaint. Kegerise moved under Rule 12(c) for judgment on the pleadings on Counts II, III, IV, VIII, IX, and X. In a memorandum of February 3, 2016, Judge William W. Caldwell agreed that many responses were inadequate but did not deem the challenged allegations admitted or award judgment. Instead the court would issue an order requiring an amended answer complying with Rule 8(b), permitted under Rule 15(a)(2). This brief covers only that answer-amendment ruling, not the lawsuit's final employment disposition.
sections.Material Facts:
Kegerise's strategy was to identify insufficient responses under Rule 8(b), have the corresponding allegations deemed admitted, and use those admissions to establish entitlement to judgment.

Three kinds of response were challenged. First, some answers responded to only part of an allegation. Paragraph 48 alleged a teacher's transfer, Rawls's intervention against the administration's decision, and his approach to a union president urging a grievance; the answer admitted the transfer and denied attempted intervention but did not respond about the union president.

Second, the defendants declined to respond to allegations on the ground that they stated legal conclusions, invoking the part of Rule 8(b)(6) that treats allegations as denied or avoided when no responsive pleading is required. Most of those allegations applied law to facts; some were purely legal, including an abstract statement of the elements of procedural due process.

Third, the defendants professed lack of knowledge about allegations that Rawls approached a union official, visited schools without advance notice, and prompted an investigation into purported nepotism.
sections.Issue: Were the defendants' partial responses, refusals to answer allegations characterized as legal conclusions, and professions of lack of knowledge adequate under Rule 8(b), and if not, should the allegations be deemed admitted and judgment on the pleadings granted?
sections.Holding: The United States District Court for the Middle District of Pennsylvania, 2016, Judge Caldwell. Many of the responses were inadequate under Rule 8(b): each portion of an allegation must be admitted or denied, an answer cannot avoid responding by calling an allegation a legal conclusion, and a professed lack of knowledge must satisfy honesty and reasonable inquiry. The court nevertheless did not deem the allegations admitted or grant judgment on the requested counts; it required an amended answer curing the deficiencies. Not every challenged response was defective: the court found paragraph 93 adequately answered and excepted paragraph 102 from the required amendment.
sections.Reasoning:
Rule 8(b) requires a party to admit or deny the allegations against it. A general denial is proper only if the party in good faith intends to deny everything; otherwise it must identify what it denies. When only part of an allegation is disputed, the answer must admit the true part and deny the rest. A genuine lack of sufficient knowledge or information has the effect of a denial. When a responsive pleading is required, an allegation other than the amount of damages is admitted if not denied.

First, partial responses must address the whole allegation. A denial of one portion did not silently deny everything else. The court required each portion to be admitted or denied; it did not instruct the defendants to deny all unanswered matter, because any true portion still had to be admitted.

Second, the provision the defendants invoked distinguishes pleadings that require a response from those that do not. An answer to the third amended complaint was required, so the provision did not exempt selected allegations within it merely because they involved law. If anything, failing to deny them would engage the admission rule. The court extended this to allegations consisting purely of law. The only recognized responses were admission, denial, or a proper statement of insufficient knowledge.

Third, Rawls's personal knowledge should permit answers about his own actions, and information about the investigation could be obtained with reasonable effort from district records. A party cannot use Rule 8(b)(5) to avoid information it possesses or could reasonably obtain. The court allowed a response explaining vagueness if paragraph 30 was too vague.

The court declined to decide the adequacy of responses saying that a document speaks for itself, because Kegerise identified no particular response on that ground.

CP-073.rule: Leave to amend under Rule 15(a) is to be freely given when justice requires, and the party opposing amendment bears the burden of showing prejudice, assessed in the particular circumstances rather than assumed whenever an admission is withdrawn.

sections.Parties: Jerry Beeck and his wife Judy were the plaintiffs and appellants. They sued Aquaslide 'N' Dive Corporation, the sole named defendant and the appellee, alleging that it made the water slide on which Jerry was injured. They sought damages under negligence, strict-liability, and implied-warranty theories, with a combined demand of $2,225,000. Aquaslide sought leave to amend its answer to deny that it manufactured the slide.
sections.Procedural History: District Judge Hanson permitted Aquaslide to amend its answer over the plaintiffs' objection. He then granted Aquaslide's request for a separate jury trial on whether the company designed, manufactured, or sold the slide. The jury found for Aquaslide, and the court entered summary judgment dismissing the case. The plaintiffs appealed both discretionary decisions; the jury's nonmanufacture finding itself was not challenged. The Eighth Circuit reviewed for abuse of discretion, considering the record as it stood when the amendment was allowed, and affirmed the district court's judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
Jerry Beeck suffered severe injuries on July 15, 1972, while using a water slide at a social gathering sponsored by his employer, Harker Wholesale Meats, at Kimberly Village in Davenport, Iowa. Kimberly Village had ordered an Aquaslide product in 1971 through local distributor George Boldt. The order traveled through Sentry Pool and Chemical Supply to Purity Swimming Pool Supply, whose warehouse delivered a slide that Kimberly's employees installed. It resembled an Aquaslide and lacked identifying marks.

Investigators for the employer's insurer, Kimberly's insurer, and Aquaslide's insurer all concluded that Aquaslide manufactured the slide. Aquaslide received notice of the accident in October 1972, and its insurer inspected the site in May 1973. Relying on these investigations, the company admitted manufacture in its December 12, 1973 answer and repeated the admission in June 3, 1974 interrogatory answers.

The two-year Iowa limitations period for the personal-injury claim expired July 15, 1974. About six and a half months later, Aquaslide's president and owner, Carl Meyer, inspected the slide before his deposition and concluded that it was not Aquaslide's product. Aquaslide then sought leave to amend its answer to deny manufacture. The plaintiffs continued to assert that the slide was Aquaslide's.
sections.Issue: Did the district court abuse its discretion by allowing Aquaslide to amend its answer to withdraw its admission of manufacture after the limitations period had expired, and by ordering a separate trial on the question of product identity?
sections.Holding: The Eighth Circuit, 1977, in an opinion by District Judge Paul Benson, sitting by designation, for a panel with Circuit Judges Bright and Henley, held that granting leave to amend was not an abuse of discretion and that ordering a separate trial on manufacture under Rule 42(b) was not an abuse of discretion either. The district court's judgment was affirmed, so the dismissal following the unchallenged jury finding that Aquaslide did not manufacture the slide stood. The court did not hold that the slide was safe or that the plaintiffs were barred from every conceivable claim against other parties.
sections.Reasoning:
Rule 15(a) directs courts to give leave freely when justice requires. Foman v. Davis recognized grounds that may justify refusal: undue delay, bad faith, dilatory motive, repeated failed amendments, undue prejudice, and futility. The plaintiffs, as the parties opposing amendment, bore the burden of showing prejudice.

The district court examined good faith, diligence, and prejudice. Aquaslide had relied on three independent insurers' investigations, and nobody contended that it had manipulated their conclusion. The court found no bad faith sufficient to prevent a trial on identity, regarded responsibility for the initial identification as shared, and found that the company and its carrier were not so lacking in diligence as to lose the right to contest manufacture.

On prejudice, the plaintiffs argued that expiration of the limitations period made the amendment fatal to their suit. But to accept that, the district court would have had to assume both that Aquaslide would win the identity issue and that no claim against anyone else remained possible. The record did not justify both assumptions at that stage. If another slide had been substituted in the distributor chain, fraud or contract claims might have different unexpired limitations periods, and equitable estoppel might affect a limitations defense. Refusing amendment could impose liability on a company without letting it prove it did not make the product.

On the separate trial, Rule 42(b) authorizes separate trials for convenience, economy, expedition, or avoidance of prejudice while preserving the jury-trial right. Product identity was potentially dispositive. Proof of Beeck's severe injuries could take several days and could prejudice the jury's consideration of the nonmanufacture defense. The plaintiffs still received a jury determination of identity. No separate opinion is reported.

CP-074.rule: The verification requirement for shareholder derivative actions does not justify dismissing a bona fide complaint because the shareholder does not personally understand it, when she verified it in good faith reliance on careful investigation by trusted advisers and counsel.

sections.Parties: Dora Surowitz was a shareholder in Hilton Hotels Corporation who brought a derivative action alleging injury to the corporation; she was the plaintiff and the petitioner. The defendants included corporate officers and directors accused of enriching themselves through transactions harmful to Hilton. Surowitz sought review after her action was dismissed because she could not personally explain its allegations at her deposition.
sections.Procedural History: Before requiring the defendants to answer, the district court permitted them to depose Surowitz. They then moved to dismiss on the grounds that the pleading was a sham and that she was not a proper plaintiff. Despite supplemental affidavits, the district court treated her verification as false and a nullity and dismissed with prejudice. The Seventh Circuit affirmed, while acknowledging the seriousness of the allegations and the substantial investigation. The Court granted review, reversed, and remanded to the district court for proceedings on the merits.
sections.Material Facts:
Surowitz was a Polish immigrant with little formal education and limited English. She had invested slightly more than $2,000 of her savings in Hilton stock on the advice of her son-in-law, Irving Brilliant, an investment adviser trained in law and economics. When she received a notice concerning Hilton's proposed repurchase of its stock, she asked him to explain it. He and lawyer Walter Rockler investigated for months before recommending suit.

The complaint alleged that insiders used stock purchases at inflated prices to transfer corporate money to themselves, through both Hilton's repurchase of its own shares and its purchase of shares in an affiliated credit corporation. These were unproved fraud allegations. Rockler signed the lengthy complaint under the version of Rule 11 then in force. Surowitz verified it, partly on information and belief, after Brilliant read and explained it to her.

At her deposition, Surowitz could not explain the legal relationships, transactions, defendants, or detailed allegations. She did know that she owned the stock, that dividends had stopped, and that her trusted adviser believed management had harmed the corporation. Affidavits from Rockler and Brilliant described their extensive investigation and the basis for filing.
sections.Issue: Did the verification requirement for shareholder derivative actions compel dismissal with prejudice because the shareholder did not personally understand the complaint, when she authorized the suit in good faith on advice grounded in an extensive investigation?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States, 1966, in an opinion by Justice Black. On this record, the verification requirement did not justify summary dismissal. A shareholder's limited personal comprehension did not nullify a bona fide derivative complaint based on reasonable beliefs arising from careful investigation by trusted advisers and counsel. The Court read the rule in light of its purpose of discouraging abusive suits while preserving legitimate protection for shareholders. It reversed and remanded for proceedings on the merits; the asserted fraud had not been proved, and the decision restored the lawsuit rather than awarding recovery.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority examined the complete record rather than the deposition in isolation. Surowitz's inability to describe complex transactions was consistent with her limited language and financial knowledge. Her reliance on Brilliant was understandable, and his and Rockler's affidavits supplied a substantial investigative basis for the complaint. The verification reflected good-faith reliance, not evidence that the claims were knowingly invented.

The Court distinguished this action from a suit filed without regard to truth merely to pressure management into paying a settlement. Surowitz sought to protect her actual investment, and her adviser's longstanding family investments also supported the conclusion that this was not an effort to harm the corporation through a baseless claim. The rule's anti-abuse purpose therefore did not support excluding her simply because she lacked sophisticated personal knowledge.

The majority stressed the Federal Rules' role in letting genuine disputes reach fair adjudication. Reading verification as an absolute financial-literacy requirement would create a procedural obstacle for precisely the small investors derivative litigation could protect. The Court reserved whether a different record of false verification could ever justify dismissal; it did not eliminate verification or approve sham pleadings generally. The opinion addresses former Rule 23(b)'s derivative-action verification requirement, which the casebook places with Rule 23.1.

Justice Harlan concurred on a narrower ground: the rule required an oath but did not specify that the shareholder personally had to supply it, and Rockler's affidavit was an adequate verification by counsel in these circumstances. Chief Justice Warren took no part in the consideration or decision, and Justice Fortas took no part in the decision. No dissent is printed with the opinion.

CP-075.rule: Under the 1993 version of Rule 11, sanctions sought by a party require a separate motion served twenty-one days before presentation to the court, giving a safe harbor to correct or withdraw, and a lawyer may rely on objectively reasonable client information.

sections.Parties: George Hadges, a harness driver, trainer, and owner, was the plaintiff and appellant. He sued Yonkers Racing Corporation (YRC), the defendant and appellee, in an independent action seeking relief from a 1990 judgment on the ground of fraud on the court. His lawyer, William Kunstler, was censured by the district court and challenged that censure on appeal. YRC had requested sanctions against them.
sections.Procedural History: In 1990 a federal court granted YRC summary judgment on Hadges's § 1983 due process claim because YRC's conduct was not state action, and that judgment was affirmed. A 1992 New York state action alleging blackballing and other claims failed, and a separate federal action against the state-run Meadowlands, begun in 1993, settled. Hadges then brought this independent action for relief from the 1990 judgment. YRC requested sanctions inside its dismissal papers. The district court denied relief, fined Hadges $2,000 under Rule 11 for misrepresentation, and censured Kunstler for inadequate investigation and failure to disclose the pending state litigation. The Second Circuit affirmed the denial of Rule 60(b) relief and reversed both the sanction on Hadges and the censure of Kunstler.
sections.Material Facts:
Hadges's state racing license, first issued in 1972, was revoked in 1974, restored in 1976, and suspended for six months in 1989. After reinstatement in September 1989, YRC independently denied him permission to work at its track. In the 1990 litigation YRC manager Galterio stated that other regional tracks remained available. Meadowlands manager Garland later explained that a 1992 resolution made exclusion at another track a basis for exclusion there, and Hadges argued this exposed Galterio's statement as fraud on the court.

In this action Hadges said he had not worked for more than four years. YRC produced records of five races at Monticello in 1991 and seven in 1993; he then admitted those appearances in an affidavit sworn twelve days after the sanctions request, explaining their minimal earnings. He also supplied an undated scratch sheet to support an alleged 1989 exclusion by state racing judges; YRC showed it concerned a 1987 event. Hadges corrected the date, and Kunstler said he had not known it was wrong.

YRC sought sanctions within its dismissal papers, not by a separate motion served twenty-one days before presentation to the court. The 1993 amendment to Rule 11 had taken effect five days before the complaint was filed and fifteen days before the request.
sections.Issue: Did Hadges show fraud on the court sufficient to support an independent action for relief from the 1990 judgment? Could Rule 11 sanctions be imposed on Hadges and his lawyer when YRC had not complied with the 1993 rule's separate-motion and safe-harbor requirements, and did the lawyer have adequate evidentiary support?
sections.Holding: The Second Circuit, 1995, in an opinion by Judge Feinberg for a panel with Judges Kearse and Altimari, with no separate writing. The court affirmed the denial of relief from the 1990 judgment, because the asserted fraud did not approach the serious impairment of adjudicative integrity that fraud on the court requires. It reversed the $2,000 sanction on Hadges and the censure of Kunstler: the unsuccessful merits claim did not justify disregarding the 1993 rule's separate-motion, safe-harbor, notice, and evidentiary-support requirements. Hadges did not obtain a new adjudication of his exclusion from Yonkers Raceway.
sections.Reasoning:
More than one year had passed since the judgment, foreclosing a motion under Rule 60(b)(3), but the rule's savings clause preserved an independent action for fraud upon the court. That category is narrower than ordinary fraud on an adversary. Reviewing for abuse of discretion, the court found no adequate showing. Meadowlands adopted its resolution and excluded Hadges in 1992, after the 1990 litigation; Galterio denied contrary knowledge; and one state track's later reliance on a private track's decision did not establish concerted blackballing. The action was not frivolous, but relief was properly denied.

On sanctions, the 1993 amendment governed. YRC's request was not a separate motion and gave no twenty-one-day safe harbor. That mattered concretely, because Hadges admitted the Monticello racing and corrected the scratch-sheet date promptly; a proper correction opportunity could have avoided the sanctions. The district court also relied on an allegedly unwarranted disqualification motion, but the amended rule prohibited monetary sanctions against a represented party for that legal-contention violation. Nor could the result be recast as court-initiated, since the court said it acted on YRC's request and court initiation required a specific show-cause order.

Kunstler likewise lacked the safe harbor. On the substance, a lawyer may rely on objectively reasonable client information, assessed in context. He had the client's sworn account, the undated scratch sheet, another lawyer's affidavit, and his own experience litigating the Meadowlands exclusion, and much of the material dating the scratch sheet belonged to YRC. Nondisclosure of the state case was an improper ground: the court's own notice of potential sanctions omitted it, though disclosure would have been wiser. The trial judge's remarks also appeared personally directed at Kunstler and activist lawyers.

CP-076.rule: Under the Kansas real-party-in-interest statute, once an insurer has fully paid a loss the subrogated claim belongs wholly to the insurer, which must bring the action in its own name; the insured cannot sue for the insurer's benefit.

sections.Parties: Ellis Canning Company was the plaintiff and the appellant. It sued International Harvester Company, the defendant and appellee, for negligence in its own name, expressly for the use and benefit of Potomac Insurance, which had insured and fully paid the loss. International Harvester denied negligence and asserted that Potomac, not Ellis, was the real party in interest.
sections.Procedural History: Ellis sued International Harvester in a Kansas trial court. The answer denied each alleged negligent act but admitted the allegations about insurance, the amount of loss, and full payment, and its third paragraph asserted that Potomac was the real party in interest and that Ellis lacked the right to maintain the action. Ellis moved to strike that paragraph and demurred to it, arguing that it stated neither a sufficient defense nor facts showing that Ellis was an improper plaintiff. The trial court denied both challenges, and Ellis appealed those rulings. The Kansas Supreme Court affirmed. There had been no factual determination of negligence and no award of damages.
sections.Material Facts:
Ellis Canning alleged that International Harvester negligently started a fire while servicing Ellis's tractor, causing $479.79 in damage. Potomac Insurance insured the loss under a policy containing a subrogation clause and paid the loss in full. Ellis then sued International Harvester in Ellis's own name, expressly for the use and benefit of Potomac.

Negligence remained disputed, but the procedural issue rested on agreed pleadings about payment and subrogation. Both parties agreed that the sole issue on appeal was whether an insured already reimbursed for its entire loss could nonetheless sue in its own name for the insurer's benefit. Kansas General Statutes 1949, § 60-401 required prosecution in the name of the real party in interest, subject to exceptions the court said did not apply here.
sections.Issue: May an insured that has been fully reimbursed for its property loss by its insurer maintain a negligence action against the alleged wrongdoer in its own name for the insurer's benefit, consistently with the Kansas statute requiring prosecution in the name of the real party in interest?
sections.Holding: The Kansas Supreme Court, 1953, in an opinion delivered by Justice Parker, held that it may not. After an insurer has fully paid a property loss, the insured cannot maintain a negligence action in its own name for the insurer's benefit under § 60-401; the insurer holds the entire claim and may and must bring the action if it is to be maintained. The answer's allegations therefore supported the real-party-in-interest defense, and the trial court correctly refused both the motion to strike and the demurrer. The judgment was affirmed. The court gave no ruling on an insurer that pays only part of a loss.
sections.Reasoning:
Full payment mattered because Ellis no longer had a direct interest in recovering compensation for the loss. The subrogated reimbursement claim belonged wholly to Potomac. Merely declaring that the lawsuit was for Potomac's benefit did not make Ellis the holder of the claim or satisfy the statute's direction about the name in which the action must proceed.

The difficulty lay in precedent rather than in the facts. Earlier Kansas cases, including Railroad Co. v. Insurance Co. and Klingberg, treated the insurer as the sole real party in interest after full reimbursement. But Hume v. McGinnis and City of New York Insurance Co. v. Tice had allowed the insured to sue for the insurer's benefit, so Ellis could point to existing language supporting its choice of plaintiff. The court acknowledged the conflict.

It chose the rule followed in its more recent Campbell, Hill, and Mehl decisions: full reimbursement leaves the insurer with the entire claim against the alleged wrongdoer. The court declined a detailed effort to distinguish or harmonize the inconsistent cases. It expressly overruled Hume and disapproved whatever in Tice could be understood to permit an insured owner whose loss had been fully paid to maintain the action for the insurer's benefit.

The report contains no separate writing. The casebook's later questions about Federal Rule 17 are editorial context, not holdings of this decision.

CP-077.rule: Under the Kansas code, causes of action arising from the same transaction may be joined in one petition even though they fall in different categories, such as injury to the person and injury to character.

sections.Parties: James Avery was the plaintiff in the district court. He sued John Harris, the defendant, in a petition pleading false imprisonment and slander arising from one encounter in Fort Scott. Harris demurred on the ground that the petition improperly joined several causes of action, and after the demurrer was overruled he sought correction of that ruling in the Kansas Supreme Court.
sections.Procedural History: Avery filed a petition in the district court pleading false imprisonment and slander, and expressly alleging that both claims arose from the same transaction. Harris demurred on the ground that the petition improperly joined several causes of action. The district court overruled the demurrer, and Harris sought appellate correction of that ruling. The Kansas Supreme Court affirmed the order overruling the demurrer. Avery could proceed with the combined petition, but he had not yet won a judgment establishing the alleged torts or awarding damages.
sections.Material Facts:
Avery alleged that Harris encountered him in Fort Scott, called him a thief in front of others, accused him of possessing a stolen horse, took that horse and kept it for four or five days, and arrested and confined him with felons in the county jail for approximately the same period. The pleaded detention involved no process. The court recounted these allegations only to decide a pleading objection; it did not decide whether the accusation was true or whether Harris owed damages.

Section 89 of the Kansas code permitted legal and equitable causes to be joined within listed classes, including causes arising from the same transaction or transactions connected with the same subject of action. Harris's objection depended on a distinction between injuries to the person, to which false imprisonment belongs, and injuries to character, to which slander belongs.
sections.Issue: May claims for false imprisonment and slander be joined in one petition under the Kansas code's same-transaction provision, even though one is an injury to the person and the other an injury to character and they could not have been joined under the common-law forms of action?
sections.Holding: The Kansas Supreme Court, 1869, in an opinion by Justice Valentine in which all the justices concurred, held that false imprisonment and slander could be joined because the petition showed that they arose from the same transaction. The order overruling Harris's demurrer was affirmed. The court thought it debatable whether the facts even made up more than one cause of action under the code, but because nobody asked it to resolve that question it assumed two causes of action for purposes of deciding joinder.
sections.Reasoning:
The court acknowledged that the distinct categories of injury to the person and injury to character might prevent joining the claims if they arose from unrelated transactions. But the same-transaction category supplied an independent basis for joinder. The accusation, the taking of the horse, and the detention were parts of one episode.

Justice Valentine reviewed the common-law rules to show why they were a poor guide to the code. Joinder had depended heavily on the form of action, the pleas available, and the judgment to be entered. Claims classified together could sometimes be combined though they arose at different places and times, while injuries from a single encounter could be separated if their forms differed.
