CP-107.rule: After adequate time for discovery, a summary-judgment movant need not negate an element on which the opponent bears the trial burden; it may point to the absence of supporting evidence in the record, and the opponent must then designate specific facts showing a genuine issue.

sections.Parties: Myrtle Nell Catrett, administratrix of the estate of her husband Louis H. Catrett, was the plaintiff. She sued fifteen corporations that allegedly manufactured or distributed asbestos products responsible for his death. Celotex Corporation was one defendant and the petitioner in the Supreme Court; it had won summary judgment in the district court. Catrett was the respondent, defending the court of appeals' reversal of that summary judgment.
sections.Procedural History:
Catrett filed her complaint in September 1980. Celotex first sought summary judgment in September 1981; the dissent describes an earlier motion that was withdrawn and later renewed. In July 1982 the District Court for the District of Columbia granted the defendants' pending motions, including Celotex's, stating that exposure to Celotex products had not been shown in the District of Columbia or elsewhere within the statutory period. Catrett appealed only the judgment for Celotex.

A divided D.C. Circuit panel reversed, reading Rule 56 and Adickes v. S. H. Kress & Co. to require Celotex to support its motion with evidence negating exposure before Catrett had to respond; it did not reach the adequacy or admissibility of her materials. Judge Bork dissented. The Supreme Court granted review to resolve a circuit disagreement about the movant's burden, and reversed and remanded.
sections.Material Facts:
Louis Catrett died in 1979. His widow's complaint alleged negligence, breach of warranty and strict liability arising from asbestos exposure. To recover against Celotex she needed proof connecting him to its products. Celotex moved for summary judgment on the ground that she had failed in discovery to identify a witness who could testify to that exposure. Its motion included no affidavit affirmatively establishing that no exposure had occurred. The motion came about a year after the action began, and discovery had occurred.

Catrett identified three documents supporting exposure in Chicago in 1970-1971: her husband's deposition from a workers' compensation proceeding, a letter from an official of a former employer, and an insurer's letter to her attorney. The casebook identifies the product as Firebar, made by a Celotex predecessor, and the employer as Anning-Johnson. The employer's official, T. R. Hoff, was a potential trial witness. Celotex contended that the documents were inadmissible hearsay. According to Justice Brennan's dissent, Catrett had supplied the documents in response to the earlier motion and Celotex knew of them when it renewed its motion.
sections.Issue: When the opposing party will bear the burden of proof at trial on an essential element, must a party moving for summary judgment submit affidavits or other affirmative evidence disproving that element? What must the movant identify, and what response is then required of the opponent?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States, in 1986, in an opinion by Justice Rehnquist for himself and Justices White, Marshall, Powell and O'Connor, held that no affirmative negation is invariably required. After adequate time for discovery, a party that fails to make a sufficient showing on an essential element on which it bears the trial burden may face summary judgment. The movant must identify the basis for its motion and the parts of the record showing the absence of a genuine material dispute, and may do so by pointing out the absence of evidence. The opponent must then identify specific facts beyond the pleadings. The Court reversed and remanded without deciding whether Catrett's actual showing sufficed. Justice White concurred; Justice Brennan, joined by Chief Justice Burger and Justice Blackmun, and Justice Stevens dissented.
sections.Reasoning:
The trial burden explains the result. If Catrett had to prove exposure to a Celotex product and could produce no sufficient evidence of it after discovery, disputes about other matters would not make a trial necessary. Rule 56's text refers to affidavits "if any" and allows motions with or without supporting affidavits; depositions, interrogatory answers and admissions can show that the opponent lacks evidence. The movant still bears an initial responsibility to identify what the motion challenges and the supporting parts of the record. A motion can be properly supported under Rule 56(e) by the existing record without a new affidavit, and the nonmovant cannot then rest on the complaint.

The opponent need not produce material in the form that would be admissible at trial; the question includes whether the material can support admissible proof, so the form of Catrett's documents was not conclusive. Adickes did not require the categorical rule adopted below, and the 1963 amendment did not enlarge the movant's burden. Adequate opportunity for discovery mattered, with then-Rule 56(f) protecting against premature motions. Summary judgment lets parties show before trial that a claim or defense lacks factual support.

Justice White, concurring, stressed that a conclusory assertion of no evidence is insufficient and that a movant cannot ignore an identified witness. Justice Brennan agreed that affirmative negation is not always required, but said a movant relying on insufficiency must engage with supporting evidence already in the record; because Celotex's renewed motion overlooked the documents and Hoff, he would have affirmed. Justice Stevens would have affirmed on the narrower ground that the motion addressed only exposure within the District of Columbia; the majority read the district court's ruling as reaching other locations.

CP-108.rule: A judgment entered on proof after a defendant who has answered fails to appear at trial is a judgment on the merits, not a default judgment, so the notice of application for default required by Rule 55(b) does not apply.

sections.Parties: Paul Smith was the plaintiff, suing Nicholas Coulas and William Bray on an open account and a promissory note. Bray denied liability and crossclaimed against Coulas. Coulas answered both the complaint and the crossclaim and counterclaimed against Smith for $18,000. Coulas, against whom judgment was entered when he did not appear at trial, moved to vacate the judgment and was the appellant.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court heard evidence on December 10, 1958, in the absence of Coulas and his counsel, and entered judgment on December 11, 1958. Smith obtained judgment against Coulas on both counts and against Bray on the note, and Bray obtained judgment against Coulas on the note. On October 29, 1960, nearly two years later, Coulas moved to vacate. The superior court denied the motion and he appealed. The Supreme Court of Arizona, sitting en banc, affirmed the denial of the motion to set aside and vacate the judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
Smith sued Coulas and Bray on an open account for $669.32 and a promissory note with an alleged balance of $3,666.67. Bray crossclaimed against Coulas for any amount Smith recovered against him, an alleged $4,000 debt, and $500 in attorney fees. Coulas answered the complaint and the crossclaim and asserted an $18,000 counterclaim, to which Smith replied, so the pleadings put the claims in dispute.

The court first set trial for October 10, 1958. On October 6 counsel for Smith and Bray stipulated to December 10, and the court reset the trial. Coulas's counsel neither attended nor joined that stipulation. The court's records showed notification to all counsel, but Coulas and his lawyers denied receiving notice of the new date, and neither appeared on December 10. The court heard evidence, including Bray's testimony and the promissory note. Its minute entry used the word default but also recorded a trial on the issues and evidence. Coulas argued that the judgment was void because he had not received the three-day notice of an application for default judgment that Arizona Rule 55(b) requires for a party who has appeared.
sections.Issue: Did the absence of the notice required for an application for default judgment invalidate a judgment entered after a defendant had answered but failed to attend trial?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of Arizona, in 1964, in a unanimous opinion by Chief Justice Udall in which Justices Lockwood, Struckmeyer, Bernstein and Scruggs concurred, held that it did not on this record, because the judgment was a judgment on the merits following proof, not a default judgment under Rule 55. Default under Rule 55 concerns failure to plead or otherwise defend. Once Coulas answered on the merits, his denial required proof of the claims against him, and his failure to attend trial did not turn the denial into an admission. At most the judgment was voidable, not void, so the six-month limit of Arizona Rule 60(c) barred the attack.
sections.Reasoning:
The plaintiffs could proceed in Coulas's absence but still had to prove their claims, and the judgment that resulted from that hearing lay outside Rule 55(b)'s notice requirement. Calling the event a default in a minute entry did not change its legal character. The court relied on Bass v. Hoagland and Klein v. Rappaport, both of which distinguish a pleading default from nonattendance after the case is at issue. The phrase otherwise defend covers preliminary defensive steps, such as jurisdictional attacks or motions, that prevent default without an answer; it does not require a party who has answered to be present at every trial call to avoid confessing the complaint.

In a part of the opinion omitted from the assigned excerpt, the court addressed Phoenix Metals Corp. v. Roth, on which Coulas relied for the statement that notice is required before a default judgment against a party who has answered. That case involved an answer mistakenly attached to the wrong file. To the extent its language suggested that default was appropriate after an answer on the merits, the court called the implication incorrect; the proper route is proof and a merits judgment.

Coulas's objection to the stipulation resetting trial failed because setting trial is the court's function under Rule 40, and he had an opportunity to object to the court's order. His claim of missing notice lacked support in the minutes, and the court presumed that the clerk performed the duty to notify under Rule 77(h) absent a contrary showing; attending on the original date would also have revealed the change. The court did not treat an actual failure of notice, adequately shown on another record, as categorically immaterial. The conclusions arise under the Arizona rules as they stood in 1964.

CP-109.rule: When legal and equitable claims in one action share common factual issues, the court's discretion over the order of trial must be used to preserve the jury right on the legal claim, which can be lost through a prior equitable determination only in the most imperative circumstances.

sections.Parties: Beacon Theatres, the operator of a new drive-in theater, was the defendant in the underlying action, asserted an antitrust counterclaim and cross-claim for treble damages, demanded a jury, and was the petitioner for mandamus. Fox West Coast Theatres, operator of a competing first-run theater, had begun the underlying action for declaratory and injunctive relief. Another theater operator intervened and was the target of Beacon's cross-claim. District Judge Harry C. Westover was the respondent because Beacon sought to control his proposed trial procedure; he was not a party to the commercial dispute.
sections.Procedural History: Beacon demanded a jury on the issues in its damages claim. The district judge directed that Fox's supposedly equitable issues be tried to the court first, with the counterclaim and cross-claim to follow, invoking Rules 42(b) and 57. Beacon petitioned the Ninth Circuit for mandamus. The court of appeals denied relief, reasoning that the declaratory and injunctive claims could be treated as equitable and that the district judge had discretion over the order of trial. The Court granted certiorari and reversed the Ninth Circuit's judgment denying mandamus.
sections.Material Facts:
Fox operated a theater in San Bernardino, California, under distribution arrangements giving it first-run rights and clearances, periods during which competing exhibitors could not show a film after its first run. Beacon opened a drive-in about eleven miles away. Whether the theaters were in substantial competition mattered because a clearance restricting a theater outside the relevant competitive relationship could be unreasonable under the antitrust laws.

Beacon contended that Fox's arrangements restrained its access to films and warned that it could sue for antitrust treble damages. Fox responded by suing for a declaration that the clearances were reasonable and did not violate the antitrust laws, and sought to restrain Beacon from bringing antitrust litigation while the declaratory action was pending. The Ninth Circuit read the complaint as seeking broader relief against threats interfering with Fox's business relationships. Beacon denied the allegations and asserted a counterclaim against Fox and a cross-claim against the intervening exhibitor alleging an antitrust conspiracy and seeking treble damages. The claims raised overlapping factual questions, so the judge's earlier findings on the reasonableness of the clearances or on competition could bind the common issues and restrict what the jury would later decide.
sections.Issue: May a court try a plaintiff's declaratory and injunctive antitrust claims without a jury before a defendant's compulsory treble-damages counterclaim, when the first trial could conclusively determine facts common to the legal claim? Does discretion over sequencing or the plaintiff's earlier filing justify that effect, and can mandamus protect the jury right?
sections.Holding: The Court, in 1959, in an opinion by Justice Black for five Justices, with Justice Stewart dissenting joined by Justices Harlan and Whittaker and Justice Frankfurter taking no part, held that the equitable-first procedure could not, in the circumstances presented, deprive Beacon of a jury determination of factual issues common to its legal damages claim. Discretion over sequencing is narrowly confined by the duty to preserve the jury right; only the most imperative circumstances could justify losing jury determination of legal issues through a prior equitable adjudication, and the Court anticipated none here. Fox could not gain priority by filing first for a declaration of nonliability and adding an injunction request. Mandamus was available to correct the denial.
sections.Reasoning:
An action for antitrust treble damages is a legal claim carrying a jury right, and Fox's request for a declaration of nonliability anticipated that controversy. The Declaratory Judgment Act supplies a procedure for earlier resolution; it does not let a party eliminate the jury right that would attend the coercive action. Otherwise the right would depend on who reached the courthouse first.

The Court assumed the Ninth Circuit's broader reading of the injunction request. Even a genuine equitable component did not itself justify deciding the common legal issues first without a jury; the adequacy of the legal remedy had to be judged in light of modern procedure. Older cases let equity go first because separate procedural systems made it hard to settle the whole controversy at law. The Federal Rules' single civil action, joinder provisions and the declaratory judgment changed those conditions.

A later jury would not protect Beacon if the judge had already conclusively resolved the facts that mattered. A practicable alternative existed: submit the common issues to the jury as part of the legal claim, then let the judge decide any remaining equitable matters consistently with the jury's findings, with temporary equitable relief available in an appropriate case. Rule 42(b) discretion is constrained by the constitutional jury right and Rule 38(a). The All Writs Act supplied authority for mandamus.

Justice Stewart, dissenting, would have sustained the denial of mandamus. In his view Fox's complaint sought equitable protection of existing contractual and business relationships, properly invoked equity jurisdiction did not disappear because the defendant later asserted a legal counterclaim, the merged rules could not enlarge the jury right beyond its historical scope, and the trial court's discretion over sequence had not been shown to be abused. The Court did not decide whether the clearances were lawful.

CP-110.rule: The Seventh Amendment applies to statutory causes of action that enforce legal rights and seek legal remedies in the ordinary courts, so either party may demand a jury in a federal Title VIII action for actual and punitive damages.

sections.Parties: Curtis, a Black woman who had sought to rent an apartment, was the plaintiff below and the petitioner in the Court. The white landlords, the Loethers, were the defendants and respondents. The landlords demanded a jury trial, which the district judge denied; Curtis sought to preserve the judge's disposition against their jury objection. The lower-court decisions were captioned Rogers v. Loether; the caption changed after the petitioner married while review was pending.
sections.Procedural History: The landlords timely requested a jury in their answer. The District Court for the Eastern District of Wisconsin concluded that neither Title VIII nor the Seventh Amendment required one and tried the case without a jury, awarding punitive damages and denying Curtis's request for attorney's fees and costs. The Seventh Circuit reversed on the jury-trial issue, concluding that the Seventh Amendment entitled the landlords to a jury and construing the statute consistently with that requirement. Curtis sought review. The Court affirmed the Seventh Circuit on the constitutional ground; the affirmance sustained the reversal of the bench-trial disposition, not the district court's award.
sections.Material Facts:
Curtis alleged that the landlords refused to rent an apartment to her because of her race, in violation of the fair housing provisions of Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968. Section 812 then authorized private civil actions and permitted injunctions, actual damages, and punitive damages up to $1,000. Her complaint asked for injunctive relief and punitive damages; a compensatory claim was later included in the issues to be tried, though the pleadings were not formally amended.

After an evidentiary hearing the district court temporarily prohibited the landlords from renting the apartment to anyone else. About five months later Curtis found other housing and consented to dissolving the injunction, leaving actual and punitive damages for trial. Her proposed proof of actual loss was excluded because she had not complied with a pretrial discovery order. The district judge found discrimination but no proven actual damages and awarded $250 in punitive damages.
sections.Issue: Does the Seventh Amendment apply to a newly created federal statutory cause of action seeking damages for housing discrimination, so that either party is entitled to a jury when the statute authorizes ordinary federal-court actions for actual and punitive damages, even though the action also involved a request for equitable relief?
sections.Holding: The Court, in 1974, in an opinion by Justice Marshall for a unanimous Court, held that it does. The Seventh Amendment reaches federal statutory actions that enforce legal rights and seek legal remedies in ordinary courts of law, and is not confined to causes of action bearing forms or names recognized in 1791. A private Title VIII claim for compensatory and punitive damages is sufficiently analogous to a tort action, and its remedies are traditional legal relief, so either party is entitled to a jury on proper demand in federal court. Joining an equitable claim does not eliminate the jury right on the legal claim or on common factual issues. The Court did not decide the jury status of Title VII backpay or whether juries are required in state court.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court began with the distinction between legal and equitable rights, not with whether Congress had used a familiar cause-of-action label. A legislature's creation of a new duty does not exempt an ordinary suit enforcing it from the Amendment, and prior cases had repeatedly applied the jury guarantee to statutory actions. The housing claim had the character of a tort action: the statute imposed a duty not to refuse to rent on discriminatory grounds and authorized compensation for breach, with analogies to the duties of innkeepers and actions for dignitary injuries. Actual damages compensate for injury and punitive damages punish wrongful conduct; both are traditional relief in courts of law.

Curtis relied on decisions letting the National Labor Relations Board award backpay and a bankruptcy court order surrender of a preference without a jury. The Court distinguished them as involving administrative enforcement or a specialized equitable tribunal, where a jury could conflict with the statutory scheme; Congress had instead authorized an ordinary civil action in federal district court. On Title VII backpay, which courts of appeals had characterized as part of an equitable remedy under different statutory language, the Court expressly declined to endorse or reject those holdings.

The earlier injunction request did not change the result. If only damages remained, the right was plain; if the suit combined legal and equitable claims, Beacon Theatres and Dairy Queen preserved the jury right on the legal claim and shared issues, and damages could not be called incidental to the injunction. Concerns about delay and jury prejudice were acknowledged, and the Court pointed to expedition requirements, preliminary injunctions, and the judge's power to direct a verdict, set aside a verdict or order a new trial, but those concerns could not overcome the constitutional right. The Court rested on the constitutional ground because its existing decisions settled the question and doing so did not invalidate the statute. The statutory provisions and damages limit are those described in the 1974 opinion.

CP-111.rule: The Seventh Amendment inquiry examines the nature of the action or issues and the nature of the remedy, giving greater importance to the remedy; damages sought from a union for breach of the duty of fair representation are legal relief triable to a jury.

sections.Parties: Terry and twenty-six other truckdrivers, all members of Local 391, sued their employer, McLean Trucking Company, and their union. They alleged that McLean violated the collective bargaining agreement and that the union breached its duty of fair representation in handling their grievances. By the time of Supreme Court review, the employer and the requests for injunctive relief had been dismissed. The union was the petitioner, seeking to strike the employees' jury demand; the employees were respondents, seeking a jury on their remaining damages claims.
sections.Procedural History:
The employees sued in July 1983, alleging a contractual violation under section 301 of the Labor Management Relations Act and a breach of the union's fair-representation duty. They sought restoration of proper seniority, an injunction against further unlawful conduct, and compensatory relief including lost wages and health benefits. McLean filed for bankruptcy in 1986, and the employees voluntarily dismissed the employer and all injunctive claims, leaving monetary relief sought from the union.

The union moved to strike the jury demand. The district court denied the motion, and the Fourth Circuit affirmed on interlocutory appeal. The Court granted review to resolve a disagreement among circuits and affirmed. The judgment under review concerned entitlement to a jury before a merits trial, not a damages verdict or a final finding of unfair representation.
sections.Material Facts:
In 1982 McLean reorganized its operations and transferred the employees to its Winston-Salem terminal, agreeing to give them special seniority rights relative to inactive drivers who had previously been laid off. After approximately six weeks the transferred drivers began experiencing repeated layoffs and recalls. They challenged McLean's treatment of their seniority and its practice of stripping the special rights from a transferred driver upon layoff.

The first grievance proceeding produced an order directing McLean to recall the affected transferred drivers, lay off certain recalled inactive drivers, and preserve the transferred drivers' special rights until the inactive drivers were properly recalled. McLean initially complied, but then recalled inactive drivers in a manner restoring their superior seniority, and in later layoffs the transferred drivers again lost their jobs first. They filed a second grievance alleging circumvention of the first decision; the union representative presented the competing positions of both groups, and the committee concluded that McLean had not violated its earlier decision.

The employees filed a third grievance as layoffs and recalls continued. The union declined to refer it to a committee, stating that the relevant questions had already been decided. The employees claimed that this representation wrongfully deprived them of wages and health benefits.
sections.Issue: Does the Seventh Amendment entitle employees to a jury when they seek damages from their union for lost wages and benefits allegedly caused by breach of the duty of fair representation? How should the claim be classified when its historical analogies include an equitable trust action and a legal malpractice or contract action, and when the requested payment is described as backpay?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 1990, with Justice Marshall announcing the judgment, held that the employees were entitled to a jury on all issues presented in their suit. Six Justices joined the remedial analysis and the judgment: the requested compensation was legal relief, because it sought wages and benefits the employees would have received from their employer rather than money the union wrongfully held, and it was not intertwined with a remaining request for an injunction. Only four Justices joined the historical comparison in Part III-A, so that comparison is not an undivided majority holding that the claim is governed by trust law. Justice Kennedy dissented, joined by Justices O'Connor and Scalia. The Court did not decide that either underlying breach had occurred.
sections.Reasoning:
The union's duty arises from its exclusive authority to represent the bargaining unit. The employees' damages case required proof of both McLean's breach of the agreement and the union's breach of its duty, even after McLean left the case.

In the plurality portion, Marshall rejected the union's analogy to an equitable proceeding setting aside an arbitration award, because the grievance committee had never adjudicated the union's alleged breach. The four Justices joining Part III-A found the trust analogy more persuasive than the lawyer-client analogy, but Marshall found the historical inquiry inconclusive because the employees also had to prove the employer's contractual breach, an issue analogous to a legal contract claim.

The six-Justice remedial analysis reasoned that the union was not holding the lost wages and benefits; the employer would have paid them had the grievances been handled successfully, so the award lacked a restitutionary feature. Nor did it accompany an injunction. The term backpay did not settle the question: Congress had expressly described Title VII relief in equitable terms, while the fair-representation duty lacked a comparable designation. The Court assumed without deciding that a Title VII plaintiff seeking backpay had no jury right.

Justice Brennan, concurring, would eliminate the search for a comparable eighteenth-century cause of action and classify only the relief. Justice Stevens, concurring, preferred the malpractice analogy. Justice Kennedy, dissenting, accepted the trust analogy as controlling and would have denied a jury, noting that monetary relief making a beneficiary whole had historically been available in equity.

CP-112.rule: Construction of a patent, including technical terms within its claims, is the exclusive responsibility of the court; the Seventh Amendment jury right attached to an infringement action does not make every subsidiary issue a jury question.

sections.Parties: Markman owned a patent for an inventory-control system used by dry-cleaning businesses and was the infringement plaintiff and Supreme Court petitioner. He sued Westview Instruments, which supplied the accused system, and Althon Enterprises, a dry-cleaning operator using it; the opinion refers to the defendants collectively as Westview. They were respondents defending a judgment as a matter of law entered in their favor after a jury verdict for Markman.
sections.Procedural History: A jury in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania found infringement of independent claim 1 and dependent claim 10. The district court nevertheless granted Westview's deferred motion for judgment as a matter of law, one ground being its construction of inventory and the accused system's inability to track clothing through the cleaning process or report garments' location and status. Markman appealed, arguing that the judge had improperly replaced the construction the jury presumably adopted. The Federal Circuit affirmed, holding claim interpretation to be the court's responsibility and rejecting the Seventh Amendment objection. The Court granted review and affirmed, leaving the judgment for Westview in place; it did not reinstate the infringement verdict or order a new jury determination of the patent's meaning.
sections.Material Facts:
Markman's patent described a system that monitored the status, location, and movement of clothing through a dry-cleaning establishment. A keyboard and data processor generated transaction records, including bar codes read by optical detectors as employees logged the clothing's progress. Westview's system also used a keyboard, processor, bar-coded tickets, and optical readers, but Westview maintained that it tracked invoices, charges, and receivables rather than the physical articles of clothing.

The dispute turned in part on the patent's use of the word inventory. Independent claim 1 referred to maintaining an inventory total and detecting improper additions and deletions. Markman's witness testified about the meaning of the language. The meaning of inventory determined whether the accused device's inability to track garments placed it outside the patent. The district judge construed the patent to require tracking physical clothing as well as cash inventory; on that construction, a system that tracked only receivables and transaction totals lacked the specified capability.
sections.Issue: Although a patent-infringement action of this kind carries a right to a jury, must the jury also construe disputed terms of art in the patent claims when expert testimony bears on their meaning, or may the judge determine the meaning of inventory as part of construing the patent document?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 1996, in a unanimous opinion by Justice Souter, held that construction of the patent, including technical terms within its claims, is the exclusive responsibility of the court. Allocation of a particular issue requires examining historical practice or appropriate analogies and, where those are not decisive, precedent, institutional competence, and relevant statutory policies. Those considerations supported judicial construction of inventory. The Court retained the distinction between interpreting the scope of the patent and deciding whether the accused product infringed under the governing construction, and its holding did not remove every factual question in a patent case from the jury.
sections.Reasoning:
Patent-infringement actions seeking legal relief descended from actions tried at law, and their jury character was undisputed. The distinct question was the subsidiary task of claim construction; protecting the substance of the jury right does not require assigning every step in a legal action to the jury.

Modern claim practice lacked an eighteenth-century counterpart, so the Court examined specification construction as the closest historical practice. The surviving cases did not establish that juries construed disputed patent terms; judges ordinarily construed written instruments. Markman's argument about terms of art rested on nineteenth-century statements that did not establish a controlling practice at the founding. The Court left open whether its treatment of technical terms should extend to other written instruments.

Precedent reinforced the allocation: Winans v. Denmead had separated judicial construction from the jury's determination of infringement, and Souter distinguished Bischoff v. Wethered and Tucker v. Spalding as cases using evidence to understand the accused things. The need for expert testimony did not make interpretation a jury function, because a proposed meaning still had to fit the patent as a whole, and the Court expected most credibility judgments to be embedded in that evaluation. Uniformity was a further reason: judicial construction permits precedential reasoning and appellate supervision, while issue preclusion would not bind new defendants. The Court did not promise complete uniformity.

The brief addresses only the judge-jury allocation decided in 1996, not later questions about standards of appellate review.

CP-113.rule: A prospective juror biased or prejudiced for or against a party, including bias about the subject matter of the litigation, is disqualified as a matter of law, and the juror's assurance of fairness in response to leading questions does not cure it.

sections.Parties: Billie Charlene Flowers filed for divorce from her husband, R.A. Flowers, and the two disputed custody of their three daughters, then aged two to ten. The appeal concerned the trial court's overruling of the mother's challenge for cause to a prospective juror, along with other rulings.
sections.Procedural History: The mother filed for divorce in January 1964. The parties agreed, with the judge's approval, to present only custody evidence and issues to the jury, leaving divorce, support, and property matters to the court. The trial court overruled the mother's challenge for cause to prospective juror Mrs. Schmidt and refused to hear another prospective juror's tendered testimony on motions for mistrial and a new trial. The Texas Court of Civil Appeals at Amarillo reversed and remanded for a new trial; it did not itself award custody to either parent. The report notes that rehearing was denied on December 6, 1965.
sections.Material Facts:
The case was tried in a small community where several prospective jurors had heard rumors about the dispute. On voir dire, the mother's lawyer disclosed that the evidence would show social drinking and one or two occasions of excessive consumption. Mrs. Schmidt initially said she knew the family through their church but had formed no opinion. Further questioning revealed categorical opposition to drinking and a willingness to hold any drinking against a parent's fitness. When the judge asked whether she would deny either parent custody if that parent drank, she answered affirmatively. Later leading questions elicited more equivocal assurances.

An affidavit from another prospective juror, Mrs. Philpot, described Schmidt's preselection statements expressing sympathy for the father and stating that the mother had previously run off and left him. The mother's counsel testified that eleven panel members were undesirable from her perspective and that fuller disclosure of Schmidt's views would have changed the allocation of peremptory challenges; a marked jury list supported that testimony.
sections.Issue: Did Schmidt's expressed prejudgment require her disqualification despite her responses to the judge's rehabilitative questions?
sections.Holding: The Texas Court of Civil Appeals at Amarillo in 1965, in an opinion by Justice Chapman, held that it did. Texas's jury guarantee required impartiality, and Article 2134 disqualified a person biased or prejudiced for or against either party. Disqualifying bias could concern the subject matter of the litigation rather than personal hostility alone. Once statutory disqualification was established, the issue was one of law rather than trial-court discretion. The court reversed and remanded for a new trial.
sections.Reasoning:
A preference rises to disqualifying bias when it naturally implies that the juror would not act impartially, and prejudice means prejudgment. Schmidt's categorical views about drinking, coupled with her statements about the family, showed that she had prejudged matters central to parental fitness, so the record established statutory disqualification as a matter of law. Alternatively, even if bias had remained a factual question for the trial judge, her established views could not be erased by agreeing to a leading assurance that she could decide on the evidence, and retaining her was an abuse of discretion. The opinion's footnote explains that the cited law required disregarding a biased juror's assurance of being able to put bias aside. The court also stated that a complainant need not independently establish probable injury from juror disqualification, though it found supporting harm in the evidence about peremptory-challenge choices.

The complete opinion addressed other errors. The mother bore the burden on whether she was a fit custodian, yet was denied the right to open and close argument that Rules 266 and 269 ordinarily gave the party bearing the burden. The judge also refused to hear divorce evidence after the custody verdict despite having reserved that issue. The court viewed the accumulated errors as requiring a new trial and emphasized that the custody verdict was binding under the statute then applicable.

The assigned casebook excerpt principally emphasizes the bias ruling and omits these additional discussions.

CP-114.rule: A private litigant in a civil case may not use peremptory challenges to exclude prospective jurors on account of race, because exercising a peremptory challenge is governmental action, and the opposing litigant may assert the excluded jurors' equal-protection rights.

sections.Parties: Thaddeus Donald Edmonson, a construction worker, was the negligence plaintiff, appellant, and Supreme Court petitioner. Leesville Concrete Company, Inc., was the private corporate defendant and respondent. Edmonson sought compensation for a job-site injury and challenged Leesville's exclusion of two prospective jurors through peremptory challenges. The constitutional rights directly implicated belonged to the prospective jurors, although Edmonson asserted them in his own litigation.
sections.Procedural History: Edmonson sued in the Western District of Louisiana and invoked his Seventh Amendment right to a jury trial. The trial judge declined to require a race-neutral explanation for Leesville's strikes, and the jury returned a verdict producing an $18,000 recovery. A divided Fifth Circuit panel reversed, reasoning that private litigants become government actors when exercising peremptory challenges; it would have remanded for a determination whether Edmonson had established a prima facie case. The court then reheard the case en banc, displaced the panel decision, and affirmed the district court, concluding that private civil litigants' strikes were not state action. The Court granted certiorari to resolve a disagreement among the circuits, reversed the en banc judgment, and remanded for the Batson inquiry the trial court had refused to undertake.
sections.Material Facts:
Edmonson was injured at Fort Polk, Louisiana, a federal enclave. He alleged that a Leesville employee allowed a truck to roll backward and pin him against construction equipment. The government was not a litigating party.

During voir dire, Leesville used two of its three statutorily authorized peremptory challenges to exclude Black prospective jurors. Edmonson, who was Black, asked the judge to require a race-neutral explanation under Batson v. Kentucky. The judge declined because he understood Batson to apply only in criminal proceedings. The jury ultimately contained eleven white jurors and one Black juror.

The jury found for Edmonson, assessed his total damages at $90,000, and attributed eighty percent of the fault to him, producing an $18,000 recovery. The Court did not infer from the racial composition of the resulting jury alone that Leesville had discriminated.
sections.Issue: Does a private party's racially discriminatory use of peremptory challenges in a federal civil trial constitute governmental action subject to the equal-protection component of the Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause? If so, may the opposing litigant assert the excluded prospective jurors' rights, and had the record already established the discrimination necessary for relief?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 1991, in an opinion by Justice Kennedy joined by Justices White, Marshall, Blackmun, Stevens, and Souter, held that a private litigant in a civil case may not exclude prospective jurors on account of race through peremptory challenges. Federal statutory authorization, indispensable judicial participation, and the delegation of a governmental jury-selection function made the exercise of a peremptory challenge governmental action; the holding does not transform every litigation choice by a private attorney into government action. The opposing civil litigant may assert the excluded jurors' equal-protection rights. The Court did not decide whether Leesville's two strikes established a prima facie case of discrimination; that was left for further proceedings. Justice O'Connor dissented, joined by Chief Justice Rehnquist and Justice Scalia, who also wrote separately.
sections.Reasoning:
Excluding someone from jury service because of race injures that person's equal-protection rights in civil and criminal proceedings alike. Because constitutional limits ordinarily do not govern private conduct, the Court applied the two-part framework drawn from Lugar v. Edmondson Oil Co.

First, the deprivation arose from a privilege conferred by governmental authority: peremptory challenges exist only because law authorizes them, and section 1870 supplied Leesville's three. Second, Leesville could fairly be treated as a governmental actor. The government summoned jurors, set qualifications, and regulated voir dire, and the judge discharged a juror when a strike was exercised, making the private choice legally effective. Jury selection is the selection of a governmental decision-making body, and government could not avoid constitutional restrictions by delegating part of it to private litigants. The Court distinguished Polk County v. Dodson, where a public defender's role was adversarial to the government. The courtroom setting compounded the injury.

Third-party standing was satisfied because discriminatory selection injures the litigant by casting doubt on the proceeding's fairness, voir dire creates a relationship with prospective jurors, and jurors face practical obstacles to suing.

Justice O'Connor, dissenting, treated peremptory challenges as a preserved sphere of private adversarial choice; the judge's excusing the juror was acquiescence, not coercion or significant encouragement, and she regarded Dodson as controlling. Justice Scalia separately anticipated additional litigation over jury selection, burdens on trial courts, constraints on minority litigants' own use of race-conscious strikes, and implications for criminal defendants' strikes.

CP-115.rule: A plaintiff must prove by a preponderance both negligence and its proximate contribution to the injury; a jury verdict cannot stand where the evidence leaves causation to speculation among possible explanations.

sections.Parties: Betty Denman, nearly seven years old, sued through her mother and next friend. The defendant was the executrix of the estate of Joseph Ross, the driver of the other car. Betty claimed negligent driving by Ross and was the appellant, asking that the jury's verdict and judgment be reinstated.
sections.Procedural History: The case went to a jury on Betty's evidence alone; the defense offered none. The jury awarded $5,000. The trial court then granted the defendant's motion for judgment notwithstanding the verdict, and Betty appealed. A separate action against the grandmother's estate had ended in a directed defense verdict affirmed earlier, but that was background rather than the judgment under review. The Supreme Court of Mississippi affirmed the judgment notwithstanding the verdict; the award was not reinstated and no new trial was ordered.
sections.Material Facts:
Betty was riding with her grandmother Eva Denman in a Ford headed south on U.S. Highway 49E. On a rainy, foggy evening in March 1958, it collided with Ross's northbound Plymouth near Sumner. The grandmother, Ross, and a Plymouth passenger died. Betty and another passenger survived with injuries but no recollection of the collision.

Betty's father described the cars' positions after the crash and the extensive damage. No evidence established skid marks or the actual point of impact, and the photographs did not explain how the collision occurred. John Barnett testified that the Plymouth passed him about three-quarters of a mile before the collision at approximately seventy miles per hour. Hal Buckley said it passed him about two hundred yards before the crash at seventy-five to eighty miles per hour and continued without slowing; he could see its taillights but could not identify the impact's location or how the cars came together, saw no departure from the Plymouth's lane, and did not notice the oncoming Ford. Earlier testimony in which he professed no estimate of speed was used to impeach him.
sections.Issue: Was there a reasonable evidentiary basis for finding that Ross's negligence caused or contributed to the collision, so that the jury verdict could stand?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of Mississippi in 1961, in an opinion by Presiding Justice Lee in which Kyle, Arrington, Ethridge, and Gillespie concurred, held that the proof did not supply that basis. Betty bore the burden of establishing, by a preponderance, both negligence and proximate contribution to the injury, and she had proof of a negligent act but not of the causal link. The court affirmed the judgment notwithstanding the verdict for the defendant.
sections.Reasoning:
The court held Barnett's relatively remote observation inadmissible under the cited Mississippi decisions. Buckley's continuous observation over the shorter distance was competent, and the inconsistency in his testimony affected credibility rather than admissibility. His testimony permitted a conclusion that Ross drove at an excessive and negligent speed.

It did not establish causation. There was no evidence of the Ford's speed, lane position, or sudden movement, nothing located the contact point, and the photographs did not reconstruct responsibility. Evidence that the Plymouth traveled too fast was therefore not evidence of how that speed caused this particular collision. The court distinguished reasonable inference from speculation: excessive speed might have contributed under some hypothetical sequences of events, but the record gave no sound basis for choosing one as more probable than the alternatives. The court did not find that the grandmother caused the collision or that Ross drove carefully; the plaintiff had simply failed to prove a required element. The defense's choice to offer no evidence did not remove her burden. The reasoning does not announce that circumstantial evidence is generally insufficient or that negligent speed can never support a causal inference.

The casebook uses the case for the limit on a jury's power to fill an evidentiary gap with conjecture.

CP-116.rule: A prima facie case combined with sufficient evidence that the employer's stated justification is false may permit, but does not compel, an inference of intentional discrimination; under Rule 50 the court reviews the whole record without weighing evidence or resolving credibility.

sections.Parties: Roger Reeves was the employee-plaintiff, the prevailing party before the jury, and the Supreme Court petitioner. Sanderson Plumbing Products, Inc., his former employer, was the defendant, Fifth Circuit appellant, and Supreme Court respondent. Reeves alleged discharge because of age under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act. Sanderson asserted that it fired him for inaccurate attendance records and related shortcomings.
sections.Procedural History:
Reeves sued in federal district court in Mississippi in 1996. The district court denied Sanderson's motion for judgment as a matter of law. The jury awarded $35,000 in compensatory damages and found the violation willful; the court entered judgment including an equal amount of liquidated damages and separately awarded front pay. It denied the employer's renewed motion for judgment as a matter of law and alternative request for a new trial.

The Fifth Circuit reversed. It acknowledged that a reasonable jury could reject Sanderson's explanation as pretextual but treated that rejection, combined with the initial discrimination showing, as insufficient without additional evidence of discriminatory motivation. The Court granted certiorari and reversed, resolving the sufficiency question itself rather than directing further appellate consideration, and without requiring a new trial.
sections.Material Facts:
Reeves was fifty-seven when fired in 1995 and had worked for Sanderson for approximately forty years. He supervised the regular production line in the Hinge Room; Joe Oswalt, in his mid-thirties, supervised a special line, and Russell Caldwell, forty-five, managed the department. An audit of attendance records supplied the stated reason for discharging Reeves and Caldwell while retaining Oswalt. Powe Chesnut, the director of manufacturing and husband of company president Sandra Sanderson, participated in the audit and recommended discharge; the president made the formal decision. Reeves offered evidence that Chesnut was the real force behind his firing. Three employees in their thirties successively assumed his duties.

Reeves explained that the automated time clock could fail to record work, that some supposed errors occurred while he was hospitalized, and that Caldwell bore responsibility for disciplining late employees. The employer had never calculated the overpayments allegedly attributable to his errors. Reeves testified that Chesnut said he was too old to do his job. Although the two supervisors' recorded productivity was nearly identical, the employer conducted an efficiency study of Reeves's line alone and placed him on probation.
sections.Issue: May a jury infer intentional discrimination from a plaintiff's prima facie case combined with evidence that the employer's asserted legitimate reason is false, or must the plaintiff always provide additional, independent evidence of discrimination? In reviewing the verdict under Rule 50, what evidence must the court consider and credit, and could this verdict survive?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 2000, in a unanimous opinion by Justice O'Connor, held that a prima facie case combined with sufficient evidence that the employer's stated justification is false may permit a reasonable factfinder to infer intentional discrimination. The inference is permissible, not mandatory, and judgment as a matter of law can still be appropriate when the entire record would not permit a rational discrimination finding. Under Rule 50 the court reviews the whole record and draws reasonable inferences for the nonmoving party, disregarding evidence favorable to the movant that the jury was not required to believe while crediting uncontradicted, unimpeached evidence for the movant, at least when supplied by disinterested witnesses. Applied here, the jury's determination had to be sustained.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court assumed, because the parties did not contest it, that the McDonnell Douglas framework applied to this ADEA case. Reeves established the initial showing; Sanderson produced evidence of a legitimate reason, which satisfied a burden of production only. The presumption then disappeared, but the underlying evidence remained available to the jury, and Reeves kept the burden of persuasion.

A false explanation is circumstantial evidence: an employer ordinarily knows why it acted, and an untrue reason can support the inference that it is concealing an unlawful one. The Fifth Circuit mistook the rule that disbelief does not compel liability for a rule that disbelief cannot help establish liability. The Court preserved limits: other evidence might conclusively reveal a different nondiscriminatory reason, or the proof of falsity might be weak against abundant uncontroverted evidence that no discrimination occurred.

On Rule 50, the Court reconciled differing formulations by separating the evidence a judge must review, which is all of it, from the evidence the judge may treat as true. Credibility, disputed inferences, and weight remain for the jury. Reeves's evidence called the recordkeeping charge into question, and Chesnut's remarks, differential treatment, selective efficiency study, and practical authority supported finding that his motivation affected the dismissal. The Fifth Circuit had substituted its own assessment of evidentiary weight.

Justice Ginsburg, concurring, anticipated that cases requiring more than a prima facie showing and evidence of a false explanation would be uncommon.

CP-117.rule: Whether to allow jurors to submit questions for witnesses is a matter of the trial judge's sound discretion, with the judge filtering irrelevant or argumentative questions.

sections.Parties: The Securities and Exchange Commission sued James Koenig, Waste Management's former chief financial officer, over accounting methods a jury found fraudulent. Koenig was the appellant. His appeal did not contest the sufficiency of the evidence for the fraud verdict; it challenged limitations, trial practices, expert evidence, and remedies.
sections.Procedural History: The SEC filed in March 2002. After a twelve-week trial, the jury rejected Koenig's position. The district court ordered disgorgement of $831,500 in bonuses from 1992, 1994, and 1995, plus more than $1.2 million in prejudgment interest, imposed a civil penalty of approximately $2.1 million, and barred Koenig from serving as a director or top manager of a public company. The Seventh Circuit affirmed except as to calculation of the bonuses under proper accounting, and remanded for further proceedings on that calculation and any resulting remedial adjustments. It sustained the fraud judgment and the juror-questioning practice; the remand did not direct a new liability trial.
sections.Material Facts:
One of Koenig's accounting methods offset ordinary operating expenses with unusual gains, making recurring profits appear stronger. Another transferred remaining depreciation from prematurely closed landfills to other assets, postponing losses. Waste Management announced in October 1997 that its financial statements were unreliable, and its share value fell sharply. A February 1998 restatement took an approximately $1.1 billion charge for 1992 to 1996. Koenig blamed new management for an "earnings bath" designed to make its predecessors look worse.

At trial the judge allowed jurors to submit written questions for witnesses, asking some, reformulating others, and withholding inappropriate or repetitive ones. Jurors were instructed not to infer anything from the judge's decision not to ask a question. Jurors submitted 127 questions, about two-thirds of them from three jurors. Some questions were inadvertently omitted, and one witness was not recalled for additional inquiries. Koenig argued that the practice risked turning jurors into advocates or causing premature commitments, and sought reversal or a restriction to narrowly "clarifying" questions.
sections.Issue: May a trial judge allow jurors to submit questions for witnesses, and was that practice properly conducted in this trial? The complete opinion also decided whether the penalty claim was timely, whether motive and responsive evidence and the deposition of Koenig's withdrawn expert were properly admitted, and whether the remedies were properly calculated.
sections.Holding: The Seventh Circuit in 2009, in an opinion by Chief Judge Easterbrook for a panel of Easterbrook, Manion, and Wood, held that allowing juror questions was a matter of the trial judge's sound discretion and that the discretion was properly exercised here. The court also held the penalty claim timely, found no reversible error in the evidentiary rulings, and held that prejudgment interest could be included in pecuniary gain when calculating the penalty ceiling, but required review of the bonus calculations using consistently corrected accounts.
sections.Reasoning:
No statute or procedural rule prohibited juror questions, and earlier judicial cautions about risks did not amount to a categorical ban. Studies and the ABA and Seventh Circuit jury projects supported benefits to attention and comprehension, especially in a long technical trial, though those recommendations were not binding procedural law. The judge should filter irrelevant or argumentative questions, and did so. The court declined a rigid distinction between "clarifying" and other questions, because what is clear to a specialist might confuse a lay juror. The omitted questions were ordinary management glitches, and 127 questions was approximately two per trial day, so three jurors asking most of them did not show a takeover. Pointed questions did not prove disqualifying prejudgment; jurors inevitably react to evidence, and questions can alert lawyers to confusion or missing proof.

On limitations, section 2462 allowed five years from accrual for penalties; relying on the fraud-concealment doctrine, the court ran the period from discovery, and public disclosure occurred in October 1997. The "earnings bath" theme should have been excluded as irrelevant, but Koenig pressed it, so responsive evidence was invited. The SEC could use the deposition of Koenig's expert Frederick Dunbar, whose report had been disclosed; any further disclosure omission was harmless under Rule 37(c)(1). The district judge had not adequately explained the 1992 bonus, because comparing inflated prior-year earnings with corrected later-year earnings was inconsistent.

The assigned casebook extract focuses on juror participation.

CP-118.rule: Under the historical Rule 49(b), when answers to interrogatories are consistent with each other but conflict with the general verdict, the court may enter judgment on the answers, return the jury for further consideration, or order a new trial, after first attempting a fair reconciliation.

sections.Parties: The Nollenberger, Matlock, Theobald, and Thompson families were plaintiffs in wrongful-death actions against United Air Lines arising from an aircraft midair collision. The plaintiffs sought new trials for insufficiency, inadequacy, and inconsistency, and in the alternative additional jury questions or judgments calculated from the jury's answers. United moved to strike an affidavit of Chapin.
sections.Procedural History: Several related actions had previously been tried together in Nevada, with questions between the United States and United Air Lines severed from the passenger claims. Following earlier liability rulings, counsel stipulated to transferring specified actions to the Southern District of California. The families' damages cases were tried successively to one jury, with a verdict in each before the next began, and entry of judgments was withheld to permit simultaneous judgments and a uniform appeal period. Chief Judge Hall denied additional interrogatories and new trials, granted United's motions to strike, and directed preparation of judgments calculated from the answers. The casebook's notes report that the Ninth Circuit later vacated that disposition; the brief covers that later stage only through the casebook's quotation, not the complete appellate opinion.
sections.Material Facts: The collision occurred on April 21, 1958. In Nollenberger, the jury found that William Edward Nollenberger had a 25-year life expectancy and a 15-year work expectancy. It specified $235,210 in expected earnings, $100,200 in subsequent pension receipts, and $25,000 in personal services to the family, and supplied percentages for the decedent's personal expenses, income taxes, taxation of income from the eventual award, inflation, and discounting. Despite those subsidiary findings, it returned general damages of $114,655. The other families likewise received general verdicts accompanied by answers to interrogatories. In Theobald and Thompson the answers yielded substantially the same figures as the verdicts.
sections.Issue: Could the court reconcile the special answers with the general verdict, and, if it could not, could it enter damages calculated from those answers or submit additional interrogatories after the jury had returned both forms of decision?
sections.Holding: The District Court for the Southern District of California in 1963, per Chief Judge Hall, held that the eleven Nollenberger answers were internally consistent and supported by the evidence but irreconcilable with the general verdict, and reached the same conclusion for Matlock. It refused additional interrogatories and held that the court should calculate judgment from the consistent answers before granting a new trial. It directed judgments of $171,702 for Nollenberger, $207,420 for Matlock, $162,412 for Theobald, and $138,678.40 for Thompson, denying Theobald's and Thompson's requests for different awards.
sections.Reasoning:
The historical Rule 49(b) distinguished several conditions. Harmonious answers and verdict required judgment on both. Consistent answers that conflicted with the general verdict permitted judgment on the answers, further jury consideration, or a new trial. Answers inconsistent with each other and with the verdict left only resubmission or a new trial. Before finding a conflict, the court had to attempt a fair reconciliation, an obligation Hall applied from Gallick. After repeated efforts he could not harmonize the answers with the verdict. His conclusion depended on treating the answers as supplying the components necessary to compute compensation, so that arithmetic could implement the jury's findings without substituting new factual judgments.

He rejected additional interrogatories, reading the rule's authorization to return the jury for further consideration of "its answers and verdict" as confined to the questions already submitted. He reserved whether inquiry would be permissible after a jury returned only a general verdict. In calculating, he treated the application of statutory civil-service salary and step increases as legal calculation rather than factfinding, added interest to past losses, discounted future losses, and deducted personal expenses, income taxes, and pension contributions where appropriate.

The casebook's notes quote the later appellate decision, which explained that the jury instructions allowed consideration of additional factors, including the decedent's disposition to provide support and the pecuniary value of society, care, comfort, and protection, so the eleven answers did not dictate a single formula or squarely conflict with the verdict. The casebook uses the case to illustrate the danger of converting answers to damage interrogatories into a judgment different from the general verdict.

CP-119.rule: A trial judge's prompt oral findings, including findings adopted verbatim from a party's proposals, remain the court's findings and receive ordinary clear-error review, but unaddressed facts material to a distinct claim can still require remand.

sections.Parties: The Lansford-Coaldale Joint Water Authority, which supplied public water in Carbon County, Pennsylvania, was the plaintiff and appellant. It sued Tonolli Pennsylvania, which operated a lead-smelting facility, its sister corporation Tonolli Canada, and their parent IFIM, ultimately including CERCLA claims for the prospective cost of replacing or treating its water supply and for monitoring and evaluation expenses. Pennsylvania became bankrupt and was dropped. Canada defended; IFIM never answered or appeared.
sections.Procedural History: The district court bifurcated liability and damages. Within hours after the nine-day liability trial ended, it announced approximately 150 oral findings, most drawn verbatim from Canada's proposed findings submitted before trial. It entered judgment for Canada and, without explanation, IFIM. The Authority had not moved for default judgment against IFIM. The appeal concerned CERCLA, not the unappealed common-law negligence counts. The Third Circuit affirmed judgment for Canada and IFIM on replacement-water and treatment costs, vacated both defendants' monitoring-and-evaluation-cost judgments and remanded, and affirmed denial of Canada's sanctions motions.
sections.Material Facts:
Tonolli Pennsylvania's lead-smelting facility stood approximately 3,100 feet from the Authority's production wells. Tonolli Canada had created and owned Tonolli Pennsylvania, but sold its shares in 1976 to IFIM, which also became Canada's parent. After learning of hazardous-substance releases and a waste-disposal permit application, the Authority commissioned the AGES study in 1987. Its wells were normally upgradient from the industrial site; the study tested whether prolonged pumping could reverse groundwater movement and draw contamination toward them.

The Authority's expert read decreases in monitoring-well water levels and increased contaminants after a 72-hour pumping test as evidence of reversed flow. Canada's hydrogeologist, Earl, said the study lacked baseline trends necessary to isolate pumping from seasonal changes, tides, weather, other pumping, and other causes, and identified a groundwater divide and a deep discharge-zone aquifer separating the sites. The district court credited Earl's explanation and his greater hydrogeological experience.
sections.Issue: Do a trial court's findings deserve less deference because they were announced orally before a transcript was obtained, relied heavily on a party's proposed findings, and followed proposals requested before rather than after trial? Were the findings sufficient to dispose of the replacement-cost claims and the separate monitoring-cost claims?
sections.Holding: The Third Circuit in 1993, in an opinion by Judge Becker joined by Judges Alito and Roth, rejected the categorical objections and applied ordinary clear-error review to the factual findings. The finding that the smelting site did not threaten the Authority's water supply was not clearly erroneous and supported denial of replacement-water and treatment costs. The monitoring-cost claims were remanded because corporate-control questions bearing on operator liability had not been addressed. Owner liability was rejected.
sections.Reasoning:
Legal components of mixed questions received plenary review and factual components clear-error review. Rule 52(a) expressly permitted findings stated orally and recorded in open court after the evidence closed, and prompt findings promoted speedy adjudication and used the judge's fresh recollection, although a carefully prepared written opinion might often be preferable. Under Anderson v. Bessemer City, adopted findings are still those of the judge. The record showed informed, considered views, and the court reserved that it might view a different record differently. A footnote rejected reliance on Roberts v. Ross as superseded by Anderson and the circuit's Hayes decision.

On groundwater, where two views of the evidence were permissible the trial court's choice was not clearly erroneous, and the Authority bore the burden of proving the threatened contamination.

Monitoring expenses could be recoverable even without actual contamination, so the failure to prove a continuing threat did not dispose of them. For operator liability the court adopted actual substantial participation and control rather than mere authority to control. Many findings supported corporate separateness, but the district court had not sufficiently addressed shared senior officers, a document describing unified management, their signatures on an environmental consent order, or the timing of releases. The Authority could not be faulted for lacking evidence the court had reserved for the damages phase. Under Frow, the common finding of no threatened contamination prevented an inconsistent judgment against nonappearing IFIM.

The brief notes that a passage in the assigned casebook pages criticizing postdecision findings is absent from the reported opinion and should not be attributed to Becker.

CP-120.rule: A trial court does not abuse its discretion in granting a new trial where a single undifferentiated verdict on two distinct causes of action leaves liability and damages on each unascertainable, even though no party objected to the verdict form before the verdict.

sections.Parties: M. Helen Magnani sued Arnold Trogi following her husband Raymond's injury and death. As administratrix she sought $30,000 under Illinois's Wrongful Death Act; individually she sought reimbursement for medical and funeral expenses under the Family Expense Statute. Magnani appealed the order granting a new trial. Trogi cross-appealed the denial of his alternative request for judgment notwithstanding the verdict.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court submitted one verdict form without objection, and the jury returned a verdict for the plaintiff with $19,000 in damages. On Trogi's post-trial motion, the trial court set aside the verdict and judgment and granted a new trial on liability and damages. Magnani obtained leave to appeal that order. The Illinois Appellate Court, by a two-to-one division, affirmed the order granting a new trial, vacating the verdict and judgment, and denying Trogi's motion for judgment notwithstanding the verdict.
sections.Material Facts: The opinion does not narrate the underlying injury event. A wrongful-death award would be apportioned between the widow and minor son according to their dependency on the decedent; an award of family expenses would not undergo that apportionment. Neither party tendered separate verdict forms for the two claims. The jury's single verdict, returned on December 21, 1962, awarded $19,000 against the defendant. The trial court could not determine whether that amount applied to both causes of action, only to wrongful death, or reflected nonliability on the expense claim. Trogi first challenged the verdict form in a post-trial motion that the assigned excerpt identifies as filed January 15, 1963.
sections.Issue: Did the trial court abuse its discretion by ordering a new trial to resolve the ambiguity in the verdict, even though Trogi first challenged the verdict form in a post-trial motion?
sections.Holding: The Illinois Appellate Court in 1966, in an opinion by Coryn joined by Alloy, with Stouder dissenting, held that the trial judge had not abused discretion on this record. The majority expressly declined a universal rule requiring retrial whenever separate verdict forms are omitted. It did not replace the $19,000 verdict with a judicial allocation or direct judgment for the defendant.
sections.Reasoning:
The Civil Practice Act provided for separate verdicts on a party's motion when complaint counts asserted different demands on which separate recoveries could be obtained, and the majority regarded these statutory claims as separate causes of action. A new-trial motion allows the trial court to correct errors by itself or the jury, and a reviewing court disturbs that decision only on an affirmative showing of clear abuse of discretion; the trial judge is better placed to assess fairness, and greater latitude is allowed for granting than for denying a new trial.

Coryn acknowledged that Magnani's waiver argument would be valid in most circumstances. Here, however, the jury had not made its conclusions on each cause of action ascertainable. A wrongful-death liability finding seemed apparent, but any inference about liability for family expenses was conjectural, and nothing allocated the $19,000 between the claims. The jury had to make those determinations; the court could not supply its own allocation. By the time the defect was raised, the court could not reassemble the jury to correct it.

Stouder, dissenting, stated that Magnani had waived her individual interest in the verdict, eliminating the allocation dilemma, and that new-trial discretion has limits when the order depends on a legal ruling about verdict forms. In his view Trogi could not obtain relief from an error he accepted, and had not established actual prejudice; he would have gone on to examine the other asserted trial errors.

CP-121.rule: A court may mould an informal verdict so that its form implements the substance the jury agreed upon only when the jury's real purpose and intent appear clearly, sufficiently, and convincingly; an uncertain or ambiguous verdict cannot be moulded and requires a new trial.

sections.Parties: Clyde J. Robb, administrator ad prosequendum of Georgianna Robb's estate, sued John C. Hickey, Inc. and Roger W. King. The pleadings put the defendants' negligence and the decedent's contributory negligence in issue. Robb sought to set aside the verdict; the defendants sought to mould it into a defense verdict.
sections.Procedural History: After the jury's verdict was received and recorded, each side objected but sought a different remedy. Robb obtained a rule to set aside the verdict for ambiguity, inconsistency, inadequacy, and departure from the charge. The defendants moved to mould it into a verdict in their favor. The Morris County Circuit Court denied the defendants' motion to mould the verdict, made the plaintiff's rule absolute, and granted a new trial. This is a single trial judge's ruling.
sections.Material Facts: The reported decision does not describe the underlying event or the negligence evidence. The judge had instructed that, if the decedent's contributory negligence was established, the comparative degrees of fault were immaterial. In the judge's absence, the verdict was received and recorded at the clerk's desk. The jury stated that both parties were negligent, said the defendants were more negligent, and recommended $2,000 for Robb against both defendants. The defendants argued that the finding of negligence on both sides indicated their entitlement to prevail and that the recommendation of damages could be disregarded as surplusage.
sections.Issue: May the court mould a verdict that finds both sides negligent yet recommends damages for the plaintiff into a defense verdict by treating the damages recommendation as surplusage, or must the verdict be set aside?
sections.Holding: The Morris County Circuit Court in 1941, per Leyden, held that the verdict could not be moulded because the jury's intent was uncertain. The judge may correct the form of a verdict whose substance and intended result are clear, but may not choose one of two conflicting substantive results and call the other surplusage. The court did not enter the $2,000 judgment for the plaintiff or a defense judgment; it granted a new trial.
sections.Reasoning:
The court recognized that some jury recommendations can be removed without changing a verdict's substance. Suggestions outside the submitted issues, such as donating the amount in suit to charity, dividing an unrelated fund, allocating costs after the plaintiff loses, or showing leniency in a criminal case, may be irrelevant surplusage. Those examples did not resolve this case.

The recommendation of $2,000 to the plaintiff was directly pertinent to the issue submitted, which was whether the defendants were liable to him in damages. The first part of the verdict, read through the contributory-negligence instruction, indicated a defense result; the last part indicated a plaintiff result. The jury had also improperly compared degrees of negligence. The court could not tell which result the jury intended merely by accepting the defendants' preferred sentence and deleting the contrary one. Read as a whole, the verdict exposed a substantive contradiction rather than an informal way of expressing one clear outcome.

Leyden explained that a court may, and should, mould an informal verdict so that its form implements the substance actually agreed upon, but that power requires the jury's real purpose and intent to appear clearly, sufficiently, and convincingly. To mould an uncertain or ambiguous verdict would substitute the court's verdict for the jury's.

The casebook's notes pose comparisons with charitable recommendations and zero-damages verdicts; those questions are not holdings of the case.

CP-122.rule: A trial court may resubmit inconsistent special-verdict answers to a still-available jury, and must attempt to reconcile the jury's findings, including a revised verdict after resubmission, before ordering a new trial.

sections.Parties: Fernando Duk sued MGM Grand Hotel, seeking medical expenses, pain and suffering, and economic losses from inability to work in connection with a heart attack discovered after he was detained by hotel security and jailed. Duk appealed, challenging the grant of a new trial. MGM cross-appealed the resubmission to the jury, asserted an improper damages component, and challenged Duk's settlements with third-party defendants.
sections.Procedural History: The first trial, in 1998, used a Rule 49(a) special verdict. After the jury returned inconsistent answers, the judge told it to continue deliberating, and it returned a second verdict. The judge then granted MGM a new trial because the fault percentages differed between the verdicts. Before retrial, MGM added the ambulance provider and police and detention entities as third-party defendants; Duk settled with them, and the court found the settlements in good faith. The second trial produced a defense verdict. The Ninth Circuit affirmed in part and reversed in part, ordering reinstatement of the first jury's second verdict and entry of judgment for Duk with interest calculated by the district court. The opinion was amended on denial of rehearing.
sections.Material Facts:
Duk and his wife stopped at MGM's Las Vegas hotel. Duk drank heavily while gambling and became disruptive in a restaurant. Security personnel asked him to leave, then detained him after a citizen's arrest when he refused. His wife told security he was an insulin-dependent diabetic. He presented evidence that he complained of chest pain and alleged that security failed to convey that complaint to the responding paramedics, who did not check his heart rate or blood pressure.
