Police took him to jail. After release the next morning, he learned at a hospital that he had suffered a heart attack; severe damage ultimately required a heart transplant in 1995.

Under Nevada's comparative-negligence scheme, Duk could recover only if his negligence was 50% or less. The verdict form told the jury to stop if it assigned him more than 50%. The jury initially assigned Duk 65% and MGM 35%, yet went on to award $3.3 million. Twenty minutes after being told to continue deliberating, it returned a second verdict assigning Duk 49% and MGM 51%, with the damages figure unchanged.
sections.Issue: May a trial court resubmit an inconsistent Rule 49(a) special verdict to the jury even where an answer was given in violation of a stop instruction? May the court then order a new trial merely because the jury's fault percentages changed between the first and second verdicts?
sections.Holding: The Ninth Circuit in 2003, in an opinion by Judge Hawkins joined by Judges D.W. Nelson and Wardlaw, held that resubmission to the still-available jury was within the trial court's discretion even with a stop instruction, and that granting a new trial was an abuse of discretion because the second verdict was internally consistent and the change could be explained consistently with law and evidence. The court also rejected MGM's damages challenge and upheld the good-faith settlement determinations.
sections.Reasoning:
Rule 49(b) expressly authorizes further consideration of general verdicts accompanied by interrogatories, while Rule 49(a) did not expressly address resubmitting special verdicts. Circuit precedent permitted it because the rule did not prohibit it, and asking the still-present factfinder to clarify inconsistent answers promoted fairness and efficiency, provided the judge did not steer the jury toward an outcome. MGM relied on Floyd v. Laws, which treated an answer given in violation of a stop instruction as surplusage, but Floyd's jury had already been discharged. The court considered contrary Fourth Circuit authority but followed the view permitting the original jury to correct its own mistakes. The mere possibility of compromise did not defeat the presumption that jurors perform their duties properly.

The Seventh Amendment required an attempt to reconcile jury findings on a reasonable view of the evidence before disregarding them, and that obligation extended to an apparent conflict between an original verdict and one returned after resubmission. Resubmission entails renewed deliberation, so a difference between verdicts can reflect the clarification the judge requested. The trial judge rejected the second verdict as manipulation without considering a lawful change of mind. The court distinguished Riley v. K Mart, where the jury changed both liability percentages and total damages so as to preserve essentially the same net recovery; Duk's jury left total damages unchanged.

Lost earnings were properly submitted, and the settlement determinations were not an abuse of discretion. The $3.3 million is the total-damages finding; judgment was to be consistent with the revised fault allocation.

CP-123.rule: A motion for judgment notwithstanding the verdict tests legal sufficiency with the evidence viewed for the verdict winner, but on a new-trial motion the trial judge may set aside a verdict against the clear weight of the evidence, resting on false evidence, or producing a miscarriage of justice.

sections.Parties: Aetna Casualty & Surety Co. initiated a declaratory-judgment suit concerning coverage under an indemnity policy. Yeatts sought from the insurer the amount of a consent judgment entered against him in a state damages action, plus costs, interest, and attorney fees. Aetna was the appellant, challenging the denial of its post-verdict motions.
sections.Procedural History: After an earlier appeal, Yeatts amended his answer to allege the consent judgment. The jury returned a verdict in his favor. Aetna had not moved for a directed verdict or otherwise challenged sufficiency before the verdict. It then sought judgment notwithstanding the verdict and alternatively a new trial, asserting that the verdict contradicted the credible evidence. Both motions were denied, and their denial supplied the only appellate issues. This was the second appeal in the coverage litigation. The Fourth Circuit affirmed the judgment.
sections.Material Facts: Aetna denied coverage on the ground that the liability arose while Yeatts performed a criminal abortion and that the policy expressly excluded that liability. The jury decided whether he had engaged in the alleged criminal conduct. Evidence could have supported the insurer's position, but Yeatts testified himself and, if believed, had committed no criminal act. The opinion does not recount the medical evidence in detail.
sections.Issue: Was Aetna entitled to judgment notwithstanding the verdict, or to a new trial, on the ground that the verdict contradicted the credible evidence, and may an appellate court disturb the trial judge's denial of a new trial?
sections.Holding: The Fourth Circuit in 1941, in an opinion by Judge Parker for a panel with Soper and H.H. Watkins, held that judgment notwithstanding the verdict was unavailable both because no directed-verdict motion had been made and because Yeatts's favorable testimony prevented it. A trial judge may grant a new trial when the verdict is against the clear weight of the evidence even where substantial evidence prevents directing a verdict, but the denial here was within the trial judge's discretion, and the court found neither abuse nor special circumstances permitting interference.
sections.Reasoning:
Under the historical Rule 50(b), an appropriate directed-verdict motion was required as the foundation for a postverdict sufficiency challenge, and none was made; its absence also prevented appellate review of evidentiary sufficiency. Even had the request been preserved, the court had to view the evidence favorably to the party against whom judgment was sought and resolve conflicts in his favor. A judge could not reject Yeatts's testimony merely because contrary evidence appeared more credible.

Rule 59 supplied a different inquiry, governed by federal procedure and not state practice. A trial judge should grant a new trial if the verdict conflicts with the clear weight of evidence, rests on false evidence, or would produce a miscarriage of justice, even where substantial evidence prevents directing a verdict. The jury guarantee assigns credibility and weighing to the jury for purposes of deciding whether to take the case from it, but the court's historical supervisory authority permits a fresh jury trial to remedy an unjust result. Parker quoted historical authorities, including Smith v. Times Publishing Co., Bright v. Eynon, and Mellin v. Taylor, explaining that new trials protect the jury institution, and his discussion of Garrison stated the difference: the judge's disbelief cannot justify a directed verdict when substantial favorable evidence exists, but it can inform a new-trial decision.

Granting or refusing a new trial rested in sound trial-court discretion and was reviewable only in exceptional circumstances. The Fourth Circuit thought the trial judge could properly have granted a new trial, but that did not make the denial an abuse of discretion.

CP-124.rule: Under the New Jersey constitution a court may use additur, conditioning denial of a plaintiff's new-trial motion on the defendant's consent to an increased award, but its use is reviewable for abuse of discretion or manifest denial of justice.

sections.Parties: William Fisch was the plaintiff, whose stopped car was struck from behind by a truck driven by Bernard Clausi and owned by the Manger and Branin partnership, the defendants. Fisch was the appellant, challenging both the trial court's power to impose additur and the inadequacy of the increased amount.
sections.Procedural History: The jury expressly found the truck driver negligent and awarded $3,000. Fisch sought a new trial for inadequate damages. The trial court ordered that it would grant a damages-only trial unless the defendants consented to increasing the award to $7,500. They consented, and the court denied the motion. Fisch appealed, and the New Jersey Supreme Court certified the appeal on its own motion. That court reversed with directions for a new trial limited to damages.
sections.Material Facts:
On September 17, 1953, a traffic officer stopped vehicles on Amboy Avenue to let schoolchildren cross. Fisch's car was third in the southbound line and had stopped when the truck struck it from behind. Fisch and the officer testified that Clausi said his foot slipped off the brake; Clausi denied that but admitted striking the rear.

Fisch was treated for whiplash with medication, diathermy, and a neck brace. Persistent severe pain led to hospitalization, unsuccessful traction, confirmation of a ruptured disc by myelogram, and surgery. He returned to work part-time in February 1954 and full-time in September. The treating physicians connected the surgery to the 1953 accident, and the defendants offered no contrary medical testimony, though they suggested an earlier 1950 accident accounted for some injury. The record showed normal heavy work and sports between recovery from that accident and the 1953 collision. Actual medical expenses exceeded $2,200 and lost wages were approximately $620, so the $3,000 award left substantially nothing for suffering and permanent injury.
sections.Issue: Does the New Jersey constitution's jury-trial guarantee permit a trial court to use additur, and if so, was the additur to $7,500 properly used in this case?
sections.Holding: The New Jersey Supreme Court in 1957, in an opinion by Justice Jacobs, held that fair use of additur and remittitur does not violate the state constitution, but rejected the additur here because the increased award still inadequately compensated Fisch and rested on a mistaken view of his prior condition. All six participating justices voted for reversal and a damages-only new trial; Heher, joined by Oliphant, concurred only in the result, leaving four justices supporting Jacobs's reasoning.
sections.Reasoning:
Jacobs treated additur and remittitur as analogous devices for attaining substantial justice without the cost and delay of retrial. He acknowledged that Dimick v. Schiedt prohibited additur in federal courts under the Seventh Amendment while permitting remittitur, and expressed doubts about its reasoning, but those were observations; the Seventh Amendment did not apply to these state-court proceedings, so the question turned on New Jersey's constitution and history. The state jury guarantee protected substantive integrity without freezing every procedural form. New Jersey had long used remittitur, Gaffney v. Illingsworth recognized parallel discretion for additur, and the 1947 constitutional convention acted against that background of judicial controls without indicating they should be curtailed.

Constitutional permission did not validate every figure a judge selects. The trial judge had limited compensation because he believed Fisch already had a back condition, but the record indicated that the earlier condition had cleared and was unrelated to this injury. That misconception produced the insufficient $7,500 figure, so a second jury should determine damages. Liability was clearly resolved and need not be retried.

Heher, joined by Oliphant, concurring in the result, understood the state guarantee to preserve the common-law jury right as it existed in 1776. Following Dimick's distinction, he reasoned that reducing an excessive award removes an excess from an amount the jury found, while increasing an inadequate verdict adds compensation no jury assessed, and a defendant's consent does not preserve the unwilling plaintiff's right to a jury assessment.

CP-125.rule: Because liability and damages are ordinarily intertwined, a new trial granted for an error affecting liability should extend to all issues where damages are unliquidated; a limited new trial is disfavored.

sections.Parties: Helen Doutre sued Pauline and Floyd Niec, who operated a beauty shop in Flint, for injuries from a bleach-and-color treatment. Both sides appealed the trial court's order for a new trial limited to liability. Doutre argued that no retrial should occur; the defendants argued that liability and damages were too closely connected to permit a limited retrial.
sections.Procedural History: At trial the defendants were prevented from testifying about the standard of care observed by local beauty shops, and the jury awarded Doutre $10,000. On the defendants' motion, the trial court granted a new trial but limited it to liability, intending to retain the damages determination. Both sides appealed. The Michigan Court of Appeals extended the new-trial order to all issues, with costs awarded to the defendants.
sections.Material Facts: On April 19, 1962, the Niecs administered a bleach-and-color treatment to Doutre without a preliminary patch test, and she suffered injuries to her head and face. The opinion does not describe the particular chemical, the treatment of the injury, or the duration of disability. One defendant had worked in the business for 24 years and the other for 14. They had attended beauticians' conventions, observed others' practices, and said they kept abreast of the practices of Genesee County operators. Doutre maintained that they could know other Flint operators' practices only through hearsay.
sections.Issue: Was the exclusion of the defendants' testimony about local trade practice an error warranting a new trial, and if so, could the new trial be limited to liability while the original damages award was preserved?
sections.Holding: The Michigan Court of Appeals in 1965, in an opinion by T.G. Kavanagh in which McGregor and Fitzgerald concurred, held that excluding the trade-practice testimony was an error requiring a new trial, and that the new trial must extend to all issues rather than liability alone. The court did not hold the $10,000 amount excessive or inadequate, and did not resolve whether the Niecs acted negligently.
sections.Reasoning:
The premise that the defendants could know other operators' practices only through hearsay was unsupported by the record; their years in the business, attendance at conventions, and observation of others' practices supplied a basis for testimony. The court agreed with the trial judge's reconsidered ruling that the exclusion was error and stated, citing Barton v. Myers, that the testimony was admissible because no person was held to a higher standard than the industry average. The brief notes that this is the standard expressed in this 1965 opinion.

On the scope of retrial, the court described liability and damages as ordinarily intertwined. The exception then recognized by the Michigan Supreme Court permitted retrial of damages alone when liability was clear. Although the court rule authorized limited new trials, the practice was disfavored, and the court saw no compelling reason to expand the exception into a liability-only retrial. The trial judge believed the exclusion might have influenced liability but could not have affected damages; the appellate court did not share that certainty. Damages were unliquidated, and liability had been decided in a trial containing a concededly erroneous evidentiary ruling, so justice required the jury deciding liability to measure damages as well.

The casebook's comparison with Judge Freedman's dissent in Hutton v. Fisher is an editorial study aid concerning a different case, not a dissent in this one.

CP-126.rule: An execution officer must protect both creditor and debtor: real estate susceptible of division must be divided and only enough sold to satisfy the execution, and a sale of the whole in violation of that requirement may be cancelled in equity on condition of restitution.

sections.Parties: Bill Griggs, the purchaser at a sheriff's execution sale of W.A. Brookshire's farm, sued for possession and damages for withholding. Brookshire denied the claim and counterclaimed to cancel the sale and the sheriff's deed; Sheriff Powell became a third-party defendant. After Brookshire appealed and was imprisoned, Miller became trustee of his estate and was substituted as the litigant.
sections.Procedural History: Griggs sued three days after the sale. The parties and the court treated the dispute as equitable. The trial court ruled for Griggs, denied the counterclaim, and awarded $2,483.24 through judgment plus $250 per month while possession was withheld. Brookshire appealed. The Supreme Court of Missouri, adopting Special Commissioner Bohling's opinion per curiam in September 1963, conditioned cancellation of the sale on a deposit of the purchase price with interest. It modified those conditions on October 7, 1963. In a supplemental opinion of January 10, 1964, it found the conditions satisfied and reversed and remanded with directions to cancel the sheriff's sale and deed and to revest title in the trustee. The casebook excerpt retains only the original conditional decree.
sections.Material Facts:
Ray Crouch obtained a $1,966.69 judgment against Brookshire in July 1959, affirmed in December 1960; no supersedeas bond stayed execution. The sheriff levied on Brookshire's 322-acre farm, advertised it for the Crouch execution, and sold it on January 16, 1961, for $20,600. The Crouch judgment, interest, and costs totaled $2,308.16. Another creditor, Dorothy Contestible as administratrix, held a $17,000 wrongful-death judgment; the sheriff received its writ and levied before the sale but never advertised a sale under that execution.

Five days before the sale Brookshire wrote the sheriff identifying the northeast forty acres and asking that the sale be confined to them, and he protested publicly. The farm consisted of approximately eight forties and could have been offered in parcels. The sheriff acknowledged that forty acres might have been worth far more than the Crouch debt but did not intend to offer even eighty; he knew of substantial cattle and other property and chose the farm because it was easier. Even on the purchaser's lower valuation, the debtor's interest was approximately $46,000. The sheriff distributed the proceeds toward both debts.
sections.Issue: Should the execution sale of the debtor's entire divisible farm be cancelled because the sheriff failed to divide it and sell only enough to satisfy the advertised execution, and if so, on what terms of restitution to the purchaser?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of Missouri in 1963, adopting Bohling's opinion per curiam with all judges concurring, held that the sale of the undivided farm violated the protective execution requirements and called for equitable cancellation, conditioned on restitution. The original decree required a $20,600 deposit with 6% annual interest from the sale within thirty days. As modified, the period was extended to 120 days from September 9, restitution of $1,610.63 in taxes Griggs had paid with 6% interest from July 6, 1962 was added, and costs were divided equally. The trustee deposited $26,019.26, and the court reversed.
sections.Reasoning:
The governing rules allowed a debtor to identify sufficient property for levy and elect the order of sale through timely written notice, and directed division of real estate susceptible of division and sale of only enough to satisfy the execution unless the debtor requested sale of the whole. The officer retained judgment but had to exercise the care of a reasonably prudent person and protect against sacrificing property. Measured against those rules, the sheriff's sale of the whole farm for convenience, despite Brookshire's written request, was improper.

Unreleased liens in the records did not justify treating the debtor's interest as nearly worthless, because the evidence showed that a $15,000 note, a $10,000 note, and a federal tax claim had been adjusted or discharged. Receipt of the second writ produced a constructive levy but gave no authority to sell under it without the required advertisement, and the sheriff testified that he sold under the Crouch execution. The larger unadvertised judgment therefore could not justify selling more land than was proper under the advertised execution.

On restitution, the court rejected the trustee's argument that alleged purchaser wrongdoing defeated it, relying on the findings, the point's late introduction in the reply brief, and the undisputed use of the purchase money to discharge lawful obligations. Equitable cancellation could not let the debtor recover the property while keeping the benefit of paid debts.

The court also rejected attacks on the ejectment pleading and an attempt to disqualify the transferred judge, since the rule permitted only one judicial disqualification for each party.

CP-127.rule: A court may order a judgment debtor to pay installments from income after allowing for reasonable needs and may punish refusal to comply as contempt; that enforces obedience to a court order the debtor can obey and is not imprisonment for debt.

sections.Parties: Reeves, a judgment creditor, sought to collect a judgment of approximately $400 from Charles Crownshield, a federal government employee. Crownshield, the judgment debtor, was the appellant, challenging an installment-payment order and a contempt order on constitutional grounds.
sections.Procedural History: After a supplementary examination, the City Court ordered Crownshield to pay $20 monthly installments until the judgment was satisfied. When he failed to pay, it adjudged him in contempt, imposed a $20 fine, and provided for commitment if the fine was not paid. He appealed directly from the City Court on constitutional grounds, and the parties stipulated to consolidate review of the two orders. The New York Court of Appeals regarded the challenged order as a final order in a special proceeding, permitting review, and affirmed both orders with costs.
sections.Material Facts:
The supplementary examination showed that Crownshield worked for the federal government as a steamship inspector, earning $230 per month less a small pension deduction. He had no children, his wife's whereabouts were unknown, and apart from $48 rent and living expenses he had no financial obligations.

A 1935 New York enactment authorized installment orders from income in addition to existing garnishment procedures. Under Civil Practice Act section 793, the debtor had to receive notice and an opportunity to show inability to pay, and the order had to account for the reasonable requirements of the debtor and family and obligations to other creditors. Section 801 authorized punishment for contempt upon refusal to comply. Crownshield did not claim that $20 monthly payments were unjust, harsh, or inequitable in his circumstances; he asserted that a court lacked power to require any such use of his income.
sections.Issue: Does the statute authorizing installment-payment orders enforced by contempt amount to imprisonment for debt in violation of state and federal due process? Does applying it to a federal employee's salary interfere with a federal instrumentality?
sections.Holding: The New York Court of Appeals in 1937, in an opinion by Finch in which all six other judges concurred, upheld the installment order and the contempt sanction against a debtor who could comply after his reasonable living needs were considered. Contempt enforced obedience to the judicial order and was not imprisonment simply for an unpaid debt. The order did not interfere with the federal government's payment of its employee. Both orders were affirmed.
sections.Reasoning:
Finch placed the enactment among efforts to improve collection from debtors able to pay who evaded judgments. Neither constitution expressly prohibited imprisonment for debt, and the state statutory prohibition excepted cases specially authorized by law. The court left open possible due-process concerns with imprisoning a debtor without regard to ability to pay; this order concerned payments from income after allowance for reasonable needs and an opportunity to establish inability. The court characterized Crownshield's position as arbitrary refusal by someone able to comply. Without enforcement authority, the direct collection remedy would be ineffective. A quoted execution-law discussion distinguished protecting the honest poor debtor from shielding a solvent debtor who conceals assets or evades process.

On the federal-employment objection, Crownshield invoked decisions invalidating state taxes on federal officers' salaries. Finch distinguished their rationale: taxing salary reduced federal compensation and could force the government to increase its payments, whereas the installment order demanded no payment by the government and did not reduce the compensation it provided. Once paid, salary became the employee's general income; property bought with it could be subject to execution, and there was no reason to exempt the same value because it remained money. The court acknowledged the then-existing bar on garnishing federal wages but distinguished an order requiring the recipient to apply income already received. Federal employment conferred no privilege to disobey a lawful state-court order.

The casebook's later discussion of body-execution statutes is editorial context, not a holding of the case.

CP-128.rule: A determination of liability that leaves damages and other requested relief unresolved is interlocutory, and Rule 54(b) cannot make it a final decision, because a complaint asserting one legal right is a single claim even though it requests several remedies.

sections.Parties: Wetzel and the other respondents were employee-plaintiffs challenging Liberty Mutual's treatment of women under Title VII, seeking relief for themselves and the class identified in their complaint. Liberty Mutual was their employer, the defendant, the party that appealed the liability ruling, and the Supreme Court petitioner. The challenged insurance benefits and maternity-leave regulations were Liberty Mutual's own employment practices.
sections.Procedural History: On January 9, 1974, the Western District of Pennsylvania granted the employees' motion for partial summary judgment on liability. Liberty Mutual moved for reconsideration. On February 20, the court denied that motion and directed entry of final judgment on the policy violations, expressly finding no just reason for delay under Rule 54(b), while stating that it was withholding the requested injunctive order. Liberty Mutual appealed. The Third Circuit regarded the order as final under 28 U.S.C. section 1291 and affirmed on the merits. The Court granted certiorari and heard argument on the merits, but raised the jurisdictional issue on its own. It vacated the Third Circuit's judgment and remanded with instructions to dismiss Liberty Mutual's appeal.
sections.Material Facts:
The disputed policies denied disability-income benefits for pregnancy-related disabilities and required women to return to work within three months of childbirth or face termination. The plaintiffs alleged sex discrimination and sought changes to employment practices, an injunction, monetary relief including backpay and other damages, costs, and attorney's fees.

After extensive discovery, the plaintiffs sought partial summary judgment on liability alone. The district court found no material factual dispute and ruled that the pregnancy-related policies violated Title VII. The judge initially stated that an injunction would issue and invited a proposed form of order. Liberty Mutual filed a notice of appeal and sought a stay. The judge then withheld the injunction and attempted to make the liability determination immediately appealable through Rule 54(b). The order awarded no injunction, damages, or fees. Neither party had questioned the Third Circuit's jurisdiction.
sections.Issue: Can a liability-only partial summary judgment become a final, appealable decision under section 1291 merely because the district court invokes Rule 54(b), when the complaint asserts one legal right but requests several forms of relief and none has been awarded? If not, can section 1292(a)(1) or section 1292(b) sustain the employer's appeal?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 1976, in an opinion by Justice Rehnquist joined by every participating Justice, with Justice Blackmun taking no part, held that the liability determination was interlocutory and that Rule 54(b) could not convert it into a final decision by a recital that there is no just reason for delay. The assertion of one legal right under one theory and set of facts remained a single claim despite the requests for multiple remedies. Neither section 1292(a)(1) nor section 1292(b) supplied jurisdiction. The Third Circuit therefore could not adjudicate the merits, and the Court did not reach whether the practices violated Title VII.
sections.Reasoning:
Appellate jurisdiction required independent examination even though the parties had argued the merits without objection; agreement or silence cannot supply statutory authority to review a nonappealable order. The district court had neither enjoined the practices nor awarded damages or fees, and those unresolved remedies were express parts of the complaint. Counsel suggested treating the order as a declaratory judgment; the Court answered that a complaint seeking only a declaration would be a different case.

Rule 54(b) enables entry of final judgment as to fewer than all qualifying claims or parties; it does not authorize immediate appeals from every final resolution of a legal issue. Separating liability from remedy within one claim did not produce two claims. The Court did not attempt a comprehensive definition of a claim for relief. Without the certification, the ruling was ordinary partial summary judgment, which narrows but does not terminate the proceedings.

Section 1292(a)(1) did not help: no injunction had issued against Liberty Mutual, and even assuming the withholding was a refusal appealable by the employees, it was not a denial of an injunction the employer sought. Section 1292(b) required district-court certification and permission from the court of appeals; the record lacked an application within the ten-day period, and the Third Circuit, believing the appeal was of right, had not exercised discretionary permission. Allowing the procedure would make almost any liability ruling appealable on a district judge's designation, contrary to the balance Congress struck in sections 1291 and 1292.

CP-129.rule: A collateral order must conclusively determine the disputed question, resolve an important issue completely separate from the merits, and be effectively unreviewable after final judgment; a claimed right to avoid trial qualifies only when delay would imperil a sufficiently substantial interest.

sections.Parties: Richard Will and the other petitioners were federal customs agents sued individually by Susan Hallock. Hallock and her computer-software business had also pursued a separate Federal Tort Claims Act action against the United States. The agents invoked the judgment in the suit against the government as a statutory bar to the individual-capacity constitutional action and sought an immediate appeal from the refusal to apply that bar.
sections.Procedural History: The FTCA suit was filed in July 2002 in the Northern District of New York and dismissed under the exception to the waiver of sovereign immunity for detention of goods. The agents then moved for judgment in Hallock's separate action, relying on the FTCA judgment bar. The district court denied the motion because it considered the earlier dismissal procedural and therefore insufficient to activate the bar. The agents appealed immediately. The Second Circuit held that it had jurisdiction under the collateral-order doctrine and affirmed the refusal to apply the bar. The Court granted certiorari on the judgment-bar question but concluded that the court of appeals lacked jurisdiction; it vacated the judgment and remanded with instructions to dismiss the appeal.
sections.Material Facts:
According to the complaint, Susan Hallock owned a software business operated from home with her husband Richard. Someone stole information associated with Richard's credit card and used it to pay for access to a child-pornography website. Customs agents investigating the site traced the payment to his card, obtained a warrant, and seized the Hallocks' computer equipment, software, and disk drives. No criminal charges followed. When the equipment was returned, several drives were damaged and the stored data, including business records and trade secrets, had been lost; the alleged loss forced the business to close.

While the FTCA negligence suit was pending, Hallock filed a separate Bivens action against the agents, alleging deprivation of property in violation of the Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause. Once the FTCA suit was dismissed, the agents invoked 28 U.S.C. section 2676, which makes a judgment in the FTCA action a bar to an action by the claimant against the government employee arising from the same subject matter. The brief notes that the casebook's introductory summary calls the individual action a negligence suit, while the full opinion identifies it as a Bivens action.
sections.Issue: Is an order refusing to apply the FTCA's judgment bar immediately appealable under the collateral-order doctrine because the agents assert a right to avoid further trial, that is, does the defense protect an interest sufficiently important and incapable of effective later review to justify an appeal before final judgment under section 1291?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 2006, in a unanimous opinion by Justice Souter, held that an order rejecting the FTCA judgment-bar defense does not qualify for immediate collateral-order appeal. An assertion of a right to avoid trial does not by itself make an order effectively unreviewable; the loss threatened by waiting must implicate a sufficiently substantial interest, not simply the time and money spent on litigation. The Second Circuit therefore lacked jurisdiction. The Court did not decide whether the district court correctly interpreted the judgment bar.
sections.Reasoning:
The collateral-order doctrine is a practical construction of the final-decision requirement covering a small class of orders, and its narrowness is integral; if every adverse ruling could be appealed immediately, successive appeals could obstruct valid claims and undermine efficient adjudication.

Orders denying absolute immunity, qualified immunity, a state's Eleventh Amendment immunity, or a double-jeopardy defense can qualify, and the agents argued for comparable treatment. The Court rejected the inference that every defense describable as a right not to be tried is immediately appealable: limitations, jurisdictional, claim-preclusion, and pleading defenses, and a valid settlement, also let a defendant avoid trial. If the irreversibility of litigation costs were enough, almost every denial of a pretrial motion would qualify.

What distinguishes the recognized examples is the interest lost by delay: separation of powers for presidential immunity, governmental effectiveness and reasonable official initiative under unclear law for qualified immunity, a state's dignitary interests, and protection against repeated prosecution. The judgment bar is different. It arises only because a prior FTCA case reached judgment and does not turn on the clarity of the law or the reasonableness of the official's conduct. It cannot operate until an FTCA judgment exists, and Hallock could have brought the individual action alone, in which event it would never have arisen. Claim preclusion was the closer analogy, though the Court did not hold the two identical; correction after final judgment is ordinarily sufficient. That double jeopardy also depends on an earlier proceeding did not control, because the underlying interests differ.

CP-130.rule: A court of appeals that may eventually hear an appeal may issue mandamus under the All Writs Act in exceptional circumstances, and calendar congestion, complexity and trial length are not exceptional conditions permitting reference of a whole nonjury case to a master.

sections.Parties: Judge La Buy, a federal district judge in the Northern District of Illinois, was the petitioner in the Court because the Seventh Circuit had directed him by mandamus to vacate orders referring two antitrust actions to a master. Howes Leather and the other respondents were parties seeking relief from those references; all parties to the underlying cases objected to them. The underlying plaintiffs were independent retail shoe-repair businesses and wholesalers suing manufacturers, wholesalers, mail-order businesses and chain operators for monopolization, price fixing and discriminatory pricing of shoe-repair supplies. They sought injunctions, treble damages and accountings.
sections.Procedural History: After Judge La Buy refused to vacate the references, the parties petitioned the Seventh Circuit under the All Writs Act, 28 U.S.C. § 1651(a). That court agreed unanimously that it had authority to issue mandamus in an appropriate case, though it divided over whether the circumstances warranted it. It issued writs directing that the reference orders be vacated, treating the transfer of the basic adjudicative work as a refusal to try the causes in due course. Judge La Buy sought certiorari, challenging both the appellate court's power to intervene before final judgment and its conclusion that his exercise of Rule 53 discretion warranted extraordinary relief. The Court affirmed the judgment issuing the writs, without adjudicating the antitrust claims or determining any damages.
sections.Material Facts:
Both actions began in 1950. When mandamus was sought, Rohlfing involved eighty-seven plaintiffs and six remaining defendants, and Shaffer six plaintiffs and six defendants. Years of preliminary proceedings, including amended pleadings, dismissals of parties, discovery disputes, numerous depositions, hearings and rulings on summary judgment requests, had given the judge substantial familiarity with the factual and legal issues. Neither liability nor relief had been decided.

When the cases were called to reset trial in February 1955, counsel estimated that one trial would require six weeks. Judge La Buy asked whether the parties would agree to a master, received no agreement, and the next day ordered references on his own initiative. The orders assigned the master to take evidence and report findings of fact and conclusions of law on the general issues, including conspiracy, liability, damages and injunctive relief, rather than a discrete accounting after liability had been established. The judge cited an extremely congested calendar, the complexity of the cases and the expected length of trial. The parties deposited approximately $8,000 as security for costs but objected and moved to vacate; their compliance did not establish consent. The then-governing Rule 53(b) made references exceptional and, for nonjury actions other than matters of account, required an exceptional condition. The record showed that Judge La Buy had made eleven references during the preceding six years.
sections.Issue: May a court of appeals use mandamus before final judgment to direct a district judge to vacate orders referring entire nonjury antitrust cases to a master? If so, do congestion, complexity and anticipated trial length constitute exceptional conditions permitting such broad references under the then-applicable Rule 53(b), or do the orders amount to an exceptional abuse warranting the writ?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States, 1957, in an opinion by Justice Clark, affirmed by a 5-4 vote. Under the All Writs Act, a court of appeals that may eventually exercise appellate jurisdiction over a case has discretionary authority to issue mandamus in aid of that jurisdiction in proper, exceptional circumstances; the availability of review after final judgment does not categorically eliminate that authority, though the Court disclaimed indiscriminate use of writs to review interlocutory rulings. The references here were a clear abuse of the district judge's authority under the historical Rule 53(b), and their exceptional scope and circumstances justified mandamus. A later, limited reference for detailed damage accounting could be appropriate after the judge determined overall liability.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court separated the existence of mandamus power from the discretion to use it. Because the Seventh Circuit could later hear appeals in these cases, it had authority under the All Writs Act, which the 1948 recodification had not eliminated. The majority confined its approval to the exceptional circumstances presented.

Those circumstances included the breadth of the delegation. The master was to try the central disputes before conspiracy or liability had been determined, which the majority regarded as nearly an abdication of the judicial function, depriving the parties of the trial before the court to which the rule entitled them. The judge's years of preliminary rulings and antitrust experience made him particularly well placed to resolve the cases. The Seventh Circuit had warned for years that references should be rare. Congestion was too common to be an exceptional condition; accepting it would make reference routine. Complexity and length likewise failed, since they supported adjudication by an experienced regular judge rather than a temporary appointee. Once the judge resolved liability, detailed calculation of individual losses might properly go to a master. The Court acknowledged that mandamus should remain an extreme remedy and did not establish an unrestricted interlocutory appeal.

Justice Brennan, joined by Justices Frankfurter, Burton and Harlan, dissented. He argued that Rule 53 gave the judge discretion, so even a mistaken reference was an error within jurisdiction correctable on final judgment, that the All Writs Act is an auxiliary power and not an independent power to review unappealable interlocutory orders, and that the majority effectively introduced discretionary interlocutory appeals without congressional authorization.

CP-131.rule: A district court's certification under 28 U.S.C. § 1292(b) does not ensure an immediate appeal; the court of appeals may deny leave where early review would prolong rather than advance the litigation and the error can be corrected after final judgment.

sections.Parties: Electrical-company defendants applied to the Second Circuit for leave to appeal a discovery order. The plaintiffs were electricity suppliers claiming damages. The defendants wanted pretrial discovery into whether the plaintiffs had actually sustained the claimed damages or had shifted them to their customers.
sections.Procedural History: The district court sustained the plaintiffs' objections to the defendants' interrogatories, effectively preventing pretrial discovery into the proposed pass-on defense. It certified the order under 28 U.S.C. § 1292(b) as involving a controlling legal question with substantial ground for disagreement, and noted that the Seventh Circuit had permitted an appeal from a similar order. The defendants then applied to the Second Circuit for leave to appeal. The reported decision is this short application ruling, not a merits adjudication of the broader electrical-equipment litigation or an appeal from a final damages judgment. The application for leave to appeal was denied.
sections.Material Facts: The defendants sought interrogatory answers about whether the plaintiff electricity suppliers actually sustained the claimed damages or passed them on to their customers. Their proposed defense was that the plaintiffs should not recover damages to the extent the defendants could prove those losses had been passed on. The district court sustained objections to the interrogatories and then certified its order for interlocutory appeal.
sections.Issue: Should the court of appeals grant leave to appeal a discovery ruling that the district court has certified under § 1292(b) as involving a controlling and disputed legal question, when deciding that question before trial may delay rather than advance the cases?
sections.Holding: The Second Circuit, 1964, per curiam, with Judges Waterman and Moore participating and Judge Friendly taking no part, denied leave to appeal. District-court certification under § 1292(b) did not ensure an immediate appeal. Resolving the disputed discovery issue before trial would likely prolong rather than advance the cases, and the defendants could seek correction after an adverse final judgment. The court expressed no opinion on whether the discovery ruling or the asserted pass-on defense was legally correct.
sections.Reasoning:
The court refused to isolate the legal question from the litigation as a whole. Many important legal questions would arise, but importance and disagreement alone did not answer whether this one should be decided before trial; the practical question was whether immediate review was feasible and advisable in the context of the cases as a whole.

Allowing the requested discovery could generate numerous full-scale inquiries into electricity rates, dwarfing even the already extensive pretrial proceedings in time and testimony. If the discovery ruling later proved erroneous and contributed to an adverse judgment, the defendants could seek correction together with other asserted errors in a final appeal. The court doubted that later discovery or hearings on the extent of passed-on damages, if the doctrine applied, would be more burdensome than conducting them immediately. Denial did not eliminate the defense or prejudice the defendants' ability to raise it on an ultimate appeal, whereas immediate appellate intervention threatened to delay final disposition. The opinion does not state a categorical ban on interlocutory discovery appeals; it evaluates the consequences in these proceedings. There was no dissent.

CP-132.rule: A prevailing party ordinarily may not appeal a favorable judgment to challenge unnecessary findings, but may appeal to have an unnecessary adverse adjudication removed from the operative decree itself.

sections.Parties: Thomas & Betts and the other respondents were the plaintiffs in an equity suit alleging patent infringement. Electrical Fittings and the other petitioners were the accused infringers. Although the suit ended in the defendants' favor, they appealed the portion of the decree that formally adjudged one patent claim valid, seeking to have that adverse statement corrected.
sections.Procedural History: The district court held claim 1 valid but not infringed and claim 2 invalid, and dismissed the bill. The patent owners did not appeal. The defendants appealed to the Second Circuit solely from the portion of the decree adjudicating claim 1 valid. The court of appeals dismissed the appeal because the defendants had obtained all the relief to which they were entitled and the litigation had ended in their favor; it also reasoned that the validity determination would not bind them in later litigation. The Court granted certiorari because of an asserted conflict among appellate decisions. It reversed the dismissal and remanded with instructions to entertain the appeal and direct the district court to reform its decree.
sections.Material Facts: The infringement action concerned two patent claims. The district court determined that claim 1 was valid but not infringed and that claim 2 was invalid. Its decree did more than dismiss the complaint: it expressly adjudged claim 1 valid while dismissing the bill because infringement had not been proved. The finding of noninfringement already sufficed to defeat the suit, so an adjudication of validity was unnecessary to the disposition. The patent owners did not appeal and filed a disclaimer of claim 2 in the Patent Office. The report does not describe the invention, the accused device, or the evidentiary basis for the determinations.
sections.Issue: May a defendant who has defeated an infringement suit appeal an unnecessary adverse adjudication of patent validity contained in the decree itself, even though a prevailing party ordinarily cannot appeal merely to challenge unfavorable findings? If so, should the appeal produce a decision on the patent's validity or a narrower revision of the decree?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States, 1939, in an opinion by Justice Roberts with no separate opinion reported, held that although a party ordinarily may not appeal a favorable judgment merely to obtain review of findings it considers erroneous and that are unnecessary to the judgment, a party may seek elimination of an unnecessary adverse adjudication contained in the operative decree itself. The defendants were entitled to removal of the decree's declaration that claim 1 was valid, and the appellate court could entertain the appeal for that purpose without adjudicating validity on the merits. The Court did not hold claim 1 invalid or disturb the defendants' success.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court started from the rule limiting appeals by prevailing parties. Appellate review ordinarily concerns an adverse judgment, not every statement or finding in the reasoning that a successful party would prefer to erase, and the Court expressly retained that principle.

The operative decree made this case different. The district court had included a formal adjudication of claim 1's validity even though the failure to prove infringement already required dismissal. The adverse matter was therefore not merely an unnecessary explanation in an opinion; it stood in the decree as a judicial adjudication of a litigated issue, and the defendants were entitled to have it removed. The court of appeals' belief that the declaration would not bind the defendants later did not justify leaving it in place, and the Court did not resolve the range of possible future preclusion consequences.

The remedy also confined the appellate court's role. Entertaining the appeal did not authorize a determination that claim 1 was invalid; the appeal could be resolved by directing reformation of the decree, leaving validity undecided. That kept the exception from becoming a general license for prevailing litigants to obtain review of unnecessary findings.

CP-133.rule: An appellee may defend a judgment on any ground supported by the record, including one the trial court rejected, but must cross-appeal to enlarge its own rights or diminish the opponent's rights under that judgment.

sections.Parties: International Ore & Fertilizer Corp. (Interore), a fertilizer seller, sued SGS Control Services, the inspection company it had engaged to inspect a vessel's holds and certify their suitability for cargo. Interore pleaded contract, warranty, negligence and negligent misrepresentation. SGS appealed the judgment against it; Interore cross-appealed the contributory-negligence finding but did not cross-appeal the dismissal of its contract claim. SGS's counsel, Charles B. Updike and Scott M. Riemer, were sanctioned under Rule 11.
sections.Procedural History: After a bench trial on liability, Judge Tenney dismissed the contract claim, reasoning that the small fee and informal transaction did not warrant large consequential liability, and rejected negligence because SGS's inspection duty arose from contract. He imposed liability for negligent misrepresentation in the certificate and attributed half the responsibility to Interore for not warning SGS about New Zealand's strict requirements. A later damages proceeding before Magistrate Judge Gershon produced a judgment of $713,666.27. SGS appealed; Interore cross-appealed only the contributory-negligence finding. The Second Circuit affirmed the judgment and the sanctions.
sections.Material Facts:
Interore sold 22,202 metric tons of fertilizer to East Coast Fertilizer in New Zealand for $4,118,287, including cost and freight. It chartered the vessel Adelina and engaged SGS to inspect the holds and certify their suitability. The vessel had carried coal immediately before and barley before that; cleaning and painting left barley behind structural stringers. A Swedish SGS affiliate inspected two holds. SGS's Tampa inspector spent about half an hour on the other three, walking through without looking behind the stringers; he later learned of the earlier cargoes but did not return. SGS issued a certificate of readiness and charged $150 for the Tampa inspection.

In New Zealand, authorities found barley contamination and would permit unloading only if buyers were informed and restrictions protected barley-growing areas. East Coast refused the shipment. After efforts to find other buyers failed, Interore sent the fertilizer to Antwerp and sold it in smaller lots, incurring additional expense and losses. SGS neither owned the vessel nor undertook the transportation; the brief notes that the casebook editors' bracketed introduction inaccurately describes SGS as transporter and shipowner.
sections.Issue: Could the contract claim that the district court rejected sustain the existing judgment when Interore had not cross-appealed its dismissal, and could the award be increased to full contract damages? Separately, did SGS owe an independent tort duty supporting negligent misrepresentation, and were the Rule 11 sanctions on its counsel proper?
sections.Holding: The Second Circuit, 1994, in an opinion by Judge Winter joined by Judge Van Graafeiland, with District Judge Mishler concurring in part and dissenting in part, rejected the negligent-misrepresentation theory but affirmed the $713,666.27 award on a contract theory. The contract governed SGS's duty, no independent tort duty existed, and SGS breached its obligation to inspect with reasonable care. Because Interore had not appealed the dismissal of its contract claim, the court declined to increase the award to full contract damages. It also affirmed the sanctions on SGS's lawyers for repeatedly relitigating causation.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority held that the same inadequate inspection could not coherently be a tort while being excused as a contractual failure. Certification was the service's central purpose, and SGS could foresee that cargo interests would rely on it. A low fee alone did not excuse foreseeable consequential loss, since SGS could price the risk or insure against it. The court did not decide whether federal maritime or New York law controlled because the result was the same.

On the appellate problem, under the rule drawn from American Railway Express an appellee may defend a decree on any ground supported by the record, including one the district court rejected, but a cross-appeal is required to enlarge the appellee's rights or diminish the opponent's. Substituting contract for tort liability preserved the award already entered; increasing the damages would change the parties' rights and was unavailable. Interore's challenge to the contributory-negligence finding did not supply the missing appeal.

The sanctions survived abuse-of-discretion review: causation had been resolved in the liability phase, yet counsel repeatedly tried to reopen it, and they had notice and an opportunity to respond.

Judge Mishler agreed on the tort theory, the cross-appeal point and sanctions, but dissented from imposing contract damages and would have dismissed the complaint, citing the disparity between the $150 charge and the claimed loss and Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 351(3).

The casebook uses the case to show that appellate relief turns on the judgment's effect on the parties, not on whether the appellate court accepts the trial judge's reasoning.

CP-134.rule: A statute authorizing a reviewing court to set aside a verdict as against the manifest weight of the evidence and require a new jury trial does not violate the state constitutional right to jury trial, provided the power is exercised within strict limits.

sections.Parties: John Corcoran sued the City of Chicago for personal injuries and won a jury verdict. After the Appellate Court reversed, he sought review in the Illinois Supreme Court by writ of error, challenging the constitutionality of the statute under which the Appellate Court had acted. The city sought dismissal of the writ.
sections.Procedural History: The jury awarded Corcoran $5,000, and the superior court denied a new trial and entered judgment. The Appellate Court reversed, finding the verdict against the manifest weight of the evidence, and initially remanded for another trial. Corcoran asked the Appellate Court to strike the remand, stating by affidavit that another trial would involve the same issues and that he had no additional or different evidence. Striking the remand made the order final and allowed him to seek Supreme Court review by a common-law writ of error. The Illinois Supreme Court denied the city's motion to dismiss the writ and affirmed the Appellate Court's judgment.
sections.Material Facts: Corcoran alleged that depressions, holes, obstructions and uneven places in a city street made travel unsafe and caused the automobile in which he was riding to overturn. Some evidence supported the alleged dangerous condition; other evidence indicated that the street was reasonably well maintained. The jury awarded him $5,000. The Appellate Court reversed under § 92(3b) of the Illinois Civil Practice Act, which authorized review when a judgment was unsupported by the evidence or against its weight. Corcoran first raised his constitutional objection on rehearing in the Appellate Court.
sections.Issue: Does § 92(3b) of the Illinois Civil Practice Act, by allowing appellate judges to set aside a jury's resolution of conflicting evidence as against the weight of the evidence, deprive the prevailing litigant of the jury trial guaranteed by the state constitution? Preliminarily, could Corcoran raise that challenge by writ of error after himself having the remand struck?
sections.Holding: The Illinois Supreme Court, 1940, in an opinion by Justice Murphy with no separate concurrence or dissent, held that the statutory authorization for appellate review of a verdict's evidentiary weight did not violate the state constitutional right to jury trial. The power permitted a reviewing court to require another jury to consider the case, subject to strict limits protecting the first jury's role. The court affirmed the appellate judgment but stated that it lacked jurisdiction to determine whether the Appellate Court had correctly weighed the evidence in this case.
sections.Reasoning:
The court first rejected the city's objections to the writ. Removal of the remand did not prevent a constitutional challenge to the power exercised; rehearing was Corcoran's first opportunity to know that the Appellate Court would reverse for factual error under this provision; and the state constitution independently supplied Supreme Court review where statutory validity was involved.

On the merits, the court traced Illinois practice to an 1837 enactment allowing exceptions to denials of new trials and appellate assignments of error based on those rulings. Earlier decisions had reversed verdicts manifestly against the evidence, and the modern provision substantially continued that practice. Cases invalidating a different power, appellate substitution of contrary findings followed by final reversal without remand, did not control; Corcoran's own request, not the statute, had removed the remand.

Because the guarantee preserved jury trial as historically understood, the court examined common-law practice. A judge at nisi prius tried the case and returned the verdict to the court at Westminster, whose judges could grant a new trial on the record without having heard the witnesses. The mechanism let another jury reconsider the dispute rather than making reviewing judges the final factfinders.

That justification required restraint. Slight differences in the balance of testimony were insufficient; precedents required a clearly wrong verdict, a strong preponderance of contrary evidence, or circumstances in which justice demanded intervention. Unrestricted appellate substitution would itself deprive parties of jury trial. The casebook excerpt emphasizes the historical foundation and omits much of the jurisdictional analysis and limiting discussion.

CP-135.rule: Rule 52(a)'s clearly erroneous standard governs a finding of discriminatory intent, with no exception for ultimate facts, and when a legal error has caused the trial court to omit findings the appellate court must ordinarily remand rather than find the facts itself.

sections.Parties: The respondents were Black employees of Pullman-Standard's railway-car manufacturing plant in Bessemer, Alabama, who challenged employment practices and the departmental seniority arrangement under federal civil-rights law. Pullman-Standard and the United Steelworkers of America, with its local union, were the petitioners defending the system. A different union, the International Association of Machinists, represented other departments, and its role in creating the plant's bargaining structure was important evidence about the system's origins.
sections.Procedural History: The employees filed suit in 1971; by the time of the Court's review the litigation had involved three trials and two appellate reviews. After the intervening Teamsters decision, the district court considered the seniority system's bona fides, found that the employment differences it produced did not result from an intention to discriminate, and held it protected by § 703(h). The Fifth Circuit reversed. It stated that it was firmly convinced a mistake had occurred, but also invoked circuit precedent treating discrimination as an ultimate fact that could be determined independently on appeal, and concluded that discriminatory purpose had been established. The Court granted review on the standard of appellate review and the criteria governing the seniority determination, declining to review separate rulings on job assignments and selection of foremen. It reversed the Fifth Circuit and remanded to that court for further proceedings.
sections.Material Facts:
Pullman-Standard had maintained racially discriminatory job assignments before Title VII became effective. The seniority rules ordinarily measured accumulated service within a department, and an employee transferring to another department generally lost the seniority accumulated in the old one. The employees contended that the rules discouraged movement and preserved disadvantages created when Black workers were assigned to less desirable jobs.

The departmental structure developed through the plant's unionization history. By 1954 the plant had 28 departments, 26 represented by the Steelworkers and two by the Machinists. The seniority arrangement had shifted between departmental and occupational bases before returning to a departmental base in 1954. A 1972 agreement with the Department of Labor allowed specified Black employees to transfer without losing seniority.

The district court examined whether transfers were discouraged equally, whether the departmental structure was rational and consistent with industry practice, whether the system originated in racial discrimination, and whether it was negotiated and maintained free of unlawful purpose. It found no discriminatory intent. The employees pointed to unequal job desirability, the division of departments along racial lines, and the Machinists' role.
sections.Issue: May a court of appeals independently decide whether a seniority system was adopted or maintained with discriminatory intent because intent is the ultimate fact determining liability? When a trial court has omitted findings because it treated relevant evidence as legally irrelevant, may the appellate court make those findings itself, or must it ordinarily remand?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States, 1982, in an opinion by Justice White, held that Rule 52(a)'s clearly erroneous standard applies to findings of discriminatory intent under § 703(h) and contains no general exception for ultimate facts. Intent here means actual motive, a factual question for the trial court even though it determines liability. When an erroneous legal view has caused the district court to omit material findings, the usual remedy is a remand; appellate resolution without remand is appropriate only when the record permits one resolution of the factual issue. The Fifth Circuit appeared to make an independent determination and supplied findings about the Machinists and Steelworkers that the district court had not made. The Court did not itself decide that the seniority system was lawful.
sections.Reasoning:
Under the Court's construction of § 703(h), a seniority system could produce racially disparate consequences without being unlawful if they did not result from discriminatory purpose. Adverse impact could be circumstantial evidence of motive but could not replace the required finding, so the intent inquiry was factual.

Nothing in Rule 52(a) creates one standard for subsidiary facts and another for the fact that ultimately determines liability; allowing independent review whenever a fact was labeled ultimate would remove much of the Rule's operation. An appellate court need not defer to a mistaken view of the law or of what evidence is relevant. The Court expressly declined to settle the general standard for mixed questions, holding only that actual discriminatory motive under this provision was a pure question of fact.

The Fifth Circuit's quotation of the definite-and-firm-conviction formula was insufficient given its opinion as a whole and its reference to independent review of ultimate facts. More fundamentally, its view that the district court had not properly considered the Machinists' role could justify setting a finding aside, but not deciding the omitted issue itself. A discriminatory motive of the Machinists could not simply be imputed to the Steelworkers, and acquiescence was not automatically discriminatory purpose.

Justice Stevens concurred in part, reserving his separately expressed views on the burden in seniority-system challenges. Justice Marshall dissented, joined by Justice Blackmun except as to Part I, which renewed his objection to requiring proof of discriminatory purpose. He accepted that Rule 52(a) governed but argued the Fifth Circuit had respected it and that the largely documentary record permitted only one result.

CP-136.rule: A single wrongful act that causes both personal injury and property damage to the same person gives rise to one cause of action with different items of damages, so a judgment on part of it bars a later action for the rest.

sections.Parties: The plaintiff sued the City of Maple Heights, first for property damage and then, in a separate action, for personal injuries from the same motorcycle accident, alleging negligent street maintenance. The city appealed the personal-injury judgment against it, arguing that the plaintiff had improperly split one cause of action.
sections.Procedural History: According to the casebook editors' account, the plaintiff first obtained a $100 municipal-court judgment for property damage, which was affirmed. In a separate personal-injury action arising from the same accident, she invoked the earlier negligence determination to secure trial on damages alone, recovered $12,000, and prevailed on appeal. In the Ohio Supreme Court the city's eighth assignment of error was that allowing separate actions for property and personal injuries improperly split one cause of action. The court found that objection dispositive and did not reach the other assigned errors. It reversed the personal-injury judgment and entered final judgment for the city, not a new trial.
sections.Material Facts: The casebook editors supply the factual background. The plaintiff fell from a motorcycle. She first recovered $100 in municipal court for property damage caused by the city's negligent street maintenance. She then brought a separate action for personal injuries from the same accident, used the earlier negligence determination to obtain a trial on damages alone, and recovered $12,000. No insurer was involved. Ohio precedent at the time, paragraph four of the syllabus in Vasu v. Kohlers, Inc., declared that personal and property injuries invaded different rights and were distinct causes of action.
sections.Issue: Does a single negligent act that injures both the person and the property of the same plaintiff give rise to one cause of action or two, so that a plaintiff who has recovered judgment for property damage may or may not bring a second action for personal injuries?
sections.Holding: The Ohio Supreme Court, 1958, in an opinion by Justice Herbert with six justices supporting reversal and Justice Zimmerman dissenting, held that one wrongful act causing personal injury and property damage to the same person produces one cause of action with different items of damages. Once the plaintiff obtains judgment on that claim, she cannot bring another action for the omitted damages. The court overruled paragraph four of Vasu's syllabus, reversed the personal-injury judgment, and entered final judgment for the city.
sections.Reasoning:
The court confronted Vasu v. Kohlers, where an insurer that had paid automobile damage and taken an assignment sued the tortfeasor and lost, and the insured was later allowed to sue for personal injuries. Vasu's syllabus also declared personal and property injuries to be distinct causes of action.

Justice Herbert examined the competing definitions of a claim. Under the majority rule elsewhere, the single wrongful act supplies the cause of action and the injuries to person and property are its consequences; requiring all damages in one suit prevents repeated litigation, expense and delay. The alternative rule focused on different protected rights or different evidence, a distinction the court found unpersuasive under modern code pleading: different damage evidence does not turn one tort into several wrongs.

The court distinguished Vasu's subrogation setting. The issue necessary there was the effect of an insurer's separately acquired interest on the insured, not whether one plaintiff could divide her own recovery. Jurisdictions adopting the one-claim rule commonly let an insurer separately recover what it has paid, and Ohio's real-party-in-interest statute supported that treatment. Rush involved no insurer. Winning the first action did not preserve the rest: the plaintiff tried to use the first negligence finding in her favor, but claim preclusion barred the second suit itself.

Justice Stewart concurred, emphasizing that Vasu's two-claim discussion was unnecessary to its decision. Justice Zimmerman dissented on grounds of stability, noting that a unanimous court had announced the earlier rule less than thirteen years before and that no changed conditions justified reversal.

CP-137.rule: A claim consists of the facts of an occurrence or transaction, not the legal theory chosen, so a judgment on that transaction bars a later suit on new theories, including one against principals whose liability derives from the agents sued first.

sections.Parties: Joseph Mathews, proceeding pro se, sued New York Racing Association, which operated Jamaica Race Track, and Thoroughbred Racing Protective Association, a private detective agency the track retained for security. He sought damages and injunctions against interference with his attendance at racetracks, libelous publication, and purported exercise of peace-officer authority. The corporate defendants moved for summary judgment on the ground of res judicata.
sections.Procedural History: In an earlier federal action Mathews sued three individuals, of whom only two were properly served; those two were employees of the present corporate defendants. He pleaded assault and libel, sought damages and injunctive protection for racetrack attendance, and tried the case before Judge Palmieri without a jury. Judgment entered June 30, 1960 rejected relief. In the present action, an earlier ruling had found the new complaint sufficient. The corporations then moved under the then-existing Rule 56(b), relying on the earlier judgment as res judicata. The district court granted the defendants' motion for summary judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
Mathews alleged that Thoroughbred's employees assaulted, kidnapped, falsely arrested and imprisoned him at the track on April 4, 1958, and that the defendants maliciously caused his disorderly-conduct prosecution and conviction on April 10. These were allegations; the court did not accept them as established.

The earlier action had already tried the April 4 removal and the statements associated with the April 10 proceeding. The earlier judge specifically found that Mathews physically resisted removal and that the employees used no more force than reasonably necessary. That action also included three separate claims based on different facts. Mathews had been given an opportunity to consolidate this action with the earlier suit and had been advised to retain counsel in another related action.
sections.Issue: Could the corporate defendants invoke a judgment won by their employees in the earlier action, and did the new complaint, pleading false arrest and malicious prosecution instead of assault and libel, concern the same claim already adjudicated?
sections.Holding: The United States District Court for the Southern District of New York, 1961, Judge MacMahon, granted summary judgment for the defendants. The new suit against the corporate principals sought to relitigate the same racetrack removal and ensuing prosecution already adjudicated in the action against their employees. The corporations and their agents were identified in interest for the derivative liability asserted, and the factual transaction defined the claim. Changing from assault and libel theories to false arrest and malicious prosecution did not create a new opportunity for recovery.
sections.Reasoning:
The court identified two connected questions. On the first, the track owner acted through Thoroughbred, which acted through the individual employees. Because the corporate liability alleged depended on those agents' actionable wrongdoing, the principals stood or fell with them. The opinion applied this to the specific respondeat-superior claim rather than declaring that every employer and employee share preclusion for all disputes.

On the second, a claim consists of the facts of an occurrence or transaction rather than the legal theory selected. Although the events were nearly a week apart, the removal was the subject of the disorderly-conduct trial and the events were sufficiently interconnected to form one claim. The witnesses to the removal gave the same account whether it was called assault or false arrest, and the employees' statements were the same whether the theory was libel or malicious prosecution. A litigant cannot reserve alternative grounds for recovery from the same alleged invasion and try them serially after losing. Preclusion reached issues tried and others that could have been raised within the claim.

The court also relied on the earlier actual findings, describing Mathews as estopped both directly and collaterally. His pro se status did not require another trial; the court acknowledged the lack of counsel but emphasized that fair adjudication must eventually end litigation. The casebook's note that the summary-judgment provision later moved to Rule 56(a) is editorial and not part of the 1961 judgment.

CP-138.rule: When an unconditional acceleration clause has made every installment of a note due, the debt is a single indivisible claim, and a creditor who takes judgment for only part of it cannot later sue for or rely on the remainder.

sections.Parties: William Jones, the buyer of an automobile, sued Morris Plan Bank of Portsmouth for conversion after the bank's agent took the car and the bank sold it. The bank held the note and the conditional-sales agreement by assignment and endorsement from the dealer. Jones lost at trial and sought reversal.
sections.Procedural History: The bank first sued in Suffolk's Civil and Police Court for the May and June installments only; Jones did not appear, the bank obtained judgment, and Jones paid the execution in full. The bank then sued for July's installment, Jones pleaded res judicata, and the bank took a nonsuit. After the bank repossessed and sold the car, Jones brought this conversion action. After he presented his evidence, the trial court struck it on the bank's motion, producing a defense verdict. On review, the court reversed and remanded solely to determine the amount of damages.
sections.Material Facts:
Jones bought a Plymouth sedan for $595. He traded in a car valued at $245 and financed the balance with a charge of $78.40, executing a $428.40 note payable in twelve monthly installments of $35.70. The note provided that nonpayment of any installment immediately made the unpaid whole due. A conditional-sales agreement reserved title until payment and secured the note. The dealer assigned the agreement and endorsed the note to the bank.

Jones missed the May and June installments. The bank sued for those two payments only, obtained judgment, and was paid in full. Its later suit for the July installment ended in a nonsuit after Jones pleaded res judicata. On September 7, 1935, while the car was parked outside Jones's home and he retained its key, the bank's agent took it during the night without his consent. The bank sold the car and applied the proceeds to the note. The bank did not dispute that the acceleration clause had matured every installment.
sections.Issue: Where a note's acceleration clause automatically made all installments due on default, could the creditor sue for two installments, collect the judgment, and still treat the remaining debt as outstanding so that title to the car stayed with it and Jones could not prove ownership in conversion?
sections.Holding: In 1937 the Virginia court, in an opinion by Justice Gregory with no separate writing or dissent, held that a creditor who obtains judgment and satisfaction for only part of an automatically accelerated installment obligation cannot retain the remaining debt as a basis for repossessing the security. All installments were due when the bank first sued, and that single claim could not be divided. Title to the automobile passed to Jones when the bank lost its right to pursue the balance, so he owned the car when it was taken. The conversion judgment for the bank was reversed, with remand limited to damages.
sections.Reasoning:
Jones argued that default matured the whole note, so the first judgment extinguished any claim for the omitted installments, and that because the title-retention agreement existed only to secure the debt, it ended too. The bank answered that the full price had never been paid, so retained title remained with it, and that the note and agreement were divisible obligations allowing successive suits.

The court rejected divisibility. An ordinary installment obligation may support separate actions as installments mature, but this note contained an unconditional acceleration clause without the usual option letting the holder choose to accelerate. Every installment had become payable before the first suit.
