The note and conditional-sales agreement formed one contract, and the agreement's sole function was to retain title until the note was discharged.

The court used identity of supporting evidence as an important test of an indivisible demand: the evidence supporting the two installments would also support the entire accelerated balance. A party cannot choose part of one presently enforceable claim, obtain judgment, and then litigate the residue. The rule protects defendants against repeated expense and harassment and gives litigation an end, and it applies even if the form of the later demand changes. The opinion distinguishes installments that accrue separately from installments already due when the action begins.

The bank could not avoid the bar by asserting the unpaid remainder defensively in the conversion action. Once its first judgment was satisfied and the omitted installments were barred, it no longer had a debt-based right to retain title.

CP-139.rule: A party who knowingly uses part of an entire, indivisible demand as a defense to defeat an opponent's suit cannot reserve the remainder of that demand for a later affirmative action.

sections.Parties: Mitchell, a Beaufort County farmer, sued the Federal Intermediate Credit Bank, South Carolina Agricultural Credit Company and W. E. Richardson for an accounting of crop proceeds. The bank pleaded a completed federal judgment in bar. The credit company and Richardson did not appear, were insolvent and in default, and were disregarded for the appeal. Mitchell appealed the order sustaining the bank's plea.
sections.Procedural History: The bank sued Mitchell on his notes in federal court in August 1926. Mitchell contested jurisdiction and pleaded the crop-proceeds facts as a complete defense, but requested no affirmative judgment by counterclaim. After jurisdiction was resolved for the bank, a January 1930 trial ended in a verdict for Mitchell, affirmed on appeal. His state accounting suit, begun in October 1926, had been held in abeyance by agreement during the federal litigation. When it resumed, the bank obtained permission to plead the federal judgment in bar. The state judge tried that defense separately on the federal record, sustained it, and refused to treat Mitchell's notice of appeal from the preliminary trial order as a stay. The South Carolina Supreme Court affirmed the circuit-court judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
Mitchell alleged that arrangements with the bank, the credit company and Richardson required him to borrow through the credit company and market his crop through a growers' cooperative, assigning the proceeds as security. He borrowed $6,000 in November 1925 and $3,000 in January 1926, giving two notes and crop mortgages. He alleged that his vegetables yielded at least $18,000 and that one or more defendants received those proceeds without accounting to him. The bank denied the alleged agency relationship and said it bought his notes and mortgages for value before maturity.

In the federal action on the notes, Mitchell used the crop-proceeds facts as a complete defense and won. In the state action he admitted that both actions concerned the same transaction and sought only the surplus of the proceeds beyond the offset against the notes.
sections.Issue: May a party who pleaded facts defensively to defeat an opponent's suit on notes, without counterclaiming, later bring an independent action on the same transaction for the excess? Put as the court framed it, may one claim be divided between defense in the first action and offense in the second?
sections.Holding: The South Carolina Supreme Court, 1932, in an opinion by Justice Stabler joined by Chief Justice Blease, Justices Carter and Bonham, and acting Associate Justice Featherstone, held that a litigant who knowingly uses part of an indivisible claim to defeat an opponent's suit cannot reserve the remainder for a later affirmative action. Mitchell's success in the federal action on his notes did not preserve a second recovery for the excess crop proceeds involved in the same transaction. The court affirmed the plea barring his accounting action.
sections.Reasoning:
The court first rejected the procedural challenge. The plea raised legal questions that could dispose of the whole action, so a separate hearing was within the judge's statutory discretion; an automatic stay would undermine that sequencing, and Mitchell could still challenge the order on appeal from final judgment.

On preclusion, the governing principle requires the holder of an entire, indivisible demand to present its whole scope rather than litigate piecemeal, and it applies to use of a claim as a setoff or defense as well as to successive plaintiff's suits. Mitchell's alleged injury was the failure to account for approximately $18,000 in crop proceeds, one demand against the bank. When the bank sued for approximately $9,000, he could invoke that demand defensively or seek affirmative judgment for the balance. Having chosen the defensive use and gained the benefit of defeating the notes, he could not later enforce the remainder. The absence of a prior award for the excess resulted from the relief he chose to request.

The court distinguished Mitchell's authorities. In Kirven the earlier defendant had withdrawn the defense before later suing; Ludlow involved uncertain pleadings and possible innocent lack of knowledge. The court recognized exceptions such as a court's own limitation of recovery or lack of knowledge, and found none here. Cases from other jurisdictions applied the same principle; winning on the defense creates no exception.

The brief cautions that the holding concerns a known indivisible demand actually used to defeat the earlier suit, not a universal rule that every unused counterclaim is barred. The casebook excerpt focuses on the defense-to-affirmative-claim problem.

CP-140.rule: A final judgment on the merits bars a later action on the same claim as to every ground that was or could have been raised, but in an action on a different claim it is conclusive only of matters actually litigated and determined.

sections.Parties: Cromwell sued the County of Sac, Iowa, to collect on county bonds and attached interest coupons. He was the plaintiff below and sought reversal in the Court. The county defended on the ground that a prior judgment denying recovery on other coupons barred the claim. Samuel C. Smith had been the named plaintiff in that first suit, and the county offered evidence that Smith had pursued it solely for Cromwell's use and benefit.
sections.Procedural History: Smith first sued the county on earlier interest coupons. The court made findings about the courthouse transaction and the absence of proof of value, entered judgment for the county, and the Court affirmed. When Cromwell brought the second action on other instruments in the federal Circuit Court for the District of Iowa, the county introduced the earlier judgment and evidence that Cromwell was the beneficial owner of the Smith suit. The trial court treated the judgment as preclusive, excluded Cromwell's offered proof that he acquired the instruments for value before maturity, and entered judgment for the county. On writ of error, the Court reversed and remanded for a new trial.
sections.Material Facts:
The county's voters had authorized $10,000 in bonds to finance a courthouse. The county judge issued the bonds to a contractor, Meserey, who immediately gave one bond to the judge as a gratuity. The courthouse was never built under the contract. These circumstances had been held to show fraud and illegality in the bonds' inception, requiring a holder seeking enforcement to prove acquisition for value before maturity.

The present suit concerned four $1,000 bonds and four $100 interest coupons. The bonds were issued in 1860, payable to bearer in New York in successive years from 1868 through 1871, with annual interest of ten percent. The prior Smith suit concerned 25 earlier-maturing coupons. In that action the claimant had not proved that value was given for the coupons, and recovery was denied. In the later action Cromwell offered evidence that he had acquired the particular bonds and coupons now sued upon before maturity for value.
sections.Issue: When a prior action between the same real parties ended in a judgment on the merits, does that judgment bar every ground that could have been presented in a later suit on different bonds or coupons? Specifically, did failure to prove value in the earlier coupon action prevent Cromwell from proving that he gave value for the distinct obligations now in suit, and could the county show that the earlier named plaintiff had litigated for Cromwell's benefit?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States, in an opinion by Justice Field reported in 1876, with Justice Clifford dissenting, held that a final merits judgment on the same claim or demand bars a later action on that claim, including grounds of recovery or defense that could have been presented, but that in a later action on a different claim preclusion extends only to matters actually litigated and determined. The prior judgment conclusively established the original fraud or illegality affecting the bonds; it did not establish that Cromwell failed to give value for other instruments in the series. Excluding his evidence was reversible error. The evidence identifying him as the beneficial party to the earlier action was admissible.
sections.Reasoning:
Justice Field separated two questions obscured by the broad term res judicata. When the same claim returns, the original judgment settles the demand as a whole, and a party cannot reopen it with an available but omitted defense or ground of recovery; after a judgment on a promissory note, later assertions of payment, forgery or lack of consideration cannot ordinarily reopen the claim.

Different claims require a narrower inquiry into the point actually disputed and decided. A fact common to both suits may be settled, but its possible relevance to the earlier pleadings is not enough. A determination of title necessary to a trespass judgment can settle title in an action for a different trespass, whereas a general verdict on several counts does not necessarily decide the validity of a contract alleged in one. The Court gave a practical reason: a litigant may refrain from pressing a point because the first claim was small, evidence was hard to obtain, or litigation was expensive.

Applying this, the first judgment established that the issuance was fraudulent or illegal, which Cromwell could not contradict. But the earlier failure of proof concerned acquisition of the particular coupons then sued upon; whether value was paid for another bond or coupon was a different fact, not even presumptively established. The finding that Smith held and owned the coupons established legal title and was compatible with a beneficial interest in Cromwell.

Justice Clifford, dissenting, considered the bonds and coupons dependent on the same title and transaction, and argued that the first claimant could have proved value and should not hold proof in reserve for a later action.

CP-141.rule: A party invoking a prior judgment as an estoppel must show, from the record or consistent extrinsic evidence, the precise question necessarily decided; if the judgment could rest on any of several distinct matters and the uncertainty is not removed, it is not conclusive of any one.

sections.Parties: Russell was the patentee and complainant seeking equitable relief against Place and the other defendants for alleged infringement. He had previously recovered a damages judgment against them in an action at law and invoked it to prevent them from contesting infringement and patent validity. The defendants acknowledged the earlier judgment but denied that it necessarily resolved the issues in the later suit.
sections.Procedural History: In the earlier action at law, the defendants pleaded the general issue and gave the statutorily required notice of their novelty and prior-use defenses. A jury returned a damages verdict for Russell and judgment was entered on it. Russell then brought an equity suit for subsequent infringement in the federal Circuit Court for the Northern District of New York, relying on the earlier judgment as an estoppel. The Circuit Court entered a decree adverse to the relief he sought, and he appealed. The Court explained that the case otherwise resembled Russell v. Dodge, decided on substantially the same testimony, and addressed only the preclusive effect of the prior judgment. It affirmed the decree.
sections.Material Facts:
The patent concerned an asserted improvement in preparing leather. It contained two claims: one for use of fat liquor generally in treating leather, the other for a particular compound and method for treating bark-tanned lamb or sheepskin. The original patent had been surrendered because its description was allegedly defective or insufficient, and a reissued patent supplied an amended specification.

Russell's earlier damages action alleged generally that the defendants made and used the invention and caused others to do so. The verdict and record did not reveal whether the jury found infringement of the first claim, the second, or both, and no outside evidence was introduced in the second proceeding to resolve that uncertainty.

The later equity suit alleged further unlicensed manufacture, use and sale, and sought an injunction and an accounting of gains and profits. The defendants challenged novelty, asserted public use more than two years before the patent application, and contended that the reissue differed from the original invention.
sections.Issue: Does a general judgment for damages for infringement of a patent containing two claims conclusively establish validity and infringement in a later suit when neither the record nor extrinsic evidence identifies which claim necessarily supported the first recovery? What must a party show to establish the particular issue determined by an earlier judgment?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States, in an opinion by Justice Field reported in 1876, with Justice Clifford dissenting, held that a prior judgment is conclusive in a later action between the same parties on a question directly involved and determined in the first action, but the party relying on it must establish, from the record or consistent extrinsic evidence, the precise question necessarily resolved. When several distinct matters could support the judgment and the uncertainty is not removed, the judgment does not conclusively determine any particular one. The earlier verdict did not show which patent claim supported recovery, so the defendants could contest infringement and validity. The decree was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court accepted that a question directly determined by a competent court cannot be litigated again between the same parties. The obstacle was evidentiary: a judgment establishes a result but may not identify each issue essential to it, so the party asserting estoppel must connect the proposition asserted to a necessary determination in the first case.

Sometimes the record makes the connection evident. When it does not, extrinsic evidence may explain what was submitted and necessarily decided, but it must be consistent with the record and cannot enlarge the adjudication by showing that another issue could have been raised. The Sickles litigation illustrated the point: a general verdict on several counts might rest on ordinary money claims rather than the special contract later said to be settled.

Russell's record had the same defect. The declaration alleged infringement generally without saying whether the unlawful act was use of fat liquor itself or use of the particular patented process, and the jury could have found for Russell under either claim. Because a patent can be valid as to one claim and invalid as to another, a verdict supporting one did not necessarily reject every defense directed at the other. With no extrinsic evidence, the Court could only conjecture, and conjecture was insufficient for estoppel. Because the second suit addressed subsequent conduct, the precise adjudicated question had to be shown, not every defense that could have been offered earlier.

The report records that Justice Clifford dissented but gives no reasoning. The brief notes that, read with Cromwell, the case adds an identification requirement to issue preclusion.

CP-142.rule: A finding in an earlier action does not bind a party in later litigation unless it was a material basis for the earlier judgment; a finding adverse to a party who won the judgment, and so could not appeal it, is not conclusive.

sections.Parties: Rios sued Davis in district court for personal-injury damages arising from an automobile collision. Davis asserted contributory negligence and relied on findings and a judgment from an earlier action in which he had joined Rios as a third-party defendant. Rios appealed after the district court sustained Davis's preclusion plea.
sections.Procedural History: Popular Dry Goods Company first sued Davis in the County Court at Law for damage to its truck. Davis pleaded Popular's contributory negligence, joined Rios as a third-party defendant, and sought damages for his own automobile. On jury findings that all three had been negligent, that court entered judgment on December 17, 1962 denying Popular recovery against Davis and denying Davis recovery against Rios. Rios then sued Davis in district court. Davis pleaded the earlier findings and judgment as res judicata and collateral estoppel; the district court sustained the plea and entered judgment for Davis. The Court of Civil Appeals reversed and remanded.
sections.Material Facts: The dispute arose from an automobile collision on December 24, 1960. In the first suit Popular sought $443.97 for damage to its truck and Davis sought $248.50 from Rios for damage to his own automobile. The jury found that Popular, Rios and Davis had each been negligent in a manner proximately causing the collision; the findings against Rios were that he failed to maintain a proper lookout and drove on the left side of the roadway. Under the then-operative contributory-negligence consequences, Davis was denied recovery against Rios. Rios then sued Davis for $17,500 in alleged personal-injury damages.
sections.Issue: Is a party bound in a later action by a jury finding of his own negligence made in an earlier action when the judgment in that earlier action was in his favor and rested on the other party's negligence?
sections.Holding: The Texas Court of Civil Appeals at Eastland, 1963, in an opinion by Justice Collings, held that a prior factual finding does not bind a party in later litigation when it was unnecessary to the prior judgment. The earlier jury had found Rios negligent, but the judgment denied Davis recovery against him because Davis was also negligent, and that favorable judgment left Rios no opportunity to appeal the adverse finding. The court reversed the judgment barring his personal-injury suit and remanded. The opinion contains no separate writings and does not state a numerical vote.
sections.Reasoning:
As between Davis and Rios, the controlling reason for the first judgment was Davis's negligence. The findings that Rios failed to keep a proper lookout and drove on the left side of the roadway did not supply a basis for denying Davis recovery; had they controlled independently of Davis's own negligence, they would have pointed toward a different judgment. Actual litigation and express jury findings were therefore not enough: the findings also had to be a material basis for the judgment invoked as preclusive.

The court tied that requirement to appellate fairness. Rios could appeal a judgment against him, not isolated findings in a judgment in his favor. Even an unsupported finding of his negligence would not have given him a right to appeal, and it would be unfair to make an unreviewable finding conclusive in the next case. Drawing on Word v. Colley and other authorities, the court located the estoppel in the judgment, not automatically in every verdict answer.

Davis relied on Rio Bravo Oil, which described preclusion as extending to questions directly in issue and passed upon in arriving at judgment. The court found no conflict, since that authority also limited issue estoppel in a different claim to matters on which the prior result depended.

The reversal was not a finding that Rios was free from negligence or entitled to damages; those questions remained to be litigated. The casebook editors' following question, whether Davis would be bound by the earlier finding of his own negligence, is a question for analysis and not a holding of the case.

CP-143.rule: Because each tax year is a separate claim, a prior tax judgment operates in a later year only as collateral estoppel, which requires an identical matter and unchanged controlling facts and legal rules.

sections.Parties: The Commissioner of Internal Revenue sought to tax royalties as the income of Sunnen, an inventor and controlling shareholder, although Sunnen had assigned the royalty contracts to his wife. Sunnen was the taxpayer and the respondent in the Court. His wife received the payments and reported them on her own returns. Sunnen Products Company, the licensed manufacturer, paid the royalties under contracts Sunnen had negotiated with it.
sections.Procedural History: In 1935 the Board of Tax Appeals held that Sunnen was not taxable on royalties paid to his wife under a 1928 agreement during 1929 through 1931. In the present litigation over 1937 through 1941, the Tax Court held Sunnen taxable on the royalties paid to his wife except for $4,881.35 attributable to the 1928 agreement, as to which it considered the 1935 decision conclusive. The Eighth Circuit upheld that exemption and reversed the rulings taxing the other royalties, thinking the assignments effective to shift the income; it therefore did not decide Sunnen's argument that preclusion also covered the other contracts. The Commissioner obtained review. The Court reversed the Eighth Circuit and remanded for further proceedings in light of its opinion.
sections.Material Facts:
Sunnen owned 89 percent of the company's stock and his wife ten percent. He was president and a director. The five-member board required three votes to act, and directors were elected annually by shareholders, so his voting ownership gave him continuing control over who served.

Sunnen granted the company nonexclusive licenses to manufacture and sell devices covered by his patents or patent applications, at a royalty of ten percent of gross sales. The contracts required no minimum production or minimum royalties, and either party could cancel without liability after a specified notice period. Sunnen assigned his interests in the contracts to his wife as gifts, and the corporation paid her the royalties. He retained the patents and patent applications.

One license agreement dated from 1928 and had been the subject of the 1935 Board decision. Of the 1937 through 1941 payments, $4,881.35 received in 1937 arose under that same agreement; the remaining royalties arose under other agreements.
sections.Issue: How does a prior tax judgment affect later litigation between the same taxpayer and the government over different taxable years? Does a favorable decision about one royalty agreement control other similar agreements, or later payments under the same agreement, when intervening decisions of the Court have substantially developed the assignment-of-income principles? On the merits, did the assignments shift tax liability despite Sunnen's retained powers?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States, 1948, in an opinion written by Justice Murphy, held that because each income-tax year creates a separate liability, litigation over another year ordinarily invokes only collateral estoppel, which requires that the matter be identical and that the controlling facts and applicable legal rules remain unchanged. The prior judgment on the 1928 agreement did not control other separable license contracts, even with similar terms. For the later payment under the same agreement, the intervening Clifford-Horst line of cases had sufficiently developed the governing principles to defeat collateral estoppel. On the merits, Sunnen's retained powers and economic interests supported taxing the royalties as his income.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court began with the distinction articulated in Cromwell: a merits judgment ends the same cause of action as to grounds that were or could have been presented, but its effect on another cause of action is limited to issues actually determined. Liability for one year's income is a different claim from another year's.

Preclusion of an unchanged issue promotes finality, but extending an old legal conclusion into every later tax year when the controlling law or facts have changed would give one taxpayer a continuing exemption unavailable to comparable taxpayers. The relevant change can come from legislation, regulations, a controlling state-court determination, or substantial development in the Court's doctrine.

The other license contracts were separate instruments the Board had never examined; similarity of terms might make the earlier decision persuasive as precedent, but stare decisis differs from collateral estoppel. The $4,881.35 payment was closer because agreement, parties and issue were the same, but intervening decisions on intra-family assignments, emphasizing effective control and economic benefit, defeated estoppel.

On the merits, Sunnen's stock control let him procure cancellation of the contracts; the absence of minimum royalties let the company raise, lower or stop payments; he kept the patents and could license competitors; and the payments stayed within the family economic unit.

Justices Frankfurter and Jackson filed a short statement that the Tax Court's judgment was supported by substantial evidence and consistent with law and that they would affirm it. The casebook excerpt concentrates on separate tax years, identity of issues, and changes in governing law.

CP-144.rule: The preclusive scope of a consent judgment is measured by the parties' intent, but a claim is reserved only if the reservation is explicit, mutual, incorporated in the offer of judgment, and the reserved claim is part of the original complaint.

sections.Parties: Robert C. Anderson, Inc., a prospective liquor-store tenant, sued Hanover Logansport, Inc., which owned premises in a South Bend shopping center, for failing to deliver the leased premises. Spatz & Company was Hanover's leasing agent. Hanover, the defendant, appealed the denial of its motion to dismiss; Anderson maintained that it had reserved a claim for further damages.
sections.Procedural History: Anderson filed its complaint in July. Before trial, Hanover tendered a Rule 68 offer of the leased premises, which Anderson accepted with qualifying language. Hanover requested judgment in accordance with the accepted offer, and both parties filed an agreed entry directing that the stipulated judgment be recorded. Hanover later sought dismissal, and the trial court denied it. The record did not show that judgment had actually been entered; because entry was required and the appellate disposition would direct it, the appellate court proceeded as though it had been. The court reversed and remanded with instructions to enter judgment on the offer and grant Hanover's motion to dismiss.
sections.Material Facts:
The parties signed a lease on February 23, 1984 for nine years and eleven months beginning May 1. Hanover agreed to remove the existing tenant, Discount Liquors, but that tenant remained. Anderson alleged that occupancy was necessary to transfer its liquor license and that the failure exposed it to a one-year bar on a renewed license application. Its complaint requested occupancy under the lease or, alternatively, $500,000 in profits over the lease term, and alleged that reliance on the lease had cost it another location.

Hanover offered the leased premises under Rule 68. Anderson accepted subject to the lease's licensing conditions and added that acceptance was only for mitigation, not settlement of breach damages. Anderson took possession around July 1, 1985. On appeal Anderson clarified that it wanted profits lost during the delay in delivery, while Hanover understood the continuing demand as profits over the entire lease term.
sections.Issue: After a plaintiff accepts an offer of judgment giving it one of the alternative remedies it pleaded, may it continue to litigate for additional damages on the strength of its own reservation in the acceptance? More generally, what determines the preclusive scope of a consent judgment?
sections.Holding: The Indiana Court of Appeals, 1987, in an opinion by Judge Staton in which Robertson concurred and Hoffman concurred separately, adopted party intent as the measure of a consent judgment's preclusive scope but required an explicit, mutual reservation grounded in the existing complaint. Anderson's unilateral acceptance language did not preserve a previously unpleaded delay-damages claim. The court reversed the denial of Hanover's motion to dismiss and directed entry of judgment on the offer and dismissal of the remaining action.
sections.Reasoning:
Judge Staton explained that a consent judgment has a dual character: it embodies an agreement and also invokes judicial authority. A judgment-centered approach stresses finality, avoidance of harassment and conservation of resources. An agreement-centered approach asks what the parties actually settled; requiring settlement of every possible issue could deter compromise because a party might inadvertently surrender something. After considering divergent federal decisions and distinguishing Indiana cases attacking the validity of earlier consent judgments, the court adopted the agreement-centered approach, noting that Rule 68's structure also allows settlement of part of a controversy.

That approach did not make Anderson's private intention controlling. Both parties had to agree, and the reserved matter had to be precise. The court required that the reservation be incorporated into the offer of judgment itself and that the reserved claim be an inherent part of the original complaint. The complaint here asked for specific performance or profits over the lease term; it stated no claim for profits lost during delayed delivery, and the acceptance's general reference to breach damages did not show Hanover's assent to that residual claim.

The court's notes extend the reservation requirement to an issue or another cause of action, not just damages, and bar curing the deficiency by later amendment: the claim had to be in the complaint when the parties agreed and the consent judgment was entered. Judge Hoffman concurred on the authority of General Discount Corp. v. Weiss Machinery without a developed alternative analysis. The casebook excerpt omits the qualification that judgment had not actually been entered.

CP-145.rule: A judicially adequate administrative adjudication can have issue-preclusive effect, even across agencies, but only against a party or privy, on an identical issue, and from the earlier final decision, which remains final while an appeal is pending.

sections.Parties: Karen Holmberg, a former employee of the State of Alaska's Division of Risk Management, sought permanent total disability benefits under workers' compensation from the state as her employer. She argued that a later decision of the Public Employees Retirement Board in her favor conclusively established her inability to do her job. Retirement and Benefits had appeared before that board for the Public Employees Retirement System. Holmberg was the appellant.
sections.Procedural History: The Alaska Workers' Compensation Board awarded Holmberg temporary total disability benefits on February 18, 1988 but denied permanent total disability; she appealed in March. Meanwhile the retirement system's administrators awarded nonoccupational disability benefits but initially denied occupational benefits. On her appeal, the Public Employees Retirement Board ruled on April 20 that she was permanently and totally disabled because of work accidents and awarded occupational disability benefits. Holmberg added that decision to the record of her workers' compensation appeal. The superior court affirmed the workers' compensation ruling, and she appealed again. The court affirmed the superior court.
sections.Material Facts:
Holmberg began working in the Division of Risk Management in 1979. She had a history of back injuries and surgeries but reported a long period without back pain before her condition worsened during this employment. Her work involved prolonged sitting, and she had additional falls and work-related knee injuries. The employer supplied a standing desk, a reclining chair, and secretarial help with bending and lifting, and allowed considerable control over work arrangements. She resigned because of back pain on June 30, 1987.

The workers' compensation board found that she could perform her duties, relying on a vocational counselor's job analysis and two physicians' conditional approval of that work. The retirement board later found her permanently and totally disabled. Before the retirement board, Retirement and Benefits appeared for the retirement system, an independent retirement plan funded by participating employers and employees.
sections.Issue: Did the Public Employees Retirement Board's later finding that Holmberg was physically unable to work at Risk Management preclude the contrary determination of the workers' compensation board? That turned on whether one agency's adjudication can preclude another's, whether the state as employer was in privity with the retirement system, and which decision was the earlier final judgment.
sections.Holding: The Alaska court, 1990, in an opinion by Justice Moore for a five-member court with no separate opinion or dissent, accepted that judicially adequate administrative proceedings can produce issue preclusion, including across different agencies. It denied preclusion here for two independently sufficient reasons: the state as employer was not in privity with the retirement system represented in the other proceeding, and the workers' compensation decision was the earlier final judgment despite its pending appeal. The court also found substantial evidence supporting the workers' compensation decision and affirmed.
sections.Reasoning:
The court distinguished the two statutory disability standards from a shared factual issue. Workers' compensation looked to ability to earn wages in the same or other employment; the retirement system looked to the employee's usual duties or a comparable job offered by the employer. Holmberg's refined argument concerned the narrower fact of physical ability to work at Risk Management.

The court rejected a categorical barrier between administrative tribunals. Retirement board hearings provided evidence, testimony and cross-examination, and the two boards had no materially different expertise on this narrow question.

Preclusion still required a party or privy, an identical issue, and a final merits determination. Retirement and Benefits appeared for the retirement system, not for the state in its separate capacity as employer. The state's interest as one contributor to the common fund gave only nominal representation, not adequate assurance of notice, opportunity to be heard, and protection of its interests.

Independently, the workers' compensation decision came first, and a final judgment keeps its preclusive effect while an appeal is pending. Treating an appeal as suspending finality would invite duplicate proceedings and let a later favorable adjudication overturn an earlier loss collaterally. A second tribunal can sometimes stay proceedings, and a judgment resting on a later-reversed judgment can be attacked under Rule 60(b)(5).

On substantial evidence, the job analysis and the physicians' conditional approval supported the board, and Holmberg had not shown the work description was inaccurate. The casebook excerpt omits this final evidentiary discussion.

CP-146.rule: Mutuality is not required for issue preclusion: a judgment may be invoked by a stranger to it, so long as the issue is identical, the judgment was final on the merits, and the party against whom it is asserted was a party or privy.

sections.Parties: Helen Bernhard, a beneficiary of Clara Sather's estate who became administratrix with the will annexed, sued Bank of America, successor to the San Dimas bank, claiming the estate remained entitled to a deposit because Sather never authorized its withdrawal. The bank pleaded consent and the preclusive effect of a probate determination. Bernhard appealed the judgment for the bank.
sections.Procedural History: Charles Cook, as executor, submitted an account in probate that omitted the transferred money, and resigned. Bernhard and other beneficiaries objected. After a hearing, the probate court settled the account and expressly determined that Sather had given the deposit to Cook during her lifetime. After Cook's discharge, Bernhard became administratrix and sued the bank. The trial court accepted the bank's preclusion defense and entered judgment for the bank. On appeal Bernhard contested preclusion, the admission of the probate record, and the validity of the gift. The judgment for the bank was affirmed.
sections.Material Facts:
Clara Sather, an elderly woman in failing health, moved into the home of Charles and Mrs. Cook in 1933. She authorized Cook and her physician to draw jointly against her Los Angeles commercial account. Cook separately opened a San Dimas account styled Clara Sather by Charles O. Cook, without authorization from Sather to that bank. Later, in the presence of bank officers, Cook and her physician, Sather signed by mark an authorization transferring $4,155.68 from her Los Angeles savings account for credit to her own account at the San Dimas bank. The bank credited the Cook-styled account. Cook withdrew the balance, placed it in an account for himself and his wife, and later moved it to another bank in their names.

Sather died that November and Cook became executor. Years later the probate court found that Sather had made a gift of the deposit to Cook. The bank had not been a party to the probate proceeding.
sections.Issue: May a defendant who was neither a party to nor in privity with a party to an earlier proceeding, and who would not have been bound had the finding gone the other way, invoke that proceeding's final determination of an issue against a plaintiff whose interests were represented there?
sections.Holding: In 1942 the California court, in a unanimous opinion by Justice Traynor, rejected mutuality as a condition for invoking issue preclusion. Due process protects the person to be bound by requiring participation or privity in the first proceeding; it does not require that the party invoking the judgment also have been bound by it. The bank could therefore use the probate court's final finding of ownership against the estate, whose same interests had been represented in the probate hearing. The court overruled Estate of Smead, Silva v. Hawkins, and People v. Rodgers to the extent inconsistent.
sections.Reasoning:
Bernhard's central objection was that the bank had not been a party or privy in probate and would not have been bound by a contrary finding, so traditional mutuality would deny it the benefit of the judgment.

Justice Traynor separated two questions the traditional formula combined: who may assert a judgment and against whom it may operate. No one can lose rights through a judgment without the notice and opportunity to participate that due process requires, so the person against whom preclusion is invoked must have been a party or privy. But another person's absence from the first litigation does not erase the first party's fair adjudication, and a litigant who has had the opportunity to contest an issue should not reopen it merely by choosing another adversary. Existing exceptions for derivative liability, such as principal and agent or employer and servant, already reflected that reasoning despite the absence of mutuality.

The court stated three inquiries: whether the issue was identical, whether there was a final judgment on the merits, and whether the person against whom preclusion is asserted was a party or privy to the earlier adjudication. Ownership of the money was identical in both proceedings and had been adjudicated on the merits when the probate court settled the account. Bernhard's change from objecting beneficiary to administratrix did not change the right represented, since in both capacities recovery was sought for the estate's legatees and creditors. An intervening California decision established the probate court's jurisdiction despite Cook's resignation. The court did not retry whether Sather made a valid gift.

The brief notes that the case illustrates nonmutual defensive issue preclusion and does not itself settle offensive use.

CP-147.rule: Federal trial courts have broad discretion to permit offensive nonmutual issue preclusion unless the plaintiff could easily have joined the earlier action or its use would be unfair to the defendant, and applying it to an issue decided in an equitable action does not violate the Seventh Amendment.

sections.Parties: Shore, a Parklane shareholder, brought a private securities class action against Parklane Hosiery Company and thirteen officers, directors and shareholders. He was the plaintiff below and the respondent in the Court; the defendants were the petitioners. Shore sought damages, rescission and costs arising from an allegedly misleading proxy statement. The Securities and Exchange Commission was the plaintiff in a separate earlier adjudication against the same defendants, in which it sought equitable relief.
sections.Procedural History: Shore sued before the SEC began its own action. In the SEC case, after a four-day bench trial the district court found the proxy statement materially false and misleading and entered a declaratory judgment; the Second Circuit affirmed. Shore then moved in his private action for partial summary judgment based on collateral estoppel. The district court denied the motion, believing preclusion would deprive the defendants of their constitutional jury right. The Second Circuit reversed, holding that the defendants had fully and fairly litigated the issue and could be bound despite the absence of a jury in the first action. The Court granted certiorari and affirmed the Second Circuit.
sections.Material Facts:
Parklane issued a proxy statement soliciting shareholder approval of a merger that would take the company private. Shore alleged that the statement contained material falsehoods and omissions. The SEC subsequently charged that the same statement violated federal securities law and requested injunctive relief. The defendants contested the SEC case through a four-day bench trial and an appeal, and lost: the statement was found materially false and misleading.

Shore then sought to treat that finding as established in his damages action. The requested preclusion would not decide every issue; injury and damages, among other matters, remained for adjudication. The defendants had no Seventh Amendment right to a jury in the SEC's equitable action. They objected that Shore had not been a party to the first case and would not have been bound had the SEC lost, and that applying the bench-trial determination would keep a jury from redetermining the issue.
sections.Issue: May a private plaintiff who was not a party to an earlier SEC action use the judgment in that action to prevent the same defendants from relitigating an issue they fully contested and lost? What limits govern this offensive use of nonmutual issue preclusion? Does the Seventh Amendment require a fresh jury determination because the first proceeding was equitable and tried to a judge?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States, 1979, in an opinion by Justice Stewart joined by seven other Justices, with Justice Rehnquist dissenting, held that federal courts may permit offensive nonmutual issue preclusion, subject to broad trial-court discretion to prevent unfairness. A court ordinarily should refuse it when the new plaintiff could easily have joined the earlier action or when its application would be unfair to the defendant. Neither concern applied here. The Seventh Amendment did not require the defendants to retry the settled issue before a jury, because a valid equitable adjudication can have preclusive consequences in a later legal action. The Court did not award damages or resolve the remaining issues.
sections.Reasoning:
Traditional mutuality limited estoppel to those who would have been bound had the first judgment gone the other way. The Court distinguished that from the due process protection owed to the person against whom preclusion is asserted; Parklane and its officers had themselves defended the SEC action.

Offensive use raises concerns that defensive use does not. Defensive estoppel encourages a plaintiff to join all defendants in one action, whereas offensive estoppel may reward a plaintiff who waits to see whether another claimant wins, benefiting from victory without risking preclusion from defeat. Fairness to the defendant adds limits: a weak incentive to defend a small first suit, inconsistency with earlier judgments favorable to the defendant, or procedural opportunities in the second suit, unavailable in the first, that could readily produce a different result.

None applied. Shore's action was already pending, and federal law restricted consolidation of private litigation with an SEC enforcement action without the Commission's consent. The defendants had ample incentive to defend and did so through trial and appeal; there was no inconsistent prior judgment; and the change from judge to jury was not itself a procedural advantage requiring relitigation.

On the Seventh Amendment, the Court answered the argument from 1791 mutuality by saying the Amendment preserves the substance of the jury right without freezing every procedural incident, and that historical practice recognized the preclusive effect of an equitable decree in a later legal action. Beacon Theatres concerned sequencing within one action. The Court rejected the Second Circuit's waiver rationale.

Justice Rehnquist dissented: abandoning mutuality here removed a contested factual question from the jury entirely, and even if that were constitutional he would have refused estoppel as a matter of discretion.

CP-148.rule: A person is not bound by a judgment in litigation to which he was not a party; knowledge of the suit and a chance to intervene impose no duty to intervene, so parties who want to bind an outsider must join him.

sections.Parties: Wilks and other white Birmingham firefighters were plaintiffs in the later employment-discrimination suit and respondents in the Court. They sued the City of Birmingham and the Jefferson County Personnel Board, alleging that promotion decisions denied them equal employment treatment. Black firefighters and other beneficiaries of earlier consent decrees intervened to defend the decrees. Martin was among the petitioners; the consolidated proceedings also included petitions associated with the city and the Board. The earlier suits had been brought by black individuals, an NAACP branch and the United States.
sections.Procedural History: Litigation beginning in 1974 produced consent decrees. The Birmingham Firefighters Association objected at the fairness hearing as an amicus; it and two members later sought intervention, which was denied as untimely, and a separate group of seven white firefighters sought and did not obtain an injunction against approval of the decrees. In the later Wilks action, the district court treated decree-required promotion decisions as immune from challenge and, after finding the disputed decisions were taken pursuant to the decrees, dismissed. The Eleventh Circuit reversed, rejecting the theory that nonparties were precluded from attacking employment decisions merely because they implemented the earlier judgments. The Court affirmed the Eleventh Circuit, leaving the claims for further proceedings.
sections.Material Facts:
Beginning in 1974, litigation challenged the city's and Board's hiring and promotion practices under Title VII and other federal law. It produced consent decrees containing goals for hiring black firefighters and promoting black employees. The decrees were a judicially approved resolution of the claims before the court, but their implementation affected the employment opportunities of people outside the original litigation.

The later plaintiffs had not been parties to the proceedings in which the decrees were entered. They alleged that they were denied promotions because of race in favor of less qualified black candidates. The Court recounted that as their allegation; it did not find the selected candidates less qualified or decide that the promotions were unlawful. The city and Board defended on the ground that the contested decisions implemented the decrees. On review of the earlier intervention ruling, the Eleventh Circuit had indicated that independent discrimination claims remained available.
sections.Issue: May persons who were not parties to employment-discrimination consent decrees be denied an opportunity to litigate their own discrimination claims because they knew about the earlier proceedings and could have sought intervention? Should the burden rest on outsiders to intervene under Rule 24, or on existing parties to join affected persons under the rules governing required parties?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States, 1989, in an opinion by Chief Justice Rehnquist joined by Justices White, O'Connor, Scalia and Kennedy, with Justice Stevens dissenting joined by Justices Brennan, Marshall and Blackmun, held that a person ordinarily is not bound by an in personam judgment in litigation to which that person was not a party. Knowledge of pending litigation and an opportunity to intervene do not impose an obligation to intervene or extinguish a later independent claim. Existing litigants who want a judgment to bind another person ordinarily must join that person, subject to recognized exceptions. The Wilks plaintiffs could not be barred merely because the challenged decisions implemented decrees to which they were not parties. The Court did not decide whether the promotions were unlawful.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority began with the ordinary limit on a judgment's reach: a litigant is entitled to a hearing on his own rights, and a decree binding its parties does not dispose of an outsider's separate federal claim.

The petitioners proposed a duty to intervene when a person knew or should have known that pending litigation might affect his interests. The Court found no such duty in Rule 24, which makes intervention available, not compulsory; appearing as an amicus or having a chance to object differs from being a party. Rule 19 addresses persons whose interests may be affected, and the parties negotiating a decree know the relief sought and are positioned to identify those they wish to bind. A mandatory-intervention rule would force outsiders to monitor litigation and would generate later disputes over notice and foreseeability, shifting burdens to those less informed. The value of settling complex employment disputes did not let the original parties settle claims they did not own. The Court preserved exceptions for representative proceedings and special statutory schemes. The decree defendants could still contest the later claims on the merits; decree compliance could not automatically replace that inquiry.

Justice Stevens agreed that a judgment does not bind nonparties but read the record differently: the district court had heard and rejected the white firefighters' claims on the merits, and a decree can supply a legitimate explanation for employment decisions without extinguishing an outsider's right to sue. He would have vacated and remanded.

The brief separately notes that Congress added 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(n) in 1991, restricting certain challenges to practices implementing discrimination judgments or orders, so Martin is not a complete statement of present employment-decree law.

CP-149.rule: A person is ordinarily not bound by a judgment in litigation to which that person was not a party; nonparty preclusion must rest on an established ground, not on an open-ended virtual-representation balancing of relationships and aligned interests.

sections.Parties: Brent Taylor was the plaintiff in the second Freedom of Information Act action and the petitioner in the Supreme Court. The Federal Aviation Administration, represented through its administrator, was the government defendant. Fairchild, the aircraft manufacturer's successor, intervened to protect its asserted interest in technical documents. Greg Herrick, Taylor's friend, had brought the earlier, unsuccessful FOIA action for the same materials. Taylor sought the documents in his own suit and challenged the preclusion ruling; the FAA and Fairchild argued that Herrick's loss barred Taylor through a doctrine called virtual representation.
sections.Procedural History:
Herrick lost his FOIA suit in federal district court in Wyoming, and the Tenth Circuit affirmed. When the FAA did not respond to Taylor's own request, Taylor sued in the District of Columbia; Fairchild intervened and asserted preclusion. The district court entered summary judgment against Taylor on preclusion grounds. The D.C. Circuit affirmed under a multi-factor virtual-representation test requiring identity of interests and adequate representation plus an additional connection such as a close relationship, substantial participation, or tactical maneuvering. It relied on the requesters' aligned objectives and close association and did not definitively find tactical manipulation.

The Court vacated the D.C. Circuit's judgment and remanded, leaving open only whether Taylor was pursuing his suit as Herrick's agent. It did not decide that such an agency existed, order disclosure, or resolve Exemption 4.
sections.Material Facts:
Herrick owned a vintage Fairchild F-45 airplane and sought FAA-held technical drawings to help restore it. The manufacturer had supplied the materials to the agency during certification, and the agency withheld them under FOIA Exemption 4, which protects specified commercial information including trade secrets. Herrick relied on a 1955 letter authorizing public access for replacement-parts purposes to argue that trade-secret protection had been waived. The Tenth Circuit concluded that the 1955 authorization had removed the documents' secret status but affirmed based on Fairchild's later objection to disclosure and the arguments Herrick had preserved; it did not decide whether trade-secret protection could legally be restored or whether restoration after a FOIA request would be effective.

Less than a month after that judgment, Taylor made his own request for the materials. He was president of an antique-aircraft association to which Herrick belonged. Herrick had asked Taylor to help restore the plane, but they had no contract or agreement for his participation. The record showed friendship, a shared lawyer, and the transfer of litigation documents. It did not show that Taylor controlled or financed Herrick's suit, participated in it, agreed to be bound, or even knew about it while it was being litigated. Herrick had not purported to sue on Taylor's behalf.
sections.Issue: May a court bind a nonparty to a prior judgment based on an equitable assessment of shared interests, friendship, common counsel, and related litigation objectives, without a recognized representative relationship or other established exception? And if the second litigant may be acting as the first litigant's agent, what must the courts examine and who bears the burden of proving preclusion?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 2008, in an opinion by Justice Ginsburg for a unanimous Court, rejected the expansive virtual-representation doctrine and vacated and remanded. Federal common law governs the preclusive effect of a federal-question judgment, subject to due process, and must operate within established grounds for binding nonparties. The Court organized those grounds into six categories: agreement to be bound; certain preexisting substantive legal relationships; adequate representation in an appropriate representative proceeding; control of the earlier litigation; a later suit pursued as an agent or proxy for a bound party; and a special statutory scheme consistent with due process. The categories were a framework for analysis, not an asserted exhaustive code. Taylor had not been adequately represented in Herrick's suit. Whether Taylor was acting as Herrick's agent required further consideration, and the defendants bore the burden of pleading and proving the affirmative defense.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court distinguished the finality owed to a judgment from the identity of the people it can bind. Claim and issue preclusion protect against repetitive litigation and inconsistent results, but a person who did not receive the relevant opportunity to litigate generally retains a claim even when someone else sought similar relief unsuccessfully. The recognized exceptions depend on relationships or procedures, such as succession to property, a properly conducted class action, or actual control of another's lawsuit, that require more than two people caring about the same outcome.

The D.C. Circuit's flexible test let shared interests and close relationships substitute for an actual representative arrangement, which could produce the equivalent of a class action without certification, notice, representation, and court supervision. Adequate representation generally requires aligned interests and either an understanding that the first party was acting representatively or protective measures taken by the first court; some settings also require notice. General language about justice and equity in earlier cases, including Blonder-Tongue, concerned parties who had already litigated, not unrelated nonparties. A multi-factor inquiry also weakened predictability.

FOIA's public purpose did not make every requester the representative of all others: the statute gives relief to the person making the request, and Congress had imposed no general restriction on successive suits by different requesters. Precedent and litigation costs adequately discourage repetition, and the FAA had not identified a pattern of abusive suits.

Applying the categories, the Court found no agreement to be bound, substantive legal relationship, control of the first suit, or special statutory scheme, and nothing showed that Herrick understood himself to represent Taylor, that Taylor knew of the case, or that the Wyoming court protected his interests. On agency, a bound party cannot avoid preclusion by controlling a second suit in another's name, but a suggestion of tactical maneuvering is insufficient; the inquiry turns on whether the later case is subject to the bound party's control. Preclusion is an affirmative defense, so the FAA and Fairchild had to establish it.

CP-150.rule: Under New York's Schwartz formulation, a party is precluded from relitigating an identical issue that was necessarily decided earlier and is decisive now if that party had a full and fair opportunity to contest it, even when the present claimants were absent from the earlier action.

sections.Parties: Landano and Kirchstein were New York plaintiffs suing American Airlines over a 1965 crash; they and their decedents were New York domiciliaries. The reported opinion bears the Hart caption together with Landano and Kirchstein but decides the latter plaintiffs' motions. The plaintiffs cross-moved for summary judgment on liability based on a Texas federal judgment against the airline. American, the defendant, moved to have the liability issues tried jointly with twenty other cases.
sections.Procedural History:
Numerous suits followed the crash in state and federal courts. The first completed trial, Creasy in the Northern District of Texas, lasted nineteen days and produced a plaintiff's verdict against the airline; that judgment was affirmed on appeal. In New York, an earlier decision by Justice Quinn in the Hart matter, affirmed without opinion, had refused to apply New York collateral-estoppel law for nonresident dependents of a deceased nonresident breadwinner with no significant New York contacts. American then sought to have the Landano and Kirchstein liability issues tried jointly with twenty other cases already grouped under an Appellate Division order, and the plaintiffs cross-moved for summary judgment.

On October 7, 1969, Justice Frank of the New York Supreme Court, New York County, sitting as a trial court, granted the plaintiffs' cross-motion on liability, denied the airline's joint-trial motion, and directed that an order assessing damages be settled.
sections.Material Facts: On November 8, 1965, an American Airlines aircraft traveling from La Guardia to an airport in Covington crashed in Kentucky. Fifty-eight of the sixty-two people aboard died. In Creasy, the Texas federal court applied Kentucky's wrongful-death statute and substantive negligence law, and after a nineteen-day trial the jury returned a plaintiff's verdict against the airline. Landano and Kirchstein's New York actions asserted the same airline-liability issue arising from the same crash. They had not been parties to the Texas action.
sections.Issue: May New York claimants who were absent from an earlier Texas federal action use that court's judgment establishing American Airlines' liability for the same crash to obtain summary judgment on liability in their own New York suits, despite the airline's objections based on the earlier Hart ruling, full faith and credit, mutuality, and fairness?
sections.Holding: The New York Supreme Court, New York County, a trial court and not the state's highest appellate court, held in 1969, in an opinion by Justice Frank alone, that the New York claimants were entitled to the benefit of the Texas federal judgment establishing the airline's liability. The plaintiffs' summary-judgment cross-motion on liability was granted and American's joint-trial motion was denied, with damages left for assessment. The ruling did not fix individual damage awards or decide every pending crash claim.
sections.Reasoning:
The court applied the New York Court of Appeals' recent Schwartz formulation: an identical issue must have been necessarily decided and be decisive in the current action, and the party to be bound must have had a full and fair opportunity to contest it. The airline's liability for the crash met the identity requirement, and the court viewed a common airplane-crash liability question as lacking the participant-specific complications of a multi-vehicle collision. The airline bore the burden of showing it lacked a full opportunity in the nineteen-day Texas trial and did not meet it.

Justice Frank distinguished the earlier Hart ruling because these plaintiffs and their decedents were New York domiciliaries. In his interest analysis, New York had the superior interest in the preclusion question affecting its own residents, and Texas had no legitimate interest in imposing its restrictive preclusion rule on them. He rejected the full-faith-and-credit objection by distinguishing enforcement of the Texas judgment itself from use of its liability determination in the New York suits, which he characterized as implementing New York policy against repeatedly trying a fully contested issue and producing inconsistent findings.

Mutuality had already been abandoned in the controlling New York decisions. A New York trial would likewise apply Kentucky substantive conduct law because the crash occurred there, which the court distinguished from using New York's preclusion doctrine. Conjectures that the Texas verdict reflected prejudice against corporations or sympathy lacked evidence, and the jury's supposed ignorance of the consequences for other claimants did not matter because negligence did not depend on the number of claims.

The casebook excerpt abbreviates the earlier Hart comparison and some fairness objections; its editors then pose the broader choice-of-preclusion-law question and describe competing approaches. The case serves as a historical example of nonmutual offensive preclusion across judicial systems.

CP-151.rule: The Parental Kidnaping Prevention Act does not impliedly create a private federal cause of action to determine which of two conflicting state custody decrees is valid; whether a statute implies a remedy turns on congressional intent.

sections.Parties: David Thompson, the father of Matthew Thompson, was the federal plaintiff and the petitioner in the Supreme Court. The child's mother, Susan Clay, formerly Susan Thompson, was the defendant and respondent. Each parent had obtained a custody decree favorable to that parent in a different state. The father sought federal declaratory and injunctive relief resolving which decree controlled.
sections.Procedural History: The father filed the federal action in 1983. The district court dismissed for lack of subject-matter and personal jurisdiction. The Ninth Circuit disagreed with the district court's jurisdictional analysis but affirmed because the complaint failed to state a claim: the PKPA did not create the private federal cause of action the father asserted. The Court granted review to resolve disagreement over whether the PKPA supplied an implied federal remedy for competing state custody decrees, and it affirmed the Ninth Circuit's judgment. It did not decide which custody decree was valid or who should have custody.
sections.Material Facts:
In July 1978, the mother petitioned a California court to dissolve the marriage and sought custody of Matthew. The court initially awarded joint custody and provided that she would have sole custody once she left for Louisiana, pending its investigator's report. She moved with Matthew in December 1980; the Court did not find that she had unlawfully abducted the child. On April 7, 1981, a Louisiana court enforced the then-existing California award in the mother's favor and modified visitation. After receiving the investigative report, the California court later awarded sole custody to the father, so the decrees appeared to give conflicting custody rights.

The father's federal suit asked a district court to declare the Louisiana decree invalid, require recognition of the later California decree, and grant corresponding injunctive relief. He relied on the Parental Kidnaping Prevention Act of 1980, 28 U.S.C. § 1738A, which directs states to enforce qualifying sister-state custody determinations and limits modification and competing jurisdiction. He had not first sought enforcement of the later California decree in Louisiana.
sections.Issue: Does the PKPA impliedly create a private federal cause of action permitting a parent to obtain a district-court judgment determining which of two conflicting state custody decrees is valid? Do the statute's text, context, and legislative history show that Congress intended a new federal remedy rather than a rule governing interstate recognition in state proceedings?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 1988, in an opinion by Justice Marshall joined by Chief Justice Rehnquist and Justices Brennan, White, Blackmun, and Stevens, held that the PKPA does not supply the asserted private federal cause of action, and affirmed. Justice O'Connor joined except for the first full paragraph of Part II and concurred in part and in the judgment; Justice Scalia concurred in the judgment. The controlling inquiry was whether Congress intended to create the remedy. The absence of a district-court remedy does not make the statute unenforceable: its requirements govern state custody proceedings, and federal questions can ultimately receive Supreme Court review. The Court did not validate the Louisiana decree, invalidate the California decree, or award custody.
sections.Reasoning:
The PKPA did not expressly authorize the remedy, so the Court examined congressional intent, treating the familiar considerations from implied-right cases as evidence of that intent rather than a license to devise a remedy. Custody judgments had presented special full-faith-and-credit difficulties because they were modifiable, so a second state might issue a competing determination, and differing jurisdictional rules encouraged forum selection and instability. The PKPA responded by prescribing which state determinations qualify for recognition, restricting simultaneous proceedings, and limiting modification. Those provisions impose obligations on adjudicating states and do not identify a district court as a new custody-review forum.

Placement reinforced that reading: Congress added § 1738A alongside § 1738, which directs recognition of judgments without ordinarily supplying an independent federal cause of action. The legislative history was particularly significant. A proposal associated with Representative Fish would have created federal diversity jurisdiction for specified custody-enforcement disputes; it met objections that federal courts lacked domestic-relations expertise and that a new forum would add complexity, and Congress chose state-court enforcement instead. The father's supposedly narrower remedy would still require federal judges to examine state-law jurisdiction and custody questions, including the child's best interests, and risked district courts directly reviewing state judgments. The Court declined to presume that state courts would be unable or unwilling to implement the Act and noted Supreme Court review for intractable conflicts.

Justice O'Connor adopted Part I of Justice Scalia's concurrence, emphasizing that the factors from earlier implied-right cases are tools for discerning intent. Justice Scalia objected to the majority's statement that Congress need not actually have had the creation of a remedy in mind, and proposed that the Court announce that private causes of action would not be implied in statutes enacted thereafter, a categorical proposal the Court did not adopt.

CP-152.rule: Section 1983 does not displace conventional issue-preclusion principles or 28 U.S.C. § 1738; federal courts generally give a state judgment the preclusive effect the rendering state would, provided the party had a full and fair opportunity to litigate the issue.

sections.Parties: Willie McCurry, previously a defendant in a Missouri criminal prosecution, was the plaintiff in the later federal civil-rights action and the respondent in the Supreme Court. He sought $1 million in damages from officers Allen and Jacobsmeyer, other unidentified officers, the City of St. Louis, and its police department. The petitioning officers asserted that an issue resolved against McCurry in the criminal proceeding could not be relitigated in the damages suit.
sections.Procedural History:
In the state criminal case, the judge partly granted and partly denied McCurry's suppression motion; a jury convicted him and the conviction was affirmed. In McCurry's later federal suit, the district court understood the complaint principally as challenging the search and seizure and granted summary judgment to the officers based on collateral estoppel. The Eighth Circuit reversed. It acknowledged that preclusion ordinarily applies in civil-rights cases but reasoned that McCurry needed access to a federal forum because Stone v. Powell foreclosed federal habeas review of a Fourth Amendment claim where a full and fair state opportunity had existed, and it directed proceedings unencumbered by collateral estoppel, subject to a separate abstention instruction.

The Court reversed the Eighth Circuit and remanded. It did not decide how Missouri preclusion law, § 1738, or the ordinary qualifications to collateral estoppel applied to each allegation in the complaint.
sections.Material Facts:
Undercover officers went to McCurry's house after an informant reported heroin dealing. Allen and Jacobsmeyer asked to purchase heroin. McCurry returned from inside the house firing a pistol, seriously wounding them. Following a gun battle and his surrender, officers entered without a warrant, purportedly to search for other people. They seized contraband in plain view and additional evidence from dresser drawers and tires on the porch. The Court took this account from the court of appeals.

In the criminal proceeding, McCurry moved to suppress the seized evidence under the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments. The state judge excluded the material found in the drawers and tires but admitted the evidence in plain view. A jury convicted McCurry of heroin possession and assault with intent to kill.

His later federal complaint alleged a conspiracy to violate his Fourth Amendment rights, an unconstitutional seizure of his house, and an assault after arrest and handcuffing. Not all of those allegations were necessarily resolved by the suppression ruling, and McCurry argued he could seek damages for conduct the state court had found unlawful. The Court expressly left those issue-specific questions unresolved.
sections.Issue: Does 42 U.S.C. § 1983 prevent application of ordinary issue-preclusion principles to a constitutional issue previously litigated in state criminal proceedings? In particular, does the absence of a federal habeas remedy for McCurry's Fourth Amendment claim entitle him to relitigate that issue without preclusion in a federal damages action?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 1980, in an opinion by Justice Stewart joined by Chief Justice Burger and Justices White, Powell, Rehnquist, and Stevens, held that § 1983 creates a federal cause of action but does not categorically displace conventional preclusion principles or the full-faith-and-credit obligations of 28 U.S.C. § 1738. Federal courts generally must give state judgments the preclusive effect the rendering state's courts would give them; a party must have had a full and fair opportunity to litigate, and the other applicable conditions and exceptions remain relevant. Stone v. Powell's limit on federal habeas relief creates no exception allowing unrestricted relitigation through § 1983. The Court held the Eighth Circuit's categorical reason for withholding estoppel erroneous; it did not hold that a full and fair opportunity is the only element of estoppel. Justice Blackmun dissented, joined by Justices Brennan and Marshall.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court distinguished claim preclusion, which can bar grounds that could have been presented, from issue preclusion, which concerns a matter actually decided and necessary to the earlier judgment; this case involved the latter, and the Court reserved questions about federal issues that could have been but were not raised earlier. Finality protects reliance on judgments, avoids inconsistent determinations, limits repeated litigation, and, for state judgments, supports the relationship between state and federal tribunals. Congress reinforced those principles in § 1738.

The text of § 1983 did not address preclusion or purport to repeal the predecessor of § 1738, and repeal by implication is disfavored. The majority acknowledged that the 1871 legislation responded to serious failures by state institutions but read the history as adding supplementary federal protection, not stripping competent state adjudications of all effect. The full-and-fair-opportunity limitation addresses inadequate state procedures, as distinct from ordinary alleged error within an adequate adjudication.

Stone addressed the costs and benefits of the exclusionary rule in habeas proceedings; it did not amend § 1983 or determine the preclusive effect of state judgments, and the unavailability of one remedy did not free another of its defenses. Nothing in the Constitution guarantees every federal-right claimant one unrestricted district-court adjudication, and a criminal defendant's involuntary presence in state court did not alone remove the normal effect of issues actually litigated there.

Justice Blackmun, dissenting, would have affirmed. He argued that preclusion must be compatible with the remedial purpose of the 1871 legislation, that modern nonmutual issue preclusion differed from the mutuality-bound doctrine Congress knew, and that a criminal defendant cannot realistically be described as freely choosing the state forum.

The casebook centers on § 1738, § 1983, and the competing views of the federal forum.

CP-153.rule: Federal common law governs the claim-preclusive effect of a federal diversity judgment and ordinarily incorporates the preclusion law of the state where the federal court sat, unless that law is incompatible with a federal interest; Rule 41(b) does not itself prescribe that effect.

sections.Parties: Semtek was the plaintiff asserting state-law business claims, the appellant from the Maryland dismissal, and the petitioner in the Supreme Court. Lockheed Martin was the defendant and respondent. Semtek sought to pursue its claims in Maryland after a California federal court had dismissed them under California's limitations law. Lockheed argued that the earlier federal judgment barred the second action altogether.
sections.Procedural History:
Semtek sued in California state court; Lockheed removed to the Central District of California on diversity grounds and obtained a limitations dismissal, which the Ninth Circuit affirmed. Semtek then sued in Maryland state court. Lockheed unsuccessfully asked the California federal court to enjoin that action and removed it on federal-question grounds, but the Maryland federal court remanded because the federal issue appeared only as a defense; diversity removal was unavailable because Lockheed was a Maryland citizen. The Maryland trial court dismissed on claim-preclusion grounds. Semtek unsuccessfully sought amendment of the California order in the district court and Ninth Circuit. The Maryland Court of Special Appeals affirmed, reasoning that federal law gave the federal merits dismissal preclusive effect irrespective of California's treatment of its own limitations judgments, and Maryland's highest court declined review.

The Court reversed the Maryland Court of Special Appeals and remanded.
sections.Material Facts:
Semtek sued in California state court for inducement of breach of contract and other business torts. After removal, the federal court dismissed under California's two-year limitations period, adopting language proposed by Lockheed declaring the claims dismissed in their entirety on the merits and with prejudice. The grounds for dismissal concerned time limits, not a trial or finding that the alleged conduct was lawful. Semtek initially did not challenge the on-the-merits designation.

Semtek then brought the same causes of action in a Maryland state court, where the applicable three-year limitations period had not expired. Lockheed relied on the federal judgment's express wording and Rule 41(b), arguing that an adjudication upon the merits necessarily precluded the claim in every other court.
