CP-COMP-CB-BE2.rule: Operating an interactive website accessible in a state does not establish specific personal jurisdiction there; the defendant must have purposefully exploited the forum market through its own deliberate conduct, and a default judgment entered without personal jurisdiction is void.

sections.Parties: The plaintiffs and appellees were two companies operating the dating website be2.com: a Delaware LLC headquartered in Delaware and its German parent, be2 Holding, A.G. The defendant and appellant was Nikolay Ivanov, a New Jersey resident alleged to be the cofounder and CEO of be2.net. Plaintiffs sought relief for trademark infringement; Ivanov sought to vacate a default judgment as void for lack of personal jurisdiction.
sections.Procedural History: The plaintiffs sued Ivanov in federal court in Illinois. He failed to answer and did not attend a scheduled status hearing, and the district court entered default under Rule 55(a) and then a default judgment under Rule 55(b)(2). Ivanov then appeared through counsel and moved to vacate the judgment as void for lack of personal jurisdiction. The district court denied relief, treating a list of Chicago registrations as sufficient Illinois contacts attributable to him. Ivanov appealed, representing himself. On April 27, 2011, amended May 19, 2011, the Seventh Circuit reversed the order denying his postjudgment motion and remanded with instructions to vacate the default judgment and dismiss the complaint for lack of personal jurisdiction. The amendment deleted a footnote that had classified the motion under Rule 59(e).
sections.Material Facts:
be2.com initially served European singles and expanded to about fourteen million users in thirty-six countries, including the United States. The complaint asserted Lanham Act trademark claims, federal common-law claims, and claims under the Illinois Uniform Deceptive Trade Practices Act. It alleged that Ivanov, who previously offered matchmaking through sladurana.com, moved that service in December 2006 to be2.net, deliberately adopting a domain and presentation confusingly similar to be2.com.

In support of damages, plaintiffs submitted their co-CEO Andreas Etten's declaration with Internet printouts. One printout, made a year before the hearing, showed ten men and ten women with Chicago addresses registered on be2.net, listing nicknames, ages, reported cities, and desired relationships. Other pages described Ivanov as a cofounder and CEO and advertised free dating services. Ivanov's affidavit claimed that he merely volunteered for Sladur, a Bulgarian company that owned be2.net, said the initials CEO meant “Centralized Expert Operator,” and said he had never entered Illinois.
sections.Issue: Did the registration of twenty people with Chicago addresses on be2.net, together with the site's accessibility in Illinois, give Ivanov minimum contacts supporting specific personal jurisdiction in Illinois, so that the default judgment against him was valid?
sections.Holding: The Seventh Circuit in 2011, in an opinion by Judge Hamilton for a panel of Judges Flaum, Wood, and Hamilton, with no separate opinion, held that on this record requiring Ivanov to defend these claims in Illinois would violate due process. It reversed the order denying his postjudgment motion and remanded with instructions to vacate the default judgment and dismiss the complaint for lack of personal jurisdiction. A default judgment entered without personal jurisdiction is void, and denying a motion to vacate it is necessarily an abuse of discretion. The court did not adjudicate infringement or clear Ivanov of wrongdoing.
sections.Reasoning:
Because Ivanov knew of the litigation and chose to default, he bore the burden on his postjudgment challenge to personal jurisdiction, but his default was not a submission to Illinois jurisdiction. The Lanham Act supplied no nationwide service of process, so Rule 4(k)(1)(A) required a basis under Illinois law, and because Illinois's long-arm statute extends to constitutional limits, the due-process question was dispositive.

The court asked whether Ivanov had purposefully exploited the Illinois market. An Internet defendant must have a forum connection attributable to its own deliberate conduct; merely operating an interactive website accessible there is insufficient. Otherwise random, attenuated contacts or third parties' unilateral choices would expose a defendant to suit everywhere the Internet reaches. The court compared a case involving a substantial Illinois advertising campaign, hundreds of thousands of customers, and millions of dollars in annual revenues. Here there was no evidence of targeting Illinois or of interaction between Ivanov and the people whose profiles listed Illinois addresses; they might have found the site on their own and clicked a button that automatically published their preferences. The printout did not establish twenty paying Illinois customers or an Illinois advertising campaign, and it was uncertain whether those people remained active users and Illinois residents. This was a failure of the demonstrated connection, not a rule that twenty customers can never suffice.

The court agreed that parts of Ivanov's affidavit were implausible, but disbelieving his explanation could not supply the missing Illinois connection.

The casebook note emphasizes the possibility that the twenty Chicago registrations resulted from users' unilateral activity, and poses a question about where to sue.

CP-COMP-CB-BENSUSAN.rule: A website accessible in the forum state, without an effort by its operator to advertise, promote, sell, or otherwise target the forum, satisfies neither New York's long-arm statute nor due process as a basis for personal jurisdiction over an out-of-state defendant.

sections.Parties: Bensusan Restaurant Corporation, a New York corporation that created the Blue Note jazz club in New York City and owned the federally registered mark, was the plaintiff. Richard King, who lived in Columbia, Missouri and owned a small club there also called the Blue Note, was the defendant. Bensusan alleged trademark infringement, dilution, and unfair competition; King moved to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(2).
sections.Procedural History: Bensusan sued King in the Southern District of New York, and King moved to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction. No discovery or evidentiary hearing had occurred. On September 9, 1996, District Judge Stein granted the Rule 12(b)(2) motion and dismissed the complaint. The court did not resolve the parties' competing trademark rights. The brief addresses only this district-court decision, not a later appellate stage.
sections.Material Facts:
In April 1996 King placed a website on a Missouri server to promote his club. The site allegedly displayed a logo substantially similar to Bensusan's. Anyone with Internet access could view its club information, event calendar, and ticketing instructions without an access code. The instructions listed Columbia ticket outlets and a telephone number for charging tickets; tickets ordered by telephone had to be collected at the Missouri box office on the night of the show, and King did not mail or transmit tickets to New York customers.

Initially the site distinguished the Missouri club from the famous New York club, recommended visiting the latter when in New York, and linked to Bensusan's website. After Bensusan objected, King removed the recommendation and hyperlink. King's affidavit stated that ninety-nine percent of patronage and revenue came from local Columbia residents, primarily university students. Bensusan relied on King's presentation of nationally known bands.
sections.Issue: Did King's Missouri-based website, accessible in New York, support personal jurisdiction under New York's long-arm statute, either § 302(a)(2) for an in-state tortious act or § 302(a)(3)(ii) for an out-of-state tort causing in-state injury, and would exercising jurisdiction comport with due process?
sections.Holding: The Southern District of New York in 1996, per District Judge Stein, found neither an adequate New York long-arm basis nor constitutionally purposeful contacts, granted the Rule 12(b)(2) motion, and dismissed the complaint. Section 302(a)(2) did not apply because the website and telephone number were not an infringing offer for sale in New York, and several components of § 302(a)(3)(ii) were missing. Independently, jurisdiction would violate due process even if the long-arm statute were satisfied. The court did not find that Internet information could never help establish an in-state tort, and it did not find that King's mark or logo was lawful.
sections.Reasoning:
Bensusan needed only a prima facie showing, and the court read its complaint and affidavits favorably, but the long-arm statute still had to be satisfied. For § 302(a)(2), the court applied authority locating trademark infringement where a product is passed off to a deceived purchaser; an infringing offering for sale in New York could suffice. Here a New York user had to find and access the site, telephone Missouri, and collect a ticket in Missouri, so any resulting transaction would occur in Missouri. Merely learning about an allegedly infringing product differs from a defendant's effort to advertise, promote, sell, or otherwise target it in New York.

Section 302(a)(3)(ii) required substantial revenue from interstate or international commerce, which Bensusan did not allege. King's knowledge that Bensusan operated in New York did not establish a reasonable expectation of forum consequences without a discernible effort to serve the New York market, and a conclusory allegation of loss in New York, based only on the injured business's domicile, did not establish the relevant injury. Foreseeability that New Yorkers would access the site, and failure to restrict access, were insufficient; the court did not resolve whether restriction was technically feasible.

On due process, King had not purposefully sought New York's benefits; he had simply made a site available to anyone able to find it. The court analogized creating a site to placing a product into the stream of commerce, citing the purposeful-direction reasoning of an Asahi plurality, and distinguished CompuServe, where a Texas user subscribed to an Ohio service, agreed to sell software through it, advertised through it, and repeatedly sent software to Ohio.

The casebook contrasts Bensusan with Inset's willingness to infer contacts from online advertising and a telephone number; it describes the statute as requiring substantial revenue from in-state activity, whereas the provision the court applied requires revenue from interstate or international commerce.

CP-COMP-CB-BLACK-HORSE.rule: For a corporate Rule 30(b)(6) deposition, a designee who attends but is unprepared and unable or unwilling to supply the noticed information can be treated as not appearing, permitting Rule 37(d) monetary sanctions without a prior order compelling discovery.

sections.Parties: Black Horse Lane Associates, assignee of the buyer United States Land Resources, together with related entities and their principal, the lawyer Lawrence Berger, were the plaintiffs and appellants. They sued over the sale of contaminated New Jersey property by Essex, whose stock Dow acquired in 1988, alleging breach of contract through unreasonable cleanup delay, breach of good faith, CERCLA response costs, New Jersey Spill Act relief, and related damages. Essex counterclaimed for permission to employ institutional and engineering controls.
sections.Procedural History:
The purchasers sued in 1997. A magistrate judge's June 30, 1999 order barred positions or evidence inconsistent with Berger's deposition testimony and imposed the fees and costs associated with the deposition and the sanctions motion. The district court separately granted the defendants summary judgment on August 10, then on December 16 affirmed the sanctions and dismissed the counterclaim without prejudice for lack of a ripe controversy. The plaintiffs appealed both orders; the defendants did not cross-appeal the counterclaim dismissal.

The Third Circuit reviewed the merits and the counterclaim rulings on a plenary basis and the sanctions for abuse of discretion. It affirmed both orders: dismissal of the complaint with prejudice, denial of the plaintiffs' counterclaim summary-judgment motion, dismissal of the counterclaim without prejudice, and the monetary discovery sanctions.
sections.Material Facts:
Essex sold the property to United States Land Resources for $3.6 million in 1985, and the buyer assigned its rights to Black Horse Lane. Paragraph 16 of the sale agreement required Essex, at its own expense, to implement the state-approved cleanup plan and obtain Department of Environmental Protection approval. The buyers knew of the contamination. Soil remediation finished within two years; groundwater work continued.

The noticed corporate deposition covered the sale agreement, the cleanup work, and expenditures. The plaintiffs designated Berger as their Rule 30(b)(6) representative. His deposition began on October 2, 1998; after scheduling disputes he was ordered to resume on October 13 and did not appear. An October 15 order imposed costs for that absence and the application and set October 19 for continuation. At later sessions he appeared physically but repeatedly gave evasive answers, disclaimed knowledge of the deposition notice and of his representative role, and refused to prepare. He claimed no recollection of an agreement he signed and likely negotiated, could not explain cleanup expenditures or consultant invoices relevant to the plaintiffs' own CERCLA claim, professed ignorance of Rule 30(b)(6), and ultimately admitted that he had not read the notice. The testimony ran seventeen hours.
sections.Issue: Does physical attendance preclude Rule 37(d) sanctions when a corporation's designated Rule 30(b)(6) representative is unprepared and unable or unwilling to supply the noticed information? The complete opinion also decided whether summary judgment on the contract, good-faith, and CERCLA claims, and dismissal of the counterclaim, were proper.
sections.Holding: The Third Circuit, in 2000, in an opinion by Greenberg joined by Barry and Weis, held that physical attendance does not preclude Rule 37(d) sanctions: for a corporate Rule 30(b)(6) deposition, inadequate preparation can amount to nonappearance. Adopting the Fifth Circuit's functional approach in Resolution Trust Corp. v. Southern Union Co., it upheld the monetary sanctions on this record. The holding concerned an organizational designee, and the court did not decide that every incomplete answer automatically warrants sanctions. It declined to reach the challenge to the Rule 37(b) preclusion sanction because the entire complaint was properly dismissed on summary judgment. The summary judgment and the dismissal of the counterclaim without prejudice were also affirmed.
sections.Reasoning:
The corporation bears responsibility for selecting and preparing a witness who can testify about the designated subjects; the procedure is intended to obtain the organization's information without successively deposing officers who each deny personal knowledge, and physical presence alone does not fulfill that responsibility. Rule 37(d), unlike Rule 37(b), did not require a prior order compelling discovery before the monetary sanction, and under the rule text then in force the good-faith-conference certification did not apply to a motion arising from nonappearance. Berger's education, professional status, and repeated opportunities reinforced the finding of deliberate noncooperation, which seventeen hours of testimony did not cure.

On the merits, the court rejected one district-court rationale: New Jersey law implied a reasonable time for cleanup performance despite the requirement of state approval, since otherwise Essex could delay indefinitely. But the plaintiffs produced no adequate evidence that a reasonable time had expired. The good-faith claim failed because questioning soil standards in a letter to regulators did not establish bad faith, particularly when the soil cleanup was timely completed. The consultant expenses were litigation-related rather than necessary CERCLA response costs; the consultant reviewed Essex's reports but did not investigate the property or perform cleanup. The counterclaim was unripe because Essex had not applied for, and could not yet obtain, a Classification Exception Area.

The casebook cites the case for the corporate-deponent holding and the district judge's quoted criticism, omitting the contract, statutory, and counterclaim rulings.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-009.rule: A supplemental instruction may urge jurors in the minority to reconsider their views in light of the majority's, so long as it preserves the requirement that the verdict reflect each juror's own judgment rather than mere submission to others.

sections.Parties: Allen was the defendant in a federal prosecution for killing Philip Henson in the Cherokee Nation of the Indian Territory, and he challenged his conviction in the Supreme Court through assignments of error directed at the jury charge. The United States was the prosecuting party. No brief or appearance was filed for Allen; the Solicitor General appeared for the United States.
sections.Procedural History: The federal Circuit Court for the Western District of Arkansas tried and convicted Allen in 1893, and the Court set that conviction aside. A second trial produced another conviction in 1894, which the Court again reversed. A third trial produced a conviction carrying a death sentence. Allen challenged numerous parts of the jury charge, and the 1896 decision briefed here reviewed that third conviction only. The Court affirmed the Circuit Court's judgment, leaving the third conviction and death sentence in place.
sections.Material Facts:
The opinion refers readers to the earlier reports for the full narrative but reproduces enough of the instructions to show the competing theories. On the prosecution's theory, supported by the testimony of two Erne boys, Allen approached a fence with a pistol, crossed into the wheat field where Henson stood, struck him, attempted to fire, and ultimately shot him in the side and back. The trial judge framed that account conditionally: if the jury believed those witnesses, the circumstances permitted findings of willfulness and malice.

After the main charge, the jury returned, apparently seeking further instructions. The judge gave a supplemental charge asking jurors to examine the case candidly, respect one another's views, and decide it if they could conscientiously do so. A juror in a minority favoring acquittal was asked to reconsider whether a doubt was reasonable when it did not persuade a much larger group of equally honest and intelligent jurors; a minority favoring conviction was likewise asked to reconsider a judgment not shared by a majority favoring acquittal. The instruction also stated that the verdict must reflect each juror's own judgment rather than mere submission to other jurors.
sections.Issue: Was it error to give a supplemental instruction, after the jury returned, urging jurors in the minority to reconsider their position in light of the majority's views? The complete opinion also resolved challenges to instructions on intent, manslaughter, self-defense, flight, false testimony, and reasonable doubt.
sections.Holding: The Court, in 1896, in an opinion by Justice Brown, held that the supplemental instruction was not error and affirmed the conviction. The report contains no separate writing and identifies no numerical vote. The approved charge preserved the requirement of an individual verdict while urging a minority to test its position against others' reasoning. The opinion did not say that numerical superiority itself establishes guilt, that agreement must be reached at all costs, or that a juror should abandon a conscientious judgment merely to end deliberations. The Court also rejected the other principal challenges to the charge.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court's premise was that individual judgment and deliberative reconsideration are compatible. Unanimity is to emerge from comparing views and arguments, and a juror may change an opinion after that process. The Court rejected the idea that a juror must keep the opinion held on entering the jury room or refuse to listen to equally honest and intelligent colleagues, and it noted that the instructions followed charges approved in Massachusetts and Connecticut cases. The distinction supporting the result is between persuasion through deliberation and acquiescence without conviction.

On the other assignments, the Court approved the instruction permitting, rather than commanding, an inference of willfulness and malice if the jury accepted the prosecution's narrative. It accepted that the intent constituting malice aforethought need not exist for a fixed interval before the killing. It held that provocative words alone did not reduce murder to manslaughter and that justification required circumstances leading a reasonable person to believe life was imperiled, and it accepted the retreat instruction in this case, distinguishing Beard and Alberty. It accepted flight as evidence tending to show guilt; although that instruction was not accurate in every respect, its substance could not have misled the jury. It accepted the instruction on fabricated testimony, and it rejected a requested additional reasonable-doubt instruction because the judge had already instructed on reasonable doubt and the presumption of innocence, distinguishing Coffin.

The casebook introduces Allen through the expression "dynamite charge" and asks whether the Court adequately answered objections to the instruction; that label and question are the casebook's, not the Court's.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-016.rule: A plaintiff who has recovered damages for a battery cannot bring a further action for later physical consequences of the same battery; the first recovery compensates the whole damage and bars the second suit.

sections.Parties: Fetter was the plaintiff. He had already recovered £11 against Beal in an action for battery and brought a further special action seeking additional relief for what his counsel characterized as a distinct maim. Beal, the defendant, pleaded the previous recovery as a bar.
sections.Procedural History: Fetter brought a further special action alleging the earlier recovery and the subsequent loss. Beal pleaded the previous recovery as a bar, and Fetter demurred, arguing that the different subsequent injury permitted the new action. The first report records judgment for the defendant, with the qualification "nisi, &c." that the casebook's excerpt elides. A second reported proceeding records counsel's renewed attempt to obtain judgment for Fetter and states that he could not obtain it because the court inclined strongly against him. The reports do not supply a modern appellate sequence.
sections.Material Facts:
Fetter recovered £11 against Beal in an action for battery. Later, a part of Fetter's skull came out as a consequence of that same battery. He then sued again, alleging the earlier recovery and the subsequent loss, and sought relief for what his counsel called a distinct maim rather than merely the bruising and battery compensated before. The reports give no new damages figure and no exact injury date.

In the second reported account, Chief Justice Holt recalled trying the original cause eight years before, when both parties appeared to have been drinking and the jury was uncertain which was at fault, resulting in lesser damages. That recollection is not in the casebook's excerpt of the first report.
sections.Issue: Could a plaintiff who had recovered damages for a battery bring another action for later physical consequences of the same battery, on the theory that the later loss constituted a different injury?
sections.Holding: The King's Bench held that the prior recovery barred the further action and gave judgment for Beal. The casebook dates the case to 1697; a historical collection captions the two reported proceedings 1698 and 1701, and the brief preserves that discrepancy. The court treated the earlier jury's award as compensation for the damage caused by the wound; the later manifestation did not supply a new actionable battery. The court attributed the resulting difficulty to the plaintiff's having proceeded too hastily in the earlier action. The £11 remained the earlier recovery and was not awarded anew.
sections.Reasoning:
In the first account, Fetter's counsel compared the new claim to successive periods of taking and detaining goods and to later property damage after a roof was uncovered. The court rejected that proposed escape from the first recovery, and its unanimous treatment of the wound and the resulting damage supported Beal's plea in bar.

In the separately reported later argument, counsel used continuing nuisance and a sea-wall example to suggest that subsequent damage could support another action. Chief Justice Holt responded that the battery supplied this action's foundation and that its probable consequences increased the damages for that action. Those consequences could and should have been put in evidence before their physical manifestation. A nuisance could differ because each new dropping of water was a new nuisance, while the maiming could already have been proved in the battery action.

The decision is a historical application of finality to a single battery and its consequences; it does not decide the availability of a new action for a genuinely new wrongful act. The casebook uses the case to ask whether finality is fair to either party, which is the editors' question rather than the court's.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-019.rule: A passenger on an ordinary commercial aircraft flying through the regular navigable airspace above a state is within that state's territorial limits and may be personally served there under then-Rule 4(f).

sections.Parties: Preston and Charlotte Grace, Arkansas citizens, were the plaintiffs. They sued John MacArthur, an Illinois citizen, Ronnie Smith, a Tennessee citizen, and Bankers Life & Casualty Company, an Illinois corporation authorized to conduct insurance business in Arkansas, for breach of a written property-exchange agreement and, alternatively, specific performance. MacArthur was the company's controlling shareholder, chairman, and president. The two individual defendants moved to quash service.
sections.Procedural History: The complaint and summons issued July 21, 1958, in the federal court for the Eastern District of Arkansas. The corporation was served through Arkansas's Insurance Commissioner and did not challenge that service. MacArthur and Smith each moved to quash service on distinct grounds, which the court treated separately. On February 16, 1959, the court denied Smith's motion, reserved MacArthur's motion until trial, and required both individual defendants to answer within ten days after receiving the memorandum and order. MacArthur remained free to renew his personal-jurisdiction contentions in his answer.
sections.Material Facts:
The complaint alleged that Smith acted for himself and as agent for both other defendants; those were allegations, not findings. MacArthur was served through Arkansas's Secretary of State under a statute reaching certain nonresidents who did business or performed work or services in Arkansas. Smith was personally served aboard Braniff Flight 337, a nonstop flight from Memphis to Dallas. The marshal's return stated that delivery occurred at 5:16 p.m. while the aircraft was directly above Pine Bluff in the Eastern District of Arkansas.

Smith did not dispute where and how he was served. He argued that a person in an aircraft above the state was outside its "territorial limits" for purposes of then-Rule 4(f). MacArthur denied doing business or work in Arkansas and denied any valid statutory basis for service on him through the Secretary of State.
sections.Issue: Was a passenger on a commercial aircraft flying over Arkansas within the state's territorial limits, so that he could be personally served under then-Rule 4(f)? Separately, was MacArthur validly served under the Arkansas statute reaching nonresidents who did business or performed work in the state?
sections.Holding: The federal district court for the Eastern District of Arkansas, in 1959, per District Judge Henley, denied Smith's motion to quash. A passenger on an ordinary commercial aircraft traveling through the regular navigable airspace above Arkansas was within Arkansas's territorial limits and could be personally served under then-Rule 4(f). The court expressly limited its discussion to the ordinary navigable airspace of 1958 and did not resolve service at hypothetical future altitudes. It did not decide MacArthur's motion, which it reserved until trial, and it neither found that Smith was MacArthur's agent nor finally determined that MacArthur was subject to personal jurisdiction.
sections.Reasoning:
Then-Rule 4(f) generally confined service in a simple diversity case to the state in which the district court sat, and no federal statute extended the service territory here, so the question was whether the aircraft's position fell inside that territory. The court approached it through the state's continuing jurisdiction over airspace. Earlier decisions recognized state authority over persons and aircraft above state territory, subject to controlling federal powers, and Arkansas's aeronautics legislation addressed crimes, torts, contracts, and passenger injuries in aircraft over the state, which presupposed that the aircraft and occupants were within its boundaries.

Smith's federal-airspace argument did not change the result. Congress had asserted national sovereignty over navigable airspace and regulated air traffic, but, relying on the Supreme Court's Braniff tax decision, the court distinguished national regulation under the commerce power from elimination of all compatible state authority. An interstate traveler is not exempt from personal service merely because he is passing through, whether by car, bus, train, or aircraft; flight might shorten the presence, but that was a difference in degree rather than principle.

MacArthur's objections concerned the Arkansas statute, including a claim that it discriminated unconstitutionally against nonresidents. The court considered them potentially serious but deferred ruling because the disputed agency question overlapped the merits, dismissal would not dispose of the action against the others, and developing the evidence could clarify or eliminate some questions.

The casebook cites the case for the in-flight service on a passenger and the refusal to quash it.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-020.rule: A state may render a personal judgment against its domiciliary who is absent from the state if he is served by a statutory method reasonably calculated to give actual notice and an opportunity to be heard, and another state cannot refuse that judgment recognition by reexamining its merits.

sections.Parties: Milliken, the petitioner, had obtained a Wyoming personal judgment against Meyer for withheld profits from Colorado oil properties and asserted that the judgment was entitled to full faith and credit. The respondent, Meyer's administratrix, was on the side that brought the later Colorado action seeking recovery of the sums paid under the Wyoming judgment, an injunction against its enforcement, and a declaration that it was void.
sections.Procedural History: Milliken sued in Wyoming, and on July 11, 1931 the Wyoming court entered a personal judgment against Meyer, who did not appear. In 1935 the respondent's side brought a Colorado action attacking that judgment. The Colorado trial court found that Meyer was domiciled in Wyoming when the Wyoming suit began, found the substituted-service statute constitutional and the judgment within Wyoming's jurisdiction, and dismissed the challenge. The Colorado Supreme Court reversed on a different ground without deciding the jurisdictional questions: it thought the Wyoming judgment contained an irreconcilable inconsistency. Milliken sought review, and the Court granted certiorari because the full-faith-and-credit question was substantial. The Court reversed the Colorado Supreme Court's judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
Transcontinental Oil Company contracted in 1922 to pay Meyer four sixty-fourths of the profits from Colorado oil properties, and Milliken claimed an interest in that share. A 1924 settlement gave Milliken two sixty-fourths and included an assignment to Transcontinental of his claims against Meyer. Milliken later sued in Wyoming, alleging a joint venture and a conspiracy to defraud him and seeking cancellation of the settlement and an accounting.

Meyer was alleged to be a Wyoming resident but was personally served in Colorado. Wyoming's statutes allowed publication in specified situations involving an absent or concealed resident and allowed personal service outside Wyoming where publication was authorized. Meyer did not appear; Transcontinental appeared and answered.

The Wyoming court found the 1924 contracts valid and dismissed the action against Transcontinental with prejudice, but found a joint venture between Milliken and Meyer, concluded that Meyer had withheld one sixty-fourth of the profits due Milliken, and entered a personal judgment for those profits and interest. It also barred Transcontinental from paying, and Meyer from receiving, more than three sixty-fourths. The disputed share was thereafter paid to Milliken's assignee rather than Meyer. The Colorado challenge alleged that Meyer had ceased residing in Wyoming before service.
sections.Issue: Could Wyoming render a personal judgment against its domiciliary who was absent from the state and personally served in Colorado under Wyoming's statute? And could Colorado refuse to recognize that judgment because it found the Wyoming court's reasoning inconsistent on the merits?
sections.Holding: The Court, in 1940, in an opinion by Justice Douglas with no separate writing or numerical vote reported, reversed the Colorado Supreme Court. Wyoming could render a personal judgment against its domiciliary despite his physical absence, using an appropriate statutory method of service: domicile supplied the adjudicatory relationship, and reasonable notice and an opportunity to be heard supplied the procedural protection. Substituted service must be reasonably calculated to provide actual notice and an opportunity to be heard. Once jurisdiction exists, full faith and credit prevents the recognizing court from reopening the merits, the consistency of the reasoning, or the correctness of the legal principles used.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court tied the duties of citizenship to its benefits. A state protects its domiciliary and permits him to invoke its laws; it may correspondingly require him to answer proceedings even during an absence. Mere travel or residence elsewhere for a time does not by itself dissolve domicile or that relationship. The Court compared this to the national government's authority over absent citizens in Blackmer, while treating adequacy of notice as a separate requirement. Here service was more than a hope that published notice would reach Meyer: he actually received personal service in Colorado under Wyoming's statutory arrangement, which the Court found adequate under due process. The basis of authority was Meyer's domicile, established by findings the Colorado Supreme Court had not impaired; the decision does not hold that receipt of a summons alone lets a state bind any nonresident, and it does not approve every publication scheme.

On recognition, a judgment remains open to challenge in another state for want of personal or subject-matter jurisdiction, but when it appears to be the judgment of a court of general jurisdiction those elements are presumed unless the record or outside evidence disproves them. Legal error within a competent court's judgment does not make it void for collateral purposes. Even assuming a mistake in upholding the assignment while awarding relief against Meyer, that was a merits objection that Colorado could not use to declare the judgment void. The Court did not itself decide that Wyoming's analysis was substantively correct.

The casebook cites the case for the passage on domicile and the reciprocal duties of an absent resident.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-021.rule: A United States citizen residing abroad remains subject to American laws made applicable to him, including the duty to return and testify when properly summoned, and may be penalized for refusal after appropriate notice and an opportunity to be heard.

sections.Parties: Harry M. Blackmer, a United States citizen living in Paris, was the witness held in contempt and the petitioner in the Supreme Court; he challenged the statute and the two contempt decrees. The United States had obtained subpoenas requiring him to return and testify for the government at a criminal trial and relied on his continuing allegiance, a citizen's duty to give evidence, and the statute's notice and hearing protections.
sections.Procedural History: The Supreme Court of the District of Columbia, which was the court issuing the subpoenas and not the United States Supreme Court, issued two subpoenas that were served on Blackmer in France. He failed to respond, and separate contempt proceedings followed. They were heard together and resulted in two fines of $30,000, with costs, to be satisfied from his property seized within the United States. The District's Court of Appeals affirmed, and the Court granted certiorari. The Court affirmed both decrees, preserving the two fines and associated costs.
sections.Material Facts:
Blackmer moved his residence to France in 1924 but retained American citizenship. The two subpoenas required him to appear at different times at a criminal trial that the casebook identifies with the Teapot Dome scandal. They were personally served on him in France under the Act of July 3, 1926.

That statute allowed a judge, on a proper governmental showing, to order a subpoena for a witness abroad who was an American citizen or domiciled in the United States. A consul was to serve it personally, first tendering the necessary expenses of travel and attendance. On proof of service and default, the court could issue an order to show cause, direct seizure of domestic property as security, and require personal service of that order and publication. Only after a hearing and proof sustaining the charge could the court impose a fine of up to $100,000 and authorize satisfaction from the seized property.

Blackmer did not respond to either subpoena. The second trial was continued from April 2 to April 9, 1928.
sections.Issue: Could Congress require a citizen residing abroad to return and testify, with consular service of the subpoena in a foreign country, and could a court fine him for contempt in his absence and satisfy the fine from his seized domestic property consistently with due process and the Fourth Amendment?
sections.Holding: The Court, in 1932, in an opinion by Chief Justice Hughes, with Justice Roberts not participating and no separate writing or vote tally reported, affirmed both contempt decrees. Moving abroad did not end Blackmer's obligations to the United States; he remained subject to American laws made applicable to him, including the duty to attend court and testify when properly summoned. Judicial power to enter a personal judgment still required appropriate notice and an opportunity to be heard, which the statute's subpoena and show-cause procedure supplied. Seizure of his domestic property was a provisional remedy securing the fine, not the source of his duty.
sections.Reasoning:
Whether a law applies abroad to citizens is a question of statutory construction rather than of legislative power; the usual presumption of territorial application is interpretive and does not limit Congress's power over its citizens abroad. One continuing duty of citizenship is to assist the administration of justice by attending courts and testifying, and Congress could prescribe that duty and penalize refusal.

The Court separated legislative obligation from judicial process. Citizenship made Blackmer subject to the law, but a personal judgment required notice and an opportunity to be heard. A footnote distinguishes cases in which the obligations inherent in allegiance are absent.

Consular delivery was simply communication of the government's requirement to its own citizen; it did not invade France's rights or require a treaty grant, and Blackmer lacked standing to assert any injury to the foreign government. The show-cause order gave adequate notice of the contempt proceeding. A hearing and judgment in his absence did not violate due process, the Court characterizing contempt proceedings as distinct from criminal prosecutions within the Sixth Amendment's ordinary meaning.

The liability arose from disobedience, not from owning reachable property, so there was no unconstitutional classification between witnesses with and without domestic assets, and the authorized levy did not violate the Fourth Amendment. Blackmer could not raise criminal defendants' compulsory-process rights on their behalf. The government's showing sufficed to issue the subpoenas, which need not state their statutory source, and the continuance of the second trial did not excuse his never responding.

The casebook cites the case, following Milliken, for citizenship as a continuing jurisdictional relationship supporting personal service abroad.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-028.rule: Under the plurality's formulation, a state may constitutionally apply its own law only if it has a significant contact or significant aggregation of contacts with the parties and the occurrence or transaction, creating state interests, so that choosing its law is neither arbitrary nor fundamentally unfair.

sections.Parties: Mrs. Hague, as personal representative of her husband Ralph Hague's estate, was the plaintiff. She sought a Minnesota declaration permitting the uninsured-motorist coverage on three automobiles to be combined, or stacked. Allstate Insurance Co., the insurer, sought application of Wisconsin law, which the Minnesota courts understood to prohibit stacking.
sections.Procedural History: Proceedings began in Minnesota on May 28, 1976. The Minnesota district court applied Minnesota law and granted summary judgment for Mrs. Hague. The Minnesota Supreme Court affirmed, using Professor Leflar's five choice-influencing considerations and emphasizing Minnesota's stacking rule and, on rehearing, the mobility of automobiles and insurance risks. The United States Supreme Court reviewed only the constitutionality of that choice of law; personal jurisdiction over Allstate was unquestioned. The case was argued October 6, 1980, and decided January 13, 1981. The Court affirmed the Minnesota Supreme Court's judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
Ralph Hague lived with his wife in Hager City, Wisconsin, about one and one-half miles from Red Wing, Minnesota, where he had worked for fifteen years and to which he commuted daily. He died from injuries suffered while riding as a motorcycle passenger in Pierce County, Wisconsin. Both vehicle operators were Wisconsin residents, and neither carried valid insurance. The accident did not occur during his commute or in Minnesota and did not involve any of his three insured automobiles, but the policy's uninsured-motorist protection was not limited to occupancy of those automobiles.

Hague had paid separate premiums, including separate uninsured-motorist premiums, on coverage of $15,000 for each automobile; stacking would yield $45,000. The policy offered continental coverage and contained no Wisconsin choice-of-law provision. Allstate was present and doing business in Minnesota.

After the accident and before the action began, Mrs. Hague moved to Red Wing. She was appointed the estate's personal representative in Minnesota. She remarried a Minnesota resident on June 19, 1976, after the proceedings began, and moved to Savage. The plurality understood the stipulated circumstances to show bona fide residence without a litigation-driven move.
sections.Issue: Did application of Minnesota's stacking law to this insurance dispute violate the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause or Article IV's Full Faith and Credit Clause, given the accident, original residence, and policy connections to Wisconsin?
sections.Holding: The Court, in 1981, affirmed by five votes to three, with Justice Stewart not participating. Justice Brennan's opinion was a plurality joined by Justices White, Marshall, and Blackmun; Justice Stevens concurred in the judgment on separate reasoning. Applying Minnesota law was constitutionally permissible. Under the plurality's formulation, the state must have a significant contact or significant aggregation of contacts with the parties and the occurrence or transaction, creating state interests, so that selecting its law is neither arbitrary nor fundamentally unfair; Minnesota's contacts collectively met that standard. The plurality did not decide whether Hague's Minnesota employment and Allstate's Minnesota presence would suffice without Mrs. Hague's residence and appointment, and a post-accident move alone remains insufficient.
sections.Reasoning:
The plurality reviewed earlier decisions through the forum's contacts and resulting interests: Dick and Yates involved no significant forum connection, while Alaska Packers, Cardillo, and Clay II showed sufficient connections outside the place of injury or policy issuance. Three Minnesota contacts operated together. First, Hague belonged to Minnesota's workforce and commuted there regularly, giving the state interests in his welfare and in vindication of his estate. Second, Allstate was present and doing business in Minnesota, which weakened any claim of unfair surprise. Third, Mrs. Hague's bona fide Minnesota residence and appointment as representative supported Minnesota's compensatory interest. More than one state's law may constitutionally govern the same dispute, and constitutional permission does not establish which law is best under ordinary conflicts principles.

Justice Stevens separated the two clauses. Full faith and credit protects other states' sovereignty, and Allstate had shown no unjustified infringement of Wisconsin's legitimate interests. Due process protects litigants against fundamental unfairness, and nationwide coverage and Allstate's Minnesota business made application of another state's law reasonably foreseeable. He thought the choice unsound as conflicts law and regarded the widow's move as irrelevant and the employment as adding nothing independently.

Justice Powell, joined by Chief Justice Burger and Justice Rehnquist, dissented. He agreed that no reasonable expectations were frustrated but found no legitimate Minnesota policy sufficiently connected to the stacking question; the inquiry required a reasonable connection to the policy advanced by the particular law, not a tally of physical contacts.

The casebook uses Hague to distinguish constitutional limits on choice of law from adjudicative jurisdiction.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-043.rule: In this historical New York trial ruling, a nonresident individual who continuously and substantially conducted business in New York and derived substantial revenue there was held subject to jurisdiction under CPLR 301 on a claim unrelated to that business.

sections.Parties: ABKCO Industries, Inc., the plaintiff, brought two actions involving the Beatles and their companies, seeking commissions, compensation for services, repayment of advances, and other relief on claims exceeding $24 million. The defendants included Richard Starkey, better known as Ringo Starr, George Harrison, McCartney, Boreham, Apple Corps Ltd., Harrisongs Ltd., Python Music Publishing, and other corporations. They challenged personal jurisdiction, the convenience of New York, the pleadings, and nonjoinder, and sought stays and disqualification of ABKCO's lawyers.
sections.Procedural History:
In July 1974 the parties consented to a reference to Dean Joseph McLaughlin to hear the jurisdictional issues and report recommendations; the court reviewed his findings and decided whether to confirm them. George Harrison's jurisdictional motion was withdrawn after personal service in New York. The trial court decided the motions on October 17, 1975, with a supplemental decision on November 25, 1975. It confirmed the reports to the stated extent, denied personal-jurisdiction dismissal for Apple Corps, Harrisongs, and Starkey, granted it for the other moving corporations, and retained attachment jurisdiction except over Python. There was no final merits judgment.

At a separate later stage, the Appellate Division, First Department, on June 8, 1976, sustained jurisdiction over Starkey and Apple Corps and the refusals of forum dismissal and disqualification, but ordered pleading-based dismissal of McCartney and Boreham.
sections.Material Facts:
An English action alleged that ABKCO breached its management agreement and fiduciary duties; a September 1975 affidavit placed that English trial in early January 1977. Apple Corps Ltd. had New York and California affiliates, both doing business in New York. Harrisongs Ltd. acted in New York through agents and representatives. Starkey, an English individual, continuously and substantially conducted business through his New York connections, derived substantial revenues from the state, and maintained geographically extensive professional activities; the action was unrelated to that New York business, and the court did not find him domiciled in New York.

Funds of Startling Music held by Fox were attached; the attachment, served January 21, 1974, reached at least $12,383.58. ABKCO conceded that there was no jurisdiction of any kind over Python. ABKCO's lawyers had represented the Beatles or their companies during 1969 to 1973.
sections.Issue: Could New York exercise jurisdiction over an English individual whose sustained New York business was unrelated to the action? Could the court retain the corporate defendants, and should the cases proceed despite the English litigation and the lawyers' former representation of the defendants?
sections.Holding: The New York Supreme Court, Special Term, New York County, in 1975, per Justice Jacob Markowitz, denied Starkey's motion under a general-jurisdiction conception of CPLR 301, departing from the referee's account of then-existing New York law. The ruling was explicitly limited to the circumstances presented. The court confirmed the referee's corporate findings: Apple Corps's affiliates were its alter egos and Harrisongs itself acted in New York, so dismissal was denied as to them and granted as to the other moving corporations, whose contacts were too remote or legally insufficient. The supplement kept those corporations, apart from Python, in the actions on quasi in rem jurisdiction over attached property. The court otherwise declined dismissal, stays, and disqualification.
sections.Reasoning:
The referee read prior law to require that a nonresident individual's cause of action arise from that individual's New York business. The judge accepted that this could accurately describe the existing cases but declined to follow it for Starkey. Given his continuous and substantial New York business and revenues, the judge treated defending an unrelated action there as compatible with fair play and substantial justice and as imposing no demonstrated handicap. The ruling did not make every nonresident who conducts any business in New York subject to all-purpose jurisdiction.

The November supplement stated that quasi in rem jurisdiction had been conceded over the corporate defendants apart from Python, and the court denied vacatur of the attachments, so failure of personal jurisdiction did not end every basis for keeping those corporations in the actions. The Business Corporation Law section 1314(b) objection also failed.

The English litigation did not support dismissal under the prior-action-pending provision, and the court was not satisfied the actions involved the same cause. On forum non conveniens, the defendants showed no undue hardship sufficient to deny a domestic corporation with substantial New York activity access to its courts, and the possible application of English law did not require an English forum. Former representation alone did not disqualify ABKCO's lawyers: the defendants showed no significant relationship between the interests formerly protected and the present issues and identified no confidential information that would be used against them.

On the later appeal, Silverman dissented only on personal jurisdiction over Starkey. The casebook uses the Starkey ruling as a historical example and asks whether it survives Goodyear and Daimler; that question is the editors', and the brief does not certify the holding as current law.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-049.rule: Compliance with a state's service procedures, including registering to do business and appointing a service agent, does not itself establish constitutional jurisdiction over claims that arose elsewhere and are unconnected with the corporation's limited forum activities.

sections.Parties: Annie and Henry Ratliff, Florida residents, sued Cooper Laboratories, Inc., a Delaware corporation headquartered in Connecticut, over injury allegedly caused by drugs. In the companion case, Alice Nichols, an Indiana resident, sued Sterling Drug Company, a Delaware corporation headquartered in New York. The drug companies were the defendants and the appellants; they sought to set aside service and dismiss the complaints.
sections.Procedural History: Both actions were filed in the South Carolina federal district court. Cooper was served under the state long-arm procedure and Sterling through its appointed state agent. The district court denied the companies' motions to set aside service and dismiss. The Fourth Circuit heard a consolidated interlocutory appeal under 28 U.S.C. section 1292(b). The procedural sufficiency of service was not disputed; the question was whether the court had adjudicatory power over these out-of-state claims. The Fourth Circuit reversed, holding that both motions should have been granted, and left undecided the companies' defense under South Carolina's door-closing statute.
sections.Material Facts:
Annie Ratliff purchased the drugs in Florida and did not consume them in South Carolina. Cooper's South Carolina activities consisted of mailed solicitation to dealers and wholesalers and promotional mailings to approximately 650 physicians.

Nichols's drug was manufactured in New York, and the parties stipulated that purchase, consumption, injury, treatment, and hospitalization occurred in Indiana. Sterling had more South Carolina activity than Cooper: it obtained authority to do business there, appointed a service agent, and employed five resident promotional representatives called detail men, who contacted doctors and drugstores and occasionally took orders but whose primary function was promotion rather than sales.

Neither company maintained an office, warehouse, bank account, or directory advertising in the state, and neither held property there except the samples and materials used by Sterling's promotional employees. The plaintiffs chose South Carolina solely for its six-year limitations period; the periods had expired in Florida, Indiana, New York, Connecticut, and Delaware. Neither plaintiff had any other connection with South Carolina.
sections.Issue: Were the drug companies' South Carolina activities, including Sterling's registration to do business and appointment of a service agent, extensive enough to permit a South Carolina court to adjudicate claims brought by nonresidents, arising elsewhere, and unconnected with those activities?
sections.Holding: The Fourth Circuit, in 1971, in an opinion by Circuit Judge Craven for a panel with Winter and District Judge Miller, with no separate writing reported, held that these forum activities did not supply sufficient contacts for the unrelated claims and reversed. Compliance with service procedures did not itself establish constitutional jurisdiction. Sterling's registration and appointment of a service agent did not change the result: in this factual setting, mere compliance with the domestication statute carried no special weight, and the five representatives did not tip the balance. The court did not decide that every registration statute or every form of expressly given consent must produce the same result.
sections.Reasoning:
South Carolina's service law had been construed to reach the outer limits allowed by International Shoe, so the constitutional inquiry controlled. A footnote explains that the incorporation of state law into federal amenability had generally been understood to include the constitutional restraints on the state's authority. The panel applied International Shoe's inquiry into the quality and nature of the activities in relation to the fair administration of the laws, rather than a mechanical count of visits or a notion of physical presence, and observed that expanding interstate business did not eliminate jurisdictional limits.

The claims lacked a rational connection to South Carolina. For an injury unconnected with forum conduct, the panel required other contacts extensive enough to justify the burden of defending there. The companies had no office, warehouse, bank account, or directory advertising in the state, and national medical-journal advertisements reaching South Carolina did not create the substantial forum relationship these claims needed. As to Sterling, the panel distinguished obtaining permission to do business from actually exercising that privilege to a constitutionally sufficient degree.

The panel found persuasive the First Circuit's similar Seymour case, which distinguished an enterprise that had made the forum a major business center or substantially entered its business life from a more limited pattern of advertising and sales solicitation.

The casebook places Ratliff in its discussion of consent through corporate registration, a later debate that is the editors' commentary rather than the panel's analysis.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-063.rule: A state may apply property within its borders, including a bank deposit owed to a nonresident, to an obligation such as alimony if the property is within the state, seized at the commencement of proceedings, and the owner has an opportunity to be heard.

sections.Parties: Pennington, the husband, was the plaintiff in an independent Ohio action to recover his deposit from the Fourth National Bank of Cincinnati, and he sought review in the Supreme Court after losing. The bank, the defendant, had paid the deposit to Mrs. Pennington under orders in her divorce and alimony proceeding and refused to pay him.
sections.Procedural History: Mrs. Pennington obtained a divorce in an Ohio state court and sought alimony in the same proceeding, joining the bank. After the court-directed payments to her, the husband brought a separate Ohio action against the bank for the deposit. Judgment went to the bank, and both the Hamilton County appellate court and the Ohio Supreme Court affirmed. The U.S. Supreme Court reviewed that judgment and affirmed it on March 6, 1917.
sections.Material Facts:
Mrs. Pennington sued for divorce and alimony in Ohio and joined the Fourth National Bank of Cincinnati, which held her husband's deposit. When she filed suit, the court enjoined the bank from paying out any of the money. Later orders directed payments to the wife; ultimately the bank was permanently restrained from paying the husband and ordered to pay the remaining balance to the wife, and it complied.

The husband was not an Ohio resident. He had not been personally served within Ohio and had not appeared voluntarily; notice to him was by publication alone. After the payments, he presented a check for the full amount of his original deposit, arguing that the orders deprived him of property without due process and that the bank knew the jurisdictional circumstances. The bank refused payment. The validity of the divorce itself was admitted.
sections.Issue: Did applying a nonresident husband's Ohio bank deposit to alimony, on notice by publication alone and after an injunction against the bank at the start of the divorce suit, deprive him of property without the due process required by the Fourteenth Amendment?
sections.Holding: The Court, in 1917, in an opinion by Justice Brandeis with no separate writing or numerical vote reported, affirmed the Ohio judgment for the bank. It treated the alimony decree as a charge against the seized property rather than an enforceable personal judgment against the absent husband. The Court identified three essentials: the property must be within the state, it must be seized at the commencement of proceedings, and the owner must have an opportunity to be heard. When those conditions were satisfied, the alimony decree was valid to the same extent as a judgment on a debt against the seized property.
sections.Reasoning:
Justice Brandeis distinguished jurisdiction over a person from jurisdiction over property. The opinion's historical premise was that a state could exercise jurisdiction over property within its borders despite the owner's absence or nonresidence, and that premise covered intangible property: the debt a resident bank owed its nonresident depositor counted as property within the state. Publication did not supply a basis for a judgment in personam, but garnishment and foreign attachment operated quasi in rem, seizing the defendant's property and applying it toward the obligation.

The husband argued that alimony differed from ordinary garnishment because an ordinary debt already exists when suit begins, while the alimony obligation arises through the proceeding itself. The Court found the distinction immaterial. Jurisdiction over the seized property did not depend on whether the claim was admitted or contested, liquidated or unliquidated, or already mature rather than inchoate and dependent on time or judicial action; the court could determine the obligation as part of the proceeding.

The opening injunction satisfied the seizure requirement. It immobilized the deposit as effectively as customary garnishment or trustee process, and equity could reach property unavailable to attachment at law. The reasoning did not authorize collection against the husband's other assets as a personal obligation established by publication.

The casebook presents the case in its section on jurisdiction based on power over property; its accompanying question about the situs of corporate stock is the editors' problem, not an issue decided in Pennington.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-064.rule: Where local law permits garnishment, personal service on a garnishee found within the state, even temporarily, gives its courts power to condemn the debt he owes, provided the garnishee's own creditor could have sued him there.

sections.Parties: Balk, a North Carolina resident, sued Harris, also of North Carolina, to recover a $180 debt. Harris, the defendant and the party seeking review in the Supreme Court, defended on the ground that he had already paid the debt under a Maryland judgment obtained by Jacob Epstein, a Baltimore resident who claimed that Balk owed him more than $300.
sections.Procedural History: Epstein began a Maryland foreign-attachment proceeding against Balk, garnishing Harris. Balk brought his own North Carolina action against Harris on August 11; the Maryland judgment condemning the debt was entered thereafter. North Carolina awarded Balk $180 with interest. Its Supreme Court treated the debt as situated in North Carolina and regarded Harris's temporary Maryland presence as insufficient to give the Maryland court jurisdiction over it. The United States Supreme Court reviewed that refusal to recognize the Maryland judgment under the Full Faith and Credit Clause. It reversed the Supreme Court of North Carolina and remanded for proceedings consistent with its opinion.
sections.Material Facts:
Harris had borrowed $180 from Balk in 1896 and verbally promised to repay it; there was no written instrument. When Harris traveled to Baltimore to purchase merchandise, Epstein sought to collect from Balk by attaching the money Harris owed him. On August 6, 1896, Harris was personally served in Baltimore with a Maryland foreign-attachment writ and a summons, and the sheriff posted the summons and short declaration against Balk at the courthouse door as Maryland law required.

Harris returned to North Carolina before the writ's return day. He acknowledged his $180 debt in an August 11 affidavit, and his counsel consented to condemnation of that debt in the Maryland proceeding. Judgment was entered thereafter, and Harris paid Epstein's North Carolina attorney after its entry. The report gives no precise Maryland judgment date.

Maryland procedure required restitution security before execution where the parties did not appear and allowed the defendant a year and a day to challenge the attaching creditor's claim. Balk learned of the attachment and judgment promptly through his own suit, yet the record showed no such challenge. He admitted in the North Carolina case that he had owed Epstein approximately $344 at the time of attachment.
sections.Issue: Could Maryland validly garnish an ordinary debt owed between two North Carolina residents when the garnishee was personally served during a temporary Maryland visit, so that North Carolina had to give full faith and credit to the resulting judgment and Harris's payment of it?
sections.Holding: The Court, in 1905, in an opinion by Justice Peckham, with Justices Harlan and Day dissenting without a written opinion, reversed and remanded. Attachment depended on local law, but where local law permitted it, personal service on a garnishee found within the state gave the court power to condemn the debt, provided that the garnishee's own creditor could sue him there; temporary presence did not defeat that power. Maryland's condemnation of the $180 was therefore jurisdictionally valid, and Harris's consent to the judgment did not make his payment merely voluntary. The reasoning was directed to ordinary debts such as this one.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court rejected the attempt to make an ordinary debt's original location decisive. An obligation to pay was enforceable against the debtor wherever he could be sued and did not become unenforceable because he crossed a state boundary for a short visit. Unlike a tangible object, a debt could not be physically seized; garnishment arrested the obligation through notice to the debtor and a direction not to pay his original creditor.

Maryland satisfied both parts of the test. Balk could have sued Harris there despite their shared North Carolina residence, which the Court connected to the privileges and immunities of citizens of the several states. Maryland's attachment provisions covered credits in another person's hands, and personal service supplied power over Harris. The attaching creditor was treated as representing the garnishee's creditor in reaching an obligation the latter could himself enforce in Maryland.

Harris admittedly owed the debt and had no defense to condemnation once jurisdiction was acquired, so consenting to the judgment Epstein was entitled to obtain did not strip the payment of its protective effect.

The Court added a qualification. A garnishee owes his own creditor notice so that the creditor can contest the attaching claim, and negligently failing to give it could prevent the garnishee from relying on the judgment and payment. On this record Balk learned of the judgment promptly, had a year and a day to challenge it, and did not, so there was no basis to deny Harris the judgment's protection.

The casebook calls the notice discussion dictum; the brief notes that the opinion develops the qualification and applies it to the facts. The brief explains the historical decision without certifying its rule as current law.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-066.rule: Jurisdiction requires a sufficient relationship among the particular defendant, the forum, and the litigation; garnishing an insurer's obligation to defend and indemnify cannot supply an insured's missing contacts, and contacts cannot be aggregated among defending parties.

sections.Parties: Savchuk, injured as a passenger in a car driven by Rush, was the plaintiff in a Minnesota tort action. Rush, the defendant driver, and State Farm, the insurer of the car and the garnishee, moved to dismiss. Savchuk sought $125,000 in damages, later reduced to the policy's $50,000 limit.
sections.Procedural History: Savchuk sued in Minnesota on May 28, 1974. Rush and State Farm moved to dismiss; the trial court denied the motion and permitted a supplemental complaint adding State Farm as garnishee. The Minnesota Supreme Court affirmed in Savchuk I in 1976, treating the insurer's obligation as attachable property. The U.S. Supreme Court vacated and remanded for reconsideration after Shaffer. Minnesota again upheld jurisdiction in Savchuk II in 1978, reasoning that the policy was closely connected to the litigation and that the procedure served resident plaintiffs. On appeal from that renewed judgment, the Court reversed the Minnesota Supreme Court.
sections.Material Facts:
Savchuk was injured as a passenger in a car driven by Rush in Elkhart, Indiana, on January 13, 1972. Both were Indiana residents at the time. Rush's father owned the car, and State Farm insured it under an Indiana liability policy. Indiana's guest statute would have barred Savchuk's claim. Savchuk moved with his parents to Minnesota in June 1973 and sued there after Indiana's two-year limitations period had expired.

Rush had no Minnesota contacts that would support personal jurisdiction and was personally served in Indiana. Savchuk sought quasi in rem jurisdiction by garnishing State Farm's contractual obligation to defend and indemnify Rush. State Farm did business in Minnesota and nationwide. The insurer denied owing anything to Rush.
sections.Issue: Can the insurer's Minnesota business and the attachment of its defense-and-indemnity obligation support jurisdiction over an insured who otherwise has no contacts with Minnesota, in a suit arising from an Indiana accident?
sections.Holding: The Court, in 1980, in an opinion by Justice Marshall joined by Chief Justice Burger and Justices Stewart, White, Blackmun, Powell, and Rehnquist, with Justices Brennan and Stevens dissenting separately, held that it cannot and reversed. Under International Shoe and Shaffer, jurisdiction requires a constitutionally sufficient relationship among the particular defendant, the forum, and the litigation, and attachable property does not eliminate that inquiry. State Farm's contacts could not supply Rush's missing contacts merely because it insured him and would conduct the defense; the requirements must be met for each defendant. The Court did not decide negligence, damages, coverage, or whether Minnesota tort law could constitutionally apply.
sections.Reasoning:
Seider-type jurisdiction combined two fictions: a debt is located wherever its debtor can be found, and a corporation is present wherever it does business. The majority assumed without deciding that the obligation was garnishable under state law and treated its constitutional significance as a separate question. The insurer's decision to do business in Minnesota was not purposeful Minnesota activity by Rush, who had no control over it and would not reasonably expect an Indiana insurance purchase to expose him to suit wherever a later plaintiff moved. The policy was not the subject matter of the negligence claim or connected to the accident; it concerned how the litigation would be defended and paid.

The direct-action analogy failed because Minnesota's procedure first needed power over the insured to bring in the insurer as garnishee, unlike the statute in Watson. Insurance did not necessarily eliminate the insured's own stake, and the plaintiff's Minnesota residence and the state's interests could not replace Rush's missing forum connection.

Justice Brennan's dissent, shared with World-Wide Volkswagen, read International Shoe as an inquiry into practical fairness giving greater weight to forum interests and the actual burden of defending; he viewed Rush's added burden as slight, since State Farm controlled the defense and would bear liability up to the policy limit. Justice Stevens treated the Minnesota procedure as functionally a direct action against the insurer that could proceed so long as Minnesota exercised no power over Rush individually.

The casebook cites the case, in a note to Shaffer, for the attachment holding and the separation of the insurer's contacts from the tortfeasor's.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-069.rule: A defendant that specially appears, fully litigates personal jurisdiction, loses, and lets the judgment become final cannot relitigate that jurisdictional question by collateral attack when the judgment is sued upon elsewhere, absent fraud.

sections.Parties: Baldwin, the petitioner, sued in the federal court for Southern Iowa to enforce a judgment previously entered against the Iowa State Traveling Men's Association in the federal court for Western Missouri. The association, the defendant, resisted enforcement on the ground that the Missouri court had lacked personal jurisdiction over it.
sections.Procedural History: The original action began in a Missouri state court and was removed to the federal district court, which denied the association's motion contesting personal jurisdiction and later entered judgment for the amount claimed. The association did not seek to set aside that judgment or seek appellate review. Baldwin then sued on the judgment in the Iowa federal district court, which admitted the jurisdictional challenge over Baldwin's objection that the issue had already been adjudicated, sustained the defense after a hearing without a jury, and dismissed the action. The Eighth Circuit affirmed. The Court reversed and remanded for further proceedings consistent with its opinion.
sections.Material Facts:
In the Missouri action the association appeared specially and moved to quash service and dismiss. The court initially quashed service but refused dismissal. After an alias summons was returned served, the association again appeared specially, asking that the service and return be set aside and the action dismissed for lack of personal jurisdiction. The court heard the question on affidavits and briefs, denied the motion, and allowed thirty days to plead. The association filed no plea, and judgment was eventually entered for the amount claimed.

When Baldwin sued on that judgment in Iowa, the association renewed the same objections: it was an Iowa corporation, had never been present in Missouri, and the person served there was not an agent upon whom service could bind it. Those were the association's assertions; the Supreme Court did not resolve them afresh.
sections.Issue: May a defendant that specially appeared, fully contested personal jurisdiction, lost that contest, and allowed the resulting judgment to become final relitigate the same jurisdictional question when the judgment is sued upon in another federal court?
sections.Holding: The Court, in 1931, in an opinion by Justice Roberts with no separate opinion reported, held that it may not. A full adjudication of the defendant's personal-jurisdiction objection can itself become conclusive. A special appearance preserves an objection for direct review; it does not entitle the defendant to repeat a fully heard jurisdictional contest through a later collateral attack. Finality applies, in the absence of fraud, where the party voluntarily submitted the issue and was fully heard. The Court reversed the judgment rejecting Baldwin's enforcement action; it did not affirm the Missouri judgment on a fresh examination of its jurisdictional merits.
sections.Reasoning:
The constitutional arguments did not resolve the dispute. Baldwin invoked the Full Faith and Credit Clause, but neither court concerned was a state court. The association invoked Fourteenth Amendment due process, but due process does not provide a right to litigate the same question twice. The controlling question was the preclusive effect of the prior adjudication of jurisdiction.

The special appearance mattered for the manner of obtaining review, not as an immunity from the eventual adjudication. The association could have preserved its objection while proceeding on the merits and challenged the jurisdictional ruling on appeal. Instead it obtained a full hearing of the objection and then took no further steps, and its deliberate submission of the issue justified treating the determination as settled.

The Court distinguished a defendant that never appears: it has never had its day in court on jurisdiction and can raise the issue in an action on the default judgment. The association's later failure to plead did not put it in that category, because it had already appeared to contest jurisdiction and been heard. The Court also distinguished National Exchange Bank v. Wiley, where an unauthorized attorney had purported to appear and confess judgment, and Bank of Jasper v. First National Bank, where the issue later raised had not been litigated.

The casebook develops the case in its discussion of challenging personal jurisdiction; its question about requiring an objection in the initial forum is an editorial hypothetical that Baldwin does not adopt.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-071.rule: A personal money judgment resting only on newspaper publication against a defendant who has left the state intending not to return is void, in the rendering state as well as elsewhere; substituted service must be the form most likely to reach the defendant.

sections.Parties: McDonald, the plaintiff, sued Mabee on a promissory note and sought review in the Supreme Court. Mabee, the defendant, relied on an earlier Texas judgment that McDonald himself had obtained on the same note as a bar to the second suit, while McDonald denied that the earlier judgment had personal effect.
sections.Procedural History: McDonald had earlier obtained a Texas judgment on the note that purported both to bind Mabee personally and to foreclose a lien securing the note. In McDonald's second suit on the note, the Texas Supreme Court held that publication satisfied state law and that the earlier judgment was a valid personal judgment, rejecting McDonald's federal due process objection to giving it that effect. The Court reversed the Texas Supreme Court's judgment on March 6, 1917; the reported disposition is "Judgment reversed," without an express remand.
sections.Material Facts: When the first suit began, Mabee was technically domiciled in Texas but had left intending to establish a home elsewhere. His family still lived in Texas. He returned briefly and later established a Missouri domicile. The only service in the first suit was publication in a local newspaper, once weekly for four successive weeks after his final departure. He never appeared. The first judgment purported to bind him personally and to foreclose a lien securing the note. In the second suit on the same note, Mabee's material defense was that earlier judgment.
