sections.Procedural History: The owners invoked diversity jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a)(1) in federal district court. The district court concluded to a legal certainty that not every individual owner had damages exceeding $10,000, found that defining a class of only those owners with qualifying claims was not feasible, and, reading Snyder v. Harris as requiring each owner's separate claim to satisfy the amount requirement, refused class treatment. A divided Second Circuit affirmed. The Court granted review and affirmed the Second Circuit's judgment sustaining the refusal to permit the proposed class action.
sections.Material Facts:
The owners alleged that discharges from International Paper's New York pulp-and-paper plant flowed through Ticonderoga Creek into Lake Champlain, polluting the water and damaging the value and utility of nearby properties. The Court did not decide whether the company had caused the alleged pollution or what damages particular owners were owed.

At that time the statutory amount in controversy had to exceed $10,000, exclusive of interest and costs. Each named plaintiff satisfied that requirement, but not every member of the proposed class did. The distinction from Snyder was central: in Snyder no plaintiff had a claim large enough to create original diversity jurisdiction, whereas the named plaintiffs here did. The dissent described approximately 240 proposed claimants, a description distinct from the majority's account of the named owners and 200 others.
sections.Issue: Under the jurisdictional law then applied, could unnamed class members with separate claims below the statutory minimum proceed in a Rule 23(b)(3) diversity class action when the named plaintiffs' claims exceeded the minimum?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States, in 1973, in an opinion by Justice White for six Justices, with three dissenting, held that they could not. Each plaintiff in a Rule 23(b)(3) action asserting a separate and distinct claim had to satisfy the jurisdictional amount, and a qualifying plaintiff's claim could not supply jurisdiction for another plaintiff's independently deficient claim. The Court did not dismiss the named owners' independently sufficient claims or adjudicate the pollution merits.
sections.Reasoning:
Justice White located the rule in the statutory phrase "matter in controversy." He distinguished separate and distinct demands joined for convenience, where each plaintiff must meet the amount, from a single title or right in which plaintiffs share a common and undivided interest, which may be considered collectively. Damage to individual lakefront properties fell in the first category; a common source of harm did not make the claims one undivided right. Clark v. Paul Gray, which entertained the one qualifying plaintiff's claim while directing dismissal of the others, showed that the rule barred deficient claims from accompanying a qualifying one. Snyder had already rejected the argument that the 1966 revision of Rule 23 changed the statutory rule, and Congress had repeatedly adjusted the dollar threshold while leaving the operative language intact. The majority saw no reason to give unnamed class members an exemption unavailable to original plaintiffs, and left any change to Congress.

Justice Brennan, joined by Justices Douglas and Marshall, dissented. He accepted that at least one qualifying plaintiff was needed for original jurisdiction, but argued that the court could then exercise ancillary jurisdiction over related claims of absent class members, a theory that did not depend on aggregation. He relied on Supreme Tribe of Ben-Hur, on the use of ancillary jurisdiction for compulsory counterclaims and intervention as of right, and on the cost of separate pollution suits.

The casebook presents Zahn before contrasting Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Allapattah Services, in which the Court stated that § 1367's text overruled Clark and Zahn; Zahn's each-member rule is therefore to be studied as the historical rule.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-162.rule: A federal court has no ancillary jurisdiction to enforce a settlement agreement after dismissing the suit unless the dismissal order incorporated the settlement's terms or expressly retained jurisdiction over it; otherwise enforcement needs an independent basis of federal jurisdiction.

sections.Parties: Kokkonen had been a general agent of Guardian Life Insurance Co. of America under an agency agreement that Guardian Life terminated. He sued Guardian Life on state-law claims, and Guardian Life asserted state-law counterclaims. After the suit settled, Guardian Life moved to enforce the settlement and Kokkonen objected that the court lacked subject-matter jurisdiction. Two other corporate defendants had been dismissed before trial; Guardian Life alone was the respondent in the Court.
sections.Procedural History: Kokkonen sued in California state court, and Guardian Life removed on diversity grounds. After closing arguments but before jury instructions, the parties settled, and in April 1992 they executed a stipulated dismissal with prejudice under the then-numbered Rule 41(a)(1)(ii), which the judge signed on April 13. Guardian Life later moved in the same federal court to enforce the settlement. The district court asserted inherent power and ordered enforcement, and the Ninth Circuit affirmed on a theory of inherent supervisory authority. Kokkonen's appeal relied solely on his jurisdictional objection. The Court reversed the Ninth Circuit and remanded for further proceedings consistent with its opinion.
sections.Material Facts:
The parties reached an oral settlement of all claims and counterclaims and recited its substance on the record before the district judge in chambers. The stipulated dismissal with prejudice was signed by the judge with the notation that it was ordered. The document did not refer to the settlement, incorporate its terms, or reserve jurisdiction to enforce it.

A later dispute concerned Kokkonen's obligation under the settlement to return files. Guardian Life sought enforcement of the agreement in the federal court that had dismissed the case. The question before the Court was the federal court's power to adjudicate the settlement dispute, not whether Kokkonen actually owed the files or whether the settlement was a valid contract.
sections.Issue: Whether a federal district court that dismissed a suit under a stipulated dismissal that neither incorporated the parties' settlement nor retained jurisdiction over it has inherent or ancillary jurisdiction to enforce that settlement agreement.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States, in 1994, in an opinion by Justice Scalia for a unanimous Court, held that it does not. A federal court's jurisdiction over the original lawsuit did not automatically give it jurisdiction to enforce the parties' later settlement contract, and this dismissal order neither incorporated that contract nor retained enforcement jurisdiction. Enforcement belonged in state court unless an independent basis of federal jurisdiction existed. The decision did not resolve the file-return dispute or foreclose a separately supported federal action.
sections.Reasoning:
Federal courts possess limited jurisdiction granted by Constitution and statute; the party asserting jurisdiction must establish it, and a judicial decree cannot enlarge it. Neither Rule 41 nor any other identified provision supplied jurisdiction over every contract that produces a stipulated dismissal. The Court distinguished enforcing the settlement from reopening the original suit under Rule 60(b)(6), a question on which appellate courts disagreed and which the Court did not decide. Enforcement, meaning damages or specific performance of the new agreement, required its own jurisdictional basis.

Guardian Life relied on broad language in Julian v. Central Trust Co., but that case involved a decree that expressly reserved jurisdiction. The Court identified two purposes of ancillary jurisdiction: allowing one court to dispose of factually interdependent claims, and allowing a court to manage its proceedings, vindicate its authority, and effectuate its decrees. Neither applied. The facts of the agency dispute and of the settlement breach had nothing to do with one another, and the only judicial command was that the action be dismissed, which a breach of a private settlement did not violate.

The result would differ if the order had incorporated the settlement's terms or expressly retained jurisdiction, because a breach would then violate the order. The judge's awareness and approval of the settlement were not enough. Under Rule 41(a)(2) the court could impose such a term in its discretion; under Rule 41(a)(1)(ii) it could do so if the parties agreed.

The casebook frames the case as a question about residual ancillary jurisdiction after §1367; the opinion cites §1367 only comparatively and its holding is narrower.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-172.rule: When a defendant removes a case in part under §1442 or §1443, the exception in §1447(d) permits appellate review of the district court's entire remand order, including every removal ground the order rejected.

sections.Parties: Baltimore's mayor and city council were the plaintiffs. They sued energy companies, including BP P.L.C., in Maryland state court on state-law causes of action. The companies, defendants, removed the suit to federal court and, after the district court remanded, appealed. They wanted appellate review of all their grounds for removal; Baltimore resisted that broader review.
sections.Procedural History: Baltimore sued in Maryland state court in 2018. The companies removed, invoking several grounds. The district court examined and rejected each ground and remanded the case to state court. The Fourth Circuit accepted that it could review the rejection of the §1442 federal-officer theory and affirmed that rejection, but declined to review the other removal theories, reading the statutory exception as ground-specific. A circuit disagreement over that appellate scope brought the case to the Court, which vacated the Fourth Circuit's judgment and remanded for further proceedings, leaving the other removal grounds to the Fourth Circuit in the first instance.
sections.Material Facts:
The complaint asserted state-law claims concerning promotion of fossil fuels, alleged concealment of environmental consequences, and resulting injuries. Whether those allegations were true was outside the appeal.

The companies asserted federal-officer removal under §1442 on the ground that some of the challenged exploration, drilling, and production occurred at the federal government's behest. They also invoked federal-question, Outer Continental Shelf, admiralty, and bankruptcy grounds. These were theories asserted by the defendants, not findings by the Court that any was satisfied.

Section 1447(d) generally prohibited appellate review of remand orders but expressly excepted cases removed pursuant to the federal-officer provision, §1442, or the civil-rights provision, §1443. By the time the case reached the Court, the dissent noted, the companies no longer pressed their §1442 ground.
sections.Issue: When a defendant premises removal in part on §1442 or §1443, does the exception in §1447(d) allow appellate review of only that removal ground, or of the district court's entire remand order?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States, in 2021, in an opinion by Justice Gorsuch for seven Justices, with Justice Sotomayor dissenting and Justice Alito not participating, held that the entire remand order is reviewable, including the other grounds for removal addressed in it. The holding concerns the scope of appellate jurisdiction after remand. It did not uphold removal, establish the validity of any particular removal ground, decide the merits of the climate claims, or determine whether fee-and-cost awards in remand orders are separately appealable.
sections.Reasoning:
The word "order" was central. The statute authorized review of an order remanding a case, and here that order rested on rejection of all the companies' theories; because courts ordinarily must exercise the jurisdiction they have, the district court could not remand while leaving a valid basis unresolved. Review of the order therefore reached each rejected basis.

A case is removed "pursuant to" §1442 when the defendant follows §1446's procedure and asserts that statute as a ground. The majority rejected Baltimore's argument that a court must first hold the federal-officer ground valid. Reliance on several statutes did not change the result: elsewhere Congress spoke of cases removed "solely" under a provision, and §1447(d) has no such limit. Exceptions deserve a fair reading rather than a narrow one.

The Court treated Yamaha as the closest analogy, since §1292(b) review of a certified "order" reaches issues fairly included in it. It found no broad and unquestioned consensus of earlier decisions that Congress could have ratified in 2011 when it added §1442. Efficiency and manipulation concerns did not override the text; §1447(c)'s cost-and-fee provisions and Rule 11 sanctions answer frivolous removal arguments, and further adjustment belongs to Congress.

Justice Sotomayor, dissenting, found the multiple-ground situation ambiguous and would have limited review to the §1442 or §1443 ground, relying on decades of appellate decisions and the policy against delaying state litigation. She warned that defendants could add a weak federal-officer theory, too weak to pursue but not sanctionable, to obtain review of unrelated grounds.

The casebook cites the case in a note on review of remand orders.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-173.rule: A district court's error in failing to remand a case improperly removed for lack of complete diversity does not require vacating a final judgment on the merits if complete diversity existed when judgment was entered.

sections.Parties: James David Lewis, a Kentucky citizen, was the plaintiff. He sued Caterpillar Inc., incorporated in Delaware with its principal place of business in Illinois, and Whayne Supply, a Kentucky corporation, on state-law claims arising from a bulldozer injury. Liberty Mutual, incorporated and headquartered in Massachusetts, intervened as a plaintiff seeking reimbursement of workers' compensation benefits. Caterpillar removed the case and won at trial; Lewis sought to have the judgment set aside because the removal was improper.
sections.Procedural History: Lewis sued in Kentucky state court on June 22, 1989. Caterpillar removed on June 21, 1990. Lewis promptly moved to remand, and the district court denied the motion. After Whayne Supply was dismissed in June 1993, a six-day jury trial in November ended in a verdict and judgment for Caterpillar. The Sixth Circuit vacated the judgment because complete diversity had been lacking at removal, and did not reach Lewis's other appellate issues. The Court reversed the Sixth Circuit and remanded for proceedings consistent with its opinion, leaving those other issues unresolved.
sections.Material Facts:
Lewis was injured while operating a bulldozer and asserted defective-manufacture, negligent-maintenance, warning, and warranty claims against Caterpillar and Whayne Supply. Kentucky citizenship on both sides prevented complete diversity. Liberty Mutual's subrogation claims ran against both defendants.

Lewis settled his own claims against Whayne Supply within a year, but Liberty Mutual's claim against that company remained. Caterpillar removed one day before the then-applicable one-year removal limit, assuming the settlement would produce Whayne Supply's dismissal. Lewis sought remand, pointing to Liberty Mutual's unresolved claim; the district court denied the motion without addressing that argument.

In June 1993 Liberty Mutual settled with Whayne Supply, which was then dismissed, so complete diversity existed before trial and at judgment. By then the one-year limit had expired. For its review the Court accepted as given that the district court wrongly treated Whayne Supply as gone at removal and that diversity was then incomplete.
sections.Issue: Whether a final judgment on the merits must be vacated because the case was removed when complete diversity was lacking and the plaintiff's timely motion to remand was wrongly denied, where the nondiverse defendant was dismissed before trial and jurisdiction was complete at judgment.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States, in 1996, in an opinion by Justice Ginsburg for a unanimous Court, held that the judgment stands. The district court should have remanded when diversity was incomplete, but its final merits judgment survived because the nondiverse defendant had been dismissed before trial and no jurisdictional defect remained at judgment. The holding did not retroactively make the original removal proper or treat Lewis's preserved objection as waived.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court began by accepting the removal error rather than excusing it. Earlier cases favored preserving some judgments despite improper removal but did not control: in American Fire & Casualty Co. v. Finn jurisdiction remained deficient at judgment, and in Grubbs v. General Electric Credit Corp. no party had objected before trial. Lewis had promptly sought remand and then appealed.

Dismissal of Whayne Supply cured the jurisdictional deficiency, but it did not erase Caterpillar's statutory failure to remove a case fit for federal adjudication at the time of removal. Nor had Lewis waived his objection. His timely remand motion preserved it; he was not required to seek a discretionary §1292(b) interlocutory appeal, a requirement that would be inconsistent with the final-judgment system. His complaint was concrete, since proper adherence to the removal rules would have kept the case in state court.

The controlling consideration was the cost of undoing a completed diversity trial that applied state substantive law and ended with all federal jurisdictional requirements met. Finality, efficiency, and economy weighed strongly against sending the case back, and Newman-Green supported the result. The boundary was essential: had a jurisdictional defect remained at the end, the judgment would have to be vacated.

Lewis warned that the rule would invite premature removal. The Court expected district courts to enforce the removal requirements and thought defendants unlikely to gain from gambling that a defect would escape detection and disappear before judgment.

The casebook presents the case before a contrasting account of Grupo Dataflux; the brief notes that this contrast is the casebook's editorial comparison.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-174.rule: Diversity is determined by the facts when the suit is filed; a change in a continuing party's citizenship after filing cannot cure a lack of diversity, unlike the dismissal of a dispensable nondiverse party.

sections.Parties: Atlas Global Group, L.P., a limited partnership organized under Texas law, was the plaintiff. It sued Grupo Dataflux, a Mexican corporation, in federal district court for breach of contract and quantum meruit, seeking more than $1.3 million. Dataflux was the defendant; after losing a jury verdict it moved to dismiss for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction. Atlas wanted the verdict preserved.
sections.Procedural History: Atlas sued in November 1997, alleging diversity between a Texas citizen and a Mexican citizen. After nearly three years of pretrial litigation the parties consented to a jury trial before a magistrate judge, and on October 27, 2000 the jury returned a $750,000 verdict for Atlas. Before entry of judgment, Dataflux moved to dismiss for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, and the magistrate judge dismissed. The Fifth Circuit reversed and directed entry of judgment for Atlas, relying on Caterpillar to create a limited exception. The Court reversed the Fifth Circuit.
sections.Material Facts:
A partnership's citizenship includes that of every partner. When Atlas filed suit it had two Mexican partners, so it shared Mexican citizenship with Dataflux despite its additional Texas and Delaware citizenship, and the required diversity was absent. Atlas did not contest that initial defect on appeal.

In a September 2000 transaction, completed before trial, the Mexican partners left the partnership. As the dissent explained, the transaction was unrelated to the suit, and it also involved a withdrawing general partner, a limited liability company with Mexican members. Atlas remained the same partnership and the same plaintiff throughout.

Dataflux had admitted jurisdiction in its answer and raised the defect only after the verdict, as the dissent stressed. The Fifth Circuit's exception applied where the defect was not raised until after a verdict or dispositive ruling and had disappeared before that resolution. Atlas had filed and then voluntarily dismissed a second action.
sections.Issue: Whether a party's change in citizenship after filing, here a partnership's loss of its nondiverse partners before trial, can cure a lack of diversity jurisdiction that existed when the suit was filed, at least where the defect is raised only after a verdict.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States, in 2004, in an opinion by Justice Scalia for a five-Justice majority, with four dissenting, held that it cannot. The withdrawal of the Mexican partners changed Atlas's citizenship but did not cure the absence of diversity at filing, because the same partnership remained the plaintiff. Dismissal for lack of jurisdiction was the available disposition for this action. The Court did not decide the contract claims or bar a properly supported new action.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority started from the longstanding rule that diversity is determined by the facts at commencement, a rule applied whether the defect is found early, after trial, or on appeal. The recognized exception is for dropping a dispensable nondiverse party, as Rule 21 and Newman-Green allow. Caterpillar likewise involved dismissal of a nondiverse defendant before trial; its language about finality and economy addressed whether an earlier statutory removal violation required undoing a judgment after jurisdiction had been cured, not whether efficiency itself cures a diversity defect.

Atlas was a single artificial entity whose composition, and so its citizenship, changed. That was a change in the condition of a continuing party, not a change in the parties. Looking through a partnership to its members determines the entity's citizenship under Carden; it does not make each member a party, and no court could drop members from the partnership as litigants.

The Fifth Circuit's distinction based on when the defect was discovered had no jurisdictional basis: if the change cured the defect, timing would not matter, and if it did not, a verdict could not supply jurisdiction. Treating Dataflux's silence as forfeiture would let litigation conduct expand subject-matter jurisdiction. A fixed rule also avoids litigation over uncertain efficiency exceptions.

Justice Ginsburg, joined by Justices Stevens, Souter, and Breyer, dissented. She viewed the time-of-filing rule as a judicial policy rule, thought the membership change trimmed away the spoilers and resembled Caterpillar and Newman-Green, and would have affirmed to avoid wasteful relitigation.

The casebook presents the case immediately after its Caterpillar comparison.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-175.rule: Parties who had notice and an opportunity to contest a court's jurisdiction, including the constitutionality of the statute conferring it, cannot collaterally attack the final decree; res judicata reaches jurisdictional objections that could have been raised.

sections.Parties: Baxter State Bank and the other respondents were bondholders who sued Chicot County Drainage District, a district organized under Arkansas law, in federal district court on fourteen $1,000 bonds. The District, the defendant, relied on a prior federal debt-readjustment decree that canceled the old bonds. The bondholders won in both lower courts, and the District sought review in the Court.
sections.Procedural History: In March 1936 a federal district court entered a debt-readjustment decree for the District under the federal Municipal Debt Readjustments Act of May 24, 1934; no direct review of that decree was sought. The bondholders later sued in the same federal court on their old bonds. The parties stipulated to a trial without a jury. The district court ruled for the bondholders and the Eighth Circuit affirmed, both treating the decree as void because the Court had since invalidated the 1934 statute in Ashton v. Cameron County District. The Court reversed and remanded to the district court with directions to dismiss the complaint.
sections.Material Facts:
The District issued bonds in 1924 and defaulted in 1932. The 1936 decree recited approval of a fair and equitable plan by holders of more than two-thirds of the outstanding indebtedness. The District issued $193,500 in new bonds to the Reconstruction Finance Corporation, which had purchased and exchanged a much larger amount of outstanding obligations, and funds were deposited for the remaining old obligations. Holders had one year to present those obligations to share in the plan and the fund or be barred. Subject to that opportunity, the decree canceled the old bonds and enjoined claims on them.

In the later bond action the evidence established the respondents' ownership of the bonds and their notice of the readjustment proceeding. They were parties to it with a full opportunity to object and apparently did not raise the constitutional question. After the decree, the Court held the 1934 statute unconstitutional in Ashton, a case involving a Texas district.
sections.Issue: Whether bondholders who were parties to a federal debt-readjustment proceeding, with notice and an opportunity to object, may collaterally attack the final decree on the ground that the statute under which the court acted was later held unconstitutional in another case.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States, in 1940, in an opinion by Chief Justice Hughes, held that they may not. Bondholders who had notice and an opportunity to challenge the proceeding could not evade its final decree by later attacking the statute's constitutionality, and the statute's later invalidation in another case did not automatically erase the completed adjudication. The Court confined its decision to the res judicata question; it did not reapprove the 1934 statute or announce a universal rule on the retroactive effects of invalidation.
sections.Reasoning:
The bondholders' theory was that an unconstitutional statute is as though it never existed, so there was no jurisdiction and no binding decree. The Court rejected that as too absolute. A statute's actual existence before it is invalidated is an operative fact with consequences for conduct, status, settled rights, and final adjudications, and a later declaration cannot necessarily erase the past.

Apart from Ashton, the elements of the District's preclusion defense were present. The earlier proceeding complied with the statute, its regularity was unchallenged, and the bondholders were parties with notice who could have contested the plan's fairness, the decree's terms, or the statute's validity. Their failure to raise an available objection did not preserve it for a separate action.

The bondholders stressed that the federal court sat in bankruptcy with only statutory jurisdiction. The Court agreed that lower federal courts have limited jurisdiction but denied that every jurisdictional error makes their judgments nullities. A court that has the parties before it consistently with due process has authority to determine whether it may entertain the case, including to construe the statute under which it acts, and that determination is open to direct review, not collateral attack. This applies whether the claim is that the court exceeded a valid statute or that the enabling statute was unconstitutional. Had the bondholders litigated validity and lost, the ruling would have been final; silence could not put them in a better position. Res judicata extends to matters that could have been presented, not only those actually argued.

The casebook cites the case in a note on collateral attack and says the notified parties chose not to appear; the brief notes that the opinion itself establishes party status, notice, and opportunity but does not narrate an appearance history.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-177.rule: Under its bankruptcy power, Congress may by a specific statute withdraw another court's power to proceed against a protected debtor, so that its later actions are void and open to collateral attack even if the debtor never contested jurisdiction or appealed there.

sections.Parties: Ernest Newton Kalb and his family were Wisconsin farmers whose farm was foreclosed. In one case the Kalbs sued the purchasers of the farm in equity for restoration of possession and cancellation of the sheriff's deed. In the other, Ernest Kalb sued the mortgagees, the sheriff, and the county judge for damages. The mortgagees had bought the farm at the sheriff's sale. The Kalbs lost in the Wisconsin courts and appealed to the Court.
sections.Procedural History: These were two consolidated appeals from the Supreme Court of Wisconsin. In No. 120, the Kalbs' equitable action was dismissed on demurrer and the Wisconsin Supreme Court affirmed. In No. 121, Ernest Kalb's damages action also ended in a final dismissal affirmed by the state supreme court. A prior appeal to the Court had been dismissed for lack of a final judgment. The Wisconsin court reasoned that §75 of the Bankruptcy Act was not an automatic stay and, on rehearing, that the confirmation order was at most erroneous, not void. The Court reversed the judgments in both cases and remanded to the Supreme Court of Wisconsin.
sections.Material Facts:
The mortgagees began foreclosure of the Kalbs' Wisconsin farm on March 7, 1933 and obtained a foreclosure judgment on April 21. The sheriff sold the property on July 20, 1935. Ernest Kalb's farmer-bankruptcy petition had been filed and approved in October 1934, dismissed in June 1935, and reinstated on September 6, 1935 under the second Frazier-Lemke Act, with the dismissal vacated. The petition was therefore pending when the state county court confirmed the sale on September 16, 1935.

Neither the state court nor the bankruptcy court had been asked for, or had granted, a separate stay. The mortgagees obtained a writ of assistance on December 16, and the sheriff enforced it on March 12, 1936, ejecting the Kalbs and their family. The Kalbs had not appealed in the foreclosure proceeding or challenged the county court's jurisdiction there. The jurisdictional question concerned the confirmation and later enforcement while the petition was pending, not the original 1933 foreclosure judgment.
sections.Issue: Whether, under §75 of the Bankruptcy Act, a pending farmer-bankruptcy petition automatically deprived the state court of power to confirm a foreclosure sale and dispossess the farmer, so that those actions were void and open to collateral attack although no stay was sought and jurisdiction was not contested in the foreclosure proceeding.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States, in 1940, in an opinion by Justice Black, held that it did. Under the specific farmer-bankruptcy statute, the pending petition deprived the state court of power to confirm the sale and dispossess the farmer without the bankruptcy court's consent, and the resulting state actions were void and subject to collateral attack. The Court did not decide personal tort liability, which depended on state law, or the appellees' immunity and other state-law contentions.
sections.Reasoning:
The appellees argued that the Wisconsin court's view that the order was merely erroneous, with no appeal taken, was an adequate nonfederal ground. The Court disagreed: whether the state court's actions were erroneous or beyond its power depended on the meaning of the federal statute, a federal question, and if Congress ousted jurisdiction the lack of a direct appeal could not validate the prohibited actions.

The Court acknowledged the normal presumption of regularity and protection against collateral attack for judgments of competent courts, citing Chicot among other decisions. But Congress's bankruptcy power allowed it to create a specific exception making judicial actions concerning protected debtors or property nullities, and state control of local procedure could not authorize disregard of federal bankruptcy law.

Section 75 did so. Subsection (n) placed the farmer and his property, including unexpired redemption rights and unconfirmed sales, under the bankruptcy court's exclusive jurisdiction. Subsection (o) prohibited commencing or maintaining foreclosure and possession proceedings unless the bankruptcy judge consented after a prescribed process. Subsection (p) applied those prohibitions to judicial and official proceedings. The 1935 amendments and committee reports reinforced this. The scheme aimed to rehabilitate distressed farmers, who did not have to hire counsel; requiring them to seek separate stays would undermine an automatic safeguard. Because the statute itself withdrew power, the confirmation, deed, writ, and ejection lacked authority, and whether the farmer had contested or could have contested jurisdiction was immaterial.

The casebook contrasts the case with Chicot; the brief adds that Kalb is a statutory exception to ordinary finality, not a rule permitting collateral attack whenever jurisdiction is disputed.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-178.rule: A judgment is entitled to full faith and credit even on questions of subject-matter jurisdiction when the second court's inquiry shows those questions were fully and fairly litigated and finally decided in the court that rendered it.

sections.Parties: The Durfees sued Duke in Nebraska to quiet title to bottom land along the Missouri River and won. Duke then sued the Durfees in Missouri to quiet title to the same land, alleging it lay in Missouri. In that second suit Duke was the plaintiff and the Durfees the defendants, who relied on the Nebraska judgment. The Durfees lost in the court of appeals and sought review in the Court.
sections.Procedural History: In 1956 the Durfees sued in a Nebraska trial court, which quieted title in them after a hearing. On Duke's appeal the Nebraska Supreme Court tried the matter de novo on the existing record and found that Nebraska had jurisdiction and that the Durfees owned the land; Duke did not seek review in the Court. Two months later Duke sued in Missouri, and the case was removed to federal district court on diversity. The district court held the Nebraska judgment res judicata. The Eighth Circuit reversed, allowing renewed examination of Nebraska's jurisdiction. The Court reversed the court of appeals and affirmed the district court. The brief notes that the casebook account attributes the allowance of collateral attack to the district court, whereas the opinion shows that the court of appeals allowed it.
sections.Material Facts:
The main channel of the Missouri River formed the Nebraska-Missouri boundary. Nebraska's subject-matter jurisdiction over the quiet-title suit depended on whether the land was in Nebraska, which depended on whether a shift in the river's course had occurred by avulsion or accretion. The parties did not dispute that this factual distinction controlled the jurisdictional issue.

Duke appeared through counsel in Nebraska and expressly contested subject-matter jurisdiction. The Nebraska Supreme Court found that the avulsion rule applied, that the land remained in Nebraska, that Nebraska's courts had subject-matter jurisdiction, and that the Durfees owned the land. Personal jurisdiction was uncontested because Duke had generally appeared and initiated the appeal. There was no dispute that Nebraska would give the judgment full preclusive effect.

In the Missouri suit, the federal district court heard evidence and expressed the view that the land was in Missouri, but held itself bound by the Nebraska judgment.
sections.Issue: Whether Duke could relitigate Nebraska's subject-matter jurisdiction in a second suit in Missouri after the parties had fully litigated that issue in Nebraska and obtained a final decision on it.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States, in 1963, in an opinion by Justice Stewart, with Justice Black concurring separately, held that she could not. A second court may inquire whether the first court had jurisdiction, but a judgment receives full faith and credit even on jurisdictional questions when that inquiry shows they were fully and fairly litigated and finally decided in the original court. Those conditions were met, so the location of the land could not be redetermined as between these parties. The Court did not itself weigh the river evidence or redraw the boundary.
sections.Reasoning:
The Full Faith and Credit Clause and §1738 generally require a judgment to receive at least the res judicata effect it would have in the rendering State, and the statute binds federal courts as well as state courts.

Duke relied on precedents allowing a judgment rendered without jurisdiction to be challenged elsewhere. The Court accepted the principle but said it did not define the scope of the second court's inquiry. Decisions on both personal and subject-matter jurisdiction had established that a jurisdictional issue already contested and decided is binding. After parties present evidence and argument and obtain a decision, a second court's reconsideration is not inherently more reliable, and litigation must end at some point. A footnote distinguished Chicot County, where an available jurisdictional objection was not actually litigated; here there was an express contest and final decision, so the Court did not need to decide the consequences of silence or default.

That the dispute concerned land did not justify an exception. A court ordinarily cannot directly determine title to land in another State, but where the land lies, like where a person is domiciled, may itself require judicial determination, and the same litigants cannot relitigate that fact once it is fairly decided. The Court recognized possible overriding exceptions, including federal preemption and sovereign immunity, and noted that in Kalb jurisdiction had not actually been litigated in the original forum. The Nebraska judgment settled title only between the parties; it did not bind either State as to its boundary.

Justice Black concurred on the understanding that the Court was not deciding whether Duke would remain bound if a later interstate proceeding or compact placed the tract in Missouri.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-180.rule: A state venue rule that treats corporations differently according to their State of incorporation does not violate equal protection if it rationally furthers the legitimate end of balancing plaintiffs' forum choices against defendants' litigation convenience.

sections.Parties: William Ford and Thomas Johnson were employees of Burlington Northern Railroad Co. who each sued the railroad under the Federal Employers' Liability Act (FELA) in the state trial court for Yellowstone County, Montana. Burlington, the defendant, was incorporated in Delaware with its principal place of business in Fort Worth, Texas. It moved to transfer both cases to Hill County and, when that failed, challenged Montana's venue rules as a denial of equal protection.
sections.Procedural History: The state trial court denied Burlington's motions to change venue. Burlington took interlocutory appeals, which the Montana Supreme Court consolidated and affirmed. That court found rational-basis review satisfied, at least in these FELA cases, by the federal policy of facilitating injured workers' recovery, and observed that the employees could have sued in federal court in Yellowstone County. The Court granted certiorari, noted that the state decision was final for §1257(a) review despite its interlocutory posture, and affirmed the judgment of the Montana Supreme Court on a different rationale, leaving the FELA merits for further proceedings.
sections.Material Facts:
Ford and Johnson alleged injuries sustained while working at the railroad's premises in Sheridan, Wyoming. Burlington claimed that its principal place of business within Montana was in Hill County and sought transfer there.

Montana generally placed trial in a county where a defendant resided when the action began; if no defendant resided in the State, the plaintiff could designate any county. State decisions treated a corporation as a Montana resident for venue purposes only if Montana was its State of incorporation, and a Montana corporation resided in the county of its principal place of business. Together these rules ordinarily confined suits against domestic corporations to one county while allowing suits against foreign corporations in any of Montana's 56 counties.

Burlington did not seriously challenge the any-county rule for individual nonresidents or for foreign corporations with no fixed Montana place of business. Its narrower objection was that its Montana office should be treated like a domestic corporation's principal office.
sections.Issue: Whether Montana denied equal protection by giving a corporation incorporated elsewhere fewer venue protections than a Montana corporation, even when the foreign corporation maintained a significant place of business in Montana.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States, in 1992, in an opinion by Justice Souter for a unanimous Court, held that it did not. The venue rules neither deprived Burlington of a fundamental right nor classified along suspect lines such as race or religion, so they survived if they rationally furthered legitimate state ends, and they bore a rational connection to balancing plaintiffs' forum choices against defendants' litigation convenience. The holding concerned incorporation and venue under rational-basis review.
sections.Reasoning:
Venue rules adjust competing interests in where litigation takes place, and balancing those interests is a legitimate state concern. A State may give plaintiffs wide choice or temper it when a reasonable assessment of defendants' interests justifies doing so; equal protection does not require the single most convenient arrangement.

Montana could reasonably protect a resident defendant from the tactical disadvantage of trial far from its residence, and could regard the difference among Montana counties as less significant for a nonresident already litigating far from home. A corporation's home office could reasonably matter more to litigation convenience than a regional office. Montana could assume that foreign corporations were unlikely to have their principal offices in Montana and that its domestic corporations probably would, and on this record those assumptions were not irrational.

Using the actual principal place of business would have been more precise than using incorporation, but rational-basis review tolerates imperfect categories. Incorporation is more readily verified, and Montana could avoid collateral litigation over headquarters at the cost of some imprecision. Burlington's own headquarters were outside Montana, so a rule keyed to corporate domicile would not have helped it.

Burlington relied on Power Manufacturing Co. v. Saunders, which invalidated an Arkansas venue distinction. The Court distinguished it: the Arkansas foreign-corporation category was limited to corporations authorized to do business there, most of which probably had an Arkansas business location, so that distinction fit the convenience considerations less precisely. The Court assumed without deciding that Saunders remained good law.

The casebook quotes the case in a note for the balance of interests in venue and poses questions about other classifications, which are the casebook's questions, not holdings.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-188.rule: In a diversity case, a §1404(a) transfer carries the transferor court's choice-of-law rules to the transferee court whether the plaintiff or the defendant sought the transfer.

sections.Parties: Albert Ferens and his wife, Pennsylvania residents, were the plaintiffs. They sued John Deere Co., incorporated in Delaware with its principal place of business in Illinois, after Albert Ferens lost his right hand, allegedly in a combine harvester manufactured by Deere. Deere was the defendant. The Ferenses wanted Mississippi's longer limitations period applied to their tort claims after the transfer to Pennsylvania.
sections.Procedural History: The Ferenses filed contract and warranty claims in the Western District of Pennsylvania and tort claims in the Southern District of Mississippi. The Mississippi court granted their unopposed §1404(a) motion to transfer the tort case to Pennsylvania, where it was consolidated with the warranty case. The Pennsylvania court applied Pennsylvania's limitations period and dismissed the tort claims. The Third Circuit affirmed on a due-process theory; the Court vacated in light of Sun Oil; on remand the Third Circuit again affirmed, holding that a plaintiff-initiated transfer does not preserve the transferor forum's rules. The Court reversed and remanded.
sections.Material Facts:
Albert Ferens lost his right hand in Pennsylvania when, he alleged, it became caught in a Deere combine harvester. He did not sue in tort before Pennsylvania's two-year limitations period expired. In the third year the Ferenses filed a diversity action in Pennsylvania on contract and warranty claims whose limitations periods had not run.

They also filed negligence and products-liability claims in federal court in Mississippi, where diversity jurisdiction and venue were proper. Under Klaxon that court would use Mississippi's choice-of-law rules, which selected Pennsylvania substantive law but Mississippi's six-year tort limitations period. Mississippi's borrowing statute did not displace that period because, as the parties agreed, Deere was already a corporate resident there before the claim accrued.

The Ferenses then moved under §1404(a) to transfer the tort case to Pennsylvania. Their home, the accident, witnesses, documents, and the pending warranty action were all there, and the tort claim had no connection to Mississippi. Deere did not oppose the transfer.
sections.Issue: Whether, in a diversity case, a transfer under §1404(a) requested by the plaintiff carries the transferor forum's choice-of-law rules to the receiving federal court, as Van Dusen held for transfers requested by defendants.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States, in 1990, in an opinion by Justice Kennedy for a five-Justice majority, with four dissenting, held that it does. A §1404(a) transfer in a diversity case does not change the governing law merely because the plaintiff, rather than the defendant, requested it, so Mississippi's statute of limitations continued to govern the tort claims. The Court did not decide that the harvester was defective or that the Ferenses would prevail.
sections.Reasoning:
The text of §1404(a) authorizes transfer for the convenience of parties and witnesses and in the interest of justice; it says nothing about choice of law and does not distinguish plaintiffs from defendants. Van Dusen treated the provision as changing courtrooms without defeating the state-law advantages of the original permissible forum, and reserved the plaintiff-transfer question.

First, preserving the transferor law is consistent with Erie. The plaintiff could already litigate in the favorable forum; transfer removes inconvenience without removing legal advantages. The defendant loses only the practical advantage of forcing litigation in a distant forum, which §1404(a) does not protect. Second, the Ferenses did not acquire favorable law through transfer; they kept law already available through their initial choice. The majority acknowledged forum shopping but did not read §1404(a) as a device for punishing permissible forum choices. Third, a stable governing law keeps the convenience decision separate from predictions about legal prejudice, and plaintiffs would otherwise resist useful transfers. Convenience matters to witnesses, courts, and the justice system, not only the movant. Finally, a single rule avoids complications with joint requests, court-initiated transfers, and multiple plaintiffs. Transfer still requires a convenience and interest-of-justice determination and is not automatic.

Justice Scalia, joined by Justices Brennan, Marshall, and Blackmun, dissented. Starting from the Rules of Decision Act and Klaxon's principle of uniformity between state and federal courts within a State, he argued that Van Dusen's rationale does not support a plaintiff who uses a distant forum as a temporary stop to bring its law home, since the Pennsylvania federal court would apply law unavailable in Pennsylvania state court.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-193.rule: Under New York's forum non conveniens statute, CPLR 327, the availability of an alternative forum is an important consideration but not an absolute prerequisite to dismissal; no single factor controls.

sections.Parties: The Islamic Republic of Iran was the plaintiff. It sued the former Shah of Iran and the Empress in New York, seeking recovery of funds they allegedly misappropriated, exemplary damages, an accounting, and a constructive trust over assets throughout the world. The Shah and Empress, defendants, challenged justiciability, service or personal jurisdiction, and the suitability of New York as the forum. Iran appealed the dismissal of its action.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court dismissed on forum non conveniens grounds and a divided Appellate Division affirmed. The Shah died while the dismissal motion was pending, and because no representative was substituted the Court of Appeals dismissed Iran's appeal as to him under CPLR 1021 without reaching the forum issue. The court had earlier dismissed the Empress's cross-appeal on personal jurisdiction because she was not aggrieved by the judgment, without deciding its merits. On Iran's appeal as against the Empress, the Court of Appeals affirmed the order with costs, and it dismissed the appeal concerning the Shah without costs.
sections.Material Facts:
Iran alleged that the Shah and Empress had accepted bribes and misappropriated approximately $35 billion during the Shah's thirty-eight-year reign, in violation of duties owed to Iran. It sought recovery of the funds and $20 billion in exemplary damages. These were allegations, not adjudicated findings.

In November 1979 the Shah, who was undergoing cancer treatment at New York Hospital, received substituted service. The Empress was personally served at the New York residence of the Shah's sister, Princess Ashraf.

The litigation concerned decades of Iranian governmental management, foreign witnesses, and assets in numerous countries. The parties' brief presence in New York supplied little connection between the State and the transactions challenged. Iran's lists of property extended well beyond New York, and the existence of relevant New York assets had not been established. Much relevant evidence was in Iran, under the plaintiff government's control. Iran also invoked the January 1981 Algerian Accords, which resolved the hostage crisis.
sections.Issue: Whether a New York court must retain an action based on a foreign controversy whenever the plaintiff may have no alternative forum, so that an available alternative forum is a prerequisite to forum non conveniens dismissal; and whether the Algerian Accords required New York courts to hear the action.
sections.Holding: The New York Court of Appeals, in 1984, in an opinion by Judge Simons for a five-judge majority, with Judge Meyer dissenting as to the Empress and Judge Kaye not participating, held that an available alternative forum is an important consideration but not an absolute prerequisite to dismissal under New York law. The lower courts had not abused their discretion as a matter of law in dismissing the action. The court did not adjudicate the alleged misappropriation or order any asset recovery.
sections.Reasoning:
CPLR 327 authorizes a court, on motion, to stay or dismiss an action on just conditions when substantial justice calls for its resolution elsewhere. The defendant bears the burden. The considerations include the burden on New York courts, hardship to the defendant, the availability of another forum, the parties' nonresidence, and where the underlying transaction occurred, and no single factor controls.

Here Iranian law would probably govern important questions, a New York court's ability to impose an effective constructive trust on foreign property was uncertain, and much of the evidence was in Iran beyond New York's compulsory process. Iran relied on decisions describing an alternative forum as indispensable. The majority treated the relevant language in Gulf Oil as dictum and read New York precedent as making availability one pertinent factor; an absolute requirement would force New York to hear foreign actions unrelated to the State whenever another forum could not or would not. The court did not find that every other forum was unavailable. It said Iran had not established that, and that dismissal was permissible even assuming it. Iran was a sovereign with control over its own legal system and the evidence, not a private claimant shut out of court. An unconditional dismissal was justified.

On the Accords, the United States' undertakings regarding the Shah's assets and enforcement of judgments were not a promise that a New York court would adjudicate the claim, and language about facilitating recovery did not displace ordinary forum rules.

Judge Meyer, dissenting, regarded an available alternative forum as a threshold condition that the defendant must establish, and suggested a conditional stay.

The casebook cites the case in a note; the brief says its account states the absence of an alternative forum more definitively than the opinion does, and that this state-law holding is not the federal adequate-alternative-forum inquiry.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-194.rule: An adequate alternative forum does not by itself require forum non conveniens dismissal; the defendant must also show that the balance of private and public interests strongly favors the foreign forum, and a resident plaintiff's choice receives deference.

sections.Parties: Nilo Tuazon, a Philippine citizen who had immigrated to Washington, was the plaintiff. He sued R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co., headquartered in North Carolina, alleging that it took part in a worldwide conspiracy to conceal the addictive and harmful effects of cigarettes. Reynolds, the defendant, challenged personal jurisdiction and sought dismissal in favor of the Philippines under forum non conveniens. Reynolds was the appellant in the Ninth Circuit.
sections.Procedural History: Reynolds moved in the district court to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction and for forum non conveniens. The district court denied both requests and certified its order for immediate appeal, and the Ninth Circuit permitted the appeal. The panel affirmed the denial of dismissal on both grounds, although it rejected the district court's conclusion that the Philippines was not an adequate alternative forum.
sections.Material Facts:
Tuazon began smoking Salem cigarettes at seventeen and continued for more than forty years while living in the Philippines. He developed a chronic cough and was diagnosed with chronic obstructive pulmonary disorder in 2003. That year he immigrated to Washington through a petition supported by his daughter, a United States citizen, and settled with relatives in Renton, where Seattle-area physicians confirmed the diagnosis and continued his treatment. The alleged conspiracy originated in the United States and operated abroad through affiliates and local entities, including the Philippine distributor of Reynolds brands. The court did not adjudicate those allegations.

Reynolds had been licensed in Washington since 1940, maintained an office and permanent employees there, advertised in local publications, researched the market, supported university research, and took part in political activity on tobacco regulation. Its annual net Washington sales in the relevant period were approximately $145 to $240 million.

On the Philippine forum, a former Philippine appellate judge supplied an affidavit describing available tort and contract relief, discovery, and procedure. Tuazon asserted corruption and delays reaching thirty years and relied on State Department reports.
sections.Issue: Whether Washington could exercise general personal jurisdiction over Reynolds for claims arising from conduct outside the State, and whether the suit should be dismissed for forum non conveniens in favor of the Philippines.
sections.Holding: The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, in 2006, in an opinion by Judge McKeown with no separate writing, affirmed the denial of dismissal for lack of personal jurisdiction and for forum non conveniens. Reynolds's sustained presence in Washington supported general jurisdiction under the framework the court then applied. The Philippines was an adequate alternative forum, but adequacy alone did not establish that litigation there would be more convenient, and the district court's balancing of private and public interests was sustained. The court did not decide conspiracy, causation, damages, or choice of law.
sections.Reasoning:
Because the claims arose from conduct outside Washington, the panel examined general jurisdiction, for which Tuazon needed a prima facie showing. Washington's statute treated continuous and substantial participation in its markets as doing business. Under the circuit's then-applied due-process framework the panel weighed the longevity, continuity, volume, economic impact, physical presence, and local integration of Reynolds's activities, and distinguished sporadic or isolated sales. Reynolds then had the burden of a compelling case of unreasonableness and identified no specific hardship in defending where it had operated for decades. The brief notes that this describes the court's 2006 analysis and does not certify that its general-jurisdiction formulation governs today.

Forum non conveniens requires an adequate alternative and a balance of interests strongly favoring dismissal, with the burden on the defendant. The panel read the record as showing Reynolds's alternative consent to service in the Philippines. The affidavit established potential redress; smaller damages did not make the remedy nonexistent. Tuazon identified no civil proceeding he had personally observed to support his claims of corruption and delay, and the State Department reports principally concerned human rights and criminal justice. The court did not hold that corruption or delay could never defeat adequacy.

Adequacy did not require dismissal. Tuazon's lawful Washington residence entitled his choice to the deference owed a resident plaintiff, and review of the balancing was for clear abuse of discretion. Both parties resided in the United States; evidence of the alleged conspiracy would largely be American and current medical evidence was in Washington; bringing selected Philippine witnesses to Washington would cost less than moving the case abroad. Washington had a local interest in its resident, and the possible application of Philippine law was one factor, not a command to dismiss.

The casebook cites the case in a note; the brief says its suggestion that the Country Report was the plaintiff's only evidence compresses the record.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-195.rule: A defendant seeking forum non conveniens dismissal from the plaintiff's home forum bears a heavy burden; an equal or marginal balance does not suffice, and a court abuses its discretion by clearly misweighing the materiality of witnesses and claims.

sections.Parties: Chimene Nandjou was the plaintiff. She sued Reluxicorp, the Canadian owner of a Residence Inn in Montreal, and two American Marriott entities after her husband William and their two-year-old son Menelik drowned in the hotel pool. She sought damages including punitive damages. The defendants sought dismissal for lack of personal jurisdiction and for forum non conveniens in favor of Canada. Nandjou appealed the forum non conveniens dismissal.
sections.Procedural History: Nandjou sued in Massachusetts state court in September 2018, and the defendants removed on diversity grounds. The district court initially denied their motion to dismiss, then on reconsideration upheld personal jurisdiction but dismissed for forum non conveniens, subject to the defendants' continued submission to Canadian jurisdiction. Nandjou already had a parallel Canadian action. On appeal the defendants offered lack of personal jurisdiction as an alternative basis for dismissal. The First Circuit affirmed the denial of dismissal for lack of personal jurisdiction and reversed the forum non conveniens dismissal, with each party bearing its own costs.
sections.Material Facts:
Nandjou, her husband William, and their three children lived in Lynn, Massachusetts. They received numerous Marriott mailings, including at least three promoting a Residence Inn in Montreal and describing its pool. After reviewing the advertisements, William booked a stay. On April 20, 2016 he took the children to the pool. Holding two-year-old Menelik, he began drowning. The surviving children, ages eight and four, tried unsuccessfully to rescue them, and nobody else was present. An Arizona guest later arrived and summoned help, and emergency personnel began arriving about twenty minutes later. William died that day and Menelik was declared brain dead two days later.

Nandjou asserted wrongful death, vicarious liability, the surviving children's emotional distress, and Menelik's conscious pain and suffering. She had since moved to Georgia. The district court emphasized approximately twenty-five Canadian third-party witnesses, including responders, physicians, police, and inspectors. Three American guests, the Arizona rescuer and two Massachusetts residents, could describe the immediate aftermath.
sections.Issue: Whether the district court abused its discretion in dismissing for forum non conveniens in favor of Canada, and whether Massachusetts could exercise specific personal jurisdiction over the Marriott entities and Reluxicorp on the basis of direct mailings sent to the family's home.
sections.Holding: The United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit, in 2021, in an opinion by Judge Barron for himself and Judge Thompson, held that the district court stated the correct standard but erred in applying it, and that the defendants had not met their heavy burden to displace the plaintiff's home forum. It also held that Nandjou made a prima facie showing of specific jurisdiction over all defendants. Judge Torruella heard argument but did not participate in issuance. The court decided neither negligence nor damages.
sections.Reasoning:
A court first asks whether an adequate alternative forum exists and then balances public and private interests; a balance that is equal or only marginally favors the foreign forum does not suffice. Review is for abuse of discretion, which includes clearly erroneous weighing of proper factors. Massachusetts remained Nandjou's home forum despite her move to Georgia. Canada's adequacy and the neutral weight of the public interests were undisputed, so private convenience was decisive.

The district court overlooked that the vicarious-liability claims required proof of the relationship between the American Marriott entities and the Canadian franchisee, evidence that was not predominantly Canadian. On the remaining claims, it counted Canadian witnesses but undervalued the two surviving children, who alone saw the drowning and the pool conditions beforehand, and for whom returning to Canada was an emotional burden. It also undervalued the American guests and American damages witnesses. Liability testimony is not inherently more important than damages testimony; the relevant question is the need for live testimony, and the defendants had not explained why each of their estimated twenty-five witnesses had to appear live.

On jurisdiction, the Marriott entities contested only relatedness, arguing the mailings were at most a but-for cause. Circuit precedent preferred proximate causation without imposing it rigidly. Marriott cultivated this family's business by direct mail to their Massachusetts home promoting this hotel and its pool, and the record supported inducement of the reservation; those contacts were sufficiently related to the claims. On agency-by-estoppel principles the mailings were attributable to Reluxicorp, given its branding, its contract authorizing marketing including direct mail, and its failure to correct the impression of a Marriott-owned hotel.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-196.rule: An alternative forum is inadequate for forum non conveniens purposes when a successful plaintiff would have no enforceable right to receive any award; a less generous remedy is adequate, but one so unsatisfactory that it amounts to none is not.

sections.Parties: Hiwot Nemariam and other plaintiffs sued the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia and the Commercial Bank of Ethiopia in federal district court in Washington, D.C., seeking recovery for property damage arising from the Ethiopia-Eritrea border war. Ethiopia, the defendant, sought forum non conveniens dismissal in favor of a Claims Commission in The Hague. The plaintiffs appealed the dismissal.
sections.Procedural History: Nemariam filed a two-count complaint in June 2000, invoking the international-takings exception of the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act, 28 U.S.C. § 1605(a)(3). The district court granted Ethiopia's motion to dismiss for forum non conveniens, finding the Commission an adequate alternative and the convenience factors strongly in its favor. The dismissal was without prejudice and allowed reinstatement for good cause if Eritrea failed to submit the plaintiffs' claims despite a timely request. The D.C. Circuit reversed the judgment dismissing the case.
sections.Material Facts:
Armed conflict between Ethiopia and Eritrea began in May 1998. Nemariam alleged that Ethiopia expelled Ethiopian citizens of Eritrean descent, including her, and confiscated the property they left behind. Bank regulations allowed withdrawal only when the account holder presented a passbook in person, which expulsion prevented. These were allegations, not findings that a taking occurred.

In December 2000 the two countries signed a peace agreement creating a Claims Commission in The Hague, whose five arbitrators would decide specified war-related claims under international law. Only the governments could appear, though each could bring claims on behalf of nationals and persons of Ethiopian or Eritrean origin. The Commission's exclusive jurisdiction excepted claims filed elsewhere before the agreement's effective date, as Nemariam's had been. The agreement allowed the governments to negotiate settlements. Individual claimants could not appear independently or require an award to be paid directly to them. By the time of the appeal, Eritrea had submitted claims covering the plaintiffs and the Commission had scheduled an evidentiary hearing.
sections.Issue: Whether the Claims Commission was an adequate alternative forum when a successful individual claim might yield only an award controlled by a government, with no enforceable individual entitlement to payment.
sections.Holding: The United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, in 2003, in an opinion by Chief Judge Ginsburg with no separate writing, held that the Commission was not an adequate alternative forum on this record, so the adequacy determination could not support dismissal even under deferential review for clear abuse of discretion. The court called adequacy a close question. It did not reach the plaintiffs' other objections, decide whether the FSIA exception established jurisdiction, categorically disqualify international tribunals, or resolve the merits of the alleged takings.
sections.Reasoning:
The court recited the forum non conveniens sequence: identify an adequate forum with jurisdiction over the whole case, weigh private interests with a presumption for the plaintiff's choice, assess public interests, and ensure the plaintiff can reinstate the suit in the alternative forum without undue prejudice. Adequacy was dispositive. A less generous remedy does not defeat adequacy, but a remedy so unsatisfactory that it amounts to none does.

The Commission could award relief only to Ethiopia or Eritrea, and Eritrea would control any award made on Nemariam's behalf. Under international law a state may abandon, settle, retain, or barter its claim, and the agreement expressly permitted direct negotiations between the governments. Eritrea could therefore offset the claim or an award against Ethiopian claims even if Nemariam's grievance were entirely meritorious. The court agreed that the record did not suggest a planned setoff, but that was not the controlling question: the governments had the option, no legal barrier prevented it, and Ethiopia had not negated the possibility.

Ethiopia pointed to Eritrea's announced intention to pass compensation for private property directly to victims. The court distinguished a voluntary governmental intention from an enforceable right; the Commission could not compel Eritrea to honor that intention. Ethiopia also cited Gonzalez, where limited Mexican wrongful-death recovery made litigation economically unattractive; a modest legal entitlement differs from possibly receiving nothing despite success. By contrast, assuming the district court had jurisdiction, success there would produce relief enforceable by the plaintiff herself.

The casebook cites the case in a note; the brief says the casebook's quotation omits that jurisdictional qualification.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-197.rule: A foreign forum can be an adequate alternative for forum non conveniens purposes if it offers a meaningful remedy for the same injury, even where its law channels liability to a party other than the defendant sued.

sections.Parties: Four individuals and six business entities from Fukushima Prefecture sued General Electric Co. in Massachusetts on behalf of putative classes of homeowners and businesses for property damage and economic harm from the 2011 Fukushima nuclear disaster. They sought compensatory and punitive damages. GE, the defendant, sought dismissal on several grounds including forum non conveniens. The plaintiffs appealed the dismissal.
sections.Procedural History: The plaintiffs filed in November 2017 and amended in May 2018. GE invoked the Convention on Supplementary Compensation for Nuclear Damage as a jurisdictional objection, Japanese liability channeling and Massachusetts time bars as merits defenses, and forum non conveniens. The district court assumed jurisdiction and dismissed for forum non conveniens, finding an adequate Japanese alternative and a strong balance of convenience favoring Japan. On appeal the plaintiffs challenged only availability and adequacy, waiving any challenge to the balancing. The First Circuit left the Convention question unresolved under Sinochem and affirmed dismissal of the amended complaint.
sections.Material Facts:
GE designed the plant's six reactors, constructed three, and provided designs and expertise for the others. The plaintiffs alleged defective reactors and safety systems, poor siting of emergency equipment, inadequate backup power, and failure to warn of earthquake and tsunami risks. The court treated this as allegation and did not adjudicate GE's negligence. The earthquake-induced tsunami disabled power and cooling systems, followed by explosions and radioactive releases.

Japan's nuclear-damage statute channeled liability to the plant operator, Tokyo Electric Power Company (TEPCO), which was strictly liable without a damages cap, though claimants still had to prove causation and damages. Victims had three nonexclusive avenues: suing TEPCO in Japanese courts, submitting claims directly to TEPCO, or mediating through the publicly established Nuclear Damages Dispute Resolution Center. There was no American-style class mechanism for these claims, but claimants could join cases, and substantial groups had obtained judgments or settlements. Mediation had no filing fee. Japan had given significant financial support to TEPCO and the compensation system.
sections.Issue: Whether Japan could be an available and adequate alternative forum when its law channeled liability to TEPCO and so prevented recovery against GE itself, and whether the district court could rely on Japan's administrative compensation mechanisms in finding adequacy.
sections.Holding: The United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit, in 2020, in an opinion by Judge Torruella with no separate writing, held that Japan was an available and adequate alternative forum on this record. A remedy for the injury need not come from the same defendant: Japan's coordinated system addressed the same injuries and let the plaintiffs obtain relief from TEPCO. The court did not establish GE's liability, decide the Convention's jurisdictional effect, or reassess the waived convenience objections.
sections.Reasoning:
A defendant seeking foreign-forum dismissal must ordinarily show that the alternative can address the dispute and that the defendant is amenable to process there. A less favorable remedy does not defeat adequacy; it must be so inadequate that it amounts to none. The defendant must also show that convenience and judicial efficiency strongly favor the alternative. Discretionary judgments are reviewed deferentially and legal errors de novo.

The plaintiffs argued that GE's willingness to accept service in Japan was empty because the channeling statute barred recovery against it. The court accepted that consent to service did not by itself resolve the channeling issue, but found that Japan's system addressed the same injuries. Japanese courts remained open to the damage claims against TEPCO, many putative class members had already recovered, and the plaintiffs gave no basis to find compensation effectively nonexistent. Gulf Oil's reference to two forums in which the defendant is amenable to process did not bar every scheme that redirects liability to another party; its concern was a meaningful absence of jurisdiction and relief. Full and fair compensation for the same injury can suffice whoever pays, which the panel analogized to complete recovery from one of two jointly liable tortfeasors. The court also observed, as a supporting inference only, that Massachusetts choice-of-law rules would likely select Japanese law.

The panel upheld reliance on direct claims and mediation, finding instructive the precedents that accept no-fault or administrative systems. The plaintiffs did not challenge the specific adequacy findings about those mechanisms.

The brief stresses that this is not a categorical ruling that any administrative fund is adequate or that a defendant's consent always cures a foreign forum's deficiencies. The casebook cites the case in a note.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-198.rule: In a forum non conveniens analysis a plaintiff's United States residence earns deference to the choice of a United States forum even outside the plaintiff's home district, and dismissal requires that private and public interests strongly favor the foreign forum.

sections.Parties: The plaintiffs were three Nigerian emigres, including Owens Wiwa and Blessing Kpuinen, and a woman proceeding as Jane Doe. They sued Royal Dutch Petroleum Co., incorporated and headquartered in the Netherlands, and Shell Transport, incorporated and headquartered in England, holding companies whose group included a Nigerian subsidiary. The plaintiffs appealed the forum non conveniens dismissal; the defendants challenged personal jurisdiction as an alternative ground.
sections.Procedural History: The plaintiffs sued in the Southern District of New York. A magistrate recommended dismissal for lack of personal jurisdiction or, alternatively, for forum non conveniens in favor of England. The district judge found jurisdiction through the defendants' investor-relations office but dismissed for forum non conveniens. On reconsideration she conditioned dismissal on the defendants' consent to English service, compliance with discovery, payment of any judgment, and waiver of a security bond and of a limitations defense. The Second Circuit upheld personal jurisdiction, reversed the forum non conveniens dismissal, and remanded for further proceedings, including consideration of the unaddressed Rule 12(b)(6) motion.
sections.Material Facts:
The plaintiffs alleged grave abuses against themselves or deceased relatives in retaliation for opposition to oil development in Nigeria's Ogoni region: that Nigerian authorities imprisoned, tortured, or killed protesters and that the defendants, through their Nigerian subsidiary, instigated and supported these actions. Ken Saro-Wiwa and John Kpuinen were executed after convictions allegedly based on fabricated evidence. The court assumed the allegations without implying any view of their truth. The complaint sought relief under the Alien Tort Claims Act, RICO, international law, Nigerian law, and state tort law.

Two of the four plaintiffs, Blessing Kpuinen and Owens Wiwa, lived in the United States when suit began; none lived in the Southern District of New York, and Owens later moved to Canada.

The defendants maintained a New York investor-relations office nominally administered through Shell Oil. Its manager and activities were devoted to the parents, who reimbursed its expenses of approximately $500,000 annually and approved important decisions. Their shares or depositary receipts traded in New York.
sections.Issue: Whether the defendants' New York investor-relations office subjected them to general personal jurisdiction in New York, and whether the district court properly dismissed for forum non conveniens in favor of England.
sections.Holding: The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, in 2000, in an opinion by Judge Leval with no separate writing, upheld personal jurisdiction under the New York doing-business and due-process framework it then applied, and reversed the forum non conveniens dismissal. Assuming without deciding that England was an adequate forum, it held that the district court erred by not crediting two plaintiffs' United States residence and that the defendants had not shown the interests strongly favored England. The judgment did not establish a viable cause of action or liability.
sections.Reasoning:
On jurisdiction, an in-state representative's activities can be attributed to a foreign corporation when they are important enough that the corporation would perform them itself without the representative. The office worked entirely for the parents, was funded by them, and cultivated access to capital markets. Listing securities and the tasks ancillary to it do not alone establish general jurisdiction, but this permanent, staffed operation went beyond that. There was no compelling unfairness given the defendants' resources and American presence.
