A nineteen-day trial produced a finding that the ice terms were not Labatt trademarks and verdicts rejecting Labatt's submitted counterclaims. Labatt prevailed against Anheuser-Busch's false-advertising claim, but Anheuser-Busch prevailed on injurious falsehood, and the jury awarded it one dollar in compensatory damages and $5 million in punitive damages. The district court set aside the punitive award because Anheuser-Busch had not adequately disclosed its demand, and refused declaratory and injunctive relief.

The Eighth Circuit affirmed except for the omission of declaratory relief, and remanded to amend the judgment to include an appropriate declaration. The punitive award remained set aside, and the nominal compensation and the refusal of an injunction remained.
sections.Material Facts:
In 1993 Labatt began selling an ice beer in Canada and then negotiated with Anheuser-Busch about bringing Labatt's beer to the United States. The negotiations involved confidential marketing and process information protected by two agreements. Anheuser-Busch also investigated developing its own brewing process and repeatedly communicated that possibility to Labatt's president. A prototype was produced in late July, and on August 4 Anheuser-Busch announced it would market its own beer. It began United States sales in October, followed shortly by Labatt. Labatt's November 30 infringement accusation prompted the suit. Labatt's advertising slogan claimed that beer other than Labatt's was not ice beer. The court recounted these facts in the light favorable to the verdict.

On punitive damages, Anheuser-Busch had not mentioned them in its pleadings or interrogatory answers. It first raised them in supplemental instructions one week before trial. Labatt expressly resisted submission of punitive damages through written and preserved oral objections.
sections.Issue: Whether the district court properly set aside a jury's punitive-damages award because the demand was not disclosed in the pleadings or interrogatory answers, and whether Rule 15(b) saved the demand; the appeal also raised trademark, contract, verdict-consistency and equitable-relief questions.
sections.Holding: The Eighth Circuit, 1996, in an opinion by Judge Bowman for a panel with Chief Judge Richard S. Arnold and District Judge John B. Jones, with no separate writing, upheld the decision setting aside the $5 million punitive award: the finding of inadequate notice was not clearly erroneous, and Rule 15(b) did not save the demand. It also declined to disturb the jury's findings that the ice terms were not trademarks and its verdicts on the other claims, upheld the refusal of an injunction, and held that Anheuser-Busch was entitled to a declaration, remanding to add one.
sections.Reasoning:
Missouri law governed the reduction or elimination of punitive damages on the Missouri injurious-falsehood claim, with the trial judge's discretion reviewed for abuse. Because Anheuser-Busch had not mentioned punitive damages in its pleadings or interrogatory answers and first raised them in supplemental instructions a week before trial, the finding of inadequate notice was not clearly erroneous. Rule 15(b)'s treatment of unpleaded issues tried by consent did not apply where Labatt expressly resisted submission through written and preserved oral objections; trying the issue over objection was not consent or waiver.

On the other issues, the instructions and special verdict adequately presented the trademark and genericness questions, and surveys and earlier generic uses supported the verdict that the ice terms were not trademarks. The verdict for Labatt on federal false advertising and against it on injurious falsehood could be reconciled because the claims had different elements. The confidentiality agreement was ambiguous, so its meaning was for the jury.

The court separated a declaration from an injunction. The verdicts entitled Anheuser-Busch to a declaration that Labatt lacked protected rights in the ice terms, and no countervailing equity justified denying it. An injunction required irreparable harm and inadequacy of legal remedies, and the one-dollar award, Labatt's success on false advertising, and Anheuser-Busch's market performance permitted its refusal.

The casebook uses the case, in a note on the prayer for relief, to examine notice of a demand for punitive damages; its question connecting the result to Rules 8(a)(3), 9(g) and 54(c), which the opinion did not cite in its punitive analysis, is the editors' prompt.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-284.rule: Rule 12(f) does not authorize a court to strike a claim for damages on the ground that the damages are precluded as a matter of law; that challenge belongs under Rule 12(b)(6) or Rule 56.

sections.Parties: California-based Whittlestone, Inc. was the plaintiff and appellant. It sued Missouri-based Handi-Craft Company for breach of a written twenty-year purchase agreement, seeking more than $250,000 in damages and restitution. Handi-Craft, the defendant, moved under Rule 12(f) to strike the damages allegations.
sections.Procedural History:
Handi-Craft moved under Rule 12(f) on October 9, 2008 to strike the damages allegations, arguing that paragraph 20(d) of the contract barred them. The district court granted the motion on November 18. Without choosing between Missouri and California law, it concluded that the limitation was enforceable under either and that the contract clearly excluded the requested damages. Reconsideration was denied, and Whittlestone appealed.

The Ninth Circuit reversed and remanded, with instructions not to dismiss the lost-profits and consequential-damages claim under Rule 12(f).
sections.Material Facts:
In March 2006 Whittlestone and Handi-Craft entered a written twenty-year agreement under which Handi-Craft undertook minimum annual unit or dollar purchases of Whittlestone products for resale. The term would last twenty years unless ended under the agreement's provisions. Paragraph 20 authorized termination by mutual written consent, by one party upon the other's insolvency or material breach after notice and an opportunity to cure, and following a change in the other party's ownership under specified conditions. Paragraph 20(d) limited compensation arising from termination or nonrenewal, including anticipated sales, prospective profits, and expenditures connected with either party's business.

Handi-Craft unilaterally withdrew in June 2008, two years into the relationship. Whittlestone sued for breach, seeking more than $250,000 in damages encompassing lost contract value, profits, consequential damages, and credits or discounts, as well as restitution. That amount was the relief demanded, not an award.
sections.Issue: Whether Rule 12(f) authorizes a district court to strike a plaintiff's claim for damages on the ground that the damages are legally unavailable, here because a contract provision allegedly excluded them.
sections.Holding: The Ninth Circuit, 2010, in an opinion by Judge N. R. Smith for a panel with Judges Reinhardt and Fletcher and no separate writing, held that Rule 12(f) does not authorize striking a damages claim merely because the defendant says those damages are legally unavailable. It also concluded that Whittlestone's reading of the contract was sufficiently plausible to survive a Rule 12(b)(6) analysis. It reversed and remanded without resolving the parties' ultimate contractual rights, and did not hold that the damages must be recovered or that the exclusion is invalid.
sections.Reasoning:
A decision to strike under Rule 12(f) is ordinarily reviewed for abuse of discretion, but whether the rule authorized the action at all was a question of interpreting the Federal Rules, reviewed de novo.

Rule 12(f) covers five categories: an insufficient defense, or redundant, immaterial, impertinent or scandalous matter. The damages claim fit none. It was not a defense, did not duplicate another claim, and directly concerned the relief sought and the harm alleged, so it was neither immaterial nor impertinent; no one claimed it was scandalous. A contention that damages fail as a matter of substantive law does not bring a pleading within these categories.

Handi-Craft was effectively seeking dismissal of part of the complaint or summary judgment, the functions of Rules 12(b)(6) and 56. Letting Rule 12(f) do the same work would duplicate those mechanisms and produce inconsistent appellate review, with abuse-of-discretion review under one label and de novo review under the other.

In a footnote the court added a case-specific reason. Reading the agreement as a whole, the twenty-year term and the enumerated termination methods supported Whittlestone's position that paragraph 20(d) applied to a termination authorized by the agreement rather than every unilateral abandonment; withdrawal alone was not a listed method. Whittlestone's reading was at least as plausible as Handi-Craft's.

The casebook's note describes the ruling as an abuse of discretion, whereas the opinion distinguishes ordinary discretionary review from the de novo question of the rule's authority.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-288.rule: A general denial is read in light of counsel's good-faith certification, so it will not be construed to deny a fact the defendant plainly knows to be true, such as its own state of incorporation, and that allegation stands admitted.

sections.Parties: Eleanor Biggs, alleged to be a Pennsylvania citizen, was the plaintiff. She sued Public Service Coordinated Transport, a bus company alleged to be a New Jersey corporation, for personal injuries and property damage from a collision with its bus. Robert Washington, the driver of her car, became a third-party defendant and had independent counsel at trial. The bus company was the appellant.
sections.Procedural History: The jury found the bus company negligent and Washington not negligent, and awarded Biggs $15,000. Approximately three months after trial, the district court reopened the record on Biggs's motion, without the defendant's participation, to admit a New Jersey Secretary of State certificate showing the defendant's New Jersey citizenship. The defendant appealed, without contesting the amount of damages as such. The Third Circuit affirmed the district court's judgment on July 5, 1960; rehearing was denied July 25, 1960.
sections.Material Facts:
On April 2, 1956, Biggs was a passenger in her own car, driven by Washington, when it collided with the defendant's bus on the Camden Plaza side of the Benjamin Franklin Bridge, below its New Jersey exit. She suffered substantial injuries.

Her eight-paragraph complaint alleged that she was a Pennsylvania citizen and the bus company a New Jersey corporation, with an amount in controversy exceeding the then-applicable $3,000 threshold. It separately alleged the defendant's ownership of the bus, the driver's relationship to the company, the collision and negligence, and damages. The answer admitted ownership and the driver's relationship, asserted insufficient knowledge about the damages paragraphs, and generally denied the remaining allegations. It specifically disputed the amount in controversy. Another defense objected to the company's name, but the parties stipulated to correct it to Public Service Coordinated Transport.

The defendant characterized the later ex parte reopening of the record as a violation of the Fifth and Seventh Amendments.
sections.Issue: Whether a defendant's qualified general denial put in issue the allegation of its own New Jersey corporate citizenship, and whether the ex parte reopening of the record to admit a certificate proving that citizenship required reversal.
sections.Holding: The Third Circuit, 1960, in an opinion by Judge Goodrich for a panel with Chief Judge Biggs and Judge Kalodner and no separate writing, held that the citizenship allegation stood admitted under then-Rule 8(d), because a fair reading of the general denial did not include the company's own corporate citizenship. Reopening the record ex parte to admit the certificate was error, but harmless, since the certificate established only facts already admitted. The court also rejected the defendant's challenges to the evidence, the trial judge and the jury instructions, and affirmed.
sections.Reasoning:
The court agreed that reopening a case for additional evidence should not occur ex parte at one litigant's request; discretion to reopen a record in the interest of fairness did not justify the procedure used.

The error was harmless because of how the answer had to be read. Counsel's signature carried the historical Rule 11 certification that counsel had read the pleading and believed there was good ground to support it. The panel would not interpret an experienced lawyer's answer as a good-faith denial that the lawyer's own client was a New Jersey corporation. The citizenship allegation was therefore admitted, and the later certificate was redundant evidence rather than a new jurisdictional fact. A footnote drew an analogy to decisions rejecting a lack-of-knowledge disclaimer about a fact a party's own circumstances make available to it. The court did not hold that every general denial admits every allegation, since this answer specifically disputed the monetary threshold, nor that parties may create federal jurisdiction by agreement.

On the remaining points, the negligence arguments depended on which witnesses the jury believed, and conflicting testimony does not permit displacing a verdict unless the credited account is inherently improbable. Reviewing the whole trial, the court found the judge impartial, and the charge as a whole, despite some unnecessary comments, did not divert the jurors.

The casebook quotes the citizenship reasoning in a note; its question about a court's independent jurisdictional obligation is the editors', not something the panel expressly decided.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-289.rule: Rule 8(b) allows only an admission, a denial, or a good-faith disclaimer of knowledge or information; an answer that neither admits nor denies and demands strict proof is none of these, and the allegations so answered are deemed admitted.

sections.Parties: King Vision Pay Per View, Ltd. was the plaintiff. It sued J.C. Dimitri's Restaurant, Inc. and James Chelios, the defendants, whose answer to the complaint prompted the court's order.
sections.Procedural History: The defendants filed a response to the complaint. Senior District Judge Shadur of the Northern District of Illinois, on his own initiative, issued a memorandum opinion and order on June 17, 1998 addressing the answer's effect. The court held the affected allegations admitted and directed that the action proceed on that basis. This was not a final judgment awarding damages or resolving every aspect of the underlying claim, and the order imposed no monetary sanction.
sections.Material Facts: The defendants' response contained thirty-five paragraphs. According to the court, thirty of them, including material incorporated by reference, responded by neither admitting nor denying the allegations and demanding strict proof. The opinion identifies direct uses of that formula in paragraphs 6-12, 17, 25-26 and 33-34, with incorporation in paragraphs 19 and 28. The opinion does not develop the underlying commercial events or establish liability facts; the conduct relevant to the decision was the defendants' way of answering the complaint.
sections.Issue: Whether an answer that neither admits nor denies the complaint's allegations but demands strict proof complies with Rule 8(b), and what consequence follows for the allegations answered that way.
sections.Holding: The United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois, 1998, in a memorandum opinion and order by Senior District Judge Shadur, held that the neither-admit-nor-deny, strict-proof formula failed to comply with Rule 8(b). Under the historical Rule 8(d), the affected allegations were admitted, and the action would proceed on that basis.
sections.Reasoning:
Rule 8(b) gave defendants three ways to address an allegation: admit it, deny it, or state the rule's lack-of-knowledge-or-information disclaimer when that could be done in the objective and subjective good faith demanded by Rule 11. A proper disclaimer then operates as a denial. Declining both admission and denial while demanding proof was none of these, and the demand did not excuse compliance or place an allegation in issue.

The court distinguished a genuine disclaimer, which communicates that the party lacks knowledge or information sufficient to form a belief about the allegation's truth, from the defendants' formula, which made no such representation. The demand for strict proof had no recognized function in modern federal pleading, in the judge's account. A claimant's ordinary obligation to prove contested facts does not give an answering defendant a fourth option.

The judge explained that he applied the admission consequence, rather than merely directing a correction, because he had encountered similar defective answers for years and had repeatedly addressed them in orders, published opinions and educational programs. Historical Rule 8(d) treated allegations requiring a responsive pleading as admitted when not denied, with an exception for allegations concerning the amount of damages. The court stressed that the clarity of the rule mattered more than the age or number of cases reiterating it, and it gave notice of similar treatment for future violators.

The casebook uses the case to illustrate the difference between an effective denial and a nonresponse.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-294.rule: Under Rule 15(c) as it then stood, an amendment changing the party sued related back only if the new party received notice within the limitations period itself, not within the additional time allowed for service; the rule was later amended.

sections.Parties: Three libel plaintiffs each sued in federal district court in New Jersey over a Fortune magazine cover story. Their complaints named Fortune as defendant, but Fortune was only a trademark and an internal division of Time, Incorporated, a New York corporation, which the plaintiffs later named by amendment. The plaintiffs lost in the district court and the Third Circuit and sought review in the Supreme Court; Time defended the dismissals.
sections.Procedural History: Each plaintiff filed a diversity action on May 9, 1983. The district court found that the amended complaints adequately identified Time but held that Time had not received notice of the suits within the limitations period, as then-Rule 15(c) required for relation back. It rejected an assertion that Time had deliberately misled the plaintiffs and denied reconsideration. The Third Circuit consolidated the appeals and affirmed, refusing to include the service period in the rule's notice deadline. The Supreme Court affirmed the Third Circuit's judgments, leaving the dismissals intact.
sections.Material Facts:
The alleged libel appeared in Fortune's May 31, 1982 cover story about charges against Reagan's Labor Secretary. The complaints named Fortune and described it as a foreign corporation with offices at the Time and Life Building. No party claimed that Fortune was a separate legal entity capable of being sued, and the magazine's masthead identified Time as publisher.

New Jersey's libel statute allowed one year after publication. Subscription copies were mailed on May 12 and received May 13-19, newsstand copies went on sale May 17, and press materials had gone out on May 11. The Third Circuit concluded that limitations expired by May 19, 1983 at the latest. The complaints were timely filed, but counsel did not mail them to Time's registered agent until May 20. The agent received them May 23 and refused service because Time was not named. In July the plaintiffs amended to designate Fortune also known as Time, Incorporated, and the amended complaints were served July 21.
sections.Issue: Whether, under the then-existing Rule 15(c), an amendment naming Time related back to timely complaints that had named only Fortune, when Time first received notice after the limitations period expired but within the period allowed for service of process.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court, 1986, in an opinion by Justice Blackmun joined by Justices Brennan, Marshall, Powell, Rehnquist and O'Connor, with Justice Stevens dissenting joined by Chief Justice Burger and Justice White, held 6-3 that the amendment naming Time did not relate back, because Time did not receive notice within the limitations period, and affirmed. The Court neither adopted nor categorically rejected an identity-of-interest exception. It did not decide whether the article was libelous. The brief notes that this notice deadline was later changed by the 1991 amendment to Rule 15(c).
sections.Reasoning:
The majority first addressed identity of interest, under which some appellate decisions imputed notice to a related party later added. Even assuming that exception applied, it could not help: neither Fortune nor Time had received notice before limitations expired, so there was no timely notice to impute.

The majority then stated four requirements under the old Rule 15(c). The amended claim had to arise from the original conduct; the new party had to receive notice sufficient to avoid prejudice in defending; it had to know or have reason to know that a mistake about identity explained the failure to name it; and the notice and knowledge requirements had to be satisfied within the limitations period. The fourth failed, because Time first learned of the suits after May 19.

The Court declined to add Rule 4's service time to the limitations period. Rule 4 concerned process, whereas Rules 3 and 15(c) concerned commencement, and the rule's reference to the period provided by law for commencing an action meant the limitations period, as the 1966 Committee Note confirmed. General commitments to merits adjudication could not overcome the rule's specific language, and the majority acknowledged the resulting arbitrariness.

Justice Stevens, dissenting, argued that the amendment merely corrected the description of a defendant already identified rather than adding a new party, and that in any event the period for commencing an action includes the time allowed to serve process, so the majority demanded earlier notice from a misnamed defendant than an accurately named one would receive.

The casebook discusses the case in its note on the relation back doctrine as applying the federal rule rather than New Jersey's more permissive approach.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-296.rule: Federal Rule 15, not contrary state law, governs whether a plaintiff's later-acquired representative capacity may be pleaded and relate back to a timely federal complaint, and leave may not be denied for mere delay without prejudice.

sections.Parties: Jimmy Davis, appointed in Alabama as executor of Dallas Hardy's estate, sued Piper Aircraft Corp. for wrongful death in federal court in North Carolina. Piper, the defendant, sought dismissal or summary judgment because Davis lacked the representative capacity North Carolina law required. Davis was the appellant, seeking leave to plead his later North Carolina qualification; Piper defended the dismissal.
sections.Procedural History: Davis filed the federal complaint on October 7, 1976. Piper's March 7, 1977 answer sought dismissal or summary judgment for lack of capacity. Davis obtained appointment as North Carolina ancillary administrator on July 6 and sought leave to amend the next day. The district court accepted that federal rules governed amendment and relation back but refused leave as a matter of discretion and dismissed for lack of capacity. The Fourth Circuit reversed and remanded, expressly allowed the proposed pleading, and gave it relation-back effect to the commencement of the action.
sections.Material Facts: Dallas Hardy, his wife Betty, and Toni Sellars died when a Piper aircraft crashed during takeoff in North Carolina on October 13, 1974. In separate Alabama proceedings, representatives of the Sellars and Betty Hardy estates sued Hardy's estate and Piper; the Sellars action produced a judgment against both defendants and the Betty Hardy action settled. Davis, the Alabama executor of Dallas Hardy's estate, then sued Piper in federal court in North Carolina on October 7, 1976, before the two-year limitations period expired. An Alabama appointment did not give him the capacity North Carolina law required. He qualified as North Carolina ancillary administrator on July 6, 1977, and sought leave to amend the next day, about nine months after the complaint and four months after Piper identified the defect. The district court's reasons for refusing leave were that Davis had not asserted the claim in either Alabama case, had delayed, could not obtain the same relief in state court, and faced evidence of Hardy's negligence from the Alabama proceedings.
sections.Issue: Whether federal pleading rules, rather than a North Carolina rule assumed to forbid it, allowed Davis's later qualification as ancillary administrator to be pleaded and to relate back to his timely complaint, and whether the district court's reasons justified denying leave.
sections.Holding: The Fourth Circuit, in 1980, in an opinion by Judge James Dickson Phillips joined by Judge Widener, with Judge K. K. Hall dissenting, reversed and remanded. Federal amendment rules controlled the conflict with state law, the later North Carolina qualification could be pleaded and related back to the timely federal complaint, and refusing leave on this record was an abuse of discretion. Because the appointment came after filing, the pleading was technically supplemental under Rule 15(d), but the majority considered that distinction noncritical for relation back where Rule 15(c)'s test is satisfied. The decision restored the action; it did not establish Piper's liability.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority did not dispense with North Carolina's capacity requirement, which Rule 17(b) made a matter of state law. The separate question was whether federal rules could give the later qualification relation-back effect. Piper argued that under Guaranty Trust Co. v. York as applied in Ragan the state rule, which treated an unqualified representative's action as a nullity, had to apply; Davis relied on Hanna and Rule 15. The majority assumed without deciding that North Carolina law would prevent the amendment.

First, Rule 15(c) was broad enough to address the same problem as the state rule, so under Hanna it controlled unless invalid under the Rules Enabling Act or the Constitution, which no one suggested. Ragan differed because the federal commencement rule there did not itself answer the state tolling question. Second, even if Rule 15(c) did not fully cover the issue, the need for a later capacity amendment does not ordinarily drive the choice of forum, uniform federal procedure outweighed any discernible state interest, and Piper already had practical notice of the claim.

Third, discretion under Rule 15(a) had to serve the rule's purposes as identified in Foman. No prejudice was found; mere delay without prejudice or intent to harass was insufficient, and Piper itself had taken about five months to answer. The state-court bar was not a proper reason once federal law was chosen, and conjecture about an eventual negligence defeat was not a clear futility determination. The proposed pleading addressed the same occurrence, so relation back was satisfied.

Judge Hall, dissenting, regarded qualification and filing as separate substantive tolling requirements under state law, thought Ragan controlled and Hanna was distinguishable, found Rule 15(d)'s silence on relation back and Rule 17(b)'s reference to state law significant, and would have upheld the district court's discretion. The casebook cites the case for the majority's footnote treating a supplemental pleading like an amendment for relation-back purposes.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-300.rule: Under the 1983 version of Rule 11, a represented party who signs a pleading or other court paper undertakes an objective duty of reasonable inquiry; relying on counsel and subjective good faith do not excuse the failure.

sections.Parties: Business Guides, Inc., a publisher of directories covering eighteen specialized retail trades, was the plaintiff. Represented by the law firm Finley, Kumble, it sued competing directory publisher Chromatic Communications Enterprises for copyright infringement, conversion and unfair competition and sought a temporary restraining order. Chromatic sought Rule 11 sanctions. Business Guides, sanctioned below, sought review in the Supreme Court.
sections.Procedural History:
The district court denied the temporary restraining order, stayed proceedings, and referred possible Rule 11 violations to a magistrate, who held three evidentiary hearings and found the client's inquiry deficient. The district court adopted the recommendations, dismissed the suit with prejudice, and imposed $13,865.66 in legal expenses and out-of-pocket costs. Chromatic withdrew its motion against Finley, Kumble without prejudice because the firm had dissolved and entered bankruptcy.

The Ninth Circuit upheld the reasonable-inquiry requirement and the findings concerning signed submissions, but rejected oral testimony as an independent Rule 11 basis and vacated the sanctions for reconsideration. The district court reaffirmed the dismissal and the monetary sanction. The Supreme Court affirmed the Ninth Circuit's judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
To detect copying, Business Guides planted inaccurate entries (seeds) in its directories. Its October 31, 1986 filings sought an immediate temporary restraining order; a lawyer and the company's president signed the initial application, and a declaration identified ten entries as copying evidence. Before the scheduled November 7 hearing, the district judge's law clerk asked which information was false. After counsel contacted research director Michael Lambe, Business Guides withdrew three alleged seeds. The clerk then spent about an hour checking the entries and found nine of the ten to be accurate. Lambe's supplemental affidavit identified seven alleged seeds, and he crossed out a fourth inaccurate allegation before signing.

At the first two hearings the publisher and its lawyers defended the accurate entries as coincidences. At the third they explained that the master seed list had been compiled after publication by comparing initial customer questionnaires with the finished directory, assuming the questionnaires were correct; proofreading had corrected input errors, so the supposed seeds were accurate entries. As to the one genuinely fictitious listing, Chromatic said a Business Guides employee had planted it in Chromatic's directory, and the district court treated the failure to deny this as a tacit admission.
sections.Issue: Whether, under the 1983 version of Rule 11, a represented party who signs a paper filed in court is held to an objective standard of reasonable inquiry, or may be sanctioned only on a showing of bad faith, and whether so reading the rule violates the Rules Enabling Act.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court, 1991, in an opinion by Justice O'Connor for five Justices (Chief Justice Rehnquist and Justices White, Blackmun and Souter joined her), held that a represented party who signed a pleading or other court paper undertook an objective duty to make a reasonable inquiry, and that employing counsel did not excuse a sophisticated publisher's failure to check the copying evidence on which its signed submissions depended. Justice Kennedy dissented, joined by Justices Marshall and Stevens and in part by Justice Scalia. The Court affirmed, expressly reserving when a nonsigning party could be sanctioned.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court read the certification sentence's reference to an attorney or party according to its ordinary breadth. The rule elsewhere expressly distinguished represented from unrepresented parties but did not insert that qualification into the certification sentence, so a party's signature could certify a document's factual and legal basis even when voluntarily supplied. Applying the personal-responsibility principle of Pavelic & LeFlore, signing brought responsibility for the submission home to the signer, who could not escape it by delegating verification to counsel. The Court declined to resolve definitively the corporate-signature objection because it had not been raised below.

Subjective good faith was not enough. The 1983 rule applied one reasonable-inquiry standard to attorneys and parties, and rulemaking had replaced the former subjective standard. A client may know the facts better than counsel; here the publisher could check its own directory evidence while its lawyers urgently sought relief. Reasonableness still depended on circumstances, and a sophisticated publisher operating since 1948 was not measured as a small, inexperienced litigant.

The Rules Enabling Act objection failed. Rule 11 regulates discrete litigation submissions, principally serving deterrence and the integrity of federal procedure; it did not create a fee-shifting rule or a new tort, and incidental substantive effects did not invalidate it.

Justice Kennedy, dissenting, read the certification provision in light of the specified attorney and unrepresented-party signatures and the rule's lawyer-centered history, and would have required subjective bad faith to sanction a represented party; in a part Justice Scalia did not join he raised federalism and rulemaking concerns.

The casebook presents the case for the objective standard and Kennedy's objection, and separately describes the 1993 revision of Rule 11.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-302.rule: Under the 1983 version of Rule 11, a filing with a reasonably supportable legal and factual basis is not sanctionable merely because counsel failed to label an argument as one for changing the law or to discuss adverse authority.

sections.Parties: Golden Eagle Distributing Corp. sued Burroughs Corp. over an allegedly defective computer system. Kirkland & Ellis represented Burroughs, the defendant, and was sanctioned by the district court. The law firm was the appellant, challenging the sanctions; the appeal did not concern any judgment on Burroughs's liability.
sections.Procedural History: Golden Eagle sued in Minnesota state court. Burroughs removed on diversity grounds and obtained transfer to the Northern District of California, then moved for summary judgment. The district court denied the motion and, on its own initiative, required defense counsel to explain why Rule 11 sanctions should not follow. After briefing and argument it imposed $3,155.50 in attorney's fees against Kirkland & Ellis. On the firm's appeal, the Ninth Circuit reversed the imposition of sanctions.
sections.Material Facts: Golden Eagle asserted fraud, negligence, and breach of contract. Burroughs's summary judgment motion argued that California's limitations law applied and barred the claims, and that California law did not permit the economic-loss negligence recovery sought. On limitations, counsel portrayed Van Dusen as supplying a forum-non-conveniens exception under which the transferee court could use California rather than Minnesota law, although the Supreme Court had left that question open; the district judge thought the motion presented the position as established law. On economic loss, counsel relied on Seely; the district court pointed to J'Aire's later special-relationship approach and to the intermediate cases Pisano and Huang. Counsel discussed J'Aire in reply after Golden Eagle raised it but omitted the two intermediate cases. The district court considered the arguments supportable but treated the presentation and omissions as breaches of candor under professional-conduct standards and, in turn, Rule 11.
sections.Issue: Whether, under the 1983 version of Rule 11, a motion that had a supportable basis could be sanctioned because counsel did not identify an argument as one for law reform rather than existing law and did not discuss adverse authority as an ethical obligation.
sections.Holding: The Ninth Circuit, in 1986, in an opinion by Judge Schroeder for a panel including Judges Reinhardt and Beezer, with no dissent or concurrence, reversed the sanctions. The district court had accepted that the motion had a supportable basis but imposed additional requirements to label an argument as law reform and to discuss adverse authority as an ethical obligation. Under the panel's interpretation of the 1983 rule, those requirements did not independently establish a Rule 11 violation. The panel assumed without deciding that the omitted authorities were directly contrary. It preserved sanctions where omitted authorities render a position unsupportable.
sections.Reasoning:
The 1983 rule certified reasonable inquiry into factual and legal support and the absence of an improper purpose, made sanctions mandatory for a violation, and used an objective reasonableness standard. Its aim was to curb frivolous or abusive filings without chilling creative arguments or spawning satellite litigation. The panel reviewed de novo whether the conduct violated Rule 11, disputed facts for clear error, and the choice of sanction for abuse of discretion.

Argument identification was not a textual condition. The rule allowed a filing supported either by existing law or by a good-faith argument to extend, modify, or reverse it, and nothing in the text or its history required counsel to say which. Once a motion had a reasonably supportable basis, an imperfect description of how established the law was did not create an additional violation. Whether an argument applies or extends precedent can itself be the contested issue, and mandatory sanctions on that characterization would set counsel's reputation and finances against forceful representation and invite hindsight. The district court had made no finding of knowing misrepresentation. The panel also read the 1983 rule as addressing the paper itself, so an unmeritorious supporting argument did not alone make an otherwise nonfrivolous filing sanctionable.

Ethical disclosure duties were not automatically Rule 11 duties. Lawyers should not misstate law or conceal directly adverse authority, but turning Rule 11 into review of whether every adverse precedent was adequately discussed would multiply burdens, conflate advocacy with adjudication, and duplicate professional-discipline procedures.

The casebook describes the sanctioned advocate as plaintiff's counsel, but the opinions identify the firm as defense counsel for Burroughs. The casebook quotes the panel's rejection of mandatory argument labeling and asks, as an editorial question about later law, whether the 1993 amendment changes the result.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-304.rule: A court may impose an attorney-fee sanction under its inherent power only on an explicit finding of bad faith supported by clear evidence, and only after giving counsel prior notice and an opportunity to be heard.

sections.Parties: Robert Wilson was the plaintiff in the underlying suit against Citigroup and other defendants. The appellants were his lawyers, the firms Langrock Sperry & Wool and Lankford & Reed, which the district court ordered to pay Citigroup's fees for preparing its reply. Citigroup, the defendant that received the fee award, defended the sanction on appeal.
sections.Procedural History:
On September 13 the district court granted the firms' motion for leave to file their opposition late, expressly finding good cause, but required counsel to pay Citigroup's reasonable fees and costs for preparing the reply, ostensibly to cure prejudice from the delayed filing. Citigroup claimed $24,398.83. The firms objected and requested reconsideration; the judge ordered prompt payment, which the firms made on October 21. After the complaint was dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, the firms appealed only the sanctions.

The Second Circuit reversed the district court's orders. It had already issued a December 12, 2012 order reversing the sanctions and directing return of the money, and the December 26 published opinion explains that result.
sections.Material Facts:
Wilson sued in March 2011 over his alleged exclusion from profits generated by investments in Brazilian companies. When Citigroup moved to dismiss, the firms obtained opposing counsel's consent to extend their July 11 opposition deadline to July 28, with a corresponding reply extension. Their July 7 electronic stipulation was rejected under local filing procedures, and they emailed it to the clerk the next day. The judge denied it without explanation at that time.

On July 11 counsel faxed a renewed request detailing competing trial preparation, depositions, discovery, pretrial deadlines, court appearances and professional obligations. The court did not promptly decide that request. Counsel filed their opposition on July 15 with a motion for leave to file late: four days after the original deadline, but before the date opposing counsel had accepted. The district court made no explicit finding of bad faith, and counsel received no notice or opportunity to defend against sanctions before the fee order.
sections.Issue: Whether the district court abused its discretion by using its inherent power to order counsel to pay the opposing party's fees for a four-day-late filing, without an explicit bad-faith finding and without prior notice and an opportunity to be heard.
sections.Holding: The Second Circuit, 2012, in a per curiam opinion for Judges Katzmann, Parker and Wesley, reversed the $24,398.83 fee sanction against the two law firms: the record warranted no sanction, the district court made no explicit bad-faith finding, and counsel received no prior notice or opportunity to defend against sanctions. The holding concerns the inherent-power attorney-fee sanction reviewed here, and the opinion did not revive or decide Wilson's underlying claims.
sections.Reasoning:
The court reviewed the exercise of inherent sanctions authority for abuse of discretion, noting that deference does not dispense with restraint or a supported legal basis, especially when counsel are sanctioned through their opponents' legal bills.

First, the conduct supplied no substantive justification. The firms sought an agreed schedule, explained good cause before the deadline expired, and filed before the agreed extended date. The court found no disobedience of an order and no prejudice to opposing counsel.

Second, an inherent-power fee sanction required an explicit bad-faith finding, and the district court made none. The circuit's cases required clear evidence that the challenged conduct lacked a legitimate basis and served harassment, delay or another improper purpose, supported by specific findings. The timely consented request, the renewed explanation, and the later good-cause finding contradicted any inference of improper delay.

Third, due process independently required notice and an opportunity to respond. Counsel had to know the particular conduct alleged to be sanctionable, the standard, and the authority invoked, and have a chance to defend before sanctions were imposed. An opportunity to object after the fee order was not the required prior process.

The court rejected Citigroup's argument that counsel waived the bad-faith issue by not raising it below, because counsel had had no timely opportunity to make the point in the district court.

The casebook cites the case, in a note placing inherent authority beside Rule 11 and section 1927, for the four-day interval, the lack of prejudice, the missing bad-faith finding and the absence of notice.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-305.rule: Attorneys who file and keep pursuing litigation without an objectively reasonable inquiry into its legal and factual premises, or for an improper purpose, may be sanctioned under Rule 11, § 1927 and inherent authority, whatever their asserted personal belief.

sections.Parties: Registered Michigan voters and Republican presidential-elector nominees sued Governor Gretchen Whitmer, Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, and the Board of State Canvassers. The City of Detroit, the Democratic National Committee and Michigan Democratic Party, and voter Robert Davis intervened. The State Defendants, the City and Davis sought sanctions against the plaintiffs' nine lawyers, including Sidney Powell and L. Lin Wood, who opposed them.
sections.Procedural History: The complaint was filed late on November 25, 2020, and amended on November 29. On December 7 the court denied emergency injunctive relief. Counsel appealed and petitioned the Supreme Court, then voluntarily dismissed in January. The City served its Rule 11 motion on December 15 and filed it on January 5, and also sought § 1927 sanctions; the State Defendants and Davis sought sanctions as well. After a hearing of almost six hours on July 12, 2021, Judge Linda V. Parker on August 25, 2021 granted the State Defendants' and City's motions and granted Davis's motion except as to his own fees and costs. A separate order of December 2, 2021 fixed the fee amounts and stayed payment pending any appeal.
sections.Material Facts:
The plaintiffs alleged constitutional and Michigan Election Code violations in the presidential election and asked the court to decertify Michigan's results, certify a result favoring Donald Trump, impound voting machines, and order a recount. The allegations rested on hundreds of pages of exhibits, including affidavits recycled from earlier election challenges and purported expert analyses. In denying emergency relief the court identified sovereign immunity, laches, standing, mootness, and abstention obstacles and a deficient evidentiary foundation. Counsel appealed and petitioned the Supreme Court; in seeking extraordinary relief they themselves said that effective relief would be unavailable after December 14, when presidential electors voted, yet they continued the district-court proceedings afterward.

The affidavits did not say what counsel claimed. Jessy Jacob said people voted in person after applying for absentee ballots, not that they had also voted absentee. A dog-walker saw bags with unseen contents transferred at a post office. Melissa Carone saw vans. Articia Bomer expressed a belief that workers were changing votes, which counsel labeled eyewitness testimony. Russell Ramsland's turnout figures conflicted with readily available official data. At the sanctions hearing the lawyers could obtain counsel, answer questions, and file briefs and affidavits; none filed the offered post-hearing affidavit.
sections.Issue: Whether the plaintiffs' attorneys could be sanctioned under Rule 11, § 1927, and the court's inherent authority for filing the election suit without reasonable inquiry into its legal and factual basis, for an improper purpose, and for continuing it after their own asserted deadline for effective relief.
sections.Holding: The Eastern District of Michigan, in 2021, in an opinion by Judge Linda V. Parker, held that the attorneys could be sanctioned under Rule 11, § 1927, and inherent authority; neither political importance nor asserted personal belief displaced those obligations. Nine lawyers were ordered jointly and severally to pay the State Defendants' and City's reasonable fees and costs, to complete at least twelve hours of continuing legal education each, and were referred to their licensing jurisdictions for investigation and possible suspension or disbarment. The plaintiffs themselves were not sanctioned. The December order awarded $21,964.75 to Whitmer and Benson and $153,285.62 to Detroit.
sections.Reasoning:
Rule 11 required an objective inquiry: what a reasonable attorney should have investigated before presenting the assertions. Honest belief did not convert speculation into evidentiary support, and the court assessed Rule 11(b)(1), (2), and (3) separately. Under § 1927 the court applied the Sixth Circuit's objective standard, requiring more than negligence but less than subjective bad faith, and focused on the failure to dismiss after December 14, which forced further motions and work; the interlocutory appeal had not divested the district court of the case. Inherent-authority fees required meritless claims, actual or constructive knowledge of that, and an improper purpose, and had to be caused by the misconduct.

The court rejected attempts by Wood, Newman, and Rohl to distance themselves, refusing categorical exemptions for named consenting cocounsel, limited hours, or local-counsel status, and noting that the post-1993 rule reaches counsel who later advocate a paper. It rejected safe-harbor objections: the City's motion identified its grounds, and no brief had to be served with it. The Rule 11 sanctions rested on the City's motion, not on the court's own initiative, since no show-cause order had issued.

On the law, the court found threshold barriers and no nonfrivolous path to the relief sought, and counsel had treated suspicions as legal violations without checking the governing rules. On the facts, the recurring defect was the gap between what an affidavit said and the stronger proposition counsel claimed; copying affidavits from other cases did not shift the duty of inquiry. The findings did not depend on proving every affiant a liar, and the court reserved whether fraud actually occurred. Improper purpose rested on, among other things, using litigation to create a public political narrative; court submissions carry professional obligations that public political speech does not.

The casebook's figure of more than $175,000 corresponds to the two December awards together.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-307.rule: An assignee holding legal title to a money claim has Article III standing to sue on it in federal court even though it has promised to remit all recovered proceeds to the assignor.

sections.Parties: The respondents were aggregators, billing and collection firms to which about 1,400 payphone operators had assigned their claims for unpaid dial-around compensation. They sued Sprint, AT&T, and other long-distance carriers. The carriers, petitioners in the Supreme Court, argued that the aggregators lacked standing; the aggregators sought to keep the litigation going.
sections.Procedural History: The aggregators sued the carriers in federal district court. The district court first accepted AT&T's standing objection but reconsidered in light of the longstanding treatment of assignees for collection. A divided D.C. Circuit panel initially accepted standing but rejected a statutory private right of action. The Supreme Court vacated that judgment for reconsideration after Global Crossing recognized the cause of action, and on remand the D.C. Circuit affirmed the district court orders permitting the litigation to proceed. The carriers obtained review of the standing question, and the Court affirmed.
sections.Material Facts:
A customer making a long-distance call from a payphone with an access code or 1-800 number paid the long-distance carrier, though the payphone operator connected the call. Federal law required the carrier to compensate the operator for these dial-around calls, and operators could sue for unpaid compensation. Individual suits were expensive and often worth little, so operators assigned their claims to aggregators.

Each Assignment and Power of Attorney Agreement transferred all rights, title, and interest in the operator's dial-around compensation claims for periods since October 1, 1997, appointed the aggregator attorney-in-fact, required litigation in the operator's interest, and barred revocation without the aggregator's written consent. A separate agreement required the aggregator to remit all proceeds to the operator, which paid for the service, typically through a quarterly charge. Legal title to the claim was thus transferred, but the aggregator kept no share of the recovery.
sections.Issue: Whether an assignee that holds legal title to a claim for money, but has promised to remit all proceeds of the litigation to the assignor, has Article III standing to pursue the claim in federal court, and whether prudential concerns bar the suit.
sections.Holding: The Court, in 2008, in an opinion by Justice Breyer joined by Justices Stevens, Kennedy, Souter, and Ginsburg, affirmed five to four. An assignee holding legal title to a claim for money could pursue it in federal court even though it had promised to remit all recovered proceeds to the assignor; the transferred claim and the established tradition of collection assignments sufficed for Article III standing. The Court also rejected the carriers' prudential objections on this record. The decision let the litigation continue; it did not decide whether compensation was actually unpaid.
sections.Reasoning:
The unpaid compensation was a concrete injury caused by the carriers that a recovery would remedy; the question was whether the aggregators could invoke an injury the operators originally suffered. History showed why legal title mattered. Early English law restricted assignments, but equity recognized them and courts of law came to allow suit on legal title even where the beneficial interest lay elsewhere. Many nineteenth-century state decisions accepted suits by assignees who held legal title but had promised to account for the proceeds, though the majority acknowledged contrary decisions. Waite, Spiller, and Titus added support, though Breyer said they did not conclusively resolve the Article III issue.

Modern doctrine pointed the same way. The operators transferred their claims completely, and Vermont Agency recognized that an assignee may invoke the assignor's injury. Redressability asks whether a favorable judgment remedies the injury asserted, not what the plaintiff later does with the money, as with suits by trustees, guardians, receivers, and executors. An assignment conveys a property right, unlike merely hiring counsel, and the carriers' line would turn on a small retained interest without changing the dispute.

On prudential objections, the complete assignments made the claims the aggregators' own legal rights, not third parties' rights; class actions are permissive and other aggregation methods exist; and discovery, preclusion, and counterclaim difficulties could be handled by other devices. No bad-faith assignment was alleged.

Chief Justice Roberts, joined by Justices Scalia, Thomas, and Alito, dissented. He would require a personal, tangible stake in the recovery, which the aggregators lacked because their fees did not depend on the outcome, and he found the historical tradition equivocal and too late to establish Article III's original meaning.

The casebook describes the arrangement as remitting recovery less a flat fee; the opinion describes remittance of all proceeds with the service paid for separately.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-309.rule: Liberal permission to join claims in one complaint does not require trying them together; a court should sever when a combined trial would confuse the jury or prejudice a party's substantial right.

sections.Parties: The plaintiffs, including Harry Sporn, were occupants of an automobile that collided with a bus operated by Hudson Transit Lines, the defendant. They asserted five negligence causes of action, and Sporn alone asserted a sixth for malicious prosecution. Hudson, the appellant, sought to sever the malicious-prosecution cause from the negligence causes.
sections.Procedural History: Hudson applied at Special Term to sever the malicious-prosecution cause from the five negligence causes. Special Term denied the application, and Hudson appealed that order. The Appellate Division, First Department, unanimously reversed the order insofar as appealed from, with twenty dollars costs and disbursements, and severed the negligence causes from the malicious-prosecution suit.
sections.Material Facts: An automobile carrying the plaintiffs collided with a bus operated by Hudson Transit Lines. The complaint alleged that negligent operation of the bus caused the collision and asserted five negligence causes of action seeking compensation for personal injuries, loss of services, and property damage. In a sixth cause of action, Harry Sporn alleged that after the collision Hudson maliciously caused his arrest for reckless driving. These were allegations in the complaint; none had been resolved on the merits. Section 258 of New York's Civil Practice Act, added in 1935, allowed a plaintiff to unite two or more causes in one complaint but let a court, on application, direct severance or separate trials when the interests of justice required.
sections.Issue: Whether liberal statutory permission to join claims justified trying the negligence and malicious-prosecution causes together despite the risk of jury confusion and prejudice to the bus company.
sections.Holding: The New York Appellate Division, First Department, in 1942, in an opinion by Justice Cohn for a unanimous five-justice panel, held that the negligence causes should be severed from the malicious-prosecution suit. Broad permission to put claims in one complaint did not settle whether they should be presented together to one jury. The court did not dismiss the malicious-prosecution cause, decide the negligence claims, or revive an absolute prohibition on pleading the two kinds of claim in the same complaint.
sections.Reasoning:
Section 258 was understood to eliminate technical barriers, unnecessary multiple actions, and delay, but it expressly allowed severance when the interests of justice required, and § 96 supported severance when joinder would prejudice a substantial right or produce confusion at trial. The discretion to separate claims existed because efficiency could come at the expense of a fair trial.

First, negligence and malicious prosecution involved different rules, different proof, and different measures of damages. A single jury would have to sort which testimony went to which cause and apply different instructions to each, and the court saw a danger that jurors would confuse the rules of law and the testimony belonging to each type of action.

Second, there was a more specific prejudice. If the malicious-prosecution evidence established malice and lack of probable cause, jurors might become hostile to Hudson, and that hostility could spill into the negligence causes, inflating damages there to punish the company instead of compensating the plaintiffs. The court stated this as a risk, not a prediction.

Those risks outweighed the policy against multiple suits. Severance reconciled the liberal joinder statute with its fairness qualification.

The casebook quotes the passage on different rules, testimony, and damages and asks whether a federal court would reach the same result; it uses the case to distinguish permissive joinder at the pleading stage from later control of the trial.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-311.rule: A counterclaim arises out of the transaction that is the subject matter of the suit when it is logically related to the opposing claim, even though the facts are not identical; transaction is a flexible term.

sections.Parties: Moore, as president of the Odd-Lot Cotton Exchange, brought a federal bill under the antitrust laws against the New York Cotton Exchange and other defendants, seeking cancellation of their quotation-distribution contract and an order compelling ticker service. The New York exchange defended its refusal and counterclaimed for an injunction against Odd-Lot's allegedly unlawful taking of its quotations. Odd-Lot lost below and appealed to the Supreme Court.
sections.Procedural History: Both sides requested interlocutory injunctions. The district court denied Odd-Lot's request and granted the defendants' request, and the Second Circuit affirmed both orders. By stipulation, it then directed entry of a final decree dismissing the bill and making the counterclaim injunction permanent. Because nothing remained below except ministerial compliance with that mandate, the Supreme Court treated the decree as final for appeal. The Court affirmed the decree.
sections.Material Facts:
Members of the New York Cotton Exchange contracted for future delivery of cotton through open bidding at its New York premises. The exchange collected the resulting price quotations and contracted with Western Union to distribute them only to recipients it approved; Western Union paid $27,500 annually for this business, and applicants agreed not to use the quotations in connection with a bucket shop or pass them to others. Western Union's controlled subsidiary, Gold & Stock Telegraph Company, supplied ticker service.

Members of the Odd-Lot Cotton Exchange contracted for future delivery of cotton in lots of 10 to 100 bales. Odd-Lot applied for service but was refused because the New York exchange withheld consent. The explanation given was that an investigation linked Odd-Lot to a predecessor convicted of operating a bucket shop, with many of the same members, and that Odd-Lot had been organized as a cover for continuing that activity.

The exchange's counterclaim alleged that Odd-Lot nevertheless obtained the quotations unlawfully, directly or through another person, and distributed them to members who supplied bucket shops. Odd-Lot had stipulated that the affidavits supporting preliminary relief could be treated as testimony on the counterclaim.
sections.Issue: Whether the bill stated an antitrust violation, and whether the federal court could adjudicate the exchange's counterclaim after the bill failed: specifically, whether dismissal of the bill eliminated federal jurisdiction and whether the counterclaim arose out of the transaction that was the subject matter of the suit under Equity Rule 30.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court, 1926, in an opinion by Justice Sutherland with no separate writing, held that the bill failed on the merits rather than for want of jurisdiction, and that the counterclaim arose out of the transaction that was the subject matter of the suit under Equity Rule 30, so it was properly adjudicated. The pleadings and affidavits supported making the injunction permanent, and the Court affirmed the decree. It expressly left unresolved whether a counterclaim not arising from the same transaction requires independent federal jurisdiction.
sections.Reasoning:
On the merits, the Court put aside the unfair-competition claim because relief under the Federal Trade Commission Act had to begin before the Commission, and found no violation of Sherman Act §§ 1 or 2. The exchange's trading was local, the exchange remained the real distributor of its own information with Western Union acting as its agency, and selective sale of its own news was an ordinary private-business choice whose effect on interstate commerce was indirect and incidental.

Jurisdiction survived the bill's failure. A substantial, nonfrivolous federal statutory claim invokes the power to decide its legal sufficiency even if it ultimately fails; only a claim plainly lacking any color of merit would not. Odd-Lot had made a serious though insufficient attempt to allege an antitrust violation, so the bill was dismissed on the merits.

Equity Rule 30 distinguished a counterclaim arising from the transaction that was the suit's subject matter, which had to be stated, from an optional counterclaim. This counterclaim fell in the first category. The connection was logical even though the allegations were not identical: Odd-Lot sought to compel delivery of quotations, and the exchange defended its refusal and sought to stop Odd-Lot from obtaining them unlawfully despite that refusal. The refusal was an essential link in both controversies. Requiring complete factual identity would drain the transaction-based rule of practical meaning, since opposing claims rarely depend on precisely the same facts. The injunction completed the relief.

The casebook cites the case for the flexible, logical-relationship understanding of transaction; its note says the defendant counterclaimed for damages, whereas the opinion describes a counterclaim for an injunction.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-314.rule: Where federal law forces related claims to be litigated in two different districts, Rule 13(a) does not require a counterclaim common to both to be asserted in whichever action received the first responsive pleading; once adjudicated in one, it cannot be reasserted in the other.

sections.Parties: Samuel J. Pickard, doing business as Pickard Engineering, was the plumbing and heating subcontractor and the plaintiff. He sued Southern Construction Co., the federal government's prime contractor, and its Miller Act surety, Continental Casualty, for amounts allegedly due on two projects. Southern sought a credit for a payment it had made to Pickard's supplier. Southern lost on that credit in the Sixth Circuit and sought review in the Supreme Court.
sections.Procedural History:
In December 1956 Pickard sued Southern and Continental in Georgia on both projects, and Southern answered and counterclaimed in January 1957. Because the Miller Act required suit in the district where the contract was performed, Pickard brought a Tennessee action in April 1957 and amended the Georgia complaint to remove the Tennessee claim. The Georgia action went to trial in 1959 but still lacked a final judgment; Southern obtained a new trial on its counterclaim in September 1961.

In Tennessee, the district court allowed Southern a $34,520 credit and found Pickard entitled to no recovery. The Sixth Circuit reversed on the credit issue, treating the payment as a compulsory counterclaim in Georgia. The Supreme Court reversed the Sixth Circuit's judgment insofar as it concerned this counterclaim and remanded to that court.
sections.Material Facts:
Southern was prime contractor for rehabilitation of barracks at Fort Campbell, Tennessee, and Fort Benning, Georgia, under three Georgia contracts and one Tennessee contract. Pickard was the subcontractor on both projects, and Atlas Supply was his principal supplier. Pickard's men left the Tennessee work before completion in December 1955 and shortly afterward left the Georgia work. Atlas asserted unpaid accounts of $34,520 on Tennessee and $104,000 on Georgia. Following an August 1956 conference, Southern paid Atlas $35,000 for a complete release covering both projects.

Southern's Georgia counterclaim asserted expenditures exceeding the contract price and included the $35,000 Atlas payment. The Tennessee district court later found that Southern had dropped the Atlas payment from its Georgia counterclaim before that trial. In Tennessee Southern initially included the payment in an affirmative counterclaim, and Pickard responded that it was barred by res judicata. Southern later waived affirmative relief and sought only a $34,520 credit, the amount Atlas had attributed to the Tennessee project. After certiorari, Southern amended its Georgia counterclaim to include the payment again, but further Georgia proceedings awaited this decision.
sections.Issue: Whether, when federal law required related construction claims to be split between two districts, Rule 13(a) made a counterclaim common to both compulsory in the action where the first responsive pleading was filed, so that it could not be asserted in the other.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court, 1962, per curiam with no separate writing, held that on these circumstances Rule 13(a) did not require the common counterclaim to be asserted in whichever action received the first responsive pleading. It reversed the Sixth Circuit as to this counterclaim and remanded. The Court accepted for purposes of decision the lower court's determination that the payment had not been allocated between the projects and could have been asserted in either case. It added that once the counterclaim was adjudicated in one action, it could not be reasserted in the other.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court asked what the compulsory-counterclaim requirement was designed to accomplish: avoiding multiple actions and resolving common disputes in one suit. It particularly targeted a defendant who omitted a counterclaim and then began a second affirmative action using the omitted claim as its complaint.

That rationale did not fit this record. Pickard himself first tried to combine the project claims, and federal law compelled their fragmentation into Georgia and Tennessee cases. Southern then faced two actions brought against it, with a settlement relevant to both. Asserting the settlement in Tennessee did not create the needless additional action the rule sought to prevent, and Southern had reason to regard the credit as particularly connected to the Tennessee project, since the requested $34,520 corresponded to Atlas's asserted Tennessee balance.

The Court therefore rejected the mechanical proposition that the first responsive pleading determines where the common counterclaim may be used. The holding expressly rested on these circumstances and did not create a general option to ignore compulsory counterclaims whenever a defendant prefers another forum. A footnote supplied the limit: permission to select a proper pending forum did not authorize double recovery or repeated adjudication once the claim had been resolved.

The casebook quotes the Court's rationale in a note and asks whether the exception should be limited to claims that substantive law requires to be split across districts; that is the editors' question, not a holding.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-316.rule: Under Rule 13(g) a coparty is any party who is not an opposing party, so an original defendant may crossclaim against a third-party defendant whom a different defendant impleaded.

sections.Parties: Earle M. Jorgenson Co., the plaintiff, sued seven defendants, including T.I. United States, Ltd. and Leonard V. Reed, over contaminated property. T.I. United States impleaded Robert T. Tosti as a third-party defendant. Reed, an original defendant, crossclaimed against Tosti for contribution and indemnity. Tosti moved to dismiss Reed's crossclaim; Reed sought to maintain it.
sections.Procedural History: On October 9, 1990, T.I. United States impleaded Tosti for indemnity and contribution. Three days later Reed crossclaimed against Tosti on the same types of derivative liability, and also crossclaimed against other original defendants. Tosti moved to dismiss on November 16, arguing that an original defendant and a third-party defendant could not be coparties. The Eastern District of Pennsylvania denied Tosti's motion to dismiss.
sections.Material Facts: Jorgenson sought cleanup costs, other damages, and declaratory relief concerning contaminated property in Bristol, Pennsylvania, and its complaint included CERCLA claims against seven defendants. T.I. United States had been A.B. Murray Corporation's sole shareholder until 1984; A.B. Murray formerly owned part of the site. Reed owned 81 percent of Reed Management, which was A.B. Murray's sole shareholder from 1984 to 1990. Jorgenson alleged that active participation, control, operation, and management during hazardous-substance releases left it, as A.B. Murray's successor, with response costs; those were complaint allegations, not findings of liability. Tosti had been A.B. Murray's vice-president of operations from 1983 to 1986. Reed had not impleaded Tosti and did not already formally oppose him on any pleaded claim; only T.I. United States had sued Tosti by third-party complaint.
sections.Issue: Whether an original defendant and a third-party defendant impleaded by a different defendant are coparties under Rule 13(g), so that the original defendant may crossclaim against the third-party defendant for contribution and indemnity.
sections.Holding: The Eastern District of Pennsylvania, in 1991, in a memorandum by Judge Ludwig, denied the motion to dismiss. An original defendant could crossclaim for contribution and indemnity against a third-party defendant whom another defendant had impleaded, because parties not already formally opposing each other on a pleaded claim could be coparties under Rule 13(g). Adopting Georgia Ports Authority's approach, the court treated a coparty as a party who is not an opposing party. The ruling permitted the crossclaim to be litigated; it did not decide CERCLA responsibility or order Tosti to pay anything.
sections.Reasoning:
The rules did not define coparty, and the authorities gave no single answer. A Third Circuit statement that crossclaims involve parties on the same side of the main litigation arose in a different setting, and Schwab classified a third-party plaintiff and the third-party defendants it had sued as opposing parties, which did not settle the relationship with a different original defendant. District cases diverged: Hansen rejected such a crossclaim, while Capital Care allowed it if the relationship was sufficiently nonadverse. Judge Ludwig thought that test helpful but not decisive, because any crossclaim introduces adversity between the parties to it.

He then read the defendant's claims together. A counterclaim runs against an opposing party, a third-party claim under Rule 14(a) against a person not already a party, and a crossclaim against a coparty. Tosti was already a party, so Reed could not simply implead him again. Under Tosti's reading Reed would generally need a separate action, which would frustrate the policy of resolving related disputes together, arbitrarily favor whichever defendant impleaded first, and conflict with Rule 1's goal of just, speedy, and inexpensive adjudication. The court noted other possible routes and separate trials as a response to confusion but did not order them.

Parties formally opposing each other on an existing pleaded claim, such as an original plaintiff and defendant or a third-party plaintiff and the third-party defendant it sued, are opposing parties. Reed and Tosti had no such relationship. A footnote added that once Reed pleaded the crossclaim he became an opposing party to Tosti, so a responsive claim from the same transaction would have to be assessed as a counterclaim, including under Rule 13(a).

The casebook quotes the definition of opposing parties and observes, as editorial context, that the issue remains unsettled.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-317.rule: Rule 13(g), as the Third Circuit read it in 1958, allows a crossclaim only as ancillary to a claim already asserted against the crossclaimant, so coplaintiffs cannot crossclaim against each other on an independent claim from the same accident.

sections.Parties: The Danner and Weintraub families, all Pennsylvania citizens, were coplaintiffs suing William Anskis, a New Jersey citizen, for personal injuries from a car collision. The Weintraub plaintiffs then tried to crossclaim against Mrs. Danner and her husband. The Weintraubs were the appellants; the Danners had moved to dismiss the crossclaim.
sections.Procedural History: The families filed suit on October 1, 1954. On April 1, 1957, Anskis was defaulted for failing to appear, plead, or defend. Three weeks later the Weintraub plaintiffs attempted to crossclaim against the Danners. The district court granted the Danners' motion to dismiss because the claim was not a proper Rule 13(g) crossclaim and lacked another federal jurisdictional basis, and it also relied on the Pennsylvania limitations period. The Weintraubs appealed, and the Third Circuit affirmed the dismissal order.
sections.Material Facts: The suit arose from a two-car collision in Bucks County, Pennsylvania. Mrs. Danner drove the car occupied by three Danner children and their mother and two Weintraub children and their mother. The complaint attributed the collision to Anskis's negligent driving and sought personal-injury damages. All plaintiffs were Pennsylvania citizens and Anskis was a New Jersey citizen, which supplied diversity for the original suit. After Anskis was defaulted, the Weintraubs' proposed crossclaim alleged that Mrs. Danner's negligent operation caused the same injuries. No claim had been asserted against the Weintraubs themselves. More than the statutory two-year period had passed before the crossclaim was served.
sections.Issue: Whether Rule 13(g) authorized plaintiffs jointly suing an outside defendant to crossclaim against their coplaintiffs on an independent claim arising from the same accident, and whether that claim had any independent basis of federal jurisdiction.
sections.Holding: The Third Circuit, in 1958, in an opinion by Judge Maris for a panel of Maris, Kalodner, and Staley, with no separate writing, affirmed. Rule 13(g), as the court then understood it, did not authorize plaintiffs jointly suing an outside defendant to crossclaim against each other on an independent claim arising from the same accident, and the proposed claim lacked an independent diversity basis because its adverse parties were all Pennsylvania citizens. The court did not hold that a plaintiff can never use Rule 13(g), and it expressly declined to decide the limitations issue.
sections.Reasoning:
Rule 13(g) authorizes a claim against a coparty arising from the transaction or occurrence underlying the original action or a counterclaim, or relating to property involved in the action. The Weintraubs' claim plainly concerned the same collision, but the court treated transactional connection as insufficient by itself.

The court understood a crossclaim as ancillary to a claim already asserted against the crossclaimant. A defendant can crossclaim against a codefendant about the underlying transaction, and a plaintiff facing a defendant's counterclaim can crossclaim against a coplaintiff about that counterclaim's transaction. The Weintraubs faced no previously pleaded claim against themselves; their affirmative claim against the Danners was independent of the families' shared complaint against Anskis.

The court tied that construction to jurisdiction. An unrestricted reading could extend district-court jurisdiction beyond the federal judicial power, contrary to Rule 82. Putting two Pennsylvania plaintiffs in a diversity case against a New Jersey defendant did not authorize a separate controversy between those plaintiffs, and treated as an independent suit the claim lacked diverse adverse parties. On limitations, the court noted only that the Danners could have raised the defense in a responsive pleading had the dismissal been reversed.

The casebook's questions challenge the court's reading of Rule 13(g), suggest considering § 1359, and ask about later § 1367 supplemental jurisdiction; those are editorial prompts, and the 1958 court neither made a finding of collusion nor interpreted the later supplemental-jurisdiction statute.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-322.rule: A person whose rights would inevitably be affected by the judgment is an indispensable party who must be joined, even in an action framed only as one for damages against someone else, and refusal to join her warrants dismissal.

sections.Parties: Barbara Ruth Warner, the current wife of attorney Caryl Warner, was the plaintiff and appellant. She sued only Pacific Telephone & Telegraph Co., which had published a directory listing for Caryl's divorced wife, Jeanne, as Mrs. Caryl Warner, and sought damages. Jeanne was not made a party. The telephone company demurred.
sections.Procedural History: The company demurred to Barbara's third amended and supplemental complaint, one ground being her failure to join Jeanne as an indispensable defendant. An earlier ruling had identified that defect, and Barbara amended twice afterward without adding Jeanne. The final demurrer was sustained without leave to amend, and she appealed the ensuing dismissal.
