Criminal contempt was appealable as a final judgment, and because discovery orders ordinarily are not immediately appealable, accepting the risk of contempt furnished a route to review; if the order had been upheld the Academy would have faced the sanction.

On discovery, Rule 37's authority to order production had to be applied with the protective and sequencing powers of then-existing Rules 26(c) and 26(d), which required evaluating the hardship to each side. The court rejected complete First Amendment immunity for the files but recognized an associational interest in candid evaluations, while withholding every file could leave the doctors unable to prove their case. It identified alternatives: private judicial inspection of the doctors' own files first, redaction of members' names with judicial comparison against originals, and initial examination of redacted files by counsel. It also considered sequencing nonsensitive discovery first where the case might fail on other elements, and stressed the danger of sensitive discovery being used as settlement leverage. These were possible methods, not a required sequence for every dispute.

On preclusion, Posner reasoned that the doctors could have asserted an Illinois antitrust theory in their first litigation and that state and federal liability standards were materially equivalent here. Judge Flaum supported dismissal on a different rationale requiring substantially contemporaneous litigation of related theories. Judge Bauer concurred in the result. Judge Eschbach agreed the discovery order was an abuse of discretion but opposed barring the federal claims. Judge Wood, joined by Judges Cummings and Cudahy, would have sustained the contempt and thought the confidentiality compromise within the district court's discretion. Judge Cudahy, joined by Judges Cummings and Wood, argued that § 1738 requires applying the rendering state's rules. The casebook develops the discovery dispute, quotes the private-inspection and redaction proposals, and asks as an editorial question how it would be assessed under the 2015 proportionality factors.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-370.rule: Initial disclosure under Rule 26 covers only witnesses and documents the disclosing party may use to support its claims or defenses; other material must be sought through properly framed discovery requests, and a Rule 30(b)(6) notice cannot compel testimony from a particular employee.

sections.Parties: Gregory Cummings and his wife, whom the caption calls Trace and the opinion Tracey, were the plaintiffs; they sued General Motors, alleging defective seat and seat-belt design and inadequate warnings in a 1995 Pontiac Grand Am. GM disputed defect and causation. The plaintiffs appealed from the judgment on a defense verdict and from the denial of relief from judgment.
sections.Procedural History: Discovery disputes produced three motions to compel and several protective-order requests. The magistrate denied the plaintiffs' motions and granted GM protection and fees, and the district court affirmed on de novo review. At trial both sides moved under Rule 50(a); both motions were denied, the jury returned a defense verdict, and the plaintiffs filed no post-verdict motion. Seven months after learning of certain GM test videos, the plaintiffs sought relief under Rule 60(b)(3), which the district court denied for delay and failure to establish misconduct. The Tenth Circuit consolidated the appeals from the judgment and that denial and, in a decision of April 28, 2004, modified on partial grant of rehearing June 2, 2004, affirmed in all respects and denied all outstanding motions.
sections.Material Facts:
On September 13, 1998, Gregory Cummings drove the Grand Am through a partially obscured stop sign at a rural Oklahoma T-intersection, and the car crossed a ditch into a field. His wife sustained a vertebral compression fracture and paraplegia; the other passengers suffered minor injuries. Their children were in the rear seats, including a three-month-old in a child seat behind the wife. GM asserted that her posture and reclined position explained her injuries. The parties disputed whether her seat was reclined about 25 degrees or 40 to 45 degrees, and whether the child seat was rear-facing, which the plaintiffs said prevented greater recline, or forward-facing, as GM's evidence suggested.

A month after the verdict the plaintiffs learned of six GM child-safety-seat acceleration-test videos already produced in unrelated litigation. They argued the videos would undermine GM's forward-facing-seat theory because their infant had escaped injury. GM described the videos as involving older child dummies, different seats and different cars, and had not planned to use them at trial.
sections.Issue: Did the district court abuse its discretion in its discovery rulings, including on the scope of initial disclosure and Rule 30(b)(6) depositions? Were the plaintiffs entitled to relief under Rule 60(b)(3) because GM had not produced the test videos? And had the plaintiffs preserved their Rule 50 challenges?
sections.Holding: The United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit, in 2004, in an opinion by Judge Paul Kelly, Jr., joined by Judges McKay and Henry, affirmed in all respects. The discovery rulings were within the district court's discretion. Initial disclosure reached only individuals and material the disclosing party might use to support its claims or defenses. The Rule 60(b)(3) motion was properly denied because of unjustified delay and because, assuming the videos were relevant, the plaintiffs' requests did not encompass them and GM had no automatic duty to disclose them. The plaintiffs' Rule 50(a) motion preserved the misuse issue but not a general sufficiency challenge to liability.
sections.Reasoning:
On Rule 50, liberal construction dispenses with technical precision but not with adequate notice of the particular grounds, so the broader liability challenge was reviewed only for plain error, and none was found. Under then-binding circuit precedent, failure to renew after verdict did not bar review of an issue raised before submission to the jury, though only a new trial could be granted. Evidence supported both sides on misuse, so submission to the jury was upheld. The casebook records that the decision was abrogated on other grounds by Unitherm Food Systems, Inc. v. Swift-Eckrich, Inc., so this Rule 50(b) rule is not current law.

On discovery, the plaintiffs identified no record support for their general claim of inadequate responses, and their imprecise requests had contributed to the disputes. Rule 30(b)(6) lets the corporation select its representatives; a particular undesignated employee had to be subpoenaed like any other nonparty witness. Under the 2000 amendments to Rule 26, initial disclosure did not require automatic disclosure of every favorable or unfavorable witness or document the party did not intend to use; that narrower obligation is distinct from responding to properly framed requests. Protection against overly broad, duplicative and unduly burdensome database searches was also upheld.

On Rule 60(b)(3), filing within one year did not by itself make the motion timely; the rule also required a reasonable time, and seven months went unexplained. Independently, relief required clear and convincing proof of fraud, misrepresentation or misconduct that substantially interfered with trial preparation. The identified requests were overly broad or directed to specified components and did not cover the videos, and GM did not plan to use them. The holding did not authorize withholding responsive material merely because it was unfavorable. The casebook cites the case for the narrower automatic-disclosure obligation and how further requests should follow initial disclosure.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-373.rule: A court may allow tightly protected discovery from an unidentified nonparty blood donor through written deposition questions under Rule 31, as modified by a Rule 26(c) protective order, where the plaintiff's need outweighs a minimal intrusion on the donor's privacy.

sections.Parties: Cynthia Watson, as administrator for her deceased infant son Trevor, sued the Red Cross and the hospital for wrongful death. She sought the identity of a blood donor or access to the donor through an intermediary. The Red Cross, appellant on interlocutory appeal, argued that the donor discovery should be prohibited under Rule 26(c) or the federal or South Carolina constitutions.
sections.Procedural History: A magistrate proposed limited questioning of the donor through a court-appointed lawyer, and the district court adopted a protective arrangement in an order signed February 6 and entered February 7, 1991. The Red Cross obtained a stay and permission for an interlocutory appeal under 28 U.S.C. § 1292(b). The appeal was held in abeyance pending resolution of federal jurisdiction over cases involving the Red Cross; after the Supreme Court's charter-jurisdiction decision the court vacated the abeyance order. The Fourth Circuit, in a decision of August 28, 1992, amended November 2, 1992, affirmed the limited discovery order.
sections.Material Facts:
Trevor, a premature infant, received transfusions in 1985, tested positive for HIV in 1986, developed AIDS, and died in 1988. Of the six donors associated with the transfusions, only one was identified as possibly HIV-positive when donating. One negligence theory challenged the way employees screened that donor. The nurses had been deposed but could not remember the donor years later, and the Red Cross had supplied nonidentifying information and a redacted questionnaire.

The district court's order required the Red Cross to deliver the donor's name and address privately to the judge within ten days, to be sealed by the clerk and opened only with express court approval. A lawyer appointed at the plaintiff's expense, whose identity would also remain confidential, would represent the donor, and approved questions would pass through that lawyer. Verified answers would be sealed, with the parties receiving copies with the verification redacted. The eighteen approved questions covered matters such as awareness that blood transmits disease, prior deferrals, the information supplied by staff, literacy and education, and motivations for donating. Watson could seek leave for one follow-up set.
sections.Issue: Should the particular discovery from the implicated blood donor, conducted through written questions and a court-appointed lawyer under a protective order, be prohibited under Rule 26(c) or the federal or South Carolina constitutions?
sections.Holding: The United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit, in 1992, in an opinion by Judge Hall, with Judge Widener concurring in the result and Judge Russell dissenting, affirmed the limited discovery order. The written questions to the nonparty donor were properly treated as Rule 31 depositions, modified by a Rule 26(c) protective order, not Rule 33 interrogatories. The court found no clear error in the district court's factual findings and no abuse of discretion in approving the questions. It did not decide negligence or authorize unrestricted disclosure of the donor's identity.
sections.Reasoning:
The court reviewed factual findings for clear error, legal conclusions de novo, and the exercise of discovery discretion for abuse.

On the blood supply, the district court had rejected the premise that this confidential discovery would dangerously reduce voluntary donations. The Red Cross's expert offered no empirical support beyond a theory of behavior, while Watson's expert predicted no measurable adverse effect, so there was no clear error. The court also rejected the argument that threatened litigation would encourage volunteer donors to lie during screening.

On privacy, Judge Hall accepted the Red Cross's standing to assert the donor's constitutional interests. He concluded that the tightly confined disclosure did not violate those interests and, alternatively, that any minimal intrusion was outweighed by Watson's need and the public interest in compensation for injuries. The identity would reach only the court and the appointed lawyer, with sealed records and redacted verifications. Broader disclosure was reserved.

On need and relevance, the donor was the one person who might remember what happened during screening, and questions about risk knowledge, past deferrals, motivation, literacy and education could illuminate the adequacy of the employees' actual screening.

Judge Widener, concurring, rejected third-party constitutional standing, which had not been briefed, and thought the Rule 26 limitations afforded at least the protection warranted. Judge Russell, dissenting, would have prohibited discovery identifying the donor even to intermediaries, regarding deterrence of donations as a common-sense risk and the incremental discovery as not worth the risks to privacy and the blood supply. The casebook presents selected questions as an example of deposition by written questions and raises editorial questions about oral depositions and Rule 33.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-375.rule: Electronic data is discoverable and the responding party presumptively pays for production; cost shifting may be considered only for relatively inaccessible data, such as backup tapes, under a seven-factor test in which marginal utility weighs most.

sections.Parties: Laura Zubulake sued UBS entities for sex discrimination and retaliation under federal, state and city law. She moved to compel production of responsive emails at UBS's expense. UBS denied discrimination.
sections.Procedural History: Zubulake filed an EEOC charge on August 16, 2001, and sued on February 15, 2002. After UBS's limited email production she moved to compel production at UBS's expense. On May 13, 2003, District Judge Shira A. Scheindlin of the Southern District of New York ordered UBS to produce all responsive emails on its optical disks and active servers at its own expense and to restore and produce responsive emails from any five backup tapes selected by Zubulake, initially at UBS's expense, then submit an affidavit on the results, time and money spent. The cost-shifting analysis would follow, and a conference was set for June 17, 2003. The brief concerns only this order, commonly called Zubulake I.
sections.Material Facts:
Zubulake was hired in August 1999 as a director and senior salesperson on the Asian Equities Sales Desk. She alleged that a male supervisor appointed in December 2000 belittled and excluded her. She was fired October 9, 2001, with two weeks' notice.

Her document request sought communications concerning her. UBS produced approximately 350 pages, including 100 pages of emails. A September 12, 2002 agreement focused retrieval on five employees' communications between August 1999 and December 2001, but UBS produced no additional emails and had searched neither its backup tapes nor its optical archives. Zubulake herself had approximately 450 pages of emails. UBS estimated restoration at approximately $175,000, excluding attorney review time. Zubulake estimated potential damages at up to $13 million.

UBS backed up email to tapes: daily tapes were kept twenty working days, weekly tapes a year and monthly tapes three years. Ninety-four tapes contained potentially responsive material, and restoring one server's monthly tape typically took five days. Optical disks separately preserved external email of designated registered traders and could be searched without restoration; internal messages were not archived there.
sections.Issue: Were the responsive electronic messages discoverable, and did their electronic form justify shifting the costs of production to Zubulake, the requesting party?
sections.Holding: The United States District Court for the Southern District of New York, in 2003, through Judge Scheindlin, held that the emails were discoverable and that electronic form alone did not justify shifting costs. The usual presumption requires the responding party to pay; cost shifting may be considered for relatively inaccessible data after examining the actual system and obtaining a factual basis for the expense and likely value. UBS's active servers and searchable optical disks were accessible, so their production costs stayed with UBS, while its backup tapes warranted consideration of cost shifting after a five-tape sample. No final allocation for the remaining tapes was made.
sections.Reasoning:
Rule 34 covered electronic data, including recoverable deleted material. UBS could not establish completeness by pointing to its search of employees' current files, and Zubulake's possession of some messages did not show she had the rest.

The court distinguished five storage categories: active online data, near-line data, offline storage or archives, backup tapes, and erased or fragmented data. The first three generally were accessible; the last two generally required restoration or processing. Electronic discovery could be cheaper and easier than paper discovery, and automatically shifting costs threatened to price plaintiffs out of meritorious cases.

Revising Rowe's eight-factor approach, the court set out seven factors: how specifically the request targets relevant information; whether other sources can supply it; production cost compared with the amount in controversy; production cost compared with each party's resources; each party's ability and incentive to control cost; the importance of the issues in the litigation; and the relative benefit to each party. They are not weighed equally. The first two form the central marginal-utility inquiry, the next three address expense and who can bear it, the sixth arises infrequently but could predominate, and the seventh is least important. The court rejected absolute cost and relative wealth as sufficient measures and generally discarded the purpose for which data was retained. The guiding question was whether the request imposed undue burden or expense relative to the information's importance.

Sampling supplied actual evidence of responsive material and restoration expense, and the court rejected requiring advance proof that discovery would yield a gold mine. The casebook reproduces the seven factors and the $175,000 estimate; the brief notes that it omits the accessible and inaccessible distinction, the unequal weighting and the five-tape sample.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-376.rule: Counsel must confer and cooperate in developing electronic search methodology, including search terms, under Rule 26(f)(3)(C) and local rules; and a motion to compel production filed before the response deadline has expired is premature.

sections.Parties: Pyle, the plaintiff, sued Selective Insurance Co. of America in an action the casebook identifies as employment discrimination. Selective, the defendant, filed two discovery motions: one for Pyle's medical records and executed HIPAA authorizations, and one for her cooperation in selecting electronic search terms. Pyle opposed both.
sections.Procedural History: Two motions by Selective were before Senior District Judge Terrence F. McVerry of the Western District of Pennsylvania: ECF 22, seeking medical records and HIPAA authorizations, and ECF 24, seeking the plaintiff's cooperation on search terms or, alternatively, relief from any obligation to produce electronically stored information. In an order of September 30, 2016, the court denied ECF 22 as premature and granted ECF 24 insofar as it required conferring and agreement on search terms. No merits judgment or sanction was entered.
sections.Material Facts:
On medical discovery, Pyle's initial disclosures named three treating doctors, and Selective later learned of a fourth. Selective's counsel requested records by letter on July 7, provided releases on August 30, and formally served a document request on September 6. No records or releases had yet been produced, but the thirty-day response period had not expired, and Pyle represented that they would be supplied within it.

On electronic discovery, Pyle's July 28 request sought emails, correspondence, memoranda and other documents from various Selective employees relating to her employment and benefits. Selective produced some documents and retrieved additional email archives. It asked opposing counsel to agree on search terms and renewed the request on September 6. Pyle's counsel refused, saying she had not requested direct account access requiring a protocol and that Selective had shown neither supporting authority nor burden.
sections.Issue: Should production of medical records and authorizations be compelled before the deadline to respond to the document request has passed? And may counsel refuse to cooperate with the opposing party in selecting search terms for electronically stored information?
sections.Holding: The United States District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania, in 2016, through Senior District Judge McVerry, held that the medical-records motion was premature and that counsel could not refuse to cooperate over search methodology. It compelled Pyle to confer and reach agreement on terms for searching the identified additional email archives. It did not grant Selective a blanket exemption from producing electronically stored information, and it set no specific deadline for agreement, though it expected prompt resolution.
sections.Reasoning:
Electronic discovery should ordinarily be driven by the parties. Rule 26(f)(3)(C) expressly requires counsel to confer about disclosure, discovery and preservation of electronically stored information, including the forms of production. The court drew on Romero and its quotation of Trusz concerning practical agreement on terms, dates and relevant people. Local Civil Rule 26.2(C) more specifically required counsel to confer and attempt agreement on protocols, including filters such as terms and date ranges. Cooperation was consistent with these obligations, and the court should not need to manage every search detail. Pyle's argument that no authority supported cooperation therefore failed. The order did not prescribe particular terms, decide the adequacy of a completed search, require predictive coding, or establish that every document matching a keyword must be produced.

On the medical motion, a party's expected compliance is not yet a failure warranting a preemptive production order. The court expected timely compliance and allowed Selective to raise the issue again if Pyle failed to comply when due. It did not uphold permanent withholding or decide any privilege objection.

The casebook presents the search-term ruling in a note on cooperation over electronic discovery; the brief adds that the casebook's remark that the federal rules do not directly prescribe this methodology should be read alongside the order's reliance on the general federal conference duty and the more specific local rule.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-381.rule: A party instructing a deposition witness not to answer must expressly identify the privilege claimed with enough information to evaluate it; privileges that were, without justification, not asserted at the deposition cannot be relied on later in opposing a motion to compel.

sections.Parties: Donald J. Moloney sued the United States under the Federal Tort Claims Act for alleged medical malpractice by Dr. Lisa Adams of Neponset Health Care Center. He moved to compel further deposition testimony from Adams. The United States, the defendant, had instructed her not to answer and opposed the motion on privilege grounds.
sections.Procedural History: The suit was filed February 25, 1999. At Adams's deposition, defense counsel instructed her not to answer certain questions, and Moloney moved to compel further testimony. On November 6, 2001, Chief Magistrate Judge Collings of the District of Massachusetts allowed the motion to compel, ordered the United States to pay the plaintiff's reasonable expenses of bringing the motion, including attorney's fees, and ordered it to pay the costs, including reasonable attorney's fees, of plaintiff's counsel attending Adams's continued deposition. The opinion fixed entitlement, not a dollar amount; affidavits were due November 23, 2001, with a response by December 7. The court did not decide negligence or damages.
sections.Material Facts:
Adams worked at Neponset Health Care Center, a subsidiary of Harbor Health Services, which had been designated a federally supported facility and Public Health Service employee under 42 U.S.C. § 233(g). Moloney's and Adams's accounts of a February 1997 consultation differed; he later underwent surgery for perforated sigmoid diverticulitis with fecal peritonitis and suffered serious complications.

At her deposition Adams was asked about three conversations with her immediate medical supervisor, Dr. Robert Baratz, about her treatment of Moloney, one within days of treatment and two in summer 1998, and about one or two conversations with Harbor Health's chief operating officer, Dan Driscoll, months after the treatment. Defense counsel instructed her not to answer questions about their substance, asserting attorney-client privilege and work-product protection. Plaintiff's counsel repeatedly asked which privilege was being asserted and reserved a motion to compel. In opposing the motion, the United States made no effort to justify those two protections and instead invoked federal self-critical-analysis and medical-peer-review privileges and Massachusetts General Laws chapter 111, §§ 203 and 204.
sections.Issue: Could counsel block deposition testimony under two stated privileges, abandon their justification, and then rely on three different privileges, never asserted at the deposition, in response to the motion to compel?
sections.Holding: The United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts, in 2001, through Chief Magistrate Judge Collings, held that on these facts it could not. The original protections were foreclosed when the government failed to justify them, and its unjustified failure to assert the later protections at the deposition prevented reliance on them afterward. The motion to compel was allowed, and expenses were awarded because the opposition was not substantially justified. The court did not decide the existence or scope of the newly asserted privileges.
sections.Reasoning:
The rules then in force governed. Rule 26(b)(5) required an express claim of privilege or trial-preparation protection and a description enabling other parties to evaluate it without revealing protected information; the court read that requirement as applying to depositions as well as documents. Rule 30(d)(1) required concise, nonargumentative, nonsuggestive objections. The privilege had to be identified with enough supporting information for meaningful evaluation, and a blanket claim was insufficient.

At the deposition defense counsel repeatedly named only attorney-client privilege and work product. Although she promised further inquiry and said her position might change, she never identified self-critical analysis, peer review or the Massachusetts statute, and that statement did not make the unstated claims express. The failure deprived opposing counsel of the opportunity to explore whether the actual privileges applied and to develop a useful record. The court rejected using one protection to stop testimony and then researching an entirely different one after a motion to compel, a sequence that defeated the notice requirements and their purpose.

Ignorance of the law was no excuse: the statutes were at least nine years old and the cited cases went back to 1970. Counsel's asserted ignorance of the conversations was also inadequate, because Baratz and Driscoll should have been identified in response to an interrogatory served in June 2000, before the February 2001 deposition. The court also relied on American Hangar for the proposition that a party instructing a witness not to answer on privilege grounds should seek a protective order instead of forcing the opponent to move to compel.

The ruling was tied to the unjustified failure on these facts and did not announce that every late or imperfect privilege assertion automatically waives protection. The casebook cites the case for counsel's switch from the privileges asserted at the deposition to different ones when opposing the motion.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-382.rule: Under the 1993 version of Rule 26, work-product material supplied to a retained testifying expert and considered by the expert in forming an opinion must be disclosed, whether or not the expert ultimately relied on it.

sections.Parties: Angela Lamonds, the plaintiff, alleged that a design defect in a General Motors automobile caused her severe injuries in an accident. General Motors, the defendant, moved to compel production of two memoranda her legal team had created and supplied to her retained experts, George Greene and Byron Bloch. Lamonds resisted on work-product grounds.
sections.Procedural History: The district court had previously denied General Motors' summary-judgment motion. Magistrate Judge B. Waugh Crigler examined the documents and denied the motion to compel, concluding that General Motors already possessed the requested information in other forms and so could not show inability to obtain the substantial equivalent elsewhere. General Motors filed timely objections. Reviewing the nondispositive order under 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)(1)(A) and Rule 72(a), Senior District Judge Michael of the Western District of Virginia held the magistrate judge's approach contrary to law, reviewed the documents in camera, and on July 2, 1998 granted the objections and the motion to compel.
sections.Material Facts: Lamonds's legal team created two memoranda and supplied them to retained experts George Greene and Byron Bloch. Both experts admitted receiving and reading the memoranda before forming their opinions, and there was no evidence that they had received the materials without reading, reflecting on or thinking about them. Lamonds argued that neither expert had actually relied on the memoranda. The judge's own in camera inspection showed that the two memoranda contained only an insignificant amount of opinion work product.
sections.Issue: Did work-product protection permit Lamonds to withhold materials furnished to experts who considered them in forming opinions for trial, despite the expert-disclosure requirements of the then-governing Rule 26?
sections.Holding: The United States District Court for the Western District of Virginia, in 1998, through Senior District Judge Michael, held that it did not. Work-product material supplied to a retained expert and considered in formulating testimony had to be disclosed. Both experts had considered the memoranda, and Lamonds's denial of actual reliance did not defeat that finding. The court ordered Memorandum I and Memorandum II produced in unredacted form under Rules 26(a)(2) and 26(b)(4). It did not decide the merits of the product-liability claim.
sections.Reasoning:
The court began with the interests protected by Hickman v. Taylor and codified in Rule 26(b)(3): lawyers need room to prepare without surrendering their investigation and analysis. Fact work product ordinarily required substantial need and inability to obtain its equivalent without undue hardship, and opinion work product in the Fourth Circuit approached immunity except in rare and extraordinary circumstances.

But Rule 26(b)(3) was subject to the expert-discovery provisions of Rule 26(b)(4). Read with the 1993 version of Rule 26(a)(2)(B), those provisions required disclosure of information an expert considered in forming an opinion. The Fourth Circuit had not squarely resolved the interaction, so the court treated the 1993 amendments and their Advisory Committee Note as controlling guides. The note explained that material furnished for use in forming an opinion could not be withheld simply because the expert did not ultimately rely on it, and it drew no distinction between fact and opinion work product in that setting.

Policy supported disclosure. An expert's apparent expertise makes effective cross-examination important, particularly where an advocate may have selected the information presented, and the opponent needs to know whether the expert assessed the facts independently or worked from a lawyer's account. Counsel can control the consequence by keeping private legal analysis separate from what is given to the expert. A test confined to actual reliance would require inquiry into the expert's internal thought processes and leave counsel uncertain, so the operative inquiry was consideration.

The small amount of opinion work product in the memoranda reinforced the result; the ordinary substantial-need test was not the governing basis. The casebook reproduces the disclosure rule and cross-examination rationale and then asks, as editorial commentary, whether the rule survives Rule 26(b)(4)(C), adopted in 2010; the brief presents the case as an interpretation of the rules then in force.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-384.rule: Dismissal under Rule 37(b)(2) for disobeying discovery orders is within the district court's discretion where the record supports findings of willfulness, bad faith or fault, and severe sanctions serve to deter other litigants as well as to punish the offender.

sections.Parties: The respondents, Metropolitan Hockey Club and others, were plaintiffs who brought an antitrust action against the National Hockey League and other petitioners. The district court dismissed their action as a discovery sanction; a divided court of appeals reversed that dismissal.
sections.Procedural History: The district court dismissed the action under Rule 37(b)(2), finding flagrant bad faith by the plaintiffs and callous disregard of professional responsibilities by their counsel, and supported the dismissal with a comprehensive memorandum reviewing the discovery record. A divided Third Circuit reversed for abuse of discretion; it did not dispute the district court's factual findings but gave weight to extenuating circumstances. The Court granted certiorari and, in a per curiam decision of June 30, 1976, reversed the Third Circuit's judgment, leaving the dismissal sustained.
sections.Material Facts:
Crucial court-ordered written interrogatories remained substantially unanswered for seventeen months. During that period the district court granted numerous extensions, including late ones, issued admonitions and received promises of compliance. The plaintiffs had been warned that noncompliance could lead to Rule 37 sanctions. When a definite June 14, 1974 deadline passed, the plaintiffs failed to perform and waited five additional days before moving for relief. The answers ultimately submitted were grossly inadequate.

The extenuating circumstances the Third Circuit relied on were that discovery had not been pressed until a consent decree resolved the claims of other original plaintiffs roughly a year into the litigation, that the respondents' current attorneys took over after that decree and had difficulty obtaining some information, and that lead counsel had assured the judge he would not knowingly or willfully disregard the final deadline.
sections.Issue: Was the court of appeals correct to conclude that dismissal of the action exceeded the district court's discretion under Rule 37 on this record of persistent noncompliance with discovery orders?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States, in 1976, in a per curiam opinion, with Justices Brennan and White dissenting without written explanation and Justice Stevens not participating, so that the judgment was 6 to 2, held that it was not. The question was not whether the appellate judges or the Court would have chosen dismissal in the first instance, but whether the trial judge abused the discretion Rule 37 confers. The Court found no abuse in either the bad-faith assessment or the choice of dismissal as the sanction.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court began with two limits. Rule 37 authorizes only such sanctions as are just, with dismissal among the listed options. And Societe Internationale established that a failure attributable to inability, as opposed to willfulness, bad faith or fault, does not support dismissal; no one suggested that amendments to Rule 37 had displaced that principle. The decision therefore does not authorize dismissal merely because a party could not comply, or require dismissal for every missed deadline.

The full record supported the district court's assessment. It had been exceptionally patient and had given ample opportunity to answer, and the respondents not only missed deadlines but ultimately submitted grossly inadequate answers. The district court's detailed memorandum showed that it had considered the full record. Mitigating circumstances and lenity mattered, but they could not entirely displace the other purposes of Rule 37.

The Court then explained why the prospect of future compliance did not justify reversal. A reviewing court may naturally recoil from dismissal and reason that the dismissed litigant has been chastened and would now comply. But sanctions also serve general deterrence: other litigants need reason to obey discovery orders before a court reaches the limit of its patience. If severe sanctions were regularly reversed once they had produced contrition, others could feel freer to disregard orders until threatened with termination. The availability of dismissal in an appropriate case thus serves both to punish the present misconduct and to deter similar conduct elsewhere. The Court tied that purpose to the supported findings of bad faith and counsel's disregard; deterrence alone did not replace the need for an appropriate factual basis.

The casebook quotes the passage distinguishing deterrence of the particular respondents from deterrence of other litigants.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-385.rule: A fee award imposed under a federal court's inherent authority through civil procedures must be compensatory, not punitive: it is limited to the fees the innocent party would not have incurred but for the misconduct.

sections.Parties: Leroy, Donna, Barry and Suzanne Haeger sued Goodyear after their motorhome swerved off the road and overturned, alleging that a Goodyear G159 tire failed; they also sued the motorhome and chassis manufacturers. After settling, the Haegers sought sanctions against Goodyear for discovery fraud. Goodyear challenged the amount of the resulting fee award.
sections.Procedural History: The parties settled shortly before trial for an undisclosed sum. After the Haegers later sought sanctions, the district court found a years-long course of bad-faith conduct by Goodyear and its lawyers and, using its inherent authority, awarded approximately $2.7 million in fees and costs, with a contingent $2 million award in case appellate review required a causal link. The Ninth Circuit affirmed the larger award, reasoning that fees incurred while Goodyear acted in bad faith could be shifted; Judge Watford dissented. The Court reversed the Ninth Circuit's judgment and remanded, directing the court below first to decide whether Goodyear had waived further challenge to the $2 million award and, if not, to have the fees reassessed under the proper causation requirement.
sections.Material Facts:
The Haegers alleged that the G159 tire was not designed to withstand the heat generated by motorhome use at highway speeds. They repeatedly requested Goodyear's internal G159 testing data. Discovery continued for years, with slow and uninformative responses and disputes requiring judicial intervention. Months after the settlement, the Haegers' lawyer learned from a newspaper account that Goodyear had disclosed relevant heat tests in another lawsuit; the tests showed unusual heating between 55 and 65 miles per hour. Goodyear then acknowledged that it had withheld them here despite repeated requests for all testing data. Goodyear did not contest the bad-faith finding in the Court.

Because the action had settled, the district court could not enter the default judgment it otherwise wanted to impose. Its $2.7 million award covered all fees and costs from Goodyear's first dishonest discovery response onward; it believed particularly egregious behavior justified recovery even of expenses lacking a causal connection, and thought timely disclosure probably would have produced a substantially earlier settlement. For the contingent $2 million award it subtracted, using Goodyear's estimates, approximately $700,000 for expenses related to other defendants and the Haegers' medical damages.
sections.Issue: May a federal court imposing a fee sanction under its inherent authority through civil procedures shift expenses beyond those caused by the sanctioned party's misconduct?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States, in 2017, in an opinion by Justice Kagan for all eight participating Justices, Justice Gorsuch not participating, held that it may not. Such an award must compensate the injured litigant, so the innocent party may recover only the fees it would not have incurred but for the misconduct. The $2.7 million award could not stand because neither lower court had applied that causal standard. The Court did not itself uphold the $2 million award, eliminate every sanction, or decide tire-defect liability.
sections.Reasoning:
Federal courts have inherent authority to sanction bad-faith abuse of the judicial process, and reimbursing the opposing party's legal expenses is one permissible sanction. But when a court uses ordinary civil procedures, the award must compensate and not punish; punishment requires the procedural protections applicable to criminal proceedings. Compensation follows the injury actually caused. If the same work would have been necessary even with proper discovery, shifting its cost adds punishment. The Court drew this framework from Fox v. Vice.

The test does not require perfect accounting. A trial judge may estimate, allocate percentages or treat a category of expenses as caused entirely by the misconduct, and appellate review is deferential, but flexibility in calculation does not dispense with causation. An award of every fee can satisfy the test in an exceptional case, for example where the whole suit was brought in bad faith, where a defendant's entire course of conduct was a scheme to defeat a valid claim, or where the court finds that proper disclosure would have produced settlement at a specific point. These apply the but-for rule; they are not exceptions for extreme behavior.

Here the district court let severity replace causation, and the Ninth Circuit used the period of bad faith as its limit; concurrent timing was not enough. The Court declined to supply a finding that timely disclosure would have ended the suit: the district court had said only that settlement probably would have come much earlier, and Goodyear retained plausible defenses, such as that the tire failed from striking road debris. The district court's own alternative award recognized that roughly $700,000 would have been incurred regardless.

The casebook cites the case for the compensatory limit and the rejected comprehensive award; the brief notes that the casebook's statement that Rule 37 sanctions were unavailable because the suit had settled is editorial explanation.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-386.rule: Reasonable corrective-discovery costs caused by an opponent's discovery misconduct may be shifted as a compensatory sanction even when they exceed the likely damages on the underlying claim; that disproportion does not make the sanction punitive.

sections.Parties: Klipsch Group sued ePRO, a Chinese company operating DealExtreme, for selling counterfeit headphones. ePRO admitted some infringing sales but maintained that its liability was small. Both sides appealed: ePRO challenged the discovery sanctions, the evidence and the asset restraints, and Klipsch challenged the refusal to find spoliation of structured sales data.
sections.Procedural History: Klipsch sued in August 2012. The magistrate judge first let ePRO correct its discovery failures with its own vendor, declined immediate sanctions, and later authorized Klipsch's own forensic examination, initially at its expense. Klipsch sought default and larger restraints. After a four-day evidentiary hearing in January 2015, Judge Broderick found willful spoliation of unstructured information but not proven destruction of structured sales data, denied default, reduced the hold tied to underlying sales to $25,000, and ordered discovery sanctions, eventually awarding $2.68 million for corrective discovery along with jury instructions and measures preserving payment. The Second Circuit took interlocutory jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1292(a)(1) over the asset-restraining injunction and pendent jurisdiction over the sanctions issues, and on January 25, 2018 affirmed in all respects, including rejection of Klipsch's cross-appeal.
sections.Material Facts:
By March 2013 ePRO had produced fewer than 500 documents. Its chief executive acknowledged that it had not implemented a litigation hold, and documents it had denied possessing, including original transaction records, turned out to exist. Its vendor's work generated roughly 40,000 documents, including 1,236 original transaction records, but ePRO restricted the vendor's access. The supplemental production led Klipsch to take a second round of depositions in Hong Kong, costing approximately $550,000, which disclosed continued failures to impose a proper hold despite court instructions and counsel's warnings.

The record of unstructured-information spoliation included 4,596 manually deleted documents, all recovered; seven employees' use of wiping software, resulting in 31 unrecoverable documents; operating-system upgrades by eighteen employees that destroyed usage data; missing email accounts; and refusal to permit access to 32 of 36 private messaging accounts.

The district court's $2.68 million award was accompanied by a corresponding asset restraint of roughly $2.7 million and an additional $2.3 million in security for potential treble damages and Lanham Act attorney's fees, based on a finding that ePRO, a foreign company with few American ties that repeatedly disregarded court orders, posed a dissipation risk.
sections.Issue: Can reasonable corrective-discovery costs caused by a party's discovery misconduct be shifted to that party even if they exceed the likely damages on the underlying claim, without making the sanction impermissibly punitive?
sections.Holding: The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, in 2018, in an opinion by Judge Lynch joined by Judge Jacobs and District Judge Crotty, sitting by designation, held that they can. Costs reasonably incurred, assessed when the corrective steps were undertaken, may be shifted when they were caused by the opponent's discovery misconduct, and they do not become punitive merely because the investigation uncovers fewer infringing sales or less spoliation than expected. All the challenged orders were affirmed. The monetary award rested on inherent authority, not Rule 37.
sections.Reasoning:
The court reviewed for abuse of discretion. The record supported a cumulative finding of willful failure to preserve unstructured information, and recovery of one class of documents did not negate other losses. ePRO could not avoid its preservation duty by insisting that employees used personal accounts when those accounts contained company business. The jury would be told that ePRO destroyed relevant unstructured information after its preservation duty arose and could, but need not, infer that the evidence favored Klipsch. Exclusion of ePRO's late expert report was within discretion. Klipsch's cross-appeal failed because direct proof of sales-record destruction was absent and missing backups did not compel an inference about their contents.

The monetary award was compensatory. It covered costs caused by ePRO's failures, beginning with the second Hong Kong depositions, and the court approved successive remedial steps after ePRO had opportunities to correct its conduct. The forensic examination was reasonable when ordered even though it did not substantiate every suspected problem. Klipsch's partial failure on structured information did not require a proportional reduction, and a potentially small merits recovery did not excuse compliance with disclosure and preservation duties. The court distinguished damages-oriented and civil-rights fee analogies from reimbursement of expenses the wrongdoer caused. Citing Goodyear v. Haeger, it noted that a compensatory inherent-power award must reimburse costs that would not have been incurred but for the misconduct, a limit satisfied here, so it did not reach the procedural requirements for punitive sanctions. Inherent sanctions required bad faith, and the court had no occasion to decide whether the December 2015 amendments to Rule 37 applied. It did not endorse unnecessarily broad initial discovery.

The casebook cites the case for the monetary holding, using a rounded $2.7 million figure and identifying inherent authority as its basis.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-387.rule: A court may dismiss on its own initiative only by a fair procedure, generally notice and a meaningful opportunity to respond, and a party must have a full and fair opportunity to discover information essential to opposing summary judgment.

sections.Parties: Audrey Miller, a former tenure-track psychology professor, was the plaintiff and appellant. In one suit she sued Sam Houston State University (SHSU) and the Texas State University System (TSUS), alleging sex discrimination, retaliation, hostile environment and Equal Pay Act violations. In a second she sued the University of Houston Downtown (UHD) and the University of Houston System (UHS), alleging retaliatory refusal to hire. On appeal she challenged the dismissal of the two systems, the denial of reconsideration and the discovery restrictions, and asked for reassignment to another judge.
sections.Procedural History: Miller filed the two suits in September and October 2015. The district court handled them jointly without formally consolidating them. At the initial January 2016 conference the judge required Miller to choose two of the four defendants and dismissed both systems with prejudice; reconsideration was denied the day after it was sought. The court repeatedly refused Miller permission for discovery and in September 2019 granted summary judgment. Miller appealed. The Fifth Circuit reversed the systems' dismissal and the universities' summary judgments, remanded for further proceedings, and directed reassignment to another district judge.
sections.Material Facts:
Miller became a tenure-track psychology professor at SHSU in 2007. She disputed her workload and treatment, while the university described problems with collegiality. SHSU denied tenure in March 2013, she pursued administrative discrimination charges and a grievance, and her employment ended in May 2014. She also applied to UHD. Its search committee rated her highly and recommended an offer, but UHD changed course after its department chair Jackson called SHSU department chair Christopher Wilson about her tenure denial, and it hired three candidates with lower hiring-metric scores. The record did not establish what was said on the call.

Initial orders required court permission for discovery. At the January 2016 conference the judge dismissed both systems without permitting meaningful discussion, briefing or amendment, made statements suggesting prejudgment, and threatened counsel with an adverse result when both parties opposed consolidation. The court repeatedly refused Miller written discovery or depositions while allowing defendants to depose her in the judge's jury room, where the judge attended parts of the deposition and participated. After summary-judgment briefing and argument he allowed one deposition, of Dean Fulton, limited to two hours, and refused further examinations of the relevant chairs and search participants.
sections.Issue: Whether the sua sponte dismissal with prejudice of the two university systems was procedurally fair; whether the district court's refusals of discovery before summary judgment were an abuse of discretion affecting Miller's substantial rights; and whether the cases should be reassigned to another district judge on remand.
sections.Holding: The Fifth Circuit in 2021, in an opinion by Judge Cory T. Wilson joined by Judges Jolly and Southwick, reversed the dismissal of the systems and the summary judgments for the universities, remanded for further proceedings, and directed the Chief Judge of the Southern District of Texas to reassign both cases. Even assuming the abrupt conference exchange was notice, Miller lacked an adequate opportunity to respond or amend, and the cumulative, nearly blanket refusal of necessary discovery denied her a fair opportunity to present her claims. The court did not determine that Miller had proved discrimination, retaliation, unequal pay or damages.
sections.Reasoning:
Reviewing the dismissal de novo, the court said a court may dismiss on its own initiative when the procedure is fair. Notice and a meaningful opportunity to respond generally are required, although notice is not invariably necessary once a plaintiff has fairly presented her best case; the court rejected the argument that Miller had already done so. Forcing her to rely on reconsideration after an immediate dismissal did not cure the unfairness, and reconsideration was prematurely denied because whether the systems were employers is a fact-specific inquiry into control over hiring, firing, supervision, schedules and the economic realities of employment. The court did not decide either system's ultimate employer status.

Discovery rulings were reviewed for abuse of discretion, with reversal requiring arbitrary or clearly unreasonable restrictions affecting substantial rights. District courts retain broad management discretion, but a party must have a full and fair opportunity to discover information essential to opposing summary judgment. The opening management orders alone were not condemned; the error was the cumulative refusal. The Jackson-Wilson call illustrated actual prejudice: UHD reversed its proposed hiring decision after the call, yet neither participant could be deposed. Records from an earlier Texas public-information request did not answer the need.

Reassignment is an extraordinary remedy. The cumulative prejudicial remarks and peremptory rulings satisfied both the stricter test and the more lenient test, which asks whether an objective observer reasonably would question impartiality, and reassignment would not create disproportionate waste because full discovery had not occurred.

The casebook cites the case for the excessive discovery restrictions and the judge's participation in Miller's deposition.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-391.rule: Issues identified at the pretrial conference and incorporated into the pretrial order supersede the pleadings, and pretrial orders and amendments should be construed liberally where the adversary suffers no surprise.

sections.Parties: Howard, a Detroit beverage-plant employee, was the plaintiff and appellant. He sued Kerr Glass Manufacturing Co. in diversity, alleging negligent manufacture and failure to inspect, and sought also to proceed on an implied-warranty theory. Kerr was the defendant and appellee.
sections.Procedural History: The parties discussed a joint pretrial document with the court at a January 1981 conference. At the jury trial about six weeks later the judge prohibited the warranty theory. After the first trial day Howard sought leave to amend, which was denied. The jury rejected negligence, and Howard appealed. The Sixth Circuit remanded solely to let Howard proceed on the asserted breach-of-warranty theory; negligence issues were expressly foreclosed.
sections.Material Facts:
Howard injured his right hand when a bottle or bottles he was handling exploded. Identification of Kerr as the manufacturer and proof of proximate cause depended essentially on circumstantial evidence.

The original complaint did not plead warranty. The parties' joint pretrial document included implied warranty of merchantability and foreseeability as factual issues, and implied warranty of fitness among Howard's claims and theories. Counsel assembled it and discussed it with the court at the January 1981 conference. Howard did not then amend his complaint. The judge had not signed the joint document at the conference, but both parties and the court knew of the warranty theory, the judge treated the document as part of the record, and he later signed it.

At trial the judge limited questioning of the plant's quality-control manager about Kerr's earlier visits, although interrogatory answers establishing visits had already been read to the jury, and refused a requested adverse-inference instruction about Kerr's unused expert. Howard did not seek judgment notwithstanding the verdict under Rule 50(b).
sections.Issue: Whether Howard should have been permitted to proceed on the implied-warranty theory disclosed in the pretrial document despite omitting it from the original complaint, and whether he could obtain appellate relief on the rejected negligence theory.
sections.Holding: The Sixth Circuit in 1983, per curiam on a panel of Judges Krupansky and Wellford and Senior Judge Brown, held that the pretrial procedure and order, or alternatively leave to amend, should have allowed the warranty theory. It held that Howard could not obtain relief on negligence: his failure to seek judgment notwithstanding the verdict under Rule 50(b) prevented appellate consideration of his directed-verdict challenge, and the other trial rulings did not justify reopening negligence. The court did not find warranty liability or award damages, and it did not reopen the entire trial.
sections.Reasoning:
Issues identified at the pretrial conference and incorporated into its order supersede the pleadings, and Rule 16's purposes include considering desirable amendments. Kerr had ample notice of the warranty theory, could not claim surprise, and should have prepared for it. Howard received no adverse indication at the conference that warranty would be excluded. The judge's later signature implied approval that the issue had been presented; the court discussed a possible nunc-pro-tunc analogy rather than announcing that every unsigned proposal automatically binds a judge. Pretrial orders should be construed liberally, as should amendments where the adversary suffers no surprise.

On negligence, the restriction on questioning the quality-control manager did not seriously impair the claim, because the interrogatory answers were before the jury and Howard could argue foreseeability; the court held only that any error did not require remand. Refusing the adverse-inference instruction was not error: Kerr's unused expert was neither its employee nor under its control, Howard did not show the testimony necessarily bore on manufacturer identification, the thin-wall theory or plant procedures at the time of injury, and his own listed expert also did not testify.

The casebook uses Howard to show that a pretrial order can prevail over the original pleading.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-392.rule: A party that fails to identify an issue for trial at the pretrial conference or in the pretrial order can waive its right to litigate that issue, even where the opposing party would bear the burden of proving it.

sections.Parties: McLean Contracting Co., which was replacing a bridge that was struck by a barge, was the plaintiff and appellee; it brought a maritime claim to recover its repair costs. Waterman Steamship Corp., whose vessel had discharged the barge, was the defendant and appellant; it sought to avoid liability on the ground that those who secured the barge were independent contractors.
sections.Procedural History: McLean sued Waterman in the Eastern District of Virginia. The parties consented to trial before a magistrate judge under 28 U.S.C. § 636(c)(1). A final pretrial order was entered February 23, 2001. A few days before trial, Waterman's proposed findings and conclusions first asserted the independent-contractor defense; on McLean's objection the magistrate excluded evidence supporting it. After a bench trial, judgment favored McLean. Waterman appealed both the exclusion and the application of the maritime presumption of fault. The Fourth Circuit affirmed, with no remand.
sections.Material Facts:
McLean was replacing the Newport River Railroad Bridge at Morehead City, North Carolina. Waterman's vessel discharged cargo barges there on August 22, 1998, including CG-5151. Waterman hired James River Towing to supply tugs and labor and Captain Glander to oversee securing the barges. During Hurricane Bonnie on August 27, CG-5151 broke loose and struck the bridge. McLean repaired the damage, incurring approximately $17,562.33 in out-of-pocket expenses.

The final pretrial order identified trial issues and factual contentions. Waterman stipulated that it operated CG-5151. Its disputed issues concerned McLean's standing, economic-loss recovery, an act-of-God defense, and reasonable securing of the barges. The order did not dispute agency or identify the towing company or Glander as independently responsible. Waterman never sought modification of the pretrial order, and it supplied no evidence identifying why its barge escaped its moorings.
sections.Issue: Whether it was an abuse of discretion to bar an independent-contractor defense that was omitted from the pretrial order, and whether the court could apply the maritime presumption of fault to Waterman on this record.
sections.Holding: The Fourth Circuit in 2002, in an opinion by Judge Williams joined by Judges Wilkinson and Gregory, held that excluding the defense was not an abuse of discretion, because Waterman knew agency was integral to McLean's liability theory and failed to identify it as disputed. It also held that, after proper exclusion of the unpreserved defense, the magistrate reasonably assumed the parties securing the barge were Waterman's agents and could impute their fault to it under the presumption. The court did not decide whether an independent-contractor relationship would have been proved had the evidence been admitted.
sections.Reasoning:
The burden to identify an issue for trial differs from the burden to prove it once disputed. McLean ordinarily would bear the burden of proving agency, and requiring Waterman to disclose that it disputed agency did not shift that burden. It served Rule 16's function of defining the actual controversy so the parties and the court could prepare efficiently. A party that fails to identify a trial issue at the pretrial conference or in the order can waive its right to litigate it. The court examined the order as a whole rather than finding waiver from one isolated omission: the pleadings and pretrial order made McLean's imputed-liability theory clear, Waterman conceded its awareness, and it listed other issues and stipulated operation without disputing agency. Because Waterman never sought modification of the order, the court expressly reserved whether a requested modification would have been proper.

Under The Oregon presumption, a moving vessel striking a stationary, visible object is presumed at fault. The presumption does not ordinarily impose personal liability on a barge owner for independent contractors' fault; Waterman was correct about that rule but could not use it to revive its waived agency defense. An established act-of-God cause could also defeat the presumption, but the magistrate rejected that defense and Waterman did not appeal that finding.

The casebook uses the case to present waiver of an issue omitted from the pretrial order.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-402.rule: Under Rule 41(a)(2), voluntary dismissal without prejudice should ordinarily be permitted unless the defendant will suffer clear legal prejudice beyond the prospect of another suit, and the possible loss of a limitations defense, absent bad faith, is not by itself such prejudice.

sections.Parties: Reta McCants, administratrix of Johnny McCants, was the plaintiff and appellee; she alleged that a defect in a military jeep manufactured by Ford caused his death and sought voluntary dismissal without prejudice so that she could sue in Mississippi. Ford Motor Co. was the defendant and appellant; it opposed dismissal or, alternatively, sought protective conditions.
sections.Procedural History: McCants first sued AM General in Alabama on July 20, 1983; the court denied her leave to amend to name Ford and dismissed that action without prejudice. She filed the present action against Ford on November 14, 1983. Ford moved for summary judgment on limitations on August 24, 1984. McCants moved for voluntary dismissal on January 15, 1985. The district court denied summary judgment and then dismissed without prejudice, imposing no conditions and explaining neither decision. Ford appealed. The Eleventh Circuit vacated and remanded for an express ruling on Ford's requested conditions, retaining appellate jurisdiction. This brief concerns the February 1986 decision; a later post-remand opinion is a separate stage.
sections.Material Facts:
Johnny McCants died on July 24, 1982, while serving a two-week Army Reserve assignment in Mississippi. His administratrix initially sued AM General, believing it had manufactured the jeep, and sued Ford after learning that Ford was the manufacturer.

Ford initially omitted a limitations defense from its answer. Discovery continued from December 1983 through 1984. Ford amended its answer on July 18, 1984, to assert Alabama's one-year limitations period and then moved for summary judgment. McCants disputed that limitations barred her claim. She moved for voluntary dismissal without prejudice three days before the scheduled summary-judgment hearing, intending to sue in Mississippi under its longer limitations period. Summary judgment was denied the day before dismissal.

Discovery and depositions had generated considerable expense. Ford also asserted that a discovery order would have prevented McCants from presenting experts and asked to preserve that benefit in later litigation. Ford's January opposition memorandum was absent from the appellate record.
sections.Issue: Whether the prospect of losing a limitations defense in a later forum, alone or combined with litigation expense, requires denial of voluntary dismissal under Rule 41(a)(2), and whether the unconditional dismissal was adequately justified.
sections.Holding: The Eleventh Circuit in 1986 held that Ford's potential loss of its limitations defense did not itself make dismissal an abuse of discretion, and that Ford's substantial litigation expense did not require a different result when dismissal was considered apart from its conditions. But the record did not permit review of the district court's implicit rejection of Ford's requested conditions, so the court vacated and remanded for a ruling on that request with supporting findings and conclusions. It did not direct dismissal with prejudice, finally award fees, or mandate another evidentiary hearing.
sections.Reasoning:
After the defendant has answered, voluntary dismissal requires a court order on terms the court considers proper. The district court exercises broad equitable discretion, principally to protect the defendant from unfair consequences. Dismissal ordinarily should be permitted absent clear legal prejudice beyond the prospect of another suit, and a possible tactical advantage to the plaintiff does not itself require refusal.

The court assumed, without deciding, that Alabama's one-year period barred this suit and that Mississippi's longer period would permit a new action. Authorities differed on whether loss of a limitations defense is legal prejudice. The court favored decisions allowing dismissal absent intentional abuse and found support in binding former Fifth Circuit precedent, Durham, where voluntary dismissal could let a plaintiff pursue a claim overcoming an advantageous contributory-negligence defense. The record showed no bad faith by McCants or counsel.

Whether dismissal is permissible does not establish that unconditional dismissal properly protects the defendant. A plaintiff ordinarily cannot dismiss without prejudice after putting a defendant to considerable trial-preparation expense without reimbursing at least some litigation expenses, which may include reasonable attorney fees; where a similar action is contemplated, reimbursement may be limited to work that will not be useful in the later case. Nonmonetary conditions may also protect the defendant. Without an explicit ruling or explanation, and unable to tell which work was wasted or reusable, the court could not assess the district court's exercise of discretion.

The casebook describes McCants as filing in Mississippi; the opinion describes only her intention to do so.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-403.rule: A district court abuses its discretion under Rule 41(a)(2) if it allows a voluntary dismissal that would cause the defendant plain legal prejudice, which includes losing a limitations defense that state law treats as a vested right extinguishing the cause of action.

sections.Parties: Bonnie Wojtas and her husband, who claimed a marital-property interest in her IRA funds, were the plaintiffs and appellants. They sued Capital Guardian Trust, later known as Capital Bank & Trust, the original custodian of the IRA, for negligence and breach of fiduciary duty, and later sought dismissal without prejudice so they could refile in Illinois. Capital was the defendant and appellee and sought judgment on the pleadings.
sections.Procedural History: The plaintiffs sued in state court, and Capital removed to federal court in the Western District of Wisconsin on diversity grounds. Capital answered and moved for judgment on the pleadings under Rule 12(c). The plaintiffs requested dismissal without prejudice under Rule 41(a)(2). The district court denied voluntary dismissal and entered judgment on the pleadings, dismissing the suit with prejudice as untimely. The plaintiffs appealed both decisions. The Seventh Circuit affirmed.
sections.Material Facts:
Bonnie Wojtas owned an IRA held by Capital. In April 1999 she directed Capital to transfer the investments to an IRA managed by Insurance Planning & Design. An employee of the successor company converted the funds and was later convicted of mail fraud. The plaintiffs alleged that Capital should have checked whether the successor they selected was qualified by the IRS to act as custodian.

Capital's Rule 12(c) motion argued that both claims rested on the same alleged fiduciary breach and were barred by Wisconsin's two-year limitations period, because the complaint came more than two years after the plaintiffs said they learned of their injury through the successor employee's indictment. Alternatively, it argued it owed no duty to investigate their selected successor. The plaintiffs answered the no-duty argument but offered no response to the limitations argument. They instead requested dismissal without prejudice, proposing to refile in Illinois under a longer limitations period.
sections.Issue: Whether the plaintiffs waived opposition to the limitations argument by failing to respond to it, and whether the district court abused its discretion by refusing a Rule 41(a)(2) dismissal without prejudice that would have let the plaintiffs refile where a longer limitations period applied.
sections.Holding: The Seventh Circuit in 2007, in an opinion by Judge Sykes for a panel with Chief Judge Easterbrook and Judge Manion, affirmed the denial of voluntary dismissal and the judgment on the pleadings dismissing both claims with prejudice on limitations grounds. The plaintiffs' failure to oppose the limitations argument was a waiver, and losing a limitations defense that Wisconsin law makes a vested right would have been plain legal prejudice to Capital, so refusing dismissal was not an abuse of discretion. The court did not decide Capital's alternative no-duty contention or whether Capital committed an actionable breach.
sections.Reasoning:
On appeal the plaintiffs argued that their negligence claim remained timely under Wisconsin's six-year property-injury provision because Capital's motion supposedly addressed only the fiduciary-duty claim. The court rejected that description: the motion unambiguously sought dismissal of both claims and argued that negligence merely relabeled the same alleged breach. The plaintiffs' silence supported the district court's inference that they acquiesced in the proposed limitations treatment.

Because Capital had answered, a Rule 41(a)(2) dismissal required a court order, and the district court had discretion over whether to allow dismissal and over its terms. Allowing dismissal that would cause the defendant plain legal prejudice would abuse that discretion. The plaintiffs relied on Bolten, where voluntary dismissal allowed refiling in a state with a longer limitations period. The court gave two answers. First, Bolten's treatment of dismissal as a right, with discretion confined to conditions, had been expressly rejected by later circuit decisions. Second, the limitations bar in Bolten concerned only the remedy in that forum, whereas Wisconsin law extinguished the cause of action as well as the remedy and created a vested right in the defendant to insist on the bar. Losing that substantive protection went beyond the ordinary expense and annoyance of defending a second lawsuit.

The casebook's account says the plaintiff filed a new Illinois action; the opinion reports only a request to dismiss so the plaintiffs could refile.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-404.rule: Under Rule 41(d) a court may stay a refiled action until the plaintiff pays the costs of the earlier dismissed action and may dismiss the whole action for noncompliance; attorney fees count as such costs only where the underlying statute defines costs to include fees.

sections.Parties: Gerald Esposito, a federal pretrial detainee, was the plaintiff and appellant; he alleged that St. Clair County jail nurses were deliberately indifferent to his serious medical needs and sought reinstatement of his entire second suit. The defendants in that suit were six nurses, including Ron Smith and Francis Piatrowski, who had been defendants in his first action.
sections.Procedural History: In the first § 1983 action Esposito voluntarily dismissed Smith by stipulation; the court dismissed Piatrowski without prejudice and converted that to dismissal with prejudice in January 1997 when Esposito failed to amend. He neither appealed nor sought Rule 60(b) relief. He filed a second action in April 1997. Piatrowski obtained dismissal on claim-preclusion grounds. On March 4, 1998, on Smith's Rule 41(d) request, the district court adopted a magistrate judge's recommendation, ordered a bill of costs and stayed the proceedings. In July 1999 it dismissed the second action without prejudice for want of prosecution, and the judgment encompassed all six defendants. Esposito appealed. The Seventh Circuit affirmed.
sections.Material Facts: Esposito's second action named six nurses, including Smith and Piatrowski, and alleged misconduct from April 1995 through January 1996. Two defendants were never served. Smith requested costs from the first action under Rule 41(d), with a stay pending payment. After the district court ordered a bill of costs and stayed the proceedings, Smith submitted a $6,758.91 bill that included fees and other expenses. Esposito paid nothing, unsuccessfully sought reconsideration, and ignored a September compliance-report order. He asserted an inability to pay. No finding had been made that his action was frivolous, unreasonable or groundless.
sections.Issue: Whether failure to pay Rule 41(d) costs owed to one repeat defendant can support dismissal of the entire second action, including new defendants, and whether attorney fees are automatically recoverable as Rule 41(d) costs.
sections.Holding: The Seventh Circuit in 2000, in an opinion by Judge Coffey for a panel with Judges Easterbrook and Evans, held that the whole second action could be stayed and then dismissed for want of prosecution when Esposito paid none of the costs ordered, and affirmed. It held that attorney fees are not automatically recoverable as Rule 41(d) costs; reasonable fees are allowed where the underlying substantive statute defines recoverable costs to include fees, subject to that statute's requirements. The court did not hold that the entire fee-inclusive bill was authorized and did not decide Piatrowski's preclusion defense.
sections.Reasoning:
Rule 41(d) authorizes costs when a previously dismissed claim is brought against the same defendant and permits a stay of the action pending compliance; its language does not limit the stay to that defendant's claims. Rule 41(b) permits dismissal for failure to prosecute or comply with a court order, reviewed for abuse of discretion. Staying and dismissing the whole action protected both the repeat defendant and the new defendants from the consequences of disregard for the payment order.

On fees, the court applied the American Rule and borrowed Marek's treatment of Rule 68: an undefined reference to costs incorporates fee recovery when the underlying statute makes fees part of costs. Rule 41(d) itself does not generally displace the American Rule. The result accords with Rule 41(a)(2)'s allowance of fee conditions and with Rule 41(d)'s deterrence of forum shopping and vexatious litigation.

Esposito's § 1983 action implicated § 1988, under which a prevailing defense may obtain fees only on a finding that the action was frivolous, unreasonable or groundless. No such finding had been made, so fees could not properly be included on that basis. But the appeal concerned dismissal of the second suit rather than the deferred costs award, and Esposito had paid no costs at all, so the improper fee component did not require reversal. The court distinguished a case in which a plaintiff paid ordinary costs while refusing only attorney fees. His asserted inability to pay did not excuse complete noncompliance.

The casebook cites the case for dismissal extending to all defendants, though it compresses the chronology: the costs-and-stay order was entered in the second action after refiling.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-406.rule: A federal trial court has inherent power to dismiss an action with prejudice for failure to prosecute on its own initiative, without a defendant's motion under Rule 41(b), and a client is bound by the acts and omissions of freely chosen counsel.

sections.Parties: William Link was the plaintiff and the petitioner in the Supreme Court; he brought a diversity negligence action seeking compensation for injuries from a collision between his vehicle and a Wabash train. Wabash Railroad Co. was the defendant and respondent. Link challenged the district court's power to dismiss his case on its own initiative and its exercise of that power.
sections.Procedural History: Link filed suit in August 1954. The district court entered judgment on the pleadings for the railroad; the Seventh Circuit reversed in 1956, and the Court denied the railroad's petition in 1957. After further trial settings and continuances, the district court on October 12, 1960 dismissed the case on its own initiative, invoking inherent authority and failure to prosecute, when Link's counsel did not attend a pretrial conference.
