sections.Holding: The Connecticut Appellate Court in 2007, in an opinion by Judge Peters with Judges DiPentima and Lavine concurring, held that service on the reinsurers' contractually designated agents satisfied the governing service requirement and entitled the plaintiffs to a judicial determination of security; that the industrial-insured exclusion did not apply to these reinsurance contracts; and that the amount of security required an evidentiary hearing at which both sides could present evidence. It reversed the denial of security and remanded. It fixed no amount and awarded neither contract damages nor a default judgment.
sections.Reasoning:
On service, section 38a-25 supplied substituted service through the commissioner, but its subsection (e) preserved service in any other legally permitted manner; reading the statute to exclude a designated agent would leave that subsection without work. The court acknowledged a textual difficulty, because section 38a-27 also cross-referenced other sections that a broad reading could make redundant. It resolved the difficulty by reading the connected provisions as remedial legislation meant to protect Connecticut insureds from having to pursue unauthorized insurers in distant forums. Liberal construction supported contractual-agent service, and it would be illogical to exclude a contractually authorized method likely to reach the insurers promptly.

On the industrial-insured objection, the defendants relied on section 38a-271(c)(5), but subsection (b)(2) excluded lawful reinsurance transactions from sections 38a-271 through 38a-278. Read together, that exclusion prevented the defendants from applying the industrial-insured exception to these reinsurance contracts.

On the amount, section 38a-27 did not say hearing, but its requirements of court approval and a court-fixed amount were construed to include one, avoiding the constitutional danger of a literal reading. Under Doehr's prejudgment-remedy analysis the court considered the private interest affected, the risk of error and useful safeguards, and the interest of the party seeking the remedy. Prepleading security impairs a defendant's use of property before liability is determined, much as prejudgment attachment does. The closely similar New York statute, upheld with safeguards including an opportunity to be heard, was persuasive support.

The casebook uses the case for the hearing requirement; the brief notes that the casebook omits the two statutory holdings needed to reach it.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-474.rule: A defendant's cross-complaint reduces or defeats a prejudgment attachment only if the defendant shows the probable validity of its own claim; merely filing a larger offsetting claim does not bar attachment.

sections.Parties: Lydig Construction, the plaintiff and a general contractor, sued its rebar subcontractor Martinez Steel Corporation and Martinez's owner for breach of contract and applied for a prejudgment attachment. Martinez and its owner opposed the application and Martinez filed a cross-complaint alleging amounts exceeding Lydig's claims. Martinez appealed from the right-to-attach order; Lydig defended it.
sections.Procedural History: Lydig sued in March 2013, alleging breach and damages exceeding $200,000, and applied for attachment in April. On May 14 Martinez and its owner answered and opposed the application. By stipulation Martinez filed its cross-complaint on May 20, and the court heard the attachment application that day, heard argument about the offsets, and took the matter under submission. It later granted attachment against Martinez only, for $203,315, and Lydig obtained writs in Riverside, Los Angeles, and San Bernardino counties. Martinez appealed from the right-to-attach order. The Court of Appeal affirmed and awarded Lydig its appellate costs.
sections.Material Facts:
Lydig won the 2010 general contract to expand San Bernardino County's Adelanto Detention Center, relying partly on Martinez's rebar bid. Their subcontract became effective January 14, 2011. Martinez could not provide the required payment and performance bonds, and Lydig accepted its owner's personal guaranty instead. By February 2012 Martinez's steel supplier required cash, so Lydig bought steel and shipped it to Martinez. In June 2012 Lydig discovered that Martinez had diverted 100,000 pounds of that steel to other projects. After a formal substitution process and an August county hearing, the county authorized termination of the subcontract, and Lydig engaged another supplier.

Lydig supported its attachment application with employee declarations, business records, and a verified copy of the county hearing officer's findings. Martinez's employee Harry Williams asserted retained payments, work billed after termination, disputed change orders, and more than 200,000 pounds of uncredited steel deliveries, without rebutting the application's specific factual account. Lydig's reply supplied testimony about delayed pours, accounting records defeating the retention claim, and a contemporaneous steel-delivery log contradicting the claimed additional deliveries.
sections.Issue: Did the filing of a cross-complaint alleging an offset larger than the plaintiff's claim deprive the trial court of power to grant a prejudgment attachment, or must the defendant establish the probable validity of its offsetting claim?
sections.Holding: The California Court of Appeal, Fourth District, Division One, in 2015, in an opinion by Acting Presiding Justice Benke in which Justices Haller and McDonald concurred, held that a cross-complaint alleging a larger offset does not automatically defeat attachment. The defendant must establish the probable validity of its claim, and Martinez's conclusory declaration, contradicted by Lydig's business records, did not meet that standard. The court affirmed the orders authorizing attachment of $203,315 against Martinez only and awarded Lydig its appellate costs. This was review of provisional security, not a final award of contract damages.
sections.Reasoning:
An appellant must show reversible error on an adequate record, silence in the record supports presumptions favoring the order, and a trial court's resolution of factual conflicts in affidavits is not disturbed on appeal.

Attachment generally required a money claim on an express or implied contract for a fixed or readily ascertainable sum of at least $500. Section 484.090 required an eligible claim, probable validity, a proper purpose, and an amount to be secured greater than zero; under section 481.190 probable validity means the claimant is more likely than not to obtain judgment. Section 483.015(b)(2) required the secured amount to be reduced by an indebtedness asserted in a filed cross-complaint if the defendant's claim was itself one upon which an attachment could issue.

That qualifying language decided the case. A claim upon which attachment could issue must satisfy the same probable-validity requirement. Otherwise any defendant could defeat a well-supported attachment by asserting a speculative counterclaim, frustrating the Legislature's provision of prejudgment security.

The trial judge implicitly found Martinez's claims insufficient. The record showed the judge noticed the offsets, heard argument, and said the documentation would be considered, so the appellate court presumed the pertinent evidence was considered. Williams's conclusory assertions about retained funds and 200,000 pounds of steel were contradicted by accounting records and contemporaneous delivery logs. Lydig's own showing was supported by declarations and documentation. The decision does not forbid offsets generally; it requires evidence meeting the statutory standard.

The casebook uses the case as an unsuccessful attempt to defeat attachment through an offset exceeding the applicant's claim; the brief notes that the casebook's term for the standard should be read as probable validity.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-475.rule: A preliminary-injunction applicant must show likely success on the merits, likely (not merely possible) irreparable harm without preliminary relief, a favorable balance of equities, and that an injunction is consistent with the public interest.

sections.Parties: Environmental organizations and individuals sued the Navy under NEPA and other environmental laws, seeking to restrict the Navy's use of mid-frequency active sonar in training exercises off Southern California because of asserted harm to marine mammals. The Navy, enjoined below, challenged two of the injunction's restrictions in the Court.
sections.Procedural History:
The district court initially prohibited active-sonar use. The Ninth Circuit found that remedy overbroad and directed a narrower injunction permitting training with mitigation. On remand the district judge imposed six additional restrictions. The Navy then obtained executive relief: the President granted a statutory exemption from Coastal Zone Management Act requirements, and the Council on Environmental Quality approved alternative NEPA arrangements on a finding of emergency circumstances. The district court refused to dissolve the challenged restrictions and the Ninth Circuit affirmed, questioning the validity of the emergency arrangements, finding likely success on the NEPA claim, and treating a possibility of irreparable injury as sufficient where merits prospects were strong.

The Court reversed the Ninth Circuit and vacated the preliminary injunction only to the extent challenged by the Navy.
sections.Material Facts:
The Navy conducts integrated strike-group exercises and regarded training with mid-frequency active sonar as essential to certifying strike groups for deployment, because quiet diesel-electric submarines can evade passive detection. The waters off Southern California were particularly useful but contained at least thirty-seven species of marine mammals. Plaintiffs maintained that sonar could cause serious injuries and behavioral disruptions; the Navy disputed the harm and emphasized forty years of regional training without a documented sonar-related mammal injury.

A 2007 national-defense exemption from the Marine Mammal Protection Act required mitigation, including lookouts, graduated power reductions, and complete sonar shutdown within 200 yards. The Navy prepared an environmental assessment for fourteen exercises scheduled through January 2009 and found no significant environmental impact, rather than completing an environmental impact statement before the exercises.

The two restrictions the Navy challenged were shutdown when a mammal was detected within 2,200 yards and a six-decibel power reduction during significant surface ducting, an ocean condition affecting sound propagation. Four other mitigation restrictions were not challenged.
sections.Issue: What showing of irreparable harm a preliminary injunction requires, and whether the two challenged restrictions on Navy sonar training could stand given the balance of equities and the public interest.
sections.Holding: The Court in 2008, in an opinion by Chief Justice Roberts joined by Justices Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas and Alito, held that a preliminary-injunction applicant must show likely irreparable harm, not a mere possibility, along with likely success on the merits, a favorable balance of equities, and consistency with the public interest. Here the balance of equities and the public interest independently required removal of the two challenged restrictions, even assuming plaintiffs had shown irreparable injury and could prevail on the environmental claim. The Court reversed the Ninth Circuit and vacated the injunction only to the extent the Navy challenged it; it did not resolve the underlying NEPA claim or the legality of the executive arrangements.
sections.Reasoning:
A preliminary injunction is extraordinary relief, not an entitlement that follows automatically from a plausible legal claim, and a mere possibility of harm is too permissive a standard. The Court did not simply find that plaintiffs had proved no environmental danger: it was uncertain whether the Ninth Circuit's incorrect verbal standard affected its analysis, since that court had also affirmed a finding of near-certain harm, and the lower court had not reassessed residual harm after the four unchallenged restrictions. It held that even a showing of irreparable injury would not overcome the balance of equities and public interest on this record, and so did not resolve likely merits success.

The majority credited detailed declarations from senior Navy officers. Courts must give appropriate deference to military judgments about readiness, though military interests do not invariably prevail. The 2,200-yard shutdown radius increased the covered surface area more than one hundredfold over the 200-yard requirement, and one interruption could waste a scenario that took days to develop. Surface ducting was rare, which made training under it harder to replace, and a six-decibel reduction was a seventy-five-percent power reduction. The same balance would preclude a permanent injunction imposing these restrictions; a court could consider declaratory relief or relief tailored to preparation of an environmental impact statement.

Justice Breyer, joined by Justice Stevens in Part I only, also concluded the challenged injunction lacked adequate support, but in Part II would have retained the modified mitigation conditions of the Ninth Circuit's temporary stay until an acceptable statement was complete. Justice Ginsburg, joined by Justice Souter, would have affirmed, emphasizing NEPA's requirement of review before action and defending equitable flexibility and a sliding-scale approach.

The brief notes that the casebook accurately states the four factors and the rejection of a mere possibility of irreparable injury, but that its short account should not be read as a finding that plaintiffs lacked likely injury or that the Navy prevailed on NEPA compliance.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-478.rule: A federal district court lacks equitable authority to issue a preliminary injunction freezing an unsecured debtor's assets before judgment in a suit for contract damages where the plaintiff claims no lien or equitable interest in those assets.

sections.Parties: The respondent investment funds, holders of approximately $75 million of unsecured notes, sued Grupo Mexicano de Desarrollo, a Mexican holding company, in federal court in New York for $80.9 million in contract damages and sought a freeze on its assets. Grupo, the defendant debtor, challenged the preliminary injunction on appeal. The United States supported the funds.
sections.Procedural History: The district court entered a temporary order and then a preliminary injunction against transfers of the toll-road notes, requiring the funds to post a $50,000 bond. The Second Circuit affirmed. While that interlocutory appeal proceeded, the district court granted the funds summary judgment, dismissed Grupo's counterclaims, ordered payment of approximately $82.44 million through assignment or transfer of toll-road assets, and converted the restraint into a permanent injunction. Grupo abandoned its appeal from the permanent injunction, although its appeal from the payment order remained pending. The Court reversed the Second Circuit and remanded.
sections.Material Facts:
Grupo, a Mexican holding company involved in toll-road construction, issued $250 million in unsecured notes in 1994, guaranteed by four subsidiaries. The notes ranked equally with other unsecured, unsubordinated debt. Economic problems undermined the toll-road program, and under a Mexican government rescue program Grupo expected approximately $309 million of toll-road notes.

Grupo missed the August 1997 interest payment. It announced transfers of rights to toll-road notes for employee compensation and to the Mexican government, apparently for taxes, while negotiations with the funds failed. On December 11 the funds accelerated their debt, and on December 12 they sued in New York, a forum to which Grupo had consented. They alleged that Grupo was insolvent or approaching insolvency and was preferring Mexican creditors by disposing of its principal assets, and sought a freeze to preserve assets from which a future judgment might be collected. The district court found near-certain success on the contract claim, irreparable injury, and a serious risk that dissipation would frustrate collection. The funds claimed no lien or equitable interest in the assets.
sections.Issue: Whether the challenge to the preliminary injunction was moot once a permanent injunction issued, and whether a federal district court has authority to freeze an unsecured debtor's assets before judgment in a suit seeking contract damages.
sections.Holding: The Court in 1999, in an opinion by Justice Scalia, held unanimously that Grupo's potential claim on the injunction bond kept the challenge alive, and held 5-4 on the merits that the district court lacked authority to freeze an unsecured debtor's assets before judgment in a contract-damages suit where the plaintiffs claimed no lien or equitable interest in those assets. It reversed the Second Circuit and remanded. It did not disturb the debt judgment or decide liability on the bond, and it expressly reserved the effect of state fraudulent-conveyance statutes.
sections.Reasoning:
On mootness, a permanent injunction ordinarily supersedes a preliminary one, but Grupo asserted a potential bond claim for harm from an unauthorized pre-judgment freeze. Winning the contract suit did not show that the earlier asset dispositions were unlawful, so a restraint designed to secure a future judgment could be wrongful even if the eventual judgment was valid.

On the merits, federal equity power under the Judiciary Act derives from the traditional principles and remedies of English Chancery at the founding, and Rule 65 regulates procedure without enlarging the available remedies. The historical creditor's bill generally required a creditor first to obtain a judgment; an unsecured claimant had no cognizable interest in particular debtor property. That requirement protected substantive property rights, and merging law and equity did not eliminate it. The majority distinguished Deckert, which sought equitable rescission and restitution, and First National City Bank, which involved a tax-enforcement statute and a governmental equitable lien, and noted De Beers's warning against unrelated asset freezes. England's Mareva injunctions emerged in 1975 as a substantial departure from earlier practice. Whether to authorize so substantial a new remedy, with its effects on state attachment rules, creditor races and bankruptcy law, was a policy choice for Congress.

Justice Ginsburg, joined by Justices Stevens, Souter and Breyer, agreed on mootness but would have affirmed. She read the grant of equity power as incorporating adaptable principles rather than freezing remedies at eighteenth-century practice, and emphasized safeguards such as a strong merits showing, substantiated danger of noncollection, and a bond.

The brief notes that the casebook describes the freeze as pending adjudication of the plaintiffs' "right to a lien," whereas no lien or equitable interest was claimed, a premise central to the majority's reasoning.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-480.rule: A receivership is an extraordinary remedy to preserve property that is the subject of the litigation; a court may not place a litigant's unrelated property in receivership to pay unsecured creditors or to control vexatious litigation conduct.

sections.Parties: Netsphere and Munish Krishan, the plaintiffs, sued Jeffrey Baron and Ondova Limited Company to enforce a memorandum settling disputes over an internet domain-name joint venture. Daniel Sherman, the Chapter 11 trustee in Ondova's bankruptcy, moved for a receiver over Baron's property. Baron, as appellant, sought to undo the receivership; the receiver and the trustee defended it. Novo Point and Quantec, entities owned by a trust of which Baron was beneficiary, were covered by the receivership.
sections.Procedural History: Krishan and Netsphere sued in May 2009; a June injunction compelled compliance with the settlement memorandum. On the eve of a July contempt hearing Ondova filed bankruptcy, staying the district court litigation, and the bankruptcy court appointed a Chapter 11 trustee. A July 2010 global settlement was approved by the bankruptcy court on July 28. The trustee moved on November 24, 2010 for a receiver, and the district court granted the motion that day without notice to Baron; it later held a January 2011 evidentiary hearing and denied vacatur. Twelve consolidated appellate proceedings followed, with jurisdiction over the appointment order under 28 U.S.C. section 1292(a)(2). The Fifth Circuit reversed the appointment and directed vacatur, discharge of the receiver, and winding up.
sections.Material Facts:
Baron and Krishan had a joint venture involving internet domain names. At least seven lawsuits and four mediation efforts preceded an April 2009 settlement memorandum. The July 2010 global settlement divided the domain portfolios, with odd-numbered names going to Quantec for Baron's benefit and even-numbered names to Krishan-controlled Manila Industries.

Meanwhile Baron's repeated hiring and firing of lawyers created unpaid fee claims. At a September hearing the trustee's lawyer presented a chart identifying forty-five unpaid lawyers, and former counsel Gerrit Pronske testified about six months of unpaid work and planned offshore transfers. The Village Trust in the Cook Islands owned Novo Point and Quantec, and Baron was its beneficiary. The bankruptcy court ordered a $330,000 security deposit and later recommended Peter Vogel as special master to mediate fee claims. After another firing, the trustee sought the receivership.

The district court stressed delay, increased costs, unpaid counsel, ignored orders, and possible offshore transfers, but did not find that Baron had failed to transfer the domain names the settlement required. The receivership reached phones, computers, mail, home keys, accounts, and requests for medical-care funds.
sections.Issue: Did the district court abuse its discretion by appointing a receiver over a litigant's personal property and controlled entities, which were not the subject of the underlying dispute, in order to pay unsecured attorney fee claims and control vexatious litigation? If so, who bears the receivership's expenses?
sections.Holding: The Fifth Circuit in 2012, in an opinion by Judge Southwick for a panel with Judges DeMoss and Higginson, held that the district court abused its discretion by using a receivership over property outside the underlying dispute to pay unsecured attorney claims and control vexatious litigation. It reversed the appointment and directed vacatur, discharge, and winding up. Reasonable receivership expenses could nevertheless be charged to existing receivership cash after reconsideration, but further asset sales were forbidden. The court also dismissed a law firm's appeal, denied a challenge to a subpoena for counsel's IOLTA records as moot, and held a recusal-affidavit issue waived.
sections.Reasoning:
Receivership is an extraordinary means of preserving property pending disposition, justified by a clear need to protect an interest in property, inadequate lesser remedies, and benefits exceeding burdens. The recognized examples did not authorize seizing unrelated personal assets merely to secure potential judgments or to manage a litigant.

The court took the three asserted justifications in turn. As to preserving jurisdiction, the All Writs Act permits measures supporting jurisdiction actually exercised. The underlying business was settlement enforcement and domain transfers, and no record evidence showed Baron had failed to transfer the names or threatened to move them beyond reach; the evidence supported concern about fees, not loss of the subject property. As to paying attorneys, unsecured contract creditors ordinarily lack a substantive interest in the debtor's property. Their claims were not judgments or the subject matter of the suit, and they could file bankruptcy claims or collection suits. The court applied to receivership the equitable limits that Fredeman, De Beers, and Grupo Mexicano place on freezing unrelated assets. As to controlling litigation, docket control and frustration with ordinary remedies created no receivership power; the court pointed to contempt, fines or imprisonment for violating a specific lawful order, or requiring Baron to keep existing counsel or proceed pro se.

On fees, allocation was equitable. The bankruptcy court recommended the appointment, the trustee sought it accordingly, and the panel found no bad faith; although the receivership did not benefit Baron, his own conduct substantially created the circumstances. Reasonable expenses could therefore be paid from cash already held, with all fees reconsidered.

The casebook cites the case for the limit on reaching unrelated property.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-481.rule: State officers may arrest and hold a person only with authority under state law; Massachusetts common law and statutes give court officers no power to hold an otherwise releasable person solely on a federal civil immigration detainer.

sections.Parties: Lunn, who was kept in a Boston Municipal Court holding cell after his criminal case was dismissed until federal officials took custody, petitioned a single justice of the Supreme Judicial Court the next morning for release, alleging that court officers lacked authority to detain him on a federal civil immigration detainer. The Commonwealth was the respondent, and the Sheriff of Suffolk County intervened. The United States urged that state officers had inherent authority to cooperate.
sections.Procedural History: Lunn was arraigned in the Boston Municipal Court in October 2016. On February 6, 2017, the judge dismissed the charge for lack of prosecution and declined to act on counsel's request for release. The next morning counsel filed a supervisory petition under G. L. c. 211, section 3. Lunn was by then in federal custody, making the requested release moot, but the single justice reserved and reported the issues as important, recurring, time-sensitive, and likely to evade review. The full court remanded to the county court for a judgment dismissing the case as moot and declaring that Massachusetts law provides no authority to hold an otherwise releasable individual solely on a federal civil immigration detainer.
sections.Material Facts:
Lunn was arraigned on an unarmed-robbery charge, later reduced with his consent to larceny from a person. A federal immigration officer had issued a civil immigration detainer the day before arraignment. It asked state custodians to keep him for up to forty-eight hours after he otherwise became entitled to release so that federal authorities could assume custody. Bail was set at $1,500 and later reduced to $750; Lunn could afford the lower amount but did not post it because he believed the detainer would prevent release anyway.

At the second scheduled trial date the Commonwealth was not ready, and the judge dismissed the case. With no Massachusetts charge pending, counsel asked for release and the judge declined to act. Court officers kept Lunn in a holding cell until federal officials took custody several hours later; the record did not give the exact duration. The detainer was a civil request concerning possible removal, not a criminal warrant, criminal detainer, or charge, and the record did not establish that Lunn had committed an immigration crime. No written 287(g) agreement was involved.
sections.Issue: Could Massachusetts court officers arrest and hold a person who was otherwise entitled to release solely on the basis of a federal civil immigration detainer, either under Massachusetts common law or statutes, an inherent authority, or 8 U.S.C. section 1357(g)(10)?
sections.Holding: The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court in 2017, in an opinion by the court with seven Justices participating and no separate writings, held that they could not. Neither Massachusetts common law nor its statutes authorized such an arrest, the court declined to create inherent or implicit authority, and it rejected reading 8 U.S.C. section 1357(g)(10) as an independent grant of arrest power absent state authority. It remanded for a judgment dismissing Lunn's case as moot and declaring the absence of state authority. It reserved detention under a written 287(g) agreement and cases where an officer has probable cause of a federal crime, and did not decide whether such an arrest, if authorized, would comply with the federal or Massachusetts constitutions.
sections.Reasoning:
Federal detainers request cooperation and impose no mandatory obligation on the states, as the United States conceded. But voluntariness answers only whether federal officials can require cooperation, not whether state officers have lawful power to give it. Holding Lunn after the state basis for custody ended was a new arrest under Massachusetts law, as the government acknowledged.

Court officers on courthouse premises have the arrest powers of Massachusetts police officers. Common law authorizes warrantless arrests for felonies on probable cause and, in specified circumstances, for misdemeanors involving a breach of the peace in the officer's presence. It supplies no general power to arrest for civil matters or for civil immigration matters. The statutes authorizing particular noncriminal detention, such as protective custody, emergency hospitalization, civil contempt, and material-witness detention, did not cover this case, and enumerated authority for particular civil custody does not create a general civil-arrest power.

The court assumed without deciding that the United States' inherent-authority theory remained viable under federal law, but refused to adopt it as Massachusetts law. Silence in state law could not create an undefined arrest power lacking the protections available to other arrestees; otherwise an officer would have more authority to arrest for a federal civil matter than for a state misdemeanor. Any carefully defined new authority was for the legislature.

Section 1357(g)(10), read in context, preserved cooperation that state law authorizes and state officers choose to provide; it did not confer arrest power state law withholds. Federal administrative warrants, issued without judicial authorization, did not supply state authority either.

The casebook uses Lunn to illustrate the need for state authority for civil arrest.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-485.rule: A statute authorizing imprisonment of a tort judgment debtor until the judgment is paid denies equal protection even under rational-basis review, because jailing an indigent debtor punishes without advancing collection.

sections.Parties: Kinsey, the plaintiff, sued Preeson for breach of contract and fraud after investing $7,500 with him. She won compensatory and punitive damages, attorney's fees, and an order imprisoning Preeson until he paid. Preeson, the defendant and appellant, challenged the constitutionality of Colorado's body-execution statute, the punitive damages, and the fee award.
sections.Procedural History: Kinsey sued in November 1983. After a bench trial the judge awarded $7,500 compensatory and $7,500 punitive damages, fixed attorney's fees at $3,306, and ordered imprisonment for one year or until payment. Written judgment was entered November 1, 1984; Preeson's new-trial motion, which raised the constitutional issue, followed November 16 and was denied December 5. The appeal went to the Court of Appeals and was transferred to the Colorado Supreme Court because a statute's constitutionality was challenged. That court reversed the imprisonment order, affirmed the punitive damages, and reversed the fee award and remanded for further proceedings on fees. The opinion was modified on denial of rehearing.
sections.Material Facts:
Preeson's letter of October 19, 1981 promised to form Chief Motorhome Rentals, Inc., a Delaware corporation, and give Kinsey five percent of its stock for $7,500. He promised European promotional work, weekly reports, and monthly payments equal to ten percent of business income until her investment was repaid. No return came.

The trial judge found Kinsey an unsophisticated investor with limited English, raised and educated in Okinawa. The judge found that Preeson had failed to form the corporation or perform the contract and had fraudulently obtained her money, disbelieved Preeson's testimony, and regarded the negligence defense as frivolous.

Counsel submitted a fee affidavit and prepared the judgment. The proposed order left the length of confinement blank; apparently the judge inserted one year and mailed it. There was no preincarceration hearing and no finding about Preeson's economic condition, and he had no opportunity to present indigency, although trial testimony described him as broke. Section 13-59-103 authorized body execution after specified tort findings involving malice, fraud, willful deceit, or reckless or willful negligence.
sections.Issue: Does Colorado's body-execution statute, which authorizes imprisoning a tort judgment debtor until the judgment is paid, violate equal protection? Were the punitive damages and the attorney-fee award against Preeson properly entered?
sections.Holding: The Colorado Supreme Court, en banc, in 1987, in an opinion by Justice Vollack with Justice Rovira not participating, held section 13-59-103 unconstitutional under the Fourteenth Amendment's equal protection guarantee even under rational-basis review, and reversed the order imprisoning Preeson. It invalidated the statute rather than merely directing an indigency hearing under it. It affirmed the $7,500 punitive damages, and reversed the $3,306 attorney-fee award and remanded for further findings. The compensatory award was not reversed. The court reserved whether personal liberty was a fundamental right in this setting or whether a suspect class was implicated.
sections.Reasoning:
Colorado's constitution allowed certain exceptions to the prohibition of imprisonment for debt, but that provision was not self-executing, so legislative authorization was needed, and the statute's age and presumptive validity did not insulate it. Wealth alone was not generally a suspect classification, but the court did not need to choose a stricter standard because the statute failed rational-basis review.

The statute's coercive purpose was to obtain payment. An indigent debtor cannot comply, so confinement punishes without achieving collection, leaves the debt outstanding, and prevents gainful employment. A solvent debtor can buy release; the apparent equal opportunity to pay is illusory for someone who is indigent. Williams and Tate reinforced the discriminatory effect of turning inability to pay into incarceration. The court declined the narrower approach of saving the statute by requiring a prior ability-to-pay hearing: the statute was penal, required strict construction, and lacked a poor-debtor oath mechanism. It did not hold that every contempt sanction for willful refusal to obey a feasible payment order is invalid.

On punitive damages, the fraud complaint was pleaded with particularity under Rule 9(b), a promise of future conduct is actionable when made with a present intention not to perform, and the oral ruling and credibility findings met the required standard of proof beyond a reasonable doubt.

On fees, the judge had not examined the statutory factors, including finances, or whether the actual trial defense was frivolous, and Preeson had no chance to contest the reasonableness of the amount.

The casebook cites the case for the body-execution ruling; the brief notes that the casebook labels it a state-constitutional invalidation although the opinion rests on the Fourteenth Amendment.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-486.rule: Postjudgment body execution against a tort debtor is constitutional only with findings of probable cause that the debtor is fleeing or concealing assets, and with a prompt hearing on the debtor's petition for release.

sections.Parties: Grimes, a judgment debtor who had been jailed for forty-nine days under North Carolina's body-execution procedure, sued under section 1983. The defendants were Patricia Miller, the judgment creditor, Hugh Shepherd, the clerk, and Paul McCrary, the sheriff. Grimes sought personal and class relief declaring the scheme unconstitutional and $100 from Miller.
sections.Procedural History: In Miller's state suit the Grimes defendants were served and failed to answer; after default, Judge McConnell entered judgment and authorized execution against Grimes's person if property execution failed. Property execution returned unsatisfied, and body-execution writs issued January 15 and May 23, 1975. Grimes was arrested July 30, unsuccessfully sought habeas relief, and was released September 17 under the insolvent's oath provisions. He then brought this federal action before a three-judge court. That court dismissed the prejudgment challenge for lack of standing, upheld the postjudgment scheme with required findings, held the twenty-day notice requirement invalid insofar as it barred preliminary release, required notice of the counsel right, and denied class certification, an injunction, damages against Miller, and section 1988 fees.
sections.Material Facts:
Patricia Miller, a professional stockcar racer, delivered her 1972 Pinto to Grimes in 1973 for rebuilding, engine replacement, and racing improvements. He instead stripped its parts, leaving the frame and body shell when she recovered it in May 1974. Her state complaint alleged intentional fraud and malicious conversion, and separately that he had transferred an $18,000 dragster to his wife to defeat creditors.

After default the state judge found intentional, willful, malicious, fraudulent conversion, the car's value having fallen from $6,500 to $150, and awarded $6,350 for the loss and $5,000 punitive damages. He made no findings about the alleged fraudulent asset transfer.

Grimes temporarily fled to Florida and was arrested on July 30. His wife at first failed to find counsel; a lawyer eventually took the matter without a fee and petitioned under the insolvent's oath provisions. After twenty days' creditor notice and an examination, the clerk found no assets beyond $50 and released him. He had spent forty-nine days in jail, and the state had not provided him counsel.
sections.Issue: Does North Carolina's postjudgment body execution against a tort judgment debtor violate due process, equal protection, or the Eighth Amendment, and what findings, hearing, and notice of counsel does the Constitution require before and during such confinement? Did Grimes have standing to challenge prejudgment arrest?
sections.Holding: A three-judge court of the Middle District of North Carolina in 1977, in an opinion by Circuit Judge Craven with Chief District Judge Gordon and District Judge Ward, upheld postjudgment body execution only with an additional protective construction. Execution requires facts establishing probable cause that the debtor was about to flee to avoid creditors, had fraudulently concealed or diverted assets, or would do so unless immediately detained. The twenty-day creditor-notice requirement was unconstitutional insofar as it barred preliminary release: the debtor must receive an actual hearing within three days of petitioning for release, or be released. The warrant must give notice of the statutory right to counsel. The prejudgment challenge was dismissed for lack of standing, and other relief was denied.
sections.Reasoning:
Grimes lacked standing to challenge prejudgment arrest because his own arrest came after judgment and he identified no threatened prejudgment proceeding. His postjudgment claim was not moot: he had other outstanding debts and a reasonable risk of recurrence, and a confinement like his could end before federal adjudication, so the injury was capable of repetition yet evading review.

The court characterized the legislative objective as compelling disclosure and preventing concealment of assets by debtors adjudged guilty of fraud or similar wrongs, not jailing ordinary indigent debtors for inability to pay. On that construction it found no substantive due process, equal protection, or Eighth Amendment violation; rich debtors concealing assets could also remain jailed.

But findings of the original tort alone were not a constitutionally sufficient basis for civil detention, since confinement would then punish the wrong without criminal procedural protections. The added probable-cause findings connect detention to preserving recovery. The court acknowledged that it could not authoritatively construe state law and predicted that North Carolina's highest court would adopt this saving construction.

The twenty-day notice rule could keep a debtor obviously without assets confined, letting vengeance rather than disclosure drive detention. Preliminary release differs from final discharge: the creditor can continue investigating, and a later finding of fraudulent concealment could lead to imprisonment until full disclosure.

A state statute supplied counsel to indigent persons in civil arrest proceedings, so the court did not decide whether there was an independent constitutional right to counsel. Miller had acted in good faith, so damages against her were denied.

The casebook cites the case for the probable-cause safeguards; the brief notes that the casebook measures the three days from arrest, while the opinion measures them from the petition for release.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-488.rule: In a multiple-claims action, a final decision on an individual claim is appealable under section 1291 when the district court expressly determines there is no just reason for delay and expressly directs entry of judgment under Rule 54(b).

sections.Parties: Mackey and his company, Time Saver Tools, the plaintiffs, sued Sears, Roebuck & Co. in federal court in Illinois in 1953. The plaintiffs appealed the dismissal of two of their claims. Sears, the defendant, moved to dismiss that appeal for lack of appellate jurisdiction and, after the Seventh Circuit refused, sought review in the Supreme Court.
sections.Procedural History: The district court dismissed Counts I and II without leave to amend while leaving Counts III and IV unresolved on the answers. It expressly determined there was no just reason for delay and directed entry of judgment. The plaintiffs appealed, and Sears moved to dismiss the appeal for lack of appellate jurisdiction. The Seventh Circuit denied that motion, relying on section 1291 and amended Rule 54(b). The Court reviewed only jurisdiction, not the sufficiency of the dismissed claims, and affirmed the Seventh Circuit's denial of the motion to dismiss the appeal.
sections.Material Facts:
The operative controversy involved four claims. Count I alleged Sherman Act violations damaging three ventures: a nursery-lamp business, a commission arrangement for selling another company's tools, and Time Saver's business in carbide-tipped lathe bits and other products. Mackey sought $570,000 in trebled damages on alleged losses of $190,000, plus equitable relief. Count II invoked diversity and sought ordinary damages for destruction of the lamp business and Mackey's losses on guaranteed obligations. Count III asserted unlawful inducement of breach of the commission agreement, and Count IV asserted unfair competition and patent infringement damaging Time Saver. Count V was abandoned and Count VI duplicated others, so the Court disregarded them. These were allegations, not findings.

The district court finally dismissed Counts I and II and certified them under amended Rule 54(b) while Counts III and IV remained pending. Count I shared some facts with Counts III and IV but rested on the Sherman Act, while those counts relied largely on common-law rights; Count II was clearly independent of the remaining claims.
sections.Issue: Did section 1291 permit an appeal from the final dismissal of some claims in a multiple-claims action, supported by a proper Rule 54(b) certification, while other claims remained pending, and did amended Rule 54(b) impermissibly enlarge appellate jurisdiction?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 1956, in an opinion by Justice Burton, held that the appeal was proper. Amended Rule 54(b) preserves the requirement that an individual claim be finally adjudicated while allowing the district judge to release that final decision for appeal before the whole action ends. Both genuine finality and the express certification are necessary; labeling an order final is not enough. The rule did not enlarge the jurisdiction granted by section 1291. The Court affirmed the Seventh Circuit's denial of Sears's motion to dismiss the appeal. Justice Frankfurter, joined by Justice Harlan, concurred in the judgment.
sections.Reasoning:
Earlier practice generally treated the whole controversy as the unit for appeal. Liberal federal joinder multiplied the claims that could sit in one case, and original Rule 54(b) allowed review of sufficiently separate claims, but whether a claim was independent enough was uncertain, so parties risked losing appeal time or filed protective appeals.

The amended rule gave a definite trigger: an express determination that there is no just reason for delay and an express direction for entry of judgment. Without those, partial dispositions remain subject to revision. The trial judge acts as a dispatcher, deciding when an already final decision on a claim is ready for appeal, and a party is assured that appeal time will not run without certification.

A district judge cannot create jurisdiction by fiat. An appellate court can still ask whether a cognizable claim was decided, whether its disposition was truly final, and whether certification was an abuse of discretion. Here the dismissed claims were cognizable, fully disposed of, and could be decided independently despite some factual overlap, and there was no abuse of discretion.

The rule did not relax the finality required of an individual decision or supersede the statute; it administered the statutory requirement for multiple claims. The Court did not reach an alternative ground under the injunction-appeal provision.

Justice Frankfurter, joined by Justice Harlan, concurred in the judgment by a different route. He viewed separateness and independence as the statutory boundary: Count II was independent, and Count I could be reviewed as an interlocutory denial of injunctive relief. He warned that the majority's approach could invite piecemeal appeals.

The casebook excerpt emphasizes the dispatcher function, preserved finality of the individual claim, and appellate scrutiny of certification.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-489.rule: Under amended Rule 54(b), a finally adjudicated claim may be certified and appealed even though an unresolved counterclaim arises partly from the same transactions; the relationship is a factor for the district court's discretion, not a jurisdictional bar.

sections.Parties: Cold Metal Process Co. and United Engineering & Foundry Co. were parties to a 1927 patent agreement. Cold Metal began the principal proceeding in 1934 to enjoin United's patent suits elsewhere and determine a license payment; United later asserted a counterclaim. After judgment on the accounting, both appealed. Cold Metal challenged the court of appeals' jurisdiction over the appeal and sought review of the Third Circuit's rejection of that objection.
sections.Procedural History: Cold Metal sued in 1934. After trial the district court upheld the contract and directed an accounting, and in 1939 the appellate court largely sustained United's position and sent payment questions to a master. United's claims, first offered in 1941, were refiled in 1949 as an ancillary cross-complaint; the district court dismissed it, but the Third Circuit reversed in 1951 and treated it as an ancillary counterclaim. The district court adopted the master's 1954 report in 1955. Both parties appealed; when Cold Metal objected that there was no Rule 54(b) certification, the district court, with appellate permission, added one. Both appealed again, and the Third Circuit rejected Cold Metal's renewed jurisdictional objection. The Court affirmed that jurisdictional ruling before the circuit decided the merits.
sections.Material Facts:
Under the 1927 agreement the two companies pooled claims from their patent applications to secure a patent for a type of steel rolling mill in Cold Metal's name and an exclusive license for United, with the license payment to be negotiated or arbitrated. After the patent issued in 1930, Cold Metal argued that no license existed until the fee was determined and paid; United maintained that an enforceable license existed.

United's counterclaim alleged that Cold Metal's conduct violated the 1939 appellate resolution. It sought protection of United's licensees against Cold Metal's infringement suits, an accounting of payments Cold Metal collected within the exclusive field, and a setoff against United's own payment obligations.

The district court's 1955 judgment on the master's report entered $387,650 against United with six-percent interest from the filing of the report. Both parties had asked to deal with the master's report before trying the counterclaim, recognizing that appellate resolution might make its trial undesirable. The district court continued the pretrial conference on the counterclaim indefinitely and removed it from the trial calendar without prejudice.
sections.Issue: Could the court of appeals review a finally adjudicated accounting claim, certified under amended Rule 54(b), although an unresolved counterclaim arising partly from the same transactions remained pending in the district court?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 1956, in an opinion by Justice Burton, held that it could under section 1291 and amended Rule 54(b). The transactional relationship between the adjudicated claim and the pending counterclaim remained relevant to the certification decision but did not categorically bar appeal. The Court affirmed the Third Circuit's jurisdictional ruling, allowing it to decide the pending merits appeals. It did not decide whether the accounting was correct or anything about the counterclaim. Justice Frankfurter, joined by Justice Harlan, dissented.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court applied the reasoning of its same-day decision in Sears, Roebuck & Co. v. Mackey. Historically the entire litigation was generally the unit for appeal. Original Rule 54(b) allowed a limited departure for separate, independent claims, which could make appealability turn on whether a counterclaim was permissive or compulsory, and those distinctions generated uncertainty. The amended rule expressly grouped claims, counterclaims, cross-claims, and third-party claims within one certification framework, so the Court found it unnecessary to decide whether United's claim was compulsory or permissive.

A claim's relationship to an unresolved counterclaim thus became a factor for the district judge rather than an automatic jurisdictional prohibition. Where a genuinely final claim is certified with no just reason for delay and the appellate court finds no abuse of discretion, the judgment can be reviewed even though the pending claim shares a transaction. Here the accounting claim was finally adjudicated, the judge certified it, and the Third Circuit found the certification proper.

The Court also rejected the argument that broader appealability made the amended rule invalid. The rule still required final disposition of an individual claim and did not let a judge call an incomplete claim final, so it did not impair section 1291 and was within the rulemaking authority.

Justice Frankfurter, joined by Justice Harlan, dissented in a shared opinion printed with Sears. For him early appeal required a completed portion separate and independent of the remaining litigation, and United's counterclaim arose substantially from the same transactions. He also objected to leaving a statutory jurisdictional boundary to district judges under an abuse-of-discretion label.

The casebook presents the case for the unresolved related counterclaim and the dissenters' different position in Sears.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-490.rule: Under Rule 54(b) a district court first determines that a claim is finally decided and then whether there is any just reason for delay; a pending nonfrivolous counterclaim does not bar certification, and the court's weighing of equities receives substantial deference.

sections.Parties: Curtiss-Wright Corp., the plaintiff, sued General Electric Co. in diversity in 1976 over contracts for components and won summary judgment on a claim for an unpaid balance. General Electric, the defendant, counterclaimed and appealed the certified judgment. After the Third Circuit dismissed that appeal and ordered certification vacated, Curtiss-Wright sought review in the Supreme Court to reinstate the certification.
sections.Procedural History: The district court awarded Curtiss-Wright summary judgment for $19 million plus statutory prejudgment interest at six percent. An earlier certification request had failed because prejudgment interest was unresolved; on a renewed request the district judge expressly directed final judgment, found no just reason for delay, gave a written explanation, and stayed enforcement without bond pending appeal. A divided Third Circuit panel dismissed for want of an appealable order and directed the district court to vacate the certification; rehearing was denied with four judges dissenting. The Court vacated the Third Circuit's judgment and remanded.
sections.Material Facts:
Between 1968 and 1972 General Electric entered twenty-one contracts worth approximately $215 million with Curtiss-Wright for components used in nuclear-powered naval vessels. Curtiss-Wright alleged fraud, misrepresentation, and breach, sought damages and reformation, and also sought an outstanding $19 million balance on work already performed. General Electric counterclaimed for $1.9 million in costs allegedly incurred helping Curtiss-Wright avoid default and $52 million in alleged unjust enrichment.

Most claims involved disputed facts, but the balance claim turned on an isolated question about a contractual release. General Electric did not dispute the amount or that it would eventually have to be paid; it argued that payment could await the other claims. The district court, applying New York law, rejected that argument.

In certifying, the district judge found the claim separate from the remaining claims and counterclaims, so that review would not be mooted or duplicated later. The judge also relied on the large liquidated sum, the difference between market and statutory interest rates, and the likely length of the remaining litigation. Both parties appeared financially sound. The judge considered the possible counterclaim setoff but found the other factors outweighed it.
sections.Issue: Did the district court abuse its discretion by certifying the $19 million judgment under Rule 54(b) despite unresolved counterclaims and a possible setoff, and may a court of appeals require unusual or harsh circumstances before such a certification is allowed?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 1980, in a unanimous opinion by Chief Justice Burger, held that the district court did not abuse its discretion. A nonfrivolous counterclaim does not categorically prevent certification, and the court of appeals had improperly substituted its own assessment of the equities for a reasonable district-court judgment. The Court vacated the Third Circuit's judgment and remanded. It did not enter judgment on the unresolved claims or counterclaims.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court separated finality from timing. First, the district court must have an ultimate disposition of a cognizable individual claim in a multiple-claims action; certification cannot make an unfinished claim final. Second, once finality exists, the judge decides whether any just reason warrants delay, acting as a dispatcher in the interest of sound judicial administration. Not every separable final claim qualifies for immediate appeal.

The second step weighs administrative interests and the parties' equities. Separability and the risk of repeated appellate consideration matter because of the policy against piecemeal appeals, though even a possibility of repeated review is not an absolute bar, and the Court declined a rigid checklist.

Counterclaims, compulsory or permissive, are evaluated by their interrelationship with the certified claim, not their label or mere presence. Here the district court found factual and legal severability, which the court of appeals did not dispute. The possible setoff was a factor to weigh, not an automatic prohibition. The Third Circuit had wrongly turned the Advisory Committee's phrase about the infrequent harsh case into a restrictive standard. Appellate courts scrutinize the relationships among claims, but once those juridical concerns are met, the district court's assessment of the equities gets substantial deference and is disturbed only if clearly unreasonable.

The interest-rate differential was a permissible consideration, alongside the large liquidated debt, the lack of dispute over it, and the length of remaining litigation. Solvency was reasonably treated as neutral, since neither party was likely to become insolvent. The Court also noted that a certifying court could stay enforcement and prescribe protections under Rule 62(h).

The casebook note develops the counterclaim and deferential-review reasoning and identifies the interest-rate differential and likely delay.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-493.rule: Disclosure orders adverse to the attorney-client privilege are not immediately appealable as collateral orders under 28 U.S.C. section 1291, because postjudgment review and other established mechanisms sufficiently protect the privilege.

sections.Parties: Norman Carpenter, a former shift supervisor at Mohawk, sued the company in federal court in Georgia in 2007, alleging unlawful termination under 42 U.S.C. section 1985(2) and state law. Mohawk, the defendant, sought immediate appellate review of an order requiring it to disclose information it claimed was protected by the attorney-client privilege.
sections.Procedural History: Carpenter sought discovery about his meeting with Mohawk's lawyer and the termination decision. The district court agreed the information was privileged but found implicit waiver through Mohawk's representations in the Williams litigation and ordered disclosure. It declined to certify the order under section 1292(b) but stayed it so Mohawk could explore other review. Mohawk filed both an appeal and a mandamus petition. The Eleventh Circuit dismissed the appeal because the order was not an appealable collateral order and denied mandamus because it found no clear usurpation of power or abuse of discretion. The Court granted review of the collateral-order question only and affirmed the Eleventh Circuit's judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
According to Carpenter's complaint, he told human resources that Mohawk employed undocumented immigrants. He did not then know that another pending case, Williams, alleged a conspiracy to depress legal employees' wages through such hiring. Mohawk directed Carpenter to meet the lawyer it had retained in Williams. Carpenter alleged that the lawyer pressured him to recant and that the company fired him under false pretenses when he refused. These were allegations, not findings by the Court.

The Williams plaintiffs sought a hearing to investigate Carpenter's allegations. Mohawk responded in that litigation by denying them and giving its own account: Carpenter had tried to get the company to hire an undocumented worker, the company investigated, retained counsel interviewed him, and it fired him for violating company policy. Those disclosures in the other case became the basis for the district court's finding that Mohawk had implicitly waived the privilege.
sections.Issue: Whether a disclosure order rejecting a claim of attorney-client privilege qualifies for immediate appeal under the collateral-order doctrine.
sections.Holding: The Court in 2009, in an opinion by Justice Sotomayor for eight Justices, with Justice Thomas joining Part II-C and concurring in the judgment, held that disclosure orders adverse to the attorney-client privilege are not immediately appealable as collateral orders under section 1291. Postjudgment review and other established mechanisms sufficiently protect the privilege. All nine Justices agreed to affirm. The Court resolved only the effective-unreviewability condition and did not decide whether Mohawk had actually waived the privilege.
sections.Reasoning:
Section 1291 ordinarily postpones appeal until a final decision. Cohen permits a small class of orders that conclusively decide important questions separate from the merits and are effectively unreviewable after final judgment, but the exception must not swallow the rule, because piecemeal appeals delay litigation and burden courts. The inquiry is categorical: whether waiting so imperils the interest that immediate appeal should be available for the whole class of orders, not whether one litigant suffers hardship.

The Court acknowledged the privilege's importance but concluded that postjudgment remedies generally suffice: an appellate court can vacate an adverse judgment and order a new trial excluding the improperly disclosed material and its fruits. It doubted that deferring review meaningfully reduces clients' candor, since clients weigh the privilege's scope and exceptions rather than the remote chance of an erroneous order.

Other safeguards remain for serious errors: section 1292(b) certification, mandamus for exceptional usurpation or clear abuse, and refusing disclosure and incurring sanctions or, in appropriate circumstances, contempt. Protective orders can limit spillover. The costs of successive appeals outweighed the limited benefits. The Court declined to decide the government's proposal concerning certain governmental privileges. Any further avenue of appeal should come through the rulemaking process Congress authorized.

Justice Thomas agreed with the outcome but declined the remaining Cohen analysis, considering Congress's choice of rulemaking sufficient reason not to add this category of appeals.

The brief says the casebook's account accurately identifies the adverse privilege disclosure order and the availability of postjudgment review, while omitting the alternative review mechanisms and reservations.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-494.rule: An order disqualifying counsel in a civil case is not a collateral order subject to immediate appeal under 28 U.S.C. section 1291.

sections.Parties: Anne Koller, through her guardians, sued Richardson-Merrell, alleging that the manufacturer's antinausea drug Bendectin, taken by her mother early in pregnancy, caused her birth defects. Richardson-Merrell, the defendant, moved to disqualify Koller's lead trial counsel, James Butler and Nicholas Allis, and their Los Angeles firm. Koller appealed the disqualification.
sections.Procedural History: After evidentiary hearings and a show-cause process, the district court revoked the pro hac vice admissions of Butler and Allis and their firm's appearance. Koller appealed immediately. The D.C. Circuit stayed the entire trial-court proceeding, accepted jurisdiction under section 1291, and held the disqualification invalid. No post-disqualification motion for section 1292(b) certification apparently followed. The Court granted review of both jurisdiction and the merits of disqualification but decided only jurisdiction. It vacated the D.C. Circuit's judgment and remanded with instructions to dismiss the appeal for want of jurisdiction.
sections.Material Facts:
Koller was born in 1979 without normal arms or legs. The Los Angeles firm Butler, Jefferson, Dan & Allis led trial preparation, and at least eight lawyers from four firms were counsel of record as trial approached.

In December 1982 Allis's secretary, Krystyna Janowski, called the defense firm and said the suit was fraudulent and the mother had not taken Bendectin during the crucial period. Allis later visited her, once with an investigator who secretly recorded the conversation, and obtained a signed statement denying that she had heard anyone say the mother had not taken the drug. Janowski subsequently recanted that statement.

Separately, after the trial court excluded evidence about other children with superficially similar birth defects, Butler submitted Drug Experience Reports about those children to the FDA, urged removal of Bendectin from the market, and gave materials to a newspaper reporter. After the anticipated jury pool had been called, the newspaper published an article discussing the case and the excluded reports.

The district court found that Allis had attempted to obstruct investigation of a crucial witness and that Butler had sought to prejudice the defense and circumvent evidentiary rulings, noting that other competent counsel already represented Koller.
sections.Issue: Whether an order disqualifying counsel in a civil case qualifies for immediate appeal as a collateral order under section 1291.
sections.Holding: The Court in 1985, in an opinion by Justice O'Connor, with the participating Justices dividing 7-1, held that a civil-case order disqualifying counsel is not immediately appealable as a collateral order. It vacated the D.C. Circuit's judgment and remanded with instructions to dismiss the appeal for want of jurisdiction. The Court expressed no view on the merits of the district court's disqualification and did not decide whether prejudice is required for reversal after an erroneous disqualification.
sections.Reasoning:
The collateral-order doctrine is narrow and requires a conclusive determination, an important issue completely separate from the merits, and effective unreviewability after final judgment.

The D.C. Circuit had stressed that disqualification is disruptive, that lawyers may need to vindicate their reputations, and that disqualification motions can be used tactically. The Court acknowledged these concerns but refused to treat them as an independent source of jurisdiction. Interlocutory civil appeals themselves cause delay, as the stay here showed. A lawyer's wish for vindication may diverge from the client's interest. Section 1292(b) certification, exceptional mandamus, and review after final judgment remain available. If mistakes and added expense alone justified immediate appeal, the exception would overwhelm finality.

Applying the reasoning of Flanagan, the criminal-disqualification decision: if erroneous disqualification requires no showing of prejudice for reversal, it can be reviewed as effectively after final judgment as before trial; if prejudice must be shown, the inquiry into its effect on the outcome is inseparable from the merits. On either premise a collateral-order requirement fails. Civil disqualification orders also often overlap the merits, as with lawyer-witness and misconduct issues, and the analysis is categorical.

Justice Brennan concurred on the understanding that appellate courts would develop review standards effectively protecting a litigant's qualified right to chosen counsel. Justice Stevens dissented: he considered the loss of chosen counsel separate from the merits and practically impossible to remedy later, and would have affirmed the D.C. Circuit. Justice Powell did not participate.

The brief says the casebook uses the case to show that the difficulty and cost of replacing counsel do not create collateral-order appealability.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-495.rule: Neither the denial of an extradited defendant's claim of immunity from civil service of process nor the denial of a forum non conveniens motion to dismiss is an immediately appealable collateral order under 28 U.S.C. section 1291.

sections.Parties: Biard, a Brussels resident, sued Van Cauwenberghe, a Brussels broker, in a federal civil action asserting RICO, fraud and related state claims arising from a loan. Van Cauwenberghe, the defendant, moved to dismiss and sought immediate appeal when his motions were denied.
sections.Procedural History: Van Cauwenberghe moved to dismiss on two grounds: that his extradition made him immune from civil process, and forum non conveniens. The district court summarily denied both motions. The Ninth Circuit dismissed his appeal for lack of jurisdiction. The civil litigation continued while the appeal was pending, and a later summary judgment awarded $1.8 million in RICO treble damages and $75,000 in fees; that judgment was not under review. The Court affirmed the Ninth Circuit's dismissal for lack of appellate jurisdiction.
sections.Material Facts:
Van Cauwenberghe encouraged Biard to discuss an investment with Alan Blair in the United States. At a Los Angeles meeting, Blair described Three B Investment Associates' renovation of a Kansas City-area townhouse complex. At Van Cauwenberghe's urging, Biard lent the partnership $1 million for three years at twenty percent interest, secured by a mortgage on the complex. The partnership had a purchase contract and deposit but never acquired title; it defaulted and the mortgage proved worthless. Biard claimed he had been misled about ownership.

Federal prosecutors indicted Van Cauwenberghe, Blair and another person. Van Cauwenberghe was arrested in Geneva under the United States-Switzerland extradition treaty and delivered to Los Angeles, where a jury convicted him of wire fraud and causing interstate transportation of a fraud victim. In January 1986 he received a term of one year and one day satisfied by pretrial confinement, restitution of $34,501.26, and probation barring departure until restitution was paid.

A week before the criminal trial, Biard filed the civil action. About two weeks after sentencing, Van Cauwenberghe was served while arriving for a probation appointment.
sections.Issue: Whether the interlocutory denial of a motion to dismiss based on an extradited person's claimed immunity from civil service of process, or of a motion to dismiss for forum non conveniens, may be appealed immediately under the collateral-order doctrine.
sections.Holding: The Court in 1988, in a unanimous opinion by Justice Marshall, held that neither denial was an immediately appealable collateral order and affirmed the Ninth Circuit's dismissal for lack of appellate jurisdiction. The claimed service immunity could be effectively vindicated after final judgment, and forum non conveniens determinations generally are not completely separate from the merits. The Court assumed without deciding that Van Cauwenberghe had a substantial immunity claim, and did not decide whether extradition actually gave him immunity or whether the forum motion should succeed.
sections.Reasoning:
Section 1291 ordinarily permits appeal only after a decision ends the litigation on the merits. Cohen's small collateral category requires conclusiveness, an important issue completely separate from the merits, and effective unreviewability after final judgment, and all three must be met.

On immunity, Van Cauwenberghe relied on the extradition principle of specialty and analogized his claim to qualified immunity, which protects against trial itself. The Court asked whether freedom from the burdens of trial was an essential feature of the claimed protection; otherwise every potentially successful dismissal argument would support immediate appeal. Specialty chiefly governs treaty obligations between states, and a private civil trial does not significantly implicate them before a binding judgment is enforced. Unlike a prosecution, it involves no pretrial detention or bail. He conceded that proper service abroad, or service during unrelated business in the United States, could have required him to defend the same suit. The claim was therefore a right not to be subjected to a binding judgment without valid personal jurisdiction, which later review can vindicate.

On forum non conveniens, weighing access to evidence, witnesses, local interests and applicable law requires examining the underlying allegations and defenses, so the question generally overlaps the merits. Appealability is decided for categories of orders, not individual cases, and asserted obvious error creates no exception. Section 1292(b) provides a discretionary route.

The brief notes that the casebook's account recounts the extradition-based immunity argument and the rejection of collateral appeal but does not develop the forum non conveniens ruling.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-496.rule: The denial of a motion to dismiss based on a contractual forum-selection clause is not immediately appealable under the collateral-order doctrine, because the right to litigate in a particular forum can be adequately vindicated on appeal after final judgment.

sections.Parties: Passengers on the Achille Lauro, and representatives of passengers' estates, sued the vessel's Italian owner, Lauro Lines, in federal court in New York. They sought compensation for injuries from the hijacking and for the wrongful death of Leon Klinghoffer. Lauro Lines, the defendant, sought dismissal under a forum-selection clause and appealed when dismissal was denied.
sections.Procedural History: Lauro Lines moved to dismiss based on the forum-selection clause in the passenger tickets. The district court denied the motion, holding that the ticket as a whole did not reasonably notify passengers that they were waiving suit in a domestic forum. The company appealed without seeking certification under section 1292(b). The Second Circuit dismissed the appeal because the denial was interlocutory and was not a collateral final order under section 1291. The Court granted review to resolve a disagreement among circuits and affirmed the Second Circuit's dismissal of the appeal.
sections.Material Facts: The claims arose from the hijacking of the Achille Lauro in the Mediterranean in October 1985. Each passenger's ticket contained a clause purporting to require that litigation connected with the contract be brought in Naples, Italy, and to renounce suit elsewhere. Lauro Lines invoked that clause to seek dismissal of the New York suit. The question before the Court concerned appellate access to the forum ruling, not liability for the hijacking or Klinghoffer's death.
sections.Issue: Whether a district court's denial of a motion to dismiss based on a contractual forum-selection clause is immediately appealable under the collateral-order doctrine.
sections.Holding: The Court in 1989, in a unanimous opinion by Justice Brennan, held that the denial was not immediately appealable because the asserted contractual right remained sufficiently vindicable on appeal after final judgment. It affirmed the Second Circuit's dismissal of the appeal. The Court expressly left the first two collateral-order conditions undecided, and did not decide whether the clause was enforceable or whether the district court's notice ruling was correct.
sections.Reasoning:
Denying dismissal kept the litigation going, so the company needed the narrow collateral-order exception: a conclusive decision, an important issue entirely separate from the merits, and effective unreviewability after final judgment. Failure of the third condition disposed of the case.

The company argued the contract gave it both a right to trial in Italy and a right not to be sued elsewhere, and that an appeal after a New York trial could not undo the inconvenience and expense. The Court acknowledged that later correction would not perfectly preserve the bargain, but that is true whenever an interlocutory ruling is mistaken; litigation costs do not overcome Congress's finality requirement. The exception requires a right essentially destroyed by postponing vindication.

The Court contrasted rights not to be tried at all, such as double jeopardy, Speech or Debate protection and civil immunity from suit, with rights to insist on litigation elsewhere. Even on the company's most favorable formulation, a right to be sued only in Naples is not a right to avoid suit altogether, and it is at least as vindicable after judgment as an objection to personal jurisdiction. The federal policy favoring forum-selection clauses invoked under The Bremen goes to enforceability on the merits, not to the timing of review.

Justice Scalia joined the opinion and concurred separately: later reversal does not literally preserve the right to avoid a New York trial, but later vindication is legally adequate because the law does not regard this forum right as important enough to overcome the policies against interlocutory appeals.

The brief says the casebook's account correctly describes the request for an Italian forum and the refusal to allow immediate collateral-order appeal.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-498.rule: An order imposing discovery-expense sanctions on an attorney under Rule 37(a)(4) is not a final decision immediately appealable under 28 U.S.C. section 1291, even when the attorney no longer represents a party in the case.

sections.Parties: Attorney Cunningham represented the plaintiff, Darwin Lee Starcher, in a civil-rights action against Hamilton County defendants arising from his son Casey's suicide while confined at the Hamilton County Justice Center. Cunningham, sanctioned for discovery conduct and later disqualified as counsel, sought to appeal the sanctions order. The county was the opposing party on appeal.
sections.Procedural History: A magistrate judge supervising discovery granted sanctions against Cunningham and directed payment of $1,494 to the county treasurer for costs and fees incurred by county counsel. The district court affirmed the sanction and disqualified Cunningham as counsel because she was a material witness. While the underlying action remained pending, Cunningham appealed the sanctions order. The Sixth Circuit dismissed for lack of appellate jurisdiction, concluding that review was not completely separate from the merits and that the end of her representation did not make the order immediately appealable. The Court granted certiorari on appealability and affirmed the dismissal.
sections.Material Facts:
The complaint alleged that defendants ignored their duty to care for Casey despite a known history of suicide attempts. Starcher later died, and Casey's sister became administrator of Casey's estate.

After the deadline for responding to interrogatories and document requests expired, the magistrate judge ordered complete responses by July 12, 1996, and scheduled four depositions for July 25. Cunningham did not produce the requested documents, gave incomplete responses to some interrogatories, and objected to others. She noticed one deposition for a different day and declined to withdraw the notice after reminders. Although the order conditioned depositions of individual defendants on complete discovery responses, she moved to compel their appearances.

The magistrate judge characterized the conduct as egregious and imposed the $1,494 sanction. He expressly did not conduct a contempt hearing or find Cunningham in contempt. Another $2,432 award for other defendants was later satisfied through settlement and was not part of the appeal.
