The court treated federal law as governing the effect of the prior federal ruling, while saying the outcome would be the same under Arizona law. It did not finally choose between describing the attempted preclusion as offensive or defensive, and lack of complete identity of plaintiffs did not alone defeat preclusion.

The critical defects were finality and necessity. A consent judgment implementing a settlement does not necessarily make earlier evidentiary rulings essential to the judgment; seatbelt nonuse affected allocation of damages, not whether General Motors caused the accident by designing a defective van. Finality for issue preclusion can extend beyond an ordinary appealable final judgment, and this ruling was not tentative, but it was neither independently appealable nor independently reviewable, so giving it conclusive force could shield it from review and perpetuate error. Settlement incentives reinforced the conclusion: defendants facing related suits might refuse early compromise if every adverse preliminary ruling bound them later. The court also worried that shared counsel could file one passenger's case where a favorable ruling was likely and export it to others, but expressly did not find that this was counsel's motive.

On choice of law, under Arizona's most-significant-relationship approach the place of injury supplied only an initial preference. The passengers' domicile and the rental relationship centered in Arizona, and Idaho's role as the place of injury was largely fortuitous. Arizona had a substantial interest in its residents' injury prevention, medical care, rehabilitation and support; Idaho had comparatively little interest in maximizing recovery for nonresident plaintiffs against nonresident defendants. The casebook's note emphasizes the preclusion reasoning.

CP-COMP-CB-GOLDEN-EAGLE-DISTRICT.rule: As the district court read the 1983 Rule 11, in a ruling later reversed on appeal, counsel violates the rule by presenting an argument for extending the law as though it were established law, or by failing to research adverse authority adequately.

sections.Parties: Golden Eagle Distributing Corp. was the plaintiff; it sued computer manufacturer Burroughs Corp. for fraud, negligence and breach of contract over an allegedly defective computer system. Burroughs was the defendant, represented by Kirkland & Ellis and by local counsel Crosby, Heafey, Roach & May. The sanctions ruling was directed at Burroughs's lawyers.
sections.Procedural History: Golden Eagle sued in Minnesota state court. Burroughs removed on diversity grounds and obtained a section 1404(a) transfer to the Northern District of California. Burroughs then moved for summary judgment. The district court denied the motion for lack of merit and ordered the responsible defense lawyers to explain why Rule 11 sanctions should not follow. On September 19, 1984, Judge Schwarzer found a Rule 11 violation and ordered sanctions. This entry covers that district ruling only; the Ninth Circuit reversed the sanction in 1986.
sections.Material Facts:
Burroughs sought summary judgment on the premise that California limitation periods, rather than Minnesota's longer period, barred the claims. It contended that Minnesota courts would have dismissed this otherwise unrelated dispute for forum non conveniens, so a transferee federal court should not apply Minnesota's limitation period, and its memorandum portrayed that exception as following from Van Dusen. In its later sanctions memorandum, counsel acknowledged that the Supreme Court had left the question open.

Burroughs also sought dismissal of the economic-loss negligence claim under California law, relying on Seely v. White Motor Co. The later California Supreme Court decision J'Aire Corp. v. Gregory allowed recovery under a special-relationship analysis, and intermediate decisions Pisano and Huang addressed J'Aire's effect on Seely. Counsel distinguished J'Aire in reply after Golden Eagle cited it, but did not discuss the intermediate cases while asserting that Seely had never been overruled.

A Kirkland associate acknowledged responsibility for preparing the motion; local counsel signed it but had not actively participated in preparing it or deciding to file it.
sections.Issue: Whether defense counsel violated the 1983 version of Rule 11 by presenting an argument for developing the law as already-established law and by failing to research and address adverse authority.
sections.Holding: The United States District Court for the Northern District of California, 1984, Judge Schwarzer. The court found a Rule 11 violation on both grounds. It directed Golden Eagle's counsel to document the reasonable expenses and fees incurred opposing the motion, with the amount to be fixed in a later order, and directed Kirkland & Ellis to pay without reimbursement from Burroughs. Both defense firms had to certify that their partners and associates received the opinion. This was the district court's position; the Ninth Circuit later reversed the sanction, so it is not the appellate rule.
sections.Reasoning:
The judge accepted that the arguments in counsel's sanctions memorandum were clear, fair and acceptable as efforts to develop the law. His objection was to how the original motion presented them and to the research behind it.

On limitations, the original memorandum presented a forum-non-conveniens exception as established when the question was open. The judge thought the Rule 11 certification would have little function if a lawyer could disguise a request to extend the law as a statement of existing law. Subjective good faith and the absence of a delaying purpose were irrelevant under what he called the rule's first prong.

On economic loss, the statement that Seely had never been overruled was technically correct yet misleading. Counsel's claimed unawareness of the intermediate cases was no excuse: citation checking of the principal authority would have disclosed Pisano. A failure to find adverse authority after a reasonable search could sometimes be excusable, but no such search was shown.

The judge treated candor as a corollary of the Rule 11 certification, invoking the ABA Model Rules and Model Code provisions on false statements of law and undisclosed adverse authority; a tribunal cannot fairly decide if counsel misleads it about the law. He declined further sanctions against local counsel beyond criticism.

The Ninth Circuit later rejected the derivation of the argument-labeling and ethical-disclosure requirements from Rule 11. The casebook quotes the district court's rationale; it calls the sanctioned lawyers plaintiff's counsel, but the opinions identify Kirkland & Ellis as counsel for defendant Burroughs.

CP-COMP-CB-GULFSTREAM.rule: An order denying a Colorado River stay or dismissal is not immediately appealable under § 1291's collateral-order doctrine or as an injunction under § 1292(a)(1); the Enelow-Ettelson doctrine is overruled.

sections.Parties: Gulfstream Aerospace Corp., an aircraft manufacturer, sued Mayacamas Corp. in Georgia state court for breach of a contract to buy an aircraft. Mayacamas then brought its own federal diversity action against Gulfstream in Northern California on the same contract. In the federal case Gulfstream was the defendant; it moved for a stay or dismissal, lost, and was the appellant in the Ninth Circuit and the party seeking review in the Supreme Court.
sections.Procedural History: Gulfstream asked the federal district court to stay or dismiss the proceeding under Colorado River. The district court found the circumstances insufficient and denied the motion. Gulfstream appealed, asserting jurisdiction under § 1291 or § 1292(a)(1), and alternatively asked the Ninth Circuit to treat its notice of appeal as a mandamus application. The Ninth Circuit dismissed for lack of appellate jurisdiction and declined to treat the notice as a mandamus application; one judge disagreed on appealability but would have affirmed the stay denial. The Court took the case to resolve a division among the circuits and affirmed the Ninth Circuit's judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
Mayacamas agreed to purchase an aircraft manufactured by Gulfstream, intending to resell it while demand was high. It later refused payments, alleging that Gulfstream had frustrated the transaction's purpose by increasing aircraft production and availability. Gulfstream sued for breach of contract in Georgia state court. Mayacamas answered and counterclaimed there rather than removing the suit. About a month later it brought its own diversity action against Gulfstream in federal court in Northern California for breach of the same contract.

Gulfstream moved to stay or dismiss the federal action under Colorado River, which permits that response to parallel state litigation only in exceptional circumstances. The district court denied the motion. Gulfstream argued, among other things, that Mayacamas's choice to forgo removal and file a separate federal suit itself required a stay or dismissal.
sections.Issue: Whether an order denying a motion to stay or dismiss a federal action under Colorado River is immediately appealable under § 1291 or § 1292(a)(1), and whether mandamus was warranted.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States, 1988. Justice Marshall wrote an opinion joined by all eight participating Justices; Justice Scalia also concurred separately, and Justice Kennedy did not participate. The Court held that the denial was not appealable under § 1291, because it failed the conclusiveness requirement of the collateral-order exception; the Court did not decide the other two requirements. It was not appealable under § 1292(a)(1), and the Court overruled the Enelow-Ettelson doctrine, so stays of "legal" proceedings on "equitable" grounds are not automatically appealable. Gulfstream also failed to show an entitlement to mandamus.
sections.Reasoning:
The order plainly did not end the litigation, so Gulfstream needed the collateral-order exception, which requires a conclusive determination, an important question separate from the merits, and effective unreviewability after final judgment. An order granting a Colorado River stay was treated as appealable in Moses H. Cone because the federal court expected the state proceeding to resolve the whole dispute. A denial carries no such expectation: the court may reassess as the litigation develops, so the denial is inherently tentative.

Under § 1292(a)(1), an order regulating only the conduct of the issuing court's own proceedings is ordinarily not an injunction. Gulfstream invoked the Enelow-Ettelson doctrine, under which a stay of a historically legal action on equitable grounds was treated as an appealable injunction. The Court overruled it. The doctrine rested on the separation of law and equity, a fiction with even less connection to practice after merger. It was hard to administer and its distinctions did not track whether prompt review was needed. Actual injunctions, orders with an injunction's practical effect and serious consequences, the collateral-order doctrine, § 1292(b) and mandamus all remain available where their requirements are met.

Mandamus requires a clear and indisputable entitlement. Colorado River puts the burden of showing exceptional circumstances on the party seeking to halt federal litigation; it does not require deference whenever a defendant files a separate federal action.

Justice Scalia cautioned against resting finality solely on the possibility of reconsideration.

The casebook cites the case for the point that such stays are not automatically appealable as injunctions; the casebook prints § 1291(a)(1) where the decision uses § 1292(a)(1).

CP-COMP-CB-HAEGER-REMAND.rule: Preserving an objection to the legal standard for a fee sanction does not preserve entry-specific objections under that standard that the party never presented to the district court.

sections.Parties: The Haegers sued Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co. on a products-liability theory and later sought reimbursement of their litigation expenses as a sanction for Goodyear's discovery misconduct. Goodyear disputed responsibility for its attorneys' acts and wanted another opportunity to challenge whether the remaining fees were caused by misconduct. Basil Musnuff, Graeme Hancock and Fennemore Craig, the lawyers involved, were also participants in the sanctions proceedings.
sections.Procedural History:
The Haegers sued in 2005 and the case settled in 2010. Almost a year later, information about Goodyear's withholding of internal testing led to sanctions proceedings. The district court originally awarded essentially all the requested fees, and also made a contingent alternative award confined to expenses directly attributable to the sanctionable conduct. The Ninth Circuit upheld the broader award. The Supreme Court required a compensatory, but-for causal connection between the misconduct and the shifted fees, and left the district court to consider whether Goodyear had waived further challenges to the contingent award.

On remand, in this March 7, 2018 order, the district court concluded that Goodyear was vicariously liable and had waived additional causation objections, ordered the parties to address the remaining amount of the award and any other remaining issues, and set a March 13, 2018 status conference. The order did not itself enter a new final judgment fixing the award.
sections.Material Facts:
The district court had previously found a corporate strategy to conceal test results, including testimony by a corporate representative denying that relevant results existed. Goodyear's associate general counsel, Ms. Okey, retained final approval over discovery decisions, knew about the bad-faith conduct, and participated in decisions central to the concealment.

In the original sanctions proceedings Goodyear examined the plaintiffs' billing entries and assigned several objection codes, including one for lack of causation. Its causation objections totaled $722,406.52 against a request approaching $2.8 million. The court told the parties it would make an alternative award limited to directly caused expenses and invited their guidance; Goodyear supplied no additional causation objections, and the contingent award deducted the entire amount of its identified objections. Goodyear later argued on appeal that other entries also lacked the necessary connection.

A September 2016 covenant resolved the plaintiffs' claims against Musnuff and Fennemore Craig while preserving claims against Goodyear, and in July 2017 plaintiffs' counsel stated that the law firms' further participation was unnecessary.
sections.Issue: Whether Goodyear was responsible for its attorneys' sanctionable acts; whether the lawyers' continued participation was needed once Goodyear itself was responsible; and whether maintaining the legal position that only incremental fees could be recovered also preserved objections to additional individual billing entries.
sections.Holding: The District of Arizona in 2018, District Judge G. Murray Snow, held that Goodyear was vicariously liable for its attorneys' acts and had waived additional causation objections to the contingent sanctions award. The court excused Musnuff, Hancock and Fennemore Craig from further participation. The vicarious-liability holding is tied to the agency relationship and the existing misconduct findings, not a proposition that every client bears every sanction imposed on counsel, and the ruling excusing the lawyers did not announce immunity for attorneys generally.
sections.Reasoning:
Applying Arizona agency principles, the court treated a principal as responsible for acts undertaken by its agents within the scope of their work and in furtherance of the principal's business. The attorney-client relationship did not make Goodyear a passive stranger to the misconduct: its associate general counsel approved discovery decisions, knew of the bad-faith conduct and took part in the concealment, and earlier findings established Goodyear's direct involvement.

Because the plaintiffs had settled with Musnuff and Fennemore Craig and represented that their participation was unnecessary, the court excused the lawyers once Goodyear was held responsible.

On waiver, the court separated two issues. One was the governing legal measure: incremental fees caused by wrongdoing rather than all fees incurred after a particular point. The other was which specific billing entries failed that measure. Goodyear preserved the first, but that did not automatically preserve entry-specific objections it had never presented. Its own detailed coding showed it knew how to identify causation objections; the court had warned of the alternative award and invited guidance; Goodyear offered nothing more and received every deduction it sought. The additional challenges first appeared on appeal, and the court applied the ordinary rule against considering arguments first raised there, finding persuasive the distinction emphasized in Judge M. Smith's earlier dissent. Winning the legal standard in the Supreme Court did not entitle Goodyear to redo objections it could have made, which would reward strategic withholding.

The casebook cites the order for the remand determinations of waiver and vicarious responsibility; the brief notes that the casebook's reference to an alternative $2 million award is shorthand, since the order left the remaining amount for further proceedings.

CP-COMP-CB-HOWMEDICA.rule: Atlantic Marine's forum-selection presumption applies to the parties who agreed to the clause, not the whole lawsuit; courts analyze contracting and noncontracting parties separately and then consider jurisdiction, joinder, severance and transfer.

sections.Parties: Howmedica Osteonics, a New Jersey medical-device company and Stryker subsidiary, sued five former California sales representatives (Keegan Freeman, Michael Nordyke, Brett Sarkisian, Taylor Smith and Bryan Wyatt), competitor DePuy, and DePuy's regional distributor Golden State, on contract and tort claims. All defendants sought transfer to the Northern District of California. Howmedica petitioned the Third Circuit for mandamus to undo the transfer.
sections.Procedural History:
Howmedica filed in New Jersey against the representatives and DePuy, later joining Golden State as an allegedly necessary party. A magistrate judge granted transfer of the whole case on April 20, 2015, and also found that New Jersey lacked personal jurisdiction over Golden State; the district judge affirmed the transfer on August 26, 2016 without resolving that issue. Meanwhile Golden State pursued a California declaratory action attacking the noncompetition agreements; the California court related the actions and entered scheduling orders, and proceedings were later stayed pending the mandamus petition, which Howmedica filed twenty-seven days after the district court's order.

On August 15, 2017 the Third Circuit issued a writ vacating the whole-case transfer order and instructed the district court to sever the claims against DePuy and Golden State under Rule 21, transfer those claims to the Northern District of California under section 1404(a), and retain the claims against all five representatives.
sections.Material Facts:
The representatives' employment agreements restricted competition and disclosure of confidential information. Four agreements selected New Jersey for litigation; Nordyke's selected Michigan. DePuy and Golden State had signed no applicable clause. Following disagreements about management and compensation, the representatives resigned and became independent contractors working for DePuy and Golden State, and customers followed them. Howmedica alleged that the representatives and the corporations had conspired before the resignations to divert business; these were allegations, not adjudicated findings.

On appeal the defendants waived objections based on improper statutory venue, the representatives waived personal-jurisdiction objections, and DePuy had not raised that defense below; Golden State's jurisdictional objection remained. No party challenged the validity of the forum clauses themselves. Neither Nordyke nor Howmedica sought to enforce the Michigan clause.
sections.Issue: How section 1404(a) should operate when a lawsuit combines defendants bound by a forum-selection clause with defendants who never agreed to it, and whether mandamus could correct the transfer after the California court had begun managing the case.
sections.Holding: The Third Circuit in 2017, Judge Krause writing for a panel of Krause, Scirica and Fuentes, retained mandamus jurisdiction and found clear legal error. Atlantic Marine's treatment of contracting parties does not remove noncontracting parties' ordinary private-interest arguments. Courts must analyze the two groups separately, consider jurisdiction and joinder constraints, and then assess severance and transfer. Applying that framework, the claims against DePuy and Golden State go to California and the claims against all five representatives stay in New Jersey. The court did not decide the contract or conspiracy merits.
sections.Reasoning:
On mandamus, the All Writs Act permitted review, and transfer orders can be reviewed for legal and procedural error. The California court's related-case and scheduling orders had not advanced the case beyond the level previously held compatible with transferor review, and the petition was prompt; the court declined to define the event that divests transferor jurisdiction. Transfer orders as a class satisfy the no-adequate-remedy and irreparable-injury requirements under circuit precedent, so the question was clear error.

Without a forum clause, section 1404(a) balances private and public interests. Atlantic Marine changes that for parties who agreed to a valid clause: their private interests are deemed to favor the selected forum and only public factors remain. Nonsignatories have not surrendered their private interests, so the clause can neither control the entire case nor be irrelevant to it.

The court set out four steps. First, presume that claims involving contracting parties belong in the agreed forum, absent an unusual case. Second, independently balance the noncontracting parties' private and public interests. Third, examine threshold constraints on severance, including jurisdiction, venue, joinder and indispensable parties. Fourth, if several outcomes remain, compare efficiency, other public interests and prejudice to noncontracting parties, displacing contractual expectations only when countervailing interests overwhelmingly outweigh them.

Applied here, Howmedica's closely-related-parties theory did not bind the corporations. Their interests and Nordyke's favored California, and Golden State could not remain in New Jersey for lack of contacts; it was not a required party under Rule 19, so severance was permissible. DePuy belonged with Golden State and Nordyke with the other representatives, whose contractual expectations his limited finances did not overwhelmingly outweigh. The casebook's note uses the case for the point that the Atlantic Marine presumption applies to agreeing parties rather than an entire lawsuit.

CP-COMP-CB-HYCITE.rule: Website interactivity is not a substitute for ordinary minimum-contacts analysis; jurisdiction turns on actual forum-directed conduct and its connection to the claim, not a site's potential to transact everywhere.

sections.Parties: Hy Cite Corp., a Wisconsin company based in Madison that sold cookware, dinnerware, glassware and related goods under its Royal Prestige mark, sued badbusinessbureau.com, L.L.C., the operator of the Rip-Off Report consumer-complaint website, for unfair competition, false advertising, disparagement and trademark infringement. The defendant, a limited liability company organized in St. Kitts/Nevis, challenged personal jurisdiction by motion.
sections.Procedural History: Hy Cite sued in the Western District of Wisconsin, and the defendant challenged personal jurisdiction. For purposes of the motion Hy Cite had to make a prima facie showing, with relevant factual conflicts resolved in its favor. On January 8, 2004 the court granted the defendant's motion, directed entry of judgment for it and closed the case. It did not decide whether the consumer complaints were false, whether infringement occurred, or whether the operator was liable for publishing them.
sections.Material Facts:
The defendant had no Wisconsin assets, offices or employees. Its website displayed consumer submissions about businesses: at least 61,000 complaints overall and thirty to forty concerning Hy Cite's products. Companies could respond, with a $25 charge for posting more than four rebuttals; no Wisconsin company had purchased one.

In June 2003 Hy Cite emailed the operator to ask about resolving the complaints. The operator responded about its Corporate Customer Advocacy Program and quoted an initial $30,000 fee plus a later $20,000 payment. Hy Cite declined to enroll, and no other Wisconsin company had enrolled.

The site also offered advertising, linked to a book for purchase, requested donations, recruited volunteer reporters and offered to contact complainants about possible class actions. No Wisconsin business had bought advertising, one Wisconsin resident had bought the book, Wisconsin donations were not established, and the operator had organized no Wisconsin class action. The operator admitted it could be sued in Arizona, where it had a distribution center.
sections.Issue: Whether a Wisconsin federal court could exercise general or specific personal jurisdiction, consistent with due process, over an out-of-state website operator on the basis of its website's commercial and interactive features, one book sale, communications initiated by the plaintiff, and alleged intentional harm to a Wisconsin company.
sections.Holding: The Western District of Wisconsin in 2004, Chief Judge Crabb, held that neither general nor specific jurisdiction was consistent with due process. The court declined to adopt the Zippo interactivity spectrum as a replacement for ordinary minimum-contacts principles, while retaining interactivity as potentially relevant evidence of purposeful availment. It did not decide whether Wisconsin's long-arm statute, section 801.05, applied or was coextensive with the Constitution, because the failure under due process made that unnecessary.
sections.Reasoning:
The court reviewed early decisions inferring jurisdiction from broadly accessible online advertising and noted their danger: any operator might become suable everywhere. Zippo's spectrum of commercial, interactive and passive sites could not reliably answer the question, since a passive site might intentionally target harm in a state while an interactive commercial site might not target it at all. Flexible minimum-contacts principles already accommodate changing technology, and the Supreme Court had rejected mechanical tests.

General jurisdiction failed because nearly all the alleged website contacts were possibilities rather than actual Wisconsin dealings; one book sale and communications with Hy Cite came nowhere near continuous and systematic contacts.

Specific jurisdiction by purposeful availment failed because the defendant sent no unsolicited Wisconsin communications and did not advertise there, Hy Cite initiated the advocacy-program discussions and no sale followed, and the claims did not arise from the book sale; that the sale and the disputed statements appeared on the same website was too tenuous a connection.

The Calder effects theory failed as well. The record did not show that the operator wrote the complaints, and putting a company's trademark on a website did not itself show targeting of its state. An undeveloped metatag argument was treated as waived. Nor would the court infer that Wisconsin suffered the brunt of the harm simply because Hy Cite's headquarters were there, distinguishing the Indianapolis Colts case. It did not reach the reasonableness factors.

The casebook uses the case for interactivity's limited role, potential versus actual contacts, and the failure to establish forum targeting or concentrated injury.

CP-COMP-CB-INSET.rule: In this early Internet decision, continuous online advertising and a toll-free number accessible in the forum counted as repeated solicitation under the long-arm statute and as purposeful contacts supporting personal jurisdiction.

sections.Parties: Inset Systems, Inc., a Connecticut corporation operating from Brookfield that developed and marketed computer software and related services, sued Instruction Set, Inc. (ISI), a Massachusetts corporation based in Natick that provided computer technology and support, for infringing its INSET trademark. Inset sought damages and injunctive relief; ISI sought dismissal for lack of personal jurisdiction and improper venue.
sections.Procedural History: Inset filed the action on June 30, 1995 in the District of Connecticut under federal trademark law, state unfair-competition and infringement principles, a Connecticut dilution provision and the Connecticut Unfair Trade Practices Act. ISI moved to dismiss under Rules 12(b)(2) and 12(b)(3). On April 17, 1996 the court denied the motion. The ruling permitted the litigation to proceed; it was not a finding of trademark liability or a damages award.
sections.Material Facts: Inset applied to register its INSET trademark in August 1985 and received the registration in October 1986. ISI later obtained the domain INSET.COM and used it to advertise its goods and services. Inset discovered the address in March 1995 when trying to acquire that domain for itself. ISI also advertised through the toll-free number 1-800-US-INSET. Inset had authorized neither use. ISI had no Connecticut office or employees and did not regularly conduct business there. The court described approximately twenty to thirty million Internet users worldwide and at least ten thousand connected users in Connecticut, figures that are the opinion's 1996 premises.
sections.Issue: Whether ISI's Internet advertising and toll-free number brought it within Connecticut's long-arm statute, section 33-411(c)(2), as repeated solicitation of business in the state; whether exercising jurisdiction satisfied Fourteenth Amendment due process; and whether venue in Connecticut was proper.
sections.Holding: The District of Connecticut in 1996, District Judge Covello, held that ISI's continuous Internet advertising was repetitive business solicitation under Connecticut's long-arm statute, that ISI had constitutionally sufficient purposeful contacts with Connecticut and jurisdiction was fair, and that venue was proper because a corporation subject to personal jurisdiction in the district was deemed to reside there. The court ordered no transfer.
sections.Reasoning:
The plaintiff had to make a prima facie showing, and the inquiry had two separate steps: the long-arm statute and due process.

On the statute, section 33-411(c)(2) subjected a foreign corporation to a resident's suit arising from business repeatedly solicited in the state. ISI did not specifically contest it. Earlier district decisions had found repeated solicitation in advertisements in publications circulated in Connecticut, and the court treated continuous Internet advertising as at least sufficiently repetitive, since users in the state could access the same advertisement repeatedly, with greater reach than discarded printed materials. The court did not require evidence of completed Connecticut sales.

On due process, ISI argued that its Massachusetts base and lack of Connecticut presence defeated minimum contacts. The court applied purposeful availment and reasonable anticipation of litigation, and inferred that ISI directed its online advertising and telephone number toward every state, including Connecticut; nationwide reach did not exclude purposeful direction to this state. Jurisdiction was also fair given the minimal distance from Massachusetts, Connecticut's interest in its own common-law and statutory claims, and efficient resolution. ISI had not developed a distinct fairness objection.

On venue, the then-applicable section 1391(b)(1) permitted suit where a defendant resided, and section 1391(c) deemed a corporate defendant resident where it was subject to personal jurisdiction when the action began.

The casebook presents Inset as an early Internet-jurisdiction decision; the brief treats its reasoning as historical and not as a current rule that every accessible website establishes jurisdiction everywhere.

CP-COMP-CB-JACOBSON.rule: A judgment conclusively settles the demand adjudicated, but in a later suit on a different demand it binds only on points actually litigated and determined, not on a fact admitted merely by a pleading omission.

sections.Parties: Miller sued Gunzburg and Jacobson for rent under an asserted lease. Jacobson, against whom Miller recovered judgment in the second suit, sought review in the Supreme Court of Michigan, contending that he could deny execution of the lease.
sections.Procedural History: Miller first sued in 1877 for earlier rent installments and obtained judgment. He later sued for later installments. The trial judge treated the first suit's files, verdict and judgment as conclusive proof of the lease's execution and rejected Jacobson's proposed evidence, and Miller again recovered judgment. On June 11, 1879 the Supreme Court of Michigan reversed with costs and ordered a new trial.
sections.Material Facts:
The asserted lease covered premises in Grand Rapids for three years at $1,400 annual rent, payable monthly in advance. The first suit sought rent allegedly accruing between October 15, 1875 and April 9, 1877. The defendants pleaded the general issue but did not deny execution of the lease under oath, so Circuit Court Rule 79 prevented them from disputing execution in that case; the lease was received without evidence for or against execution. Jacobson offered evidence that Gunzburg alone occupied the premises.

The second suit sought rent accruing from July 1877 through April 1878. This time Jacobson submitted an affidavit denying that he had signed, executed or delivered the lease or authorized anyone else to do so, which ordinarily required Miller to prove execution. Miller instead introduced the first suit's record. The judge also rejected Jacobson's proposed evidence of a December 1875 arrangement under which Miller allegedly accepted Gunzburg as the tenant, and an attempted showing of a later surrender.
sections.Issue: Whether a judgment for earlier rent installments, in a suit where execution of the lease was admitted only by the defendants' failure to deny it under oath, conclusively established execution of the lease in a later suit for different installments.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of Michigan in 1879, Justice Cooley writing with Chief Justice Campbell and Justice Marston concurring and Justice Graves concurring separately, held that it did not. Jacobson could dispute execution when the later installments were sought, although he could not reopen liability for the earlier installments. The court did not decide that Jacobson never executed the lease or that a surrender terminated liability; those matters were left for the new trial.
sections.Reasoning:
Justice Cooley distinguished two kinds of conclusiveness. A judgment settles the subject matter of the litigation, the right one party asserted against the other, and a later suit cannot reopen that demand, including through a defense that should have been raised originally. A judgment can also settle a point of fact or law necessarily adjudicated, but that requires attention to what the first proceeding actually put in dispute and determined.

The judgment for the earlier rent stood whether correct or erroneous, contested or obtained by default. The present suit, however, concerned later rent, a different demand. By failing to submit the sworn denial, the defendants conceded execution for the purposes of the first litigation and removed it from the issues the court and jury could consider; even a special finding on execution would have been surplusage. The prior judgment therefore rested on a procedural admission without resolving the fact for later actions. Had execution actually been contested and determined, that determination could bind in later litigation under the same lease, but an opportunity to contest a fact does not show it was determined when the second action concerns a different demand. Cooley drew on Cromwell. Finality protects the judgment made, not an adjudication that could or should have been made.

On surrender, the court declined to prescribe instructions in advance; evidence that Miller received a store key and offered the premises for rent could bear on surrender but was not conclusive.

Justice Graves, concurring, likened the first proceeding's effect to an agreement to decide that particular case regardless of whether the instrument had genuinely been executed. The casebook places the case near a discussion of common-law compulsory counterclaims and asks whether possible landlord reliance should preclude the defense.

CP-COMP-CB-JOHNS-MANVILLE-1996.rule: A federal court may not abstain from deciding an uncertain state-law question merely because it is difficult, and a mandatory class restructuring a trust need not offer opt-out rights where the court has jurisdiction over the trust and representation is adequate.

sections.Parties: The case concerned the restructuring of the Manville Personal Injury Settlement Trust. Six subclasses were designated: present claimants, future claimants, claimants with settlements or judgments before November 19, 1990, codefendant manufacturers, MacArthur distributors, and other Manville distributors. On appeal, parties contested the deferral of the Maryland setoff rule, approximately 150 District of Columbia claimants sought exclusion from the settlement, and the insurer USF&G, an intervenor that denied covering MacArthur's asbestos claims, objected to a fund for the MacArthur distributors.
sections.Procedural History:
The trust was created in 1988 under a bankruptcy-approved reorganization plan. Its insolvency prompted restructuring litigation in 1990. An earlier restructuring settlement was vacated in Findley II. On remand a trial began but stopped when the parties settled nearly all issues. Judge Weinstein, sitting in both federal districts, and Chief Bankruptcy Judge Lifland approved the revised settlement after fairness proceedings, culminating in the January 19, 1995 judgment appealed here. The trial courts deferred the Maryland setoff question to the Maryland courts and denied the District of Columbia claimants' opt-out request.

On February 21, 1996 the Second Circuit vacated and remanded the Maryland deferral, dismissed USF&G's appeal for lack of standing, and otherwise affirmed.
sections.Material Facts:
The trust assumed health claims and other asbestos obligations, including contribution and indemnity claims by manufacturers and distributors, and the bankruptcy court enjoined further litigation against Manville itself. Expected lifetime claims had been approximately 83,000 to 100,000; by December 1994 approximately 240,000 had been filed.

The Trust Distribution Process assigned values across seven disease categories and initially paid ten percent of a claim's liquidated value, with assets and liabilities reevaluated at least every three years. Setoff rules determined how much a plaintiff's recovery against another manufacturer would be reduced because of the trust's responsibility, generally by reference to local law (pro tanto, pro rata or apportionment). Maryland claims were expressly excluded from the general setoff provisions pending a trial-court determination; injured claimants favored pro tanto treatment and codefendant manufacturers and distributors favored pro rata.

A separate $10 million MacArthur fund exchanged those distributors' releases of claims against Manville and the trust for reimbursement of specified litigation expenses, including insurance-coverage litigation. USF&G had not paid MacArthur's claims.
sections.Issue: Whether the trial courts properly declined to decide which Maryland setoff rule governed; whether District of Columbia claimants were entitled to opt out of the trust-restructuring settlement under Shutts or for inadequate representation; and whether USF&G had standing to appeal.
sections.Holding: The Second Circuit in 1996, Judge Kearse writing for a unanimous panel with Judges Winter and Cabranes, held that the refusal to decide the Maryland question was an improper abstention and remanded without selecting the Maryland rule; that Shutts did not require opt-out rights in this equitable trust restructuring and denying the opt-out was not an abuse of discretion; and that USF&G lacked a concrete injury and so lacked standing to appeal. The brief notes that this is the panel's 1996 resolution of this restructuring, not a statement that every mandatory mass-tort settlement satisfies Rule 23.
sections.Reasoning:
On Maryland, announcing that Maryland law applied did not answer which Maryland rule governed in this settlement. The court treated the deferral as abstention, reviewed rigorously, with legal premises receiving plenary review. Only Burford abstention was potentially relevant, and it protects important state regulatory or administrative arrangements from disruptive federal intervention; none was identified. Maryland's ordinary interests in compensating injured persons and distributing tortfeasor liability did not turn difficult contribution law into a reason to decline jurisdiction. Federal courts had to predict how Maryland's highest court would rule, and difficulty alone did not excuse decision. The panel rejected the distributors' claim that Maryland clearly required a pro rata release whenever a settling tortfeasor could not pay its full share, but left the final answer to the trial courts.

On the District of Columbia claimants, who objected that a trust settlement could yield only ten percent while reducing recovery against another defendant by the trust's entire pro rata share, the panel adhered to Findley II: this was an equitable trust restructuring, not simply an action for money judgments, and in rem and quasi in rem jurisdiction existed over beneficiaries of the New York bankruptcy-created trust. That conclusion depended on adequate Rule 23 representation, which the record showed: experienced counsel, no demonstrated neglect, and no distinction between the objectors and many similarly situated claimants who accepted. The trial courts reasonably concluded that exclusions would upset the settlement's balance.

On USF&G, an intervenor still needs a concrete, actual or imminent injury traceable to the challenged action and redressable. Having paid nothing, it had no present subrogation right, and having denied coverage it could not prevent its insured from settling and releasing claims.

The casebook uses the case to illustrate bankruptcy-funded asbestos trusts, equity ownership and an ongoing payment source.

CP-COMP-CB-JOHNSON-HUFFPOST.rule: A website's accessibility, interactivity, and unrelated advertising or merchandise sales in the forum do not support specific jurisdiction over a libel claim unless the publisher purposefully directed the allegedly wrongful conduct at the forum.

sections.Parties: Charles Johnson, a Texas citizen, sued TheHuffingtonPost.com, Inc. (HuffPost) for libel. HuffPost was a citizen of Delaware and New York with no Texas office, employees or property, and it contested personal jurisdiction. Johnson was the appellant, seeking reversal of the dismissal or, alternatively, jurisdictional discovery; HuffPost was the appellee.
sections.Procedural History: Johnson sued in the Southern District of Texas and amended his complaint to emphasize HuffPost's virtual connections with Texas. The district court dismissed for lack of personal jurisdiction because the story was not directed at Texas or based on Texas events or sources, and it denied jurisdictional discovery. Johnson appealed. On December 23, 2021 the Fifth Circuit affirmed the dismissal, with one judge dissenting.
sections.Material Facts:
HuffPost published a story about Johnson meeting two members of Congress in Washington, D.C., describing him as a Holocaust denier and white nationalist. The story said nothing about Texas, recounted no conduct there, and relied on no Texas sources.

Johnson alleged that Texans could read the story on the site, that HuffPost marketed merchandise and an ad-free experience to readers including Texans, that Texas advertisers contracted for space, and that the site collected visitors' locations so advertisers could display relevant ads. Reading HuffPost was free; the optional payment removed advertisements. Johnson conceded that he could not establish general jurisdiction. He did not allege that HuffPost reached into Texas to attract readers to the site or the story, for example through geographically targeted advertisements elsewhere.
sections.Issue: Whether a Texas court had specific personal jurisdiction over an out-of-state online publisher for a libel claim based on the website's interactive and commercial features and Texas readership, when the story itself had no Texas focus; and whether denying jurisdictional discovery was an abuse of discretion.
sections.Holding: The Fifth Circuit in 2021, Judge Jerry E. Smith writing for himself and Judge King with Judge Haynes dissenting, held that the pleaded connections were inadequate for specific jurisdiction because HuffPost had not aimed either the alleged libel or its website at Texas, and that denying jurisdictional discovery was not an abuse of discretion. The majority did not establish a comprehensive rule about what additional online targeting would suffice, and did not decide whether the descriptions were true, defamatory or actionable.
sections.Reasoning:
Specific jurisdiction required purposeful forum contacts, a claim arising out of or relating to them, and fairness. The majority treated the circuit's Revell Internet-libel precedent as controlling: interactivity is a prerequisite to the analysis, not a sufficient showing, and Revell applied Calder's focus on the story and forum-related harm. The story lacked Texas connections. Johnson's distinction between features on the same page as the libel and features elsewhere was unpleaded and in any event wrong, because the inquiry is the relationship between the forum contact and the claim.

Independently, ordinary principles required dismissal. Merchandise sales and advertisements, including location-based ones, concerned unrelated goods and did not relate to the reputational injury. Showing tailored ads to people who had already visited a universally accessible site is not soliciting Texas readers. Treating unrelated advertising as enough would collapse specific into general jurisdiction. The majority read Ford as requiring a meaningful connection between the forum market and the product underlying the injury, and Keeton as resting on an affirmative decision to distribute the publication in the state. Discovery would only confirm more of the same legally insufficient contacts.

Judge Haynes, dissenting, distinguished Keeton's publication-circulation route from Calder's effects analysis for individual authors and argued the majority erased the former. She viewed HuffPost's substantial Texas circulation and Texas-specific advertising as deliberate commercial exploitation, read Ford's relationship principle as supporting Johnson because an online newspaper's core product is its articles, and would have vacated and remanded.

The casebook excerpts the majority and dissent for the dispute over purposeful market exploitation.

CP-COMP-CB-KATZ-LILLY.rule: When investigation conducted without compulsory process gives a factual basis to believe a judgment offered as offensive collateral estoppel rested on a compromise verdict, jurors with relevant information may be deposed to resist its preclusive use.

sections.Parties: Benna Katz sued Eli Lilly & Co. for negligence in testing and distributing diethylstilbestrol (DES) and for breach of warranty, seeking $5 million. After she died in 1977, her mother, Esta Katz, brought the wrongful-death action as administratrix. Katz moved to quash subpoenas and vacate deposition notices directed to jurors from another DES case; Lilly wanted the jurors' testimony.
sections.Procedural History: Katz sued in 1975 in the Eastern District of New York. During discovery, a different DES plaintiff, Joyce Bichler, obtained a $500,000 verdict against Lilly after a seven-week state-court trial ending July 16, 1979; that judgment remained on appeal. Lilly noticed depositions of two Bichler jurors and obtained subpoenas. Katz moved under Rules 26 and 45 to quash the subpoenas and vacate the notices. On November 29, 1979 the court denied the motion.
sections.Material Facts:
Katz alleged that her mother took DES before her birth in 1953 and that she later developed vaginal adenocarcinoma. Katz intended to invoke the Bichler judgment to prevent Lilly from relitigating liability issues.

At the end of the Bichler trial the state judge told jurors they were free to discuss deliberations or decline. Lilly's lawyers contacted juror Margaret Donnelly, who initially agreed to talk. According to counsel, she said her liability vote depended on damages being reduced by averaging each juror's proposed award. Information from juror Willie Bowman also suggested compromise. These accounts were allegations supporting discovery, not judicial findings. Donnelly later declined to sign an affidavit. Bowman was served with a subpoena, but Donnelly could not be served. After Donnelly complained of harassment, the state judge barred further contact with the Bichler jurors pending the federal court's resolution. Lilly's counsel represented that the testimony was sought only to resist the judgment's collateral-estoppel effect in Katz, not to attack the Bichler verdict itself.
sections.Issue: Whether a defendant facing offensive collateral estoppel may depose jurors from the earlier trial about a possible compromise verdict, despite the rule against using juror testimony to impeach a verdict, where the testimony is sought only to resist the judgment's preclusive use by a stranger to the first action.
sections.Holding: The Eastern District of New York in 1979, District Judge Neaher, held that when permissible investigation conducted without compulsory court process establishes a factual basis for believing that a judgment offered as collateral estoppel rested on a compromise verdict, depositions of jurors shown to possess relevant information are warranted under the Federal Rules. The court did not determine that the verdict was a compromise, finally refuse preclusion, authorize depositions on mere suspicion in every case, or decide the merits of the DES claims.
sections.Reasoning:
The court began with a limitation: had Lilly's purpose been to invalidate the Bichler verdict, both state and federal law would require granting the motion, and federal discovery could not be taken for use in a pending state action. The testimony was sought for a distinct federal proceeding.

The then-applicable discovery rule allowed relevant, nonprivileged matters beyond the exact issues framed by the pleadings, and Katz's motion papers showed the intended estoppel argument. New York law controlled issue preclusion in this diversity action. Mutuality was not required, but offensive use depended on the defendant having had a full and fair opportunity to litigate, which required examining the realities of the earlier litigation, including indications of a compromise verdict. The information was therefore relevant to a foreseeable defense.

Katz argued that the rule against juror impeachment of verdicts, reflected in Rule 606(b), made the information inadmissible. The court recognized those policies but distinguished disturbing a verdict's finality from limiting its use against a party in litigation with a stranger to the original action, and found no authority directly controlling.

Collateral estoppel is an equitable doctrine governed by fairness. A judgment may remain conclusive between the original parties despite an erroneous compromise, but offensive use by a stranger raises a different fairness question: Katz sought not to escape repeated litigation of her own dispute but to avoid litigation altogether. Where there was a factual basis to suspect compromise, the defendant needed a reasonable opportunity to investigate before preclusion was decided, and counsel's voluntary interviews supplied that basis.

The casebook's note asks whether the distinction between undermining the verdict and restricting its effect holds, and whether investigating the verdict defeats preclusion's economy.

CP-COMP-CB-KOREAN-AIR-1987.rule: A multidistrict transferee court deciding a question of federal law should consider the transferor circuit's precedents but is not bound by them; Van Dusen's preservation of transferor law applies to state law in diversity cases.

sections.Parties: Plaintiffs in wrongful-death actions arising from the loss of Korean Air Lines Flight 007 sued Korean Air Lines. The plaintiffs sought partial summary judgment denying the carrier the $75,000 Warsaw/Montreal liability limitation and were the appellants; Korean Air Lines sought to invoke the limitation.
sections.Procedural History: The wrongful-death actions were consolidated for pretrial proceedings in the District of Columbia under 28 U.S.C. section 1407. On July 25, 1985 Chief Judge Aubrey E. Robinson Jr. denied the plaintiffs' motion for partial summary judgment and their request for immediate payment of $75,000. After certification under section 1292(b), the D.C. Circuit allowed an interlocutory appeal and, on January 30, 1987, remanded for clarification of the ruling's scope. Robinson's May 7, 1987 memorandum explained that his interpretation applied to all categories of actions, including those originating in New York. On September 25, 1987 the D.C. Circuit affirmed the determination that Korean Air Lines could invoke the limitation, expressly adopting the district court's opinion on that question.
sections.Material Facts: A Soviet aircraft shot down Korean Air Lines Flight 007 on September 1, 1983. The passengers' tickets contained the notice of limited liability in eight-point type, although the Montreal Agreement specified ten-point type. The Second Circuit had accepted an argument that noncompliance with the ten-point requirement deprived a carrier of the limitation, while the District of Columbia court independently rejected that interpretation. Some of the consolidated actions originated in New York, so whether the transferee court had to apply the federal-law interpretation of the circuit where an action originated bore directly on the plaintiffs' potential recovery. The $75,000 figure was a maximum, not a guaranteed minimum, and individual damages remained disputed.
sections.Issue: Whether a multidistrict transferee court must apply the transferor circuit's interpretation of federal law, by extension of Van Dusen v. Barrack, and whether printing the liability notice in eight-point rather than ten-point type deprived the carrier of the Warsaw/Montreal damages limitation.
sections.Holding: The D.C. Circuit in 1987, Judge Ruth Bader Ginsburg writing for a panel with Judges Stephen F. Williams and Douglas H. Ginsburg, held that a transferee court should consider the transferor circuit's federal precedents but is not bound by them under stare decisis, and affirmed that Korean Air Lines could invoke the $75,000 limitation. The holding did not displace transferor state law in diversity cases. The court did not decide the plaintiff-initiated transfer question or conclusively decide how a transferor court must treat a multidistrict ruling after return.
sections.Reasoning:
The court rejected the extension of Van Dusen. That case concerned defendant-initiated transfer of diversity litigation under section 1404(a) and preserved the transferor state's law, including its choice-of-law rules, for an Erie-based purpose: preventing a federal transfer from producing a result unavailable in the state courts where the action was filed. That justification gives no entitlement to a particular circuit's interpretation of one body of federal law. A venue rule selects a convenient location, not a favored federal interpretation. Each federal court must apply federal law according to its own reasoned judgment; other circuits' decisions deserve careful consideration but do not bind merely because an action began there. Automatic adherence to every transferor circuit would institutionalize the inconsistency centralization sought to reduce, and the Supreme Court can resolve a genuine conflict. The court thought law-of-the-case principles should bind later proceedings, while acknowledging it could not have the last word on that.

On the merits, the adopted district opinion distinguished failure to deliver a ticket from an irregularity in a delivered ticket. The Montreal Agreement, an intercarrier agreement, required ten-point notice but did not say that a violation forfeited the limit, and it expressly waived Article 20 defenses without any express waiver of the damages limitation. Dissatisfaction with the treaty did not authorize judges to rewrite it.

Judge Douglas H. Ginsburg, concurring and joined by Judge Williams, found no instruction in section 1407 that the transferee judge simulate the transferor judge's rulings, discussed the unresolved problem of a case returning to a circuit with contrary precedent, and canvassed possible legislation.

The casebook uses the case for the contrast between transferor state law and independent interpretation of federal law, and uses the concurrence to question the structure of multidistrict coordination.

CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-015.rule: In this case-management order the court declined to pick a deposition site itself and directed counsel to settle that logistical question by one game of rock, paper, scissors, subject to place, time and review limits.

sections.Parties: Avista Management, Inc., doing business as Avista Plex, was the plaintiff, and Wausau Underwriters Insurance Company was the defendant. Avista moved for the court to designate the location of a Rule 30(b)(6) deposition.
sections.Procedural History: In consolidated litigation in the Orlando Division of the Middle District of Florida, Avista filed a motion asking the court to designate the location of a Rule 30(b)(6) deposition. On June 6, 2006 the court denied the motion in a two-page order and instead prescribed a procedure for counsel to resolve the question.
sections.Material Facts:
The order describes the motion as another dispute the parties had been unable to untangle without federal-court assistance. It gives no account of the underlying insurance claims, the competing preferred locations, or the parties' arguments.

The court directed counsel to meet at 4 p.m. on June 30, 2006 at a mutually acceptable neutral site and, if they could not agree on one, on the front steps of the Sam M. Gibbons U.S. Courthouse in Tampa, to play a single game of rock, paper, scissors. Each lawyer could bring one paralegal as attendant and witness. The winner could choose the deposition site, but only somewhere in Hillsborough County, and the deposition was to occur during July 11-12, 2006. Either party could dispute the outcome at a hearing before the same judge in Orlando on July 7, 2006 at 8:30 a.m., which the order called an appeal. The order does not show whether counsel actually played, who won, or whether anyone sought the hearing.
sections.Issue: Where the Rule 30(b)(6) deposition should be held, the parties having been unable to agree on a location.
sections.Holding: The Middle District of Florida in 2006, District Judge Gregory A. Presnell, denied the motion to designate a location and directed counsel to resolve that limited question through a single game of rock, paper, scissors. The order is a case-management direction; it decided no underlying merits question and announced no legal test validating games or chance procedures.
sections.Reasoning:
The order cites no authority and supplies no broader legal test. The brief explains that the practical reasoning is apparent from the court's description of repeated unnecessary intervention: the court sought a simple mechanism for a logistical disagreement while preserving geographic, timing and judicial-review constraints.

The brief notes that the casebook summarizes the order as one to meet on the courthouse steps, whereas the order made that site conditional on failure to agree on a neutral location. The casebook cites the order to ask whether using a children's game was appropriate and whether drawing lots would differ; those are the editors' questions, which the order does not resolve.

CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-039.rule: A municipal ordinance that bars a person from occupying property solely because of race is not a legitimate exercise of the police power and violates the Fourteenth Amendment's protection of the rights to acquire, use and dispose of property.

sections.Parties: Buchanan, a white seller, sued Warley, a Black purchaser, for specific performance of a contract to sell a Louisville lot. Warley defended on the ground that Louisville's racial residential ordinance prevented him from residing there. Buchanan contended that the ordinance violated the Fourteenth Amendment and brought the case to the Supreme Court on writ of error.
sections.Procedural History: Buchanan sued in the Chancery Branch of the Jefferson Circuit Court for specific performance. The Kentucky trial court and the Kentucky Court of Appeals treated the ordinance as constitutional and a complete defense. The Supreme Court reviewed the Kentucky Court of Appeals judgment on writ of error and, on November 5, 1917, reversed and remanded for further proceedings consistent with its opinion. It did not itself enter a decree of specific performance.
sections.Material Facts:
Buchanan agreed to sell Warley a lot at 37th Street and Pflanz Avenue in Louisville. Warley's written offer stated that he intended to build a home there and would not have to accept a deed or pay unless Kentucky and Louisville law permitted him to occupy the property as his residence. When they contracted, eight of the block's ten residences were occupied by white people and two, the nearest to the lot, by Black people.

The ordinance, approved May 11, 1914, prohibited a Black person from moving into a residence or assembly place on a block with more white-occupied than Black-occupied properties, and a parallel provision prohibited a white person from moving into a predominantly Black block. Existing occupancy and previously acquired occupancy rights were protected, and servants and employees could live in their employers' residences. Violation was an offense. The ordinance regulated occupancy rather than expressly prohibiting a deed, but its practical effect controlled this sale.
sections.Issue: Whether a white seller could challenge the ordinance when the restriction fell on a Black purchaser, and whether a city may, under the police power, forbid occupancy, and so in practice purchase and sale, of property solely because of the intended occupant's race.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 1917, in an opinion by Justice Day with no separate writing, held that Buchanan could raise the challenge because his own ability to dispose of his property was impaired, and that the ordinance's racial restriction was not a legitimate exercise of the police power and could not stand under the Fourteenth Amendment. The opinion did not treat all regulation of land transactions as forbidden and did not announce the invalidity of every form of segregation.
sections.Reasoning:
On the threshold objection, the Court accepted that a litigant must show injury to his own rights. Buchanan did: the state courts denied enforcement solely because the ordinance prevented his purchaser from occupying the lot, so his own right to dispose of property was impaired.

On the merits, the Court recognized broad state power to regulate health, safety and welfare and rejected the idea that ownership confers an absolute right to every use. But the police power is subject to the Constitution. Property includes the rights to acquire, use and dispose of a thing, and the Fourteenth Amendment protects them. Although phrased as an occupancy rule, the ordinance meant a buyer forbidden to live there could not ordinarily buy for residential use, so the racial classification directly burdened the white owner's disposition and the Black purchaser's acquisition.

Justice Day relied on the Reconstruction Amendments and on the federal civil-rights enactments of 1866 and 1870, which secured equal rights to purchase, sell, hold and convey property and equal contractual rights.

The defenders' justifications failed. The Court distinguished rather than overruled Plessy v. Ferguson, describing it as providing separate but equal accommodations without denying transportation altogether, and distinguished Berea College as resting on Kentucky's authority over a corporate charter. Racial hostility could not justify sacrificing constitutional rights to preserve public peace. Racial purity did not fit a case about sale and residence, especially when the ordinance allowed Black servants in white homes. Protecting white property values was insufficient, since undesirable white neighbors or lawful disagreeable uses could have similar effects.

The casebook cites Buchanan for the invalidation of municipal racial zoning under the Due Process Clause; its discussion of later restrictive covenants, Hansberry and Shelley is the editors' historical context.

CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-044.rule: Under code pleading, an allegation that a draft was accepted for valuable consideration states an ultimate, issuable fact rather than a legal conclusion, and the particular consideration need not be pleaded.

sections.Parties: California Packing Corp. sued Kelly Storage & Distributing Co. in contract on an accepted draft and obtained a warrant of attachment. Phoenix and Third National Bank of Lexington, Kentucky, a third party to the underlying dispute, moved to vacate the attachment. California Packing was the appellant in the Court of Appeals, defending the attachment and disputing the bank's standing.
sections.Procedural History: California Packing obtained a warrant of attachment on its complaint and accompanying affidavit. The bank moved under Code of Civil Procedure section 682 to vacate it. Special Term denied the motion. The First Department reversed and vacated the attachment. California Packing appealed by permission on three certified questions. On January 27, 1920 the New York Court of Appeals reversed the Appellate Division's order, awarded costs in that court and the Court of Appeals, and affirmed Special Term's order.
sections.Material Facts: California Packing alleged that it drew a draft upon Kelly Storage and Distributing Company and that Kelly accepted it for valuable consideration. The draft was not alleged to be negotiable. The complaint did not plead the particular consideration, and the reported opinion gives no transaction amount or description of the actual consideration. California Packing relied on the complaint and affidavit to obtain the attachment in its contract action.
sections.Issue: Whether the bank could move to vacate the attachment; whether alleging acceptance for valuable consideration stated a fact or a legal conclusion under the Code's requirement of a plain, concise statement of facts; and whether the papers sufficiently showed a cause of action.
sections.Holding: The New York Court of Appeals in 1920, Judge Pound writing for a unanimous seven-judge court, held that the bank could make the motion, that the allegation of acceptance for valuable consideration was factual rather than a legal conclusion, stating an ultimate, principal, issuable fact that allowed proof of the actual consideration, and that the complaint and affidavit sufficiently showed a cause of action to support the attachment.
sections.Reasoning:
The First Department had repeatedly treated such an allegation as a mere legal conclusion, while the Third Department regarded a more detailed statement as unnecessary. Judge Pound adopted the latter approach. Section 519 required liberal construction of pleadings toward substantial justice. Established common-law forms had permitted pleading according to legal effect, and precedent accepted value received as an adequate averment on a nonnegotiable note. A pleader could safely rely on a form stabilized by authority rather than risk error by devising a more elaborate account.

Negotiable instruments supplied a comparison: statute presumed consideration for a negotiable instrument, allowing pleading by copy without a separate consideration averment, and comparable language in an action on a nonnegotiable draft sufficiently alleged the corresponding ultimate fact. The allegation was not defective merely because it summarized the underlying transaction.

The papers showed a contract cause of action with liquidated damages on which attachment could rest. The court did not hold that evidence was unnecessary or that every generalized allegation would suffice, but requiring meticulous recital of the facts ultimately proved at trial would obscure the real issue without furnishing a useful safeguard against oppression.

The casebook cites the case within Professor Cook's discussion of statements of fact under code pleading; Cook's broader critique of the fact/law distinction is scholarly commentary, not the court's reasoning.

CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-051.rule: A party opposing summary judgment need not present evidence in final trial-admissible form; a genuine issue exists if the record, taken cumulatively, would let a jury return a verdict for the nonmoving party.

sections.Parties: Myrtle Nell Catrett, administratrix of her husband Louis's estate, sued fifteen asbestos manufacturers or distributors after his death. Celotex was the only defendant before this panel. Catrett was the appellant, seeking reversal of summary judgment for Celotex; Celotex contended she had shown no exposure to its products.
sections.Procedural History: Catrett sued in 1980. Celotex first sought summary judgment in September 1981, then withdrew that motion and requested transfer to Illinois. On a renewed motion, after a July 1982 hearing, the district court granted summary judgment orally without a written opinion, finding no showing of exposure in the District of Columbia or elsewhere within the statutory period. The D.C. Circuit initially reversed because Celotex had not supported its motion with affirmative evidence. The Supreme Court reversed that ruling in Celotex Corp. v. Catrett and remanded for consideration of Catrett's actual showing. On that remand, on August 7, 1987, the D.C. Circuit reversed the district court's judgment and remanded for further proceedings, with one judge dissenting.
sections.Material Facts:
Louis Catrett died in 1979 after a construction career involving asbestos products. The disputed link was whether he had encountered an asbestos product for whose liabilities Celotex was responsible.

Catrett's interrogatory responses identified his employment with Anning-Johnson and his work as a fireproofer. Opposing summary judgment she relied on three documents: Louis's earlier workers' compensation testimony, a letter by Anning-Johnson assistant secretary T. R. Hoff, and an insurer's letter repeating Hoff's information. Hoff's letter said Louis supervised and trained crews applying Firebar. She supplemented her interrogatory answers to identify Hoff as a trial witness.

Celotex's own transfer papers included purchase orders showing Firebar shipments to Anning-Johnson during 1971 from Carey-Canadian Asbestos, a Panacon division, and its interrogatory answers acknowledged that Panacon merged into Celotex in 1972 and that Celotex assumed Panacon's ordinary liabilities. At the hearing Celotex challenged the admissibility of Louis's prior testimony; the judges disagreed about whether it also objected to Hoff's letter. Catrett still had not answered detailed exposure interrogatories, and a motion to compel had never been decided.
sections.Issue: Whether the record, as it stood when the district court granted summary judgment, contained a genuine factual issue about Louis Catrett's exposure to Celotex-related asbestos.
sections.Holding: The D.C. Circuit in 1987, Judge Starr writing for himself and Chief Judge Wald with Judge Bork dissenting, held 2-1 that the record raised a genuine issue of exposure and that summary judgment was improper. The panel expressly reserved whether a better-developed record might later justify summary judgment; it established neither proven exposure nor that the case must be tried, and did not adjudicate Celotex's ultimate liability.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority treated the Supreme Court's majority opinion as controlling the moving party's initial burden. Under Rule 56 and Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, a genuine issue requires enough evidence for a jury to return a verdict for the nonmoving party, an inquiry parallel to directed verdict. The opposing party need not present evidence in final trial-admissible form, though whether the material could become admissible remained important.

The majority evaluated the cumulative chain. Hoff's letter and the supplemental answer naming Hoff as a witness, read together, indicated a witness capable of giving admissible testimony about exposure; a bare witness name alone would not automatically suffice. The court did not decide that the letter met the business-records exception. It found inadmissibility uncertain and concluded that Celotex had not timely objected: counsel discussed the letter, the judge requested and examined it, and that consideration implicitly overruled any unclear objection. Celotex's purchase orders placed Firebar at Anning-Johnson while Louis worked there, and its merger admissions connected Carey-Canadian, Panacon and Celotex. The majority did not rely on the compensation testimony, to which Celotex specifically objected, or on the insurer's letter, which merely repeated Hoff. Catrett's unanswered interrogatories were a matter for discovery enforcement.

Judge Bork, dissenting, would have affirmed. Listing Hoff and describing general duties did not show a witness with personal knowledge of exposure; the letter was unsworn hearsay prepared for litigation, and he read counsel's statements as an objection to it. He thought the majority effectively granted an unrequested extension of discovery and weakened the directed-verdict standard.

The casebook's note excerpts the dispute over the Hoff letter and Bork's objection.

CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-073.rule: A class action under California section 382 requires an ascertainable class and a well-defined community of interest in questions of law and fact; it does not require a common fund or a single indivisible recovery.

sections.Parties: David Daar sued Yellow Cab Company of California, the only appearing defendant, for alleged taxicab overcharges on behalf of himself and two classes of riders: those who paid with coupons from Yellow Cab script books and those who paid cash. He sought damages and an accounting. Yellow Cab demurred. Daar was the appellant.
sections.Procedural History: Daar sued on November 20, 1964. Yellow Cab demurred for failure to state a claim or a proper class action, nonjoinder, uncertainty and lack of subject-matter jurisdiction. The superior court's January 28, 1965 minute order sustained the jurisdictional demurrer without leave to amend and transferred the case to municipal court, effectively treating Daar's own small claim as all that remained. No formal judgment appeared in the record. On November 15, 1967 the California Supreme Court treated the order as a final judgment for purposes of appeal, reversed it, and directed the superior court to overrule the demurrer on every specified ground except uncertainty, which the trial court had never ruled on. Other attempted appeals were dismissed.
sections.Material Facts:
The complaint, whose allegations were accepted for testing its sufficiency, covered the four years before suit. Daar alleged that the company's written franchise required fares at rates fixed by the Los Angeles Public Utilities Commission, but that its meters were adjusted to charge higher rates. The proportion of overcharge was allegedly uniform, and company information could establish the total.

Script books and individual coupons bore corresponding serial numbers, and the complaint alleged that company records could identify purchasers and users and determine their overcharges. For cash riders, it alleged that the amount of the overcharge was known to Yellow Cab and ascertainable at trial. Daar claimed to have spent $100 on script books and $100 in cash fares. Each count alleged aggregate overcharges exceeding $100,000. Small individual losses allegedly made separate lawsuits economically infeasible.
sections.Issue: Whether the order sustaining the demurrer was appealable, and whether the complaint stated a proper class action under Code of Civil Procedure section 382 when class members could not all be identified at the outset and each rider's recovery would be a different amount.
sections.Holding: The California Supreme Court in 1967, Justice Sullivan writing for a unanimous court, held that the order was appealable because it effectively dismissed the claims of every class member except Daar, and that the complaint sufficiently pleaded an ascertainable class and a well-defined community of interest. The ruling went only to the sufficiency of the allegations; it awarded no overcharge damages. The court expressly declined as premature to decide an amicus proposal for handling recovered overcharges and did not approve a fare-reduction remedy.
sections.Reasoning:
On appealability, the court looked to the order's legal effect rather than its label; otherwise destruction of the class action would evade review.

Section 382 reflects equity's doctrine of representative litigation, and precedent required both an ascertainable class and a well-defined community of interest. Identifying every member at the outset is different from showing an ascertainable class; an inability presently to name all people affected by common issues does not foreclose a representative suit, and a later claimant would still have to identify himself and establish his entitlement.

The court rejected Yellow Cab's argument that community must extend to common relief. No common fund or single indivisible recovery is required; individual calculations can be subsidiary to common questions. What matters is whether numerous substantial individual questions would remain. The court distinguished cases where each person's right to recover depended on unique facts from cases where basic liability questions were shared and amounts could be determined mathematically. The 1966 revision of federal Rule 23 was a useful comparison but not controlling.

Applied to the complaint, both groups faced a uniform overcharge from the same pricing practice, and an accounting could establish amounts from company records.
