Separate actions would likely cost more than each rider could recover, and without a class procedure Yellow Cab might retain the benefits of the alleged wrongdoing. The court declined judicial notice of fare structures and tipping practices offered to discredit the uniform-overcharge allegation, because they were not beyond reasonable dispute.

The brief notes that the casebook attributes to this citation an order lowering fares for all riders for a period; that may concern later events, but it is not the judgment in the 1967 opinion.

CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-087.rule: Where only some named plaintiffs in a Title VII action satisfy the statute's special venue requirements in the chosen district, a court may cure the defect by dismissing the improperly venued plaintiffs rather than dismissing or transferring the whole action.

sections.Parties: The plaintiffs were six named plaintiffs bringing employment-discrimination claims under Title VII against Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. in the Northern District of California. Wal-Mart, the defendant, sought dismissal for improper venue or, alternatively, transfer to the Western District of Arkansas. The casebook account does not identify each plaintiff.
sections.Procedural History: The plaintiffs filed in the Northern District of California. Wal-Mart moved to dismiss for improper venue or to transfer. On December 3, 2001, the district court denied the motion and cured the venue defect by dismissing the four improperly venued named plaintiffs, leaving the action in California. The complete 2001 decision was not recovered; this account rests on the casebook and on a later court opinion quoting the ruling. This venue stage is separate from the later Supreme Court decision on class certification.
sections.Material Facts: The claims were employment-discrimination claims under Title VII, which has a special statutory venue provision. The plaintiffs filed in the Northern District of California. Wal-Mart sought transfer to the Western District of Arkansas, where the casebook places its headquarters. Of the six named plaintiffs, four did not satisfy Title VII's venue requirements in the chosen district and two were properly venued. The casebook account does not describe each employee's workplace or discrimination allegations, and the full factual record of the order is not available.
sections.Issue: Whether, when four of six named plaintiffs do not satisfy Title VII's venue requirements in the chosen district, the court should dismiss or transfer the entire action or instead dismiss only the improperly venued plaintiffs.
sections.Holding: The United States District Court for the Northern District of California, 2001. According to the casebook, the court denied Wal-Mart's motion and cured the venue defect by dismissing the four improperly venued named plaintiffs rather than the entire action, leaving the litigation in California with the properly venued plaintiffs. The ruling did not determine liability for discrimination or certify a class. The exact terms of the individual dismissals are not known without the original order.
sections.Reasoning:
The only recovered reasoning comes from a later Maryland opinion, International Painters and Allied Trades Industry Pension Fund v. Miller Painting Co., Inc., which quotes the 2001 ruling. As quoted there, the court explained that dismissing or transferring the entire action would be too severe when two of six plaintiffs were properly venued, and chose instead to dismiss the improperly venued plaintiffs and permit the California plaintiffs and the action to remain. The later opinion relates this to dropping or transferring parties. The rest of the court's reasoning, including any rejected arguments, cannot be given because the complete December 2001 opinion was not recovered.

The casebook uses the outcome to raise questions about representative lawsuits: whether the dismissed named plaintiffs could participate as absent class members, whether pendent venue could fill the gap, and whether geographically diverse named plaintiffs would better represent a nationwide class. Those are the editors' questions, not answers given by the court.

CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-125.rule: A federal court applying state law must decide as the state's highest court would, and may follow that court's recent considered dicta over an older contrary holding when the dicta signal the old rule no longer stands.

sections.Parties: F. O. Grey, a cotton grower in Yazoo County, Mississippi, sued Hayes-Sammons Chemical Co., a Texas insecticide manufacturer, for crop damage, alleging breach of warranty, negligence and a settlement agreement. Grey won a jury verdict, lost it on the manufacturer's motion for judgment notwithstanding the verdict, and appealed.
sections.Procedural History: Grey sued in state court for $11,423.75, and Hayes-Sammons removed the action. The district judge withheld the settlement claim from the jury, refused a res ipsa loquitur instruction, and gave warranty instructions without expressly addressing privity. The jury awarded $8,750. On the manufacturer's motion the judge entered judgment notwithstanding the verdict, reasoning that the label's disclaimer shifted all risk to Grey and that Mississippi warranty law ordinarily did not protect consumers lacking privity outside the food-product exception. On November 7, 1962 the Fifth Circuit reversed and directed entry of judgment for Grey in accordance with the verdict.
sections.Material Facts:
In 1957 Grey farmed a 45.6-acre tract and a 19-acre tract. He sprayed his cotton with Hayes-Sammons insecticides bought through T. A. Quinn Chemical & Fertilizer Company in sealed five-gallon cans. The first two drumloads covered the larger tract and the northern quarter of the smaller one; a third partial load finished the job. Late in July the cotton showed damage that was severe and uniform across the land covered by the first two drumloads and slight on the rest. The manufacturer's division manager, Andrew White, and an entomologist agreed the symptoms indicated a growth-hormone herbicide such as 2-4D or 2-4-5T. The empty cans could not be tested.

Grey shared the spraying equipment with his brother and was sure his brother used weed killer. The manufacturer described careful separation of herbicides from its insecticide operations.

Quinn received a 7.5 percent sales commission and a $300 monthly salary, sold only Hayes-Sammons insecticides, and held them under a written consignment agreement; the manufacturer retained title until withdrawal for sale and fixed prices and territory. The can's label listed the ingredients, directed use against cotton insects, and carried a nonwarranty clause addressing use and handling.
sections.Issue: Whether Mississippi's older privity decisions required judgment for the manufacturer on negligence; whether negligence was pursued and res ipsa loquitur could support it; whether the distributor's relationship to the manufacturer satisfied privity for warranty; whether the label's disclaimer covered a foreign contaminant; and whether circumstantial evidence of causation sustained the verdict.
sections.Holding: The Fifth Circuit in 1962, Judge Wisdom writing for a panel with Chief Judge Tuttle and Judge Rives, held that Mississippi would no longer require privity for a negligence claim against a manufacturer; that negligence was pleaded and pursued; that Quinn acted as the manufacturer's agent, establishing privity with Grey for warranty purposes; that the disclaimer did not cover contamination by an undisclosed herbicide; and that the damage pattern was adequate evidence of causation. The court did not reach whether an enforceable settlement existed.
sections.Reasoning:
Mississippi law controlled, and the court had to decide as a Mississippi court would, considering prior holdings and later indications from the state's highest court. In Ford Motor Co. v. Myers, Mississippi had declined to follow MacPherson. But in E. I. Du Pont de Nemours & Co. v. Ladner the Mississippi Supreme Court, while resolving the case on causation, deliberately and approvingly discussed the modern principle allowing remote consumers to recover for a manufacturer's negligence. The First Circuit's Mason decision had read that discussion, with the overwhelming modern trend, as signaling abandonment of Ford's rule, and this court agreed, acknowledging that it was unusual to prefer recent considered dicta to an older contrary holding.

Negligence was in the case: the complaint alleged contamination when the product was manufactured, packaged and sealed, counsel argued negligent packaging, and Grey requested a res ipsa instruction. Sealed-container contamination could support res ipsa under Mississippi principles, subject to the plaintiff's burden.

On warranty, the overall sales relationship made Quinn a selling agent despite the agreement's terminology, so privity was satisfied through agency, not abolished. Disclaimers must clearly identify the warranties excluded and are construed against the seller; this clause addressed hazards of using the described insecticide, not an undisclosed foreign herbicide. On causation, residue from the brother's use should have diminished after the first drumload, so uniform severe damage across two loads supported an inference that the second can replenished the herbicide. A new trial would serve no useful purpose.

The casebook uses Grey to illustrate state-law prediction after Mason; the brief notes that its statement that lack of privity did not bar the claim compresses the two distinct routes.

CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-186.rule: Rule 23 governs in federal court despite a state statute barring private class actions on a state-created claim, because allowing the class changes only the mode of litigating existing rights, not the substantive rights themselves.

sections.Parties: Robert Lisk, a homeowner, sued Lumber One Wood Preserving, LLC, the supplier of allegedly defective treated fence wood, under Alabama's Deceptive Trade Practices Act (ADTPA) and for breach of express warranty, seeking to represent a nationwide class. Lumber One moved to dismiss. Lisk was the appellant.
sections.Procedural History: Lisk invoked federal jurisdiction under the Class Action Fairness Act, his individual claim not exceeding $75,000. Lumber One argued that Alabama forbade private ADTPA class actions, that no sufficiently pleaded warranty ran to a remote purchaser, and that without the class claims no jurisdictional basis remained. The district court dismissed the complaint. On July 10, 2015 the Eleventh Circuit, reviewing de novo, reversed and remanded. It did not certify the class.
sections.Material Facts:
The facts are the complaint's allegations, accepted for evaluating dismissal. Lisk hired Clean Cut Fence Company to install a fence at his home. The contract required treated wood and stated that manufacturers supplied the warranties on fencing materials. Clean Cut bought wood through Capitol Wholesale Fence Company, a distributor supplied by Lumber One. Lumber One's website, advertising and labels represented that the wood was pressure-treated using licensed MCA technology that would resist rot, fungal decay and termites for at least fifteen years. Lisk's posts allegedly rotted within three years, and Clean Cut said other customers had similar problems.

The ADTPA authorized consumer relief but reserved representative actions to the Alabama Attorney General or district attorneys and prohibited private class actions. The parties assumed, and the court accepted for the appeal, that Alabama substantive law governed.
sections.Issue: Whether Rule 23 or Alabama's statutory ban on private class actions governs an ADTPA class claim in federal court, and whether a remote purchaser plausibly pleaded an express-warranty claim as an intended third-party beneficiary of the manufacturer's warranty to its distributor.
sections.Holding: The Eleventh Circuit in 2015, District Judge Robert L. Hinkle sitting by designation and writing for a panel with Circuit Judges Marcus and Jill Pryor, held that Rule 23 governs the proposed ADTPA class claim and that Lisk plausibly pleaded an express-warranty claim as an intended third-party beneficiary. The court expressly left unresolved which of the broader Shady Grove opinions supplies the binding rule. Neither liability nor class certification was adjudicated.
sections.Reasoning:
The Rules Enabling Act permits federal procedural rules but forbids abridging, enlarging or modifying substantive rights, and a valid Federal Rule displaces conflicting state provisions. Applying Rule 23 changed the mode of litigating existing ADTPA rights without changing the rules of liability: Lumber One remained obliged to represent its product accurately and buyers kept the same right to redress.

On Shady Grove, Justice Stevens had joined Parts I and II-A of Justice Scalia's opinion, giving those portions five votes, and all five justices supporting the result agreed that Rule 23 governed the New York statutory-penalty class claim. The panel saw no meaningful distinction between that claim and the Alabama one: both were state-created rights with individual recovery permitted but private collective recovery restricted, and Alabama even allowed public officials to bring representative actions. That the Alabama ban sits within the statute creating the claim was not controlling, since reorganizing a code cannot change whether a Federal Rule alters substantive rights. Because the result was consistent with both the Scalia and Stevens approaches, the panel did not choose between them, noting the difficulty of applying Marks.

On warranty, Alabama required intent at contract formation to confer a direct benefit, intended-beneficiary status and breach, and Lisk alleged each. It was plausible that a manufacturer would warrant its product to end users to increase demand, and Alabama's Harris Moran seed case supported the analogy. If the manufacturer-distributor agreement expressly excluded end-user warranties, that might establish a defense in later proceedings.

The casebook cites the case for the refusal to choose between the Shady Grove rationales; its account of Alabama's 2016 legislative response is the editors' later context.

CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-224.rule: A cy pres distribution of class settlement funds must be guided by the objectives of the underlying statutes and the interests of the absent class members, including the class's geographic reach.

sections.Parties: Four plaintiffs brought a class action against AOL, LLC on behalf of approximately 66 million current AOL members. Darren McKinney, an objector, challenged the settlement's charitable distributions and appealed its approval; AOL defended the settlement.
sections.Procedural History: The class action was filed in August 2009 and settled. The district court provisionally certified the class and approved notice. Over McKinney's objections it approved the settlement, and Judge Snyder declined to recuse. McKinney appealed on the cy pres distribution, recusal and notice. On November 21, 2011 the Ninth Circuit reversed in part, affirmed in part and remanded: approval of the cy pres distribution was reversed and the denial of recusal affirmed. It declined to decide the sufficiency of notice and ordered each side to bear its own costs.
sections.Material Facts:
The plaintiffs alleged that AOL inserted promotional footers into emails sent by its subscribers, and asserted electronic-communications privacy, unjust-enrichment, California consumer-protection and contract claims. The settlement provided notifications of the advertisements and an opportunity to opt out. The parties considered individual damages small and hard to ascertain: an approximately $2 million maximum trial recovery would yield about three cents per member, less than the cost of distribution.

Instead, at the mediator's suggestion, AOL agreed to donate $25,000 to each of three recipients: Los Angeles Legal Aid, the Federal Judicial Center Foundation, and the Boys and Girls Club, shared between Los Angeles and Santa Monica chapters. Separate donations totaling $35,000, $8,750 for each named plaintiff's designation, went to charities chosen by the representatives, for total donations of $110,000. Judge Snyder's husband served as a volunteer on Los Angeles Legal Aid's approximately fifty-member board.
sections.Issue: Whether the district court abused its discretion in approving cy pres donations to charities with no demonstrated connection to the claims or to the nationwide class, and whether the judge was required to recuse because her husband sat on the board of one recipient.
sections.Holding: The Ninth Circuit in 2011, Circuit Judge N. Randy Smith writing for a panel with Judge Betty B. Fletcher and District Judge James S. Gwin sitting by designation, held that the district court applied the wrong standard and abused its discretion in approving the cy pres distribution, and that recusal was not required. The panel did not itself choose a charity or order payment to the Treasury.
sections.Reasoning:
Cy pres permits an indirect, next-best use of settlement funds that are unclaimed or impracticable to distribute, but a good charitable purpose is not enough. The distribution must be guided by the underlying statutory objectives and the absent class members' interests, including the class's geographic reach; without that nexus the choice may serve the preferences of the parties, lawyers or court and create an appearance of impropriety. Under Six Mexican Workers, a distribution must address the statutory objectives, target the plaintiff class, and give reasonable certainty that members will benefit.

These donations failed. The recipients had no demonstrated connection to the electronic-communications and commercial-email interests underlying the claims. Two-thirds of the principal donations went to local Los Angeles charities despite a nationwide class, and the Federal Judicial Center Foundation, though national, had no apparent connection to the statutory purposes. AOL's plea for deference to the settlement as fair, reasonable and adequate confused two inquiries: the adequacy of the settlement as a whole and the validity of its distribution. The standards apply whether the parties or the judge select recipients, and a mediator's involvement does not remove the nexus requirement. Suitable beneficiaries were not impossible to find, since all members used the internet; organizations protecting internet users from online fraud were plausible. If none could be identified, the district court should consider escheat to the Treasury.

On recusal, a reasonable informed observer would not necessarily question the judge's impartiality merely from her husband's volunteer board membership, and Legal Aid was not a party; remote or speculative benefits did not create a disqualifying interest.

The casebook cites the case for the nexus failure; the brief notes that the footers were appended to subscribers' outgoing messages and that the wrongdoing was alleged, not adjudicated.

CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-238.rule: Class notice must be the best practicable under the circumstances, not a guarantee of actual receipt, and a settlement reached before certification is also examined for signs of collusion before approval.

sections.Parties: Richard Noll and Rhythm Motor Sports, LLC, who sold items on eBay, sued eBay, Inc. on behalf of sellers who paid recurring fees on Good 'Til Cancelled listings, seeking refunds of disputed renewal fees. The plaintiffs sought final approval of a class settlement, attorneys' fees, expenses and class-representative payments; three objections to the settlement were filed.
sections.Procedural History: The 2011 complaint included contract, consumer-protection, unjust-enrichment, fraud and declaratory claims. Motions to dismiss narrowed the case, and the court dismissed the automatic-renewal statutory count with prejudice in 2013. After amended pleadings, discovery, expert work and a class-certification motion, the parties settled following two mediations before retired judges; the agreement was executed January 14, 2015. On September 15, 2015 the court certified a settlement class, approved the settlement, overruled the objections, awarded fees and expenses, and reduced the requested class-representative payments.
sections.Material Facts:
Good 'Til Cancelled listings renewed every thirty days until ended or sold, with insertion fees and optional-feature fees. The sellers alleged that eBay's fee schedules did not adequately disclose the monthly recurring charges. The settlement class periods ended June 19, 2012.

The settlement fund was $6.4 million, with no claims process: active accounts would receive automatic credits and inactive or closed accounts checks. Uncashed amounts would go to two nonprofit organizations rather than revert to eBay. The fund exceeded 71 percent of first-renewal fees and was about 9 percent of all renewal fees at issue. The report identified 1,192,947 unique user IDs.

Notice combined individual email with a linked settlement website, mailed notices where email was missing or failed, a press release and toll-free support. The administrator mailed 20,739 notices for missing or invalid email addresses and further notices after 170,746 emails were returned; the court reported that 98.57 percent appeared to have received direct notice. Ninety-seven exclusions and three objections were filed, and no state Attorney General responded to the Class Action Fairness Act notice.
sections.Issue: Whether a settlement class should be certified under Rule 23(a) and (b)(3); whether the notice plan was adequate; whether the settlement was fair and free of collusion; and what attorneys' fees, expenses and representative awards were warranted.
sections.Holding: The Northern District of California in 2015, District Judge Edward J. Davila, certified the class for settlement purposes, approved the notice plan and the settlement, and found no collusive arrangement. The court awarded $1.6 million in fees, 25 percent of the fund, and $72,923.16 in expenses, and awarded each class representative $5,000 instead of the $15,000 requested. Approval did not establish liability on the underlying claims.
sections.Reasoning:
On certification, numerosity was undisputed. The common user agreement, fee schedules and listing system generated common questions; the representatives suffered the same alleged injury; and uniform allocation and experienced counsel supported adequacy. Common contractual questions predominated for settlement purposes and small individual recoveries made separate suits uneconomical, though the court acknowledged that contested litigation could require individualized evidence.

On notice, the court approved the combined email, website, postal, press and support plan under the best-practicable-notice standard and Rule 23(e); reasonable efforts did not guarantee each member's actual receipt.

On fairness, the court weighed the eight Churchill factors. Prior dismissals and disputed contractual understandings posed real risks, and extensive discovery, experts and mediated negotiations supported an informed compromise. The low numbers of exclusions and objections and the absence of governmental objection supported approval.

Because settlement preceded formal certification, the court separately examined the Bluetooth indicators of collusion. Counsel sought the 25 percent benchmark, the fee and representative awards were not conditions of settlement, reductions would increase class funds, and nothing reverted to eBay.

The fee was checked against a lodestar exceeding $1.035 million for approximately 2,600 hours, an approximately 1.6 multiplier. The $15,000 representative awards were not justified as an upward departure. The objections failed: the awards were not contingent on supporting the settlement, counsel's out-of-state location was no bar, and one objector was late and outside the class.

The casebook quotes the notice methods and poses questions about Internet-only notice, which are the editors' questions and not the court's holding.

CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-243.rule: A pleading must state facts rather than legal conclusions or evidence: a defendant's belief that a publication was true does not plead truth, and absolute privilege must be shown by pleaded facts, though it need not be named.

sections.Parties: Daniel O'Regan, former Hudson County prosecutor, and William George, former assistant prosecutor, each sued the twenty-three members of the county's December 1944 grand jury for libel, each complaint demanding $100,000 from each defendant. The grand jurors, defended by the Attorney General, filed a joint answer in each action containing fourteen separate defenses. Plaintiffs moved to strike the answers or particular defenses; defendants' supplemental answers operated as cross-motions to strike the complaints.
sections.Procedural History:
The two libel actions were substantially identical. Plaintiffs moved to strike the answers or particular defenses. At oral argument defendants obtained leave to supplement their answers with an objection that the suits were premature, and plaintiffs elected to attack the supplemental matter as part of their existing motions. Because the pleadings were practically identical, Supreme Court Commissioner Ackerson considered the motions together as though one joint action. The decision concerns which allegations and defenses could remain; it was not a trial of the publication's truth or a final damages judgment.

The court denied the motion to strike the fourteenth defense, struck a number of other defenses or parts of them, denied the attack on the reserved prematurity objection without prejudice, and directed an order implementing its mixed rulings. Plaintiffs were allowed to amend their damages demand and defendants to amend paragraph eight of the first defense and the sixth, tenth, and twelfth defenses, on or before November 25, 1946.
sections.Material Facts:
O'Regan and George served as prosecutor and assistant prosecutor from February 4, 1934, through February 4, 1944. The complaints alleged that the grand jurors published a report accusing them of suppressing the Hartkorn report and failing to call Hartkorn as a witness in criminal proceedings against John Longo, thereby withholding potentially exculpatory material. The quoted accusation invoked Canon 5's obligation to seek justice rather than merely convictions. These were allegations about the publication, not a judicial finding that either prosecutor suppressed evidence.

Each complaint charged a joint tort in one count but demanded $100,000 from each defendant. The complaints alleged only that defendants composed and published the defamatory material; they did not allege an official presentation to the court.

Among the defenses, one paragraph alleged that the jurors believed the report true and recited the evidence producing that belief. The second defense alleged the statements were substantially true; the third alleged they were true and was not attacked. The fourteenth defense alleged that the jurors were investigating allegations of suppressed evidence in a particular prosecution, that the prosecutors appeared and testified under oath, and that the publication resulted from an official presentation to the court.
sections.Issue: Which allegations and defenses in the libel pleadings were sufficient: in particular, whether a defendant's belief in the truth of the publication, with the evidence behind it, pleads a defense of truth or privilege, and whether the facts pleaded showed that the grand jurors' report was absolutely privileged as a judicial act.
sections.Holding: Supreme Court Commissioner Ackerson, in a 1946 decision in the New Jersey Miscellaneous reports, held that belief in truth is not a complete defense of truth and struck the challenged substance of that paragraph while preserving its express denials. The second defense of substantial truth was technically insufficient, and the fair-comment and several other defenses were stricken as deficient. The fourth and seventh defenses were stricken because grand-juror status alone does not protect every publication, but the motion to strike the fourteenth defense was denied: the statements it described were pertinent to an official investigation and absolutely privileged. The complaints' damages demand was technically defective and could be amended, and the Attorney General could defend the former grand jurors.
sections.Reasoning:
Facts, not legal labels, determine the sufficiency of a pleading. Because the complaints alleged only composition and publication, defendants had to plead the facts supporting privilege in their answer; inserting conclusions such as clear absence of jurisdiction would not change that.

Honest belief might be pleaded in mitigation when punitive damages were claimed, but that purpose had to be clear and the pleading should not detail the underlying evidence. The paragraph instead appeared to assert belief as complete justification, and it failed as qualified privilege because belief in truth did not establish absence of malice. Truth required an averment that the words were true in substance and in fact. Fair comment needed allegations that the underlying facts were true, the subject was of public interest, and the comments were fair, in good faith, and without malice. The Rule 40 prematurity objection functioned like a demurrer, so a motion to strike was not the way to test it.

A party did not have to name absolute or qualified privilege if pleaded facts established it. The fourth defense failed to show an official investigation and judicial act and the seventh failed to identify the circumstances of publication. The fourteenth supplied those facts, accepted for the limited purpose of the motion. Grand juries exercise judicial functions, and judicial immunity turns on the distinction between a clear absence of all jurisdiction and an erroneous or excessive exercise of actual or colorable jurisdiction. Even assuming the document was only a report without an intended indictment, composing and presenting it remained a judicial act. Expunction of a report was a distinct question from civil damages.

The casebook cites the case, in a note contrasting factual pleading with pleading legal conclusions, for its refusal to infer truth from a defendant's belief and the evidence behind it.

CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-256.rule: Parties to a class settlement may agree in advance that money remaining after class members have been compensated, here by treble damages, will go to related charities, and a court does not abuse its discretion in approving that disposition.

sections.Parties: The plaintiffs were a consumer subclass of the Medicare Part B Co-Payment Class in multidistrict litigation over average wholesale prices, suing AstraZeneca over the drug Zoladex under state consumer-protection statutes. M. Joyce Howe, individually and for her husband's estate, and Leroy Townsend were the AstraZeneca subclass representatives. Howe, a named plaintiff, objected to the settlement and appealed its approval.
sections.Procedural History: A coalition sued in Massachusetts in December 2001, and related actions were consolidated there in April 2002. The district court organized the litigation into two tracks and three Track One classes. After an August 2005 order deferred certification until representatives were found, the court certified a Rule 23(b)(3) class in January 2006, excluding residents of nine states whose consumer-protection statutes did not create the relevant action. The parties settled in May 2007 on the eve of trial. Howe objected, and the judge considered her objections at a May 2008 fairness hearing, required changes sending more money to class members, and finally approved the settlement on December 15, 2008. Howe appealed. The First Circuit affirmed the approval of the settlement.
sections.Material Facts:
Pharmaceutical companies published an average wholesale price that insurers and Medicare used to calculate payments to physicians and patients' co-payments. The alleged wrong was a widening spread between that figure and physicians' much lower acquisition costs, with co-payments tied to the inflated benchmark. Zoladex commonly treated prostate cancer. Medicare generally covered 80 percent of the cost; most members' Medigap coverage paid 80 percent of the 20 percent co-payment.

Plaintiffs' expert estimated losses of $31,128,851. AstraZeneca agreed to pay $24 million in compensation, and the settlement expanded the class to include the nine previously excluded states in exchange for comprehensive peace. Distribution costs and attorneys' fees were separate obligations. Because many patients were elderly, deceased, or hard to locate, the agreement used a simple claims process, with recovery initially set at twice estimated actual loss. Money left after claims would go to mutually acceptable charities funding cancer research or patient care, subject to court approval of recipients.

The judge required treble compensation, first for the strongest claims and later, in October 2008, for all members if money remained, and reduced fees to 30 percent of recovery. The amended agreement kept a $10 million combined limit on additional treble payments and the charitable remainder. A February 2009 expert projection anticipated $17.2 million in claims and $6.8 million for charity; those were estimates.
sections.Issue: Whether the district court abused its discretion in approving a class settlement under which money remaining after payment of class members' treble damages would go to charities, and whether Howe's other objections, including conflict of counsel, the insurance assumption, the claims process, and the class definition, required reversal.
sections.Holding: The First Circuit in 2009, in an opinion by Chief Judge Lynch for a panel with Judges Torruella and Howard and no separate opinion, affirmed approval of the $24 million settlement. Its principal holding allowed the parties to agree in advance that money remaining after payment of class members' treble damages would go to related charities. It rejected Howe's conflict, insurance-assumption, and equal-check objections, and treated her fee-negotiation and class-definition objections as waived or raised for the first time on appeal. The court did not decide the distinct controversy over court-created charitable distributions outside a settlement and did not approve every possible charitable recipient.
sections.Reasoning:
Settlement approval was reviewed for abuse of discretion, with legal conclusions considered de novo. Arm's-length negotiation after sufficient discovery supported a presumption of reasonableness, but the judge still had to balance benefits, costs, litigation risks, and attainable alternatives.

The court distinguished two settlement uses of cy pres: substituting charitable payments where individual distribution is economically infeasible, and disposing of a remainder after compensation. This case involved the latter. Although the parties planned the remainder's use before administration ended, requiring them to wait would elevate timing over substance. Claimants could receive more than their actual damages before charity received anything, and the existence of members unlikely ever to claim supported an agreed disposition of the residue. The ALI's proposed Principles of Aggregate Litigation, on which Howe relied, were guidance and not the binding test; their concern that members recover fully before strangers benefit was met by treble compensation. Paying a larger total also prevented AstraZeneca from escaping its agreed obligation.

There was no evidence that the advocacy organization counsel had earlier represented existed to promote such funds, and it did not fit the cancer-research or patient-care description. Accounting for supplemental insurance matched actual losses; Howe's own policy paid 50 percent, but double or treble recovery still exceeded actual damages. Mailing equal checks from the CMS database would pay some nonmembers and overpay or underpay members. On the class definition, discussed for guidance, Rule 23(c)(1)(B) does not require complete restatement of earlier orders; incorporation was sufficient.

The casebook uses the case as an example, describing the $24 million settlement and the estimated $6.8 million charitable remainder.

CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-275.rule: Where individual suits over a defendant's uniform rules could impose incompatible standards of conduct on it or impair absent members' interests, a class may be certified under Rule 23(b)(1) without opt-out rights, even if it would also qualify under Rule 23(b)(3).

sections.Parties: Seventy-eight named players or former players, financially supported by the Players Association, sued the National Football League on behalf of 5,706 current and former professional players on antitrust claims. Class counsel also represented the association. Fifteen active players and one inactive player objected to the settlement and appealed its approval, seeking Rule 23(b)(3) treatment so that they could opt out. The class also moved on appeal for a remand or stay.
sections.Procedural History: The litigation followed Mackey v. NFL, which had held the Rozelle Rule unlawful under the Sherman Act's rule-of-reason analysis. The NFL, the association, and class counsel negotiated a class settlement of past antitrust claims at the same time as a collective bargaining agreement on future player movement; the NFL withdrew its pending certiorari petition in Mackey as part of the settlement. After hearings noticed for April 25 and July 5, District Judge Earl R. Larson certified the class under Rule 23(b)(1) and approved the $13,675,000 settlement. The objectors appealed. The Eighth Circuit denied the motion for remand or a stay and affirmed the order approving the settlement.
sections.Material Facts:
Under the Rozelle Rule, when a player's contract expired and he joined another team, the new club owed compensation to the former club, and if the teams could not agree the commissioner could award players or draft choices. Mackey treated player-movement restrictions as a mandatory bargaining subject but rejected the labor exemption because the rule had not resulted from bona fide arm's-length bargaining.

In this action plaintiffs had sought changes to league rules as well as damages. The settlement provided $13,675,000 in damages for past claims; a covenant not to sue was also challenged. The separately negotiated labor agreement adopted a new first-refusal and compensation arrangement for future player movement; 453 of 478 eligible voting union members ratified it. The district court found that the labor agreement was not consideration for the class settlement. Evidence showed that money otherwise available to the union pension fund had increased the class settlement fund.

The objectors argued that active and retired players needed subclasses, that the notices did not announce judicial review of the labor agreement, and that the new arrangement was more restrictive than the Rozelle Rule. On appeal the class cited purported new evidence that teams interpreted the labor agreement differently from the association.
sections.Issue: Whether the district court abused its discretion in certifying the class under Rule 23(b)(1), without a right to opt out, and in approving the antitrust settlement over objections about notice, subclasses, conflicts of interest, and the covenant not to sue; and whether the court had to supervise the separately negotiated labor agreement.
sections.Holding: The Eighth Circuit in 1978, in an opinion by Chief Judge Gibson for a panel with Judges Heaney and Bright and no separate opinion, affirmed. It sustained certification under Rule 23(b)(1), rejected the objections concerning notice and representation, found no abuse of discretion in the compromise or its distribution formula, and denied the motion seeking remand or a stay for judicial supervision of the labor agreement. The court did not hold that unequal damages awards alone establish incompatible conduct.
sections.Reasoning:
Review was for abuse of discretion, with substantial weight given to the trial judge's familiarity with the litigation; his findings were not clearly erroneous.

On certification, the court looked to the action's broader remedial scope. Plaintiffs had sought changes to league rules as well as damages, and individual injunctions governing uniform player-movement practices could impose incompatible obligations on the NFL, which satisfied Rule 23(b)(1)(A). Collective bargaining had removed the need for that equitable remedy by the time of settlement, but that did not erase the action's original scope. Under Rule 23(b)(1)(B), individual changes to common league rules would apply across the league and could impair others' interests. The case also appeared eligible under (b)(3), but where both applied, proceeding exclusively under (b)(1) was generally appropriate to avoid inconsistent adjudication.

The court could not set aside the labor agreement in these suits; complaints about representation in bargaining could be raised in an action for breach of the union's duty of fair representation. Notice under then-Rule 23(e) was adequate and did not have to announce a review of the labor agreement that was not before the court. The division between members interested in past damages and those interested in future rules was theoretical and did not show an actual conflict; any bargaining tension had been resolved in favor of damages. The covenant not to sue was superfluous: old Rozelle Rule claims would meet res judicata, and future claims could encounter the labor exemption, which the panel thought highly likely but did not decide. The dispute over interpretation of the labor agreement belonged in arbitration and labor-law channels.

The casebook uses the case as an example and quotes its incompatible-standards reasoning.

CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-289.rule: A court approving a class settlement must still find Rule 23's certification requirements met, and may approve a provision sending cash left after class claims to charity rather than back to the defendant.

sections.Parties: Ethan Shaw and Clive D. Moon sued Toshiba America Information Systems and NEC Electronics, with additional Toshiba and NEC entities later added, on behalf of owners and lessees of Toshiba laptop and notebook computers. They sought relief for an alleged defect in floppy-diskette controllers. Toshiba denied any defect or liability. Fewer than thirty objections to the settlement were filed.
sections.Procedural History: Shaw and Moon filed suit on March 5, 1999, in the Eastern District of Texas. After extensive briefing, the court denied partial-summary-judgment motions in August 1999 and ordered mediation, while discovery continued on an accelerated schedule. The parties announced a settlement on October 28. The court conditionally certified a class, preliminarily approved the agreement, protected its jurisdiction against competing litigation, and set a January 19, 2000 fairness hearing. In this opinion of January 28, 2000, following that hearing, District Judge Heartfield certified the settlement class, approved the settlement, and approved class counsel's fees, expenses, representative payments, and compensation for objectors' counsel. This is the final-settlement decision, distinct from the earlier summary-judgment rulings.
sections.Material Facts:
Plaintiffs alleged defective microcode in floppy-diskette controllers. The controller was supposed to signal overruns or underruns during a read or write operation; the alleged condition prevented a signal when the problem occurred only on the last byte of a sector, potentially causing undetected data loss, corruption, or system failure. The claims invoked the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, 18 U.S.C. section 1030, and warranty law. Toshiba denied that its laptops were defective or that any user had lost data, and the settlement imposed no admission of liability.

The class covered qualifying United States citizens or residents, including businesses and governments, who owned or leased Toshiba laptop or notebook computers, about five million units, about three million under warranty. Relief depended on purchase timing and warranty status: cash payments for units bought new on or after March 5, 1998; a software patch and a $225 Toshiba-product coupon for units under warranty on or after March 5, 1999, with a hardware option and a $200 coupon; and a patch and a $100 coupon for others. Consequential-damage claims were reserved.

The package had an aggregate face value of approximately $2.1 billion. Toshiba had to establish a $597.5 million cash fund for class claims. Only cash remaining after class claims would go to a charity buying Toshiba computers for schools, churches, nonprofit organizations, libraries, hospitals, and poor recipients; none would revert to Toshiba.
sections.Issue: Whether the proposed nationwide settlement class satisfied Rule 23's certification requirements, whether the settlement, including its coupon relief and its provision sending residual cash to charity, was fair, adequate, and reasonable, and whether the requested attorneys' fees were reasonable.
sections.Holding: The Eastern District of Texas in 2000, District Judge Heartfield, certified an opt-out settlement class, mainly under Rule 23(b)(3), found the approximately $2.1 billion settlement package fair, adequate, and reasonable, and approved $147.5 million in class counsel's fees as fair, just, and reasonable. The court also approved up to $3 million in litigation expenses, $25,000 for each representative, and $6 million for counsel whose objections helped extend coupon validity, and it revoked the pro hac vice admission of one objector's lawyer for inappropriate conduct. The settlement decided nothing about defect or liability.
sections.Reasoning:
Settlement did not dispense with Rule 23's requirements. Applying Amchem, the court found the millions of owners too numerous for joinder; the existence of the same controller problem and its legality were common questions; Shaw and Moon invoked the same theories as absent owners and had no conflicting interests. Predominance rested on the single alleged source of economic injury and common liability questions; individual damages could vary, warranty principles were sufficiently uniform across states, and reserving consequential-damage claims avoided future-injury conflicts. Class treatment was superior because many claims were worth less than the cost of individual litigation. The court added that the injunctive and warranty claims were sufficient for (b)(2) treatment.

On fairness, the court examined six factors: fraud or collusion; complexity, expense, and duration; litigation progress and discovery; prospects of success; possible recovery; and the views of counsel, representatives, and members. It found arm's-length bargaining after extensive discovery, and technical uncertainty, a relatively new statutory theory, and difficulty collecting against Japanese assets supported compromise. The coupons were transferable and aggregatable, which supported economic value, though their Toshiba-only restriction reduced it.

The residual-charity provision was tied to addressing the digital divide and improving computer skills. The court rejected three alternatives: reversion, which would give an incentive to discourage claims; extra fees; and additional payments that could create a windfall. The charity followed satisfaction of claims and did not replace individual remedies.

For fees the court tested the request under lodestar, percentage, and hybrid approaches, valuing the common fund conservatively at $1 billion to $1.1 billion; the request fell within all three ranges.

The casebook cites the case for its residual-charity provision, which it quotes; its figures for the foundation's later totals are editorial history, not findings of this opinion.

CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-293.rule: A forum court in a multistate class action must examine the law of each state whose law is claimed to conflict; where that examination shows no outcome-changing conflict, the same result may stand under each state's law.

sections.Parties: Irl Shutts and Robert and Betty Anderson sued Phillips Petroleum Co. in Kansas on behalf of approximately 28,100 royalty owners, seeking interest on gas royalties Phillips had suspended. Phillips was the defendant and, after the district court on remand again ruled for the class, the appellant in the Kansas Supreme Court.
sections.Procedural History: An earlier case, Shutts I in 1977, involved 6,400 owners and a different suspension period. In the present action the original trial judgment was entered May 20, 1983, and in Shutts II in 1984 the Kansas Supreme Court accepted jurisdiction over nonresident plaintiffs, awarded interest under equitable principles at the rates in Phillips's federal undertaking, and imposed Kansas's fifteen-percent post-judgment rate. In 1985 the United States Supreme Court upheld jurisdiction but rejected the Kansas rationale for applying forum law to every claim, leaving the examination of conflicts and the choice of law to the Kansas courts. On remand the Seward County district court found no conflict on liability and the pre-judgment rate, adopted the prior result, and entered a new judgment on April 30, 1986. Phillips appealed. The Kansas Supreme Court affirmed the judgment as modified and remanded for calculation of each plaintiff's interest and entry of judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
Phillips collected tentative gas-price increases while awaiting Federal Power Commission approval but withheld the associated royalty increases unless owners provided indemnity and security against possible refunds. After approval it paid the suspended royalties without interest despite having used the money in its business. The opinion recounts payments of $3.7 million in 1976, $4.7 million in 1977, and $2.9 million in 1978.

Phillips's FPC undertaking set interest at seven percent before October 10, 1974, nine percent through September 30, 1979, and thereafter the average prime rate compounded quarterly. Its indemnity offers required owners to promise repayment with interest and to obtain an acceptable irrevocable bank letter of credit.

Although the gas came from eleven states, Phillips briefed conflicts only for Texas, Oklahoma, Louisiana, New Mexico, and Wyoming; the court treated arguments about other jurisdictions as abandoned. Phillips argued that the district court had not obeyed the mandate, that state laws genuinely differed, and that the fifteen-percent post-judgment award was error.
sections.Issue: On remand from the United States Supreme Court, whether the laws of Texas, Oklahoma, Louisiana, New Mexico, and Wyoming conflicted with the Kansas result on Phillips's liability for interest on suspended royalties and the applicable rate, and what post-judgment interest rate and starting date applied.
sections.Holding: The Kansas Supreme Court in 1987, in an opinion by Chief Justice Schroeder with Justice Allegrucci not participating, held that all five contested states would impose liability and imply an agreement to compensate owners at the rates in Phillips's federal undertaking, so recovery of pre-judgment interest at those rates was sustained. It modified the post-judgment award: post-judgment interest begins April 30, 1986, and Kansas's fifteen-percent rate does not apply automatically to leases in the five states. The court directed the lesser of the implied-contract federal rate or eighteen percent for Texas, fifteen percent for Oklahoma, seven for Louisiana, fifteen for New Mexico, and ten for Wyoming, with fifteen percent for Kansas leases and all other jurisdictions.
sections.Reasoning:
The court did not repeat a preference for forum law. It examined statutes and decisions in each contested state, often predicting the answer where no state court had decided this precise royalty question. Its common premise was that Phillips's role as stakeholder and its actual use of the money supported compensation under equitable principles of unjust enrichment.

For Texas, the court relied on decisions recognizing an equitable exception to the common-law restriction on interest and rejected Phillips's purchaser-versus-producer distinction because Phillips undertook royalty disbursement and used the retained funds. Conditional indemnity offers were not an unconditional tender and did not stop interest from accruing. Oklahoma authorities similarly allowed compensation for another's use of money, and the federal undertaking could be viewed as an implied contractual obligation. For Louisiana, the court treated the undertaking as a third-party-beneficiary stipulation, acknowledging confusing authorities. New Mexico allowed interest for loss of the use of money. Wyoming's ordinary notice requirement was impractical because Phillips itself computed and withheld the royalties.

The federal rates remained the measure because Phillips could never keep the suspended principal outright, and its own indemnity demands used the same federal interest framework. The court found no outcome-changing conflict on these obligations in these circumstances; it did not say every state's interest law is identical.

On post-judgment interest, a full reversal wipes out a judgment. The court construed the Supreme Court's choice-of-law reversal as vacating the original award, so post-judgment interest ran from the new judgment.

The casebook cites the remand decision in a note for the point that the choice-of-law analysis produced no change on liability and the pre-judgment rate; its statement that the five states embraced 97 percent is an editorial compression, since the report associates that figure with six states including Kansas.

CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-312.rule: Under Rule 23(e) a class settlement must be fair, adequate and reasonable even without overt collusion; courts must scrutinize attorney's fees and unexplained larger payments to selected class members, though reasonable, individually justified incentive awards to named representatives are permitted.

sections.Parties: African-American employees of the Boeing Company, including thirty-two named plaintiffs, brought an employment-discrimination class action against Boeing under Title VII, § 1981 and other claims. The plaintiffs and Boeing agreed to a consent decree settling the case. Objecting class members challenged certification and the settlement.
sections.Procedural History: The class action was filed in 1998. After negotiations beginning in November 1998, the parties announced an agreement in January 1999. Objectors challenged certification, the allocation of damages, counsel fees, notice, limited discovery and the prospective relief. The district court permitted some discovery into alleged collusion, held two fairness hearings, found no direct collusion, and in September 1999 certified the settlement class and approved the decree. On appeal the Ninth Circuit issued a majority opinion on November 26, 2002, then withdrew it and substituted the April 29, 2003 opinion, denying rehearing and rehearing en banc. The court found no abuse of discretion in certification but reversed approval of the consent decree and remanded.
sections.Material Facts:
The plaintiffs alleged discrimination in promotion, compensation, career development and working conditions. The class ultimately included approximately 15,000 employees across twenty-seven states. Little formal discovery had occurred when settlement talks began, though class counsel had interviewed more than 1,300 employees.

The consent decree provided $7.3 million in monetary relief, with about $6.5 million actually payable. A group of 264 named plaintiffs and other participating class members, reduced to 237 after opt-outs, would receive more than half the nominal monetary award. Class counsel selected these recipients and assigned them awards of $5,000 to $50,000, averaging about $16,500; the group largely overlapped people who had signed individual retainer agreements and contributed toward counsel's expenses. Approximately 3,400 other members claimed under a points system, with average awards around $1,000. One recipient, Cordell Bolder, was acknowledged not to be a class member.

Boeing also agreed to about $4.05 million in fees and costs, which the parties defended as roughly 28 percent of a putative common fund that included a valuation of the prospective relief. That relief consisted largely of consultation and monitoring, often leaving Boeing free to decide whether to adopt changes. The release reached beyond race-discrimination claims.
sections.Issue: Whether the district court abused its discretion in certifying the settlement class under Rule 23(a), and whether the consent decree, with its attorney's fee provision and its much larger payments to a selected group, was fair, adequate and reasonable under Rule 23(e).
sections.Holding: The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, 2003. Judge Berzon wrote for herself and Judge Lay; Judge Trott dissented, so the panel divided 2-1. The court upheld certification of the settlement class but reversed approval of the decree. The fee award had not been justified under either a statutory lodestar method or a proper common-fund method, and the large differential payments to the identified group lacked adequate support. The court did not ban reasonable incentive awards to named representatives. On remand the parties may try to justify the existing allocation and fees or renegotiate; the court cannot impose altered terms.
sections.Reasoning:
On certification, numerosity was undisputed, and counsel's interviews and more than 200 documented experiences across locations supported commonality and typicality. The court declined to bar classes mixing supervisors with nonsupervisors or employees from different facilities.

Rule 23(e) separately requires that the whole settlement be fair, adequate and reasonable. The absence of overt collusion does not settle that question, because counsel and selected participants can respond to incentives that disadvantage absent members without any secret agreement.

On fees, Boeing's formally separate payment did not remove the class's interest, since a defendant negotiates the cost of the whole package. Fees may be negotiated as statutory fees and justified under lodestar principles, or awarded by the court from a settled common fund; either approach must keep its own safeguards. Here the parties fixed the fee as a settlement term but defended it as a percentage of a supposed fund. Speculative injunctive relief could not ordinarily inflate that fund; without it the fee was about 38 percent, well above the circuit's 25 percent benchmark, which is not an automatic maximum.

On distribution, the roughly sixteenfold difference in average payments was unsupported by direct evidence. Incentive awards require individualized scrutiny of the representatives' actions, the benefit to the class, time and effort, and reasonable fears of retaliation. Unexplained special benefits give knowledgeable participants an incentive to maximize their own recoveries rather than test the settlement for the class.

Judge Trott would have affirmed, stressing deferential review and the district court's finding of no collusion.

The casebook quotes the incentive-award reasoning; the broader prohibition in the casebook's separate Johnson account is a later Eleventh Circuit rule, not this case's holding.

CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-321.rule: Lawful permanent residence does not make an alien a United States citizen for diversity purposes, so section 1332(a)(2) gives no jurisdiction over a suit between two aliens, and a treaty's access-to-courts provision does not supply it.

sections.Parties: Benjamin Tagger, an Israeli citizen living in Brooklyn as a lawful permanent resident of the United States, sued without counsel. The defendant was Strauss Group Ltd., an Israeli corporation headquartered in Israel; Sabra Dipping Co., LLC appears in the caption as an additional defendant, but the jurisdictional discussion concerns Strauss. Tagger was the plaintiff and appellant; Strauss sought dismissal and was the appellee.
sections.Procedural History: Tagger sued in the Eastern District of New York, invoking diversity jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. section 1332(a). Strauss sought dismissal on several grounds, including lack of subject-matter jurisdiction and forum non conveniens. Judge Cogan dismissed: Tagger's lawful permanent residence did not make him a New York citizen for diversity purposes in a suit against another alien, and Israeli courts were the more appropriate forum. Tagger appealed, relying not on the statute but on the United States-Israel Treaty of Friendship, Commerce and Navigation. The Second Circuit affirmed the district court's judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
Tagger was an Israeli citizen domiciled in New York as a lawful permanent resident. Strauss was incorporated and headquartered in Israel, and its foreign status was undisputed. Tagger brought common-law contract and tort claims, alleging that Strauss had falsely initiated legal proceedings against him in Israel, causing him to be prohibited from leaving that country. The Second Circuit did not decide whether those allegations were true.

In 1988 Congress had added a provision deeming an alien admitted for permanent residence a citizen of the state where the alien was domiciled. In 2011 the Federal Courts Jurisdiction and Venue Clarification Act removed that provision and instead denied section 1332(a)(2) jurisdiction in actions between a citizen of a state and a foreign citizen lawfully admitted for permanent residence and domiciled in the same state.

Article V(1) of the 1951 treaty promises national and most-favored-nation treatment regarding access to courts and administrative tribunals.
sections.Issue: Whether section 1332(a)(2) permits a suit by an Israeli citizen who is a New York-domiciled lawful permanent resident against an Israeli corporation, and whether the 1951 United States-Israel treaty independently confers federal jurisdiction over his claims.
sections.Holding: The Second Circuit in 2020, in a per curiam opinion by Judges Kearse, Calabresi, and Pooler with no separate opinion, answered both questions no and affirmed. Permanent-resident status did not transform Tagger into a United States citizen for alienage jurisdiction; both relevant parties were aliens, so section 1332(a)(2) did not supply diversity jurisdiction. The treaty guaranteed equal access and treatment and did not remove the jurisdictional requirements governing access to federal court. The stated grounds concerned subject-matter jurisdiction, not the merits of the contract and tort claims.
sections.Reasoning:
The court reviewed jurisdictional factual findings for clear error and legal conclusions de novo. Although Tagger did not challenge the district court's statutory reading on appeal, the panel explained it.

The court distinguished residence from the citizenship the diversity statute requires. An individual's diversity citizenship ordinarily follows domicile, but Tagger remained an Israeli citizen. The statutory history answered whether permanent residence supplied United States citizenship. Courts had disagreed over whether the 1988 deeming provision let a permanent resident sue another alien in diversity. The 2011 Act removed that provision and substituted an exception that restricts jurisdiction in the same-state situation without declaring a permanent resident a United States citizen. The legislative history explained that eliminating deemed citizenship avoided anomalous results and possible Article III problems. Tagger and Strauss were therefore both aliens, and section 1332(a)(2) did not authorize the suit. That formulation concerns this posture and is not a prohibition on every action with aliens on both sides.

On the treaty, relying on its earlier decision in Blanco and the Supreme Court's explanation in Sumitomo Shoji, the panel distinguished procedural equality from substantive entitlement. Access provisions protect matters such as filing fees, representation by lawyers, legal aid, and security for costs. National treatment means treatment equal to domestic nationals; most-favored-nation treatment means treatment no less favorable than that of another country's nationals. Neither exempts a litigant from otherwise applicable jurisdictional rules. The court did not say a treaty can never create a ground of federal jurisdiction.

The casebook cites the case in a parenthetical following its discussion of the permanent-resident amendments.

CP-COMP-CB-MACDERMID.rule: A nonresident who knowingly accesses a server located in the forum state to carry out the alleged wrong uses a computer in that state under its long-arm statute, and jurisdiction over her satisfies due process.

sections.Parties: MacDermid, Inc., a specialty chemical company based in Waterbury, Connecticut, sued Jackie Deiter, a former account manager of its Canadian subsidiary who lived and worked in Canada. MacDermid was the plaintiff and appellant, alleging unauthorized computer access and misuse and misappropriation of trade secrets under Connecticut law. Deiter was the defendant and appellee and sought dismissal for lack of personal jurisdiction.
sections.Procedural History: MacDermid sued in Connecticut federal court, with subject-matter jurisdiction resting on diversity. The district court dismissed under Rule 12(b)(2) without an evidentiary hearing, reasoning that Deiter had used only computers in Canada: she had essentially sent email from one Canadian computer to another. It did not reach due process. MacDermid appealed. The Second Circuit reversed the dismissal and remanded for further proceedings.
sections.Material Facts:
MacDermid's Canadian subsidiary employed Deiter as an account manager from May 2008 until April 2011. MacDermid stored its confidential and proprietary electronic information on servers in Waterbury, and employees of the Canadian subsidiary could retrieve it only by accessing those servers. Employees were informed that the email system and protected data were housed there. Deiter had agreed in writing to safeguard the information and was not authorized to transfer it to a personal email account.

After learning that she would be terminated effective April 7, 2011, Deiter allegedly forwarded confidential files from her company email account to her personal account shortly before termination. To obtain and send those files she necessarily accessed the Waterbury servers.

Deiter submitted no affidavit testimony with her motion, so MacDermid's uncontroverted complaint allegations and opposing affidavit were assumed true, including that she accessed the Connecticut servers and knew the email system and confidential information were located there.
sections.Issue: Whether Deiter's remote operation of servers in Connecticut from Canada counted as using a computer located in Connecticut under Connecticut General Statutes section 52-59b(a)(5), and, if so, whether exercising personal jurisdiction over her was consistent with due process.
sections.Holding: The Second Circuit in 2012, in an opinion by Judge Barrington D. Parker for a panel with Judges Newman and Raggi and no separate opinion, held that section 52-59b(a)(5) authorized jurisdiction on the accepted facts and that exercising it satisfied due process. It reversed the dismissal and remanded. The court reserved MacDermid's alternative arguments under subsections (a)(2) and (a)(3) because subsection (a)(5) sufficed. It did not find Deiter liable, and it did not hold that server location alone or a generic Internet connection suffices in every case.
sections.Reasoning:
Review was de novo. Because the motion was decided without an evidentiary hearing, MacDermid needed only a prima facie showing.

On the statute, the incorporated definition of a computer covered equipment that automatically performs operations on data and communicates the results, so a server was itself a computer. The statutory language located the computer in Connecticut, not necessarily the person operating it. Deiter's remote access caused the Connecticut servers to retrieve and communicate protected files, which was use of a Connecticut computer. Limiting subsection (a)(5) to users physically in Connecticut would make it largely redundant, because subsection (a)(2) already reached an in-state tort. The long-arm statute did not incorporate the computer-crimes definition of use that Deiter invoked, and her conduct met it anyway.

On due process, which the court could address because it had been pressed or passed upon below, the accepted allegations showed purposeful conduct tied to Connecticut. Deiter knew the company centralized its email and confidential information in Waterbury, she retrieved and sent the files through those servers, and the email transfer was itself the alleged tort. Her conduct was also directed at a Connecticut corporation, which complemented the knowing server use without substituting for it. Physical presence was unnecessary. The court acknowledged that most Internet users may not know where their servers are, which made the pleaded knowledge important.

Jurisdiction was reasonable: travel from Canada was a burden but not enough alone, MacDermid and most corporate witnesses were in Connecticut, and the state had an interest in enforcing its laws.

The casebook reproduces the statutory and constitutional reasoning at length in a note; its questions about an employee who did not know the server's location or a claim not involving an intentional tort are editorial hypotheticals.

CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.rule: Under § 1738 a federal court must first determine a state judgment's preclusive effect under the rendering state's law; only if state law would bar the claim does the court ask whether a federal statute creates an exception, even where the later claim is exclusively federal.

sections.Parties: Drs. Marrese and Treister, board-certified orthopaedic surgeons, were the plaintiffs in a federal antitrust action against the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, which had denied their membership applications. The Academy, the defendant, moved to dismiss on claim-preclusion grounds based on the doctors' earlier state suits. The Academy prevailed in the Seventh Circuit en banc, and the doctors sought reversal in the Supreme Court.
sections.Procedural History: Treister sued in an Illinois circuit court in November 1976 and Marrese filed a similar action. The Illinois Appellate Court held that Treister's complaint failed to state a cause of action, the Illinois Supreme Court declined review, and the circuit court then dismissed Marrese's complaint. In March 1980 the doctors sued in the Northern District of Illinois. The district court denied the Academy's motion to dismiss and initially declined to certify that ruling under § 1292(b). It entered a criminal-contempt judgment against the Academy in a discovery dispute and, while the contempt appeal was pending, certified the preclusion question. The Seventh Circuit, en banc, held the federal claims barred, with no majority opinion on the preclusion reasoning, and reversed the contempt judgment. The Court granted review only of the preclusion ruling, reversed, and remanded.
sections.Material Facts:
The Academy denied the two surgeons' membership applications without a hearing or explanation. Their Illinois suits alleged interference with associational rights protected by Illinois common law. Neither alleged a state antitrust violation, and neither brought a federal antitrust case at the same time. The state actions ended in dismissals with prejudice.

The doctors' later federal complaint, as amended, alleged that the Academy possessed monopoly power and excluded them to discourage competition, a boycott forbidden by § 1 of the Sherman Act. The Academy argued that the state actions involved the same events and so barred the federal suit. The district court reasoned that state courts lacked jurisdiction over federal antitrust claims, so their judgments could not bar those claims. In the Seventh Circuit, a plurality stressed the availability of a materially similar Illinois antitrust cause of action.
sections.Issue: Whether a prior state-court judgment can preclude a later federal antitrust claim that the state court had no jurisdiction to hear, and by what law that question is decided.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States, 1985. Justice O'Connor wrote for six Justices; Chief Justice Burger concurred in the judgment, and Justices Blackmun and Stevens did not participate. The Court held that the lower courts erred by determining the effect of the Illinois judgments under independent federal preclusion rules without first examining Illinois law. Under § 1738, a federal court first asks whether the rendering state's law would bar the claim; only if it would does the court consider whether a federal statute creates an exception. The Court did not decide whether Illinois law barred the claims or whether the Sherman Act creates an exception.
sections.Reasoning:
Section 1738 ordinarily gives a state judgment the preclusive effect it has under the rendering state's law, and exclusive federal jurisdiction over Sherman Act claims does not remove that first step. If state law would not bar the claim, there is no need to reach any federal exception. If it would, the exception question turns on congressional intent, the particular statute, and the nature of the claim, not on a general preference for federal adjudication.

Exclusive jurisdiction does not make state judgments irrelevant: issue preclusion may attach to an issue a state court resolved. Claim preclusion is different where the first court lacked jurisdiction over the omitted theory, and most state rules recognize that limit, but the federal court must examine the actual state rule.

The Seventh Circuit had suggested that federal courts could give the state judgments greater effect than Illinois would. Migra foreclosed that. Efficiency and repose are legitimate interests, but Congress directed respect for the scope states give their own judgments. Moitie was not to the contrary because it involved a prior federal judgment. On jurisdiction, the appeal from criminal contempt, a separate proceeding, did not transfer the whole case, so the district court could still certify the preclusion question.

Chief Justice Burger agreed that state law must be consulted but thought the majority gave too little guidance where state law is indeterminate; he favored considering a federal rule asking whether the plaintiff had a full and fair opportunity to pursue equivalent rights.

The casebook cites the case for this two-step approach and for why jurisdictional-competency rules often avoid the exception question.

CP-COMP-CB-MATSUSHITA-EPSTEIN.rule: Under 28 U.S.C. section 1738, a state-court judgment approving a class settlement gets the preclusive effect the rendering state would give it, even where it releases claims within exclusive federal jurisdiction, unless a federal statute creates an exception.

sections.Parties: Shareholders of MCA, a Delaware corporation, sued MCA's directors in Delaware over Matsushita's 1990 tender offer, and other shareholders, including the respondents, sued Matsushita in a California federal court under the federal securities rules. The question in the Court was whether the Delaware settlement judgment barred the respondents' federal claims against Matsushita.
sections.Procedural History: The California federal court denied class certification, granted Matsushita summary judgment, and dismissed the case on April 15, 1992; the plaintiffs appealed. Meanwhile the Delaware Chancery Court, having rejected an initial settlement in April 1991, approved a second class settlement whose release covered the pending federal case, and Delaware's Supreme Court affirmed. The respondents did not opt out, object, or appear. The Ninth Circuit nevertheless refused to treat the settlement as a bar, limiting state settlement preclusion to claims that could have been extinguished through issue preclusion from an adjudication of the state claims, and ruled on the federal securities claims. The Court reviewed the preclusion question, and it reversed and remanded.
sections.Material Facts:
Matsushita's 1990 tender offer sought MCA. In Delaware, shareholders alleged fiduciary breaches by MCA's directors; their amended complaint also alleged waste through exposure to federal securities liability and Matsushita's conspiracy and assistance in the breaches. These were state causes of action. In the California federal suit, shareholders alleged violations of SEC Rules 10b-13 and 14d-10. Federal jurisdiction over those Exchange Act claims was exclusive under section 27.

The Chancery Court rejected a first settlement that offered shareholders no money, sought substantial counsel fees, and lacked an opt-out right. The second settlement had a $2 million fund, which after deductions would yield only a few cents per share, a release encompassing the pending federal case, and an opportunity to opt out. The court found the monetary benefit meager and barely adequate but approved it, reducing the attorney fee to $250,000. Suspicion of collusion was reported but collusion was not found proved.

Notice was mailed twice and published in the Wall Street Journal. The respondents did not opt out, object, or appear at the approval hearing.
sections.Issue: Whether a federal court may refuse full faith and credit to a Delaware judgment approving a shareholder class settlement solely because its release included securities claims within exclusive federal jurisdiction.
sections.Holding: The Court in 1996, in an opinion by Justice Thomas for seven Justices, answered no. Justice Stevens joined Parts I, II-A, and II-C but not Part II-B or the judgment. Section 1738 generally required the judgment to receive the effect it would have in Delaware; Delaware would treat this settlement as preclusive, and section 27 of the Securities Exchange Act did not create an implied exception. The Court reversed and remanded. It expressly reserved the respondents' constitutional challenge to the adequacy of representation and their argument about failure to opt out, and it did not decide whether Matsushita violated the securities rules.
sections.Reasoning:
A judgment incorporating a class settlement is the product of a judicial proceeding under section 1738; neither settlement nor the exclusively federal character of the released claims exempts it. Marrese supplied two steps: first determine the judgment's effect under the rendering state's law; then, if that law would bar the action, ask whether the federal statute creates an exception to section 1738.

At the first step, the Court read Delaware decisions to permit settlements releasing related claims that the Chancery Court could not itself have adjudicated, where they share the factual predicate of the settled litigation. The release expressly identified the California action and the respondents had remained in the class.

At the second step, section 27 has no express exception, so an implied partial repeal required irreconcilable conflict.
