Section 27 reserved adjudication of Exchange Act claims to federal courts but did not prohibit parties from releasing them in a state settlement of a suit properly within state jurisdiction. Assessing the claims' value to judge fairness was not adjudicating them. The exception for a court lacking jurisdiction did not apply because Delaware had jurisdiction over the state suit and the parties.

Justice Stevens agreed that section 27 did not impliedly repeal section 1738 but wanted the lower federal court to decide Delaware preclusion law first. Justice Ginsburg agreed remand was appropriate but opposed the Court's first-instance resolution of Delaware law; her Part II-B, joined by Justices Stevens and Souter, stressed that adequate representation of absent class members remains a constitutional requirement that notice and an opt-out opportunity do not replace. She did not find the respondents' allegations established.

The casebook cites the case in a note for the settlement-release holding and for Justice Ginsburg's due-process concern.

CP-COMP-CB-MAVRIX.rule: A website operator that commercially exploits a national audience, including a substantial forum audience, and intentionally posts infringing material harming the plaintiff in the forum has expressly aimed at it and is subject to specific, though not general, jurisdiction there.

sections.Parties: Mavrix Photo, Inc., a celebrity-photo agency incorporated in Florida and principally based in Miami, sued Brand Technologies, Inc., an Ohio corporation principally based in Toledo that operated the website celebrity-gossip.net, and its CEO Brad Mandell. Mavrix, the plaintiff and appellant, alleged copyright infringement and sought an injunction and actual and statutory damages. Brand, the defendant and appellee, moved to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction.
sections.Procedural History: Mavrix sued in the Central District of California. Brand moved to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction. The district court denied jurisdictional discovery and dismissed, and Mavrix appealed. The Ninth Circuit reversed the dismissal and remanded for further proceedings.
sections.Material Facts:
Mavrix paid photographers for candid pictures and licensed them to celebrity publications such as People and Us Weekly. It maintained a Los Angeles office, used local photographers, had a California registered agent, and paid California franchise fees.

Brand's website offered photos, videos, and short stories, and visitors could comment, vote in polls, receive a newsletter, join a membership club, and submit tips and photographs. Brand's marketing materials claimed more than twelve million unique U.S. visitors and seventy million U.S. page views per month; the record had no precise count of California visitors. Brand earned advertising revenue; some third-party ads promoted California jobs, hotels, or vacations, and the site linked to a ticket seller offering California events. Brand had relationships with California companies but no California office, real property, or staff, was not licensed there, and paid no California taxes.

In 2008 a Mavrix photographer took thirty-five photographs of singer Stacy Ferguson, known as Fergie, and actor Josh Duhamel vacationing in the Bahamas. Mavrix registered copyright and posted them on its own website. It alleged that Brand soon reposted them without authorization, destroying their market value.
sections.Issue: Whether Brand's contacts with California through its nationally accessible commercial website supported general jurisdiction, and whether its alleged reposting of Mavrix's copyrighted photographs was purposefully directed at California so as to support specific jurisdiction.
sections.Holding: The Ninth Circuit in 2011, in an opinion by Judge William A. Fletcher for a panel with Judge Wardlaw and District Judge Barbara M. Lynn sitting by designation, with no separate opinion, held that Brand was subject to specific jurisdiction, but not general jurisdiction, in California. Mavrix had made a prima facie showing of purposeful direction sufficient to survive the motion. The court reversed the dismissal and remanded. It did not decide that the copyright allegations were true.
sections.Reasoning:
Review was de novo. Because the motion rested on written materials, Mavrix needed a prima facie showing, with uncontroverted allegations accepted. California's long-arm statute was coextensive with federal due process.

General jurisdiction failed. Applying its precedents and the Supreme Court's recent Goodyear decision, the court asked whether Brand's contacts approximated an in-state presence and made it essentially at home. Third-party advertisements were less probative, the only ticket sale shown was to Mavrix's counsel, and the other relationships were doing business with California residents, not substantial operations in California. The court rejected Zippo's interactivity scale as a substitute for general-jurisdiction analysis.

Specific jurisdiction required purposeful direction, a claim arising from forum activity, and reasonableness; only the first was disputed. For this tort-like copyright claim the court applied Calder's effects test: an intentional act, express aiming at the forum, and harm the defendant knew was likely there. The reposting was an intentional act. On express aiming, accessibility alone was not enough; the most important feature was Brand's use of the photos as part of its commercial exploitation of California's audience. By analogy to Keeton, Brand cultivated a national audience for profit, including a substantial California audience, and advertisements directed to Californians supported the inference that it knew of and exploited those users. Its focus on the California-centered celebrity and entertainment industries supported the same inference. A local newspaper, an individual, or an unpaid blogger would not necessarily be treated alike. The harm was foreseeable in California because a substantial part of the photographs' market value came from California readers.

The casebook cites the case in a note, describing the result as purposeful availment and highlighting third-party advertising and foreseeable injury; its question about consistency with McIntyre is editorial.

CP-COMP-CB-MF-GLOBAL.rule: Under 28 U.S.C. section 1407, differing legal theories do not defeat centralization of actions that share substantial factual questions; the degree of coordination or consolidation is left to the transferee judge.

sections.Parties: Jon Corzine, Bradley Abelow, Henri Steenkamp, and Laurie Ferber, defendants in litigation arising from the bankruptcy of MF Global Holdings, moved to centralize the actions in the Southern District of New York. The plaintiffs were two groups: investors in securities and holders of commodities futures customer accounts. The Sapere commodities customer plaintiff opposed centralization altogether, and customer plaintiffs in Illinois and Montana opposed combining customer and securities litigation. Other defendants and the securities lead plaintiffs supported centralization in New York.
sections.Procedural History: Three actions were formally before the Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation: Henning-Carey Proprietary Trading v. Corzine in the Northern District of Illinois, and Joseph Deangelis v. Corzine and Sapere CTA Fund v. Corzine in the Southern District of New York. The motion had initially covered twelve actions; eight were closed when New York cases were consolidated, and an Eastern District of Michigan action had been dismissed. The Panel had also been notified of twelve potentially related actions. By order of April 23, 2012, the Panel transferred the action pending outside the Southern District of New York to that district and, with that court's consent, assigned it to Judge Victor Marrero for coordinated or consolidated pretrial proceedings with the listed New York actions.
sections.Material Facts:
The bankruptcy of MF Global Holdings and related entities generated litigation by investors in securities and by holders of commodities futures customer accounts. The proceedings shared factual questions about the collapse and a reported estimated $1.6 billion customer-account shortfall; that estimate was background, not an adjudication.

The principal objection was that securities-law claims and Commodities Exchange Act and related customer claims were legally distinct, so that a shared proceeding would be inefficient and would slow the customer litigation. Several customer plaintiffs supported New York centralization while opposing actual consolidation of securities and customer actions before the transferee judge.

MF Global Holdings and several defendants were headquartered in New York, and the related bankruptcy proceedings were under way there. Judge Marrero already presided over both kinds of actions.
sections.Issue: Whether actions by securities investors and by commodities customers, resting on different legal theories but arising from the same corporate collapse, should be centralized in a single proceeding under section 1407 or kept in separate proceedings.
sections.Holding: The Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation in 2012, in a transfer order issued by Acting Chairman Kathryn H. Vratil with no separate opinion and Judge Heyburn not participating, held that disparate legal theories do not defeat transfer where the cases share substantial factual questions. It ordered the Schedule A action pending outside the Southern District of New York transferred there and assigned to Judge Marrero for coordinated or consolidated pretrial proceedings. The order did not resolve any substantive wrongdoing, certify a class, or expressly transfer the potential tag-along actions.
sections.Reasoning:
Section 1407 centralization requires common factual questions and a determination that coordinated or consolidated pretrial proceedings will serve convenience and the just and efficient conduct of the actions. These actions arose from the same corporate collapse and account shortfall and would focus on many of the same events, defendants, and witnesses. Separate statutory theories did not eliminate that overlap.

The Panel declined to prescribe how the proceedings should be organized. Its usual practice was to avoid separate proceedings for different claims arising from a common factual background and to leave the degree of coordination or consolidation to the transferee judge's discretion. That answered part of the efficiency objection: centralization created a common judicial setting without requiring every pretrial task or claim to proceed identically.

The Panel found that centralization would avoid duplicative discovery, reduce inconsistent pretrial rulings, including class-certification rulings, and conserve the resources of litigants, counsel, and the judiciary.

New York was appropriate because numerous parties supported it, MF Global Holdings and several defendants were headquartered there, and the bankruptcy proceedings were there. Judge Marrero had multidistrict experience, already presided over both kinds of actions, and had taken steps to streamline them.

The casebook cites the order for the point that shared facts justify centralization despite different legal theories, with coordination left to the transferee judge; its questions about administrative costs, counsel control, fees, and settlement leverage are editorial.

CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2014.rule: Before granting preliminary approval of a class settlement, a court must have a record that lets it judge whether the proposal falls within the range of possible approval; the parties' assurances that a capped fund is adequate do not suffice.

sections.Parties: Retired professional football players sued the NFL and NFL Properties LLC, alleging failure to protect them from, and concealment of, the chronic risks of head injuries. The plaintiffs moved for preliminary approval of a class settlement and for class certification; the NFL parties did not oppose the motion. The Riddell defendants were also sued but did not participate in the proposed settlement.
sections.Procedural History: Players began suing in July 2011, and more than 4,500 former players filed substantially similar cases. The Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation consolidated the cases for pretrial proceedings in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania before Judge Anita B. Brody. She directed mediation before retired federal judge Layn Phillips in July 2013; the parties signed a principal-terms agreement in August. In December she appointed Perry Golkin under Rule 53 to help assess the financial arrangements. Plaintiffs filed the proposed class complaint and settlement motion on January 6, 2014. On January 14, 2014, the court denied the motion for preliminary approval and class certification without prejudice. This decision concerns the original capped settlement, not the later uncapped settlement or the appeal.
sections.Material Facts:
The proposed nationwide class included retired NFL players, authorized representatives of deceased or legally incapacitated players, and derivative claimants; the NFL's records indicated more than 20,000 members. One subclass was players without qualifying diagnoses, the other those already diagnosed.

The NFL parties would pay $760 million over twenty years: $75 million for baseline neurological assessment, $675 million for monetary awards, and $10 million for education and injury prevention. Maximum awards were $1.5 million for early dementia, $3 million for moderate dementia, $3.5 million for Alzheimer's or Parkinson's disease, $5 million for ALS, and $4 million for death with CTE, subject to reductions. Up to $37.5 million of further funding was available on a shortfall, but the fund remained capped. Notice expenses of up to $4 million and attorneys' fees and costs of up to $112.5 million were additional. The monetary fund had a 65-year lifespan.

The settlement would release claims against the NFL parties, and recipients of monetary awards would have to dismiss or refrain from cognitive-injury litigation against the NCAA and other collegiate, amateur, or youth organizations.

The parties said experts had modeled incidence rates and that funding was adequate, but the analyses themselves were not given to the court.
sections.Issue: Whether, on the record submitted, the proposed capped settlement could receive preliminary approval under Rule 23(e), that is, whether it had no obvious deficiencies and fell within the range of possible approval.
sections.Holding: The Eastern District of Pennsylvania in 2014, Judge Anita B. Brody, denied the motion for preliminary approval and class certification without prejudice and required the parties to submit their supporting financial analyses through the Special Master. The court held that this proposed arrangement and evidentiary submission had not earned preliminary approval. It did not find collusion, did not hold that an uncapped fund was the only permissible structure, and did not decide whether to conditionally certify the class.
sections.Reasoning:
Rule 23(e) permitted approval only on a finding that the settlement was fair, reasonable, and adequate. Preliminary approval is a less demanding inquiry than final approval, asking whether there are obvious deficiencies or preferential treatment and whether the proposal is within a possible approval range, but it still requires comparing the value offered with the members' expected recovery.

That scrutiny could not be a formality. Class judgments can preclude absent members, and once representatives and defendants agree, the adversarial process may no longer expose weaknesses affecting absentees, so the judge must guard their interests. A settlement negotiated before certification called for especially careful scrutiny, and catching a conspicuous deficiency before notice avoids costly and futile notice and hearings.

The court found no indication that negotiations lacked good faith or arm's-length dealing. The problem was that it could not tell whether all eligible retired players would be paid before the fund ran out. With a 65-year fund, roughly 20,000 potential members, and substantial maximum awards, even a hypothetical ten-percent diagnosis rate raised serious questions about the capped fund. That was a concern requiring evidence, not a finding that depletion was certain. The mediator's declaration and counsel's confidence rested on analyses the court had not seen, and conclusions could not substitute for documentation that the judge and Special Master could test. A footnote added concerns about the assessment program and the release of claims against amateur football organizations.

The casebook discusses this ruling in its note on the NFL litigation, combining it with the later negotiations, the 2015 approval, and the 2016 appeal.

CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2015.rule: A settlement class must independently satisfy Rule 23(a) and (b)(3); separately represented subclasses and an uncapped, inflation-protected fund can resolve the conflict between presently injured and future claimants, and the settlement must be fair, reasonable, and adequate under Rule 23(e).

sections.Parties: Retired professional football players, with representatives of deceased or incapacitated players and derivative claimants, sued the NFL, alleging that it knew of the long-term neurological dangers of repeated head impacts but concealed them and failed to protect players. Kevin Turner and Shawn Wooden filed the settlement class complaint and served as subclass representatives. The parties' amended settlement was before the court for class certification and final approval; 205 objectors joined eighty-three written objections. Claims against helmet manufacturer Riddell were outside the settlement.
sections.Procedural History: The first concussion case was a July 19, 2011 California suit by seventy-three players; the multidistrict litigation came to include more than 300 lawsuits and approximately 5,000 players. The NFL argued by motion that collective-bargaining agreements preempted the claims under section 301 of the Labor Management Relations Act; the court stayed discovery, heard argument in April 2013, and did not resolve the motion. It ordered mediation in July 2013. In January 2014 the court refused preliminary approval of a proposed $765 million arrangement. After the parties removed the monetary-award cap and narrowed the releases, the court granted preliminary approval in July 2014, held a fairness hearing in November, and required further improvements, incorporated in February 2015. On April 22, 2015, Judge Brody certified the class and subclasses, approved the amended settlement, and entered final judgment dismissing the class complaint and related lawsuits with prejudice. This is the district court's final-approval stage; the 2014 refusal and the Third Circuit's 2016 affirmance are distinct.
sections.Material Facts:
The lawsuits asserted negligence and fraud, among other state-law theories. Players reported dementia, Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, ALS, and other symptoms, and survivors invoked postmortem diagnoses of chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE.

The class of approximately 20,000 was divided into two independently represented subclasses: players without a qualifying diagnosis before preliminary approval, and those already diagnosed. Turner had ALS; Wooden had no qualifying diagnosis.

The monetary-award fund was uncapped, adjusted for inflation, and available for sixty-five years. Players with a qualifying diagnosis did not have to prove that NFL football caused the condition. Maximum awards ranged from $1.5 million for Level 1.5 neurocognitive impairment to $5 million for ALS, with $4 million for death with CTE before final approval; awards varied with age at diagnosis and credited seasons and were subject to offsets, and a player whose condition worsened could seek a supplemental award. A separate $75 million baseline-assessment program and a $10 million education fund were included.

Releases covered head, brain, and cognitive injury claims against the NFL parties, not claims against the NCAA, amateur or youth football organizations, or Riddell. The NFL promised not to oppose fees up to $112.5 million, to be paid separately. Notice was mailed to more than 30,000 addresses and supplemented by publication. The court reported 208 remaining opt-outs.
sections.Issue: Whether the proposed settlement class could independently satisfy Rule 23(a) and Rule 23(b)(3) despite different diseases, career histories, and present versus future injuries, and whether the amended settlement was fair, reasonable, and adequate under Rule 23(e), with adequate notice and an opportunity to opt out.
sections.Holding: The Eastern District of Pennsylvania in 2015, Judge Anita B. Brody, answered both questions yes. Settlement did not dilute Rule 23's certification requirements. The court certified the class and subclasses under Rules 23(a) and 23(b)(3), approved the whole amended agreement under Rule 23(e), and entered final judgment. Approval did not adjudicate the NFL's liability, and the court postponed the decision on attorneys' fees, leaving objectors an opportunity to contest a later petition.
sections.Reasoning:
Numerosity was readily met. Commonality rested on the NFL's alleged shared conduct in withholding information and failing to protect players; the court distinguished the decentralized employment decisions in Wal-Mart. Turner's and Wooden's claims were typical of their subclasses.

On adequacy, the court found experienced counsel, sustained adversarial negotiation, and genuinely separate subclass representation. Fees were negotiated after the substantive terms and would be paid separately. The decisive question was whether differently situated players were sacrificing one another's interests. Unlike a fixed fund that present claimants could exhaust, an uncapped fund with inflation protection and supplemental awards protected later claimants, and different awards reflected the severity, value, and litigation risks of different claims. More subclasses were unnecessary and could defeat a workable settlement. Common questions predominated, the court distinguishing Amchem's more heterogeneous asbestos population, and class resolution was superior to decades of repetitive litigation.

Notice was adequate in content and distribution; the notice expert estimated it reached ninety percent of the class, and the later amendments only improved class benefits, so no second notice was required.

On fairness, the judge acted as a fiduciary for absent members and applied the Girsh and relevant Prudential factors. Causation and preemption were uncertain, evidence would be hard to develop, and impaired players needed timely help. The NFL's ability to pay was neutral.

On CTE, the most contested objection, the court evaluated the scientific record available in 2015 and concluded that many associated cognitive symptoms would qualify for dementia-based awards; the death-with-CTE benefit compensated families of players who died without notice to obtain a qualifying diagnosis.

The decision illustrates how subclass structure, an uncapped fund, informed negotiation, effective notice, and active judicial supervision can address the concerns raised by Amchem and Ortiz. The casebook covers it in its note on the NFL litigation, which compresses the several procedural stages.

CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2016.rule: A mass-tort settlement class may be certified under Rule 23(b)(3) where the defendant's alleged common course of conduct supplies commonality and predominance and separately represented subclasses with an uncapped fund protect future claimants; approval is reviewed for abuse of discretion.

sections.Parties: Retired NFL players, with representative claimants for deceased or incapacitated players and derivative claimants, were the plaintiff class suing the NFL for failing to protect and warn them about the long-term risks of repeated head impacts. Objectors appealed the district court's final certification of the settlement class and approval of the settlement, in twelve consolidated appeals. Claims against helmet manufacturer Riddell were outside the appeal.
sections.Procedural History: After removal, hundreds of actions were consolidated before Judge Brody for pretrial proceedings. The NFL sought dismissal on federal labor-law preemption grounds, a defense still unresolved when the parties settled. Court-ordered mediation began in July 2013, and an August term sheet proposed a capped settlement. In January 2014 the district court declined preliminary approval because the monetary fund might not pay all eligible claims; the parties then uncapped the fund. Preliminary approval followed in July 2014, a fairness hearing in November, and further improvements in February 2015. An earlier Rule 23(f) petition was unsuccessful. The April 22, 2015 final approval generated twelve consolidated appeals. The Third Circuit affirmed certification and settlement approval in full.
sections.Material Facts:
The players asserted negligence, fraud, concealment, medical-monitoring, and related claims. The class, exceeding 20,000, included players retired before July 7, 2014. One subclass was players without a qualifying diagnosis before that date; the other was those with one. The two subclasses had separate representatives and separate counsel; Wooden represented undiagnosed players and Turner diagnosed players.

The agreement created an uncapped, inflation-adjusted Monetary Award Fund lasting sixty-five years, a $75 million Baseline Assessment Program, and a $10 million education fund. Six qualifying diagnoses could produce awards: two levels of neurocognitive impairment, Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, ALS, and death with CTE for players who died before final approval. A claimant did not have to prove that NFL play caused the diagnosis. Maximum awards ran from $1.5 million to $5 million, subject to reductions. The parties were to meet in good faith every ten years about possible scientific changes to the qualifying diagnoses.

Class members released concussion-related claims against the NFL. About one percent objected and about one percent opted out. The NFL agreed not to oppose a fee-and-cost award up to $112.5 million, paid separately; fees had not yet been awarded. Objectors argued that Arnold Levin, counsel for the future-injury subclass, also represented presently injured players.
sections.Issue: Whether the district court abused its discretion in certifying the Rule 23(b)(3) settlement class, given differences among players and the conflict between present and future claimants, and in approving the settlement as fair, including its notice, its treatment of CTE, and the deferral of the fee petition.
sections.Holding: The Third Circuit in 2016, in an opinion by Judge Ambro for a unanimous panel with Judges Hardiman and Nygaard, affirmed final certification of the Rule 23(b)(3) settlement class and approval of the settlement in full. Rule 23(a)'s prerequisites and Rule 23(b)(3)'s predominance and superiority requirements still applied to a settlement class and were met; representation was adequate; notice was sufficient; the settlement was fair notwithstanding its treatment of CTE; and deferring the fee petition did not violate Rule 23(h) or due process here. Approval did not adjudicate the NFL's liability.
sections.Reasoning:
Review was for abuse of discretion. On commonality and typicality the panel distinguished Wal-Mart: the NFL allegedly injured players through the same course of conduct, so what it knew, concealed, or did could be resolved commonly even though injuries differed. Predominance was supplied by the alleged league-wide conduct and shared scientific causation questions; Amchem did not categorically bar mass-tort settlement classes, and its asbestos class was much larger and more varied.

Amchem's central concern was that presently injured people would maximize immediate payments while future claimants needed a durable fund. Here there were separate representatives and counsel, an uncapped and inflation-adjusted fund, and periodic meetings on the science. Subclass counsel could come from the existing steering committee. The record did not establish that Levin's other clients had qualifying diagnoses, so the panel did not find that he actually represented both subclasses.

Notice explained benefits, releases, objections, and opt-out rights and did not have to reproduce every detail. On fairness, the district court properly applied the Girsh and Prudential factors; formal discovery was not invariably required, and players faced substantial preemption and causation risks.

On CTE, the panel upheld the district court's scientific findings under clear-error review: on the record then, CTE could be diagnosed only after death and its link to living symptoms was uncertain, while many associated impairments were compensable independently. The pre-approval death benefit was a proxy for diagnoses deceased players could not obtain while living. A clear-sailing fee provision warranted careful scrutiny, not automatic rejection.

The casebook's note on the NFL litigation describes this appeal; its statement that counsel represented both subclasses is broader than what the panel found.

CP-COMP-CB-PFAU-2009.rule: On a petition by the Chief Administrative Judge, a New York court ordered debt-collection respondents to show cause under CPLR § 5015(c) and (d) why default judgments tied to one process server's affidavits should not be vacated unless service was independently proved.

sections.Parties: Chief Administrative Judge Ann Pfau, acting in her administrative capacity and represented by the Attorney General, was the petitioner in a special proceeding. The respondents were Forster & Garbus and numerous other law firms, lawyers and collection respondents. Pfau sought to have default judgments vacated; the respondents were directed to show cause why that relief should not be entered.
sections.Procedural History: Pfau brought a special proceeding in the Supreme Court of New York, Erie County, on a petition verified July 9, 2009. On July 21, 2009, the court granted an order to show cause directing the respondents to appear before Part 8 and respond. That order is the only judicial source recovered, and it is not a final adjudication. The casebook says the action later settled by consent; the consent instrument was not recovered, and its terms are not given here.
sections.Material Facts:
The casebook places the proceeding in its account of "sewer service", in which a process server allegedly fails to deliver process but files a false affidavit of service, and the creditor then obtains a default judgment. According to the casebook, Pfau sought to vacate tens of thousands of judgments allegedly resting on false service affidavits; that is the casebook's description of the allegations, not a finding in the order.

The order recites the verified petition, an Assistant Attorney General's affirmation dated July 17, and affidavits from court-system auditors, court personnel and Attorney General investigators. The relief requested covered proceedings throughout New York's judicial districts in which the respondents appeared as party or counsel, American Legal Process served the initiating papers, and a default judgment had been entered or an application for one was pending. Exhibits A and B were electronic databases containing personally identifying information about New York residents.
sections.Issue: Whether the respondents should be required to show cause why relief should not be entered under CPLR § 5015(c) and (d), including vacatur of default judgments in proceedings where American Legal Process served the initiating papers.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of New York, Erie County, 2009. The court ordered the respondents to show cause why the requested relief should not be entered and gave directions on the record, confidentiality and answering papers. It did not grant the requested vacatur. The order is not a reasoned final opinion finding fraud against any respondent.
sections.Reasoning:
The order contains no reasoned opinion. Its numbered paragraphs describe the relief to be considered rather than relief already granted. Respondents would identify the affected proceedings; notice would go by first-class mail to each interested party's last known residence or actual business address; respondents would give the court a schedule of recipients, addresses, judgment amounts and amounts paid after entry; and interested parties would have an opportunity to be heard.

The principal requested remedy was vacatur of the identified default judgments, or denial of pending default applications, unless the party seeking the judgment established proper service at the hearing without relying on an American Legal Process affidavit of service. The petition also sought restitution after vacatur, and a bar on further defaults against persons served through that company until independent evidence of service was supplied.

What the court actually directed was narrower. Pfau was to file and serve the exhibits; the clerk was to seal the two databases and restrict inspection to a party or someone authorized by court order, while providing them to respondents. The court set the timing of answering papers under CPLR § 403(b) and deemed service of the order at respondents' actual business addresses sufficient.

The casebook cites the proceeding in its discussion of sewer service and says it was resolved by consent, linked to a later Erie County matter numbered 2166/11; that statement is the casebook's and could not be checked against the consent instrument.

CP-COMP-CB-PFAU-2011.rule: Effective service is the procedural foundation for obtaining a default judgment, and a remedy for suspect defaults may involve vacatur and a fresh opportunity to answer rather than a determination that the underlying debts do not exist.

sections.Parties: New York's Chief Administrative Judge initiated a special proceeding, titled Matter of Pfau v. Forster & Garbus, against debt-collection attorneys. The asserted problem was default judgments allegedly supported by false affidavits of service.
sections.Procedural History:
The casebook identifies a 2009 commencement, and a July 2009 order to show cause containing eight requests for relief was recovered separately. The editors say the proceeding then settled through a consent order, part of which established a procedure for vacating illegally obtained default judgments, and they cite Supreme Court, Erie County, Index No. 2166/11 (2011) for that procedure.

The brief covers only the casebook's account of the 2011 procedure. The complete order under that index number has not been recovered, and its signing judge, exact date, exact disposition and full conditions are not given.
sections.Material Facts:
Debt-collection attorneys had obtained default judgments that were allegedly supported by false affidavits of service.

Two other court opinions give context without reproducing the Pfau order. In Legal Servicing, LLC v. Lunghi, a filed opinion on a different defendant's motion to vacate a judgment in a different court refers to papers in the Pfau proceeding under Index No. 2166/11 and describes a process server's affidavits purporting to place him at different locations at the same time. In North Fork Bank v. Porri, decided February 24, 2011, Judge Hirsh describes a consent-related affidavit and stipulation sent to defendants in cases involving American Legal Process service; the reproduced form connected requested vacatur with renewed service, a time to answer, limitations concessions and a release of certain claims. Porri does not establish that this form is the complete order entered under Index No. 2166/11, so its terms cannot simply be transferred to the 2011 order.
sections.Issue: Not given in the brief.
sections.Holding: Supreme Court, Erie County, 2011. The brief reports no adjudicated ruling. According to the casebook editors, the proceeding settled through a consent order, and part of the relief established a procedure for vacating illegally obtained default judgments. The account supports only that such a procedure was created in this litigation. It does not certify every consent term, it is not an adjudication that every challenged judgment was invalid, and it supplies no merits judgment on the debts.
sections.Reasoning:
No court reasoning is given, because the consent order and any accompanying reasons were not recovered.

The brief's teaching point is limited. Effective service is the procedural foundation for obtaining a default judgment, and a remedy for suspect defaults may involve vacatur and a fresh opportunity to answer rather than a determination that the underlying debts do not exist. Requested relief, consent terms and rulings in individual later debt cases remain distinct: the eight requests in the July 2009 order to show cause should not be described as relief granted in the later consent disposition, and in Porri Judge Hirsh refused a proposed consent-based order after the defendant altered its terms and separately evaluated defective service and insufficient proof supporting the default judgment.

The casebook cites the proceeding for the procedure it established for vacating illegally obtained default judgments.

CP-COMP-CB-PINCAY-PANEL.rule: Under Appellate Rule 4(a)(5), as this 2003 panel applied it, a lawyer's reliance on a nonlawyer clerk's misreading of the unambiguous appeal deadline is not excusable neglect, because the lawyer cannot delegate responsibility for knowing the rule.

sections.Parties: Pincay and McCarron were the plaintiffs, who sued Andrews and related defendants over financial injuries under RICO and California law. Andrews, having missed the deadline to appeal the judgment against him, obtained an extension of time from the district court. Pincay appealed that extension order and wanted it reversed; Andrews defended it.
sections.Procedural History: Plaintiffs sued in 1989, and a 1992 jury found for them on both theories. Required to elect a remedy, they chose RICO; that judgment was reversed in a prior appeal as time-barred. On remand they elected the state remedy, and judgment was entered July 3, 2002. Andrews noticed an extension motion on August 25 and filed a notice of appeal on August 27, twenty-five days late. The majority states that the district court granted the extension on August 30, making the notice timely retroactively; the dissent's footnotes give the order's date as September 3, 2002. Pincay appealed the extension order. The Ninth Circuit panel reversed the district court's retroactive extension. This is the 2003 panel decision; the later en banc decision in 2004 reached the opposite result on the extension.
sections.Material Facts:
On July 10, a nonlawyer calendaring clerk sent the judgment to defendants' supervising lawyer, who was out of the office. Asked when the appeal period ran, the clerk mistakenly used sixty days and ultimately proposed September 3 after adjusting for Sunday and Labor Day. The lawyer asked for an earlier calendar date of August 29 and later confirmed it had been entered. The ordinary thirty-day deadline was actually August 2.

On August 22, counsel handling Andrews's Connecticut bankruptcy told the lawyer that Pincay had represented the judgment as final because the appeal time had expired. Andrews then moved for an extension and filed the notice of appeal. Counsel offered reliance on the clerk as the excuse, without stating that he had read or misremembered the appeal rules.
sections.Issue: Whether counsel's reliance on a calendar clerk's erroneous reading of the appeal deadline was excusable neglect permitting the district court to extend the time to appeal under Appellate Rule 4(a)(5).
sections.Holding: The Ninth Circuit in 2003, in a panel opinion by Judge Noonan joined by Judge Wardlaw, with Judge Kleinfeld dissenting, held that it was not excusable neglect and reversed the extension order. The majority found no good cause, rejected the asserted neglect as excusable, and treated the district court's acceptance of counsel's excuse as an error of law. The panel did not review the merits of the underlying claims.
sections.Reasoning:
Appellate Rule 4(a)(1)(A) generally required filing within thirty days, and Rule 4(a)(5) allowed an extension on a timely motion showing excusable neglect or good cause.

The majority recognized Pioneer's flexible conception of neglect, which includes carelessness, but emphasized Pioneer's statement that ignorance or misinterpretation of rules ordinarily is not excusable. It relied on Kyle's treatment of a mistake about an unambiguous rule and distinguished Marx, Briones, and Bateman on their circumstances. The decisive distinction was between delegating work and delegating professional responsibility: nonlawyer help can be efficient, but the lawyer remains responsible for knowing the governing rule. Ignorance of the rule, compounded by delegating knowledge of it, was inexcusable here. The majority said the ignorance-of-law principle was not a per se rule.

Judge Kleinfeld, dissenting, would have affirmed. He argued that negligence, including ignorance of a rule and negligent delegation, can still be excusable neglect after an equitable assessment under Pioneer's factors: prejudice, length of delay, reason for delay, and good faith. In his account the district court considered each, finding no significant prejudice, a delay of a few weeks, and no bad faith. He also argued that extension decisions are committed to the district court's discretion and that the majority avoided deference by labelling the equitable assessment a legal error; he read the majority's reasoning as a categorical exclusion incompatible with Pioneer.

The casebook quotes this panel opinion's reasoning rejecting excusable neglect; it omits the dissent and does not explain that the 2004 en banc decision upheld the district court's discretion and rejected categorical treatment of delegation.

CP-COMP-CB-POITRA.rule: A witness is otherwise made known during discovery under Rule 26(e) only if the information is the functional equivalent of a proper disclosure; a passing deposition mention does not qualify, and Rule 37(c)(1) bars the undisclosed witness unless the omission was substantially justified or harmless.

sections.Parties: Michael Poitra, the plaintiff, sued Denver's school district and supervisor Anita Marchant after his 2013 termination, alleging employment discrimination and other violations. The school district, a defendant, moved for sanctions, seeking to exclude undisclosed witnesses and to recover its motion expenses. Poitra opposed, wanting to call employee Rebecca Ortega at trial.
sections.Procedural History: Discovery closed January 5, 2015. Poitra's April 30 proposed pretrial order listed Ortega among forty-one witnesses; the district objected to seven undisclosed witnesses and raised the issue at the May 5 final pretrial conference, where the magistrate judge declined to rule without a written motion. A May 8 order set trial for January 11, 2016. A separate September 2015 summary-judgment order dismissed the retaliation, due-process, and tortious-interference claims and left race, gender, and age discrimination claims for trial. The district moved for sanctions on November 16. By the December 16 hearing Poitra had removed the other three people named in the motion. On December 21, 2015, Magistrate Judge Shaffer granted the motion to exclude Ortega as a substantive or merits witness and denied attorney's fees and costs.
sections.Material Facts:
Poitra did not identify Ortega in his initial disclosures or in any written supplement before the final pretrial conference. His counsel learned about her around the December 2014 deposition and interviewed her near the discovery cutoff, but formally designated her only months later.

In deposition, Poitra mentioned Ortega's dissatisfaction with her job, fear of losing it, dislike of Marchant, and earlier workplace allegations. Marchant made one limited reference to Ortega's harassment complaints and their investigation. The testimony later proposed for Ortega concerned observations of Poitra, disciplinary practices, Marchant, Montgomery, and Worden.

Poitra argued that the deposition references gave sufficient notice under Rule 26(e)'s exception for information otherwise made known during discovery, and pointed to the final pretrial order and the requirement to disclose trial witnesses at least thirty days before trial. Defense counsel knew of the disputed witnesses in April and May but waited until trial approached to move. Counsel conceded that Rule 37(c)(1) was the proper basis for the motion.
sections.Issue: Whether mentioning Ortega during depositions satisfied the duty to supplement disclosures when those references did not adequately disclose her intended role as a supporting witness and her testimony, and, if not, whether she should be excluded and the district awarded its expenses.
sections.Holding: The District of Colorado in 2015, Magistrate Judge Craig B. Shaffer, held that the deposition references were insufficient. Information otherwise made known must be the functional equivalent of a proper disclosure, provided in time for meaningful discovery and trial preparation. The court excluded Ortega from substantive or merits testimony, preserved her possible use solely for impeachment, and denied the district's requested attorney's fees and costs. The court made no finding that the nondisclosure was willful.
sections.Reasoning:
Rule 26(a)(1)(A)(i) required identifying individuals likely to have discoverable information that the party might use to support its claims or defenses, with the subjects of their information. Rule 26(e)(1)(A) imposed a timely duty to supplement unless equivalent information had otherwise been communicated.

The deposition references did not match the testimony later proposed. Knowing that Ortega existed was different from knowing that Poitra intended to rely on her as a supporting witness with specified information. The court rejected a reading that would require an opponent to investigate every passing name despite deposition limits and proportionality, and distinguished Llewellyn, where deposition questioning made the witness's relevant information clear. The thirty-day trial-witness requirement of Rule 26(a)(3) applies in addition to the earlier disclosure duties and does not replace them. The court found no substantial justification.

Under Rule 37(c)(1), undisclosed testimony generally cannot be used unless the omission was substantially justified or harmless, and the court considered prejudice or surprise, ability to cure, trial disruption, and bad faith or willfulness. The omission prejudiced preparation; a last-minute deposition, reopened discovery, or a postponed trial would each be costly. No evidence showed willfulness or bad faith, but that alone did not make the omission harmless.

The court criticized the district for waiting passively and moving only as trial approached. Poitra's disclosure failures outweighed that delay for purposes of exclusion, but awarding expenses would appear to reward the district's dilatory conduct.

The casebook reproduces the disclosure rationale in a note and says the motion to strike and for sanctions was granted, a shorthand that omits the denial of expenses and the impeachment exception.

CP-COMP-CB-QUERCIA.rule: A federal trial judge may comment on the evidence and express an opinion on the facts if the jury is told the facts are theirs to decide, but may not distort or add to the evidence; a disclaimer does not cure such an addition.

sections.Parties: Quercia was the defendant in a federal criminal prosecution under the Narcotic Act and the petitioner in the Court, challenging the trial judge's charge to the jury. The United States was the prosecuting party. The Solicitor General did not oppose certiorari, acknowledged that part of the charge was improper, and submitted the matter without arguing for affirmance or reversal.
sections.Procedural History: Quercia was tried and convicted under the federal Narcotic Act. The trial court denied a directed-verdict motion and related requested rulings, and Quercia excepted to the judge's charge. The First Circuit affirmed the conviction. On certiorari, which the Solicitor General did not oppose, the Court reversed the judgment affirming the conviction. The opinion gives no detailed remand instruction.
sections.Material Facts:
Government agents testified against Quercia, and he took the stand to deny the charges generally. His testimony was not reproduced in the appellate record.

The judge instructed on innocence and reasonable doubt and told jurors generally that his opinions on the evidence were not binding. He then pointed to the defendant's wiping of his hands while testifying and asserted that the mannerism almost always indicated lying. He described that proposition as fact although he could not explain its basis, and said that everything Quercia had said, except where he agreed with the government's witnesses, was a lie. He repeated that his opinion was not binding and that jurors who disagreed should acquit.
sections.Issue: Whether a federal trial judge may use his claimed experience with a defendant's demeanor to denounce the defendant's testimony as a lie, where he also tells the jury that his opinion is not binding on them.
sections.Holding: The Court in 1933, in an opinion by Chief Justice Hughes with no separate opinion reported, held that the charge improperly added to the evidence and was highly prejudicial, and that the disclaimer did not cure it because the unsupported factual assertion and forceful denunciation remained. It reversed the judgment affirming the conviction. The Court did not adopt a rule of judicial silence and did not say jurors may never consider demeanor.
sections.Reasoning:
A federal trial judge governs the trial, decides legal questions, and may help jurors understand the evidence. That help can include discussing important evidence and expressing an opinion on the facts, provided the judge makes clear that factual decisions belong to the jury. The Court described this as a common-law judicial prerogative maintained in federal courts under the Constitution.

The power has corresponding limits. A judge may analyze and dissect the evidence but may not distort it, add to it, or assume the role of a witness. Because of the judge's influence, even a slight intimation can carry unusual persuasive force, so comments must avoid one-sided presentation, unwarranted deductions, and conjectural facts unsupported by evidence. In a criminal trial, hostile comment must not empty the defendant's opportunity to testify of practical value. The Court illustrated the limits with other cases, such as treating flight as conclusive proof of guilt.

The judge's remarks about hand-wiping crossed from evaluating the record into supplying a supposed fact from personal experience, placed against the accused with the authority of his office. He then swept aside everything the defendant said that conflicted with the government's case. The unsupported generalization combined with the blanket denunciation made the error highly prejudicial.

The reminder that jurors could disagree did not withdraw the factual assertion; its definiteness and the force of a judge's words made it likely to stay in jurors' minds and prevent fair evaluation.

The casebook reproduces the challenged charge in a note and asks readers to compare it with the civil jury commentary in Nunley, a comparison that is the editors' question, not a ruling of the Court.

CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.rule: Due process ordinarily requires notice and a hearing before a creditor may attach a debtor's property before judgment; a statute allowing summary attachment without limits tied to extraordinary need, and reaching necessities of life, is unconstitutional.

sections.Parties: A collection agency sued Joseph Randone and his wife, individually and doing business as Randone Trucking, on an assigned debt, and attached their bank account. The Randones, defendants in that action, moved to dissolve the attachment and then petitioned the California Supreme Court for an original writ against the Appellate Department of the Superior Court of Sacramento County. The agency defended the attachment statute.
sections.Procedural History: The agency sued on February 16, 1970, and on March 17 obtained a writ of attachment from the municipal court clerk. On March 31 the Randones moved to dissolve the attachment as a deprivation of property without due process; the municipal court heard and denied the motion on April 3. The superior court's appellate department affirmed without a written opinion on October 29 and refused certification to the Court of Appeal on November 5. The Randones then sought an original writ in the California Supreme Court, which issued an alternative writ because the constitutional question was important and lower courts disagreed. The court ordered a peremptory writ of mandamus directing the appellate department to order the trial court to dissolve the attachment.
sections.Material Facts:
The agency alleged that it held an assigned debt for $490 in legal services, plus $130 interest. After obtaining the writ from the clerk it levied on the Randones' checking account, and the bank withheld the account's $176.20 pending an order releasing the attachment. No judicial determination of the alleged debt came first. The Randones' affidavit stated that unemployment insurance was their sole source of income.

Code of Civil Procedure section 537, subdivision 1, generally authorized attachment in qualifying unsecured contract actions for the direct payment of money. Once the plaintiff filed the required declaration and undertaking, a clerk could issue the writ without judicial scrutiny, prior notice, or an opportunity for the debtor to contest it. The creditor chose the property. Earnings were excluded by a 1970 amendment, but the scheme reached almost every other kind of property, and the restraint could last three years unless released earlier. Debtors could post security, win the suit, or seek an exemption, but those remedies put the burden on them.
sections.Issue: Whether the due-process principle of Sniadach v. Family Finance Corp. extends beyond wage garnishment to prejudgment attachment generally, and whether section 537, subdivision 1, which allowed attachment without notice or hearing and reached necessities of life, was constitutional.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of California in 1971, in a unanimous opinion by Justice Tobriner, held section 537, subdivision 1, facially unconstitutional under the state and federal due-process provisions because it broadly allowed seizure without notice and hearing, lacked limits tied to extraordinary need, and permitted deprivation of necessities. It declined to rewrite the statute and ordered the attachment dissolved. The court did not decide whether the Randones owed the underlying debt, and it reserved the constitutionality of a provision confined to restraints, such as a lien on real estate, that do not significantly impair use.
sections.Reasoning:
The court rejected the agency's reading of Sniadach as limited to wages. Its recent Blair v. Pitchess decision had applied the same reasoning to claim and delivery, and federal and California decisions reflected a general requirement of an opportunity to be heard before a significant deprivation, subject to exceptional countervailing interests. The property interest at stake was use of the property before judgment; calling attachment temporary did not remove that interest or the hardship of losing it.

Summary action can be justified, as in banking and public-health cases involving urgent public protection and tailored statutes. Section 537(1) lacked that tailoring: it made security available broadly without proof that delay would frustrate collection. The agency's claim that attachment was essential to available credit was unsupported on the record. An actual danger of flight or concealment could support a carefully limited summary remedy, but the statute required no particularized showing and none was made here.

The statute also reached necessities. Bank funds needed by an unemployed family could be as vital as wages, and the creditor's power to choose the property allowed the greatest settlement pressure. Such deprivation could undermine the later hearing itself by forcing a debtor to settle even a meritorious defense. A creditor's private security interest did not justify taking necessities before a hearing on the validity of the claim, and post-attachment exemptions did not cure the problem.

The court contemplated a valid scheme protecting necessities, ordinarily permitting attachment after notice and a hearing on probable validity, with safeguarded exceptions for demonstrated risk of concealment or flight.

The casebook cites the case in its attachment note as the decision invalidating the summary attachment statute; its description of later legislation is editorial context.

CP-COMP-CB-REF-007.rule: A default judgment entered without valid service is void for lack of personal jurisdiction and must be vacated; actual receipt of the papers cannot by itself cure delivery to someone who is not the defendant's officer or authorized agent.

sections.Parties: The American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA) sued Affinity Card, Inc. for breach of contract, alleging that Affinity withheld fee information and failed to make required payments, and obtained a default judgment. Affinity, the defendant, moved to vacate that judgment, arguing that ineffective service deprived the court of personal jurisdiction and made the judgment void.
sections.Procedural History: AICPA filed its complaint in the Southern District of New York on March 24, 1998, and a process server delivered the summons and complaint on March 30. Affinity failed to answer or move in time, and a default judgment was entered on May 11. Affinity then moved under Rules 55(c) and 60(b)(4). On July 16, 1998, District Judge Scheindlin granted the motion to vacate the default judgment, conditioned on Affinity's agreement to accept service through its attorney. AICPA was to make that service within seven days, and a conference was scheduled for August 12.
sections.Material Facts:
AICPA, Affinity and Marine Midland Bank entered a contract on November 5, 1992, establishing a Visa program marketed to AICPA members. Marine Midland issued the cards, Affinity assisted with promotion, and AICPA and Affinity shared participant fees.

On March 30, 1998, process server Peter Murphy delivered the summons and complaint to Patrick McDonald at the shared Wellesley, Massachusetts office suite where Affinity did business. The affidavit of service called McDonald Affinity's assistant vice president, but he held that title at Primecard Corporation and did not work for Affinity. Four companies shared the suite and reception area, and Greg Miller was president, treasurer and at least a partial owner of all four.

Murphy said he asked for Miller, explained he had important legal papers for Affinity and Miller, and asked who could accept them, and that McDonald agreed to deliver them, viewed them and gave his title. McDonald said Murphy did not identify or show the papers or ask whether he could accept service, and handed him a sealed envelope. McDonald put it in Miller's mailbox that day.
sections.Issue: Could delivery of the summons and complaint to an employee of a different corporation sharing the defendant's office suite support a default judgment against Affinity, under Rule 4(h)(1) or New York or Massachusetts law, and did Miller's actual receipt of the papers or an alter-ego theory cure any defect?
sections.Holding: The United States District Court for the Southern District of New York, 1998, Judge Scheindlin, held that service was ineffective under the federal rule and under both New York and Massachusetts law, so the default judgment was void for lack of personal jurisdiction. Actual receipt could not by itself cure ineffective service, and the alter-ego argument failed. The court granted the motion to vacate, stated that it lacked jurisdiction over Affinity until proper service occurred, and, recognizing AICPA's good-faith belief that it had served the company, conditioned vacatur on Affinity's agreement to accept service through its attorney. It did not decide the contract allegations.
sections.Reasoning:
The court distinguished this motion from discretionary relief for excusable neglect. A judgment entered without personal jurisdiction is a nullity, relief from it is mandatory, and the movant need not show a meritorious defense. Valid service is a prerequisite to personal jurisdiction. Invoking the circuit's preference for decisions on the merits, the court said equally plausible conflicting accounts should be resolved for the party seeking vacatur when the record gives no basis to choose, and so credited McDonald's version. This was its approach to this default-vacatur record, not a universal rule.

Under Rule 4(h)(1), the plaintiff must supply a basis for inferring authority to accept process. Job titles are not conclusive, and service can reach a representative sufficiently integrated into the organization to know what to do with the papers, but that requires a meaningful relationship with the defendant. McDonald had worked for Primecard only a few months, had no Affinity responsibilities, had never heard of Affinity, and on the credited account did not hold himself out as its representative. Hellenic Challenger differed because its recipient was the defendant's well-integrated employee familiar with receiving summonses.

Miller's actual receipt that day was important, but knowledge of the lawsuit and delivery to a legally appropriate recipient are distinct requirements. The alter-ego argument failed under Massachusetts corporate law, which requires substantially more than common officers, some shared employees, an address and a telephone number. Service also failed under New York law, which permits reasonable reliance on an employee's representation of authority, and under Massachusetts law, whose categories are construed restrictively.

The casebook cites the case for the point that actual notice does not inevitably cure defective service.

CP-COMP-CB-REF-010.rule: Unless Congress clearly classifies a threshold restriction on a statute's coverage as jurisdictional, courts treat it as a nonjurisdictional element of the claim; Title VII's fifteen-employee requirement is therefore an element, not a limit on subject-matter jurisdiction.

sections.Parties: Jenifer Arbaugh, a bartender and waitress at the Moonlight Cafe in New Orleans, sued the restaurant's owner, Y & H Corporation, under Title VII and Louisiana law, alleging that an owner, Yalcin Hatipoglu, sexually harassed her and caused her constructive discharge. Arbaugh was the plaintiff and won a jury verdict. Y & H, the defendant, then sought dismissal of the whole action for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction.
sections.Procedural History: Arbaugh sued in November 2001, invoking federal-question jurisdiction and supplemental jurisdiction over the state claims. After the parties consented to a magistrate judge's adjudication, a two-day jury trial produced a verdict for Arbaugh, and judgment was entered on November 5, 2002. Two weeks later Y & H moved under Rule 12(h)(3) to dismiss for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction. After posttrial discovery the trial court, though it called the timing unfair and wasteful, considered dismissal mandatory: it vacated the judgment, dismissed the federal claim with prejudice and dismissed the state claims without prejudice. The Fifth Circuit affirmed under its precedent treating the employee minimum as jurisdictional. The Court took the case to resolve a circuit conflict, reversed the Fifth Circuit and remanded.
sections.Material Facts:
Arbaugh worked at the Moonlight Cafe from May 2000 through February 2001. Y & H admitted the jurisdictional allegations while contesting the merits. The pretrial order likewise acknowledged federal jurisdiction and did not identify the number of employees as a disputed issue, and no workforce objection arose before or during trial. The jury found sexual harassment and constructive discharge under federal and state law and awarded $5,000 in backpay, $5,000 in compensatory damages and $30,000 in punitive damages.

Two weeks after judgment, Y & H asserted for the first time that it lacked the fifteen employees necessary to qualify as a Title VII employer. Title VII defines an employer as a person in an industry affecting commerce with fifteen or more employees for each working day in twenty or more calendar weeks in the current or preceding year. Posttrial discovery focused on eight delivery drivers, two owner-managers and their shareholder spouses; counting either the drivers or the four owners would have met the threshold. The trial court concluded that none of them counted as employees.
sections.Issue: Is Title VII's requirement that an employer have fifteen or more employees a limit on federal subject-matter jurisdiction, which can be raised at any time including after trial and judgment, or an element of the plaintiff's claim, which cannot be raised for the first time after trial?
sections.Holding: The Court, 2006, in an opinion by Justice Ginsburg joined by every participating Justice (8-0; Justice Alito did not participate), held that Title VII's fifteen-employee threshold is an element of the claim rather than a restriction on federal subject-matter jurisdiction. Congress must clearly classify a threshold restriction on statutory coverage as jurisdictional for courts to treat it that way; without such classification the restriction is nonjurisdictional. The Court reversed the Fifth Circuit and remanded. It did not decide whether Y & H actually had fifteen employees.
sections.Reasoning:
Federal-question jurisdiction came from 28 U.S.C. § 1331 and Title VII's own authorization for district courts to hear actions under the Act, and neither grant incorporated the employee minimum. The minimum appears in a separate definitions section that does not speak in jurisdictional terms or refer to district-court jurisdiction.

The classification matters. A true subject-matter defect cannot be waived or forfeited and can be raised after trial and judgment, while Rule 12(h)(2)'s failure-to-state-a-claim defense survives through trial on the merits but not beyond it. The Court identified three consequences of a jurisdictional label: courts would have an independent duty to investigate employer size, though nothing in Title VII indicates Congress intended that; judges can sometimes resolve jurisdictional facts, whereas contested facts about a claim element belong to the jury; and jurisdictional dismissal would require dismissing the entire complaint, including already-tried state claims, rather than permitting discretionary supplemental jurisdiction.

The Court acknowledged imprecise use of the word jurisdiction in its own decisions and said a label used without considering whether an issue actually concerned adjudicatory authority has no precedential force on that question; Hishon, Arabian American Oil and Walters did not decide the point. Congress remains free to impose jurisdictional requirements, as with diversity jurisdiction's monetary floor. The rule does not eliminate dismissal for want of jurisdiction where a federal claim is manufactured solely to obtain jurisdiction or is wholly insubstantial and frivolous, which Arbaugh's was not.

The casebook cites the case for the point that the workforce objection came too late because it concerned substantive coverage.

CP-COMP-CB-REF-013.rule: A state may constitutionally exercise personal jurisdiction over a nonresident director of its corporation, under a director-consent statute, in an action for breach of fiduciary duty to that corporation, where the director accepted the office after the statute took effect.

sections.Parties: Shareholders brought two consolidated derivative actions on behalf of Morrison-Knudsen, a Delaware corporation, against its directors, alleging breach of duties owed to the corporation in transactions repurchasing its stock from Crane Company. The individual director defendants, none of whom lived in Delaware, entered limited appearances challenging personal jurisdiction and were the appellants.
sections.Procedural History: After Shaffer invalidated Delaware's earlier sequestration procedure, the legislature enacted section 3114. The plaintiffs served the directors under that statute. The directors entered limited appearances challenging jurisdiction, the Court of Chancery rejected their objection, and the Delaware Supreme Court accepted an interlocutory appeal. On October 29, 1980, it affirmed in part and reversed in part: the rejection of the jurisdictional challenge stood for three directors, and six others should have been dismissed. The ruling decided no question of fiduciary liability.
sections.Material Facts:
Morrison-Knudsen was incorporated in Delaware but had its principal place of business in Boise, Idaho, and did no Delaware business beyond what was necessary to maintain its corporate status. None of the individual defendants lived in Delaware, no board meeting had occurred there, and the complaints alleged no Delaware connection beyond the directors' relationship with the corporation.

Section 3114 treated specified acceptance of, or service in, a Delaware corporate directorship as consent to appointing the corporation's registered agent, or the Secretary of State if there was none, for service in designated corporate or fiduciary-duty actions. One clause covered service as a director after June 30, 1978; the summonses here had issued before that date. The other covered acceptance of election or appointment after September 1, 1977. Armstrong, McMurren, Stuart, Morrison, Scott and Spencer had been elected to their then-current terms before September 1, 1977. Lilly, McCabe and Woodhead had been elected at the annual meeting in early May 1978.
sections.Issue: Did section 3114 authorize service on each director, given its timing provisions, and if so, was it constitutional under Shaffer's minimum-contacts requirement for Delaware to exercise jurisdiction over nonresident directors whose only Delaware connection was their directorship in a Delaware corporation?
sections.Holding: The Delaware Supreme Court, 1980, Justice McNeilly writing for a three-justice panel that also included Justices Quillen and Horsey, held that section 3114 did not reach the six directors elected to their terms before September 1, 1977, who should have been dismissed, and that it did reach Lilly, McCabe and Woodhead, elected in May 1978. The court upheld the statute as applied to those three: exercising jurisdiction over them in this fiduciary-duty action was constitutional. The judgment was affirmed in part and reversed in part.
sections.Reasoning:
The court addressed the statute before the Constitution. The service-after-June-30-1978 clause could not justify jurisdiction because the summonses had issued earlier, and the acceptance clause covered only the three directors elected in May 1978.

Those three argued that Shaffer required minimum contacts and that director status alone could not supply them. The court agreed their contacts were numerically slight but assessed their quality and connection to the litigation. The directorships existed under Delaware corporation law, and the suits challenged conduct undertaken through powers that law conferred. Accepting the position after the statute's effective date gave express notice that a director might be called to defend in Delaware. The office carried benefits available under Delaware statutes, including management authority, opportunities for interest-free unsecured corporate loans, and indemnification rights. If the allegations were true, the directors' acts had foreseeably injured a Delaware corporation even though they occurred elsewhere.

Delaware had a substantial interest in supervising duties created by its corporate law and in giving shareholders an effective forum; other states might decline to apply Delaware law, interpret it inconsistently, or impose procedural obstacles, and no single alternative state might have jurisdiction over all directors. The court considered much of Shaffer's discussion of officers and directors unnecessary to its sequestration holding, and distinguished a director's knowing acceptance of a fiduciary position under an explicit statute from jurisdiction based on shares constructively located in Delaware. The reasoning was tied to corporate or fiduciary-duty litigation and does not authorize jurisdiction over unrelated personal disputes.

The casebook uses Armstrong as an example of jurisdiction over nonresident directors whose relevant Delaware connection was their directorship; its mention of a 2004 extension to high officers is the editors' later history.

CP-COMP-CB-REF-038.rule: A mutual settlement for consideration of remaining individual claims after continued litigation, expressly reserving specified issues for appeal, produces a final judgment under 28 U.S.C. section 1291; Microsoft v. Baker's bar on manufactured finality does not apply.

sections.Parties: Silken Brown, joined on appeal by Mario De La Rosa, was the plaintiff in a class complaint against Cinemark USA, Inc. and Century Theatres alleging wage-and-hour violations. Brown and De La Rosa were the appellants, challenging rulings they had reserved in a settlement. Cinemark and Century Theatres, the defendants and appellees, moved to dismiss the appeal for lack of jurisdiction.
sections.Procedural History: The defendants removed Brown's action to federal court, where it was consolidated with similar litigation, including De La Rosa's action. The district court dismissed Brown's individual direct wage-statement claim and denied certification of several proposed classes, and the remaining individual claims were set for trial. On the defendants' summary-judgment motion the court issued a tentative ruling granting it in part and denying it in part. The parties stipulated to that ruling and settled all remaining individual claims, reserving certain issues, and Brown and De La Rosa appealed. While the appeal was pending the Supreme Court decided Microsoft Corp. v. Baker, and the defendants moved to dismiss. The Ninth Circuit denied the motion and retained jurisdiction to consider the appeal on the merits; other issues were addressed in a separate memorandum disposition.
sections.Material Facts:
The district court denied certification of proposed classes for meal and rest breaks, reporting pay, off-the-clock work, derivative wage statements, and direct wage statements. Brown and De La Rosa went on litigating their individual claims after that denial. After the tentative summary-judgment ruling, the parties stipulated to it and settled all remaining individual claims. Their settlement reserved the right to challenge the denial of certification of the direct wage claim and the dismissal of Brown's individual direct wage-statement claim.

The defendants argued that settling the remaining claims, like the voluntary dismissal in Baker, could not create a final decision permitting review of an interlocutory class ruling. In Baker the plaintiffs, after losing class certification and being denied Rule 23(f) review, had voluntarily dismissed their own individual claims to create a final judgment.
sections.Issue: Whether Microsoft Corp. v. Baker deprives a court of appeals of jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. section 1291 when the parties resolve the remaining individual claims through a mutual settlement for consideration and expressly preserve specified issues for appeal.
sections.Holding: The Ninth Circuit in 2017, in an order issued by Chief Judge Sidney R. Thomas and Judges Stephen Reinhardt and Kathleen M. O'Malley, sitting by designation, with no separate writing, held that it does not in these circumstances. The settlement produced a valid final judgment, the motion to dismiss was denied, and the court retained jurisdiction to consider the reserved appeal on the merits. The order neither affirmed nor reversed the certification ruling.
sections.Reasoning:
The panel accepted Baker's rule. The Supreme Court there rejected the tactic of voluntarily dismissing individual claims to obtain review of a class ruling because it undermined section 1291's protection against piecemeal appeals and circumvented Rule 23(f)'s procedure for discretionary interlocutory review. The question was whether this litigation and settlement presented the same problem.

The panel found material differences. Brown and De La Rosa kept litigating their individual claims after certification was denied; some claims were resolved in the defendants' favor and others were settled. The agreement was a mutual exchange for consideration, not a unilateral abandonment of claims designed to manufacture appellate jurisdiction. It reserved specific claims for appeal, and the record disclosed no sham tactic to obtain a nominal final judgment. Those circumstances brought the remaining trial-court litigation to a genuine end while leaving a concrete appellate dispute over the reserved matters.

The reasoning is narrower than a rule that every dismissal accompanied by a reservation of appeal is effective. The court looked to the course of actual merits litigation, the nature of the exchange, and the absence of the circumvention that drove Baker; a reservation by itself was not identified as enough to make an interlocutory order final. Here the mutual settlement did not implicate Baker's concerns.

The casebook cites the case in a note for the distinction between a mutual settlement and a unilateral dismissal and for the finding that no sham tactic was shown.

CP-COMP-CB-REF-098.rule: Under Rule 4(f)(3) a court may authorize email service on foreign defendants without first requiring other methods, if no international agreement prohibits it and the email addresses are shown to be reasonably calculated to give notice.

sections.Parties: The plaintiffs were the publishers Cengage, Elsevier, McGraw-Hill and Pearson. The defendants were foreign retailers alleged to have sold counterfeit copies of the publishers' textbooks in the United States through eBay storefronts; thirteen were named foreign defendants, eight based in Malaysia, including the corporate entity Akitrade, and five in China. The publishers sought permission to serve their amended complaint by email.
sections.Procedural History: The publishers filed the original complaint in the Southern District of New York against twenty unidentified defendants on August 17, 2017, and obtained an ex parte temporary restraining order, expedited discovery and an order to show cause; a preliminary injunction followed in September. Under those orders they emailed the original complaint and injunction materials to addresses associated with the storefronts, and no foreign defendant responded. They amended the complaint on January 29, 2018, to name the defendants, and on February 2 moved for leave to serve it by email. On March 12, 2018, Magistrate Judge Gabriel W. Gorenstein granted the motion.
sections.Material Facts:
