The alleged listings used the legitimate books' names, authors, cover images, trademarks and ISBNs. The sellers received proceeds through PayPal or another payment system. Although many allegedly gave eBay fictitious names or physical addresses, they supplied working email addresses to operate their accounts. Before suing, the publishers made purchases from the storefronts and obtained associated email addresses.

The publishers subpoenaed eBay and PayPal, which supplied account information in December 2017. That information identified the defendants but showed multiple changing or incomplete physical addresses, and the publishers represented that they could not determine the defendants' true locations. Their motion asked to serve the amended complaint by email to all addresses that eBay and PayPal identified as associated with the defendants' business accounts, and proposed tracking delivery through a service such as ReadNotify. These were allegations underlying the service request, not an adjudication of copyright or trademark liability.
sections.Issue: May a court authorize email service of an amended complaint on foreign defendants in Malaysia and China under Rule 4(f)(3), without requiring an attempt at Hague Convention service, consistent with international agreements and due process?
sections.Holding: The United States District Court for the Southern District of New York, 2018, Magistrate Judge Gorenstein, granted the alternative-service motion and authorized email service on the thirteen specifically listed foreign defendants, including Akitrade. It directed use of an email tracking service to preserve the maximum information about effectiveness in case that became relevant later. The order resolved only the permitted method of service; it entered no default judgment, established no infringement liability and awarded no damages.
sections.Reasoning:
Rule 4(f) provides several methods for serving individuals abroad, and Rule 4(h)(2) incorporates them for foreign corporations such as Akitrade. Following Rio Properties and related decisions, the court rejected a mandatory hierarchy requiring exhaustion of subsections (1) and (2) before subsection (3): court-ordered alternative service is an available method in its own right, though it must respect international agreements and due process and remains discretionary. Some judges require reasonable service attempts and a demonstrated need for intervention; the court treated those as discretionary safeguards, not a categorical command.

Malaysia was not a Hague Service Convention signatory at the time, and no other agreement barred email service there. China was a party, but service through its Ministry of Justice required an address, the defendants' incomplete and shifting addresses frustrated that, and Article 1 excludes cases where the recipient's address is unknown. China had objected to postal-channel service under Article 10, but the court accepted district-court decisions treating that objection as not extending to email.

Due process asks whether the method is reasonably calculated, under the circumstances, to inform the defendants of the suit and let them object. The court did not presume any discovered address would suffice. It relied on these defendants' online business operations and regular customer communication through functional addresses tied to their eBay and PayPal accounts, supported by the publishers' purchases, account discovery and declaration. Because the defendants used those channels to conduct the very business at issue, email was the method most likely to notify them.

The casebook quotes the case for the connection between functioning business email accounts and the likelihood of meaningful notice.

CP-COMP-CB-REF-106.rule: A court may order email service abroad under Rule 4(f)(3) when no international agreement prohibits it and the movant supplies facts showing that process sent to the address is likely to reach the defendant.

sections.Parties: Richard Y. Fisher, the plaintiff, owned a painting he claimed was Petr Petrovich Konchalovsky's 1920 oil painting Still Life with Grinder, and alleged that the defendant Petr Konchalovsky Foundation, a Russian corporation based in Moscow, had wrongfully declared it inauthentic. Fisher sought court permission to serve the Foundation by an alternative method.
sections.Procedural History: Fisher filed the action in the Southern District of New York on December 17, 2015. On January 14, 2016, he sought permission to serve the Foundation through United States Post Office International Mail. The court denied the postal request and required him either to explain why it should depart from the district's contrary authority or to propose another method. He proposed email on January 28. On March 10, 2016, District Judge Alison J. Nathan granted the request to serve by email and denied international-mail service.
sections.Material Facts:
An attorney experienced in international process submitted an affidavit identifying the Foundation as a Russian corporation based in Moscow and explaining that Russia no longer effected service through its Hague Convention Central Authority. The opinion also cited Russia's suspension of civil and commercial judicial cooperation with the United States in 2003. Russia had objected to Article 10 postal-channel service.

Fisher's attorney, David Steiner, enlisted Paris art dealer Valère Lamblot to contact the Foundation. Lamblot emailed an authentication inquiry about a purported Konchalovsky painting. Alexander Konov, whom Fisher's affidavit identified as the Foundation's director, replied the same day from konov@pkonchalovsky.com, recommending art experts in Geneva or Moscow and providing their institutes' websites. Steiner later emailed Konov himself but received no response.
sections.Issue: Could the court authorize email service on a Russian corporate defendant under Rule 4(f)(3), that is, was email compatible with international agreements despite Russia's objection to postal-channel service, and was the proposed address reasonably calculated to give the Foundation notice?
sections.Holding: The United States District Court for the Southern District of New York, 2016, Judge Nathan, granted Fisher's request to serve the Foundation by email and denied service by international mail. It held that no international agreement barred email service, that Russia had not explicitly objected to electronic service, and that Fisher had supplied sufficient evidence that email to the designated address was likely to reach the defendant. The order did not decide the painting's authenticity or the Foundation's liability.
sections.Reasoning:
Rule 4(f)(3) permits a court to order another method of foreign service if international agreement does not prohibit it, and Rule 4(h)(2) incorporates the Rule 4(f) methods for corporations abroad. The court applied two requirements: compatibility with international agreements and constitutional due process.

On the postal request, a country's failure to execute Convention requests did not establish that it consented to service by mail, so the court would not disregard Russia's Article 10 objection. On email, the court followed decisions reading an objection to Article 10's enumerated methods as not expressly rejecting email. It acknowledged Agha v. Jacobs, which treated postal-channel language as potentially encompassing email, but adopted the contrary interpretation. Russia had not explicitly objected to electronic service, and the court knew of no other international agreement or Russian law prohibiting it.

Due process requires a method reasonably calculated, under the circumstances, to inform the defendant of the action and permit objections. Identifying an email address is not enough; the movant must supply facts indicating that process sent there would likely reach the defendant. Konov's prompt reply within the preceding two months showed recent use of the address by the person identified as the Foundation's director, and the exchange concerned authentication of a Konchalovsky painting, the very type of activity at issue in the suit. The court contrasted Fortunato, where a Facebook profile's listed address lacked facts showing it was operational and accessed, and the SEC's China Intelligent Lighting application, where the record neither linked the addresses to the individuals nor showed continued use.

The casebook cites the order for the points that no international agreement barred email service, Russia had not objected to it, and Fisher showed the email was likely to reach the defendant.

CP-COMP-CB-REF-154.rule: Rule 4(f)(3) court-directed service is an available method rather than a last resort, and a court may authorize service on foreign defendants through their United States counsel when that is not prohibited by international agreement and is reasonably calculated to give notice.

sections.Parties: I.M. Wilson, Inc., a Pennsylvania corporation selling dancewear including pointe shoes, sued Nicolai Grishko, the Russian limited-liability company OOO Grichko, and the Czech limited-liability company Grishko Dance, S.R.O., alleging infringement of its United States rights in the GRISHKO brand. Wilson, the plaintiff, moved for permission to serve all three defendants through Brian Kinder, the Russian defendants' United States lawyer.
sections.Procedural History: Wilson sued in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania and had a pending preliminary-injunction motion. It moved for alternative service on all three foreign defendants through their United States counsel, proposing email delivery. On December 10, 2018, District Judge Gene E.K. Pratter granted the motion in a memorandum and a separate one-page order, authorizing service by delivering hard copies of the summons and complaint to Kinder at his business address under Rule 4(c). The court did not decide the preliminary-injunction motion or the merits.
sections.Material Facts:
In the late 1980s Wilson entered an agreement with Nicolai Grishko to develop and sell a pointe-shoe brand in the United States; Wilson developed the plans and marketed the brand, and Grishko, through Grishko, Inc., developed the shoes. Wilson alleged that it owned the GRISHKO brand in the United States and that, nearly thirty years into the relationship, the defendants infringed its rights by selling GRISHKO-branded products to United States customers through Internet sales and Canadian distributors.

Grishko was the principal owner and operator of the Russian and Czech entities and had a Moscow business address; he was the Czech company's sole director and board member. Kinder was reportedly actively representing OOO Grichko and Grishko in opposition and cancellation proceedings before the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board concerning the same marks, and Wilson had communicated with him and had his correct contact information. According to the State Department, Russia suspended judicial cooperation with the United States in 2003 and returned service requests unexecuted. Wilson expected Hague Convention service in the Czech Republic to take two to four months.
sections.Issue: May a court, under Rule 4(f)(3), authorize service on Russian and Czech defendants by delivery to the United States lawyer who represents the Russian defendants in related proceedings, consistent with international agreements and due process, and may that delivery be made by email?
sections.Holding: The United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, 2018, Judge Pratter, granted the alternative-service motion and authorized service on OOO Grichko, Nicolai Grishko and Grishko Dance by delivering hard copies of the summons and complaint to Kinder at his business address under Rule 4(c). It rejected Wilson's proposed email delivery because an email could be caught by a spam filter or otherwise fail. It did not decide the preliminary-injunction motion, enter default or determine infringement.
sections.Reasoning:
Following Rio Properties and Knit With, the court treated Rule 4(f)(3) as an available method rather than extraordinary relief available only as a last resort. A court may in its discretion require attempted service and a demonstrated need for intervention, but the rule does not invariably impose that requirement. The method chosen must be compatible with international agreements and due process, and its purpose is meaningful notice in time for the defendants to answer and present defenses.

The obstacles differed by country. For the Russian defendants, the court relied on the State Department's account that requests sent through diplomatic channels or Russia's Hague Central Authority were returned unexecuted. For the Czech defendant, a Convention signatory's process would take two to four months, a delay Wilson said was particularly harmful while its preliminary-injunction request was pending; the court accepted the urgency and the proposed domestic channel as reasons for an alternative. As far as the court was aware, service through American counsel was not prohibited by Russian law or international agreement, or by Czech law.

Kinder's ongoing representation of OOO Grichko and Grishko in proceedings about the same marks, and counsel's duties, supported the expectation that he would notify the Russian clients. Because Grishko was the Czech company's sole director and board member and Kinder already represented him, serving Kinder was reasonably calculated to convey notice to Grishko Dance; the court did not find that Kinder independently represented the Czech company. Prompt notice also let the defendants protect their interests in an accelerated proceeding.

The casebook cites the case for the distinction between authorizing service through United States counsel and refusing email as the delivery medium.

CP-COMP-CB-REF-180.rule: Rule 23(c)(2)(B) requires individual notice to all class members identifiable through reasonable effort; the expense or size of a search does not excuse it where available records can identify actual members, and an accurate partial list requires notice even when a complete one is impracticable.

sections.Parties: Consumers sued over flat early-termination fees in cellular-service contracts, alleging illegal penalties under federal communications and state consumer-protection law. The operative complaint's five class representatives were people charged Sprint fees, and Sprint was the settling defendant; AT&T remained in the caption but was not part of the settlement or the appeal. Objectors, including the Galleguillos objectors and Jessica Hall, challenged the class notice, the representatives' adequacy and the settlement.
sections.Procedural History: The District of New Jersey preliminarily approved the settlement and conditionally certified a Rule 23(b)(3) class in December 2008. After the initial fairness hearing it found the proposed notice inadequate and required a new plan identifying reasonably accessible subsets of class members for individual notice. Sprint and class counsel proposed an amended plan, which the court approved after twelve days. On January 15, 2010, it rejected the objections and approved certification and settlement. On June 29, 2012, the Third Circuit vacated the certification-and-settlement order and remanded for further proceedings.
sections.Material Facts:
Until late 2008 Sprint used flat early-termination fees of approximately $200 that did not decline as the contract neared its end. After five months of negotiation supervised by a retired district judge, the parties agreed in December 2008 to a $17.5 million settlement: $14 million in cash and $3.5 million in activation-fee waivers, additional minutes and credit forgiveness. Relief varied among four categories; Category IV, for claims arising after notice but before January 1, 2011, offered only noncash benefits.

The district court first found that a complete class list for 1999-2008 might take six to twelve months and at least $1 million, but said that did not excuse identifying reasonably accessible subsets. The amended plan offered bill inserts to current customers, notice to 194,461 members of another California class, and notice to about 90,000 otherwise identifiable subscribers, but Sprint and class counsel declined to search Sprint's billing records. A declaration by Scott Rice estimated that obtaining recent records would cost approximately $100,000. The objectors estimated 4.2 million discoverable customers, and Sprint acknowledged that its records could identify millions of class members. All five representatives were former customers when the settlement was made.
sections.Issue: Did the district court abuse its discretion in approving a class notice plan that required no search of the defendant's billing records for identifiable class members, and did it adequately examine whether the class representatives had the incentive to represent the whole class under Rule 23(a)(4)?
sections.Holding: The United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit, 2012, Judge Jordan writing for a panel with Chief Judge McKee and Judge Fuentes, held that approving the notice plan without requiring any billing-record search, on little explanation beyond the cost declaration, was an abuse of discretion. It vacated the January 15, 2010 certification-and-settlement order and remanded for reassessment on a fuller record, leaving the final reasonable-effort determination to the district court. It urged renewed analysis of the representatives' adequacy without finally deciding it, and did not decide whether the settlement was fair, reasonable and adequate.
sections.Reasoning:
Rule 23(c)(2)(B) requires individual notice to all members identifiable through reasonable effort. The court assumed the Rice declaration was admissible; even so, the refusal to require any search could not stand.

The court distinguished finding recipients from paying to deliver notice. Eisen treated individual notice to reasonably identifiable members as mandatory, not dispensable because of expense. Oppenheimer addressed who bears identification costs and did not eliminate the need to obtain available identifying information. Expense, anticipated results and the amount involved inform reasonable effort, but size alone does not excuse effort, because a large class may require a large search. Domestic Air involved a list whose relationship to class membership was highly uncertain, whereas Sprint acknowledged its records could identify millions of actual members. An accurate partial list requires notice even when a complete one is impracticable. The district court had originally recognized that, then changed course with little explanation.

The costs reinforced the point: if the $100,000 search identified two million members, identification would cost about five cents each, or about forty-three cents with mailing. These were hypothetical calculations. The people who had paid the fees stood to receive much of the settlement yet were generally no longer current customers reachable by bill inserts.

On adequacy, Rule 23(a)(4) involves both freedom from conflicts and the ability and incentive to represent the class vigorously. The district court stressed the absence of antagonism but did not adequately examine whether former customers had an incentive to prevent continued fee enforcement against current subscribers, some of whom could receive only Category IV's noncash benefits.

The casebook quotes the court's cost reasoning; the brief notes that the casebook summarizes it as a refusal to order a search, while the opinion left the reasonable-effort decision to the district court on remand.

CP-COMP-CB-REF-206.rule: Where personal jurisdiction is lacking, a district court has discretion to refuse a transfer in the interest of justice even though the statute of limitations has run elsewhere, if the plaintiff was on notice of the defect and failed to protect the claim.

sections.Parties: Robert McFarlane, an admitted public figure who had served in senior Reagan Administration roles, sued freelance writer Craig Unger and the publishers Esquire Magazine and Hearst Corporation for defamation, alleging that an article falsely portrayed him as an Israeli spy and a traitor. McFarlane was the plaintiff and the appellant; Unger and the publisher were defendants and prevailed below.
sections.Procedural History: McFarlane sued in federal district court in Washington, D.C. After discovery, the district court found no personal jurisdiction over Unger, refused to transfer the claim against him, and granted summary judgment for Esquire because no reasonable jury could find actual malice by clear and convincing evidence. On January 30, 1996, the D.C. Circuit affirmed: it sustained the jurisdictional dismissal and transfer denial as to Unger and the actual-malice summary judgment as to the publisher.
sections.Material Facts:
An October 1991 Esquire article described an alleged conspiracy by members of the Reagan-Bush campaign to delay release of American hostages in Iran. Unger wrote it and delivered it to Esquire in New York. It relied heavily on Ari Ben-Menashe, a self-described former Israeli spy, and attributed to him assertions connecting McFarlane with Israeli intelligence and the Jonathan Pollard espionage affair. The article also disclosed substantial doubts about Ben-Menashe's credibility.

Unger wrote for national publications circulated in the District and had written two articles for Washington-based publications, one of them, for the Washington Post, after the complaint. McFarlane acknowledged that Unger was an independent contractor. New York's defamation limitations period apparently had expired. Unger's answer had alerted McFarlane to the jurisdictional defense, and McFarlane's counsel had not filed a protective action in New York.
sections.Issue: Did the D.C. long-arm statute reach Unger; if not, was the district court required to transfer the claim against him because the New York limitations period had apparently expired; and could the evidence support a finding of actual malice by Esquire, including by imputing the freelancer's state of mind to the publisher?
sections.Holding: The United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, 1996, Judge Stephen F. Williams writing for a panel also comprising Judges Ginsburg and Randolph, affirmed. D.C. Code § 13-423(a)(3) and (4) did not reach Unger's contacts. The district court was within its discretion in denying transfer, because Unger's answer had alerted McFarlane to the jurisdictional defense and counsel had inexplicably failed to file a protective New York action. Summary judgment for the publisher was proper because the evidence could not support the required finding of actual malice.
sections.Reasoning:
Subsection (3) of the D.C. statute requires both an injury and an act within the District. Unger wrote and delivered the article in New York, and treating the reputational injury as an in-forum act would erase the statute's distinction between act and injury. Subsection (4) requires an in-District injury plus regular business, a persistent course of conduct, or substantial revenue; writing for national publications and two articles for Washington publications did not show regularity or persistence, and the writer's contacts were assessed separately from the publisher's distribution.

On transfer, courts disagreed whether § 1406(a) or § 1404(a) applies when venue is unchallenged but personal jurisdiction is absent. The panel left that unresolved because both involve abuse-of-discretion review and the interest of justice. Dismissal was a serious penalty given the apparently expired limitations period, but McFarlane had notice and failed to protect the claim. The panel criticized the district court's reasoning that Esquire's insurance left McFarlane unprejudiced, since a claim against Unger might have been an easier route to vindication, but sustained the denial anyway.

On actual malice, the panel doubted that a nonemployee's state of mind could be imputed to a publisher, and in any event McFarlane showed no evidence that Esquire supervised how Unger converted raw information into the article. Assuming the editors' knowledge could be aggregated, the evidence was insufficient: the editors published many attacks on Ben-Menashe's credibility, the handling of Elliot Richardson's statements could reflect confusion rather than recklessness, slanted presentation did not show subjective belief in falsity, and changing a denial to a refusal to comment was careless but not shown to be purposeful.

The casebook cites the transfer ruling as a qualification to the usual preference for preserving claims through transfer.

CP-COMP-CB-REF-219.rule: A class representative must show enough interest, credibility and understanding of the suit that he is not merely lending his name to litigation controlled by lawyers; the plaintiff bears the burden of proving adequacy with evidence at certification.

sections.Parties: Larry Monroe, the plaintiff and appellant, brought a § 1983 action against the City of Charlottesville and police officers, including Officer Mooney, who had approached him at his home to request a DNA sample during a serial-rape investigation. He alleged equal-protection and Fourth Amendment violations and sought class treatment of the equal-protection claim. The City and officers were the defendants and appellees.
sections.Procedural History: The district court dismissed Monroe's racial-classification theory but let a different-investigatory-methods theory continue; it dismissed the encounter-as-seizure theory, let a bodily-fluids claim proceed, and after an amended complaint dismissed the encounter theory again. It set July 13, 2007 as the deadline for certification memoranda, held a hearing on July 20, refused as untimely an affidavit Monroe filed on July 23, and denied class certification for lack of adequacy. Monroe then obtained voluntary dismissal of his remaining individual claims, agreeing not to bring them again, and appealed the certification denial and the dismissed constitutional theories. On August 31, 2009, the Fourth Circuit affirmed.
sections.Material Facts:
Charlottesville police investigated a serial rapist beginning in spring 2002. Several victims consistently described a youthful-looking Black male, and police had composite images and the assailant's DNA. Over several years officers contacted 190 Black men matching the general description and asked for DNA samples. Officer Mooney approached Monroe at his home. The amended complaint added the officer's uniform, the absence of advice that Monroe could decline, the home setting, and Monroe's beliefs about police relations with minority communities.

At certification, an officer's affidavit reported that Monroe said his lawyers did not return calls, that they had approached him about suing, that he learned the action was filed in his name from a newspaper, that the suit made him look bad, and that he was not interested in damages against Mooney. Monroe did not attend the hearing or provide a responsive affidavit by then. His lawyer testified that she returned calls and that Monroe had approached her, submitted his deposition, and told the judge no further evidence would be offered. The deposition showed that Monroe could not recognize the complaint and knew little about the litigation.
sections.Issue: Did the district court abuse its discretion in refusing a late affidavit and finding Monroe an inadequate class representative under Rule 23(a)(4)? Did his allegations about the encounter at his home plausibly plead a Fourth Amendment seizure, and did police reliance on victims' descriptions of the suspect amount to an express racial classification?
sections.Holding: The United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit, 2009, Senior Judge C. Arlen Beam writing for a panel with Judge Shedd and District Judge Joseph F. Anderson, Jr., affirmed. The district court acted within its discretion in rejecting the late affidavit and finding Monroe inadequate to represent the class. His home-encounter allegations did not plausibly establish a Fourth Amendment seizure. On the record described, police use of several victims' suspect descriptions was not the express governmental racial classification asserted, and the panel added that the investigation would satisfy strict scrutiny on the undisputed facts.
sections.Reasoning:
Rule 23(a)(4) protects absent members through a representative who can fairly and adequately pursue their interests. The plaintiff bears the burden, certification is an evidentiary inquiry that does not simply accept the complaint as true, and the district court's assessment receives considerable deference. The court may set and enforce deadlines; the prehearing deadline, the completed hearing and counsel's statement that no further evidence remained justified refusing the later affidavit, which in any event would not have changed the result. Adequacy does not require mastery of every legal intricacy, but it does require enough interest, credibility and understanding to avoid a person merely lending a name to litigation controlled by lawyers. The officer's evidence, Monroe's inability to recognize his own complaint and his lack of knowledge about the filing raised serious questions that his lawyer's limited rebuttal did not resolve.

On the seizure claim, reviewed de novo under Twombly, a police approach and questions are not alone a seizure; the question is whether a reasonable person would feel unable to disregard the officer and end the encounter. Monroe's subjective beliefs did not control, and a uniform, a home visit and the failure to announce a right to refuse describe many consensual encounters.

On equal protection, the victims consistently described their actual assailant; police did not invent a racial profile or decide to investigate Black people as a group, but used a description with several characteristics plus further leads. Alternatively, protecting the public from crime was compelling and the investigation was narrowly tailored on the undisputed facts.

The casebook uses Monroe's learning of the suit from a newspaper and his inability to recognize the complaint as examples of an inadequate representative.

CP-COMP-CB-REF-285.rule: When an affected property owner's name and address are known or easily ascertainable, newspaper publication and posted notices are constitutionally inadequate; notice must be reasonably calculated, in the actual circumstances, to inform the owner of the proceeding.

sections.Parties: The appellant owned a house and three and one-half acres on the Neversink River in Orange County, New York. She brought an equitable action against New York City, alleging that she had not been notified of the City's condemnation proceedings to divert the river's water. She sought an opportunity to present a compensation claim, not a right to stop the diversion. The City relied on its compliance with the statutory publication and posting procedure.
sections.Procedural History: The appellant filed no damages claim within the three-year statutory period. In January 1960 she brought an equitable action. The trial court granted the City's motion for judgment on the pleadings, treating the conceded statutory compliance as constitutionally adequate. The Appellate Division affirmed, and the New York Court of Appeals affirmed over two dissenting votes. Although the complaint requested an injunction against diversion, the New York courts construed it as a means of challenging notice and asserting a right to be heard on damages, and in the Supreme Court the appellant conceded she was not entitled to an injunction. The Court heard the federal constitutional appeal under the then-applicable section 1257(2). It reversed the New York Court of Appeals and remanded for further proceedings consistent with its opinion.
sections.Material Facts:
The appellant's family occupied the property only in July and August. In 1952 New York City began proceedings under the Water Supply Act to acquire the right to divert some of the river's water at a point in Sullivan County, about twenty-five miles upstream. The statute required six weeks of newspaper publication in the City Record, two New York City newspapers and two newspapers in each affected county, plus handbills in at least twenty conspicuous places along the aqueduct or near the affected property. Damages claims were barred after three years.

The City complied. It posted twenty-two notices on trees and poles along a seven- or eight-mile stretch of river near her premises, but none was on her property and she never saw any. The postings occurred in January, when the summer home was vacant. The two Orange County newspapers were published in small communities many miles away. The City could readily have found her name and address in deed records and tax rolls. The notices did not name her or any other owner, explain how to seek compensation, or reveal the filing deadline. She alleged she learned of the proceedings and her right to claim damages only on consulting a lawyer in 1959.
sections.Issue: Did the City's statutory procedure of newspaper publication and notices posted near the property reasonably notify a readily identifiable owner whose compensation claim would be barred, or was that notice constitutionally inadequate?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 1962, in an opinion by Justice Stewart with no separate writing, held that the City's publications and postings were constitutionally inadequate in this setting. The City made no effort to contact a readily identifiable owner personally, and mailing a single letter would have discharged its obligation in these circumstances. The Court awarded no damages and ordered no halt to the diversion; the appellant gained an opportunity to pursue the notice and compensation issues without the deficient notice being treated as sufficient.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court began with Mullane, which required notice reasonably calculated, in the actual circumstances, to inform affected parties of the proceeding and allow them to present objections. Notice is tied to the right to be heard: an owner cannot choose whether to contest a proceeding without learning that it exists. The standard is contextual, and missing or unknown persons can make personal notification impracticable.

The reasons for relying on publication weaken sharply, however, when an affected person's identity and address are known or easily ascertainable. A small newspaper announcement depends heavily on chance, particularly outside the paper's normal circulation area and when it does not name the intended recipient. Walker supplied a closely analogous condemnation case, in which newspaper notice was inadequate for an owner known to the city and listed in official records. Adding notices on trees and poles did not cure the deficiency here, because no sign appeared on the appellant's property or reached her.

The Court rejected the New York Court of Appeals' assumption that the diversion's effects must have become apparent before the deadline. The pleadings contained no such allegation, and even awareness that the river looked different would not tell an owner that the City had diverted it or that she had a right to seek compensation. The Court's conclusion about a letter concerns an adequate method directed to this owner; it does not guarantee that every recipient actually reads the communication.

The casebook cites the case in a note on Mullane to illustrate why newspaper publication and notices posted near property can fail when the government can readily identify and contact the affected owner.

CP-COMP-CB-REF-287.rule: A court will not order alternative service under Rule 4(f)(3), even where conventional service appears impracticable, unless competent evidence shows the proposed method is reasonably calculated to reach the particular defendant.

sections.Parties: The Securities and Exchange Commission, the plaintiff, alleged fraud and other securities-law violations against China Intelligent Lighting and Electronics, Inc. (CIL), NIVS IntelliMedia Technology Group, Inc. (NIV), and two executives, Xuemei Li and Tianfu Li. The SEC sought permission to serve the two individuals, Chinese nationals residing in China, by newspaper publication and email.
sections.Procedural History: In an enforcement action in the Southern District of New York, the SEC moved on January 6, 2014 for Rule 4(f)(3) service on Tianfu Li and Xuemei Li only. On January 30, 2014, District Judge Jesse M. Furman denied the motion without prejudice to a new application supported by affidavits or other appropriate evidence. The ruling did not address the merits of the securities claims.
sections.Material Facts:
Xuemei Li was CIL's CEO, president, chairman and a 28% shareholder. Tianfu Li was NIV's CEO, chairman and a 30% shareholder. The SEC proposed publication in the International New York Times and email to two addresses it associated with the two individuals.

The SEC's memorandum asserted that CIL's auditor had used one address to communicate with Xuemei Li and that NIV had produced the other in response to a subpoena as Tianfu Li's contact information, but those assertions were unsworn. For the first address, the only supporting item was an email copied to it on March 23, 2011, and nothing in that email linked the address to Xuemei Li. For the second, the SEC supplied an undated spreadsheet that appeared to list NIV executives' contact information, including a “Li Tianfu.” The SEC gave no information about the newspaper's circulation, its circulation within China, where it was distributed there, or the languages in which it appeared.
sections.Issue: Were the SEC's proposed methods of alternative service under Rule 4(f)(3), publication in an international newspaper and email to two addresses, shown to be reasonably calculated to give the two individual defendants in China notice and an opportunity to object?
sections.Holding: The United States District Court for the Southern District of New York, 2014, Judge Furman, denied the Rule 4(f)(3) motion without prejudice to a new application supported by affidavits or other appropriate evidence showing that the proposed methods, or other alternatives, were reasonably calculated to give these defendants notice and an opportunity to object. The SEC had not supplied competent evidence that either method would likely reach them. The court did not dismiss the action or permanently foreclose email or publication.
sections.Reasoning:
The court accepted that alternative service was appropriate in principle: the SEC had exercised due diligence in pursuing Hague Convention service, there was reason to believe that route would not work, and the court saw no other apparent method apart from Rule 4(f)(3).

A court-directed alternative must be both unprohibited by international agreement and consistent with due process. Publication and email met the first requirement; following Pecon Software, the court treated China's Article 10 objections as not barring email, while acknowledging the contrary approach in Agha v. Jacobs.

The separate constitutional question was whether the means were reasonably calculated, in the particular circumstances, to notify these defendants. A method's legal availability does not substitute for evidence of its expected effectiveness. Without basic information about the newspaper's circulation, distribution in China and languages, or anything connecting it to the defendants, the court could not evaluate publication. As to the first email address, nothing tied it to Xuemei Li, and even if it had been hers in 2011 there was no evidence of continued use. As to the second, even assuming the spreadsheet was authentic, it had no date or other information permitting an inference that Tianfu Li still used the address. These were evidentiary deficiencies, not a categorical holding against publication or email.

The casebook quotes the deficiency in the undated spreadsheet.

CP-COMP-CB-REF-306.rule: In an action filed originally in federal court, the amount demanded in a defendant's compulsory counterclaim may be counted toward the diversity amount in controversy when the defendant answers and counterclaims without first moving to dismiss.

sections.Parties: Spectacor Management Group, a Pennsylvania joint venture managing stadiums, arenas and other public facilities, sued its former executive vice-president, Matthew Brown, a New Jersey citizen, to recover payments made following his termination. Brown, the defendant, denied subject-matter jurisdiction in his answer and asserted compulsory counterclaims for severance, commissions, bonus and other amounts. Brown won judgment at trial and was the appellant.
sections.Procedural History: Spectacor filed in federal district court under diversity jurisdiction. Brown did not move to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(1); he answered, expressly denying subject-matter jurisdiction, and counterclaimed. After a bench trial the district court entered judgment for Brown, but for substantially less than he demanded, and he appealed. On November 24, 1997, the Third Circuit affirmed the district court's judgment, with one judge dissenting in favor of a remand for jurisdictional inquiry.
sections.Material Facts:
Spectacor alleged that it paid Brown $42,500 in benefits and $4,921.04 for medical insurance, totaling $47,421.04, less than the $50,000 diversity threshold applicable when the suit was filed. It added $3,287.21 in payroll taxes, claiming $50,708.25 exclusive of interest and costs. Spectacor maintained that the payments were recoverable advances against a settlement that was never concluded.

Brown argued that the tax component was a contrivance to obtain federal jurisdiction and prevent his intended state-court suit, and that Spectacor's own concessions showed it owed him more than it sought. His compulsory counterclaims demanded $135,000 in severance, $837,000 in commissions, $70,720 in bonus, and $17,550 in unused vacation and unreimbursed expenses, amounts exceeding the threshold.
sections.Issue: Could the amount demanded in Brown's compulsory counterclaim be considered toward the diversity amount in controversy when he answered and counterclaimed without first obtaining consideration of a motion to dismiss, even though his answer disputed jurisdiction?
sections.Holding: The United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit, 1997, Judge McKee writing for a majority joined by Judge Greenberg, with Senior Judge Wellford dissenting, held that it could. By bringing a compulsory counterclaim before the court in these circumstances, Brown placed that demand into the controversy whose amount the court measured. The majority therefore did not decide whether the payroll taxes properly counted in Spectacor's own demand, and it affirmed the merits judgment, finding no clear error. The holding was confined to compulsory counterclaims in an action filed originally in federal court.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority began with the usual rule that the amount is measured from good-faith allegations in the complaint, subject to a legal-certainty challenge. But the complaint is not necessarily the entire controversy. Brown's compulsory counterclaim arose from the same transactions, the parties' obligations under the employment arrangement and the payments resulting from termination, and so was part of what was actually at stake. The majority drew support from Home Life, Roberts Mining, Fenton and Motorists Mutual, distinguishing a counterclaim that only reduces the original amount through a setoff. A sufficiently large compulsory counterclaim could have supported an independent suit with the parties reversed, so measuring the connected controversy avoids making jurisdiction turn on who reached federal court first.

The majority expressly rejected any theory that litigants can confer subject-matter jurisdiction by agreement or waiver; its point concerned which claims had become part of the controversy before the court. Brown could have filed a Rule 12 motion before answering and counterclaiming and did not. The majority declined to extend the holding to permissive counterclaims and distinguished removal cases, which involve a separate statutory framework and a policy of narrow construction protecting the state forum. It discussed Horton v. Liberty Mutual but did not rely on it.

Judge Wellford, dissenting, would have remanded for a fuller determination of jurisdiction. He stressed that jurisdiction is ordinarily assessed when the action is filed, that the invoking party must establish it when challenged, and that filing a counterclaim the rules required should not strip Brown of the objection he made in his answer; he also questioned the payroll-tax allegation.

The casebook cites the majority's holding in a note on compulsory counterclaims and the jurisdictional amount, and asks separately about removal.

CP-COMP-CB-REF-308.rule: Under the 1962 version of Rule 24(a)(2), a shareholder has no right to intervene in a corporation's suit unless he may be legally bound by the judgment and representation may be inadequate; disagreement over how to conduct the litigation is not inadequate representation.

sections.Parties: Harry Stadin, a holder of forty-three of Union Electric Company's more than eleven million common shares, sought to intervene in two treble-damages antitrust actions Union had brought against electrical-equipment manufacturers, in order to add derivative claims for additional equipment categories. Union, the plaintiff in those actions, opposed intervention. Stadin was the appellant.
sections.Procedural History: Union sued Westinghouse and General Electric in December 1961 over turbine-generator overcharges and, with two other utilities, sued those companies and Sangamo in January 1962 over meter overcharges. Stadin applied to intervene in both cases. The district court denied intervention; its final order consolidated the cases for appeal and made a Rule 54(b) determination, an earlier request for § 1292(b) review having been denied. On November 15, 1962, the Eighth Circuit affirmed the order insofar as it denied intervention of right and dismissed the appeal insofar as it concerned permissive intervention.
sections.Material Facts:
Following criminal antitrust judgments entered in Philadelphia in February 1961, in which the suppliers had pleaded guilty or no contest, Union sued under the Clayton Act. Before Union filed, Stadin proposed a shareholder resolution directing pursuit of the company's rights against convicted suppliers. Management omitted it from proxy materials as not a proper subject of shareholder action under Missouri law; Stadin presented it at the annual meeting, where it lost overwhelmingly. Four days later he threatened a derivative suit unless Union pursued its remedies. Union eventually sued concerning eight equipment categories, while purchases in eleven others remained under investigation.

Stadin's proposed complaints incorporated Union's allegations and demanded recovery for the additional categories, not the turbine-generators or meters already at issue. He argued that management's earlier resistance showed bad faith and condonation of price-fixing, that Union's general counsel, also a director, was not friendly with him, and that organizing litigation by defendants rather than equipment categories would be more efficient. Union's affidavits described ongoing investigation of thousands of items.
sections.Issue: Was a minority shareholder entitled to intervene of right under the historical Rule 24(a)(2) in the corporation's antitrust suits, was denial of permissive intervention under Rule 24(b)(2) an abuse of discretion, and did his applications meet the requirements for a derivative proceeding under then-Rule 23(b)?
sections.Holding: The United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit, 1962, Judge Blackmun writing for a panel of Judges Sanborn and Blackmun and District Judge Register, held that Stadin had no right to intervene because he showed neither that he was or might be bound by a judgment in the actions nor possible inadequate representation. It found no abuse of discretion in refusing permissive intervention and found the derivative-suit requirements unmet. The court affirmed the order insofar as it denied intervention of right and dismissed the appeal insofar as it concerned permissive intervention.
sections.Reasoning:
The court assumed well-pleaded allegations true but distinguished concrete allegations from conclusory descriptions such as bad faith, and considered the opponents' uncontroverted material facts.

Historical Rule 24(a)(2) required both potentially inadequate representation and that the applicant was or might be bound by the judgment. Stadin's proposed claims involved different equipment and facts from the pending ones; his concern was that adverse decisions would make separate litigation harder as precedent. Relying on Sam Fox, the court said practical difficulty or comity is not the requisite legal binding effect.

Nor was representation shown to be possibly inadequate. Inadequacy can arise through collusion, an adverse interest, or failure to perform the representative's duty. Stadin alleged no collusion with suppliers; management's earlier vote did not establish refusal to bring the cases now pending; and counsel's alleged unfriendliness and disagreement over structuring the lawsuits did not show an interest of Union adverse to Stadin's. If a mere difference of opinion among attorneys were inadequate representation, intervention of right would become almost automatic. Union needed a reasonable opportunity to act before failure of duty could be inferred.

Permissive intervention required weighing delay and prejudice, and adding numerous equipment categories would bring more witnesses, discovery, longer trial and confusion to two already complicated suits. On the derivative theory, the court assumed without deciding that a derivative suit could be instituted through intervention, but suits in eight categories and continued investigation of the rest did not show an unwarranted refusal or breach of trust; litigation decisions remained within management's discretion.

The casebook cites the case for the adequacy point: disagreement over conducting litigation, without a showing of failure of duty to shareholders, does not create a right to intervene.

CP-COMP-CB-REF-347.rule: A property owner is entitled to a hearing on just compensation, and newspaper publication alone is constitutionally inadequate notice of that hearing when the owner's name is known to the condemning authority and appears in official records.

sections.Parties: Lee Walker owned land in Hutchinson, Kansas. The City of Hutchinson condemned part of it for opening, widening and extending city streets. Walker brought an equitable action against the City, challenging notice by publication as insufficient under the Fourteenth Amendment and seeking to restrain the City's entry onto his property, along with other appropriate relief. Walker was the appellant in the Supreme Court; the City and the State defended the statutory publication procedure.
sections.Procedural History: In 1954 the City instituted condemnation proceedings in the Reno County district court, which appointed three commissioners to appraise the property. Walker did not appeal their award within the thirty days allowed. He later brought an equitable action. The trial court denied relief after a hearing because it considered the statutory publication constitutionally sufficient, and the Kansas Supreme Court affirmed. The Supreme Court heard an appeal under the then-applicable section 1257(2). It reversed the Kansas Supreme Court and remanded for further proceedings consistent with its opinion.
sections.Material Facts:
Under section 26-201 the court appointed three commissioners to appraise Walker's property and assess other damages. Section 26-202 required at least ten days' notice of the assessment hearing but allowed either written notice or a single publication in the official city newspaper. The City used publication and gave Walker no written notice. The commissioners fixed compensation at $725, which was deposited with the city treasurer for Walker's benefit. An appeal from the award had to be taken within thirty days after the report was filed, and Walker did not appeal in that time.

Walker alleged that he had received no notice and knew nothing of the condemnation until the appeal period had expired. His amended petition alleged that he had owned the property since 1905, that the City filed its application on April 12, 1954, that the only notice was an April 14 newspaper publication, and that he did not learn of the effort to take the land until about mid-August. These are the petition's allegations, not Supreme Court findings. Walker's name was known to the City and appeared in official records. In 1955 Kansas amended the statute to require mailing a copy of the newspaper notice to an owner's last known residence unless diligent inquiry could not locate it.
sections.Issue: Was a single newspaper publication constitutionally adequate notice of the proceeding to fix compensation for a resident owner whose name was known to the City? The majority treated the question as the adequacy of notice for the compensation hearing, not every aspect of the City's power to take the land.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 1956, in an opinion by Justice Black, with Justices Frankfurter and Burton dissenting separately and Justice Brennan not participating (6-2), held that publication alone was inadequate for this known resident owner in the compensation proceeding. The fact that the statute permitted publication did not establish that the method met the federal constitutional standard. The Court did not award a higher sum, hold the condemnation itself invalid, or direct issuance of the permanent injunction sought in the petition.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority first accepted the construction it inferred the Kansas Supreme Court had given the pleading: because Kansas required actual damage to maintain an equitable suit and the state court had addressed section 26-202, the petition was treated as sufficiently alleging monetary harm from lack of notice about compensation, not only an attack on the taking.

An owner whose property is taken for public use must have a hearing on just compensation, and notice makes that hearing meaningful. Applying Mullane, the Court required a feasible method reasonably calculated to inform the affected person. It rejected a rigid formula and acknowledged that missing or unknown people can make personal notice impracticable. Those obstacles were absent: Walker's name was known and in official records, and the Court found no compelling or even persuasive reason why direct notice could not be given. Newspaper publication rarely reaches the individual concerned; even a letter would have told Walker his property was about to be taken and that he needed to appear. The Court distinguished Huling, which sustained publication for a nonresident owner, and expressly declined to decide how far Mullane had undermined it. The governmental character of condemnation did not diminish the right to be heard; without notice, authorities could effectively set the amount one-sidedly.

Justice Frankfurter, dissenting, read the petition as seeking to keep possession and permanently prevent entry, without alleging that $725 was less than fair value; he saw no actual controversy over compensation and would have affirmed or returned the case to Kansas for a construction of the pleading. Justice Burton, dissenting, considered the length and method of notice largely within state legislative discretion and would have affirmed.

The casebook cites Walker in a note on Mullane for the known resident owner given newspaper-only notice.

CP-COMP-CB-REF-348.rule: A defendant's uniform payment methodology does not by itself establish commonality or predominance; the plaintiff must prove that its legality can be decided classwide, which requires accounting for differences in class members' contractual rights and circumstances.

sections.Parties: The Wallace B. Roderick Revocable Living Trust, which held royalty interests in eight wells under five leases, sued XTO Energy, Inc. as representative of a proposed class of Kansas royalty owners, claiming XTO underpaid royalties by deducting expenses that Kansas law required the producer to bear. The Trust was the plaintiff and appellee; XTO, the defendant, appealed class certification.
sections.Procedural History: The Kansas action alleged breach of contract and unjust enrichment and sought an accounting; Colorado claims initially proposed had been dropped, and Oklahoma claims had been severed and transferred. The district court certified a class under Rule 23(b)(3), relying on one asserted common issue. The Tenth Circuit permitted a Rule 23(f) appeal, in which XTO challenged commonality, typicality, adequacy and predominance. On July 9, 2013, the Tenth Circuit vacated the certification order and remanded for further proceedings.
sections.Material Facts:
XTO produced natural gas and constituent products from Kansas wells. The proposed class covered roughly 650 leases and more than 300 wells across ten fields, with Kansas production from January 1, 1999 onward. The Trust's theory rested on Kansas's implied duty of marketability: unless the contract provides otherwise, a gas lessee bears the costs of gathering, compression, dehydration, treatment and processing needed to make gas marketable. The Trust maintained that gas from every class well required one or more of those services; XTO said some gas was sold directly into interstate pipelines without processing.

XTO calculated royalties through its Avatar accounting system, which did not adjust payments according to an owner's lease language; payment depended on XTO's marketing contract with the gas purchaser. XTO's expert grouped a sample of one-fifth of the leases into twenty categories of royalty provisions, some allegedly eliminating the implied duty or authorizing particular deductions. Roughly 430 leases had not been examined by the Trust or the court. The district court certified on the single common issue of whether XTO's uniform payment methodology breached the implied duty of marketability.
sections.Issue: Did XTO's uniform method of calculating royalty payments establish commonality under Rule 23(a) and predominance under Rule 23(b)(3) for a class of royalty owners, given variations in lease language and in the point at which gas from different wells became marketable?
sections.Holding: The United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit, 2013, Judge Kelly writing for a panel with Judges McKay and Matheson, held that a uniform payment system did not, on this record, establish that its legality could be decided for the entire class in one stroke. The plaintiff had to prove shared contractual rights and address potentially different points of gas marketability. The district court's relaxed commonality standard, possible shift of the burden to XTO, and brief predominance analysis were inconsistent with rigorous certification analysis. The court vacated the certification order and remanded, without deciding the merits or holding that certification could never be justified.
sections.Reasoning:
Rule 23 requires proof of actual compliance, not allegations or a presumption favoring certification, and a common question must be capable of producing an answer central to each claim. The inquiry could not stop at whether every payment ran through the same software, because a deduction was wrongful only if the owner had the asserted contractual right and the gas had not already reached marketable condition when the cost was incurred.

The district court assumed a marketability duty in every lease because XTO had not identified a provision unambiguously negating it. That had the burden backward: given known variations, the Trust had to establish that the duty existed throughout the class. A chart grouping lease terms could help on remand, and the district court might conclude that no category displaced the duty. Marketability was a second potential difference, since gas might be marketable at one well but need further services at another. The court was also “not so sure” XTO had conceded that it uniformly charged owners for making gas marketable. Because commonality, typicality and adequacy overlap, those requirements were to be reconsidered too.

Predominance is more demanding than commonality; focusing only on the defendant's common conduct is insufficient where owners may hold different rights or face different defenses. Individual damages calculations do not alone defeat certification but matter if their complexity would overwhelm common issues; subclasses or liability-only proceedings might preserve class treatment.

The court declined to estop XTO based on its settlement of the Fankhouser royalty class action, which involved different facts and was certified before Wal-Mart and Comcast.

The casebook cites the case for the point that a common calculation methodology did not establish commonality, and asks what more Wal-Mart requires.

CP-COMP-CB-ROBINSON-MEYER.rule: When all the facts necessary to a legal consequence have been pleaded and contested, a court may apply that consequence, including a statute, even though the party did not expressly plead the legal conclusion; stating it is proper and desirable but not mandatory.

sections.Parties: The plaintiffs brought a quiet-title action against the defendants, their neighbors, over a triangular tract adjoining Bolton Road in Vernon, Connecticut, lying between the two properties. The plaintiffs relied on deeds describing their lot's western boundary; the defendants relied on estoppel, occupation and monuments. The plaintiffs lost at trial and appealed, seeking a new trial.
sections.Procedural History: The plaintiffs filed their quiet-title action in February 1947. The trial court rendered judgment rejecting their claim, holding that a deed in their chain of title was void as to the tract under the ouster statute, and finding that the owners of both properties had accepted the defendants' asserted boundary since 1933. The plaintiffs appealed, arguing that they first learned of the statutory theory on receiving the trial court's memorandum of decision. The Connecticut Supreme Court of Errors found no error; no new trial or remand was ordered.
sections.Material Facts:
The plaintiffs' deeds described their lot's western boundary as perpendicular to Bolton Road. The original deed carved the lot from a larger property in 1932, and later deeds repeated the description. Under the plaintiffs' claimed line, half of the defendants' house, with their garage and driveway, stood on land the plaintiffs claimed. Both houses were built in 1932; a predecessor of the defendants built the garage and driveway on the disputed area in 1944.

The occupation by the defendants and their predecessors was open, visible and notorious and would establish adverse possession if continued uninterruptedly for fifteen years. In the plaintiffs' chain of title, Howard Hastings conveyed the disputed land to Ruth Evelyn Robinson on February 10, 1934, after a predecessor of the defendants had ousted him from its possession. Under the governing statute, General Statutes, Revision of 1930, § 5020, that ouster made Hastings's deed void as to the tract. The defendants' amended answer alleged facts adequate to establish adverse possession if they existed for the requisite time. The plaintiffs filed no formal reply but denied the allegation in open court, and considerable evidence on use and occupation was introduced. The plaintiffs said that with earlier notice they would have offered evidence that Hastings had not actually been ousted when he conveyed.
sections.Issue: Could the trial court apply the deed-invalidating ouster statute when the defendants had pleaded the relevant possession facts but had not expressly pleaded that legal consequence or called the statute to the court's attention at trial?
sections.Holding: The Connecticut Supreme Court of Errors in 1949, in an opinion by Justice Jennings in which the other four members of the five-judge court concurred, found no error. The quality of ouster that makes a grantor's deed void is the same quality required for adverse possession. When all necessary facts were pleaded and contested, expressly stating the resulting legal conclusion was proper and desirable but not mandatory, so the trial court could apply the statute.
sections.Reasoning:
The court found the result plainly just but still examined whether the plaintiffs' procedural objection required a new trial. The defendants' amended answer alleged facts adequate to establish adverse possession if continued for the requisite time. The plaintiffs denied that allegation in open court, considerable evidence on use and occupation was introduced, and the court's examination of the record confirmed that the facts underlying the defense were actually litigated.

Those same pleaded facts established the ouster that invalidated Hastings's 1934 deed. The trial court therefore was not deciding on an unpleaded factual basis; it supplied the legal effect of facts already put in issue. Naming the statute might have clarified the defense, but its omission did not prevent the court from applying it. Because the plaintiffs had joined issue on the underlying question, applying the statute caused no procedural injustice warranting a new trial. The opinion cited other Connecticut cases applying statutory consequences in comparable circumstances.

The court did not find that the full fifteen-year adverse-possession period had run. The occupation's potential to ripen into title explained the character of the possession, while the statutory ouster invalidated an intervening deed.

The casebook describes the case as an inference of adverse-possession title from facts establishing ouster; the brief notes that this compresses the actual mechanism, which was that Hastings's deed was void under the ouster statute, and that the case illustrates how a court may supply legal consequences to adequately pleaded facts.

CP-COMP-CB-ROURKE-AMCHEM.rule: A forum state must give another state's judgment the preclusive effect the rendering state would give it, so a judgment from a state that retains mutuality cannot be used for offensive nonmutual issue preclusion in the forum.

sections.Parties: The plaintiffs were Maryland asbestos personal-injury and wrongful-death claimants covered by a global settlement. They sued the Center for Claims Resolution (CCR), which asbestos manufacturers created to administer and settle claims, and its twelve then-current members, including Amchem Products, for declaratory and monetary relief. The defendants moved to compel arbitration. The plaintiffs, who lost below, argued that a Virginia judgment precluded the defendants from relitigating arbitrability.
sections.Procedural History: The plaintiffs sued in a Maryland circuit court, and the defendants moved to compel arbitration. The circuit court compelled arbitration and entered no order on the motion to dismiss CCR. The Court of Special Appeals affirmed, applying Virginia's mutuality requirement to deny preclusion and construing the settlement letter as leaving arbitration intact. Maryland's highest court also affirmed the order compelling arbitration.
sections.Material Facts:
In April 2000 plaintiffs' law firms negotiated a global settlement with CCR for 882 Maryland claimants, with an anticipated aggregate of about $10.1 million payable in three installments. The Settlement Agreement made each member liable only for its individual share, specified options if a member defaulted, required binding arbitration of unresolved disputes arising while implementing the agreement, and selected Maryland law.

Because required releases acknowledged full payment before some clients would actually receive it, CCR's claims officer, Michael Rooney, sent an October 31, 2000 letter explaining that the releases did not establish full satisfaction. A claimant not fully paid could pursue a contract remedy for the deficiency, with interest and reasonable collection fees and expenses, including collection "by lawsuit or otherwise."

After payment shortfalls and member defaults, the plaintiffs argued that the letter imposed joint and several liability and authorized a judicial collection action. They also invoked a Virginia Supreme Court decision construing a similar agreement and letter against arbitration. The Maryland plaintiffs were not parties to the Virginia case; only three of the Maryland defendant members, with CCR, had been actual parties there. Alleged privity for other defendants was not contested on appeal, and the court did not decide it. Virginia retained the mutuality requirement.
sections.Issue: Could Maryland apply its own preclusion principles to give a Virginia judgment offensive nonmutual issue-preclusive effect that Virginia itself would not give it? If the Virginia judgment was not binding, did the later letter displace the settlement's arbitration clause?
sections.Holding: Maryland's highest court in 2004, in an opinion by Judge Wilner over a dissent by Chief Judge Bell joined by Judge Cathell (5-2), held that Maryland must give the Virginia judgment the effect Virginia would give it. Because Virginia retained mutuality and would not bind these defendants at the request of different plaintiffs, the Virginia judgment did not foreclose litigating arbitrability in Maryland. Deciding arbitrability itself, the court held that the letter did not displace the arbitration clause and affirmed the order compelling arbitration. It did not decide whether the nondefaulting members owed all deficient payments.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority grounded its result in both full faith and credit and Maryland's common-law conflicts rule. It read § 1738 and Supreme Court precedent as requiring the rendering state's preclusion rules, ordinarily giving the judgment neither greater nor lesser preclusive force; the forum cannot substitute its own policy because its rules might give broader consequences.

Policy reinforced this. Whether to dispense with mutuality is a state's choice about fairness, litigation incentives and reliance on its judgments. Offensive preclusion can reward waiting for another plaintiff's victory, expose defendants to disproportionate consequences from a first small-stakes case, and disregard inconsistent judgments. Virginia had affirmatively retained mutuality, and Maryland could not defeat that choice. The majority also said Maryland had not formally embraced offensive nonmutual preclusion and declined to do so here. The contractual choice of Maryland law did not change the result, because Maryland's own law pointed to Virginia's rules for the effect of a Virginia judgment.

On arbitrability, whether the later letter displaced the clause was a question for the court. Reading the documents harmoniously under Maryland's objective interpretation principle, a "remedy in contract" could be an arbitration remedy, and the letter's purpose was to protect clients whose releases preceded full payment. Collection "by lawsuit or otherwise" could refer to litigation against defaulting members, coexisting with arbitration as to nondefaulting members. Ambiguities were resolved in favor of arbitration.

Chief Judge Bell, dissenting, viewed issue preclusion as the forum's tool for controlling repeated litigation, so giving the Virginia judgment added collateral consequences would not deny it full faith and credit. At minimum he would have remanded for review of offensive preclusion on its merits.

The casebook cites the case in a note for the majority-dissent disagreement on interstate preclusion.

CP-COMP-CB-RUDELL.rule: Failure to raise a defense or noncompulsory counterclaim ordinarily does not bar a later action, but a later action is barred if it would nullify the earlier judgment or impair rights it established and the party had a full and fair opportunity to raise the matter earlier.

sections.Parties: Glenn and Jean Rudell, franchisees in a computerized-accounting business, sued the franchisor, Comprehensive Accounting Corp., and its officers Leo and Christopher Lauzen, alleging fraudulent inducement of the franchise agreement. Their bankruptcy trustee was added as a plaintiff, and they also claimed to represent other franchisees. The Rudells were plaintiffs below and appellants; Comprehensive and the Lauzens sought dismissal on the ground that earlier arbitration and confirmation proceedings precluded the suit.
sections.Procedural History: Comprehensive invoked arbitration in September 1983 and obtained an award. The district court confirmed the award under the Federal Arbitration Act on January 3, 1984, and the Seventh Circuit affirmed in a separate 1985 decision concerning the asserted invalidity of the arbitration provision. Before that appellate decision, the Rudells filed the present action. Treating the defendants' motion to dismiss as one for summary judgment, the district court held the action precluded by the earlier arbitration and confirmation proceedings. The Seventh Circuit affirmed the summary judgment. It also granted Comprehensive's motion to strike a late-raised argument but denied its request for fees and costs of that motion.
sections.Material Facts:
The Rudells became franchisees on September 5, 1980. Their license agreement, sales agreement, finance agreement and collateral note, together treated as the franchise agreement, provided for mandatory, binding arbitration of disputes. When Comprehensive invoked arbitration in September 1983, alleging default, the Rudells neither appeared nor sought to stop it. The arbitrator awarded Comprehensive damages and equitable relief.

When Comprehensive sought judicial confirmation, the Rudells objected and requested vacatur, alleging among other things that the franchise agreement had been procured by fraud and misrepresentation, but offered no evidence. The confirming judge offered an opportunity to present the fraud allegations, warning that unreasonable prolongation could lead to sanctions under § 1927; the Rudells again supplied no proof.

The present action alleged fraudulent inducement of the entire franchise agreement under RICO, two Illinois statutes, and common-law fraud and deceit. The requested damages measured the difference between the Rudells' current position and the projected position they would have occupied had they never purchased the franchises. The Rudells conceded that fraudulent inducement could have been asserted as a defense in arbitration.
sections.Issue: Does a franchisee's failure to present a fraudulent-inducement defense in arbitration and confirmation proceedings bar a later affirmative fraud action whose success would undermine the rights established by the judgment confirming the award, and did the franchisees have a full and fair opportunity to raise the fraud earlier?
sections.Holding: The Seventh Circuit in 1986, in an opinion by Judge Harlington Wood, Jr., for a panel with Judges Posner and Fairchild and with no separate opinion, affirmed summary judgment for the defendants. The later suit sought relief that would undermine the rights established by the judgment confirming the arbitration award, and the Rudells had a full and fair opportunity to present their fraud allegations earlier. The court did not decide whether Comprehensive actually committed fraud, and it did not decide whether the RICO claim could or should have been arbitrated.
sections.Reasoning:
The court began with the ordinary rule: failure to assert a defense or a noncompulsory counterclaim does not bar a later affirmative action simply because both rest on the same facts, and fairness may let a defendant choose a later time and forum. There is, however, a limited class of common-law compulsory counterclaims: a later action cannot be used to nullify the earlier judgment or impair rights it established. The court applied its Martino and Lee precedents and Restatement § 22(2)(b), emphasizing the integrity of judgments. Comprehensive did not have to show that it acted in reliance on the award.

The Rudells argued that they sought affirmative compensation for fraud, not avoidance of the adjudicated obligations. The court found the distinction untenable on this complaint. Proving the contract fraudulently procured and voidable would undermine the contract rights enforced through the award, and making the Rudells whole on their damages theory would presumably include compensation for the arbitration award itself. The availability of treble damages under RICO did not remove the conflict.

On full and fair opportunity, the court distinguished fraud directed at the arbitration clause from fraud concerning the rest of the contract; the latter could have been presented to the arbitrator, but the Rudells chose not to participate. The confirming judge had also actually offered an opportunity to present the allegations, and a warning against wasteful proceedings did not make it inadequate. Genuine inadequacy would defeat preclusion. The argument that the Lauzens were not parties or privies was waived because it was raised too late, as was an objection about the absence of class-action and third-party-discovery procedures in arbitration.

The casebook uses Rudell in a note as an example of a later action barred because it could undermine a confirmed award.

CP-COMP-CB-SMITH-BARRY-REMAND.rule: A timely informal brief can serve as a notice of appeal only as to judgments it designates, read liberally in its procedural context; liberal construction cannot supply notice of an appeal from an order the paper neither names nor indirectly mentions.

sections.Parties: William Smith, an inmate at the Maryland State Penitentiary, sued correctional administrators, seven officers, two staff psychologists and Dr. Wayne Barry, a private physician, under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, alleging deliberate indifference to his medical needs through denial of a wheelchair, and separately excessive force. Smith was the plaintiff and appellant. On remand he sought review of Barry's dismissal and of the directed verdict for six guards: Victor, Turner, Hall, Brown, Jackson and Wilkins.
sections.Procedural History: The district court dismissed Barry on December 26, 1984. At trial it directed verdicts for the administrators, Commander Carpenter and the six remaining guards on the deliberate-indifference claim; the jury found the two psychologists liable and awarded $15,000. Judgment was entered February 29, 1988. Smith filed a pro se notice on March 22 while a motion for judgment notwithstanding the verdict was pending, and on May 4 submitted an informal brief. The Fourth Circuit dismissed the appeal, believing an informal brief could not substitute for a notice. The Court reversed that categorical ruling in 1992 and directed examination of whether the brief supplied what Rule 3(c) requires. On remand, on February 8, 1993, the Fourth Circuit affirmed in part and dismissed in part.
sections.Material Facts:
Smith suffered from a painful psychogenic disorder that prevented him from walking.
