Forbearance still had to be sufficient consideration. Drawing on Hartle v. Stahl and Restatement of Contracts § 76(b), the court required both subjective honesty and an objective reasonable basis for believing the claim possibly valid. A person could not manufacture consideration by threatening a claim known to have no factual or legal foundation merely to be paid for relief from annoyance.

The authorities showed that uncertainty or later failure of a paternity claim did not necessarily defeat a settlement honestly made without fraud or oppression. Here there was no proof of fraud or unfairness, and Boehm's testimony indicated good faith when she made the charge. The court therefore upheld the amended pleading and the denial of a directed verdict.

On the jury instructions, Fiege's only preserved exception was a general objection, and Maryland's procedural rule confined review to objections distinctly identified before the jury retired, so his more specific appellate challenge was not preserved.

The casebook cites the case in its note 'The Claimant's Belief'; that note prints the date as 1951 and places the agreement after the birth, whereas the decision is from 1956 and the pleading and testimony put the agreement before the birth.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-012.rule: Consideration requires a bargained exchange; past contributions cannot support a later promise, and a promise framed as recognition and appreciation for a gift, rather than as exchanged for it, is gratuitous and unenforceable.

sections.Parties: The Meyer and Anna Prentis Family Foundation, Inc., a donor, sued the Barbara Ann Karmanos Cancer Institute for breach of an undertaking to name a cancer center after Meyer L. Prentis, and sued the law firm Honigman, Miller, Schwartz and Cohn (HMSC) for its conduct in connection with the arrangement. The Foundation appealed the dismissal of HMSC and of its damages claim against the Institute; the Institute separately appealed the determination that it breached the naming agreement.
sections.Procedural History: The Foundation sued on July 27, 2000. The trial court dismissed HMSC, held a bench trial on equitable matters, and determined that the Institute breached the naming agreement. The first judge found rescission unjustified and restitution unavailable in connection with it, and a later summary-disposition ruling dismissed the Foundation's legal damages claim as speculative. Both sides appealed. The Michigan Court of Appeals affirmed in part and reversed in part: the Foundation's challenges failed, while the Institute prevailed on standing, consideration and breach. The judgment contains no express remand instruction.
sections.Material Facts:
A 1985 endowment agreement called for a $1.5 million charitable fund, contributed to Wayne State University in annual installments of at least $300,000 over no more than five years beginning in 1985, to support cancer research exclusively. A second provision recognized the Foundation's longstanding leadership and financial contributions and expressed appreciation for the newly created fund. It then stated that the University, the center and the Michigan Cancer Foundation agreed to rename the center the Meyer L. Prentis Comprehensive Cancer Center of Metropolitan Detroit. The casebook's problem adds that the payments were completed in 1990.

The Michigan Cancer Foundation merged with the center. The Foundation's board representative attended discussions of the merger in 1994 and discussions and voting concerning the Karmanos gift and renaming in 1995. A 1993 letter had already alerted that representative to a prospective donor who would receive name recognition. The Foundation had not provided for return of the funds if the name did not change.
sections.Issue: Whether the Foundation's contribution was exchanged for an enforceable promise to name the center, so that renaming it breached the agreement; whether the Foundation, as donor, had standing to enforce the charitable gift; and whether HMSC owed the Foundation fiduciary duties.
sections.Holding: The Michigan Court of Appeals in 2005, in a unanimous per curiam opinion before Judges Markey, Fitzgerald and Owens, affirmed in part and reversed in part. It held that the naming undertaking was gratuitous and legally unenforceable for want of consideration, that the trial court erred in finding breach because nothing showed the money was used for anything but cancer research, and that the Foundation lacked standing to enforce the charitable trust. It affirmed dismissal of the claims against HMSC and of the damages claim, and denied HMSC's sanctions request. This was the court's interpretation of this agreement, not a holding that every charitable naming undertaking is unenforceable.
sections.Reasoning:
Reviewing the unambiguous agreement de novo, the court sought intent in the language used. Consideration required a bargained exchange involving a benefit or detriment. The clause's reference to years of past contributions could not provide consideration for a subsequent agreement, and its reference to the new fund used words of recognition and appreciation rather than language indicating that payment was exchanged for the naming provision. The court rejected the Foundation's unilateral expectations as a basis for rewriting the document. With the naming provision unenforceable, the enforceable restriction was exclusive use for cancer research, and the record showed no improper use.

On standing, a charitable donation created a charitable trust regardless of the donor's motive. Enforcement could be sought by the Attorney General, a co-trustee, or a person with a special interest, but not by the settlor merely in that capacity.

On HMSC, counsel for a corporation represents the corporation, not its shareholders or agents, and trust and reliance could not be inferred merely because the Foundation's representative served on the center's board. The Foundation identified no action showing that HMSC represented it independently, and HMSC produced letters showing disclosure of and consent to its potential conflict. The fiduciary-duty claim was also time-barred under the three-year period, because the Foundation should have known of a possible claim by 1995 and fraudulent-concealment tolling required affirmative concealment, not mere silence.

The court also held that the Institute could rely on the Foundation's jury demand on the legal claims, and that the damages claim was properly dismissed as speculative.

The casebook presents the case as a problem inviting analysis without stating the appellate result.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-013.rule: Participating in a free promotional contest can be consideration for the promoter's promise of a prize when the participant's requested acts, such as visiting, waiting and supplying information, are what the promoter sought to induce.

sections.Parties: Rena and Sheldon Gottlieb, Pennsylvania residents, sued Tropicana Hotel and Casino, claiming it refused to pay a $1 million promotional prize Rena said she won on its Fun House Million Dollar Wheel. They pleaded breach of contract, misrepresentation, fraud and deceit, and consumer-protection claims. Tropicana denied that they won and moved for summary judgment; it had also asserted third-party claims against its insurer and two insurance brokers under a prize-indemnity policy.
sections.Procedural History: This was a federal diversity action in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, not an appeal. The New Jersey consumer-fraud claim in Count V had been voluntarily dismissed. On July 5, 2000, the district court decided Tropicana's summary-judgment motion against the plaintiffs, without resolving the third-party coverage dispute. It granted the motion against Sheldon on all counts and against Rena on Count IV, the Pennsylvania consumer-protection claim, and denied it against Rena on breach of contract, misrepresentation, and fraud and deceit. The brief covers only this ruling and not any eventual jury outcome.
sections.Material Facts:
The Gottliebs were in Atlantic City during summer 1999 and visited Tropicana on July 24 after dinner with friends. The casino's free Diamond Club required an application and identification, collected contact information, and issued each member a uniquely numbered card. Swiping the card during play supplied information about gambling habits, which the casino's marketing department used to tailor promotions. Rena had been a member for several years.

Members received one free spin per day on the Fun House Million Dollar Wheel, with a possible $1 million prize. Rena waited approximately five minutes. The parties agreed that she presented her card, an attendant swiped it, and she pressed a button that started the wheel.

They sharply disputed what followed. Rena claimed the wheel landed on the million-dollar prize and that the attendant immediately swiped another card and restarted the wheel, producing two show tickets instead. Tropicana claimed the wheel simply landed on the lesser prize and denied any intervention. Tropicana relied on computer records; Rena relied in part on her own testimony and her husband's eyewitness testimony. There was no evidence that the Gottliebs saw the casino's advertisements.
sections.Issue: Whether a patron's participation in a casino's free promotional spin supplies consideration for the casino's promise of a prize, under New Jersey or Pennsylvania law, and whether that same consideration makes the contract an unenforceable illegal lottery.
sections.Holding: The Eastern District of Pennsylvania in 2000, per District Judge Bartle, held that Rena's requested acts in taking part in the promotion were consideration supporting a contract, and that the contract was not unenforceable as an illegal lottery because she paid no statutory 'something of value' for the chance. Whether the wheel landed on the jackpot was a factual dispute for a jury, so summary judgment was denied on her contract, misrepresentation and fraud counts. It was granted on her Pennsylvania consumer-protection count and on all of Sheldon's claims. The ruling did not award the $1 million or find that she won.
sections.Reasoning:
Applying Pennsylvania's conflicts rules as the forum's, the court first asked whether the two States' laws actually conflicted. Both required a bargained exchange that could consist of a benefit to the promisor or a detriment to the promisee. Tropicana's New Jersey authority was an unpublished 1985 trial ruling on whether promotional games were illegal gambling, which applied the statutory requirement that participants transfer something of value and did not decide that participation could never be contract consideration. New Jersey's Lucky Calendar decision and Pennsylvania's Cobaugh decision both recognized that a participant's requested act and the resulting publicity or patronage could be consideration, so there was no conflict to resolve.

Rena's acts were requested as part of the opportunity to win: going to the casino, waiting, presenting her card and permitting collection of gambling information, and taking part in the casino's entertainment. The promotion sought commercial patronage and excitement. Those detriments and benefits supported an exchange although no price was paid for the spin; the distinction from a conditional gift rests on what the casino sought to induce.

On illegality, the court refused to equate ordinary contract consideration with the more restrictive statutory phrase something of value, crediting a 1983 New Jersey Attorney General opinion that the legislature meant to exclude the kind of personal inconvenience sufficient for a contract.

The consumer-protection count failed because the statute gave a private claim to a person who purchased or leased goods or services, and Rena had done neither. Sheldon's claims failed because he had not participated in the game, and the motion against him was uncontested.

The casebook's note 'The Million-Dollar Swipe' quotes the consideration passage accurately but describes recent club enrollment and a remand, whereas Rena was an established member and the ruling was a partial denial of summary judgment by a district court.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-014.rule: Consideration may be a benefit to the promisor or a detriment to the promisee, so listening to a radio station because of its promised reward can be consideration for the station's promise even though the listener pays nothing.

sections.Parties: Steve Jennings, a prisoner proceeding without counsel, sued Radio Station KSCS and its individual employees on an oral-contract claim for a $25,000 payment the station had promised if it failed to play at least three songs consecutively. Jennings was the plaintiff and appellant. The defendants argued that his pleaded facts disclosed no legally recognized duty to him and, on appeal, that no consideration flowed to the station.
sections.Procedural History:
The defendants filed special exceptions asserting failure to state a cause of action. Jennings filed a rebuttal but declined further amendment. The defendants then obtained summary judgment, and Jennings filed no written response to the motion. He appealed. On May 8, 1986, the Texas Court of Appeals at Fort Worth reversed and remanded to the trial court, without a $25,000 award.

The brief also reports a later stage: according to the Texas Supreme Court's 1988 opinion in Radio Station KSCS v. Jennings, there was a second summary judgment and a second appeal, and the Supreme Court reversed the later appellate judgment and affirmed the trial court's judgment for KSCS because Jennings's affidavit did not satisfy the personal-knowledge requirement. The intervening 1988 court-of-appeals opinion was not separately read for the brief.
sections.Material Facts: These are the allegations whose legal sufficiency was at issue, not findings. Jennings alleged that radio was his only contact with the outside world and that he regularly listened to KSCS. The station repeatedly announced a guarantee of at least three songs consecutively, with a $25,000 payment if it failed. His petition complained that the station's five-song sequences consisted of three songs, a short commercial and two songs; it also alleged that on specific occasions he contacted the station after fewer than three consecutive songs, but it refused payment. He alleged that he then stopped listening.
sections.Issue: Whether the single ground in the defendants' summary-judgment motion, that the facts pleaded disclosed no legally recognized duty to Jennings, which the station elaborated on appeal as an absence of consideration flowing to it, supported judgment as a matter of law.
sections.Holding: The Texas Court of Appeals at Fort Worth in 1986, in an opinion by retired Justice Ashworth sitting by assignment on a panel with Justices Burdock and Hughes, reversed the summary judgment and remanded. It held that Jennings's petition sufficiently alleged a contract claim to require proceedings on the merits, because his listening in the hope of the promised reward could be consideration. It did not hold that any existing listener automatically accepted any broadcast promise, resolve whether a breach occurred, or award damages.
sections.Reasoning:
Because Jennings filed no response, review under Texas Rule of Civil Procedure 166-A(c) was limited to whether the grounds expressly presented in the written motion could support judgment as a matter of law; his silence did not turn an insufficient legal ground into an entitlement to judgment.

The court stated that sufficient consideration could be a benefit to the promisor or a loss or detriment to the promisee, and that action to one's detriment in reliance on a promise could bind the promisor. From Jennings's allegation that he stopped listening after nonpayment, it inferred that he had listened because of the promised reward. He could have chosen another station but selected KSCS in the hope of payment if the station failed its guarantee. The station also benefited, because the promotion attracted listeners hoping to win. The absence of a monetary payment for radio programming therefore did not itself defeat consideration.

The later Texas Supreme Court ruling rested on evidentiary insufficiency, not on repudiation of the listening-as-consideration analysis.

The casebook uses the 1986 consideration ruling in its 'Jailhouse Rock' problem and calls the station's motion a motion to dismiss, although the actual appeal concerned summary judgment after special exceptions.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-015.rule: An advertisement that requests a specified performance without further communication is an offer of a unilateral contract, and the bargained-for act is consideration regardless of equivalence of values, but the offeree must give reasonable notice of performance when the offeror could not otherwise learn of it.

sections.Parties: The plaintiffs were three-year-old Joshua Gnaizda, to whom Time, Inc.'s mailing was addressed, and Mark Harris and Richard Baker, recipients of the same mailing. They sued Time on contract, statutory advertising, promissory-estoppel and fraud claims, seeking declaratory and injunctive relief, compensatory damages measured by the watch's value, and $15 million in punitive damages for a consumer fund. Time, the defendant, argued there was no offer, no adequate consideration and no notice of performance.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court sustained a demurrer to the contract, estoppel and fraud claims without specifying its grounds, then granted summary judgment on the advertising claims and entered dismissal. The plaintiffs appealed and abandoned the estoppel and fraud claims; the appellate court treated the premature notice of appeal as filed immediately after judgment. On April 27, 1987, California's First District Court of Appeal, Division Five, affirmed dismissal of the entire action, with each party to bear its own appellate costs. Part I of the opinion, which addressed the advertising claims, was excluded from publication and was not available for the brief, so the brief covers only the published reasoning.
sections.Material Facts: These facts were allegations reviewed for pleading sufficiency, not findings. A mailing addressed to Joshua Gnaizda displayed, through a window in its envelope, a promise of a free calculator watch, apparently conditioned only on opening the envelope before February 15, 1985. His mother opened it. The window had concealed additional instructions requiring the mailing of a certificate, and the certificate required a Fortune subscription. The complaint alleged that Joshua's father demanded the watch without a subscription and Time refused. The complaint did not allege comparable demands by Harris and Baker. The plaintiffs did not claim that Time failed to supply watches to people who subscribed.
sections.Issue: Whether the visible promise on the envelope was an offer, whether opening the envelope was adequate consideration, whether the plaintiffs had to and did give notice of their performance, and whether dismissal should nonetheless be affirmed.
sections.Holding: The California Court of Appeal, First District, Division Five, in 1987, in an opinion by Justice King in which Presiding Justice Low and Justice Haning concurred, held that on the complaint's allegations the mailer was an offer of a unilateral contract and opening the envelope was consideration, and that Joshua's pleaded demand gave the required notice of performance while Harris and Baker had alleged none. It nevertheless affirmed dismissal of the entire action under Civil Code section 3533's principle that the law disregards trifles. The affirmance is not a holding that opening an envelope can never be consideration.
sections.Reasoning:
An advertisement ordinarily invites bargaining, but one that requests a specified performance without further communication or negotiation can offer a unilateral contract. The visible promise fell within that exception: it promised the watch for the requested act of opening the envelope.

On consideration, a bargained-for act ordinarily suffices without equivalence of values, an additional benefit to the promisor, or additional detriment to the promisee. Opening the envelope exposed the recipient to Time's sales pitch, which the court considered valuable to Time even if insignificant to the recipient.

Because Time could not otherwise learn that an envelope had been opened, the court required reasonable notice of performance. Joshua's demand supplied it; Harris and Baker had alleged no notice before suit, so their contract allegations were insufficient. The plaintiffs argued that the concealed subscription requirement was an anticipatory breach excusing notice, but the court applied California precedents declining anticipatory-breach relief for unilateral contracts and found no compelling reason to depart from binding state supreme court precedent.

The court then affirmed on a different ground from the technically supported contract claim. It emphasized the absence of alleged loss beyond the time and effort of opening the envelope, contrasted that with the $15 million sought, and considered the litigation an excessive use of judicial resources.

The casebook reproduces the envelope facts as a problem asking what follows from Time's want-of-consideration motion.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-016.rule: Consideration is distinguished from a conditional gift by reciprocal inducement: the promise must induce the detriment and the detriment must induce the promise, and no actual negotiation over the terms is required.

sections.Parties: Pennsy Supply, Inc., a paving subcontractor, sued American Ash Recycling Corp. of Pennsylvania, which had supplied it free with AggRite, a treated-ash aggregate that Pennsy used in a paving job that later cracked. Pennsy, the plaintiff and appellant, pleaded breach of contract, three warranty counts and promissory estoppel, seeking its remedial and disposal costs. American Ash demurred to all five counts.
sections.Procedural History: Pennsy filed its complaint on November 18, 2004, and requested leave to amend if any demurrer were sustained. The trial court sustained demurrers to all five counts and dismissed the action, treating the free material as a conditional gift, holding that a gift was not a sale of goods, and rejecting promissory estoppel. Pennsy appealed. On March 17, 2006, the Pennsylvania Superior Court reversed the order and remanded for further proceedings, relinquishing jurisdiction. The decision concerns only the sufficiency of the complaint; it did not award damages or finally determine product defects, breach or reliance.
sections.Material Facts:
These are the complaint's allegations, accepted as true on demurrer. Northern York County School District engaged general contractor Lobar to build a high school, and Lobar subcontracted paving of driveways and a parking lot to Pennsy. The project specifications required specified aggregates but allowed substitution of AggRite. They included notice that American Ash offered AggRite free and a letter to the architect confirming availability on a first-come basis. Pennsy told American Ash it needed about 11,000 tons, collected the material, and used it in the work.

Pennsy completed paving in December 2001, and extensive cracking appeared in February 2002. Pennsy performed remedial work in summer 2003 without charging the District. Removing and properly disposing of the AggRite was part of that work because the material was classified as hazardous waste. American Ash did not arrange removal and disposal when asked. Pennsy alleged $251,940.20 in remedial work and a further $133,777.48 in disposal costs.

Pennsy expressly alleged that American Ash promoted AggRite for use in construction and supplied it free to induce others to dispose of it, avoiding American Ash's own disposal costs. The complaint did not expressly allege that the parties discussed disposal costs or that Pennsy understood American Ash's motive.
sections.Issue: Whether Pennsy's taking of free AggRite, which relieved American Ash of disposal costs, could be consideration for a contract rather than a condition of a gift when the parties did not bargain over those costs; and whether the transaction could be a sale supporting Article 2 warranties and the complaint could support promissory estoppel.
sections.Holding: The Pennsylvania Superior Court in 2006, in an opinion by Judge Orie Melvin before Judges Joyce and Tamilia with no separate writing, reversed the order sustaining the demurrers and remanded. It held that the complaint adequately alleged consideration, because the facts pleaded showed reciprocal inducement and actual negotiation over the terms was unnecessary. It also held that relief from disposal costs could be the price for a sale of goods, so the warranty counts could not be dismissed for absence of a sale, and that the promissory-estoppel count was adequately pleaded.
sections.Reasoning:
Well-pleaded facts and fair inferences were accepted as true, and dismissal was proper only if recovery was clearly precluded.

The court distinguished a detriment merely incidental to receiving a gift from a detriment sought in exchange for the promise. Benefit to the promisor can indicate an exchange but is not a conclusive test; what matters is reciprocal inducement. Accepting Pennsy's allegation, the promise of free supply induced Pennsy to collect and take title, while the transfer and relief from disposal obligations induced American Ash to offer the material. The transaction could therefore be an exchange instead of a gift with a collection condition. Facts showing reciprocal inducement could establish bargained consideration without any discussion of disposal costs. The court also rejected the possible alternative ground that the oral agreement's terms were insufficiently pleaded.

On the warranty counts, AggRite was a movable good, and Article 2 defined a sale as transfer of title for a price payable in money or otherwise, so relief from disposal costs could be the nonmonetary price. American Ash's alleged promotion of AggRite as a building material differed from abandoning garbage for anyone to retrieve. The court did not hold that every warranty requirement had been proved.

On promissory estoppel, the complaint alleged direct assurances of suitability at an August 2, 2001 project meeting, before the alleged agreement around August 21, and earlier reliance on the specifications did not rule out further reliance on that assurance. A second route was that American Ash allegedly made representations to the architect, who used them in specifications on which Pennsy relied; Restatement (Second) § 90 reaches expected action by a third person.

The casebook uses the case in its 'One Person's Trash' problem, which poses the consideration question without stating the appellate result.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-017.rule: A unilateral contract becomes enforceable when the requested performance is rendered, so an employer's promise to at-will employees, even if illusory when made, binds once the employees complete the performance it asked for.

sections.Parties: The plaintiffs, original employees of American Energy Services (AES), sued the company for breach of an alleged oral promise to share five percent of the value of any sale or merger among the original employees still employed at that time. They lost on summary judgment in the trial court and in the court of appeals. AES, the defendant, argued that the promise was illusory because the employees were at will.
sections.Procedural History: AES sought summary judgment on two grounds: that the promise was illusory and that the oral agreement violated the statute of frauds; it later expressly abandoned the statute-of-frauds defense. The trial court granted summary judgment. The court of appeals affirmed on the view that the purported unilateral contract required at least one nonillusory promise. On December 18, 2009, the Texas Supreme Court reversed the court of appeals' judgment and remanded to the trial court for further proceedings.
sections.Material Facts:
The description of the promise rests on the employees' allegations, taken favorably to them on review of summary judgment. AES was formed in summer 1996 and hired the employees that year. At a June 1997 operational meeting they voiced concern to vice president John Carnett about the company's continued viability and complained of long hours and antiquated equipment. They alleged that, to induce them to remain, Carnett promised that the original eight employees still employed when AES was sold or merged would share five percent of the transaction's value.

They were at-will employees, free to leave. AES Acquisition, Inc. acquired AES in 2001, and seven of the original eight remained. They demanded their share, and the company refused.
sections.Issue: Whether an employer's alleged promise to pay at-will employees a bonus if they are still employed when the company is sold is unenforceable as illusory, because the employer could have fired them before the sale and they were free to leave, even though they stayed until the sale.
sections.Holding: The Texas Supreme Court in 2009, in an opinion delivered by Justice Green with no separate writing, reversed and remanded. It held that, assuming AES made the alleged offer, the employees accepted it by remaining employed through the acquisition, which made the promise enforceable regardless of whether it was illusory when made. The court did not finally determine that the oral offer was made or fix any recovery, and it did not address revocation during partial performance, a pre-sale dismissal, or a sale that never occurred. The brief gives no vote because the opinion identifies no voting lineup.
sections.Reasoning:
AES and the court of appeals relied on Light v. Centel Cellular Co. of Texas and Alex Sheshunoff Management Services, L.P. v. Johnson, both about covenants not to compete. The court explained that Light dealt with whether a noncompete covenant was ancillary to an otherwise enforceable agreement, and that Sheshunoff later rejected the reading of Light that would permanently exclude a unilateral arrangement made enforceable by later performance merely because it was unenforceable when made. Those cases did not require an exchange of enforceable promises for every contract accepted by performance.

A bilateral contract exchanges promises. A unilateral contract offers a benefit in return for actual performance or forbearance and becomes enforceable upon that performance. The court of appeals' formulation, one illusory promise and one nonillusory promise, addressed whether a failed bilateral exchange could be salvaged; it did not describe unilateral contracts generally.

Even assuming AES's promise was illusory when made, the question was whether it had become enforceable by the time of the alleged breach. By staying through the acquisition the employees had done what the offer requested, and AES's earlier ability to end their employment could not erase the completed performance. A house-painting illustration contrasted a proposed payment before performance with a binding obligation after it.

The existing salary did not defeat consideration: at-will employees were not already obligated to remain, so continued service could support both salary and the additional promised compensation. Requiring a separate binding promise to stay would also imperil ordinary arrangements such as pensions, vacation leave and bonuses earned through a term of service.

The casebook uses the case in its problem 'A Revolting Development,' whose variations about long-term contracts and signed documents are modifications for discussion, not facts of the case.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-018.rule: Under Sherman Act section 1, concerted action turns on economic substance: an agreement that joins independent decisionmakers pursuing distinct economic interests on the challenged decision, here franchise restaurants' hiring, is concerted action despite a common enterprise.

sections.Parties: Jarvis Arrington, Geneva Blanchard and Sandra Munster, who had worked at Burger King franchise restaurants, sued Restaurant Brands International, its subsidiary Burger King Worldwide, and Worldwide's subsidiary Burger King Corporation, together called Burger King. The employees alleged that a no-hire provision in the standard franchise agreement violated the Sherman Act by blocking moves among restaurants and depressing wages. They appealed the dismissal of their claim; Burger King defended it as a single enterprise incapable of conspiring.
sections.Procedural History: Burger King moved to dismiss. The district court held that Burger King and each franchisee were one economic enterprise incapable of conspiring under Sherman Act § 1; having rejected that first element, it did not reach unreasonable restraint or restraint of interstate or foreign trade, and it denied leave to amend as futile. The employees appealed. On August 31, 2022, the Eleventh Circuit, reviewing de novo under the plausibility standard, reversed the dismissal to the extent it rested on the concerted-action element and remanded for further proceedings.
sections.Material Facts:
These are pleading-stage allegations, not findings. More than 99 percent of Burger King restaurants worldwide were independently owned franchises; the corporation operated about fifty United States restaurants, all around Miami. From at least 2010 through at least September 13, 2018, the standard franchise contract contained a provision under which Burger King Corporation and each franchisee agreed not to entice another's employees to leave, or to employ them within six months after their employment ended, unless the former employer gave prior written consent. The corporation could terminate a franchise for breach.

The franchise agreement classified franchisees as independent contractors and made each solely responsible for its employees, free to hire, discipline, promote, discharge and set wages, hours, benefits and employment policies without corporate approval. A franchise covered one restaurant at a specified site with no protected territory, and the disclosure document warned of competition from other franchisees and corporate restaurants.

Arrington had been a line cook at an Illinois franchise until August 2017; Blanchard had worked for a New Orleans franchise since 2013; Munster had worked fifteen years for another Illinois franchise, rising to general manager. They alleged that the agreement prevented moves among Burger King restaurants, depressed wages, reduced benefits and restricted mobility.
sections.Issue: Whether the employees plausibly alleged concerted action under Sherman Act § 1, that is, whether Burger King and its independently owned franchisees were separate economic actors capable of conspiring when they agreed not to hire one another's employees, or instead a single enterprise.
sections.Holding: The Eleventh Circuit in 2022, in an opinion by Judge Rosenbaum for a unanimous panel with Judges Wilson and Hull, held that the employees plausibly alleged that independently operated Burger King restaurants joined otherwise independent hiring decisions through the no-hire agreement, which was enough to plead concerted action. It reversed the dismissal to that extent and remanded. The court did not decide whether the restraint was unreasonable, choose among per se, quick-look or rule-of-reason analysis, certify a class, or award relief, and it did not hold that franchise businesses act in concert for every purpose.
sections.Reasoning:
Section 1 reaches concerted action among separate actors and treats unilateral conduct differently. Under Copperweld and American Needle the inquiry concerns economic substance rather than legal form: whether an agreement joins independent decisionmakers pursuing distinct economic interests and so removes independent centers of decisionmaking from the marketplace. The focus is the challenged decision, not all of an enterprise's activities taken together.

American Needle illustrated the point. NFL teams shared an interest in promoting their league yet kept separate economic interests in licensing their own intellectual property, so their common licensing arrangement could involve concerted action.

Applying that, the court found the employees' position plausible. The independent-contractor language supported it, but the express allocation of hiring and employment decisions to each franchisee was particularly significant. The complaint and proposed amendment also described different recruitment approaches, including one franchise's managerial bonuses, another's emphasis on wages, benefits and scheduling, and a third's use of Burger King's website for applications. Absent the agreement, independently operated restaurants could pursue their own interests by offering different terms or enticing employees from competitors; the restriction joined those hiring choices and reduced independent decisionmaking.

Burger King asked the panel to affirm on the alternative ground that any restraint was reasonable, but that would have required selecting and applying a mode of antitrust analysis, which the panel left to the district court in the first instance.

The casebook mentions the case in its discussion of recent restraints on worker mobility.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-019.rule: The temporary restraining order states no general rule; it shows only that a court granted interim relief directing a hiring hospital either to lend staff to, or to stop hiring from, the employer whose team was leaving.

sections.Parties: ThedaCare, Inc., a healthcare employer, moved for a temporary restraining order against Ascension NE Wisconsin, Inc., the named defendant, which was hiring seven members of ThedaCare's interventional radiology and cardiovascular team. The order is addressed to Ascension, not to the individual workers.
sections.Procedural History: The brief covers only the initial temporary restraining order, document 11 in Outagamie County Circuit Court case 2022CV000068, signed by Circuit Court Judge Mark J. McGinnis on January 20, 2022, and filed January 21. The order granted ThedaCare's motion and remains effective, by its terms, unless and until terminated by a subsequent court order. Later stages, including any dissolution, later hearing or final resolution, are not part of the brief.
sections.Material Facts:
According to the casebook's account, an interventional radiology and cardiovascular team sought to move from ThedaCare to Ascension during the pandemic, and ThedaCare's complaint alleged that Ascension had 'shockingly' chosen to poach the employees; that is an allegation by ThedaCare's lawyers, not a finding.

The order identifies seven people resigning their ThedaCare employment to join Ascension: Amber Kohler, Andrew Kohler, Samantha Baltus, Timothy Breister, Kailey Young, Michael Preissner and Paul Winter. The order does not recite the parties' contracts or identify any promise by a worker.
sections.Issue: Whether ThedaCare was entitled to a temporary restraining order against Ascension in connection with the departure of the seven named employees.
sections.Holding: The Outagamie County Circuit Court, by Judge Mark J. McGinnis, granted ThedaCare's motion in January 2022, citing Wis. Stat. § 813.02. It directed Ascension to choose between two alternatives: make available to ThedaCare one invasive radiology technician and one registered nurse from the group, with their support including on-call responsibilities, or cease hiring the named individuals until ThedaCare had hired adequate staff to replace the departing team members. A violation by Ascension was made immediately punishable by contempt. The order sets no fixed number of days and does not direct the employees themselves to work for ThedaCare.
sections.Reasoning:
The written order contains no developed findings explaining why temporary relief was justified. It states only that the motion is granted based on the filings and evidence submitted. It does not determine that the employees lost their right to quit, set out a tortious-interference or no-poaching rule, or reproduce Ascension's response or the evidence. It is an interim command, not a final award of damages, a permanent injunction, or a judgment enforcing a noncompetition covenant.

The casebook uses the dispute, under the heading 'Essentially At-Will,' to ask whether calling workers essential changes what an employer can obtain when at-will employees seek work elsewhere; that question is the casebook's, and the order itself establishes no general rule answering it.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-020.rule: Definite handbook provisions, such as disciplinary procedures, distributed to an at-will employee can become a binding unilateral contract when the employee keeps working with knowledge of them, the continued service supplying both acceptance and consideration.

sections.Parties: Pine River State Bank sued its former loan officer, Richard Mettille, on two defaulted notes. Mettille counterclaimed for discharge without cause and denial of required disciplinary procedures. The bank was the appellant, seeking to overturn the judgment for Mettille on the contract counterclaim; Mettille, who had also sought a new trial below, did not appeal.
sections.Procedural History: The bank sued in November 1980. At the January 1982 trial the jury found a contract restricting discharge without good cause, a discharge without good cause, and $27,675 in damages. After deducting the debt owed to the bank, the trial court entered judgment of $24,141.07 for Mettille. Both sides unsuccessfully sought a new trial, but only the bank appealed. The Minnesota Supreme Court affirmed the denial of the bank's post-trial motions and sustained the judgment for Mettille.
sections.Material Facts:
Mettille, then unemployed and nearly forty-eight, accepted an oral offer from the bank in early 1978 at $1,000 a month, moved from St. Paul, and began work on April 10. Neither permanence nor a fixed term was discussed, and he understood he remained free to leave. After a six-month probation he held the loan-officer title. Late that year the bank distributed a printed handbook that President E. A. Griffith had drafted from a seminar model; Griffith testified that he intended information and internal guidance, not a contractual commitment. Its job-security section praised the stability of banking employment. Its disciplinary section was more specific: an oral reprimand, a written reprimand for a second offense, a further written reprimand and meeting with a possible five-day unpaid suspension, and discharge if conduct did not improve, with every discharge reviewed by an executive officer.

Mettille received a seven-percent raise after his April 1979 review. In September state examiners identified exceptions in loan files; the bank characterized fifty-eight of eighty-five reviewed files as containing serious exceptions and assigned fifty-seven to Mettille, characterizations he contested. When he returned from illness on September 28, Griffith fired him without reviewing the exception list with him or following the disciplinary steps. He received two months' severance; evidence showed no prior reprimands.
sections.Issue: Whether definite disciplinary procedures in a handbook distributed after hiring could become contractually binding through an at-will employee's continued service, despite the bank's objections that at-will status should prevail, that consideration beyond ordinary services was required, and that the employee's freedom to leave defeated mutuality.
sections.Holding: The Minnesota Supreme Court, sitting en banc in 1983 in an opinion by Justice Simonett, with Justice Coyne not participating, affirmed. Definite disciplinary procedures in a handbook distributed after hiring could become binding through an at-will employee's continued service. The bank's general job-security statements were only policy, but its definite disciplinary policy was an offer of termination procedures, which Mettille's continued work accepted and supported. The operative holding was that applicable, enforceable procedures were not followed; the court did not announce a general tort prohibition on bad-faith discharge or a guarantee of lifetime employment. Lost wages through trial were supportable, and there was no reversible evidentiary error.
sections.Reasoning:
An employment promise of indefinite duration can create a unilateral contract if it is sufficiently definite as an offer, communicated, and accepted through performance. Objective manifestations, not the employer's undisclosed intention, decide whether there is an offer, and general assurances of a career or stability are insufficient. Distribution of a handbook can communicate definite terms, and an employee who stays with knowledge of them, although free to leave, both accepts and supplies consideration, so a later handbook can modify an earlier arrangement. Employers can reserve discretion or amendment rights in the handbook's language; not every handbook statement is binding.

The court rejected each of the bank's objections as a categorical bar. At-will employment is a presumption for interpreting an indefinite hiring, not a prohibition on agreed restrictions. Additional consideration can help show that genuine permanent employment was intended but is not the only way to support a clear termination provision, since one performance can support multiple promises. Once consideration is present, no separate mutuality requirement invalidates the employer's undertaking. A note distinguished post-hiring noncompete promises, which the cited cases treated under a different public-policy rule requiring independent consideration.

The jury had been told to find that the bank intended to be bound, an incorrectly subjective test, but the bank chose to retain that instruction, making it the law of the case. The handbook did not use the words good cause, and whether the contract allowed summary dismissal for good cause was not presented for decision. Mettille might have corrected his deficiencies if given warning, so the protections had substantive value, and the record did not show he would lawfully have been terminated before trial. His request for a new trial on mental-anguish damages was not before the court because he filed no notice of review.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-021.rule: An employer may change a generally applicable written discharge-for-cause policy to at-will employment without having reserved the right to do so, provided reasonable notice of the change is uniformly given to affected employees.

sections.Parties: Kenneth Bankey, a salesman discharged by Storer Broadcasting Co., sued Storer alleging a longstanding just-cause policy on which he had relied. Storer, the defendant, appealed a jury verdict for Bankey to the Sixth Circuit, which certified a question of Michigan law to the Michigan Supreme Court. Storer argued that continued work after a policy change accepted a new offer; Bankey argued that modifying an existing obligation required mutual assent.
sections.Procedural History: Bankey sued in Michigan state court in July 1982, and Storer removed on diversity grounds. After Storer moved for a directed verdict at the close of Bankey's case, the district court ruled that the 1980 digest created a for-cause employment obligation under Toussaint that could not unilaterally be altered for existing employees. The jury awarded Bankey $55,000. Storer appealed, and the Sixth Circuit certified the question. On June 6, 1989, the Michigan Supreme Court answered the certified question affirmatively. It did not affirm or reverse Bankey's federal judgment or decide whether Storer's actual notice was adequate; application was left to the federal proceedings.
sections.Material Facts:
The facts came from the Sixth Circuit's certification, not from a state-court examination of the trial record. Bankey worked thirteen years as a salesman for Storer Broadcasting and was discharged on March 23, 1981, for asserted poor performance. A 1980 Personnel Policy Digest said that an employee could be discharged for cause. The January 1981 replacement instead declared employment at the company's will.

The certified question assumed an obligation arising through employees' legitimate expectations grounded in written policy statements, not an individually negotiated express promise, and asked whether an employer could later adopt a generally applicable at-will policy without having announced its right to do so at the outset.
sections.Issue: Whether an employer whose written policy statements created a legitimate-expectations obligation to discharge only for cause may unilaterally change that generally applicable policy to employment at will without having reserved in advance the right to make the change.
sections.Holding: The Michigan Supreme Court in 1989, in a majority opinion by Justice Griffin joined by Chief Justice Riley and Justices Brickley and Cavanagh, answered yes: a generally applicable written discharge-for-cause policy based on legitimate expectations may be changed to at-will employment without an advance reservation of amendment power, provided reasonable notice of the change is uniformly given to affected employees. Justice Boyle concurred in the result, joined by Justice Archer, and Justice Levin wrote separately. The answer was confined to the prospective termination policy; the majority reserved a possibly different answer for benefits already vested or accrued, such as pensions or severance.
sections.Reasoning:
Toussaint recognized two paths to for-cause protection: express agreement and legitimate expectations generated by employer policies. It did not settle how long a policy-based expectation remained legitimate after the employer changed the policy.

The majority found neither party's contract theory adequate. Storer's unilateral-contract explanation would artificially treat each day's work as completion of a new contract. Bankey's mutual-assent position could not explain an obligation that, under the legitimate-expectations branch, arose without mutual agreement in the first place.

The majority instead grounded enforcement in the benefit an employer obtains by cultivating an orderly, loyal, cooperative workforce and a climate of fair treatment. That collective benefit could create an obligation without individualized assent or detrimental reliance. The obligation required consistent application of the policy while in force but did not make it permanent; withdrawing the policy also withdrew the benefit and the rationale for enforcing it.

Requiring renegotiation with every employee could produce conflicting policy regimes depending on hiring date and handbook version, and could tie employers indefinitely to outdated rules because they had not anticipated Toussaint. Changes applicable to the whole workforce or particular classifications were therefore permitted. The majority disclaimed approval of bad-faith manipulation, such as temporarily suspending a for-cause policy to fire one targeted employee, and required reasonable notice uniformly communicated before revocation took effect.

Justice Boyle emphasized that the legitimate-expectations branch rested on the court's common-law authority to recognize enforceable noncontractual obligations, so traditional contract theory was inappropriate. Justice Levin agreed employers could change policies but argued that long-serving employees might retain legitimate expectations deserving additional relief, and he questioned the court's constitutional authority to answer certified questions.

The casebook's 'Administrative Law Model?' account emphasizes consistent application but omits the separate requirement of reasonable notice of the actual change.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-022.rule: A promise is not illusory, and supplies consideration, when the promisor surrenders a legal freedom he otherwise had, even if reserved powers and contingencies may reduce the practical value the promisee receives; the existence of consideration is distinct from its adequacy.

sections.Parties: Nancy Harrington, the plaintiff, sued to foreclose two mortgages on the farm of her former husband, Gerald Harrington. Gerald, the defendant, resisted on the ground that Nancy had agreed to release the mortgages and the underlying note, and his answer asked that she be required to satisfy them. The Farmers Home Administration disclaimed an interest, the Security State Bank of Hannaford appeared, and the remaining defendants did not appear. Nancy challenged the resulting judgment in the North Dakota Supreme Court.
sections.Procedural History: Nancy brought the foreclosure action on October 3, 1983. The district court held that she was contractually bound to release the mortgages and the debt, dismissed her complaint, and required satisfaction of the mortgages; its judgment allowed Gerald's attorney to apply for a court-ordered satisfaction if she refused. On April 1, 1985 the North Dakota Supreme Court affirmed the dismissal of the foreclosure action and the order requiring her to satisfy the two mortgages.
sections.Material Facts:
Nancy and Gerald divorced in 1981. Their property settlement gave Gerald the farm in exchange for $150,000 to Nancy: a $10,000 initial payment and fifteen annual installments, on a promissory note secured by two farm mortgages. Gerald made the initial payment but only $3,000 afterward. He needed refinancing, which Nancy's encumbrances prevented, and late in 1981 asked her to release the mortgages. Their son Ronn farmed with Gerald, who had remarried and whose wife was pregnant; Nancy worried Ronn might not inherit the farm.

Under an agreement prepared by Gerald's attorney and signed December 30, 1981, Nancy would satisfy both mortgages and release liability on the note, and Gerald would make Ronn sole devisee of the farm land Gerald had owned before January 1, 1978. Ronn would take subject to encumbrances and would owe Gerald's widow twenty-five percent of the crops annually while she had farm-related debt. Gerald could convey a portion to continue farming if future economic exigencies required it, with Ronn holding a first option on land sold. On April 1, 1982 Gerald made a holographic will devising the land to Ronn, conditioned on Nancy's performance. He obtained refinancing and kept farming with Ronn. Nancy did not satisfy the mortgages.
sections.Issue: Was Gerald's promise to devise the farm to Ronn illusory, and so no consideration for Nancy's release, because he kept power to convey or encumber the land and his current wife kept a statutory elective share? And was the order to satisfy the mortgages improper specific performance because of Rule 13(a), an unshown inadequacy of legal remedies, or inadequate consideration?
sections.Holding: The North Dakota Supreme Court, in 1985, in an opinion by Justice Gierke for a unanimous five-member court, affirmed. Gerald's agreement to devise the farm to Ronn supplied consideration for Nancy's release despite the reserved powers and the contingencies affecting what Ronn might ultimately inherit. Specific performance was also proper: the issue of her failure to release the mortgages had been tried and decided, so Rule 13(a) was no bar; damages would not remove the encumbrances; and Nancy had not shown the inequity needed to deny equitable relief. The court did not award Ronn a present farm interest or adjudicate any eventual probate distribution.
sections.Reasoning:
The court distinguished the existence of consideration from its adequacy. Contractual detriment concerns surrender of a legal freedom, not whether the promisee is certain to receive a valuable practical result. A promise is illusory if its apparent commitment disappears on examination because the promisor has committed to nothing. Gerald surrendered his otherwise available freedom to choose another devisee, and that legal restriction was consideration even though later events could reduce the devise's value. The reserved powers were limited: Gerald had to act in good faith under the cited statute and could not convey or encumber the farm simply to evade the promised devise. The possibility that his wife, who had not waived her elective share, might later elect did not eliminate his commitment.

On pleading, Gerald's answer did not label a counterclaim, though its prayer asked that Nancy be required to satisfy the mortgages. Rule 15(b) permits an unpleaded issue tried by express or implied consent to be treated as pleaded. The pleadings gave sufficient notice of the relief demanded, and damages could not accomplish removal of the encumbrances.

On fairness, adequacy of consideration may be scrutinized when specific performance is sought, but mere inadequacy does not defeat it absent unfairness or overreaching. Reviewing for abuse of discretion, the court said the agreement was not a model of balanced bargaining, yet neither it nor the trial court found undue influence or coercion in Gerald's warning that he and Ronn might have to stop farming.

The casebook uses the case in a problem concentrating on illusoriness.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-023.rule: Under UCC § 2-306 a seller's obligation under an output contract is measured by the output that actually occurs in good faith, so a seller may stop producing only in good faith, and merely earning less profit than expected does not justify cessation.

sections.Parties: Fred Feld, who operated the Crushed Toast Company, was the buyer and plaintiff; he sought summary judgment on liability. Henry S. Levy & Sons, Inc., which conducted a wholesale bread-baking business, was the seller and defendant; it sought summary judgment dismissing the claim, arguing that it had promised only to sell whatever bread crumbs it actually produced, not to continue producing them. Both parties appealed to the New York Court of Appeals.
sections.Procedural History: Special Term denied both parties' motions for summary judgment. A divided Appellate Division affirmed, and both parties appealed on a certified question. On July 8, 1975 the New York Court of Appeals affirmed the Appellate Division's order, without costs, and answered the certified question affirmatively. The seller's good faith in discontinuing production remained a factual issue for further proceedings; the court neither awarded the buyer damages nor conclusively found a breach.
sections.Material Facts:
A written agreement of June 19, 1968 required Levy to sell, and Feld to buy, all bread crumbs produced at Levy's Brooklyn factory through June 18, 1969, renewing automatically for successive one-year terms. Either party could cancel on at least six months' notice by certified mail; neither did. Feld supplied the required performance bond and later a continuation certificate for the term beginning June 19, 1969.

The crumbs were deliberately manufactured: stale or imperfect loaves had their labels removed, went through two grinders, were toasted in a drum placed in an oven, and were bagged. Levy sold Feld more than 250 tons before stopping production around May 15, 1969. Its comptroller said the oven was too large for the drum and the operation very uneconomical. Levy did not then try to obtain more economical equipment. The oven was intentionally broken down, partially rebuilt, and completely dismantled that summer, and the space became a computer room. Levy indicated it would resume production if the agreed six-cent price rose to seven cents per pound, and afterward sold the raw materials to animal-food manufacturers. The record did not establish production costs, crumb profits or losses, or the return from the animal-food sales.
sections.Issue: Does an output contract leave the seller free to cease production altogether, so that dismantling its equipment ends any delivery obligation, or does the duty of good faith limit when the seller may stop? On this record, could either party obtain summary judgment?
sections.Holding: The New York Court of Appeals, in 1975, in a unanimous opinion by Judge Cooke, held that an output contract does not fail for want of a fixed quantity or mutuality, and that the seller's obligation is measured by actual output occurring in good faith. Until cancellation under the six-month notice clause, Levy had to perform in good faith. Bankruptcy or a genuine threat to the entire business would justify stopping the crumb line; merely earning less profit than expected would not. Whether Levy stopped in good faith was a question of fact, so neither side was entitled to summary judgment.
sections.Reasoning:
The court rejected the premise that an output contract fails merely because it fixes no quantity or lacks mutuality. UCC § 2-306 measures the seller's obligation by actual output occurring in good faith, subject to its restriction on disproportionate quantities, and the official comment ties that standard to commercial fair dealing and reasonably foreseeable output. The court also reproduced subsection (2), imposing best efforts under an exclusive-dealing agreement unless otherwise agreed. It read the agreement against its commercial background and the then-applicable UCC § 1-203 duty of good-faith performance.

The court acknowledged the general rule that a good-faith cessation of production can end an output seller's further obligations. But Levy had not stopped its principal bread-baking business, only a single product line, and calling continued production uneconomical or economically infeasible was conclusory. The six-month cancellation clause gave a contractual way to end a relationship that proved less profitable than anticipated, and gave the other party time to find another outlet or source. Because the crumb line was one facet of the enterprise and the contract provided that mechanism, good faith could require production even without profit until cancellation. The court did not impose an absolute duty to run a ruinous line: without additional justification, losses exceeding the trivial could justify a good-faith cessation before cancellation. The proposed price increase, the dismantling and the animal-food sales bore on motive, but the missing financial figures prevented a final determination.

The casebook adapts the case into a hypothetical problem with different parties and terms; those are problem facts, not the facts of Feld.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-024.rule: Services performed gratuitously, without expectation of payment, are past consideration and cannot support a later promise to pay for them; a promise made because assistance has already occurred, rather than to procure it, is unenforceable for lack of consideration.

sections.Parties: Peter Dementas, the claimant and plaintiff, sought $50,000 from the estate of his close friend Jack Tallas on the strength of a notarized memorandum in which Tallas said he owed him that sum for past help. The estate, through its personal representative, First Security Bank, denied the claim and defended the suit. Dementas appealed after losing at trial.
sections.Procedural History: Dementas timely presented a $50,000 claim to the estate with copies of the Greek and English documents. The personal representative denied it, and he sued. A pretrial order disposed of quantum meruit, a contract to make or modify a will, and gift causa mortis, so the case went to trial on the memorandum as, at best, an acknowledgment of an existing debt from an earlier oral contract. After extensive testimony the trial court found no enforceable commitment supported by consideration, rejected account stated because the presented claim had not named that theory, and alternatively found no account stated proved. On November 17, 1988 the Utah Court of Appeals affirmed the judgment dismissing the claim, with each party bearing its own appeal costs.
sections.Material Facts:
Tallas immigrated from Greece in 1914, lived nearly seventy years in Salt Lake City, succeeded as an insurance agent and landlord, and spent his last years at the Little America Hotel. Over fourteen years his close friend Dementas gave him at least some personal assistance. On December 18, 1982 Tallas dictated a memorandum in Greek stating that he owed Dementas $50,000 for past help, including collecting mail, grocery shopping and managing rental properties, and proposing to change his will to make Dementas an heir for that sum. Tallas kept the Greek document, prepared an English version, notarized it with his own seal, and delivered the documents three days later. The English version described a father-and-son-like relationship, family dinners, transportation, gasoline expenditures and property assistance. Tallas died on February 4, 1983 without changing his will. His existing will only asked that Dementas and another person collect rents and manage the properties for reasonable compensation.

The trial court found that the documents were executed without fraud, duress or undue influence, but that the memorandum expressed appreciation for gratuitous services and an intention to compensate Dementas later.
sections.Issue: Must a claim presented to an estate name every legal theory on which the claimant later relies? And can a written, notarized acknowledgment of a $50,000 debt for services already performed be enforced as a contract or as an account stated when the services were rendered gratuitously?
sections.Holding: The Utah Court of Appeals, in 1988, in an opinion by Judge Orme for a unanimous panel, affirmed on the merits while correcting the trial court's notice reasoning. Dementas had adequately notified the estate of his demand, and failure to name account stated as a theory did not invalidate the claim. But he could not prove consideration or an underlying debt: a notarized acknowledgment of gratitude for services already performed gratuitously established neither an enforceable contract nor an account stated. The court did not order testamentary changes, award restitution, or treat notarization as a substitute for consideration.
sections.Reasoning:
On notice, Utah's claim-presentation statute required a written statement of the claim's basis, claimant and amount, and the Probate Code called for liberal construction. Since a claimant could instead start an action satisfying ordinary notice pleading, it would be anomalous to demand more detail in the less formal presentation. The amount, the assertion of indebtedness for services, and the attached acknowledgment let the representative investigate.

On the merits, the court did not decide whether the memorandum was ambiguous or integrated. Even a writing that appears completely integrated can be accompanied by evidence showing whether its promise has consideration, and the plaintiff bore the burden of establishing consideration. Existence of consideration differs from adequacy: any genuinely bargained-for detriment could suffice even if economically slight, so the value of the services was not the decisive problem. The decisive finding, not shown erroneous, was that the services were performed gratuitously, without expectation of payment. The later promise responded to completed events rather than inducing them, which is why past consideration is ordinarily no consideration. The court acknowledged criticism of the rule and efforts elsewhere to enforce some promises through moral obligation; Utah had not embraced that exception, and the gratuitous-services finding would defeat the claim under that approach anyway.

An account stated requires prior monetary transactions creating indebtedness, agreement on the balance, and a promise to pay. The trial court found no existing accounts or liquidated debts, and because account stated is itself contractual, the label could not manufacture an obligation from gratuitous assistance.

The casebook uses the case in a problem on personal assistance and a notarized writing.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-025.rule: A gratuitous bailee who promises, as part of the bailment, to insure the goods and then receives them has entered on the undertaking and must perform that term; the bailment entered upon, not reliance alone, supplies the consideration.

sections.Parties: William Siegel, the plaintiff, had bought furniture on installments from Spear & Co., the defendant, which held chattel mortgages on it and stored it for him without charge. Siegel sued for the loss of the furniture by fire after Spear's creditman, McGrath, failed to procure promised insurance. Spear challenged the judgment on the grounds of want of consideration and McGrath's lack of authority.
sections.Procedural History: Siegel sued in the City Court of New York City for the loss caused by the failure to insure, and prevailed below on a jury finding that the promise had been made. The Appellate Division certified a question of law for review by the Court of Appeals. On January 16, 1923 the New York Court of Appeals affirmed the judgment for Siegel, with costs. The opinion does not state a separate dollar amount for the recovery beyond describing recovery of the loss.
sections.Material Facts:
Siegel bought household furniture from Spear in August 1917 and January 1918 for $909.25. Two chattel mortgages secured monthly installments and prohibited removal from his apartment without the mortgagee's written consent. By May 1918 he had paid $295. Planning to leave the city for the summer and give up his apartment, he arranged with McGrath to send the furniture to Spear's storehouse, where storage would be free.

According to Siegel, McGrath suggested transferring an insurance policy to the warehouse. Siegel said he had never insured the furniture and would arrange coverage through his life-insurance agent before delivery. McGrath answered that he would procure the insurance more cheaply because he handled considerable insurance business, and that Siegel could pay the insurance bill with the next installment. The furniture went to the warehouse around May 15 and was destroyed by fire around June 15. No insurance had been obtained.
sections.Issue: Is a promise to procure insurance on goods, made by a party who then receives the goods for storage without pay, enforceable despite the gratuitous character of the bailment?
sections.Holding: The New York Court of Appeals, in 1923, in a unanimous opinion by Judge Crane, held Spear liable. The insurance promise was part of an undertaking that Spear began performing when it received the furniture in a gratuitous bailment; having entered on the undertaking, it was obliged to perform that term as well as to care for the goods. The court left open whether Siegel's refraining from obtaining insurance himself was independent consideration, and whether it would follow Thorne v. Deas when the issue properly arose. The challenge to McGrath's authority was not raised by a sufficient exception.
sections.Reasoning:
Spear's mortgage did not change its status as a bailee without pay. Under the historical bailment rule the court described, an ordinary gratuitous bailee was not responsible for fire damage absent gross neglect, and none existed here, so liability did not arise simply from storage, the mortgage, or the fire. It arose from the additional insurance undertaking linked to receipt of the property.

McGrath promised insurance while the furniture was still in Siegel's possession; delivery followed the promise and began execution of the entrusted undertaking. The court treated the insurance promise as a term of the overall bailment transaction, and the gratuitous character of the storage did not reduce the accepted undertaking to nothing.

The court distinguished Thorne v. Deas, where one joint owner of a vessel promised another to obtain insurance, failed, and was held not liable after the vessel was lost: there the other owner transferred neither possession nor an interest to the promisor. It distinguished Brawn v. Lyford the same way. Authorities on voluntarily accepted trusts and bailments, including Rutgers v. Lucet and Hammond v. Hussey, supported the line between an unexecuted gratuitous promise and an undertaking actually entered upon. These did not establish that every gratuitous promise becomes enforceable upon any reliance.

Because the executed-bailment reasoning supplied consideration, the court did not decide the alternative theory based on Siegel's forbearance. The casebook places Siegel within the history of reliance-based enforcement, although the opinion itself explains the result through the accepted bailment and its associated undertaking.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-026.rule: A charity's acceptance of part payment on a pledge conditioned on a memorial to the donor implies a return promise to maintain and publicize the memorial, and that implied promise is consideration making the unpaid balance of the pledge enforceable.

sections.Parties: Allegheny College, a liberal-learning institution in Meadville, Pennsylvania, was the plaintiff; it sued to recover the unpaid $4,000 balance of a $5,000 pledge made by Mary Yates Johnston. The defendant was Johnston's executor, the National Chautauqua County Bank of Jamestown, which resisted payment; Johnston had notified the college before her death that she repudiated the pledge. The college lost in both lower courts and appealed.
sections.Procedural History: Thirty days after Johnston's death the college sued her executor for the remaining $4,000. The Trial Term gave judgment for the executor and the Appellate Division did the same. On November 22, 1927 the New York Court of Appeals, by five to two, reversed both judgments and ordered judgment for the college as prayed in its complaint, with costs in all courts.
sections.Material Facts:
The college was conducting a $1.25 million endowment campaign. On June 15, 1921 Johnston signed and delivered a $5,000 estate pledge. Its face referred to her interest in Christian education and to others' subscriptions, directed payment from her estate thirty days after death, and permitted endowment use or use under the instructions on the reverse. Spaces for an interest rate and commencement date were left blank. The reverse required a Mary Yates Johnston Memorial Fund whose proceeds would educate students preparing for the ministry in the United States or abroad, and conditioned validity on first satisfying the provisions of her existing will.

Although payment was deferred until after death, Johnston paid $1,000 on account in December 1923. The college set it aside as a scholarship fund for prospective ministers. In July 1924 she notified the college that she repudiated the pledge.
sections.Issue: Was Johnston's charitable pledge supported by consideration, so that her estate was bound to pay the balance despite her repudiation, where she attached a memorial condition and the college accepted a part payment?
sections.Holding: The New York Court of Appeals, in 1927, in an opinion by Chief Judge Cardozo joined by Judges Pound, Crane, Lehman and O'Brien, with Judge Kellogg dissenting joined by Judge Andrews, held the pledge enforceable. By accepting part of the pledge the college impliedly promised to maintain and publicize the donor's memorial, and that return promise was consideration for the unpaid balance, producing a bilateral agreement. The court discussed promissory estoppel in charitable-subscription cases at length but did not rest the recovery on it, and did not hold that every restricted charitable pledge is enforceable without consideration or actual reliance.
sections.Reasoning:
Cardozo acknowledged New York cases holding unsupported charitable promises unenforceable and others finding enforceability where older formulations of consideration might suggest none. Detriment induced by a promise is not alone consideration: promise and detriment must each purport to induce the other, at least in part, and merely changing position in anticipation of a gift is not a bargain. He described promissory estoppel as an exception or substitute recognized in the charitable-subscription cases, declined to decide how far it modified New York's general law, and disclaimed any abandonment of consideration.

The donor wanted her name perpetuated. On taking the $1,000 the college assumed an obligation to do what was customary and reasonably necessary to maintain the memorial, including identifying the donor in scholarship announcements; it could not keep the payment while disclaiming that responsibility. The duty went beyond applying funds to a corporate purpose, it benefited the donor through remembrance, and even a small requested obligation can be consideration. Conduct can communicate a promise, so acceptance yielded a subscription promise on one side and an implied-in-fact return promise on the other. Cardozo recognized that restrictions on a gift are sometimes only conditions of a gratuitous promise, with benefit to the promisor a useful but nonconclusive guide; here the memorial objective, the payment and the acceptance supported the inference of a requested undertaking.

Kellogg, dissenting, read the memorial language as a donor's wish, not a request for a promise. Even assuming an offer, it sought actual memorializing acts, which had not occurred, and death had withdrawn it.

The casebook identifies consideration as the ground of decision and the reliance commentary as dictum.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-027.rule: In Massachusetts a charitable pledge is enforceable only if there is a promise to transfer property for a charitable purpose and that promise is supported by either consideration or reliance.

sections.Parties: Coretta Scott King, as administratrix of the estate of Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. and individually, was the plaintiff; she sued for conversion, asserting that the estate owned papers Dr. King had deposited with Boston University. The Trustees of Boston University, the defendant, claimed ownership of the papers under Dr. King's 1964 letter. The estate appealed after a jury verdict for the university; the university cross-appealed.
sections.Procedural History: Mrs. King sued for conversion in December 1987. The trial judge removed the university's defenses of completed gift, gift of a future interest, and charitable trust. The jury considered contract, charitable pledge, limitations and laches; by special answers it found a promise in the letter and consideration or reliance supporting a charitable pledge, but no contract, and so did not reach limitations or laches. The judge denied judgment notwithstanding the verdict or a new trial. The Supreme Judicial Court granted direct appellate review and, on April 12, 1995, affirmed the judgment sustaining the university's ownership. It did not reach the university's cross-appeal claims.
sections.Material Facts:
In 1963 Boston University planned expanded library special collections, and its director, Howard Gotlieb, sought papers from Dr. King, an alumnus of its graduate school. Other institutions, including Morehouse College, also approached him. Coretta Scott King testified that he believed Boston offered safety but worried about criticism for removing papers from a Black institution in the South.

Dr. King's signed letter of July 16, 1964 named the university's library the repository of his correspondence, manuscripts, other papers, awards and research materials. It authorized immediate removal of most specified materials, including correspondence through 1961, and contemplated later annual shipments. The materials would remain his legal property until otherwise indicated; the university would exercise scrupulous care and was released from responsibility for loss or damage despite that care.
