He stated an intention to identify portions each year as outright gifts until all were given, and that at his death all materials deposited there would become the university's absolute property.

The university indexed the papers, made them available to researchers, employed trained staff to care for them, and held a convocation at which Dr. King spoke about selecting it. The facts were summarized favorably to the university as the nonmoving party.
sections.Issue: Was there sufficient evidence to submit to the jury whether Dr. King's letter contained a promise to transfer ownership of the papers to the university and whether that promise was supported by consideration or reliance? Did the Statute of Wills or Statute of Frauds bar enforcement, and were the instructions correct?
sections.Holding: The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court, in 1995, in an opinion by Justice Abrams with no separate writings or recorded dissent, affirmed. The letter and the bailment it created were sufficient evidence to put the promise question to the jury, and the university's conduct, such as indexing, could be found to go beyond scrupulous custodial care and furnish consideration or reliance. The letter was a promise of absolute title during life or at the latest at death, not a contract to make a will, so the statutory formalities did not bar it. The instructions correctly stated the pledge elements.
sections.Reasoning:
A charitable pledge required a promise to transfer property for a charitable purpose and consideration or reliance supporting it. Massachusetts had declined the approach of Restatement § 90(2), which dispenses with proof of induced action or forbearance for charitable subscriptions, and this case did not change that. Donor intention, assessed from the entire instrument and surrounding circumstances, remained central.

Read alone, the statement that Dr. King intended future gifts might convey only an expectation. But the letter and actual deposit established a consensual bailment in which the university took custody and a stated standard of care while title stayed with Dr. King. A factfinder could view the deposit as security for a promised future gift and so as further evidence of intent to be bound. The court limited the inference: deposit with a charity creates no irrebuttable presumption of donative intent and does not override express conditions. A contemplated tax appraisal and later shipments consistent with the letter were additional evidence.

Both parties agreed the letter could not operate as a will because it lacked the statutory witnesses, but the Statute of Wills did not prohibit a contractual arrangement for disposition at death. Even assuming the Statute of Frauds for agreements to make testamentary dispositions applied, the signed writing could state all terms; the annual-gift and death provisions together let the jury treat death as the latest date for completing the transfer.

The charge, read as a whole, distinguished a nonbinding present intention from a statement committing the speaker to specified conduct. An objection about the retained-title passage was unpreserved.

The casebook discusses the case in its account of charitable subscriptions.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-028.rule: The detriment required for promissory estoppel is not measured only by comparing financial gains and losses; forgone alternatives and nonfinancial burdens assumed in reliance on the promise can make the reliance substantial, and whether they do is a question of fact.

sections.Parties: Soloman Vastoler, the plaintiff and appellant, was a retired employee of American Can Co., the defendant. He sought a pension calculated with credit for his service back to 1937, both under the pension plan itself and on a promissory-estoppel theory based on a promise he said the company made to induce him to accept promotion to supervisor. The company disputed the pension promise.
sections.Procedural History: The district court rejected Vastoler's claim under the plan's express terms and granted the company summary judgment on promissory estoppel. For that purpose it assumed the promise had been made and that Vastoler had no notice that pension credit began in July 1958 rather than March 1937, but it found no substantial detriment. On February 23, 1983 the Third Circuit affirmed rejection of the claim under the plan, reversed the summary judgment on promissory estoppel, and remanded for trial. It did not establish ultimate liability or award increased benefits.
sections.Material Facts:
Vastoler worked for American Can during several periods from 1937 until he retired at fifty-nine on December 31, 1978. Apart from three years of military service, he was an hourly employee from 1937 to 1946, 1947 to 1952, and 1958 to 1963. His 1952 resignation cancelled pre-1958 accredited service under the plan's express provisions. In April 1963 the company sought to promote him from lithographer to salaried supervisor. On the record viewed favorably to him, he reluctantly accepted primarily on a promise of pension credit for past service.

An internal memorandum by plant manager Joe Choborda, who negotiated the promotion, supported his account of service-credit discussions and acknowledged that the company had needed to sell him on the benefits because he initially gained no financial advantage from promotion. The company granted past-service credit for other benefits but not the pension. With a 1958 start date his benefits were $656.14 monthly until sixty-two and $580.20 thereafter; with 1937 credit they would be $875.23 monthly from retirement. As supervisor he became responsible for approximately fifty workers. He testified that, had he known of the lower pension, he would have increased contributions to his Amalgamated Lithographers of America pension.
sections.Issue: Could the district court conclude on summary judgment that Vastoler suffered no substantial detriment in relying on the alleged pension promise because the financial advantages of fifteen years as a salaried supervisor exceeded the lost pension credit?
sections.Holding: The Third Circuit, in 1983, in an opinion by Judge A. Leon Higginbotham, Jr. on a panel with Judges Gibbons and Becker, who concurred separately, held that summary judgment on promissory estoppel was improper. The record permitted a finding of substantial detrimental reliance on the alleged promise, including forgone alternatives and potentially burdensome supervisory responsibilities, and whether intervening compensation eliminated detriment was for the factfinder. The court sustained the rejection of the claim under the plan's express terms.
sections.Reasoning:
The district court had weighed fifteen years of gains, including extra paid leave, stock purchases, better insurance, a $2,000 retirement payment, higher compensation, freedom from union dues, and retention while hourly workers faced layoffs, against the pension shortfall and found no detriment. Rule 56 required favorable inferences for the employee.

The majority identified an unsupported assumption that without promotion Vastoler would necessarily have remained an hourly employee at American Can. Possible alternatives extended beyond the company. His testimony that the pension induced him to stay and that he would otherwise have increased his union pension contributions supported a possible reliance loss in forgone employment opportunities and retirement planning; their existence and significance were trial issues.

The district court had also ignored the potential stress of supervision. Vastoler moved from responsibility for individual tasks to responsibility for assignments, discipline, and possible recommendations for dismissal or layoffs, and a jury could find additional emotional burdens. The majority rejected a purely financial measure but did not say promotion inherently establishes substantial detriment. Even the financial picture was disputed, given Choborda's memorandum and Vastoler's testimony.

Becker, concurring, stressed that the employee's account was accepted only for reviewing summary judgment; that failure to deliver the promised credit could not itself be the reliance detriment, since breach and detrimental reliance are distinct; and that New Jersey law probably permits stress and anxiety as one relevant factor.

The casebook's suggestion that the court used reliance to enforce the promise is a teaching question; the judgment required a trial and did not finally enforce increased pension payments.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-029.rule: Promissory estoppel requires an actual, clear and definite promise that induces reasonable reliance; expressions of expectation, statutory eligibility representations, and corporate promotion made in seeking a tax abatement are not such a promise.

sections.Parties: The Charter Township of Ypsilanti, the plaintiff, sued General Motors Corp. to stop it from moving production out of its Willow Run plant after receiving tax abatements. Washtenaw County joined voluntarily, and Michigan, which first appeared as amicus, was added as a plaintiff by the trial court. General Motors, the defendant, challenged the injunction entered against it in the Michigan Court of Appeals.
sections.Procedural History: The township sued on April 29, 1992, asserting statutory and conduct-based contract theories, promissory estoppel, unjust enrichment and misrepresentation. After a lengthy trial the circuit court found that the abatement statute and application created no contract, but held on promissory estoppel that GM must keep Caprice production at Willow Run as long as it made that model. Its February 9, 1993 injunction barred transfer of the sedan and specified station-wagon production. On August 3, 1993 the Michigan Court of Appeals, per curiam, reversed the injunction and allowed GM to tax costs. It expressed no opinion on the unjust-enrichment claim, which had not been decided below.
sections.Material Facts:
GM's Hydra-Matic and Willow Run plants employed approximately 9,000 and more than 4,000 people. The township granted eleven abatements over time, three for Willow Run, under a statute encouraging job creation or retention. On July 17, 1984 it approved a twelve-year, fifty-percent personal-property tax abatement for a $175 million investment. In April 1988 GM announced a new rear-wheel-drive Chevrolet Caprice project at Willow Run, and its October 7 application sought another twelve-year, fifty-percent abatement for a $75 million investment, which the township approved after public hearings.

Plant manager Harvey Williams's prepared statement said that completion of the project and favorable market demand would allow Willow Run to continue production and maintain continuous employment. County chairman Dillard Craiger asked for a duration commitment and complained that none existed. At the hearing comptroller Russell Hughes warned about job losses from declining market share, Craiger repeated that GM would not say whether or when it might move, and other speakers said GM was promising nothing. Township officials did not contradict them, and the township unanimously approved the abatement without conditioning it on operation for any period.

On December 18, 1991 GM announced it would consolidate Willow Run and Arlington, Texas production at Arlington, citing record losses and declining Caprice demand.
sections.Issue: Did General Motors, in seeking and obtaining the Willow Run tax abatements, make a clear and definite promise to continue production there on which the township reasonably relied, so that promissory estoppel could support an injunction against moving the work?
sections.Holding: The Michigan Court of Appeals, in 1993, in a per curiam decision with no separate writing or dissent recorded, held that the trial court clearly erred in finding a definite promise of continued production. Williams's statement was a qualified expectation of what the investment would enable, not a commitment to keep those lines at Willow Run. Even assuming a promise, reliance on it would have been unreasonable in light of what was said at the hearing. The court reversed the injunction; it did not order repayment of abatements.
sections.Reasoning:
Promissory estoppel required an actual, clear, definite promise inducing reasonable action or forbearance, with enforcement necessary to avoid injustice. Reviewing the trial court's findings for clear error, the court concluded that neither equitable concern nor community expectations established such a promise, although the trial court had called the loss of thousands of jobs after substantial tax concessions grossly unfair.

Seeking abatements with assurances about jobs was consistent with the legislation's purpose and not itself evidence of a commitment to operate indefinitely or for a set term. The statute required certification that the project had a reasonable likelihood of creating or retaining employment; that eligibility representation differed from a guarantee of continued production. Corporate hyperbole and promotion did not necessarily create a binding undertaking. The history of plant tours, lunches and presentations showed efforts to obtain a statutory benefit, and much of it concerned Hydra-Matic. The State Tax Commission's concerns were its own expectations, Hughes's statement about roughly 5,000 employees described history, and the assessor's confidence that GM had kept its word was the assessor's own assessment.

Williams's words spoke of what project completion and favorable demand would allow; statements about cooperation and future investment added promotional language rather than a definite duration obligation.

On reliance, the hearing record showed Craiger and others saying openly that GM would not commit to staying, with no contradiction from township officials and no condition attached to the approval.

The casebook presents the speech and the injunction as a problem and leaves the appellate result for analysis.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-030.rule: Section 230(c)(1) bars state-law claims that treat an interactive computer service as the publisher of another's content, but not a promissory-estoppel claim whose duty arises from the provider's own enforceable promise to remove that content.

sections.Parties: Cecilia Barnes, the plaintiff and appellant, sued Yahoo!, Inc. over its failure to remove unauthorized profiles of her posted by a former boyfriend after a Yahoo employee said the matter would be taken care of. She sought to hold Yahoo liable for negligent undertaking and on its promise. Yahoo, the defendant, relied on the immunity in § 230(c)(1) and indicated it would contest her allegations.
sections.Procedural History: Barnes sued in Oregon state court, and Yahoo removed the case to federal court. The district court dismissed under Rule 12(b)(6) on Yahoo's § 230(c)(1) defense. The Ninth Circuit issued an opinion in May 2009, amended it in June, deleting Part II of the original and replacing a footnote, and denied both parties' rehearing petitions; a September order corrected one phrase. In the amended opinion the court affirmed dismissal of the Oregon negligent-undertaking theory, reversed dismissal of the promissory-estoppel theory, and remanded, with each party bearing its own costs.
sections.Material Facts:
These are allegations accepted for purposes of dismissal, not findings. After Barnes ended a relationship in late 2004, her former boyfriend posted unauthorized Yahoo profiles containing nude photographs taken without her knowledge and an apparent solicitation for sex. Posing as Barnes in chat rooms, he directed men to the profiles, which gave her workplace's physical and electronic addresses and telephone number. Strangers contacted and visited her workplace expecting sexual encounters.

Following Yahoo's procedure, Barnes mailed her photo identification and a signed statement denying involvement and requesting removal. After a month without response she wrote again, and the following month sent two more requests. With a local television report imminent, Yahoo's communications director, Ms. Osako, called and asked Barnes to fax her earlier statements directly. Osako said she would personally take them to the division responsible for unauthorized profiles and that it would take care of the problem. Barnes alleged that she relied on this assurance and took no further action. After approximately two more months she sued. The profiles disappeared shortly after the lawsuit.
sections.Issue: Does § 230(c)(1) bar a state-law negligent-undertaking claim based on a provider's failure to remove third-party content it undertook to remove? Does it bar a promissory-estoppel claim based on the provider's promise to remove that content?
sections.Holding: The Ninth Circuit, in 2009, in an opinion by Judge O'Scannlain for Judges Graber and Callahan, held that § 230(c)(1) barred the negligent-undertaking theory, because the undertaking was removal of third-party profiles, itself a publisher's function, but did not bar the contract theory based on promissory estoppel, because that duty arises from a commitment voluntarily assumed as a promisor rather than from publishing status. The court did not decide that Barnes had established an enforceable promise or that Yahoo lacked a different defense under § 230(c)(2).
sections.Reasoning:
Section 230(c)(1) prevents treating a provider of an interactive computer service as the publisher or speaker of information supplied by another, and with § 230(e)(3) protects it against inconsistent state-law claims imposing liability in that capacity. Yahoo's eligibility and the former boyfriend's responsibility for the profiles were undisputed, so the question was the source of the asserted duty. Relabelling a claim cannot avoid the statute if liability still depends on reviewing, editing, publishing or withdrawing another's content.

Barnes's tort theory was that Yahoo, having undertaken removal, had to use reasonable care. The court rejected that distinction: the statutory bar would be ineffective if a plaintiff could evade it by describing a failure to withdraw publication as negligent performance of services. The statute was not confined to defamation, nor limited to providers that actively screen.

Oregon promissory estoppel required a promise, reasonably foreseeable inducement of the conduct that occurred, actual reliance, and a substantial change of position. The court treated it principally as a means of enforcing a contract without consideration. The contractual duty arose from an enforceable commitment, so promising to remove content could create a different legal obligation even though performance would be an ordinary publishing act. This did not turn every helpful response or monitoring policy into a contract: a definite promise and objective manifestations of intent to be bound remained necessary, Yahoo could disclaim that intent, and formation defenses remained available. Neither the availability nor the measure of damages was decided.

The casebook's account invites a separate analysis under § 90; the court itself reserved whether the contract claim was viable.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-031.rule: An employee whose suggestion is rejected under a program making a committee's decision final has no express contract claim, but may pursue unjust enrichment if the employer in fact used the idea, since a failed attempt to contract does not foreclose an obligation imposed by law.

sections.Parties: Schott, the plaintiff and appellant, was a Westinghouse employee who submitted a cost-saving suggestion under the company's employee suggestion program. He sought an accounting of the savings and damages, alleging that the company used his idea after rejecting it. Westinghouse Electric Corp., the defendant, maintained that its committee's rejection was final and that its redesign resulted from independent action without knowledge of his suggestion.
sections.Procedural History: Schott's first complaint was dismissed with leave to amend. He then pleaded separate contract and unjust-enrichment counts. The trial court dismissed again on demurrer, reasoning that the committee's rejection controlled, without separately addressing the new restitution count. On November 28, 1969 the Pennsylvania Supreme Court upheld the rejection of the express-contract count, reversed the dismissal of the unjust-enrichment count, and remanded for further proceedings. No damages were awarded.
sections.Material Facts:
From 1962 through 1965 Westinghouse invited employees to submit practical suggestions to improve production or reduce costs. Its forms offered cash awards of $5 to $15,000 for adopted suggestions. Immediately above the employee's signature was an agreement that the local Suggestion Committee's decisions on the suggestion, award eligibility and amount would be final. Rejected suggestions could be reopened within twelve months or resubmitted afterward.

In May 1962 Schott proposed replacing cast-aluminum circuit-breaker panels with fabricated heavy-gauge steel. The committee rejected the proposal because design, model and testing expenses would exceed the savings, but said it would consider the idea if breaker redesign later began for other reasons. He resubmitted in September 1963; the January 1964 rejection added a need for nonmagnetic materials and referred to an independent cost-reduction study. Schott alleged that the company nevertheless used his recommendations, probably in 1964. Its May 1965 response acknowledged application of the same basic idea in a redesign but said the change resulted from independent action. That was the company's position, not an adjudicated fact.
sections.Issue: Do the pleaded facts state a claim for an award under an express contract when the suggestion committee, whose decision the employee agreed would be final, rejected the suggestion? If not, can the employee still state a claim in unjust enrichment for the company's alleged use of his idea?
sections.Holding: The Pennsylvania Supreme Court, in 1969, in a majority opinion by Justice Pomeroy for four judges, with Justices Roberts and O'Brien concurring in the result and Chief Justice Bell dissenting, held that the first count failed to establish an express contract, because on either view of the program the committee's good-faith rejection meant no contract was completed. The unjust-enrichment count could proceed: the allegations allowed the possibility that a benefit was unjustly retained to be tested. The court did not find that Westinghouse had actually appropriated a novel idea.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority did not need to classify the program as a unilateral offer or an invitation for employees to make offers. If the company offered a unilateral contract, it requested a suggestion its committee in good faith would deem acceptable, not the mere act of submitting one, and that performance had not occurred. If Schott's submission was the offer, a good-faith rejection prevented acceptance. Schott did not allege fraud or bad faith that would release him from the finality clause.

The majority distinguished formal adoption by the committee, which mattered to the contract count, from practical appropriation by operating personnel, which could matter to restitution. Unjust enrichment is unavailable where an express agreement governs the relationship, but no completed contract had been found here, and quasi-contract can operate without assent and even despite a defendant's contrary intention. A demurrer could defeat the claim only if the pleaded facts left no doubt that recovery was legally impossible. The exhibits connected an invitation for suggestions, a promise to reconsider on future redesign, and later use of the same basic idea, and Schott alleged resulting savings; his submission could not be conclusively called gratuitous or officious. Thomas v. R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co., requiring a concrete and novel idea, concerned failure of proof at trial; at the pleading stage those matters could be inferred and left to proof.

Roberts, joined by O'Brien, would permit a contract claim through acceptance by conduct but not restitution outside the program's limits. Bell would treat the written terms as conclusive.

The casebook's problem refers to two judges approving a contract route, which is the Roberts and O'Brien concurrence, not the majority's holding.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-032.rule: An express contract bars quasi-contractual recovery only on the subject matter it covers, so a party may recover in quantum meruit for a distinct benefit the contract left unaddressed, or where a contractual waiver was induced by fraud and is avoided.

sections.Parties: Jesse 'The Body' Ventura, the plaintiff, was a wrestler and commentator for Titan Sports, Inc., the defendant, which operated the World Wrestling Federation. Ventura sought the reasonable value of royalties for Titan's videotape exploitation of his commentary and for other merchandise. Titan appealed the judgment against it, and the denial of interest for the period before suit was also reviewed.
sections.Procedural History: Ventura sued in December 1991 for fraud, appropriation of publicity rights, and quantum meruit. He abandoned the separate fraud counts before trial, and only quantum meruit went to the jury, with a special verdict addressing misrepresentation. The jury found fraud and assessed $801,333.06 for videotape exploitation of commentary plus $8,625.60 for other merchandise. The district court then concluded the equitable claim carried no right to a jury, vacated the verdict, and entered its own consistent findings and conclusions, awarding interest from filing but denying prefiling interest. On September 11, 1995 the Eighth Circuit affirmed in all respects; rehearing and rehearing en banc were denied October 26.
sections.Material Facts:
Titan's 1984 licensing arrangements led to toys and other merchandise, and its video agreements produced approximately ninety videotapes involving Ventura. He began wrestling under an oral agreement in spring 1984. After medical problems he returned as a commentator under a separate oral arrangement paying $1,000 weekly, with no discussion of videotape licenses or royalties. A written Wrestling Booking Agreement effective January 1, 1985 governed his resumed wrestling. He left in March 1986 for acting and returned later that year as a commentator under another oral agreement silent about videotape royalties.

In 1987 his agent, Barry Bloom, negotiated unsuccessfully with Titan's production partner, and then Titan's business-affairs vice president, Dick Glover, represented that royalties went only to performers featured in their own videotapes. Wanting the job, Ventura accepted commentary agreements waiving royalties; Bloom asked again in later annual negotiations and Glover repeated the policy. In fact Titan paid royalties to numerous wrestlers on tapes without a single featured performer. The district court credited Bloom and Ventura, found the representations false, and found Ventura would not have accepted the waiver had he known the truth.
sections.Issue: Under Minnesota law, could Ventura recover in quantum meruit for Titan's videotape use of his commentary despite his agreements with Titan, both for the period when the agreements were silent on royalties and for the period when he had expressly waived them? Was the denial of prefiling interest proper?
sections.Holding: The Eighth Circuit, in 1995, in an opinion by Judge Magill joined by Senior Judge John R. Gibson, with Judge Morris Sheppard Arnold dissenting in part, affirmed. For the earlier period, the commentary agreements did not cover videotape licenses, so they did not bar recovery for that distinct benefit. For 1987 to 1990, fraudulent inducement permitted avoidance of the royalty waiver and restitution of the reasonable royalty value. The court upheld the expert valuation evidence and the denial of prefiling interest. Recovery was sustained for commentary only, not for wrestling governed by the written agreement.
sections.Reasoning:
Under Minnesota law, receiving a benefit alone does not establish unjust enrichment. The majority identified a benefit beyond the labor Titan had paid for: intellectual-property interests generated by Ventura's performance. It predicted that Minnesota's supreme court would recognize a right of publicity, and Titan's unauthorized use of that interest could make retention unjust. A copyright-preemption issue was held waived, not rejected on the merits.

An express contract bars quasi-contractual recovery on the same subject matter but not necessarily for a distinct benefit it leaves unaddressed. The finding that the commentary agreements did not cover videotape licenses concerned contractual intent and survived clear-error review: the parties had not discussed the rights, and initially Ventura was unaware of the impending commercialization.

The later agreements expressly covered royalties, so silence could not support recovery. Although Ventura had not pleaded this misrepresentation under Rule 9(b), Titan's answer raised the express-contract defense, and the then-applicable Rule 8(d) treated it as denied or avoided, so he could introduce inducement evidence to defeat it. The repeated policy representations, inconsistent royalty payments and credited reliance evidence supported rescission.

Market licensing rates, shown through expert Weston Anson's survey, bore on the reasonable value of the benefit. Prefiling interest required a liquidated or readily ascertainable claim, and the royalty rate, sales base and other details were unsettled.

Arnold would have denied recovery for the period before Bloom's negotiations, finding the publicity-right prediction unsupported.

The casebook's account describes an approximately $800,000 jury award and omits the later vacatur and replacement by judicial findings.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-033.rule: No contract is formed, and no action lies on a check given in the transaction, where both parties understood the whole exchange as a jest and neither intended the stated purchase and sale.

sections.Parties: Holderman was the plaintiff; he sued Keller on a dishonored $300 check that Keller had drawn on a banker in Niles. Keller, the defendant, wrote the check and received a watch in the transaction. The case reached the Michigan Supreme Court by error after judgment against Keller. The casebook's account reverses the parties' roles; the original report confirms the roles stated here.
sections.Procedural History: The case was tried without a jury in the Berrien Circuit Court. The circuit judge found the transaction was banter but held Keller liable because he had omitted a condition from the check and kept the watch, and entered judgment for the amount of the check. On May 12, 1863 the Michigan Supreme Court reversed, with costs of both courts. The report does not order a new trial or award the watch's value.
sections.Material Facts: Keller gave Holderman a $300 check drawn on a banker in Niles for an old silver watch worth approximately $15. The circuit judge found that the entire transaction was playful banter: Holderman did not expect to sell the watch, and Keller did not intend to buy it at the check's stated price. Keller had no money with the banker and had meant to put a condition on the check preventing liability, but failed to insert it. The check was dishonored. Keller took the watch and kept it until trial, when he offered to return it and Holderman refused.
sections.Issue: Can the payee recover on a check given for a watch when the trial court has found that the whole transaction was a jest and that neither party intended the stated purchase and sale?
sections.Holding: The Michigan Supreme Court, in 1863, in an opinion by Chief Justice Martin in which the other justices concurred, held that the trial court's own finding of mutual banter required the opposite conclusion from the one it reached: no contract had been made, and Holderman had no cause of action on the check. The judgment was reversed.
sections.Reasoning:
The decisive point was the trial judge's express finding about both participants' understanding: neither contemplated the stated purchase and sale. The trial court had treated the absence of a condition on the check and Keller's retention of the watch as reasons for enforcement, but those were not findings of a serious bargain, and treating the check alone as dispositive overlooked the finding about the underlying transaction.

Because the reasoning rests on what both parties understood, the opinion does not establish that a party may escape a reasonably understood serious promise merely by asserting a secret intention to joke. Nor does it hold that a price far above market value invalidates a contract for inadequate consideration; the $300 figure and $15 value are part of the reported context only.

The casebook uses the case in a note on jesting and bluffing, and its hypothetical comparisons there are editorial, not holdings of the court.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-034.rule: An advertisement is ordinarily an invitation to make offers, not an offer, and whether a communication is an offer is judged by what an objective reasonable person would understand, so an evident joke creates no power of acceptance.

sections.Parties: John Leonard, who lived in Seattle, demanded that PepsiCo, Inc. deliver a Harrier jet shown in a television commercial for its points promotion, and also asserted fraud. PepsiCo denied that the commercial was a genuine offer. Leonard was the plaintiff in the action decided in the district court and the appellant in the Second Circuit; PepsiCo, which had first filed its own declaratory action, was the defendant and appellee.
sections.Procedural History: PepsiCo filed a declaratory action in New York in July 1996. Leonard sued in Florida in August; removal and transfer brought his action to New York. The declaratory case was initially dismissed for lack of personal jurisdiction. Leonard attempted a voluntary dismissal, which was conditioned on fees later set at $88,162, and instead resumed litigation. In February 1999 the parties dismissed the intervening appeals by stipulation, Leonard consented to jurisdiction, and PepsiCo agreed not to enforce the fee award. On August 5, 1999 the district court granted PepsiCo summary judgment. On April 17, 2000 the Second Circuit affirmed, substantially for the district court's reasons.
sections.Material Facts:
Pepsi's test-market promotion ran from October 1995 to March 1996 in the Pacific Northwest. Consumers collected points from marked packages and redeemed them for branded merchandise. The commercial showed a teenager wearing a shirt, leather jacket and sunglasses, each with its point price, and ended with him landing a Harrier beside his school, wind disrupting the classroom and stripping a teacher's clothes, and a screen stating a price of seven million points. The teenager remarked that this beat taking the bus. The ad referred viewers to the catalog and to package details.

The catalog's order form listed fifty-three items and no Harrier. It required an original order form and at least fifteen original points but let additional points be bought for ten cents each. Leonard raised approximately $700,000 through acquaintances and, around March 27, 1996, submitted fifteen points, a check for $700,008.50, and an order form on which he wrote in a Harrier. The fulfillment company returned the check in May, explaining that the jet was humorous advertising and not catalog merchandise. The plane's value was roughly $23 million.
sections.Issue: Was the commercial an offer that Leonard accepted by tendering points and money? Would an objective reasonable person have understood it as a genuine offer of a jet? Did any agreement satisfy the statute of frauds, and was there fraud?
sections.Holding: The Southern District of New York, in 1999, per Judge Kimba M. Wood, granted PepsiCo summary judgment, and the Second Circuit, in 2000, in a unanimous per curiam opinion by Judges Feinberg, Jacobs and Cynthia Holcomb Hall, affirmed. The commercial was not an offer; no objective reasonable viewer would understand it as a genuine offer of a jet; and the supposed agreement did not satisfy New York's statute of frauds. The fraud claim also failed. Neither court ordered delivery of a plane or awarded damages.
sections.Reasoning:
Advertisements ordinarily invite offers rather than confer a power of acceptance. A sufficiently definite advertisement can depart from that rule, as in Lefkowitz with its specified goods, time, limited quantity and first-come terms. Pepsi's commercial reserved the details to a separate catalog and prescribed no definite means of accepting a jet offer, so Leonard's order was an offer that Pepsi never accepted; the absence of limiting terms mattered because an unlimited commercial could expose a seller to acceptances beyond its inventory. Reward cases such as Carlill involved commitments inducing completion of an identified act, not an invitation to order merchandise subject to catalog conditions.

Formation turned on a reasonable interpretation of the ad, not on Pepsi's undisclosed intention or Leonard's sincere belief. A secretly intended joke may bind if it reasonably communicates a serious offer; an evident joke does not. The extraordinary school commute, youthful pilot, physical disruption, the aircraft's military purpose, and the gap between the plane's value and the cost of buying points made the scene an adolescent fantasy. This was a contextual assessment, not a rule that an unusually favorable price invalidates a bargain. Formation could be decided on summary judgment where reasonable people could not disagree, and further discovery would not change the objective meaning of the commercial.

UCC § 2-201 required a writing signed by the party charged for goods of $500 or more; the commercial was not such a writing and the order form lacked Pepsi's signature. The fraud claim identified no collateral misrepresentation of present fact.

The casebook's account gives the tender as $700,000, which is approximate.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-035.rule: A statement of the lowest price at which a vendor would sell does not itself establish a contract to sell at that price to the person asking; the inquirer's reply agreeing to buy is only an offer requiring acceptance.

sections.Parties: The appellants, solicitors practicing together in Kingston, Jamaica, were the would-be buyers of Bumper Hall Pen. They sought specific performance against L. M. Facey, alleging that he could bind his wife Adelaide in selling the property, and an injunction preventing the municipality from taking a conveyance. The respondents contested that any contract had been formed.
sections.Procedural History: Justice Curran dismissed the action because the asserted agreement disclosed no concluded contract. The Supreme Court on appeal instead found an agreement with Facey but held that his authority to sell without his wife's concurrence had not been established; it refused specific performance, awarded forty shillings damages against him, and awarded costs in both courts. The buyers obtained leave and additional special leave to appeal, and the order expressly permitted the respondents to contest formation without separate leave. The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council advised reversal of the Supreme Court's judgment and restoration of Curran's dismissal with costs, the buyers to pay the respondents' costs of both appeals.
sections.Material Facts: In early October 1891 Facey had negotiated with Kingston's Mayor and Council over Bumper Hall Pen, offering a sale for £900. The council discussed the proposal on October 6 and deferred acceptance. On October 7, while Facey was travelling by train from Kingston to Porus, the appellants sent him a telegram asking whether he would sell them the property and requesting his lowest cash price, with the answer paid. Facey answered that the lowest price was £900. The appellants' final telegram said they agreed to buy for that sum and requested the title deed so as to obtain early possession. All three messages were received.
sections.Issue: Whether Facey's telegram stating the lowest price for Bumper Hall Pen was an offer to sell that the buyers' third telegram accepted, so that a concluded contract existed, or whether the third telegram was itself only an offer that Facey never accepted.
sections.Holding: The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, in 1893, in advice delivered by Lord Morris with no separate writing or dissent, held that there was no concluded contract. A statement of the lowest price at which a vendor would sell did not itself establish a contract to sell at that price to the person asking. The buyers' third telegram was therefore an offer requiring Facey's acceptance, and that acceptance was absent. The decision rejected the existence of a contract; it did not find a valid contract for which specific performance happened to be unavailable.
sections.Reasoning:
The initial telegram contained two distinct questions: whether Facey was willing to sell to these buyers, and what his lowest price was. The placement of the request to telegraph directed it to the price question, and Facey answered that question alone. His answer did not also communicate an unconditional willingness to sell to the inquirers, and the committee refused to imply such a commitment merely because the buyers wanted that inference.

The third telegram was accordingly an offer, not an acceptance completing a sale already offered by Facey, and the necessary acceptance was missing. The lesson concerns the distinction between a communicated price and a commitment empowering the recipient to conclude a bargain; the committee did not declare that price quotations can never be offers in other contexts. Because the formation point disposed of the case, the committee did not address further defenses, including Facey's alleged authority to bind his wife.

The casebook's summary omits the intermediate forty-shilling damages award and the provision in the appeal order permitting a formation challenge.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-036.rule: A person who fills an order addressed to someone else without disclosing the substitution acquires no contract with the buyer and cannot sue for the price, because the buyer intended to deal with the addressee.

sections.Parties: Boulton, the plaintiff, had bought the business of Brocklehurst, a manufacturer of leather pipe hose, and sued for the price of goods he supplied. The defendants, Jones and another, were customers who had regularly dealt with Brocklehurst; they pleaded that they were never indebted and sought entry of a verdict in their favor.
sections.Procedural History: The action was tried in Liverpool's Court of Passage, where the jury found for Boulton under the Assessor's direction, with leave reserved for the defendants to seek entry of a verdict in their favor. Mellish obtained a rule nisi, and counsel argued whether the defendants' receipt and retention of Boulton's goods could support the price action. On November 25, 1857, the Court of Exchequer made the rule absolute to enter a verdict for the defendants, so the verdict for the supplier did not stand.
sections.Material Facts: Boulton had served as foreman and manager for Brocklehurst. The defendants regularly dealt with Brocklehurst and had a running account with him. On the morning of January 13, 1857, Boulton bought and paid for the stock, fixtures, and business. That afternoon the defendants' servant delivered a written order addressed to Brocklehurst for three fifty-foot lengths of leather hose. Boulton supplied them without notifying the defendants of the change in supplier, and his bookkeeper struck Brocklehurst's name from the order and substituted Boulton's. When an invoice in Boulton's name arrived, the defendants replied that they knew nothing of him. The defendants had a set-off available against Brocklehurst.
sections.Issue: Whether a successor to a business who fills an order addressed to his predecessor, without telling the buyers of the change, has a contract with the buyers on which he can sue for the price, including by reason of their receipt and retention of the goods.
sections.Holding: The Court of Exchequer, in 1857, with Pollock C.B., Martin B., Bramwell B., and Channell B. each giving a short agreeing explanation, held that the plaintiff had not shown a contract with himself and made absolute the rule to enter a verdict for the defendants. The decision was not a new trial, an award of restitution, or a finding that an undisclosed principal could enforce the order. The court did not adjudicate every possible implied obligation or award the value of the goods outside the pleaded price action.
sections.Reasoning:
The pertinent question was who had contracted, not who owned the delivered goods. Boulton's counsel argued that the goods were his and that keeping them after notice of his ownership adopted a contract with him; the defendants answered that this was not an agency transaction, that the goods could have been used before the invoice came, and that a debt owed by Brocklehurst could not be set off against Boulton.

Pollock held that the written order disclosed an intention to deal with Brocklehurst, and that a successor could not acquire a contractual right simply by performing an order directed to someone else without disclosing the substitution. He suggested Brocklehurst might have adopted the supply and sued, but that was not this action. Martin likewise found no principal-and-agent arrangement and no contract with Boulton.

Bramwell stressed the practical prejudice: letting Boulton sue would deprive the defendants of their set-off against the party they intended to deal with. A counterparty's identity could matter because of personal skill, as in writing a book, or because of a financial adjustment available against that person. Channell required Boulton to establish an agreement with himself; he had executed an order to his predecessor without explaining the change, and by the time the invoice arrived the defendants might no longer have been able to return the goods, so receipt and nonreturn did not supply the missing assent.

The casebook labels the court the Exchequer Chamber, but the report supports the Court of Exchequer.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-037.rule: Whether a communication is an offer depends on what a reasonable person in the recipient's position would understand from the words and conduct in their full setting, not on the sender's undisclosed intention; a price quotation can be an offer in light of prior dealings.

sections.Parties: Southworth, a cattle rancher who owned adjoining land, was the plaintiff; he sought a declaration that Joseph and Arlene Oliver were obligated to sell him approximately 2,933 acres of ranch land in Oregon's Bear Valley. The Olivers, the defendants and appellants, denied that they had made a firm offer and said the land and their grazing permits were not offered separately.
sections.Procedural History: Southworth originally sought a declaration that the Olivers were obligated to sell. After a trial the court entered a decree of specific performance. The Olivers appealed on formation, acceptance and definiteness grounds and also filed a general demurrer in the Oregon Supreme Court asserting a statute-of-frauds defect for the first time. The Oregon Supreme Court affirmed the decree in 1978.
sections.Material Facts:
In 1976 the Olivers decided to sell some Bear Valley land and Forest Service grazing permits; for tax reasons the land sale had to provide installment payments. On May 20 Joseph approached Southworth, suggesting he would be interested in the land while a neighbor, Clyde Holliday, would be interested in the permits. They identified the land on a map without fixing price or terms; Joseph would determine the price while Southworth investigated financing. On June 13 Southworth telephoned; Joseph confirmed the plans and said he was awaiting the assessor's information, and Southworth said financing was ready.

A June 17 letter, drafted by Arlene and signed by Joseph, enclosed information on the ranch sales previously discussed. It identified approximately 2,933 acres near Seneca at a total of $324,419, with 29 percent down, the balance over five years at eight percent interest, and a sale date to be negotiated for December 1, 1976 or January 1, 1977. It separately listed two grazing permits. The material went to Southworth, Holliday and two other neighbors. On June 21 Southworth sent a letter accepting the offer for the Bear Valley land. On June 24 the Olivers denied making a firm offer and said the property and permits were not offered separately.
sections.Issue: Was the June 17 letter an offer to sell the land that Southworth could accept, although it called its enclosures information, omitted the word offer, and went to four neighbors? Did a land-only acceptance conclude a contract? Was the contract definite enough for specific performance without agreed security provisions, and could the statute of frauds be raised first on appeal?
sections.Holding: The Oregon Supreme Court, in 1978, in an opinion by Tongue for the five-member participating court with no separate opinion, held that the prior negotiations and definite sale terms made the letter an offer to Southworth, which he accepted. He could reasonably understand the land as separately available from the permits. The missing security provisions were subordinate details equity could supply. The statute-of-frauds objection failed because it was raised for the first time in the Supreme Court, not because the court found the writing sufficient.
sections.Reasoning:
The court asked what a reasonable person in Southworth's position would understand. A quotation standing alone ordinarily is not an offer, but surrounding circumstances can make it one, and distribution to several recipients is relevant, not a categorical bar. Here the letter did not arrive unexpectedly: Joseph had sought out Southworth, identified the tract, undertaken to determine its price, and been told financing was arranged. The enclosure then supplied the price and definite installment terms for the mapped property, and it went to four specific neighbors rather than an indefinite public. The labels used and the omitted word did not outweigh those dealings, and the sellers' undisclosed intention could not control.

On acceptance, the decisive point was the earlier discussion that Holliday might take the permits while Southworth took the land, so the land-only response accepted a separate land offer rather than counteroffering.

On definiteness, the court distinguished an earlier case where the buyer could not force the seller to take installments. Southworth's bargain required a down payment and five years of installments. Equity may make subordinate details certain within reasonable limits when the parties have sufficiently manifested an intent to contract; the decree called for a standard printed installment land-sale contract with customary security terms.

The statute of frauds can be waived, and an objection below could have let the plaintiff plead and prove facts overcoming it, so it could not be raised first on appeal. The court declined to decide whether the circumstances showed ratification, waiver or estoppel.

The casebook presents the case as a problem with hypothetical variations.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-038.rule: A letter quoting prices and inviting orders, without committing to sell any particular quantity, is a solicitation rather than an offer, so an order sent in response does not by itself form a contract.

sections.Parties: Moulton, a salt dealer in La Crosse, was the plaintiff and buyer; he sought $800 in damages for the refusal to deliver salt he had ordered. Kershaw and Son, salt dealers in Milwaukee, were the defendants and sellers; they demurred to the complaint and appealed when the demurrer was overruled.
sections.Procedural History: Moulton sued for damages. The defendants filed a general demurrer, which the circuit court overruled, and they appealed. The Wisconsin Supreme Court reversed the order overruling the demurrer and remanded for further proceedings according to law. This was a decision on the sufficiency of the complaint; the court did not award damages or report a final damages judgment for either party.
sections.Material Facts:
As the complaint alleged, Kershaw and Son dealt in salt, including Michigan Salt Association salt, and knew Moulton customarily bought large quantities. Their letter of September 19, 1882 described an opportunity arising from a rupture in the salt trade. It said they were authorized to offer Michigan fine salt in carloads of eighty to ninety-five barrels, delivered in his city at eighty-five cents a barrel, shipped only over the Chicago and North Western railroad. It called the price a bargain and said they would be pleased to receive his order.

Moulton received the letter September 20 and telegraphed an order for 2,000 barrels on the stated terms, asking for an answer. He alleged this was a reasonable quantity the defendants could expect given his business. On September 21 they notified him that they were withdrawing their supposed offer. He demanded delivery and offered payment; they refused.
sections.Issue: Was the sellers' letter an offer to sell any reasonable quantity of salt that the buyer could accept by telegraphing an order, or only a solicitation of orders?
sections.Holding: The Wisconsin Supreme Court, in 1884, in an opinion by Taylor with no separate writing, held that the letter solicited orders rather than making an offer that bound the sellers on the buyer's response. Because the letter was not an offer, the telegraphed order did not by itself perfect a contract, and the complaint did not show one; the demurrer should have been sustained. The court expressly declined to hold that a seller can never make a binding offer leaving quantity for the buyer to specify.
sections.Reasoning:
The correspondence was the only basis for the asserted contract. The buyer read the letter as an offer to furnish any reasonable quantity, not less than a carload, that the sellers could anticipate he would order. The court rejected that reading because no such commitment was expressed in the writings: whether an order was reasonably anticipated would require examining both businesses in each case, making the obligation depend on evidence outside the correspondence. The court also invoked the then-applicable statute of frauds for sales of personal property over $50 and would not add a contractual commitment by parol evidence.

The alternative literal reading, an offer to fill any quantity of at least one carload, was one the buyer's own counsel did not insist on. It was more reasonable to read the letter as notice that the sellers could supply salt at the stated prices and an invitation to deal. Although the letter used the word offer, it did not say the defendants offered to sell this buyer a particular quantity, any quantity he chose, or a reasonable quantity; its general language, price comparison and request for an order resembled an advertisement or circular to the trade.

The court added that had the letter promised to sell all the Michigan fine salt the buyer ordered on the stated terms, a timely order could have bound the sellers. It contrasted a grape-sale case in which the seller offered as many grapes from the year's crop as the purchaser wished, so that quantity selection was expressly delegated and the crop bounded the undertaking.

The casebook presents the case with teaching variations on the quantity term.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-039.rule: An arrangement among friends for a social outing does not manifest a bargained-for exchange and is not a contract, so a passenger on such a trip remains a guest under an automobile guest statute.

sections.Parties: Harry Mitzel, the plaintiff and appellant, was injured while riding in a car owned and driven by his friend Ronald Hauck, the defendant. Both were seventeen at the time of the accident and each appeared through a guardian ad litem. Mitzel sought damages for personal injury and tried to avoid the automobile guest statute by characterizing the trip arrangement as a contract.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court directed a verdict for Hauck at the close of the plaintiff's evidence. The South Dakota Supreme Court, in 1960, affirmed the directed verdict and judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
Five young men discussed a Sunday duck-hunting trip. Mitzel testified that he offered to use his car, but Hauck said they would use his. Mitzel then agreed to forgo work at his brother's place that afternoon and go with Hauck to look for ducks, giving his time in exchange for Hauck's taking the car. Mitzel testified that before trial he disaffirmed the agreement.

The guest statute denied an action to a person transported as a guest without compensation unless willful and wanton misconduct caused the injury. Mitzel's evidence showed a speed of approximately seventy miles per hour on a normal gravel road, rising to about seventy-four as the car approached a gradual grade. He told Hauck to take it easy. The grade hid an unmarked curve; when it came into view Mitzel shouted a warning. Hauck braked 156 feet before the turn, but according to Mitzel the brakes did not hold much. The car went through a barbed-wire fence and stopped 104 feet into a field. There was testimony that Hauck had earlier said he would get his brakes fixed and had not.
sections.Issue: Did the friends' arrangement for the hunting trip create a contract that took Mitzel out of the guest statute? Could he, as a minor, avoid guest status by disaffirming? Did his evidence show the willful and wanton misconduct a guest must prove?
sections.Holding: The South Dakota Supreme Court, in 1960, in an opinion by Biegelmeier in which all judges concurred, held that the arrangement for the hunting trip did not create a commercial bargain removing Mitzel from the guest statute, that he could not avoid the statutory classification by disaffirming a supposed contract made while a minor, and that his evidence failed to establish willful and wanton misconduct. The court did not hold that driving at seventy-four miles per hour was necessarily nonnegligent.
sections.Reasoning:
Not every agreement contemplates legally enforceable rights and duties. The court looked to the surrounding circumstances and manifestations of assent, expressly rejecting any requirement of a subjective meeting of minds. It discussed family relationships and mutually understood jokes as settings where an apparent arrangement lacks the manifestation of a bargain. It addressed Williston's suggestion that social engagements could be contracts when the ordinary requisites exist, doubted its support, and emphasized the accompanying explanation that such parties typically do not manifest an exchange of a promise for agreed consideration. The evidence showed an enjoyable pastime arising from friendship, not a commercial transaction; looking for ducks and accompanying a friend were benefits compatible with hospitality and companionship, and forgoing an afternoon's work did not make the arrangement a contractual exchange.

Because there was no such contract, the statute permitting minors to disaffirm contracts did not apply. The court added that on one version of Mitzel's theory, disaffirming the bargain that made him a compensated passenger would return him to guest status. Cases on very young children who could not choose to accept a ride did not help him: he was nearly eighteen, a high-school graduate, and owned and drove a car, and his contractual disability did not exclude him from the guest category.

On misconduct, Hauck had no prior knowledge or warning of the curve, the road appeared wide and maintained, there was no evidence of earlier careless driving, and Mitzel's opinion about the brakes did not supply the required reckless state of mind.

The casebook's note focuses on the absence of a binding social bargain.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-040.rule: Under New York law parties who contemplate a later formal writing are bound beforehand if their objective manifestations show intent to be bound, judged by any express reservation, partial performance, agreement on essential terms, and whether such a deal is ordinarily put in writing.

sections.Parties: Pennzoil Co. was the plaintiff; it claimed that Texaco, Inc. knowingly interfered with Pennzoil's agreement with Getty Oil, the Sarah C. Getty Trust, and the J. Paul Getty Museum by inducing them to deal with Texaco instead. Texaco, the defendant and appellant, denied that a binding agreement existed or that it knew of one, and attacked the jury charge, evidentiary rulings, the fairness of the trial, and the damages.
sections.Procedural History: Pennzoil sued and obtained a Texas jury judgment against Texaco for $7.53 billion in compensatory and $3 billion in punitive damages. Texaco appealed to the Texas Court of Appeals in Houston, First District; the parties agreed that New York substantive law and Texas procedural law governed. The court rejected Texaco's challenges except on the size of punitive damages. Its disposition was conditional: if Pennzoil filed a $2 billion remittitur within thirty days, the judgment would be reformed and affirmed for $7.53 billion compensatory and $1 billion exemplary damages; otherwise it would be reversed and remanded. The report notes later denials of rehearing.
sections.Material Facts:
Gordon Getty, as trustee, controlled approximately 40.2 percent of Getty Oil's shares, and the Museum approximately 11.8 percent. Pennzoil began with a public tender offer at $100 per share in late December 1983. A memorandum negotiated around January 1 and 2 proposed that Pennzoil acquire a three-sevenths interest and the Trust keep four-sevenths, with the Museum's shares acquired; Gordon, the Museum and Pennzoil signed it, but Getty Oil did not, and its board initially rejected the price. On January 3 the board voted fifteen to one for a proposal of $110 per share plus a $5 deferred payment; Pennzoil's chief executive, Hugh Liedtke, accepted, and acceptance was communicated to the board before it adjourned. Getty's January 4 press release described an agreement in principle, subject to execution of a definitive merger agreement, shareholder approval and regulatory requirements. Lawyers continued drafting.

Meanwhile Getty Oil's investment banker solicited other bidders. Texaco's advisers assessed how to stop the Pennzoil transaction, identifying the Museum as a crucial initial target. Texaco offered a higher price, obtained agreements with the Museum and the Trust, and arranged a merger with Getty Oil. The Museum required protection against claims arising from the Pennzoil transaction. Getty Oil withdrew from the Pennzoil arrangement.
sections.Issue: Was there sufficient evidence that Pennzoil and the Getty entities intended to be bound at the end of the January 3 board meeting, before a definitive agreement was signed? Did Texaco knowingly induce a breach of that agreement? Were the compensatory and punitive damages proper?
sections.Holding: The Texas Court of Appeals, in 1987, in an opinion by Justice Warren for a three-judge panel, sustained the jury's finding of a binding agreement and rejected the claim of indefiniteness; found legally and factually sufficient evidence of knowing interference and active inducement; and upheld the $7.53 billion in compensatory damages. It held punitive damages legally available but concluded that $1 billion sufficed and $2 billion was excessive, producing the conditional remittitur. Several of Texaco's defenses, including mutual mistake and the statute of frauds, failed on procedural grounds rather than on the merits.
sections.Reasoning:
Under the New York law applied, intent to be bound depends on objective manifestations in context. An express reservation against obligation before execution can be decisive; absent one, anticipating a later writing does not necessarily prevent present agreement. The court considered four factors, none automatically controlling. First, neither the memorandum nor the press release conclusively reserved all obligation until formal execution; language about a definitive merger agreement could describe conditions to consummation rather than formation, and the meaning of agreement in principle was contested, so the jury could choose between interpretations. Second, there was little partial performance, but only a short interval separated the claimed agreement and Getty's withdrawal. Third, evidence supported agreement on the essentials: ownership proportions, price, the Museum's sale, and the restructuring-or-division framework. Fourth, the transaction's size and complexity favored expecting a formal document, a substantial but not conclusive consideration.

Knowing interference required knowledge of the facts giving rise to the contractual duty, not a correct legal conclusion that they created a contract, so lawyers' assurances that the arrangement was nonbinding did not defeat liability. Inducement required more than signing with someone known to have another contract; the evidence showed active persuasion through planning, favorable terms and protections.

Damages for interference allowed the pecuniary loss of contractual benefits. Pennzoil's experts used a replacement-cost model, 1.008 billion barrels multiplied by a $7.47 difference per barrel, and Texaco offered no competing expert. Advice of counsel was a factor for the jury on punitive damages, not an automatic bar.

The casebook's note adds a later bankruptcy and $3 billion settlement, which are editorial subsequent history.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-041.rule: A store advertisement stating a sale price is an invitation to negotiate rather than an offer a shopper can accept, although a materially misleading advertisement may still give rise to statutory liability without proof of intent to deceive.

sections.Parties: Judith Geismar, the claimant, appeared without counsel in a small-claims action and sought $280 from Abraham & Straus, a department store, the defendant, which had refused to sell her a set of china at the sale price stated in its newspaper advertisement.
sections.Procedural History: This is the trial court's own small-claims decision, not an appellate ruling. On June 8, 1981 the District Court of Suffolk County, New York rejected recovery for breach of contract and found no proved actual damages, but entered judgment for Geismar for the $50 statutory minimum under the false-advertising provisions of the General Business Law.
sections.Material Facts: On February 11, 1981 Abraham & Straus placed a full-page advertisement in Newsday. A bold heading advertised discounts of forty to fifty percent on Mikasa, Sango and Yamaka china. Four sets appeared with regular and sale prices: a twenty-piece set reduced from $100 to $59.95; a forty-piece set from $140 to $59.95; a service for eight from $120 to $69.95; and the disputed service for twelve from $280 to $39.95. Geismar tried to buy the last set for $39.95, and the store refused. She sued for the entire stated regular price of $280. She did not prove that she had bought substitute dishes elsewhere and established no actual damages.
sections.Issue: Did the advertisement create a contract when Geismar offered to buy at the advertised price? If not, was the advertisement materially misleading under the General Business Law, and could she recover as an injured person without proving intent to deceive or actual damages?
sections.Holding: The District Court of Suffolk County, in 1981, per Judge Francis G. Caldeira, held that the advertisement was an invitation to negotiate rather than an offer a shopper could accept, so the contract claim failed. It held, however, that the advertisement was materially misleading, that the statute required no proof of intent to deceive for ordinary liability, and that a person misled could be an injured person without proving an actual financial loss. Geismar recovered the $50 statutory minimum; the court did not find or award the statutory enhancement for willful or knowing violation.
sections.Reasoning:
Applying the authorities it cited, the court characterized the advertisement as an invitation to negotiate, which disposed of the breach-of-contract theory. A seller's freedom from contractual liability did not make its public representations legally irrelevant. Article 22-A of the General Business Law prohibited false advertising through sections 350 and 350-a, and a provision effective June 19, 1980 let an injured person recover actual damages or $50, whichever was greater, with a discretionary enhanced award for a willful or knowing violation.

The definition of false advertising turned on whether an advertisement was misleading in a material respect, not on the advertiser's intent, and the separate enhancement for willful or knowing conduct reinforced that distinction. The unusually low price was not an obvious mistake that removed misleadingness: two listed discounts already exceeded the headline's fifty-percent ceiling, so a shopper could reasonably think the headline percentages inaccurate rather than assume the $39.95 price was an error. The court found materially misleading advertising without finding deliberate baiting or dishonesty.

On injury, limiting recovery to demonstrated monetary damages would frustrate the $50 minimum, and legislative and gubernatorial explanations identified encouragement of private suits as a purpose. The judge acknowledged the breadth of this construction and suggested legislative reconsideration. He also observed that the statutory questions had not been fully explored or argued in the small-claims proceeding.

The casebook uses the case in its account of consumer protection, contrasting the failed contract theory with the $50 statutory recovery.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-042.rule: Advertisements and general sales solicitations ordinarily invite offers; a customer's order sent in response is itself the offer, and no contract is formed until the seller accepts it.

sections.Parties: Mary and Anthony Mesaros, the plaintiffs and appellants, filed a putative class action, naming thirty-three other persons, against the United States over the Mint's failure to fill their credit-card order for commemorative gold coins. They sought damages for nondelivery or, alternatively, mandamus compelling the government to accept their order and deliver the coins. The government defendants moved to dismiss or for summary judgment.
sections.Procedural History: The plaintiffs sued in the Southern District of Georgia. On April 13, 1987 the district court granted the defendants' motion to dismiss or alternatively for summary judgment in its entirety and did not act on class certification, which was moot. The appeal went first to the Eleventh Circuit and was transferred to the Federal Circuit on the defendants' motion. On May 6, 1988 the Federal Circuit affirmed: summary judgment on the contract claim was proper, and the mandamus claim was properly dismissed for want of jurisdiction.
sections.Material Facts:
The July 1985 Statue of Liberty-Ellis Island Commemorative Coin Act authorized coin sales and limited production to 500,000 gold five-dollar coins; it directed the Secretary to accept prepaid orders before issuance at a discount. In November and December 1985 the Mint sent promotional materials to previous customers and collectors, including the plaintiffs, saying a reservation received by December 31 would qualify for a pre-issue discount. The order form asked the Mint to accept the purchaser's order, said sales were final, contemplated verification by the Mint, and reserved the right to limit shipments subject to availability. Credit-card processing, contracted to Mellon Bank, was slower than filling cash orders.

The plaintiffs alleged that Mary submitted an order on November 26, 1985 authorizing a $1,675 charge to Anthony's credit account. Anthony separately ordered eighteen more gold coins on December 30 using nine checks and family members' names; those arrived around May 1986. On February 18 the Mint wrote that it had tried but could not process the credit-card order. The plaintiffs' bank later confirmed it had authorized the transaction on December 27. Demand substantially exceeded the supply of gold coins, which sold out.
sections.Issue: Were the Mint's promotional materials an offer that the plaintiffs accepted by submitting their order, so that a contract was breached by nondelivery? Alternatively, did the Act impose a duty owed to the plaintiffs that could be enforced by mandamus?
sections.Holding: The Federal Circuit, in 1988, in an opinion by Senior Circuit Judge Skelton for a panel with Mayer and Baldwin and no separate writings, held that the promotional materials solicited offers, that the plaintiffs' order was an offer the government had not accepted, and that summary judgment on the contract claim was therefore proper. The statute imposed no duty owed to these purchasers to contract with them in any particular sequence, so the district court lacked mandamus jurisdiction. Class certification did not need to be decided.
sections.Reasoning:
The district court had Little Tucker Act jurisdiction over the pleaded contract claim, but that did not establish that a contract existed. The court applied an objective-reasonableness inquiry. Advertisements and general sales solicitations ordinarily invite offers; treating broadly distributed materials as commitments to every respondent could bind a seller beyond its supply. Congress had limited gold production, and the complete materials contemplated the Mint's later verification and acceptance. The form's request that the Mint accept the customer's order identified the order as the customer's offer.

The court distinguished Lefkowitz, which involved a specifically identified fur stole offered to the first customer at a designated opening time. The Mint's materials promised no first-come, first-served allocation or any equivalent basis binding it to every timely response, and the different payment methods made a chronological sales process impracticable. The holding concerned these materials; it did not rule out that a sufficiently definite advertisement could be an offer.

On mandamus, all authorized gold coins had been sold, and compelling further production would exceed the 500,000 statutory limit. The statute did not require contracts with these plaintiffs on a first-come, first-served basis or in any particular order; the Secretary had broad administrative discretion and the court found no abuse on this record.

The casebook raises the formation question in a problem that quotes only some of the order language.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-043.rule: A person who performs the act for which a private reward was offered cannot recover the reward unless he knew or had notice of the offer when he performed, because liability for the reward rests on contract.

sections.Parties: S. H. Broadnax, the plaintiff, claimed a $500 reward publicly offered by A. L. Ledbetter, the Dallas County sheriff, for the recapture of an escaped prisoner. Ledbetter, the defendant, demurred because the petition did not allege that Broadnax knew of the reward when he made the recapture. The casebook gives the sheriff's initials as A. H.; the original report says A. L.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court sustained Ledbetter's demurrers; Broadnax declined to amend, and the court dismissed his case with costs. On his appeal the Court of Civil Appeals for the Third District certified to the Texas Supreme Court the question whether knowledge or notice of the reward at the time of the recapture was essential to recovery. On February 27, 1907 the Texas Supreme Court answered yes. Its disposition was an answer to the certified question, not itself an affirmance.
sections.Material Facts: These are the petition's allegations, not findings. Holly Vann, convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death, escaped from the Dallas County jail on January 25, 1905 while his case was on appeal. Ledbetter publicly offered $500 to anyone who recaptured Vann and returned him to the Dallas County jail or another Texas jail or jailer. Broadnax alleged that, before the offer was revoked, he recaptured and returned Vann that evening and performed all stated conditions, and that payment was refused. The petition did not allege that he knew or had notice of the reward while recapturing and returning Vann.
sections.Issue: Is knowledge or notice of an offered reward, at the time the claimant performs the act for which it was offered, essential to his right to recover the reward?
sections.Holding: The Texas Supreme Court, in 1907, in an opinion by Associate Justice Williams, answered the certified question in the affirmative: knowledge or notice of the reward when the recapture occurred was essential to recovery. Ledbetter's liability as an individual promisor required a contract, and one who is ignorant of the offer cannot act in acceptance of it.
sections.Reasoning:
Broadnax argued that a public reward was a conditional promise binding once someone performed its conditions before revocation, and that knowledge was unnecessary because the offer did not make it a condition. Ledbetter answered that liability was contractual and knowledge essential to acceptance. The court acknowledged conflicting decisions in other states and adopted Ledbetter's position.

No general rule independently imposed payment of this privately offered reward, so any obligation had to arise through contract. An offer alone does not make a contract; the performer must accept, which a reward offer permits through the requested service. Someone ignorant of the offer could do the same physical acts but could not thereby accept, and performance without reference to the promise supplied neither assent nor the consideration the offer contemplated.

The court rejected two other explanations. Calling a reward a bounty or gratuity gave no legal basis to compel payment of a promised gift. Benefit to the offeror was not enough either, since the value of the acts is not the test of contractual responsibility; the promise had to induce the action. Knowledge of an offer is distinct from motive, which the court said might not be controlling. A supposed public policy of encouraging crime detection could not justify enforcing unknown private promises, because an unknown offer cannot stimulate conduct. The court reserved the different case of a government reward authorized by law, which might confer an entitlement independent of contract.

The casebook uses the case in its account of advertised rewards as offers, and its later hypotheticals about motive and later-acquired knowledge were not decided by the court.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-044.rule: An announced prize for a specified act is an offer for a unilateral contract, and performance with knowledge of the offer can accept it even if the performer did not act principally to obtain the reward.

sections.Parties: William and Viola Simmons sued the United States for a tax refund. They were the plaintiffs and the appellants; the federal government was the defendant, not the brewery that offered and paid the fishing prize. The Simmonses wanted back the balance of the tax paid on a $25,000 prize.
