sections.Procedural History: The Internal Revenue Service assessed a $5,230 deficiency on the ground that the payment was income under Internal Revenue Code sections 61(a) and 74(a). Simmons paid, sought a refund, and received a small refund based on deductions. He sued for the balance. The district court entered summary judgment for the government. On August 28, 1962, the Fourth Circuit affirmed.
sections.Material Facts:
American Brewery placed a tagged rockfish called Diamond Jim III in Chesapeake Bay on June 19, 1958, in cooperation with Maryland game officials. Its widely publicized Third Annual American Beer Fishing Derby promised $25,000 to whoever caught that fish and presented it with the tag and an affidavit that it had been caught on hook and line. Other tagged fish carried smaller prizes.

William Simmons caught Diamond Jim III on August 6. He initially paid little attention to the tag but recognized the prize fish when he looked again about half an hour later. He complied with the remaining conditions and received the money during a television appearance arranged by the brewery. He had known about the contest before fishing, but did not have the remote prospect of catching Diamond Jim in mind when he set out that morning.
sections.Issue: Whether the $25,000 prize was includable income, or was instead excluded as a civic achievement award under section 74(b) or as a gift under section 102, and whether it could constitutionally be taxed without apportionment. Within the gift question, the court considered whether the payment discharged an obligation under a reward contract.
sections.Holding: The Fourth Circuit in 1962, in an opinion by Chief Judge Sobeloff for a panel including Haynsworth and Boreman with no separate writing, affirmed summary judgment for the United States. It held that the $25,000 payment was taxable, did not qualify for the invoked statutory exclusions, and could constitutionally be taxed without apportionment. The reward-contract discussion was part of the analysis rejecting treatment of the payment as a gift; the court did not adjudicate a wagering-contract defense against the brewery.
sections.Reasoning:
On the achievement-award exclusion, the character of the recipient's achievement, not the donor's purpose, controlled. Civic achievement required positive, exemplary, unselfish action broadly beneficial to the community. Catching this fish was principally fortunate, and the facts could not reasonably support the requested jury finding.

Gift status turned on the donor's motivation under Duberstein. There was no personal relationship between Simmons and the brewery and no need-based charitable payment, and the publicized award supplied the publicity the brewery sought. Contract principles reinforced the conclusion. In the absence of pertinent Maryland decisions, the court reasoned that an announced prize for a specified act is an offer for a unilateral contract, and performance with knowledge of the offer can accept it. The performer need not act principally to obtain the reward: Simmons knew of the Derby, and his unrelated reason for going fishing did not prevent acceptance. A payment discharging the resulting obligation was not a gift.

The court qualified enforceability: the arrangement might be attacked as a wagering contract, which Maryland law did not clearly resolve. Even if the promise were unenforceable, advertising created a strong moral duty to pay, and a payment proceeding principally from moral or legal constraint was not a gift.

On the Constitution, the court characterized the tax as an indirect tax on receipt of money; alternatively, the receipt was income within the Sixteenth Amendment.

The casebook uses the case to contrast knowledge of the contest with the fisherman's immediate motive and to ask why Simmons, rather than the brewery, called the prize a gift.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-045.rule: A bidder bound by an irrevocable bid may rescind for a material clerical mistake not resulting from neglect of a legal duty if enforcement would be unconscionable, the other party can be restored to the status quo, and the bidder rescinds promptly.

sections.Parties: The Elsinore Union Elementary School District, plaintiff, sued contractor E. J. Kastorff and his surety for damages after Kastorff refused to execute a building contract at his submitted bid. The district sought the difference between his bid and the replacement contract, and the bid-bond amount from the surety. Kastorff and the surety, defendants, were the appellants; Kastorff pleaded honest error, prompt notice, and rescission.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court acknowledged the worksheets and an omission in transferring the plumbing and heating figures, but made adverse findings: the use of the totals column could not be ascertained, the district did not know the submitted bid differed from the intended bid, enforcing it would not be inequitable, and Kastorff had ample time to check his figures. It entered judgment for the district in the amounts sought, $12,906 against Kastorff and $4,499.60 against his surety. The contractor and surety appealed. The California Supreme Court, sitting in bank, reversed the judgment on July 1, 1960.
sections.Material Facts:
The district invited bids for additions to its school buildings, due at 8 p.m. on August 12, 1952. Kastorff received a plumbing bid for $9,285 in the afternoon and later another for $6,500. Believing the first amount was already in his total, he deducted approximately $3,000. In fact he had carried neither plumbing figure into the total, so his $89,994 bid contained no allowance for plumbing. The bid was $11,306 below the next lowest of five bids. Asked by the superintendent and four board members whether his figures were correct, Kastorff, who did not have his worksheets with him, confirmed them, and the board voted that evening to award him the contract.

The next morning Kastorff discovered the error and showed the worksheets to Rendon at the architects' office, who telephoned the superintendent that morning with Kastorff's request for release. Kastorff wrote to the board on August 14; on August 15 the board declined. Written notice of the award arrived August 28, and Kastorff returned the formal contract on September 8 with another request to withdraw. The published invitation purported to prohibit withdrawal for forty-five days. The district received additional bids and contracted with the lowest new bidder for $102,900. Kastorff's pleaded intended total was $99,494.
sections.Issue: Whether a contractor who submitted a bid subject to a nonwithdrawal condition, and who confirmed his figures at the bid opening, could rescind the bid for an honest clerical omission that he discovered and reported the next day, so as to be relieved of liability for refusing to execute the contract.
sections.Holding: The California Supreme Court in 1960, in an opinion by Justice Schauer in which Chief Justice Gibson and Justices Traynor, McComb, Peters, White, and Dooling concurred, unanimous among the seven participating justices, held that the honest clerical error and prompt rescission relieved Kastorff from the obligation to execute the contract, and reversed the judgment. It did not award reformation to substitute a higher bid or direct performance at a judicially chosen price. The court expressly reserved whether, following the rescission, the district could have accepted the original next-lowest bid before the forty-five days expired.
sections.Reasoning:
Relying on Kemper and Lemoge, the court said that a bid subject to a nonwithdrawal condition, once opened and declared, could function as an irrevocable option that ordinary unilateral withdrawal could not destroy. The bidder could nevertheless rescind if the requirements for equitable relief were met: the mistake must be material and not result from neglect of a legal duty; enforcement must be unconscionable; the other party must be capable of restoration to the status quo; and the mistaken party must promptly elect rescission and restore or offer to restore any value received. Knowledge, or reason to know, of the other party's mistake supported relief rather than a right to exploit it. Ordinary carelessness was not invariably the neglect of legal duty that defeated rescission.

The court found certain trial findings unsupported and others immaterial. The worksheets, which the court inspected itself, and uncontradicted testimony, including from the district's own architect, superintendent, and board member, established the clerical mechanism and the board's receipt of notice. Mere time and opportunity to check did not establish neglect of a legal duty. Kastorff's assurance at bid opening did not bar relief: he had no worksheets then, checked them at the earliest practicable opportunity, and promptly notified the district. The district's August 15 refusal came with knowledge of the asserted error, and the written notification came about two weeks after rescission. The district had no legitimate expectation of plumbing without charge. Whether the omission was $6,500 or $9,285, it was material relative to $89,994. Prompt withdrawal, unlike the performance followed by a reformation request in Lemoge, was central.

The brief notes that the casebook's statement that the court agreed with favorable trial findings about Kastorff is inaccurate, and that the later public-contract statute in the casebook notes was enacted after this decision.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-046.rule: Rescission for a unilateral material mistake is ordinarily unavailable where the mistaken party failed to exercise ordinary diligence or where relief would seriously prejudice the other party beyond loss of its bargain.

sections.Parties: Heifetz Metal Crafts, Inc., a kitchen-equipment subcontractor, sued general contractor Peter Kiewit Sons' Co. to rescind and cancel a subcontract on a Veterans Hospital construction project in Topeka, Kansas. Kiewit counterclaimed for breach and joined Heifetz's performance-bond surety. Heifetz and the surety were the appellants; Kiewit was the appellee.
sections.Procedural History: After a nonjury trial, the trial court denied rescission and awarded Kiewit $50,100. It found that Heifetz's president participated in selecting the plans and was responsible for the mistaken judgment, that disregarding the available specifications was a failure of due diligence, that Kiewit neither knew nor was chargeable with knowledge of the error, and that Kiewit had relied in good faith. Heifetz and the surety appealed. The Eighth Circuit affirmed on March 5, 1959; rehearing was denied April 6.
sections.Material Facts:
On bid-opening day Heifetz, with which Kiewit had never dealt, telephoned and volunteered a $99,500 quotation for the kitchen-equipment work, $52,000 below Kiewit's next lowest quotation. Kiewit specifically asked whether the figure conformed to the plans and specifications. Heifetz confirmed that it did, that it would remain firm, and that the same quotation was being given to all competing general contractors. Kiewit reduced its own general bid by $52,000 and won the $17,942,200 project by $9,000; without the reduction it would not have been the lowest bidder.

Kiewit obtained written confirmation, and several weeks later the parties executed a formal subcontract at the quoted amount. When drawings were requested, the mistake emerged: Heifetz had estimated only the principal kitchen in Building 20, although smaller installations were required in several other buildings. Heifetz's president had obtained Building 20's two blueprint sheets from another general contractor together with section 502 of the specifications, which revealed that multiple buildings were involved; no one at Heifetz checked the quote on that point. Other trades on the same project also showed significant spreads between quotations. After Heifetz refused to perform, Kiewit had to pay $50,100 more to another subcontractor.
sections.Issue: Whether a subcontractor that underbid because it estimated only part of the work could rescind the executed subcontract for its unilateral mistake, where the general contractor had relied on the quotation in its own bid and was found not to know or have reason to know of the error.
sections.Holding: The Eighth Circuit in 1959, in an opinion by Circuit Judge Johnsen for a panel with Sanborn and Van Oosterhout and no separate opinion, affirmed the judgment denying rescission and awarding Kiewit $50,100. Heifetz failed both because it was responsible for the error and because rescission would prejudice Kiewit. The holding concerns rescission of the actual executed subcontract and the breach counterclaim; the court did not decide a standalone promissory-estoppel claim on an unaccepted subcontract bid, and noted the bidding representations might have had a different legal consequence had no contract later been executed.
sections.Reasoning:
The court reviewed the nonjury findings for clear error and found substantial support for them, with added deference to credibility and good-faith evaluations. Kiewit's actual reduction of its own bid and its failure immediately to lock Heifetz into a contract supported the finding that it was not trying to exploit a suspected mistake. Kiewit's employees saw a substantial price difference but no reason to attribute it to a mistake, especially after the express assurance; the price disparity was evidence assessed in context, not a rule that low bids never impose a duty of inquiry.

The court did not need to choose between Nebraska and Kansas law because the rescission principles were the same. Equitable relief from a unilateral material mistake could be available where enforcement would be unconscionable, the mistaken party exercised ordinary diligence, and relief would not seriously prejudice the other party beyond loss of its bargain. A failure of reasonably expected diligence ordinarily would not justify rescission without some additional equitable consideration.

The available specifications could have revealed the omission. Independently, even if Heifetz had been faultless, its volunteered quotation and assurance caused Kiewit to reduce its general bid, and rescission would shift the $50,100 burden onto a party without knowledge or bad faith. Restoring the parties' former positions was central to rescission; where that was impossible, only the strongest equities could justify relief. The argument that Kiewit could absorb the loss from profit failed: there was no evidence of any profit, and Kiewit had passed the low quotation into its own bid.

The casebook note presents the bid difference and the rejection of constructive knowledge.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-047.rule: As this intermediate court reasoned before it was reversed, a dealer's advertisement of one identified car at a stated price, read with the advertised-price statute, is an offer accepted by tender, and a good-faith unilateral mistake does not necessarily erase it.

sections.Parties: Donovan, a prospective car buyer, sued RRL Corporation, whose dealership was Lexus of Westminster, after the dealer refused to sell him a used Jaguar at its advertised price. Donovan was the plaintiff; RRL, the defendant, relied on mistake.
sections.Procedural History: Donovan sued in municipal court. After a bench trial, that court found that the advertisement could produce a contract upon tender, that a good-faith unilateral mistake negated contractual intent, and that Donovan did not know of the mistake; it entered judgment for the dealer. The superior court's appellate division reversed, relying on Vehicle Code section 11713.1(e) and on Germain's allocation of mistaken transmission risk. Following certification, the Court of Appeal transferred the case for hearing and decision. On August 23, 1999, the Fourth District, Division Three, reversed the judgment for the dealer and remanded to the trial court to determine Donovan's damages, awarding him appellate costs. The California Supreme Court subsequently reversed this decision in 2001; this entry covers only the intermediate court's reasoning, not the final disposition.
sections.Material Facts:
Donovan saw a Saturday Daily Pilot advertisement listing a particular 1995 Jaguar XJ6 Vanden Plas, identified by VIN 720603, for $25,995. The next day he and his wife visited the dealership, found the car, and test-drove it. Donovan then said he would buy it for the advertised price. A representative immediately responded that the price was a mistake. Donovan accused the dealer of bait-and-switch advertising and offered to write a check for the full advertised price; the sales manager instead offered to sell for $37,016. Donovan declined and left.

The advertisement resulted from a newspaper error. The dealer had advertised the 1995 car without a price. On Tuesday its advertising manager requested another run of that advertisement; on Thursday she requested a replacement advertisement for a 1994 Jaguar XJ6 priced at $25,995. The newspaper's composing room combined the 1995 vehicle with the 1994 vehicle's price. The advertising manager did not review a proof because she did not work Fridays, when the advertisement went to press.
sections.Issue: Whether a newspaper advertisement for a specific used car at a stated price was an offer that the buyer accepted by attempting to tender the price, and whether the dealer's good-faith unilateral mistake in the advertised price defeated the contract.
sections.Holding: The California Court of Appeal, Fourth District, Division Three, in 1999, in an opinion by Justice Rylaarsdam in which Presiding Justice Sills and Justice Crosby concurred, held that the sufficiently specific used-car advertisement, read in light of California's advertised-price statute, was an offer accepted by the buyer's attempted tender. It rejected the dealer's mistake defense and itself found the dealer negligent in failing to check the advertising proof. It did not award a specified damage sum or order delivery of the car, and it did not hold that every price advertisement is an offer.
sections.Reasoning:
The court acknowledged the ordinary rule that advertisements invite bargaining. The exception requires sufficient commitment and sufficiently definite requested action without further negotiation. This advertisement identified one unique car and a price, and nothing on its face told a buyer to do more than tender the price; only one buyer could accept. Unilateral versus bilateral classification was not decisive, the dealer's refusal excused actual presentation of the money under Civil Code section 1440, and the prospect of a later written sales agreement did not necessarily prevent present formation. The court called the offer question close and relied on the advertised-price statute to tip the balance.

On the statute, the dealer did not intend the erroneous advertisement but knowingly refused the requested advertised-price sale; the statute protects the public from irresponsible as well as unscrupulous dealers. The court rejected a newspaper amicus's First Amendment objection.

On mistake, the court accepted the good-faith finding but disagreed that unilateral mistake necessarily erased the offer. It distinguished Kemper, where the accepting city already knew of the bidder's clerical mistake, and invoked objective-contract reasoning. It expressly avoided deciding whether the newspaper was the dealer's agent. Instead, using Code of Civil Procedure section 909, which allows appellate factual determinations in a case tried without a jury, it found that the advertising manager's failure to take the opportunity to review the proof was negligent, given the advertising duties imposed on automobile dealers.

The casebook's account of the case includes the stated 2001 reversal.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-048.rule: A party may rescind for a good-faith unilateral mistake of fact the other party neither caused nor had reason to know of, if the mistake concerns a basic assumption, materially affects the exchange, the mistaken party does not bear the risk, and enforcement would be unconscionable.

sections.Parties: Donovan, a prospective buyer, sued RRL Corporation, an automobile dealer, for refusing to sell him a used Jaguar at the price printed in a newspaper advertisement. Donovan was the plaintiff and had prevailed in the Court of Appeal; RRL was the defendant and had won at trial. Donovan claimed breach of contract; RRL maintained that the advertised price was a mistake.
sections.Procedural History: Donovan sued for contract breach, fraud, and negligence. The municipal court disallowed the negligence cause of action, found a good-faith mistake without deceptive intent and that Donovan was unaware of the mistake, and entered judgment for RRL, reasoning that the mistaken price negated contractual intent. Donovan confined his appeal to contract breach. The superior court's appellate department reversed and directed calculation of damages. The Court of Appeal likewise reversed after transfer, treating the advertisement as an offer and finding RRL negligent under its appellate factfinding authority. The California Supreme Court granted review and requested briefing on the applicable Uniform Commercial Code provisions. On July 30, 2001, as modified September 12, 2001, it reversed the Court of Appeal, concluding that the municipal court correctly entered judgment for the dealer. Rehearing was denied; Werdegar and Baxter favored rehearing.
sections.Material Facts:
The April 26, 1997 Daily Pilot advertisement announced a two-day used-car sale and identified a sapphire-blue 1995 Jaguar XJ6 Vanden Plas by its vehicle identification number at $25,995. It displayed the dealer's name and address, listed fifteen other cars, and expired April 27. Donovan visited a Jaguar dealership on April 26, where other 1995 Jaguars were priced $8,000 to $10,000 higher. At RRL's dealership the next day he verified the identification number and test-drove the car with his spouse. When he offered to buy at about $26,000 and showed the advertisement, the salesperson immediately identified the mistake.

The sales manager apologized and offered reimbursement for Donovan's fuel, time, and effort. Donovan declined, asserted there had been no mistake, and offered a check for the advertised price. The manager refused and offered $37,016, based on RRL's $35,000 investment. RRL later advertised the car at an intended price of $37,995 and sold it for $38,399. The intended advertisement had been for a different, 1994 Jaguar at $25,995; the newspaper inserted that price but failed to replace the 1995 vehicle description. Its staff made typesetting and proofreading errors and acknowledged them in a retraction. RRL did not check the revised proof. Its other newspaper advertisements correctly described the 1994 vehicle.
sections.Issue: Whether a dealer's advertisement for a specific used car at a stated price was an offer accepted by the customer's tender and a sufficient writing under the statute of frauds, and, if so, whether the dealer could rescind the resulting contract for its good-faith unilateral mistake about the advertised price.
sections.Holding: The California Supreme Court in 2001, in an opinion by Chief Justice George for himself and Justices Kennard, Chin, and Brown, with Justice Werdegar dissenting joined by Justice Baxter, four votes to two among the participating justices, held that the advertisement, interpreted in the setting of California's advertised-price regulation, was an offer accepted by the customer's tender and satisfied the goods statute of frauds. Nevertheless, the dealer could rescind for a good-faith unilateral mistake of fact: the substantial pricing error concerned a basic assumption, materially disadvantaged the dealer, was not a risk allocated to it, and would make enforcement unconscionable. The court reversed the Court of Appeal; the trial court's judgment was correct although its contract-formation rationale was mistaken.
sections.Reasoning:
Objective manifestations govern formation, and a price error unknown to the buyer does not itself erase an otherwise operative offer; mistake goes to avoidance. The court declined to resolve the validity of the general advertising rule. The decisive setting was a licensed dealer's advertisement of one particular vehicle under Vehicle Code section 11713.1(e) and its regulation, which required sale at the advertised price and created reasonable consumer expectations of an operative offer. The dealer's printed name served as an authenticating signature under section 2201.

On mistake, Kemper and Elsinore already authorized relief beyond the first Restatement's requirement that the other party know of or cause the mistake. The court expressly adopted Restatement Second section 153(a). The $12,000 disparity, approximately 32 percent, was material. Ordinary negligence did not necessarily constitute neglect of a legal duty under Civil Code section 1577, and the advertised-price regulation did not eliminate mistake defenses. The evidence supported good faith; relying on the newspaper's proofreading might be negligent but did not warrant allocating all pricing risk to RRL. Enforcement would cost RRL more than $9,000 of its investment and give Donovan a $12,000 unintended benefit; the immediate explanation, apology, and reimbursement offer permitted restoration of the status quo. Although RRL had not requested rescission, the majority sustained the trial judgment as correct on another ground, treating rescission as a defense.

Justice Werdegar, dissenting, agreed that a contract formed but objected to granting unsolicited rescission on an undeveloped record: the theory came from amici, and the buyer had no fair opportunity to brief it. She would have affirmed the intermediate decision or, at most, transferred for briefing and decision on rescission.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-049.rule: On this court's reasoning, an ordinary eBay auction does not, without further forum ties, purposefully direct the seller's conduct toward the winning bidder's state, because the seller cannot choose the winner's identity or location.

sections.Parties: Foley, an Illinois resident, sued Massachusetts residents Yale Turner and Samir Jaber and Yacht Management Group, Inc., alleging breach of a contract for a yacht auctioned on eBay. Turner owned the yacht and had engaged Jaber and the corporation, of which Jaber was president and treasurer, to sell it through a brokerage service. Turner, proceeding pro se, moved to dismiss.
sections.Procedural History: Foley sued in the Northern District of Illinois. Turner framed his pro se motion as one for improper venue, but its substance concerned personal jurisdiction, which the court addressed first. On July 9, 2009, the court granted Turner's motion to dismiss. The complaint remained viable against Jaber and Yacht Management Group. This memorandum covers only that jurisdictional stage; it did not decide whether an enforceable boat-sale contract existed or whether an auction agent's mistake justified rescission.
sections.Material Facts:
These facts are the plaintiff's allegations, taken from the complaint and Foley's response for the jurisdictional motion. On July 14, 2008, Foley traveled to Massachusetts, met Turner, and inspected Turner's 1987, 55-foot Hatteras Convertible, Material Girls; they did not negotiate its purchase. Defendants listed the yacht in a reserve-price eBay auction on November 13. Turner called and emailed Foley in Chicago that day to inform him of the listing and invite a bid. Foley was the highest bidder when the auction ended November 21 but did not meet the undisclosed reserve, so no sale followed.

On or about November 28 defendants listed the vessel again, with a $100,000 opening bid and no reserve. When that auction ended December 4, Foley's $135,100 bid was highest and eBay emailed confirmation that he had won. Under the sale terms a $2,000 deposit was due within twenty-four hours; Foley paid through PayPal, but defendants rejected and returned it. On December 6 he faxed and mailed a letter expressing his intention to complete the sale. Turner called him that day, but the sale was never completed.
sections.Issue: Whether an Illinois federal court could exercise specific personal jurisdiction over a Massachusetts seller whose yacht was won in an eBay auction by an Illinois bidder, where the seller had called and emailed that bidder about an earlier auction of the same yacht.
sections.Holding: The Northern District of Illinois in 2009, Judge Virginia M. Kendall, held that it lacked personal jurisdiction over Turner and consequently considered venue improper under the then-applicable section 1391(a), and granted his motion to dismiss. It granted Turner's motion alone. Its statement that the complaint remained viable against the other defendants was not a finding that a contract had been proved against them, and the opinion did not impose liability on the seller at the winning bid.
sections.Reasoning:
Foley bore the burden of a prima facie jurisdictional showing, with factual disputes resolved in his favor. In a diversity case the court asked whether an Illinois court could exercise jurisdiction; Illinois's long-arm catch-all extended to constitutional limits, so the analysis was a federal due-process inquiry. Foley did not assert general jurisdiction. The question was whether Turner purposefully availed himself of Illinois such that requiring him to defend there was consistent with fair play and substantial justice. Mere foreseeability that an out-of-state purchaser might respond to an internet auction was not enough.

The Seventh Circuit had not decided the eBay issue, so the court examined district-court decisions from other circuits and adopted their reasoning: an ordinary eBay auction does not, without further forum ties, purposefully direct the seller's conduct toward the high bidder's state, because the seller cannot choose the winner's identity or location. The connection was random, fortuitous, and attenuated. The court found the Zippo sliding scale unhelpful because it generally concerned websites owned or controlled by the defendant.

Turner's calls and emails to a known Illinois resident were insufficient because they still left the winner's identity outside his control; in McGuire, by contrast, a seller stopped an auction and sold directly to the forum buyer. The messages also concerned the first, reserve auction, while the claim arose from the later no-reserve auction.

The casebook's problem differs from the memorandum: it rounds the bid to $135,000, describes two unsuccessful reserve auctions, and attributes the no-reserve designation to an agent's error, a matter the court did not decide. The casebook uses the dispute to pose no-reserve-auction and mistake questions.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-050.rule: An order form requiring home-office acceptance can be accepted through correspondence: a letter promising attention to the order, together with a later letter cancelling that identified order, can evidence acceptance and recognize an existing contract.

sections.Parties: Hill's, Inc., a retailer, sued William B. Kessler, Inc., a clothing manufacturer, for lost profits after Kessler cancelled an order for thirty-four men's suits. Hill's was the plaintiff and prevailed at trial; Kessler, the defendant, appealed. Kessler denied that it had accepted the order.
sections.Procedural History: Hill's brought a damages action seeking lost profits of $815.83, calculated from a 66 2/3 percent markup. The trial court found that Kessler intentionally cancelled at the instigation of a large downtown Seattle retailer selling its clothing, and Hill's prevailed. Kessler appealed. On August 7, 1952, the Washington Supreme Court affirmed the judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
On May 16, 1950, Hill's ordered thirty-four suits through Kessler's salesman, using Kessler's printed form. The form stated that the order would not bind Kessler until an authorized officer accepted it at the corporation's office in Hammonton, New Jersey. On May 23, Kessler sent a form letter assuring Hill's of its best attention to the order.

On or about July 18, Kessler cancelled. Its July 18 letter identified the May 16 order placed with salesman Jacobus, said shipment was impossible because of previous commitments to other stores in town, characterized its action as cancellation, and apologized for inconvenience. By then the period for placing fall orders had passed, leaving Hill's unable to obtain comparable suits elsewhere for its fall trade. Kessler's correspondence was signed by Glenda Fitting; its treasurer testified that she was only a clerk and that the president, secretary, and treasurer alone could accept orders.
sections.Issue: Whether Kessler's letter assuring its best attention to the order, together with its later cancellation letter, showed acceptance of the order; whether Kessler could avoid liability because the correspondence was not signed by an authorized officer; and whether lost resale profits were recoverable.
sections.Holding: The Washington Supreme Court in 1952, in an opinion by Justice Mallery joined by Chief Justice Schwellenbach and Justices Grady and Weaver, affirmed. The majority held that the correspondence evidenced acceptance and recognized an existing contract, that Kessler could not defeat liability by disputing its office clerk's authority on this record, and that the retailer's lost resale profits were recoverable. Justice Donworth concurred in the result only. Five judges thus agreed on affirmance, four joining the opinion and one giving a narrower rationale.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority found Bauman v. McManus exactly in point: a promise of prompt, careful attention naturally concerns filling the order, not the supplier's private investigation of whether to accept it; otherwise a supplier could use equivocal reassuring language and later exploit it. The court did not rely exclusively on the initial letter. The later letter was independent evidence of an intention to accept, because saying Kessler needed to cancel an identified order recognized the existence of the contract it purported to terminate. The court considered the whole correspondence rather than treating "best attention" as invariably dispositive.

On authority, the trial court had examined substantial correspondence signed by Fitting and was justified in disbelieving the restrictive testimony. Applying apparent-authority principles, when a principal voluntarily puts an agent in a position that reasonably leads a person familiar with the business to assume authority for a particular act, and that person deals on the assumption, the principal cannot defeat the transaction by proving a narrower undisclosed actual authority.

On damages, travelling east to procure an equivalent order would have cost more than the lost profits, so that expenditure was unjustified as mitigation. Kessler understood the suits were for fall resale at the markup, their quality was unavailable in the West, and the cancellation came after the ordering season, so lost profits were an appropriate measure.

Justice Donworth concurred solely because the July 18 letter acknowledged a contract whose terms appeared in the May 16 order.

The casebook note asks whether these words amounted to acceptance when compared with Wucherpfennig's failure to communicate unconditional assent.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-051.rule: As this intermediate court reasoned before it was reversed, acceptance of an offer requesting a promise must be communicated unless the offeror dispenses with notice, and a letter merely acknowledging an order neither accepts nor gives that notice.

sections.Parties: International Filter Co., a manufacturer with its office in Chicago, sued Conroe Gin, Ice & Light Co. for breach of a contract to buy a water softener and filter. International Filter was the plaintiff and appellant; Conroe, the defendant and appellee, maintained that it had withdrawn its order before any contract was made.
sections.Procedural History: Following a bench trial, Judge J. M. Combs found that no effective contract existed before cancellation, that there was no evidence the letter's signer, Johnson, was an executive officer, and that the damages proof would be inadequate even if a contract existed; the court rejected Conroe's jurisdictional objection. It entered judgment that International Filter take nothing. International Filter appealed. On January 30, 1925, the Beaumont Court of Civil Appeals of Texas affirmed; rehearing was denied February 11, 1925, and a writ of error was granted April 8, 1925. This entry covers only the intermediate appeal. The later decision, the casebook's principal case, reversed this judgment and remanded to the Court of Civil Appeals to address previously unconsidered questions.
sections.Material Facts:
On February 10, 1920, Conroe's manager, Henry Thompson, signed a proposal solicited by International Filter's representative, W. W. Waterman, for a Junior No. 2 steel-tank water softener and filter to purify water of the character shown by a sample Conroe would supply. Though expressed as the manufacturer's proposal, it said it became a contract when accepted by the purchaser and approved by an executive officer at International Filter's Chicago office, and that it was subject to change without notice unless promptly accepted. Thompson's notation requested shipment by March 10. Thompson testified that he told Waterman Conroe needed an immediate definite answer because it was a rush order late in the season.

On February 13, International Filter's president, P. N. Engel, placed his dated approval on the paper. A February 14 letter signed by M. B. Johnson acknowledged and thanked Conroe for its order, repeated the specifications, and asked Conroe promptly to ship a water sample for analysis. On February 28 Conroe wrote that it wished to cancel for the time being. International Filter refused to accept cancellation and on April 6 demanded the overdue $615 first installment. The machine was never shipped.
sections.Issue: Who made the operative offer; whether Engel's approval accepted it; whether notice of that approval to Conroe was necessary; and whether the February 14 letter supplied either acceptance or notice before Conroe withdrew.
sections.Holding: The Texas Court of Civil Appeals at Beaumont in 1925, in an opinion by Justice Walker with no recorded dissent, affirmed the take-nothing judgment. It treated Conroe's signed order as an offer to purchase and Engel's approval as an acceptance, rejecting the trial court's contrary conclusion on that point, but held that the acceptance had not been communicated before Conroe withdrew its offer, so no contract was completed. It did not reach the attacks on the alternative damages ground.
sections.Reasoning:
The court determined the instrument's legal function from the reserved home-office approval rather than its introductory wording: Conroe was proposing terms on which it would buy, and the manufacturer still had to accept. Engel's endorsement communicated approval as effectively as the word "accepted"; the defect was uncommunicated acceptance.

The court distinguished an offer requesting an act from one requesting a promise. Communication was generally required for the latter, though an offeror could dispense with notice through the terms of its offer. International Filter relied on the clause making the contract effective on home-office approval. Reading both clauses together, the court reasoned that Conroe's reserved ability to change its proposal would be meaningless unless it lasted until Conroe was notified of the Chicago approval. If that reading was not compelled, the provisions were at least ambiguous and were construed against International Filter, which supplied the language. Thompson's uncontradicted account of the immediate-answer discussion was admissible.

The February 14 letter neither accepted nor gave notice of Engel's acceptance. It thanked Conroe for an order and sought the sample without declaring approval. The court relied on decisions distinguishing acknowledgment and a promise of attention from assent, including Courtney Shoe. The sample request was especially important: International Filter retained the privilege to examine the water before agreeing to furnish a suitable machine.

The later principal case rejects this notification construction and treats the February 14 letter as sufficient notice if notice were necessary. The casebook discusses this earlier judgment in its note on expressions of acceptance; the brief notes that the casebook's "Ky. App." parenthetical for it is erroneous.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-052.rule: An acknowledgment that an order has been received and will get prompt and careful attention is a promise to consider the order, not an acceptance of it, and its ordinary meaning is for the court to construe.

sections.Parties: Courtney Shoe Co., a St. Louis wholesaler, sued E. W. Curd & Son, merchants in Cave City, Kentucky, for the price of delivered stock shoes. Curd counterclaimed that the wholesaler had accepted and then breached a separate order for sample shoes, claiming $1,083.20 in damages. Courtney Shoe was the appellant.
sections.Procedural History: Curd refused to pay for the delivered stock shoes, and Courtney Shoe sued for their price. Curd counterclaimed on the sample order. The trial court submitted the intended effect of the acknowledgment card to the jury, which awarded Curd $250 on the counterclaim; the trial court entered judgment and Courtney Shoe appealed. On February 14, 1911, the Kentucky court reversed and remanded for proceedings consistent with its conclusion that the trial court should have instructed the jury peremptorily to find for Courtney Shoe for the amount of its price claim. It did not itself enter a final money judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
On Sunday, August 22, 1909, the retailers gave traveling salesman W. B. Yater two orders, dated August 21: $49.15 of stock shoes and $1,772.35 of sample shoes, for shipment as soon as possible. When the papers reached the wholesaler on August 23, it mailed a card acknowledging receipt, promising prompt and careful attention, thanking the customer, and expressing hope for future business. It shipped the stock shoes but rejected the sample order because Yater lacked authority to sell those samples. The approving officer rejected the sample order on the day it arrived.

The rejection first went to Yater with directions to return the order to the customer. Yater sent it back and asked Courtney Shoe to communicate directly. The resulting August 31 letter told Curd that the salesman had lacked authority and that the wholesaler could not accept the sample order. Curd's proof was that acknowledgment cards were often the only notice customers received before learning of shipment. Courtney Shoe's evidence described its routine: acknowledge receipt first, submit the order to the approving officer next, and dispatch the result through the salesman.
sections.Issue: Whether a card acknowledging receipt of an order and promising it prompt and careful attention was an acceptance of the order, and whether the evidence permitted the jury to treat it as one rather than having its legal effect determined by the court.
sections.Holding: The Kentucky court in 1911, in an opinion by Chief Justice Hobson with no separate writing, held that there was no acceptance of the sample-shoe order. An acknowledgment saying that an order would receive prompt and careful attention did not accept it, and the eight-day delay in conveying the wholesaler's rejection to the customer did not turn the acknowledgment into a contract. The court reversed the retailer's jury judgment on the counterclaim.
sections.Reasoning:
Ordinary words have their ordinary meaning unless technical language, an established trade usage, or context gives them a different sense. There were no technical words and no proof that a trade usage gave the acknowledgment a peculiar meaning, so its construction was for the court, not a jury question about the sender's unexpressed intention. Evidence that cards commonly preceded shipments did not establish an altered usage making a promise to consider every order an acceptance of it.

A promise of attention was a promise to consider the proposal, not assent to supply the goods, a distinction adopted from Manier v. Appling. Adding "careful" to "prompt" did not change the sense, and conventional thanks and hopes for future orders supplied no commitment. Courtney Shoe fulfilled its promise by examining and rejecting the order.

The court distinguished Jordon v. Patterson and Bauman v. McManus, where acceptance rested substantially on subsequent performance or correspondence rather than the receipt card alone. Here the salesman's sample order remained subject to the house's approval; he had no authority to bind it to sell the samples at the large discount proposed, and the house repudiated promptly. The added time before the direct letter resulted from routing the rejection through the salesman.

The buyer could countermand before acceptance, while the seller could not revoke an actual acceptance without the buyer's consent. Shipment ordinarily could accept an order, but delivery of the separate $49.15 stock order did not accept the rejected sample order.

The casebook uses this decision to test whether a courteous acknowledgment constitutes acceptance.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-053.rule: Assent to a contract modification is judged by objective manifestations, and a reply that varies the proposal is a counteroffer that the other party can accept by its response and immediate performance, including in an instant-message exchange.

sections.Parties: CX Digital Media Inc., which operated an affiliate advertising network, sued its client Smoking Everywhere Inc., a seller of electronic cigarettes, for unpaid fees under an advertising-services contract. CX Digital, the plaintiff, claimed the contract had been modified by instant messages to change the landing pages and remove a daily limit; Smoking Everywhere, the defendant, denied any binding modification.
sections.Procedural History: The case was tried in a five-day bench trial in the Southern District of Florida. The parties agreed that Delaware law governed, and the original agreement's validity was admitted. On March 23, 2011, the court issued findings and conclusions in CX Digital's favor and directed that a final judgment would be entered by separate order, which CX Digital was to propose by March 30. This entry covers the March 23 findings and conclusions, not the separate final judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
Affiliates sent prospective customers to Smoking Everywhere's offer, and a compensable "Sale" was credited after successful credit-card submission and arrival at the confirmation page. CX Digital paid affiliates even if its client did not pay it. On August 4, 2009, Smoking Everywhere's advertising vice-president, Nick Touris, signed insertion order 6921, promising $45 per qualifying registration, with a 200-per-day limit and specified destination URLs. In August the affiliates produced 670 Sales and never exceeded the limit.

On September 2, 2009, Touris and CX Digital account manager Pedram Soltani conducted a day-long instant-message exchange. They arranged two new landing pages, tracking pixels, and tests of the new links. Later Soltani sought permission to send approximately 2,000 orders per day and requested an agent-of-record arrangement giving CX Digital exclusivity. Touris answered that there was no limit; Soltani responded enthusiastically and the affiliates immediately increased performance. Between September 2 and 23 the daily average was about 1,244 Sales, peaking at 2,896 on September 22. Smoking Everywhere did not contemporaneously demand restoration of the original URLs or the 200-Sale ceiling. CX Digital removed the offer around September 23 to 24 because of nonpayment.
sections.Issue: Whether the parties modified an existing advertising-services agreement, through instant messages and subsequent conduct, to substitute new landing pages and remove the 200-per-day limit on compensated Sales, despite a clause requiring signed written modifications and a challenge to the vice-president's authority.
sections.Holding: The Southern District of Florida in 2011, Judge Cecilia M. Altonaga, found after a bench trial that the parties modified the contract through instant messages and their subsequent conduct, replacing the specified landing pages and removing the daily limit on compensated registrations. The court calculated $1,260,805 in unpaid principal, at $45 for 670 August Sales and 27,459 later Sales less a $5,000 deposit, and authorized contractual interest, attorney's fees, and costs.
sections.Reasoning:
The URL modification rested on objective manifestations: Touris helped install and test tracking on the new pages, and his asserted private understanding could not negate what the parties implemented. Assent can exist even when no single precise moment of formation can be identified.

On volume, the court rejected CX Digital's characterization of Touris's response as acceptance of the exact proposal. The proposal mentioned approximately 2,000 orders per day and exclusivity; the response authorized unlimited volume without exclusivity. It was a counteroffer that Soltani accepted through his reply and immediate performance. Delivery of more than 2,000 Sales on some days confirmed there was no new 2,000-Sale cap. The interval between messages did not cause the offer to lapse in a day-long conversation with intermittent responses.

Because the contract concerned services, the court declined to apply UCC section 2-209. Under the Delaware common-law rule applied, a requirement of signed written modification can itself be waived by later agreement or conduct, and the implemented changes supported waiver. The court alternatively relied on estoppel, since CX Digital paid affiliates for increased traffic while Smoking Everywhere accepted performance. The volume change had consideration in increased Sales for payment at the existing rate; the URL change was supported by material reliance under Restatement (Second) of Contracts section 89.

Touris had apparent authority: Smoking Everywhere presented him as the vice-president responsible for advertising, and he signed the original order and implemented the changes. The court rejected the fraud-provision, frustration, good-faith, and mutual-mistake defenses.

The casebook's problem uses a shortened version of the message exchange to study objective assent.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-054.rule: An advertisement promising a reward to anyone who performs stated conditions is an offer to the public that is accepted by performance, without advance notice of acceptance, and the requested performance supplies consideration.

sections.Parties: Carlill, a purchaser and user of the smoke ball, sued the Carbolic Smoke Ball Company for the £100 reward promised in its advertisement. She was the plaintiff and the respondent on appeal; the company was the defendant and the appellant, disputing the existence and enforceability of any contract.
sections.Procedural History: Hawkins J. held that Carlill could recover the promised £100. The company appealed, disputing the existence and enforceability of a contract rather than identifying a factual failure to use the product as directed. The Court of Appeal heard the appeal on December 6 and 7, 1892, and unanimously dismissed it, leaving the £100 judgment in place.
sections.Material Facts:
The company advertised in the Pall Mall Gazette on November 13, 1891, and in other newspapers that it would pay £100 to a person who contracted influenza, a cold, or a disease caused by taking cold after using its smoke ball three times daily for two weeks according to the directions. The advertisement stated that £1,000 had been deposited with Alliance Bank to demonstrate the company's sincerity. It also asserted that no ascertained disease case had occurred among users during the previous epidemic, described the product's price and refill cost, and promoted its usefulness to a family over several months.

Carlill bought a ball from a chemist in reliance on the advertisement. She used it as directed from November 20, 1891, until January 17, 1892, when she contracted influenza while still using it.
sections.Issue: Whether the advertisement was a legal promise capable of acceptance by a member of the public or a mere expression of confidence; whether acceptance had to be communicated before performance; whether there was consideration; whether the promise was too indefinite as to time; and whether the bargain was an unlawful wager or insurance policy.
sections.Holding: The Court of Appeal, deciding the case on December 7, 1892, with Lindley, Bowen, and A. L. Smith L.JJ. each delivering reasons, unanimously dismissed the company's appeal. The judges agreed that the advertisement was an enforceable offer, that the stipulated use supplied consideration and acceptance without advance notice, and that Carlill satisfied the conditions for payment. The wagering and insurance arguments were rejected. Their interpretations of the duration of protection were not identical, so the result does not establish a unanimous rule fixing how long a former user would remain protected.
sections.Reasoning:
Lindley began with the express promise to pay. The statement that money had been deposited to show sincerity contradicted the suggestion of mere promotional exaggeration. Reward advertisements can be offers to anyone who performs their conditions; the absence of a named offeree does not matter. Bowen distinguished an offer to the public from a contract with everyone: the advertisement became a contract only with those who performed on its faith before withdrawal, and it was unlike an advertisement that merely invites bargaining. A. L. Smith likewise found an offer intended to be acted upon.

The judges acknowledged the ordinary requirement that acceptance be notified, but the offeror can indicate expressly or by the character of the transaction that performance is sufficient. Bowen used a lost-dog reward as an illustration. Lindley regarded notice separate from performance as unnecessary here, or alternatively satisfied by notification accompanying the fact of performance. These reasons construe what this offer invited; they do not abolish notice for every unilateral bargain.

Using the smoke ball as requested involved inconvenience sufficient to support the promise, and the judges recognized the commercial benefit from public use stimulating sales. Bowen said the law does not appraise the adequacy of the inconvenience; A. L. Smith considered enhanced sales the more important consideration. Gerhard v. Bates did not establish a contrary rule.

On certainty, the advertisement did not promise lifelong immunity. Lindley preferred protection for a reasonable time after use; Bowen preferred protection while the ball remained in use; A. L. Smith identified three possible limits and declined to choose. Carlill fell ill during continued use, so the difference did not matter.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-055.rule: When an offer of guaranty invites an act that the offeror is unlikely to learn of promptly, the offeree must give notice of performance with reasonable diligence, and seasonably mailing a properly addressed, prepaid letter satisfies that requirement even if it never arrives.

sections.Parties: Bishop, of Sycamore, Illinois, sued Eaton on a guaranty, seeking reimbursement of a note he had signed as surety for Eaton's brother Harry and later paid. Bishop was the plaintiff and won at trial. Eaton, the defendant, brought exceptions, disputing acceptance and notice of the guaranty and asserting that an extension of the note discharged him.
sections.Procedural History: Bishop brought an action on the guaranty, with a writ dated February 2, 1892. Braley J. tried it without a jury, declined Eaton's requested rulings, and concluded that Bishop was entitled to judgment as a matter of law on the reported findings. Eaton excepted. On June 19, 1894, the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court sustained the defendant's exceptions and required a new trial. It neither entered final judgment for Eaton nor affirmed Bishop's judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
In December 1886, Eaton wrote from Nova Scotia inviting Bishop either to supply Eaton's brother Harry with additional money or to help him obtain it, and promising to see that the debt was paid. On January 7, 1887, Harry issued a $200 note to Stark, payable in one year; Bishop signed as surety in reliance on Eaton's letter. Shortly afterward Bishop mailed a letter describing the note and amount, properly addressed to Eaton in Nova Scotia with postage prepaid. Eaton testified that he never received it, and there was no finding that it reached him.

At maturity, payment was extended for another year; the bill of exceptions showed the extension was without Eaton's consent. In an August 1889 interview, Bishop asked Eaton to take up the note. Eaton answered that Bishop should try to get Harry to pay and that, if Harry did not, Eaton would, assuring Bishop the matter would not cost him anything. Bishop paid the note on October 1, 1891. Eaton said he first learned of the payment on December 22.
sections.Issue: Whether Bishop accepted Eaton's offer of guaranty and gave adequate notice of his performance when his mailed letter was never shown to have arrived, and whether extending the note's maturity without the guarantor's consent discharged the guaranty.
sections.Holding: The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court in 1894, in the sole reported opinion by Knowlton J., held that Bishop had adequately notified Eaton that he performed the act invited by the offer of guaranty, even though Eaton denied receiving the properly mailed letter. But an extension of the underlying note's maturity without the guarantor's consent discharged the guaranty unless Eaton later ratified it, and the trial judge had not resolved ratification under the correct rule. The exceptions were sustained.
sections.Reasoning:
The court first classified Eaton's promise as a guaranty rather than an independent primary undertaking: whether Bishop lent to Harry or helped him borrow, Harry remained primarily liable.

The letter offered a promise in exchange for an act, not for a return promise. Bishop's signing as surety accomplished the invited assistance, supplied consideration, and accepted the offer. Ordinarily an offeror who will promptly learn of the performed act needs no separate notice. Where the nature of the act or the parties' circumstances make such knowledge unlikely, the offeree must give notice with reasonable diligence after performance. Until seasonable notice the guarantor would not be bound, but performance protected the promisee against an intervening withdrawal if notice followed within a reasonable time.

The notice had to be reasonable given the transaction, the parties' locations, and prior dealings. Eaton made his offer by letter between Nova Scotia and Illinois, so he should have contemplated that word of Bishop's response would also travel by letter. Seasonably mailing a properly addressed, prepaid letter did everything reasonably required; Bishop did not assume the risk of non-arrival. The court expressly reserved how far this reasoning applies to ordinary contracts formed by correspondence. Delayed notice of Harry's later default was not a defense, at least without evidence that it injured Eaton.

Separately, extending the principal debtor's time without the guarantor's consent discharged Eaton unless he later assented and ratified. The court could not tell whether the trial judge would have found ratification under the proper rule.

The casebook features the notice issue; its note does not report the extension error that produced the new trial.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-056.rule: A school's catalog describing its admission criteria is an invitation to make an offer; tendering an application and fee is the offer, and the school's acceptance of them forms a contract to evaluate the application under the stated criteria.

sections.Parties: Robert Steinberg, a rejected applicant, sued the Chicago Medical School on behalf of himself and similarly situated applicants. He was the plaintiff; the school was the defendant. Steinberg alleged the school did not evaluate applications under its published criteria and sought relief in contract, under consumer-protection statutes, for fraud, and for unjust enrichment.
sections.Procedural History: The complaint contained four counts: breach of contract, statutory consumer-fraud and deceptive-trade-practice violations, common-law fraud, and unjust enrichment. The circuit court dismissed all four for failure to state a claim. The appellate court restored the contract count, permitted a class restricted to applicants in Steinberg's year, and affirmed dismissal of the others. On December 12, 1977, the Illinois Supreme Court affirmed in part and reversed in part both lower judgments and remanded to the circuit court for further proceedings, including class-related preliminary determinations.
sections.Material Facts: These are allegations accepted as true on review of a dismissal, not findings. Steinberg received the school's catalog, applied for the 1974-75 academic year, paid the required $15 fee, and was rejected. The bulletin said selection rested on scholarship, character, and motivation, without regard to race, creed, or sex; it specified academic achievement, admission-test results, instructors' appraisals, and a possible personal interview as evaluation criteria. Steinberg alleged that the school instead selected primarily according to financial contributions pledged or paid by applicants or their families.
sections.Issue: Whether rejected applicants stated claims for breach of contract and common-law fraud by alleging that the school accepted applications and fees while not evaluating applicants under its published criteria, and whether the proposed class could be confined to a single application year.
sections.Holding: The Illinois Supreme Court in 1977, in the sole reported opinion by Dooley J., held that the rejected applicants adequately alleged both breach of an agreement to evaluate applications under published criteria and common-law fraud. It rejected the appellate restriction of the class to a single application year. It affirmed dismissal of the statutory trade-practice and separately pleaded unjust-enrichment counts. The court did not find that the school had actually committed the alleged misconduct, did not decide that every university catalog creates an enforceable admission promise, and did not award Steinberg a place.
sections.Reasoning:
The court adopted a formation theory more precise than calling the catalog an offer of admission. The brochure invited an offer to apply on the published evaluation terms. Tendering an application and the $15 fee made that offer; the school's acceptance of both accepted it. The fee was legally sufficient consideration for evaluating the application as represented. The court analogized the sequence to a merchant's invitation to deal on advertised terms followed by the customer's offer and the merchant's receipt of payment.

The school's insistence on a subjective meeting of minds did not defeat the complaint: observable conduct can manifest assent even where a party denies an internal intention to contract. Steinberg did not demand admission; the promised service was evaluation under the stated qualifications. The court distinguished Tinkoff, where the university reserved a right to reject for any reason and the applicant sought to compel admission.

On fraud, although a statement about future conduct ordinarily does not support fraud, there is an exception where a false future promise is itself alleged to be the means of a fraudulent scheme, and the alleged use of a misleading bulletin to obtain fees fit it at the pleading stage. The statutory count failed because the applicants were not purchasers of merchandise within the consumer definition, and the unjust-enrichment count failed because no fiduciary relationship supported a constructive trust.

On the class, the court applied the newly enacted Civil Practice Act section 57.2 as procedural. The complaint was broad enough to reach applicants outside 1974-75 who paid fees in reliance on a brochure containing the alleged misrepresentations.

The casebook's problem on this case asks for the formation theory.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-057.rule: A seller's internal preparation to fill an order, such as referring it to the factory and incurring expense, is not acceptance; a buyer may cancel its order before acceptance is communicated or the goods are delivered.

sections.Parties: Doll & Smith, a seller of advertising materials in New York, sued the A. & S. Sanitary Dairy Company, the buyer, for the price of the materials. Doll & Smith was the plaintiff and appellant; the Dairy Company was the defendant, denying that a contract was formed and asserting cancellation.
sections.Procedural History: The seller's petition alleged an order, acceptance, delivery, and an unpaid price. The Council Bluffs Municipal Court, Judge Daniel H. Sheehan, entered judgment for the buyer. The seller appealed. On December 14, 1926, the Iowa Supreme Court affirmed.
sections.Material Facts:
On June 9, 1924, the Dairy Company signed an order directing shipment of specified advertising materials by express, F.O.B. New York, as soon as possible, and agreeing to pay on specified terms. The order apparently went through an agent to the seller in New York. Doll & Smith received it June 14 and referred it to the factory to be filled. They paid the agent's commission and incurred other expenses, but did not notify the Dairy Company of acceptance.

The Dairy Company telegraphed cancellation on June 16 and followed with a June 19 letter. On June 20, the seller acknowledged the telegram and objected to cancellation. Both cancellation communications used the word "contract," while the letter also called the transaction an order and stated that the Dairy Company did not wish to contract. The goods were not delivered.
sections.Issue: Whether the steps the seller took after receiving the order had made the offer irrevocable as an accepted contract before the buyer's cancellation telegram.
sections.Holding: The Iowa Supreme Court in 1926, in an opinion by Morling J. in which De Graff C.J. and Evans and Albert JJ. concurred, affirmed judgment for the Dairy Company. Internal preparation and expense did not establish a completed contract before the buyer canceled its offer, and the goods were not delivered. The court also found no pleaded or proved damages case that could sustain recovery on a different basis.
sections.Reasoning:
The court found no contract consummated on the stated facts. No acceptance was communicated, and the goods had not been delivered before the offer was withdrawn. Referring the order to the factory, paying a commission, and incurring expense did not change that conclusion. Nor could the buyer's casual use of the word "contract" in its cancellation communications change the legal effect of the sequence or prove that formation had already occurred.

The seller's price theory had an additional factual defect: notwithstanding its pleading, the goods were not delivered. The court separately stated that neither pleading nor proof made a damages case. It did not calculate reliance reimbursement, and it did not hold that every conceivable preparatory act can never constitute acceptance under different facts.

The casebook uses the case, in its note on preparation for shipment of goods as acceptance, for the distinction between preparation and the conduct that constitutes acceptance, and asks for comparison with another case.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-058.rule: Where prior dealings and a standing offer warrant a seller in sending conforming goods, the recipient's silence and retention of the goods for an unreasonable time can be found to be acceptance, because conduct importing assent counts as assent.

sections.Parties: Hobbs, of Saugus, a supplier of eel skins, sued the Massasoit Whip Company, a whip manufacturer in Westfield, for the price of a shipment of skins. Hobbs was the plaintiff and won a jury verdict. The company, the defendant, brought exceptions to a jury instruction, denying that it had ordered or accepted the skins.
sections.Procedural History: At trial, Hammond J. instructed that Hobbs could not recover for skins under twenty-two inches or in the condition described by the company's witnesses, and additionally permitted a plaintiff's verdict if the company remained silent while having reason to believe the sender understood that it was accepting the skins. The jury found for Hobbs. The company excepted to the latter instruction. On March 1, 1893, the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court overruled the exceptions, leaving the plaintiff's verdict intact.
sections.Material Facts:
Hobbs supplied eel skins to the manufacturer through Harding in Lynn. Four or five earlier shipments sent in the same way had been accepted and paid for. The manufacturer's president acknowledged prices of five cents per skin over twenty-seven inches and two cents for skins between twenty-two and twenty-seven inches, provided they were suitable for the business.

On February 18, 1890, Hobbs delivered the disputed shipment to Harding, who sent it on that day or the next. The covering letter identified 2,050 skins at five cents and 300 at two cents, totaling 2,350 skins and $108.50. Hobbs said they met the size and condition requirements. The company's witnesses said the shipment was short, badly conditioned, and useless; its president denied ordering these skins and said he promptly informed Harding in writing that they were unfit and held subject to Hobbs's directions. Hobbs denied receiving notice of rejection. The skins remained at the factory for months and were later destroyed. The parties disputed whose agent Harding was; that question went to the jury under instructions to which no exception was taken.
sections.Issue: Whether a jury could be permitted to find acceptance from the company's silence and retention of the skins, or whether such an instruction wrongly let a sender impose a purchase obligation on an unwilling recipient merely by shipping goods.
sections.Holding: The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court in 1893, in the sole opinion by Holmes J., overruled the company's exceptions. In the context of the parties' prior dealings, the jury could find that Hobbs's conforming shipment, coupled with the company's failure to reject it for an unreasonable time, manifested assent. The court did not allow a stranger to create a duty to pay merely by announcing that failure to respond would be acceptance.
sections.Reasoning:
Holmes recognized that the instruction, read in isolation, might suggest that a sender could impose a purchase on an unwilling recipient. He instead examined what the jury would understand in the evidentiary setting. Hobbs had repeatedly supplied the same kind of goods by the same route, and the company accepted and paid for them. In view of the verdict and the quality instruction, the court took the skins to be suitable and sufficiently long and took Hobbs to have received no rejection notice.

The company's own testimony supported an understanding that it would take suitable skins meeting the stated dimensions, and Holmes described a standing offer for such skins. Even if shipment alone did not complete the contract under that offer, the established relationship warranted Hobbs in sending conforming goods and called for the company to act upon receiving them. Silence combined with retention for an unreasonable time could then justify the jury in finding acceptance.

The operative principle was objective manifestation: conduct importing assent counts as assent regardless of an undisclosed contrary mental state. Silence acquired significance from the prior transactions, the understood requirements, receipt of conforming skins, and continued retention. The court did not decide an objection to the agency instructions, which had not been preserved.

The casebook discusses the case under the heading that silence is not ordinarily acceptance, quoting reasoning that emphasizes the prior dealings and asking what conduct existed beyond silence.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-059.rule: A seller that has accepted orders and then unequivocally refuses to perform them after receiving adequate assurances commits anticipatory repudiation; it cannot unilaterally rescind its acceptances, and ending a continuing relationship for future orders does not discharge orders already accepted.

sections.Parties: American Bronze Corporation, a maker of castings, sued its customer Streamway Products on an unpaid account. Streamway counterclaimed for damages after American refused to produce castings under three accepted orders. Streamway, the counterclaimant, was the appellant; American was the appellee. The appeal concerned only the counterclaim.
sections.Procedural History: After a bench trial, the trial court found that American's requested assurances had been adequately given but concluded that American had unilaterally rescinded its acceptances within commercially reasonable periods and so had not breached. It entered judgment for American on the counterclaim and a separate $9,489.64 stipulated account judgment for American. Streamway appealed the counterclaim judgment through three assignments of error. On December 16, 1982, the Ohio Court of Appeals sustained all three, reversed, and remanded on the counterclaim alone.
sections.Material Facts:
American and Streamway had dealt for more than twenty years. Streamway regularly telephoned an order, followed it with a written purchase order, and American began production. Three accepted orders were at issue. Under the November 21, 1979 order American failed to deliver 1,000 units of one casting; under the December 27 order for 13,000 castings it delivered 5,087; it delivered nothing under the January 3, 1980 order.

On January 17, American's vice-president, Gerald Goldstein, said American would accept no new orders but would produce the existing open orders. The castings were unique and custom made by American, with no duplicate tooling elsewhere. American asked Streamway to bring its account current, pay future invoices within ten days, agree on scrap prices, and hold American harmless for failure to produce. Streamway paid more than $66,000 on January 18, bringing the account current, and agreed to the ten-day term.

On January 24, Goldstein announced that American would produce none of the outstanding castings and had melted down castings already produced. Only then did Streamway remove its tooling. It obtained substitutes from Wolverine Brass Works; the trial court found additional cover and related costs totaling $25,145.41.
sections.Issue: Whether a seller that had accepted three purchase orders and received adequate assurances could unilaterally rescind its acceptances within a commercially reasonable time, or whether its refusal to produce the castings was an anticipatory repudiation and breach.
sections.Holding: The Ohio Court of Appeals in 1982, in the sole opinion by Pryatel C.J. with Parrino and Markus JJ. concurring, reversed and remanded the judgment against Streamway on its counterclaim. American had accepted three orders and then unequivocally refused to perform them after receiving adequate assurances; that refusal was anticipatory repudiation, not a permissible unilateral rescission within a commercially reasonable time. The court did not itself render a money judgment for the $25,145.41.
sections.Reasoning:
Ohio's sales provisions allow a contract to arise through any conduct sufficient to show agreement, despite uncertainty about the exact moment of formation. The established ordering procedure and American's accepted orders established contracts, and for two orders production had already begun. The court rejected Streamway's separate argument that the merchant-confirmation provision, R.C. 1302.04(B), itself proved formation: satisfying it removes the statute-of-frauds defense but does not prove that the oral agreement existed.

Anticipatory repudiation required a definite and unequivocal refusal of future performance that substantially impaired the contract's value. The January 24 announcement and the melting of the castings met that test. The repudiation breached the accepted contracts; it did not rescind them by mutual consent, and the trial court could not convert a unilateral disavowal into consensual rescission by calling the elapsed time commercially reasonable.

Nor was the conduct a termination requiring reasonable notice. Termination meant ending a contract under a legal or agreed power otherwise than for breach, and the provision for successive performances of indefinite duration did not apply to contracts for definite quantities. Ending the relationship for future orders did not discharge the accepted orders. Streamway's removal of tooling responded to the repudiation.

On assurances, reasonable insecurity permits a request for adequate assurance. Both courts regarded bringing the account current and agreeing to the ten-day term as adequate. Once American received them it remained bound to perform. The court also discussed the buyer's right to cover and recover the difference.

The casebook's account emphasizes the telephone orders, written confirmations, established practice, and unfilled orders.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-060.rule: Whether a contract forms when a service appointment is scheduled, or only when performance begins, is a question of fact that cannot be assumed; an appointment may be only an invitation to negotiate.

sections.Parties: Edith Perry, a Black woman and salon customer, sued Command Performance, a beauty salon at the King of Prussia Mall, under 42 U.S.C. section 1981 and Pennsylvania intentional-infliction-of-emotional-distress law after an operator allegedly refused to serve her because of race. Perry was the plaintiff and appellant; the salon was the defendant and appellee.
sections.Procedural History: The district court granted summary judgment for the salon. Applying Patterson v. McLean Credit Union, it concluded that the telephone appointment created a racially neutral contract and that the operator's later conduct was harassment after formation, outside section 1981. Perry appealed. On August 30, 1990, the Third Circuit, reviewing de novo with facts and inferences viewed favorably to Perry, vacated the order and remanded for further proceedings, with costs charged to the appellee.
sections.Material Facts:
These facts come from Perry's complaint and deposition, reviewed on summary judgment rather than found after trial. On October 12, 1987, Perry's husband called the salon to arrange a noon wash-and-set appointment. Perry had used the salon more than five times, with different operators. Helene Kugler, who had previously done her hair, was scheduled to serve her. After Perry arrived, Kugler said she had a bad cold and asked whether another operator could serve her, and Perry agreed.

According to Perry, Beth Abbott loudly refused when Kugler asked her to take the appointment, saying that she did not do Black people's hair and did not deal with Black people.
