Perry said she became distraught, cried, called mall security, and left with her husband. The record contained a dispute about whether Kugler offered to perform the service after Abbott's outburst. The salon later sent an apology and an offer of a free wash and set.
sections.Issue: Whether, for purposes of a section 1981 claim under the framework then governing, the district court could assume on summary judgment that a contract formed when the appointment was scheduled, so that the alleged racial refusal of service was only post-formation conduct.
sections.Holding: The Third Circuit in 1990, in an opinion by Anne E. Thompson, a district judge sitting by designation, for a panel of Sloviter, Mansmann, and Thompson with no separate writing, vacated summary judgment for the salon and remanded. The record did not support the assumption that a contract formed when the appointment was scheduled. Even if an appointment created a contract, evidence might show that its terms were themselves discriminatory. The court did not determine liability or award damages.
sections.Reasoning:
Under Patterson, as then governing, section 1981 reached racial refusal to enter contracts, or offers on discriminatory terms, but not harassment arising after formation. Timing therefore mattered.

The district court had no evidentiary basis for determining that a contract necessarily formed at the scheduling stage. An appointment could instead be an invitation to negotiate, with acceptance accompanying performance and a payment obligation arising only when service began. If so, Abbott's refusal might have occurred during formation and amounted to a refusal to contract. The court offered this as a possible account requiring factual development, not a categorical holding that every salon appointment is nonbinding. The remand permitted consideration of industry practice and the parties' expectations.

A finding of earlier formation would not end the claim. The parties also had to be allowed to present evidence whether the agreement was implicitly conditioned on the availability of an operator willing to serve a Black patron. The record could support an inference that a white patron with the same appointment would have received a replacement operator's services. Such a discriminatory term could violate the right to make contracts even under Patterson.

The district court also had not considered whether Abbott's conduct was authorized or reflected a salon policy, or determined intentional discrimination. The court did not accept Perry's argument that Patterson was confined to employment, and it did not decide the state tort claim.

The casebook's account notes that in 1991 Congress expanded "make and enforce contracts" to cover performance, modification, termination, and enjoyment of contractual benefits and conditions, so the Patterson discussion reflects the 1990 framework.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-061.rule: An offer to exchange a large bill for smaller bills is a proposed contract supported by consideration, even though the face values are equal and the business charges no fee and gains no immediate profit.

sections.Parties: James and Chris Barfield, father and son, sued Commerce Bank, N.A., under 42 U.S.C. section 1981, alleging that the bank refused to make change for African-American customers who did not hold accounts while doing so for white customers. The Barfields were the plaintiffs and appellants; the bank was the defendant and appellee.
sections.Procedural History: The Barfields sued under section 1981. While the bank's motion to dismiss was pending, the parties engaged in unsuccessful mediation and negotiations, and the Barfields sought class certification and amendment. The district court denied the plaintiffs' motions and dismissed the original action for failure to state a claim, accepting the bank's position that providing change involved no consideration. On May 1, 2007, the Tenth Circuit reversed the dismissal, affirmed the denial of permission to amend, and remanded for further proceedings. It did not grant class certification.
sections.Material Facts: These are the allegations of a complaint dismissed for failure to state a claim, not findings. Chris Barfield, an African-American man, requested change for a $50 bill at a Wichita Commerce Bank branch and was refused because he did not hold an account. The next day his father, James, sent a white friend, John Polson, to request change. Polson received it without being asked about an account. A few minutes later James requested change for a $100 bill and was refused unless he was an account-holder. James then enlisted a white news reporter and the reporter's African-American colleague. In separate visits, only the African-American visitor was asked whether he held an account.
sections.Issue: Whether a customer's request to exchange a large bill for smaller bills proposes a contractual transaction supported by consideration, so that a racially discriminatory refusal interferes with an activity protected by section 1981, or is instead a legally gratuitous service.
sections.Holding: The Tenth Circuit in 2007, in the sole opinion by McConnell J. for a panel of Kelly, McConnell, and Holmes, reversed dismissal of the section 1981 claim, affirmed denial of leave to amend, and remanded. Offering a large bill in exchange for smaller bills could constitute a proposed contract supported by consideration, even without a fee or an immediate profit for the bank. That conclusion let the discrimination claim proceed; it did not establish intentional discrimination or award damages.
sections.Reasoning:
The 1991 statutory addition extended "make and enforce contracts" to performance, modification, termination, and the enjoyment of contractual benefits and conditions. The circuit's test required membership in a protected class, intent to discriminate because of race, and interference with a protected activity; only the third was disputed. Retail customers' tangible attempts to enter transactions could trigger the statute before a purchase was completed.

Under Kansas common law, consideration could consist of a benefit, interest, right, detriment, forbearance, or responsibility bargained for in exchange. The customer proposed exchanging something of value, a large-denomination bill, for other bills the customer preferred. Equality in face value did not eliminate the exchange or make its consideration insufficient; parties could attach value to what they received without a court assigning the bargain a separate financial gain.

The bank argued that it supplied a free service. But a profit-making business may offer a transaction producing no immediate gain, or even a loss, to encourage other business, and such a transaction does not for that reason lack consideration. Potential goodwill or future dealings can carry value. The court distinguished Hampton v. Dillard Department Stores, where a niece who had neither made nor attempted a purchase failed to satisfy the terms of a coupon offer for fragrance samples; Hampton set no categorical rule excluding free samples and services.

The proposed amendment listed generalized accusations without identifying persons, dates, or incidents, and did not allege that the Barfields themselves were denied the additional services, so denying leave to amend was not an abuse of discretion.

The casebook recounts the bank visits and presents consideration as a question.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-062.rule: An offer made face to face, with no time specified, ordinarily remains open only through the conversation, and conduct by the offeree that justifies the offeror in understanding the offer was rejected ends the power to accept.

sections.Parties: Charles William Akers and William Gambill Whitsitt, engineers employed under five-year written contracts, sued their employer J. B. Sedberry, Inc., a Tennessee distributor of hammer mills, and Mrs. M. B. Sedberry, its president and principal shareholder, who had guaranteed both contracts. The employees prevailed in consolidated chancery causes; the employer and its president sought review by writ of error. The employees also challenged the denial of interest.
sections.Procedural History: The chancellor entered decrees awarding the employees damages: $17,927.75 to Akers and $4,200 to Whitsitt in salary recovery after earnings offsets, plus their contractual shares of the distributor's net profits, with the profit amounts referred to a special master. The employer and its president sought review by writ of error; the employees challenged the denial of interest. On September 9, 1955, the Tennessee Court of Appeals overruled all assignments, affirmed, directed appellate decrees for the amounts below with interest, charged costs against the defendants and their cost-bond sureties, and remanded for further proceedings.
sections.Material Facts:
Akers became chief engineer under a five-year contract beginning July 1, 1947, at $12,000 annually plus a profit percentage; Whitsitt became assistant chief engineer under a parallel contract beginning August 1, 1947, at $7,200 annually. At Mrs. Sedberry's direction they moved to Tyler, Texas, to supervise manufacturing by the separate Jay Bee Manufacturing Company, where friction developed with manager A. M. Sorenson.

Akers and Whitsitt visited Mrs. Sedberry without advance notice on Friday, September 29, 1950, for a conference lasting from 9:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Concerned that the unannounced visit might appear disloyal, they offered to resign at its outset as evidence of good faith. They testified that the offer required ninety days' notice; she disputed that. She did not accept then. She testified that she privately wanted to consult Sorenson, but she communicated no reservation of the offers for later decision. Instead she continued the business discussion, gave the engineers instructions, and had them return to Texas to carry them out. Nothing further was said about resignations. On Monday, October 2, she sent telegrams purporting to accept the resignations immediately. The engineers' October 16 letters disputed any outstanding offer.
sections.Issue: Whether the employees' offers to resign, made at the start of a face-to-face meeting and not accepted then, were still open when the employer telegraphed acceptance three days later, so as to end the fixed-term employment contracts.
sections.Holding: The Tennessee Court of Appeals in 1955, in the sole opinion by Felts J. with Hickerson and Shriver JJ. concurring, affirmed the decrees for the employees. Their face-to-face offers did not remain open beyond the meeting, and the employer's conduct had already rejected them earlier in the conversation. With no resignation offer remaining, the employer's attempt to terminate the fixed-term contracts breached them. The court did not impose a universal rule that every conversational offer expires instantly.
sections.Reasoning:
The court treated a proposed resignation from fixed-term employment as an offer to change or end the contractual relationship by mutual assent; it was not self-executing. Like other offers, it had to be accepted on its terms while still effective, and rejection or lapse ended the power to accept. Where no time was specified, reasonable duration depended on the proposed transaction, business usage, and surrounding circumstances. Ordinarily a face-to-face offer, without contrary words or circumstances, remained open only through the conversation.

Here the engineers expected an immediate response, and nothing showed an intention to preserve their offers after the meeting, so the Monday telegrams could not accept them. The court also found a more immediate ground: Mrs. Sedberry's conduct during the meeting justified the engineers in understanding that she had rejected the offers. She brushed them aside and resumed plans for their future work. Her unexpressed intent to deliberate did not outweigh that objective conduct. The ninety-day notice term was not an agreement that the offers stayed open for ninety days.

On damages, the measure was contractual salary and profit percentages for the remaining terms, less what each employee could earn elsewhere through due diligence. The court rejected an offset for the manufacturing company's losses, because the contracts did not contemplate it and the asserted parent-subsidiary relationship was not satisfactorily established. Recovery could not be limited to ninety days by the terms of an unaccepted offer. The employees' challenge to the denial of interest failed because their damages were not liquidated.

The casebook uses the case to introduce conversational lapse of an offer.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-063.rule: An offer that states no time limit lapses after a reasonable time, measured by its terms, purpose, and circumstances; a reward offer answering a particular emergency does not remain open indefinitely merely because it was never formally revoked.

sections.Parties: Loring and a co-plaintiff sued the City of Boston in assumpsit for a $1,000 reward the mayor had advertised for the apprehension and conviction of anyone setting fire to a building in the city. The plaintiffs claimed the reward for securing an arsonist's conviction; the city, the defendant, maintained that the offer had ceased before they acted.
sections.Procedural History: The plaintiffs brought assumpsit for the reward by a writ dated September 30, 1841. The parties withdrew the case from the jury and agreed that the city would be defaulted or the plaintiffs nonsuited according to the full court's determination. The only submitted question was whether the earlier offer remained effective when the Amory House burned. At the March Term 1844, the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court ordered a nonsuit of the plaintiffs. This was not an appellate affirmance of a jury verdict.
sections.Material Facts:
Mayor Samuel A. Eliot advertised a $500 reward on May 26, 1837, for apprehension and conviction of anyone setting fire to a building within the city. The following day a second advertisement doubled the reward to $1,000, describing repeated successful incendiary attempts and the need for vigorous prevention. Publication continued for about one week. No city vote or mayoral notice formally revoked the offer or specified its duration. The fire-department chief testified that alarms had been frequent before the advertisements but that few fires occurred from then through the end of 1841.

After a January 1841 Washington Street fire destroyed the Amory House and other buildings, the plaintiffs suspected Samuel Marriott. They announced their intention to pursue him to obtain the advertised reward, followed him to New York with an identifying witness, arrested him, and returned him to Boston. They supplied witnesses and evidence, secured an indictment, and helped obtain his March 1841 conviction for burning the Amory House. The brief notes that the report itself is inconsistent on the advertisement dates, the opinion's discussion saying March 26 where the reproduced advertisements say May 26.
sections.Issue: Whether a reward offer published for about a week in 1837, with no stated duration and never formally revoked, was still open to acceptance by performance when the plaintiffs apprehended and helped convict an arsonist in 1841.
sections.Holding: The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court at its March Term 1844, in the sole opinion by Shaw C.J., held that Boston's reward offer had ceased before the plaintiffs acted on it and ordered a nonsuit. Three years and eight months was beyond a reasonable duration for this temporary offer responding to a particular arson emergency, so no express reward contract supported the action. The court declined to identify a precise universal deadline for reward offers.
sections.Reasoning:
Shaw accepted that a public reward is an offer capable of acceptance through the requested service, creating an enforceable contract supported by consideration. The question was the offer's duration, which the court determined from its terms, purpose, and circumstances.

An omitted express deadline did not make the offer unlimited. The advertisement was a temporary executive response to a stated emergency, not a standing municipal ordinance, and a reasonable reader would not regard it as continuing for ten or twenty years merely because no formal revocation appeared. The plaintiffs' argument that the statute of limitations supplied the only temporal limit was mistaken: a limitations period would begin when the services created the contract, not when the unaccepted offer was published, which could leave the offer open for decades.

The court therefore implied a reasonable duration, which on the circumstances proved was a question of law. The reward's purposes were to make the public and officers vigilant and perhaps to deter offenders, and those purposes depended on the reward being publicly known and remembered. A long-discontinued advertisement would no longer operate as the intended incentive. The officers' annual tenure offered some indication of temporary character but no rigid deadline. Cessation of advertising was not itself a revocation, but it was evidence that the emergency had passed.

In these circumstances three years and eight months was too long: the emergency had passed, the public could be presumed to have forgotten the offer, and the plaintiffs could not reasonably understand it as still continuing. Their subjective motivation to earn the reward could not revive the expired offer.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-064.rule: A public reward offer can be accepted only within its own terms and while it remains open; a later news report replaying the offer does not renew it, and ratification cannot supply legal significance the replayed act itself lacks.

sections.Parties: Newman, a Missouri lawyer, sued Schiff, who promoted books and lectures asserting that federal income taxation was voluntary, to recover a $100,000 reward Schiff had promised on television. Schiff denied that Newman had satisfied the offer. It was a diversity action governed by Missouri law. Newman appealed the judgment for Schiff, and Schiff cross-appealed.
sections.Procedural History:
The district court initially found that the live offer ended with the Nightwatch program, that the rebroadcast did not extend it, and that Newman therefore had not accepted in time. After Newman requested additional findings and amendment of the judgment, the court kept the judgment but changed part of its explanation: it concluded that Schiff had ratified the morning rebroadcast by failing to object, accepting publicity, and writing his April 20 letter, and that this renewed the offer, yet Newman still responded too late because he had not done so on the morning of the rebroadcast.

Newman appealed, challenging the standard for timing a response to the supposed renewed offer. Schiff cross-appealed but did not challenge the district court's rejection of his tax theory. The Eighth Circuit affirmed the judgment for Schiff, with no costs imposed against Newman.
sections.Material Facts:
On February 7, 1983, Schiff appeared live on CBS News Nightwatch, interviewed by Karen Stone from approximately 3 to 4 a.m. Eastern Time. The program displayed its call-in number and invited viewers to speak with him on air. He promised $100,000 to anyone who called 'this show' and identified a Code section requiring an individual to file a tax return.

Newman did not watch the live program. Several hours later he saw a two-minute recorded excerpt on CBS Morning News, in which Diane Sawyer explained that Schiff had discussed his views earlier that morning on Nightwatch. Newman researched the Code at work and on February 8 called CBS Morning News, using a general CBS number rather than the Nightwatch call-in number. He cited statutory provisions and sent a letter stating that his research performed the requested consideration. CBS replied on March 3 that it had forwarded the letter to Schiff. On April 13 Newman wrote to Schiff directly. Schiff's April 20 reply acknowledged making an offer but denied that Newman had satisfied it, asserting that § 6012 did not establish a filing requirement and that the offer went to the first qualifying respondent.
sections.Issue: Whether Newman accepted a reward offer from Schiff: whether the offer made on the live Nightwatch broadcast remained open after that program ended, and whether the replay on the morning news, or Schiff's later conduct treated as ratifying it, renewed the offer so that Newman's response the next day could accept it.
sections.Holding: The Eighth Circuit, in 1985, in an opinion by Senior Judge Bright for a panel including Judges Heaney and Arnold, affirmed the judgment for Schiff. The televised promise was a potentially binding reward offer, but the only offer was the invitation to call the live Nightwatch program before it ended, and Newman did not respond to it. The morning news replay reported the earlier offer and did not renew it. The court rejected the district court's ratification analysis and declined to decide the timeliness of acceptance of a supposed renewed offer. No costs were imposed against Newman.
sections.Reasoning:
The court explained formation through manifested assent, offer and acceptance. The question is how words and conduct would reasonably be understood, not whether the parties privately shared an identical mental state, although the court cautioned against completely disregarding actual, proven assent.

Public reward cases such as Carlill and James v. Turilli showed that a broadcast format does not prevent formation. The court said a person who called Nightwatch with the Code sections Newman found would have formed a contract and called Schiff's bluff. The failure lay in the offer's temporal and program-specific scope. In context 'this show' meant the live call-in broadcast, and the offer stayed open only until that program concluded. A reasonable viewer of the later news segment would understand it as a report of what Schiff had offered, not another invitation to earn $100,000 by calling a different program.

Schiff's later conduct and letter could be considered as evidence of whether the rebroadcast objectively appeared to be an offer, but they were indefinite, continued to deny obligation, and did not change the character of the news report. Even under an agency ratification analysis the result was the same. Ratification adopts an unauthorized act done on another's behalf and relates back as authorization; it does not supply legal significance missing from the act itself. Schiff might have authorized CBS's decision to replay the interview, but authorizing a news report did not turn it into a renewed reward offer.

The court separately explained that § 6012 required individuals above specified income thresholds to file returns and commended Newman for exposing Schiff's false claim, but that approval did not replace the required acceptance. There was no separate opinion. The casebook uses the case in a note on counting the offers; its reference to an evening challenge is imprecise against the report's 3 to 4 a.m. account.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-065.rule: An oral offer made face to face ordinarily ends with the conversation unless a contrary intention appears; if the offeror invites a later answer and states no deadline, the offer remains open for a reasonable time determined by the circumstances.

sections.Parties: Yaros sued the Trustees of the University of Pennsylvania in negligence after falling at the university's skating rink. Her lawyer was Richard Haaz; the university's trial counsel was John Orlando. Yaros sought enforcement of a $750,000 settlement she said she had accepted during trial, first by oral motion before the jury deliberated and again after the defense verdict. The university, the appellant, argued that its offer had expired or been rejected before she accepted.
sections.Procedural History: Testimony began January 26, 1998, before Judge Paul Ribner. On January 29, after Yaros's acceptance was announced at sidebar, the university's counsel said he did not know whether the offer was still there. The next day, before deliberations, Yaros orally moved to enforce the settlement. Judge Ribner denied the motion pending evidentiary hearings and the verdict, and the jury then found for the university. After trial Yaros renewed the enforcement request and sought post-trial relief. Judge Ribner held one hearing; on his retirement the matter went to Judge Sandra Mazer Moss, who held further hearings in January 1999 and granted enforcement on February 22. The university appealed that order. The Pennsylvania Superior Court affirmed the order enforcing the settlement.
sections.Material Facts:
Early in the trial the university offered $750,000. Haaz told Orlando that Yaros would accept $1.5 million until she testified, after which she would not settle. Two defense witnesses testified before Yaros, and no settlement was reached.

On January 29, after the evidence concluded, Orlando again offered $750,000 during a ten-minute recess before closings. He told Haaz to get back to him, looked at the clock, and placed his palms sideways. Neither a time limit nor an expiration at the start of closing arguments was communicated. Haaz left to speak with his client, who was in the restroom; he returned without her and obtained two minutes from the judge to consult her. Orlando assumed they had not yet discussed the offer. When she returned they did not confer and arguments began immediately. The court had asked counsel to finish by 5 p.m.

During the university's closing, Yaros authorized acceptance. Haaz delivered his rebuttal and then told the court at sidebar that she had accepted. The interval was seventy minutes. Acceptance was communicated before the jury's deliberations and its defense verdict.
sections.Issue: Whether the university's oral $750,000 offer, made in a recess before closing arguments with no stated deadline, was still open when Yaros accepted about seventy minutes later after closings: whether it ended with the conversation or at the start of closings, whether proceeding with closings was a rejection, and whether the acceptance came within a reasonable time.
sections.Holding: The Pennsylvania Superior Court, in 1999, in an opinion by Judge Orie Melvin for a panel with Judges Ford Elliott and Stevens, affirmed the order enforcing the $750,000 settlement. The university had not communicated a deadline requiring acceptance before closings, and its instruction to counsel to get back to it showed that the oral offer survived the conversation. Continuing with closing arguments was not a rejection. Whether seventy minutes was a reasonable time depended on the circumstances of this negotiation, not on a rule that every offer made before closing argument automatically expires when argument starts, and competent evidence supported the trial court's finding. The later defense verdict did not remove the settlement already formed.
sections.Reasoning:
Settlement enforcement follows contract law. Legal conclusions received plenary review and the trial judge's factual findings received deference.

The university invoked Restatement (Second) § 41 comment d: in face-to-face or telephone bargaining an oral offer ordinarily ends with the conversation unless a contrary intention appears. The court agreed that this rule fit the setting more closely than the general reasonable-time rule the trial court applied, but stressed its exception: words or circumstances showing an expected intervening step can invite delayed acceptance. Orlando's direction to get back to him contemplated that Haaz would consult Yaros and return, so the offer plainly continued. A glance at the clock, hand gestures, and the general urgency of trial did not make a cutoff before closings clear, and Orlando's own uncertainty after closings undercut the claim of an unmistakable deadline. Orlando and the university's liability administrator testified that they had not set or communicated a time limit. The earlier negotiation set no convention of automatic event conditions, because Yaros's earlier condition had been expressly stated.

Proceeding through closings was not a rejection. Conduct can justify an inference of rejection, but in Smaligo the offeror had expressly said that going forward would count as rejection, and no comparable notice was given here. A rule treating the start of closings as automatic rejection would let an offeror assert, only after acceptance, that an uncommunicated trial event had ended the offer. Orlando also believed Yaros had not yet learned of the offer.

Reasonable time ordinarily depends on the transaction, relationship, course of dealing, and usages. The distinctive timing here warranted a factual determination, and a significant trial event is only one consideration. There was no separate writing. The casebook assigns a problem, Courtroom Countdown, based on this negotiation and the later defense verdict.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-066.rule: An offer unsupported by consideration is withdrawn when a communication reaching the offeree before acceptance states or implies that the offeror no longer consents to the transaction; no express words of revocation are required.

sections.Parties: Clements Paper Company, the prospective seller of real estate, sued Hoover Motor Express Company, the prospective buyer, for specific performance or alternatively damages after Hoover refused to go through with a purchase it had offered to make. Clements's vice-president, Williams, handled the dealings. Hoover, which lost in both lower courts, obtained certiorari and argued that it had withdrawn its offer before any acceptance.
sections.Procedural History: The chancellor sustained Clements's bill, finding that Hoover had breached the parties' written contract, and the Court of Appeals agreed. A reference to the master was ordered to ascertain damages, so no final damages amount had been fixed. Hoover obtained certiorari, arguing that there was no concurrent controlling finding and that any such finding lacked support under the applicable law. The Tennessee Supreme Court reversed both decrees and remanded for a decree consistent with the absence of a contract, with all costs in all courts against Clements. The caption reports that rehearing was denied August 31, 1951.
sections.Material Facts:
On November 19, 1949, Hoover delivered a written offer concerning its purchase of real estate from Clements. No consideration was paid for the offer. In December Clements authorized Williams to accept, but he withheld acceptance hoping for a substantially better bargain: he wanted Clements to retain an easement through the property and tried repeatedly to contact Hoover about it. He never actually communicated the proposed changes.

On January 13, 1950, Williams reached Hoover by telephone and said Clements was ready to proceed and that he wished to discuss the transaction. Hoover replied that he did not know whether they were ready, they had not decided, and they might not want to proceed. By Williams's own testimony Hoover also said he did not think the company would proceed, indicated it had other plans, declined positively to commit, and said he would call January 17, which he never did. Williams testified he was shocked to hear they did not plan to go through with it. Clements's complaint described this as its first information or intimation that Hoover would not or might not carry out the agreement or offer.

On January 20 Clements sent a written acceptance, closing with a demand that Hoover comply with its part of the agreement. Clements asserted no earlier acceptance.
sections.Issue: Whether Hoover's November 19 offer, unsupported by consideration, was still open when Clements sent its written acceptance on January 20, or whether the January 13 telephone conversation had already withdrawn it even though Hoover never expressly said the offer was revoked.
sections.Holding: The Tennessee Supreme Court, in 1951, in a unanimous opinion by Justice Tomlinson, reversed the decrees sustaining Clements's claim. Hoover's January 13 communication withdrew its November 19 offer before Clements attempted written acceptance on January 20. No formula expressly announcing revocation is necessary when the communication brings home to the offeree that the offeror no longer consents to the proposed transaction. Because no offer continued on January 20, the written acceptance could not form a contract. The cause was remanded for a conforming decree, with all costs against Clements.
sections.Reasoning:
The court first held that the lower courts had made concurrent findings on the controlling fact: the chancellor's finding of a contract implicitly found the offer had not been withdrawn, and the Court of Appeals found so expressly. It was bound by those findings if any material evidence sustained them and could not review the facts anew, so it examined the evidence most favorable to Clements. That made Clements's own witness decisive: even Williams's account could not reasonably support a finding that Hoover's commitment continued.

The parties agreed that an offer unsupported by consideration must be accepted before withdrawal, and the offer must still exist when acceptance occurs. Finding no Tennessee decision on the precise point, the court turned to general authority that express notice in prescribed words is unnecessary. The First Restatement of Contracts § 41 included a communication received before acceptance that states or implies that the offeror no longer intends to contract, and the court invoked Coleman v. Applegarth's quotation from Dickinson v. Dodds rejecting any requirement that the offeror actually say the offer is withdrawn.

Applying that rule, Williams learned on January 13 that Hoover no longer consented. His descriptions of the other plans, the refusal to commit, and his shock supported that meaning, and the wording of the January 20 letter showed his understanding that something had occurred that might cause Hoover to refuse. An indication that Hoover might call again did not preserve the offer. Williams's earlier authority and private intention to accept had not exercised the power of acceptance, and because he never communicated his proposed changes the court did not treat a counteroffer as the terminating event. The lower courts' error was insisting on express withdrawal language. The court did not hold that every expression of uncertainty revokes an offer. The casebook cites the case on when a communication constitutes revocation.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-067.rule: A public reward offer may be revoked before acceptance by performance, but only in the manner in which it was made or by another method giving like publicity; private acts that convey nothing to the public do not revoke it.

sections.Parties: Carr and other plaintiffs, who furnished information leading to the arrest and conviction of bank robbers, sued the Mahaska County Bankers Association, an unincorporated voluntary association, and several alleged member banks for a $1,000 reward. Taintor Savings Bank, a defendant that had displayed the reward poster, was the sole appellant and argued that it had revoked the offer by taking the poster down.
sections.Procedural History: After the jury was waived, a bench trial produced a $1,000 judgment with interest and costs against three banks. Taintor moved for a directed verdict and dismissal at the close of the plaintiffs' evidence and renewed the motion after all testimony, asserting no evidence that the association existed at the time of the robbery, that Taintor was then a member, or that Taintor had displayed a reward notice. The motion was denied. Taintor alone appealed. The Iowa Supreme Court affirmed, with no remand or new trial.
sections.Material Facts:
The association's poster offered $1,000 for capture or information leading to the arrest and conviction of robbers or burglars of any member bank in the county, and represented that the displaying bank belonged to the association. The record did not establish the poster's exact origin; the court inferred it had existed for some years before 1930. Taintor's cashier admitted that the bank joined the association and displayed an identical poster, and Taintor conceded that displaying it made the bank an offeror, because the association was not a legally suable entity.

The cashier testified that in December 1931 or January 1932 he removed the poster and threw it in the wastebasket, and at the same time refused an association sight-draft for dues; no further dues were paid. No bank resolution or minutes recorded a withdrawal from the association.

On January 10, 1935, the Farmers Savings Bank in Leighton was robbed. Carr and the other plaintiffs discovered and furnished information leading to the offenders' arrest and conviction, relying on the reward offer.
sections.Issue: Whether a bank that had made a public reward offer for future bank robberies by displaying a poster effectively revoked that offer by privately removing the poster and ceasing to pay association dues, without publicizing any withdrawal, before the plaintiffs performed.
sections.Holding: The Iowa Supreme Court, in 1936, in an opinion by Justice Richards with seven justices concurring and no separate writing, affirmed the $1,000 reward judgment, with interest and costs, against Taintor Savings Bank. Removing a reward poster without publicizing a withdrawal did not effectively revoke an offer aimed at deterring future bank robberies. The public could reasonably understand the offer as continuing even without continuous display, and the record supported a finding that Taintor did not revoke in the manner in which the offer was made or by another method providing like publicity.
sections.Reasoning:
On procedure, Taintor did not stand on its first motion but introduced its own evidence, so a deficiency at the close of the plaintiffs' case did not require reversal if competent evidence supported the case when the motion was renewed. The court reviewed the renewed motion on the full record, including the cashier's admissions. Although revocation was not strictly within the motion's grounds, both sides treated it as presented and the court did likewise.

A public reward offer ordinarily may be revoked before acceptance by performance, but the revocation must be effective against the public to whom the offer was made. In Shuey a published revocation was effective though the claimant did not know of it; Sullivan supplied the rule that revocation must use the original manner of publication or another method giving comparable publicity. Individual notice is not always needed, but private conduct that conveys nothing publicly is insufficient.

The offer's purpose affects how the public reasonably understands it. The court distinguished rewards for an existing temporary evil or a particular past crime from those looking to future events. This notice contemplated any future robbery of a county bank, and deterrence was its paramount incentive, so the trial court could find that the public reasonably assumed continuity without the poster staying constantly visible. The public could not be charged with knowledge that the cashier discarded the paper or refused a dues draft. The court suggested posting a revocation notice in the bank as one possible method, without holding it the only one.

Because liability arose from Taintor's own representation of a principal lacking legal existence, the association's alleged absence or the end of membership did not defeat the claim. The bank never claimed that a reasonable time for acceptance had expired, so the court did not decide that such rewards stay open perpetually. The casebook uses the case to ask whether taking down a bulletin-board reward is a sufficient revocation.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-068.rule: An offer to dedicate land to public use must be accepted by a manifest public act while the offer is still open; it ends by lapse after an unreasonable delay or by withdrawal through private use inconsistent with public ownership.

sections.Parties: Raymond and Jean Marx, owners of lots on either side of a platted but undeveloped road called Birch Lane, sued to vacate the road and quiet title, alleging that its dedication had never been accepted. The complaint named several defendants, including the Department of Commerce, but only Bay Township and the Charlevoix County road commission pursued the consolidated appeals, contending that the dedication had been accepted.
sections.Procedural History: In 1993 the Marxes sought vacation of Birch Lane and a declaratory judgment quieting title. The government defendants moved for summary disposition under MCR 2.116(C)(10), relying on plat approval, asserted maintenance expenditures, and an alleged assumption of road jurisdiction under the McNitt Act. The landowners responded under MCR 2.116(I)(2), asking for judgment in their favor because no acceptance had occurred and their own use was inconsistent with public dedication. The trial court granted that relief and ordered vacation. The township and the county road commission appealed. The Michigan Court of Appeals, reviewing de novo, affirmed summary disposition for the landowners and the order of vacation.
sections.Material Facts:
George and Laura Franklin platted Zenith Heights in Bay Township in August 1911, designating its streets and alleys for public use. Birch Lane lay between Lots six and seven, running from Valley Brook Avenue to Walloon Lake. The township approved the plat on August 14, 1911. The Marxes acquired Lot six in 1970, Lot seven in 1976, and Lot five in 1977; the report's factual narrative places their residence on Lot seven with a driveway encroaching on Birch Lane, while its withdrawal analysis dates the driveway on Birch Lane to 1970.

The defendants could locate no resolution assuming jurisdiction under the McNitt Act, only a purported McNitt map, which did not refer to Birch Lane, and a 1938 mileage survey, which omitted Birch Lane's mileage. There was a 1952 discussion of underwriting improvements to roads including Birch Lane, but no actual work or expenditure on it. The road commission told the owners that the township did not intend to develop the road, and the owners regularly parked on the strip and treated it as private property. In 1979 the township passed a resolution formally accepting previously unaccepted dedicated lands, specifically referring to Zenith Heights.
sections.Issue: Whether the public authorities timely accepted the 1911 offer to dedicate Birch Lane, through the McNitt Act, plat approval, expenditures, or the township's 1979 resolution, or whether by 1979 the offer had lapsed through delay or been withdrawn by the owners' inconsistent private use.
sections.Holding: The Michigan Court of Appeals, in 1996, in an opinion by Judge O'Connell for a panel with Judge Fitzgerald and assigned circuit judge T. L. Ludington, affirmed summary disposition for the landowners and the order vacating Birch Lane's dedication. The public authorities had not established a timely manifest acceptance of the 1911 dedication. The township's 1979 resolution was sufficient in form, assuming its authority, but came after the offer had both lapsed and been withdrawn. Those were separate grounds: lapse arose from unreasonable delay, and withdrawal arose from affirmative private use inconsistent with public ownership, which the court placed in 1970.
sections.Reasoning:
A valid public dedication requires a recorded plat showing the proprietor's intent and timely acceptance by the proper authority through a manifest public act, formal or informal: a resolution, actual expenditure of public money for repair, improvement and control, or public use. The requirement protects authorities from responsibility for unwanted property. The authority bears the burden of proving acceptance; the owner must prove withdrawal.

No acceptance was shown. Under Kraus even a general resolution claiming all township roads did not manifest acceptance without identifying the road or its plat, and here there was no resolution at all; the map and survey did not mention Birch Lane. On plat approval, the court followed Salzer rather than Bangle: approval without reference to accepting the dedicated property lacks the necessary manifestation. The 1952 discussion of a possible project involved no actual expenditure.

The 1979 resolution would ordinarily satisfy the form of acceptance, the court assuming the township's authority, but it came too late. An offer to dedicate may continue if not withdrawn, yet continuation depends on the circumstances. Comparing cases finding eighty-six and eighty-seven years unreasonable with one it described as allowing twenty-six, the court found sixty-eight years unreasonable on this record, without setting a fixed cutoff.

Independently, using dedicated land inconsistently with public ownership can manifest withdrawal. The unrefuted evidence of the driveway, the regular parking, and the road commission's statement showed withdrawal; complete blockage was unnecessary. A 1978 statutory presumption of acceptance was rebutted because the 1970 withdrawal preceded both the statute and the attempted acceptance. The court declined to decide road-end access arguments as unnecessary and treated a claimed public policy favoring lake access as abandoned. There was no separate writing.

The casebook uses the case to distinguish lapse from revocation; its statement that state law required a formal governmental resolution is narrower than the opinion, which recognizes informal acceptance.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.rule: A mixed contract for goods and services falls under Article 2 when its predominant factor, reasonably described, is a sale of goods with labor incidentally involved rather than the rendition of services with goods incidentally involved.

sections.Parties: Frances Bonebrake, as administratrix of the estate of her brother Woodrow Simek, a sole proprietor who dealt in bowling equipment, sued Donald and Claude Cox, operators of the Tamarack Bowl in Missouri Valley, Iowa, for the unpaid price under two contracts. The Coxes, the buyers, counterclaimed for their losses and asserted that Simek or the estate had breached first.
sections.Procedural History: The case was referred to a special master, who rejected both sides' breach positions and recommended awarding the estate the $28,000 unpaid balance less $1,000 representing the seller's value of unaccepted goods. The master excluded the April contract from Article 2, held that the buyers had waived warranty recovery by inadequate notice and by preventing cure, and concluded that the buyers breached by taking over the work. The district court entered judgment of $27,000 for the estate. Iowa law governed by an unchallenged ruling. The Eighth Circuit reversed and remanded for proceedings consistent with its holdings, without itself calculating any recovery.
sections.Material Facts:
A February 5, 1968 fire destroyed the Coxes' bowling equipment. On April 17 they agreed to pay Simek $20,000 for used lane beds, ball returns, seating, lockers, and other equipment, delivered and installed, with lane resurfacing and promises of freedom from defects. On August 23 they separately agreed to pay $35,000 for ten used Brunswick pinspotters delivered and installed, with a one-year guarantee on motors and gearboxes. Neither contract fixed a completion date, but the business depended on leagues starting in late August or early September.

By September 4 the pinspotters were in place, but the master found them inoperative, in very poor condition, and not installed. The buyers and volunteers repaired them with the advice of Simek's installer, Ilert Avery. Simek died on September 6. The court's narrative identifies $20,000 paid on the pinspotter contract and $7,000 on the April contract. Several April items were undelivered. The buyers searched for the missing equipment through Simek's warehouses, suppliers, Avery, and Bonebrake, found no one able to organize completion, and then ordered missing items and hired specialists. Their lawyer's September 17 letter described the incomplete installation, the repairs, lost income, and the records being kept for a loss claim. The alley opened October 14, allowing only three league rounds.
sections.Issue: Whether the April equipment-and-installation contract was a transaction in goods under Article 2; whether buyers who accepted defective goods lost their warranty claim through inadequate notice or by refusing the seller's cure; and whether the buyers' completion of the work was their own breach or a justified response to anticipatory repudiation.
sections.Holding: The Eighth Circuit, in 1974, in an opinion by Judge Talbot Smith, sitting by designation, for a panel with Judges Heaney and Stephenson, reversed the $27,000 judgment for the seller's estate and remanded. The April contract was governed by Article 2 because its predominant purpose was a sale of goods. Buyers who accept defective goods need only give notice that the transaction is troublesome and claimed to involve a breach, which the September 17 letter did, and they need not accept a later cure to keep a damages claim. The buyers' completion of the work was justified by the estate's anticipatory repudiation and was not their breach.
sections.Reasoning:
On notice, Iowa § 554.2607(3)(a), corresponding to UCC § 2-607(3)(a), governs accepted goods and requires notice of breach within a reasonable time after discovery. Section 554.2605(1) governs rejection and failure to particularize defects. The master had demanded the more exacting rejection notice. Notice after acceptance need not list every defect or threaten suit; the September 17 letter was more than enough. The cure ruling likewise imported rejection rules: § 554.2508 lets a seller cure a rejected tender, but these buyers had accepted and sought damages. Refusing cure could raise mitigation questions but did not eliminate the warranty claim.

On scope, Article 2 applies to transactions in goods, defined by movability at identification to the contract. The equipment was movable then, and installation services created no unstated exception. Later attachment to the alley did not make this a construction contract; the lane beds were used, prefabricated equipment previously installed elsewhere. The test for mixed contracts is whether the predominant factor, reasonably stated, is the rendition of service with goods incidentally involved, as in a contract with an artist for a painting, or a sale with labor incidentally involved, as in installing a water heater in a bathroom. This contract replaced bowling equipment destroyed by fire, so Article 2 governed.

On repudiation, the master's conclusion that the buyers breached necessarily rejected their claim, and that was clear error. The court did not hold that a seller's death always repudiates. Under § 554.2610, repudiation does not require literal impossibility or ill will; conduct reasonably indicating rejection of the continuing obligation suffices. The sole proprietor's death, the serious defects, the missing equipment, the urgent league schedule, the failed searches, and the absence of anyone able to perform supplied that indication. Any later completion offer by the administrators came after the buyers materially changed position. There was no separate opinion.

The casebook cites the case for the predominant-factor approach.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.rule: When one transaction sells both goods and non-goods, Article 2 governs the sale of the goods even though non-goods predominate, so the seller cannot use the resale-price remedy for the goods without giving notice of a private resale.

sections.Parties: Colorado Radio Corporation, the seller, brought a diversity action against Rosemary Foster, the buyer, after she failed to complete her agreement to acquire certain assets of a New Mexico radio station. The seller sought the difference between the contract price and the price on resale. Foster challenged the finding of breach and the damages.
sections.Procedural History: Shortly after filing suit, Colorado Radio privately resold the station to Walton. The trial court found that Foster had breached, treated the transaction as entirely outside the Code, and, under the parties' stipulated measure, awarded $15,750 as the difference between the contract price and the resale price, plus $500 attorney's fees as incidental damages. It also found the $5,000 escrow fund was not an exclusive remedy. Foster did not challenge the fee award. The Tenth Circuit affirmed the judgment as modified, reducing the price-difference award to $14,175 and ordering no new trial or remand.
sections.Material Facts:
The agreement, dated August 28, 1964, required Foster to make satisfactory arrangements to assume two notes and to apply to the Federal Communications Commission for transfer of the station's license; both parties were to act diligently and cooperate. Foster did not arrange to assume the notes, and the evidence fell far short of reasonable diligence on one note. She never filed the application. On November 18, about two weeks before suit, Colorado Radio telegraphed that its materials had been ready in September, demanded diligence, and said five more days was reasonable; two later telephone calls asked whether and when she would file.

The assets included the license, goodwill, real estate, studios, and transmission equipment, and also office equipment and furnishings, which Colorado Radio conceded were movables and which made up five to ten percent of the price. The seller admitted it gave no notice of its intended private resale to Walton. At trial the parties stipulated that, apart from incidental damages, the measure was the difference between the resale price and the contract price.
sections.Issue: Whether Foster breached despite the unmet conditions and the statutory demand requirement, and whether Article 2 applied to the movable office equipment and furnishings sold as a small part of a radio station, so that the seller's failure to give notice of its private resale barred the resale-price measure of damages for that portion.
sections.Holding: The Tenth Circuit, in 1967, in an opinion by Chief Judge Murrah for a panel with Judge Hickey and District Judge Christensen, affirmed the seller's judgment as modified. Foster breached. The transaction included both goods and non-goods, and Article 2 governed the movable office equipment and furnishings even though they were a small part of the business sold. Because the seller gave no notice of the private resale, it could not use the stipulated resale-price remedy for the goods portion; the remedy remained available for the non-goods. Attributing ten percent of the damages to the goods, the court reduced the award from $15,750 to $14,175 and left the $500 fee award intact.
sections.Reasoning:
On breach, the agreement placed responsibility for the note arrangements on Foster, and a party cannot use a condition's nonoccurrence to avoid liability when her own inaction caused it. New Mexico § 50-7-3 required a demand for performance before suit on certain contracts; its purpose is to give a final opportunity to perform, and the seller's demand that she file the application, the first step toward performance, satisfied it without a separate demand for the price.

On damages, the New Mexico versions of UCC § 2-706(1) and (3) allow the contract-resale difference but require reasonable notification of a private resale. The court read the stipulation as fixing the measure if the resale was legally proper, not as waiving that prerequisite. It agreed that the license, goodwill, real estate, studios, and transmission equipment were non-goods on this record. The seller argued the conceded goods were incidental to the transfer of a going concern. The court rejected that exemption: Article 2's language gives no basis to disregard a conceded sale of goods because non-goods predominate, and a business could consist almost entirely of goods apart from goodwill. Epstein, the beauty-services case, was distinguished because this was a sale of a group of assets, not the supply of a service.

The contract could therefore be viewed in two parts. For the goods, lack of notice foreclosed § 2-706, and because the parties had stipulated to that measure, the breach as to goods was unremediable in this case. For the non-goods, notice was not mandatory and the agreed measure remained. Taking the valuation testimony most favorably to Foster, the court used ten percent as the goods' share.

Foster could not go behind the stipulation with a late theory, and the escrow agreement, which said the fund did not limit damages, was admissible to resolve the contract's ambiguity. There was no separate opinion.

The casebook cites the case for bifurcating a hybrid radio-station sale.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-071.rule: In Maryland, when a commercial transaction sells consumer goods that retain that character after performance and monetary loss or personal injury arises from a defect in them, implied warranties apply to those goods even though consumer services predominate.

sections.Parties: John and Pilar Sheehan, homeowners, sued Anthony Pools, which designed and built their backyard swimming pool and designed, manufactured, and installed its diving board, after John was injured in a fall from the board. They claimed breach of the implied warranty of merchantability and strict liability. Anthony, which won at trial and lost in the intermediate court, obtained certiorari.
sections.Procedural History: At the close of the plaintiffs' evidence the trial court directed a verdict for Anthony on the warranty claim because the agreement conspicuously made its express warranties exclusive of others. The strict-liability claim went to the jury, which returned a defense verdict. The Court of Special Appeals reversed and remanded for a new trial: it regarded the swimming-pool package as consumer goods, treated the warranty exclusion as ineffective, and found an omission in the jury instructions concerning the plaintiff's conduct. Anthony obtained certiorari on the warranty question, the instruction concerning inadvertent use, and the statement that contributory negligence was not a strict-liability defense. The Maryland Court of Appeals affirmed the intermediate court's judgment, with costs payable by Anthony.
sections.Material Facts:
The Sheehans' May 25, 1976 agreement was a two-sided printed form combining a retail installment contract with a swimming-pool construction agreement. Anthony agreed both to construct the pool and to sell the related equipment; its duties ran from engineering, excavation, steel, and gunite to filtering equipment and the specified diving board. The reverse side excluded implied warranties. Nothing allocated a separate price to each item or portion of work.

The inground gunite pool measured sixteen by forty feet. Anthony also designed, manufactured, and installed a six-foot diving board over the alcove at the deep end. The work was finished by mid-June 1976. At an August 21 pool party John, by his testimony using the board for the first time, slipped from its right side and hit the coping.

The Sheehans alleged that the skid-resistant material stopped about an inch short of the board's side edges, breaching merchantability, and offered evidence that the board, particularly its placement, was unreasonably dangerous. Those were their theories, not appellate findings of defect or causation.
sections.Issue: Whether an implied warranty of merchantability, which under Maryland's consumer-warranty statute cannot be disclaimed, attached to a diving board sold as part of a swimming-pool contract in which construction services predominated, and whether the strict-liability jury instructions properly dealt with the plaintiff's own conduct.
sections.Holding: The Maryland Court of Appeals, then the state's highest court, in 1983, in an opinion by Judge Rodowsky for the six listed judges, affirmed the intermediate court's reversal and order for a new trial. Although construction services predominated, the separately identifiable consumer diving board carried an implied warranty of merchantability, and Maryland's § 2-316.1 made the contractual disclaimer ineffective, so the directed verdict was error. When consumer goods sold in a commercial transaction retain that character after performance and loss or injury arises from a defect in them, the implied-warranty provisions apply to those goods even though services predominate. The court also adopted the intermediate court's strict-liability instruction analysis. It did not find the board defective.
sections.Reasoning:
Article 2 ordinarily applies to transactions in goods, and § 2-316 permits exclusion of implied warranties. Maryland's § 2-316.1 provides that the exclusion section does not apply to consumer goods, services, or both, and that language excluding implied consumer warranties is unenforceable.

Under the predominant-purpose test the court had adopted in Burton, the Sheehans were buying construction of a finished pool, not individual materials; labor and services predominated and the board was incidental. The court did not avoid the problem by reclassifying the whole undertaking as a sale. But the board kept a distinct identity: the contract promised sale of equipment, called the Sheehans buyers, and offered the board as an optional accessory; it was movable when identified, not structurally integrated, and detachable. Bought separately, it would have carried a merchantability warranty.

Hawkland's suggested gravamen approach, which separates injury from a defective item from injury caused by deficient labor, supplied the analytical vehicle, and the Maryland statute supplied the decisive policy. An all-or-nothing classification would leave consumer goods in a services-predominant transaction with no implied warranty at all, yet § 2-316.1 expressly embraces consumer goods and services; treating the construction classification as dispositive would frustrate it. The court reserved whether goods consumed in rendering a service are covered and did not abolish predominant-purpose analysis for other Article 2 issues.

On strict liability, the court adopted Part III of the intermediate opinion. Inadvertence or failure to discover or guard against a defect does not bar recovery. A plaintiff who discovers a defect, understands the danger, and voluntarily and unreasonably encounters it may assume the risk, a subjective inquiry requiring actual awareness. The jury needed instructions drawing that distinction, and the plaintiffs still had to prove a defective, unreasonably dangerous product and causation. No separate writing appears.

The casebook cites the case in its comparison of approaches to hybrid transactions.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-072.rule: A merchant seller's implied warranty of merchantability arises by operation of law from the seller-buyer relationship, and a usage of trade excludes it only if the parties share the trade or both knew or should have known of it.

sections.Parties: Bill Cantrell, a homeowner, sued Joseph Frantz and Frantz Lumber, which he had hired to install a new shingled roof on his residence, for breach of implied warranty after the shingles curled and failed to seal. Cantrell won at a bench trial. Frantz, the appellant, contested the existence of the warranty, the evidence of breach, and the damages.
sections.Procedural History: After a bench trial the court found for Cantrell and awarded the repair or replacement cost less a credit for the roof's value and use, for a judgment of $3,904.97. Frantz appealed the existence of the warranty, the evidence of breach, and damages. The Indiana Court of Appeals, the state's intermediate appellate court, affirmed both liability and the award, with no retrial or remand.
sections.Material Facts:
In summer 1994 Cantrell hired Frantz to install a new shingled roof for $1,985.15, asking for good-quality asphalt rather than fiberglass shingles. Frantz selected a three-tab asphalt product it routinely sold, carrying a twenty-year manufacturer warranty. Installation was completed that summer, and Cantrell, seeing no defect, paid.

During the following winter he noticed curling edges and tabs that failed to seal. A Frantz representative inspected the roof, found the workmanship competent, recognized a shingles problem he had not seen before, and said he would contact the manufacturer. Frantz later sent information on cold curl, which should disappear in warmer conditions; it did not explain the failure to seal. Cantrell waited until summer 1995, but neither problem corrected itself, and he eventually sued. The roof had not leaked and no shingles had blown off. The replacement estimate was $4,897.55, a usual and customary local bid, and Frantz offered no contrary evidence. Cantrell's own expert testified that roofers traditionally gave no warranty on shingles themselves.
sections.Issue: Whether Frantz, as seller and installer of the shingles, gave an implied warranty of merchantability without any special relationship to the manufacturer; whether a claimed roofing-trade usage excluded that warranty; whether shingles that curled and failed to seal but did not leak breached it; and whether the damages were supported.
sections.Holding: The Indiana Court of Appeals, in 1999, in an opinion by Judge Kirsch with Judges Garrard and Najam concurring, affirmed the $3,904.97 judgment for Cantrell. A merchant's implied warranty of merchantability does not depend on a special relationship with the manufacturer. Frantz's experience and representations supported merchant status, and the asserted roofing-trade practice did not exclude the warranty without evidence that the homeowner knew or should have known of it. Persistent curling and failed sealing supported the finding of breach even though the roof had not leaked, and the award of replacement cost less the benefit received was supported.
sections.Reasoning:
Under Indiana's Article 2, merchantability is implied in a sales contract when the seller is a merchant in goods of that kind, unless properly excluded or modified. It arises by operation of law from the relationship between seller and buyer, so no special seller-manufacturer relationship was needed, and the manufacturer's twenty-year promise did not displace the seller's own obligation.

Frantz was a merchant. Casual or isolated sales would not qualify, but the family had been affiliated with the business since 1910, its statements advertised all kinds of building material, Cantrell came to it for its local roofing reputation, and its representative knew the products. The statutory definition covers both dealing in goods of the kind and holding oneself out as having relevant knowledge or skill.

On usage of trade under § 2-316(3)(c), a regular trade practice can sometimes modify an implied warranty, but it must be shared by the parties' trade or be one both knew or should have known. The parties were not in the same trade and nothing showed Cantrell knew or should have known of the custom.

On breach, the court would not reweigh the evidence. Frantz argued that shingles exist to keep out the elements and these had. The court rejected that narrow view: merchantable shingles must conform to ordinary standards and average grade, quality, and value and pass without objection in the trade. Tabs that fail to seal and edges that stay curled in warm weather need not meet that standard merely because no leak has occurred.

On damages, §§ 2-714(1) and 2-715 allow reasonable compensatory and foreseeable consequential damages. Replacement of the whole roof was required, and the trial court credited Frantz with half the original price, $992.58.

The casebook treats the case as an implicit gravamen approach to a hybrid roof-installation contract; that is the editors' classification, since the opinion neither names a gravamen test nor decides that services predominated.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-073.rule: An offer that seeks acts rather than a return promise is accepted without words when the offerees enter upon the requested performance, and the offeror may not then defeat their interest while they continue performing as far as permitted.

sections.Parties: Joseph Brackenbury and his wife, the daughter of Sarah Hodgkin, were the plaintiffs in a bill in equity. The suit concerned the farm of Sarah Hodgkin, a widow living outside Lewiston, Maine; the defendants included her son Walter Hodgkin, to whom she had deeded it. The couple sought reconveyance, an injunction against Walter's eviction action, and a trust on the title; the defendants appealed the decree granting that relief.
sections.Procedural History: The couple filed a bill in equity seeking reconveyance from Walter to Sarah, an injunction against his eviction action, and recognition that Sarah's legal title was impressed with a trust in their favor according to the contract. After detailed findings, the sitting justice sustained the bill, granted the requested relief, and imposed costs on Walter. The defendants appealed. The Maine Supreme Judicial Court, sitting as the Law Court, dismissed the appeal and affirmed the decree with costs against Walter Hodgkin.
sections.Material Facts:
Sarah Hodgkin lived alone on her home farm. Her daughter and son-in-law lived in Independence, Missouri. After several letters, she sent them a letter dated February 8, 1915: if they moved to Lewiston, paid their moving expenses, and maintained and cared for her on the farm during her life, they would have the use and income of the property and the use of household goods, with specified exceptions, and she would keep the rooms she needed. A postscript promised them the place at her death.

The offer had not been withdrawn or modified when the couple moved to Maine in late April 1915, entered the farm, and began the specified performance. Relations became unpleasant within weeks. Sarah brought two suits against her son-in-law on matters the opinion calls trifling and ordered the couple to leave; they refused. On November 7, 1916 she deeded the premises to her son Walter, reserving a life estate. Walter knew of the agreement and took the deed for the sole purpose of evicting the couple. He served a notice to quit that day and began forcible-entry-and-detainer proceedings on November 13.
sections.Issue: Whether the mother's written offer became a binding contract when the couple moved and began caring for her, without any return promise; whether that contract gave them an equitable interest in the farm enforceable against a son who took a deed with notice; and whether alleged misconduct or an adequate legal remedy barred equitable relief.
sections.Holding: The Maine Supreme Judicial Court, sitting as the Law Court, in 1917, in an opinion by Chief Justice Cornish with no separate writing, dismissed the defendants' appeal and affirmed the decree protecting the Brackenburys' interest in the farm. The mother's written offer was accepted by the couple's move and entry upon the promised care, followed by continued performance so far as she permitted. The contract, with performance entered upon, created an enforceable equitable interest in the land, and the finding that the couple had not forfeited it through misconduct was supported.
sections.Reasoning:
The court found a legal and binding contract clearly proven. Sarah's offer was written and definite. The court classified it as unilateral, seeking acts in return for her promise rather than a reciprocal promise, so acceptance in words was unnecessary. The couple accepted by moving from Missouri to the farm and entering upon the specified acts, and they continued performing as far as Sarah allowed. On those facts the contract was complete and valid. The court did not require them to finish a lifetime of care before having any protection, and it did not say they could stop caring for her and keep the entitlement.

The contract, with performance begun, created an equitable interest in the land. The Maine statute required a signed writing for a trust concerning land, and Sarah's signed letter met it; no particular formal document was needed if the terms and the parties' relationships were reasonably certain. Walter knew of the bargain and took the deed to evict the couple, so he was not a bona fide purchaser for value without notice, and reconveyance and restraint of the eviction suit were proper.

The defendants claimed the couple had treated Sarah unkindly and forfeited relief. The sitting justice found otherwise, and the evidence, including Sarah's own conduct and testimony, showed her to be the principal provoking cause of the difficulties. The objection that an adequate remedy at law bars equity did not apply because Maine had expressly conferred equitable jurisdiction over trusts.

The casebook assigns a problem, Move to Maine, built on these facts; its alternative letter and its hypothetical death after the couple sold a Missouri home and business are changed facts, not part of the case.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-074.rule: A general contractor's use of a supplier's quoted price in its own bid does not accept the supplier's offer, and promissory estoppel will not bind an offeror whose offer sought a return promise that was not given.

sections.Parties: James Baird Co., a Washington general contractor, sued Gimbel Bros., a New York merchant that had offered to supply linoleum for a public building, for damages for breach of a contract to sell and deliver the linoleum. Gimbel denied that any contract had been made, having withdrawn its offer after discovering a mistake in it.
sections.Procedural History: Baird sued for damages for breach of contract. The parties tried the case to a judge under a written stipulation, and the judge directed judgment for Gimbel. Contract formation was the only issue the appellate court needed to decide. The Second Circuit affirmed. Baird obtained neither damages nor a remand for a new trial.
sections.Material Facts:
Pennsylvania's Department of Highways sought bids for construction of a public building. A Gimbel employee examined the specifications and underestimated the linoleum yardage by about half. Unaware of the mistake, Gimbel on December 24 sent offers to twenty or thirty prospective general contractors, proposing two lump-sum prices depending on quality. Its language contemplated a guarantee if it was awarded the supply contract and prompt acceptance after the general contract was awarded.

Baird received the offer on December 28. Gimbel discovered the mistake that same day and telegraphed a withdrawal, saying it would substitute prices about twice as high. Baird received the telegram that afternoon, after it had submitted its own lump-sum bid in Harrisburg using Gimbel's figures. The public authorities accepted Baird's bid on December 30. Written confirmation of the withdrawal reached Baird on December 31, and Baird formally accepted the original offer on January 2. Gimbel refused to recognize a contract. The opinion gives the month and day sequence without specifying the year.
sections.Issue: Whether a general contractor's use of a supplier's quoted price in its bid for a public project accepted the supplier's offer or made it irrevocable, and, if not, whether promissory estoppel bound the supplier to its offer after the contractor relied on it.
sections.Holding: The Second Circuit, in 1933, in an opinion by Judge Learned Hand for a panel of Judges Manton, Hand, and Swan, affirmed the judgment for Gimbel. The offer had been revoked before Baird accepted it. Using the quoted price in a construction bid did not itself accept the supplier's offer, and the court declined to use promissory estoppel to supply the missing acceptance or to construe the offer as an option.
sections.Reasoning:
The court began from the ordinary rule that an acceptance communicated after withdrawal is too late. The parties could have made their dealings binding at the bidding stage, but the question was what their language and conduct actually manifested. Baird argued that Gimbel knew contractors would use its prices and commit themselves, so that use of the offer made it irrevocable or was itself an acceptance with a conditional promise to buy. Gimbel's awareness of the contractor's predicament gave the argument some force but did not establish that exchange.

Hand tested the asserted contract from the other side. Had Baird repudiated the public contract after the award, Gimbel could not have sued Baird merely because Baird had used its figures, nor proved a claim against Baird's bankruptcy estate. Use of the figures manifested no commitment to buy. The offer's terms also looked forward to an award and a later communicated acceptance, and treating that as mere notice of a contract already formed strained its natural meaning. Contractors could have secured conditional supply contracts before using the figures.

On promissory estoppel, the court assumed the First Restatement's § 90 formulation for argument's sake rather than rejecting the doctrine in every setting. It distinguished a donative promise from an offer seeking an exchange. This offer sought Baird's promise to take and pay for the linoleum, and Gimbel had not stipulated that submitting the general bid would be the equivalent. Estoppel would bind it without the counter-promise it requested.

Nor would the court read the offer as an option letting Baird accept later while free to buy elsewhere; nothing showed Gimbel intended so one-sided a commitment. Hand acknowledged that estoppel might operate if an actual option promise were established and declined to decide that question.

The casebook presents the case under Revocability and Reliance, as part of the historical development of reliance doctrine.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-075.rule: A general contractor's use of a subcontractor's price and listing of that subcontractor in its successful prime bid does not, without more, manifest acceptance of the subcontractor's offer.

sections.Parties: Holman Erection Company, a steel-erection subcontractor, sued Orville E. Madsen & Sons, Inc., a general contractor, for the profits it said it lost when Madsen, having used Holman's bid and listed Holman in its successful prime bid, gave the steel-erection work to another firm. Madsen denied that any contract had been formed.
sections.Procedural History: Holman sued in Clay County District Court for lost profits, asserting that use of its price and the public listing constituted acceptance and created a contract. The district court granted Madsen summary judgment. The underlying facts were undisputed, but Holman contended that a factfinder could infer formation from them. The Minnesota Supreme Court affirmed the summary judgment dismissing Holman's claim, awarding no lost profits and ordering no trial.
sections.Material Facts:
The City of Moorhead sought bids for a wastewater treatment facility, to be opened publicly on January 22, 1981. Madsen invited potential subcontractors, including Holman, to bid. Two or three hours before the prime bid deadline, Holman telephoned its price and proposed scope to Madsen's office. Holman submitted the identical bid to six other general contractors competing for the project.

Madsen used Holman's figures to prepare its prime bid. The city required bidders to identify proposed subcontractors, so Madsen listed Holman for steel erection, about two percent of the project; the requirement came from the awarding authority, not a statute.
