Madsen received the general contract on February 2. There was no further communication promising Holman the work.

After the award, Madsen contacted Van Knight Steel Erection, asked about its minority-business qualifications, and eventually selected it. Federal minority-business regulations required an effort to assign part of the project to minority businesses. Van Knight qualified and offered significant materials and some labor outside Holman's bid, at a slightly higher price. Holman learned it had been the low bidder and had been listed, telephoned Madsen, and was told another firm would get the work. Those two calls were the parties' only communications.
sections.Issue: Whether a general contractor accepts a subcontractor's bid, forming a contract, merely by using the subcontractor's price and listing the subcontractor in its successful prime bid, and whether fairness requires that result because a subcontractor can be bound to its bid through the general contractor's reliance.
sections.Holding: The Minnesota Supreme Court, in 1983, in an opinion by Justice Yetka with no separate writing, affirmed summary judgment dismissing Holman's claim for lost profits. A general contractor's use of a subcontractor's price and listing of that subcontractor in its successful public bid does not, without more, accept the subcontractor's offer. Because the undisputed facts did not establish acceptance, no permissible inference from them changed the outcome. The decision concerns mere use or listing in these circumstances and does not say a general contractor can never bind itself through further assent.
sections.Reasoning:
Acceptance requires an objective manifestation of assent. Written words, oral words, or conduct can each suffice, but under Restatement (Second) § 19 and comment c the actor must know or have reason to know that its conduct could communicate assent. Listing a proposed subcontractor, without an additional acceptance communication, is not such a manifestation. Decisions from Idaho, California, Washington, Arizona, and federal appellate courts had rejected formation from mere use or listing of a subcontract bid, and Holman's efforts to distinguish them did not undermine their reasoning. Holman had shown no additional communication, detrimental reliance, or loss apart from the hoped-for profits.

Holman argued for reciprocal obligations because Minnesota precedent can bind a subcontractor to its bid through promissory estoppel when a general contractor justifiably relies on it. The court rejected the symmetry because that obligation rests on reliance, not on a reciprocal contract, and the parties' reliance positions differ. A general contractor awarded the prime contract is committed to its price, so a subcontractor's withdrawal can cause it loss. Holman prepared one bid for several contractors and incurred its ordinary bidding overhead whoever won; it spent nothing further in reliance on the listing.

The court noted commentators' proposals to bind general contractors at the listing stage and acknowledged that bid shopping is undesirable. But subcontractors submit bids shortly before the deadline in a hectic process, detailed terms are left for later, and selection depends on reliability, quality, capacity, and minority-business obligations as well as price. Binding Madsen to every listed subcontractor could have prevented the adjustment needed to meet those obligations. The court left any general change to the legislature.

The casebook discusses the case in a note titled Subcontractor Reliance?

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-076.rule: An oral contract to pay money after the promisor's death can be valid where a promise is given for a promise, and an offeror's immediate face-to-face assent to qualifications the offeree adds can produce agreement on the qualified terms.

sections.Parties: Benjamin A. Earle, the plaintiff, sued Charles A. Angell, executor of Earle's aunt Mary Dewitt, for $500 that he said she had promised him during her lifetime in exchange for his promise to attend her funeral. The executor, the defendant, offered no evidence and won a directed verdict; Earle brought exceptions.
sections.Procedural History: The case was tried before Maynard, J. The executor offered no evidence. After Earle rested, the trial judge directed a verdict for the executor, and Earle alleged exceptions. The question was whether his proof permitted the contract claim to go forward. The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court sustained the exceptions; it did not itself find a binding contract or award the money.
sections.Material Facts:
Earle testified about a conversation with his aunt in Oxford, Massachusetts, in August 1883. She recalled his journey from the Philadelphia area to his uncle's funeral in a severe snowstorm and, concerned that few family members remained, asked him to attend her own funeral if he outlived her, offering $500 and his expenses. In a more specifically reciprocal version, she offered payment if he would agree to come. Earle said he promised on his honor, provided he remained alive, received timely notice, and was able to travel.

He also testified that she reminded him of the agreement in 1885, and he renewed his assurance. Dewitt died in 1887, and Earle attended her funeral because of his promise. Soon after, he received a sealed writing in her handwriting, dated August 14, 1883, directing her executor to pay $500 if he attended her funeral. These were Earle's account of events, not jury findings.
sections.Issue: Whether Earle's testimony could support a finding of a binding contract, made in the aunt's lifetime, to pay $500 after her death in exchange for his promise to attend her funeral, even though he added qualifications to his promise, so that directing a verdict for the executor was error.
sections.Holding: The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court, in 1892, in an opinion by Holmes with no separate writing, sustained Earle's exceptions to the directed verdict. His testimony could support a finding that the aunt promised payment in exchange for his present promise to attend her funeral, and that she assented to any qualifications he added. An oral contract to pay money after the promisor's death could be valid. The court neither awarded the $500 nor conclusively determined that the parties had exchanged enforceable promises.
sections.Reasoning:
Holmes explained that an oral contract to pay money after the promisor's death could be valid; postponing payment until death does not by itself defeat an otherwise binding lifetime contract. The aunt's request for a promise to attend, and Earle's stated promise in return, could provide a bilateral exchange, with attendance a condition of payment under that agreement. The analysis rested on the present exchange about her own funeral, not on the earlier visit to the uncle's funeral as consideration, and the opinion did not hold that the handwritten direction independently created a testamentary gift.

The executor's side suggested that Earle's response varied from the offer because it added conditions about notice and ability. Holmes emphasized that the parties spoke face to face and apparently separated in agreement, so a jury could find that the aunt assented at once to any variation. The response could thus lead to agreement on qualified terms rather than ending the discussion without a contract. That possible finding was enough to defeat the directed verdict.

If the jury found the reciprocal agreement Holmes described, the aunt's death would come after formation, and her estate could owe the payment when the condition was met. The court did not hold that death generally leaves an unaccepted offer open or that attendance after death accepts a new unilateral offer.

The casebook places the case under death of an offeror and bases its In Memoriam problem on it, changing the amount to $5,000 and compressing the timeline; those changed facts are the editors', not the court's.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-077.rule: A response to an offer that proposes different terms rejects the offer, and the offeree cannot afterward revive it by tendering an acceptance unless the offeror renews the offer or assents to the change.

sections.Parties: The Minneapolis & St. Louis Railway Company, the buyer and plaintiff, sued the Columbus Rolling-Mill Company, an Ohio manufacturer and the defendant, for breach of an alleged contract to sell 2,000 tons of iron rails. The mill denied that any contract had been formed. The railway, having lost at trial, brought the case to the Court by writ of error.
sections.Procedural History: The railway alleged a December 19 contract for 2,000 tons and sued for breach in the federal Circuit Court for the Southern District of Ohio. The mill denied formation. A jury returned a verdict for the mill, and the railway took exceptions and sought a writ of error. The Court affirmed the judgment for the mill, ordering no new trial.
sections.Material Facts:
On December 5, 1879, the railway asked the mill for prices on specified quantities of steel and iron rails for March 1880 delivery. On December 8 the mill replied that it did not make steel rails but would sell 2,000 to 5,000 tons of fifty-pound iron rails at $54 per gross ton, for cash, free on board cars at its mill, and that it expected notice of acceptance before December 20.

On December 16 the railway telegraphed an order for 1,200 tons, referring to the December 8 offer; its letter of the same day repeated that quantity and price and requested a written contract. On December 18 the mill replied that it could not book the order at that price. The next day the railway requested 2,000 tons under the original letter and asked for a written contract. After further inquiries, the mill on January 19, 1880 denied that any contract existed. The parties admitted that the letters and telegrams were sent on those dates and received in due course.
sections.Issue: Whether the railway's order for 1,200 tons, a quantity below the minimum in the mill's offer, rejected that offer, so that the railway's later request for 2,000 tons, made before the stated acceptance deadline, could not form a contract.
sections.Holding: The Court, in 1886, in an opinion by Justice Gray, affirmed the judgment for the rolling mill. The railway rejected the seller's offer by attempting to order a quantity below the stated minimum, and its later attempt to accept within the original quantity range could not revive the terminated offer. The December 19 request for 2,000 tons came before the stated deadline but after the earlier negotiation had closed, and it created no contract.
sections.Reasoning:
Gray stated the common-law requirement of mutual assent: an ordinary offer imposes no obligation until accepted according to its terms. A response proposing different terms rejects the original offer unless the offeror renews it or assents to the change, and the offeree cannot afterward restore the rejected offer simply by tendering an acceptance. A stated acceptance deadline does not itself keep an ordinary offer irrevocably open; while open, the offer can be accepted, rejected, or withdrawn before the deadline.

The mill's offer gave the railway a choice of any quantity from 2,000 to 5,000 tons, and the 1,200-ton order was outside that range. Both the telegram and the letter referred to the original offer and its terms, so the Court treated them as a qualified response to that offer rather than an independent proposal that left it undisturbed. That response rejected the original terms, and the mill then declined the reduced order.

Given that legal effect of the writings, the Court did not need to decide whether the trial instructions had treated rejection as a question of law or of fact. Submitting a question of law to the jury is no ground for reversal when the jury reaches the correct result.

The casebook uses the case for the rejection rule; its footnote flags a later UCC § 2-207 qualification, and its follow-on option and firm-offer problems are hypotheticals, not facts of the case.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-078.rule: An attempt to negotiate additional terms does not terminate an option supported by consideration, because the option is itself a binding contract; the holder may still exercise it according to its terms within the option period.

sections.Parties: Humble Oil & Refining Co., holder of a paid option to buy land, sued Westside Investment Corp., the optionor, for specific performance. Westside argued that Humble had rejected and terminated the option. Realtor Marvin H. Mann intervened, claiming $1,260 in brokerage charges. Ray Ellison and Boyce Gaskin were Westside's stipulated successors in interest.
sections.Procedural History: Humble sued on February 10, 1965, for specific performance, and Mann intervened for his brokerage claim. All three parties sought summary judgment. The trial court granted Westside's motion and denied Humble's and Mann's, and the court of civil appeals affirmed. The Texas Supreme Court severed Humble's cause from Mann's, reversed the trial and appellate judgments as to Humble, and rendered judgment requiring Westside and its successors to specifically perform. It separately reversed the judgments against Mann and remanded his brokerage cause for a new trial. All costs were assessed against Westside and its successors.
sections.Material Facts:
On April 5, 1963, Westside gave Humble an exclusive, irrevocable option to buy five subdivision lots outside San Antonio for $35,000. Humble paid $50 as consideration for the option. It could exercise by notice before 9 p.m. on June 4, 1963, accompanied by $1,750 earnest money paid then or within ten days, leaving $33,200 due as the balance.

On May 2 Humble wrote that it exercised the option, but also asserted that Westside had agreed to extend gas, water, sewer, and electricity before closing; the letter purported to amend the sale agreement accordingly and asked Westside to sign and return a copy accepting the amendment. On May 14 Humble sent a second communication exercising the option without qualification and allowing Westside to disregard the proposed amendment, and it paid $1,750 to the designated escrow agent. The parties agreed that this notice and payment timely exercised the option unless the May 2 letter had already destroyed it. Most relevant facts were stipulated or established through summary-judgment affidavits.
sections.Issue: Whether Humble's May 2 letter, which purported to exercise a paid option while proposing an added term about utilities, rejected and terminated the option so that its unqualified exercise on May 14, within the option period, was ineffective.
sections.Holding: The Texas Supreme Court, in 1968, in an opinion by Justice Smith with no separate writing, reversed the judgments for Westside and rendered specific-performance relief for Humble. Humble's attempt to negotiate additional sale terms did not terminate its supported option, and Humble later exercised the option unconditionally and on time. Westside and its successors had to deliver a general warranty deed and a $35,000 owner's title-insurance policy when Humble paid the $33,200 balance. Mann's separate commission claim required a trial and was remanded.
sections.Reasoning:
The court distinguished the ordinary rule that a qualified acceptance rejects an offer from the effect of a counterproposal under a paid option. An ordinary offer has not yet produced a contract. A supported option is an independently completed agreement binding the optionor to keep the purchase opportunity open for a stated time, and the holder creates the purchase obligation by satisfying its conditions. The court's quotation from James on Option Contracts explains why an ordinary rejection rule cannot automatically destroy rights already purchased under such a contract.

The court relied on Cerbo v. Carabello, where unsuccessful negotiation for a lower price did not show abandonment of an existing option. Parties can abandon or modify an agreement by words or conduct, but negotiation alone does not establish that. Humble had not surrendered its paid right to elect to purchase; it stayed free to negotiate sale terms while keeping the option, and Westside stayed bound to honor the option through its period. The unqualified May 14 exercise therefore operated on a still-binding option. Corbin's discussion reinforced the distinction, and Westside's authorities involved mere offers, no fixed option period, or no consideration. The court did not hold that every attempted acceptance with new terms completes a purchase.

On the brokerage claim, the contract required Westside to pay a six-percent commission to Clarence Jones Realty. Mann alleged he had procured the agreement while associated with Jones and was entitled to sixty percent of the commission. Westside did not deny this, but Jones Realty was not a party and Mann's entitlement remained unresolved, so neither side could have summary judgment on it.

The casebook presents the May 2 and May 14 communications and asks whether the purchase agreement survived; its alternative in which Humble first said it had decided not to buy is a hypothetical.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-079.rule: An offeror who makes an offer by post is treated as making the same offer throughout the letter's journey, and the offeree's acceptance completes the contract without the offeror first having to receive it.

sections.Parties: The plaintiffs, woollen manufacturers at Bromsgrove, Worcestershire, were the buyers; they sued for nondelivery of wool. The defendants, wool dealers in St. Ives, Huntingdonshire, were the sellers; they had offered the wool by letter and then sold it to someone else. The buyers won a verdict at trial, and the sellers sought a new trial on the ground that there was no binding contract.
sections.Procedural History: The buyers sued for nondelivery according to the agreement. At the Worcester Lent assizes before Burrough, J., the judge directed that the sellers' mistake required the jury to regard the answer as arriving in due course of post, and the buyers recovered a verdict; the report gives no damages amount. The sellers obtained a rule nisi for a new trial in Easter Term, contending there was no binding contract. The King's Bench proceeding is identified as June 5, 1818. The court's disposition was 'Rule discharged', so the sellers did not obtain a new trial and the buyers' verdict stood.
sections.Material Facts:
On Tuesday, September 2, 1817, the sellers wrote to the buyers offering 800 tods of wether fleeces of specified quality at 35 shillings and sixpence per tod, deliverable at Leicester, with payment by a two-month bill and weighing by the buyers' agent within fourteen days. The offer requested an answer in the course of post.

The sellers misdirected the letter to Bromsgrove in Leicestershire, so it did not reach the buyers in Worcestershire until 7 p.m. on Friday, September 5. That evening the buyers wrote accepting on the offered terms. Mail between Bromsgrove and St. Ives traveled through London, and the sellers received the response on Tuesday, September 9. They had expected an answer on Sunday, September 7, the ordinary time had their own letter been correctly addressed. Having received none, they sold the wool to another person on Monday, September 8.
sections.Issue: Whether a contract made by post was complete when the buyers wrote accepting the sellers' offer, or only when the sellers actually received the acceptance, which was after they had sold the wool to someone else; and who bore the delay caused by the sellers' misdirected letter.
sections.Holding: The Court of King's Bench, in 1818, discharged the sellers' rule for a new trial, leaving the buyers' verdict undisturbed. The report attributes the reasoning to the court collectively. The sellers were treated as making the same offer throughout the letter's journey, and the buyers' acceptance completed the contract; receipt of the acceptance did not have to come before the sellers' later resale for the agreement to bind. Because the delay arose wholly from the sellers' addressing mistake, the buyers' reply was taken, as against the sellers, to have been received in the course of post.
sections.Reasoning:
Counsel for the buyers began to argue that acceptance bound the sellers on Friday evening; the court stopped that argument and called on the sellers' counsel to support the rule. Relying on Payne v. Cave and particularly Cooke v. Oxley, the sellers contended that an offer did not bind them until they actually received the acceptance, so that the Monday resale withdrew the offer before Tuesday's receipt. That was the sellers' characterization of the resale, not a holding that a secret resale is a communicated revocation.

The court rejected making completion of a postal contract turn on receipt. On the sellers' premise, if they were not bound until they received the buyers' answer, the buyers likewise could await notice that the sellers had received and assented to it, followed by further confirmations indefinitely. The court instead treated the sellers as making the same offer throughout the time the letter was travelling, with the buyers' acceptance completing the contract.

On the timing condition in the offer, any delay in notification arose entirely from the sellers' own mistake in addressing the letter, so as against them the answer was taken as received in the course of post.

The case does not decide the operation of email, instantaneous communications, option contracts, or a later overtaking rejection by the offeree. The brief is based on a reproduction of the report in an 1898 collection of contract cases; the original report volumes were not directly collated. The casebook's account says 800 tons, where the report says 800 tods.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-080.rule: Under Pennsylvania's Chanoff v. Fiala, where use of the mail is authorized or implied, posting an option exercise completes it, although the general rule recognized by the court is that an option exercise takes effect on receipt.

sections.Parties: Pennsylvania Academy of Fine Arts (PAFA), which had acquired the lease of a Center City Philadelphia parking lot, sued to enforce the lease's purchase option. The defendant and appellant was the lessor, Thelma Grant, as trustee of Max Grant's residuary trust, who contended that PAFA's notice exercising the option was untimely and alleged environmental and tax breaches of the lease.
sections.Procedural History: PAFA sued to enforce the lease. Grant challenged the timeliness of the notice and alleged environmental and tax breaches. The trial court granted PAFA summary judgment, and Grant appealed. The Pennsylvania Superior Court affirmed the order on March 21, 1991; reargument was later denied. The opinion supplies no damages award or detailed conveyance decree.
sections.Material Facts:
PAFA acquired Mellon Bank (East), N.A.'s lease of the parking lot on January 30, 1989. The lease expired July 31, 1989 and permitted purchase if the lessee exercised the option at least six months before expiration. Section 801 required written notices to be delivered or mailed by certified or registered mail. A letter dated January 30 announcing PAFA's exercise, accompanied by the necessary deposit check, was mailed January 31 by prepaid certified mail with return receipt requested. Grant received it on February 3, five months and twenty-eight days before expiration. On February 28 she returned the check, asserting that receipt after the six-month cutoff made the exercise ineffective.

Grant also alleged that an underground 10,000-gallon gasoline tank, installed by the predecessor lessee Mellon Bank, violated environmental requirements, and that delinquent city use and occupancy taxes breached the lease. These are the opinion's January and February dates, not the July and August dates in the casebook's account.
sections.Issue: Whether the exercise of a lease purchase option, sent by certified mail as the lease's notice clause allowed, took effect when it was mailed, before the six-month deadline, or when the lessor received it, after the deadline; and whether Grant's breach defenses raised a factual dispute preventing summary judgment.
sections.Holding: The Pennsylvania Superior Court, in 1991, in an opinion by Judge Montemuro for a panel with Judges Wieand and Hester, affirmed summary judgment for PAFA. Although the court recognized the general rule that exercise of a leasehold option becomes effective on receipt absent contrary intent, it held itself constrained by the Pennsylvania Supreme Court's decision in Chanoff v. Fiala to treat PAFA's January 31 mailing as an effective exercise. Grant's environmental and tax defenses, supported only by defective affidavits, established neither a material breach nor a disputed material fact.
sections.Reasoning:
The operative dates were not in dispute, so the effect of the notice was a legal question. The trial court found no lease term saying when notice became effective: section 801 prescribed a method of communication but did not declare dispatch or receipt the effective event. The court recognized the general option rule, supported by Restatement (Second) § 63 comment f and treatises, that absent contrary intent the exercise of a leasehold option is effective on receipt.

The complication was Chanoff v. Fiala. There a buyer mailed a deposit check the day before an option expired and the seller received it afterward; the Pennsylvania Supreme Court applied the mailbox rule, that when use of the mail is authorized or implied, posting an acceptance through normal channels completes acceptance, and a registered-mail notice provision supported authorization. Grant pointed to factual differences: a course of dealing suggesting lax attention to deadlines, a mailing one day before expiration, and the seller's deposit of the check. None was part of the Supreme Court's stated rationale, and the Superior Court's own view of the general rule did not authorize departure from the higher court. The reasoning is thus a jurisdiction-specific application of controlling precedent, not a claim that the Restatement adopts dispatch for options.

On the other defenses, the record showed no legal action over the tank, only possible liability that might never materialize, and the taxes involved a former tenant, not PAFA, and created no liability for Grant as landlord. Grant's own accusatory affidavits and an attorney's affidavit resting on third-party hearsay failed Rule 1035(d)'s requirements of personal knowledge and admissible facts.

The casebook's note on the case gives July 30, July 31, and August 3 for the letter, mailing, and receipt, which differs from the report's January and February dates.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-081.skip: The brief is a source-limited account of a casebook problem's settlement chronology and questions; the court's opinion was not recovered, so no holding, reasoning, or disposition is given.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-082.rule: An acceptance must be definite and unequivocal; an acceptance made conditional on added terms is a counteroffer, but an acceptance accompanied by a request stands if it is clearly independent of whether the request is granted.

sections.Parties: Ernest Ardente, the prospective buyer of a Newport residential property, sued the owners, William and Katherine Horan, for specific performance of an alleged agreement to sell it to him. The Horans, the defendants, denied that a contract had formed and obtained summary judgment. Ardente appealed.
sections.Procedural History: Ardente sought specific performance. The Horans answered and moved for summary judgment under Superior Court Rule 56. After affidavits from both sides and a hearing, the trial justice held that the letter accompanying Ardente's signed agreement made his response a counteroffer, and that because the sellers never accepted it no contract formed. Ardente appealed, challenging both the propriety of summary judgment and the interpretation of his response. The Rhode Island Supreme Court denied and dismissed the appeal, affirmed the judgment, and remanded the case to the Superior Court.
sections.Material Facts:
The Horans offered their Newport residential property for sale in August 1975. Ardente bid $250,000 through their attorney. After telling Ardente that the price was acceptable, the attorney prepared a purchase-and-sale agreement at the Horans' direction and sent it to Ardente's attorney for signature. The document lacked the sellers' signatures. Ardente investigated conditions of title and signed.

His attorney returned the agreement with a $20,000 deposit check and a letter dated September 8, 1975 seeking confirmation that a dining-room set and tapestry wall covering, fireplace fixtures, and sun-parlor furniture were included in the transaction. The letter described replacing these items as difficult. The Horans declined to include them, never signed the agreement, returned both the document and the deposit, and refused to sell.
sections.Issue: Whether Ardente's return of the signed purchase agreement, accompanied by a letter seeking confirmation that certain furnishings were included in the sale, was an acceptance of the sellers' assumed offer or a conditional acceptance operating as a counteroffer, and whether summary judgment was proper.
sections.Holding: The Rhode Island Supreme Court, in 1976, in an opinion by Justice Doris, Justice Paolino not participating, denied and dismissed Ardente's appeal and affirmed the judgment for the Horans. Assuming without deciding that delivery of the purchase-and-sale document was the Horans' offer, the court held that Ardente's signed agreement and accompanying letter, read together, were a conditional acceptance. That response rejected the offer and was a counteroffer the sellers never accepted, so no contractual obligation arose. Summary judgment was proper because Ardente had not presented specific facts showing a genuine dispute.
sections.Reasoning:
Summary judgment is a drastic remedy but is proper when no genuine dispute of material fact exists and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. Ardente argued on appeal that there was a factual question whether the preliminary oral agreement was itself a binding contract. He had not presented the trial court with specific facts establishing that dispute; at the hearing he argued only the interpretation of his letter, which the court treated as a legal question. A party opposing summary judgment cannot rest on pleading allegations or denials. He later conceded in an appellate memorandum that no factual dispute existed.

For the acceptance analysis the court assumed, favorably to Ardente, that delivery of the agreement was the Horans' offer. If it was not, his signed return could itself be only an offer the Horans never accepted. On the assumed premise, formation required an overt communication of acceptance, not a private intention. The only communicated response was the signed agreement with the September 8 letter, so the court read them together. An effective acceptance must be definite and unequivocal; a conditional or limited acceptance is a counteroffer requiring the original offeror's acceptance.

The court rejected a mechanical rule that every request for a change defeats formation. Citing Williston and Corbin, it said an offeree can accept unequivocally while suggesting an addition or modification, provided the acceptance clearly stands whether or not the request is granted. The question is whether the added language is a condition of assent or an independent collateral inquiry.

Ardente's letter sought confirmation that the items were part of the transaction and did not say he would buy without them. Its emphasis on the difficulty of replacing them reinforced their importance to his proposed bargain. The response was therefore conditional. The Horans did not raise the statute of frauds, and the court would not raise it for them.

The casebook asks whether the letter's language could instead have been read as merely suggestive, which is the editors' question.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-083.rule: A counteroffer rejects the original offer, but a mere inquiry whether the offeror would consider different terms does not, so the offeree may still accept the original offer after the inquiry is refused.

sections.Parties: Jeffrey Rios, a criminal defendant facing eleven charges in Prince George's County, moved to enforce a plea agreement he said his attorney, Ronald Schwartz, had reached with the assigned prosecutor. The State of Maryland denied that any agreement had been formed. Rios appealed the denial of his motion; the State moved to dismiss the appeal as interlocutory.
sections.Procedural History: On May 23 Rios moved to enforce the agreement and dismiss all charges but reckless endangerment. The circuit court denied the motion after a June 13 hearing, treating Schwartz's question about a nolo plea as a counteroffer that rejected the outstanding Alford offer rather than a mere inquiry. Rios appealed on July 7 without having entered the plea, and the trial was continued pending appeal. The State moved to dismiss the appeal as interlocutory. The Maryland appellate court denied the State's motion, vacated the order denying enforcement, and remanded for proceedings consistent with its opinion, with costs payable by Prince George's County.
sections.Material Facts:
Rios was charged with three counts each of first-degree assault, second-degree assault, and using a handgun in a crime of violence, plus reckless endangerment and unlawful handgun carrying. Schwartz negotiated with the prosecutor for about two weeks. Before the week of April 7, 2008, the prosecutor offered a plea to handgun possession and reckless endangerment with time served. Around April 8 Schwartz rejected that and said he could recommend an Alford plea to reckless endangerment with time served. The prosecutor agreed, but Schwartz said he needed to discuss it with Rios and respond. Rios then authorized acceptance.

Schwartz left voicemail messages on April 18 and 21, which the motions court found did not communicate unconditional acceptance. When the prosecutor returned the call on April 22, Schwartz asked whether he would consider a nolo plea to reckless endangerment. The prosecutor refused and said police and his superiors were pressuring him not to offer a bargain. Schwartz then communicated acceptance of the Alford arrangement. The prosecutor responded that he did not think he could offer a plea, and later that week said no offer would be made. The parties stipulated to these negotiation facts.
sections.Issue: Whether the order refusing to enforce the alleged plea agreement was immediately appealable, and whether defense counsel's question whether the prosecutor would consider a nolo plea was a counteroffer that rejected the outstanding Alford plea offer or a mere inquiry that left it open for acceptance.
sections.Holding: The Maryland appellate court, in 2009, in an opinion by Judge Meredith for a panel also including Judges Deborah Eyler and Zarnoch, held the order appealable under the collateral-order doctrine and vacated it. On the stipulated facts, Schwartz's question about a nolo plea was a mere inquiry, not a conditional acceptance or a substituted offer, and it left the Alford offer open. Schwartz communicated acceptance before the prosecutor attempted to withdraw, so the parties formed an agreement binding on the State, subject to court approval. The court did not itself enter a plea or dismiss the other charges.
sections.Reasoning:
On appealability, Maryland's collateral-order doctrine has four strictly construed conditions. The order conclusively rejected the alleged agreement; the issue was important, since enforcement would remove all but one charge and avoid trial; the agreement's existence was separate from guilt or innocence; and waiting for a verdict would destroy a substantial benefit of the bargain, the avoidance of trial. The State's distinction that formation was disputed and Rios had not relied failed because Clark v. Elza, a civil settlement case, also concerned formation without detrimental reliance.

On the merits, plea negotiations involve fair play, equity, and due-process safeguards, not contract law alone, but with no detrimental reliance or unfair conduct suggested, ordinary formation principles could decide whether an agreement existed. Rios argued that Schwartz made an offer on April 8 which the prosecutor accepted then. The court disagreed: Schwartz conditioned his proposal on client approval, so it was not an offer capable of immediate acceptance. The prosecutor's approval was the outstanding offer, and the client's acceptance had to be communicated; given the unchallenged finding on the voicemails, that happened in the April 22 conversation.

A counteroffer rejects the original offer and makes a later attempted acceptance ineffective. But Restatement (Second) § 39 comment b distinguishes a counteroffer from a tentative inquiry about better or different terms. A counteroffer must itself meet the requirements of an offer and propose substitution rather than keeping the original under consideration. The Restatement's example is a buyer who asks a land seller to take less, is refused, and then accepts the original offer. Schwartz asked whether the prosecutor would consider a nolo plea; that was an inquiry. The substantive difference between the two pleas did not make every question about switching them a rejection. There was no separate writing.

The casebook's account labels the case State v. Rios and calls the result reversed; the caption is Rios v. State and the disposition was vacatur and remand.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-084.rule: Under North Carolina law a contract can be accepted through a course of conduct without a signed writing, and a party who performs knowing the other side has consistently rejected a proposed term may be found to have accepted a counteroffer omitting it.

sections.Parties: Mechanical Plant Services (MPS), a supplier of precision millwrights who built and repaired metal surfaces and rotating machinery, was the plaintiff and the appellant. It sought $901,280 in liquidated damages from its customer under a clause in its labor quotation forms. Dresser-Rand, the customer, was the defendant and appellee. It maintained that it had consistently rejected the clause and that MPS's later provision of labor accepted a counteroffer omitting it.
sections.Procedural History: MPS brought a diversity action alleging that Dresser-Rand had hired its employees in violation of the clause. The district court granted Dresser-Rand summary judgment because MPS's performance accepted an offer excluding the clause. The Fourth Circuit heard argument on June 4, 1997 and decided the appeal on June 27, 1997 in an unpublished per curiam opinion that stated its own nonbinding status under the local rule then in force. Over Judge Hamilton's dissent, the court affirmed summary judgment for Dresser-Rand.
sections.Material Facts:
Dresser-Rand requested a labor quotation in 1990. MPS's March 7 quotation included a clause barring Dresser-Rand for one year from employing MPS workers who had been terminated, released, or voluntarily quit, or from using them through another labor broker or vendor. Violation purportedly required payment equivalent to 2,000 manhours per employee at the straight-time invoice rate.

Dresser-Rand's March 19 purchase order expressly took exception to that term, and MPS refused the next day to acknowledge the exception. Dresser-Rand's March 26 letter said it did not intend to employ MPS's active employees but had a problem signing the clause, and proposed discussion. Telephone negotiations followed. MPS vice-president Wayne Henry eventually told Dresser-Rand manager R. M. Jennings that no employees would be sent unless the clause was included. MPS nevertheless began supplying workers without a document signed by Dresser-Rand. Over the ensuing five-year relationship MPS sent a form containing the clause each time labor was ordered, Dresser-Rand never signed, and MPS continued supplying workers for whom Dresser-Rand paid.
sections.Issue: Whose proposed terms governed a relationship in which both sides performed while repeatedly disagreeing over a restriction: did Dresser-Rand's acceptance of labor accept MPS's forms including the clause, or did MPS's provision of labor, despite Dresser-Rand's continuing objection, accept a counteroffer omitting it?
sections.Holding: The Fourth Circuit in 1997, in an unpublished per curiam opinion by a panel of Chief Judge Wilkinson and Judges Wilkins and Hamilton, with Judge Hamilton dissenting, held that MPS's course of conduct in supplying labor while knowing of Dresser-Rand's consistent objection showed willingness to transact without the disputed restriction and effectively accepted Dresser-Rand's counteroffer. The clause was therefore not part of the contract, and summary judgment for Dresser-Rand was affirmed. MPS's damages demand was a claim, not an award.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority did not treat the absence of a signature as automatically fatal. North Carolina law recognized enforceable agreements and acceptance through a course of conduct without an executed writing, so the question was what the conduct meant in light of the parties' communications. Dresser-Rand's initial express objection and continued refusal to sign were consistent throughout, and its receiving and paying for labor did not establish agreement to a term it had consistently rejected. MPS, by contrast, supplied labor knowing of that continuing objection; its ultimatum was never accepted, yet it performed anyway. The result turns on express resistance combined with performance. The court did not hold that the physically last form always settles a dispute or that every unsigned term fails.

North Carolina's suspicion of restraints on employee mobility reinforced the majority's caution. The clause would indirectly prevent MPS millwrights, who were not parties to the agreement, from moving to customer employment, a purpose MPS acknowledged. The majority treated that policy as consistent with its formation conclusion and did not separately adjudicate the clause's reasonableness as to time or territory.

Judge Hamilton, dissenting, thought the record supported two equally plausible interpretations and required a factfinder: after the March 26 letter MPS insisted that performance depended on the restriction, and Dresser-Rand then accepted the services while MPS's written terms continued to include it. He added that North Carolina's rule concerned unreasonable restrictions and the district court had never assessed reasonableness. He would have vacated and remanded.

The casebook note uses the case for its competing forms, the performance, the majority's reasoning, and the employee-mobility concern.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-085.rule: Under UCC 2-207 an additional term in an acceptance between merchants that materially alters the bargain, meaning one to which consent cannot reasonably be presumed, does not become part of the contract unless the other party actually consents to it.

sections.Parties: Union Carbide, a seller of plastic sausage casings, was the plaintiff and appellant. It sought reimbursement from its buyer for back taxes and interest it had paid to Illinois, relying on tax language in its invoices and price books. Oscar Mayer, the buyer, was the defendant and appellee and denied that the language obliged it to reimburse later tax assessments on completed purchases.
sections.Procedural History: Union Carbide brought a diversity contract action against Oscar Mayer. The district court granted Oscar Mayer summary judgment. On appeal Union Carbide did not dispute that Oscar Mayer's purchase orders were offers and its own invoices acceptances, or that the price book, even if an offer, had never been accepted. The Seventh Circuit, in an opinion dated November 15, 1991, found no breach and affirmed the judgment for Oscar Mayer.
sections.Material Facts:
Union Carbide's prices included two one-percent taxes applicable to sales originating in Chicago. In 1980 a competing supplier began receiving orders outside Chicago and cut its price by one percent, believing one tax no longer applied. When Oscar Mayer raised that discount, Union Carbide likewise directed orders to an address outside Chicago, stopped paying both taxes, and removed both charges from its invoices. Eight years later Illinois assessed Union Carbide $88,000 in back taxes on the Oscar Mayer sales and $55,000 in interest. Union Carbide paid and sought reimbursement under invoice and price-book language requiring the buyer, in addition to the purchase price, to pay governmental taxes the seller might be required to pay concerning the goods' production, sale, or transportation.

The transactions used four documents. Oscar Mayer sent standing purchase orders, telephoned quantity requests as inventory was needed, and after delivery sent a shipment-specific release order on its usual purchase-order form; Union Carbide sent an invoice around the same time. The tax clause appeared on invoice backs and in periodic price books. Oscar Mayer's purchase-order form had space for sales tax, and it had paid invoice taxes without protest. It had no requirements contract and could stop buying from Union Carbide.
sections.Issue: Did the tax language oblige the buyer to indemnify the seller for back taxes and interest assessed years after delivery, and, if it could be so read, did that term become part of the contract under UCC 2-207 or was it a material alteration to which Oscar Mayer never consented?
sections.Holding: The Seventh Circuit in 1991, in an opinion by Judge Posner on a panel with Judges Flaum and Manion, rejected Union Carbide's reading of the tax clause as an indemnity for later assessments, finding it too weakly supported to require a trial against the natural reading that the seller could add applicable taxes to the agreed purchase price, so summary judgment was proper on interpretation alone. Alternatively, even if the clause were construed as an indemnity, it materially altered the bargain and Oscar Mayer had not consented to it expressly or impliedly. The court found no breach and affirmed.
sections.Reasoning:
The court first rejected Union Carbide's interpretation. The text could linguistically accommodate its claim, but it also naturally allowed the seller simply to add applicable taxes to an agreed price, which differs substantially from open-ended liability for retroactive taxes and interest years after delivery because the seller miscalculated its obligations. Economic context favored that reading: Union Carbide, the taxpayer dealing with Illinois, was better placed than its customer to prevent a tax mistake, and Oscar Mayer sought a competitive price reduction, not a discount that might later be reclaimed with interest. Union Carbide's proposed meaning was too weakly supported to require a trial.

Alternatively, under 2-207 an acceptance can form a sales contract despite additional terms, and between merchants such terms may become part of the agreement, but a material alteration does not enter automatically. The court described materiality as an alteration to which consent cannot reasonably be presumed, equivalent to unreasonable surprise, and criticized treating hardship as an independent criterion; hardship ordinarily followed from the alteration. Materiality and actual acceptance were separate questions. A buyer could accept even a material change, expressly or by silence against a course of dealing supporting an inference of consent, but the proposer needed evidence beyond the term itself.

Applying this, Oscar Mayer's acknowledged obligation to pay taxes shown on invoices differed from an incalculable obligation to reimburse later assessments on completed purchases. Because the clause was at best ambiguous about indemnity, silence in response to successive invoices could not show assent to Union Carbide's reading.

The casebook note focuses on surprise versus hardship and on the document sequence.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-086.rule: When expressly conditional and inconsistent forms fail to form a written contract and the parties' conduct establishes one, section 2-207(3) alone determines its terms: those on which the writings agree plus supplementary terms supplied by other Code provisions.

sections.Parties: Malden Mills, a textile manufacturer, and its property insurers, Commerce & Industry and Federal Insurance, were the plaintiffs. They sued Bayer and numerous other defendants over a factory fire, alleging against Bayer negligence and breaches of the implied warranties of merchantability and fitness. Bayer, which sold nylon tow to Malden Mills, was a defendant and the appellant; it sought to compel arbitration under language printed in Malden Mills's own purchase orders. Malden Mills refused to arbitrate.
sections.Procedural History: The civil action began on December 3, 1998. Bayer moved to compel arbitration and stay the litigation. Superior Court Judge S. Jane Haggerty denied the motion, holding that conduct formed the sales contract but the parties' writings did not agree on arbitration, and that equitable estoppel did not supply the missing obligation. The denial was immediately appealable under G.L. c. 251, section 18(a)(1), and the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court granted direct appellate review. On February 21, 2001 it affirmed the order denying the motion to compel arbitration and stay litigation. The appeal did not adjudicate responsibility for the fire.
sections.Material Facts:
An explosion and fire destroyed several buildings at Malden Mills's facility on December 11, 1995. The plaintiffs alleged that static electrical discharge ignited nylon tow sold by Bayer, manufactured by a French entity, and used in producing flocked upholstery fabric; these were allegations, not findings.

Malden Mills ordered nylon by sending a purchase order or by telephoning and then sending its standard order. The reverse side required arbitration in New York or Boston under either AAA or General Arbitration Council of the Textile Industry rules, the choices belonging to Malden Mills. Another provision declared the order the entire agreement regardless of the seller's forms and permitted modification only in a writing signed by an authorized buyer representative.

Bayer forwarded orders to the manufacturer, usually directing shipment straight to Malden Mills, and then sent invoices. Capitalized invoice language made acceptance subject to a mutually executed contract or, absent one, Bayer's prices and printed conditions. Paragraph fourteen disclaimed being an acceptance or confirmation under section 2-207 and expressly conditioned acceptance on the buyer's assent to additional or conflicting invoice terms. The invoice said nothing about arbitration or any other method of resolving disputes. Malden Mills ordinarily paid within thirty days.
sections.Issue: When expressly conditional and inconsistent forms fail to form a written contract, does an arbitration provision appearing only in the buyer's form become part of the contract later established by delivery, acceptance, and payment?
sections.Holding: The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court in 2001, in an opinion by Justice Greaney for a court of five with no separate writing, held that on this record it does not. G.L. c. 106, section 2-207(3) exclusively determines the terms of a contract formed by conduct: the terms on which the writings agree, together with supplementary terms supplied through other applicable Code provisions. Subsection (2)'s test for additional or different terms cannot be imported to preserve a term in a contract the writings never formed. The order denying arbitration was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning:
The court distinguished three routes. Divergent forms can establish a contract under subsection (1) when the seller's acceptance is not expressly conditional. An expressly conditional invoice instead requires affirmative acceptance of the counteroffer. If the forms do not establish a contract but shipment and acceptance recognize one, subsection (3) supplies the contract and its terms. Bayer conceded the third route governed: its conditional invoice was never affirmatively accepted, and Malden Mills's purchase order also restricted acceptance to its own terms.

Bayer argued that arbitration caused no surprise or hardship and was not a material alteration, relying on language in JOM suggesting that subsection (3) implicitly incorporated subsection (2) and on official comment 6. The court rejected this because the route to formation determines the available term-selection rule. Subsection (2) governs terms in contracts formed through writings or confirmations of oral agreements and cannot itself serve as another Code provision supplying terms. Official comment 7 addresses contracts formed by conduct and points to subsection (3).

Subsection (3) can incorporate terms established by course of dealing, performance, or trade usage, but Bayer showed none; it conceded it had never previously arbitrated a dispute with Malden Mills and offered no evidence of industry custom. Policies favoring arbitration presuppose an agreement to arbitrate. Equitable estoppel also failed: Bayer did not establish an intention to remain bound to the buyer's arbitration language absent a final written contract, or inequity from proceeding in court.

The casebook presents the case as a problem illustrating the distinction between a contract's existence and its contents.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-087.rule: A buyer who keeps mail-order goods beyond the stated return period assents to the terms enclosed with them, but an arbitration term whose costs effectively leave consumers without an accessible forum can be unenforceable for substantive unconscionability alone.

sections.Parties: The plaintiffs and appellants were purchasers of Gateway computers who sought compensatory and punitive damages for themselves and similarly situated consumers. They asserted seven causes of action, including warranty, contract, fraud, and unfair-trade-practice claims. Gateway 2000, which sold computers and software directly by telephone or mail, was the defendant and invoked the arbitration agreement enclosed with its shipments.
sections.Procedural History: By an order of October 21, 1997, Justice Beatrice Shainswit of the Supreme Court, New York County, dismissed the complaint based on the agreement to arbitrate. The purchasers appealed. On August 13, 1998 the Appellate Division, First Department, modified the order on the law and facts by vacating the requirement to arbitrate before the International Chamber of Commerce, granted leave to seek appointment of an arbitrator under 9 U.S.C. section 5, remanded for that purpose, and otherwise affirmed, without costs. The decision did not reach the truth of the purchasers' claims or any entitlement to damages.
sections.Material Facts:
Beginning July 3, 1995, Gateway's shipments included a Standard Terms and Conditions Agreement and warranties. A boxed customer notice, in slightly larger type, said that keeping the system beyond thirty days after delivery accepted the enclosed terms. The four-page agreement had sixteen paragraphs; paragraph ten required exclusive, final arbitration under International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) rules before a sole arbitrator in Chicago. The appellants relevant to the decision bought after July 3, 1995.

The purchasers alleged that Gateway promised free around-the-clock technical assistance, software support, and certain on-site services, while reaching a technician was virtually impossible. They objected that the clause was not part of their original bargain, was obscure and adhesive, and imposed an inaccessible, costly process. The ICC was headquartered in France. For claims under $50,000, ICC advance fees were $4,000, including a $2,000 registration fee not refunded even to a successful claimant, while counsel estimated individual damages at no more than $1,000. ICC rules also exposed an unsuccessful consumer to Gateway's legal fees. Gateway claimed it had since offered customers a choice between the AAA and the ICC; the parties agreed the AAA required a nonrefundable filing fee of at least $500.
sections.Issue: Did the purchasers assent to the arbitration clause enclosed with the computers by keeping them beyond thirty days, or was it a material alteration of an existing agreement under UCC 2-207? If they assented, was the clause unenforceable as a contract of adhesion or as unconscionable?
sections.Holding: The Appellate Division, First Department, in 1998, in an opinion by Justice Presiding Milonas in which Justices Nardelli, Mazzarelli, and Saxe concurred, held that retaining the product beyond the stated thirty days manifested assent to the enclosed contract, so the arbitration clause was a provision of the single agreement eventually accepted and not a material alteration under UCC 2-207. The agreement was not invalid as adhesive and had no procedural defect, but the ICC designation was substantively unconscionable because of its cost and was vacated, leaving the arbitration obligation itself in place.
sections.Reasoning:
On formation, the court adopted the reasoning of Hill and ProCD while acknowledging those Seventh Circuit decisions were not controlling New York authority. Neither the initial order nor receipt of the goods completed the contract; the proposed agreement stayed open for rejection by return until the retention period ended. Decisions about arbitration language added to an existing oral contract therefore did not govern.

Unequal bargaining power alone did not make the agreement adhesive. Purchasers could buy a competitor's product and had an unqualified opportunity to return the merchandise within thirty days for any reason. Failing to read or understand the agreement did not undo assent.

New York ordinarily required both procedural and substantive unconscionability. The court found no procedural defect: the heading was conspicuous, the agreement short, the type uniform, and arbitration was not hidden in a complex document. Chicago's inconvenience alone was insufficient. The ICC costs were different: excluding consumers from court while demanding fees out of proportion to their claims effectively left them without an accessible forum, and sufficiently severe substantive unconscionability alone could make that portion unenforceable.

Gateway's claimed substitution of the AAA did not moot the problem. The purchasers had not accepted the amendment, the court invoked UCC 2-209 in rejecting any supposed acceptance, and the record lacked the AAA rules and cost information needed to assess unconscionability. The court also rejected the argument, first raised on appeal, that the false-advertising claims about technical support fell outside arbitration.

The casebook uses the case twice, once on formation and once on the costly forum and substitution.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-088.rule: When the Government repudiates or substantially breaches a contract, the other party may obtain restitution of the payments it made, even if the contract would not ultimately have been profitable, provided it has not waived that right.

sections.Parties: Mobil and Marathon were companies that had paid the United States for offshore leases and sued it for breach of contract, seeking restitution of their up-front bonus payments. They were the petitioners in the Supreme Court. The United States, the lessor and the respondent, contended that the leases' incorporated statutes and regulations authorized its conduct, that the companies had waived restitution, and that they could never have obtained all the necessary permits anyway.
sections.Procedural History: The companies joined a contract action in the Court of Federal Claims in October 1992. On summary judgment that court found repudiation and awarded restitution of the bonus payments. A divided Federal Circuit reversed because North Carolina's consistency objection would have prevented exploration regardless of Interior's failure to approve the plan. The Court considered both companies' petitions together and, on June 26, 2000, reversed the Federal Circuit and remanded both cases for proceedings consistent with restitution of the $156 million in bonus payments.
sections.Material Facts:
Mobil and Marathon paid approximately $156 million in up-front bonus payments for ten-year renewable leases issued in 1981 covering exploration and development off North Carolina's coast. The leases did not guarantee permission to drill. They gave the companies an opportunity to seek permissions under incorporated statutes and regulations, including the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act and the Coastal Zone Management Act. Interior had to consider an Exploration Plan and approve a qualifying plan within thirty days; a drilling permit also required a coastal-zone consistency certification, subject to state objection and possible Commerce override.

The companies submitted their final Exploration Plan and consistency certification on August 20, 1990. Two days earlier the Outer Banks Protection Act (OBPA) had taken effect. It barred plan approvals and drilling permits for at least thirteen months and required a report from a new Environmental Sciences Review Panel, Interior certification to Congress, and a further congressional-session period. Interior told Mobil that the plan satisfied existing law and could not properly be disapproved under it, but that OBPA prevented approval; it suspended the leases instead. North Carolina objected to consistency in November 1990. Commerce rejected the companies' override request in 1994, relying substantially on the new Panel's findings. Congress repealed OBPA in 1996.
sections.Issue: Did the Government's refusal to approve the Exploration Plan under the procedures the leases promised, because of a later statute, amount to a repudiation or substantial breach entitling the companies to restitution of their bonus payments, and had the companies waived that right?
sections.Holding: The Court in 2000, in an opinion by Justice Breyer for eight Justices with Justice Stevens dissenting, held that the Government repudiated the leases by announcing that it would follow OBPA in place of the promised approval process, that the breach substantially impaired the value of the contracts, and that the companies had not waived restitution. They were therefore entitled to restitution of their bonus payments whether or not the venture would ultimately have produced a profit or all permits. The Court did not order drilling, invalidate OBPA, or decide every possible additional expense claim.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court applied ordinary contract principles that govern when the Government contracts. Under Restatement section 373, repudiation or nonperformance amounting to total breach supports restitution; section 250 defines repudiation and section 243 requires substantial impairment of contractual value. Not every delay or minor breach gives a refund. Once the threshold is met, restitution restores the advance payment even if performance would have been financially disadvantageous.

The Government's incorporated-law defenses failed. An OCSLA suspension provision required a lessee's request. An existing regulation permitting suspension for environmental analysis could not import every analysis a future statute demanded. The leases included certain future regulations under identified statutes, but their general catchall did not incorporate unknown requirements of a later statute such as OBPA. Authority to suspend for serious environmental harm did not apply, since Interior itself said the plan complied with existing standards.

Because the United States was the contracting obligor, communicating that it would follow the incompatible statute communicated an intention to depart from the leases. The Court declined to reopen the sovereign-acts defense, which the trial court had rejected and the Government did not contest. The breach was material: timely consideration under agreed procedures was a gateway to exploration rights, and an announced delay of at least thirteen months, ultimately at least four years, substantially narrowed it. Urging a repudiating party to perform does not waive restitution, and the Government showed no acceptance of significant post-repudiation performance. The state's objection went to compensatory damages, not restitution.

Justice Stevens agreed that failing to approve the plan within thirty days was a breach but disputed repudiation, materiality, and the remedy. He thought at most modest delay damages were appropriate and a $156 million refund disproportionate.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-089.rule: As the Appellate Division held at this stage, an agreement granting an exclusive right is void for want of mutuality and consideration where the grantee's only promises depend on acts the writing does not require him to perform.

sections.Parties: Otis Wood was the plaintiff and the respondent on appeal. He sued on a written fashion-marketing agreement that gave him exclusive rights to place Lucy, Lady Duff-Gordon's endorsements and to sell or license her designs, claiming she had breached it. Duff-Gordon, a creator of fashion, was the defendant and appellant. She argued that the writing lacked mutuality and consideration because Wood had not promised the essential revenue-producing activity.
sections.Procedural History: The pleadings consisted of Wood's amended complaint and Duff-Gordon's demurrer. New York Special Term denied Duff-Gordon's motion for judgment on the pleadings by an order entered January 6, 1917, and she appealed. On April 20, 1917 the Appellate Division, First Department, reversed the order with ten dollars costs and disbursements and granted her motion with ten dollars costs. This brief covers only that intermediate stage. The casebook reproduces it in a footnote to the later Court of Appeals opinion, which took a different interpretive approach and found a reasonable-efforts promise implied in the writing.
sections.Material Facts:
The written agreement, reproduced in Wood's amended complaint, recited Duff-Gordon's position as a creator of fashion in America, England, and France and the monetary value of endorsements carrying her name, and described Wood's organization as suited to placing endorsements she approved. Wood received the exclusive right to place endorsements he considered advantageous and those approved by Duff-Gordon or her adviser, and the exclusive right to sell or license the manufacture and sale of certain articles she created.

Wood would collect the profits and revenues from endorsements, sales, and licenses. Duff-Gordon would receive half, and he would keep the remainder after paying the costs of obtaining the revenues. He had to account monthly. He would also obtain patents, copyrights, and trademarks he considered necessary and take protective proceedings he considered appropriate, with the latter expenses shared equally.

The complaint alleged that Duff-Gordon placed endorsements herself for consideration without Wood's consent, defeating his exclusive right and depriving him of his revenue share. That was an allegation, not a trial finding.
sections.Issue: Did the complaint state a sufficient cause of action on the writing, or was the agreement unenforceable for want of mutuality and consideration because Wood had not bound himself to obtain endorsements, make sales, or grant licenses?
sections.Holding: The Appellate Division, First Department, in 1917, in an opinion by Justice Davis in which Presiding Justice Clarke and Justices Laughlin, Dowling, and Shearn concurred, held the contract void for want of mutuality and consideration. Duff-Gordon had granted the exclusive opportunity, but Wood had supplied no binding reciprocal undertaking to exploit it. The court reversed the order and granted judgment on the pleadings for Duff-Gordon. It was a ruling on the sufficiency of the pleaded contract claim, not a damages calculation after trial.
sections.Reasoning:
The court distinguished collecting and distributing revenue from undertaking to create the transactions that produce it. Wood's promise to collect and account would bind him if he placed an endorsement, made a sale, or granted a license. But the court found no provision obligating him to obtain endorsements, make sales, or grant licenses in the first place, and Duff-Gordon could not compel those preliminary acts. His downstream promises therefore depended on an act he had not agreed to perform.

The patent and protective-proceeding language did not solve the problem. Those promises concerned endorsements he was under no duty to place, and their performance was left to his judgment. In the court's reading, no provision could be enforced against him if he simply did nothing. It drew support from the proposition in Commercial Wood & Cement that a plaintiff who had obligated itself to do nothing could never breach.

The court did not determine how much effort a binding reasonable-efforts promise would require; its premise was that the agreement created no such enforceable obligation.

The casebook reproduces this intermediate court's reasoning in an editorial footnote within its account of the Court of Appeals decision, which expressly took a different approach, to show the conflict between literal dependence on optional acts and implication from the arrangement's context.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-090.rule: Under Indiana promissory estoppel a conditional promise can be enforced where the promisor should reasonably have expected the general nature and extent of the reliance it induced, with recovery limited to reliance damages.

sections.Parties: D & G Stout, Inc., formerly General Liquors, a liquor distributor in northern Indiana, was the plaintiff and sought the costs of relying on an assurance that it would remain a Bacardi distributor. David and Georgia Stout were individual plaintiffs who claimed only losses on the Fort Wayne warehouse. Bacardi Imports, a supplier whose line accounted for thirty percent of General's sales and twenty-three percent of its profit, was the defendant.
sections.Procedural History: The district court had granted summary judgment for Bacardi, and the Seventh Circuit reversed. On remand District Judge Miller conducted a nonjury trial and made findings under Rule 52(a). The appellate decision remained controlling on its interpretation of Indiana law but did not establish the contested facts. By a memorandum of October 21, 1992, the court directed judgment for D & G Stout against Bacardi for $510,450, being $394,050 in reliance damages plus $116,400 in prejudgment interest, directed judgment for Bacardi on the Stouts' individual claims, and assessed costs against Bacardi. This brief covers only that judgment after trial on remand.
sections.Material Facts:
In 1987 two suppliers withdrew important product lines from General on customary thirty-day notice under at-will arrangements. General's president, David Stout, concluded that General could stay profitable if it kept Bacardi, Hiram Walker, and a third supplier and closed its Fort Wayne facility. At a July 9 meeting Stout said General needed Bacardi to remain in business. Bacardi's marketing vice president, William Tovell, assured him that General would remain a distributor if it kept meeting sales expectations and market conditions did not change, and regional manager Ned Russo reaffirmed that in later calls. The court found a conditional promise, not the unconditional commitment assumed on appeal.

National Wine & Spirits made a July offer to buy General. Stout seriously considered it but decided to keep operating, a decision the court placed around July 21. Contrary to the summary-judgment assumptions, Bacardi did not know of the National negotiations before the offer was rejected. Bacardi then chose Olinger as its statewide distributor, announcing the selection July 29 and informing General July 30. Stout reopened negotiations with National, which now held the stronger bargaining position, and the resulting August asset sale was less favorable than the July offer.
sections.Issue: Could Bacardi's conditional assurance to an at-will distributor support promissory estoppel under Indiana law when Bacardi did not know of the specific purchase offer General rejected in reliance on it, and if so, what reliance damages were recoverable?
sections.Holding: The Northern District of Indiana in 1992, in a memorandum by District Judge Miller after a nonjury trial, held that Bacardi's conditional promise satisfied Indiana's elements of promissory estoppel. Bacardi reasonably should have expected General to keep operating and so forgo alternatives requiring it to leave the distribution business, and General's reliance was reasonable, definite, and substantial. The court awarded $394,050 as the difference between the rejected July offer and the August sale proceeds, plus $116,400 in prejudgment interest, and denied the Fort Wayne warehouse expenses.
sections.Reasoning:
The court applied Indiana's five elements: a promise, an expectation of reliance, induced reasonable reliance, reliance of a definite and substantial nature, and injustice avoidable only by enforcement. Bacardi's conditions did not eliminate the promise; a promise supporting section 90 need not satisfy every requirement of a contractual offer.

Bacardi argued it could not reasonably expect General to reject an offer it did not know existed. The court distinguished the exact opportunity forgone from the general nature and extent of the reliance. Bacardi knew General's survival depended on its line and was asked for a commitment for that reason, so it need not know which purchase offer General would reject. Remaining in business was foreseeable reliance; buying additional assets to expand would not have been.

Reliance was reasonable despite at-will status. Neither sales performance nor market conditions changed between July 9 and July 23; what changed was Bacardi's assessment and business plan. The promise was not perpetual, but an announcement three and a half weeks later contradicted the short-term assurance. General sought the costs of reliance on the additional assurance, not damages for breach of the at-will distributorship. Rejecting National's firm offer was definite and substantial forbearance, and the industry's handshake relationships supported the conclusion that enforcement was needed.

On damages, Fort Wayne warehouse expenses were excluded because General had planned to close that facility before the assurance; awarding them would put it in a better position than performance. Prejudgment interest was allowed only on the $291,000 of losses ascertainable by mathematical comparison, at eight percent simple interest for five years.

The casebook's account of the outcome on remand reports the $394,050 in reliance damages but omits the interest and the resulting $510,450 judgment.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-091.rule: An executory agreement that one party may cancel at any time lacks mutuality and is unenforceable as to future performance, and equity will not specifically enforce it at the suit of the party who holds the power to revoke.

sections.Parties: Miami Coca-Cola Bottling Co., the licensee, was the complainant and the appellant. It sought an injunction against cancellation of its license and specific performance of it. Orange Crush Co., the licensor, was the defendant and appellee; it had given written notice that it would no longer be bound by the license.
sections.Procedural History: Miami Coca-Cola filed a bill in equity. District Judge Rhydon M. Call dismissed the bill. The Fifth Circuit reviewed that equity decree and, in an opinion of February 19, 1924, affirmed the decree dismissing the bill.
sections.Material Facts:
Orange Crush granted Miami Coca-Cola the exclusive right within a designated territory to manufacture orange crush, bottle it, and distribute it under Orange Crush's trademark. Orange Crush promised to supply its concentrate at stated prices and undertake certain advertising. Miami Coca-Cola agreed to purchase a specified quantity of concentrate, maintain a bottling plant, solicit orders, promote sales, and develop increasing sales volume. The license was described as perpetual, but Miami Coca-Cola could cancel the agreement at any time; the report gives no notice period or other restriction on that power.

The bill alleged that Miami Coca-Cola purchased concentrate, manufactured the beverage, and was performing its obligations when, about a year after formation, Orange Crush gave written notice that it would no longer be bound. These were the pleading's allegations, not findings after trial.
sections.Issue: Could a licensee that held an unrestricted power to cancel the license at any time obtain an injunction and specific performance compelling the licensor to continue performing it?
sections.Holding: The Fifth Circuit in 1924, in an opinion by Judge Bryan on a panel consisting of Judges Walker and Bryan, held that the agreement lacked mutuality and was unenforceable insofar as it remained executory, because Miami Coca-Cola's unrestricted power to cancel meant it had not committed itself to future performance. The court affirmed the dismissal of the bill. It did not finally reject every possible damages claim arising from the period already performed.
sections.Reasoning:
Although the license listed substantial activities for the bottler, the unrestricted cancellation proviso let it withdraw at any time. The promised consideration was a promise for a promise, and Miami Coca-Cola's ability to cancel meant it had not committed itself to the future performance the licensor sought in exchange. The reasoning depends on the cancellation power, not on any absence of particular tasks.

Miami Coca-Cola could not preserve the arrangement by treating it as a continuing option. An enforceable option needed supporting consideration, and the court found none binding the grant of that continuing privilege.

The court distinguished the period already performed. It conceded that Orange Crush might be liable for damages for that period, but those damages had an adequate remedy at law, and the suit under review sought prospective equitable relief.

The court added an equitable ground from Express Co. v. Railroad Co.: equity would not intervene where a party held the power of revocation, because that party could render the court's action a nullity. Here the bottler could cancel the very arrangement it wanted the court to compel the licensor to perform.

The casebook's termination-clause note uses the decision to illustrate an unrestricted power to withdraw; the note's ensuing discussion of restricted cancellation and the Uniform Commercial Code is editorial material, not a holding of this opinion.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-092.rule: A pension promise made after an employee has independently decided to retire is not supported by bargained-for consideration and is not enforceable by promissory estoppel, because the promise did not induce the retirement or other forbearance.

sections.Parties: Edward J. Hayes, a retired general manager of Plantations Steel, was the plaintiff. He sued to enforce what he claimed was the company's promise of a pension, and cross-appealed the denial of attorney's fees under ERISA. Plantations Steel Co., his former employer, was the defendant and the appellant on liability; it had stopped making annual payments to him.
