sections.Procedural History: Hayes sued in December 1977. After a nonjury trial the Superior Court found an implied-in-fact contract for a lifetime pension, treating voluntary retirement as consideration, and alternatively found promissory estoppel. It awarded $5,000 annually for 1977 through 1979 and rejected Hayes's ERISA attorney-fee theory. Plantations appealed the liability judgment and Hayes cross-appealed on fees. On January 6, 1982 the Rhode Island Supreme Court sustained Plantations's appeal, reversed the Superior Court judgment, and remanded the papers to that court. Because liability failed, it did not decide the cross-appeal.
sections.Material Facts:
Hayes worked for Plantations from 1947 until 1972, beginning as an estimator and draftsman and becoming general manager. In January 1972 he announced that he would retire the following July, at sixty-five. He testified that he expected a pension and would not otherwise have retired, but no company statement or conduct had induced the January decision.

About a week before the retirement, officer and shareholder Hugo R. Mainelli, Jr., told Hayes that the company would take care of him. It was their first and only conversation about pension payments, and no amount or salary percentage was specified. The shareholders and directors had not formally authorized payments. The company had no pension provision for employees outside its union arrangement, and Hayes was not a union member. Mainelli testified that his father authorized the first payment as appreciation for past service.

Plantations paid $5,000 annually from January 1973 through January 1976, totaling $20,000. Hayes took no other employment. Each year he visited, thanked Mainelli for the prior check, and asked how long payments would continue. After poor business years and a shareholder dispute that ended with the DiMartino family in control, payments stopped after 1976.
sections.Issue: Was the company's assurance that it would take care of Hayes enforceable as an implied-in-fact contract supported by consideration, or under promissory estoppel, when Hayes had announced his retirement before the assurance was given?
sections.Holding: The Rhode Island Supreme Court in 1982, in an opinion by Justice Shea, held that the promise was enforceable on neither theory. Hayes's retirement and past service were not bargained for and were not induced by the promise, so there was no consideration; the promise was a gratuity acknowledging completed service. Promissory estoppel failed because the assurance did not cause his retirement or any additional definite and substantial forbearance. The court reversed the judgment for Hayes.
sections.Reasoning:
For analysis the court assumed that Plantations had made a legally relevant promise. An implied-in-fact agreement requires consideration just as an express contract does; the difference lies only in how assent is manifested. Consideration must be bargained for and must induce the return act or promise, and past conduct undertaken without reference to the later promise cannot supply the exchange. Hayes announced his retirement well before the assurance, and his earlier years of service were likewise not induced by it. The promise neither encouraged him to stay at work nor induced long service from the start.

The court distinguished Bredemann, where the employer wanted the employee to retire and made a concrete offer to pay if she did so immediately; Plantations had not sought Hayes's retirement. It distinguished Ulmann, where the employee's agreement not to compete supplied the principal consideration. That some work occurred after the assurance did not establish a bargain.

The court recognized promissory estoppel as a substitute for consideration under the Restatement formulation it had adopted, so the absence of a bargain did not alone dispose of that theory. The decisive defect was causation. Hayes had decided to retire on his own initiative before Mainelli spoke. The court contrasted Feinberg and the Restatement annuity example, where an announced pension induced the later retirement. Failing to seek another job showed no change of position, because the premise of his retirement was that he would stop working, and receiving payments did not itself show reliance, particularly as he repeatedly asked whether another payment could be expected.

The casebook presents the case as a problem asking whether this pension promise differs materially from Feinberg.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-093.rule: A party claiming an express or implied contract to be paid for services must prove an actual mutual intention to contract, and services rendered within a family household are explained by the family relationship and do not by themselves imply a hiring.

sections.Parties: John Hertzog was the plaintiff. He sued his deceased father's estate for the value of services he and his wife rendered on the father's farms and for money lent, and he obtained a verdict at trial. The estate was the defendant and brought the case to the reviewing court by writ of error, challenging the trial court's instructions to the jury.
sections.Procedural History: At trial the estate requested an instruction requiring proof that the relationship was one of master and servant and not ordinary parent and child. The trial court agreed that wages could not be recovered without a mutual understanding to compensate, but told the jury it could infer such an agreement from the testimony of two witnesses. It also permitted a quantum-meruit count to be added and ruled that John could sue for his wife's money without joining her. The jury returned a verdict of $2,203.97 for John, and judgment followed. On the estate's writ of error, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court reversed the judgment and awarded a new trial.
sections.Material Facts:
John reached majority around 1825 but continued to live with his farmer father and work on his farms, apart from a temporary absence in Virginia. In 1842 he married and brought his wife into his parents' home. His father later placed him on another farm the father owned and then moved there with his own wife. They lived together until the father's death in 1849. The father managed the farm in his own name, and no accounts were kept between father and son. The reviewing court presumed the son and his family received their living from the father.

Witness Adam Stamm heard the father say he would pay John for his labor. Daniel Roderick testified that John had repeatedly asked his father for payment and been put off; when Roderick approached the father at John's request, the father said he intended to make John safe.

There was also a $500 loan claim. Evidence indicated that the father had received money belonging to John's wife when buying a farm in 1847. The reviewing court treated the evidence of the loan and its date as indistinct.
sections.Issue: Could the jury infer a contract to pay wages from an adult son's work on his father's farm while living in the father's household, together with the father's statements that he would pay the son and intended to make him safe?
sections.Holding: The Pennsylvania Supreme Court in 1857, in an opinion by Justice Lowrie, held that the trial court erred in authorizing the jury to infer a contract from this testimony. The family relationship explained the services without implying a hiring, and the father's statements showed at most an intention to reward the son, not an existing agreement to pay wages. The court also said, conditionally, that if the $500 was lent before the 1848 married-women's law, John could sue without joining his wife. The judgment was reversed and a new trial awarded.
sections.Reasoning:
Justice Lowrie began by separating relationships commonly gathered under the label implied contract. A true contract rests on the parties' mutual intention: it is express when the terms are openly stated and implied when actual intention is inferred from circumstances. A constructive contract, by contrast, is a legal fiction used to enforce a duty through a contract remedy even when the parties had no intention to contract; its duty comes from law. The court said this case asserted a proper express or implied agreement, not a constructive obligation, so the quantum-meruit count did not let the jury replace proof of the agreement with a general belief that payment would be fair.

Ordinary work for a stranger may support an inference of hiring because the relationship otherwise calls for an explanation. An existing relationship may supply that explanation, as with neighbors helping to save a burning house. Family association likewise could account for a son's work for his father. A party claiming a contract must prove it, and circumstances equally explained by the family relationship are insufficient. Here the shared household, the father's management, the absence of accounts, and the presumed support supplied the family explanation. Relatives were not incapable of contracting: accounts, periodic wages, or a settlement of wages might show an express contract, but none was present.

The father's statements acknowledged that the son deserved a reward while leaving unproved any existing agreement, and John's repeated unsuccessful requests suggested he wanted an agreement, not that one existed. John's argument on review that the farm was run jointly with profits divided had no evidence behind it.

The casebook note cites the case for its treatment of family services and refusal of restitution; the brief notes that Lowrie identified the theory before him as one requiring a real contract and did not decide every unjust-enrichment theory.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-094.rule: The at-will presumption may be rebutted by an implied-in-fact agreement to discharge only for good cause, but breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing in an employment contract does not give rise to tort remedies.

sections.Parties: Daniel D. Foley, a discharged branch manager, was the plaintiff and sought compensatory and punitive damages from his former employer on three theories: discharge contrary to public policy, breach of an implied-in-fact agreement to discharge only for good cause, and tortious breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing. Interactive Data Corporation, the employer, was the defendant and had prevailed in both lower courts.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court sustained demurrers to Foley's second amended complaint without leave to amend and entered judgment for the employer. The Court of Appeal affirmed all three dismissals. On December 29, 1988 the California Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Appeal's judgment as to dismissal of the public-policy and tortious-covenant causes of action, reversed it as to dismissal of the implied-in-fact good-cause contract claim, and remanded for proceedings consistent with the opinion. No damages were awarded and no employment contract was finally found.
sections.Material Facts:
The facts were allegations assumed true on demurrer. Interactive Data hired Foley in June 1976 as an assistant product manager at $18,500. It required an agreement restricting competition and requiring disclosure and assignment of computer-related information and innovations for one year after termination; that writing did not define permissible grounds for discharge. Over six years and nine months Foley allegedly received promotions, raises, bonuses, favorable evaluations, and assurances of continued employment while he performed adequately. He became Los Angeles branch manager, earning $56,164 annually, and received a $6,762 merit bonus two days before discharge. Written termination guidelines allegedly prescribed grounds for dismissal and a mandatory seven-step procedure, and Foley allegedly declined other employment in reliance on job security.

In January 1983 Foley privately told former supervisor Richard Earnest that his new supervisor, Robert Kuhne, was under FBI investigation for embezzlement from Bank of America. Earnest told him to disregard the rumors. In March Kuhne announced that Foley would be replaced for performance reasons and possibly transferred. Later discussions offered continued branch management under a performance plan, but at the meeting meant to present the plan Kuhne instead gave him a choice between resignation and discharge.
sections.Issue: Did the complaint state a claim for discharge in violation of public policy? Could an implied-in-fact promise to discharge only for good cause be enforced despite the at-will presumption of Labor Code section 2922 and the one-year statute of frauds? Does breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing in an employment contract support tort damages?
sections.Holding: The California Supreme Court in 1988, in an opinion by Chief Justice Lucas, held three things. By six to one, the public-policy claim failed because Foley's disclosure served the employer's private interest and not a fundamental duty benefiting the public. Unanimously, the allegations were sufficient to permit proof of an implied-in-fact agreement to discharge only for good cause, and the statute of frauds did not bar it. By four to three, breach of the implied covenant of good faith in an employment contract does not give rise to tort damages. Justices Broussard and Kaufman dissented on the third point, and Justice Mosk on the first and third.
sections.Reasoning:
On public policy, section 2922's at-will presumption does not authorize a discharge that violates fundamental public policy, and Tameny allows a tort claim based on a duty imposed by law. But the complaint had to implicate a fundamental duty benefiting the public, not only a particular employer or employee. The majority found that Foley's disclosure served the employer's private interest, unlike refusing to commit crimes, reporting wrongdoing to authorities, or disclosing unsafe conditions.

On implied contract, section 2922 supplies a presumption only when no contrary agreement exists. The court rejected any requirement of separate consideration beyond services, since one consideration can support several promises, and any need for equivalent limits on the employee's right to leave. Relevant evidence included personnel policies and practices, longevity of service, assurances of continued employment, and industry practice; the totality alleged could support the claimed understanding. The court did not find a contract or decide whether good cause existed.

On the statute of frauds, the one-year provision applies only to contracts that by their terms cannot possibly be performed within a year. An indefinite good-cause agreement could be completed within a year if the employee left or was discharged for cause.

On the covenant, the majority distinguished contract law's enforcement of agreed expectations from tort law's enforcement of broader social duties and found ordinary employment insufficiently like insurance: a dismissed employee can seek replacement work, and employers do not sell protection against loss. Predictability and existing protections counseled caution. The covenant protects benefits actually agreed upon and cannot itself turn an at-will relationship into a good-cause contract.

Justice Broussard, dissenting in part, viewed the tort remedy as established by appellate authority and the insurance analogy as persuasive. Justice Kaufman would recognize tort remedies for willful, malicious discharge. Justice Mosk also thought that reporting a supervisor's potential criminal wrongdoing benefited society.

The casebook uses the case for the rejection of automatic transfer of the insurance model.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-001.rule: Efforts made in negotiating a deal that are ordinary attempts to secure one's own business advantage, conferring at most an incidental benefit on the other side, do not support recovery in unjust enrichment.

sections.Parties: Songbird Jet and Jet Leasing, which bought, sold, brokered, and serviced business aircraft, were the plaintiffs. Their principals were Alan Rosefielde and William Handy. They claimed breach of a contract to sell them a Falcon 50 jet, breach of a separate brokerage contract, fraud, and unjust enrichment. Amax, a mineral and energy business that was reducing its corporate aircraft fleet, was the defendant; it denied that any contract existed, asserted counterclaims, and moved for summary judgment.
sections.Procedural History: The plaintiffs sued in January 1983 in a diversity action. Amax asserted counterclaims against the plaintiffs and their principals and moved under Rule 56 for summary judgment dismissing the plaintiffs' claims. New York substantive law was undisputed. In 1984 Judge Edward Weinfeld of the Southern District of New York denied the motion on the sales-contract claim and granted it on all the other claims. The opinion neither dismissed the whole action nor resolved Amax's counterclaims.
sections.Material Facts:
These are competing evidentiary accounts, not facts resolved at trial. Amax owned an undelivered Falcon 50, serial number 108, under construction. The plaintiffs' evidence described a June 1982 meeting under which they would find a buyer for the 108 and earn the difference between their purchase and resale prices. By September they had found L.R. French, who wanted to trade in a Lear jet. Rosefielde proposed that the plaintiffs buy the 108, take the Lear in their resale to French, and let Amax sell the tax benefits separately. According to Rosefielde, Amax's David Ayres announced about October 28 that they had a deal at $8,850,000, conditioned on a $250,000 deposit applicable to the price and a French resale agreement acceptable to Amax.

The plaintiffs furnished the French agreement and tendered the deposit under a letter making it refundable on request and creditable toward the price should an agreement be finalized. Amax's lawyers prepared several drafts, but neither side signed. Jet Leasing sent personnel to monitor the plane's completion. On December 22 Amax denied that a contract existed; it sold the tax benefits on December 29 and returned the deposit on January 3, withholding $53,789.68 as a disputed debt. Amax described a different June arrangement, an inseparable package of transactions, which it said the plaintiffs repudiated.
sections.Issue: On Amax's motion for summary judgment, did material issues of fact require a trial on the alleged oral contract to sell the aircraft, including authority, intent to be bound, and the statute of frauds, and could the plaintiffs maintain claims for a separate brokerage contract, fraud, or unjust enrichment for their negotiation, tax-structuring, and monitoring services?
sections.Holding: The Southern District of New York in 1984, per Judge Weinfeld, held that disputed facts about the executives' authority, the parties' intent to be bound before a formal writing, and whether the $250,000 was accepted as part payment under UCC 2-201(3)(c) required a trial of the sales-contract claim. It granted summary judgment dismissing the brokerage, fraud, and unjust-enrichment claims. The court did not adjudge that a sale existed or award damages.
sections.Reasoning:
On the sales claim, the July board resolution's reference to an agreement or agreements did not conclusively establish a nonseverable package, and evidence of the executives' duties, a directive permitting adjustments within ten percent of board-approved prices, and prior dealings could support implied or apparent authority. On intent, if parties intend no obligation before formal execution, execution is necessary; if they intend an immediate bargain later to be memorialized, lack of signatures does not negate formation. Which model applied was a question of fact. No sufficient Amax-signed writing satisfied the UCC statute of frauds, but section 2-201(3)(c) allows enforcement where payment has been made and accepted, and for an indivisible item accepted part payment can support the whole oral sale. Whether the deposit was accepted toward the price had to be tried.

The brokerage count failed because the evidence showed the plaintiffs buying for their own resale, setting French's price and bearing the resale risk. The fraud count failed for lack of evidence that Amax made a promise with a contemporaneous undisclosed intent not to perform.

Unjust enrichment required both a benefit to Amax and injustice between the parties. Locating French, negotiating the resale, and exchanging information were ordinary efforts to secure the plaintiffs' own business advantage, and the risk of losing negotiation costs did not make an incidental benefit unjust. The tax-benefit idea was neither novel nor original. Monitoring completion was closer, since the plaintiffs might have believed they held a contract, but the services were voluntary and protected their own resale profit.

The casebook uses the case for its unjust-enrichment account; the brief notes that its description of negotiations falling through should be read with the fact that the sales claim remained open.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-002.rule: Where parties intend not to be bound until a formal writing is executed no contract arises from their oral dealings, but one whose services were designed to benefit the other side, and did enrich it, may recover in unjust enrichment.

sections.Parties: On the plaintiffs' side were Precision Testing Laboratories (PTL), owned by Asher Hiesiger, a lawyer and real-estate investor, and Arthur Ellis, who operated Texas Coach in Houston and had developed emissions systems. The plaintiffs claimed that the defendants breached an oral joint venture and alternatively sought restitution. The defendants were Kenyon Corporation of America (KCA) and its sole owner, Lawrence Kenyon, who denied that any binding agreement had been reached.
sections.Procedural History: The plaintiffs brought the diversity action in July 1984. Judge Irving Ben Cooper of the Southern District of New York tried liability without a jury from February 10 through February 14, reserving damages for a later phase. In an opinion of August 26, 1986 the court rejected the defendants' request to dismiss Kenyon individually, dismissed the complaint in its entirety except for Ellis's right to recover from both defendants the portion of money earned by his services in certifying KCA's test car, and directed the parties to try to agree on a reasonable amount, failing which a damages trial limited to Ellis would be set. No dollar amount was awarded.
sections.Material Facts:
The parties sought to develop emissions systems for imported gray-market automobiles. KCA held small-volume-manufacturer status but lacked a successful certification vehicle. The plaintiffs claimed that discussions culminated in a binding joint venture on February 17, 1984. The evidence supported discussion of a 50-25-25 stock split, with each plaintiff paying $5,000 for a quarter interest, and numerous other proposals; some were accepted and others, particularly assumption of corporate liabilities, remained disputed. At the meeting's close the parties telephoned Kenyon's attorney to arrange formal documents. Kenyon and the attorney said any arrangement required a writing and counsel's approval, and Hiesiger himself raised an unresolved control problem, the risk of deadlock.

Work continued. Ellis's technicians spent 93 hours preparing a coast-down test, and Ellis spent five weeks at an Ohio testing laboratory, performing most of the physical work and supplying the intellectual contribution responsible for success. KCA paid the laboratory's bills. The vehicle achieved certification levels on April 13. Formal negotiations in May left ownership, management, salary, financing, and transfer restrictions unresolved. A $10,000 check delivered in June was never negotiated. KCA received conformity certificates in August 1984 and January 1985. Hiesiger had separately advanced $100,000 to Ellis without telling Kenyon.
sections.Issue: Did the parties' oral discussions create a binding joint venture under New York law before any formal instrument was executed, and if not, could the plaintiffs recover in unjust enrichment for what they contributed to KCA's certification?
sections.Holding: The Southern District of New York in 1986, per Judge Cooper after a bench trial on liability, held that the parties did not intend to be bound before executing formal documents and that, in any event, two essential elements of a New York joint venture were missing, so there was no recovery for breach. It held that Ellis could recover in unjust enrichment from both defendants for his services in certifying KCA's test car, but it allowed no restitution for the advances, payments, and apartment use attributed to Hiesiger and PTL.
sections.Reasoning:
Under New York law parties may bind themselves orally, but an expressed intention to await a formal instrument must be respected. The court balanced four factors, none decisive: reservation of the right not to be bound, agreement on all terms, the complexity and magnitude of the transaction, and partial performance. Counsel's involvement and the parties' conduct showed they reserved final commitment. The stock split, a deadlock solution, sharing of risks and liabilities, and other material terms were unsettled. The venture was substantial and complicated, with at least fifteen terms discussed and six documents being prepared. Some acts were performance, notably Ellis's technical work, but much promised performance never occurred.

As a second ground, even assuming intent to be bound orally, a joint venture required agreement to create one, sharing of profits and losses, joint control, and contributions. No definite arrangement governed profits and losses, and the parties had not resolved who would direct and manage KCA.

Unjust enrichment required enrichment of the defendants that was unjust at the claimant's expense. Ellis's staff's work and his own engineering effort were essential to the certification vehicle, and he had received no monetary compensation. His services were designed to benefit KCA, which distinguished Songbird's ordinary negotiation and self-protective resale activities. For Hiesiger, the $100,000 advanced privately to Ellis was not shown to have funded KCA's success, PTL's $15,055.41 payment bought parts for Texas Coach, and the apartment he let Kenyon use caused him no corresponding expense. Benefit and expense had to be proved for the particular claimant.

The casebook uses the case for the restitution comparison with Songbird.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-003.rule: A promise of one's own future conduct that is made to deceive, without intent to perform it, can support an action for fraud, each element of which must be proved by clear, cogent, and convincing evidence.

sections.Parties: The plaintiff and appellant was Auburn Industrial Center, a fifteen-member partnership that owned an industrial property and sued its tenant for unpaid rent. ABC Transfer & Storage Co., the tenant, was the defendant and respondent. It denied liability and counterclaimed for damages caused by the partnership's deceptive assurances that its warehouse lease would be renewed.
sections.Procedural History: The partnership sued for unpaid rent, and ABC counterclaimed over the renewal representations. The trial court made findings for ABC and entered judgment on the counterclaim, stated in the report as $114,934.92. The partnership appealed with fourteen assignments of error, ten directed at factual findings. The Washington Supreme Court rejected the other assignments, which concerned attorney fees, refusal to reopen, waiver, and Boeing's dismissal, without developed discussion. In 1969 it affirmed the trial court's judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
The partnership leased two warehouse buildings to ABC for three years from September 15, 1962, with no renewal provision. ABC's principal customer, Scott Paper, used the facility as an important distribution point. ABC's president, Francis Bury, began renewal negotiations with partner Sidney Eland in February 1965, while Scott Paper was considering a new three-year arrangement with ABC that depended on ABC's ability to remain. The trial court found that Eland assured Scott Paper's representative, with Bury present, that Scott could have anything it wanted, which the parties understood to assure a three-year renewal, and that Bury reasonably relied on it. In June another partner accepted Bury's proposal for five bays at $7,312.50 monthly through September 1968, and ABC paid the increased rent in June and July.

Meanwhile the partnership secretly negotiated with an agent for an undisclosed purchaser and on July 1, 1965 granted an option to sell the facility for $4 million. The purchaser, Boeing, exercised the option. ABC learned of the sale from an August 25 letter requiring it to vacate by September 15. With timely notice ABC could have moved Scott Paper's goods gradually for no more than $1,000 plus $18,281.25 in rent. Instead it incurred $45,598.99 in expenses and lost Scott Paper's business, producing $91,127.88 in lost profits.
sections.Issue: Did the record support actionable fraud and misrepresentation by clear, cogent, and convincing evidence, where the partnership argued that its renewal assurances were only unenforceable predictions about the future, and were the resulting damages established?
sections.Holding: The Washington Supreme Court in 1969, in an opinion by Hale in which Chief Justice Hunter, Hill, Rosellini, and Armstrong, sitting pro tempore, concurred, held that the findings of fraud were supported. The partnership's assurances concerned its own future conduct and were made in circumstances that turned them into commitments, and a promise made without intent to perform and intended to deceive can support deceit. The department's decision was unanimous, and the judgment on the counterclaim was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning:
Fraud required proof of an existing factual representation, materiality, falsity, the speaker's knowledge of falsity or ignorance of truth, intended action by the recipient, the recipient's ignorance, actual and rightful reliance, and consequent damage. Each element had to be established by clear, cogent, and convincing evidence, more than a mere preponderance, and fraud was not presumed.

A prediction of future events, without an undertaking to bring them about, would not suffice. But these assurances concerned the partnership's own future conduct. The court characterized the promise as an undertaking, supported by consideration, to renew for three years and negotiate rent in good faith. It explained that a promise intended to deceive and made without intent to perform could support deceit, and that a related rule covered a promise made without care whether it would be kept when the promisor knew or should know it would induce detrimental action or inaction. The opinion therefore did more than impose liability for the bare failure of negotiations.

The evidence corroborated the promise and the reliance: testimony, the repeated lease changes, the increases negotiated during the secret sale discussions, and the owner's economic motives. Continued occupation by a nationally known customer helped the sale effort, and if the sale failed the owner would keep its tenant and rental income. The court found substantial support for the findings and presumed the trial court had applied the heightened standard for fraud.

The casebook emphasizes the case for precontractual reliance losses; the brief notes that the full opinion rests on fraud findings and a supported renewal undertaking and includes lost profits from the existing Scott Paper relationship as consequential reliance loss.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-004.rule: Promissory estoppel does not require reimbursing negotiation expenses where the contemplated transaction was subject to contingencies that could have left those expenses unrecovered even had the promise been kept, because enforcement is then unnecessary to avoid injustice.

sections.Parties: Gruen Industries, a watch manufacturer, and its subsidiary Gruen Industries International were the plaintiffs and appellants. They sought to buy the Windsor Group and sued for breach of an alleged oral stock-sale contract, alternatively for their reliance expenses, and for tortious interference. The defendants and appellees were Earl Biller and Robert Hersch, who each owned 170,000 of Windsor's 400,000 shares, and Premium Corporation of America (PCA), the competing buyer to which the owners sold.
sections.Procedural History: Gruen sued in October 1975 for breach of the alleged stock-sale contract, alternatively for reliance expenses under promissory estoppel, and against PCA for tortious interference. The district court granted summary judgment on every count. It treated the alleged sale as unenforceable under Wisconsin's securities statute of frauds, denied reliance recovery, and reasoned that an unenforceable contract could not support the interference claim. In 1979 the Seventh Circuit affirmed summary judgment for all defendants on all three counts.
sections.Material Facts:
Gruen's vice president Charles Evans approached Windsor's owners early in 1975 about an acquisition. Gruen alleged that the parties orally agreed in early May to an asset sale. Evans and board chairman Peyser stated in affidavits that they warned they would not incur drafting expenses without a firm commitment and that Hersch assured them they had one.

The parties then employed lawyers. On May 20 they restructured the transaction, for the sellers' tax purposes, as a share purchase involving the principal owners and some minority shareholders. Signing was planned for mid-July, and the unsigned draft contemplated completing the sale on or before November 1. The document ran to 58 pages and, according to Gruen, drafting was virtually finished in early July. On July 17 PCA offered a higher price, and the owners sold to PCA. The Gruen document was never signed. When PCA submitted its proposal it was expressly told that no agreement had been made and its offer would be considered.

The proposed sale contained contingencies: a decline in Windsor's net worth could permit termination, at least 75 percent of the minority-held shares had to be sold, and encumbrances on the principal owners' shares had to be discharged.
sections.Issue: Did the sellers' statements amount to an admission of a contract sufficient to overcome the securities statute of frauds? If not, could Gruen recover its attorneys' fees and other preparation expenses under promissory estoppel? Did the evidence raise a factual issue of intentional interference by PCA?
sections.Holding: The Seventh Circuit in 1979, in an opinion by Judge Pell for a panel that included Chief Judge Fairchild and Senior District Judge Bonsal, held that no genuine issue existed as to a sufficient admission under Wisconsin section 408.319(4), so the contract count failed. Assuming the alleged firm-commitment assurances were made, reimbursement of Gruen's expenses was not necessary to avoid injustice, so promissory estoppel failed. PCA had no actual knowledge or sufficient notice of a contract, so the interference claim failed.
sections.Reasoning:
The statute permitted enforcement without a signed writing where the party charged admitted in court a contract for a stated quantity of described securities at a defined or stated price. An admission need not concede the legal conclusion and could describe circumstances permitting an inference of agreement. But the statements Gruen relied on, nearly all from Hersch's deposition, were too vague or described interest if the professionals could assemble a satisfactory deal. Hersch's $2,000 advance was conditioned on closing, and draft schedules came with caveats. Where parties understand they will be bound only on executing the contemplated writing, settling individual details does not form the contract.

On promissory estoppel, Wisconsin's Hoffman v. Red Owl test asked whether the promisor should reasonably expect definite and substantial action, whether the promise induced it, and whether enforcement alone could avoid injustice, the last being a judicial policy determination. Because of the contingencies, Gruen's expenses could have gone unrecovered even if the owners honored their assurances. Reimbursement would place Gruen in a better position than if the conditional transaction had proceeded and failed at closing. The assurances were also informal, formal documentation was contemplated, experienced businesspeople represented Gruen, and no unjust enrichment of the sellers was alleged. Ordinary negotiation costs were a business risk. This was a case-specific evaluation, not a categorical rule against recovery by businesses.

On interference, the court left open whether PCA could invoke the owners' statute-of-frauds defense. Wisconsin required a purpose to interfere, supported by actual knowledge or sufficient notice of a contract, and PCA knew only of advanced negotiations. The court declined to impose a duty of inquiry on every potential buyer.

The casebook discusses the case in a note after Hoffman, where its caption reads Green Industries.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-005.rule: Under Restatement section 90 an employer whose definite job offer foreseeably induces a person to resign from existing employment may be liable for that person's reliance losses, even though the promised employment would have been terminable at will.

sections.Parties: John Grouse, a pharmacist, was the plaintiff and appellant. He sued for damages after resigning from his job in reliance on a job offer that was then withdrawn. Group Health Plan, Inc., which made the offer and then filled the position with someone else, was the defendant and respondent.
sections.Procedural History: Grouse sued for damages. The trial court entered judgment for Group Health on the ground that he had failed to state an actionable claim. The appellate question was whether that conclusion was correct, not the amount of any loss. The Minnesota Supreme Court reversed and remanded for a new trial on damages.
sections.Material Facts:
Grouse, a 1974 pharmacy graduate, worked at Richter Drug in Minneapolis about forty-one hours weekly at $7 an hour and wanted a hospital or clinical position. After applying to Group Health in September 1975, he interviewed with its chief pharmacist, Cyrus Elliott, and later with general manager Donald Shoberg.

On December 4 Elliott offered Grouse a pharmacist position at Group Health's St. Louis Park Clinic. Grouse accepted, explaining that he needed to give Richter two weeks' notice. That afternoon he declined an offer from a Veterans Administration hospital in Virginia because he had accepted Group Health's position. Elliott later called to confirm that Grouse had resigned.

Only afterward did Elliott tell Shoberg that he had hired, or was considering hiring, Grouse. Shoberg required a favorable written reference, a background check, and general-manager approval. Two faculty members declined to give references, and former work contacts reported insufficient experience with Grouse to evaluate him. Unable to obtain a favorable reference, Shoberg hired someone else. On December 15, when Grouse reported that he was available to start, Elliott told him the position had been filled. Grouse had difficulty regaining full-time employment and lost wages. The opinion called these facts essentially undisputed.
sections.Issue: Did a person who resigned from his job and declined another offer in reliance on a definite offer of at-will employment, which the employer then withdrew before he started, state an actionable claim?
sections.Holding: The Minnesota Supreme Court in 1981, in an opinion by Justice Otis, held that he did, under promissory estoppel. Because either side could terminate at will, the court said the parties' promises were illusory and no contract existed in fact, but section 90 imposed an obligation implied in law because Group Health should have expected its definite offer to induce Grouse to resign and it would be unjust to deny relief. Damages were to be measured by reliance. The court reversed and remanded for a new trial on damages.
sections.Reasoning:
The parties had argued the case as anticipatory repudiation of an at-will employment arrangement, and Group Health contended that recovery would anomalously favor a person turned away before starting over an employee discharged after one day. The court instead located the remedy in promissory estoppel. Section 90 permitted an obligation implied in law where foreseeable, induced action or forbearance made enforcement necessary to avoid injustice.

Group Health should have expected its definite offer to cause Grouse to resign. He did so, and Elliott verified the resignation. It would be unjust to refuse any relief after the employer induced that surrender and denied him even an opportunity to perform. Grouse could reasonably assume he would receive a good-faith opportunity to do the job to the employer's satisfaction; that opportunity, not guaranteed permanent employment, was what the promise protected.

The court rejected the proposed dividing line between before and after starting work: in appropriate circumstances section 90 could also apply after employment had begun. But it cautioned that its conclusion did not impose liability whenever an employer discharged an at-will employee.

On remedy, relief under section 90 could be limited as justice required and measured by reliance. Because the prospective employment could have ended at any time, the focus was less on what Grouse would have earned at Group Health than on what he lost by quitting Richter and declining at least one other offer. The opinion gave a direction for recovery, not a calculation or award.

The casebook discusses the case in a note on at-will employment and treats the firm offer here as a definite employment offer, separate from the merchant-offer provision of UCC 2-205.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-006.rule: A lowest responsible bidder wrongfully denied a public contract may recover its reasonable bid preparation costs from the public entity under promissory estoppel, but not the profits it expected to earn from performing the contract.

sections.Parties: Kajima/Ray Wilson, a bidder for a public construction contract, was the plaintiff. It sought injunctive and writ relief and damages after the contract was awarded to a higher bidder. The Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA), the public entity that solicited the bids, was the defendant and petitioned the California Supreme Court for review of the damages awarded against it.
sections.Procedural History: After a bench trial the court issued a peremptory writ requiring MTA to stop using its five-percent broker policy and awarded Kajima $44,869 in second-round bid expenses, $89,223 in second-round protest expenses, $300,000 in overhead, $350,000 in lost profits, and $139,829.74 in prejudgment interest, a judgment of $923,921.74. The Court of Appeal affirmed, approving lost profits as an available equitable remedy. On MTA's petition the California Supreme Court considered only bid preparation costs and lost profits; review of protest costs and overhead was waived. It reversed the Court of Appeal's judgment and remanded to that court. Rehearing was denied August 23, 2000.
sections.Material Facts:
MTA sought bids in April 1994 for construction of the Hollywood/Highland station and tunnels on the Los Angeles Metro Red Line. After a protest over the disadvantaged-business-enterprise (DBE) participation goal, MTA determined that no bid was responsive and rejected all bids.

MTA solicited new bids in November with a DBE participation goal of thirty percent of the total bid. Kajima bid $68,912,089, Tutor-Saliba $69,887,867, and Kiewit-Shea $72,970,345. MTA nevertheless selected Tutor-Saliba, explaining that Kajima had failed the participation requirement. The difference came from how the two designated the same firm, Manual Tejeda Trucking: Kajima described it as a broker, Tutor-Saliba as a subcontractor. MTA had an unwritten policy crediting only five percent of amounts assigned to brokers but one hundred percent of amounts assigned to subcontractors. Had Kajima received the same credit, it would have exceeded the thirty-percent goal.

Kajima requested $93,411 for first-round bid and protest expenses, $134,092 for second-round bid and protest expenses, $1,298,589 in unabsorbed overhead, and $1,544,034 in lost profit. The Court of Appeal held the differential credit policy arbitrary, contrary to federal regulations, and an abuse of discretion, and MTA did not challenge that determination.
sections.Issue: Where effective injunctive relief is no longer available, may a lowest responsible bidder wrongfully denied a public contract obtain monetary relief from the public entity, and if so, does that relief include the profit it expected from performing the contract?
sections.Holding: The California Supreme Court in 2000, in an opinion by Justice Brown for a unanimous seven-member court, held that reasonable bid preparation costs were recoverable under promissory estoppel for this wrongful public award, but expected profits were not. It reversed the Court of Appeal and remanded. It did not enter a new damages judgment, decide the waived protest-cost and overhead issues, or authorize recovery for every disappointed bid.
sections.Reasoning:
The public contracting statutes did not expressly address a disappointed bidder's damages. The court declined to read that silence as a prohibition, since it could equally reflect an assumption that existing promissory-estoppel principles supplied relief, and found no statutory barrier to a valid equitable theory.

Under Restatement section 90, when a public entity solicits bids it represents, consistently with its statutory obligation, that if it awards the contract the award will go to the lowest responsible bidder, and bid preparation expenses are incurred in reliance on that representation. MTA did not dispute that these circumstances appeared to establish the elements; Kajima conceded it had neither a tort nor a breach-of-contract claim. The fit with ordinary promissory estoppel was imperfect, because the court was chiefly furthering the public policies behind competitive bidding. Earlier decisions denying reimbursement after a valid rejection of all bids were distinguishable as an ordinary risk of pursuing public work.

Preparation costs were reasonably incurred in reliance on fair evaluation. Expected profits were not expenditures incurred in reliance and were uncertain; awarding them could put the bidder in a better position than performance. Public policy independently limited the remedy: competitive bidding primarily protects taxpayers, and paying the higher contractor and also an unperformed contract's profits would compound the public loss. Large profit awards could encourage opportunistic litigation. Rules for ordinary private breach-of-contract damages did not control because Kajima had no contract with MTA. The court surveyed other jurisdictions, many of which allow preparation costs but not profits. Its reasoning does not prohibit lost profits in all private promissory-estoppel actions.

The casebook discusses the case in a note; the brief notes that its compressed account says the appealed decision had denied preparation costs, whereas the full opinion records the trial award and the Court of Appeal's affirmance.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-007.rule: A promise to pay a fair share of profits is too indefinite to enforce where nothing identifies the share or a method of determining it, though one who has performed may seek the reasonable value of the services in quantum meruit.

sections.Parties: George Varney, an architect and draftsman, was the plaintiff and appellant. He sued his former employer for $1,680, made up of $40 weekly for November 7 through December 31 and a fair percentage of net profits from February 1 through the end of the year. Isaac Ditmars, an architect and Varney's employer, was the defendant and respondent; he denied any agreement and had discharged Varney.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court dismissed the complaint at the close of Varney's case. The Appellate Division affirmed, and Varney appealed to the New York Court of Appeals. In 1916 that court affirmed the dismissal, with costs, by four to three.
sections.Material Facts:
Varney began working for Ditmars in October 1910 at $35 weekly, after asking for $40. When Varney reported another employment offer, Ditmars encouraged him to stay and help clear the office's accumulated work. On February 1, 1911 Ditmars offered Varney and another employee a $5 weekly increase and promised to close his books the following January and give them a fair share of profits if they continued their efforts and got stalled jobs moving. Varney took charge of drafting, helped reorganize personnel, and worked overtime, Sundays, and holidays, and he received $40 weekly. The alleged agreement rested on Varney's testimony; he was the only witness to it.

Before election day, November 7, Ditmars asked employees to work if possible. Varney said he wished to attend an election where he lived. He became ill that afternoon and could not work until sometime after December 1. A November 11 letter discharged him, accusing him of disloyalty and insubordination and of telling other employees to stay away; those were the employer's stated grounds. After recovering, Varney offered to return on an unspecified date, and Ditmars refused. Varney earned about $50 from other work before January 1.
sections.Issue: Was a promise to give an employee a fair share of the employer's profits definite enough to be enforced, and could Varney's claim for salary through the end of the year go to a jury on this record?
sections.Holding: The New York Court of Appeals in 1916, in an opinion by Chase joined by Collin, Cuddeback, and Pound, with Cardozo dissenting and joined by Chief Judge Willard Bartlett and Hogan, held four to three that the profit promise was too indefinite to enforce, because nothing identified a share or a method for determining it. It also held that the salary claim could not go to the jury on this record. The dismissal was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning:
Nothing in the parties' words, documents, or another transaction identified a share of profits or a way to determine it. The minds of the parties had not met on that element, which remained subject to the employer's will or further negotiation. Calling the share fair did not let a jury choose whatever amount it found satisfactory.

The court rejected the contention that every agreement using fair or reasonable compensation, or omitting a fixed price, is unenforceable. A fair market price for goods can be established by competent testimony, and contracts for goods or services often imply a reasonable price. The profit-sharing promise differed because its amount rested on conjecture, not an identified objective standard.

The majority preserved the distinction between enforcing an executory bargain and restitution for completed performance. A person who performed under an indefinite arrangement could, in a proper quantum-meruit action, recover the reasonable value of the services, so if Varney's work was worth more than $40 weekly a proper complaint could seek that value less what he had been paid. This was a conditional explanation, not a finding.

On salary, Varney performed no services during his illness, did not establish when he offered to return, and earned $50 elsewhere. The arrangement was conditional and did not unqualifiedly guarantee employment through January.

Cardozo, dissenting, agreed that this plaintiff had not supplied the data to measure profit damages but rejected the premise that a fair share of profits could never be determined, since custom might supply a percentage on another record. He read the promise as employment through the year-end closing of the books, found evidence that the discharge lacked cause, and would have reversed and ordered a new trial.

The casebook uses the case for indefiniteness and separately revisits its conditional explanation of restitution.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-008.rule: The parol evidence rule does not bar proof of an oral promise made alongside a written agreement where the writing, viewed in its setting, does not integrate all the parties' promises and the oral promise is not one they would ordinarily have put in it.

sections.Parties: Harold Lee and his sons Lester and Eric were the plaintiffs and appellees. They owned fifty percent of Capitol City Liquor Company, a Washington, D.C., wholesale distributorship, and sued for breach of an oral promise to relocate them to another distributorship. Joseph E. Seagram & Sons, whose brands generated a substantial part of Capitol City's sales, was the defendant and appellant and sought to overturn the jury's verdict.
sections.Procedural History: The Lees sued fifteen months after the asset sale closed. Judge Tenney denied Seagram summary judgment, entered judgment on a $407,850 jury verdict for the Lees, and denied Seagram's Rule 50(b) motion for judgment notwithstanding the verdict. Separate antitrust claims had been dismissed by directed verdict and were not on appeal. Both parties assumed New York law, and the court applied it. In 1977 the Second Circuit affirmed the judgment, including the $407,850 award and the denial of post-verdict relief.
sections.Material Facts:
Harold Lee had worked for Seagram for thirty-six years, had bought Seagram's Capitol City shares in 1958, and had known executive vice president Jack Yogman for thirteen years. Harold's brother and nephew owned the other half of Capitol City. In May 1970, when the owners wanted to sell, Harold discussed a sale with Yogman, conditioning his proposal on Seagram's relocating himself and his sons to another distributorship. Another Seagram officer, John Barth, then negotiated the purchase of Capitol City's assets on behalf of a replacement distributor, Carter. The asset sale closed September 30 under a written agreement that did not contain the relocation promise and had no integration clause.

The Lees maintained that they had performed by agreeing to the asset sale and that Seagram failed to provide the promised business despite opportunities to do so. Under the unchallenged instruction, the jury found a commitment to provide a Seagram distributorship within a reasonable time, in a location acceptable to the Lees, at a price requiring approximately the capital they received from selling their Capitol City interest. The court described its value and profit potential as approximately half Capitol City's.
sections.Issue: Did the parol evidence rule bar proof of the oral relocation promise, was that promise too indefinite or illusory to enforce, and was the evidence of damages speculative or incompetent?
sections.Holding: The Second Circuit in 1977, in an opinion by Judge Gurfein for a panel including Judges Medina and Oakes, held that the written asset-sale agreement did not exclude the oral promise, which was a collateral undertaking the parties would not ordinarily have put in that writing. The promise as the jury found it was definite enough to enforce and was not illusory, and the damages evidence was sufficient. The court affirmed the judgment for the Lees.
sections.Reasoning:
The parol evidence rule is substantive law but does not exclude every oral promise associated with a written transaction. The court asked whether the writing, objectively considered in its setting, integrated all the parties' promises and whether the asserted undertaking was one they would ordinarily put in that writing. Several features favored the Lees. The writing governed a corporate asset sale, while the oral promise benefited particular individuals who held only half the ownership. The long relationship between Harold and Yogman made reliance on a handshake plausible. The written negotiations were conducted by other officers. The agreement lacked a customary integration clause despite substantial boilerplate, and the oral promise did not change the money consideration paid to the corporation. This was a contextual decision, not a rule that any inducement omitted from a writing is enforceable.

On definiteness, the credited evidence supplied objective content: a business of about half Capitol City's value and profit potential for a comparable investment, with industry practice valuing a distributorship at book value plus three times the previous year's after-tax net profit. Performance within a reasonable time was permissible, particularly as Seagram knew the Lees needed to reinvest within one year for tax reasons.

The promise was not illusory. The Lees' consideration, agreeing to the asset sale and franchise assignment, had been performed, and their discretion over location was constrained by good faith; a tender of reasonable performance would discharge Seagram even if they refused it.

On damages, prospective profits could support recovery, even for a business not yet operating, where an established comparator gave a reasonable basis. Seagram's breach had made exact proof harder, so it bore that uncertainty.

The casebook presents the case in a note whose questions about the Lees' discretion are answered by the opinion's good-faith and reasonable-tender discussion.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-009.rule: An employee claiming an agreement that alters presumptive at-will employment must prove by clear and convincing evidence a promise with ascertainable, definite terms; general assurances of job security are not enough.

sections.Parties: The plaintiffs were employees of cable systems in West Virginia who had been hired by Cablentertainment when it bought their former employer and were later discharged. They sued for breach of alleged oral employment contracts guaranteeing continued employment for an indefinite period. Cablentertainment, the employer, was the defendant and the appellant; it argued that the proof did not establish such an agreement and alternatively relied on the statute of frauds.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court bifurcated liability and damages. At the March 1991 trial it directed a verdict against Charles Chesser after the employees' evidence and against Mary Wamsley after the employer's evidence, and let the other claims go to the jury. On two special interrogatories using a clear-and-convincing standard, the jury found an oral agreement to employ the remaining plaintiffs and its breach around November 1, 1982. The April 24 judgment upheld the verdict, and in June the court denied a new trial and stayed the damages proceedings pending appeal. The Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia reversed the decision of the Circuit Court of Harrison County.
sections.Material Facts:
Cablentertainment purchased Midwest CATV in August 1981 and hired the employees working at its West Virginia cable systems. They remained employed until November 1982, when a newly adopted nepotism policy prompted their discharge. Apparently the employees were related to one another, and they alleged that Cablentertainment already knew of those relationships when it bought Midwest.

The employees' descriptions of the promised duration differed. Some believed they could leave at any time while the company remained irrevocably obliged to retain them. They could not identify exact contract terms or when and where the assurances were made. They had no written contracts with either operator and no contemporaneous memoranda, and the parties agreed that no relevant employee handbooks existed. The strongest assurance described was that the employees would not lose their jobs because a new company was buying the business.

One witness denied receiving a promise of continued employment absent wrongdoing. Another described hopes of employment until retirement but admitted no period had been stated. Wamsley described faith in assurances of security but acknowledged that no duration had been given.
sections.Issue: Could the employees' testimony about oral assurances of job security establish, by clear and convincing evidence, a definite agreement altering presumptive at-will employment, and did the statute of frauds for contracts not performable within one year bar the claim?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia in 1992, in an opinion by Justice Workman, held that the testimony was legally insufficient to prove by clear and convincing evidence an agreement with ascertainable, definite terms altering at-will status, so the case should not have gone to the jury. On the statute of frauds, the court applied its rule that an oral agreement not actually performed within one year must be shown by clear and convincing evidence before submission to the jury, and that threshold was not met. The circuit court's decision was reversed.
sections.Reasoning:
West Virginia presumed that employment of unspecified duration was terminable at will, and the employee claiming otherwise bore the burden of rebutting the presumption. The handbook decisions showed that an employer could make a sufficiently definite promise limiting discharge to specified grounds. The absence of a handbook was not automatically fatal to an oral promise, but the court used those formation principles to require ascertainable, definite terms in any claimed alteration of at-will status. Lifetime employment was an extraordinary commitment requiring clear and unequivocal language.

A permanent employment contract or comparable substantial employment right had to be proved by clear and convincing evidence. The court found the testimony legally insufficient under that standard even though the jury had answered interrogatories that invoked it. None of the witnesses identified job security for a specific period or continued employment on specified conditions. A possible promise that the buyout would not itself cost the employees their jobs did not establish an undertaking to retain them for life, and their employment for more than a year did not supply the missing terms. The decision separates an employee's expectation or trust from proof of an ascertainable promise. It does not hold that oral employment promises can never bind or that every enforceable restriction needs a fixed calendar term.

On the statute of frauds, the employees invoked the capable-of-performance exception, arguing that misconduct could have led to discharge for cause within the first year. The court retained that exception but applied its Thompson rule requiring clear and convincing evidence where the agreement was not actually performed within a year. It did not rest on a categorical ruling that potential discharge could never take an employment agreement outside the statute.

The casebook discusses the case in a note on offers of job security; the note's questions about an offer accepted by continued work are editorial.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-010.rule: At-will employment is a rebuttable construction of unspecified-duration arrangements, and an employment manual and surrounding circumstances can create an implied-in-fact contract term limiting discharge, without separate consideration or symmetrical termination rights.

sections.Parties: Shirley Berube, a former assistant manager at Fashion Centre's Ogden store, sued her employer, Fashion Centre, Ltd., and by amendment added Western States Polygraph, the company that administered her first polygraph examination. She claimed defamation, wrongful discharge, emotional distress, and breach of employment contract. Berube was the appellant; she challenged a statutory ruling, the dismissal of her polygraph-related negligence claim, and the refusal of jury instructions on exceptions to at-will employment.
sections.Procedural History:
Berube sued in October 1983. The trial court allowed her to add Western States but refused a claim under Utah Code § 34-37-16(2). It granted summary judgment to Western States on all claims and to Fashion Centre on all claims except defamation and wrongful discharge. A jury then found Fashion Centre not liable. Berube appealed to the Utah Supreme Court. Although she had not objected to the specific instructions, she had renewed her challenge to their overall statement of employment law, and the court considered it in the interests of justice under Rule 51.

The court affirmed the statutory and negligence rulings, reversed in part, and remanded for retrial on breach of an implied employment-contract term. Rehearing was denied April 28, 1989.
sections.Material Facts:
Fashion Centre hired Berube as a sales clerk in April 1979 and promoted her to assistant manager in 1981. Her reviews ranged from good to superior, and a manager told her she could eventually manage a store. She acknowledged that her employment had no specified duration. The company's disciplinary policy promised warnings and an opportunity to improve except for listed grounds, including dishonesty, falsification of records, gross misconduct, and refusal to take or failure to pass a polygraph.

In fall 1981 an apparent inventory shortage exceeding three percent prompted an investigation. Berube signed a consent releasing Fashion Centre and Western States from claims related to the first polygraph. That examination indicated apparent deception only when she denied knowing for certain who had stolen; the examiner explained the reaction as suspicion of others, and sent the result and the explanation to the employer. Without explanation, Fashion Centre required a second examination by another company, which she passed. It then required a third, again without explanation. Berube became distressed, sought a postponement, offered a doctor's statement, and was told she must take the test or lose her job. After her shift she said she could not take it and was directed to sign termination papers. Her later willingness to take the examination did not avert discharge.
sections.Issue: Did Utah Code § 34-37-16 bar discharge for refusing a nonsurreptitious polygraph? Was the negligence claim over the first polygraph properly dismissed? And could an employee of unspecified duration go to a jury on the theory that the employer's disciplinary policy and surrounding circumstances created a contractual limit on its power to discharge her for refusing a third polygraph?
sections.Holding: The Utah Supreme Court, in 1989, in a lead opinion by Justice Durham joined throughout by Justice Stewart, affirmed the statutory and negligence rulings, reversed in part, and remanded for retrial limited to an implied-in-fact contract theory. All five justices agreed in the relevant affirmances and the remand, with different employment rationales. Section 34-37-16 protected only refusal to consent to or cooperate with surreptitious examinations. The negligence dismissal was affirmed on Berube's signed release. On remand, Fashion Centre could contest the existence of the term, show an express disavowal, or establish that the third examination was essential and reasonable; if Berube proved breach, general and foreseeable consequential contract damages could be awarded. No final liability or damages amount was entered.
sections.Reasoning:
On the statute, the court agreed with the employer that the subsection had to be read within a provision concerning surreptitious examinations; an expansive ban on polygraph screening would ordinarily have been stated directly. The court reserved whether employment polygraphs were lawful under other theories. On negligence, the trial court had relied on proximate cause, but the Supreme Court affirmed instead on the release, whose scope and validity Berube did not challenge on appeal, without resolving proximate cause.

On employment, Justice Durham treated at-will employment as a rebuttable construction of unspecified-duration arrangements, not a rule overriding proven contractual intent. Promises limiting dismissal could arise from a manual and surrounding circumstances, and separate consideration and symmetrical termination rights were not required; Justice Zimmerman expressly agreed on those points. Durham found the manual, favorable reviews, advancement, and representations sufficient prima facie to support contractual limits, and rejected Berube's argument that "a polygraph" permitted only one test in a career; the question was reasonable use in the circumstances.

Justice Howe, joined by Chief Justice Hall, concurred only in the results in Parts IV and V of the lead opinion, confining the analysis to the manual as part of the employment agreement and leaving to a fact finder whether discharge without warning violated it. Justice Zimmerman reasoned that a jury could find an implied-in-fact term prohibiting discharge for a reasonable refusal, since reading the policy to permit unlimited examinations would effectively restore at-will power.

Only Durham and Stewart supported a broader implied-in-law good-faith covenant; Zimmerman declined to recognize it as lacking predictable limits, and Howe and Hall found it unnecessary. The lead opinion's public-policy exception discussion acknowledged that it did not apply to Berube's case.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-012.rule: A contractual duty to negotiate in good faith, read as honesty in fact, forbids trickery but does not require concessions, disclosure of one's reservation price or strategy, or giving up commercial advantages the contract allocates.

sections.Parties: PSI Energy, Inc. was the buyer and Exxon Coal USA, Inc. the seller under a long-term coal supply contract. PSI contended that Exxon's last price offer for 1993 through 1997 was incomplete and made in bad faith, and wanted a lower Base price; Exxon wanted its $30-per-ton last offer to govern. PSI prevailed in the district court on remand, and the appellate court reversed.
sections.Procedural History:
A 1993 appeal held that the coal contract remained in effect, held that PSI's competing offer from Black Beauty did not qualify under the contract, and remanded to determine the Base price for 1993 through 1997. The brief treats that earlier appeal only as procedural history. On remand the district court found Exxon's last offer incomplete and its bargaining dishonest, and declared a Base of $23.266, the figure Exxon had offered to match Black Beauty if that offer qualified.

On the second appeal the Seventh Circuit found the judgment final and appealable because all issues presented in this suit had been resolved; damages for PSI's failure to accept deliveries were the subject of a separate action by Exxon. The court reversed and determined that the Base for 1993 through 1997 was $30 per ton. Rehearing and rehearing en banc were denied March 21.
sections.Material Facts:
The contract required price renegotiation every five years. Section 7.03 required each side to negotiate in good faith. If they could not agree, PSI had to accept Exxon's last offer or present a firm, written competing offer from another supplier for the remaining supply, which Exxon could meet; if Exxon declined to match a qualifying offer, the contract would end. Section 7.05 confined renegotiation to Base and Exhibit A, which translated changes in twelve cost categories into Price adjustments. Base and the delivered Price were related but distinct defined terms.

After an April 1992 stalemate, PSI asked for a formal last offer. Exxon proposed a $30 Base, F.O.B. PSI's Gibson generating station, effective January 1, 1993, promised updated Exhibit A figures, and specified interim adjustments for union welfare, taxes and fees, and new laws or regulations. During negotiations Exxon had given PSI a handout listing about forty existing long-term utility contracts drawn from regulatory filings, with prices from $22.97 to $50.48 and an average of $31.70. Exxon's own assessments suggested a market price of approximately $20.50 at the mine or $25 delivered. PSI's negotiator immediately recognized many of the listed contracts as old and discounted them. PSI bought Black Beauty coal from January through July 1993, resuming Exxon deliveries only after the first appellate decision.
sections.Issue: Was Exxon's $30-per-ton last offer sufficiently complete under the contract even though it did not include a completed, updated Exhibit A? And did Exxon breach its contractual duty to negotiate in good faith by presenting accurate data on higher-priced contracts while privately expecting the market price to be lower?
sections.Holding: The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit, in 1994, in an opinion by Judge Easterbrook for a panel that also included Judges Bauer and Reavley, with no separate writing, reversed. Exxon's $30 Base was a valid and complete last offer, and the finding of bad faith could not stand. The governing Base for 1993 through 1997 was $30 per ton, subject to the contractual adjustment system. The court did not award damages in Exxon's separate delivery-refusal suit and did not adopt $30 as an unadjustable all-in delivered Price.
sections.Reasoning:
Contract interpretation was reviewed plenarily because the parties agreed the agreement was unambiguous; the bad-faith finding was reviewed for clear error.

On completeness, the district court was right that Base and Exhibit A were both needed to calculate a delivered Price, but wrong that all future numerical adjustments had to accompany the offer. Section 7.03 contemplated agreement on a Base followed by updates to the adjustment factors, and the original contract had been formed the same way. Matters might differ had the parties been negotiating a change to Exhibit A's structure, but PSI made no concrete proposal about the schedule. Even the district court's $23.266 figure assumed the remaining adjustments could be worked out afterward.

On good faith, the court applied the obligation consistently with the UCC's then-applicable honesty-in-fact formulation. It did not require kindness, concessions, or disclosure of reservation prices or strategy, though it still prohibited trickery and certain obstinate misconduct. Departure from a market figure did not by itself show dishonesty, and the three-million-ton annual commitment could command a premium. The bad-faith finding rested on alleged lies about market prices, but the handout's data were accurate, with no finding of doctored figures or selective omission; treating them as false was clear error, and treating their presentation as bad faith because Exxon expected to settle lower amounted to requiring it to reveal its bargaining floor. The district court had also found neither deception of PSI nor a risk of it.

Finally, the contract did not adjust automatically to market price; it gave the seller's last offer priority unless the buyer obtained the specified competitive offer, and a general fairness adjustment would rewrite that risk allocation. The casebook uses the case in a note and for its good-faith quotation.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-013.rule: An oral agreement is within the one-year provision of the statute of frauds only if its terms make full performance within a year impossible; the possibility that it will end within a year through breach does not count as performance.

sections.Parties: D & N Boening, Inc., the company through which Joseph Boening's sons carried on a Yoo-Hoo subdistributorship, sued American Beverage and Kirsch Beverages, Inc., the successive holders of the principal franchise, for contract damages or, alternatively, specific performance, alleging unilateral termination without cause. The defendants sought dismissal under the statute of frauds.
sections.Procedural History: The defendants separately moved to dismiss under CPLR 3211(a)(5), relying on General Obligations Law § 5-701(a)(1). Special Term denied dismissal because it considered the arrangement terminable at any time and thus capable of ending within a year. The Appellate Division unanimously reversed and dismissed the complaint because the pleaded agreement could end within a year only through breach. The New York Court of Appeals affirmed, with costs. The decision addresses the agreement as pleaded, not facts found after trial.
sections.Material Facts: In 1955 Minck Beverages, the principal distributor of Yoo-Hoo, orally granted Joseph Boening and his sons exclusive subdistribution rights in Nassau County and part of Suffolk County. They were required to stop distributing a competing chocolate beverage. Their exclusivity was to continue while they distributed satisfactorily, used their best efforts, and acted in good faith. American Beverage acquired the principal franchise in 1963. After Joseph's death in 1965, his sons continued through D & N Boening. They sought a writing; American refused but orally agreed to continue on satisfactory-performance terms. Kirsch bought American in 1982 and assumed its obligations. That year Kirsch told Boening it would terminate the arrangement and distribute Yoo-Hoo itself.
sections.Issue: Is an oral exclusive distribution agreement that is to continue for as long as the distributor performs satisfactorily, with no cancellation option and no fixed expiration, within the one-year provision of the statute of frauds, when it could end within a year only if the distributor breached?
sections.Holding: The New York Court of Appeals, in 1984, in an opinion by Judge Jasen in which Chief Judge Cooke and Judges Jones, Wachtler, Meyer, Simons, and Kaye concurred, unanimously affirmed the dismissal. The alleged oral agreement had no permitted route to completion within a year: it could end in that period only through breach, which is not performance. It was therefore within the one-year provision and unenforceable without a writing. No damages or specific performance were awarded.
sections.Reasoning:
The statute requires a writing subscribed by the party to be charged when an agreement's terms prevent performance within one year. The court acknowledged the statute's antifraud purpose and the imperfect connection between a contract's duration and when litigation might arise, and so retained a narrow construction: an agreement is within the provision only if its terms make full performance within a year impossible in fact and law. Expected duration, actual years of performance, or practical improbability of quick completion is not enough; the inquiry is what the parties' terms require or permit.

The court catalogued agreements outside the provision because they offered genuine avenues for completion, such as an option to terminate on seven months' notice, a permitted discontinuation of the underlying business, and employment terminable for a sufficient business reason. A cancellation option makes completion possible because exercising it carries out what the contract permits. Breach instead fails to do what the contract requires, and treating any possible breach as completion would effectively eliminate the one-year provision.

Here the sole condition limiting the pleaded subdistributorship was Boening's obligation to distribute satisfactorily, use best efforts, and act in good faith. Neither party had an independent cancellation option, and no event or expiration would end their duties. Failure to perform would be breach, not an agreed alternative mode of fulfillment, so the arrangement continued indefinitely unless Boening failed to perform; its indefinite duration did not make it at-will. A footnote adds that an agreement terminable for just cause is not necessarily outside the statute if just cause can only mean the other party's breach.
