The court said only that the plaintiff's other arguments lacked merit. The casebook asks how the franchise outcome fits the narrow possible-performance rule.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-014.rule: Whether an oral agreement can be performed within one year turns on the terms the parties actually agreed to, not on a party's ability to perform sooner; and a voice on a secret recording is not an electronic signature without intent to sign.

sections.Parties: Barbara Sawyer, who had performed marketing and research services for Melbourne Mills's practice, sued Mills to recover the unpaid balance of an orally promised bonus. Mills defended on the statute of frauds. Sawyer won a jury verdict, lost it on Mills's motion for judgment notwithstanding the verdict, and sought review in the Kentucky Supreme Court.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court denied summary judgment so the evidence could be developed at trial. After four days, the jury found an agreement, found that it could be completed within one year, and awarded the $900,000 unpaid balance. The trial court granted Mills's motion for judgment notwithstanding the verdict under Kentucky's statute of frauds, and the Court of Appeals affirmed. The Kentucky Supreme Court granted discretionary review and affirmed the judgment for Mills. It did not decide Sawyer's request for prejudgment interest.
sections.Material Facts:
Sawyer met Mills in 1991 and helped his practice secure mass-tort clients. In 1994 he promised a large bonus if one of his class actions produced a big payday. From 1994 through 2001 she performed marketing and research services and received compensation. In 1997 she suggested and helped publicize the Fen-Phen litigation; about 2,600 claimants responded.

After the Fen-Phen settlement in May 2001 and receipt of fees in June, Mills gave substantial bonuses to several employees; Sawyer initially received approximately $1,300. On June 25 she and her husband invited him to their art studio and secretly recorded the conversation. She proposed a $1,065,000 bonus: $1 million plus $65,000 for a car. Although able to pay immediately, Mills rejected a lump sum and agreed to monthly payments of $10,000, expressing concern that other employees would learn of the payment. A lawyer later prepared a written memorialization using 107 monthly installments, but Mills never signed it.

His periodic payments, including $10,000 on June 25, totaled $65,000, and he made a separate $100,000 payment in October. The last payment was in February 2002. Sawyer's employment ended on March 31, 2002, when she had received $165,000. The work said to justify the bonus had been completed before the June 25 conversation, and her later hourly employment was separately compensated.
sections.Issue: Was the oral bonus agreement, payable in monthly installments over roughly ten years, within the one-year provision of Kentucky's statute of frauds? If so, was it saved by Sawyer's full performance, by the secret recording as an electronic signature under the federal E-SIGN Act, by Mills's signed checks, or by promissory estoppel?
sections.Holding: The Kentucky Supreme Court, in 2009, in an opinion by Justice Noble in which all justices sitting concurred, affirmed the judgment notwithstanding the verdict for Mills. The agreed payment terms brought the agreement within KRS 371.010(7); the services invoked as consideration had already been performed; and neither the secret recording, the checks, nor the claimed reliance supplied an enforceable alternative. The court did not resolve whether promissory estoppel can ever defeat the statute of frauds, holding only that Sawyer's proof was insufficient even assuming it could.
sections.Reasoning:
The court described the demanding standard for setting aside a verdict but concluded that the agreed terms, not Mills's abstract capacity to pay earlier, controlled the one-year inquiry. Sawyer could not replace the actual arrangement with an imagined lump sum: the conversation repeatedly contemplated installments over approximately ten years, and Mills specifically refused immediate payment. The jury's contrary special finding could not save the oral agreement.

The full-performance exception did not apply because her relevant services preceded the June promise; they were not rendered in performance of that agreement and could not be consideration for it. Her continued employment was compensated separately, and the bonus was not shown to depend on it. This past-services problem was an additional ground.

Under the E-SIGN Act the tape was an electronic record, but an electronic signature requires a sound, symbol, or process executed or adopted with intent to sign. Identifying Mills's voice showed who spoke, not an intent to adopt a recording he did not know existed, and the later plan for a writing he refused to sign reinforced that. The court did not bar a recording the parties knowingly agree will embody their contract. The checks did not cure the problem: decisions accepting checks as memoranda involved references to contract terms or other connected writings, whereas these checks were as consistent with a gratuitous bonus as with an exchange and could not be joined to an unadopted recording.

On promissory estoppel, even assuming preservation and an available exception, Sawyer's claim that she stayed and declined other opportunities was unsubstantiated beyond her own account; there was no showing that Mills conditioned payment on continued employment or asked her to decline other work, and she received both the $165,000 and hourly pay during the roughly nine additional months. The casebook uses the case as a short illustration of an oral bonus payable over ten years.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-015.rule: Under Texas law as applied by the Tenth Circuit, when an employee keeps working after a written contract of more than one year expires, an implied renewal on an indefinite or month-to-month basis is not barred by the one-year provision of the statute of frauds.

sections.Parties: W. Clayton Rash, the former manager of the Tulsa division of J.V. Intermediate, Ltd. (JVIC), sued JVIC on his employment contract, claiming that understated profits and equity had reduced his bonuses. JVIC raised the statute of frauds and counterclaimed for breach of fiduciary duty and breach of the duty of loyalty based on Rash's undisclosed outside businesses. JVIC challenged on appeal the rejection of its fiduciary-duty counterclaim, its statute-of-frauds defense, and equitable forfeiture.
sections.Procedural History:
This was a diversity action applying Texas law. The district court rejected JVIC's statute-of-frauds argument before trial. At trial it granted Rash judgment as a matter of law on the fiduciary-duty counterclaim, leaving a duty-of-loyalty counterclaim for the jury. Rash requested $564,993 and received $444,933 on his contract claim; JVIC requested $143,000 and received $71,500 for breach of loyalty. The court denied JVIC's posttrial motions, including equitable forfeiture.

The Tenth Circuit reversed the determination that Rash owed no fiduciary duty, remanded for a jury determination of fiduciary-duty damages and a judicial determination of possible compensation forfeiture, and affirmed the rejection of the statute-of-frauds defense.
sections.Material Facts:
JVIC operated industrial-plant maintenance businesses. It hired Rash to establish and manage its Tulsa division under a written two-year contract running from 1999 to 2001. He received a $125,000 base salary, 20 percent of the division's net profits, and a termination bonus of 20 percent of its equity, and he promised to devote his full working time and efforts to JVIC. He continued managing the division, without a signed extension, until he resigned in July 2004. JVIC's president testified that they kept going under the agreement, and Rash described an assurance that it remained effective while he worked for JVIC.

Beginning in 2001, JVIC alleged, Rash owned or participated in several undisclosed businesses. He held a significant interest in Total Industrial Plant Services (TIPS), a scaffolding company that bid for JVIC subcontracts, and he was instrumental in selecting subcontractors. TIPS received more than $1 million from JVIC between 2001 and 2004, while JVIC's own scaffolding services were never used by the Tulsa division. His ownership, his participation in subcontract selection, and his nondisclosure were uncontroverted.
sections.Issue: Did Rash, as branch manager, owe JVIC a fiduciary duty as its agent under Texas law, and did his undisclosed interest in a subcontractor he helped select breach it? And did the statute of frauds bar his contract claims for the period after the written two-year term expired, when the parties simply continued without a signed extension?
sections.Holding: The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit, in 2007, in an opinion by Judge Tymkovich for a panel with Judges McConnell and McKay and no separate opinion, held that Rash was JVIC's agent, owed it a fiduciary duty as a matter of law, and breached that duty as a matter of law by his undisclosed ownership in TIPS while selecting it for subcontracts. Damages and possible compensation forfeiture were remanded. The court affirmed that the statute of frauds did not bar Rash's post-2001 contract claims, because the parties' conduct renewed the contract on an indefinite or month-to-month basis. It did not hold that every implied renewal is enforceable or that renewed fixed terms exceeding a year avoid the statute.
sections.Reasoning:
Texas recognizes informal fiduciary relationships and also formal ones, including principal and agent, that create duties as a matter of law. The district court relied on Meyer v. Cathey, which refused to impose an informal fiduciary relationship, but that case did not eliminate duties arising from agency. Rash managed essentially every aspect of the Tulsa startup, solicited and reviewed subcontract bids, and set customer rates; on the undisputed facts he was JVIC's agent. The scope of an employee's fiduciary duty is tied to the transaction, but an agent must disclose personal interests affecting the principal's business. Generalized approval of outside ventures was not informed consent to his ownership in TIPS.

The loyalty verdict did not make the error harmless, because the fiduciary instruction imposed broader duties and put the burden on Rash. A jury had to determine damages, accounting for the $71,500 loyalty recovery, with total collection not to exceed $143,000. Forfeiture, which Texas permits for a clear and serious breach, was for the trial judge to decide on remand.

On the statute of frauds, Texas Business and Commerce Code § 26.01(b)(6) requires a writing for an agreement not to be performed within one year, and the original two-year contract was within it. But the district court's finding of a month-to-month renewal was reasonable. JVIC argued that Farone v. Bag'n Baggage barred any implied renewal of a contract originally within the statute. The court read Farone more narrowly, as involving renewal of the entire contract including its term exceeding one year. The statute does not require every extension to be written, Texas excludes indefinite employment agreements from the one-year provision, and applying the statute to an indefinite or short renewal solely because the original term was longer would not advance its antifraud purpose. The casebook uses the case to illustrate this distinction for informal employment extensions.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-016.rule: Under Texas law as stated in this decision, an employment agreement for a term longer than one year is within the statute of frauds, and it cannot be enforced through successive implied renewals without a further signed writing.

sections.Parties: Robert Farone, the former president of Bag'n Baggage, sued for damages for breach of his employment arrangement and for breach of an alleged oral promise to compensate him for stock options. The defendants obtained summary judgment, and Farone appealed. Other claims were settled and were not part of the appeal.
sections.Procedural History: The defendants obtained partial summary judgment on the employment-contract and stock-option compensation claims, which became final after the parties resolved the other issues. The trial court did not specify its grounds. On appeal the Eastland Court of Appeals applied the traditional summary-judgment standard of Rule 166a(c), not the no-evidence rule, taking evidence favorable to Farone as true. It affirmed the judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
Caribbean Marine bought the closely held Bag'n Baggage corporation in 1983. On June 17, 1985, Bag'n Baggage agreed in writing to employ Farone as president for 24 months, subject to earlier termination for death, permanent disability, or specified breaches, with termination for material breach on 30 days' written notice. The agreement contained no renewal clause. A simultaneous written option agreement allowed him to purchase ten percent of the company's shares within three years; he exercised options for five percent.

When the business was converted into a partnership, he accepted Caribbean Marine stock of equal value for his shares and bought a one-percent limited partnership interest for $10,000. He alleged that he told Caribbean Marine's president, Bill Bowen, that the conversion could destroy his remaining options, and that Bowen orally responded that he would be compensated for them when Bag'n Baggage was sold or Farone left.

Bowen died in 1996. Farone continued working long after the written term expired, with no successive written employment agreement. Most of the board became dissatisfied with his performance, voted to discharge him in December 2000, and informed him on January 11, 2001.
sections.Issue: Could the discharge limits of a written two-year employment agreement be enforced years after its term expired, on the theory of implied renewals, without a further writing satisfying the statute of frauds? And was an oral promise that Farone would be "compensated" for his remaining stock options definite enough to enforce?
sections.Holding: The Texas Court of Appeals at Eastland, in 2005, in an opinion by Justice Jim R. Wright for a panel with Chief Justice Arnot and Justice McCall, with no separate writings, affirmed summary judgment for the defendants. The original two-year agreement was subject to the statute of frauds, and it could not be enforced through successive implied renewals without further writings; without an enforceable restriction, Farone was an at-will employee. The promise to compensate him for stock options lacked essential terms.
sections.Reasoning:
Texas Business and Commerce Code § 26.01 requires a signed writing for an agreement not to be performed within one year. The original term was two years. Its provisions for death, disability, and performance failures did not make full performance possible within a year; the court distinguished those methods of termination or excusable nonperformance from completion of the promised term.

The court assumed without deciding that the initial contract limited discharge to the specified conditions. That assumption did not extend the restriction indefinitely. An original agreement that could not be performed within a year could not be enforced through successive implied renewals without further writings. Implied agreements to continue may have existed, but they were unenforceable under the statute, and the original writing neither authorized renewal nor memorialized the later arrangements. Farone's authorities were distinguishable: they involved an original one-year term, monthly extensions of noncompetition arrangements, indefinite oral promises, or employment lasting only while performance remained satisfactory. Without an enforceable continuing limitation, the at-will presumption allowed discharge for good cause, bad cause, or no cause.

The option claim failed for a different reason. Even accepting the alleged assurance, the evidence showed no agreement on the price, whether compensation would be cash or equity, how equity would be valued, or which entity's equity it would be. These were essential terms, and courts cannot create a contract the parties did not make.

The casebook presents Farone alongside the later federal decision in Rash, which construed Farone's broad language in light of renewal of a term exceeding one year and distinguished a month-to-month or indefinite continuation; that narrowing is Rash's characterization, not Farone's own qualification.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-017.rule: The suretyship provision of the statute of frauds applies to promises to answer for another's future as well as existing debt, but a suretyship promise made mainly to serve the promisor's own pecuniary or business interest falls outside the writing requirement.

sections.Parties: Rosewood Care Center, Inc., a nursing facility, sued Caterpillar, Inc. to recover charges for the skilled nursing care of Caterpillar's injured employee, Betty Jo Cook, asserting contract, promissory-estoppel, and quantum-meruit claims; it also sued Cook. Caterpillar sought dismissal on the ground that its alleged oral promise to pay lacked the writing required by the Frauds Act. Caterpillar petitioned the Illinois Supreme Court after the appellate court reinstated the complaint.
sections.Procedural History: Caterpillar moved under section 2-619(a)(7) to dismiss the contract and estoppel counts and separately sought to strike quantum meruit. The circuit court granted those requests and made its orders immediately appealable under Rule 304(a). The appellate court reversed, reading Williams v. Corbet and Hartley Bros. v. Varner to exclude from the statute a promise made before the underlying debt arose; Justice Lytton specially concurred to criticize that supposed requirement. The Illinois Supreme Court accepted Caterpillar's petition and affirmed the appellate judgment on other grounds, returning the case to the circuit court.
sections.Material Facts:
The facts come from Rosewood's complaint and exhibits, not findings after trial. Cook suffered a workplace injury on October 21, 2001, was hospitalized until January 30, 2002, and filed a workers' compensation claim. On January 3 Caterpillar asked Rosewood's management agent to admit her at a fixed managed-care rate; Rosewood declined. On January 10 Dr. Norma Just, the Caterpillar employee responsible for workers' compensation medical care, allegedly told the agent that Caterpillar would cover 100 percent of Cook's skilled nursing care, pay Rosewood directly, and impose neither a deductible nor a maximum limit, and said Cook was precertified for four weeks.

Rosewood's agent faxed a confirmation of admission and four weeks' treatment, which Just signed and returned; Rosewood did not argue that this document satisfied the writing requirement. On admission Cook assigned insurance benefits and acknowledged responsibility for unpaid services. Caterpillar's health-care manager later authorized care on eight dates through June 4. Cook remained until June 13, generating charges of $181,857. Monthly bills went to Caterpillar without objection, but it ultimately refused payment. Rosewood alleged that it admitted Cook only because of Caterpillar's promise.
sections.Issue: Does the suretyship provision of the Illinois statute of frauds apply only when the other person's debt already exists at the time of the promise? If not, could Caterpillar's alleged oral promise be held unenforceable on a motion to dismiss, or did the main-purpose rule and the question whether the promise was an original undertaking require factfinding?
sections.Holding: The Illinois Supreme Court, in 2007, in an opinion by Justice Burke joined by Chief Justice Thomas and Justices Freeman, Fitzgerald, Kilbride, Garman, and Karmeier, unanimously affirmed the reversal of dismissal but rejected the appellate court's rationale. Illinois has no rule that a debt must already exist when a guaranty is made before the suretyship provision can apply. Factfinding was nevertheless required to determine whether Caterpillar's alleged promise was a suretyship and, if so, whether its main purpose was Caterpillar's own economic advantage. The court did not award the nursing charges or find Caterpillar liable.
sections.Reasoning:
The suretyship provision of 740 ILCS 80/1 requires a signed writing for a special promise to answer for another's debt, default, or miscarriage. Its text does not require that the debt exist before the promise, and reading in that condition would conflict with its ordinary language. The policy of requiring more secure evidence applies equally to future debt, which can expose a promisor to an amount not yet known. The older cases did not compel otherwise: Williams turned on to whom credit was extended and deferred to a jury's resolution of conflicting testimony, and Hartley Bros. simply relied on Williams. Neither established a categorical preexisting-debt rule, so nothing needed to be overruled.

Even a suretyship promise falls outside the writing requirement if its main purpose or leading object is to promote the promisor's own pecuniary or business interests, a rule Illinois has recognized since 1873. Where the consideration chiefly benefits the promisor, the transaction lacks the gratuitous character that makes a guaranty vulnerable to fabricated claims. The impetus for a promise is generally a fact question, with indicators such as the relationship between the benefit and the promised amount and the principal obligor's absence from negotiations. The allegations alone did not permit a determination of Caterpillar's main purpose.

Rosewood also argued that Caterpillar contracted directly rather than guaranteeing Cook's obligation. Whether the undertaking was an original obligation or a suretyship likewise required factual determination. A footnote notes that Rosewood did not challenge the appellate court's statement that an applicable statute of frauds would also bar the estoppel and quantum-meruit claims, so the court did not separately adjudicate that point. The casebook uses the case as a problem asking how to characterize the promise and what evidence would illuminate it.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-022.rule: Part performance takes an oral land contract out of the statute of frauds only on clear and convincing proof of definite terms and acts exclusively referable to the contract; restitution for benefits conferred remains available, measured by the value to the recipient.

sections.Parties: Ross and Wes Wilberg sued their grandfather, Albert Hyatt, and Clyde Magnuson, to whom Hyatt had sold Rock Canyon Ranch. The grandsons sought to enforce an alleged oral promise that the ranch would pass to them and, alternatively, restitution for unjust enrichment. They were the appellants.
sections.Procedural History: After Hyatt sold the ranch, the grandsons filed a lien for irrigation contributions and sued both men. The district court granted partial summary judgment for Hyatt on the contract claim, which also disposed of the claims against Magnuson because those depended on an enforceable earlier contract. After a bench trial the court rejected unjust enrichment. The Utah Court of Appeals affirmed the summary judgment on the oral land promise, reversed the rejection of the unjust-enrichment claim concerning irrigation installations, and remanded that limited claim for reconsideration. The rejection of the claim for general farm labor was not challenged and stood. The court denied appellate attorney fees.
sections.Material Facts:
The grandsons alleged that Hyatt promised Ross that Rock Canyon Ranch would pass to them if they worked for Hyatt until his death and then cared for his son, their uncle, until the uncle's death. They asserted nearly daily work and management over about a decade without compensation. They also furnished labor and materials for irrigation at Rock Canyon Ranch and labor for a similar system at Hyatt's Clawson Ranch. Ross used federal irrigation funding available to him subject to a lifetime limit; it covered 90 percent of predetermined costs, compared with Hyatt's 75 percent eligibility. The Clawson materials came from funding available to Hyatt and his daughter.

The grandsons relied on later will, trust, and LLC documents. The trust and LLC were never finalized or funded; the LLC gave Hyatt 99 percent ownership and sole management authority, including discretion to dispose of land, and the trust authorized him to sell property. Hyatt had worked extensively on the Wilberg family's own ranch and allowed use of his machinery and equipment, before and during the relevant period. Hyatt then sold Rock Canyon Ranch to Magnuson.
sections.Issue: Could the grandsons enforce the alleged oral promise of land under the part-performance exception to Utah's statute of frauds? And was their unjust-enrichment claim for the irrigation installations properly rejected because they did not allocate their proof between the two ranches and because federal funds paid much of the cost?
sections.Holding: The Utah Court of Appeals, in 2012, in an opinion by Judge Roth, with Judge Christiansen concurring and Judge Orme joining and writing separately on the scope of remand, affirmed summary judgment against the oral land-contract claim and reversed the rejection of the irrigation unjust-enrichment claim. Neither the grandsons' proof of the contract nor their reliance conduct reached the clarity the part-performance exception requires. The restitution claim ran against Hyatt for benefits on both properties, and the benefit did not vanish because the resources were government-funded. The court ordered reconsideration, not conveyance of the ranch or a damages award.
sections.Reasoning:
Utah's land-transfer statute generally requires a subscribed writing. Equity can enforce a partly performed oral agreement, but the claimant must establish clear and definite terms and clear acts in reliance, ordinarily exclusively referable to the bargain. The doctrine rests on estoppel. Strong independent proof or admission of a definite contract can relax the need for otherwise unexplained reliance acts, but when the contract is disputed and unclear, exclusively referable conduct becomes vital. The ultimate standard is clear and convincing evidence, and summary judgment turned on whether a reasonable factfinder could meet it.

The will, trust, and LLC documents preserved Hyatt's control and ability to sell, so they did not strongly corroborate an unconditional duty to transfer the ranch at death. The work was not exclusively referable to the bargain because it could reasonably be explained as reciprocal family labor. The court also found no abuse of discretion in treating the moving papers' noncompliance with Rule 7's format as technical, since the grandsons identified no prejudice.

Unjust enrichment requires a benefit the recipient knows of or appreciates under circumstances making uncompensated retention unjust, measured by the value of the benefit to the recipient. The trial court recognized that Hyatt benefited from the irrigation but denied recovery because the proof was not allocated to Rock Canyon. That misunderstood the claim, which sought restitution from Hyatt for both installations. If the observation that the grandsons were not out any cash contributed to the denial, it was error; Ross had also exhausted much of his limited lifetime entitlement.

Judge Orme, concurring, read the existing benefit finding as leaving only valuation on remand and would have directed the trial court to fix restitution. The casebook uses the case as a problem on part performance, estoppel, reciprocal family work, and restitution; the opinion analyzes estoppel within part performance rather than as a separate promissory-estoppel claim.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-023.rule: A contract for the sale of goods still requires a bargain in fact; silence in response to an unsigned confirmation is not acceptance unless the parties' relationship or course of dealing justifies expecting a reply.

sections.Parties: Cargill Incorporated, a supplier of agricultural products and risk-management services, sued Jorgenson Farms, which raised corn and soybeans, seeking arbitration or damages on an alleged contract for the farm to deliver 80,000 bushels of corn. The farm denied ever making that contract and sought summary judgment and sanctions. Cargill was the appellant.
sections.Procedural History: Cargill requested National Grain and Feed Association arbitration in September 2004; the farm answered that it had made no contract containing an arbitration agreement. Cargill served a complaint on January 18, 2005, delayed filing it, and filed in July with a motion to compel arbitration. The farm moved for summary judgment and sanctions, having warned Cargill in March that the claim lacked a contractual basis. At the August 26 hearing Cargill orally requested more discovery time. The district court denied that request, granted summary judgment, denied arbitration, and awarded $5,000 in sanctions. The Minnesota Court of Appeals affirmed on August 8, 2006.
sections.Material Facts:
Cargill asserted that the farm had agreed to deliver 80,000 bushels of corn in December 2003. Ben Presthus, the farm's exclusive Cargill contact during the period, had authority to make contracts. His usual practice was to record each agreement in his diary, notify accounting, and have Cargill send a confirmation for signature and return. He identified two July 17, 2003 contracts, for 100,000 and 135,000 bushels, that the farm performed. He denied negotiating the additional 80,000-bushel transaction, found no diary entry for it, and described the confirmation as a clerical error. Co-owner James Jorgenson likewise denied any oral or written agreement. He acknowledged receiving an October 2003 information packet containing the document but said harvest work delayed his attention to it.

Cargill's confirmation directed the seller to sign and date the original and attached copy, return the original, and keep the copy. Jorgenson neither signed nor returned it. Cargill relied on that July confirmation, an October put-option addendum, internal emails among its employees, and affidavits from manager Kurt Peterson and supervisor Brad Morrison, who disputed that he had agreed no contract existed. In the roughly seven months after serving its complaint Cargill served no interrogatories, document requests, requests for admission, or deposition notices.
sections.Issue: Did Cargill produce evidence from which a rational factfinder could find that Jorgenson Farms agreed to sell the disputed 80,000 bushels, where the farm never signed or returned the confirmation and the only witnesses with direct knowledge denied the agreement? Were the denial of further discovery, the refusal to compel arbitration, and the fee sanction proper?
sections.Holding: The Minnesota Court of Appeals, in 2006, in an opinion by Judge Dietzen for a panel with Presiding Judge Stoneburner and Chief Judge Toussaint and no separate opinion, affirmed summary judgment for Jorgenson Farms because Cargill had not produced evidence from which a rational factfinder could find an agreement. It also affirmed the denial of further discovery, the refusal to compel arbitration, and the $5,000 attorney-fee sanction. The court expressly declined to decide the statute-of-frauds defense because no contract had been formed.
sections.Reasoning:
The court viewed the record favorably to Cargill, but unsupported conclusions, speculative future evidence, and mere doubt about an opponent's witnesses do not create a material factual dispute. Minnesota's UCC allows agreement through language or conduct and treats course of dealing, performance, and trade usage as relevant, but still requires a bargain in fact.

The only witnesses identified as having direct knowledge, Presthus and Jorgenson, denied the agreement. Under the confirmation's own terms, which required signature and return, the unsigned document had not formed a contract. Silence ordinarily is not acceptance unless the parties' relationship justifies expecting a reply or imposes a duty to respond, and Cargill produced no course-of-dealing evidence making the farm's silence assent. The October addendum was not accepted in writing or orally, and an email between Cargill employees could not show the farm's agreement. Cargill's suggestion that Presthus was related to the Jorgensons and tied to a competitor was unsupported speculation.

Denying a discovery continuance was within the district court's discretion given Cargill's seven months of inactivity; waiting on arbitration was no excuse, because arbitration itself depended on the disputed contract. Without the contract there was no arbitration agreement to enforce. The sanction under section 549.211, subdivision 2(1) did not require an express bad-faith finding, and Cargill had continued the claim without discovery despite notice of Presthus's denial.

The court quoted the merchant-confirmation provision, section 336.2-201(2), but did not decide whether the farm was a merchant, whether the packet satisfied that provision, or whether silence under it could create an agreement. The casebook uses the dispute as a problem posing those confirmation questions, while the actual judgment resolves the anterior formation issue.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-024.rule: Under Pennsylvania law as described in this decision, a minor's contracts other than for necessaries are voidable, and shelter is not invariably a necessary; it depends on the minor's situation and whether a parent or guardian is able and willing to supply it.

sections.Parties: Carmen Rivera, a minor who was denied admission to public housing, sued the Reading Housing Authority and its executive director. She sought a change in the authority's policy requiring applicants under eighteen to obtain a judicial emancipation decree, admission to public housing, and monetary compensation under section 1983. The defendants defended the policy.
sections.Procedural History:
The complaint, filed December 23, 1991, initially named three plaintiffs and proposed a class. The court denied class certification in April 1992, and the other two named plaintiffs dismissed their claims without prejudice, leaving only Rivera's claims. She elected not to pursue an Age Discrimination Act claim. After discovery the parties agreed the material facts were undisputed and submitted cross-motions for summary judgment; the authority alternatively sought dismissal.

On January 25, 1993, the district court granted the defendants' summary-judgment motion, denied Rivera's, denied the alternative motion to dismiss as moot, and entered judgment for the defendants. The brief covers only the district court's decision, not any later appellate judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
The authority operated eight low-income housing projects under a contract requiring compliance with HUD regulations and the Public Housing Occupancy Handbook. In March 1991 it revised its admissions policy; HUD approved the revision on July 2, and it took effect July 23. The revised policy required an applicant under eighteen to obtain a judicial decree declaring emancipation and entitlement to contract for necessities. The parties stipulated that the authority sought to ensure enforceable leases, establish need for housing, and establish capacity to comply with a lease and live independently.

Rivera, born January 17, 1975, had been raised by paternal grandparents; her parents were separated and largely absent. In April 1991, while pregnant, she and David Gonzalez left her grandparents' Reading apartment for a place of their own, paying $260 monthly plus utilities and receiving public assistance. They applied for public housing on May 21, 1991. The authority put Rivera on a waiting list pending an emancipation decree and notified her of the requirement on August 9. She did not seek a decree; her attorney argued that Pennsylvania minors could make enforceable contracts for necessaries. The authority denied admission on September 9. Rivera gave birth in November, and in February 1992 the family moved to a larger apartment costing $400 monthly, where they encountered rats.
sections.Issue: Did the housing authority's requirement that applicants under eighteen obtain a judicial emancipation decree violate the United States Housing Act, HUD regulations, or the Fourteenth Amendment, given Rivera's argument that Pennsylvania minors can make enforceable contracts for necessaries such as housing?
sections.Holding: The U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, in 1993, per District Judge Van Antwerpen, entered summary judgment for the Reading Housing Authority and its executive director. The court upheld the decree requirement and rejected Rivera's challenges under the Housing Act, HUD regulations, and the Fourteenth Amendment. It ordered neither admission nor compensation. The court did not decide whether housing was a necessary for Rivera herself.
sections.Reasoning:
The court read the Housing Act as serving both the provision of safe, decent housing and local responsibility for efficient administration, including rent collection; it did not guarantee admission to every needy applicant. The HUD regulations forbade automatic exclusion of a category of otherwise eligible applicants, but the policy did not exclude every minor, since a minor could qualify through a decree, and its premise was the legal ability to disaffirm a lease, not an assumption that minors were irresponsible. The court also relied on HUD Handbook language permitting minimum ages to avoid leases unenforceable under state law, while noting that a July 1991 revision had inadvertently omitted the minor provisions.

Pennsylvania generally treated a minor's contracts, other than for necessaries, as voidable rather than void. Whether something was a necessary depended on the minor's situation and the ability and willingness of a parent or guardian to supply it, so the court rejected the proposition that shelter was invariably a necessary. A footnote explained that even necessary lodging could create liability only for reasonable rent during actual occupancy, not the whole lease term, so the category did not give an authority the security of an ordinary enforceable lease.

Rivera was right that emancipation from parental control alone does not end a minor's right to disaffirm, but the court distinguished an adjudication directed specifically to contractual capacity. It accepted an uncontroverted affidavit from Judge Arthur Grim describing a nonstatutory Berks County procedure for such a petition, and found that referral to a court gave greater contractual certainty than the authority's own assessment.

On due process, Rivera called the rule an irrebuttable presumption. The court applied rational-basis scrutiny; overinclusion or underinclusion did not make a welfare rule unconstitutional, and protecting scarce housing and rent collection through enforceable leases was a rational justification. The casebook quotes the court's policy discussion of minority and necessaries.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-025.rule: Legal services can fall within the class of necessaries that overcomes an infancy defense, but whether particular services were actually necessary is a question of fact, and if they were the minor owes only their reasonable value.

sections.Parties: Robert Zelnick, an attorney, represented Jonathan Adams, then a minor, under a one-third contingent-fee retainer signed by Jonathan's mother. Jonathan's father sued on his behalf to invalidate the fee contract; after reaching majority Jonathan intervened, replaced his father, and disaffirmed. Zelnick sought to keep his fee. Both sides appealed, and this opinion addressed Zelnick's appeal.
sections.Procedural History: In March 1998 Jonathan's father sued on his behalf to invalidate the fee contract. After majority Jonathan intervened and expressly disaffirmed, and in April 2000 he sought summary judgment. The trial court declared the contract void and held the necessaries doctrine inapplicable, reasoning that Jonathan had been a minor and that the matter could have awaited majority. It nonetheless awarded Zelnick $60,000 in quantum meruit with prejudgment interest from the January 1998 consent decree. Both sides appealed. The Supreme Court of Virginia decided Zelnick's appeal in this opinion and resolved Adams's companion appeal by separate order. It reversed the judgment and remanded for evidence on actual necessity.
sections.Material Facts:
Jonathan Adams was born April 5, 1980, to unmarried parents, Mildred Adams and Cecil Hylton Jr. An agreed September 1995 Florida order established paternity. Jonathan's grandfather had died in 1989, leaving trusts under a will that gave executors or trustees authority to determine whether persons claiming descent outside marriage were his issue. Two grandchildren's trusts contemplated potential distributions in 2014 and 2021.

In July 1996 Jonathan's mother consulted Zelnick after hearing that grandchildren might already be receiving distributions; her own inquiries had produced no useful information about whether Jonathan would be recognized. Unable to afford an hourly fee, she requested contingent representation, and on July 19 she signed a retainer for one-third of the recovery in Jonathan's claim against the estate. Zelnick wrote the executors demanding recognition; estate counsel responded that the claim should be evaluated when distributions became payable. Zelnick filed a declaratory and accounting suit in May 1997. A January 23, 1998 consent decree declared Jonathan the grandfather's issue and entitled to benefits payable to grandchildren under the will and trusts, without fixing any amount. Zelnick testified to approximately 150 to 200 hours at a $200 hourly rate.
sections.Issue: Can a contract for legal services made on a minor's behalf fall within the necessaries doctrine so as to defeat the minor's infancy defense, and could the trial court hold the doctrine inapplicable on summary judgment yet still award the attorney quantum meruit?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia, in 2002, in an opinion by Justice Lemons with no separate writing, held that legal services fall within the general class of necessaries that can overcome an infancy defense, but that whether these particular services were necessary required factfinding. It reversed and remanded. If the doctrine did not apply, the contract would be avoided and no award made; if the evidence defeated the infancy plea, the trial court was to hear evidence of reasonable value. The court neither enforced the one-third contingent fee nor preserved the $60,000 award.
sections.Reasoning:
A minor's contract under Virginia law is ordinarily voidable, not void. Following Bear, the court separated the judge's threshold decisions from the factfinder's. The judge first decides whether the goods or services can belong to a general class of necessaries and whether there is enough evidence of actual necessity to submit the question. If both tests are met, the factfinder considers the minor's position and condition, all the circumstances, and whether the minor was already sufficiently supplied.

Legal services can belong to the class, including protection of liberty, reputation, personal injury claims, or property interests, because a minor's ability to protect those interests can depend on counsel being reasonably compensated. But classification does not prove that every legal service benefits a minor enough to warrant recovery.

Even when necessity defeats the infancy plea, the minor is bound on an implied obligation to pay reasonable value, not automatically on the express agreement. Conversely, if the services were not necessary and the infancy defense succeeds, a court may not get around that result with an independent quantum-meruit award. Quantum meruit here is the measure of recovery under the necessaries-based implied contract, and so was properly before the trial court without a separate pleading.

The trial court erred twice. Minority at signing could not exclude the doctrine, since it is the very condition that makes the exception relevant. And the conclusion that the suit could have awaited majority was a factual determination unsupported by the summary-judgment record; necessity is assessed in the circumstances when services were rendered, without a hindsight burden on the supplier. On remand a contingent award at an appropriate percentage was not categorically excluded, but any award required full evidentiary support.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-026.rule: Under Pennsylvania law, a minor's contract, except one for necessities, is voidable if the minor disaffirms it within a reasonable time after reaching majority.

sections.Parties: Darko Milicic, a Serbian basketball player, sued The Basketball Marketing Company, doing business as AND 1, for temporary, preliminary, and declaratory relief after he disaffirmed an endorsement agreement he had signed as a minor. He sought to stop the company from interfering with his efforts to obtain other endorsement contracts. The company appealed the preliminary injunction entered against it.
sections.Procedural History: Milicic sued for temporary, preliminary, and declaratory relief. After a temporary restraining order, a hearing, and briefing, the trial court issued a preliminary injunction restraining the company from interfering with his efforts to obtain endorsement contracts. The company appealed. The Superior Court of Pennsylvania affirmed the order on August 25, 2004. The appeal concerned only whether apparently reasonable grounds supported interim relief, not a final adjudication of the declaratory action or of tort damages.
sections.Material Facts:
The company marketed basketball apparel and related products from Pennsylvania. Milicic signed its endorsement agreement on June 15, 2002, when he was sixteen. The company would supply money and products in exchange for endorsements. Two amendments changed compensation and payment recipients but kept the other provisions, including a Pennsylvania choice-of-law clause. Initially little known in the United States, Milicic became a prominent 2003 NBA prospect and the Detroit Pistons' second overall draft pick, which made a more lucrative endorsement possible.

In June 2003 the parties discussed a buyout, and his proposal was rejected. Shortly after turning eighteen he sent an unequivocal disaffirmance letter and began returning the money and products he had received, or their equivalent value. AND 1 refused to treat the letter as ending the agreement. On July 11 it wrote to Adidas and Reebok, asserting that its agreement remained valid and enforceable for several years. Adidas stopped advanced negotiations, preventing execution of a nearly completed endorsement agreement. The company had produced no evidence that counsel advised Milicic and had not obtained a guardian to protect his interests.
sections.Issue: Did apparently reasonable grounds support a preliminary injunction barring the company from interfering with Milicic's endorsement negotiations, given that he had disaffirmed shortly after majority an agreement signed at sixteen, and were the company's letters to competitors actionable interference?
sections.Holding: The Superior Court of Pennsylvania, in 2004, in an opinion by Judge McCaffery for a panel with Judges Hudock and Popovich and no separate writing, affirmed the preliminary injunction. All four prerequisites were satisfied: a strong likelihood of success, immediate irreparable injury not compensable in money, greater injury from denial than from grant, and restoration of the status quo. Milicic's disaffirmance letter supplied more than a reasonable probability of success in the declaratory action. The decision entered no final declaration that the contract was invalid and fixed no damages.
sections.Reasoning:
The court did not decide the ultimate merits. It asked whether the record supplied apparently reasonable grounds for the trial court's action. Several of the company's issues were waived: its objection to supposed premature findings and its commercial-speech argument were not properly developed below, and its choice-of-law challenge was omitted from its concise statement of issues.

Pennsylvania law generally made a minor's contract voidable, except for necessities, if disaffirmed within a reasonable time after majority, and Milicic's letter supplied more than a reasonable probability of success in the declaratory action; that likelihood supported interim relief and was not a final declaratory judgment. On irreparable harm, his agent explained that the period after the NBA draft in which publicity can be converted into endorsements is short, and that blocking a principal endorsement could impair secondary deals; the loss could be estimated only conjecturally. In balancing the harms the trial court relied on the protective policy behind the infancy rule, noting that the experienced company had not shown that counsel advised Milicic and had obtained no guardian. The public interest included protecting minors from immature mistakes and adult overbearance. Enjoining further interference returned the parties to their position before the letters.

AND 1 argued that its letters merely reported publicly known litigation. The court refused to separate the communication from the underlying contract dispute: the likely effectiveness of the disaffirmance bore on whether AND 1 had any justification for telling competitors its contract remained enforceable. The elements of intentional interference with prospective contractual relations were supported, since the Adidas negotiations were active, the letters were aimed at stopping them, and an affidavit from Adidas's general counsel showed they did.

The casebook uses the case for disaffirmance and the return of benefits.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-027.rule: Where a statute prescribes a parent's written consent as the means of authorizing use of a minor's image, a consent that meets the statute binds the child, who cannot later disaffirm it under the common-law infancy rule.

sections.Parties: Brooke Shields, a child model, sued photographer Garry Gross in tort and contract for damages and a permanent injunction against all further use of photographs he took of her at age ten under written consents signed by her mother. Gross relied on the consents. Both sides appealed to the New York Court of Appeals: Gross sought restoration of the trial judgment, and Shields sought broader relief, retention of the appellate order, or a new trial.
sections.Procedural History: Special Term initially issued a preliminary injunction. After a nonjury trial, the court found the consents unrestricted in time and use and dismissed the complaint, but on Gross's stipulation it permanently barred use in pornographic magazines or publications predominantly appealing to prurient interests. The Appellate Division accepted the unrestricted-consent findings but, in several opinions, added a permanent injunction against advertising or trade uses. On cross-appeals, the Court of Appeals on March 29, 1983 modified the Appellate Division's order by striking the added advertising-and-trade injunction and affirmed as modified, with costs to Gross. The trial court's narrower stipulated injunction remained.
sections.Material Facts:
Shields obtained modeling work through Ford Model Agency. In 1975, when she was ten, Gross photographed her for a project financed by Playboy Press, initially called Portfolio 8 and later Sugar and Spice. Her mother and legal guardian, Teri Shields, signed two consents before the sessions. The written permission covered use and reuse, publication and republication through different media for any purpose, and waived approval of the finished photographs and their eventual use. The fee was $450.

The photographs appeared in the intended publication and, with the knowledge of mother and daughter, in other publications and enlarged store-window displays. Shields herself later used them in a book after her mother obtained Gross's authorization. In 1980 she learned of publication in a French magazine and of contemplated further uses, and she tried unsuccessfully to buy the negatives. In 1981 she sued. The trial court found the photographs nonpornographic.
sections.Issue: May a minor disaffirm unrestricted written consents that her parent executed in compliance with sections 50 and 51 of the New York Civil Rights Law, and then obtain statutory relief against publication of her photographs within the terms of those consents?
sections.Holding: The New York Court of Appeals, in 1983, in an opinion by Judge Simons for Chief Judge Cooke and Judges Jones and Wachtler, with Judge Jasen dissenting in part joined by Judges Fuchsberg and Meyer, a 4-3 division, held that a child model could not disaffirm unrestricted written consents her mother executed under sections 50 and 51 and then obtain statutory relief against publication within their terms. The court struck the Appellate Division's added injunction and otherwise affirmed. It awarded Shields no damages and did not decide unconscionability, which had not been raised at trial.
sections.Reasoning:
New York had no common-law privacy cause of action; the Legislature created the protection in sections 50 and 51. Section 50 specified written consent by the person depicted or, for a minor, the parent or guardian, and section 51 made consent so obtained a bar to the civil remedy. The majority construed the statutory remedy strictly. Once written consent was obtained, use was permissible within its terms.

The majority acknowledged that an infant ordinarily could disaffirm consent given personally or on the infant's behalf, but the Legislature could alter that right. Having created a new cause of action and prescribed how a minor's consent is obtained, it made a parent's conforming written consent binding; no express prohibition of disaffirmance was needed. This was a conclusion about statutory consents, not a declaration that every agreement a parent makes binds a child.

The lack of prior court approval under General Obligations Law section 3-105 did not invalidate the consents. That provision covered performing artists and professional athletes, and court approval was impractical for session-by-session modeling at modest fees; parental judgment was the Legislature's substitute. Shields had not claimed the photographs were obscene, and the stipulated injunction already barred pornographic uses. A parent could limit the authorized uses, and a user could not exceed those limits.

Judge Jasen, dissenting in part, would have affirmed the broader Appellate Division protection. He stressed that Shields sought to prevent future uses, viewed parental consent and common-law disaffirmance as complementary safeguards, and found no legislative intent to remove the child's later protection against a parent's poor judgment or exploitation.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-028.rule: A minor's contract is voidable, but after reaching majority the former minor ratifies it by failing to disaffirm within a reasonable time or by a distinct, decisive act clearly showing affirmation, and a ratified contract can no longer be avoided.

sections.Parties: Kirsten Fletcher sued her former boyfriend and co-tenant, John Marshall, in small claims for $2,500 plus costs as contribution toward rent she had paid on their jointly leased apartment after he moved out. Marshall defended on the ground that he was a minor when he signed the lease. Fletcher appealed the judgment for Marshall.
sections.Procedural History: After a bench trial, the circuit court of Lake County entered judgment for Marshall because it regarded his minority at signing as preventing joint liability under the lease. Fletcher unsuccessfully sought reconsideration, invoking both necessaries and ratification. Her sole argument on appeal was ratification through post-majority possession and payment, so the appellate court did not decide whether the apartment was a necessary. The Illinois Appellate Court, Second District, reversed and remanded for a hearing to determine Fletcher's damages.
sections.Material Facts:
Fletcher and Marshall dated in high school. After his parents expelled him from their home following graduation, he moved in with Fletcher and her parents. The couple agreed to rent an apartment and share expenses. A lease dated April 29, 1991 called for $525 monthly rent from July 1, 1991 through June 30, 1992. Marshall said he signed on April 29, while seventeen; Fletcher and her mother said it was not signed until June 30. His father established May 30 as his birthday, and the trial court found that he signed while still a minor.

The couple paid an extra half month's rent and moved in before the stated term. Marshall acknowledged making rent payments and paying at least part of the security deposit. He moved into the apartment and paid rent about two weeks after turning eighteen, stayed approximately a month and a half, and did nothing before leaving that indicated disaffirmance. He left because the relationship was not working and he had a college opportunity; the witnesses disputed whether he left on August 2 or August 15. Fletcher remained and paid the full rent for the remaining ten months.
sections.Issue: Did Marshall ratify a lease he signed as a minor by moving into the apartment and paying rent after turning eighteen, so that he could not later disaffirm it by moving out and refusing to pay?
sections.Holding: The Illinois Appellate Court, Second District, in 1994, in an opinion by Justice Bowman with Justices Doyle and Quetsch concurring and no separate writing, held that Marshall ratified the lease by moving in and paying rent after turning eighteen. Those acts prevented him from later disaffirming by moving out and refusing further payment. He remained liable for the rest of the lease term and, on the contribution theory, for payments Fletcher made on his behalf. The court reversed and remanded for a hearing on damages; it did not itself award the $2,500 demanded.
sections.Reasoning:
Common-law contribution required compulsory payment by a joint obligor of more than that person's share of a common obligation, so whether Marshall remained bound on the lease was the prerequisite to Fletcher's claim.

A minor's contract is voidable, not void. After majority the former minor may disaffirm or ratify. Failure to disaffirm within a reasonable time, or a distinct, decisive act clearly showing affirmation, can establish ratification, and once ratified the obligation can no longer be avoided on the ground of minority.

Fletcher asked for de novo review because the conduct was undisputed. The court declined: intent can require factual inferences even from undisputed acts, so ratification is generally a question of fact, and the judgment would be disturbed only if against the manifest weight of the evidence.

The court compared three Illinois Supreme Court decisions, Rubin, Schlig, and Shepherd, in which post-majority conduct recognizing an earlier transaction, such as installment payments or collecting rent, made it binding without a newly signed promise. Here Marshall moved in and paid rent about two weeks after turning eighteen, stayed about a month and a half, and gave no sign of disaffirmance before leaving. The court found no basis in the record for reading those acts as anything other than unequivocal ratification, and so reversed even under the deferential standard. His later departure and refusal to pay could not undo an obligation already ratified. The conclusion rested on the combined conduct in this record, not on a rule that any single payment always ratifies a minor's contract.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-029.rule: On the quoted Nebraska reasoning, a minor's position on disaffirmance is not defeated because services received cannot be returned; the resulting loss falls on the adult, to discourage adults from contracting with minors.

sections.Parties: The quoted passage identifies the minor as Travis and identifies Mizerski as the person who supplied paint and body work on the minor's vehicle. The brief gives nothing further about the parties or their roles in the litigation, because the complete opinion was unavailable.
sections.Procedural History: The complete unpublished opinion of the Nebraska Court of Appeals was unavailable. An official Nebraska appellate reporter index identifies the case as No. A-93-403, lists the result as affirmed, and identifies Mues as the judge. The index does not show which trial judgment was affirmed, what sum was involved, or what other issues were raised.
sections.Material Facts: The brief rests only on a short judicial quotation reproduced in the casebook. Mizerski supplied paint and body work on a vehicle belonging to Travis, a minor. Because of the character of that performance, Travis had nothing to return. The passage does not give the contract price, the date of the agreement, Travis's exact age, any parental participation, or any award amount.
sections.Issue: When a minor has received services that by their nature cannot be returned, does the inability to restore them defeat the minor's position against the adult who supplied them?
sections.Holding: The Nebraska Court of Appeals, in 1995, in a decision the official index attributes to Judge Mues, affirmed. The quoted reasoning supports the conclusion that the inability to return the paint and body work did not defeat the minor's position merely because the adult provider suffered a loss. The remainder of the holding could not be verified because the full opinion was unavailable.
sections.Reasoning:
The reproduced reasoning recognizes the apparent injustice to Mizerski, who furnished work that could not be given back. It explains that Nebraska law imposes that consequence on adults who contract with minors as a means of discouraging such contracts. The quotation does not disclose every legal condition of disaffirmance or state a rule for every transaction with a minor, and the opinion's other reasoning, any footnotes, and any separate writings were not available.

The casebook places the case in its discussion of restitution following a minor's disaffirmance; the distinction it draws between goods that remain in the minor's hands and services that cannot be restored is the casebook editors' framing of the quoted reasoning.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-030.rule: A minor who disaffirms a fair purchase made without overreaching, after paying money and using the article, may recover the price only subject to the seller's reasonable compensation for use, depreciation, and willful or negligent damage.

sections.Parties: Joseph Dodson, who was sixteen when he bought a used pickup truck, sued the sellers, Burns and Mary Shrader, who ran the dealership, to rescind the purchase and recover the price he paid. The Shraders refused to take back the truck without compensation for depreciation.
sections.Procedural History: Dodson sued in general sessions court to rescind and recover his payment. That court dismissed the warrant, and he took a de novo appeal to circuit court. In November 1988 the circuit judge, reluctantly following earlier common-law decisions, ordered the sellers to refund $4,900 upon tender and delivery of the truck. The Court of Appeals affirmed in an opinion by Judge Todd, with Judge Cantrell concurring separately and Judge Koch dissenting. The Tennessee Supreme Court, on January 27, 1992, adopted a new rule and remanded for further proceedings under it, displacing the lower courts' unconditional full refund; appellate costs were divided equally.
sections.Material Facts:
In April 1987 Dodson, then sixteen, bought a used 1984 pickup truck from the Shraders' dealership for $4,900 in cash borrowed from his girlfriend's grandmother. The sellers did not ask his age and he did not misrepresent it; Mr. Shrader testified that he believed Dodson was eighteen or nineteen.

In December the truck developed mechanical problems. A mechanic suspected a burnt valve but would have needed to inspect the engine to be sure. Dodson either did not want to pay for repairs or lacked the money. He kept driving, and the engine failed in January. He parked the truck at his parents' home and asked the sellers to rescind and refund the price. They refused. Before the circuit-court trial, a hit-and-run driver struck the parked truck's left front fender. Mr. Shrader estimated the truck's value at trial at $500 because of the engine and body damage.
sections.Issue: When a minor disaffirms a purchase and returns the article, must the seller refund the full purchase price, or may the recovery be reduced to account for the article's loss in value while in the minor's hands?
sections.Holding: The Tennessee Supreme Court, in 1992, in an opinion by Justice O'Brien in which Chief Justice Reid and Justices Drowota, Daughtrey, and Anderson concurred, unanimously held that where the contract is fair and reasonable, there is no overreaching or undue influence, and the minor has paid money and taken and used the article, the minor may not recover the amount paid without allowing the seller reasonable compensation for use, depreciation, and willful or negligent damage while the article was in the minor's hands. The court remanded for factual determinations and did not set Dodson's net refund.
sections.Reasoning:
The court traced Tennessee law from older distinctions among beneficial, prejudicial, and uncertain contracts to the modern view that a minor's contract is voidable rather than void. Voidability lets the minor keep advantageous bargains and disaffirm injudicious ones. The doctrine protects immature judgment from exploitation, but equitable principles resist turning that shield into a means of injuring good-faith counterparties.

The court compared two minority approaches in other states. One reduces recovery by the benefit the minor actually received through use; the other allows deductions for use, depreciation, or deterioration. It adopted a modified version of the Oregon approach. The common law can adapt, the court reasoned, and modern minors often work, earn, and spend money independently; merchants should be able to deal fairly with them without invariably refunding the whole price after an article has been used or destroyed. The change went to restitution only and did not make minors generally capable of binding contracts.

The rule does not apply if the seller practiced fraud or imposition, the contract was unfair, or an unfair advantage induced the purchase. Whether the seller overreached and the fair market value of the returned property are questions for the trier of fact.

Several matters were left for the trial court: whether Dodson's continued driving after learning of the engine problem was gross negligence or intentional conduct; the amount of the hit-and-run damage and its allocation between buyer and sellers, given that it occurred after the first tender was refused; and the truck's fair market value at tender. The casebook labels the result a reversal, while the opinion's final directive is a remand.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-031.rule: A contract is voidable for mental incapacity if the person cannot reasonably understand the nature and consequences of the transaction, or cannot act reasonably in relation to it and the other party has reason to know of the condition.

sections.Parties: Viola Farnum, a ninety-year-old woman, acting through her nephew and later guardian Harry Gove, sued Joseph Silvano, the twenty-four-year-old who had bought her house, seeking rescission of the conveyance. Silvano defended the sale. Farnum's side appealed after the Probate Court upheld the conveyance.
sections.Procedural History: The action was commenced April 6, 1987. The Probate Court found that Farnum was coherent or in a lucid interval when she signed, treated that as sufficient capacity, and ruled for Silvano. On June 30, 1989, the Massachusetts Appeals Court vacated the judgment and remanded for a judgment of rescission with an appropriate restitutionary accounting. It accepted the trial judge's supported findings but held that the judge had applied an insufficient measure of contractual capacity.
sections.Material Facts:
On July 14, 1986, Farnum conveyed her South Yarmouth house to Silvano, who had mowed her lawn and done landscaping and whom she trusted. The price was $64,900 for property appraised at $115,000, and the agreement included furniture and furnishings. Silvano obtained a $65,000 bank mortgage at the closing. Her nephew, Harry Gove, had warned Silvano not to proceed because of the inadequate price and her mental disability.

Farnum's competence had seriously declined since 1983. She wondered why deceased sisters did not contact her, repeatedly locked herself out, became lost, and had offered the house to a neighbor for $35,000. Her sister and nephew helped pay her bills. A May 1985 scan disclosed organic brain disease. In January 1987 she was hospitalized for dementia and seizure disorder and then discharged to a nursing home.

Silvano selected and paid the lawyer who represented Farnum in the conveyance. At the closing in her home she was cheerful, made coffee, and appeared aware of the event. The trial judge found she could be coherent and then confused two minutes later. After the closing she told her sister and nephew she still owned the house.
sections.Issue: Is a seller's momentary awareness that a closing is taking place enough to establish capacity to contract, or may the conveyance be avoided where she could not act reasonably in relation to the transaction and the buyer had reason to know of her mental condition?
sections.Holding: The Massachusetts Appeals Court, in 1989, in an opinion by Judge Kass for a panel with Judges Warner and Fine and no separate writing, held the deed voidable under Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 15(1)(b). A moment in which the seller understood that a closing was taking place did not establish reasonable understanding of the transaction and its consequences, and Silvano's knowledge of her impaired ability to act reasonably was decisive. The court vacated the judgment and remanded for rescission, without resolving the alternative theories of fraud, undue influence, or constructive trust.
sections.Reasoning:
The court distinguished testamentary from contractual capacity. A person of unsound mind may be able to execute a will at a particular moment, and a choice among beneficiaries can be arbitrary. A contract creates reciprocal obligations and requires reasonable comprehension of its nature, significance, and consequences, so transient awareness of the event is not enough.

The court invoked the two branches of Restatement § 15(1): inability to understand the transaction's nature and consequences in a reasonable manner, or inability to act reasonably in relation to it where the other party has reason to know of the condition. Using Ortelere, it separated knowing that a transfer is occurring from comprehending its consequences in one's actual circumstances. Farnum could know she was selling below value without understanding why disposing of a major asset so cheaply was unreasonable when rent, home-care, and nursing-home costs were approaching.

The findings showed that missing understanding. Her disease appeared in irrational conduct and was confirmed diagnostically. Silvano was neither family nor a long-term caregiver. His claim that he let her remain in the house was unpersuasive because the agreement and deed were silent on it, and the lawyer he procured concentrated on completing the transaction. The decisive factor was Silvano's awareness: he knew the price was about half the home's value and had received the nephew's specific warning.

On remand Silvano was to convey the property to Farnum's guardian in return for the consideration he paid, with an accounting for possession or rental value and for benefits such as taxes he paid; improvements and mortgage payments ordinarily would not be credited. The casebook uses the case for the distinction between testamentary and contractual capacity; the brief notes that the casebook's statement that the mortgage exceeded the home's market value does not match the opinion's figures.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-032.rule: As the federal court predicted New Jersey law, a gambler has no dram-shop tort claim against a casino for losses incurred while intoxicated, but intoxication so complete that he could not appreciate the nature and consequences of his act remains a contract defense to the casino's credit claim.

sections.Parties: Hakimoglu, a gambler, sued Trump Taj Mahal Associates and other defendants to recover gambling losses exceeding $2 million, on a common-law dram-shop theory that the casino served him alcohol and let him keep gambling while visibly intoxicated. The casino counterclaimed for $700,000 advanced on credit markers. Hakimoglu defended the counterclaim on the ground that intoxication deprived him of capacity to contract.
sections.Procedural History:
On March 31, 1994, the district court held that it had subject-matter jurisdiction but dismissed Hakimoglu's affirmative claims, predicting that New Jersey would not recognize a dram-shop action for gambling losses. After the Third Circuit's September 6 decision in Greate Bay Hotel & Casino v. Tose, the court invited briefing on reconsideration. The casino separately moved for partial summary judgment on the unpaid markers.

On December 23, 1994, the court denied reconsideration, denied the casino's partial-summary-judgment motion without prejudice, and certified the dismissal for immediate appeal under Rule 54(b). The brief covers only this district-court stage; there was no trial, finding of incapacity, or recovery on the markers.
sections.Material Facts:
The facts on the tort claims are the complaint's allegations, accepted for purposes of the motion to dismiss. Hakimoglu alleged that the defendants enticed him to gamble at the Taj Mahal on numerous occasions in 1992 and 1993, provided free alcohol in his hotel room, and continually supplied complimentary four-to-five-ounce gin martinis while he gambled. He alleged that they kept serving him after he became visibly and substantially intoxicated, let him keep gambling, and permitted additional credit markers, and that he lost more than $2 million.

The casino's counterclaim sought $700,000 advanced through five counterchecks executed during gambling on April 25, 1993. The checks were deposited on May 12 and returned unpaid on May 20 marked "account closed." Shortly before returning to the Taj Mahal, Hakimoglu had consulted counsel about alcohol-related gambling losses and sent a letter threatening litigation against Caesars. Hakimoglu testified that he had warned his casino host about excessive service and intoxication, though the record did not show when.
sections.Issue: Did the Third Circuit's intervening decision in Greate Bay require reconsideration of the prediction that New Jersey would not recognize a dram-shop claim for gambling losses? And was the casino entitled to summary judgment on its credit markers on the theory that equitable estoppel barred Hakimoglu's intoxication defense?
sections.Holding: The U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey, in 1994, per Judge Simandle, denied reconsideration, leaving the dismissal of the dram-shop claims in place; denied without prejudice the casino's motion for partial summary judgment on the markers; and granted Rule 54(b) certification. A casino enforcing a credit marker remains subject to ordinary contract defenses, including incapacity caused by intoxication. Visible intoxication is not enough for that defense; the court quoted the requirement of intoxication so excessive and complete that the person could not realize and appreciate the nature and consequences of the act.
sections.Reasoning:
Sitting in diversity, the court had to predict New Jersey law. New Jersey dram-shop law protected persons injured by negligent alcohol service, but the court found no state authority extending it to gambling losses, which differ from drunken-driving injuries, falls, and fights.

Greate Bay decided only that the Casino Control Commission lacked exclusive primary jurisdiction and expressly reserved whether a cause of action existed; its remark that a reasonable argument could be made for a duty warranted careful consideration, not a change in the law. The court gave several reasons against expanded liability: the patron chooses to gamble; baccarat turns on chance; causation is difficult because sober patrons may lose and intoxicated ones may win; a claim brought years later lacks contemporaneous evidence; and regulation, together with the unenforceability of credit extended to a person lacking capacity, already deters misconduct.

On the markers, the Casino Control Act did not abrogate contract defenses such as incapacity from intoxication, duress, and unconscionability. Equitable estoppel can apply to contracts, but it requires justified and reasonable detrimental reliance by an innocent party. The casino offered no affidavits establishing what it knew about Hakimoglu's drinking and gambling, and his testimony about warning his host raised factual issues. The court also rejected the argument that the markers were binding because gambling enjoyment could not be restored: the consideration was $700,000 in chips, and if the defense succeeded the casino would get neither the money nor reimbursement.

Certification was proper because the dismissal resolved all of Hakimoglu's affirmative claims and the two sets of claims used different intoxication standards. The casebook's note describes a remand and quotes language about a burden of producing evidence of intoxication; the brief reports that neither appears in this district-court opinion.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-033.rule: An agreement fixing a spouse's economic rights on divorce, made mid-marriage under the other spouse's threat to divorce, arises in an inherently coercive setting and is enforced only if fair both when signed and when enforcement is sought.

sections.Parties: Antonio Pacelli filed for divorce from his wife, Francesca Pacelli, and sought to enforce a mid-marriage agreement limiting her to fixed payments in place of equitable distribution and alimony. Francesca challenged the agreement and appealed its enforcement. Antonio cross-appealed on credit for interim support and on the admission of recordings concerning an alleged cancellation of the agreement.
sections.Procedural History: Antonio filed for divorce in 1994. After a plenary trial the court entered an October 25, 1996 order upholding the agreement, finding no coercion, finding it fair as measured in 1985, and finding no credible proof of Francesca's claimed 1989 mutual cancellation. A divorce judgment followed on July 9, 1997. On March 9, 1999, the Appellate Division reversed the enforceability order, vacated the paragraph of the judgment awarding $35,000 in counsel fees, affirmed the divorce judgment in all other respects, dismissed Antonio's cross-appeal as moot, and remanded for equitable distribution, alimony, and other economic determinations.
sections.Material Facts:
The couple married in June 1975, when Antonio was forty-four and Francesca twenty; she had immigrated from Italy at fourteen. He was a builder, developer, and restaurant owner.
