Prohibition was available where the facts showed an excess of jurisdiction apparent as a matter of law and no adequate legal remedy existed, as with an unambiguous covenant and an injunction demonstrably broader than its terms.

The casebook cites the case for the five-mile office restriction and the retained freedom to make calls or treat people from the area at an outside office.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-088.rule: Contractual intention is determined as of the time the agreement was made, and statutes then in effect become part of the contract, so a promise lasting until majority refers to the age of majority when the parties contracted.

sections.Parties: Alberta Wilcox, the mother with custody of the parties' daughter Brenda Sue, and Garland Wilcox, the father, were divorced spouses. Garland moved to be relieved of further child-maintenance payments under their settlement contract once the daughter turned eighteen. The appeal challenged the judgment granting him that relief.
sections.Procedural History: The divorce action began on November 14, 1951, and judgment was entered on November 24, approving the settlement contract and incorporating it into the judgment. After Kentucky lowered the age of majority, Garland moved to be relieved of further payments. The trial court held that the change ended his duty at eighteen. Kentucky's Court of Appeals reversed on March 25, 1966, and returned the case for proceedings consistent with its opinion. The report records denial of rehearing on October 7, 1966.
sections.Material Facts:
In the 1951 divorce, the mother received custody and control of the daughter, Brenda Sue. A settlement contract provided that the father would make child-maintenance payments until the daughter reached majority or became self-supporting. The court approved the agreement and incorporated it into the divorce judgment. At that time Kentucky's age of majority was twenty-one.

Effective January 1, 1965, the legislature lowered it to eighteen. KRS 2.015 declared eighteen the age of majority generally, retaining twenty-one for alcoholic-beverage purchases and the care and treatment of handicapped children. When the dispute arose, Brenda was eighteen, attended college full time, and was not self-supporting. The trial court identified the support obligation as $40 monthly and the amount in controversy as $1,440, representing thirty-six months. Its policy would continue support only for a child still in high school, through graduation. The report treated the facts as undisputed.
sections.Issue: Where a 1951 settlement contract required child-maintenance payments until the daughter reached majority or became self-supporting, did the later statutory reduction of the age of majority from twenty-one to eighteen end the father's obligation at eighteen?
sections.Holding: Kentucky's Court of Appeals, in 1966, in an opinion by Judge Hill recording no dissent or separate writing, reversed. The contract's reference to majority meant twenty-one, the legal age when the parties made their agreement, so the father remained obligated until the daughter turned twenty-one or became self-supporting. The case was returned for consistent proceedings; the court did not itself order an itemized arrears award.
sections.Reasoning:
The court explained that contractual intention governs and must be determined by asking how the parties meant the agreement to operate when they entered it. It also invoked the principle that constitutional and statutory provisions in effect when a contract is made become part of that contract. When these parties used the word majority in 1951, its legal referent was twenty-one. The later statutory revision did not substitute eighteen as the endpoint of their existing promise.

The alternative self-support condition mattered: the court did not hold that age twenty-one was the only possible termination event. Nor did it deny that eighteen had become the statutory age of majority for general purposes. Its ruling identified the duration of a contractual promise made under the earlier law, and the trial court's high-school extension policy did not replace that promise's original endpoint.

The casebook uses the decision to ask how incorporated or legally defined terms respond to later changes in the law; its short account omits the self-support alternative and the contract's incorporation into the divorce judgment.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-089.rule: A party who knows the meaning the other party intends for an ambiguous term and accepts on that basis without communicating a different interpretation is bound by the known meaning, and the rule construing ambiguity against the drafter does not apply.

sections.Parties: Fredrick C. Hamann, a teacher at Garden City Community Junior College, sued college officials, including President Crouch, seeking damages or mandamus compelling a contract for 1970-71. He appealed the denial of reinstatement and the limits on his damages. The college officials cross-appealed the finding of liability.
sections.Procedural History: Hamann filed suit on June 12, seeking damages or mandamus. The trial court construed the ambiguous leave policy against the college as drafter, found a guarantee of reemployment, and awarded $9,928 less $3,600 in mitigation, a $6,328 judgment, while refusing reinstatement. Hamann appealed the denial of reinstatement, the mitigation calculation, and the denial of additional damages including attorney fees; the college cross-appealed. The Kansas Supreme Court reversed with directions to enter judgment for the college defendants.
sections.Material Facts:
Hamann had taught at the college since 1965. His March 17, 1969 contract covered nine months from September 1 at $9,928 and incorporated the college's rules and policies. The leave regulation said professional employees granted leave would, if possible, be reinstated in positions similar to those held when leave began. Hamann read the qualification as applying only to similarity; the college understood reinstatement itself to depend on an available position.

Hamann applied on his own for a year's teacher training at Oak Ridge Associated Universities. After acceptance on May 20, he consulted his neighbor, attorney Fleming, then not knowing the college's interpretation. His May 23 request anticipated returning to his present position; a May 26 letter granted leave according to the policy. He then spoke with President Crouch and board chairman Edwin S. Hooper, who fully informed him that reinstatement depended on an available position. He did not tell either that he read the provision differently, saying only that under that interpretation he did not feel they had a leave policy at all. He accepted leave, acknowledging at trial that he knew he was taking a chance.

In February 1970 he asked to return. Before March 15 the college notified him that no position was available. The trial court found no exactly similar position available without changing schedules, creating classes, or dismissing another teacher.
sections.Issue: Where a leave policy is ambiguous and the employee accepts leave knowing the employer's interpretation without disclosing his own, is the employee bound by the employer's known meaning, or must the ambiguity be construed against the employer as drafter?
sections.Holding: The Kansas Supreme Court, in 1973, in an opinion by Justice Kaul with no separate opinion in the report, reversed with directions to enter judgment for the college defendants. Because Hamann accepted leave knowing the college's conditional meaning of its policy, he was bound by it, and with no position available the college owed neither reinstatement nor damages. The court treated the college's first contention, that his knowledge bound him to its meaning, as dispositive.
sections.Reasoning:
Both sides conceded ambiguity. The court accepted that ambiguities ordinarily may be construed against a drafter but held that the trial court misapplied that rule to these facts. Interpretation seeks the parties' intention. Where actual ambiguity exists, oral testimony showing an operative interpretation is admissible and can be controlling. A party who knows the meaning the other intends cannot accept on that basis while silently reserving a different interpretation and later ask a court to enforce the uncommunicated version. The court cautioned that this principle cannot be a device for writing a new contract; the facts must warrant it, and here the findings and Hamann's own testimony established the required knowledge and acceptance.

Leave was discretionary, not an unconditional entitlement. Hamann could have rejected the college's conditions or stated his own position. Granting and accepting leave released him from teaching for the ensuing year and released the college from its corresponding obligations, so his remaining rights arose from the leave regulation rather than the teaching contract or the continuing-contract statute. The lawyer's earlier advice, given without knowledge of the college's meaning, was of little value.

Whether a vacancy existed involved enrollment, space, qualifications, budgets, and schedules. No finding or evidence showed fraud, bad faith, or arbitrary action, so the trial court could not replace the board's administrative judgment with its own staffing arrangements.

The casebook's problem describes Hamann consulting counsel after learning the college's interpretation, whereas the opinion places the consultation before that knowledge.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-090.rule: A usage of trade can modify or exclude an implied warranty without actual knowledge, binding those in the trade or who should be aware of it; where buyer and seller are in different trades, the seller must show the buyer knew or should have known.

sections.Parties: Hall Farms, Inc., a watermelon grower, sued Martin Rispens & Son, the retailer that sold it seed, and Petoseed, which grew the seed, for breach of express and implied warranties, negligence, and strict liability after its crop was damaged. Hall Farms sought transfer to the Indiana Supreme Court to restore the trial court's broader denial of summary judgment.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court denied the defendants summary judgment. On interlocutory appeal, the Court of Appeals directed judgment on most claims, preserved a strict-liability claim against Petoseed and one express-warranty claim against Rispens, and treated both defendants' seed-price limitations as effective for contract and tort claims. The Indiana Supreme Court granted transfer, vacated the Court of Appeals opinion, and remanded with instructions to enter summary judgment against Hall Farms on every claim except the express-warranty claims against both defendants and the implied warranty of merchantability claim against Rispens.
sections.Material Facts:
Hall Farms operated roughly 1,400 acres in Knox County and had used Prince Charles watermelon seed since 1982 or 1983. In August 1988 it ordered forty pounds from Rispens at $85.40 per pound; Rispens delivered sealed one-pound cans in February 1989. Petoseed grew the seed, the lots originating in China and Mexico.

Hall Farms germinated the seed in April. Yellow lesions appeared on about fifteen seedlings on April 25; they did not inhibit growth. The asymptomatic seedlings went into the fields in early May. A purple blotch appeared on a watermelon in early July, spread rapidly, and had ruined a significant portion of the crop by harvest. Purdue plant pathologist Richard Latin believed bacteria arrived through the seed.

Petoseed described its product as top-quality seed with high vitality, vigor, and germination. Rispens' purchase order promised strictly high-grade seeds properly fitted for seeding purposes. Rispens' disclaimer omitted merchantability and was on the unsigned reverse of the order. Petoseed's can label and Rispens' reverse-side conditions limited damages to the seed's purchase price. Mark Hall testified that he read the top of the can but not its side limitation, and had not read the reverse of the order or similar disclaimers from another seller.
sections.Issue: Which of Hall Farms' express-warranty, implied-warranty, negligence, and strict-liability claims survive summary judgment; in particular, did a seed-trade usage disclaiming warranties bind a farmer, and were the purchase-price damage limitations enforceable as a matter of law?
sections.Holding: The Indiana Supreme Court, in 1993, in a majority opinion by Justice Krahulik joined by Chief Justice Shepard and Justices DeBruler and Givan, held that express-warranty claims against both defendants and the merchantability claim against Rispens raised factual issues, that the remedy limitations did not fail of their essential purpose and were not unconscionable merely because the defect was latent but raised factual issues of assent, and that the defendants were entitled to summary judgment on strict liability and Petoseed on negligence. Justice Dickson dissented from dismissal of the strict-liability claim. No breach was established and no damages were awarded.
sections.Reasoning:
Applying Article 2 of the UCC, the court said that whether wholly written representations create express warranties is a question for the court. Top-quality seed was puffery, but high vitality, vigor, and germination described performance, and whether disease impaired that performance was a factual question. Rispens' purchase-order language was ambiguous as to latent disease, and Rispens, as movant, had not shown the absence of a factual issue.

Rispens' written disclaimer omitted merchantability and was inconspicuous. A usage of trade could still exclude the warranty, and actual knowledge is not always necessary. But Rispens sold seed while Hall Farms planted it and produced crops, so Rispens had to show that Hall Farms knew or should have known of the usage, not merely that seed merchants followed it. The affidavits and Mark Hall's testimony left that in dispute.

The limitations' purpose was to restrict liability to the seed price, and that purpose would be fulfilled; parties may allocate the risk of latent defects. A seller could not knowingly supply nonconforming goods while hiding that knowledge, but the evidence did not conclusively show it. Assent to the unread limitations remained a factual issue.

Under the then-applicable Indiana statute, physical harm included sudden, major property damage but not gradually evolving damage; the disease developed over months, and the loss was damage to the product itself. The negligence claim sought economic loss from inferior product performance.

Justice Dickson would have let a factfinder decide suddenness and rejected treating the crop as simply the purchased product.

The casebook quotes the trade distinction and asks whether buying seed should place the farmer within the same trade.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-091.rule: The parties' later discussions and conduct are strong evidence of what they understood their contract to require, and a claimed trade usage is tested in the particular market where the transaction occurred and must be shown by regular observance.

sections.Parties: Ray G. Williams of Georgia, who packaged, loaded, and sold produce grown by others, was the seller. Thomas A. Curtin of New York, who bought, stored, and sold cabbage primarily for coleslaw processing, was the buyer. Both were licensed under the Perishable Agricultural Commodities Act, or PACA. Williams claimed an unpaid $24,121.02 for delivered cabbage; Curtin counterclaimed for short delivery. Williams was the appellant.
sections.Procedural History: Williams commenced a PACA reparation proceeding when Curtin refused payment, and Curtin counterclaimed. The Department of Agriculture's judicial officer ruled for Curtin. On a trial de novo, in which the Secretary's findings were prima facie evidence, the district court adopted the supported findings after hearing testimony, including additional witnesses, and upheld the award. Williams appealed. The D.C. Circuit affirmed on December 23, 1986; the affirmed award was $47,435.10, with the interest and attorney-fee components the district court described.
sections.Material Facts:
In January 1982 Curtin visited Williams in Georgia. They agreed on roughly thirty acres of cabbage, expected to yield 600-800 tons, at $136 per ton, delivered f.o.b. between May 1 and June 15. Curtin stated a preference for large heads, twelve or fewer in a fifty-pound sack, and advanced $4,000. Williams arranged for the Baker brothers to grow the crop.

The final writing, a contract dated March 8 with Curtin's changes, referred to approximately thirty acres or 600-800 tons of slaw cabbage, at $120 per ton loose and $136 bagged, with $10,000 in advances. It contained no express numerical head-size limit.

Cabbage prices then rose from roughly $3-$4 per sack in January to as much as $12 in May. On May 6 Curtin visited; they inspected the field and found most heads not reaching the desired size. Curtin said he wanted all the cabbage he could get and would be satisfied with 400 tons. Williams did not object that only large heads qualified, and accepted another $6,000.

The field produced 518.4 tons. Williams delivered only the 152.42 tons of large cabbage to Curtin and sold the smaller heads elsewhere at about $10 a sack, against an average $3.07 for cabbage supplied to Curtin. Curtin bought on the open market at an average $400 per ton.
sections.Issue: Did the contract for slaw cabbage oblige Williams to deliver only large heads, either as the parties' actual intention or under a trade usage; and should usage be tested only by the Georgia market where the cabbage was grown and packed?
sections.Holding: The D.C. Circuit, in 1986, in an opinion by Senior District Judge Jameson, sitting by designation, for a panel with Circuit Judges Silberman and Williams and no dissent or separate opinion, affirmed. The adopted findings that the contract was not limited to large heads were not clearly erroneous; the relevant usage inquiry was the interstate coleslaw-processing market, not Georgia alone; and the finding that Williams' asserted size usage was unproved was supported by substantial evidence. The court did not need to decide choice of law.
sections.Reasoning:
The court rejected the premise that the district court ignored intention merely because it made no express finding using that word; it had adopted the judicial officer's findings about what the contract required. Later discussions and conduct were strong evidence of the parties' understanding: when both could see that too little large cabbage was growing, they discussed reducing overall tonnage, and Williams did not insist that size excluded smaller heads. His acceptance of the second advance reinforced this. Curtin's preference for large cabbage was therefore distinguishable from a contractual condition. The district court treated the May conversation as a modification reducing quantity to 400 tons, and damages were measured from the 152.42 tons received against that figure.

Williams relied on UCC section 1-205(5), on local usage where performance occurs, arguing that growing, cutting, sizing, and bagging all took place in Georgia. The court identified the pertinent performance as delivery into an interstate market: the parties lived in separate states, both were licensed for interstate produce commerce, and Williams regularly sold to out-of-state buyers. Usage requires regular observance sufficient to justify an expectation in the transaction.

On the evidence, only Williams testified to the usage before the agency; the district court found Curtin's experienced processing witnesses more persuasive; and earlier transactions between the parties used the words large cabbage rather than slaw cabbage. Because Georgia and New York had identical versions of section 1-205, choice of law did not need deciding.

The casebook simplifies the facts into a slaw-cabbage problem asking which usage would apply if both could be established.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-092.rule: A buyer's precontract examination excludes the implied warranty of merchantability only for defects that the examination ought, in the circumstances, to have revealed, and the warranty survives compliance with buyer specifications that are consistent with it.

sections.Parties: Garlock Sealing Technologies, LLC, which designed and sold industrial seals, sued its Taiwan manufacturer Mao Shun, later named NAK Sealing Technologies Corp., and Sunrise Trading, the manufacturer's American intermediary, after Garlock settled its customer Rockwell's suit over defective seals. Garlock sought damages and indemnity. Both Garlock and Mao Shun appealed the trial judgment.
sections.Procedural History: Rockwell sued Garlock in federal court in August 2001; Garlock's attempt to join Mao Shun failed for lack of personal jurisdiction in South Carolina, and Garlock settled. Garlock sued Mao Shun and Sunrise in October 2002. After a bench trial it obtained $1,870,424 plus interest and costs against Mao Shun. The court denied Garlock's indemnity claim, held Sunrise to be Mao Shun's agent, ordered that Garlock take nothing against Sunrise, and required Mao Shun to reimburse Sunrise's defense costs. The California Court of Appeal, Third District, affirmed the damages judgment and the reimbursement obligation, reversed only the denial of implied contractual indemnity, and remanded for reconsideration.
sections.Material Facts:
Garlock resold Mao Shun's seals to Rockwell for gear reducers used in conveyor systems. Garlock supplied physical-property and dimensional specifications known as RA-37 and requested the manufacturer's standard brown viton compound, without prescribing the formula or a particular pigment. Mao Shun furnished sample seals and a material slab. Garlock checked dimensions, configuration, and standard ASTM physical properties, and the samples complied. It did not functionally test them in an operating gearbox; its engineer explained that such testing normally applied to a newly configured component using a new compound. Mao Shun formulated the compound itself and neither sifted nor tested the pigment for particle size.

The brown seals produced almost a thirty-percent leakage rate, sometimes failing after 150 operating hours. Investigators found grooves in hardened steel shafts, and laboratory analysis identified hard, sharp-edged magnetite particles in the brown pigment. Green viton replacement seals cut leakage to one or two percent and eliminated grooving.

Garlock settled with Rockwell for $2.2 million cash, $150,000 in refunds and discounts, and potential further discounts of $530,000, a stated value of $2.88 million.
sections.Issue: Did the manufacturer's compliance with the buyer's specifications, or the buyer's precontract examination of samples, displace the implied warranty of merchantability for a latent abrasive defect? Were consequential damages recoverable, was Sunrise the manufacturer's agent, and does implied contractual indemnity require proof of negligence?
sections.Holding: The California Court of Appeal, Third District, in 2007, in an opinion by Justice Cantil-Sakauye with Acting Presiding Justice Raye and Justice Butz concurring, held that merchantability survived both the specifications and Garlock's reasonable inspection, that the breach finding and consequential damages were supported, and that Sunrise was Mao Shun's actual agent. It held that implied contractual indemnity does not require proof of negligent breach and remanded that claim, declining to award indemnity itself or decide its ultimate equitable merits.
sections.Reasoning:
Mao Shun argued that complying with the buyer's specifications displaced merchantability. Even assuming the specifications created an express warranty in addition to the warranty by sample the trial court found, the warranties were reasonably consistent and cumulative under California UCC section 2317. Garlock specified standard material and dimensions and left the chemical formulation to the manufacturer. The court confined this to a standard component whose ingredients and potential flaws were unknown to the buyer.

Section 2316(3)(b) removes an implied warranty for defects that a precontract examination ought, in the circumstances, to have revealed. The trial court found the abrasiveness latent and not reasonably discoverable through applicable testing practices. Mao Shun's challenge attacked the evidence for a factual finding, and its incomplete and misleading summary forfeited it; the court also rejected it on the merits. The test is what examination ought to reveal, not whether a more elaborate test conceivably could detect a flaw.

A seal that abraded shafts and prematurely lost oil failed its ordinary purpose. Under section 2715(2)(a) the seller needed reason to know of requirements and exposure to loss, not foresight of this precise defect; a longtime seal manufacturer could anticipate that abrasive seals would damage shafts. The $1,678,267 consequential component applied a 73.79-percent share to a $2,274,383 valuation of the settlement payment.

Substantial evidence, including a 1981 written agreement, supported Sunrise's actual agency.

Implied contractual indemnity derives from contractual responsibilities and a breach foreseeably causing the indemnitee's third-party loss, so breach of merchantability could support it without unreasonable care.

The casebook uses the case as a latent-defect problem that simplifies the supply chain and assumes unmerchantability uncontested.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-093.rule: Unconscionability is evaluated as of the time the bargain is made, not in hindsight from the work eventually required or the result eventually achieved.

sections.Parties: The accounting partnership Langrall, Muir & Noppinger sued its clients Harry and Virginia Gladding to collect compensation under a contingent-fee agreement. The Gladdings defended on nonperformance and unconscionability and counterclaimed for return of the retainer. The Gladdings were the petitioners in the Maryland Court of Appeals.
sections.Procedural History: The partnership sued in the Superior Court of Baltimore City. After a nonjury trial, Judge Basil A. Thomas resolved all issues for the partnership and entered judgment for $30,639. The Court of Special Appeals affirmed in an unreported decision, and the Court of Appeals granted certiorari. There the taxpayers abandoned the contention that the accountants had breached their performance obligation. The Court of Appeals affirmed on May 28, 1979, with costs on the petitioners.
sections.Material Facts:
An IRS audit report dated June 16, 1969 assessed the Gladdings and corporations they owned or controlled approximately $1.3 million in additional taxes and penalties for 1961 through 1966. On the advice of his personal attorney, John Demyan, Harry contacted Herbert Langrall, senior partner of the accounting firm, who proposed bringing in Jacques Schlenger of the law firm Venable, Baetjer and Howard. At an early January 1970 meeting of Gladding, Demyan, Schlenger, and Langrall, the participants orally agreed to employ both firms; separate written agreements followed several weeks later.

The accountants' agreement provided a $10,000 retainer and a contingent payment of four percent of the first $700,000 in tax savings and three percent of savings above that. It promised best efforts and denied any guarantee of results. The law firm's agreement provided a $20,000 retainer and sixteen percent of the first $700,000 saved plus twelve percent of additional savings.

The IRS's internal review procedures produced a settlement saving the taxpayers $1,121,000, largely through the law firm's work. The accountants' time records showed only seventeen professional hours and a minimal contribution. The taxpayers refused the claimed balance, described as $30,639 allegedly due after crediting the retainer; the report does not reconcile that credit with the fee clause's wording.
sections.Issue: Did the disparity between the accountants' modest work, seventeen professional hours, and their substantial contingent compensation make the fee agreement unconscionable?
sections.Holding: The Maryland Court of Appeals, in 1979, in an opinion by Judge Digges with no separate writing, affirmed the judgment enforcing the accountants' contingent fee. Unconscionability must be evaluated when the bargain is made, and the taxpayers made no assertion that the agreement was unfair when negotiated. The court assumed without deciding that rescission or cancellation could be asserted in an action at law and raised through general-issue pleas.
sections.Reasoning:
The court held that unconscionability is judged at the time of the bargain, not retrospectively from the work eventually required or the outcome achieved. Later circumstances can make a bargain much more favorable to one party without making its original terms unconscionable. The court relied on Maryland's rescission and cancellation decisions and referred by analogy to the commercial statute's formation-time treatment of unconscionable goods contracts.

The taxpayers' objective when contracting was relief from an extraordinary tax assessment, not the purchase of a set number of professional hours. Choosing contingent compensation reflected willingness to pay for a favorable outcome, and both sides took a chance on the degree of success. That the law firm did most of the work was undisputed, but it did not defeat the accountants' contractual right once the breach contention was abandoned.

The court also noted that the two firms' combined contingent percentages would not exceed twenty percent of the savings and that the taxpayers had their own attorney's advice throughout negotiation. These supported the result here.

The taxpayers argued that the special scrutiny given attorney-client fee agreements should extend to accountants. The court rejected the equivalence because the judicial interest in lawyers' fees arose from their status as officers of the court. Even assuming comparable confidentiality could attach to accountant-client relations, the relationship here did not exist until after the contract was formed.

The casebook presents the case for the disproportion between seventeen hours and the fee and for the distinction between supervision of lawyers' and accountants' fees.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-094.rule: Under the False Claims Act as then worded, a demand on a grantee or other recipient is a claim if the United States provided any portion of the money; and a staffing figure appearing only in a cost estimate is not a contractual commitment.

sections.Parties: The relators, DRC, Inc., a subcontractor, and its managing director Robert Isakson, sued on behalf of the United States under the False Claims Act against the contractor Custer Battles, LLC and individual defendants. Former employee William Baldwin separately claimed whistleblower retaliation. The government declined to intervene but participated as amicus. The relators were the appellants.
sections.Procedural History: The district court dismissed a conspiracy count, limited the currency-contract fraud claims to a $3 million Treasury-funded advance, and severed the airport-contract claim, on which it granted summary judgment. A jury found the defendants liable under the then-existing sections 3729(a)(1) and (a)(2), awarded $3 million in fraud damages, and awarded Baldwin $165,000 for retaliation. Before judgment on the fraud verdict, the district court granted a deferred Rule 50(a) motion for judgment as a matter of law, considering presentment insufficient. The Fourth Circuit reversed the currency-claim restriction and the Rule 50 judgment, affirmed summary judgment on the airport claim, and remanded.
sections.Material Facts:
The Coalition Provisional Authority governed Iraq from May 2003 until June 28, 2004, staffed largely from the United States but also from other coalition countries. On August 27, 2003 it contracted with Custer Battles to build, equip, and service three currency-exchange hubs at Baghdad, Mosul, and Basra for actual costs plus twenty-five percent for overhead and profit. The Authority advanced $3 million by a Treasury check drawn on seized Iraqi assets and later paid roughly $12 million from the Development Fund for Iraq, which included $210 million in Iraqi bank funds confiscated by the United States and transferred to it. Invoices usually reached American contracting officers detailed to the Authority.

After an October 18, 2003 meeting, Michael Battles accidentally left a spreadsheet comparing actual costs with billed amounts, including two trucks costing $18,000 billed at $80,000 and generators costing $74,000 billed at $400,000.

The separate airport-security contract was a fixed-price undertaking for $16,840,832, beginning August 31, 2003. The relators alleged fraudulent inducement because staffing dropped below about 138 personnel. A 138.5-person figure appeared only in the contractor's cost estimate supporting its price.
sections.Issue: Did demands paid from the Development Fund for Iraq qualify as claims under the False Claims Act though the United States did not pay the contractor directly; was presentment to American personnel detailed to the Authority sufficient; and did the airport contract's cost-estimate staffing figure support a fraudulent-inducement claim?
sections.Holding: The Fourth Circuit, in 2009, in an opinion by Judge Niemeyer for a unanimous panel with Judges Shedd and Duncan, held that the false demands under the currency contract qualified as claims and that the evidence permitted a jury to find presentment, and reversed. It affirmed summary judgment on the airport claim because the staffing figure was not a contractual commitment. On remand the relators could elect a new currency trial; if they declined, the district court was to consider the remaining Rule 50 grounds and enter judgment on the verdict only if it rejected them.
sections.Reasoning:
The district court treated only the $3 million advance as American property. Under section 3729(c) as then applicable, a claim included demands on a grantee or other recipient if the United States provided any portion of the money requested. A claim paid from a grantee's mixed funds could therefore qualify in full, and the inclusion of grantees defeated any requirement that the government keep title or control after transfer. The contract's statement that no coalition country's funds would be obligated did not answer the statutory question, which asked whether the United States had provided funds; the $210 million contribution supplied the connection. Nor was privity with the United States required.

Qualifying claims and recoverable damages were distinct: damages were limited to loss sustained by the United States, which the court could not resolve on appeal.

On presentment, the district court assumed that personnel detailed to an international Authority stopped acting in their American official capacities. The evidence permitted the opposite conclusion: contracting officer Patricia Logsdon was paid by the Army Contracting Agency, held a government contracting warrant, and reported to an American colonel. The court did not have to hold that the Authority was an American instrumentality. Allison Engine, decided after the district court's ruling, rejected a presentment requirement for section (a)(2).

On the airport claim, neither the proposal nor the operative agreements fixed a staffing level, no personnel-cost invoices were submitted under the fixed-price arrangement, and the responsible minister confirmed that payment did not require particular staffing.

The casebook's account calls the currency ruling summary judgment, describes the government as appellant, and gives a $20 million contract; the opinion differs on each point.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-095.rule: An employee's salary is consideration for her promise to arbitrate without a matching employer promise, and section 2 of the FAA bars states from burdening arbitration clauses more than other terms in form contracts.

sections.Parties: Oblix, Inc., an employer with its principal place of business in California, brought a declaratory action to require its former employee Felicia Winiecki to arbitrate her claims. Winiecki counterclaimed for substantive relief, asserting unpaid compensation and that her discharge and other conduct violated Title VII. Oblix appealed the refusal to compel arbitration.
sections.Procedural History: The federal district court in Illinois denied arbitration on April 23, 2003, believing further discovery and litigation were needed to determine unconscionability, and invited reconsideration in light of the Supreme Court's PacifiCare decision. Oblix moved on May 19; the district court again refused arbitration on July 1, and Oblix appealed on July 3. The Seventh Circuit held the appeal timely, reversed, and remanded with instructions to refer the parties to arbitration and dismiss Winiecki's counterclaim.
sections.Material Facts: Winiecki began working for Oblix in September 2000 and signed an employment agreement requiring arbitration. One clause specifically covered disputes over salary, severance, and similar amounts; another required binding AAA arbitration of disputes relating to interpretation, construction, performance, or breach of the employment agreement. The agreement selected California law. It was offered on a take-it-or-leave-it basis and did not require Oblix to arbitrate every claim it might have against the employee; for example, Oblix could seek a judicial forum for an alleged taking of trade secrets. Winiecki was terminated in April 2002.
sections.Issue: Was the arbitration clause in a take-it-or-leave-it employment agreement unenforceable for want of consideration or as unconscionable because the employer was not bound to arbitrate all of its own claims, and could California law impose additional requirements on employment arbitration consistently with the FAA?
sections.Holding: The Seventh Circuit, in 2004, in an opinion by Judge Easterbrook for a panel with Judges Diane P. Wood and Williams and no dissent or concurrence, reversed. The agreement covered Winiecki's compensation and discriminatory-discharge claims and was enforceable under ordinary contract rules: her salary supported the arbitration promise, a matching employer promise was unnecessary, and the take-it-or-leave-it character of the offer did not make it unconscionable. The court decided the forum only, not the merits of her claims.
sections.Reasoning:
On timeliness, the reconsideration motion did not toll the thirty-day period, but the July 1 refusal was independently appealable under the FAA, and circuit precedent treated a refusal to direct arbitration while conducting arbitrability discovery as an appealable denial.

The clauses' wording covered the compensation and discharge disputes. The court distinguished broad substantive coverage from delegation of arbitrability itself; the wording did not commit arbitrability to the arbitrator, so the panel addressed scope and unconscionability.

The panel rejected the idea that salary was consideration for work but not for the accompanying arbitration promise. Winiecki did not dispute that her salary supported the obligation: the employment exchange purchased several promises together. A matching promise by the employer to arbitrate every claim was not needed. The court compared the arbitration term to a nonnegotiable salary offer: unwillingness to negotiate does not entitle the employee to substitute better terms after accepting the package.

Invoking Prima Paint, the panel said a generalized objection to standard-form contracting attacked the entire bargain and could itself go to arbitration, but it nonetheless addressed and rejected the unconscionability argument.

Section 2 of the FAA prevents states from imposing on arbitration clauses special burdens not imposed on other form-contract provisions; California enforces other standard terms such as releases and indemnity provisions. Winiecki read Armendariz to require extra protections for employment arbitration; the court treated the competing readings of that decision as immaterial given the federal bar on special disfavor of arbitration.

The casebook uses the case twice, once for salary as consideration and once for asymmetry and FAA equal treatment; a linked casebook note sets the court's arbitration observations beside later empirical studies.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-096.rule: Under Mississippi precedent a proved oral agreement to devise real property does not support specific performance; the promisee who relied may recover money, here through a constructive trust for the amount invested plus interest.

sections.Parties: Grandchildren Christine Ladner, called Christy, and Theodore Bilbo, called Ted, petitioned for specific performance of their late grandfather Richard Horrigan's oral promise that his house and garage apartment would pass to them, and alternatively for a constructive trust, quantum meruit, or restitution. His widow Eunice, called Sue, daughter Eunice LeBlanc, and Roy Horrigan denied any agreement and sought rent. The family appealed and the grandchildren cross-appealed.
sections.Procedural History: LeBlanc sought probate in September 1996; Christy filed a caveat, later withdrawn, and the original will was reinstated before trial. In May 1997 the grandchildren petitioned for specific performance and related relief. After an October 1998 trial, Chancellor Thomas Teel granted specific performance, set aside a conveyance of one lot to LeBlanc, and ordered the grandchildren to pay $600 monthly rent for the house, but not the apartment, from judgment. The Mississippi Supreme Court affirmed repayment of the renovation investment with interest through a constructive trust, reversed the award of ownership interests, sustained the rent obligation, and remanded. Rehearing was denied on March 16, 2000.
sections.Material Facts:
Richard Horrigan promised Christy and Ted that if they invested their funds in renovating his house and garage apartment, the property would pass to them after he and his wife Sue died. The grandchildren alleged the agreement was made in 1989. They invested $22,178, a majority of their savings. Richard had served as their Louisiana tutor, a role the opinion equates with guardianship in Mississippi, and was responsible for funds awarded after their mother's death. The grandparents urged them to use money of which they had previously been unaware for the improvements. Their father co-signed the expenditure checks, and the tutor's legal duties ended when they reached Louisiana majority.

Richard died testate on March 5, 1996. His will did not implement the oral arrangement. Sue denied the arrangement, but the fact finder credited contrary testimony. A purported witness to a supposed holographic will could not recall its words. Demands for rent arose after the will contest and its litigation expenses.
sections.Issue: Could the grandchildren obtain specific performance of an unwritten promise to leave them real property on which they had relied, or were they limited to recovering their investment; and could they be charged rent for occupying the house?
sections.Holding: The Mississippi Supreme Court, in 1999, in an opinion by Justice McRae, with five justices concurring, two concurring only in the result, and Justice Cobb concurring in part and dissenting in part without opinion, held that the oral agreement was proved but could not be specifically enforced. The grandchildren were entitled to a constructive trust for $22,178 plus interest from the date of their last payment, dissolved on repayment, and not to ownership of the property. They had to vacate the house or pay Sue, as life tenant, $600 monthly from November 1998; the apartment remained rent-free.
sections.Reasoning:
The chancellor believed the oral agreement existed and relied on a supposed holographic will to treat the promise as irrevocable. The court separated the two. There was no substantial proof of a holographic will, since there was no sufficient evidence of its contents or execution. But that did not undo the supported finding that the grandparents promised the property and induced the investment.

The court said detrimental reliance and complete performance justified equitable estoppel, but preserved a remedial limit: under Mississippi precedent, proof of an unwritten agreement to devise real property did not permit specific performance, and agreements to exchange property for services without an executed will could support quantum meruit rather than a compelled conveyance. The court therefore gave monetary protection against unjust enrichment and refused the promised ownership.

Constructive trusts require clear and convincing proof and more than the bare existence of a family or confidential relationship; the court discussed the need for abuse of confidence or substantial overreaching. Despite the countervailing circumstances, it relied on the grandfather's tutor role, the grandparents' solicitation of the savings, the promise-induced investment, and the unfair enrichment that would otherwise result. The contribution was admitted by the family's attorney at oral argument.

On rent, the court upheld the finding that the grandchildren were to have the apartment without rent but rejected a right to occupy the house indefinitely rent-free; nothing showed $600 was unfair.

The casebook notes emphasize the contrast between repayment and specific performance; their description of a repayment lien simply affirmed on review compresses the actual sequence.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-097.rule: To avoid a release for economic duress a party must show involuntary acceptance, no reasonably available alternative, and circumstances resulting from the other party's coercive conduct; its own financial difficulty or a disparity in size is not enough.

sections.Parties: Undersea Engineering & Construction Co., a subcontractor, and Shelton Engineering, its sub-subcontractor, sued International Telephone & Telegraph Corp., the prime contractor on a Navy project, and Healy-Tibbitts, another subcontractor. Undersea asserted contract, unjust-enrichment, and mooring-damage tort claims and alleged economic coercion to avoid a settlement release. Shelton sought $88,290.15 in quasi-contract from ITT. The plaintiffs appealed.
sections.Procedural History: Undersea and Shelton sued in November 1967 in federal district court in Hawaii. District Judge Martin Pence, in a decision signed August 26, 1968, granted the defendants summary judgment on all claims and dismissed the defendants' counterclaims; the court also rejected a judicial-bias affidavit and imposed costs and attorney fees as a sanction. The Ninth Circuit, per curiam, affirmed the summary judgment and the disqualification and sanctions orders, expressly adopting the district court's reasoning and reproducing its decision as an appendix. Rehearing was denied on July 21, 1970.
sections.Material Facts:
ITT held a Navy contract to install an offshore hydrophone system near Kauai and on June 10, 1966 subcontracted work to Undersea. Disputes arose over support services, delay, price, modifications, and quality. Undersea claimed overhead and lost profit for support services ITT did not use, and standby charges and more pay because a cable-laying vessel expected in August 1966 arrived in February 1967, for reasons outside ITT's control. ITT rejected the demands and asserted defective-work claims.

Undersea kept performing and negotiating while threatening suit. Its vice president David Glickman, a California lawyer, wrote in August 1967 threatening about $200,000 in compensatory and $100 million in punitive damages, worldwide distribution of legal papers, and complaints to federal agencies, while offering to settle for $108,000. Undersea was capitalized at $25,000.

In September 1967 ITT offered $40,000 for claims apart from the fixed-price portion and $5,000 for that portion, conditioned on a release of all claims connected with the subcontract. Undersea accepted by cable and confirmed its release by letter of October 3. ITT mailed the $45,000 check on October 5; its endorsement identified final payment and release. Undersea alleged that ITT deliberately withheld payment and exploited its impending bankruptcy to secure a cheap settlement.
sections.Issue: Could Undersea avoid its release on the ground of economic duress, and, apart from the release, could it recover for the mooring damage or Shelton recover in quasi-contract from the prime contractor?
sections.Holding: The Ninth Circuit, in 1970, in a per curiam opinion by Judges Jertberg, Browning, and Hufstedler with no separate writings, affirmed, adopting the district court's reasoning. The unambiguous release covered Undersea's contract, restitution, and tort demands connected with the subcontract, and the undisputed record lacked the facts needed to establish duress. The claim against Healy-Tibbitts and Shelton's restitution claim also failed. The bias affidavit was legally insufficient and the sanction lay within the district court's discretion.
sections.Reasoning:
The merits reasoning is the district court's, adopted on appeal. The release unambiguously covered claims arising in connection with the subcontract, without resort to extrinsic evidence, so coercion was the central route to avoiding it.

The court required facts showing involuntary acceptance, no reasonably available alternative, and circumstances resulting from ITT's coercive conduct. Assertions of financial difficulty or reluctance did not establish those elements. The record showed Undersea initiating negotiations, pressing its demands for almost six months, and keeping litigation available; settlement was its chosen alternative to suit, not its only reasonable choice.

Coercion could not be inferred from relative size alone. Even assuming bankruptcy motivated acceptance, the claimant had to connect that pressure to wrongful and oppressive acts of the opponent rather than its own necessities. The claims and counterclaims had remained unliquidated and disputed for months, and an alleged isolated statement that ITT would break Undersea financially was insufficient in the documented context.

On the mooring, the court discussed the then-applied joint-tortfeasor release rule and separately found no damages: Undersea had been paid the full $28,000 subcontract price and ITT replaced the mooring at its own expense.

Shelton's theory ignored ITT's admitted payment of about $247,000 to Undersea. Shelton had an express subcontract with Undersea and no alleged contractual dealings with ITT; absent legislation specifically permitting recovery, no implied payment obligation would be imposed on the prime contractor merely because it benefited.

On disqualification, filing an affidavit does not automatically disqualify a judge, who may determine its legal sufficiency.

The casebook note observes that Undersea itself applied extensive pressure, which is accurate but not the complete legal test.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-001.rule: An instrument diminishing legal rights that would otherwise exist, such as an exculpatory clause, is construed strictly against the party invoking it and must state the parties' intention with particularity.

sections.Parties: The plaintiff, Galligan, was a tenant in the defendants' apartment building. She sued the defendant landlords in trespass, alleging that their negligence caused her injury. The landlords pleaded an exculpatory clause in her lease as a defense. The tenant appealed after judgment was entered for the landlords.
sections.Procedural History: The tenant sued in trespass. The defendants pleaded new matter asserting that an exculpatory clause in the lease relieved them of liability, and the trial court entered judgment on the pleadings for the landlords. The Pennsylvania Supreme Court reversed on April 19, 1966, with a procedendo, returning the action for further proceedings rather than awarding damages or finding negligence established.
sections.Material Facts: On August 4, 1961, the plaintiff tripped on the lawn in front of the defendants' apartment building, where she was a tenant, and was injured. Her lease contained a clause requiring the tenant to relieve the lessor of liability for injuries associated with the use, misuse, or abuse of elevators, hatches, openings, stairways, fire escapes, hallways, and the sidewalks surrounding the buildings. The clause also included language about defective construction, failures of utilities and equipment, weather, and other causes on the premises, and expressly referred to negligence by the lessor or its agents. The plaintiff argued that the lawn was not within the specified locations and that the clause was invalid as contrary to public policy.
sections.Issue: Did the exculpatory clause in the lease, which listed seven locations including the sidewalks surrounding the buildings, bar on the pleadings a tenant's negligence action for a fall on the lawn in front of the building?
sections.Holding: The Pennsylvania Supreme Court, in 1966, in an opinion by Justice Cohen, reversed the judgment on the pleadings. Of the seven justices, five supported reversal, Justices Eagen and Roberts concurring in the result, and Chief Justice Bell and Justice Jones dissented without published explanation. Strictly construed, the clause did not reach the fall: none of its seven listed locations included a lawn, so it did not support judgment against the plaintiff at the pleadings stage.
sections.Reasoning:
The court held that an instrument diminishing legal rights that would otherwise exist must be construed strictly against the party invoking it and must state the parties' intention with particularity. It also applied the rule construing a written instrument strictly against its maker. Either rule, the opinion said, was enough to require reversal. Without the clause the plaintiff could not properly suffer judgment on the pleadings, so the claimed surrender of her right to recover for negligent injury had to fit this occurrence precisely.

None of the seven listed locations included a lawn. A lawn and a sidewalk are different places, and neither encompasses the other. The court distinguished Bryans v. Gallagher, where an injury on a driveway fell within a similarly worded provision because the driveway was the sole means of ingress and egress and had been agreed to be the sidewalk the clause contemplated; there was no comparable agreement here. The opinion does not separately analyze the clause's general references to causes on the premises.

Justice Cohen then added what he expressly called personal observations unnecessary to the decision: standardized apartment leases contain a provision landlords will not delete, leaving the tenant without bargaining power, and a rule premised on free bargaining should not be extended to that setting. He did not dispute the existing rule enforcing negligence covenants made by private individuals in their personal affairs.

Justice Roberts, concurring in the result, considered the clause a contract of adhesion lacking a meeting of the minds, contrary to public policy, and without legal effect. Justice Eagen gave no reasons.

The casebook uses the case to illustrate strict construction of an exculpatory provision.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-004.rule: Under Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 211, a standardized term is not part of the agreement if the drafter has reason to believe the adhering party would not assent if aware of it.

sections.Parties: Darner Motor Sales operated an automobile sales, service and leasing business. It brought third-party claims against Universal Underwriters Insurance Co. and Doxsee, a full-time employee and agent of Universal who had solicited Darner's insurance business. Darner sought to hold them responsible for lessee coverage at $100,000 per person and $300,000 per accident under four related theories: equitable estoppel, reformation, negligent misrepresentation and fraud.
sections.Procedural History:
After a judgment against one of its renters left a shortfall above the lessee limits Universal paid, Darner brought third-party claims against Universal and Doxsee. Both lower courts rejected the claims, principally through the policy terms and a duty to read; summary judgment went against Darner, and the Court of Appeals issued a memorandum decision and an appellate attorney-fee award.

The Arizona Supreme Court decided the case on March 29, 1984, and denied reconsideration on May 22. It vacated the Court of Appeals' memorandum decision, reversed summary judgment on equitable estoppel, reformation, negligent misrepresentation and fraud, and vacated the appellate attorney-fee award, allowing the disputed claims to proceed to trial.
sections.Material Facts:
In 1973 Doxsee solicited Darner's insurance business. The November 1973 U-Drive policy provided limits of $100,000 per person and $300,000 per accident for Darner but $15,000/$30,000 for lessees. In April 1975 Darner acquired Universal's Unicover umbrella package and renewed the U-Drive coverage.

Joel Darner wanted lessees covered at $100,000/$300,000, and Darner's rental form promised those limits. He read the U-Drive limits and contacted Doxsee about the discrepancy. Darner and sales manager Hadley testified that Doxsee assured them the umbrella would supply the higher coverage; Doxsee did not recall the conversation but denied he would have made such an assurance. These were disputed accounts on summary judgment, not findings.

The umbrella later arrived as a lengthy loose-leaf book, which Darner did not read. The actual umbrella policy was absent from the appellate record, so the court assumed against Darner that it clearly and unambiguously excluded lessees from the definition of insured.

About twenty months after the transaction, renter Crawford, using an older rental form promising the higher limits, negligently injured a pedestrian, who recovered $60,000 against him. Universal paid $15,000; Darner had paid or was liable for the remaining $45,000.
sections.Issue: Do unread standardized policy terms and the duty to read bar, as a matter of law, an insured's claims for equitable estoppel, reformation, negligent misrepresentation and fraud based on the insurer's agent's alleged assurance of coverage that the boilerplate, assumed to be clear and unambiguous, excludes?
sections.Holding: Arizona Supreme Court, 1984, Justice Feldman, 4-1. No. The court adopted Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 211 and rejected a categorical rule that estoppel can never establish insurance coverage beyond printed limitations. If the factfinder determined that Darner and Doxsee agreed to $100,000/$300,000 lessee coverage and Darner justifiably relied on the assurance without knowing of the umbrella exclusion, Universal could be estopped from asserting the boilerplate definition excluding lessees. Summary judgment was also improper on reformation, negligent misrepresentation and fraud. The court did not finally reform the policy, award damages or establish additional coverage.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority criticized treating an insurance form as though every provision reflected an individually negotiated intention: standardized agreements serve necessary commercial functions, but most boilerplate is neither negotiated nor read. Creating fictitious ambiguity to escape an unjust result was unsatisfactory. The better starting point was to ask what expectations had actually been induced by a promise or conduct; a policyholder's mere hope of coverage does not qualify.

Under § 211, a person who assents to a writing known to be a standardized agreement is ordinarily bound, but a particular term is not part of the agreement if the drafter has reason to believe the adhering party would not assent if aware of it. Prior negotiations and surrounding circumstances may show that reason, as may a term that is bizarre or oppressive, defeats expressly agreed terms, or eliminates the transaction's dominant purpose. The court did not abolish writings, integration or the duty to read.

Estoppel requires conduct inducing a belief, justifiable reliance and resulting injury; reasonableness was a factual question, and delivery of the policy before the loss did not automatically defeat the claim. Reformation for one party's mistake requires fraud or inequitable conduct by the other, and the disputed evidence could show the writing differed from the actual agreement. Doxsee, though Universal's agent and not Darner's fiduciary, still owed reasonable professional care; failure to read did not conclusively bar negligence. Fraud required all nine elements; the evidence appeared especially weak but was not wholly without merit.

Justice Cameron, concurring, stressed that standardized forms still bind and that only expectations induced by words or conduct matter. Chief Justice Holohan, dissenting, saw the majority as abandoning precedent and letting oral accounts undermine written limits. The casebook cites the case for the § 211 limitation on an undisclosed standardized term contradicting the bargain.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-005.rule: Under Mississippi law as the Fifth Circuit read it, illiteracy does not defeat a signed agreement; a signer who cannot read must obtain assistance, and the other party need not explain the document.

sections.Parties: Washington Mutual Finance Group, a lender, and four insurers that intervened sought to compel arbitration. The opposing parties were six borrowers (John Phinizee, Willie Curry, Beulah Tate, Violet Smith, John Bailey and Helen Spellman) and John Phinizee's wife, Miriah, who had sued the lender and insurers in Mississippi state court and resisted arbitration. The lender and insurers were the appellants in the Fifth Circuit.
sections.Procedural History:
The borrowers and Miriah Phinizee sued the lender and insurers in Mississippi state court. The lender responded with separate federal actions under FAA § 4 seeking arbitration and a stay of the state cases; the insurers intervened, and the federal district court consolidated the actions.

The district court found the six borrowers illiterate and found that the lender had not specifically told them they were signing arbitration agreements. Treating that combination as procedural unconscionability, it denied the motion to compel and the insurers' summary-judgment motion and granted the borrowers' motion to dismiss. It also refused to compel Miriah because she had not signed an arbitration agreement.

On March 19, 2004, the Fifth Circuit reversed the refusal to compel arbitration and the dismissal of the lender's federal action, and remanded for entry of an order compelling arbitration for every party to the action.
sections.Material Facts:
Six borrowers obtained loans from Washington Mutual Finance or its predecessors and bought associated insurance from four insurers. Each signed an agreement to arbitrate disputes with the lender. The arbitration agreement was a separate document with a prominent capitalized alternative-dispute-resolution heading.

The borrowers and Miriah Phinizee later sued in state court, primarily alleging that they had been sold and charged for insurance they neither needed nor wanted; those were allegations, not findings of the appellate court. The district court found the six borrowers illiterate. The borrowers argued that they had told the lender they could not read and had asked what they were signing, and that the documents were described as insurance and finance papers. None of the borrowers obtained a reading of the arbitration agreement.

Miriah had obtained no loan or insurance herself. Whether she co-signed her husband's loan and insurance papers was disputed; it was undisputed that she had not signed the arbitration agreement. All her claims depended on rights arising from those transactions.
sections.Issue: Under Mississippi contract law, are arbitration agreements that the borrowers admittedly signed unenforceable as procedurally unconscionable because the borrowers were illiterate and the lender did not specifically tell them they were signing arbitration agreements, or because of an allegedly fraudulent description of the documents? And can a nonsignatory spouse whose claims depend on the transactions be compelled to arbitrate?
sections.Holding: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, 2004, Judge E. Grady Jolly for a panel with no separate writing. The arbitration agreements were enforceable. Mississippi precedent did not make inability to read sufficient to defeat a signed agreement, and the lender's failure to give a specific oral explanation did not change that. The fraudulent-description defense failed on its merits. Miriah Phinizee was bound to arbitrate by equitable estoppel although she had not signed. The decision enforces the forum agreements and does not decide whether the underlying insurance practices were wrongful.
sections.Reasoning:
Reviewing the § 4 determination de novo, the court asked whether the parties agreed to arbitrate and whether a federal statute or policy made the claims nonarbitrable; none was asserted. Both sides agreed Mississippi contract law governed formation and validity.

The borrowers' challenge went to the process of formation. There was no coercion allegation, and print, complexity and bargaining power were not disputed on appeal; the district court's grounds were illiteracy and the absence of specific oral disclosure. Mississippi decisions charged signers with knowledge of the documents they executed and did not permit avoidance because they had neither read the document nor had it read to them. An illiterate signer therefore had to obtain assistance, and illiteracy did not shift that responsibility to the other party. Because proof of illiteracy would not alter the result, the court left unresolved the objection that the district court used material outside the pleadings.

On fraud, the record showed only general inquiries about the package of documents and a general response that was not plainly misleading, and any inaccurate impression would have been corrected by reading or obtaining a reading. The court could decide this defense itself because it was directed specifically to the arbitration agreement, not the entire contract.

As to Miriah, a claimant could not seek benefits from a transaction while disavowing its arbitration burden solely because she had not signed. Marriage alone was not the basis; the dependence of her claims on the contractual transactions was. The court applied federal substantive arbitrability law to that question and saw no reason to expect a different result under Mississippi law.

The casebook uses the case to illustrate signed borrowers' duty to read or obtain a reading under Mississippi law.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-006.rule: A private act amending an insurer's charter will not be read as silently exempting that insurer from a general statute protecting insureds against avoidance for innocent misstatements; the two acts are harmonized.

sections.Parties: Randolph DeLancey, the insured and plaintiff, sued Rockingham Farmers' Mutual Fire Insurance Co. on an insurance policy. DeLancey invoked a general statute protecting insureds against avoidance for misstatements not intentionally and fraudulently made. The insurer defended on the ground that his inaccurate description of his title voided the policy under a later special provision of its charter.
sections.Procedural History: DeLancey sued on the policy. He testified, over the insurer's exception, about the understandings and payments behind the title transfers, and a jury found his interest sufficiently valuable for the amount insured. The New Hampshire report places the decision in June 1873. The court directed judgment for the plaintiff on the policy; it did not order a new trial to determine whether the insurer committed fraud. The report does not specify the amount of the judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
DeLancey's policy, dated November 19, 1866, purported to insure his house, clothing and provisions. The property's title involved the estate of Moses Hobbs, whose widow, three brothers and sister (DeLancey's wife) held interests. The widow conveyed her interest to the siblings in February 1866; two brothers conveyed to DeLancey in April; the remaining interests reached him through conveyances in April 1867. The house was worth $2,883.33 when insured; the application estimated $1,400 and the policy insured $1,050.

The signed application described the property as his and unencumbered. As Justice Doe analyzed it, he held absolute legal title to only part, as a tenant in common. The application agreed to the charter and bylaws, and the policy incorporated the application and annexed the charter, its 1862 amendment and the bylaws. The promise to insure was in prominent legible print; restrictive material was in small, compact, difficult print.

An 1855 general statute prevented avoidance for an error, mistake or misrepresentation unless intentionally and fraudulently made. An 1862 private act amending this insurer's charter stated that a policy would be void if the insured held less than an unencumbered fee and the true title was not stated. DeLancey's inaccurate title description was not intentional and fraudulent.
sections.Issue: Did the 1862 private act amending the insurer's charter exempt this company from the 1855 general statute, so that an innocent misdescription of title voided the policy? And did the insured, by agreeing to the annexed charter, waive the statutory protection?
sections.Holding: The New Hampshire court, June 1873, principal opinion by Justice Doe; the report gives no numerical vote. Section 3 of the 1862 amendment did not exempt the company from section 6 of the 1855 statute, so DeLancey's innocent title description did not invalidate the policy, and judgment was directed for the insured. The waiver argument failed as well. The court did not hold that any small-print contract is automatically void, and it did not strike down the amendment as unconstitutional.
sections.Reasoning:
Doe treated legislative purpose as essential to deciding whether the private act silently restored the problem the general act had remedied. He described a public belief that some insurers collected premiums through technically dense documents but evaded payment through hidden conditions; he said it was unnecessary to decide whether the belief was warranted, because the belief explained the legislation.

It was implausible that the legislature, after years of general protection against innocent misstatements, gave one company an unexplained immunity. Legislative history, the remedial purpose and constitutional principles favoring common benefit and equal rights supported a presumption against such a discriminatory exemption, though sufficiently explicit words could show a contrary intent. The private act's title and body referred to amending the company's charter, not the general insurance law; it repealed specified charter sections but had no general repeal clause and no express reference to the 1855 protection. The former charter's statement that signed policies bound the company "in all cases" necessarily operated subject to general insurance law, and the substituted provision had to be read with the same qualification.

Waiver failed for the same reason: even if the annexed charter became part of the contract, it did so according to its legal construction, which left it subject to the general protection.

Justice Hibbard concurred in the result on a different ground, reading the application as insuring only DeLancey's undivided half, which he owned in fee simple, so that the statutory conflict did not arise.

The casebook cites the case for Doe's criticism of tiny crowded print and his remark that there was ground for a premium payer to argue that the print alone was competent evidence for a jury of a fraudulent plot; the judgment itself turned on construction of the statutes, not on that observation.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-007.rule: A court will refuse to enforce an exculpatory clause as a matter of law when it is printed so that the customer cannot read it, apart from any question of unconscionability.

sections.Parties: McCarthy Well Co., a well contractor, sued St. Peter Creamery, Inc. for the unpaid balance of its bill for restoring the creamery's artesian well, ultimately seeking $23,422.02 plus interest. The creamery counterclaimed, alleging negligent work and misrepresentation of the time required. McCarthy was the appellant, challenging the judgment and the denial of a new trial.
sections.Procedural History:
McCarthy sued on March 12, 1980, and the creamery counterclaimed. The trial court excluded the reverse side of McCarthy's form, which contained an exculpatory provision, because it was illegible. A jury found both parties negligent, found $190,000 in creamery damages and assigned 75 percent of the fault to McCarthy. McCarthy appealed the judgment and the denial of a new trial. The Court of Appeals upheld the challenged rulings, treating the clause as unconscionable and, alternatively, as not confined to negligence.

The Minnesota Supreme Court decided the case on August 7, 1987. Its formal disposition was "Affirmed in part; reversed in part": it sustained the recovery and the refusal to enforce the clause but rejected the intermediate court's characterization of the clause as unconscionable. The published disposition does not separately direct a new trial or state a revised dollar judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
St. Peter Creamery engaged McCarthy Well to restore its artesian well to its original capacity. The creamery's manager contacted the company in June 1979; McCarthy sent an acknowledgment-of-order form in August and began work two weeks later. It removed a copper liner, airlifted sand, televised the well, tried unsuccessfully to remove a donut from the casing, blasted with dynamite, and in late October installed a turbine pump. The November bill was $34,573.27, including $8,329.45 for the pump. The creamery paid only part.

The pump shaft broke three days after McCarthy sued, was repaired, and broke again in April; after another failure in August the creamery hired another company to install a pump. That pump failed in January 1981, inspection disclosed a casing hole, and the creamery dug a new well.

The reverse of McCarthy's form contained extensive terms, including a provision disclaiming any other damage or liability arising from its work. Two columns covered the whole reverse of an eleven-by-eight-and-one-half-inch page in tiny print, apparently about three-point type, on dark paper with no highlighting, and the exculpatory term lay in the middle of the dense text. The court itself resorted to enlargement to decipher it.
sections.Issue: Is an exculpatory clause printed in unreadable type on the back of a contractor's form enforceable against the customer? The court also decided whether the bar on recovering economic loss in negligence applied to this mixed goods-and-services contract, and whether a voir dire question about an insurer or late disclosures required a new trial.
sections.Holding: Minnesota Supreme Court, 1987, Justice Scott, with no concurrence or dissent. The exculpatory clause was unenforceable as a matter of law because the customer could not know the terms; they were unreadable. The court refused to call the clause substantively unconscionable, left undecided the objection to its breadth, and did not decide whether the same language, presented readably, would be enforceable. Because services predominated in the contract, Article 2 did not govern and the economic-loss bar did not preclude the creamery's negligence recovery. There was no reversible prejudice from the jury inquiry or the late disclosures.
sections.Reasoning:
On the clause, the physical presentation mattered: dense two-column tiny print on dark paper, no room for amendments, no highlighting, the term buried mid-text, and type about half the size of newspaper classified print. The court suspected larger print had been reduced to fit the page. The defect was not that clearly disclosed terms had excessively harsh consequences; it was the practical inability to identify the terms at all.

On economic loss, McCarthy invoked Superwood's prohibition on recovering economic losses through negligence or strict products liability in commercial transactions. The court explained that the prohibition rests on protecting the rights and remedies of Article 2 of the U.C.C., so for this doctrine a commercial transaction means one governed by that article. For a mixed agreement the court applied the predominant-purpose test. The object was restoring the well through extensive services, with the pump, $8,329.45 of a $34,573.27 bill, one part of a single agreement and not a separate transaction.

On trial procedure, the judge asked the panel once whether anyone had an interest in Great American Insurance Company, without identifying it as McCarthy's insurer; that was within discretion. The creamery disclosed more specific negligence grounds and two experts five days before trial, but the subjects had been explored in depositions, the permitted expert had been deposed as a fact witness, and no prejudicial surprise appeared.

The casebook uses the case for the distinction between unreadability and the usual conception of unconscionability.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-008.rule: A party's failure to read a clearly stated contract term printed in the same size type as the rest of the document does not establish mutual mistake for reformation or unfair surprise for unconscionability.

sections.Parties: Fraass Surgical Manufacturing Co., a manufacturer of medical and surgical equipment, was the plaintiff contractor. It sued the United States in the Court of Claims to recover the amount it had borne for government-furnished property destroyed in a fire, asking that the contract's risk-of-loss clause be replaced with one imposing liability only for fault or wrongdoing. The government defended on limitations and on the merits.
sections.Procedural History: Fraass filed suit on September 21, 1973. A 1974 decision on the government's summary-judgment motion dismissed portions of the petition and remanded for trial of an accrual dispute affecting the six-year limitations defense and, if the suit was timely, the mutual-mistake claim. Fraass later added unconscionability. After trial, Trial Judge David Schwartz issued a recommended decision on September 30, 1977. Fraass filed neither a notice of intention to except nor exceptions within the allowed time, and the government moved to adopt the recommendation. On February 22, 1978, the Court of Claims, per curiam and without oral argument, adopted the recommended decision as the basis of its judgment and dismissed the petition.
sections.Material Facts:
Fraass contracted to produce airmen's survival kits for the Air Force. Government-furnished material worth approximately $126,220 was on its premises when a fire on January 9, 1967 destroyed the plant. The fire occurred without Fraass's fault, but the contract assigned the contractor the risk of loss of government property. Fraass turned over $75,000 in insurance proceeds with rights reserved, and the government offset the remainder against contract payments.

Fraass's president assumed, without reading the 1966 contract, that it contained the less demanding risk term used in the parties' 1960 and 1963 contracts.
