The clause appeared in the same size print as the rest of the document and stated its allocation clearly. Fraass had reduced its insurance shortly before the fire.

Under the procurement regulations, fixed-price contracts ordinarily used the strict risk clause; the less demanding clause applied to fixed-price contracts requiring certified cost or pricing data, which were not required where there was adequate price competition. The government had solicited fifteen firms and received six bids, from $11.97 to $39.50 per unit. The trial judge found that no preaward survey occurred and that certified data were neither solicited nor furnished.

On limitations, a withheld $12,382.02 invoice payment was described as tentative withholding; the government set off the remainder on October 19.
sections.Issue: Was the suit timely under the six-year limitations period? If so, was Fraass entitled to reformation of the risk-of-loss clause for mutual mistake, or to relief from the clause as unconscionable, where its president had not read the contract and assumed it matched earlier contracts?
sections.Holding: U.S. Court of Claims, 1978, per curiam (Judges Davis, Kunzig and Bennett), adopting Trial Judge Schwartz's opinion; no concurrence or dissent. The suit was timely, because a tentative withholding was not a final offset. On the merits the petition was dismissed. The strict clause was the correct one under the regulations, so there was no government mistake, no mutual mistake and no basis for reformation. The clause was not unconscionable: it was neither an unfair surprise nor oppressive.
sections.Reasoning:
On limitations, the advice of payment referred to authorization for tentative withholding, with funds going into escrow pending final determination, so the contractor could treat it as temporary postponement. No actual payment by Fraass or offset was shown before October 10, within six years of suit.

Reformation ordinarily corrects a mutual factual mistake that makes the writing depart from the parties' actual intention, and the claimant must show the government would have agreed to the proposed contract. Failure to read does not invariably foreclose reformation, but nonreading alone cannot establish the government's mistake or make a unilateral misunderstanding mutual. Fraass said the government selected the wrong clause. Contracting officials had determined there was adequate price competition, a discretionary judgment reviewable for arbitrariness, caprice or abuse, and the number and range of bids and the experienced suppliers supported it. The trial judge rejected Fraass's account of a preaward survey and cost data. The strict clause was therefore correct, which made it unnecessary to decide Fraass's own alleged mistake.

Unconscionability addresses oppression and unfair surprise, not redistribution of risk merely because bargaining power differed. The experienced president's assumption that earlier contracts controlled, without reading this one, supplied no acceptable surprise defense. Nor was the allocation oppressive: Fraass could insure the property, and its underinsurance was not the government's fault. The court also rejected a claim of unconstitutional discrimination against small contractors, since insurance was available to large and small contractors alike.

The casebook note cites the case for the unread-term passage. The report says Schwartz's separate findings of fact were adopted but not printed, and the brief does not cover them.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-009.rule: A forum-selection clause in an online membership agreement binds a subscriber who had the opportunity to scroll through the terms and clicked to accept, where the clause was reasonably presented and not concealed.

sections.Parties: Four subscribers to MSN, two living in New Jersey, one in Ohio and one in New York, sued Microsoft Network and Microsoft Corporation in New Jersey and sought to represent approximately 1.5 million subscribers nationwide. Microsoft sought dismissal under the membership agreement's forum-selection clause. The subscribers were the appellants in the Appellate Division.
sections.Procedural History:
The original complaint was filed February 24, 1997, and first amended March 5. Microsoft's March 26 federal removal petition was withdrawn April 24. After the subscribers sought multistate class certification in May, Microsoft moved to dismiss on the forum clause, and the subscribers sought to strike a supporting certification and depose its author. On November 13, Judge Fitzpatrick dismissed the complaint, denied those cross-motions in consequence, and denied class certification as moot; a December 19 order modified a passage of his opinion.

On July 2, 1999, the Appellate Division of the New Jersey Superior Court affirmed the dismissal.
sections.Material Facts:
The subscribers' eighteen-count amended complaint asserted contract, common-law fraud and consumer-fraud theories arising from the alleged conversion of memberships to more expensive plans without notice or permission. These were allegations; the court did not find Microsoft liable.

Paragraph 15.1 of the membership agreement provided that Washington law governed and that subscribers consented to exclusive jurisdiction and venue in King County courts for disputes arising from MSN use or membership. The clause was the first item in the last paragraph, in the same lower-case presentation as most terms; a few other paragraphs used capital letters.

Before joining, a prospective subscriber encountered multiple information screens, including the membership agreement in a scrollable window beside "I Agree" and "I Don't Agree" choices. Either could be clicked at any point while scrolling. Registration could proceed only after an opportunity to view the agreement and affirmative assent, and charges began only after that process and the agreement click. The system did not force the subscriber to read every line or scroll to the bottom.
sections.Issue: Is the exclusive King County, Washington forum-selection clause in MSN's online membership agreement valid and enforceable against the subscribers, and in particular did they receive adequate notice of the clause so that it became part of the contract?
sections.Holding: Appellate Division of the New Jersey Superior Court, 1999, Judge Kestin for a panel with Judges Long and Wefing, no separate writing. The forum clause was valid and enforceable, and dismissal of the New Jersey action was affirmed. On this record reasonable notice was a question of law for the court, and the subscribers' showing did not overcome it. This was a determination of where the claims must proceed, not a merits judgment, and it did not establish that every electronic assent system or forum provision gives adequate notice.
sections.Reasoning:
The court applied New Jersey's general rule that forum-selection clauses are prima facie valid, with the objector bearing the burden of showing fraud or overweening bargaining power, conflict with strong state public policy, or serious inconvenience of trial. Corporate size alone did not show unfairly exploited bargaining inequality: MSN operated in a competitive market, customers could choose another service, and the agreement could be rejected without charge. The clause was clear and contained no material misrepresentation.

On public policy, earlier New Jersey decisions invalidating forum provisions rested on policies not applicable here, and the subscribers gave no reason to conclude Washington's consumer protections were materially different or narrower. On inconvenience, with named plaintiffs in several states and a proposed nationwide class, Washington was no more inconvenient than another location.

On notice, the court said Carnival Cruise Lines v. Shute did not itself resolve the question, because the passengers there had essentially conceded reasonable communication of the clause. The electronic medium did not materially change the comparison with a printed form. Subscribers could scroll through the terms before accepting, and nothing about the clause's placement or presentation showed unfair concealment or de-emphasis. Rejecting it on that basis would undermine identically presented terms generally, though the subscribers necessarily knew they were entering a contract. Unread form terms may bind a party where there is reasonable presentation and an opportunity to reject. The court excluded a CD-ROM version in the record because none of these plaintiffs used it to join. Affirmance left the parties free to litigate other issues in another jurisdiction.

The casebook's account emphasizes the scrolling opportunity, the ordinary presentation and the affirmed dismissal.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-010.rule: An advertisement is deceptive if a representation is likely to mislead reasonable consumers and is material; strong health claims require competent and reliable scientific evidence, and a placebo response does not substantiate a claim of inherent effectiveness.

sections.Parties: The Federal Trade Commission was the plaintiff. The defendants were three corporations, QT, Inc., Q-Ray Company and Bio-Metal, which marketed a metal bracelet; Que Te Park, also known as Andrew Park, who was president of all three; and Jung Joo Park, an officer and Park's wife. The FTC sought monetary relief and permanent relief against deceptive advertising under three counts.
sections.Procedural History:
The FTC sued on May 27, 2003. An asset-freeze temporary restraining order followed on May 29 and a stipulated preliminary injunction on June 11. The parties consented to magistrate-judge jurisdiction, and a seven-day bench trial was held between June 6 and July 11.

On September 8, 2006, Magistrate Judge Denlow issued a memorandum opinion and order containing Rule 52 findings and conclusions. It directed judgment for the FTC against the three corporations and Que Te Park on all three counts, jointly and severally, and judgment for Jung Joo Park on all counts. It ordered monetary relief, directed permanent relief against deceptive conduct, and required the parties to submit a proposed final judgment for later entry. Claims about a newer November 2005 infomercial were outside this trial.
sections.Material Facts:
The defendants marketed a C-shaped metal bracelet manufactured in Spain. Park began American sales in 1996 and direct-consumer infomercials in 2000. Retail prices ranged from $49.95 to $249.95, against wholesale costs of $7.50 to $28.

Four versions of lengthy infomercials, with websites, brochures and packaging, promoted immediate, significant or complete relief from many kinds of pain. Testimonials claimed vanished back, joint and other pain, and hosts presented purported scientific explanations and demonstrations. The advertisements also promised an unconditional thirty-day refund.

The studies offered as substantiation had weak blinding, unexplained populations and measurements, absent raw data, no valid comparison groups and uncertain product identity. A first study by graduate student DeAnn Trapp included pain and placebo data that did not substantiate the benefit; at the company's request the report supplied to QT was altered to omit that material. A Mayo study found improvement in both the active and placebo groups without a statistically significant difference, and QT continued the challenged infomercial after learning the results. Park gave contradictory accounts of ionization and could not explain or substantiate the manufacturing process.

The thirty-day guarantee did not match the policies actually imposed on many online purchasers and some bracelet styles; a less visible website link disclosed a shorter period.
sections.Issue: Did the sellers engage in deceptive advertising in violation of §§ 5 and 12 by claiming the bracelet relieved pain without a reasonable basis, by claiming that tests proved pain relief, and by advertising a thirty-day refund guarantee they did not honor? Were the two individual defendants personally liable, and what relief was appropriate?
sections.Holding: U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois, 2006, Magistrate Judge Denlow, after a bench trial. All three counts were proven against the three corporations and Que Te Park. The pain-relief claims lacked a reasonable basis and were materially misleading under §§ 5 and 12; the claim that tests proved pain relief was materially misleading; and the refund guarantee was false. Jung Joo Park was not liable. The court ordered disgorgement of $22.5 million in profits plus interest and refund eligibility for purchasers from January 1, 2000 to June 30, 2003, with total restitution capped at $87,019,840, and directed permanent injunctive relief against further deceptive conduct.
sections.Reasoning:
The court examined each infomercial's overall impression. Brief, inconspicuous disclaimers did not undo the message, and the efficacy and proof claims were express or conspicuous enough that no consumer survey was needed. An advertisement is deceptive if a representation, omission or practice is likely to mislead reasonable consumers and is material; express claims and important health-related claims were presumptively material.

On Count I, the defendants had to identify their substantiation and the FTC bore the burden of proving it inadequate. For these strong medical claims the court required competent and reliable scientific evidence, specifically a well-conducted, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study, a requirement tied to the advertised health benefit. The studies offered were deficient, anecdotes could not fill the gap, and the proposed ionization mechanism was unsupported. Following Pantron and Acu-Dot, the court rejected placebo response as substantiation for a representation of inherent effectiveness. On Count II, a claim that tests prove a benefit is itself a representation of scientific substantiation, and the studies did not provide the proof claimed. On Count III, the false guarantee and its nonretroactive correction were decisive; ordinary processing delays were not treated as a separate violation.

The bracelet was a device because its advertised intended use was to mitigate pain; intended use depended on promotion, not actual operation. A directed verdict for Park in a prior Illinois consumer class action did not preclude the FTC, which was not a party or privy and vindicated a public interest. Individual liability required participation or authority to control plus knowledge; Park's approval of advertising and control satisfied it, while Jung Joo Park's title as secretary and bank-signature authority did not. On relief, the court rejected an absolute net-profit limit on restitution; the monetary remedies overlapped and were not cumulative.

The casebook's account describes the decision as enjoining sale and ordering refunds along with disgorgement; the opinion's injunction was the narrower one against deception.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-011.rule: When a sale of goods is unconscionable under UCC § 2-302 and the buyer keeps the goods, the seller recovers its net cost plus a reasonable profit and reasonable charges, not the contract price.

sections.Parties: Frostifresh Corp., the seller of a refrigerator-freezer on an installment contract, was the plaintiff. It sued the buyers, Reynoso and a second buyer, for $1,364.10, comprising the asserted balance, attorney fees and a late charge. The appeal concerned the trial judgment that limited its recovery.
sections.Procedural History:
The case was tried in Nassau County District Court before Judge Francis J. Donovan. When unconscionability emerged during trial, the court adjourned to give both parties a reasonable opportunity to present evidence about the contract's commercial setting, purpose and effect. On November 15, 1966, it refused to enforce the price and credit terms and gave judgment against both buyers for $316, with interest from December 26, 1964.

On May 24, 1967, the Supreme Court, Appellate Term, Second Department, in a per curiam opinion, unanimously reversed without costs and ordered a new trial limited to assessing the seller's damages and entering judgment. No later damages assessment is covered by the brief.
sections.Material Facts:
The agreement set a $900 cash price for the appliance plus a $245.88 credit charge, totaling $1,145.88. The buyers had paid only $32. The seller admitted its own cost for the appliance was $348.

Negotiations were conducted in Spanish with a Spanish-speaking salesman. Reynoso told him that only one week remained on his job and he could not afford the appliance. The salesman said referral bonuses or commissions of $25 on sales to friends and neighbors would make the appliance cost them nothing. The trial court described that conduct as distracting and deluding the buyers. The written installment form was entirely in English and was neither translated nor explained. The trial court found the buyers disadvantaged in their understanding of the commercial setting and the form's terms. The buyers kept the appliance. These were findings after a completed trial.
sections.Issue: Was the installment sale unconscionable under UCC § 2-302, and if so, what may the seller recover when the buyers retain the appliance: only its own cost, or something more?
sections.Holding: Appellate Term of the New York Supreme Court, Second Department, 1967, per curiam and unanimous (Justices Schwartzwald, Fanelli and Beckinella). The evidence clearly warranted the finding of unconscionability, but the remedy was wrong. The seller should recover its net cost plus a reasonable profit, necessarily incurred trucking and service charges, and reasonable finance charges. The court did not validate the original $900 price, award the claimed charges in full or specify a new dollar judgment; a limited new trial was to determine damages under that formula.
sections.Reasoning:
At trial, fraud had not been pleaded as a defense, so the trial court treated it as unavailable. Unconscionability remained independently available under UCC § 2-302. The trial court found the price and terms shocking to the conscience and the charge oppressive in conjunction with the buyers' limited understanding and the foreign-language form. Invoking the Code's protection against oppression and unfair surprise, and its comment's discussion of Campbell Soup, it refused to enforce the written price and credit provisions.

Because the buyers retained the appliance, the trial court required reimbursement of the seller's admitted $348 cost and allowed nothing for sales commissions, attorney fees, service charges or other overhead; deducting the $32 already paid produced the $316 judgment.

The Appellate Term left the unconscionability assessment intact but rejected reimbursement limited to acquisition cost, substituting net cost plus a reasonable profit and reasonable charges. Avoiding the oppressive terms did not entitle the buyers to keep the appliance free, and the appeal allowed reasonable seller compensation without restoring the original bargain.

The casebook cites the case in a remedies note. The brief notes that the casebook calls $348 the purchase price, when the trial report identifies it as the seller's cost and the buyers' cash price as $900, and that the casebook's scholarly comments about deterrence and consumer credit are editorial reactions, not judicial opinions.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-012.rule: A rent-to-own agreement that transfers ownership after a series of payments for no further consideration is in substance a credit sale and security transaction, and charging disguised interest above the statutory limit is an unconscionable commercial practice.

sections.Parties: Green and Levine, consumers who had obtained furniture and appliances from Continental Rentals under agreements styled as leases, were the plaintiffs in consolidated damages actions. Continental was the defendant. The New Jersey Attorney General intervened. The consumers and the intervenor sought rulings that the agreements were covered by consumer-credit statutes and violated the Consumer Fraud Act; Continental sought summary judgment on the common-law fraud claim.
sections.Procedural History: The consolidated actions came before Judge Alterman of the New Jersey Superior Court, Law Division, Passaic County, on cross-motions for partial summary judgment. On March 25, 1994, the court granted the consumers' and the intervenor's motions and denied Continental's motion directed to common-law fraud because fraudulent intent remained genuinely disputed. Plaintiffs were directed to submit an order on five days' notice. This is a trial-court decision; the report contains no final damages amount and describes no later proceedings.
sections.Material Facts:
Continental supplied furniture and appliances through agreements styled as short-term leases, each renewing when the customer paid the next periodic charge. Completing a specified series of payments transferred ownership without further consideration. A customer could end the arrangement by returning the goods and paying rental charges then due, and bore the risk of loss, theft and destruction. Early purchase credited forty percent of prior payments toward the price; a customer who left before completion lost the equity accumulated toward ownership.

Green entered five agreements in 1988-1989 for furniture, a stereo and freezer, a washing machine, and a dinette and hutch. She paid from April 1988 through August 1989, a total of $3,335.86 against combined cash prices of $2,785.12; completing every schedule would have cost $6,663.85. Continental spread partial payments among the agreements and, after default, repossessed all the items on August 28, 1989. Levine contracted for a washer and dryer through seventy-eight weekly payments of $23.95, defaulted after forty-three, and the goods were repossessed.

Continental derived total installments by multiplying wholesale cost by 3.5 and set the cash price at forty percent of that product. The difference was called the cost of leased services, although no such services existed.
sections.Issue: Are rent-to-own agreements, terminable by the customer at each renewal but transferring ownership after a series of payments, credit sales and security transactions subject to TILA, the New Jersey Retail Installment Sales Act and the UCC? Do their terms and pricing amount to an unconscionable commercial practice under the Consumer Fraud Act?
sections.Holding: New Jersey Superior Court, Law Division, 1994, Judge Alterman. The agreements were security transactions subject to TILA, RISA and the UCC, and they violated the Consumer Fraud Act. The difference between total installments and cash price was interest, and the effective rates substantially exceeded the thirty-percent annual statutory limit the court identified, which was an unconscionable practice. Actual deceit or fraudulent intent was not essential to that ground. The common-law fraud claim was left for further litigation.
sections.Reasoning:
TILA's definition of a credit sale included certain leases in which the lessee contracts to pay an amount substantially equal to or exceeding the property's value and becomes owner for no or nominal further consideration. Courts were divided: one line treated the consumer's ability to terminate after a week as decisive, the other looked to the transaction's substance, the ownership incentive and the forfeiture of accumulated equity. A Regulation Z amendment excluding leases terminable without penalty did not end the disagreement. The court adopted the view that forfeiture of accrued equity is a penalty, identifying the forty-percent early-purchase credit as the consumers' equity; Federal Reserve interpretations deserved substantial deference but were not binding as the seller claimed.

RISA posed a parallel question, and New Jersey provisions coordinating it with TILA supported a similar reading. Relying on the statutes' remedial purposes, the court looked through the lease label and found an economic sale, since the customer's object and incentive were eventual ownership.

Under the UCC provision then in force, a provision granting ownership on compliance for no additional or nominal consideration created a security interest, and these agreements said exactly that, so the contract language decided the point as a matter of law.

The Consumer Fraud Act covered rental transactions and prohibited unconscionable commercial practices. The court emphasized the consumers' minimal bargaining power and the unfairness of the arrangement. Statutory first-in, first-out allocation of payments would have kept Green from losing everything. The seller's right to require payment or return was forbearance in substance, so the so-called cost of leased services was interest.

The casebook's note emphasizes the disguised interest and the unconscionability determination.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-013.rule: Under the Indian Claims Commission Act, disparity in price alone establishes unconscionable consideration only where there is a very gross inequality, judged on each case's facts and circumstances and not by a mechanical percentage formula.

sections.Parties: The Nez Perce Tribe of Indians was the claimant and appellant. It sought additional compensation from the United States, the respondent, for reservation lands ceded under an 1893 agreement, relying on section 2, clauses (3) and (5), of the Indian Claims Commission Act, and it also sought interest on any additional recovery.
sections.Procedural History:
The Tribe brought its claim before the Indian Claims Commission. The Commission said the evidence could support $4 per acre as a maximum value, considered the difference between that figure and the price paid insufficiently large to be unconscionable, and found no proven fraud, duress or unfair and dishonorable dealing. Commissioner Scott wrote separately at the Commission stage.

The Tribe appealed to the United States Court of Claims, which decided the case on July 15, 1966. The court agreed that fraud, duress and unfair and dishonorable dealings had not been established, rejected the Commission's treatment of unconscionable consideration, rejected the claim to interest, and reversed and remanded for further proceedings conforming to the opinion.
sections.Material Facts:
By an agreement of May 1, 1893, ratified August 15, 1894, the Tribe ceded 549,559 acres of its northern Idaho reservation, which had contained approximately 762,000 acres, after provision for individual allotments and tribal trust lands. The price was $2.97 per acre as the opinion describes it. Total consideration was $1,626,222: $626,222 payable per capita as soon as practicable after ratification, and $1 million held in trust at five percent interest.

August 15, 1894 was the agreed valuation date. The Tribe maintained the lands were worth $12.63 per acre; the government argued for $1.29. The Tribe's appraiser, William C. Brown, reached $11.89; the government's appraiser, Homer Hoyt, reached $1.29. The Commission found Brown too optimistic and Hoyt too pessimistic.

Slightly more than half of the ceded area was best suited for agriculture, somewhat less than a quarter was timberland, and the rest was grazing land; access varied, and the allotted lands tended to include the more favorable tracts. When the ceded lands opened to settlement in November 1895, there were 507 homestead filings in thirteen days. The agreement and proclamation set prices of $3.75 for agricultural acres and $5 for stone, timber and mineral acres, though much land was later acquired free under the homestead laws.
sections.Issue: Was the consideration paid for the ceded lands unconscionable within clause (3) of section 2 of the Indian Claims Commission Act, where the Commission treated $4 per acre as the maximum value? And if additional compensation is due, is the Tribe entitled to five percent interest on it?
sections.Holding: U.S. Court of Claims, 1966, Judge Laramore; no voting lineup is given. Substantial evidence supported the $4 figure, but the overwhelming weight of the evidence required treating it as a minimum, not a ceiling, and on that footing the Commission's rejection of unconscionable consideration could not stand. The court reversed and remanded without requiring a particular higher value or awarding a damages sum. The Tribe was not entitled to interest on the additional recovery. The finding that fraud, duress and unfair and dishonorable dealings were not proved was left intact.
sections.Reasoning:
On value, the court agreed with the Commission's criticisms of both appraisers but gave greater weight to Brown's basic approach. It explored adjustments to his comparable-sales analysis: about twenty-five percent for improvements, and further allowances of twenty to twenty-five percent each for remoteness and for the tract's immense size. These were exploratory tools, not discounts imposed on remand. A rough illustration starting around $20 per acre produced $5 to $7 after discounts of sixty-five to seventy-five percent, so even substantial allowances supported $4 as a floor.

On unconscionability, precedent required a very gross inequality before price disparity alone could suffice, but supplied no mechanical percentage formula; each case turned on its facts. Earlier decisions involving disparities above one hundred percent did not make smaller ones automatically exempt, and the Commission had relied too heavily on the percentage gap. Three features mattered. The $1.03 difference between the price and the minimum $4 value, over 549,559 acres, came to $566,045.77, a substantial sum in 1894. Additional consideration paid then would likely have earned trust interest, very roughly estimated near $200,000. Most importantly, $4 was the bare minimum a reasonable willing seller would have accepted, with the legitimate range of disagreement extending upward from there.

On interest, claims against the United States ordinarily bear interest only with express statutory or contractual authorization, apart from the constitutional taking exception. The agreement prescribed an exact total and made only its $1 million remainder interest-bearing; it did not create an open-ended trust covering a later judicial determination of fair value.

The casebook uses the case in a historical-price problem. The brief notes that no original Court of Claims reporter facsimile was recovered.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-014.rule: Whether an attorney's fee is unconscionable depends on the value of the services to the client measured against the market for comparable lawyers, not on the law firm's cost or profit margin.

sections.Parties: Marcy Shaffer, a contract staff attorney at Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher and not a party to the underlying action, petitioned for a writ of mandate against the Superior Court's discovery order. The opposing party was Jeremy Simms, a former client suing the firm, who wanted to compel Shaffer to disclose the hourly compensation the firm paid her in order to show an unconscionable markup.
sections.Procedural History:
In January 1993 Simms sued the firm for breach of contract, fraud, breach of fiduciary duties and professional negligence. At Shaffer's deposition, counsel objected to a question about her hourly compensation on relevance and privacy grounds and instructed her not to answer. Simms moved to compel and requested sanctions. A discovery referee recommended disclosure and $1,100 in sanctions. On August 12, 1994, the trial court adopted the report but reduced sanctions to $900; an October 21 amendment explained that the client's need outweighed Shaffer's privacy interest.

Shaffer sought mandate. The Court of Appeal issued an alternative writ; her separate attempted appeal was dismissed because the order was nonappealable. On March 30, 1995, the court discharged the alternative writ and ordered a peremptory writ compelling the trial court to vacate its order, disapprove the referee's report and deny the motion to compel. Supreme Court review was denied June 15, 1995.
sections.Material Facts:
On June 13, 1989, Simms retained Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher for advice about disputes with Alan Robbins and possible litigation. His fees were to equal the time of the individuals performing services multiplied by their generally applicable hourly rates when the work was performed. The firm represented him in the Robbins matters into 1991. He alleged that he paid $2,018,067.63 in bills from July 1989 through December 1990, about $51,000 of it for other work, and that further bills of approximately $250,700 followed. These allegations were not adjudicated in this proceeding.

Shaffer's services were billed to Simms at $215 to $250 an hour for approximately 1,800 hours, apparently about nineteen percent of the time billed on the Robbins matters. She had been a full-time associate at the firm from 1980 into 1983 and returned as a contract attorney doing research, analysis and writing. She testified that she had no permanent office or dedicated secretary, used temporarily vacant offices and sometimes the library, and did most of her own typing.
sections.Issue: Is the hourly compensation a law firm paid its contract attorney relevant, and therefore discoverable, on a client's claim that the fees the firm charged for her work were unconscionable?
sections.Holding: California Court of Appeal, Second District, Division Three, 1995, Justice Croskey for a unanimous panel. No. The compensation the firm paid Shaffer was irrelevant to the client's claim that the firm's fees were unconscionable, so the motion to compel had to be denied. The court resolved the matter on relevance and expressly declined to decide her constitutional privacy claim. This was a ruling about discoverability of the firm's costs, not a determination that its fees were conscionable or its representation competent.
sections.Reasoning:
Discovery reached unprivileged matter relevant to the action, and privacy balancing did not eliminate the threshold requirement of relevance.

The court set out the ordinary distinction between procedural unconscionability, meaning oppression from unequal bargaining power or surprise from hidden terms, and substantively harsh allocations, with a sliding relationship between them. For legal fees, former Rule of Professional Conduct 4-200 gave more specific, nonexclusive factors; the pertinent ones were the fee's relationship to the value of the services, the attorney's experience and ability, and informed client consent. None made the firm's profit margin an appropriate measure.

The pertinent question was what Simms received for the $215 to $250 charged: the quality and necessity of Shaffer's services and their value compared with similar work by lawyers of comparable experience and ability in the community. A fee substantially consistent with that market was difficult to call unconscionable merely because the firm bought the labor cheaply. That did not foreclose a challenge based on deficient, unnecessary or otherwise unjustifiably priced services.

A profit analysis would require an accounting inquiry with no stable stopping point, covering revenue, accounting methods, allocation of overhead, and the value of reputation and goodwill. A firm that operated efficiently would face greater scrutiny for providing the same valuable services at lower cost, and courts would end up regulating profit margins. The court drew support from Copeland and Margolin, which rejected a cost-plus method of awarding reasonable fees in public-interest litigation.

The casebook's account raises a comparison with freezer-sale profits as an editorial question. The brief notes that the casebook misdescribes the procedure as a client's appeal from a denial of discovery.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-015.rule: Under New York's price-gouging statute, a prima facie case of an unconscionably excessive price may be shown by comparing the challenged price with the seller's usual pre-disruption price; a single violation suffices, and the seller may rebut by proving added costs.

sections.Parties: The People of the State of New York, through the Attorney General, petitioned against Quality King Distributors, Inc., a wholesaler supplying grocery and discount stores, and its CEO. The Attorney General sought an injunction, accounting, restitution, disgorgement and civil penalties for alleged price gouging on Lysol. Quality King denied gouging, alleged increased costs and asserted that the statute was unconstitutionally vague. Both sides appealed.
sections.Procedural History:
In May 2020 the Attorney General commenced a special proceeding under General Business Law § 396-r and Executive Law § 63(12). After answering, Quality King moved to dismiss under CPLR 3211(a)(1) and (7). The trial court's September 23, 2020 order denied the petition, dismissed it against the CEO, and effectively dismissed the whole proceeding. Both sides appealed the order and a so-ordered oral-argument transcript.

On August 23, 2022, the First Department reversed on the law, without costs, reinstated the petition and answer, and remanded for further proceedings. It dismissed Quality King's separate appeal, because Quality King was not aggrieved by an order dismissing the proceeding, and dismissed both transcript appeals as redundant.
sections.Material Facts:
The product was Lysol disinfectant in 19-ounce spray cans. Consumer complaints in February and March 2020 prompted the Attorney General to investigate and obtain Quality King's sales and purchase records. The petition alleged that median monthly prices for twelve-packs rose from $51 before the crisis despite relatively stable acquisition costs, and identified at least 432 sales between February 1 and April 7, involving 3,835 twelve-packs. These were allegations, not appellate findings.

Demand for disinfectants had sharply increased and strained supply; Quality King acknowledged that the manufacturer had sold out and could not keep pace by February, if not earlier. The Governor declared an emergency on March 7; federal health officials had declared a public-health emergency on January 31; CDC warnings on February 26 made imminent community spread explicit.

The transaction records showed, for example, that Jack's American Outlet paid $60 to $66.09 per case on February 24 and $88.42 on March 16; CVS paid $62.40 on February 26 and later $84.01, $91.56 and $95.96; and Clinton Variety's February prices of $56.09 and $61.96 rose to $108.99 on April 1.
sections.Issue: Did the Attorney General make a prima facie showing that Quality King sold a vital and necessary good at unconscionably excessive prices during an abnormal market disruption, so that dismissal was error? When did the disruption begin, how are prices to be compared, and is the statute unconstitutionally vague?
sections.Holding: New York's First Department, 2022, opinion by Higgitt, with Manzanet-Daniels, Shulman and Rodriguez concurring. Dismissal was error. An abnormal market disruption existed from February 26, 2020; Lysol was vital and necessary; and the customer-specific price comparisons established prima facie gross disparities on several occasions. The statute was not unconstitutionally vague. The court left cost justification, the full extent of violations and appropriate relief for the trial court, and did not set a restitution amount or impose a penalty.
sections.Reasoning:
Under the pre-June 2020 statute, the Attorney General had to show an abnormal market disruption, goods vital and necessary for consumers' health, safety and welfare, and an unconscionably excessive price. A prima facie case could compare the challenged price with the seller's usual pre-disruption price, and the seller could rebut by proving additional costs outside its control.

A Governor's declaration was one listed cause of disruption, not a prerequisite. The court chose February 26, 2020, rejecting January 31 because the federal declaration did not yet establish a national emergency in the statute's ordinary sense, and March 7 because waiting would leave earlier emergency pricing outside a remedial statute. Lysol was vital and necessary from the perspective of consumers facing the emerging pandemic; later disagreement about surface transmission did not undo that reasonable early belief, and the exceptional demand created a temporary imbalance in bargaining power.

Because prices varied with customer type, order size and location, each post-February 26 purchase should generally be compared with the same customer's price immediately before the disruption, not with monthly medians. The example transactions showed gross disparities, but did not resolve which other sales violated the law or whether costs justified increases. Section 396-r could reach an individual violation without a uniform practice; repeated or persistent illegality remained relevant to Executive Law § 63(12). Disputed issues warranted a trial, and the trial court could order an accounting, a hearing or both.

On vagueness, considered as an alternative ground to affirm, the statute regulated economic conduct through civil remedies and received relaxed review; its contextual standards gave adequate notice, and the absence of a fixed numerical threshold was not fatal.

The casebook cites the case as an example of price-gouging enforcement being upheld, which the brief says should be read with the prima facie findings and remand.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-016.rule: Unconscionability under UCC § 2-302 can apply between merchants; the primary consideration is the substantive reasonableness of the term, and unequal bargaining power alone will not invalidate a reasonable provision.

sections.Parties: Gianni Sport Ltd., a New York manufacturer and distributor of women's clothing, was the plaintiff. Gantos, Inc., a retailer headquartered in Grand Rapids, was the defendant. Gianni sought payment for a holiday clothing order that Gantos had canceled and then accepted at a reduced price. Gantos appealed the trial court's refusal to enforce its cancellation clause; Gianni cross-appealed for additional damages on other transactions.
sections.Procedural History: After a bench trial in Kent Circuit Court, Gianni obtained a $27,290 judgment. The trial court found the cancellation clause unconscionable and invalidated the price concession that the clause had made necessary. Gantos appealed the unconscionability determination. Gianni cross-appealed findings concerning a price reduction on a separate shipment that arrived two weeks late and a $2,000 advertising allowance. On April 28, 1986, the Michigan Court of Appeals, per curiam, affirmed the judgment in all respects and rejected the cross-appeal.
sections.Material Facts:
The parties had dealt with each other for more than two years. On June 10, 1980, Gantos ordered holiday clothing for delivery on October 10. The back of its purchase order reserved a right, by notice, to terminate all or part of the order for goods not yet shipped, or goods not timely delivered for any reason. Gantos canceled in late September. The trial court found that Gianni then agreed to a fifty-percent price reduction to induce Gantos to accept the goods anyway.

The holiday order represented twenty to twenty-two percent of Gianni's business in 1980, and Gantos's total sales were approximately twenty times Gianni's. Gianni manufactured the goods especially for Gantos, in an industry where styles changed rapidly. Mr. Gianni testified that he had not read the clause and would not have done business with Gantos had he read it. There was no evidence the provision could be negotiated, though Mr. Gantos acknowledged that some manufacturers wanted to negotiate it. The trial court credited the explanation of the retailer's buyer that buyers controlled the industry and could impose these provisions on small independent manufacturers.
sections.Issue: Was a retailer's purchase-order clause allowing it to cancel an order for unshipped goods by notice unconscionable under Michigan's UCC § 2-302 when imposed on a small manufacturer of custom seasonal clothing, even though both parties were merchants?
sections.Holding: Michigan Court of Appeals, 1986, per curiam (Presiding Judge D. F. Walsh, Judge Hood and Circuit Judge K. N. Hansen). Yes. The trial court's assessment of the cancellation clause's substantive unfairness was not clearly erroneous, so its refusal to enforce the clause, and its invalidation of the fifty-percent concession the clause had made necessary, stood. On the cross-appeal, there was no clear error in crediting Gantos's witnesses about the late shipment and the advertising allowance. The $27,290 judgment was affirmed in all respects.
sections.Reasoning:
Section 2-302 required an opportunity to present evidence about a disputed term's commercial setting, purpose and effect, and the inquiry examined one-sidedness against the trade's commercial background and needs at formation. The official comment emphasized preventing oppression and unfair surprise while preserving reasonable risk allocation despite superior bargaining power. Although the opinion described unconscionability as a question of law, it applied the clearly-erroneous standard to the trial court's determination.

Michigan decisions asked about the parties' economic strength, bargaining power and alternatives, and the challenged term's substantive reasonableness. The court made reasonableness the primary consideration: unequal power alone would not invalidate a reasonable provision. Gantos argued that two experienced merchants had merely allocated risks through a standard clause.

The differences in size mattered but were not decisive alone. The decisive commercial problem was that the goods were made especially for Gantos in a fast-changing fashion trade. Last-minute cancellation left the small manufacturer absorbing the loss or bargaining with the same retailer to take completed goods at a deep discount, and the fifty-percent concession showed how the power operated. The court did not turn Mr. Gianni's failure to read into a general excuse; it also weighed the absence of negotiability and the buyers' control of the industry.

Cardinal Stone did not require enforcement: there the parties were experienced businessmen who knowingly accepted a cancellation risk, with no sign of unequal power or lack of alternatives and no analysis of substantive reasonableness. Johnson v. Mobil Oil, involving an illiterate dealer and a consequential-damages limitation, was also inapposite.

The casebook uses the case to illustrate that unconscionability can apply between businesses.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-017.rule: A service-station lease and dealer agreement form one franchise relationship, and public policy reads into it a restriction that the franchisor may not terminate, cancel or refuse to renew without good cause, meaning the dealer's failure substantially to perform.

sections.Parties: Shell Oil Co. controlled a service-station site in Fort Lee and supplied its products; Frank Marinello operated the station under a lease and dealer agreement. Marinello sued in Chancery for an injunction and reformation after Shell gave notice of termination. Shell brought a summary dispossess action claiming he was holding over without permission. Shell was the appellant in the New Jersey Supreme Court.
sections.Procedural History:
Marinello sued in Chancery. On June 1, 1972, Shell brought a summary dispossess action, which was transferred, consolidated with the Chancery suit and tried for nine days. The trial court ruled for Marinello: the new Franchise Practices Act did not apply directly to his earlier renewals; an implied good-cause covenant should be inserted by reformation; and he had substantially performed. It also sustained an alternative unclean-hands defense.

Shell appealed, and the New Jersey Supreme Court certified the matter directly while it was pending unheard in the Appellate Division. On July 11, 1973, the court modified the judgment to conform to its opinion and affirmed as modified. It declined to review reformation doctrine or the alternative unclean-hands findings.
sections.Material Facts:
In 1959 Shell leased the station at Route 5 and Anderson Avenue to Marinello and a partner and simultaneously made a dealer agreement. The partnership dissolved in 1965 and Shell approved Marinello's continuing alone. The one-year documents were renewed for matching terms. The latest agreements, dated April 28, 1969, ran three years through May 31, 1972, and then year to year. The lease let Marinello terminate on ninety days' notice and let Shell terminate at the end of the primary or a later annual term on thirty days' notice. The dealer agreement permitted termination at any time on ten days' notice.

Shell's letter of April 14, 1972 gave notice that both agreements would end on May 31.

Marinello testified that Shell originally told him the station was run down but a good operator could build a future there. Shell's own witnesses acknowledged a company policy of terminating dealers only for deficient operation. Shell's representatives complained about cleanliness, operating hours and stagnant gasoline sales; Marinello offered contrary evidence and attributed the conflict to his rejecting a requested price reduction in a local gasoline-price war and to insufficient purchases of tires, batteries and accessories. The trial court found substantial performance and no just cause.
sections.Issue: May an oil company terminate a service-station operator's lease and dealer agreement under their express termination provisions without good cause, or does public policy restrict that power? If good cause is required, did Shell show it?
sections.Holding: New Jersey Supreme Court, 1973, Justice Sullivan, unanimous. The lease and dealer agreement formed one franchise relationship. The absolute ten-day termination power violated public policy, and a restriction against termination, cancellation or nonrenewal without good cause, meaning the operator's failure substantially to perform his obligations, had to be read into the existing documents and into future agreements negotiated in good faith between these parties. Shell had not established good cause. Marinello's franchise, including the lease, could continue while he substantially performed. The court reached this result without specific reformation of the documents.
sections.Reasoning:
Shell argued the lease was independent of the dealer agreement and its landlord rights could not be restricted. The court disagreed: the documents were executed together, shared commencement and expiration dates, and referred to the same station, creating one business relationship that was fundamentally a franchise.

New Jersey public policy, drawn from Henningsen and Ellsworth Dobbs, opposed grossly unfair provisions imposed through seriously disproportionate bargaining power that tend to injure the public, and motor-fuel distribution had recognized public importance. The Franchise Practices Act prohibited termination, cancellation or nonrenewal without good cause. Its effective date kept it from applying directly to these earlier agreements, but its restrictions reflected an existing public policy addressing longstanding abuses; the court used that policy and did not apply the Act retroactively.

Shell controlled both the supplies and the location, yet Marinello's service and efforts generated the station's clientele and goodwill. Once an operator had invested years building the trade, a threat of nonrenewal left him little practical ability to negotiate. The nominal availability of termination to both sides did not create equal power: Shell could install a replacement and keep the going business, while Marinello would lose his clientele. The almost-at-will provisions were grossly unfair in that setting.

On good cause, the record amply supported the trial court's finding of substantial performance.

The court did not freeze the operational terms; revision to conform to current area dealer practices remained possible. It reserved whether the relationship would survive Marinello's death or disability and what remedy would apply if Shell in good faith chose to operate the station itself.

The casebook presents the case for its good-cause conclusion; the brief notes that the casebook compresses the facts by saying Shell terminated on ten days' notice.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-018.rule: A clearly disclosed franchise provision permitting termination without cause on reasonable notice is not inherently unconscionable, and exercising it openly is not by itself bad faith.

sections.Parties: Bernard and Elaine Zapatha, franchisees who operated a Dairy Mart convenience store, were the plaintiffs. They sued Dairy Mart, Inc., the franchisor, to enjoin its termination of their franchise agreement. Dairy Mart was the appellant in the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court, seeking reversal of judgments that barred termination without good cause.
sections.Procedural History: The franchisees sued to enjoin termination. The trial court held the termination clause unconscionable, found the termination contrary to good faith and to chapter 93A, and declared that Dairy Mart could terminate only for good cause. A separate chapter 93A judgment apparently awarded only costs and attorney fees. Dairy Mart applied for and obtained direct appellate review. On August 5, 1980, the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court reversed the judgments.
sections.Material Facts:
Bernard Zapatha had a year of college, evening courses in business administration and business law, and substantial managerial experience; he lost his job in May 1973. Dairy Mart gave him sales assurances and a brochure describing independence, security and ownership, and presented its form agreement on November 8, 1973. Its representative read and explained the termination term, recommended legal advice, and said the terms were nonnegotiable. The couple signed without consulting a lawyer. Bernard testified that he understood every word but took the clause to permit termination only for cause.

Dairy Mart provided the equipped premises, paid rent, utilities and some other expenses, licensed its name and methods, and took a percentage of gross sales. The franchisees bought and maintained inventory and paid wages and taxes. After the first twelve months either side could end the agreement on ninety days' written notice. On termination without cause, Dairy Mart agreed to repurchase saleable inventory at retail price less twenty percent. In 1974 the couple moved to a Springfield store and signed an identical form.

In November 1977 Dairy Mart proposed a new agreement with some less favorable terms, which Bernard refused. On January 20, 1978, Dairy Mart gave ninety days' notice, offered to buy inventory and invited discussion of a new agreement. The trial judge found the refusal to sign was the sole reason for termination.
sections.Issue: Was the franchise agreement's provision allowing either party to terminate without cause on ninety days' notice unconscionable? Did Dairy Mart's termination, after the franchisees refused a replacement agreement, violate the obligation of good faith or chapter 93A's prohibition of unfair or deceptive conduct?
sections.Holding: Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court, 1980, Justice Wilkins, with no separate opinion or dissent. On this record the disclosed ninety-day termination provision was not unconscionable, and exercising it after the franchisees refused a replacement agreement was not shown to violate good faith or chapter 93A. Dairy Mart lawfully terminated, and the judgments were reversed. The decision rejects an automatic good-cause requirement for this kind of franchise; it does not eliminate good-faith limits on all termination clauses.
sections.Reasoning:
The court did not apply UCC Article 2 directly. About seventy percent of inventory came from other suppliers, Dairy Mart's return came chiefly from its franchise fee, and the arrangement licensed a whole business format. The court instead applied the Code's principles of unconscionability and good faith by common-law analogy.

Unconscionability was a legal issue measured at formation, looking to commercial context, unfair surprise and substantive oppression. Section 2-309's reasonable-notice provision indicated that termination without an agreed cause was not inherently unconscionable, and no one suggested ninety days was unreasonable. There was no unfair surprise: the provision was plainly stated, specifically explained and not hidden in fine print, the franchisees had time to consider it and declined recommended legal advice, and Bernard's experience made his mistaken reading insufficient. Nonnegotiability did not override those facts. Nor was there oppression: Dairy Mart supplied the business, equipment and premises, the franchisees' investment was inventory that Dairy Mart would repurchase at eighty percent of retail value, and nothing showed forfeited investment or a need for more time to recoup expenses.

On performance, a term fair when agreed could still be used unfairly, but termination without cause was not bad faith by itself. No evidence identified violated commercial standards. Dairy Mart openly exercised a clear right; even if arbitrary, that was not shown to be dishonest. The brochure's assertions about owning a business were misleading but did not prove the violation asserted. Unlike Fortune, Dairy Mart had not appropriated earned income, and there was no showing of goodwill built in the franchisees' own name. Massachusetts had not imposed cause requirements on all franchises; the court noted New Jersey's different approach in Shell v. Marinello without adopting it.

The casebook excerpts the absence of surprise and the inventory-repurchase protection.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-019.rule: A mandatory employment arbitration agreement may cover FEHA claims only if it preserves the employee's unwaivable statutory rights, and an adhesive agreement is unconscionable if it requires arbitration of the employee's claims but not the employer's corresponding claims without a reasonable business justification.

sections.Parties: Marybeth Armendariz and Dolores Olague-Rodgers, former supervisors in the Provider Relations Group of Foundation Health Psychcare Services, were the plaintiffs. They sued their former employer, alleging a FEHA violation and three other tort and contract causes of action for wrongful termination, and seeking general and punitive damages, injunctive relief, attorney fees and costs. Foundation Health, the defendant, moved to compel arbitration.
sections.Procedural History:
Foundation Health moved to compel arbitration under Code of Civil Procedure section 1281.2. The trial court found an adhesion contract with substantively one-sided provisions, particularly the employee-only arbitration obligation and the backpay-only remedy, declined to strike individual terms, and refused to enforce the agreement. The Court of Appeal agreed that the contract was adhesive and its damages limitation unlawful but concluded that the rest of the agreement should be enforced.

On August 24, 2000, the Supreme Court of California reversed the Court of Appeal and remanded with directions to affirm the trial court's refusal to compel arbitration. It did not decide the discrimination or wrongful-termination claims.
sections.Material Facts:
Foundation Health hired the two employees in July and August 1995; they later became supervisors earning $38,000 annually. On June 20, 1996, the employer told them their positions were being eliminated and terminated them. They alleged sexually based harassment and discrimination and termination because of their perceived or actual heterosexual orientation. These were allegations, not findings.

Both signed application forms containing an arbitration clause and later signed separate agreements repeating it. As a condition of employment, each promised to arbitrate a contention that her termination was wrongful, violated employment conditions or an express or implied term or covenant, or otherwise violated her rights. The agreement incorporated California's arbitration statutes. It limited the employee's exclusive remedy to the wages she would have earned between discharge and the arbitration award, excluding any other legal or equitable remedy, including reinstatement or injunctive relief.

The agreement did not require the employer to arbitrate its own claims against the employees arising from the same termination. It was imposed without an opportunity to negotiate. The employer later said it was willing to accept mutual arbitration and full remedies.
sections.Issue: May an employer require employees, as a condition of employment, to arbitrate FEHA claims, and on what conditions? Was this agreement, which limited remedies to backpay and bound only the employee's wrongful-termination claims to arbitration, unconscionable, and if so could the defects be severed?
sections.Holding: Supreme Court of California, 2000, Justice Mosk for a five-justice majority, with Justice Brown concurring separately, joined by Justice Chin. FEHA claims may be arbitrated if the forum preserves the employees' unwaivable statutory rights. This agreement, however, unlawfully restricted remedies and unjustifiably required arbitration of employee claims while leaving corresponding employer claims outside the required forum. It was procedurally and substantively unconscionable, and its defects could not be cured by permissible severance, so the whole arbitration agreement was unenforceable.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority rejected the view that the Civil Rights Act of 1991 or FEHA barred mandatory arbitration, and declined to decide whether the Federal Arbitration Act applied because the California Arbitration Act also enforced agreements subject to general contract defenses.

FEHA's protections serve the public and cannot be waived by private agreement. Drawing on Cole, the court endorsed safeguards: a neutral arbitrator, adequate discovery, a written decision, all relief available in court, and no improper arbitration costs. The backpay-only clause was unlawful because it excluded statutory remedies. Discovery sufficient to vindicate the claims and a written decision revealing essential findings were implied in the agreement. The employer must bear costs unique to arbitration; the agreement's silence on costs was construed that way.

Unconscionability requires both a procedural and a substantive element on a sliding scale. The agreement was imposed as an employment condition without negotiation. Substantively, a stronger party may not force the weaker into arbitration while reserving its own corresponding claims for litigation unless it establishes a reasonable business justification, and none was shown. Backpay through the award also excluded front pay with no comparable limit on the employer.

Under Civil Code section 1670.5, two features supported refusing the whole arrangement: the two defects together indicated a systematic inferior forum favoring the employer, and the lack of mutuality could not be cured by deleting a term; the court would have to add an employer obligation, which the statute did not authorize. The employer's later willingness to arbitrate mutually was at most an unaccepted modification offer.

Justice Brown, joined by Justice Chin, concurred in the judgment and most of the reasoning but would leave apportionment of arbitration costs to the arbitrator, subject to judicial review.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-021.rule: A procedurally unconscionable employment arbitration agreement is still enforced where its only substantively unconscionable term can be deleted without adding obligations or undermining the agreement's central purpose.

sections.Parties: Kristy Shubin, an employee of William Lyon Homes, Inc., was the plaintiff; she filed a sex- and pregnancy-discrimination and harassment complaint against her employer. William Lyon Homes, the defendant, moved to compel arbitration under an employee agreement and was the appellant after the trial court denied the motion.
sections.Procedural History:
After obtaining a Department of Fair Employment and Housing right-to-sue letter, Shubin filed her complaint in July 1999. The employer moved in September to compel arbitration. On October 8, 1999, before Armendariz was decided, the trial court denied arbitration, finding unequal court access, discovery limits especially harmful to the employee, and the possibility that she would owe the employer's costs and fees even after prevailing in court or an administrative forum.

On November 14, 2000, the California Court of Appeal, First District, Division Four, reversed and directed the trial court to sever the words "or administrative" from the final sentence of the arbitration clause and enforce the remainder. The reported text was later omitted from the reporter on direction of the California Supreme Court by order dated March 14, 2001, so the brief describes a historical decision and not currently published precedent.
sections.Material Facts:
William Lyon Homes hired Shubin as a receptionist in April 1998 and promoted her to escrow coordinator in December. She alleged that after she announced her pregnancy in January 1999 she met hostility, was demoted to receptionist and was refused accommodations. The court did not determine whether the alleged discrimination occurred.

Shubin declared that office manager Kathy Sampson brought several documents to her desk late in the day, said they needed to be signed for headquarters, stood by and indicated where to sign or initial. Asked what the papers were, Sampson described them as company records showing Shubin's hiring and promised to explain them later. Shubin said she had no time to read everything, felt she had no choice, received no copies and was never told she was agreeing to arbitration. Sampson recalled giving her the agreement to read and sign and said Shubin never asked for more time.

The two-page agreement required arbitration under JAMS/Endispute rules of employment disputes, expressly including discrimination and harassment. It excepted workers' compensation, unemployment, and claims concerning confidential information. Its final sentence allowed the responding party to recover costs, expenses and attorney fees if the other party pursued a legal or administrative action on a matter within the arbitration clause.
sections.Issue: Was the employment arbitration agreement unconscionable, procedurally and substantively, under Armendariz, and if any term was substantively unconscionable, should the court refuse to enforce the agreement or sever the offending term and compel arbitration?
sections.Holding: California Court of Appeal, First District, Division Four, 2000, Justice Sepulveda, with Presiding Justice Hanlon and Justice Reardon concurring. Procedural unconscionability was established, but only a removable part of one provision was substantively unlawful: the cost-and-fee penalty as applied to administrative actions. Deleting "or administrative" cured the defect, so the order denying arbitration was reversed and the remaining agreement enforced. The court did not adjudicate the discrimination merits or hold that procedural unconscionability was sufficient by itself.
sections.Reasoning:
The agreement was adhesive: a standardized employment condition with no realistic opportunity to negotiate. The employer's reliance on a signer's obligation to read was insufficient, because Sampson's words and conduct were evidence of pressure, and the trial court could credit Shubin's declaration and infer a hurried process with no meaningful chance to read. A later incident, in which another office manager refused to let Shubin take a second agreement home or consult counsel, corroborated the inference about the employer's practices.

Applying Armendariz, the court separated defects that interpretation could address from those needing severance. Agreement to arbitrate FEHA rights implied adequate discovery and a written decision, and the employer had to bear costs unique to mandatory arbitration; incorporation of JAMS rules did not defeat those inferences.

On mutuality, the court rejected the trial court's unequal-access analysis. Unlike the employee-only clause in Armendariz, the confidentiality exception did not expressly distinguish employer from employee, and the employee too could seek declaratory relief in court. The workers' compensation and unemployment exceptions involved statutory administrative processes.

On the fee penalty, the court reasoned that Civil Code section 1717 made recovery bilateral for the prevailing party in a court action on a contract. But that statute did not appear to reach administrative proceedings, so an employee legitimately pursuing a complaint before the state enforcement agency could still face the penalty. Armendariz preserved access to that agency, and the penalty would chill it.

Only that component was unlawful, and it could be removed without adding obligations, unlike the multiple defects and nonmutual scope in Armendariz.

The casebook's account covers the pressure to sign and the procedural finding.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-022.rule: Unconscionability remains a generally applicable contract defense to an arbitration agreement after Concepcion, and a court may refuse to sever where multiple one-sided terms show arbitration was structured as an inferior forum favoring the stronger party.

sections.Parties: Salome Samaniego and Juventino Garcia, carpet installers who worked or had worked for Flooring Install, alleged to be an affiliate or subsidiary of Empire Today, LLC, were the plaintiffs in a putative class action raising Labor Code claims. Empire, the defendant, moved to stay the action and compel arbitration and was the appellant after the trial court refused.
sections.Procedural History:
The workers filed a putative class action. Empire moved to stay and compel arbitration. The trial court found serious procedural unfairness and several substantive defects and denied the motion; it also refused reply declarations Empire filed on the hearing date, and denied reconsideration sought after Concepcion was issued. Empire appealed.

On April 5, 2012, the California Court of Appeal, First District, Division Three, affirmed the order denying Empire's request to stay the action and compel arbitration. The California Supreme Court denied Empire's petition for review on July 11, 2012. The underlying wage and classification claims were not adjudicated on their merits.
sections.Material Facts:
The workers were required to sign form agreements to obtain and later keep their work. Garcia could not read English; Samaniego could read only simpler English. They asked for Spanish translations and were told none were available. The original paperwork was not given to them after signing. When presented with a later agreement, Samaniego was told to sign immediately and could not take it home; Garcia received twenty-four hours.

The second agreement was eleven single-spaced pages of small print and complicated legal terminology. Arbitration appeared in section 36 of 37, without individually flagged headings or initials. It required a single arbitrator under American Arbitration Association commercial rules, which were neither attached nor supplied. It exempted claims for declaratory or preliminary injunctive relief under provisions on proprietary information and noncompetition or nonsolicitation. Other clauses shortened the installers' time to sue to six months, waived contrary limitations periods, and required them to pay attorney fees Empire incurred to enforce its rights, with no reciprocal obligation. The contract selected Illinois law and Chicago jurisdiction and venue.

The complaint alleged unlawful independent-contractor classification, unpaid minimum and overtime wages, denied expense reimbursement, unlawful deductions, denied meal periods and unpaid termination wages.
sections.Issue: Was the arbitration provision in the installers' form agreement unconscionable and unenforceable under California law despite the contract's choice of Illinois law? Should the offending terms have been severed, and does Concepcion preempt the unconscionability analysis?
sections.Holding: California Court of Appeal, First District, Division Three, 2012, Justice Siggins for a unanimous court. The order denying arbitration was affirmed. The court upheld the findings of procedural and substantive unconscionability, the application of California law in place of the chosen Illinois law, the refusal to sever the multiple unfair provisions, and the exclusion of the unexplained late declarations. Concepcion did not preempt the generally applicable contract analysis used here.
sections.Reasoning:
Procedural unconscionability requires oppression or surprise, substantive unconscionability an objectively unreasonable or unexpected allocation of risk; both are needed on a sliding scale. The nonnegotiable work condition, limited English literacy, denied translations, rushed signing, dense format and absent rules together justified the procedural finding. Roman was distinguished as involving only minimal unfairness. The court did not hold that adhesion alone always invalidates employment arbitration.

Substantively, the six-month limitation was judged against statutory wage claims for which employees otherwise had three or four years to sue. The employer-only fee term and the exemption for claims employers typically bring, alongside compelled arbitration of the workers' claims, added to the unfairness. Empire argued the one-way fee provision could not matter because it was already illegal and unenforceable; the court answered that illegality did not make an imposed term immune from the unfairness inquiry.

On choice of law, a forum may decline a choice clause imposed through improper means or one whose enforcement would cause substantial injustice to the weaker party, and the same formation pressures and substantive defects warranted California law. The court expressly declined to decide whether Illinois law would actually compel arbitration.

On severance, Empire had not asked the trial court to exercise that discretion. Independently, the multiple defects supported an inference that arbitration had been structured as an inferior forum favoring the stronger party, so refusal was within discretion.

On preemption, Concepcion rejected the Discover Bank rule but retained generally applicable defenses such as fraud, duress and unconscionability, and the present analysis fell within that surviving category.

The casebook's account concentrates on the signing circumstances, format, absent rules and the continued unconscionability analysis after Concepcion.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-023.rule: Arbitration terms are subject to ordinary contract defenses; place-and-manner terms that are procedurally and substantively unconscionable in their commercial setting may be severed, leaving the agreement to arbitrate enforceable, where unconscionability does not permeate the agreement.

sections.Parties: Florence Bolter, Sandra Valdez and Stephen Knight, who bought Chem-Dry carpet-cleaning franchises in the early 1980s and operated them in Orange County, sued in the superior court and were the petitioners for a writ of mandate in the Court of Appeal; their state complaint added A.Y.S., Inc. Harris Research was the franchisor. The franchisees sought damages and declaratory relief for contract and good-faith breaches and resisted arbitration in Utah. Harris wanted the disputes arbitrated in Salt Lake City and the litigation stayed.
sections.Procedural History:
The franchisees filed their complaint in April 1998. Harris commenced separate Utah arbitrations and sought removal to federal court; the franchisees then dismissed their federal action and filed an identical state complaint. They declined to participate in the AAA hearings, and three appointed arbitrators found the disputes arbitrable. On March 2, 1999, Judge Firmat denied Harris's requested stay and temporarily stopped arbitration. The superior court later granted Harris's motion to confirm the arbitrators' rulings, but vacated that order after an earlier appellate alternative writ required an independent judicial determination of arbitrability. It then ordered arbitration in Utah and dismissed the case on April 18, signing findings that the provisions, even if adhesive, were neither unconscionable nor unreasonably burdensome. The franchisees filed a further writ petition and the Court of Appeal temporarily stayed arbitration.

The Court of Appeal granted the petition, directed the superior court to vacate its judgment and enter a new order striking the provisions requiring arbitration in Utah, dissolved its stay and awarded petitioners appellate costs. Rehearing was denied and the opinion modified on March 30, 2001; Supreme Court review was denied June 13, 2001.
sections.Material Facts:
When the franchisees bought their franchises, Harris was headquartered in California and the agreements contained no arbitration provision. The franchisees periodically signed renewals or replacement agreements. Harris later moved to Utah and required dispute proceedings there; the franchisees claimed that increasingly restrictive terms were imposed under threats of franchise termination.

The clause required disputes to be submitted to the Salt Lake City AAA office and heard there by one arbitrator under commercial rules. It selected the FAA for arbitration matters and Utah law for the franchise agreement, excluded exemplary or punitive damages, required individual rather than class proceedings and barred consolidation with other arbitrations. Harris alone retained an election to litigate claims relating to its marks.

Harris did not refute its characterization as a wealthy international franchisor, and the franchisees' limited means were undisputed. Valdez personally handled advertising, administration, sales, customer calls and scheduling from home. Knight personally administered three franchises and feared losing business if forced to leave California. Bolter was sixty-six, solely responsible for running her franchises, cared for a severely ill husband and had recently declared bankruptcy. Valdez said a franchise bought for $32,500 might sell for only $10,000 to $15,000. The underlying grievances, including an obligation to buy an allegedly overpriced water-extraction system, were not adjudicated by the writ decision.
sections.Issue: Whether provisions requiring established, financially constrained California franchisees to arbitrate in Utah were unconscionable and, if so, whether they could be severed from the agreement to arbitrate. The court expressly avoided the parties' dispute over a California statute prohibiting out-of-state franchise venue and its possible FAA preemption, and decided under generally applicable contract principles.
sections.Holding: The California Court of Appeal, Fourth District, Division Three, in 2001, in an opinion by Justice O'Leary in which Acting Presiding Justice Crosby and Justice Bedsworth concurred, held that the place-and-manner arrangement was oppressive in this setting but that the provisions placing all arbitrations in Salt Lake City could be removed while leaving a complete agreement to arbitrate. It granted the writ and ordered the Utah-location provisions struck.
