Its operative relief did not separately order deletion of the consolidation and damages restrictions or expressly authorize class arbitration, and it left the application of Business and Professions Code section 20040.5 and FAA preemption unresolved.
sections.Reasoning:
The court rejected the premise that arbitration is immune from ordinary contract defenses. Both the federal and California arbitration statutes preserve grounds applicable to contracts generally, and Civil Code section 1670.5 permits rejection or limitation of unconscionable terms. Procedural and substantive unconscionability must both be present, on a sliding scale, and the evaluation looks to commercial setting, purpose and effect, not just contract wording. Adhesion alone does not make arbitration unconscionable.

The procedural concern was that existing owners had to accept the newer terms to continue their businesses. Unlike a prospective purchaser able to reject a franchise at the outset, they had already committed to ongoing small operations and could not realistically negotiate the new place and manner requirements.

Substantively, Utah proceedings would require travel and lodging, interruption of daily operations and added expense for counsel familiar with Utah law. The consolidation prohibition prevented the franchisees from sharing those costs, and the damages restriction limited possible recovery. The court regarded the arrangement as oppressive, with no justification beyond maximizing Harris's advantage and potentially preventing claims. It did not declare every out-of-state arbitration clause, every individual-proceeding clause or arbitration itself unconscionable; its conclusion depended on the combined restrictions and these franchisees' circumstances.

On severance, the franchisees argued the agreement was specifically to arbitrate in Utah and could not survive removal of that element. The court disagreed: section 1670.5 authorizes severance where unconscionability does not permeate the agreement, the requirement to arbitrate was not intrinsically unfair, and curing the defect did not require adding obligations. The casebook uses the case to illustrate severance of the oppressive Utah requirement while retaining arbitration.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-027.rule: A cardholder whose agreement authorizes amendment on notice is bound by a clearly noticed arbitration amendment he had a meaningful opportunity to reject and did not, unless he establishes a generally applicable contract defense to the arbitration agreement itself.

sections.Parties: Bank One, N.A., identified as an Ohio corporation, brought this separate federal action under section 4 of the Federal Arbitration Act to compel arbitration. The defendant, Coates, a Mississippi resident, had financed a home satellite system through a Bank One revolving credit-card plan and, with thirty-seven others, was suing Bank One and additional defendants in Mississippi state court. Bank One wanted arbitration compelled. Coates wanted the court to abstain, to join additional parties and dismiss, and to allow discovery before any ruling.
sections.Procedural History:
On October 20, 1999, Coates and thirty-seven others sued Bank One and additional defendants in the Circuit Court of the Second Judicial District of Bolivar County, Mississippi. On November 22, Sky Scanner Satellite removed the case to the Northern District of Mississippi; Bank One did not remove it. Judge Neal Biggers remanded on August 23, 2000. Bank One had been served on May 1 and answered on June 2.

On September 7, Bank One commenced this separate action against Coates in the Southern District of Mississippi and filed identical actions against the other thirty-seven state plaintiffs. The state plaintiffs then sought a trial setting, and the state judge directed mediation. Coates asked the district court to abstain, alternatively sought to join additional parties including the local agent or employee S. Broadwater, whose joinder would defeat diversity, and requested discovery. On January 2, 2001, the court denied Coates's motions for joinder and dismissal, abstention and discovery and granted Bank One's motion to compel arbitration.
sections.Material Facts:
The credit application Coates signed stated immediately above the signature that he agreed to abide by the Account Agreement and Disclosure Statement issued from time to time. The agreement selected Ohio law. Its amendment provision authorized the bank to change or amend the agreement's terms upon fifteen days' prior written notice if required by law.

On March 8, 1998, Bank One sent cardholders a notice adding arbitration. The provision covered claims by either party against the other, its employees, agents or assigns, arising from or relating to the agreement or account, including the applicability of the arbitration provision or the validity of the agreement. It designated the National Arbitration Forum and its code, provided for a hearing in the federal judicial district containing the customer's billing address, invoked the FAA, and expressly warned that claims otherwise litigable in court or through representative litigation would have to be arbitrated. The amendment took effect April 15, 1998; a cardholder could reject it by mailing written notice with identifying account information by that date.

Coates did not reject. He did not dispute these facts or contend his claims fell outside the clause; he did not recall the notice but did not specifically deny receipt. His position was that he never agreed to arbitration and that the purported agreement was unenforceable. His affidavit said the salesperson had not informed him he was signing for a Bank One credit card.
sections.Issue: Whether the court had an independent basis of federal jurisdiction, had to join absent participants in the underlying transaction, or should abstain in favor of the parallel state litigation; and whether an arbitration agreement was validly formed by the amendment and was enforceable despite Coates's requests for discovery and his claims of fraud, procedural and substantive unconscionability, and the asserted need for a separate clear waiver of jury trial.
sections.Holding: The United States District Court for the Southern District of Mississippi, in 2001, per Chief Judge Tom S. Lee, held that diversity jurisdiction existed, that the local participant need not be joined under Rule 19, that abstention was not justified, and that discovery was unnecessary. It held that Coates was bound by the arbitration amendment on the actual amendment language, notice, rejection mechanism and his failure to reject, that the agreement was not unconscionable, and that no distinct jury-trial waiver was required. It compelled arbitration. It did not decide the truth of the financing allegations, award damages, or expressly enjoin the pending state litigation.
sections.Reasoning:
The FAA does not itself supply jurisdiction, but diversity existed with more than $75,000 in controversy. The action sought only to decide whether Bank One and Coates had to arbitrate their claims against each other, so other alleged joint tortfeasors were not indispensable. Abstention under Colorado River and Moses H. Cone requires exceptional circumstances; neither the prospect of piecemeal proceedings nor the earlier state filing overcame the FAA's policy of enforcement.

Discovery was unnecessary because the agreement, the notice and the incorporated Forum rules were available. Coates's fraud claim attacked procurement of the overall credit agreement rather than the agreement to arbitrate, so under Prima Paint and the Fifth Circuit authorities the court applied it belonged to arbitration; the court did not find that fraud occurred. An unsupported declaration that a party never agreed does not establish a genuine dispute over the making of the agreement.

On assent, the signed application incorporated the agreement, whose first amendment sentence gave broad authority that the following sentence on fees and rates did not restrict, and Ohio banking law allowed the parties to agree to amendments. The notice concerned arbitration alone, prominently warned of its effect and explained how to reject. Small, consistent, legible print did not alone establish procedural unconscionability under Ohio law, which the court read to require both procedural and substantive unconscionability.

A valid agreement to arbitrate necessarily removes the judicial jury trial. Applying Green Tree Financial v. Randolph, Coates had to establish the likelihood of prohibitive expense; the Forum code allowed remedies available under substantive law, modest fees and neutral arbitrators, and his bias claim was speculation.

The casebook builds an adapted problem about depositors, signature cards and a monthly statement announcing arbitration on this case; those are not the facts of Coates.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-028.rule: A party that satisfies a contract's express terms may still be liable in contract damages for breaching the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing if it deliberately acts to destroy the other party's contractual benefits for its own advantage.

sections.Parties: Hilton Hotels Corp., the plaintiff and appellant, had contracted with Dynamic Duo, Inc., a corporation formed by boxing promoters Butch Lewis and Don King, to present boxing events at the Las Vegas Hilton. Hilton sued on breach-of-contract, conspiracy and intentional-interference theories, alleging that Dynamic Duo and its agents intentionally defeated the benefits it expected from the contract. The defendants prevailed before the jury and defended the judgment on appeal.
sections.Procedural History: The jury found for the defendants on all claims, judgment followed, and the district court denied Hilton's motion for a new trial. Hilton appealed the judgment and the denial order, challenging jury misconduct, the contract instructions, and the exclusion of testimony either as rebuttal or upon reopening its case. The Nevada Supreme Court rejected the objections based on jury tampering and the contract instructions, but reversed the defendants' judgment and remanded for a new trial on Hilton's claim for breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing because critical rebuttal evidence had been excluded. Rehearing was denied August 28, 1991.
sections.Material Facts:
Hilton contracted with Dynamic Duo to present the final four events in a heavyweight Unification Series, intended to select a single champion from the titleholders recognized by three boxing organizations. Michael Spinks then held the International Boxing Federation championship. Hilton contended the bargain contemplated his participation throughout the four events. The written contract's recital identified Spinks for the first event in September 1986, but its provision requiring Dynamic Duo to supply boxers for each event did not name particular fighters.

Before the final Ultimate Unification Bout, Spinks forfeited his IBF championship and became ineligible for the series. Hilton alleged that Dynamic Duo and its agents intentionally brought about the forfeiture to pursue more profitable fights outside the series.

At trial Hilton's evidence of Lewis's intentions consisted of newspaper accounts, several quoting him taking credit after the fact for higher purses outside the series. In rebuttal Hilton offered testimony from Duane Ford, then chairman of the Nevada Athletic Commission, that Lewis had said in September 1986, before the Spinks-Cooney arrangement, that he planned to withdraw Spinks from the series to make more money elsewhere. The trial court excluded it as material that belonged in Hilton's case-in-chief and as more prejudicial than probative.
sections.Issue: Whether the jury instructions on contract interpretation or the alleged jury tampering required a new trial; whether, apart from any express obligation to supply Spinks, the promoters owed a duty under the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing not to deliberately defeat Hilton's contractual benefits; and whether excluding Ford's rebuttal testimony was prejudicial error.
sections.Holding: The Nevada Supreme Court, in 1991, in an opinion by Justice Springer in which Chief Justice Mowbray, Justices Steffen and Young and Senior Justice Zenoff concurred, held that there was no instructional error warranting a new trial on ordinary contract breach and no reversible error in the handling of the alleged jury tampering. It held, however, that although Dynamic Duo had no established contractual obligation to supply Spinks for all four events, it had a duty not deliberately to interfere with his ability to participate, and that excluding Ford's testimony as rebuttal was erroneous and prejudicial. The remand did not establish that the promoters deliberately caused the forfeiture or award Hilton damages.
sections.Reasoning:
The trial court declined Hilton's proposed instruction on implied terms but told the jury to determine the parties' intention from the contract's words and the surrounding circumstances, including negotiations, precontract statements and the transaction's object. That gave the jury a fair opportunity to find a mutually understood obligation to produce Spinks throughout, and the court declined to infer that obligation itself after the jury rejected it.

Compliance with the literal terms did not dispose of the separate contention that the promoters deliberately defeated the contract's purpose. Relying on A.C. Shaw Construction, the court explained that contract damages are recoverable for performance contravening the bargain's intention and spirit even where express requirements are satisfied. It distinguished this contractual claim from the narrower tort remedy, which requires special reliance or a fiduciary element. The duty to refrain from such manipulation was distinct from a promise guaranteeing a particular fighter's continued championship; whether Lewis intentionally caused Spinks to lose his title remained a factual question. Although Hilton had not specifically pleaded the covenant claim, the theory apparently had been tried by consent through an unobjected-to instruction.

The newspaper accounts did not clearly establish a prior design to cause the forfeiture. The defense maintained that Lewis and Dynamic Duo had done nothing to interrupt Spinks's title; Ford's proffer directly answered that position and supplied powerful evidence of earlier intention. The defendants could cross-examine him or offer contradictory material, and Lewis remained present. The court was reluctant to find an abuse of discretion in refusing to reopen the case; its holding rested on rebuttal.

The casebook presents the dispute as the Dynamic Duo account, compressing the agreement as silent about Spinks.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-029.rule: A party breaches the implied duty of good faith in every contract when it knowingly exploits its contracting partner's mistake during performance, as distinct from merely remaining silent or having superior knowledge.

sections.Parties: Market Street Associates Limited Partnership, whose general partner and manager was William Orenstein, was the plaintiff. It had taken an assignment of J.C. Penney's leaseholds and sought conveyance of the West Allis, Wisconsin property for $216,336.13 plus interest and $658,590 in monetary damages. The defendants were the General Electric Pension Trust, the lessor, and its five trustees, who resisted the purchase option.
sections.Procedural History: The district court entered summary judgment for the trust on October 3, 1990. The Seventh Circuit reversed in 1991 because the evidence had not been construed favorably enough for the nonmovant Market Street and because Orenstein's state of mind required live testimony; the remand did not itself establish dishonest intent. After a bench trial, Senior District Judge Reynolds of the Eastern District of Wisconsin issued findings of fact and conclusions of law on April 6, 1993. He denied specific performance, ordered judgment for the trust and its five trustees, and dismissed the action on the merits. The brief covers this judgment after remand, not the earlier appellate ruling.
sections.Material Facts:
On January 15, 1968, J.C. Penney sold four properties to the trust and leased them back. Paragraph 34 let the lessee request financing for additional improvements costing at least $250,000; the lessor promised reasonable consideration and good-faith negotiations, and if the parties could not agree the lessee could elect within sixty days to repurchase at the lessor's unamortized cost plus specified accrued interest. On October 30, 1987, Penney assigned the leaseholds to Market Street.

In spring 1988 Market Street negotiated with Phar-Mor for a West Allis addition and wanted to buy the property. After calls and a June 8 letter about purchasing, the trust quoted $3 to $3.1 million on June 29, which Orenstein considered inflated. His July 28 letter described the addition, estimated at $2 million, and requested discussion of financing without mentioning the lease or paragraph 34. The trust, which routinely rejected deals below $10 million, sent an August 10 form rejection saying the proposal did not meet current investment criteria. After receiving it, Orenstein discussed with his son the possibility that the trust did not know he was proceeding under paragraph 34. On August 16, before receiving that rejection, he had sent a second letter asking about financing under the lease without identifying the paragraph; on August 22 he accepted that the trust was not interested. Only the September 27 letter exercising the option identified paragraph 34. Investment manager David Erb testified he had not known of the paragraph until then.
sections.Issue: Whether, as the Seventh Circuit had framed the decisive question, Market Street tried to trick the trust and succeeded, exploiting its contracting partner's mistake during performance in breach of the implied duty of good faith, so that it was not entitled to specific performance of the purchase option.
sections.Holding: The United States District Court for the Eastern District of Wisconsin, in 1993, per Senior District Judge Reynolds after a bench trial, held that Orenstein knowingly exploited the pension trust's misunderstanding during contractual performance, breaching the duty of good faith. Market Street was not entitled to specific performance; the court ordered judgment for the trust and all five trustees and dismissed the action on the merits, awarding neither the discounted conveyance nor the monetary damages requested. The conclusions did not decide the case on the trust's assertion that the purchase option was personal to Penney and could not be assigned.
sections.Reasoning:
Exercising diversity jurisdiction and applying Wisconsin substantive law, the judge invoked the implied duty of good faith in every contract and answered the question framed by the Seventh Circuit against Market Street.

The court distinguished Orenstein's initial assumption from his later realization. He initially expected the trust to review the lease and to respond with reference to paragraph 34; he said he believed the trust must have read the lease when offering a sale price. But the trust screened hundreds of proposals through general investment criteria and treated his request accordingly. Once the form rejection arrived, Orenstein recognized that it reflected general investment screening rather than consideration under paragraph 34. He nevertheless accepted the rejection in ambiguous correspondence, still without identifying the option provision, and did not alert the trust until he exercised the discounted option. He testified that the August 22 letter created a file record of seeking other financing because of the trust's action and that he feared the trust might offer financing later.

That knowing sequence, rather than silence or superior knowledge alone, constituted bad-faith performance. There were no separate writings.

The casebook quotes this postremand finding in a note following its excerpt of the earlier appellate decision; the adjacent discussion of opportunism is the casebook's and not another holding by Judge Reynolds.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-030.rule: Intended will beneficiaries may sue the drafting attorney in negligence and as third-party beneficiaries despite lack of privity, but an attorney is not liable for an error on a legal question that competent lawyers may reasonably regard as doubtful.

sections.Parties: The plaintiffs and appellants were some of the beneficiaries under Eugene H. Emmick's will. The defendant was attorney L. S. Hamm, whom Emmick had retained for consideration to prepare a will and codicils and who later acted for the executors. The beneficiaries sought damages for an allegedly invalid trust provision and for inadequate releases in a will-contest settlement; Hamm argued, among other things, that they lacked contractual privity.
sections.Procedural History: A general demurrer to the beneficiaries' second amended complaint was sustained without leave to amend, and the action was dismissed. On September 5, 1961, the California Supreme Court affirmed the dismissal. Rehearing was denied October 4, 1961.
sections.Material Facts:
These are allegations reviewed on demurrer. The beneficiaries were to receive 15 percent of the residue through a trust under paragraph Eighth of the will, which would terminate at noon five years after the probate court entered its order distributing property to the trustee. They alleged this language violated California's then-applicable perpetuity and alienation restrictions. After probate, Hamm allegedly advised the executors and beneficiaries that the trust was invalid and that they should settle with blood relatives; the beneficiaries alleged a $75,000 loss from the settlement.

A third count concerned Hamm's later work for the executors in settling a will contest based on lack of testamentary capacity. A tentative settlement, subject to court approval, had the estate pay $10,000 for appropriate releases. After the releases were executed and sent to escrow, but before approval, other counsel allegedly warned Hamm of the perpetuity problem and requested releases of all claims against the estate. Hamm allegedly refused to modify the releases or bring the recommendations to the probate court's attention. The compromise was approved, the contestants received $10,000 and later joined an attack on the trust's validity. The beneficiaries alleged broader releases would have left them another $15,000.
sections.Issue: Whether intended beneficiaries of a will, who are not in privity with the attorney who drafted it, may recover from him in negligence or as third-party beneficiaries of his contract with the testator; and, if so, whether these beneficiaries pleaded actionable professional negligence or breach in the drafting of the trust or the handling of the releases.
sections.Holding: The California Supreme Court, in 1961, in a unanimous opinion by Chief Justice Gibson, held that intended will beneficiaries may pursue an attorney in negligence and as third-party beneficiaries of the attorney's contract, overruling Buckley v. Gray. It held, however, that these plaintiffs had not pleaded actionable professional negligence or breach: the first two counts did not and could not state a cause of action on the alleged drafting error, and the release count also failed. It affirmed the dismissal. The court expressly did not decide that the trust was actually invalid.
sections.Reasoning:
Following Biakanja v. Irving, the court asked whether liability to a nonclient was appropriate by weighing the transaction's intended effect, foreseeability of harm, certainty of injury, the connection between conduct and injury, and the policy of preventing future harm, and whether the duty would unduly burden the profession. A principal purpose of hiring a lawyer to draft a will is to transfer the estate as the client directs, failure foreseeably injures the intended recipients, and the estate ordinarily suffers no corresponding loss. Recognizing the claim imposed no greater standard than the attorney already owed the client.

Separately, Civil Code section 1559 permits enforcement of a contract made expressly for a third person's benefit. 'Expressly' excludes merely incidental benefits but does not require a formal declaration naming the beneficiary. The court disapproved language in Smith v. Anglo-California Trust Co. and Fruitvale Canning Co. v. Cotton to the extent it conflicted.

Neither theory relieved the plaintiffs of showing deficient performance. An attorney must use the skill, prudence and diligence ordinarily possessed by lawyers and, without a special undertaking, is not an insurer. The alleged defect arose in the exceptionally difficult interaction of perpetuity and alienation law, and invalidity depended on the remote possibility that distribution would be delayed beyond a life in being plus sixteen years; an ordinarily skilled lawyer could miss it.

On the releases, the complaint did not allege the contestants would have given up other attacks for the same $10,000, nor that Hamm failed to ask for broader releases, and the plaintiffs did not claim they could amend.

The casebook cites the case both for the beneficiary-duty principle and for the limitation that recognizing a right to sue does not establish breach.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-031.rule: Whether a best-efforts obligation requires exclusivity depends on the circumstances, including trade usage; a distributor breaches it by taking on a directly competing product where doing so would necessarily dilute the promised effort.

sections.Parties: Joyce Beverages of New York, Inc., a bottler holding long-term exclusive territorial franchises from Royal Crown Cola Co. covering parts of New York, New Jersey and Connecticut, was the plaintiff. It sought a preliminary injunction preventing Royal Crown from terminating its franchises and appointing another distributor. Royal Crown, the defendant, licensed trademarks and sold secret concentrates to independent bottlers and wanted to terminate because Joyce had agreed to distribute a competing cola.
sections.Procedural History: Joyce sued on December 21. After accelerated discovery, an evidentiary hearing on the preliminary-injunction application began January 11, 1983. On January 18, 1983, Judge Milton Pollack of the Southern District of New York denied preliminary relief in all respects. The opinion supplies findings and conclusions under Rule 52(a) for that provisional application only; it does not enter a final damages judgment or dispose of every claim and counterclaim.
sections.Material Facts:
Joyce's older Royal Crown and Diet-Rite agreements required best efforts to build, maintain and expand sales satisfactorily to Royal Crown. Updated agreements for RC-100 and Decaffeinated RC expressly prohibited substantially or reasonably similar drinks and required best efforts to achieve maximum distribution and sales. Royal Crown's cola brands were about five percent of national cola sales in 1981. Joyce also distributed lemon-lime Seven-Up and other non-cola products.

The Seven-Up Company introduced LIKE, a decaffeinated cola. Early in 1982 Royal Crown warned Joyce it would have to choose between LIKE and Royal Crown's colas. In November Seven-Up offered Joyce partial coexistence in New York and demanded a decision by Thanksgiving. Royal Crown repeated its objection at a November 8 meeting and in a letter warning that it would terminate if Joyce chose LIKE. Joyce signed on November 22. Its president told Royal Crown on November 30 that no decision had been made, then acknowledged the agreement the next day while refusing to surrender the Royal Crown licenses. Seven-Up expected introduction by February 7, 1983. Joyce began soliciting retailers to carry LIKE and planned large free giveaways. Seven-Up's national advertising disparaged caffeine; Joyce's Chicago and Washington affiliates had sponsored that campaign, and Joyce had not committed to reject it in New York.
sections.Issue: Whether Joyce was entitled to a preliminary injunction against termination, which turned on whether taking on the competing LIKE cola breached its best-efforts obligations to Royal Crown, whether the exclusivity arrangement violated section 3 of the Clayton Act or section 1 of the Sherman Act, and whether Joyce showed irreparable injury and a favorable balance of hardships.
sections.Holding: The United States District Court for the Southern District of New York, in 1983, per Judge Milton Pollack, denied the preliminary injunction. It read best efforts as exclusive efforts in these circumstances, found a material breach by Joyce, and concluded that Royal Crown's proposed cancellation would not breach its own obligations. It expressly declined a categorical rule that taking a competitive product line always breaches best efforts. It found no likelihood of success or fair ground for litigation on the antitrust alternative, no irreparable injury, and a balance of hardships favoring Royal Crown.
sections.Reasoning:
Joyce conceded that its conduct violated the Decaffeinated RC agreement unless antitrust law supplied a defense, but claimed it could represent both colas evenhandedly under the older language. The court found a breach from the hearing record. Bottlers compete for limited shelf space, displays, advertising features and promotions; Joyce was already persuading retailers to devote budgets and space to LIKE and would control both brands' local pricing and discounts. That would necessarily dilute its effort for Royal Crown, and keeping Royal Crown merely alive fell short of an undertaking to expand its sales vigorously. Preserving confidential competing marketing strategies posed a further conflict, and the caffeine campaign sought to draw consumers away from Royal Crown's caffeinated products. The court noted that Bloor v. Falstaff did not equate evenhanded effort with best effort.

Industry usage reinforced the conclusion: the record showed a longstanding practice of one cola franchise per bottler, and the newer express exclusivity language reflected the existing understanding rather than a new obligation. The bare signature of another cola agreement was not by itself decisive.

On antitrust, the arrangement did not substantially lessen competition. LIKE had other viable routes into the area, Joyce was Seven-Up's first choice but not its only one, and Royal Crown was a small competitor behind Coke and Pepsi. Separate bottlers would preserve rivalry between the brands.

The transition was a difficult adjustment, not destruction of Joyce's business, while an injunction would leave Royal Crown dependent on a distributor unable and unwilling to promote it.

The casebook uses the case for the contextual nature of exclusivity and the caffeine advertising; the disputed product was LIKE cola, not ordinary Seven-Up.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-032.rule: As the Appellate Division held before being reversed, a release of ordinary negligence cannot defeat personal-injury liability that the exceptions in New Jersey's equine-activities statute preserve, because those exceptions are part of the legislature's allocation of risk.

sections.Parties: Gloria Hubner, who was injured when a rented horse fell at Spring Valley Equestrian Center, and her husband Michael Hubner, who claimed consequential loss, were the plaintiffs and the appellants in the Appellate Division. Spring Valley, the stable operator, was the defendant and relied on the statutory protection for inherent equine risks and on a release Gloria had signed.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court granted summary judgment for Spring Valley, concluding that the statutory allocation of equine risks barred Gloria's personal-injury claim and Michael's consequential-loss claim and accepting the ordinary-negligence release as an independent defense. On August 4, 2009, the New Jersey Appellate Division reversed summary judgment on both grounds. The New Jersey Supreme Court subsequently reversed this appellate decision in 2010 and reinstated summary judgment on the statutory ground, expressly leaving the release question undecided. This entry covers the Appellate Division stage.
sections.Material Facts:
The court stated the facts in the light most favorable to plaintiffs. Gloria and Michael Hubner and four others visited Spring Valley to ride its horses on trails under an employee's guidance. Gloria signed a rental agreement and a release covering injury caused by the stable's ordinary negligence in relation to its premises and operations, excluding gross negligence and willful and wanton misconduct. In the barn were an open mounting area, movable mounting steps, and six to eight pine poles lying parallel on the floor about fifteen feet from the mounting area, roughly six inches in diameter and fourteen to sixteen feet long, used to simulate trail obstacles.

Trail guide Kate Martin brought Gloria the horse Lady, and Gloria mounted from the ground. After Martin led Lady away from the mounting area, horse and rider faced away from the poles; the opinion did not resolve whether Martin or Lady had turned. Martin went for another horse. Lady whinnied, moved her head and backed up. Martin told Gloria to release the reins, which she did, but Lady backed into the poles, tripped and fell, throwing Gloria onto the movable steps and landing on her. Gloria suffered fractures and other injuries. Plaintiffs' expert Andrew Elder attributed the accident to unsecured poles near the mounting area and behind the horses.
sections.Issue: Whether the evidence permitted a jury to find that the accident fell within the equine-activities statute's exceptions for knowingly supplying faulty equipment or negligent disregard for participant safety, rather than being an assumed inherent risk; and whether a release of ordinary negligence could be enforced against claims within those statutory exceptions.
sections.Holding: The New Jersey Appellate Division, in 2009, in an opinion by Judge Grall on a panel with Judges Graves and Ashrafi, held that Elder's opinion about the unsecured poles and the placement of poles and steps created a sufficient jury question under the faulty-equipment or negligent-disregard exception, and that, absent further legislative direction, the release could not defeat personal-injury liability within section 5:15-9. It reversed summary judgment on both grounds. This was a ruling that plaintiffs could proceed, not a finding of negligence, and the Supreme Court later rejected this application of the statute.
sections.Reasoning:
The statute allocates to participants the inherent risks of equine activities, dangers operators cannot practically eliminate, and makes those risks a complete defense, but section 5:15-9 preserves operator liability in specified circumstances notwithstanding the participant's assumption of risk. The court distinguished dangers integral to equine activities from every danger found on a riding track or in a barn. The statutory examples did not make dangerous conduct or instrumentalities within an operator's control necessarily inherent. An operator could knowingly provide faulty equipment by using it improperly installed or for an inappropriate purpose, and positioning equipment to create an unnecessary risk could be negligent disregard even where the general possibility of collisions is inherent. A participant would still have to prove the exception's elements and causation. Spring Valley's broader reading would leave little incentive to eliminate known, unnecessary risks readily within an operator's control.

On the release, the language was broad enough to cover the claim, so the question was enforceability. Exculpatory clauses receive close scrutiny for public-policy conflicts and unconscionability, though voluntarily signing a release to engage in recreation does not generally make it unenforceable. The controlling point was the legislative allocation of risks: the exceptions were an important component of the balance the legislature adopted, and allowing a release to eliminate the liability they authorized would upset it. The opinion did not invalidate every recreational release or every part of this agreement.

The casebook cites the 2009 decision and its 2010 reversal but attributes the exception finding and the quoted release reasoning to the Supreme Court; that public-policy passage is this Appellate Division's reasoning.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-033.rule: Under New Jersey's Equine Activities Liability Act, exceptions to the bar on claims from inherent risks are strictly but reasonably construed: faulty equipment means equipment itself faulty, and negligent disregard requires a breach of a recognized operator duty that caused the injury.

sections.Parties: Gloria Hubner, injured when her horse fell at Spring Valley Equestrian Center, was the plaintiff; her husband Michael was also a plaintiff. Spring Valley, the defendant stable, sought reinstatement of summary judgment in the New Jersey Supreme Court after losing in the Appellate Division. The Farm Bureau and Horse Council supported a protective construction of the statute.
sections.Procedural History: The Law Division granted summary judgment for Spring Valley because the horse's unpredictable movement and collision with the rails were inherent risks covered by the Act, finding the rails were not faulty equipment but part of the ring; as an alternative ground it enforced the release. The Appellate Division reversed and remanded, reasoning that equipment placement could support a statutory exception and that the expert report created a factual issue, and it rejected enforcement of the exculpatory clause in those circumstances. Certification followed. On July 28, 2010, the New Jersey Supreme Court reversed the Appellate Division and reinstated the Law Division's summary judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
On September 3, 2005, Gloria Hubner visited Spring Valley with her husband, relatives and friends for horseback riding. She signed a release before entering the ring for training before a trail ride. Employee Kate Martin instructed her on steering and handling the horse. Wooden rails, or cavaletti, lay near the ring's center for a planned exercise preparing riders for trail conditions, and a portable mounting block was nearby. Gloria declined the block and mounted from the ground with Martin's help. Martin led horse and rider away from the mounting area, leaving them facing the rails and block while other riders mounted.

The horse slowly turned about 180 degrees, putting the equipment behind it, then moved its head, whinnied and backed up. Gloria screamed and pulled back on the reins. Martin told her to stop and she complied, but the horse continued backward, accelerated, tripped over a rail and fell. Gloria was thrown against the mounting block and injured. The court treated these circumstances as undisputed.

Andrew Elder's proposed expert report attributed the accident to unsecured rails near the mounting area and behind the horses and to the block left behind the horse. Elder had never been formally offered as an expert, and his qualifications had not been litigated.
sections.Issue: Whether Gloria Hubner's injury resulted from an inherent risk of equine activity for which the Equine Activities Liability Act bars recovery, or whether the placement of the rails and mounting block brought the claim within the Act's exceptions for knowingly supplied faulty equipment or negligent disregard for participant safety.
sections.Holding: The New Jersey Supreme Court, in 2010, in an opinion by Justice Hoens joined by Justices Long, LaVecchia, Albin, Wallace and Rivera-Soto, with Chief Justice Rabner not participating, unanimously held that the Act barred the claim because the injury resulted from an inherent risk. Good-condition rails were not faulty equipment, and the record showed no supported breach within a statutory exception causing the injury. It reversed the Appellate Division and reinstated summary judgment for Spring Valley, expressly without deciding whether the contractual release was valid.
sections.Reasoning:
The Act's findings allocate to participants risks essentially impractical or impossible to eliminate. Its nonexhaustive definition of inherent risks includes horses' propensities and unpredictable reactions, collisions, and a participant's failure to maintain control; claims from those risks are completely barred notwithstanding comparative negligence, subject to exceptions in section 5:15-9. Each provision looked plain in isolation, but broad exception language could eliminate the broad protection altogether. That latent ambiguity required harmonizing the whole enactment, so the court construed the exceptions strictly but reasonably in light of the statute's purpose.

Because the legislative history did not resolve the interaction, the court looked to the related Ski and Roller Skating Rink Acts and to the distinction in Meistrich between primary assumption of risk, an inherent risk for which the operator owes no duty, and secondary assumption, a risk negligently created by an operator who owes a duty.

The protection does not excuse every act: assigning a beginner to a known difficult horse or furnishing a saddle with a known broken strap could implicate an exception. But faulty equipment means the equipment itself is faulty, so improper placement must be judged under the negligent-disregard exception, which requires breach of a recognized duty that caused the injury. A participant cannot recast an inherent-risk injury as an operator's omission.

Elder's placement theory depended on a premise the record contradicted. The employee did not position the equipment behind horse and rider; Gloria faced the rails before and after mounting, and they came to be behind her only because the horse turned. The turning, backing and collision were defined inherent dangers.

The casebook attributes an exception-based result and a quotation about unenforceable releases to this court, but those were the Appellate Division's reasoning.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-034.rule: Under the clean-hands doctrine, equity will refuse to enforce a valid contract for a plaintiff whose misconduct is serious and sufficiently related to the transaction, including misconduct in which continuing the employment relationship necessarily involved the employee.

sections.Parties: North Pacific Lumber Co., a Portland lumber wholesaler, was the plaintiff and appellant. It sued its former hardwood trader and assistant manager, Oliver, to enforce a noncompetition covenant, seeking an injunction, damages and attorney fees. Oliver challenged the covenant as unreasonable, asserted unclean hands, counterclaimed for attorney fees, and cross-appealed the amount of the fees awarded to him. Tree Products, his new employer, was named but never served.
sections.Procedural History: North Pacific sued in May 1976. After a lengthy trial, the court found the contract valid but refused enforcement because of North Pacific's misconduct and dismissed the complaint with prejudice. It rejected Oliver's claim that the contract was oppressive, denied quantum-meruit wages, and, applying the reciprocal-fee statute, ORS 20.096, awarded Oliver $105,000 in fees. North Pacific appealed the dismissal and the award; Oliver cross-appealed the amount. On June 19, 1979, the Oregon Supreme Court, reviewing de novo, affirmed dismissal of the complaint, modified the decree to delete the fee award, and allowed neither party costs. Rehearing was denied September 5.
sections.Material Facts:
North Pacific wholesaled lumber, principally by telephone trading from Portland. It hired Oliver in February 1967 as a hardwood trader and promoted him to assistant manager in 1969. His contract prohibited defined competition after departure for the shorter of his employment period or two years, and gave the company a right to an injunction, damages and attorney fees. Oliver left voluntarily in April 1976 and soon worked for competing Tree Products. He stopped actively soliciting sales when he learned of the suit. By the time of the appeal the noncompetition period had expired.

Oliver accused North Pacific of many kinds of misconduct; the principal ones became telephone monitoring and profits from settling customer claims. The company had equipment and practices for listening to employees' calls, and one episode sought information about Oliver after he left. As to settlements, traders handling complaints about defective lumber would minimize the deficiency to induce a buyer to accept a small settlement, then exaggerate it to the supplier to obtain a larger payment, and North Pacific kept the difference. The company acknowledged improper profits and encouragement by lower management. Oliver supervised those departmental activities and was paid a salary and a percentage of departmental profit.
sections.Issue: Whether an employer's misconduct during the employment relationship, rather than in forming the covenant itself, can bar equitable enforcement of a valid noncompetition covenant under the clean-hands doctrine; and whether an employee who knowingly participated in that misconduct can recover attorney fees under the reciprocal-fee statute after successfully defending.
sections.Holding: The Oregon Supreme Court, in 1979, in an opinion by Justice Holman, held that the settlement-profit practice sufficiently affected the parties' equitable relations to justify refusing North Pacific's claims, although the telephone monitoring did not. It also held that Oliver, who knowingly participated in and profited from the improper settlements, was barred from affirmative contractual relief, and that ORS 20.096 did not give him a fee right free of the clean-hands objection. It affirmed dismissal of the complaint, deleted the $105,000 fee award, and left the parties where it found them.
sections.Reasoning:
The court distinguished a covenant's validity from its enforceability in equity. Clean hands protects the integrity of the court rather than punishing the plaintiff or rewarding a deserving defendant. The misconduct need not invalidate the agreement or violate a statute, but it must be serious enough and sufficiently related to the transaction; general bad character or unrelated wrongdoing does not suffice.

North Pacific argued that the covenant itself must have arisen from the wrongdoing. The court declined to confine the relevant transaction to contract formation: later performance of the employment relationship can create the connection, and misconduct toward outsiders can matter if the employer used the employee's position to involve him in it. The critical question was whether continuing the employment made the employee's participation in the wrongful practices necessary. The defense did not depend on the employee's moral innocence.

Monitoring failed that test because there was no showing that North Pacific monitored Oliver's own conversations or required him to monitor others. The settlement practice met it: the court found the practice occurred and was knowingly encouraged in departmental meetings and the instruction manual, and Oliver could not remain assistant manager while avoiding responsibility for carrying it out.

On fees, a successful defense did not entitle Oliver to affirmative relief free of the same objection. ORS 20.096 makes one-sided fee rights reciprocal, but equalizing contractual rights does not give a party more than an express bilateral fee provision would, and such a provision would itself be subject to clean hands.

The casebook uses the case in its clean-hands account to contrast the monitoring with the settlement-profit scheme and the different results on enforcement and fees.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-035.rule: A seller's mere knowledge that a buyer follows an unlawful occupation does not bar recovery of the price of an ordinary lawful article with legitimate uses, where the seller did not sell to aid that business or participate in an unlawful use.

sections.Parties: Fineman, a retail dealer in pianos and talking machines, was the plaintiff seller suing on a purchase-money note. The defendant was J. B. Faulkner, administrator of the estate of the purchaser, Mamie Faulkner, who resisted enforcement of the note on the ground that the transaction was contrary to public policy.
sections.Procedural History: The parties agreed on the material facts, and judgment was entered for the seller against the administrator. On September 12, 1917, the North Carolina Supreme Court affirmed.
sections.Material Facts: Mamie Faulkner conducted prostitution at her home in Princeville, across the river from Tarboro. On September 18, 1916, Fineman sold her an Edison talking machine and records, delivered them to that home, and obtained the purchase-money writing, which was secured in the machine. He knew her occupation by general reputation. The stipulation also established that he had no interest in her business and gave no aid in its conduct beyond whatever incidental assistance the mere sale might furnish. The terms were those of his ordinary transactions, and the instrument was of a generally used kind without a slot attachment. After her death the administrator refused to pay and did not offer to return the goods. The report states no dollar amount for the unpaid balance.
sections.Issue: Whether the seller's knowledge that the purchaser engaged in prostitution made an ordinary sale of a talking machine and the purchase-money note unenforceable on public-policy grounds.
sections.Holding: The North Carolina Supreme Court, in 1917, in an opinion by Chief Justice Clark, held that knowledge of a purchaser's unlawful occupation does not by itself defeat the seller's claim for the price of an article having legitimate uses, where he has not sold to aid that business or participated in an unlawful use. On the agreed facts the estate could not use the purchaser's occupation to defeat the seller's lawful claim, and the judgment was affirmed. The opinion did not decide the different case of a seller intentionally financing, supplying or otherwise participating in an unlawful undertaking.
sections.Reasoning:
The court adopted, with a modification, the distinction offered by the seller's counsel between an unlawful sale, an article usable only for an unlawful purpose, and the ordinary lawful sale of an article having legitimate uses. The first two could prevent recovery of the price; the third does not. The test looks to the claimant's own participation and the legality of the transaction rather than treating the buyer's occupation as a universal disability to incur ordinary commercial obligations.

Allowing the defense would either encourage people in illegal occupations by freeing them from paying for ordinary goods or effectively bar them from obtaining such goods at all, and neither was the law's intended result. The court gave the example of ordinary provisions or clothing sold to someone known to distill or retail liquor unlawfully. It compared a prior land sale in which the vendor knew the buyer intended an immoral use; lack of the vendor's participation and control did not excuse payment. Fineman's position was stronger in one respect, since knowing the purchaser's occupation did not establish that he knew this machine would be put to an immoral use.

The administrator's authorities on gambling notes, usurious agreements and transactions supporting the Confederate government involved an illegal consideration, an unlawful transaction, or the seller's participation in the prohibited purpose. A case denying compelled telephone service to premises used for prostitution involved a service almost necessarily aiding the illegal business. The security in the machine did not alter the analysis.

The casebook presents the case, within its discussion of degrees of involvement, for the distinction between knowledge and participation in an ordinary credit sale.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-036.rule: A contract obtained through bribery cannot sustain claims before a tribunal as a matter of public policy, and a contract procured by bribing the other party's agent is voidable at that principal's option until informed affirmation.

sections.Parties: World Duty Free Company Limited, an Isle of Man company managed by Nasir Ibrahim Ali, was the claimant. The Republic of Kenya was the respondent. The company sought restoration of its airport duty-free complexes with associated financial relief, or alternative compensation around $500 million. Kenya denied breach and applied to dismiss on illegality grounds. Former President Daniel arap Moi was not a party, and the tribunal had no jurisdiction over him.
sections.Procedural History: The claimant commenced ICSID proceedings in June 2000. After it disclosed the payment in its December 2002 memorial, Kenya applied in March 2003 to dismiss on illegality grounds and, in its April 18, 2003 counter-memorial, expressly avoided the agreement. The tribunal, composed of President Gilbert Guillaume, Andrew Rogers, QC, and V. V. Veeder, QC, confined a preliminary merits hearing to whether Kenya was entitled to avoid and had avoided the contract, whether it had lost that right, and whether public policy barred the pleaded claims; breach and damages were excluded. The hearing was held January 18, 2006. The award of October 4, 2006 dismissed the claim, with each side bearing its own legal costs and half the arbitration costs.
sections.Material Facts:
On April 27, 1989, Kenya agreed with House of Perfume to construct, maintain and operate duty-free complexes at Nairobi and Mombasa airports for ten years, with an option for another ten, at $1 million annually. A May 11, 1990 amendment substituted World Duty Free. Ali signed for the companies and managed the project. Article 9 consented to ICSID arbitration and directed the tribunal to apply English law; Article 10(A) said Kenyan law governed construction of the agreement.

Ali's own written statement and hearing evidence supplied the payment facts. While seeking permissions for the investment, he consulted intermediary Rashid Sajjad, who arranged an audience with Moi and said that a $2 million personal donation in cash was required for doing business with the government. Ali transferred $2 million through the intermediary. He described $500,000, converted into Kenyan shillings, being brought in a briefcase to the president's residence; after the meeting he found corn in place of the money. He said the payment had appeared to him to be a bribe but that he was told it was lawful and necessary for the contract. Kenya did not deny the payment circumstances.

The company alleged it had spent approximately $27 million developing the facilities and that later actors seized its control and assets and caused Ali's arrest and deportation. These were allegations, not findings.
sections.Issue: Whether the payment to the president was a bribe that procured the investment agreement; whether public policy, transnational or under the applicable English and Kenyan law, barred the claimant's contractual claims; and whether Kenya was entitled to avoid the agreement, had avoided it, and had not lost that right through affirmation.
sections.Holding: The ICSID tribunal, in its 2006 award signed by all three arbitrators, found that the payment was bribery procuring the 1989 agreement and held that the claimant could not maintain its pleaded claims under transnational public policy or the public policy of the applicable law. It also held that Kenya had validly avoided the agreement and had not lost that right beforehand. It dismissed the claim and declined ordinary successful-party cost shifting. There was no damages award, restitution order or recovery of the bribe, and no award against Moi.
sections.Reasoning:
The claimant characterized the payment as a gift of protocol or a Harambee contribution. The tribunal rejected that explanation for concealed payments intended above all to obtain presidential approval for the investment.

On transnational public policy, the tribunal warned that it required objective support rather than an arbitrator's personal moral judgment. It considered criminal prohibitions, international anticorruption instruments, national decisions and arbitral precedents; conventions postdating the transaction served only as confirmation of an existing condemnation of bribery, and Kenya's own law prohibited the conduct in 1989. Widespread corrupt practice did not make procurement bribery acceptable.

Under the chosen laws, it found no material difference between English and Kenyan law on the issues. The bar to a claim founded on illegality protects the public rather than rewarding the defendant. Ali was the alter ego of both contracting companies, the bribe was intrinsic to the whole transaction, and it could not be severed as a collateral bargain. The tribunal found no authority for balancing comparative misconduct and said the facts would not favor the claimant in any event: Ali had no investment held hostage and freely chose to bribe. It acknowledged the disturbing feature of Kenya invoking its former president's corruption.

On avoidance, a contract procured by bribing the other party's agent is voidable at the principal's option. Moi's corrupt knowledge was not attributed to the state; Kenya first learned of the payment from the December 2002 disclosure and promptly avoided in April 2003.

Neither side argued that the bribe specifically procured the arbitration clause, so the tribunal assumed it remained valid.

The casebook calls this a 2007 arbitration decision; 2007 is the publication year.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-037.rule: Absent a statute directing return of bribe money, a briber cannot recover it through the courts, whether the attempted corruption succeeded or failed, because agreements to commit a crime are illegal and void.

sections.Parties: The State of Maryland was the appellant, challenging an order returning bribe money. James Linwood Strickland, who had pleaded guilty to bribery, was the appellee; he had moved in the circuit court for return of the $2,500 he had paid and moved to dismiss the State's appeal.
sections.Procedural History: Strickland was indicted, pleaded guilty and received a four-year prison term. When the plea was accepted on November 17, 1977, the State offered the cash as an exhibit and the court admitted it. Judgment was entered March 1, 1978, and Strickland did not appeal. Almost three months after trial he moved for sentence modification or reduction, return of property and other relief. After a hearing, the circuit court ordered return of the money on August 10, 1978, and the State appealed that portion. On April 19, 1979, Maryland's Court of Special Appeals denied Strickland's motion to dismiss the appeal, reversed the return order and charged appellate costs to him. It did not review his unappealed conviction and sentence.
sections.Material Facts: Strickland sought to induce District Court Judge Sylvania W. Woods to show leniency toward a friend with a pending case. Woods promptly contacted the State's Attorney, and the opinion describes an apparent request that the judge cooperate with the investigation until payment occurred. Strickland delivered $2,500 to Woods, who immediately handed it to agents of the State's Attorney. The State later placed the cash in evidence at the guilty-plea proceeding. In seeking its return, Strickland testified that he did not intend a gift. The hearing judge viewed the State's retention of the money as an unconstitutional forfeiture of estate resulting from conviction under Article 27 of Maryland's Declaration of Rights.
sections.Issue: Whether the State could appeal an order, entered under a criminal docket, returning money used as an exhibit; and whether a convicted briber is entitled to recover the bribe money, under the exhibit-withdrawal rule, the constitutional prohibition on forfeiture of estate, or a theory that the illegal bargain was unperformed.
sections.Holding: Maryland's Court of Special Appeals, in 1979, in an opinion by Chief Judge Gilbert for a panel with Judges Thompson and Wilner, held that the State could appeal because the property claim was civil in nature, and that Strickland was not entitled to the money. Its express rule was that, absent a statute directing return of bribe money, the briber cannot recover it whether the attempted corruption succeeded or failed. The return order was reversed.
sections.Reasoning:
On appealability, Strickland argued that the order arose in a criminal case and fell under the restricted statutory authority for State criminal appeals. The court distinguished the nature of the claim from where it was filed. The demand sought a determination of ownership or entitlement to possession of personal property, in the nature of replevin or of trespass or trover to determine title, and was civil either way.

Rule 1217(f)(2) on withdrawal of exhibits did not help him. Withdrawal means taking back what one supplied; the State, not Strickland, had supplied the exhibit, and the rule did not restore his title.

On forfeiture, the court reasoned that Strickland freely relinquished possession and title when he delivered the money to Woods, who received it as the State's agent, so title passed to the State. Because he no longer owned an interest in the money, retaining it did not forfeit his estate.

On contract, agreements to commit a crime are illegal and void, and courts do not award damages for their breach. Even assuming for argument that Woods had breached such an agreement or that the consideration had wholly failed, Strickland could not obtain judicial help to recover payment made for an illegal act. An Attorney General opinion stating a general rule of returning property to the person from whom it was taken did not establish a contrary right. Public policy independently forbade courts from assisting a person who voluntarily paid to corrupt judicial action, and the court emphasized the damage judicially ordered refunds of bribes would do to public confidence.

The casebook uses the case, under the heading of judicial bribery, for illegality and failed consideration.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-038.rule: A disappointed bidder's claim that the government denied its proposal fair and honest consideration accrues when the bidder has notice of the alleged concealed manipulation, not merely when it learns it lost the award.

sections.Parties: L-3 Communications Integrated Systems, L.P., successor in interest to Raytheon E-Systems, was the plaintiff in a bid protest against the United States. Lockheed Martin Aeronautics Company, which had won the contracts, intervened to defend its awards. L-3 sought $2,564,397 in bid-preparation and proposal costs. The United States and Lockheed Martin moved to dismiss as untimely, and Lockheed Martin also moved to dismiss for failure to state a claim.
sections.Procedural History: L-3 filed this protest in the United States Court of Federal Claims on May 16, 2006 and amended its complaint in February 2007. The United States and Lockheed Martin filed Rule 12(b)(1) timeliness motions, and Lockheed Martin filed a Rule 12(b)(6) motion. Judge Williams issued the opinion under seal on November 16, 2007 and reissued it with redactions on November 26. The court denied all the motions and directed a status conference for further proceedings. This was an interlocutory decision permitting the protest to continue, not a judgment finding corruption or awarding costs. The brief is based on the public, redacted opinion.
sections.Material Facts:
The Air Force solicited proposals in August 1998 for work in its C-5 Galaxy avionics modernization program. Raytheon and Lockheed Martin were the only proposers. Raytheon learned on January 22, 1999 that Lockheed Martin had won the two contracts and received a debriefing January 28, which disclosed that senior Air Force acquisition official Darleen Druyun had acted as source selection authority and had changed evaluation ratings.

In 2002 Druyun recused herself from matters involving Lockheed Martin and Raytheon, entered employment discussions with Lockheed Martin and verbally agreed to accept a position there. She separately negotiated for Boeing employment, later joined Boeing, and in April 2004 pleaded guilty to a conflict-of-interest conspiracy. Her conviction concerned Boeing dealings, not this procurement.

A Defense Department study reviewed 407 acquisitions and selected eight anomalies, including the C-5 procurement. On February 28, 2006, the Inspector General issued a report identifying inadequately documented source-selection decisions, an unsupported reassignment of selection authority to Druyun, and unjustified ratings changes favoring Lockheed Martin's higher-cost proposal. L-3 alleged that Druyun improperly appointed herself, manipulated ratings and concealed the denial of fair consideration. It did not accuse Lockheed Martin of knowing about or participating in the alleged misconduct.
sections.Issue: Whether L-3's claim was barred by the six-year limitation in 28 U.S.C. section 2501 because it accrued at the January 1999 award or debriefing rather than when the investigation disclosed the alleged irregularities; and whether the complaint stated a claim despite the presumption that government officials act in good faith.
sections.Holding: The United States Court of Federal Claims, in 2007, per Judge Williams, held that the fair-consideration claim accrued when the Inspector General report provided notice in February 2006 and was timely, and alternatively that the accrual-suspension rule applied because of the alleged concealment. It held that the pleading alleged more than an unsupported conclusion and could support bid-preparation and proposal costs if proved. It denied all the dismissal motions. It expressly did not resolve whether equitable tolling is available under section 2501.
sections.Reasoning:
The court treated section 2501 as jurisdictional under then-binding Federal Circuit authority, so L-3 bore the burden of establishing timeliness. Judge Williams reasoned that the Administrative Dispute Resolution Act supplied broader statutory protest jurisdiction and removed the need for the implied contract of fair consideration as a jurisdictional predicate, while leaving unfair consideration actionable; the court acknowledged the Federal Circuit had not resolved whether the implied-contract theory survived the Act.

On accrual, the court distinguished knowing one had lost a procurement from knowing the consideration process had allegedly been secretly manipulated. Raytheon knew Druyun served as selection authority and changed ratings, but neither action was unlawful on its face; a source selection authority ordinarily may exercise independent judgment and disagree with subordinate evaluators. Officials act under a presumption of good faith, and bidders were not obliged to assume secret bias. A speculative protective protest in 1999 could have disrupted the procurement without assuring discovery. Alternatively, accrual suspension protects a claimant where government conduct was concealed or the injury inherently unknowable; that is distinct from equitable tolling. Using the report's issuance to establish notice did not accept its assertions as proof of wrongdoing.

On the merits motion, the court agreed that a clear-and-convincing burden applies to allegations of fraud or comparable quasi-criminal misconduct, but the eventual evidentiary burden did not permit weighing likely success at the pleading stage. The allegations tied together Druyun's Lockheed Martin dealings, employment ambitions, unauthorized assumption of selection authority and ratings manipulation; although the connections were indirect, they met Twombly's requirement of factual allegations above speculation.

The casebook uses the case under its heading on undoing official corruption; its summary ties the claim to Druyun's Boeing favors, though the awards went to Lockheed Martin.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-039.rule: A seller who procures sales by secretly bribing the buyer's purchasing agent cannot recover the price, because public policy forbids enforcing contracts obtained through corruption of an agent, even if the buyer keeps the goods.

sections.Parties: Samuel Sirkin, the seller, was the plaintiff and sued for $1,555.81, the purchase price of hosiery and wrappers sold and delivered. The Fourteenth Street Store, a New York department-store corporation, was the defendant buyer and the appellant; it pleaded as a separate defense that Sirkin had obtained the orders by bribing its purchasing agent.
sections.Procedural History: At trial in the City Court, Sirkin proved orders, delivery and nonpayment and moved for judgment on the evidence and pleadings, arguing the separate defense was legally insufficient. The store objected and asked to prove its allegations. The City Court directed a verdict for the price plus interest, and the Appellate Term affirmed. On February 14, 1908, the Appellate Division, First Department, by a vote of three to two, reversed the Appellate Term's determination and the seller's judgment and ordered a new trial, with costs to the appellant to abide the event.
sections.Material Facts: Because the defense was excluded, the facts are those the store alleged. The store's separate defense alleged that, without its knowledge or consent, Sirkin promised its purchasing agent five percent of the price of goods the agent ordered, that the orders resulted from that arrangement, and that Sirkin paid the agent $75 after delivery solely in return for placing those orders. The store characterized the bribe and the sales as parts of an illegal transaction. The City Court reasoned that although the agreement to pay the agent was contrary to public policy, the buyer could not retain the goods without paying. Section 384r of the Penal Code, enacted in 1905, criminalized specified secret gifts, promises and commissions intended to influence an agent's conduct in the principal's business, with a fine between $10 and $500 or such a fine and imprisonment for up to one year; it did not expressly state that the resulting sales contract was void.
sections.Issue: Whether a buyer's pleaded defense that the seller obtained the orders by secretly promising and paying a commission to the buyer's purchasing agent is legally sufficient to bar the seller's action for the price of goods delivered and retained.
sections.Holding: The New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division, First Department, in 1908, in an opinion by Justice Laughlin joined by Justices McLaughlin and Clarke, with Justice Scott dissenting joined by Presiding Justice Patterson, held that the buyer must be permitted to prove its pleaded commercial-bribery defense and that, if established, the defense would prevent the seller from enforcing the resulting sales contracts. It ordered a new trial. The decision was not a finding that the alleged bribe had been proved.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority treated the promise of a percentage of every order as an inducement to place the orders and consideration for doing so, and refused to isolate a formally ordinary sales agreement from the unlawful method by which it was allegedly obtained; later orders given pursuant to the promise remained connected to it.

Although the statute did not declare the sales void, the majority treated it as an authoritative declaration and extension of public policy against corrupting agents. Denying only the commission would inadequately deter the practice. The principal had purchased faithful service, and a secret payment tempted the agent to overpay or accept inferior goods; the injury did not depend on proving an overcharge. Enforcing the seller's net share after subtracting the bribe would itself give effect to the illegal arrangement. The agent's accountability to the principal was an inadequate remedy because secrecy made detection difficult.

Retaining the goods was not ratification: unlike ordinary fraud, this transaction implicated a public policy that forbade ratification as well as formation. Nor could the seller avoid the defense by presenting a prima facie case that did not expose the bribe. The majority accepted that a buyer might keep delivered goods without an enforceable price obligation.

Justice Scott, dissenting, would have affirmed. He saw the illegal agreement between seller and agent as distinct from the lawful, completed sale, which was at most voidable for fraud, and thought adding forfeiture of the price to the statutory penalties was a legislative decision.

The casebook uses the case for commercial bribery and the public-policy bar, and its editors separately criticize the majority's broad licensing analogy.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-040.rule: A party may be denied recovery on a contract lawful on its face when its performance involved gravely immoral and illegal conduct, such as commercial bribery, that is directly connected to the obligation sued upon and central to the performance.

sections.Parties: McConnell, the plaintiff, sued Commonwealth Pictures Corp. for further commissions and an accounting under a written agreement to pay him for negotiating motion-picture distribution rights. Commonwealth, the defendant and the appellant in the Court of Appeals, pleaded two affirmative defenses alleging that McConnell obtained the rights by commercial bribery and that recovery was barred by public policy. McConnell disputed the allegations and moved to strike the defenses.
sections.Procedural History: Special Term struck both defenses because the agreement McConnell sued upon was lawful in itself. The First Department affirmed that part of the order despite a dissent. Commonwealth appealed. On March 31, 1960, the New York Court of Appeals reversed the appealed order, awarded costs in all courts, remitted the matter to the Appellate Division for proceedings consistent with its opinion, and answered the certified question in the negative, so that McConnell's motion attacking the two defenses was to be denied. Whether Commonwealth could prove the defenses remained for later, and the sufficiency of its counterclaims was not before the court.
sections.Material Facts:
The allegations were accepted as true only to test the legal sufficiency of the defenses. Commonwealth agreed in writing to pay McConnell $10,000 if he negotiated an agreement obtaining motion-picture distribution rights for it, followed by a percentage of gross receipts. According to the dissent, the rights concerned forty western feature films and four serial films associated with Universal Pictures, and the later payment was twenty percent of gross receipts after Commonwealth recouped $100,000 from sixty percent of gross receipts. McConnell obtained the distribution agreement, Commonwealth paid the initial $10,000, and it later refused his demand for further commissions and an accounting.

Commonwealth's answer alleged that McConnell obtained the rights by secretly promising and paying $10,000 to a representative of the producer, without the knowledge of Commonwealth or the producer. One defense characterized the payment as commercial bribery contrary to Penal Law section 439; the other repeated the conduct and invoked public policy. Commonwealth also counterclaimed, including for recovery of the initial $10,000.
sections.Issue: Whether a defendant may plead commercial bribery central to the plaintiff's performance as a defense to compensation under an agreement lawful on its face, even though the defendant did not direct the bribery and the plaintiff might prove his prima facie contract claim without mentioning it.
sections.Holding: The New York Court of Appeals, in 1960, in an opinion by Chief Judge Desmond joined by Judges Dye, Fuld, Burke and Foster, with Judge Froessel dissenting and Judge Van Voorhis joining that dissent in a separate memorandum, answered yes and reinstated the two defenses. A party can be denied recovery on a facially valid contract where its performance involves gravely immoral, illegal conduct, provided the illegality bears a direct connection to the obligation sued upon and is central to or a dominant part of the performance. The court did not decide that McConnell actually paid a bribe.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority began with the public policy against using courts to obtain the rewards of crime or to profit from one's own fraud. That policy would fail if a plaintiff could avoid it merely by drafting a lawful promise and then performing through central corruption. Assuming the defenses were true, the commissions resulted from the bribery used to obtain the rights. The concern was whether enforcement would let the plaintiff collect the fruits of corruption, not whether the defendant had a superior moral claim.

The court thought the conduct appeared to fall within section 439 but also relied on common-law public policy. Sirkin had refused recovery to a seller who secretly paid the buyer's purchasing agent, and Reiner denied compensation for services performed through fraud on a third party; bribing the producer's representative did not differ in principle. It was not decisive that McConnell could prove his claim without exposing the bribe.

Answering the windfall objection, the majority rejected any rule that small illegality forfeits compensation: minor or merely incidental wrongdoing does not erase contractual rights, and the pleaded bribery lay at the dominant end of the spectrum. Southwestern Shipping was distinguished as an exception protecting against a mere depository or escrow holder exploiting illegality.

Judge Froessel would have affirmed: the agreement was lawful when made and not itself obtained through bribery, Commonwealth kept the benefits, Sirkin involved the very contract sued upon, and the majority's gradations were unworkable. Judge Van Voorhis added that the rule might encourage breaches of faith rather than discourage bribery.

The casebook uses the case to expose the tension between refusing judicial aid to central corruption and letting the defendant keep the contractual benefit.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-041.rule: A contract made by a contractor lacking a statutorily required license is null and void, and an agency's relaxed enforcement or the other party's knowledge does not validate it; the contractor may recover only its actual costs through unjust enrichment.

sections.Parties: Trade-Winds Environmental Restoration, Inc., a remediation contractor, was the plaintiff suing for the asserted unpaid balance on work at Heritage Plaza in Metairie. The defendants and movants were Stewart Development, LLC, the building's owner; Stirling Properties, Inc., which managed leasing and acted as the owner's agent; and Travelers Indemnity Company of Connecticut, the property insurer. They sought partial summary judgment, Stewart Development arguing that the contract was invalid because Trade-Winds lacked the required licenses at formation.
sections.Procedural History: Trade-Winds filed suit on June 27, 2006. The defendants filed a motion for partial summary judgment on December 11, 2007. In an order signed January 24, 2008, Judge Ivan L. R. Lemelle of the Eastern District of Louisiana granted the motion. The order dismissed Trade-Winds' breach-of-contract claim against Stewart Development and its claims against Stirling and Travelers, leaving its claims against Stewart Development limited to unjust enrichment for the actual cost of materials, services and labor.
