sections.Material Facts:
RaDec became general contractor on a $5,275,800 bid, including $404,269 allocated to earthwork. The original plan required importing 100,000 cubic yards of fill. The contract incorporated American Institute of Architects general conditions; section 12.1.4 authorized the architect to determine the cost of a change when the parties could not agree, based on reasonable expenditures and savings attributable to it.

After contracting, architect Wilscam, Mullins, Birge revised the plan so that no imported fill was needed. RaDec sought reductions from its earthwork subcontractor, Wiekhorst Brothers, and Wilscam rejected proposed reductions of $30,100 and then $80,000 as unfair to the district. The district invoked section 12.1.4. At a meeting, grading subcontractor Negus-Sweenie proposed a $203,500 cost for earthwork without imported fill. Two months later, at a meeting attended only by district and architect representatives, Wilscam issued a $189,018 contract deduction, removing the $407,888 earthwork figure in the payment schedules and substituting Negus-Sweenie's $203,500 plus profit.

RaDec objected that rebuilding the whole earthwork price from the bottom up ignored costs already incurred and exceeded the architect's authority to price the change. It refused to sign the change order but finished the school.
sections.Issue: What standard governs judicial review of an architect's contractually authorized determination of the cost of a change, and whether the architect's repricing of the earthwork here could be set aside under that standard.
sections.Holding: Nebraska Supreme Court, 1995, in an opinion by Justice Connolly; no separate writing or vote is reported. The court held that the architect's contractual decision was ordinarily binding absent fraud, gross mistake necessarily implying bad faith, or failure to exercise honest judgment. Although the district correctly argued for that demanding standard, the architect's reduction was patently erroneous and thus legally equivalent to bad faith for this dispute. The $80,269 judgment was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning:
The court agreed with the district about the governing rule: a designated third person's decision on construction disputes can be binding, subject to fraud, a gross mistake necessarily implying bad faith, or a failure of honest judgment. A court may not merely substitute what it regards as a better calculation. But decisions without a reasonable basis, or patently erroneous ones, can constitute the equivalent of bad faith and the necessary gross mistake.

The evidence supported the trial court's finding that Wilscam used Negus-Sweenie's figures without verifying a reasonable relationship to actual costs. RaDec had supplied an accounting that accurately reflected the savings from eliminating imported fill, but Wilscam did not use it. That was more than a disagreement over professional discretion: the method was patently erroneous for the contract change being evaluated.

Because this was a law action tried without a jury, the trial court's findings had the effect of a jury verdict and would be reversed only if clearly wrong. Under that review the gross-mistake conclusion stood, and the district's correct statement of the stricter rule did not require reversal.

The casebook asks whether grossly erroneous but potentially honest judgment can satisfy the bad-faith limitation; the brief notes that the court reasoned by legal equivalence and made no finding of conscious dishonesty.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-059.rule: When a contract conditions final payment on an architect's certificate, the architect's wrongful refusal to issue a certificate that has been earned excuses the condition, and the owner need not have participated in the refusal.

sections.Parties: Saverio Rizzolo, a building contractor, was the plaintiff. He sued Poysher as builder and Alfred Stahl as owner of the property, claiming the final payment and extras under a building contract and asserting a mechanics' lien. In the Court of Errors and Appeals the dispute concerned the special judgment against the owner's property.
sections.Procedural History: The Circuit Court entered a general judgment against the builder and a special judgment against the owner. During trial the owner moved to nonsuit for inadequate lien particulars, and the judge permitted amendments to six extra-work items. On intermediate appeal the Supreme Court sustained the builder judgment, which was not appealed further, but reversed the special property judgment, reasoning that a deficient bill of particulars could not support a lien as to only part. New Jersey's Court of Errors and Appeals reversed the Supreme Court's judgment and affirmed the Circuit Court judgment for Rizzolo, without ordering a new trial.
sections.Material Facts:
Rizzolo asserted performance of an October 29, 1912 building contract and of separately agreed extras. His claim included the $1,500 final payment and specified additional work and materials, with a stated aggregate claim of $2,056. The work was claimed completed April 29, 1913; the lien claim was filed June 26 and suit brought July 1.

The defendants pleaded that no architect's certificate had been obtained. The architect's own testimony permitted an inference that he was ready to certify, but that the defendants wanted several hundred dollars withheld on a counterclaim he largely would not support. He told the contractor to pursue the money, yet refused certification when asked the day before suit because he did not want to appear to issue a certificate for litigation. The defendant had accepted the building.
sections.Issue: Whether a mechanics' lien claim fails entirely when some items in its bill of particulars are insufficiently stated, and whether a contractor can recover the final payment without the required architect's certificate when the architect wrongfully refused it and the owner did not take part in the refusal.
sections.Holding: New Jersey Court of Errors and Appeals, 1916, Justice Parker writing, with eleven members voting for reversal and none for affirmance. The court held that a lien claim containing good and bad items can stand for the good ones unless they are inseparably blended, so the motion to nonsuit the whole claim failed. It also held that the certificate condition did not defeat recovery where, on the evidence, the architect wrongfully withheld the certificate, and that the owner's participation in the refusal was unnecessary. The pleading and party amendments caused no properly presented injurious error.
sections.Reasoning:
Section 16 of the Mechanics' Lien Act required particulars of the labor, materials, price, times, credits and balance. Neither the statute nor the precedents established that one insufficiently stated item invalidates all others; older strict decisions involved bills with no supportable items, and more recent cases favored amendments. No willful or fraudulent misstatement was at issue. Reading the amended claim as a whole, the court found sufficiently specified extras and treated the original and extra work as a single undertaking, timely claimed, so at least some items belonged before the jury.

The amendment adding allegations of architect fraud and waiver put the record in shape for the issue actually tried, and the defendants took no exception. The amendment limiting Poysher to builder and Stahl to owner reduced rather than enlarged liability.

On the certificate, the fraud question went to the jury under instructions to which no exception was taken. The court regarded the architect's stated reason as insufficient and his refusal, if his testimony was true, as fraudulent in the sense relevant to excusing the condition. Requiring owner participation would be unjust, because a corrupt architect could then withhold an earned certificate to extract money from the contractor.

The time-of-the-essence argument was not adequately presented, and in any event the defendant had accepted the building and could claim at most delay damages.

The casebook discusses the case under refusal without reason, concentrating on the certificate exception.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-060.rule: A contestant who agrees that the contest judges' decisions are final is bound by them absent fraud, gross mistake or lack of good faith.

sections.Parties: Randy Giunto, a sweepstakes contestant, was the plaintiff. He sued the sponsors, including Florida Coca-Cola Bottling Company, for breach of contract, claiming a $1 million hockey-shot prize. The sweepstakes was sponsored by Coca-Cola, Blockbuster and the Florida Panthers. Giunto appealed an order granting a new trial; the sponsors cross-appealed the denial of a directed verdict and of judgment notwithstanding the verdict.
sections.Procedural History: Giunto sued for breach. A jury found for him, but the trial judge granted a new trial. Giunto appealed that order, and the sponsors cross-appealed the denials of directed verdict and judgment notwithstanding the verdict. Florida's Third District Court of Appeal decided the cross-appeal first, reversed, and remanded with directions to enter judgment for the sponsors, which made Giunto's appeal from the new-trial order moot.
sections.Material Facts:
Giunto entered a March 1994 sweepstakes. The application rules selected ten people for tickets to home games and a chance to shoot a puck across the ice into and through a special small goal. They also provided that entrants would be bound by the official rules and by the judges' decisions, final in all sweepstakes matters. Giunto was chosen. Immediately before his March 18 attempt he signed a Spectator Agreement to Participate specifying that the puck had to pass completely through the target.

The target was plywood placed in front of the goal, with a bottom slot somewhat larger than a puck. From 118 feet away Giunto shot the puck into the corner of the slot; it rebounded side to side and stopped just slightly inside. The sponsors conceded that it crossed the plane of the opening, and Giunto conceded that it did not pass completely through. The contest judge declared the attempt unsuccessful. Giunto contended that the original into-and-through wording controlled and that entry of any portion of the puck satisfied it.
sections.Issue: Whether a contestant who agreed to be bound by the judges' final decisions can recover the prize in court after the judge ruled his shot unsuccessful, where the original rules said into and through and a later signed agreement said completely through.
sections.Holding: Florida Third District Court of Appeal, 1999, Judge Cope writing, joined by Judge Jorgenson, with Chief Judge Schwartz dissenting. The court held that the sponsors were entitled to judgment as a matter of law. It enforced the contestant's agreement to accept the contest judges' decisions, finding neither pleading nor proof of fraud, gross mistake or lack of good faith. It did not reach the reasons for the new-trial order.
sections.Reasoning:
Submitting the application bound Giunto to the final-decisions clause. Drawing on other contest decisions, the majority recognized that agreed tournament or award decisions remain binding absent fraud, gross mistake or lack of good faith, and a footnote likened the clause to arbitration's function of resolving disputes outside court. The judge had to apply the rules to a puck that entered but did not pass fully through, and because no disqualifying misconduct or error had been pleaded or proved, his decision bound the contestant.

The signed spectator agreement also told Giunto before the shot that the judges would read the original language to require complete passage. The majority was inclined to regard that as the ordinary meaning anyway, and said any interpretation was better given before the attempt than after. A note recorded video of five other contests using the same target, with winning pucks passing entirely through.

Schwartz, dissenting, treated the accepted offers as adhesion contracts whose conflicts must be resolved against the drafters, so the less demanding into-and-through language controlled. He would have disregarded the finality clause because the later agreement lacked one, and independently considered it unenforceable because the judge, Declan Bolger, was the Panthers' director of promotions and a sponsor could not judge its own responsibility. He would have remanded for entry of judgment on the jury's verdict.

The casebook presents the case as a problem and says Giunto insisted the puck passed completely through; the brief notes that the opinion instead records his concession that it did not.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-061.rule: Where the purpose of a notice condition is undisputedly fulfilled by timely actual notice, a court may excuse strict compliance with the prescribed method of delivery to avoid disproportionate forfeiture, unless the condition was a material part of the agreed exchange.

sections.Parties: Michael Conley and Katie Maurer, the buyers under a contract for a condominium, were the plaintiffs. They sued the seller, Mona Guerrero, and the competing purchasers, Brian Kraminitz and Michele Tanzi, seeking specific performance and other relief. The buyers appealed after their complaint was dismissed; the seller and other respondents, with the State Bar Association as amicus, defended the judgment.
sections.Procedural History: The trial judge denied temporary injunctive relief and then decided cross-motions for summary judgment because the facts were undisputed. He dismissed the buyers' complaint, regarding the deviation from the prescribed notice method as minor. The buyers appealed, demanding strict compliance. The New Jersey Superior Court, Appellate Division, reviewed summary judgment de novo and affirmed. The brief covers only this 2015 intermediate judgment and not the later 2017 Supreme Court stage.
sections.Material Facts:
The buyers signed a broker-prepared contract on January 12, 2014 for Guerrero's Bernards Township condominium at $292,000 and paid a $1,000 deposit. Guerrero signed two days later, and the executed agreement was delivered January 15. Its standard three-day attorney-review clause allowed either party's attorney to disapprove, required notice to the realtor and the other party, and prescribed certified mail, telegram or personal delivery for the realtor's notice. Because of a three-day weekend, the review period ran through January 21.

Other offers arrived. The buyers increased their offer to $298,000. Kraminitz and Tanzi offered $307,500 and signed a separate agreement with Guerrero on January 16. On January 20, a lawyer in the office of Guerrero's attorney sent the buyers' counsel a letter by email and fax declaring the seller's termination and authorizing release of the deposit; the realtor received a copy by email. Receipt by counsel and agent was undisputed. On January 23, the buyers' counsel asserted that the contract had become binding because no notice had arrived in an authorized form during the review period.
sections.Issue: Whether a seller's attorney's disapproval of a real-estate contract during attorney review is effective when it was timely and actually received but was sent by email and fax rather than by the certified mail, telegram or personal delivery the clause prescribed.
sections.Holding: New Jersey Superior Court, Appellate Division, 2015, Judge Ostrer writing for the panel; no separate writing or vote is reproduced. The court held that the seller's termination was effective: on the undisputed actual-notice facts, substantial compliance and avoidance of disproportionate forfeiture excused the deviation from the prescribed method. The panel expressly declined to establish a general rule that email satisfies the delivery provision, and it assumed without deciding that the buyers could enforce the realtor's delivery right. The complaint remained dismissed.
sections.Reasoning:
The standard attorney-review provision came from a court-approved settlement between the bar and realtors. Only the realtor's notice was subject to the specified delivery methods; any actual notice sufficed for the buyers themselves. The panel inferred that the prescribed methods protected real-estate professionals, while attorney review protected contracting parties from being bound by broker-prepared documents without legal advice. The buyers' own notice right was satisfied, and they sought to enforce a realtor delivery right about which the realtor did not complain.

The court applied the principle that a condition's nonoccurrence may be excused to avoid disproportionate forfeiture unless its occurrence was material to the agreed exchange, weighing the extent of the lost rights, the importance of the risk protected against, and how much protection excusing exact compliance would cost. Strict enforcement would forfeit Guerrero's right to disapprove and enter a different agreement, while the buyers already had the timely actual notice the delivery rule sought to ensure. The procedure was not an individually negotiated term but one imposed by the settlement, which justified more liberal substantial-compliance treatment.

Peterson, Kutzin, Romano and Gaglia were distinguished, because here there was a timely disapproval and actual notice and only the method deviated. The panel refused the amicus request to revise the standard clause for modern communications.

The brief notes that the casebook's account reverses the parties: it was the seller's counsel who disapproved and the buyers who sought specific performance.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-062.rule: A contracting officer's finding that the contract makes final and conclusive may be set aside for constructive fraud, which requires no actual dishonesty: a gross or arbitrary mistake amounting to a palpable substantial wrong is enough.

sections.Parties: Anthony P. Miller, Inc., a construction contractor, was the plaintiff. It sued the Wilmington Housing Authority over payments withheld as liquidated damages for late completion of low-rent housing under the Eastlake and Southbridge contracts, and for the cost of work it considered an extra. Both parties moved for summary judgment.
sections.Procedural History: Both the contractor and the housing authority moved for summary judgment in the federal district court for Delaware. On November 3, 1959, District Judge Layton denied both motions on both contracts. The ruling was not a final award of the sums the contractor claimed. A prior decision in the case concerned another aspect and was not redetermined.
sections.Material Facts:
Miller began work around May 26, 1952 on construction that suffered weather, strike and other delays. The contract authorized $148 per day in liquidated damages for late completion. Section 13(a) excused unforeseeable causes beyond the contractor's control and without its fault or negligence. The contracting officer would ascertain the facts and extent of delay, and his findings of fact were final and conclusive.

Miller sought extensions totaling 713 days across overlapping causes; the actual overrun was 465 days. The officer allowed approximately 304 days, leaving 161 days treated as inexcusable, and the authority ratified a $23,828 withholding. Miller requested 226 labor-shortage days and was allowed 20.93.

In his plumbing analysis the officer started with 573 days, subtracted 209.17 concurrent-delay days, halved the remaining 363.83 days to 181.92 on an assumed fifty-percent labor shortage, and then multiplied by 8.35 percent, the ratio of estimated plumbing cost to estimated total contract cost, reducing the allowance to 15.19 days. Three experienced construction witnesses gave affidavits against the formula, and the authority offered none in reply.

Miller also claimed $3,626.96 for work it considered an extra. The specifications required slabs to be reinforced with welded wire mesh of the size scheduled on the drawings; seven slab types had specified mesh sizes, while type A instead showed vermiculite and concrete in the reinforcement column.
sections.Issue: Whether a contracting officer's delay determination, made final and conclusive by the contract, can be set aside for gross error without proof of actual bad faith, and whether either party was entitled to summary judgment on the delay claim or the wire-mesh dispute.
sections.Holding: United States District Court for the District of Delaware, 1959, Judge Layton. The court held that the contracting officer had committed gross calculation errors legally characterized as constructive fraud, which permitted the court to set aside the contractual finding. It expressly found no indication of actual bad faith, dishonesty or deliberate wrongdoing. But the correct period of excusable delay still required factual and expert assessment, and the contract language on reinforcement was open to two readings, so both parties' summary-judgment motions were denied.
sections.Reasoning:
Miller argued that the officer lacked power to construe the contract; the judge declined to decide that and asked instead whether the determination was so palpably erroneous as to be constructive fraud. Agreed decisions of architects, engineers and contracting officers ordinarily receive conclusive effect, but fraud defeats that protection, and actual dishonesty is unnecessary: gross or arbitrary mistake amounting to a palpable substantial wrong, or conduct legally implying bad faith, can suffice.

The final step of the officer's calculation, multiplying by the cost ratio, was irrelevant to the delay question, since relating relative cost to performance time did not determine excusable delay, and the estimated cost figures differed substantially from actual costs. Other inconsistencies reinforced the unreliability. The judge acknowledged the caution due an officer's judgment but noted that the officer was the authority's paid agent and the ratification favored it. He attributed the mistakes to inexperience, yet precedent required the constructive-fraud label for sufficiently gross error.

Miller's argument that delays caused by the authority nullified all liquidated damages failed, because the contract itself provided extensions for such delay. Nor was Miller entitled to judgment on the 181.92-day intermediate figure, since disputed facts and questions of expert judgment remained for a jury. On the wire mesh, both readings were possible. The judge suggested, as a possible alternative only, that a bidder aware of an obvious mistake might have a duty to call attention to it.

The casebook uses the case for constructive fraud, highlighting the cost-ratio error and the absence of subjective wrongdoing.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-063.rule: Where a seller's conveyance and a buyer's payment are to be performed at the same time, the promises are dependent, and a party cannot sue on the other's promise without pleading that he performed or offered to perform his own.

sections.Parties: Goodisson, the seller of a copyhold estate, was the plaintiff. He brought an action of debt for the £21 stipulated as payable on the buyer's failure to complete the transaction. Nunn, the purchaser, was the defendant and pleaded the seller's nonperformance.
sections.Procedural History: The seller sued in debt for £21. The purchaser obtained production of the agreement and pleaded non est factum and three special pleas: that the seller did not convey by the appointed date, that he had not conveyed by that date or since, and that he had no interest in the premises enabling him to convey when the articles were made. The seller demurred generally to the three special pleas. The King's Bench gave judgment for the defendant. This was a determination on the pleadings, not a verdict following findings that either party had performed.
sections.Material Facts: The seller undertook to convey a copyhold estate on or before September 2, and the purchaser undertook to pay £210 by that date. Each party would owe the other £21 on failing to carry out his obligation. The instrument also addressed taking up the copyhold for the buyer or his wife, the seller's first taking it up for himself, and sharing the expenses; the report acknowledges that its conveyancing language was imperfectly drawn. The seller had neither conveyed nor offered to convey, nor taken a step toward conveyance, yet claimed the stipulated sum.
sections.Issue: Whether the buyer's promise to pay was independent of the seller's promise to convey, so that the seller could recover the stipulated sum without having conveyed or offered to convey, or whether the promises were dependent.
sections.Holding: King's Bench, 1792. Lord Kenyon, Chief Justice, and Justices Buller and Grose each gave reasons supporting judgment for the defendant purchaser. The court rejected the contention that the buyer owed the sum independently of the seller's conveyance or offer to convey; the seller had to plead performance or an offer to perform before maintaining the action. The judgment did not award the purchaser the reciprocal £21, did not separately rule on the plea about the seller's title, and did not decide whether either stipulated sum was enforceable as a penalty.
sections.Reasoning:
Counsel for the seller argued that each covenant was general and independent, one promise being consideration for the other, and relied on older authorities including Pordage v. Cole and Blackwell v. Nash to say that the purchaser's remedy lay in a separate action. He also suggested that the buyer had to act first by choosing what conveyance he wanted.

Kenyon thought the case clear in strict law and in justice. The reciprocal acts were to occur together: the seller would receive the price on conveyance, and the buyer the estate on payment. It would be unreasonable to make one party part with the whole consideration and rely on a separate suit against a possibly insolvent counterparty. He accepted the older principle that dependent covenants require the plaintiff to perform or offer performance, but rejected applying it as if a mere exchange of promises made the duties independent.

Buller likewise reasoned that conveyance and payment were by the nature of the sale acts to be done together, invoking Mansfield's explanation that neither side was to give the other personal credit. He answered the buyer-first argument by pointing out that Goodisson first had to take up the copyhold himself. Grose supported asking whether in reality the seller had to act first or the performances were concurrent, rather than resolving dependency by technical wording.

The casebook uses the case to introduce concurrent conditions and quotes the performance-or-offer pleading requirement; its later discussion of modern UCC tender rules is the editors' comparison. The brief was written from a reprint of the report, not the original 1792 report pages.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-064.rule: A purchaser's deficient original tender does not bar specific performance where the vendor was already in default on title and the purchaser tenders performance in its equitable pleading and offers to pay whatever further sum the court finds due.

sections.Parties: R. E. Smith and Roy Hofheinz, the purchasers of the McMillan Ranch in Brazoria County, sued the sellers, W. W. McMillan, Arthur Mandell and Herman Wright, for specific performance. The buyers maintained that the deductions they took from the price were authorized by the contract. The sellers insisted that the insufficient tender foreclosed specific performance and entitled them to rescission. Both sides sought review in the Texas Supreme Court.
sections.Procedural History:
After the buyers presented their evidence in a nonjury trial, both sides rested and the sellers moved for judgment on the inadequacy of the tender. The trial court ordered that the buyers take nothing and declared the contract void. The Court of Civil Appeals reversed and remanded for a new trial, but its three judges did not share one rationale: Justice Werlein wrote the principal opinion, Justice Coleman agreed only with reversal and remand, and Chief Justice Bell would have affirmed because he regarded the tender as insufficient. Both sides sought Supreme Court review.

The Texas Supreme Court affirmed the reversal of the sellers' judgment, displaced the general new-trial remand, and substituted a conditional remand requiring payment of the correct cash amount within thirty days after its opinion became final. Rehearing was denied on January 23, 1963.
sections.Material Facts:
On August 24, 1959, the sellers agreed to sell the ranch for $525,000, assuming 1,184 surface acres, with the price adjusted at $443.42 an acre for shortages or excesses. They promised an abstract showing good and merchantable title and a general warranty deed. Paragraph 6 required an opportunity to cure title objections and, on failure, let the buyers cancel, seek specific performance, or take the defective title and recover reasonable costs of curing it. Paragraph 7 addressed closing and title costs.

The buyers' lawyer raised twenty-five title objections. In February 1960 the sellers refused to address several and said they could not clear others. On February 29 the buyers elected to take title subject to the unresolved objections. Their proposed deed demanded a general warranty covering the entire ranch, including an alleged 36.293-acre vacancy of unpatented school land. They would assume $152,874.43 in secured debt and tender the rest after deductions totaling $27,898.12: $1,500 in anticipated legal and other expenses, the per-acre value of the alleged vacancy, and $10,305.08 as an estimate of the cost of removing three utility easements. On March 18 the sellers refused the deed and purported to rescind for insufficient tender. In court the buyers deposited $336,038.10, alleged they were ready, willing and able to perform, and offered to pay any further amount the judge found due. Their solvency was unquestioned.
sections.Issue: Whether the contract authorized the buyers' deductions from the purchase price, and, if it did not, whether their deficient original tender barred specific performance and entitled the already defaulting sellers to rescission.
sections.Holding: The Texas Supreme Court, in a 1962 opinion by Justice Greenhill, held that the contract did not allow the buyers' deductions, but that the deficient original tender did not preclude specific performance in these circumstances and did not entitle the defaulting sellers to rescission. The buyers had to supply the withheld $27,898.12, raising the cash paid into the court registry from $336,038.10 to $363,936.22, separately from their assumption of the secured debt. If they paid within thirty days after the opinion became final, the trial court was to grant specific performance through the February 29 deed; otherwise it was to enter judgment for the sellers. Curative-cost recovery, general-warranty rights and rights to any after-acquired title remained protected.
sections.Reasoning:
The court first fixed the correct contractual obligation rather than excusing the deductions through equity. Neither paragraph 6 nor paragraph 7 authorized deducting speculative future attorneys' fees and court costs; the litigation might never be needed. Paragraph 7 addressed actual closing expenses where good title was conveyed, and the election to take defective title under paragraph 6 preserved a later right to recover established curative costs, not an immediate right to deduct an unincurred estimate. As to the alleged vacancy, the buyers could exclude the acreage and abate the price, cancel, or take all the land under a general warranty while retaining curative-cost and warranty rights. They chose the third course and could not also subtract the price as if they had chosen the first. The same reasoning governed the utility easements.

The deficiency was nevertheless not an absolute bar. Courts of equity had not applied the rigid tender rules of an action at law. Where a vendor failed or refused to cure title defects so that a pre-suit tender would be useless, the purchaser's failure to make it could be excused when performance was tendered in the equitable pleading; the court relied on treatises and Burford v. Pounders. Here the sellers had defaulted first, the amount due was uncertain under a difficult contract that even the intermediate judges read differently, and the buyers had placed cash in court and offered unequivocally to supply whatever more was required. The court could thus protect the sellers' right to full payment while enforcing the buyers' right to a conveyance. This was a conditional equitable solution, not a holding that a promise to pay later always substitutes for proper tender. Because the court's analysis assumed the vacancy, the lawyer's good faith and the tender's inadequacy, the excluded evidence on those matters did not justify a general new trial.

The casebook uses the case to explain how an equitable order can secure the defendant's receipt of the plaintiff's performance.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-065.rule: Under UCC section 2.601 a buyer may reject goods that fail to conform to the contract in any respect, but conformity is measured by the parties' actual agreement and the right to reject must be exercised in good faith.

sections.Parties: Supermind Publishing Co., the buyer, sued Printing Center of Texas, the printer, seeking cancellation and a refund of its deposit after rejecting the books the printer delivered. Printing Center, the defendant at trial, appealed the judgment for the publisher, arguing that the defects were minor and that Supermind had rejected in bad faith.
sections.Procedural History: The publisher rejected the books and sought cancellation and a refund under UCC sections 2.601 and 2.711. A jury found that the books failed in some respect to conform to the contract. The county court at law awarded the $2,900 deposit, $3,000 in reasonable attorneys' fees, and a combined $1,500 in additional fees through Supreme Court proceedings. The printer appealed, challenging the attorney-billing evidence, the support for the nonconformity finding, and the court's authority to enter a judgment beyond its $5,000 jurisdictional limit. The Houston Fourteenth Court of Appeals overruled all points and affirmed on March 15, 1984; rehearing was denied April 19, 1984.
sections.Material Facts: Supermind contracted with Printing Center for 5,000 copies of a book titled Supermind Supermemory. The bid proposal of July 31, 1981 specified essential terms including quantity, trim size, paper and cover, and called for thirty-pound white newsprint. A publisher witness testified that the printer showed a white sample but delivered books with gray pages. Other evidence concerned off-center cover art, crooked and wrinkled pages, and inadequate perforation of a pull-out page. The printer knew that the books were intended for public sale. The written proposal did not expressly address the physical defects other than the paper, and no trade-usage evidence was supplied to supplement it. The publisher paid a $2,900 deposit and rejected the delivered books. At trial its lawyer's billing letters came in through a legal secretary, Patricia Burrows, as records custodian, although she lacked personal knowledge of the listed work and had not been custodian when the bills were made.
sections.Issue: Assuming Article 2 governed, whether the evidence supported the jury's finding that the books did not conform to the contract so as to justify rejection, whether the printer had shown a bad-faith rejection, and whether the fee evidence and the size of the award made the judgment erroneous or void.
sections.Holding: The Texas Court of Appeals, Houston Fourteenth District (1984), in an opinion by Justice Cannon for a panel with Chief Justice J. Curtiss Brown and Justice Draughn, with no dissent or concurrence, affirmed. Applying Article 2 on the parties' assumed theory while expressly doubting that this predominantly service transaction belonged under the UCC, the court held that perfect tender means conformity to the contract in every respect, that the sample warranty and merchantability supported the nonconformity finding, that the printer had neither proved nor preserved its bad-faith defense, and that the fee evidence was admissible and the judgment not void for want of jurisdiction.
sections.Reasoning:
The court first observed that printing involves goods, paper and ink, and services such as binding, typesetting and proofing, and that under the dominant-factor test services appeared to be the essence of the transaction. At common law a finding of any nonconformity would not itself establish a right to reject and obtain a refund. But the printer had not assigned error on whether the verdict supported the judgment, so the point was waived and the court proceeded on the doubtful assumption that Article 2 applied.

On that assumption, perfect tender meant conformity to the contract in every respect, not abstract flawlessness, and substantial compliance was insufficient under section 2.601; the court rejected a contrary holding in Del Monte Corp. v. Martin. Conformity required identifying the actual agreement, including express language and terms from course of dealing, usage of trade or course of performance. The white sample was evidence of an express warranty under section 2.313(a)(3), so the gray pages could support the finding. The known purpose of public sale supported a requirement that the books be commercially acceptable under section 2.314's merchantability standard, and the jury could find the crooked and wrinkled pages, off-center artwork and deficient perforation made them unfit for sale.

Rejection operates within the Code's duty of good faith, and a seller asserting bad-faith rejection bears the burden. A buyer seizing a minor defect in a falling market to escape a bargain might show bad faith, as in Neumiller Farms v. Cornett. Here the defects were not minor, there was no evidence that escape from a bad bargain was the publisher's primary motivation, and the printer had waived the defense by not requesting a jury issue. The secretary's lack of personal knowledge went to weight, not admissibility. Jurisdiction was acquired on the original petition's good-faith allegations, and a later amendment seeking further fees did not divest it.

The casebook uses the case to show the interaction of contractual conformity and good faith, and labels the general good-faith illustration dictum.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-066.rule: An owner's occupancy of a building and delivery of a partial list of defects do not, as a matter of law, waive or estop proof of other defects; and a builder claiming substantial performance must explain departures from the contract and prove the allowance for them.

sections.Parties: Anthony B. Cawley, a builder, sued the Weiners, the owners of the land, to foreclose a mechanic's lien for the unpaid balance of a contract to build a dwelling and garage. Cawley alleged substantial performance. The owners, who lost at trial and in the Appellate Division, appealed, arguing that the trial judge had barred material defenses without the facts needed for waiver or estoppel and had allowed full payment despite proved departures from the specifications.
sections.Procedural History: The Nassau County Court found substantial performance and awarded the builder the full amount claimed, less a small reduction concerning extras. The Appellate Division unanimously affirmed. The New York Court of Appeals accepted the binding findings of fact but reviewed whether the evidentiary rulings were lawful and whether the findings could support the judgment. On July 13, 1923 it reversed both judgments and granted a new trial, with costs to abide the event. It did not determine the owners' final liability or fix damages.
sections.Material Facts:
On January 31, 1921, Cawley agreed in writing to erect and finish a dwelling and garage for the Weiners at Port Washington, Nassau County, for $8,500. Work proceeded through June 9, with five modifications made at the owners' request and with their consent. Around June 1 the owners entered the still-unfinished bungalow on their land and gave the builder a list of seventeen items they wanted changed or supplied. After claiming completion, Cawley filed a mechanic's lien and sued.

At trial the owners sought to prove three defects not on their list: a sagging floor, omission of a specified supporting arch beneath the living-room fireplace, and a half-inch crack in the first-story brick wall. The trial judge excluded the proof because, absent a showing that an omitted defect could not then have been discovered, specifying some defects waived or estopped reliance on all others. The builder claimed no change of position induced by the list.

At the owners' request the judge also found other defects: cement bricks substituted for the specified No. 2 brick in the cesspool, omission of a bricked dome and a three-inch cement slab, drainage that backed into the house when the cesspool reached the height of the pipe, a dormer roof six inches out of level, and a sun parlor that leaked around inward-opening windows. He nonetheless awarded the full contract price.
sections.Issue: Whether owners who moved into the house and gave the builder a list of defects were barred as a matter of law from proving other defects, and whether a finding of substantial performance could support an award of the full contract balance where defects were found but no deduction was made or explained.
sections.Holding: The New York Court of Appeals (1923), in an opinion by Judge Crane with Chief Judge Hiscock and Judges Hogan, Cardozo, Pound, McLaughlin and Andrews concurring, unanimously reversed and ordered a new trial. It identified two independently sufficient errors: excluding evidence of additional construction defects on an automatic waiver or estoppel theory, and awarding the full contract balance despite findings of defects without explaining or measuring an appropriate deduction. Waiver, estoppel, the additional defects and any monetary allowance were left to be determined on the evidence at retrial.
sections.Reasoning:
The court distinguished a house built on the owners' land from a sale of goods: the owners could move into and use their house without waiving construction defects. Giving a list did not automatically estop them from proving other departures. Actual waiver is acceptance with knowledge of the defects; estoppel requires circumstances that make it unfair for the owners to rely on the omitted objections. Quoting Williston, the court explained that specifying one objection could create an estoppel if it operated as a deception on which the contractor relied, preventing complete performance that otherwise would have occurred, and that it mattered whether the additional objections, if disclosed, could readily have been remedied. Simply omitting them did not establish those facts. The trial judge should have received the evidence and decided whether there was a waiver or estoppel in fact, rather than treating the list as conclusive as a matter of law. The builder remained free on retrial to prove circumstances supporting waiver or estoppel.

On the second error, relying on Jacob & Youngs v. Kent and Spence v. Ham, the court required the builder to account for the defects the judge had found. They might or might not have been substantial. The builder bore the burden of explaining their cause, including whether they resulted from the plans rather than defective workmanship, and, if they were defects properly compensated by an allowance, of proving the reasonable cost of remedying them. An award of the full price with no deduction and no finding explaining why none was warranted could not stand. The court did not decide that every variation defeated substantial performance.

The casebook cites the case on successive objections: a builder's practical desire for a definitive list does not itself establish a legal forfeiture of unlisted defenses.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-068.rule: A buyer who notifies the seller may withhold or deduct from the price due damages resulting from the seller's material breach of the same contract, even after accepting the goods.

sections.Parties: Telerent Leasing Corporation, lessor of television equipment under a lease-purchase agreement, sued Jagdish C. Patel, owner of the Sonya Motor Inn in Jackson, for $24,445.44 as the remaining lease obligation and repossession and sale expenses, less sale proceeds. Patel, the defendant, contended that Telerent had breached by failing to complete installation. Patel won in county court, lost in circuit court, and appealed to the Mississippi Supreme Court.
sections.Procedural History: Telerent first obtained a county court replevin judgment giving it possession of twenty-two sets with radios, twenty-two locking pedestals and the theft alarm system, and bought the equipment at the public sale for a total of $2,920. It then sued in county court for $24,445.44. After a nonjury trial at which only Telerent's collection manager and Patel testified, the county judge denied Telerent relief on December 22, 1986. On appeal the circuit court applied North Carolina law, treated a completion certificate and the engraving of the motel's name on the sets as acceptance, held that Patel had not properly rejected, and rendered judgment for the lessor. Patel appealed. The Mississippi Supreme Court reversed the circuit court and reinstated the county court judgment, without a remand for a new trial.
sections.Material Facts:
On April 25, 1985, Telerent agreed to provide thirty General Electric television sets and accessories for Patel's fifty-room motel under a lease-purchase contract calling for eighty-four monthly installments of $281.16, beginning by the first of the month after the lessor completed its equipment work, with a nominal purchase option at the end. Telerent had to change existing taps in all rooms and supply an in-line amplifier, and undertook to replace or repair stolen or damaged sets on prompt report. An August addendum required theft alarms for all fifty rooms and added $27.39 a month.

Patel signed a completion certificate in June and another on October 15, but repeatedly complained that the distribution system was incomplete and the televisions could not be used before October 15. Telerent's November 11 letter acknowledged that he had refused its July bill because installation was incomplete and that it had returned to extend the system. It agreed to make the lease effective November 1 at $327.06 a month, yet claimed four months' earlier use and demanded $1,345.78 or threatened repossession. On November 17 Patel tendered $272.55 for November, subtracting $54.51 for five reported stolen sets that had not been replaced. Telerent returned the check and threatened acceleration and removal. On December 4 Patel sent the same check again, repeated his complaints, and added that the theft alarm malfunctioned and other equipment had not been properly mounted. Telerent then repossessed.
sections.Issue: Whether substantial evidence supported the county court's judgment denying the lessor's deficiency claim, and whether the lessor's incomplete installation justified the motel owner in withholding payment even if he had accepted the equipment.
sections.Holding: The Mississippi Supreme Court (1990), in an opinion by Presiding Justice Hawkins in which all the other participating justices concurred, making the disposition unanimous, reversed the circuit court's $24,445.44 judgment for Telerent and reinstated the county court judgment denying Telerent relief. It held that substantial evidence supported the county judge's result and that the lessor's material failure to install the equipment justified Patel's withholding payment. Patel received no affirmative damages award or refund; Telerent's deficiency claim was denied.
sections.Reasoning:
The court treated the lease-purchase as the functional equivalent of a sale, given the nominal purchase price at the end of the term, and applied Article 2. The parties could choose the governing state law, and the relevant Mississippi and North Carolina UCC provisions were identical.

The county court, not the circuit court sitting on appeal, was the factfinder. Its nonjury judgment was binding if supported by substantial evidence and not manifestly wrong, and it could be sustained on a correct ground even if the judge had given a different legal reason. Patel's letters and Telerent's own November concession amply supported a finding that the system remained incomplete and unsatisfactory before October 15; a certificate or the marking of the receivers could not override that evidence.

Inadequate installation was a material breach justifying withholding. Under section 2-717, a buyer who notifies the seller may deduct damages resulting from a breach from the price due under the same contract. The official comments require that the breach and the price arise under the same contract and that the notice reasonably communicate the reason for withholding, though no special formality is needed. The court also referred to section 2-609 on demands for adequate assurance, regarding Patel's requests for completion as requests for assurance for which he should not be penalized, and connected these remedies to pre-Code material-breach principles and Restatement section 237. The circuit court's acceptance analysis did not negate the defense: relying on Missouri Bag Co., the court said a buyer may accept and use defective goods and still claim an offset against the price. The result thus rested on material breach, withholding and recoupment rather than on the county judge's characterization of rejection and abandonment.

The casebook contrasts this right to withhold with the election-of-remedies problem in ARP Films.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-069.rule: After the other party's repudiation, a party may stop performing and sue for total breach or continue the contract and sue for partial breach; having elected to continue and keep the benefits, it may not withhold its own material performance.

sections.Parties: ARP Films, Inc., Amerex Films and Claude Hill, distributors of cartoons embodying Marvel-associated characters including Spiderman, sued Marvel, which removed the case and whose own separate action was consolidated with it. ARP claimed exclusive videocassette rights and damages for Marvel's licensing to others; Marvel claimed ARP's breaches entitled it to terminate the distribution license. ARP, Amerex and Hill appealed to the Second Circuit and Marvel cross-appealed.
sections.Procedural History: ARP sued in July 1986; Marvel removed on diversity grounds and its separate action was consolidated. The district court ruled on partial summary judgment that ARP's continued exploitation affirmed the agreement, and on a renewed motion that the withholding was a material breach making Marvel's September termination effective. After a six-week trial the jury found the 1976 agreement covered videocassettes but the side agreements did not, awarded ARP $1,220,000 for Marvel's competing videocassette licensing, and awarded Marvel $137,000 for other breaches. The district court also awarded ARP $293,480 in commissions under a side agreement and ordered an accounting. An earlier appeal was dismissed as premature because the accounting was unfinished. After the accounting concluded, the appeal and cross-appeal followed. The Second Circuit affirmed all challenged orders and the judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
A 1968 agreement permitted production and exploitation of the cartoons; litigation over it ended in a 1976 settlement and new agreement. Amerex was formed to distribute specified films, with ARP supplying distribution services. Amerex had to remit agreed percentages of gross receipts and furnish periodic accountings to Marvel and ARP. Paragraph 8 permitted termination of the distribution license for substantial noncompliance, expressly identifying prompt accounting, while providing that the remainder of the agreement would continue. Letters in 1979 and 1980 gave ARP additional commission-based distribution rights.

Marvel began licensing home videocassette distribution in 1981, and in 1982 ARP asserted that its rights were exclusive for that medium. On November 12, 1986, Marvel purported to terminate all distribution rights for alleged violations, offering continued distribution on a courtesy, at-will basis. ARP continued receiving proceeds from existing licenses and at first paid Marvel its share. Marvel refused approval of proposed new licenses. In February 1987 ARP stopped remitting Marvel's share, and in April it stopped reporting distribution activities; more than $400,000 was withheld. On September 2 Marvel sent a second termination letter stating that the withholding was an unjustified material breach independently terminating any rights still outstanding.
sections.Issue: Whether a party that responds to the other side's repudiation by continuing to take the benefits of the contract may withhold its own payments and accountings without committing a material breach that justifies termination.
sections.Holding: The Second Circuit (1991), in an opinion by Judge Mahoney for a panel with Judges Cardamone and Miner and no separate writing, affirmed. Although Marvel's first attempted termination was treated as a repudiation, ARP's choice to retain contractual benefits while withholding substantial payments and accountings justified the later termination of the distribution license through the second letter. That conclusion did not erase ARP's damages for Marvel's own breach or its rights to revenues from valid licenses created before termination. The license terminated; the agreement's other terms continued.
sections.Reasoning:
ARP argued that withholding payments and reports would pressure Marvel to retract its repudiation and should not count as a material breach. The court rejected that combination of continued benefits and nonperformance. After a repudiation ARP could cease performance and sue for total breach, or affirm by continuing to perform and sue for partial breach. Its continued receipt of benefits was an affirmation. Having elected, it could not keep exploiting the agreement while refusing its important reciprocal obligations over a substantial period.

Materiality was established as a matter of law. Paragraph 8 expressly made prompt accounting important to the license and authorized termination for substantial noncompliance; withholding payment is generally a material failure; and the amounts were very substantial, as the accounting confirmed.

On the other rulings, the court refused to turn Bartsch's context-specific construction of a broad grant into a universal rule giving every unreserved right to a licensee; the side agreements were short letters without comparable grant language. ARP was properly denied revenue from new licenses made without Marvel's contractually required consent, since it had not shown that refusal of any particular deal was unreasonable. Exclusion of a barter-syndication damages estimate exceeding $3 million as speculative was within the trial judge's discretion, and the mixed outcome supported the denial of costs and attorneys' fees. On Marvel's cross-appeal the court declined to disturb the jury's findings, including that ARP kept its share of revenues from valid pre-termination licenses received later.

The casebook focuses on ARP's impermissible self-help after affirming the agreement and contrasts it with the buyer's withholding in Patel.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-070.rule: In a lengthy construction contract calling for progress payments, substantial compliance with the payment terms is a condition precedent to the contractor's duty to continue work, and a clause extending time for delay does not require the contractor to stand ready indefinitely.

sections.Parties: Guerini Stone Company, a subcontractor, sued P. J. Carlin Construction Company, the federal government's general contractor for a post office and court building at San Juan, Puerto Rico, asserting total breach and also a general quantum-meruit claim for labor and materials. Guerini won a jury verdict; Carlin obtained reversal in the First Circuit; Guerini brought the case to the Supreme Court.
sections.Procedural History: This was the second review of the dispute in the Supreme Court. After the Court's earlier reversal, a new trial produced a substantial damages verdict for Guerini. The First Circuit reversed for asserted instructional and evidentiary errors. The Court rejected those grounds, examined the remaining assignments of error, 101 in total, found none warranting reversal, reversed the First Circuit's judgment and affirmed the district court's judgment for Guerini, without remanding for another trial. The opinion does not print the amount of the verdict.
sections.Material Facts:
Carlin was to complete the foundation to basement level; Guerini was to build the principal concrete structure, including walls, floors and roof, for $64,750. Carlin also exercised an option for Guerini to set supplied granite at forty cents per square foot. Paragraph 12 required monthly payments of up to eighty-five percent of the cost of work erected, on a written requisition at least twelve days before payment was required. Paragraph 11 required Carlin to supply other labor and materials without delaying Guerini's material progress. Paragraphs 6 and 7 set a 300-day completion period and extensions for specified delays.

Guerini submitted unpaid requisitions in December 1911 and January 1912. Its evidence was that around February 2 the parties agreed to a unit-price schedule. On March 9 it submitted a requisition showing $11,735.95 due; apart from a later $674 payment it went unpaid. Meanwhile the government found serious settlement of the foundation and ordered construction stopped. Carlin told Guerini of the shutdown on March 9 and confirmed it by letter two days later, without answering Guerini's request for instructions about its work force. By May 22 Guerini had received neither meaningful further payment nor permission to resume, and its evidence indicated that no one could say when work might restart. Its termination letter cited nonpayment and indefinite delay, announced it would do no further work, and claimed damages. Materials, machinery and tools worth $3,500 were left at the site and taken for Carlin's use.
sections.Issue: Whether a subcontractor was justified in ending its work and recovering damages where the general contractor substantially failed to make progress payments and the work had been stopped with no reasonable prospect of resumption, despite a contract clause extending the time for completion in case of delay.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court (1919), in an opinion by Justice Pitney, reversed the First Circuit and affirmed the district court's judgment for Guerini. The trial court's instructions on delay and payment were proper: the jury could find termination justified if by May 22 a long or indefinite delay was apparent, and a substantial failure to make the contractual progress payments could justify stopping work and recovering damages. The extension-of-time clause did not require Guerini to remain ready indefinitely after a total shutdown, and the granite work was subject to the contract's general payment terms.
sections.Reasoning:
On delay, the First Circuit read the extension-of-time clause as requiring continued readiness despite owner-caused delay, leaving only damages. The Court disagreed. Paragraph 11 required Carlin to supply a foundation on which Guerini could build without delay, an obligation that did not depend on Carlin's fault or on the government's right to stop work under a main-contract clause not incorporated into the subcontract. The protection in paragraphs 6 and 7 against late completion did not require Guerini to stay available indefinitely after a total shutdown. The instruction was judged in light of the two months that had already passed, not as permission to terminate over a brief interruption.

On payment, the progress payments were material in a lengthy project requiring large outlays; the parties could not have expected the subcontractor to finance the whole undertaking without them. Substantial compliance with the payment obligations was therefore a condition precedent to further performance, and Carlin was not entitled to an instruction limiting the remedy to interest unless it had positively refused all payment. Exercising the granite option added work to the existing contract under its general payment terms; even on the separate-contract view, the jury could find the granite work substantially complete in February.

Evidence of the materials left at the site was admissible on the quantum-meruit claim and under the damages approach of United States v. Behan. Evidence of the February unit-price arrangement was properly received; any variance from the complaint was unimportant and nonprejudicial. The Court did not endorse a possibly duplicative damages instruction on the merits, because Carlin had not specifically excepted to it.

The casebook emphasizes the progress-payment condition and asks how suspension differs from final termination.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-071.rule: A landlord who accepts late rent for years without objection may waive the right to treat that lateness as a default despite a lease clause requiring written waivers, and equity may relieve a tenant from forfeiture of a purchase option for defaults that have been cured.

sections.Parties: Dillingham Commercial Company, Inc., assignee of the tenant under a ten-year lease of Spears's general-store property, sued Spears, the landlord, for specific performance of the lease's option to purchase. Spears contended that the tenant's defaults had terminated the lease and option. In the Alaska Supreme Court Spears challenged the order of specific performance, and Dillingham cross-appealed the financial conditions attached to it and the fee award.
sections.Procedural History: The superior court granted Dillingham summary judgment compelling performance of the purchase option. It required Dillingham to pay Spears $20,016.50 in interest on the purchase price and $6,000 for insurance premiums, including interest, and awarded Dillingham $6,710 in attorney's fees and $1,737.52 in costs. Spears appealed the specific performance; Dillingham cross-appealed the financial conditions and fees. The Alaska Supreme Court affirmed the judgment in its entirety on February 19, 1982.
sections.Material Facts:
An earnest-money agreement dated January 15, 1967 provided for sale of Spears's general-store business, a ten-year lease and an option to purchase the property. The March 1 lease required $600 monthly rent and payment of all taxes and assessments. The option could be exercised during the term so long as the lease was not in default, on one month's mailed notice and payment of $20,000 toward a $79,800 price. The lease required waivers to be in writing and said waiver of one default would not waive another. Spears approved the assignment to Dillingham.

Rent was late virtually every month, and Spears accepted it without objection. In October 1975 she demanded payment of tax arrears; Dillingham paid the city $16,239.61 that November, but further amounts remained. On March 9, 1976 she again demanded cure, and on March 22 Dillingham gave notice of its intention to exercise the option. Spears answered that all defaults must first be cured. On June 18 she purported to terminate the lease and option for nonpayment of real-estate taxes and paid the city herself. Dillingham paid further taxes in July and tendered reimbursement, which she refused. On August 12 Dillingham again tendered reimbursement, July and August rent, and the $20,000 down payment. Spears refused, and Dillingham sued. Dillingham remained in possession throughout.
sections.Issue: Whether the landlord's notice terminated the lease, whether the tenant's tax and late-rent defaults barred exercise of an option conditioned on the lease not being in default, whether the sale terms were sufficiently established, and whether the tenant owed interest on the purchase price.
sections.Holding: The Alaska Supreme Court (1982), in an opinion by Chief Justice Rabinowitz with no separate writing, affirmed in full. Spears's notice did not itself terminate the lease, because the lease did not specially authorize termination by unilateral notice and she had brought no judicial action. Equity relieved Dillingham from loss of the option over the tax arrears and late rent, and Spears's prolonged acceptance of late rent waived the right to claim default from it. The sale terms were sufficiently established, and Dillingham owed interest on the full price from August 21, 1976.
sections.Reasoning:
Under Klinger, absent a special agreement, early termination of a lease required the prescribed judicial action and decree. Lease language about the tenant's rights lapsing at expiration or otherwise, and about preserving a privilege to terminate despite prior leniency, did not create a right to terminate by notice.

On the tax arrears, the taxes had been paid and Spears had been offered reimbursement; Dillingham had paid substantial rent over nine years and the lease was near its end. The superior court properly weighed those amounts in finding forfeiture inequitable. Alaska's installment-land-contract decisions supported equitable discretion, though forfeiture remained possible in extreme circumstances. A footnote distinguished an installment purchaser's equitable ownership from an option holder's contractual right but found no reason to treat them differently here.

On rent, Spears had accepted late payment without objection and raised it only when Dillingham sought to exercise the option. A clause requiring written waivers does not invariably prevent waiver by conduct, and her prolonged acquiescence was a waiver. The court also independently sustained equitable relief from forfeiture for the late rent, and, assuming two months remained unpaid, held that default did not justify forfeiture either. Her sublease and insurance grounds were not developed on appeal and were waived.

The superior court could use the earnest-money agreement's payment and interest terms as part of the parties' total agreement; Spears offered no contrary evidence. Although the superior court wrongly used the money-judgment fee schedule, the $6,710 fee was reasonable. Specific performance required an equitable accounting pairing the purchaser's rents and profits with interest owed the seller on unpaid purchase money; Dillingham could not keep both the property's benefits and interest-free use of the money. Forty-three $600 payments deposited in trust were most plausibly continuing rent and earned no credit.

The casebook uses the decision as an example of conduct overcoming an anti-waiver clause.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-072.rule: After-acquired evidence of employee misconduct serious enough that the employer would have fired for it does not bar all relief for a discriminatory discharge, but it generally forecloses reinstatement and front pay and makes the period from discharge to discovery the starting point for backpay.

sections.Parties: Christine McKennon, discharged at sixty-two after about thirty years with the Nashville Banner, sued the Nashville Banner Publishing Company under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act, alleging that age was the true reason for her discharge and seeking legal and equitable relief including backpay. The employer, which attributed the discharge to a cost-driven workforce reduction, relied on misconduct it discovered during the litigation. McKennon lost below and sought review in the Supreme Court.
sections.Procedural History: The district court granted the employer summary judgment against all relief under the Act, holding that McKennon's misconduct foreclosed backpay and every other remedy. The Sixth Circuit affirmed. Both courts treated after-acquired evidence of sufficiently serious employee misconduct as a complete bar. For purposes of summary judgment the employer conceded discrimination. The Supreme Court reversed and remanded to the Sixth Circuit for further proceedings, announcing remedial principles without awarding any sum or finding that age discrimination had occurred.
sections.Material Facts: McKennon had worked for the Nashville Banner for about thirty years and was sixty-two when discharged. The company said the discharge was part of a workforce reduction required by costs. In her deposition on December 18, 1991, she testified that in her final year as secretary to the comptroller she had copied confidential financial documents, taken them home and shown them to her husband, and that fear of an age-related discharge had prompted her to keep them for protection. A few days later the employer sent another termination letter saying that removing and copying the records violated her responsibilities and that, had it known, it would have fired her immediately. The Court reviewed the case on two premises: age was the sole reason for the original discharge, and the misconduct was grave enough that immediate discharge would have followed its disclosure.
sections.Issue: Whether an employee discharged in violation of the Age Discrimination in Employment Act is barred from all relief when the employer later discovers misconduct that would have led to her discharge on lawful grounds had it been known.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court (1995), in a unanimous opinion by Justice Kennedy, held that after-acquired evidence of misconduct is not a complete bar to relief under the Act, but that it bears on the remedy. As a general rule reinstatement and front pay are inappropriate, and the starting point for backpay is the period from the unlawful discharge to the date the new information was discovered. The employer must first establish that the wrongdoing was so severe that the employee actually would have been terminated on that ground alone had the employer known of it at the time of discharge.
sections.Reasoning:
The Act's purposes include both deterring discrimination and compensating its victims, and the private action vindicates public policy as well as an individual injury. An absolute bar based on later-discovered wrongdoing would disregard the earlier discrimination and frustrate that enforcement scheme.

The employer could not defend the discharge as a mixed-motive decision. Mt. Healthy concerned lawful and unlawful motives both operating when the employer acted. Here the misconduct was unknown at the time, and information the employer did not have could not have motivated its decision. The question was therefore the effect on relief for an assumed violation, not whether an unknown legitimate reason retroactively removed the violation.

The Court also rejected the opposite view that the misconduct was irrelevant. Unclean hands could not mechanically bar a private action serving important statutory purposes, but the Act prohibits discrimination rather than regulating all employment choices, and an employer keeps its lawful prerogatives concerning serious misconduct. Reinstating someone the employer would immediately and lawfully terminate would be inequitable and pointless. For backpay, the employer need not ignore the misconduct once learned, even if it was discovered only because the employee sued, yet eliminating all backpay would weaken the incentive to examine discriminatory motives. Extraordinary equitable circumstances affecting either party's legitimate interests could warrant further adjustment.

The Court acknowledged the concern that employers would conduct extensive discovery into work history to resist discrimination claims, and expected statutory fee awards and appropriate use of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure to deter most abuses.

The casebook uses the case in a note distinguishing a claim under the Act from the surrounding discussion of employment contracts and public-policy torts, quoting the deterrence rationale and the backpay starting point.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-073.rule: A contract whose separately priced preparatory steps exist only to secure a party's continuing readiness to perform is entire, not divisible, and that party's insolvency and assignment for creditors, disabling it from remaining ready, is a present total breach.

sections.Parties: Pennsylvania Exchange Bank and Roseman, assignees for the benefit of the creditors of Joseph Lerner & Son, sued the United States in the Court of Claims for the unpaid balance on Lerner's Army Signal Corps contract. The United States counterclaimed, contending that Lerner's assignment destroyed the bargain and seeking to recover what it had paid. Both sides moved for summary judgment.
sections.Procedural History: The assignees sued for the unpaid contract balance and the United States pleaded alternative counterclaims. On cross-motions, the Court of Claims denied the assignees' motions for summary judgment and to dismiss the counterclaim, granted the government summary judgment, and directed dismissal of the petition. The government's recovery was subject to deductions, including the value of delivered articles, which was to be determined by a commissioner unless stipulated. The opinion is dated March 4, 1959, as amended April 3. It was a ruling on liability with a specified recovery formula, not a final fixed-dollar award.
sections.Material Facts:
The Army Signal Corps wanted manufacturers prepared to supply specified components promptly in a national emergency. Lerner's contract of February 29, 1952 concerned microwave magic tees, which controlled the direction of microwave impulses. Step I required information, planning, qualification approval and a pilot manufacturing run. Step II required production planning, assuming a mobilization schedule of 2,821 units in one year. Step III required acquiring the additional tools and manufacturing aids needed for that schedule, which cost $37,907.37. Step IV contemplated volume production only after a government order in a national emergency; the government did not promise to order any units. After the first three steps Lerner had to preserve the acquired information and keep its tools in operable condition for six years.

Payment for Steps I and II was redetermined to $135,754.48. By October 1, 1953, Lerner had substantially completed Steps I through III. The government had paid $92,843.12 on the first two and had reimbursed the cost of the tools except for $1,922.23. On that date, about a year and a half after entering the agreement, Lerner made an assignment for creditors in lieu of bankruptcy. Procurement Specification 15 emphasized preparing each particular manufacturer to produce by its own methods and disclaimed collecting information to pass to another manufacturer.
sections.Issue: Whether the completed, separately priced preparatory steps were divisible from the manufacturer's undertaking to remain ready for production, so that its assignees could recover the unpaid balance, or whether the assignment for creditors was a total breach of a single bargain supported by consideration.
sections.Holding: The Court of Claims (1959), in an opinion by Judge Whitaker in which Chief Judge Jones, Judges Laramore and Madden, and Circuit Judge Bastian, sitting by designation, concurred, held the contract indivisible and Lerner's disabling assignment a present total breach. It dismissed the petition and granted the government summary judgment, recoverable against the assignees only to the extent they held Lerner assets. Recovery started at $92,843.12, less any value to the government of the Step I articles delivered and less the $1,922.23 unpaid tool-cost balance.
sections.Reasoning:
The court examined the contract's purpose rather than assuming that separate steps and listed prices made it divisible. The first three steps were incidental to the ultimate readiness to undertake Step IV; their expense would not have been incurred apart from that objective. The duty to remain ready was an essential element of one bargain, and the preparation could not be separated from it.

Preserving records and tools implicitly required this manufacturer to remain ready, willing and able to use them. Lerner's insolvency and assignment destroyed its ability to undertake the promised volume production. The government lost its bargain even if no emergency ever arose, because it had bought continuing preparedness, not merely deliveries after an emergency, and keeping the mobilization plan would require preparing another manufacturer. The court applied the implied obligation not to render oneself incapable of performance through insolvency or acts of bankruptcy, tying the conclusion to this contract's continuing readiness undertaking rather than to mere dissatisfaction with a contractor's finances.

The assignees argued that the government had merely reimbursed the first three steps, paid nothing separately for standby, and promised no purchases. The court agreed there was no purchase commitment but found consideration: government-funded preparation gave Lerner a manufacturing capability it had lacked and a chance of profit if orders came, and the government would not have paid for the preparation without the promise to remain ready. Tennessee Soap, involving failure to deliver under an agreement lacking mutual purchase commitments, was distinguished; the court did not decide what obligations would arise if the government later ordered tees and Lerner refused. The loss was described as the cost, as of October 1, 1953, of preparing another manufacturer to stand ready.

The casebook presents this as the Case of the Magic Tees, emphasizing the continuing-readiness purpose, indivisibility and total breach.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-074.rule: A promise in a sale contract to pay the prevailing party's litigation costs is divisible from the sale and remains enforceable even though the sale itself became void when its financing condition failed.

sections.Parties: Grease Monkey International, Inc., the seller under a real-estate contract, sued the buyer, Godat, for specific performance. Godat defended on the ground that the financing condition had not been satisfied and sought his litigation costs under the contract's fee clause. Grease Monkey lost at trial and appealed the denial of specific performance and the award of the buyer's litigation expenses, which was secured by a lien on the property.
sections.Procedural History: Grease Monkey sued for specific performance on September 14. After a bench trial the court found the financing condition unfulfilled and found that Grease Monkey had not shown an ownership interest sufficient to convey title. It awarded the buyer approximately $27,000 in litigation costs under the fee clause, secured by a lien on the property. Grease Monkey appealed. The Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District, affirmed the denial of specific performance and the fee award, reversed the lien, and awarded Godat a further $9,798.71 for the appeal.
sections.Material Facts:
The April 1992 agreement concerned property on Halls Ferry Road in St. Louis County. It made the sale contingent on a financing commitment by a specified deadline, otherwise declaring the contract null and void and requiring return of the deposit; the buyer could obtain conventional financing on terms satisfactory to him in his sole discretion. A separate clause entitled the prevailing party to litigation costs, including reasonable attorney's fees, in any litigation between the parties.
