A June 30 extension kept the financing condition, made the deposit nonrefundable, and set July 9 for the commitment and July 15 for closing. After Boatman's Bank denied the loan, Godat applied to Commerce Bank. On July 9 a Commerce vice president sent the seller's agent a letter saying the bank approved a loan, but he testified that it was not a commitment, which required an appraisal. The seller's own agent acknowledged the letter was not customary commitment documentation. Grease Monkey wrote that it regarded the letter as satisfying the condition; the buyer did not reply and kept pursuing financing. When closing did not occur, the seller offered an extension only on new terms: acknowledgment that the letter satisfied the contingency, another $5,000 nonrefundable deposit, and a higher price. Godat refused. The recorded owner of the property was Grease Monkey Income Limited Partnership, 1987-1, whose assets the seller said had been rolled into its parent, Grease Monkey Holding Company.
sections.Issue: Whether the financing condition was satisfied so as to entitle the seller to specific performance, whether the contract's fee clause survived the failure of that condition, and whether the fee award could be secured by a lien on property the seller claimed through its parent corporation.
sections.Holding: The Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District (1995), in an opinion by Judge Pudlowski in which Presiding Judge Ahrens and Judge Grimm concurred, affirmed in part and reversed in part. The evidence supported the finding that no financing commitment was obtained, so the sale agreement was void and specific performance was properly denied. The fee promise was an independent agreement that survived, and the buyer recovered his litigation costs from the seller. The lien was reversed because it reached the property of a separate corporation that was not before the court.
sections.Reasoning:
Reviewing the bench-trial judgment under Murphy v. Carron and deferring to credibility determinations, the court found the condition's failure supported by the buyer's uncertainty over the loan amount, the bank officer's explanation and the seller's agent's testimony. The seller's later conduct strengthened the finding: an August 24 letter accused the buyer of failing the financing provision, and its demand for different terms suggested it did not regard the original agreement as still valid. Because the seller's correspondence sought a new bargain, the court did not resolve its argument that the closing deadline existed for its benefit and had been waived. Adopting the buyer's proposed findings was not itself reversible error.

Failure of the sales condition did not erase the separate promise to pay litigation expenses. Divisibility depends primarily on intent, assessed through the agreement's language and subject matter; distinct promises capable of separate execution can operate as independent agreements even when made together. Performance of the sale did not depend on the litigation clause, and a promise covering any litigation did not condition reimbursement on the sale remaining enforceable. The buyer's failure to file a formal counterclaim did not defeat fees: he had requested them in writing and orally, and the seller itself sought fees under the same clause, so it had notice and an opportunity to respond.

A parent is not ordinarily liable for its subsidiary's acts; treating them as one requires evidence of the domination and control needed to pierce the veil. The parent was not before the court, and a lien on its alleged property imposed the subsidiary's debt on it without a hearing.

Specific performance also requires the plaintiff to remain ready, willing and able to perform. Grease Monkey refused an extension, tried to get a better deal, and sued on the old terms only when that failed; ordering performance would be inequitable.

The casebook uses the decision to illustrate an independent fee promise surviving nonoccurrence of a sales condition.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-075.rule: An attorney who cannot complete an indivisible representation because of his own disbarment may not recover contract fees or the market value of his services, but only restitution measured by the benefit conferred on the client, less what the client has already paid.

sections.Parties: David M. Somers and Associates, P.C., a law firm, sued its former client, Lori Busch, for $13,124.62 in fees for work on her divorce from September 10, 1998 through July 2, 1999. Busch denied the debt, alleged excessive and unnecessary billing, and counterclaimed under CUTPA for deceptive nondisclosure and billing practices. The firm, which lost at trial, appealed; Busch did not cross-appeal the rejection of her counterclaim.
sections.Procedural History: After a three-day bench trial the trial court rejected Busch's CUTPA counterclaim, requested supplemental briefing on restitution, and then denied the firm any further recovery. It concluded that the representation was one indivisible undertaking through final dissolution absent excusable withdrawal, that disbarment breached it, and that Busch's prior payments exceeded the benefit she received. The firm appealed; the Connecticut Supreme Court transferred the appeal from the Appellate Court and affirmed. The client received no refund, and the judgment against her on the counterclaim stood.
sections.Material Facts:
In fall 1998 Busch sought a swift, amicable divorce. She and her husband had agreed on custody and visitation for their three children and on an equal division of assets; alimony and child support remained open. She signed Somers's preprinted retainer agreement hiring the firm to process her dissolution proceedings, with a $2,500 retainer and $240 hourly attorney fees. Monthly invoices were due on receipt, and the agreement also contemplated payment of outstanding invoices from settlement or other proceeds. A separate provision let Somers demand payment within seven days and, on nonpayment, decline further representation or seek court-approved withdrawal; he never made that demand.

Somers commenced the dissolution action and represented Busch for about a year, until he was disbarred on September 15, 1999. He disclosed neither the pending disciplinary proceedings nor the disbarment; she learned of it from a friend. He then asserted that she was responsible for all incurred fees. Busch had already paid about $4,730. The trial court valued the benefit to her at no more than $3,625. Work found not to advance her goals included challenging her husband's suitability for custody without her authorization, seeking a sixty-forty asset split, and refusing a four-way conference while falsely attributing the refusal to her.
sections.Issue: Whether a retainer agreement billed by the hour was divisible so that a disbarred attorney could recover fees accrued before disbarment, whether disbarment excused his failure to complete the representation, and what measure of restitution, if any, was available to him.
sections.Holding: The Connecticut Supreme Court (2007), in an opinion by Justice Norcott in which Justices Borden, Katz, Palmer and Zarella concurred, affirmed. The agreement was ambiguous as to the duration of the representation and the trial court's finding that it was one indivisible undertaking was supported. Disbarment, a condition the attorney created himself, did not excuse his breach. Quantum meruit for the market value of the services was unavailable because an express contract governed, but a breaching party may recover restitution for the benefit conferred; since Busch had already paid more than that benefit, nothing more was owed.
sections.Reasoning:
The phrase about processing dissolution proceedings was ambiguous as to how long the representation would last, so intent was a question of fact reviewed for clear error. Five findings supported the trial court: Busch understood the representation would run from beginning to end; payment of invoices from a final award pointed to completion; Somers never made the seven-day demand needed to invoke the withdrawal provision; no one discussed a limited number of hours or further retainers; and the representation ended because of disbarment, not completion or nonpayment. A footnote added that ambiguous language is construed against the attorney who drafted it, and saw no reason to confine that rule to insurance contracts, particularly where the drafter owed fiduciary duties.

The attorney had neither fully performed nor tendered further performance. A party who creates the condition making performance impossible cannot claim that its nonperformance is legally excused, and Somers's inability to practice followed from his own actions.

On restitution, the court reviewed the choice of doctrine plenarily. Because a valid express agreement governed the work, quantum meruit did not allow recovery of reasonable market value in its place. But a breaching party can obtain restitution where the other party accepted partial performance and would otherwise keep an unpaid benefit. That recovery rests in quasi-contract and is measured by the benefit advancing the contract's objective, not the market value of the work. The court declined to create a categorical exception denying such claims to disbarred attorneys. Reasonably undertaken work furthering the client's goals can count as a benefit without producing a winning result, and whether benefit arose is for the factfinder. Here the supported value was below what Busch had paid, so she was not unjustly enriched.

The casebook cites the case in a note on licensed workers, connecting the indivisible representation and benefit-based restitution.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-076.rule: Separately itemized prices do not by themselves make a contract divisible; whether a failure to supply one listed service is a material breach of an entire contract is a question of fact, and a funeral contract can support foreseeable emotional-distress damages.

sections.Parties: Menorah Chapels at Millburn, a funeral home, sued Emanuel Needle, who had arranged his father-in-law's funeral, to collect the cost of the funeral. Needle denied liability and counterclaimed for negligence and breach of warranty causing emotional distress to the family, because the funeral home had not supplied the full vigil of watchers it promised. Needle lost on summary judgment and appealed to the New Jersey Appellate Division.
sections.Procedural History: In October 1999 Menorah sued in the Special Civil Part for the funeral cost, with a $390 deduction for the missing shifts. After a dismissal without prejudice, Menorah filed a new complaint on April 9, 2002 and Needle repeated his counterclaim. When Needle was unprepared for trial on October 16, 2002, an adjournment was conditioned on $4,877.02 in fees and costs. The motion judge declined referral to a religious court, characterized the sale as divisible, and dismissed the counterclaim. Menorah later obtained summary judgment on its complaint, plus $11,627.02 in contractual attorney's fees and $1,641.35 in costs. Needle appealed. The Appellate Division reversed the divisibility ruling, restored the contract counterclaim for trial, preserved dismissal of the untimely tort claims, affirmed the readiness sanction, vacated the contractual fee award, and remanded.
sections.Material Facts: Needle arranged services when his father-in-law, an Orthodox Jew, died on a Friday. The funeral was set for Sunday, February 21, 1999, after the Sabbath. Menorah advertised a Jewish funeral chapel and offered requested Orthodox ritual services. Its documents specified shrouds and a continuous vigil over the body, and the statement of selected services listed six shifts of watchers, or shomerim, for $900. Menorah subcontracted the watchers to a burial society. Allegedly because of the Sabbath, only three shifts appeared, beginning Saturday evening after the Sabbath ended, so the body was left unattended contrary to the requested custom. Needle and his family learned of this shortly before the funeral began. The parties' agreement selected New Jersey law and permitted litigation in the Superior Court.
sections.Issue: Whether a civil court could adjudicate the dispute without religious entanglement, whether itemized prices made the funeral agreement divisible so that the missing watcher shifts could be cured by a price deduction, and whether the contract counterclaim could seek emotional-distress damages.
sections.Holding: The New Jersey Appellate Division (2006), in an opinion by Judge Payne for a panel with Judges Skillman and Axelrad, held that the dispute could be decided on neutral contract principles, that itemized pricing did not establish divisibility, and that a jury must decide whether full provision of watchers was a material condition. If the breach was material, Menorah might still recover the value of its remaining services in quantum meruit, allowing for damages caused by the breach. The contract counterclaim could include consequential emotional-distress damages foreseeable at contracting. The court reversed and remanded.
sections.Reasoning:
The Free Exercise and Establishment Clauses did not require abstention. The dispute between secular parties was whether the promised watchers appeared at all, not the doctrinal adequacy of a ritual, and the claimed harm was distress to survivors. Neutral contract rules could resolve both the collection action and the counterclaim.

Whether the parties exchanged one entire undertaking or separate transactions depends on intent, gathered from the agreement and circumstances. Mandatory itemization of funeral services is a consumer-protection disclosure, not proof that each item was meant to be independently enforceable, and a unit rate alone does not show willingness to accept partial performance at a proportional price. Material failures such as not transporting the remains or not supplying the selected coffin could not be cured simply by deducting their listed prices, and the same could not be presumed for the vigil. Materiality was left to a jury. If Menorah were limited to quantum meruit, the listed unit prices would not be an automatic measure, since a missing material component might reduce the worth of the other services.

The record did not justify dismissal with prejudice as a discovery sanction, and that ground was vacated. The negligence, misrepresentation and fraud claims remained untimely under the two-year period. Because funeral services are intended to offer comfort and solace, breach could foreseeably cause emotional distress; the court rejected the heightened severity test for intentional infliction of emotional distress and rejected difficulty of valuation as a ground for dismissal. These rulings made a trial possible without proving any injury.

The readiness sanction was within the trial court's discretion. The contractual fee award was vacated without prejudice to an award if Menorah prevailed on its contract claim; such fees would not be available on a recovery solely in quantum meruit.

The casebook, in an account that dates the case 2008, uses it to pose restitution-offset questions; its statement that breach and entitlement to emotional-distress damages were held overstates the finality, since materiality and damages were left for trial.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-077.rule: Absent an express fee agreement, the law implies payment of the reasonable value of legal services, so a client or his estate may seek restitution of an advance exceeding the value of the services rendered, even if the client's own breach ended the representation.

sections.Parties: The administrator of the estate of Nicholas Begovich sued Neil Murphy, the lawyer who had been defending Begovich on a murder charge, to recover $4,000 of the money advanced to Murphy, plus costs and attorney fees. Murphy moved to dismiss. The administrator, having lost in the trial court, appealed to the Michigan Supreme Court.
sections.Procedural History: The trial judge dismissed the administrator's declaration on Murphy's motion, relying on a supposed definite agreement to pay Murphy $10,000 to represent Begovich at trial, an agreement that was not alleged in the declaration. The administrator appealed. The Michigan Supreme Court reversed and remanded for trial on February 26, 1960, with costs to the administrator. It did not award the refund or decide the underlying facts.
sections.Material Facts: According to the declaration, whose allegations were accepted as true for the appeal, Begovich was in the county jail on a murder charge around July 10, 1958, and Murphy was his lawyer. Murphy demanded and received $2,500, followed by a further $4,000, for the defense. Before trial, on August 7, Begovich died by suicide. The administrator alleged that Murphy's services consisted of an initial interview and consultation, an arraignment appearance waiving examination, and an appearance on the information arranging bail, and that those services were worth no more than $2,500. The estate therefore sought the remaining $4,000. The declaration alleged no express agreement fixing the fee, and nothing in it suggested the second payment was earnest money or a retainer.
sections.Issue: Whether a declaration alleging that a lawyer retained an advance exceeding the value of the services he rendered before his client's suicide ended the representation states a claim for repayment that must go to trial.
sections.Holding: The Michigan Supreme Court (1960), in an opinion by Justice Edwards in which Chief Justice Dethmers and Justices Carr, Kelly, Smith, Black, Kavanagh and Souris concurred, held that the estate's complaint could not be dismissed without trial. Read as alleging that the second $4,000 was an advance for future services that never occurred, the declaration stated a claim of unjustified retention, with the answer and trial to determine the actual circumstances. The court reversed and remanded for trial.
sections.Reasoning:
The sufficiency of the pleading had to be judged on what it alleged, not on an express fee bargain supplied by the trial court.

Michigan law ordinarily implies an obligation to pay the reasonable value of legal services when express compensation terms are absent. Most of the precedents involved lawyers seeking fees, but the court reasoned that the same principle should apply when a client seeks repayment of an advance; otherwise an advance could become an entitlement to compensation exceeding the services rendered without any express bargain supporting it. The court's footnote reproduced Court Rule No. 4 (1945), which let courts, on a client's verified complaint and after notice and hearing, require an attorney to pay money as law and justice required, and treated it as supporting the applicable public policy.

The difficult point was the suicide, which prevented completion of the defense. For purposes of this record the court presumed, as the trial judge had, that it amounted to a willful breach. Even so, absent express terms addressing that contingency and a showing of damage to the lawyer, letting him keep an unearned advance could produce a windfall. An earlier Kentucky decision allowing a lawyer to retain a fee after a client's suicide was distinguished on its trial record and contract terms.

The court endorsed the principles of Restatement of Contracts section 357, which measures restitution by the net benefit exceeding the loss caused by the claimant's own breach, and which excepts earnest money and permissible contractual retention provisions. It did not hold that every willfully breaching client recovers every unused dollar, and it did not assign a particular subsection of section 357 as the established basis for recovery.

The casebook presents the case as a short lawyer-client problem and calls Murphy's challenge a demurrer, where the decision speaks of a motion to dismiss.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-078.rule: When a contract requires written notice within a stated period, the writing must actually be received within that period; and under New York law a seller of real estate may retain a traditional ten percent down payment when the buyer defaults without excuse.

sections.Parties: Maxton Builders, Inc., the seller of a newly built house, sued the buyers, the Lo Galbos, for the amount of the $21,000 down payment after they refused to go through with the purchase and stopped payment on the deposit check. The buyers maintained that they had properly cancelled under a tax rider and, alternatively, that Maxton was limited to its actual damages. The buyers appealed to the New York Court of Appeals.
sections.Procedural History: Maxton sued on September 20, and both sides sought summary judgment. Special Term deemed the cancellation ineffective but denied Maxton summary judgment on recovery, reasoning that the size of the payment and the successful resale raised a factual issue whether claiming the deposit imposed a penalty. The Appellate Division modified and granted Maxton summary judgment for the deposit, applying New York's rule even where the seller resold at the same or a higher price. The buyers appealed on both cancellation and damages. On November 18, 1986 the Court of Appeals affirmed, with costs.
sections.Material Facts:
On August 3, 1983, the Lo Galbos contracted to buy the house from Maxton for $210,000 and tendered a $21,000 check as the escrow down payment. A handwritten rider requested by the buyers let them cancel if real-estate taxes based on a full assessment at that price exceeded $3,500, provided they gave the seller written notice within three days; cancellation would entail return of the escrow funds. The contract did not expressly make time of the essence. On August 4 Cynthia Lo Galbo and Maxton's president visited the assessor's office and obtained an estimate above $3,500.

The buyers' lawyer orally told the seller's lawyer that the buyers wished to cancel. A certified cancellation letter was mailed on Friday, August 5, but the seller's lawyer received it on August 9. The buyers also stopped payment on the check. Maxton resold the house on December 20 for the same $210,000, paying a $12,000 brokerage fee on the resale. It alleged that the breach also caused carrying charges, interest, taxes, insurance and other losses exceeding the deposit, but elected to seek the deposit rather than a separately calculated damages award. The buyers made no effort to show that the seller's actual losses were lower than alleged.
sections.Issue: Whether written notice of cancellation mailed within the three-day period but received after it was effective, and whether New York should abandon the rule of Lawrence v. Miller and limit a seller to its actual damages when a defaulting buyer has made a ten percent down payment.
sections.Holding: The New York Court of Appeals (1986), in an opinion by Chief Judge Wachtler in which Judges Meyer, Simons, Kaye, Alexander, Titone and Hancock concurred, affirmed summary judgment for the seller. The buyers had not exercised their limited cancellation right in the manner and time specified, so the contract remained in force and their refusal to perform was a breach. The court declined to abandon the longstanding New York rule permitting the seller to keep a traditional ten percent down payment after an unexcused default. A footnote reserved the question of installment payments beyond a ten percent down payment.
sections.Reasoning:
On notice, the buyers argued that because time was not expressly of the essence, mailing the writing and communicating orally within three days was reasonable notice. The court answered that when an agreement requires written notice within a stated period, the writing must actually arrive within that period. The parties bargained for a limited right to cancel and the buyers did not exercise it as agreed; that the tax estimate met the rider's threshold did not itself cancel the sale.

On restitution, the court acknowledged criticism of the broad common-law rule denying restitution to parties in default: applied to substantial or nearly completed performance, it could make the forfeiture grow as the breach became smaller. The modern approach generally allows recovery of the net benefit exceeding the injured party's loss, with the defaulting claimant bearing the burden of proof. But the court distinguished real-estate down payments. The modern Restatement itself recognizes liquidated damages and understandings or usages providing for retention of money on breach, with an illustration involving a ten percent first installment, and a proposed New York legislative reform, which was not enacted, would itself have allowed retention of a reasonable percentage.

The court gave weight to stability where settled rules structure contractual rights and reliance. A restitution rule would be no better or more workable for down payments near ten percent: an express clause allowing retention of so modest a sum would probably survive liquidated-damages analysis, and without one a defaulting buyer would face a difficult burden of showing that the payment exceeded the seller's damages. Change would often extend litigation without saving anyone from real loss. Real-estate sales are generally negotiated at arm's length, and the bargaining table is the place to alter the established consequences, absent a real risk of overreaching.

The casebook emphasizes the reservation for larger payments and the court's refusal to overrule Lawrence.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-079.rule: A purchaser of land whose breach was not willful may recover payments to the extent the seller is unjustly enriched, but bears the burden of proving the seller's damages were less than the money retained, and a ten percent liquidated-damages clause is presumptively reasonable.

sections.Parties: Euel and Etta Vines, purchasers under a contract to buy a New Canaan condominium, sued the seller, Orchard Hills, Inc., for restitution of their $7,880 down payment after they declined to take title. Orchard Hills relied on the contract's liquidated-damages clause. The buyers won at trial, and the seller appealed to the Connecticut Supreme Court.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court overruled the seller's demurrer and, after a hearing, awarded the buyers $7,880 plus interest, treating the property's rise in value by the time of the 1979 trial as a windfall to the seller that justified repayment. The seller appealed, challenging the pleading ruling, the refusal to enforce the liquidated-damages clause, and the use of a valuation as of the trial date. On July 15, 1980 the Connecticut Supreme Court upheld the overruling of the demurrer but set aside the refund judgment and remanded for further proceedings, without entering a final judgment allowing the seller to keep the money.
sections.Material Facts:
On July 11, 1973, the Vineses contracted to purchase the condominium from Orchard Hills for $78,800. By the time they signed they had paid $7,880, exactly ten percent. The default clause provided that if the purchasers failed to perform while the seller performed its obligations, the seller would retain all payments as liquidated damages and the parties' rights and liabilities would end. The buyers later declined to take title because Euel's employer transferred him to New Jersey, and they notified the seller by letter of January 4, 1974. They alleged neither nonperformance by the seller nor a legal excuse for their own failure, and no one alleged that their default was willful.

At the hearing the evidence showed that the condominium's fair market value had risen to $160,000 by the 1979 trial, an increase of approximately $80,000. Neither side supplied the property's value at the time of the breach or evidence of the seller's damages from the breach.
sections.Issue: Whether purchasers of real property who have themselves breached may recover their down payment in restitution, who bears the burden of proof, and whether a contract clause allowing the seller to retain a ten percent down payment as liquidated damages defeats the claim.
sections.Holding: The Connecticut Supreme Court (1980), in an opinion by Justice Peters in which Chief Justice Cotter and Justices Bogdanski, Healey and Parskey concurred, held that a land purchaser whose default was not willful may pursue restitution of a payment unjustly retained by the seller, but that these purchasers had not proved that entitlement. A contract permitting retention of a ten percent down payment as liquidated damages is presumptively reasonable, subject to rebuttal. The refund judgment was set aside and the case remanded for further proceedings.
sections.Reasoning:
Default alone did not make the complaint legally insufficient; whether the seller was unjustly enriched despite the agreed damages clause was a question of fact.

The court explained that a categorical bar punishes a purchaser who has partly performed more severely than one who paid nothing, though partial performance usually causes the innocent party no greater injury. Contract damages compensate the injured party's loss of bargain; retention beyond that loss can be unjust enrichment, and anti-forfeiture principles elsewhere in contract and property law supported examining it. The court did not unreservedly adopt an economic model encouraging breach, since the injured party might in practice be left uncompensated. Restitution is legal in form but equitable in nature, permitting a balance of avoiding forfeiture, incentives to perform, the character of the breach and protection of the innocent party. The holding covered a purchaser whose breach was not willful.

Permission to sue did not establish entitlement. The defaulting purchasers ordinarily had to prove that the seller's damages were less than the money received. The contract also supplied an agreed measure of damages, and because the clause was raised as a defense to the buyers' restitution claim, the buyers bore the burden of proving it invalid or unenforceable. A ten percent earnest-money allocation was presumptively reasonable. The presumption could be rebutted by showing fraud, mistake or unconscionability, or that the breach caused no damage or damage substantially below the agreed amount.

The trial court used the wrong valuation date. The seller's damages are measured at the time of breach, and later appreciation properly accrued to the seller. Because Connecticut had not previously stated the claim's availability and limits clearly, the buyers were given another opportunity to prove it.

The casebook describes the restitution rule and the rebuttable presumption; its statement that the seller was entitled to keep the deposit compresses the result, since the court remanded to let the buyers try to rebut the presumption.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-080.rule: Where a contract has no forfeiture or liquidated-damages clause, a defaulting buyer is entitled under Restatement (Second) of Contracts section 374(1) to restitution of the part of a deposit that exceeds the seller's actual damages, and bears the burden of proving the excess.

sections.Parties: Milton and Ruth Kutzin, sellers of a house in Haworth, sued the buyers, Duncan and Gertrude Pirnie, first for specific performance and then, after reselling, for damages. The Pirnies counterclaimed for return of their $36,000 deposit, arguing that the contract had been rescinded through attorney review or mutual agreement. Both sides appealed the trial judgment, and the case reached the New Jersey Supreme Court after the Appellate Division let the sellers keep the whole deposit.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court found a binding, unrescinded contract and awarded the sellers $17,325: the $12,500 shortfall on resale, $3,825 in utilities, taxes and insurance during the six-month delay, and $1,000 for a new basement carpet. It declined claimed lost interest and increased capital-gains taxes and ordered the $18,675 balance of the deposit returned. The sellers appealed, seeking the additional losses or alternatively the whole deposit; the buyers cross-appealed for the whole deposit. The Appellate Division agreed that the contract was enforceable and the interest and tax claims too speculative, but permitted the sellers to retain all $36,000. The New Jersey Supreme Court modified that judgment to restore the trial court's award and affirmed as modified.
sections.Material Facts:
On September 1, 1987, the Kutzins agreed to sell their house to the Pirnies for $365,000 on a standard realtors' form prepared by the sellers' broker. The buyers paid $1,000 and owed another $35,000 within seven days. The contract contained no forfeiture or liquidated-damages provision. Its attorney-review clause let either side's lawyer disapprove within three days, by notice to the realtors and the other party, the notice to the realtors to be sent by certified mail or telegram or delivered personally; otherwise the agreement became binding.

The sellers' attorney, Kozinn, approved the agreement except that he wanted to hold the deposit, and said so in a September 3 letter. On September 4 the buyers' attorney, Maccarone, accepted that arrangement and mailed a proposed rider. Neither letter was certified, and neither side obtained a written extension of attorney review. On September 10 the attorneys agreed on changes to the rider, Maccarone assured Kozinn that the buyers intended to purchase, and Kozinn received the additional $35,000 the next day. The sellers then left for Florida. Shortly afterward the buyers retained a new attorney, who mailed a September 28 notice that they no longer wished to purchase and wanted the deposit back. While the suit was pending the sellers sold the house to someone else for $352,500.
sections.Issue: Whether the lawyers' exchange of proposed revisions rescinded the contract under the attorney-review clause, and, if the buyers breached, whether the sellers could keep the entire deposit when it exceeded their actual damages and the contract had no forfeiture or liquidated-damages clause.
sections.Holding: The New Jersey Supreme Court (1991), in a unanimous opinion by Justice Clifford joined by Chief Justice Wilentz and Justices Handler, Pollock, O'Hern, Garibaldi and Stein, held that the buyers had breached an enforceable contract but that the breach did not entitle the sellers to retain a deposit exceeding their actual loss. Adopting Restatement (Second) of Contracts section 374(1) and overruling contrary New Jersey decisions, the court restored the trial court's $17,325 damages award to the sellers and the $18,675 repayment to the buyers.
sections.Reasoning:
The attorney-review clause was unambiguous, and communication between the lawyers did not displace its notice requirements. Neither lawyer disapproved the agreement as specified: Kozinn's letter called it satisfactory subject to the deposit arrangement, and Maccarone's proposed changes without disapproving; neither was certified or sent to all the required recipients. The contract therefore became binding at the end of the review period, modified only as to custody of the deposit, and the refusal to purchase was a breach. The court did not decide whether notice to the other party's attorney would satisfy the requirement of notice to that party.

Traditional New Jersey cases let an innocent seller keep a defaulting buyer's payment regardless of actual damages, on the premise that a contract breaker should get no judicial help from the wrong. The court explained the asymmetry of that rule: a buyer who paid nothing before breaching owed only compensatory damages, while one who partly performed could lose a sum exceeding the same injury. Keeping the excess imposes a penalty rather than making the seller whole. Tracing the restitution approach through Corbin, the first Restatement's section 357 and the broader modern section 374(1), the court adopted the latter.

The buyers still bore the burden of proving that the deposit exceeded the sellers' injury. Here the $17,325 loss had been found and was not challenged, and subtracting it from $36,000 left $18,675 to return. That the deposit was just under ten percent of the price did not change the calculation.

The court stressed that no forfeiture or liquidated-damages clause was before it. Such a clause would implicate section 374(2), which limits restitution when the agreed retention reasonably reflects anticipated loss and difficulties of proof; the court did not decide the validity of any such clause, cautioning that labeling a penalty as liquidated damages would not cure it.

The casebook cites the case for section 374 and the absence of liquidated damages.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-081.rule: A seller's tolerance of late payment does not oblige it to forbear indefinitely; absent an intentional relinquishment of the right to payment, it may insist on payment after giving notice and the cure period the contract provides.

sections.Parties: Sethness-Greenleaf, Inc., which had sold the Green River soda trademarks, secret formulas and other business assets to Green River Corporation (GRC) and continued to supply it with concentrate, sued to reclaim the trademarks and formulas held in escrow after GRC failed to pay. GRC, the company of Daniel Meyers and Cornell Wing, disputed the seller's right to demand payment and retake the escrow items, and appealed the contract judgment against it to the Seventh Circuit.
sections.Procedural History: A prior appellate decision upheld preliminary injunctive relief and identified the remaining liability question as whether the parties had orally agreed to let payment be delayed as long as it was. On return, the district court found on summary judgment that there was no such oral agreement, held that nonpayment after demand entitled the seller to reclaim the soda rights, and enjoined imitation sales. The contract judgment was certified under Rule 54(b) while calculation of Lanham Act damages remained in the district court. GRC appealed, and the Seventh Circuit affirmed on August 21, 1995.
sections.Material Facts:
In 1985 GRC arranged to acquire the Green River trademarks, secret formulas and other business assets from Sethness-Greenleaf for $75,000. The seller would keep producing concentrate, which GRC would buy; each paid gallon generated a credit, at first $3 and later $5, against the acquisition price. Until full payment the trademarks and formulas stayed in escrow as security. Section 6(b) of the escrow entitled GRC to written notice of past-due obligations and a thirty-day cure period. The deal closed in June 1985, and GRC was behind by July 1986. In June 1988 it issued notes for approximately $26,000 to cover unpaid balances.

Every shipment carried an invoice requiring payment within ten days, which GRC routinely disregarded; it received over 200 invoices without objection. Over the next fourteen months the balance grew beyond $60,000, and most of the $75,000 price remained unpaid. On August 3, 1989, Sethness-Greenleaf demanded full payment within thirty days and warned that failure would trigger escrow default and repossession. GRC did not pay. It admitted owing roughly $60,000; its November offer to pay was conditioned on dismissal of the suit and was rejected. GRC then began selling its own formulation under the Green River label.
sections.Issue: Whether the ten-day payment term on the seller's invoices bound the buyer, whether the parties had agreed to indefinite credit, and whether the seller's long tolerance of late payment prevented it from demanding payment and reclaiming the escrowed assets.
sections.Holding: The Seventh Circuit (1995), in an opinion by Judge Easterbrook for a panel with Judge Kanne and District Judge Allen Sharp, sitting by designation, affirmed the contract judgment allowing Sethness-Greenleaf to reclaim the trademarks and formulas. The invoices' ten-day term was part of the parties' agreement, there was no objective agreement for indefinite credit, and the seller's lenience did not waive its right to payment. GRC received the written notice and thirty-day cure period that the escrow agreement required and had not bargained for more.
sections.Reasoning:
GRC argued that fourteen months of arrears disproved any agreement to the ten-day deadline. Applying Illinois's UCC section 2-207, the court explained that merchants can contract through exchanged forms without negotiating each term, and that additional terms in a written confirmation become part of the agreement unless acceptance was expressly limited, the term materially alters the bargain, or there is timely objection. Both sides were merchants, GRC's orders said nothing about payment timing, and it received the invoices without objection. The term was not surprising or a material alteration, since the Code's default rule in section 2-310(a), payment on delivery, was less generous. Failure to comply did not show the obligation never existed.

Meyers's affidavit asserted that the seller's president promised credit until profitability, but at his deposition he retracted that and acknowledged the subject had not really been discussed. A private wish or expectation cannot supply the objective communications a contract requires. Course of dealing or performance can clarify an incomplete or ambiguous bargain, but here the documents cut the other way, and the long-term-credit theory appeared only well into the litigation.

Tolerating late payment did not oblige the seller to forbear indefinitely. Treating patience as such an undertaking would encourage sellers to cut off supply immediately and deprive buyers generally of lenience. The court recognized that conduct can sometimes waive a particular default or require notice before strict enforcement resumes, but distinguished that from intentional abandonment of the right to payment, of which there was no evidence. Even if the seller's early conduct encouraged complacency, it gave notice that further delay would not be accepted and allowed another thirty days.

The casebook quotes the rationale against indefinite forbearance in a note on the benefits of lenience.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-082.rule: A party whose own conduct prevents or hinders the other's performance cannot rely on the resulting nonperformance, and parol evidence of surrounding circumstances may be used to show the contract's subject matter and that conduct.

sections.Parties: Peck contracted with a military officer to furnish and deliver wood and hay to the Tongue River station in the Yellowstone region. The dispute, between Peck and the United States, was whether the government could deduct from the amount owed on his wood account the extra cost of obtaining hay from others after he failed to deliver it. The case came to the Supreme Court on cross appeals from the Court of Claims.
sections.Procedural History: The Court of Claims considered the written agreement together with the surrounding circumstances and gave judgment; cross appeals to the Supreme Court followed. The Court affirmed. The published report states neither a quantified recovery nor the results of other minor points, which the report notes were omitted at Justice Bradley's suggestion; this account covers only the published report.
sections.Material Facts:
Peck contracted to furnish and deliver specified quantities of wood and hay to the Tongue River station by a designated time. The written contract did not name the source from which he had to obtain the hay. He delivered the wood but not the hay. Others supplied the hay at increased expense, and government accounting officers sought to deduct that additional cost from the amount owed on his wood account.

The Court of Claims concluded that both sides contemplated hay gathered in the Yellowstone valley, particularly Big Meadows near the mouth of Tongue River. That was the only source Peck could obtain within hundreds of miles, and his reliance on it was known. Government officers, concerned that he might not perform and regarding the hay as indispensable, permitted other parties to cut the Big Meadows hay and use it to supply the station. Peck objected that the government both deprived him of the supply on which he relied and charged him the extra cost of obtaining it through others.
sections.Issue: Whether surrounding circumstances could be shown by parol evidence to establish the subject matter of the written contract and the government's conduct, and whether the government could charge the contractor for a failure to deliver that its own conduct had caused.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court (1880), in an opinion by Justice Bradley, affirmed the judgment of the Court of Claims. Surrounding circumstances could establish the contract's subject matter and the government's conduct preventing performance, and a party cannot invoke nonperformance that its own interference caused. The published discussion rejects the government's use of the hay default to justify deducting the increased cost from the wood account.
sections.Reasoning:
Justice Bradley identified two proper uses of parol evidence. First, it clarified the subject matter of the contract: hay to be cut and gathered in the region of delivery. Second, it established the later conduct of the government's agents. They had encouraged reliance on a particular means of performance until alternatives were no longer feasible, and then themselves removed that means. The Court treated the resulting inability as prevention and hindrance by the government rather than an unexplained failure by the supplier. It did not simply add a source term to the written bargain or excuse a contractor who independently chose an unreliable source; the reasoning tied the parties' circumstances and known reliance to the government's own actions.

The opinion cited authority permitting proof of contractual subject matter through surrounding circumstances and then explained the rule that one party's prevention excuses the other's nonperformance. Its principal analogy involved a bond requiring procurement and cancellation of a mortgage: after the obligor obtained it, the obligee directed that it be placed with a third person, and parol proof of that instruction excused incomplete literal compliance, since the preventing party could not benefit from the resulting omission. A second analogy involved a bond to convey land that was later orally rescinded and followed by a sale to another purchaser; the parties' agreement and acts discharged it although the papers were never formally surrendered. Bradley found the principles of those cases applicable to Peck.

The casebook summarizes the Big Meadows interference and quotes the prevention rule; the surrounding discussion of good faith is the casebook's framing, not language of the opinion.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-083.rule: A real-estate broker is entitled to the commission, even under a rule that ordinarily requires the sale to close, when the seller's own conduct prevents completion of a sale to a buyer the broker produced who was willing and able to perform.

sections.Parties: Charles Hosley, a real-estate broker, sued Paul Drake, the owner who had listed land with him, for his commission after Drake sold the land to other buyers through another broker. Drake argued that no commission was earned because the sale to Hosley's buyers never closed, and that Hosley had agreed to an earlier closing date and had breached fiduciary duties. Drake lost on summary judgment and appealed to the Alaska Supreme Court.
sections.Procedural History: Hosley sued for his commission, and on cross motions for summary judgment the superior court granted his motion and denied Drake's, finding that he had fulfilled the listing agreement by locating buyers who entered a binding sale during the listing period. Drake appealed. The Alaska Supreme Court affirmed on January 31, 1986; rehearing was denied on April 3.
sections.Material Facts:
On March 5, 1984, Drake signed an exclusive listing agreement authorizing Hosley to sell his North Pole land through March 30. It provided a ten percent commission on specified events, including a binding sale during the listing period or production of a buyer willing and able to purchase on Drake's terms. Hosley found three buyers. On March 23 Drake and the buyers signed an earnest-money agreement calling for closing within ten days of clear title, and an addendum confirmed the commission.

Hosley received the preliminary title commitment on April 3; the only encumbrance was a judgment owed to Drake's former wife. Drake's lawyer, Wickwire, later wanted closing by April 11, saying a discounted settlement of that judgment required payment then. Wickwire claimed Hosley agreed to that date; Hosley said only that he would try to close quickly. Hosley learned from the former wife's attorney that the deadline had in fact been extended to the end of the month. On April 11 Hosley told Wickwire the buyers lacked funds for that day and would not have them before May 1. Wickwire said he would advise cancellation and mailed a withdrawal letter. On April 12 Drake sold through another broker to different buyers. That same day Hosley presented checks totaling $33,000 from the original buyers for the down payment, which Wickwire refused.
sections.Issue: Whether the broker earned his commission although the sale to the buyers he produced never closed, and whether a disputed agreement between the broker and the seller's lawyer for an earlier closing date raised a material issue of fact precluding summary judgment.
sections.Holding: The Alaska Supreme Court (1986), in an opinion by Justice Moore for a panel that also included Chief Justice Rabinowitz and Justices Burke, Matthews and Compton, with no separate writing, affirmed summary judgment for the broker. The original buyers were willing and able to perform on the agreed terms and tendered within the ten-day closing period, and Drake frustrated that performance by selling to third parties during the period. The opinion establishes entitlement to the commission without stating its amount.
sections.Reasoning:
Alaska's statute provided that a commission is earned when a broker fulfills a written personal-services agreement. Drake urged the court to apply Ellsworth Dobbs, Inc. v. Johnson, under which a broker generally earns the commission only when the buyer performs and the sale is completed, absent seller default. The court described the traditional rule allowing a commission on production of a ready, willing and able buyer and the practical reasons for requiring performance instead: a signed agreement does not prove the buyer can pay, and the seller normally expects the sale proceeds to fund the commission. It found the Dobbs reasoning persuasive, but that approach did not help Drake, because Dobbs itself preserves the broker's right when improper or frustrating conduct by the owner prevents title from passing.

The dispute over whether Hosley promised an April 11 closing was genuine but not material. There was only a bare allegation, with no evidence, that Hosley represented the buyers or could modify their agreement; conveying a message from them did not establish agency. An agreement between the seller's lawyer and the seller's broker could not bind the buyers to an accelerated deadline. The April 12 tender fell within ten days of either the title report's April 2 typist date or its April 3 receipt, and so was timely. The court rejected the claimed ambiguity among the ten-day provision, the as-soon-as-possible language and the time-is-of-the-essence clause, and Drake's asserted unilateral power to select an earlier day. It reserved the statute-of-frauds question about an oral modification.

Drake's argument that the broker breached duties of loyalty and disclosure by acting for the buyers failed for the same lack of agency evidence. One purchaser, Hofschulte, was employed by Hosley, but that relationship had been disclosed.

The casebook cites the case in its brokerage discussion for the seller-prevention principle.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-084.rule: Under New York's prevention doctrine a party may not avoid a contractual duty by frustrating the occurrence of a condition to it, and enforcing an airline's own promised remedies through that doctrine is not preempted by the Airline Deregulation Act.

sections.Parties: Stephen Ide, Karen Steele-Clarke, Philip Tenn and Donald Dominique, customers whose British Airways flights were cancelled, sued British Airways PLC in a putative class action for breach of contract, alleging that the airline withheld the refunds its conditions of carriage promised. British Airways moved to compel Dominique to arbitrate and to dismiss the remaining plaintiffs' claims.
sections.Procedural History: British Airways moved in the Southern District of New York to compel arbitration of Dominique's claims and to dismiss the amended complaint as to the other plaintiffs. On March 26, 2021 the court compelled Dominique's arbitration and stayed the action only as to him. It denied dismissal of the other three plaintiffs' contract claims, granted dismissal of their requests for statutory, punitive or exemplary damages and injunctive relief, denied leave to amend those requests as futile, and required an answer within three weeks. This was a pleading-stage decision: the court neither certified a class nor awarded compensation, and it did not find that the airline had done what was alleged.
sections.Material Facts:
British Airways's General Conditions of Carriage promised a customer whose flight was cancelled a choice among three remedies: carriage as soon as possible on an available scheduled service, carriage later at the customer's convenience within the ticket's validity period, or an involuntary fare refund. The options did not expressly include a voucher for future travel.

The complaint alleged that after the pandemic caused mass cancellations, the airline changed its website to steer customers toward vouchers. A button labeled to cancel and refund flights led to a voucher application, and the online refund option was removed. The telephone became the only route to a refund, but many calls were disconnected and others meant hours on hold. Ide could not reach the airline, obtained a voucher as the only available relief, and later sought cash; four calls were disconnected and an agent eventually refused conversion because the voucher had issued. Steele-Clarke believed the online form sought a refund but received a voucher; her seat-selection charge was refunded but her fare was not. Tenn submitted a voucher form but asked for a refund by telephone and email before any voucher issued, and allegedly received neither. Dominique bought through Expedia, whose agreement required individual arbitration of claims against travel suppliers, and he too received neither form of relief. Ide's voucher was only part payment for a future booking, with a twelve-month travel deadline.
sections.Issue: Whether the complaint plausibly alleged breach of the conditions of carriage, either because a voucher was not one of the promised remedies or because the airline prevented customers from choosing a refund, and whether the Airline Deregulation Act preempted those claims or the relief sought.
sections.Holding: The United States District Court for the Southern District of New York (2021), Judge Jesse M. Furman, held that the three remaining plaintiffs plausibly alleged breach of contract on two theories: that the airline failed to offer a promised remedy, and that it prevented customers from exercising their contractual choice. The contract claims were not preempted by the Airline Deregulation Act. Punitive or exemplary damages were preempted, the requests for statutory damages were struck as unopposed, and injunctive relief was rejected because money could adequately compensate the alleged injury. Dominique's claims were sent to arbitration and stayed.
sections.Reasoning:
Dominique did not oppose arbitration but opposed dismissal with prejudice; applying circuit authority requiring a stay when requested, the court stayed his claims. The airline's argument that Tenn missed his outbound flight rested on a Passenger Name Record outside the complaint, which the court would not consider on a motion to dismiss or convert to summary judgment before discovery.

The existence of a contract and the plaintiffs' performance were undisputed for the motion. The damages argument, raised only in a footnote, failed in any event: restricted in-kind compensation was plausibly worth less than cash.

First, the contract unambiguously let the customer choose among three listed remedies. The airline said a voucher was essentially equivalent to later carriage at the customer's convenience, but given the limits on Ide's voucher that equivalence was plausibly disputable. Requesting a voucher did not establish modification, waiver, estoppel or accord and satisfaction on the face of the complaint; those are affirmative defenses requiring proof.

Second, the airline characterized calling for a refund as an unsatisfied condition precedent. New York's prevention doctrine bars avoiding a contractual duty by frustrating the condition's occurrence, and removing refund forms and funneling requests through inaccessible call centers allegedly did that. Whether the difficulty came from the public-health emergency or from intentional website changes was a factual dispute that could not support dismissal. Unlike plaintiffs in similar airline cases, these plaintiffs described their own unsuccessful attempts.

On preemption, Wolens permits enforcement of an airline's voluntarily undertaken contractual obligations, and Ginsberg distinguishes an implied obligation protecting the parties' bargain from a state-imposed standard that enlarges it. Under New York law the prevention doctrine serves the parties' intent and reasonable expectations, so using it to enforce the promised choice imposed no external obligation. The court did not exempt all implied-covenant claims.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-085.rule: A promisor that wrongfully prevents a condition from occurring cannot rely on its nonoccurrence to escape the promised performance, but conduct the contract authorizes, a risk the other party assumed, is not wrongful prevention.

sections.Parties: Richard Shear, who had found a purchaser for the National Rifle Association's Washington headquarters building, was the plaintiff and appellant. He sued the NRA, the defendant and appellee, on contract, fraud and rescission claims arising from a brokerage agreement that promised him $150,000 contingent on settlement of the sale. The NRA sought to uphold dismissal of the complaint.
sections.Procedural History: The district court dismissed Shear's complaint under Rule 12(b)(6) without an opinion. Shear appealed the contract, fraud and rescission claims; claims for harm to professional reputation and quantum meruit apparently were not pursued on appeal. Because the appeal tested only the pleading, the court accepted all of Shear's factual allegations, declined to decide whether he could prove them, and rejected the NRA's effort to substitute its own account of the facts. The D.C. Circuit reversed dismissal of the contract and fraud counts and remanded for further proceedings, and affirmed dismissal of the rescission count.
sections.Material Facts:
The following facts were alleged and accepted for purposes of the pleading. The NRA planned to move its headquarters from Washington to Colorado Springs, bought land, and held a groundbreaking ceremony in November 1976. Its treasurer, Binswanger, instructed Shear to obtain offers for the Washington building, and he found two prospective purchasers. On April 1, 1977, the Management Committee set up a sealed-bid procedure and promised unanimously to recommend the winning bid to the Board at its May 23 meeting. Board approval was necessary for a sale. On April 29 the committee selected the highest bid, which Shear had procured, and the purchaser and the NRA president signed a sales contract subject to Board approval. On May 6 the executive vice president signed a brokerage agreement promising Shear $150,000, instead of four percent of the sales price, contingent on settlement.

Later in May, dissident members and officers took control at the annual meeting. New bylaws prohibited moving the headquarters and stripped the Board of authority to approve a sale of NRA real property. Only afterward was the sale put to the Board; the Management Committee declined to recommend approval and the Board did not approve. No settlement occurred and no commission was paid. Shear alleged that Binswanger and other officers knew of the intended obstruction during negotiations but kept promising a favorable recommendation without disclosing it.
sections.Issue: Whether Shear's complaint stated claims for breach of contract and fraud even though the conditions of Board approval and settlement never occurred, on the theory that the NRA wrongfully prevented them; whether New York's Not-For-Profit Corporation Law left the officers without authority to make the promises; and whether the complaint stated a claim for rescission based on mutual mistake.
sections.Holding: The D.C. Circuit in 1979, in an opinion by Judge MacKinnon for a panel that also included Judge Tamm and visiting District Judge John H. Pratt, held that the complaint stated contract and fraud claims and did not state a rescission claim. On the pleaded facts Shear assumed the risk that an authorized Board might reject a recommended sale, but not the risk that the Management Committee would withdraw its promised recommendation or that new bylaws would strip the Board of power before submission. Those alleged failures supported wrongful prevention. The court awarded no commission and made no prediction about success at trial.
sections.Reasoning:
Ordinarily a conditional duty does not become enforceable before its condition occurs, but a promisor cannot wrongfully prevent the condition and then rely on its absence. The court drew this from Corbin, Williston, earlier cases, and the tentative Second Restatement provision, then numbered section 269, excusing nonoccurrence when a party's breach substantially contributes to it. Prevention must be wrongful: if the contract authorizes the conduct that stops the condition, there is no breach, so the controlling question was which risks Shear's arrangement assigned to him. The NRA's argument that it never agreed to sell missed the claim, which alleged obstruction of the agreed approval process and not an unconditional obligation to convey.

To the objection that settlement was speculative, the court answered that some counterfactual reasoning is inevitable in prevention cases, that the allegation of prevention had to be accepted at this stage, and that the tentative Restatement required substantial contribution, not strict but-for causation, while leaving the party in breach to show the condition would not have occurred anyway.

On authority, a statutory restriction on selling property did not bar hiring a broker; section 712 permitted delegation to committees; and the NRA's conduct could support apparent authority. The pleading entitled Shear to prove authority. The fraud count was sufficient because a promise made with a contemporaneous intention not to perform can be fraud, and the alleged assurance concerned the committee's recommendation, not a guarantee of Board approval. The mutual-mistake count failed because the alleged mistake was a belief about a future recommendation, not about facts existing when the agreement was made.

The casebook describes the case in shorthand as a reversal; the decision also separately affirmed dismissal of rescission.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-086.rule: A party ordinarily cannot rely on the nonoccurrence of a condition precedent when it has itself frustrated or prevented that condition, unless the other party's conduct is shown to justify the obstruction.

sections.Parties: Kooleraire Service & Installation Corp., a prequalified bidder awarded a heating and ventilation contract for J.H.S. 56 in Manhattan, sued the Board of Education for breach after the Board rescinded. The Board defended on the ground that a required comptroller's certificate had never been endorsed, and on alleged false statements in Kooleraire's prequalification application. Kooleraire was the appellant in the Court of Appeals.
sections.Procedural History: Kooleraire sued for breach. The Board pleaded two affirmative defenses: lack of certification under the contract and Administrative Code section 93c-3.0, and justification for rescission based on alleged false statements in the prequalification application. The trial court deliberately tried only the certificate issue, reserving the factual merits of the second defense, and entered judgment for the Board solely because the certificate was absent. The Appellate Division and the trial court agreed that the contractual provision, not the statute, governed the certification question. The Court of Appeals reversed the order with costs and remitted the case to Supreme Court, New York County, for further proceedings.
sections.Material Facts: Kooleraire was a prequalified bidder for heating and ventilation work at J.H.S. 56 in Manhattan. Its low bid was $418,175. The Board awarded the contract on July 21, 1965; Kooleraire executed it on August 12 and the Board on August 13. Article 44 made the agreement nonbinding until the comptroller endorsed a certificate that an unexpended, unapplied appropriation balance was sufficient to meet the estimated expense. Kooleraire began preliminary work. On November 17 the Board rescinded. No certification had occurred, although uncontradicted trial proof showed adequate funds and the certification and registration of a later contract for the same purpose. The Board itself had asked the comptroller to withhold registration, a fact it did not dispute.
sections.Issue: Whether the Board could invoke the nonoccurrence of the certification condition after it had asked the comptroller not to certify, even though sufficient funds existed.
sections.Holding: The New York Court of Appeals in 1971, in an opinion by Judge Bergan in which all six participating judges agreed (Judge Burke did not participate), held that the Board could not rely on the missing certificate on the record tried. Having induced noncertification while funds were available, the Board could not use the absent certificate to defeat contractual liability. The court awarded no damages and did not decide whether the alleged prequalification misconduct justified rescission; that reserved defense remained open for litigation on its merits.
sections.Reasoning:
The court read article 44 by its purpose. The parties could reasonably have intended a certificate confirming that adequate funds existed, and nothing in the instrument suggested an independent comptroller veto. A party ordinarily cannot rely on another's failure to satisfy a condition precedent when it has frustrated or prevented that condition. Here funds existed, but the Board induced noncertification and then sought to use the missing certificate to escape liability for a different reason, turning a funding safeguard into a means of avoiding the agreement.

The prevention rule does not make all obstruction unjustifiable; the other party's conduct can justify it. But the record held only the Board's assertion of false prequalification statements. Their truth and legal significance had not been tried, and no one had asked to litigate justification within the trial's limited scope. The Board could litigate that defense later but could not obtain a finding of justified prevention from a record that deliberately omitted the issue.

The court distinguished Albany Supply & Equipment Co. v. City of Cohoes, which involved a statute making the contract invalid and an effort by the contractor and officials to evade it. This case involved a contractual funding certification with money actually available, and the court did not announce a general power to disregard statutory municipal-contract requirements.

The casebook cites the case in shorthand as a reversal; the actual disposition was a remittal with the justification defense unresolved.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-087.rule: A signed offer to purchase that fixes the material terms can be a binding contract, if the parties so intend, even though it contemplates a later formal agreement, and a deadline for executing that agreement is a condition that can be waived by conduct.

sections.Parties: John McCarthy, the prospective buyer, sued Ann Tobin, the seller, for specific performance and damages, claiming that their signed offer-to-purchase form bound her to sell real estate. Robert and Juliann DiMinico intervened because they later contracted to buy the same property. Tobin and the DiMinicos maintained that Tobin had no obligation to sell to McCarthy.
sections.Procedural History: The motion judge granted summary judgment to Tobin and partial summary judgment to the interveners, declaring that Tobin had no obligation to sell to McCarthy. The Appeals Court vacated that judgment and directed judgment for McCarthy; the brief describes that 1998 opinion only as procedural history. On the interveners' application, the Supreme Judicial Court granted further appellate review. It vacated the judgment and remanded to the Superior Court for entry of judgment on McCarthy's specific-performance claim.
sections.Material Facts:
On August 9, 1995, McCarthy signed a standard Greater Boston Real Estate Board offer-to-purchase form, and Tobin accepted it on August 11. The form described the property, price, deposits, limited title requirements, and closing time and place. It required execution of the standard purchase-and-sale agreement by 5 p.m. on August 16 and said that document, once executed, would be the parties' agreement. A typed provision made the offer subject to a purchase-and-sale agreement satisfactory to both. The form made time essential and prominently warned that it created binding obligations.

Tobin's lawyer undertook to prepare the formal agreement but faxed the first draft only after 5 p.m. on August 16. McCarthy's lawyer proposed revisions on August 21; the lawyers discussed them the next day without mentioning an extension or objecting to the elapsed date. A revised draft arrived August 23. On Friday, August 25, McCarthy's lawyer said the agreement was acceptable and would be signed and delivered Monday. McCarthy signed on Saturday, August 26; Tobin accepted the DiMinicos' competing offer that day. McCarthy delivered the executed agreement and deposit to Tobin's broker on Monday, August 28. The next day her lawyer rejected it as late. Tobin and the DiMinicos later executed their agreement and closed.
sections.Issue: Whether the accepted offer-to-purchase form was a binding contract to sell or only an agreement to negotiate; whether Tobin waived the August 16 deadline for executing the purchase-and-sale agreement; and whether specific performance was available against the later purchasers.
sections.Holding: The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court in 1999, in an opinion by Justice Abrams, held that the accepted offer bound Tobin to sell and McCarthy to buy. The requirement of a purchase-and-sale agreement by August 16 was an unambiguous and enforceable condition subsequent, but Tobin, through her lawyer's conduct, waived it, so McCarthy's later tender was reasonable and timely. Specific performance was appropriate, and the DiMinicos, who had actual notice of McCarthy's claim, held legal title subject to an equitable obligation to convey to him on payment of the agreed price.
sections.Reasoning:
The controlling formation question was the parties' manifested intention. Contemplating a later formal writing can indicate incomplete negotiations, but need not do so when material terms have already been agreed; the final writing may memorialize an existing bargain. Here the property and price were fixed, and the requested changes were ministerial and nonessential. The printed warning reinforced that intention, and the operative language said McCarthy offered to buy and Tobin accepted. The interveners' reading, that the parties promised only to negotiate in good faith, did not account for that language. A note advised parties who intend no binding preliminary obligation to say so clearly.

Formation did not make the formal-document requirement meaningless. The court classified the August 16 deadline as a condition subsequent: without timely execution, the obligations already created would be extinguished. A time-essential deadline would ordinarily be enforced, but a condition can be waived. The lawyer's conduct, attributable to Tobin as principal, established waiver. He took on the drafting but supplied the first draft too late for timely execution, continued substantive communications and revisions without invoking the deadline, and his only express communication about execution implied a later date would suffice. Once the condition was waived, time was no longer essential. Whether the lawyer contemplated August 25 or August 28 was immaterial. Waiver is ordinarily factual, but the undisputed facts made it a legal question here.

Specific performance is discretionary but commonly granted for land because money may not adequately replace that unique interest. The DiMinicos took with actual notice and assumed the risk of an adverse outcome.

In the casebook's prevention-and-waiver discussion, the seller's late drafting matters through the holding of waiver, not a ruling that every formal-document condition is automatically excused.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-088.rule: A promise to fabricate goods by a deadline with materials the customer will furnish ordinarily implies duties on the customer to supply those materials in time and to accept the finished goods without undue delay.

sections.Parties: Kehm Corp., a contractor that had agreed to manufacture concrete practice bombs for the Navy, sued the United States in the Court of Claims for additional expenses it attributed to Government delays. The contract price had already been paid; Kehm claimed $21,737.94. The Government denied liability for delay damages.
sections.Procedural History: Kehm filed its additional-expense claim on April 8, 1944, for a period ending April 7. The contracting officer sustained its contentions on July 10. The Comptroller General disallowed the claim in January 1945 and reaffirmed that decision in September because unliquidated damages required judicial determination. In the Court of Claims, Rule 39(b) limited this phase to whether the Government was liable for any part of the claimed expenses. The court held the Government liable for breach and left the amount of recovery to further proceedings. The brief covers only this published liability ruling, not any later damages determination.
sections.Material Facts:
On October 8, 1943, Kehm agreed to manufacture 2,800 concrete practice bombs for the Navy, 2,500 weighing 100 pounds and 300 weighing 1,000 pounds, due within 45 days, by November 22. The Government was to supply tail assemblies; the writing did not specify the tail type or supply dates. Practice tails had to be cast into the concrete, while service tails could be attached afterward. Before execution the Navy told Kehm it wanted and would supply service tails.

On October 16 the Navy delivered 500 practice tails; a week was lost clarifying whether that was a mistake. The Navy again promised service tails but directed use of the practice tails. Kehm made 500 smaller bombs by the deadline. More tails came on November 19, and the 300 larger bombs were ready by the end of December. No further tails arrived until February 23, 1944, when 2,050 smaller-bomb service tails were delivered; they had not been ordered until November 12. Kehm completed the bombs within 45 days after receiving the relevant tails.

The Navy also delayed acceptance. By the end of January only 739 smaller and 96 larger bombs had been delivered, and the Navy refused further deliveries until a March 21 amendment redirected the balance to Miami; shipments ended April 12. The Navy had lost interest in the program and had difficulty finding storage.
sections.Issue: Whether the Government breached the contract, and so was liable for some part of Kehm's additional expenses, by delaying the supply of tail assemblies and the acceptance of completed bombs, notwithstanding contract provisions extending performance time for Government delay and permitting changes.
sections.Holding: The United States Court of Claims in 1950, in an opinion by Judge Howell in which all five judges agreed, held that the Government's delays breached the contract, prevented timely performance, and caused some damage. Kehm was entitled to recover the loss actually attributable to those delays but still bore the burden of proving its nature and amount. Contractor-caused loss and mitigation were left for further proceedings, and no dollar recovery was fixed.
sections.Reasoning:
A promise to fabricate goods by a deadline using materials the customer will furnish ordinarily implies complementary duties to provide the materials early enough and to accept completed goods without undue delay. Cooperation can require affirmative action needed to make performance possible, not merely refraining from active obstruction, and the implied duty binds as effectively as an express term.

The Government relied on United States v. Howard P. Foley Co., involving delayed availability of an airport site. The court explained that whether an implied duty of timely cooperation exists depends on the contract's circumstances. Foley involved governmental diligence and a setting in which both parties knew dredging, settling and grading could cause delay. Kehm, by contrast, expected to begin immediately, was prepared to meet the 45-day schedule, and had no warning that the Navy would delay ordering tails or refuse completed deliveries. Most of the tails were not ordered until ten days before the completion date, and the Government offered no adequate explanation.

Kehm could have cast service-tail bombs before the tails arrived, but whether its reluctance was justified went to mitigation and the extent of loss, not to breach, and was reserved for the damages phase.

A provision extending performance time for Government delay did not necessarily make an extension the exclusive remedy. With particular surrounding facts, as in Foley, it could show that delay was anticipated and allocated without a damages promise, but absent those circumstances a Government drafter intending immunity from delay damages would ordinarily say so expressly. The right to make changes did not justify waiting until February to furnish materials required in October or November, or forcing Kehm to store finished bombs for weeks. Nor could the claim be finally settled administratively merely because the contracting officer had considered it.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-089.rule: Where a contract conditions a duty on approval by a party's own internal division, that party must consider approval in good faith but does not promise to approve, and may rely on the condition absent bad faith.

sections.Parties: Carl and Lorraine Sutton, the principal interested plaintiffs, and previous landowners Billy and Virginia Curtis sued the State of Indiana, the Indiana State Highway Commission and a contractor, Brown, over drainage work. The Highway Commission was replaced by the Indiana Department of Transportation (INDOT) in 1990.
