The Suttons sought to enforce a settlement; the State, the petitioner on transfer, resisted enforcement because required approvals had not been given.
sections.Procedural History: The Suttons sued in 1988. Four days before the scheduled January 1997 trial the lawyers reached a settlement and told the trial court the case was settled. When the State had neither paid nor furnished the easement after 45 days, the Suttons moved to enforce. After a September hearing the trial court found a binding settlement and ordered payment, an easement and attorney's fees. The Court of Appeals affirmed enforcement but reversed the fee award; the brief treats that decision only as procedural history. The Indiana Supreme Court granted the State's transfer petition, reversed the enforcement order as to the easement provisions, and summarily affirmed the Court of Appeals' reversal of the fee award.
sections.Material Facts:
In 1985 the Suttons granted the State an easement over commercial property for drainage work along State Road 10. In 1988 they sued, alleging the work destroyed their septic system, restricted access, and made the parking lot unusable, causing lost business.

Four days before trial, the State's private lawyer, Michael Blaize, discussed settlement with the Suttons' lawyer, Gary Matthews. Blaize expressly said that money required the Governor's approval and that a septic-system easement across State property required INDOT's approval. A deputy attorney general said there was no reason to believe the Governor would disapprove, and that reassurance was relayed to Matthews. The lawyers agreed on a monetary amount, an easement to install a new septic system, and payment within 45 days. Matthews wrote and faxed the agreement, which Blaize signed and returned. Paragraph seven expressly conditioned access through the existing guardrail and the associated driveway on INDOT's approval.

After 45 days the State had not paid or furnished the easement, and neither approval had occurred. The Governor approved the monetary settlement between trial and appeal, so the outstanding approval concerned the easement.
sections.Issue: Whether the settlement's easement provisions were enforceable against the State although INDOT had not given the approval on which they were expressly conditioned, and whether the passage of the 45-day period established waiver, estoppel, or prevention of that condition. The court also addressed the Governor's statutory authority over compromise of tort claims against the State.
sections.Holding: The Indiana Supreme Court in 1998, in an opinion by Justice Boehm in which all five justices agreed, held that the State could rely on the absence of INDOT's approval. The express condition was enforceable under ordinary contract principles; the mere expiration of 45 days showed neither waiver nor bad faith; and no extreme forfeiture was shown. The Tort Claims Act independently required the Governor's approval to compromise a tort claim against the State. The court did not decide the merits of the underlying drainage suit.
sections.Reasoning:
Factual findings received deference under Trial Rule 52, but whether they established an enforceable settlement was a legal conclusion. The trial court itself found approval was required, and nothing showed INDOT had approved or relinquished the condition.

An express condition generally must occur before the duty it qualifies becomes enforceable. Waiver requires voluntary, intentional relinquishment of a known right, and the expiration of 45 days alone did not show waiver or estoppel. Failure to obtain approval was not necessarily repudiation. A condition's harsh operation alone does not excuse it; extreme forfeiture might justify excusing a nonessential condition, but none was shown and approval was essential, since an easement affecting a highway safety rail raised obvious public-safety concerns.

The prevention doctrine does not estop a party from relying on every unfulfilled condition. Parties have an implied duty to make reasonable, good-faith efforts to satisfy conditions and may not sabotage the agreement. But where the condition reserves approval to an internal division, the duty is to consider approval in good faith, not to guarantee it. The passage of time alone did not establish bad faith, and there was no other evidence of it. The approval requirement protected the State; the 45-day limit protected the Suttons by letting them revive their lawsuit. The court added that preserving real approval conditions can facilitate settlements, because expected approval differs from assured approval.

On the Governor, the court read the Tort Claims Act as reserving ultimate settlement authority to that office, which ordinary attorney-client principles could not override.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-090.rule: A contract carries an implied undertaking that neither party will intentionally prevent the other from performing, and a party who causes the other's nonperformance cannot rely on it as a defense.

sections.Parties: Benjamin Patterson, the plaintiff and appellant, had agreed in writing to sell four parcels with houses to Anna Meyerhofer, the defendant and respondent. Patterson sought a declaration that Meyerhofer held the premises in trust subject to his contract, conveyance of a fifth house, a lien, and $620 in damages. Meyerhofer denied any oral agreement or relationship of trust and argued that Patterson's known inability to perform permitted her to rescind and buy directly.
sections.Procedural History: Special Term dismissed the complaint after trial, reasoning that an ordinary vendor-purchaser agreement created no relation of confidence, so Meyerhofer could bid as a stranger and keep the property without paying Patterson the difference. The Appellate Division affirmed; the brief treats that stage only as procedural history. The New York Court of Appeals reversed both judgments and granted a new trial, with costs to abide the event. It did not itself enter a final $620 money judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
Patterson agreed in writing to sell Meyerhofer four parcels with houses for $23,000, payable partly in cash and partly by taking title subject to mortgages. Meyerhofer knew when contracting that Patterson did not own the property and expected to acquire it at a foreclosure sale. Before the sale she announced that she would not perform the contract and would buy for herself without recognizing it as binding. Patterson attended the sale able, ready and willing to purchase, and bid, but she outbid him whenever he bid. On the majority's account she acquired the four parcels for $5,595 apiece, $22,380 altogether, which was $155 below the agreed resale price for each parcel and $620 below the total contract price. She also acquired a fifth house.

Patterson alleged an earlier oral arrangement under which he would acquire all five houses, convey four to Meyerhofer, and keep the fifth. The majority emphasized that there was no finding establishing that arrangement.
sections.Issue: Whether a buyer who knows her seller must acquire the property at a particular foreclosure sale breaches the contract by deliberately outbidding him there, so that the seller may recover the profit the contract would have given him, even though his claim that she held the property in trust fails.
sections.Holding: The New York Court of Appeals in 1912, in an opinion by Judge Willard Bartlett for a four-to-three majority, held that Patterson's $620 contract-damages claim could succeed on the existing record despite the failure of his trust theory. Meyerhofer's agreement to buy from Patterson implied that she would not prevent his acquisition by deliberately bidding against him and taking the houses herself. The fifth house was left outside the remedy, and the majority allowed that she might present a better defense at the new trial.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority agreed that no trust arose. There was no proved, enforceable oral agreement about the fifth house, and Meyerhofer had not entered possession under Patterson's title before acquiring the houses; she acquired them in declared defiance of his rights. The cases treating a vendee's purchase of a superior title as held for the vendor involved purchasers already in possession and did not fit.

Failure of the equitable theory did not eliminate the pleaded contract claim. Patterson expressly sought $620, and a plaintiff should not be dismissed simply because the complaint also asked for excessive equitable relief. The contract carried an implied undertaking against intentional prevention of the other party's performance; a party responsible for causing nonperformance cannot use that failure as a defense. Meyerhofer knew Patterson had to acquire the houses at the identified foreclosure sale before he could convey them, and the absence of an express prohibition on bidding did not remove the undertaking. The majority presumed that without her interference Patterson could have bought the four houses for the price she paid and then received $620 more under the contract. Requiring her to pay that difference gave him what the contract promised and charged her no more than she had agreed to pay.

Judge Chase, dissenting with two other judges, gave a fuller chronology and thought Patterson could have secured the property with a slightly higher bid, so that his nonperformance was unnecessary acquiescence. His decisive objection was procedural: Patterson had chosen and maintained an equitable action asserting a trust, with damages only incidental, and had not sought to proceed at law, so the dismissal should be affirmed.

The casebook cites the case for the implied undertaking against deliberate prevention and asks for comparison with Iron Trade Products.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-091.rule: In a mercantile contract for goods to be shipped in stated monthly quantities, the time and amount of shipment are a condition precedent, and a materially deficient early shipment entitles the buyer to rescind the whole contract if the right is asserted distinctly and seasonably.

sections.Parties: Arthur Norrington, the seller of iron rails, sued the buyers, Wright and others, Pennsylvania citizens trading as Peter Wright & Sons, for refusing iron shipments. Norrington was the plaintiff below and brought the writ of error. The buyers defended on the ground that they had rescinded the contract because the early shipments did not comply with it.
sections.Procedural History: Norrington sued in the federal Circuit Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania. The trial court instructed the jury to find for the buyers if, when they accepted and paid for the first cargo, they lacked notice that the seller had failed to ship approximately 1,000 tons in February and, on learning of the deficiency, immediately notified him of their intention to rescind. The jury returned a verdict for the buyers. Norrington excepted to the instruction and brought a writ of error. The Court affirmed the judgment for the buyers.
sections.Material Facts:
By a contract of January 19, 1880, Norrington sold 5,000 tons of old T iron rails, to be shipped from European ports for Philadelphia at approximately 1,000 tons a month beginning in February, the whole to be shipped before August 1. The price was $45 per ton of 2,240 pounds, payable in cash on presentation of bills and weight certificates. The seller did not have to replace a parcel lost after shipment.

Actual shipments were 400 tons in February, 885 in March, 1,571 in April, 850 in May, 1,000 in June and 300 in July. The buyers received and paid for the February cargo when it arrived in March without knowing it was the entire February shipment. They first learned the amounts shipped in the first three months around May 14, when the March cargoes arrived, and then notified the broker, Edward Etting, that they declined the March and April shipments. On May 17 they said that if the early deficiencies released them from the contract they would take that advantage. On May 19 they declared that they would reject future shipments if legally entitled to do so and would accept them if not. They refused Etting's June offer of exactly 1,000 April tons. The market price had been below the contract price and kept falling.
sections.Issue: Whether a seller's shipment of materially less than the agreed monthly quantity in the first months entitled the buyers to rescind the whole contract; whether the buyers' legally conditional statements were an effective assertion of that right; and whether accepting and paying for the first cargo waived it.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 1885, in an opinion by Justice Gray (the Chief Justice took no part), held that shipping only 400 tons in February and 885 in March failed the promised early installments and gave the buyers the right to rescind the whole purchase if they asserted it distinctly and seasonably. The buyers did assert it, and their acceptance of the February cargo, made without notice or means of knowing the full February deficiency, did not waive it. The Court awarded the buyers no damages.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court treated shipment time as a material description of the promised goods in a mercantile contract, serving practical needs such as estimating arrival, arranging funds and meeting downstream contracts. It used warranty in the sense of a condition precedent: failure of the material description could justify repudiating the whole contract.

The agreement was one contract for 5,000 tons despite the monthly shipping and payment terms; the permission not to replace lost cargoes did not divide it. The schedule required approximately 1,000 tons in each month from February through June, with only slight deficiencies made up in July. Because no independently identified lot qualified the quantity, the approximation allowed only accidental, minor variations. The seller could neither force acceptance of a deficient quantity nor compel the buyers to select the stipulated amount from an excessive one.

The buyers' position, that they would reject if the law entitled them to and otherwise accept, preserved and exercised the right and did not surrender it merely because its validity was disputed. Their failure to return the February cargo caused the seller no injury, since its paid price exceeded market value.

Answering the seller's reliance on English installment cases, the Court favored authorities permitting rejection after a deficient first installment and refused to relax strict construction because a falling market made rejection advantageous. Mersey Steel, concerning a buyer's failure to pay for an installment, did not control a seller's failure to deliver one. The Court found it unnecessary to dwell on the April objection.

The casebook reproduces the buyers' conditional answer in a problem asking whether they repudiated; the Court held their assertion of the right to rescind clear and effective.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-092.rule: Under the California rule applied, anticipatory breach does not apply to a contract that is unilateral at inception or has become unilateral through one party's complete performance; the performing party must wait until the other's performance is due.

sections.Parties: Roger Diamond, an attorney representing himself and other first-time purchasers of economy season football tickets, brought a class action against the University of Southern California. He was the plaintiff and appellant and sought class damages and an attorney's fee. USC, the defendant and respondent, had obtained summary judgment.
sections.Procedural History: Diamond sued on December 9, 1968. USC moved for summary judgment on January 23, supported by the declaration of its ticket-committee chairman, Elton Phillips; Diamond filed a counterdeclaration. The trial court granted summary judgment on February 10, and judgment was entered March 4. Diamond appealed, asking for reversal so that class damages and a reasonable fee could be determined. The California Court of Appeal, Second District, Division Five, affirmed.
sections.Material Facts:
The complaint alleged that before the 1968 football season USC sold economy season tickets with a promise that each purchaser could obtain an option to buy a Rose Bowl ticket if USC's team was selected. Diamond and the proposed class had paid for such season tickets for the first time. After USC was selected for the January 1, 1969 game, Diamond received a December 4 notice that reasons beyond USC's control prevented first-time economy holders from receiving the promised applications. He sued on December 9, alleging a $12 difference between a Rose Bowl ticket's market value and the university's price, and $36,000 in aggregate damages for 3,000 tickets bought by about 600 persons.

According to Phillips's declaration, USC had ranked first-time economy purchasers last. Between December 8 and 16, enough other holders failed to exercise their options that applications could be sent to the previously excluded group, and USC mailed them on December 17. Diamond's counterdeclaration said USC's attorney did not tell him of the newly available tickets on December 16 and told him on December 19 that applications had already been mailed.
sections.Issue: Whether USC's December 4 notice refusing Rose Bowl ticket applications was an immediately actionable anticipatory breach, given that the ticket purchasers had already fully performed by paying for their season tickets.
sections.Holding: The California Court of Appeal in 1970, in an opinion by Presiding Justice Kaus in which Justices Stephens and Reppy concurred, held that the suit was premature. Anticipatory breach did not apply to a contract made unilateral by the purchasers' complete performance, so the later offer to sell Diamond a ticket defeated the cause of action just as it would have had he sued individually. Bringing a class action did not change that rule. The court declined to decide the broader class-action questions.
sections.Reasoning:
Diamond argued that the December 4 refusal was an anticipatory repudiation, that filing suit changed the class's position and ended USC's power to retract, and that supplying applications afterward improperly settled matured claims directly with class members. The court accepted only for the sake of argument that filing an action could end the power to retract; it did not hold that it had that effect.

The antecedent question was whether the December notice could be an actionable anticipatory breach at all. Under the California rule the court applied, the doctrine did not reach contracts unilateral at inception or made unilateral by one party's complete performance. The explanation was that a plaintiff with no remaining duty need not be released from future obligations and can wait until the defendant's performance is due. The purchasers had done everything required by paying; only USC's promise to provide applications remained.

The court did not hold that the short ticket supply excused the promise through impossibility, and it did not rest the judgment on a finding that the lawsuit played no causal role in the tickets becoming available. It left open questions about fees outside a common fund and direct dealings with class members.

The opinion acknowledged criticism of the unilateral-contract exception, including Corbin's objection that it permits suit by a party who has not performed while denying it to one who has, and it contemplated that a future class case with sufficient public-policy considerations might question the exception.

The casebook uses the case, as the Rose Bowl Affair, for the unilateral-contract exception and returns to it to ask about the assumed effect of filing suit in light of Seacoast.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-093.rule: As this 1839 decision held, a buyer's advance notice that he will refuse goods is not itself a breach unless the seller acts on it and rescinds, so damages are measured at the time delivery was due.

sections.Parties: The plaintiffs were Gloucester corn merchants who had contracted to sell wheat. The defendant was Evans, a Birmingham miller, the buyer. The sellers sued in assumpsit for his refusal to accept the wheat. Evans did not contest liability for the ultimate refusal but sought to have damages measured at the earlier date of his notice.
sections.Procedural History: The case was tried at the Gloucester Assizes before Alderson, where the dispute was the date for valuing damages. Alderson directed the jury to use the market at the last time the contract could have been performed, the tender for acceptance, and the jury returned £248 9s. The defendant reserved leave to move to reduce the award to £93 12s., the figure on the earlier-date calculation. That motion was the proceeding before the Exchequer; it was not a new trial or an appeal. The court refused the rule, leaving the verdict unreduced.
sections.Material Facts: In early January 1839 the sellers contracted to sell wheat to Evans, to be delivered at Birmingham as soon as vessels could be obtained to carry it. After the market began to fall, Evans notified the sellers on January 26 that he would not accept the wheat if delivered. It was already travelling by canal to Birmingham. When it arrived, the sellers tendered it and Evans again refused to accept. The report does not give the quantity, the contract price or the arrival date.
sections.Issue: Whether damages for a buyer's refusal to accept goods are measured by the market price on the date he gave advance notice that he would refuse, or by the market price at the time the goods were to be delivered and accepted.
sections.Holding: The Exchequer in 1839, with the four reported judges (Lord Abinger, Chief Baron, Parke, Alderson and Gurney) agreeing, refused to reduce the damages. The relevant time was when the buyer ought to have received the wheat. His notice did not modify the contract, and the sellers were not bound to resell on receiving it in order to reduce damages.
sections.Reasoning:
Counsel for Evans argued that the January notice conclusively refused performance, discharged the sellers' duty to deliver, and entitled them to sue at once, so that they could have sold the wheat by sample in transit and should not benefit from a further fall in the market. Alderson asked how that could be distinguished from Leigh v. Paterson, which emphasized that a mutually made contract remains open unless the plaintiff assents to ending it.

Lord Abinger found no ground to reduce the damages, considered Leigh directly applicable, and adopted its reasoning. Parke gave the fuller explanation. If the sellers could have sued immediately after the notice, the notice-date measure might follow, but no such action lay before the delivery time. Evans's undertaking was to be ready and willing to receive and pay for the goods when the contract required; an earlier declaration that he would refuse did not itself break that undertaking, because he could still accept when the wheat was due. The sellers therefore had to wait and see. Parke qualified the point: the notice was ineffective before the receipt date unless the seller acted on it in the meantime and rescinded the contract, which these sellers had not done. Alderson said again that Leigh governed, and Gurney concurred.

The brief notes that this reasoning preceded the anticipatory-breach doctrine associated with Hochster and should not be restated as a modern, universal bar on suing for anticipatory repudiation. The casebook uses the case to illustrate waiting for performance despite a refusal and compares later authorities, including Roehm v. Horst.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-094.rule: A repudiating party's power to retract ends once the other party takes definite action treating the anticipatory breach as final, such as filing suit or firmly declaring that the breach will be accepted unless withdrawn within a stated period.

sections.Parties: The United States, which had contracted with Seacoast Gas Co. for gas for a federal housing project, sued Seacoast for the loss caused by having to make a higher-priced replacement arrangement after Seacoast announced it would cancel. The government was the plaintiff and appellant. Seacoast, the defendant and appellee, contended that it had withdrawn its repudiation in time.
sections.Procedural History: After a bench trial the district court entered judgment for Seacoast, holding that its retraction cured the anticipatory breach because the November 13 assurance came before the substitute gas contract was signed. The government appealed. The Fifth Circuit reversed and remanded with directions to enter judgment for the government for the loss the breach caused; it did not fix a dollar amount. Rehearing was denied without a separate opinion.
sections.Material Facts:
Seacoast undertook to supply gas to a federal housing project from April 15, 1947, to June 15, 1948. The government's claim described an October 7 letter declaring that Seacoast would cancel as of November 15 because of an asserted government breach; the report elsewhere refers to an October 24 letter, an inconsistency the brief preserves. The government immediately disputed any right to stop performance and said it would solicit other bids if the refusal persisted.

By November 6 bids had been received, with Trion the low bidder. Zell, president of both Seacoast and Trion, attended the bid opening and refused a request to withdraw Seacoast's notice. Regional counsel sent Seacoast a registered letter addressed to Zell saying that unless the government received a written withdrawal and assurance of continued performance within three days, it would accept Trion's bid and hold Seacoast and its performance bond responsible. Seacoast did not respond within that period. Zell again refused to retract on November 10, and the government accepted Trion's bid. On November 13 Zell told regional counsel that Seacoast admitted it had no right to cancel and rescinded its notice. The new contract was signed on November 17; the uncontradicted evidence attributed the delay to Trion's failure to furnish its bond sooner.
sections.Issue: Whether Seacoast's retraction of its anticipatory repudiation was timely because it came before the government signed the substitute contract, or too late because the government had already declared it would treat the breach as final and had accepted another bid.
sections.Holding: The Fifth Circuit in 1953, in an opinion by Chief Judge Hutcheson for a panel that also included Judges Borah and Russell, held that the retraction came too late. Definite action treating the anticipatory breach as final closes the opportunity to retract. The opportunity ended with the three-day period in the government's notice, not with the later signing of the replacement contract, and acceptance of Trion's bid had occurred on November 10.
sections.Reasoning:
The parties agreed that an anticipatory breach had occurred, that without timely withdrawal Seacoast was liable for the government's loss, and that a repudiator's power to retract ends once the other party acts or relies on the repudiation. They disagreed about which action counted. Seacoast treated November 17 as the acceptance date; the court held that this confused acceptance of Trion's bid with signing the resulting contract.

Definite action treating the breach as final can consist of filing suit or of a firm declaration that the breach will be accepted if not withdrawn within a stated period. The government obtained bids, gave the three-day declaration, and then awarded the contract to the lowest bidder after Seacoast again refused to withdraw. Formal signing was not the event that first made the repudiation final.

Seacoast's claim that it never received the registered notice was immaterial on this record, for two reasons: the government need not have given any notice or grace period, and Zell personally repeated his refusal to regional counsel on November 10.

The corporate connection reinforced the equity of the result without substituting for the contract analysis. Zell was president and practically sole owner of both companies and had organized Trion specifically to take part in this bidding; he refused to withdraw at the bid opening and award and tried to withdraw only a day or two before the new contract was signed. A delayed bond could not extend the old supplier's power to undo the government's declaration and award.

The casebook uses the replacement-contract chronology to show the distinction between acceptance of a bid and later signature; its account calls the supply natural gas, while the notice in the report concerns liquefied petroleum gas.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-095.rule: A party who responds to the other's apparent renunciation by electing to keep the contract alive remains bound to perform its own side, and proved expenses of preparing to perform are recoverable when lost profits are too speculative.

sections.Parties: Bernstein, who had agreed to supply the Jarbeau Comedy Company for theater performances, sued Meech and the other defendants, who had agreed to furnish the theater, for breach of contract after they refused the company the theater. Bernstein was the plaintiff and respondent on appeal; the defendants were the appellants, arguing that his demand for a larger share had released them and that his expenses were not recoverable.
sections.Procedural History: Bernstein sued for breach and obtained a jury verdict. The trial court submitted to the jury whether the defendants had been relieved of their contractual obligation and refused to direct a verdict for them. The General Term of the Supreme Court in the Fifth Judicial Department affirmed by an order dated October 1, 1889. The defendants appealed to the New York Court of Appeals, which affirmed the judgment for Bernstein without ordering a new trial or a newly quantified award.
sections.Material Facts:
On August 4, 1887, Bernstein agreed to supply the Jarbeau Comedy Company for four performances at Buffalo's Academy of Music on December 22 to 24; the defendants agreed to furnish the theater, and Bernstein would receive half the gross receipts. Eight days later Bernstein sent a proposed replacement contract demanding sixty percent and wrote that he could not think of playing for less. On August 13 the defendants returned that paper unsigned, explaining that they already had his signed contract and needed no other agreement for the appearances.

On November 17 Bernstein's agent sent advertising clippings and asked the defendants to publicize the engagement. Their November 28 reply expressed surprise, saying they had understood the August letter to mean the company would not come and that they could no longer arrange the dates. That letter reached the agent only on December 17 or 18, when he arrived in Buffalo to prepare advertising. Bernstein and his company reached Buffalo in time and were ready to perform. The defendants had engaged the James Brown Potter Company for the same dates and refused them the theater.
sections.Issue: Whether Bernstein's letter demanding sixty percent released the defendants from the contract as a matter of law, and whether, with profits from the performances too speculative to prove, Bernstein could recover the expenses he incurred in preparing to perform or only nominal damages.
sections.Holding: The New York Court of Appeals in 1891, in an opinion by Bradley in which all concurred except Potter, who did not vote, held that the defendants were not released. Even if they could initially have treated Bernstein's letter as ending the agreement, their August 13 answer elected to preserve it, and that election bound both sides. Bernstein could recover the expenses legitimately and essentially incurred for the contemplated performance, although the expected profits could not be proved.
sections.Reasoning:
The court recognized the general principle that renunciation of an executory contract may allow the other party to act on a breach before performance is due. But it rejected the claim that Bernstein's letter necessarily ended the contract as a matter of law. Whether the correspondence and the parties' understanding justified treating it as a renunciation was properly left to the jury; the defendants had themselves asked for submission of that issue, and the instructions given covered it.

More decisively, by rejecting the replacement paper because an existing signed contract already governed, the defendants retained their contractual rights instead of accepting a termination. That election operated on both parties: Bernstein remained liable if he failed to perform, and the defendants remained obliged to furnish the theater. They could not keep a right to insist on his performance while treating their own duty as discharged. The brief notes that the holding depends on that affirmative response and does not declare that every refusal of changed terms prevents reliance on a repudiation.

On damages, the ordinary recovery would be the profits from Bernstein's half of receipts after expenses, but the receipts from the four performances were speculative and not provable. The defendants argued that only nominal damages remained. The court disagreed because that ignored a separately proved loss: the jury could find the expenditures were legitimately incurred for performance, were within the parties' contemplation, and became a loss through the refusal of the theater. The court would not assume Bernstein would have lost those amounts even had the defendants performed.

The casebook presents the case as a problem, Jarbeau's Case, about the demand for a larger percentage and the performance expenses.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-096.rule: Under Florida's UCC section 672.609, failure to give adequate assurance within a reasonable time after a justified written demand is a repudiation, and whether assurances were adequate is ordinarily a question of fact.

sections.Parties: Validsa, Inc., a Florida international food trader, sued Bariven, a subsidiary of the Venezuelan national oil company PDVSA, and PDVSA Services, Inc. (PSI), Bariven's subsidiary and purchasing agent, for payment for delivered food and damages for anticipatory repudiation of two contracts. Bariven counterclaimed for breach, unjust enrichment, implied good faith and commercial reasonableness, and an accounting. PSI and Bariven appealed; Validsa cross-appealed on damages, offset and prejudgment interest.
sections.Procedural History: Validsa sued on June 12, 2008. The district court adopted Validsa's proposed summary-judgment order, found liability on all five claims, dismissed all counterclaims, and held PSI individually liable despite its disclosed agency. A later bench trial on damages produced awards for unpaid deliveries, incidental losses and lost profits of about $40.76 million before offset of the approximately $44.58 million in advances; the court excluded certain expert testimony and the seller's consequential losses and denied prejudgment interest. Both sides appealed. The Eleventh Circuit, in an unpublished per curiam decision, affirmed in part, reversed in part and remanded: it vacated the anticipatory-repudiation summary judgment against Bariven for trial, reinstated four counterclaims, and directed judgment for PSI.
sections.Material Facts:
Bariven bought food from Validsa, using PSI as purchasing agent; purchase orders identified Bariven as purchaser, care of PSI. Two March 2008 purchases were contract 632, for 100,000 metric tons of sugar at about $44.7 million, and contract 757, for 24,000 metric tons of beef at about $103.9 million. Bariven paid thirty-percent advances totaling about $44.58 million. Deliveries were to be in installments, with seventy percent paid after each delivery and thirty percent drawn from the advance.

Validsa asserted that a businessman demanded a $2 million kickback in March; the defendants disputed this, and the court made no finding. On April 15 Validsa inadvertently received an internal email string instructing cancellation of contract 757 and suspension of payments. On April 17 it demanded a written explanation. At an April 29 meeting PSI's president proposed applying the advances to the first $44 million of deliveries and using letters of credit afterward; no agreement was reached. Validsa's counsel demanded adequate assurances on May 9. A May 16 response said the internal messages were not intended for Validsa and should not have been considered. On June 3 PSI sent a draft agreement, labeled as without legal or commercial value, with a new delivery schedule and a proposed substitution of PSI as the party responsible for payment. Validsa did not respond and sued on June 12, still holding nearly all the advances.
sections.Issue: Whether Validsa was entitled to summary judgment that Bariven repudiated the March contracts by failing to give adequate assurance of performance under Florida's UCC section 672.609; whether PSI, as agent of a disclosed principal, was personally liable; and whether the district court's rulings on the counterclaims, expert testimony, consequential damages, offset and prejudgment interest were correct.
sections.Holding: The Eleventh Circuit in 2011, in an unpublished per curiam decision by Judges Barkett and Hull and District Judge Schlesinger, held that Validsa had reasonable grounds for insecurity and made a written demand, but that a reasonable factfinder could conclude adequate assurances were given, so summary judgment on the anticipatory-repudiation claims was improper. It did not decide that Bariven's assurances were sufficient. PSI, as agent of a disclosed principal, had not expressly assumed Bariven's liabilities and was not personally liable. The exclusion of expert testimony and consequential damages, the offset, and the denial of prejudgment interest were affirmed.
sections.Reasoning:
Section 672.609 permits a written demand when reasonable grounds for insecurity arise; between merchants, commercial standards govern the grounds and the adequacy of the response; and failure to give adequate assurance within a reasonable time, capped at thirty days, is repudiation. Insecurity and adequacy are ordinarily factual but can be decided as law when only one conclusion is rational. The April 17 demand began the inquiry.

A factfinder could find adequate assurance from the April meeting, the May 16 explanation, the June draft, and Validsa's continued possession of unrecalled advances. The June proposal could be read as an attempt to escape Bariven's obligations, or as adding security by substituting a United States corporation and accommodating delays. The court also rejected the district court's April 29 repudiation date, because the statutory window after April 17 had not closed. Validsa's own earlier delivery delays did not bar its demand. If Bariven gave adequate assurances, Validsa's termination was itself a breach; if not, Bariven anticipatorily breached.

Because the breach finding no longer stood, the court reinstated Bariven's counterclaims for breach and for good faith and commercial reasonableness. It affirmed dismissal of unjust enrichment because express contracts governed, and of the accounting claim because no fiduciary relationship or complex transaction was shown.

Under Florida law an agent of a disclosed principal is not personally liable for its contract debts absent an express contrary agreement; offering a future substitution was not an express assumption of existing obligations.

The economist's excluded opinions rested on hypothetical future dealings. Losses on beef beyond the pleaded 24,000 tons were consequential, and Florida intermediate authority limits an aggrieved seller to lost profits and incidental damages. Prejudgment interest would have been an inequitable windfall because Validsa held advances exceeding the award.

The casebook's problem compresses PSI and Bariven into PSI and asks about repudiation, assurances and modified payment terms.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-097.rule: A party to a contract outside the UCC may suspend performance when the other side ignores its reasonable requests for assurance, applying the principle of UCC section 2-609 as generalized in Restatement (Second) of Contracts section 251.

sections.Parties: C.L. Maddox, Inc., a contractor on a coal-mine project, sued its subcontractor, Coalfield Services, Inc., for the added cost of completing the job after Coalfield stopped work. Coalfield counterclaimed for $103,500 for work done. Maddox was the plaintiff and appellant; Coalfield was the defendant, counterclaimant and appellee.
sections.Procedural History: In this diversity action governed by Illinois contract law, both parties moved for summary judgment; Coalfield at first maintained that no contract existed. The district judge found a contract and held Coalfield liable for abandoning it, then reconsidered who had breached. With the parties' consent a magistrate judge tried that issue without a jury, found Maddox responsible, and awarded Coalfield $103,500, considering himself bound by the district judge's supposed finding of forty-five-percent completion. Maddox appealed. The Seventh Circuit affirmed that Maddox alone breached, reversed the damages determination, and remanded for Coalfield's damages to be redetermined.
sections.Material Facts:
Maddox's January 18, 1991 contract with Zeigler/Old Ben Coal required demolishing an underground loading facility, removing its steel, and fabricating and installing a replacement. At a February site meeting Coalfield's president offered to do the non-fabrication work for $230,000 in three weeks if his crew could work around the clock; he did not inspect the facility underground. On March 19 Coalfield sent a written proposal with that price, the conditional schedule, and biweekly progress payments. Maddox asked for a noncompetition clause, which Coalfield added, and said it would sign but never did. Work began March 20.

Progress was slower than expected, and Coalfield's repeated requests that Maddox sign went unanswered. Early on April 8 Coalfield brought its crew and equipment to the surface, then faxed a demand for acceptance of the proposal and payment of a $103,500 invoice for an asserted forty-five-percent completion. Maddox apologized, questioned the percentage, and offered to accept it with ten-percent retention, apparently on condition that Coalfield sign a letter extending the schedule to four weeks but adding $1,000 a day in liquidated damages. Coalfield, expecting five or six more weeks of work, rejected the letter and said work would restart April 16. Maddox required resumption by April 9. Coalfield never resumed, and Maddox hired someone else.
sections.Issue: Whether Coalfield's stoppage of work was a breach or was excused by Maddox's silence in the face of repeated requests to confirm the agreed terms, and whether the $103,500 award could rest on an untried assumption that the work was forty-five percent complete.
sections.Holding: The Seventh Circuit in 1995, in an opinion by Chief Judge Posner for a panel that included Judge Ripple and District Judge Norgle, held that a contract existed despite the missing signature and that Coalfield was entitled to suspend performance because Maddox had ignored its reasonable requests for confirmation for about three weeks. Maddox alone was the contract breaker. The $103,500 award could not stand because the extent of Coalfield's performance had never actually been determined.
sections.Reasoning:
The unsigned paper did not defeat the contract. The presidents had agreed on job, price and schedule; Coalfield had performed a substantial portion, which took the oral agreement outside the statute of frauds; and Maddox's promise to sign implied assent to the stated terms.

The court rejected the magistrate's reasons. Unpaid progress payments could not justify the stoppage, because Coalfield sent its first invoice only after stopping. The liquidated-damages demand also came after the stoppage. And the interruption was not a pause of a few hours, since Coalfield proposed no return for eight days on a time-sensitive project; without an excuse it could be a breach.

The excuse was Maddox's silence. For about three weeks it neither signed, proposed different terms, nor answered requests about a proposal that contained nothing unusual or one-sided. Coalfield could interrupt performance instead of accumulating costs with no assurance of payment. The later liquidated-damages proposal corroborated the reasonableness of its suspicion but did not retroactively create the justification. Because this was a service contract outside the UCC, the court drew on section 2-609 and Restatement section 251, acknowledging that the Restatement is not law and that no Illinois decision discussed the section, and predicting Illinois courts would accept the principle. The requirement of a clear, unequivocal statement of intent to breach addresses repudiation by statement, not silence in response to the equivalent of a request for assurances.

Maddox's suggestion that Coalfield used the unsigned proposal as a pretext to abandon an underestimated job was not developed enough to justify reversal. The forty-five-percent figure was an assumption drawn from Coalfield's concession, not a litigated finding binding Maddox.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-098.rule: A forward contract for a crop may be specifically enforced where a shortage makes the goods unique and irreplaceable, and a ginning cutoff date in such a contract carries an implied duty to harvest and gin in good faith.

sections.Parties: Mitchell-Huntley Cotton Co., Inc., the corporate assignee of a cotton-buying joint venture, sued Alabama farmers who had each separately contracted to sell their 1973 cotton crop. The buyer sought a declaration that the contracts were enforceable, specific performance, and an injunction against delaying harvest or selling the crop elsewhere. The farmers sought to invalidate the contracts or to avoid them by delaying ginning.
sections.Procedural History: The farmers had filed an Alabama state action to invalidate the contracts or establish that they could avoid them by delaying ginning until after December 15. The buyer filed this federal diversity action on September 25, 1973. The court granted a preliminary injunction after a separate hearing. Two original defendants were removed on the plaintiff's motion and two were subject to agreed final judgments; the defenses of the remaining eight farmers were tried. In findings and conclusions of February 25, 1974, the court adjudged each contract binding, granted specific performance, made the injunction permanent, and retained jurisdiction for supplementary relief and costs.
sections.Material Facts:
On February 15, 1973, several Alabama farmers separately made identically structured contracts with the Mitchell-Huntley Cotton joint venture. Each agreed to sell all cotton planted and produced that crop year on identified Colbert County acreage at a basic thirty cents per pound, and the buyer agreed to purchase the cotton ginned through December 15. Four farmers signed supplements covering cotton planted above the legal allotment at forty cents per pound. The joint venture transferred the contracts to the corporate plaintiff, which assumed the buyer's obligations.

By September 25, when the buyer sued, cotton was maturing and being picked and ginned, and the market price exceeded eighty cents per pound. The court found a drastic shortage: most of the national 1973 crop was already committed under comparable contracts, little merchantable cotton remained from earlier years, and very little would be available on the open market. The plaintiff had contracted to deliver this cotton to Riegel Fibre, which had undertaken to produce goods at prices based on its purchase price. The farmers could store and dispose of the crop beyond the buyer's reach.
sections.Issue: Whether the forward cotton contracts were valid and specifically enforceable against the farmers despite their defenses of misrepresentation, the December 15 ginning clause, lack of mutuality, improper assignment, the bar on specific enforcement of personal-service contracts, gambling statutes, and landlords' crop-share claims.
sections.Holding: The United States District Court for the Northern District of Alabama in 1974, Judge Guin, held each contract binding and enforceable and granted specific performance. The farmers were required to pick and gin promptly as the cotton matured in normal good farming practice and to deliver cotton ginned through December 15 on payment of the contract price. The December 15 provision was a limitation subject to an implicit duty of good-faith performance, and the scarce cotton was unique and irreplaceable.
sections.Reasoning:
On misrepresentation, the farmers claimed the ginner Nathaniel Reid misled them about the buyer's financial strength and identity and the December 15 clause. The court found that on the financial inquiry Reid acted independently of the buyer on the sellers' behalf, and that the farmers showed no detrimental reliance: the price had risen and the plaintiff was ready and able to pay. Sellers insecure about payment could have demanded assurances, but no demand was shown.

The farmers did not prove Reid said they could postpone ginning past the cutoff and be free, and such a statement would in any event concern legal interpretation. The buyer's commitment to purchase eligible cotton supplied consideration, defeating the mutuality objection. Finding the December 15 language ambiguous, the court considered extrinsic evidence and trade usage of harvesting and ginning promptly, and held the farmers could not manufacture an escape by withholding normal harvesting.

The assignment and personal-service objections failed because cotton farming did not depend on these sellers' unique personal talents; merely involving human work does not make a contract one for personal services. Alabama's bucket-shop statutes targeted wagering on prices, not genuine sales with intended delivery, and UCC section 2-501 recognizes contracts for the next crop. As to landlords, the tenant held title and possession of the whole crop subject to the landlord's lien, and the judgment left landlords' claims against tenants unaffected.

The casebook uses the case to question whether a price increase alone makes damages inadequate; the findings support the decree with scarcity, limited substitutes and dependent supply commitments.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-099.rule: A court of equity will not aid a plaintiff whose bad faith relates to the very transaction for which relief is sought, even if the defendant's conduct was also improper and the plaintiff's misconduct was not independently actionable.

sections.Parties: The New York Football Giants sued the Los Angeles Chargers Football Club and Charles Flowers, a University of Mississippi football player, seeking equitable enforcement of a contract Flowers had signed with the Giants, including an order preventing him from playing for the competing club. The Giants were the plaintiff and appellant; the Chargers and Flowers, who had signed a later contract with each other, were the defendants and appellees.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court ruled for both defendants on contractual grounds, holding that the agreement was not binding until approved by the Commissioner, that approval procured contrary to the promise to delay submission did not make it binding, and that Flowers therefore had a legal right to cancel until January 1. The Giants appealed. The Fifth Circuit affirmed dismissal of the amended complaint and the costs imposed on the Giants, but struck the paragraphs of the final judgment making legal determinations about the contracts' validity, and affirmed the judgment as modified.
sections.Material Facts:
Charles Flowers was an outstanding University of Mississippi player in fall 1959 whose team was to play Louisiana State University in the January 1, 1960 Sugar Bowl. Conference and NCAA eligibility rules excluded players who had entered professional arrangements. Giants official Mara urged Flowers to sign for two seasons beginning in 1960. Flowers made clear he did not want to destroy his Sugar Bowl eligibility; Mara admitted he understood this, proposed keeping the signing confidential, and knew disclosure would prevent Flowers from playing.

Flowers signed the standard NFL form on December 1 and received $3,500 in bonus checks. The form required the Commissioner's approval before becoming binding, and Mara agreed not to submit it until after January 1. After Flowers tried to withdraw by telephone around December 5, the Giants promptly filed the document. The Commissioner approved it on December 15 but, at Mara's request, withheld the announcement until after the bowl game. On December 29 Flowers negotiated a better offer from the Chargers, wrote to the Giants withdrawing, and returned the uncashed checks. He played in the Sugar Bowl and afterward formally executed the Chargers contract.
sections.Issue: Whether the Giants could obtain equitable enforcement of Flowers's contract when they had arranged to keep the signing secret so that he would appear eligible to play in the Sugar Bowl.
sections.Holding: The Fifth Circuit in 1961, in an opinion by Chief Judge Tuttle for a panel that also included Judge Rives and District Judge De Vane, held that the Giants' misconduct in bringing about and concealing the purported agreement barred equitable assistance under the clean-hands doctrine. The court expressly declined to resolve the contract-law questions, so it did not hold either professional contract valid or invalid, and it did not decide whether an action at law would succeed.
sections.Reasoning:
The opinion opened with Judge Wright's criticism, in a different football-contract case, of recruiting practices and competing professional agreements, and concluded that in an appropriate case a federal equity court must decline to aid a transaction offensive to honest dealing in its inception.

Drawing mainly on Precision Instrument, the court explained that clean hands bars equitable relief for bad faith related to the matter in which relief is sought, even if the defendant has also behaved improperly. The plaintiff need not have been blameless in unrelated matters, and the misconduct need not be criminal or independently actionable; a willful act concerning the cause of action that transgresses equitable standards can suffice. The discretion matters especially where public interests accompany private ones, because refusing relief can prevent public injury. Deweese likewise distinguished possible rights at law from entitlement to equity's aid.

The remedy the Giants sought was tied directly to their own deception. The court treated Mara's uncontradicted testimony as evidence of a deliberate plan to deceive the coach, the university, the opposing team and the football public. The Giants asserted a binding contract while agreeing to represent, in effect, that none existed. A straightforward signing and filing would not have created the legal difficulties they asked the court to untangle. Once that testimony made the plan apparent, the suit should have been dismissed on clean-hands grounds without adjudicating the contract issues. Flowers's own participation in the scheme did not entitle the Giants to enforcement against him.

The casebook cites the case in a short clean-hands note on the Giants' failure to obtain an injunction and contrasts Houston Oilers v. Neely; that comparison is the casebook's account of another decision.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-100.rule: A court may stay litigation over a merger agreement for a defined period to let the parties close, while fixing a deadline after which the case returns promptly to trial if closing fails.

sections.Parties: Twitter, Inc. was the plaintiff. Elon R. Musk, X Holdings I, Inc. and X Holdings II, Inc. were the defendants and counterclaim plaintiffs. The defendants moved to stay the action so the merger could close; Twitter opposed the stay.
sections.Procedural History: The action was pending in the Delaware Court of Chancery. After agreeing to close the merger, the defendants moved to stay the litigation, and Twitter opposed. On October 6, 2022, the court issued a two-page letter order staying the action until 5 p.m. on October 28, 2022. The brief covers only this October 6 stage and does not infer a later closing or final disposition.
sections.Material Facts: The defendants had agreed to close the transaction contemplated by the Agreement and Plan of Merger dated April 25, 2022. They moved to stay the action in light of that agreement, telling the court that closing was expected around October 28. Twitter opposed because the defendants' agreement did not ensure that the transaction would close quickly enough. These were the positions the court recorded, not findings that financing was complete or that closing was certain.
sections.Issue: Whether to suspend the litigation to permit the parties to close the merger despite Twitter's concern about delay.
sections.Holding: The Delaware Court of Chancery in 2022, in a letter order by Chancellor Kathaleen St. Jude McCormick, stayed the action until 5 p.m. on October 28, 2022. If the transaction had not closed by then, both sides were to email the Chancellor that evening to obtain November 2022 trial dates. The order did not adjudicate the underlying contract claims and contains no breach determination, damages award or specific-performance decree.
sections.Reasoning:
The letter gives a practical case-management resolution without setting out a general test for stays or finding that specific performance was warranted. Its express purpose was to give the parties time to close. The firm expiration time and the instruction to request renewed trial dates addressed the prospect that the promised closing might not occur, preserving a prompt route back to trial. The order set neither an automatic merits judgment on October 28 nor particular November trial dates.

The casebook, in its discussion following Snow Phipps, uses the order to show how a court can structure litigation around the anticipated performance of a merger agreement; the editors' remarks about the prospect of specific performance and the speed of resolution are their teaching context, not part of the order.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-101.rule: Specific performance of a contract to sell land requires clear and convincing proof of a valid contract, the claimant's readiness, willingness and ability to perform, and a balance of equities favoring enforcement, and the decree may add interest to compensate delayed payment.

sections.Parties: The owner of a Delaware beach house, Lucille Osborn, sued through her niece and attorney-in-fact, Sharon Gillespie, and after her death her estate was substituted as plaintiff. The defendant was Michael J. Kemp, the long-time occupant. The owner sought an injunction, a declaration defeating Kemp's ownership claim, and restitution. Kemp counterclaimed for specific performance of a handwritten agreement to purchase the property.
sections.Procedural History: Suit began in the Delaware Court of Chancery in August 2007. Kemp added his specific-performance counterclaim in August 2008. Trial took place on October 29, 2008, followed by affidavits on repairs, briefing and argument. Osborn died in December 2008 and her estate was substituted in January 2009. In a post-trial memorandum opinion the court granted Kemp's counterclaim for specific performance on stated terms, directed dismissal of the estate's complaint with prejudice, and called for a proposed final judgment. The brief covers this 2009 trial-court decision only.
sections.Material Facts:
Lucille Osborn owned a two-apartment beach house in Slaughter Beach, Delaware. In November 1984 Michael Kemp, an electrician, rented the upstairs apartment for $275 a month plus utilities. Under a handwritten one-sentence agreement dated April 16, 1985, Kemp undertook twenty years of $275 monthly payments plus utilities to purchase the property for $50,000. The document appeared to bear both signatures and a notary's signature and seal; only a photocopy survived.

Kemp and his cohabitant, Roxanne Danburg, made the monthly payments through July 2005, often calling them rent, and Osborn treated them as rent on her 2004 tax return. Kemp claimed about $11,000 in improvements. The twenty-year period ended in April 2005; Kemp stopped paying after July and testified that he sought a deed in August. In May 2006 Osborn became unable to manage her affairs after a fall and progressive dementia, and Gillespie took over. Kemp did not disclose the agreement when they met in August 2006. In January 2007, after a notice demanding overdue rent and utilities, he produced the photocopy and asserted purchase rights.
sections.Issue: Whether the photocopied handwritten agreement was authentic and an enforceable contract to sell the property; whether its price term required a further $50,000 beyond the twenty years of monthly payments; and whether Kemp was entitled to specific performance despite the estate's objections about fairness, his ability to pay, and laches.
sections.Holding: The Delaware Court of Chancery in 2009, Vice Chancellor Parsons, found the agreement authentic and enforceable, construed it to require an additional $50,000 after twenty years of monthly payments, and granted Kemp specific performance. Kemp had to pay the $50,000 with interest at the legal rate from April 16, 2005, compounded quarterly until settlement, and reimburse utilities, with closing within ninety days. If he could not obtain financing within that period, specific performance would be exhausted and the contract deemed expired.
sections.Reasoning:
The original-document rule did not exclude the photocopy: the court found Osborn probably kept the original, with no persuasive evidence that Kemp destroyed it in bad faith. The notary's seal carried no statutory presumption because required elements were missing, but her testimony, other credible testimony and the parties' long course of conduct, including the unchanged monthly payment, met the clear-and-convincing standard for authenticity.

The court found intent to be bound, definite essential terms and consideration. Osborn obtained a long income stream, a tenant able to maintain the house, and continued downstairs use; asserted inadequacy of price alone did not show inequity.

On price, the court rejected Kemp's claim that $66,000 in monthly payments had already bought the property, because that reading left the separately stated $50,000 price without meaningful work. It also treated the term as ambiguous and construed it against Kemp as drafter.

On ability to perform, the court took judicial notice that financing could probably be obtained with the property as collateral and gave Kemp a reasonable opportunity to get it; this was conditional relief.

The equities favored performance: there was no showing of incapacity at formation or undue influence, the owner had received the payments for almost the whole twenty years, and the property was Kemp's long-standing home with more than nominal improvements. Laches failed because the end of payments gave at least indirect notice while Osborn was competent, and later delay was attributable equally to both sides.

The remedy aimed to place both sides as nearly as possible where an April 16, 2005 purchase would have put them. The estate could not collect further rent, but the interest compensated the seller for delayed receipt of the price.

The casebook quotes this remedy through Snow Phipps to illustrate interest adjustments when specific performance comes years after performance was due.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-102.rule: A court of equity ordinarily will not order specific performance of a construction contract where the order would be impractical to enforce and require supervising a complex project, absent special circumstances or direct involvement of the public interest.

sections.Parties: Northern Delaware Industrial Development Corp. and Phoenix Steel Corp. were the plaintiffs. They sued E. W. Bliss Co., the contractor modernizing and expanding Phoenix Steel's plant, seeking an order compelling Bliss to put 300 additional construction workers on a night shift, along with damages and other relief. Bliss moved to dismiss or stay on the basis of an asserted arbitration obligation.
sections.Procedural History: In the Delaware Court of Chancery, the plaintiffs sought specific performance, damages and other relief; consideration of damages was deferred. Bliss moved to dismiss or stay on an asserted contractual arbitration obligation. At argument the court itself raised whether it should exercise equitable jurisdiction to order specific performance of the claimed staffing provision. On July 9, 1968, it declined to do so, leaving the plaintiffs free to apply on notice for an order dismissing the specific-performance claim or removing that cause to a competent court. On July 22, 1968, it denied reargument. The arbitration question and delay damages were not decided.
sections.Material Facts:
Under a May 26, 1966 contract, Bliss agreed to provide labor, services, materials and equipment to modernize and expand Phoenix Steel's plant in Claymont. The job cost $27.5 million and covered about sixty acres. On the sparse record before the court, work had fallen behind the contractual schedule. Around the time the complaint was filed, Bliss was running a single shift of between 192 and 337 workers a day.

The claimed obligation came from an incorporated proposal by the prime subcontractor, Noble J. Dick. Its working-schedule provision quoted the work on a normal forty-hour, five-day basis, except necessary service tie-ins, and included premium time for the mill shutdown, when work in two shifts was contemplated. The plaintiffs said the industry phrase meant day and night shifts over a seven-day week, which Bliss did not deny, and inferred an entitlement to at least 300 workers on each shift. The court noted that the contract did not promise any particular number of workers.
sections.Issue: Whether a court of equity should order a contractor on a large, unfinished construction project to hire additional workers for a second shift, as specific performance of a contract provision contemplating two-shift work.
sections.Holding: The Delaware Court of Chancery in 1968, Vice Chancellor Marvel, declined to order specific performance of the proposed work schedule and then denied reargument. The staffing provision was imprecise, and the mandatory workforce order sought would be impracticable, potentially impossible, to enforce because it would commit the court to supervising a massive, complex, unfinished construction project. The plaintiffs remained able to seek legal relief for actionable building delays.
sections.Reasoning:
The court's concern was not the mere act of placing an employment requisition. Keeping a prescribed workforce on site to accelerate the project implicated continuing technical construction management. An affidavit also suggested that the extra labor might be unavailable and, even if available, could impede orderly completion; the court expressed those points cautiously on this record.

The court rejected any universal absence of jurisdiction over construction contracts. Equity can require completion of a sufficiently defined construction undertaking in a suitable case, especially when tied to a land sale and largely completed. It distinguished defined plans permitting effective judicial supervision from this attempt to accelerate general work on the plaintiffs' own property through a clause that merely contemplated a second shift. An impractical construction order ordinarily should not issue absent special circumstances or direct involvement of the public interest. City Stores did not require a different result, because it involved definite shopping-center plans and a promised tenancy whose opportunity could otherwise be lost.

On reargument the plaintiffs said they sought only the ministerial act of hiring more workers, not supervision of the whole undertaking, and asked to show that labor was available and that fewer than 300 workers might suffice. The court answered that even sustainable new factual contentions would not eliminate its authority to decline this form of equitable relief. It added that a court does not affirmatively and directly enforce performance of personal services, even unique ones, because the practical difficulties resemble those of supervising construction.

The casebook's statement that the contract required adding 300 workers compresses the plaintiffs' position, and its arbitration hypothetical following the case is the editors' own; this case did not decide whether an arbitral award of the same relief must be enforced.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-103.rule: Specific performance of a long-term output contract for goods may be decreed where damages would be conjectural because future quantities and prices are uncertain and the goods, identified by their source, cannot readily be replaced.

sections.Parties: Simon and Abram Michlovitz and David Furman, trading as Michlovitz & Co., wholesale scrap dealers, were the buyers and plaintiffs. They sued Eastern Rolling Mill Co., a sheet-steel manufacturer in the Baltimore area, for specific performance of two five-year contracts for its scrap output. Eastern, the defendant and appellant, argued that the contracts were ultra vires, unauthorized, fraudulent or unconscionable, and adequately remedied by damages.
sections.Procedural History: The buyers sued for specific performance, alleging irreparable loss. After proof taken in open court, the chancellor granted a decree specifically enforcing the two contracts. Eastern appealed. The Maryland Court of Appeals affirmed the decree with costs.
sections.Material Facts:
Eastern's manufacture of sheet steel produced crop-end scrap and bundled sheet scrap, by-products worth only about two percent of its business but accumulating daily in large quantities that needed prompt removal. Since beginning operations in 1920 Eastern had sold the scrap exclusively to the buyers, under arrangements that grew from short-term to a five-year contract beginning in 1924.

In September 1927 the parties replaced that contract with two new ones, each covering the complete output of one scrap type from October 1, 1927 through September 30, 1932. The price for each quarter was calculated from designated Philadelphia-market quotations in Iron Age, minus $3 per ton. The buyers took scrap as it accumulated, loaded by Eastern onto cars at its plant, and paid $5,000 on account at formation.

John M. Jones, Eastern's president and general manager from its inception, made these agreements. After his death around November 1, 1927, the new president sought rescission or a shorter term, while remaining willing to contract for one year on the other terms. The evidence did not show that the buyers agreed. Both sides fixed quarterly prices and performed through June 1928; Eastern then refused further performance despite demands. It did not question the buyers' willingness and ability to perform.
sections.Issue: Whether the five-year scrap-output contracts were within Eastern's corporate power and its general manager's authority and free of fraud or unfairness, and whether damages were an inadequate remedy so that the buyers were entitled to specific performance of contracts for the sale of goods.
sections.Holding: The Maryland Court of Appeals in 1929, in an opinion by Judge Parke with no separate opinion, held the contracts valid and authorized and affirmed the decree of specific performance. Damages were inadequate because neither quantity nor price was fixed for the remaining years, so a present estimate would be conjecture. The output of the designated plant constituted specific or ascertained goods under the Sale of Goods Act in the special circumstances, and the chancellor had power to decree specific performance.
sections.Reasoning:
Eastern's continued performance with knowledge of its objections suggested an election to abide by the contracts, but the court addressed the defenses on the merits. The charter expressly authorized sale of sheet steel and its by-products and imposed no limit on duration or price, so a possibly unwise term did not make the sale ultra vires. Jones acted within his managerial authority: the board habitually left sales terms to him, and a successor five-year contract at a market-based price resembled earlier authorized dealings.

There was no fraud. The evidence showed no collusion, ulterior interest, or personal benefit to Jones apart from benefits he shared as a substantial stockholder, and the company challenged the contracts only after his death. The price floated quarterly with the market. The $3 deduction had a commercial explanation: the buyers had historically paid an average of $3.37 below the quotations, and the deduction covered freight, handling, storage and resale risks, and profit. The court judged the bargain as of when it was made, not by later events that increased the buyers' profits.

On remedy, Eastern had assets to satisfy a judgment, and the court recognized the ordinary preference for damages in sales of chattels. But scrap output varied with operations, contract prices changed quarterly, and future market values were uncertain, so a jury could not fairly ascertain tonnage and prices through September 1932. Scrap of this quality and concentrated weight was unavailable in the neighborhood or the Philadelphia market, and Baltimore delivery was itself valuable. Performance required only delivering accumulated scrap, not personal skill. Under section 89 of the Sale of Goods Act, all scrap from the specified plant in the stated period became identified to the contracts when manufactured.

The casebook uses the case to ask about specific performance under later UCC provisions.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-104.rule: A wrongfully suspended employee must seek other employment and the employer is credited with replacement earnings, but the employer bears the burden of proving both lack of reasonable diligence and the availability of suitable work.

sections.Parties: Schilling and Klingler, deputy sheriffs who had been suspended and then reinstated, brought back-pay actions against their employer. The officers disputed deductions for outside earnings and sought prejudgment interest. The employer sought further mitigation credits for periods when it said the officers had not adequately looked for work.
sections.Procedural History: Schilling and Klingler successfully appealed their suspensions to the circuit court and were reinstated. In a 1972 decision the Wisconsin Supreme Court reversed an award of full back pay without deductions for outside earnings and remanded; the brief treats that decision only as procedural history. On remand the trial court deducted Schilling's outside earnings in full, found that both officers had made reasonable and diligent efforts to find other work, and denied prejudgment interest. In 1974 the Wisconsin Supreme Court affirmed the orders.
sections.Material Facts:
After the remand the parties stipulated that Klingler's back pay was $11,499.16 and that the employer should receive a $1,000 credit for his self-employment during part of the suspension. They stipulated that Schilling's gross back pay was $11,510.38 and that he had earned $3,869.13 during part of his suspension, but disagreed whether that should be deducted. The trial court deducted it, leaving $7,641.25.

The employer challenged the adequacy of Klingler's job search between September 14, 1970 and January 1, 1971, and Schilling's between September 14, 1970 and March 1971. Schilling later found work in Wisconsin and Arizona, moving to Arizona in June 1971. Schilling had worked the midnight-to-8 a.m. sheriff's shift and argued that because his substitute earnings were obtained outside those hours, none should reduce his recovery. Before his suspension in September 1970 he had also earned $3,369.24 in sheriff's-office overtime that year. The officers had never given the employer information about their earnings during the suspension.
sections.Issue: Whether the employer was entitled to further mitigation credits for periods when the officers allegedly failed to seek work; whether Schilling's earnings during suspension should be deducted even though earned outside his regular shift hours; and whether the officers were entitled to prejudgment interest on their back pay.
sections.Holding: The Wisconsin Supreme Court in 1974, in an opinion by Justice Connor T. Hansen, affirmed the orders. The employer failed to carry its burden of proving a lack of diligence and the availability of suitable work, so it received no further credits. The employer was entitled to credit for Schilling's suspension-period earnings from employment unrelated to outside or part-time work he had held before suspension, so the $3,869.13 deduction stood. Prejudgment interest was properly denied.
sections.Reasoning:
A discharged or suspended employee must seek other employment, and the employer may receive credit for earnings actually obtained or that could have been obtained. The employee need not seek or accept work of a different or inferior kind. The employer bears the burden of establishing both a lack of reasonable and diligent efforts and the availability of suitable work. The officers were not necessarily limited as a matter of law to police jobs, since each had other work experience, but the employer introduced no evidence that alternative work was available during the disputed periods. The trial court's findings of diligent effort were not against the great weight and clear preponderance of the evidence. Judicial notice could not fill the gap: the court declined to assume that work of like character, on similar terms and in a reasonably convenient location, was available to these particular employees.

On Schilling's earnings, the 1972 mandate called for considering whether earnings accrued during regular duty hours together with the amount earned outside those hours immediately before suspension; the clock alone was not decisive. The court approved the trial court's rejection of Schilling's argument, under which he could avoid third-shift work, earn elsewhere, and keep all substitute earnings alongside unreduced back pay. The brief notes that the decision does not say every preexisting side job must reduce damages.

Interest requires a fixed or readily determinable amount. The mitigation credit was not a separate unliquidated setoff that leaves interest available. The officers had disputed any allowance for outside earnings and never supplied their earnings information, so the employer could not reasonably calculate and tender the amount due.

The casebook quotes the trial court's explanation, as approved by the Supreme Court, and surrounds the case with collateral-source and lost-volume comparisons, which are its own teaching questions.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-105.rule: An express warranty requires that the seller's affirmation become part of the basis of the bargain through the buyer's reliance, and consequential damages for its breach require separate proof that the breach caused each particular loss.

sections.Parties: Dr. Luel P. Overstreet, a veterinarian who operated a standardbred horse farm in Henderson County, Kentucky, was the plaintiff buyer. He sued Norden Laboratories, Inc., the maker of the vaccine Rhinomune, for breach of warranty after vaccinated mares aborted their foals.
