Norden, the defendant, was the appellant in the Sixth Circuit, challenging the reliance instructions, causation, and the measure of damages.
sections.Procedural History: Overstreet's initial complaint was broader, and partial summary judgment disposed of some claims; the claim tried concerned six aborted foals. The jury found that Overstreet had not violated his duties in using Rhinomune and that Norden had violated "any of its warranties," without specifying an express or implied warranty, and awarded $40,500. Norden's motions for judgment notwithstanding the verdict or a new trial were denied, and it appealed. On February 3, 1982, the Sixth Circuit, sitting in diversity, reversed and remanded for proceedings consistent with the opinion. The lead opinion at first describes the judgment as vacated, but its final directive is reversal and remand.
sections.Material Facts:
Equine rhinopneumonitis produces cold-like symptoms in horses but can cause pregnant mares to abort. In spring 1973 two mares on Overstreet's farm aborted, later determined to have been caused by this virus. Around the same time Norden began marketing Rhinomune, a new vaccine promoted through advertisements, brochures, and sales representatives. A representative spoke to an associate in Overstreet's office, and Overstreet asserted that he read promotional literature and ordered the vaccine because of its representations. Twenty-three mares were vaccinated between August 10 and November 9, 1973. Six inoculated mares aborted their foals in spring 1974. The appeal did not finally establish that the vaccine caused the disease.

At trial, after liability was found, the jury was told to measure damages as the difference between each mare's value with and without her foal.
sections.Issue: Under Kentucky law, as the federal court predicted it, must a buyer's reliance be found before an express warranty arises under Kentucky Revised Statutes section 355.2-313, did the evidence support recovery on an implied warranty of merchantability, and could the loss of the foals be recovered as consequential damages without separate proof that the breach caused that loss?
sections.Holding: The Sixth Circuit, in 1982, reversed and remanded. Judge Keith wrote the lead opinion; Judges Engel and Kennedy filed a joint special concurrence that supplied the two-judge position on consequential damages. All three judges agreed that the express-warranty instructions wrongly omitted reliance and that the evidence was insufficient to establish breach of an implied warranty. The two-judge concurrence held that recovery for the aborted foals required proof of a causal connection between the breach and that particular loss, and that where an issue of alternatives was fairly raised and causally material, as here, the plaintiff bore the burden of proving an effective alternative. The court did not enter judgment for Norden.
sections.Reasoning:
No Kentucky court had construed the express-warranty provision, so the panel predicted Kentucky law from the statutory language, earlier state decisions, and commentary. Under section 355.2-313 an affirmation, promise, description, or model must become part of the basis of the bargain, so reliance as an inducement to purchase was necessary. The instructions and verdict form did not require that finding, and the nonspecific verdict could not reveal which theory the jury used. Formal warranty language was unnecessary and an advertisement could create a warranty, though mere opinion or puffing might not. Expertise did not necessarily bar reliance on a newly marketed, unique product better known to its manufacturer. Merchantability under section 355.2-314 arose by law and required no reliance, but the evidence did not establish its breach.

On damages, Engel and Kennedy concluded that the instruction treated the foals' loss as recoverable automatically on breach. Under sections 355.2-714 and 355.2-715 the buyer could recover the vaccine's difference in value and administration expenses, but the foals required proof of causation: the vaccine itself causing injury, an inferior batch, forgoing another effective preventive, or other detrimental reliance. If no effective product could have prevented the abortions and no other causal link existed, the breach had not caused the loss. They denied adopting a universal "Alternative Product Rule."

Keith disagreed on damages. He thought the liability instructions' causation language adequate and argued that the warranty itself defined the promised preventive performance; limiting recovery by the availability of another product would disadvantage consumers and reduce new-product promises to ineffective guarantees.

The casebook compares the case with Chatlos.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-106.rule: Under UCC section 2-714(2), damages for accepted goods are the difference between their value as accepted and the value they would have had as warranted; the contract price is relevant evidence of warranted value but is not controlling.

sections.Parties: Chatlos Systems, Inc., the plaintiff, acquired a computer system from National Cash Register Corp. (NCR), the defendant, and sued for breach of warranty when the system did not perform the promised functions. On this appeal NCR challenged the district court's valuation of the warranted system and the award of prejudgment interest.
sections.Procedural History: Chatlos filed in New Jersey state court, and NCR removed the diversity case to federal court. After a bench trial the district judge found breach of warranty and awarded $57,152.76 for the breach and $63,558.16 in consequential damages. On the 1980 appeal the Third Circuit affirmed liability, set aside the consequential damages, and remanded for recalculation of warranty damages. On remand the district court valued the warranted system at $207,826.50 and the delivered goods at $6,000, awarding $201,826.50 plus prejudgment interest. On January 15, 1982, the Third Circuit affirmed. Rehearing was denied February 11, with three judges dissenting from the denial, and the report records that certiorari was dismissed June 9.
sections.Material Facts:
Chatlos acquired an NCR 399/656 disc computer system intended to perform specified business functions. As Judge Rosenn's dissent describes it, the July 1974 transaction priced the hardware at $40,165 and six programs at $5,855, a total of $46,020 before tax. The programs covered accounts receivable, payroll, order entry, inventory deletion, state income tax, and cash receipts. The computer was delivered in December 1974 and payroll became operational in March 1975. NCR was still unsuccessful with order entry and inventory deletion by March 1976, and Chatlos demanded termination and removal on September 1, 1976. NCR had sold the system to a bank for $46,020 in July 1975, and Chatlos leased it from the bank. August 1975 was treated as the acceptance date.

On remand Chatlos's expert, Dick Brandon, valued a system that could perform the promised functions without limiting himself to the NCR model, and acknowledged that comparable systems were outside the delivered system's price range. NCR offered no expert valuation. NCR's programmer, Frank Hicks, had recommended an NCR 8200, and Gerald Greenstein acknowledged that the 8200 was two levels above the 399 in sophistication and price.
sections.Issue: In measuring warranty damages under New Jersey's enactment of UCC section 2-714(2), was the district court bound to treat the $46,020 contract price as the value of the system as warranted, or could it rely on expert evidence of the value of a system capable of performing the warranted functions? Was prejudgment interest properly awarded?
sections.Holding: The Third Circuit, in 1982, affirmed in a per curiam opinion for Judges Aldisert and Weis, with Judge Rosenn dissenting. The contract price is relevant evidence of market value but is not controlling, and the district court's finding that the system as warranted was worth $207,826.50 was not clearly erroneous. The award of prejudgment interest lay within the district court's discretion. The judgment of $201,826.50 plus prejudgment interest was affirmed without reduction.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority treated the bargain as a computer system with specified capabilities, not merely a named model regardless of performance. Section 2-714(2) measures the difference, at acceptance, between the value of the goods accepted and the value they would have had as warranted, and it can preserve a particularly favorable bargain even without an intervening rise in market price. NCR argued that Chatlos's expert had replaced a Ford with a Rolls-Royce; the majority preferred the analogy of equipment promised to lift one thousand pounds but able to lift only five hundred, where the cost of equipment able to lift the promised load illuminates warranted value. NCR chose not to offer valuation evidence on remand. The conflicting positions required the district judge to assess credibility and weight; Brandon was well qualified, NCR's own witnesses gave some corroboration, and the appellate court could not substitute its own valuation. Interest was upheld briefly by reference to the prior appeal.

Judge Rosenn, dissenting, read the statute to focus on the goods actually accepted in their warranted condition, not hypothetical superior goods capable of equivalent functions, and considered Brandon's estimates speculative. He would have used $46,020 as warranted value, credited $6,000 for the hardware and $1,000 for the usable payroll program, awarded $39,020, and opposed prejudgment interest on unliquidated, substantially disputed damages.

Judge Adams, joined by Judges Hunter and Garth, dissented from the denial of rehearing because the UCC valuation question reached beyond ordinary state-law error.

The casebook cites the case in a note comparing it with Overstreet, which separately addresses causation of consequential losses.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-108.rule: The cost of reinstating defective building work is recoverable only if the work is necessary to produce conformity and reasonable to undertake; where it is not, the owner may be awarded damages for loss of amenity rather than nothing.

sections.Parties: Ruxley Electronics & Construction Ltd., trading as Home Counties Swimming Pools and owned or controlled by Hall, built a swimming pool for Stephen Forsyth at his house in Kent. Ruxley sued for the unpaid balance of the price. Forsyth counterclaimed for defects and, at trial, for the pool's failure to reach the specified depth, seeking the cost of rebuilding it. Ruxley was the appellant in the House of Lords.
sections.Procedural History: Ruxley sued in January 1990 for a balance of 10,330 pounds, and an associated enclosure company brought a separate action for its own balance. Forsyth's counterclaims listed defects without mentioning depth; he first raised depth during the trial in May 1993, appearing in person. Judge Diamond QC refused the cost of rebuilding, rejected Forsyth's argument that an entire, uncompleted contract left him owing nothing, and awarded 2,500 pounds for loss of amenity and a separate 750 pounds for general inconvenience. A Court of Appeal majority, Staughton and Mann LJJ, awarded the reconstruction cost and set aside the amenity award; Dillon LJ dissented. On June 29, 1995, the House of Lords allowed Ruxley's appeal and restored the trial judge's judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
In autumn 1986 Forsyth contracted with Ruxley for a pool adjoining his house. Lord Lloyd gives the price, with extras and VAT, as 17,797.40 pounds. The specified depth was first six feet six inches; Hall later agreed, without extra charge, to increase it to seven feet six inches. There was no provision for a diving board. Work began in June 1987, but defective subcontracted work cracked the bottom, and Hall replaced the pool without charge; the replacement was finished in June 1988. Hall reluctantly agreed to a 10,000 pound reduction for disturbance, but Forsyth still did not pay the invoice. In March 1989 Forsyth discovered that the deep end was six feet nine inches rather than seven feet six inches. The speeches also refer to a depth of six feet at the relevant diving location.

The trial judge found the pool safe for diving, no diminution in its value from the shortfall, no intention or likely wish to fit a diving board, and no way to obtain the specified depth short of total reconstruction at 21,560 pounds. He found reconstruction wholly disproportionate to the benefit and was not persuaded that Forsyth's professed intention to rebuild would outlast the litigation.
sections.Issue: Where a builder delivers a usable pool shallower than specified, the shortfall causes no loss of market value, and the only cure is demolition and rebuilding, is the owner entitled to the full cost of reconstruction, or is that cost recoverable only if reasonable? If it is not recoverable, is the owner limited to nothing?
sections.Holding: The House of Lords, in 1995, unanimously allowed the builder's appeal; the five Law Lords were Keith, Bridge, Jauncey, Mustill, and Lloyd. Forsyth could not recover the 21,560 pound cost of demolishing and rebuilding his usable pool merely because that was the only way to attain the specified depth. Restoring the trial judgment preserved the 2,500 pound loss-of-amenity award. Lord Jauncey reserved the propriety of that award because the builder had not challenged it, while Lords Bridge, Mustill, and Lloyd gave affirmative reasons for recognizing such compensation.
sections.Reasoning:
Forsyth's counsel argued that cost of cure and diminution in value were the only permissible measures, so that reconstruction cost followed once diminution was zero. The House rejected a forced choice between nothing and an excessive award.

Lord Jauncey tied reasonableness to identifying the loss itself, rather than treating it merely as a choice among remedies once loss is established. A usable pool that misses one specification does not produce the loss of receiving no pool. Reconstruction cost is often the right measure for defective building work, but the work must be necessary for conformity and reasonable to undertake; the trial finding of unreasonableness meant the loss did not extend to full reinstatement. Lord Lloyd agreed that the absence of a cheaper cure did not make disproportionate spending reasonable. Personal preference is a factor, as with a collapsed ornamental folly that adds nothing to market value, but it is not exempt from reasonableness. Intention to rebuild bears on whether the cost is a genuine loss; Jauncey declined to decide whether it is always required, and Lloyd said Forsyth's later undertaking to rebuild could not create a loss that did not otherwise exist.

Lord Mustill denied that there were two exhaustive measures. The aim is compensation for true loss, and a promise may be worth more to a householder than its effect on sale value; he called this consumer surplus, and imprecision in valuing it was no reason to ignore it. Lord Bridge endorsed amenity damages. Lord Lloyd justified the award as an adaptation of the exception for contracts affording pleasure, and left open whether modest compensation is available in ordinary building cases.

The casebook builds a problem, "The Deep End," on the case with altered, hypothetical facts.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-109.rule: Where the cost of remediating land to a contractual standard is grossly disproportionate to the resulting economic benefit, damages for breach of the promise to remediate are capped at the diminution in the property's value.

sections.Parties: Fred and Zola Schneberger, owners of a 154.95-acre tract in Washita County, were the plaintiffs. They sued Apache Corp., which drilled the Schneberger 1-17 well, alleging that it breached a settlement agreement by failing to reduce contaminants to the promised levels. The owners sought the cost of remediation; Apache urged that damages be measured by diminution in value.
sections.Procedural History: In March 1984 the owners sued in federal court over contamination; a March 4, 1986 settlement resolved that action, which was dismissed with prejudice. In October 1989 the owners brought the present federal action for breach of the settlement. The federal district court certified two questions to the Oklahoma Supreme Court: the measure of damages for breach of the pollution-reduction settlement, and, conditional on cost of remediation being the measure, whether a jury could consider a remediation plan different from the one approved by the Corporation Commission. On October 25, 1994, the court answered that diminution in value was the maximum recoverable and declined to answer the second question. Rehearing was denied January 18, 1995. The court did not enter judgment or decide whether Apache had breached.
sections.Material Facts:
Apache began drilling the Schneberger 1-17 well on June 29, 1982. The owners' 1984 suit alleged contamination, property injury, and personal damages from that well and an upstream well, Rogers 1-18. In the 1986 settlement Apache paid $80,000 for damages and expenses and approximately $179,000 in attorney fees under a court order. The parties agreed that Apache would ask for a stay of Corporation Commission cleanup proceedings but, if no stay was obtained, would remain subject to the Commission's requirements. No stay occurred; the Commission ordered and monitored cleanup, and Apache spent substantial sums carrying out its approved plan.

In the 1989 action the owners alleged that Apache had not achieved the reduced contaminant levels promised in the agreement. They estimated approximately $1.3 million to remediate to the contractual standards and sought to introduce methods not contemplated by the Commission's orders. Apache estimated a $5,175 loss in market value. These were the parties' estimates, not adjudicated values. The agreement did not specify a measure of damages for breach.
sections.Issue: What is the measure of damages for breach of a settlement agreement promising to reduce water pollution to stated levels, where the estimated cost of remediation far exceeds the estimated loss in the land's market value: cost of remediation or diminution in value? If cost of remediation, may the jury consider a plan different from the one the Corporation Commission approved?
sections.Holding: The Oklahoma Supreme Court, in 1994, in an opinion by Vice Chief Justice Lavender for five justices, held that diminution in the property's value was the maximum recoverable measure in the circumstances presented. Because cost of remediation was not the proper measure, the court declined to answer the conditional second question. Justices Alma Wilson, Kauger, and Summers concurred in part and dissented in part, and Justice Opala dissented, none with a separate reasoned writing.
sections.Reasoning:
The general contract statute, 23 O.S. section 21, compensates detriment proximately caused by breach. Property-damage rules measure permanent injury by the before-and-after difference in value and reparable injury initially by reasonable restoration cost, but Oklahoma decisions limit restoration recovery. The court reaffirmed Peevyhouse's treatment of remediation costs grossly disproportionate to the economic benefit, together with statutory limits against recovering more than full performance would give and against unreasonable, oppressive damages. Peevyhouse had called the breached restoration provision incidental to the contract's main purpose; the court acknowledged that wording but noted that later cases had kept to diminution principles without that distinction.

The owners argued that environmental statutes, including the Surface Damage Act, made Peevyhouse obsolete, and relied on federal decisions predicting that Oklahoma would abandon it. The court rejected those predictions, noting that neither case had been certified to it. It viewed the Surface Damage Act as balancing two valuable resources, and its own precedents under that Act still used diminution in value. The requirement of reasonable damages applied to contract obligations, and given the disparity between $1.3 million and the presented value loss the court saw no basis to abandon its rule. The parties could have specified a contractual measure but had not.

The court distinguished private damages from public enforcement: nothing in a damages award compels the recipient to spend it on restoration, and the Commission's authority and Apache's regulatory cleanup duties were preserved.

The casebook discusses the case in a note following Peevyhouse.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-110.rule: A seller recovers lost profit as a lost-volume seller by proving capacity for both sales, that the additional sale would have been profitable, and that it probably would have been made absent the breach.

sections.Parties: R.E. Davis Chemical Corp., the buyer, contracted to purchase a magnetic resonance instrument from Diasonics, Inc., the seller, and then failed to take delivery. Davis sued to recover its down payment under UCC section 2-718(2); Diasonics counterclaimed for lost profit under section 2-708(2). On this appeal Davis challenged the damages judgment entered for Diasonics after remand.
sections.Procedural History: The district court first granted Davis summary judgment on the theory that a lost-volume seller could recover only resale-based damages under section 2-706. In the 1987 appeal the Seventh Circuit predicted that Illinois would permit lost-profit recovery and remanded for proof of capacity, profitability, and a probable second sale. After a three-day bench trial the district court found lost profit of $453,050 and entered judgment for $153,050 after crediting the retained deposit; it refused a research-grant deduction and excluded evidence on the upgrade. On February 8, 1991, the Seventh Circuit affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded for further consideration of the research-grant and upgrade issues. The brief covers only this 1991 appeal.
sections.Material Facts:
On February 23, 1984, Davis agreed to buy a .35-tesla nuclear magnetic resonance instrument from Diasonics for $1.5 million. Full payment would entitle Davis to a $225,000 research grant based on an approved development program. The agreement also offered an upgrade to a high-field/spectroscopy system by June 1, 1985, for an additional $700,000. Davis paid a $300,000 deposit but did not take delivery. Diasonics resold the MRI to a third party for the same price and refused to return the deposit.

Diasonics' MRI units were generic and interchangeable and were not assigned to particular buyers until shortly before delivery. Its capacity to manufacture one more unit was undisputed, and its controller testified that the sales force pursued every possible lead and qualified customer. Davis had not paid the full price or obtained approval of a development program. Davis had designed its MRI building for the more powerful system, and Diasonics had initially sought profits from Davis's failure to upgrade.
sections.Issue: Did Diasonics prove that it was a lost-volume seller without tracing the particular unit Davis ordered to an identified resale buyer, and was its profit accounting sufficiently certain? In computing lost profit, must the court consider whether the $225,000 research grant was in substance a rebate and whether expenses avoided on the upgrade option should reduce the award?
sections.Holding: The Seventh Circuit, in 1991, in an opinion by Judge Cudahy for a panel including Judges Cummings and Easterbrook, upheld the finding that Diasonics was a lost-volume seller and upheld its accounting methodology. It reversed and remanded for the district court to determine whether the research grant was a genuine exchange or a disguised rebate, and to consider the upgrade evidence if exercise of the option was substantially likely and its value persuasively shown. The court did not itself order a $225,000 credit or find that the option would have been exercised.
sections.Reasoning:
Lost volume means that a contract-market or resale measure fails to compensate a seller who could have made both the original and the additional sale. Davis argued that Diasonics had to trace the unit it ordered to a specific resale buyer. The court rejected that demand on this record because the units were interchangeable and unassigned until shortly before delivery. Capacity was undisputed, the controller's testimony about pursuing every lead was corroborated by Diasonics' position as a young company in a competitive market, and Davis offered no contrary proof, so the finding that another sale probably would have occurred was not clearly erroneous. The court did not treat every manufacturer with spare capacity as a lost-volume seller. Damages require reasonable certainty, not mathematical precision, and the district judge's choice between the accountants survived clear-error review.

On the grant, unmet conditions did not settle its economic nature. If the research would genuinely benefit Diasonics, the grant was an independent exchange; if both parties understood that practically worthless information would qualify for a routinely payable rebate, damages had to be reduced by $225,000, because breach does not entitle Diasonics to more than its bargain. The trial judge's explanation was too ambiguous to tell which.

On the upgrade, Illinois ordinarily requires strict adherence to an option's conditions, but the label can conceal an integral part of the original deal. The factors on remand were the option's importance to the bargain, its value relative to the $700,000 payment, and the original MRI's value relative to its $1.5 million price.

The casebook's account of the appeal after remand reports the capacity and accounting conclusions but omits the remand issues and the mixed disposition.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-111.rule: A promisee may recover necessary expenditures made in preparation for performance, but the promisor may reduce that recovery by any amount it proves the promisee would have lost had the contract been fully performed.

sections.Parties: L. Albert & Son, the seller, agreed to sell four rubber-reconditioning machines to Armstrong Rubber Co., the buyer. Albert sued for the $25,500 price. Armstrong counterclaimed for breach, seeking its reliance expenditures and claiming no lost profits. Both parties appealed to the Second Circuit.
sections.Procedural History: The trial judge found that the machines conformed to specifications or could have been made to conform with slight trouble and expense, but that the seller's delay justified rejection. He dismissed both Albert's price claim and Armstrong's damages counterclaim, but awarded Albert the value, without interest, of a motor and accessories that Armstrong had put to use. On cross-appeals the Second Circuit, on November 29, 1949, modified the judgment to add interest on the motor and to allow Armstrong a setoff for its foundation expense, subject to a further hearing at which Albert could prove that timely performance would have produced a loss, and affirmed the judgment as modified.
sections.Material Facts:
By an exchange of letters in December 1942 Albert agreed to sell Armstrong four "Refiners," machines that reconditioned old rubber, as an indivisible purchase. Two arrived in August 1943; the other two arrived on August 31 or September 8, 1945. Armstrong accepted the first two without objecting to lateness, installed them in August 1944, and on March 28, 1945 wrote asking Albert to complete the order. The machines served a wartime demand for reclaimed rubber, which the end of fighting threatened. Armstrong rejected all four in October 1945. On February 20, 1946 it put to use a 300-horsepower motor and accessories from the rejected equipment, with a fair market value of $4,590.

Armstrong sought $118,478 spent on its reclaim department, $27,555.63 spent on scrap rubber, and $3,000 spent on foundations for the refiners. It had disposed of its scrap rubber in April and May 1945 and did not attribute the department's collapse to the missing refiners until its May 1947 counterclaim.
sections.Issue: Was the buyer entitled to reject the machines for late delivery, or had it accepted them by its letters, its tax depreciation entry, or its later use of the motor? May a buyer who cannot prove lost profits recover expenditures made in reliance on the contract, and who bears the burden of showing that the contract would have been a losing one?
sections.Holding: The Second Circuit, in 1949, in an opinion by Chief Judge Learned Hand for a panel with Judges Swan and Clark, held that the buyer rightfully rejected the substantially delayed machinery and had not accepted it. The seller could recover the $4,590 value of the converted motor with interest from February 20, 1946. The buyer could not recover its reclaim-department or scrap-rubber expenses, but could set off the $3,000 foundation cost, with interest from October 1945, less any loss the seller proved the buyer would have suffered had the refiners been delivered on or before May 1, 1945.
sections.Reasoning:
Hand treated the earlier delay as waived by the March 28 letter, after which the buyer had to accept delivery within a reasonable time. Given the wartime purpose, delivery at the end of August was too late. Under the Uniform Sales Act's forms of acceptance, a bookkeeping letter acknowledging the amount of the claim did not show an intention to accept, and a depreciation entry for tax purposes was an assertion to the taxing authority, not an act against the goods. Using the motor was a conversion, but it came four months after an unequivocal rejection and did not retract it; the seller's remedy was the motor's value on a quasi-contractual basis, with interest under Connecticut law because the value was ascertainable at conversion.

On reliance, the finding that the late machines were only one possible cause of the reclaim department's failure was not clearly erroneous, and a possible causal link could not shift the whole venture's expenses to the seller. The foundations were different: they were necessary preparation for the promised machines. The buyer had not proved the refiners' prospective earnings and so had no expectation award, but that did not bar reimbursement. Unrestricted reliance recovery would make the seller insure the buyer's venture if performance would have lost money, so Hand placed on the breaching seller the burden of proving such a loss, since the breach made the inquiry necessary. He found the Connecticut authorities inconclusive and relied on the Restatement and scholarly treatments.

The casebook quotes the reliance rule; its statement that the delay caused the venture to fail is broader than the upheld finding.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-113.rule: Disgorgement of a breaching party's profits is available as restitution case by case, where the breach is conscious and substantial and damages are inadequate, but the profits must be apportioned between the parties' respective contributions.

sections.Parties: Hydrosphere Resource Consultants, Inc., a software developer, was the plaintiff. EarthInfo, Inc., which had acquired US West's interest in products Hydrosphere developed and assumed its royalty obligations, was the defendant. Hydrosphere obtained rescission and restitution of EarthInfo's net profits at trial. EarthInfo challenged the award of all net profits on review in the Colorado Supreme Court.
sections.Procedural History: After a March 1992 trial the trial court found that royalties were not owed on the derivative product but that EarthInfo's unilateral suspension of other royalties was a substantial breach. At a later hearing both parties sought rescission and restitution. The court ordered EarthInfo to return property and to repay $265,204.91 in net profits, less credits, for a judgment of $185,772.91. The court of appeals affirmed in an unpublished decision, with Judge Rothenberg dissenting on the net-profits issue. On June 30, 1995, the Colorado Supreme Court, en banc, affirmed in part, reversed in part, and returned the case to the court of appeals with directions to remand for recalculation and a new restitution order.
sections.Material Facts:
Between 1986 and 1988 Hydrosphere contracted with US West to develop CD-ROM products making public hydrological and meteorological data accessible. US West received ownership, copyrights, and patents and agreed to pay fixed hourly development fees plus royalties on net sales, quarterly. EarthInfo acquired US West's interest on February 10, 1989, agreeing to pay $60,432, and by a separate agreement with Hydrosphere assumed US West's obligations, including royalties. EarthInfo paid royalties through June 30, 1990. A dispute then arose over whether a new derivative product carried a royalty. On October 30, when third-quarter royalties came due, EarthInfo announced that it would withhold those and future royalties pending clarification. It kept paying development fees, including $19,000 after June 30. On December 12 Hydrosphere notified EarthInfo that it was rescinding the contracts.

The trial court chose June 30, 1990 as the rescission date and credited EarthInfo with the $60,432 acquisition amount and the $19,000 in fees against net profits from that date. EarthInfo had supplied marketing, packaging, enhancements, manuals, trademarks, promotional materials, and licensee lists.
sections.Issue: On rescission for a substantial breach of contract, may the court order the breaching party to disgorge its profits as restitution, and if so, may it award all net profits without distinguishing the portion attributable to the breaching party's own contributions?
sections.Holding: The Colorado Supreme Court, en banc, in 1995, in an opinion by Justice Scott, held that profit disgorgement was available in these circumstances, but that an award of all net profits that failed to distinguish the parties' contributions to those profits could not stand. It placed on the plaintiff, Hydrosphere, the burden of establishing sufficient facts for a fair apportionment in this case, and ordered further proceedings without fixing a share or amount. It declined to decide whether the rescission date was correct.
sections.Reasoning:
The court saw a tension between compensating the promisee's expectation and preventing a breaching party from keeping gains from wrongdoing. It adopted neither a rule always allowing the breacher to keep the excess nor one always requiring disgorgement; the trial court decides case by case. Rescission was warranted because the breach was substantial, damages could not repair the hostile relationship, and both parties sought it. Restitution measures the defendant's gain, not the plaintiff's loss, so it can exceed expectation damages.

Profit recovery is extraordinary. A mere breach does not make every resulting benefit recoverable, and some profit almost always comes from the defendant's own investment or effort. Relevant considerations are the seriousness of the wrongdoing, the connection between wrongdoing and profit, and the feasibility of separating contributions. EarthInfo's conscious and substantial repudiation of its existing royalty obligations, the difficulty of assessing damages, and the mutual rescission justified disgorging profits attributable to Hydrosphere's contribution. That no royalties were owed on derivatives did not excuse withholding the others.

Deducting legitimate expenses, which the defendant must prove, differs from identifying each party's contribution to the net profit. EarthInfo's own work helped create the profit, and even wrongful conduct does not justify confiscating the defendant's own investment and enterprise. The trial court needed a reasonable approximation of the respective contributions; if contributions cannot be separated, profits ordinarily should not be awarded unless the defendant is a very serious wrongdoer.

The casebook uses the case for the point that restitution must account for benefits on both sides, but it states that EarthInfo bore the burden of proving relative contributions, whereas the opinion assigns that burden to the plaintiff.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-114.rule: An injured party that has performed all of its contractual duties cannot obtain restitution in quantum meruit when all that remains due from the other party is payment of a definite sum; the agreed price is the measure.

sections.Parties: John T. Brady & Co., the contractor, and its surety, Federal Insurance, to which Brady had assigned its contractual rights, sued for unpaid construction compensation. The Urban Redevelopment Commission, the owner, and Rich-Taubman Associates, the redeveloper that would complete and operate the mall, sued for delay and defective performance. The City of Stamford, though originally named, was no longer a party. The owner and redeveloper appealed, and the surety and contractor cross-appealed.
sections.Procedural History: Brady sued in August 1982. The owner and redeveloper brought their own action seeking $3,225,907.14 beyond the remaining contract balance for delay and deficient performance. After a lengthy consolidated trial the jury found for the contractor and surety in both actions, awarding $2,612,098.84 plus $1,456,520.49 in interest, in a verdict that did not separate the issues through interrogatories. The trial court had excluded the surety's alternative quantum meruit claim. On November 19, 1991, the Connecticut Supreme Court reversed the judgment and remanded for a new trial, while approving the exclusion of quantum meruit, the restrictions on certain extras, and the trial-management ruling the contractor challenged.
sections.Material Facts:
Brady undertook to build the Stamford Town Center's nine-story parking garage and the shell of an adjacent shopping mall. The amended contract price was $36,014,993, of which $33,028,201 had been paid. The December 19, 1978 construction contract set a January 20, 1981 deadline with $3,000 in liquidated damages per day of delay, and made final payment depend on acceptance, certification, approval, and releases of claims.

A September 28, 1981 settlement, made when the project was 94 percent complete, had the owner promise $2,250,000 and Brady release its preexisting claims; the owner conditionally waived $800,000 in stipulated actual delay damages if substantial completion occurred by January 20, 1982. Brady missed that date, and the owner paid only $1,375,000 of the settlement amount. Brady assigned its contractual rights to the surety in March 1982. A June 1, 1982 completion agreement, made at 99 percent completion, required surety financing for completion by July 9; that date also passed, and the owner withheld further payments. A temporary occupancy certificate issued in October, and Brady left in January 1983 claiming completion. The owner asserted defects and hired another contractor.

At trial, for the first six weeks, the surety introduced extensive evidence blaming the owner for delays before September 1981, over repeated objections.
sections.Issue: Did the admission of extensive evidence about delay claims released in the settlement require a new trial? Could the surety recover in quantum meruit for the value of the work, as an alternative to the contract price, when the work was 99 percent complete and the complaint sought unpaid contractual sums? Did unfulfilled contract conditions entitle the owner to judgment as a matter of law?
sections.Holding: The Connecticut Supreme Court, in 1991, in an opinion by Chief Justice Peters for a unanimous five-justice court, reversed and remanded for a new trial because extensive evidence contradicted an unambiguous settlement release and was not effectively cured by the jury instructions. It upheld the exclusion of quantum meruit: under Restatement (Second) of Contracts section 373(2), a party that has performed all its contractual duties cannot obtain restitution when only payment of a definite sum remains due. The owner was not entitled to judgment as a matter of law on the unfulfilled conditions.
sections.Reasoning:
On the conditions, the evidence, viewed favorably to the verdict, permitted a finding that the owner's conduct, including withheld payments, significantly contributed to the completion difficulties, so the dispute could go to a jury.

A new trial was required because the settlement unambiguously released extra-work and delay claims arising before September 1981, and the surety had withdrawn its duress contention. The trial court eventually recognized the settlement but declined to strike the evidence or declare a mistrial, and its brief final caution months later did not effectively identify what the jury must disregard. For retrial the court cautioned against using generic fairness or equitable estoppel to displace the three agreements, and said the jury needed meaningful guidance on prejudgment interest.

On quantum meruit, the surety argued that the owner's payment failures were material breaches. The work was 99 percent complete when suit was filed, and the complaint claimed unpaid contractual sums and extras without a rescission or restitution count. Restitution ordinarily prevents the breacher's unjust enrichment and measures its gain, but after full performance the parties' agreed valuation supplies the measure and avoids judicial revaluation. The court kept a qualification for a special showing such as lack of good faith, unconscionability, or abuse of contract, and expressly reserved whether the full-performance rule applies equally to substantial performance.

On the cross-appeals, extras the engineer rejected could not be recovered where his decision was not arbitrary or in bad faith, cost estimates could not replace costs incurred and paid, and limits on the contractor's separate participation were not an abuse given its identity of interest with the surety.

The casebook quotes only the quantum meruit portion.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-115.rule: A carrier with notice of the special purpose of a shipment is liable for the shipper's definite expenditures wasted by its delay, even though the shipper would have incurred those expenses had the carrier performed and cannot prove lost profits.

sections.Parties: Security Stove & Manufacturing Co., a furnace manufacturer, was the plaintiff shipper. American Railway Express Co., the defendant carrier, appealed from a judgment reimbursing the expenses Security wasted on a convention exhibit that the carrier's late delivery frustrated.
sections.Procedural History: After a bench trial the court entered judgment for Security for its exhibition expenses; the opinion's opening describes an $801.50 principal judgment plus interest, totaling $1,000, though its later itemization totals $801.51. The carrier appealed. On May 23, 1932, the Kansas City Court of Appeals of Missouri affirmed.
sections.Material Facts:
Security made a furnace with a special combination oil and gas burner and wanted to show it at the American Gas Association convention in Atlantic City during the week beginning October 11, 1926. Its president hoped to interest the Henry L. Dougherty Company; the shipment was for demonstration, not for sale at the convention. Security reserved a booth, by which time it was too late to ship by freight. On September 18 it wrote the carrier explaining the exhibit and the need for arrival by October 8. The carrier's representative said shipment on October 4 would allow timely delivery. Security wrote again on October 1 and had the goods collected on October 2: twenty-one numbered packages. It paid the regular rate and asked for no special route, train, or preference.

The president arrived about October 11 and found the shipment at the booth without the gas manifold, the exhibit's most important part, which could not be replaced there. The missing package was in the carrier's St. Louis "over and short" department and had not arrived when the convention closed on Thursday. Ordinary transit took three or four days.

Security claimed its express charges, return freight, railway and Pullman fares, hotel charges, its president's time, an employee's wages, and booth rental.
sections.Issue: May a shipper recover from a carrier the expenses of a frustrated exhibition, including booth rental incurred before the shipping agreement, when it does not claim or prove lost profits and the expenses would have been incurred even had the carrier delivered on time? Did the claim rest on an unlawful special contract to deliver by a fixed date?
sections.Holding: The Kansas City Court of Appeals of Missouri, in 1932, in an opinion by Judge Bland in which all concurred, affirmed the judgment for the shipper. A carrier with notice of the shipment's exhibition purpose and the importance of timely arrival is liable for the shipper's definite wasted expenditures, including the booth rental, without proof of speculative profits. The claim was for failure to deliver within a reasonable time and did not depend on an unlawful preferential contract.
sections.Reasoning:
The carrier argued that the suit enforced a special promise to deliver by a fixed date, which federal interstate-commerce law forbade as discrimination among shippers. The court accepted the rule against preferential contracts but read the unchallenged petition liberally as alleging failure to deliver within a reasonable time. The October 8 date showed the ordinary time for carriage and the carrier's knowledge of the purpose; the arrangement demanded nothing another shipper could not get on the same terms.

Delay damages are ordinarily the difference in market value between timely and actual delivery, but that measure missed the known exhibition purpose. A carrier given sufficient notice of peculiar circumstances producing unusual losses can be responsible for the real loss contemplated. The numbered package's presence in the over-and-short department indicated mistake or negligence, which the carrier made no effort to explain; the court described negligence as practically conceded.

The carrier also argued that only lost profits were recoverable and that the expenses would have been incurred anyway, so refunding them restored the pre-contract position. There was no claim or evidence of lost profits, and the court held that profits were not the exclusive measure for a demonstration shipment. The breach deprived Security of the purpose for which the expenses were incurred, and without reimbursement it would receive no substantial compensation. The booth rental, though incurred before the shipping agreement, was allowed because Security arranged the exhibit in contemplation of the carrier's common-law obligation to accept and transport goods with reasonable dispatch.

The casebook presents the case as a problem asking whether the listed expenses may be recovered.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-116.rule: A party may not recover for a loss following the other party's breach that he could have avoided by taking available protective action himself.

sections.Parties: The plaintiff, Vertue, was a carrier who brought an action on an agreement to carry goods and deliver them at a place the defendant would appoint. He claimed for the death of his horses, which he attributed to the defendant's failure to appoint a place.
sections.Procedural History: The case was in King's Bench. According to the Ventris report, after a not-guilty plea and a verdict for the plaintiff there was a motion in arrest of judgment. In the Keble report, after the verdict and the staying of judgment, Holt asked the court to permit judgment for the plaintiff. Both reports end with judgment stayed. The ruling is attributed to the court collectively. Keble places the case in Trinity Term of the twenty-ninth year of Charles II, headed 1677; Ventris places it in Easter Term of that year; the casebook gives 1678.
sections.Material Facts:
Two reports survive and differ on details. In the Keble report, the agreement was to carry corn from a place identified as A. to Ipswich, Suffolk, and deliver it at a place the defendant would appoint, with no time stated. The plaintiff averred that he carried the corn on a particular day and notified the defendant, who failed to appoint a delivery place, and that this omission caused four of his horses to become diseased and die.

In the Ventris report, the carriage was of the defendant's timber to the defendant's house. The plaintiff declared that the defendant delayed six hours in specifying where to deliver, and that his horses, hot from hauling and standing in the open air, died soon afterward. That report does not say four horses. These are pleading allegations; neither report gives a carriage price or a valuation of the horses.
sections.Issue: Is a defendant who failed to appoint a place for delivery of carried goods answerable for the death of the carrier's horses, when the carrier could have taken the horses out of the cart or put the goods down rather than leave the horses standing?
sections.Holding: King's Bench, in a ruling attributed to the court collectively and reported under the twenty-ninth year of Charles II, stayed judgment for the plaintiff after verdict. The defendant was not answerable for the loss of the horses, because the plaintiff could have taken the horses out of the cart or put the corn down somewhere in Ipswich. The reports give no award or damages calculation.
sections.Reasoning:
In the Keble report, Holt argued for the plaintiff that the defendant had caused the nonperformance of the agreement and should answer for the consequential damage. The court rejected the argument because the plaintiff could have taken the horses out of the cart or laid the corn down anywhere in Ipswich; the failure to appoint a place did not make the defendant answerable for a loss the plaintiff could have prevented.

In the Ventris report, the argument on the motion in arrest of judgment was that letting the horses stand was the plaintiff's folly, and that the defendant was not bound, on pain of an action of this kind, to receive the timber or appoint a place; on a refusal the carrier could recover his agreed compensation for the carriage after doing his part, but could not maintain this action. Ventris attributes the folly explanation to the motion and reports that all the court agreed to stay judgment.

The casebook uses the case for the principle of avoidability: a promisee cannot recover a loss that reasonable protective action would have avoided. Its account combines details from both reports. Restatement section 350 and the general rules on mitigation appear in the casebook's later discussion and are not the words of either report.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-117.rule: Damages for breach of a promise to deliver stock under an option are the stock's market value at the time of the breach less the exercise price, and an issuer's earlier repudiation does not fix the breach date if the holder keeps the option alive.

sections.Parties: Charles Hermanowski, formerly chairman, president, and chief executive of Acton Corp., was the plaintiff. He sued Acton, the defendant, for refusing to honor a stock option granted when he resigned. Acton maintained that it had validly cancelled the option and asserted counterclaims. On appeal Acton was the appellant and Hermanowski cross-appealed on the calculation of the exercise price.
sections.Procedural History: After a diversity bench trial in the Eastern District of New York, Judge Glasser issued findings and conclusions on August 10, 1983, holding that Acton had breached an irrevocable five-year option, fixing damages at $415,030 with interest from November 12, 1979, and dismissing Acton's unsupported counterclaims. On March 7, 1984, a Second Circuit panel of Judges Meskill, Pierce, and Pratt, per curiam, affirmed on Acton's appeal but remanded on Hermanowski's cross-appeal for reconsideration of the exercise-price calculation alone, affirming on all other issues. The brief covers both stages.
sections.Material Facts:
Hermanowski's March 1973 employment contract paid $65,000 a year through December 31, 1976. At an April 11, 1975 board meeting he offered to resign. The board accepted and resolved, in consideration of terminating his employment agreement, to pay $25,000 and grant a five-year nonqualified option for 50,000 common shares at $2 each. A handwritten agreement signed that evening said the option would be under the terms of Acton's 1972 nonqualified stock plan, which allowed the company to terminate options on notice. In December 1975 Acton sent option certificates reciting the cancellation provision; Hermanowski signed with an express proviso that the option was noncancelable. In June 1976 Acton asserted cancellability and gave thirty days' termination notice. Hermanowski objected in July and September without response.

On September 28, 1979, within the five years, Hermanowski sent a $10,000 bank check for 5,000 shares. Acton returned it with a November 9 letter saying it found no exercisable option; he learned of the rejection on November 12. Two ten-percent stock dividends had enlarged the option to 60,500 shares. On November 12 the stock's high was $12.125 and its low $11.50. The option covered restricted stock, and the experts disagreed between a 25 and a 30 percent discount.
sections.Issue: Did the agreement's reference to the nonqualified stock plan make the option cancellable by Acton? If not, did the breach occur when Acton purported to cancel in 1975 or 1976 or when it refused the exercise in November 1979, and are damages measured at the breach date or by the highest intermediate market price within a reasonable period afterward?
sections.Holding: The Eastern District of New York, in 1983, per Judge Glasser, held that Acton had granted an irrevocable five-year option, that its attempted cancellation did not terminate it, and that its refusal in November 1979 breached the agreement as to all shares under the option. Damages were the market value on November 12, 1979, discounted 25 percent to $8.86 a share, or $536,030, less a $121,000 option price, for $415,030. The Second Circuit, in 1984, per curiam, approved the liability reasoning, the breach date, and the measure of damages, and remanded only for reconsideration of whether the exercise price should have been $100,000.
sections.Reasoning:
Acton argued that the agreement incorporated every provision of the nonqualified plan, including cancellation. Hermanowski said the reference only avoided the qualified plan's automatic termination on leaving employment. The court found it implausible that an experienced executive would give up approximately $100,000 remaining under his employment agreement for $25,000 and an illusory option. Treating the reference as ambiguous, it admitted evidence of the negotiations; directors Mamber and Koehl testified that the option was meant to be noncancelable for five years.

On timing, an option is an irrevocable offer, and Acton's unilateral withdrawal did not extinguish Hermanowski's right; good faith did not excuse repudiation. He could treat the repudiation as a present breach or ignore it and exercise when he chose, and he kept the option. Letting Acton choose the earlier date would take away the option's opportunity to speculate. The later refusal breached as to all shares, since further tender would have been futile.

On the measure, the highest-intermediate-price rule applies to conversion of property the owner already had, allowing time to replace it. Acton had converted nothing; a broken promise to deliver stock called for the ordinary contract measure at the time and place of breach.

The Second Circuit questioned multiplying $2 by the dividend-adjusted 60,500 shares; Hermanowski argued that the aggregate price remained $100,000, which would add $21,000. Unsure whether the district judge had an evidentiary reason for $121,000, it did not award the increase itself.

The casebook builds a problem on the case with simplified, hypothetical prices, and its label of the case as affirmed omits the limited remand.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-119.rule: A buyer's market-price damages for nondelivery may be limited to its actual lost resale profit where the seller knew of the resale contract, the buyer has not shown liability to its own customer, and the seller did not breach in bad faith.

sections.Parties: Allied Canners & Packers, Inc., a San Francisco exporter of food products, was the plaintiff buyer. Victor Packing Co., a Fresno fruit packer and processor, was the defendant seller, which conceded that it breached by failing to deliver raisins. Allied, though it won at trial, appealed to obtain market-price damages in place of the smaller sum awarded.
sections.Procedural History: After a bench trial, judgment was entered in July 1981 for Allied for $4,462.50, its anticipated gain on the transaction. The trial court refused the market-price formula because it regarded Allied's four-percent gain as a broker's commission and Allied as outside the buyer's remedies. Allied appealed, seeking approximately $150,000. On December 18, 1984, the California Court of Appeal, First District, Division Two, held that Allied was a buyer but affirmed the award on a different rationale, with each party bearing its own costs on appeal. Rehearing was denied with a modification on January 17, 1985, and the California Supreme Court denied a hearing on February 21, 1985.
sections.Material Facts:
On September 3 and 8, 1976, Allied contracted to buy from Victor two groups of five containers of Natural Thompson Seedless raisins, 375,000 pounds in all, for delivery FOB Oakland in October. The price was 29.75 cents per pound with a four-percent discount, giving Allied an agreed anticipated gain of $4,462.50. Allied had corresponding resale contracts with Japanese firms. Victor, as a packer, could buy reserve raisins from the federal Raisin Administrative Committee at 22 cents per pound before a cutoff at 8:30 a.m. on September 10; Allied could not buy directly. Heavy rains on September 9 damaged the crop, and the committee withdrew its offer from members who had not submitted deposits. Victor had not applied in time. On September 15 Victor announced that it would not deliver. Allied did not cover. When the market reopened in October prices were far higher: the trial court used 80 cents, and the parties stipulated to 87 cents on October 18.

One Japanese buyer agreed to rescind its three-container purchase. Shoei demanded delivery of the other seven containers, but its agreement protected Allied against liability from specified events beyond Allied's control. By the time of judgment the limitation period had expired, Shoei had never sued, and nothing showed that Allied had paid it anything.
sections.Issue: Was Allied a buyer entitled to the remedies of the California Commercial Code? If so, could it recover under section 2713 the difference between market price and contract price, $150,281.25 on the seven containers, when that sum far exceeded the $4,462.50 it would have earned had Victor performed?
sections.Holding: The California Court of Appeal, in 1984, in an opinion by Justice Rouse with Presiding Justice Kline and Justice Smith concurring, held that Allied was a buyer, not a broker, but affirmed the $4,462.50 award. Where the seller knew the buyer had a resale contract, the buyer had not shown that it would be liable in damages to its own customer, and there was no finding that the seller acted in bad faith, the policy of section 1106 limited the buyer to its actual loss.
sections.Reasoning:
The trial court's broker characterization was legal error. A buyer is one who buys or contracts to buy goods; the contracts named Allied and Victor, Victor was to deliver to Allied and would have sued Allied for nonpayment, and Allied was invoiced and paid from its own account. Back-to-back purchases and resales are ordinary middleman transactions.

Buyer's remedies therefore applied. Cover under section 2712 requires an actual substitute purchase, while section 2713 gives a market formula to a buyer who has not covered, and failure to cover does not forfeit other remedies. The court reviewed scholarship treating market damages as hypothetical cover, as a historical survival, or as a statutory baseline deterring breach, and recognized opposing lines of authority and that a market formula need not match a middleman's actual loss.

It gave effect to section 1106's principle that remedies put the injured party in as good a position as performance. Three features supported the limit: Victor knew of the resale contracts, Allied had not shown downstream liability, and there was no finding of bad faith. A prior case awarding market damages without cover was distinguished because no resale contract there defined the buyer's expected gain. The court did not hold that actual profit always caps a noncovering buyer's recovery, and it reserved what degree of bad faith might justify full market damages. It declined to infer a deliberate profitable breach, given the supply problem and Victor's efforts to obtain a release from the committee.

The casebook's account appears within the Tongish opinion, which criticizes the case.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-120.rule: A brokerage agreement that entitles the broker to a commission at the time of closing makes closing a condition precedent, so no commission is owed if the purchaser defaults before closing.

sections.Parties: Harding Realty, Inc., a real estate broker, was the plaintiff and appellant. Turnberry Towers Corporation, a condominium developer, was the defendant and appellee. Harding sued for its commission, or a share of the forfeited deposits, on two condominium sales that never closed, and alternatively sought recovery in quantum meruit.
sections.Procedural History: On undisputed facts the trial court entered final summary judgment for Turnberry on Harding's entire action. Harding appealed. Florida's Third District Court of Appeal affirmed on August 2, 1983, and denied rehearing on September 21, 1983.
sections.Material Facts:
Harding entered written brokerage agreements with Turnberry and procured two corporations as prospective purchasers of two condominium units. The purchasers signed binding purchase-and-sale contracts and paid earnest-money deposits, then defaulted without closing. Turnberry kept both deposits under the purchase contracts. Harding demanded a share and then sued for its commission. The report does not give the amounts of the deposits.

The brokerage agreement, which Harding drafted, provided that Harding would be entitled to a three-percent commission at the time of closing on sales to clients brought by its salespeople. Neither closing occurred.
sections.Issue: Did the clause entitling the broker to a commission at the time of closing merely fix when an already-earned commission was payable, or make closing a condition precedent to any right to a commission? If no commission was owed under the agreement, could the broker recover in quantum meruit?
sections.Holding: Florida's Third District Court of Appeal, in 1983, in an opinion by Judge Nesbitt for a panel with Judges Hendry and Baskin, affirmed summary judgment for the developer. The agreement expressly conditioned Harding's entitlement to a commission on closing, and because neither sale closed the brokerage contract barred recovery as a matter of law. Quantum meruit was unavailable because the law will not imply a contract where a valid express contract governs the relationship.
sections.Reasoning:
The court first characterized the agreement as employing Harding to effect a sale, not merely to find a ready, willing, and able buyer. Under the ordinary rule, a broker so employed earns the commission either by completing the sale or by presenting the seller with a binding, enforceable written purchase-and-sale agreement, and in the latter case the buyer's later default generally does not defeat the commission. So Harding could not be denied a commission merely because the purchasers defaulted.

That default rule can be varied by express language. Citing Florida decisions and noting conflicting decisions elsewhere, the court adopted what it called the greater weight of authority: provisions making the commission payable at sale, closing, or settlement make that event a condition precedent to the obligation to pay. Harding's wording was an especially strong example because it tied entitlement itself, not only payment, to closing, and Harding had drafted it. Since it was uncontroverted that neither closing occurred, producing binding purchase contracts did not satisfy the condition, and Turnberry's retention of the deposits under the separate purchase agreements did not satisfy it either.

On quantum meruit, restitution could not substitute for the express agreement's closing contingency. The court did not hold that brokerage services can never support restitution where there is no enforceable express agreement.

The casebook cites the case in a note on the closing clause and compares it with construction-payment provisions, a comparison that is the editors' question and not part of the holding.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-121.rule: Unless the parties agree otherwise, written notice exercising an option is effective only when the optionor receives it, so notice mailed on the last day of the term but received the next day is too late.

sections.Parties: John Livesey and Dwight Ziegler, doing business as Livesey Enterprises, were the plaintiffs and held an option to buy real estate from the defendant, Copps Corporation. They sought specific performance of the option after Copps refused to convey. The buyers were the appellants.
sections.Procedural History: On undisputed affidavit evidence the Portage County circuit court denied the buyers' motion for summary judgment, granted Copps's motion, and dismissed the complaint. The buyers appealed. On May 29, 1979, the Wisconsin Court of Appeals affirmed. The reporter also records that a petition for review was denied.
sections.Material Facts:
In 1975 the parties negotiated development of a shopping center on Copps's land. Their attorneys exchanged drafts by mail, and four documents were executed in Stevens Point as of October 31, 1975: Copps conveyed one parcel to Livesey, Livesey leased it back to Copps, and Copps granted Livesey an option on the adjoining parcel. The option ran for twelve months from signing and required written notice to Copps during its term. The lease-back, by contrast, expressly deemed notice delivered when registered or certified and deposited in the mail.

In 1976 the parties extended the option. Livesey retyped it, keeping the term and notice language, and mailed it to Copps, which returned executed copies by mail; the new option was signed November 15, 1976. Livesey mailed an exercise notice by certified mail on November 15, 1977. Copps received it on November 16 and refused to convey.
sections.Issue: When did a twelve-month option signed on November 15, 1976 expire, and was a written notice of exercise that was mailed on the last day of the term but received the following day effective to exercise the option?
sections.Holding: The Wisconsin Court of Appeals, in 1979, in an opinion by Presiding Judge Gartzke for a panel with Judges Bablitch and Dykman, affirmed the dismissal. The option expired at midnight on November 15, 1977, so the mailing was within the term. But because the option required written notice to Copps during its term, the notice had to be received within the term, and receipt on November 16 came too late. Copps had no obligation to convey.
sections.Reasoning:
On the expiration date, the court applied Wisconsin common-law decisions, not the statutory computation provisions. The common-law rule excludes the first day when time is measured from a specified date and includes it when measured from an event. This option ran from the date of signing, so November 15, 1976 was excluded and the option ran through midnight on November 15, 1977.

On notice, time is ordinarily essential to an option. The court recognized that an option is a continuing offer and that sending an offer by mail can imply permission to accept by mail; because Copps had returned the revised option by mail, a mailed exercise could have been effective on dispatch unless the option's terms required otherwise. The requirement of written notice to Copps during the term supplied that qualification. Wisconsin notice law generally requires actual receipt absent custom, statute, estoppel, or an express stipulation. Relying also on Corbin's explanation that notice of exercise can operate as a condition of an existing contractual duty, the court adopted the majority view that notice exercising an option must arrive unless the parties agree otherwise. The buyers' California authority rested on a codified dispatch rule that Wisconsin lacked. The lease-back's clause making notice effective on mailing reinforced the reading: when these parties wanted notice to take effect on mailing, they said so.

The casebook uses the case to illustrate strict timing for options.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-122.rule: A subcontract provision conditioning payment on the owner's payment is construed by the court as a matter of law: if unambiguous it is a condition precedent, and if ambiguous it merely fixes a reasonable time for the general contractor to pay.

sections.Parties: DEC Electric, Inc., an electrical subcontractor, sought payment for completed work from Raphael Construction Corporation, the general contractor. Raphael refused to pay because the owner had not paid it. The case reached the Florida Supreme Court on a certified question after both lower courts sustained Raphael's refusal to pay.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court determined as a matter of law that paragraph 6 of the subcontract unambiguously required payment by the owner before Raphael owed DEC anything. The Fourth District Court of Appeal affirmed, but, describing the paragraph as somewhat confusing and ambiguous and doubting whether a judge or a jury should construe it, certified the question to the Florida Supreme Court. On March 22, 1990, the Florida Supreme Court answered the certified question in the affirmative, found the provision unambiguous, and approved the district court's result.
sections.Material Facts:
DEC subcontracted with Raphael to do electrical work on a construction project. The owner later shut the project down. It was undisputed that DEC had performed satisfactorily and was entitled to $25,612 plus interest for the work, but Raphael had not been paid by the owner and refused to pay DEC.

Paragraph 6 of the subcontract dealt with sworn statements, lien waivers, interim draws, and payment according to the general contractor's estimate of completion on its billing to the owner. Its operative condition expressly provided that no funds would be owed to the subcontractor unless the owner paid the general contractor in accordance with the sworn statement. It also stated that the subcontractor understood that, on nonpayment, it had recourse against the owner through the mechanics' lien law or other procedures for the sums due.
sections.Issue: Must provisions in contracts between general contractors and subcontractors or suppliers concerning the conditions or timing of payment be construed as a matter of law by the court, and did paragraph 6 of this subcontract make the owner's payment a condition precedent to the general contractor's duty to pay?
sections.Holding: The Florida Supreme Court, in 1990, in a unanimous opinion by Justice McDonald, answered the certified question in the affirmative: such payment provisions are construed as a matter of law. Paragraph 6 unambiguously made payment by the owner a prerequisite to Raphael's obligation, so DEC could not recover the unpaid balance from Raphael despite its satisfactory work. The court approved the district court's result.
sections.Reasoning:
Raphael argued that ambiguous contract terms ordinarily raise a factual question of intent for a jury. The court accepted that proposition for most settings but kept its special rule of judicial interpretation for provisions allocating the risk of the owner's nonpayment between contractors and subcontractors. It did not turn every contractual ambiguity into a question of law.

The court's earlier Peacock decision had treated these provisions as suited to judicial interpretation because the commercial relationship is common and the usual intention does not vary materially from one transaction to the next, even if the language does. Small subcontractors generally need payment to stay in business and ordinarily do not intend to assume the risk that the owner will not pay. That supported a default against imposing the risk through ambiguous language.

There are accordingly two possible constructions. An unambiguous risk-shifting provision makes the owner's payment a condition precedent to the general contractor's obligation. An ambiguous provision instead fixes a reasonable time for the general contractor to pay. The general contractor bears the burden of clearly expressing a shift of the risk. Once the judge finds a provision ambiguous, the default settles its effect and nothing remains for a jury. The court declined to recede from Peacock or from Aetna Casualty, which applied the same approach in an action on a surety payment bond.

Reading paragraph 6 as a whole, the court found that it clearly made the owner's payment a prerequisite.

The casebook's note reproduces the certified question and the answer and explains the two constructions, but omits the project facts and the finding that paragraph 6 was unambiguous.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-123.rule: A pay-if-paid clause making the owner's payment a condition precedent to a general contractor's duty to pay a subcontractor is unenforceable as contrary to public policy, because it indirectly waives the subcontractor's protected mechanics' lien rights.

sections.Parties: Wm. R. Clarke Corporation, Barsotti's, Garvin Fire Protection, and Church and Larsen were subcontractors of Keller Construction, the general contractor on a Los Angeles building rehabilitation. They sued Safeco Insurance Company of America, the surety on Keller's labor-and-material payment bond, for work the owner never paid for. Safeco, having lost below, sought reversal in the California Supreme Court.
sections.Procedural History: After the owner stopped paying and Keller declined to pay them, the subcontractors recorded liens and brought separate actions on the bond against Safeco. Three were resolved by summary judgment and one by a bench trial; each ended in judgment for the subcontractor. The Court of Appeal consolidated the appeals and affirmed. On June 26, 1997, the California Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Appeal's judgment and remanded for further proceedings consistent with its opinion. Rehearing was denied September 3, 1997, with three justices voting to grant it.
sections.Material Facts:
In 1990 the owner of a Los Angeles commercial building hired Keller to rehabilitate it. Keller subcontracted work to the four subcontractors. Each subcontract expressly made Keller's receipt of funds from the owner a condition of its obligation to pay, whatever the reason for nonpayment, including the fault of any participant. Three subcontracts also had an addendum repeating that the contractor was not liable if unpaid and purporting to preserve mechanics' lien rights as the subcontractor's sole remedy; Barsotti's had not signed the addendum, but the parties treated all four alike on appeal.

At the owner's insistence and under the general contract, Keller obtained a $16.5 million labor-and-material payment bond from Safeco, binding Keller and Safeco to persons furnishing work or materials to the project. The recorded bond invoked the statutory payment-bond scheme and required a claimant to record a lien or give timely notice before suing. After substantial work the owner stopped paying, apparently because of insolvency, and Keller then declined to pay the subcontractors.
sections.Issue: Is a true pay-if-paid provision, which makes the owner's payment a condition precedent to the general contractor's obligation to pay its subcontractors, enforceable in California, so that a payment-bond surety may rely on it to defeat the subcontractors' claims on the bond?
sections.Holding: The California Supreme Court, in 1997, in an opinion by Justice Kennard for a four-justice majority, with Justice Chin dissenting joined by Justices Mosk and Baxter, held that the pay-if-paid provisions were unenforceable on public-policy grounds because they accomplished indirectly the waiver of mechanics' lien rights that the anti-waiver rules forbid directly. Keller therefore owed payment under the subcontracts and Safeco was liable on the bond. The majority added that Safeco would lose even on its alternative theory, because the bond covered valid lien claims independently.
sections.Reasoning:
Safeco argued that a surety's obligation cannot exceed its principal's, and that Keller's duty never arose because the owner never paid. That depended on the condition being valid. The majority distinguished clauses read as merely setting the usual time for payment, which leave an unconditional duty after a reasonable period, from true conditions that can eliminate payment altogether; this was the latter.

California's Constitution secures lien rights to those who improve property, and former Civil Code section 3262 restricted waivers to prescribed forms tied to payment. Safeco said the condition waived no lien but only prevented a right to payment from arising. The majority rejected the practical result: former section 3140 measured lien recovery by the amount due under the contract's terms, so a valid condition and an unpaid owner could leave a subcontractor with no enforceable lien despite completed work. Freedom of contract did not override that legislative policy, the clause reached nonpayment for any reason and not only insolvency, and the addendum's reservation of lien rights could be illusory.

On the bond, Keller was a principal and co-obligor, and the bond's language covered valid project lien claims whether or not the claimant had an enforceable direct claim against Keller. The court disapproved Kalfountzos to the extent it implied that a principal has no bond liability absent another payment obligation.

Justice Chin, dissenting, would have read section 3140 as fixing the lien's value at the contract amount without letting the owner's default erase the lien, so that the parties could share the risk of nonpayment. He also viewed the surety as guaranteeing only Keller's default, not the owner's, and would have reversed.

The casebook's note cites the case for California's public-policy invalidation of such clauses.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-124.rule: A merchant buyer's rejection of goods under a satisfaction clause is effective only if its dissatisfaction is genuine and in good faith, meaning honesty in fact and observance of reasonable commercial standards of fair dealing.

sections.Parties: Jonah Cornett and Ralph Moore, farmers, were the plaintiff sellers. Neumiller Farms, Inc., a potato broker, was the defendant buyer. The sellers sued after Neumiller rejected potatoes under their contract, and Neumiller appealed from the jury's verdict for the sellers.
