sections.Procedural History: A jury returned a $17,500 verdict for the sellers. Neumiller appealed. On March 9, 1979, the Alabama Supreme Court affirmed, finding evidence to support wrongful rejection and an award within the damages recoverable under Alabama's enactment of UCC section 2-708(2).
sections.Material Facts:
On March 3, 1976, the parties signed a contract for twelve loads of United States Grade No. 1 chipping potatoes, to be delivered in July and August. Each load was 430 hundredweight at $4.25 per hundredweight, or $1,827.50 a load. The potatoes also had to chip to the buyer's satisfaction. The sellers' crop yielded twenty to twenty-four loads. Neumiller accepted three loads without objection while the market price was $4.25, but rejected further loads after the market fell to $2.00, claiming they would not chip satisfactorily.

An agricultural-extension expert tested samples and found the potatoes suitable in all respects. After a demand for performance Neumiller agreed to try another load, which the sellers obtained from a grower named Hartline. Neumiller's agent had recently bought potatoes from Hartline's fields at $2.00, but expressed dissatisfaction when the sellers offered potatoes from the same fields at the contract price. When the sellers offered to get the remaining nine loads from other growers, the agent rejected any further performance and referred to being able to buy potatoes for $2.00. At the final rejection the sellers had seventeen to twenty-one loads still in the fields and had sold only about four loads despite efforts in several regional markets. This is the account the jury could have found.
sections.Issue: May a merchant buyer reject goods under a clause requiring them to perform to its satisfaction when the evidence shows the goods were suitable and the rejection followed a fall in the market price? Are the sellers' damages limited to the difference between contract and market price under section 2-708(1), or may they recover under section 2-708(2)?
sections.Holding: The Alabama Supreme Court, in 1979, in an opinion by Justice Shores with four justices concurring, affirmed the verdict. A rejection based on dissatisfaction that is not in good faith is ineffective and is a breach of contract, and the jury could find that Neumiller's claimed dissatisfaction was not in good faith. The $17,500 award was within the damages recoverable under section 2-708(2), because the market-difference measure would not have put the sellers in the position performance would have.
sections.Reasoning:
The buyer claimed the potatoes failed the satisfaction requirement. The court recognized the statutory right to reject nonconforming goods but required the dissatisfaction to be genuine and in good faith, not a device to escape an unfavorable bargain. Neumiller dealt professionally in farm products and was a merchant, so its good faith included both honesty in fact and observance of reasonable commercial standards of fair dealing. For a merchant buying fungible goods, an objective standard could test the claim. The expert's finding and the buyer's different treatment of the same grower's potatoes at different prices let the jury reject Neumiller's assertion.

On damages, Neumiller argued that section 2-708(1) limited recovery to $2.25 per hundredweight on the nine rejected loads. The court read the market formula as presupposing both an available market and an obligation on the seller to enter it. Some market remained, but the sellers had most of their crop unsold despite reasonable efforts. Requiring them to give Neumiller's nine loads priority in that limited market over their unallocated crop would sacrifice their own opportunity for the breaching buyer's benefit. The court distinguished an inventory consisting only of the contract goods, or a failure to make reasonable efforts to sell.

Subsection (2) allows profit including reasonable overhead, incidental damages, and reasonably incurred costs. The farmers had substantially performed and incurred substantially all their expenses. The nine loads' contract value was $16,447.50, and the sellers also claimed interest and freight; the verdict was within the recoverable amount.

The casebook presents the case in a note titled Cheaper Chips for the merchant good-faith analysis, and omits the mitigation and profit-measure reasoning.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-125.rule: A party whose duty is conditioned on its own satisfaction is excused if it is genuinely dissatisfied with the subject of the condition, even though other motives also make the transaction unattractive, provided it made reasonable efforts to bring the condition about.

sections.Parties: Columbia Christian College, Inc., the owner and seller of about 268 acres in east Multnomah County, Oregon, was the plaintiff and sued for specific performance of a land sale. Commonwealth Properties, Inc., the prospective buyer and developer, was the defendant and counterclaimed for return of its option payments. Commonwealth appealed the compensation award against it, and the college cross-appealed for more compensation.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court refused specific performance as impracticable but awarded the college $92,300 in equitable compensation for the period during which the land was tied up. Commonwealth appealed that award; the college cross-appealed for more but did not appeal the denial of specific performance. Reviewing the equity suit de novo, the Oregon Supreme Court on May 8, 1979 deleted the compensation award, awarded Commonwealth the return of its $35,000 in option payments, and affirmed the denial of specific performance, with costs to neither party. On rehearing, on June 19, 1979, it withdrew one explanation, adhered to its factual conclusions, and denied the petition.
sections.Material Facts:
The college's 1973 offer gave Commonwealth a 180-day option for $10,000, credited toward the price. Commonwealth was to investigate the land's suitability, seek annexation into Gresham, obtain satisfactory zoning, and seek utility permission. If it exercised an extension while applications were pending, it was required to purchase, subject to satisfactory government decisions. In February 1974 the parties agreed to a six-month extension for $25,000. Further extensions followed, including one in December 1974 supported by an increase in the proposed price from $3,800 to $4,100 per acre.

The planning commission recommended approving Commonwealth's concept plan only if concerns about drainage and offsite traffic improvements were solved in a final plan. Commonwealth estimated that the research to address them would cost another $100,000 and take six months, with approval still uncertain. It sought the December extension to ask the city council for approval without those conditions. In February 1975 the council approved the zoning ordinance conditioned on resolving the concerns in the final plan. Commonwealth then took part in document preparation and requested a title report, but in July wrote that unsatisfactory zoning ended the transaction. The college contended that the real motive was a decline in the housing market and Commonwealth's preference for smaller projects.
sections.Issue: Was Commonwealth excused from purchasing because satisfactory zoning was not obtained, even if a declining housing market also motivated its withdrawal? Did it breach its duty to make reasonable efforts to obtain satisfactory zoning by not filing a final plan? Was the college entitled to compensation, and Commonwealth to the return of its option payments?
sections.Holding: The Oregon Supreme Court, in 1979, in an opinion by Justice Howell, held that Commonwealth was in good faith dissatisfied with the conditioned zoning and had reasonably pursued approval, so it was excused from purchasing. Dissatisfaction must relate to the subject of the condition but need not be the party's only dissatisfaction. The court deleted the $92,300 compensation award, ordered the $35,000 in option payments returned to Commonwealth under the parties' proved refund agreement, and affirmed the denial of specific performance.
sections.Reasoning:
The court first held that Commonwealth had a contractual duty to purchase subject to the conditions; the different extension terms in 1974 did not free it from the original commitment.

It then separated satisfaction with the zoning obtained from the duty to make reasonable efforts to obtain it. Satisfactory zoning had not been obtained: the ordinance left wide discretion over the final plan and pointed to substantial offsite demands not contemplated at formation. A genuine contractual ground for refusing performance is not defeated because other concerns also make the deal unattractive, and here the zoning requirements themselves affected economic feasibility. Commonwealth's later document preparation, exploring whether to proceed, did not show satisfaction.

On reasonable efforts, Commonwealth did not have to spend $100,000 and six more months researching solutions for an already marginal project, or file a final plan without that research merely to go through the motions. On rehearing the court withdrew its statement that Commonwealth's knowledge of the burdens when it sought the December extension did not relate back to formation, and explained that Commonwealth could seek an extension to try for unconditional approval without committing itself either to abandon at once or to proceed whatever the council decided.

The college had bargained for the possibility that its land would be off the market without a sale, so that alone did not entitle it to compensation. The refund rested on the accepted extension letter, which contemplated return of the money if satisfactory zoning could not be obtained, and on the broker's testimony that the parties rejected a forfeiture.

The casebook quotes the case for the mixed-motive point; its example of a cheaper source of supply is the editors' hypothetical.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-126.rule: Parol evidence is admissible to show that a writing was not to take effect as a contract until a condition precedent occurred, unless the condition contradicts the writing or the writing expressly states that no outside conditions exist.

sections.Parties: The brief identifies the parties only as the plaintiff and the defendant. The defendant maintained that the writing sued on was not to operate as a contract until two approvals were given, and the plaintiff sought to exclude proof of that condition under the parol evidence rule.
sections.Procedural History: At the original trial the court excluded the defendant's testimony about the condition, and the jury answered the questions put to it. The trial court then concluded that the testimony should have been received and ordered a new trial on all issues. On appeal, the Wisconsin Supreme Court on May 8, 1951 affirmed the order granting a new trial.
sections.Material Facts: The defendant offered to prove that the writing was not to operate as a contract until both the union consented and a Mr. Quaal approved. The writing contained a clause describing it as complete in itself and stating that the first party was not bound by other terms or agreements. The brief states that the reported opinion does not give a detailed account of the underlying transaction, the amount demanded, or the jury's original result.
sections.Issue: Does the parol evidence rule, or a clause stating that the writing is complete in itself, bar testimony that the writing was not to become an effective contract until a third party consented and another person approved?
sections.Holding: The Wisconsin Supreme Court, in 1951, in an opinion by Justice Gehl, affirmed the order granting a new trial on all issues. The excluded testimony was admissible as proof of a condition precedent to the writing's effectiveness as a contract, and the completeness clause did not expressly exclude such a condition. The ruling did not decide that the defendant had proved the condition or owed nothing.
sections.Reasoning:
The court described the offered testimony as proof of a condition precedent necessary for the instrument to take effect as a contract. It was not aimed at altering the writing's contents, and the asserted condition was compatible with the written terms.

The court relied on decisions allowing extrinsic proof that a writing was not to take effect until a future event, so long as the alleged condition did not contradict the written conditions. It distinguished such proof from a condition subsequent, which would undo a contract after it had become effective. The evidence could show that the instrument never became operative as a contract at all. The court compared conditional stock subscriptions and earlier cases involving notes conditioned on a venture's profitability or on obtaining additional signatures.

The plaintiff relied on the clause describing the writing as complete in itself. The court did not find that language sufficient to exclude the condition. It distinguished Edward T. Kelly Co. v. von Zakobiel, where the writing declared itself irrevocable and stated that no conditions affecting it existed outside the document, which expressly excluded the very kind of condition sought to be proved. The court therefore did not hold that every integration clause lets in every alleged oral term.

Because the testimony was excluded, the jury had answered questions that did not properly address the issues, so a new trial on all issues was warranted.

The casebook cites the case in its note on merger clauses and conditions, for the availability of proof of an oral condition despite a completeness clause.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-127.rule: A builder who in good faith substantially performs a construction contract may recover the contract price less the reasonable cost of curing defects and omissions chargeable to the builder.

sections.Parties: Dollar, a builder, was the plaintiff. He sued O. Q. Kizziar and his wife, Mildred Kizziar, the owners of the property, for the price of constructing a medical clinic, for an additional sum under an alleged oral agreement to enlarge it, for foreclosure of his mechanics' and materialmen's lien, and for the balance on an earlier building contract. The Kizziars were the appellants.
sections.Procedural History: After a bench trial the trial court awarded Dollar the requested construction amounts less deductions, ordered foreclosure by sale, allowed $2,500 for costs and attorney fees, and awarded $902.60 on the earlier contract. The Kizziars appealed. On July 23, 1959, the Tenth Circuit accepted the finding of substantial performance and sustained several challenged findings, but remanded for additional findings and modification of the judgment on the deductions for the cooling system and uncompleted items. Rehearing was denied August 20.
sections.Material Facts:
On November 12, 1956, Dollar agreed in writing with O. Q. Kizziar to construct a building on property owned by Kizziar and his wife for $20,000. Dollar also claimed $2,863.50 under a later oral agreement to extend the planned 70-by-35-foot building to 77 feet in length, which the defendants denied. The building was a medical clinic occupied by the defendants' lessee from early April 1957, and the owners accepted the rental benefits. Changes had been made during construction at the request of the owners and the lessee.

The specifications called for a five-ply roof; Dollar installed four-ply, and adding the missing ply would cost $150. They called for a ducted Chrysler Air Temp heating and cooling system or its equal, with a duct in each room; the installed make was equivalent, but its cooling capacity was inadequate, and the trial court deducted $750 for window air conditioners. Painting, tile cleaning, mouldings, bathroom locks, and medicine cabinets had not been completed. The foundation did not conform to the specifications and the variance was not authorized, but undisputed evidence showed it was standard and adequate for the building, and there was no evidence of the cost of a conforming foundation or of a particular reason for the specified design.
sections.Issue: Under Oklahoma law, may a builder whose work departs from the specifications in several respects recover on an entire construction contract on the ground of substantial performance, and what deductions are the owners entitled to for the nonconforming foundation, the inadequate cooling system, and the uncompleted items?
sections.Holding: The Tenth Circuit, in 1959, in an opinion by Judge Pickett for a panel with Judges Murrah and Breitenstein, held that Dollar had substantially performed in good faith and could recover the contract price less the reasonable cost of curing defects and omissions chargeable to him. The adequate though nonconforming foundation was sufficient under substantial performance. The court remanded for an allowance based on an adequately functioning central cooling system and for the cost of completing the items the contract required, with the judgment to be modified accordingly.
sections.Reasoning:
The owners argued that the contract was entire and indivisible, so deficient performance barred recovery. Applying Oklahoma law, the court rejected a requirement of literal compliance with every detail where the builder made a good-faith effort and substantially supplied the building contracted for, especially where the owner has occupied and used it. It found no sign of bad faith. Substantial performance did not remove the owners' right to proper deductions.

The $150 roof deduction stood as the reasonable cost of the missing ply. The cooling system was different: the owners had bought a central system, and approval of an equivalent make did not authorize an inferior type or insufficient capacity, so a deduction for window units was inadequate. The owners were also entitled to the cost of completing required items that were neither completed nor waived, unless their own conduct had solely prevented completion.

On the foundation, the evidence of adequacy was undisputed and nothing showed the cost of conformity or a special purpose for the specified design. This was a factual application, not a holding that every structural deviation is immaterial.

The finding of the oral enlargement agreement was not clearly erroneous, given supporting testimony from the doctor who would occupy the building. A $3,500 note to the lessee signed by Dollar and Kizziar was to be paid from the judgment funds, with protection against double payment left to the trial court. The $2,500 fee allowance was sustained under Rule 15(b) although the complaint alleged $2,000.

The casebook cites the case in a note on variations on the rule, contrasting the adequate-foundation finding with a structural-defect proposition attributed to another decision.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-128.rule: Under the Sixth Circuit's prediction of Michigan law, application fraud discovered after discharge can supply just cause for the discharge if the misrepresentation was material, directly relevant to evaluating the candidate, and relied upon in hiring.

sections.Parties: Mildred Johnson, a former field relations manager, sued her former employer, Honeywell Information Systems, for breach of a just-cause employment contract and for retaliation prohibited by Michigan's Elliott-Larsen Civil Rights Act. Honeywell, the defendant, appealed after a jury verdict for Johnson on the contract claim and sought judgment in its favor. Johnson cross-appealed the directed verdict entered against her on the statutory claim.
sections.Procedural History:
Johnson sued in state court and Honeywell removed the action. Honeywell conceded a just-cause contract but sought summary judgment on two theories: that the newly discovered fraud constituted just cause, and that fraudulent inducement prevented formation of the claimed contract. The district court rejected the first theory because the fraud had not actually motivated the discharge and found factual disputes about materiality and reliance on the second. It later directed a verdict for Honeywell on the statutory claim because Johnson had not established retaliatory pretext. The contract claim produced a jury verdict for Johnson, and Honeywell's directed-verdict and postverdict motions on that claim were denied. Honeywell appealed and Johnson cross-appealed.

The Sixth Circuit reversed the denial of Honeywell's summary-judgment motion on the contract claim, affirmed the directed verdict on the civil-rights claim, and remanded with instructions to enter judgment for Honeywell on all counts. Rehearing was denied.
sections.Material Facts:
Johnson worked for Honeywell as a field relations manager from November 1976 until November 2, 1984, assisting branch managers with affirmative-action programs, EEOC charges, hiring and other personnel matters. Her reviews were generally favorable until mid-1983, when supervisors and internal clients complained about her availability, cooperation, effectiveness, flexibility and knowledge. Honeywell discharged her after she declined to resign, citing refusal to follow reasonable supervisory directions. Johnson maintained that her performance was satisfactory and that the discharge reflected conflict with managers over affirmative-action goals. Nearly a year earlier she had sent supervisors a memorandum complaining of discrimination against her; a supervisor investigated and found it without merit.

During discovery Honeywell learned that Johnson had falsely claimed a bachelor's degree from the University of Detroit, though she had completed only four courses and audited two. It also discovered false or exaggerated representations about Wayne State studies, prior jobs, and property-management work during a period of unemployment. The job advertisement required a college degree and four to six years of relevant experience, and her signed application warned that false information could cause immediate discharge later. The hiring manager stated that he relied on the claimed degree and would neither have hired nor interviewed her had he known the truth.
sections.Issue: Whether, under Michigan law, application fraud that the employer discovered only after discharge can provide just cause defeating a claim for breach of a just-cause employment contract, whether such fraud also bars relief under the Elliott-Larsen Civil Rights Act, and whether Johnson established protected opposition under that Act.
sections.Holding: The Sixth Circuit, in 1992, in an opinion by Judge Ryan for a panel of Ryan, Boggs and Senior Judge Godbold sitting by designation, held, predicting Michigan law, that sufficiently material application fraud could provide just cause even though the employer discovered it after discharge. On the evidence, reliance and materiality were established as a matter of law, so Johnson's fraud was sufficient just cause. The court also treated the after-acquired fraud as barring relief under Elliott-Larsen and, separately, held that Johnson had not established protected opposition to a violation of that Act. No separate opinion appears in the report.
sections.Reasoning:
The court found no controlling Michigan Supreme Court decision on after-acquired misconduct. It relied principally on the Michigan Court of Appeals' unpublished Bradley decision, which allowed misconduct predating termination to be substantive evidence even if discovered later, and on general contract doctrine, the rule's practical rationale, and the absence of contrary Michigan authority. It distinguished Toussaint's discussion of the jury's role in identifying an employer's true motive: that inquiry did not eliminate an independent defense based on application fraud. The court expressly recognized that the unknown facts were neither the actual nor the inducing cause of discharge.

The defense was bounded. In resume-fraud cases the misrepresentation must be material, directly relevant to evaluating a candidate, and relied upon in hiring, so that employers could not defeat otherwise impermissible discharges by searching for trivial inaccuracies. The court did not hold that every false application statement is just cause. Here Johnson admitted misrepresenting her education to obtain consideration, and the hiring manager's reliance was not genuinely disputed; the question was whether Honeywell would have hired her without the claimed degree.

On the statutory claim, the court relied on Summers' reasoning: even assuming retaliatory discharge, Honeywell showed it would not have hired Johnson and would have discharged her on discovering the fraud. Separately, complaints about resistance to affirmative-action goals did not identify practices required by Elliott-Larsen, and the memorandum showed at most one employee's alleged intolerance.

The casebook quotes the court's prediction about facts unknown at discharge in its discussion of after-acquired evidence.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-129.rule: In an employee-handbook contract action, after-acquired evidence of misconduct is a complete defense only if the employer proves by clear and convincing evidence that the misconduct was severe enough that it would in fact have fired the employee on that ground alone.

sections.Parties: Douglas Lewis, a machinist discharged by Fisher Service Company, sued Fisher in federal court for breach of its employee handbook, alleging demotion and discharge contrary to the handbook's discipline provisions. Fisher, the employer and defendant, sought judgment as a matter of law or a new trial after a jury verdict for Lewis and invoked misconduct it discovered after the discharge as a defense.
sections.Procedural History:
A June 1993 federal jury awarded Lewis $400,000 in actual damages representing back and front pay. That verdict was set aside for reasons unrelated to the certification, and a June 1994 retrial produced a $355,000 verdict. Fisher moved for judgment as a matter of law or a new trial. The district court concluded that, viewing the evidence favorably to Lewis, the original recording incident did not require overturning the verdict. To assist in disposing of the pending post-trial motion, it certified to the South Carolina Supreme Court whether South Carolina recognized an after-acquired-evidence defense in handbook cases and whether it could eliminate liability, cut off recovery at discovery, or cut off recovery at judgment.

The South Carolina Supreme Court's exact disposition was "Certified Questions Answered." It did not vacate the federal verdict, enter judgment for either litigant, or decide whether Fisher met the standard.
sections.Material Facts:
Fisher hired Lewis as a machinist in 1984 and gave him a Practices and Policies manual on his first day. The handbook promised progressive discipline but allowed immediate dismissal for violations of very serious and widely recognized behavior standards. In April 1991, when Lewis applied to become a quality-control inspector, he used a pocket recorder during an interview with supervisor Andy Simpson. The recording was later played to other employees in the break area. Fisher treated the incident as serious enough to bypass progressive discipline and discharged him. Lewis maintained that he had told Simpson of the recording and that another employee played it; Fisher claimed the recording was secret and that Lewis himself played it.

In a deposition after filing suit, Lewis admitted secretly recording a conversation with general manager David Suk and probably one with shop manager Jeff Klatt before his termination. Nondisclosure of these recordings was undisputed. Suk testified that secretly recording management was serious misconduct, that he did not know Lewis had recorded him, and that he would have immediately fired Lewis had he known. These later-discovered, earlier acts supplied the proposed defense; they were not the conduct Fisher knew about when it discharged him.
sections.Issue: Whether South Carolina recognizes after-acquired evidence of employee misconduct as a defense in an action for breach of an employee handbook, and if so whether it eliminates liability altogether or only cuts off recovery at the date of discovery or of judgment.
sections.Holding: The South Carolina Supreme Court, in 1998, in a unanimous opinion by Justice Toal in which Chief Justice Finney and Justices Moore, Waller and Burnett concurred, held that after-acquired evidence may defeat liability altogether in an employee-handbook contract action, but only upon clear and convincing proof that the misconduct was sufficiently severe that the employer actually would have fired the employee on that ground alone. The court did not decide whether Fisher met that standard; application was left to the certifying federal court.
sections.Reasoning:
The court traced the dispute over complete defenses through Summers and Wallace and then explained McKennon, which rejected a complete bar in an ADEA discrimination action and instead balanced deterrence and compensation against legitimate employer interests through remedies, generally permitting back pay until discovery while limiting reinstatement and front pay. South Carolina had adopted McKennon's approach in Baber, a statutory whistleblower action.

Reviewing other jurisdictions, the court found persuasive a distinction between private employment-contract claims and claims implicating major public interests, such as discrimination, whistleblowing or workers' compensation rights. Public protections justified refusing to let after-acquired misconduct erase liability for an employer's earlier statutory wrong. Handbook litigation concerned private rights and did not present those overriding purposes, so the court declined to prohibit absolutely the use of such evidence to defeat contractual liability. That distinction did not abolish Baber's different statutory treatment.

The court nevertheless recognized that employers sued on a handbook have an incentive to search an employee's record for minor missteps, such as previously tolerated tardiness, and that unrestricted use could make contractual promises effectively unenforceable. It therefore imposed two protections: the misconduct must be severe enough that the employee would in fact have been terminated on that ground alone had it been known at discharge, and the employer must prove this by clear and convincing evidence rather than a preponderance. A mere assertion that the employer could have fired the employee, or that the conduct violated some workplace rule, is insufficient.

The casebook cites the case in its after-acquired-evidence discussion as the handbook comparison and quotes the clear-and-convincing, would-have-terminated requirement.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-130.rule: After-acquired evidence of employee misconduct is a defense to a contract claim for discharge-related wages and benefits if the employer would have fired the employee for it, but in a wrongful-discharge tort action it limits remedies rather than barring liability.

sections.Parties: Dennis O'Day, a laid-off engineer, sued his former employer, McDonnell Douglas Helicopter Company, in federal court under the federal ADEA and the Arizona Civil Rights Act and also pleaded breach of contract and wrongful discharge in violation of public policy. McDonnell Douglas, the defendant, raised an after-acquired-evidence defense based on misconduct by O'Day that it learned of during the suit. The Arizona Supreme Court answered certified questions about the state contract and tort claims.
sections.Procedural History: After exhausting EEOC remedies, O'Day sued. The district court initially granted summary judgment for the employer on all counts under an after-acquired-evidence defense. The Ninth Circuit affirmed establishment of that defense but reversed the dismissal under McKennon's remedial principles and remanded for trial, reserving how the defense affected the state contract and tort claims. Those reserved questions prompted certification to the Arizona Supreme Court. Sitting en banc, that court answered the certified questions. It did not reverse or affirm an Arizona trial judgment, determine a damages amount, or decide the federal statutory counts.
sections.Material Facts:
McDonnell Douglas denied O'Day promotion to lead engineer on June 8, 1990. About a month later it laid him off during a general workforce reduction. O'Day was forty-six and had worked there fourteen years; he believed age motivated the adverse decisions.

The night after the promotion denial, O'Day searched his supervisor's office, took documents he thought useful to a discrimination claim, copied them, and returned the originals. McDonnell Douglas learned of that misconduct only after discovery in the suit began. The promotion denial therefore preceded the improper search and copying, while the layoff followed it. These facts supplied the setting for the certified questions; the Arizona court was not itself trying the alleged discriminatory motive.
sections.Issue: How after-acquired evidence of employee misconduct affects, under Arizona law, first a claim for breach of an employment contract and second a tort claim for wrongful discharge in violation of public policy: whether it bars liability or instead limits the available remedies.
sections.Holding: The Arizona Supreme Court, en banc, in 1998, in an opinion by Justice Martone in which Chief Justice Zlaket, Vice Chief Justice Jones, Justice Feldman and designated Judge Toci concurred (retired Justice Moeller not participating), answered that on the contract claim after-acquired evidence is a defense to discharge-related lost wages and benefits upon proof that the employer would have fired the employee had it known. On the tort claim, liability survives: if the employer shows it would have fired the employee, reinstatement and front pay are unavailable and lost past earnings run only from discharge until discovery, but other compensatory damages, including diminished earning capacity, and punitive damages remain available when supported by the evidence.
sections.Reasoning:
The court first described McKennon's balancing in statutory discrimination cases as a comparison for the distinct common-law questions before it.

On contract, it followed traditional doctrine, including Restatement section 237: an earlier uncured material failure can discharge the other party's remaining duties. The employer's ignorance of the misconduct did not eliminate the defense if it could show it would have discharged the employee had it known, and the court saw no need to revise contract doctrine merely to duplicate statutory and tort protections. The defense reached only wages and benefits lost because of discharge. It did not excuse duties already earned, equitable principles generally prevented recovering wages previously paid, and an employer that knew of the misconduct and chose to ignore it could not later rely on it. Because O'Day's promotion denial preceded his misconduct, the evidence did not bar a contract claim arising from that earlier refusal to promote.

On tort, the court rejected both ignoring the evidence, which would conflict with the employer's right to discharge, and a complete defense, which would defeat the tort's purpose of assigning consequences to the employer's wrongful conduct. A remedies-only approach gave significance to both parties' conduct. It distinguished specific future wages from this employer, lost because of the lawful basis for discharge, from general diminished earning capacity, which remained recoverable if proved.

Continuing compensatory and punitive exposure reduced the incentive to abuse the defense, and the employer still had to persuade the factfinder that it actually would have fired the employee; the court did not adopt Lewis's clear-and-convincing standard. O'Day's objection under Arizona constitutional provisions failed because they addressed enacted or statutory damage limits.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-131.rule: The clean-hands doctrine is discretionary and does not categorically bar enforcement of a professional football contract merely because the club agreed to keep the signing secret so a college player could appear in a postseason game.

sections.Parties: Houston Oilers, Inc., a professional football club in the AFL, sued Ralph Neely, a University of Oklahoma player who had signed with Houston and later signed with Dallas. Houston sought a declaration that its agreements with Neely were enforceable and an injunction restraining him from playing professional football for anyone other than Houston. Neely, the defendant, resisted on grounds of fraud, unclean hands and the statute of frauds. Houston was the appellant in the Tenth Circuit.
sections.Procedural History: Houston sued for a declaration of enforceability and an injunction. The trial court denied relief, finding fraud and a Texas statute-of-frauds problem in the service-station agreement, which it treated as too indefinite. Houston appealed. The Tenth Circuit held the agreements valid and enforceable, rejected the fraud, clean-hands and statute-of-frauds grounds for denying relief, and reversed and remanded with instructions to grant the injunction. Rehearing was denied on June 23, 1966.
sections.Material Facts:
Neely, a prominent University of Oklahoma senior, wanted a professional career and the financial benefits of competition between the AFL and NFL. On November 28, 1964, Houston acquired AFL draft rights to him and Baltimore acquired NFL rights. Advised throughout by his father-in-law Robert Forte, Neely negotiated with Houston's president, K. S. Adams, Jr. Houston offered a $25,000 bonus, a four-year no-cut contract at $16,000 annually, guaranteed off-season real-estate employment paying at least $5,000 annually, and an arrangement to build and convey a Phillips 66 service station. On December 1 Neely executed the standard player agreements for 1965 through 1968 and the ancillary agreements, which the parties stipulated formed a single transaction.

Neely insisted on payment during 1964 for tax reasons and on confidentiality so that he could play in the January 2 Gator Bowl. The bonus check was made payable to Forte as trustee and public announcement was deferred. The written player agreements declared themselves immediately binding on execution and required filing with the league commissioner within ten days; Houston inserted December 1 and filed them.

Dallas later acquired Baltimore's draft rights. Neely sent withdrawal letters dated December 29 and returned Houston's bonus check, and Dallas deposited $25,000 to his account. He disclosed his Houston dealings to his college coach, was declared ineligible on January 1, signed with Dallas that evening, and played there in 1965.
sections.Issue: Whether Houston's contracts with Neely were valid and enforceable by an injunction against his playing for another club, or whether relief was barred by fraud, by the clean-hands doctrine because of the secrecy arrangement, or by the Texas statute of frauds as applied to the service-station agreement.
sections.Holding: The Tenth Circuit, in 1966, in an opinion by Judge Pickett for a panel of Pickett, Hill and Seth, held Neely's agreements with Houston valid and enforceable and ordered an injunction restraining him from playing professional football for anyone other than Houston. There was insufficient proof of a material fraudulent representation by Houston; agreeing to keep the signing confidential did not bar equitable relief under the clean-hands doctrine; and the service-station writing satisfied the statute of frauds. The relief was a negative enforcement order, not a direction compelling Neely to play for Houston or an award of damages.
sections.Reasoning:
On fraud, Neely's position rested on an asserted understanding that the agreements would not take effect or be filed until after the bowl game. The court rejected the trial court's inference that Houston falsely represented that secrecy would preserve eligibility. The express immediate-effectiveness clause, the dated ancillary instruments, the accepted bonus and Neely's own understanding of the collegiate rules contradicted that account; everyone understood that signing and accepting money destroyed eligibility, so secrecy would only conceal existing ineligibility. Filing did not itself produce the publicity, and nothing attributed that publicity to Houston. The court criticized ruthless professional recruiting practices but emphasized Neely's competence, his advice, and his negotiations with multiple bidders. These observations explain the evidentiary conclusion and do not establish that sophisticated athletes can never prove fraudulent inducement.

On clean hands, the court recognized that equity ordinarily declines aid to a claimant whose conduct concerning the controversy is unlawful, unconscionable or inequitable, but said the doctrine does not exclude every wrongdoer and allows discretion to further justice. Neely was legally free to surrender amateur status at any time, Houston was free to contract with him, and Houston had no legal duty to announce the agreement. The court distinguished New York Football Giants v. Los Angeles Chargers, involving Charles Flowers, and disagreed with any reading of it that created a categorical bar whenever a college player signed secretly before a postseason game.

Neely's stipulated unique skill and the written exclusivity clause supported an injunction under Texas law. The station agreement was sufficiently definite because it specified the station series, Phillips-product operation, and construction, financing and site selection through Ada Oil within stated terms.

The casebook cites the case for its disagreement with a blanket secrecy rule, in a paragraph contrasting professional-athlete clean-hands decisions.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-001.rule: A clerk discharged without sufficient cause during a quarter who remains willing to serve the rest of it is treated in law as having served the whole quarter and may recover the unpaid salary as a debt for work and labour.

sections.Parties: A merchant's discharged clerk, the plaintiff, sued the merchant, the defendant, in indebitatus assumpsit for work and labour, adding the common money counts, to recover the unpaid part of a quarter's salary. Garrow and Dowling appeared for the clerk and Topping and Lawes for the merchant.
sections.Procedural History: The case was tried at nisi prius before Lord Ellenborough and reported on February 19, 1816. Ellenborough ruled on the merchant's legal objection to the form of action, and the clerk obtained a verdict for 25 pounds, the remaining half-quarter's salary. This is a trial report ending in a jury verdict rather than an appellate decision.
sections.Material Facts: The clerk's salary was 200 pounds a year, payable quarterly. After a dispute on August 11 of the preceding year, the merchant discharged him and paid 25 pounds for half the quarter, described in the report as July 1 through August 15. The following day the clerk offered to perform his duties, but the merchant declined. The cause of the underlying dispute is not described. The brief notes that the report contains an apparent transposition of the parties in one sentence, but its narrative and the ruling identify the discharged employee as the person willing to continue serving.
sections.Issue: Whether a discharged clerk can recover the unpaid part of a quarter's salary in indebitatus assumpsit for work and labour although he did not actually work throughout the quarter, or whether he needed a count specifically for salary or a special action on the contract.
sections.Holding: Lord Ellenborough, at nisi prius in 1816, held the action maintainable if the discharge lacked sufficient cause. A clerk who had served part of the quarter and remained willing to serve the rest could, in contemplation of law, be treated as having served the whole quarter, which made the employer indebted for work and labour in the unpaid amount. The ruling was expressly conditional on insufficient cause for discharge.
sections.Reasoning:
Topping, for the merchant, argued that the payment already exceeded the period of actual employment, so there was no unpaid work or labour to support the counts, and that even if more was due the clerk needed a count for salary or a special action on the contract for discharge before the quarter ended; he relied on Hulle v. Heightman. Ellenborough rejected the objection. He treated the clerk's readiness to complete the agreed service as legal performance for purposes of the debt claim, so the employer's refusal to accept the offered performance did not defeat recovery on these counts.

The ruling did not establish that every discharge creates a full-quarter entitlement. It did not calculate a general wrongful-discharge award extending beyond the quarter, decide whether other work was available, or state a rule for deducting outside earnings; the report resolves the narrower pleading and salary question.

The casebook presents the decision as an early refusal to apply mitigation and contrasts it with Howard v. Daly's later rejection of constructive service.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-002.rule: An employer asserting failure to mitigate bears the burden of proving both that substantially equivalent positions were available and that the employee failed to exercise reasonable diligence in seeking them.

sections.Parties: Anne Delliponti, administrative assistant to the chief of police of the borough of Norristown, challenged the borough's elimination of her position in a Local Agency Law appeal, and the trial court ordered her reinstated with back pay. The borough resisted, contending that she had no protected right to continued employment and that she had failed to mitigate her loss. Delliponti was the appellant in the Pennsylvania Supreme Court.
sections.Procedural History: Delliponti brought a Local Agency Law appeal. The trial court heard the dispute over whether economic necessity was the actual reason for eliminating her position; she produced no evidence of another reason, and the court found the borough acted without malice. The rest proceeded in the nature of a case stated. Common pleas held that the borough's failure to exempt her position from the charter's civil-service system protected her employment, that eliminating it without the required process was an adjudication affecting a property right, and, because the code contained no applicable layoff rules, ordered reinstatement with back pay. The Commonwealth Court reversed, reasoning that the omission had not made her a civil-service employee or constrained an economic reduction in force. Delliponti appealed. The Pennsylvania Supreme Court reversed the Commonwealth Court and reinstated the Montgomery County common-pleas order.
sections.Material Facts:
Delliponti began as a borough secretary in September 1976 and became administrative assistant to the chief of police, a confidential position. She was the most senior of four nonunion administrative assistants. On January 22, 1991, the borough told her that her position would be eliminated three days later.

Section 512D of the borough charter required civil-service rules governing appointment, discipline, removal and layoffs, while permitting affirmative exemptions. Section 513 required a comprehensive merit-based personnel system with provisions addressing reductions in force. The personnel code supplied just-cause disciplinary protections and separate economic-furlough provisions for police and fire employees. It omitted economic-layoff rules for Delliponti's position but did not exempt it.

On mitigation, the borough asserted that she had made telephone inquiries about only three advertised job openings and pursued no others, and that comparable jobs were unquestionably available. The lower courts had not resolved that defense.
sections.Issue: Whether the borough's charter and personnel code gave Delliponti a protected expectation of continued employment entitling her to notice and a hearing before her position was eliminated, and whether her back pay should be reduced or denied because she failed to mitigate.
sections.Holding: The Pennsylvania Supreme Court, in 1996, in an opinion by Chief Justice Nix, with Justices Zappala and Flaherty dissenting in a 5-2 result, held that the borough's failure to exempt Delliponti's position from the charter's civil-service system gave her a legitimate expectation of continued employment, that the three-day notification failed to provide adequate notice and a hearing, and that reinstatement with back pay was the appropriate remedy. It rejected the mitigation defense on the record because the borough had not proved that substantially equivalent positions were available. No numerical back-pay amount was determined.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority explained that public employment is not itself a property right; the employee needs an expectation of continuation arising from statute, contract or a quasi-contractual source, and an at-will employee lacks the hearing entitlement. Under Local Agency Law, an agency determination affecting protected rights is an adjudication requiring notice and a hearing. Reading the charter provisions together, the borough's failure to exempt her position afforded the protected expectation, and the council could not defeat the charter's protection through its own failure to supply the required rules. The court distinguished Hill and Sergi as involving limited statutory protections that did not cover the relevant employment action, whereas this charter specifically required rules addressing layoffs and reductions in force unless an exemption was adopted. Economic necessity therefore did not eliminate the protected interest.

On mitigation, an injured employee must make reasonable efforts to reduce loss, and damages ordinarily equal promised wages less earnings actually received or reasonably obtainable through diligent efforts to secure similar employment. But the employer bears the burden of showing avoidable loss, which requires proof both that substantially equivalent positions were available and that the employee failed to exercise reasonable diligence in seeking them. An allegation that comparable jobs existed does not establish actual vacancies available to this employee. Even assuming her efforts were inadequate, the borough had not proved availability. The decision does not approve every job search limited to three calls.

Justice Zappala, joined by Justice Flaherty, would have affirmed: a legislative body's failure to enact implementing rules did not confer the rights those rules would have created, so Delliponti remained at will. The dissent did not separately address mitigation.

The casebook cites the case for its mitigation analysis.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-003.rule: An employee suing a former employer for tortious interference with a new job need not accept reemployment from that employer to mitigate, and an offer of reemployment reduces recovery only if it does not require renewed association that circumstances make offensive or degrading.

sections.Parties: Albert Voorhees, a former outside salesman for Guyan Machinery Company, sued Guyan and its chairman, Robert Shell, for intentional interference with his employment contract with a new employer, Polydeck. Guyan, the defendant held liable at trial, appealed, challenging liability, damages, and the refusal to treat its offer of reemployment as mitigation. Shell was dismissed from the suit after the jury's findings.
sections.Procedural History: Voorhees sued Guyan and Shell in October 1991. The trial court rejected Guyan's mitigation motion. In July 1992, special jury interrogatories established that the covenant was invalid, that Guyan knew or should have known that, and that Guyan intentionally interfered. The jury also found that Shell reasonably believed he was protecting a legitimate interest, leading to his dismissal. The verdict against Guyan awarded $75,000 compensatory damages, $75,000 punitive damages, and $7,065.76 prejudgment interest running from the Polydeck discharge. Guyan appealed. The West Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals affirmed the Logan County circuit-court judgment, including the compensatory and punitive awards and interest.
sections.Material Facts:
Voorhees joined Guyan as an outside salesman in July 1981. In December 1985 he was required to sign a covenant prohibiting competition for twenty-four months after departure within a 250-mile radius of West Virginia. He resigned in July 1991 and began work for Polydeck, which manufactured urethane screens, a product representing less than one-half of one percent of Guyan's total sales. Shell notified Polydeck of the covenant and threatened litigation to enforce it. Polydeck told Voorhees to renegotiate the restriction or lose his job. Negotiations failed, and Polydeck fired him on August 14, 1991.

After Voorhees sued in October, Guyan offered him a sales position beginning November 4. He rejected it as a sham intended to induce him to abandon the lawsuit; that characterization was his position. Voorhees contacted at least twenty-two mining-industry employers, sent resumes, and incurred $695.40 in search expenses that were included in damages.
sections.Issue: Whether the evidence supported liability and punitive damages against Guyan for intentional interference with the Polydeck contract despite the asserted business justification and the jury's finding about Shell, and whether Voorhees's refusal of Guyan's offer of reemployment cut off his damages as a failure to mitigate.
sections.Holding: The West Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals, in 1994, in an opinion by Justice Neely, with Justice Workman dissenting from the punitive award and the breadth of the mitigation rule, affirmed the tortious-interference judgment. It held that the evidence defeated Guyan's justification defenses, that punitive damages could be awarded for intentional interference, and that refusal of Guyan's offer did not automatically bar later damages: the wrongful-discharge precedents did not establish a duty to accept reemployment from the interfering former employer, and even if reemployment principles applied, renewed association with Guyan in these circumstances was unreasonable to require.
sections.Reasoning:
The court applied Torbett's four elements of interference: a contractual or business relationship or expectancy, intentional interference by an outsider, resulting harm, and damages. Justification is an affirmative defense. Guyan relied on the signed covenant and protection of its business interests, but restrictive covenants require a protectible interest, such as investment in specialized training or confidential information, together with reasonable necessity and absence of undue hardship. Guyan had supplied no unique training, its customers' names were publicly available, and its overlap with Polydeck was too slight.

Guyan argued that liability and punitive damages were inconsistent with the finding of Shell's good faith. The majority reconciled the findings by distinguishing the lay chairman's reasonable belief from the corporation's responsibility to obtain competent legal advice before attempting enforcement, inferring that the jury treated entrusting the matter to an uninformed layman as reckless disregard of the employee's rights. Under Thacker, malice could be inferred from the wrongful character of the act.

On mitigation, the majority rejected an instruction that refusal of the October offer barred damages after November 1. Guyan failed to prove inadequate mitigation, given Voorhees's job search. Even assuming reemployment principles applied, an offer reduces recovery only if it does not prejudice rights under the original contract; a substantially inferior position would not suffice, nor would an offer requiring renewed association that circumstances made offensive or degrading. Guyan had caused the loss of the Polydeck job and then offered a return only after being sued.

Justice Workman, dissenting, considered the punitive reasoning inconsistent with corporate agency, since Shell's nonmalicious act was the corporation's act, and would have limited the offensive-association exception to relevant tortious conduct judged by an objective reasonableness standard.

The casebook quotes the alternative offensive-association rationale.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-004.rule: A breaching party cannot invoke the plaintiff's failure to mitigate when the defendant had the primary contractual duty to perform, an equal opportunity to take the same preventive step, and equal knowledge of the consequences.

sections.Parties: Shea-S&M Ball (Shea) and Massman-Kiewit-Early (MKE) were separate joint ventures that contracted with WMATA to build neighboring subway segments. Shea, the plaintiff and appellant, sued MKE and WMATA over flooding of its work area, claiming as a third-party beneficiary of MKE's contract with WMATA and in negligence. MKE and WMATA were the defendants. Shea appealed the limits the district court placed on its recovery.
sections.Procedural History: After a bench trial, the district court entered judgment on December 2, 1977. It found that MKE breached but awarded only $14,000, characterized as the cost of erecting and removing a dike. It treated the first flood as an act of God and restricted recovery for the later floods because Shea failed to mitigate by building a dike at the interface. It rejected the negligence claim on contributory-negligence grounds without determining whether MKE was negligent, and it rejected liability against WMATA, concluding the authority had no obligation to enforce its proposed solution. Shea appealed. The D.C. Circuit reversed the judgment and remanded for further proceedings consistent with its opinion, without setting a new dollar recovery. Rehearing was denied on September 6, 1979.
sections.Material Facts:
Shea's C-4 project comprised the tunnel south of Foggy Bottom station; MKE's C-3 work included the station and the tunnel to its north. The projects met at the station's south end. On seven occasions, water from MKE's overflowing corrugated-steel sewer flooded Shea's area, the first on June 21, 1973. MKE's contract with WMATA required it to control groundwater and protect facilities from damage caused by dewatering operations, and Shea was a third-party beneficiary of that contract.

At a February 1974 conference after the third flood, WMATA proposed that Shea build a dike and that MKE pump the accumulating water. WMATA maintained that it could only suggest, not compel, this solution. Section 1.14 of the contracts required contractors to cooperate with other project contractors, fit their work as directed, and avoid interference. The record contained neither the ordinary rainfall range for Washington nor evidence of the amount that actually fell during the relevant periods.
sections.Issue: Whether the first flood was excused as an act of God, whether Shea's contract damages could be limited because it failed to mitigate by building a dike that MKE was equally able and primarily obliged to build, and whether WMATA owed Shea a contractual duty to secure MKE's cooperation.
sections.Holding: The D.C. Circuit, in 1979, in an opinion by Senior Third Circuit Judge Van Dusen, sitting by designation, for a panel with Judges Bazelon and Robinson, held that the act-of-God defense failed on this record, that the mitigation limitation did not apply because MKE had the primary contractual obligation, an equal opportunity to build the dike and equal knowledge of the consequences, and that WMATA breached a contractual obligation owed to Shea by failing to compel cooperation. Damages could be recalculated only if Shea supplied sufficient supporting evidence. No separate opinion is reproduced.
sections.Reasoning:
Act of God. Rainfall qualifies only if unprecedented and extraordinary, of unusual proportions, and not reasonably foreseeable; heavy rain alone does not. With no evidence of ordinary or actual rainfall, the defendants supplied no basis for treating the first flood as extraordinary. A footnote added that an act of God must arise exclusively and directly from natural causes, and the district court had not determined whether MKE's negligence contributed. First-flood damages therefore required determination on remand.

Mitigation. The court recognized the usual rule against passively accumulating harm when obvious, reasonable precautions would greatly reduce it. Following S. J. Groves, however, a defendant cannot complain about the plaintiff's omission of the same preventive act when both had equal opportunity and the defendant could as reasonably be expected to act. MKE bore primary responsibility for its runoff, knew the consequences of failing to control it, and could have built the same dike, so the cost of its default could not be shifted to Shea. The court did not say an injured party never needs to mitigate merely because the defendant breached.

Negligence stayed distinct: a footnote affirmed the contributory-negligence conclusion about failure to take obvious protective steps, while directing examination of whether the first flood's danger was sufficiently obvious and foreseeable.

WMATA. Applying Hoffman, the court read the cooperation clause as obligating the contracting authority to secure cooperation for the affected contractor's benefit. Shea was entitled to expect WMATA to exercise its supervisory power, and arranging one unsuccessful meeting did not discharge that duty.

The casebook presents the equal-opportunity reasoning together with its later criticism in Cates, which is the casebook's editorial context rather than part of this decision.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-005.rule: A buyer need not cover by impractical or disproportionately expensive means or beyond its financial resources; reasonableness of cover is judged by good faith and the circumstances at the time, and the seller bears the burden of proving an unreasonable failure to avoid loss.

sections.Parties: Frederick Simeone, a collector, was the buyer and plaintiff. He sued First Bank National Association, the seller, for breach of a contract to sell repossessed rare Mercedes-Benz cars and parts; the Quante estate, which claimed one car and some parts, was also a defendant until Simeone dismissed it with prejudice. First Bank appealed the damages judgment entered on the jury's verdict for Simeone.
sections.Procedural History: The district court initially granted the sellers summary judgment for failure of a condition precedent. In an earlier decision in 1992, the Eighth Circuit vacated that ruling, held that the bank and estate breached, and remanded other claims and damages. Before the 1994 trial, Simeone dismissed the estate with prejudice. The district court ruled that the bank's conduct was not fraud but let that claim go to the jury as a precaution against a later reversal. The jury returned $1 on that claim and $2,405,000 in contract damages: $585,000 compensatory, $225,000 incidental and $1,595,000 consequential, plus prejudgment interest. The court denied the bank's new-trial, amendment and remittitur requests. On this appeal the Eighth Circuit affirmed the compensatory and consequential components, reversed the incidental component, and remanded, with prejudgment interest on the revised damages.
sections.Material Facts:
First Bank repossessed several unusually rare 1920s and 1930s Mercedes-Benz cars and thousands of scarce parts from its debtor, Gohlike. One car and some parts were also claimed by the Quante estate. On October 26, 1985, the bank contracted to sell its repossessed assets to Simeone for $400,000, with another $50,000 for the estate's claimed car and parts in the same agreement. He paid a ten-percent deposit. The collection included a unique 1929 SS Roadster and a 1928 SSK.

On the November 4 closing date, Gohlike obtained a temporary restraining order preventing the collateral sale, and the bank refused Simeone's tender. It negotiated instead with Gohlike and a neighbor, Torseth, agreeing to a slightly higher price and dismissal of Gohlike's $13 million due-process suit against the bank. Believing a contractual condition relieved it of the Simeone obligation, the bank sold to Torseth's corporation, SMB, and returned Simeone's deposit with interest. SMB ultimately resold the assets for $1,114,960, including $470,000 that Simeone paid for the SS Roadster alone.
sections.Issue: Whether the market-price, consequential and incidental damages awarded to Simeone under Minnesota's UCC were proper, including whether the appreciation losses were foreseeable and reasonably proved, and whether Simeone failed to mitigate by not repurchasing the whole collection from SMB.
sections.Holding: The Eighth Circuit, in 1996, in an opinion by Judge Ross for a panel with Judges Beam and Murphy, affirmed the $585,000 compensatory award measured in the collector market and the $1,595,000 consequential award for foreseeable appreciation, held that Simeone was not required to cover by repurchasing the entire collection for over $1 million, and reversed the $225,000 incidental award as duplicative. First Bank remained responsible for the estate-claimed car, and prejudgment interest remained available on the revised award.
sections.Reasoning:
Under UCC section 2-713, seller-breach damages ordinarily are the difference between the market price when the buyer learns of the breach and the contract price, plus incidental and consequential losses. The bank urged a market for repossessed goods at foreclosure sales. The court accepted the collector market and expert valuation because the cars and parts were rare or unique. The jury valued the assets at $1,035,000 in total; subtracting the $450,000 contract price produced $585,000.

The consequential award reflected expert estimates of appreciation two years after breach, less the breach-time market value. Section 2-715(2)(a) requires losses arising from requirements the seller had reason to know of when contracting and which could not reasonably be prevented. The bank argued that Simeone had described himself as a collector rather than a reseller, but its officer knew collectors might trade to improve their collections, Simeone testified that he disclosed possible trade or resale, and the quantity of parts supported an inference of resale or assembly into more valuable property. Foreseeability was a jury question. Minnesota law barred speculative losses but did not demand mathematical precision once loss and a reasonable basis for approximation were shown.

On cover, reasonableness depends on good faith and the circumstances when the buyer acts, not on hindsight, and the seller bears the burden of proving unreasonable failure to avoid loss. An injured buyer need not take impractical measures, incur disproportionate expense, or act beyond available financial means. The bank did not show that Simeone had the resources to repurchase the whole collection or that doing so was reasonable; he had covered in part by buying the Roadster. The holding concerns this record, not a categorical rule against cover after a price increase.

The incidental award failed because a cover-price differential under section 2-712 is distinct from incidental charges under section 2-715(1), and it duplicated the other awards.

The casebook uses the case in a problem on the cover issue; its simplified figures differ from the opinion's.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-006.rule: Notice of the purpose for which goods are wanted does not make a seller liable for remote consequences not within the parties' contemplation when contracting, but a complaint alleging a contract and its breach is not dismissible merely because the damages demanded are unrecoverable.

sections.Parties: Lorenzo Coppola, the plaintiff and appellant, alleged that he ordered two gowns for his betrothed from Isidor Kraushaar, the defendant, and sued Kraushaar for breach of the delivery contract, demanding $500 for wedding expenses allegedly rendered useless. The action was against the dress supplier, not against the betrothed for breach of a promise to marry.
sections.Procedural History: The plaintiff's complaint was dismissed at trial before any testimony was taken. He appealed. On March 3, 1905, the Appellate Division, Second Department, unanimously reversed the judgment with costs. The appellate issue concerned the adequacy of the allegations rather than facts established through evidence; the court did not award $500, enter a $10 recovery, or find the alleged facts proved.
sections.Material Facts: These are pleading allegations; no proof was heard. Coppola alleged that on January 3, 1902, he ordered two gowns for his betrothed from Kraushaar, specifying a particular model. He told the defendant that the wedding was set for January 19 and that he was incurring substantial wedding-feast expenses. The defendant allegedly promised delivery by January 18 for $50 and received $10 immediately. Coppola and his betrothed demanded the gowns on the promised date, but the defendant failed to deliver. The complaint attributed the woman's breaking off the wedding to that failure and demanded $500 for presents, wine, clothes and other expenses allegedly rendered useless. The complaint did not identify either gown as the bridal gown.
sections.Issue: Whether the wedding expenditures allegedly rendered useless by the seller's failure to deliver the gowns were recoverable as damages for breach, and whether the complaint nonetheless stated a cause of action for breach of contract so that dismissal was error.
sections.Holding: The New York Appellate Division, Second Department, in 1905, in an opinion by Justice Jenks for Presiding Justice Hirschberg and Justices Woodward, Rich and Miller, all concurring, held that the claimed $500 wedding losses were too remote to be recovered, but that dismissal was nevertheless wrong because the complaint alleged an agreement, a $10 part payment and nonperformance, which could support a breach claim for nominal damages or the part payment.
sections.Reasoning:
The wedding expenditures were neither an immediate and necessary result of the breach nor a loss shown to have been within the parties' contemplation when contracting. Telling the supplier the intended use and the delivery deadline notified him of the occasion, but did not warn him of the asserted consequence, the bride's permanent refusal to marry. The court cited the principle that notice of an object does not alone change damages unless it forms the basis of the agreement.

The allegation that the expenditures became wholly useless implied more than a postponement; gifts, wine and clothes would not necessarily become useless merely because the wedding date changed. To impose these losses, the parties would have had to contemplate that the marriage would never take place if the dresses were not delivered the day before the ceremony. The bride's disappointment might be predictable, but permanent refusal to wed was not, absent a specific warning. Applying Hadley and an intervening-agency foreseeability inquiry, the court deemed the damages too remote.

Dismissal was still error. On an objection to legal sufficiency the allegations and their reasonable implications are accepted. Nominal damages alone would have prevented dismissal, and an erroneous damages theory does not make an otherwise adequate cause of action demurrable. The allegations also required an inference of $10 actual loss from the part payment. The court observed that the plaintiff's eventual victory might be small.

The casebook's account presents the failed wedding as an event and omits the reversal that allowed nominal or part-payment recovery.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-007.rule: A shipowner cannot treat a classification society's certificate as a guarantee of the vessel's sound construction; the owner keeps its nondelegable duty of seaworthiness, and a great disparity between the fee and the loss claimed suggests the parties did not allocate that risk to the society.

sections.Parties: Sundance Cruises Corp., the shipowner, sued American Bureau of Shipping (ABS), the classification society that inspected and certified its converted cruise ship, for negligent and grossly negligent certification, misrepresentation, breach of contract and breach of an implied warranty of workmanlike performance. Sundance sought $264 million in actual and punitive damages. ABS was the defendant; Sundance was the appellant.
sections.Procedural History: The district court concluded that Bahamian law immunized ABS's governmental certifications, found insufficient evidence of gross negligence and misrepresentation, and rejected a Ryan warranty in this setting. On reargument it clarified that the immunity did not extend to the private classification certificate, but that Sundance had supplied no evidence of damage caused by errors in that certificate. Final judgments in July and September 1992 dismissed the complaint on summary judgment. The Second Circuit, reviewing de novo and construing the facts favorably to Sundance, affirmed the dismissal with prejudice of all Sundance's claims against ABS.
sections.Material Facts:
In early 1984, Sundance bought an overnight car ferry and converted it at a Swedish shipyard into a luxury cruise ship for more than seven hundred passengers. It chose Bahamian registration and needed international safety certificates, as well as a private classification certificate for insurance. A March 5 agreement engaged ABS to inspect compliance with its own class rules and conduct regulatory checks for the Bahamian government. ABS attended portions of the conversion and received many plans, but none for the grey-water piping system. On June 14 it issued provisional Load Line and SOLAS safety certificates for the government, followed shortly by a provisional private classification certificate. Sundance paid ABS $85,000.

On June 29 the ship hit an underwater rock off British Columbia. It was designed to survive flooding of any two of thirteen compartments, and the hull breach flooded two. Water then passed through two bulkhead holes and an unvalved grey-water system into other compartments, and the vessel listed and sank at a nearby pier. The missing valves violated SOLAS and the bulkhead holes violated both SOLAS and ABS rules; ABS had not reported them. The ship was a constructive total loss.
sections.Issue: Whether Bahamian law immunized ABS from liability for the safety certificates it issued on the government's behalf, and whether Sundance could recover from ABS in contract or tort for the loss of its ship on the basis of the private classification certificate.
sections.Holding: The Second Circuit, in 1993, in an opinion by Judge Pratt for a panel with Judges Timbers and Kearse, affirmed on two distinct grounds. ABS had direct statutory immunity under section 279 of the Bahamian Merchant Shipping Act for its good-faith governmental safety certifications. The private classification certificate fell outside that immunity, but Sundance showed no damage flowing from it and could not treat classification as ABS's guarantee to the owner that its own vessel was soundly constructed. No separate opinion appears.
sections.Reasoning:
The inspection and classification contracts were maritime, so federal maritime choice-of-law principles governed. Whether New York clauses printed on later invoices bound the parties was immaterial. Applying Lauritzen's contacts, the court emphasized the ship's Bahamian flag, which Sundance had voluntarily chosen, and that government's interest in the safety certifications.

Section 279 protected authorized governmental agents for good-faith performance of statutory duties. ABS was nominated as an approved classification society and specifically confirmed as acting for the government on these surveys, and the Bahamian interpretive statute included corporations within persons. The court rejected the district court's restrictive reading that would immunize individual surveyors but not their corporate principal. The immunity was tied to governmental work and did not cover the private classification certificate, which was needed for private insurance purposes.

For that certificate, the court accepted the absence-of-damage rationale. The enormous disparity between the $85,000 fee and the $264 million claim supported an inference that the parties had not allocated that risk to ABS, citing Restatement section 351 comment f. More importantly, Sundance retained control of and responsibility for conversion, repair and maintenance and its nondelegable seaworthiness duty; inspection and certification did not transfer those obligations. The court distinguished claims by an injured third party relying on a certificate: Sundance was the owner responsible for the defects, and for it the certificate's purpose was access to insurance rates for a classed ship. Both the contract and tort theories therefore failed, and the court did not decide the district court's alternative grounds.

The casebook quotes the fee-disparity point in an account of allocation of risk; that point is one component of a broader decision.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-008.rule: Where a contract excludes consequential damages, recovery for breach of a service promise is limited to the direct loss, the difference between the value of the services promised and the value of those supplied; resulting property damage is consequential even if foreseeable.

sections.Parties: Reynolds Metals Co., the buyer of a large transformer for its Texas plant, sued the seller, Westinghouse Electric Corp., to recover the cost of repairing the transformer after it failed. Reynolds was the plaintiff and prevailed at trial on a claim that Westinghouse failed to supply the promised competent service engineer. Westinghouse, the defendant, appealed.
sections.Procedural History: Reynolds sued in April 1976 and the case was removed on diversity grounds. Negligence and strict-liability theories were barred by limitations. The district court directed a verdict on nearly all warranty matters, concluding that warranty coverage began at shipment and had expired by the time of failure, while the disclaimer and damages limitation remained effective. The surviving contract theory, total failure to provide the promised competent supervising engineer, went to the jury, which found breach and proximate causation. The district court awarded the stipulated repair bill plus prejudgment interest. On appeal the Fifth Circuit affirmed the jury's breach finding, reversed the damages award, vacated prejudgment interest, and remanded for a new trial on damages.
sections.Material Facts:
In 1970, Westinghouse proposed a large transformer for approximately $250,000. The price included a competent service engineer for two full days during equipment check or startup. The proposal supplied a one-year shipment-based warranty, disclaimed other warranties, and excluded special, indirect, incidental and consequential damages. Reynolds accepted by purchase order. In January 1971, anticipating storage, Reynolds bought an additional year of warranty coverage for $2,637, conditioned on pre-startup inspection and Westinghouse startup supervision.

The unit shipped in July 1971 and was stored until installation in early 1973. Westinghouse engineer Reindl arrived for final inspection and startup and worked with Reynolds engineer Younger over roughly two months; the unit entered service in late April. Reindl had an electrical-engineering degree but limited experience with this type of transformer and regarded his role as technical assistance, not supervision.
