According to Reynolds's experts, only one of two grounding cables passed through the alarm system, a configuration that could fail to disclose internal burning.

The transformer failed April 11, 1974. The experts attributed the initial burning to a compression-ring design defect, with the alarm failure allowing damage to continue undetected. Westinghouse denied warranty coverage as expired, and Reynolds paid $109,284.82 for repair.
sections.Issue: Whether Westinghouse's failure to supply a competent supervising engineer could be a breach of contract despite the warranty disclaimer and expired warranty, and whether the transformer repair cost was recoverable as damages for that breach given the contract's exclusion of consequential damages.
sections.Holding: The Fifth Circuit, in 1985, in an opinion by Judge Higginbotham for a panel with Judges Thornberry and Reavley, upheld the jury's finding that Westinghouse failed to provide the promised competent engineering services, but held that the repair costs were consequential losses excluded by the agreement. Direct damages were the difference between the value of the competent engineering services promised and the market value of the services actually supplied. It reversed the damages award and remanded for a new damages trial. No separate opinion appears.
sections.Reasoning:
A warranty disclaimer does not necessarily excuse failure to supply the promised performance at all. Had a competent supervising engineer performed poorly, the claim would have been for breach of warranty under the district court's analysis; but a person who did not meet the promised qualification and did not undertake the promised supervisory role could amount to total nonperformance, and the jury could so find. The ruling is not an exception invalidating every warranty disclaimer whenever work is defective. Westinghouse's argument that the warranty-extension condition merely reserved its right to supervise seemed the more reasonable reading to the court, but it had not been presented below. The notice objection under section 2-607 also failed.

On damages, the agreed exclusion remained enforceable. Contract expectancy generally comprises the performance-value differential, incidental mitigation expense, and consequential losses such as foreseeable injury to property. A restriction on consequential recovery required isolating the direct value differential rather than awarding every loss proximately caused by the breach. Because the transaction was predominantly a sale, the Texas UCC governed, and by analogy to section 2-714 the court suggested the competent engineer's fee less the value of Reindl's work as a way to determine the difference. Failure to detect ground current and the aggravated burning were foreseeable, but foreseeability did not turn the repair losses into direct service-value losses. Independently, the underlying design flaw meant service-related recovery could not simply encompass every repair cost.

The court expressly declined to approve or disapprove the district court's treatment of the conflicting forms under section 2-207.

The casebook's account gives a fee-based explanation of the direct-damages measure.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-009.rule: Loss of future business with a known customer may be a foreseeable consequence of delivering seriously defective goods, but lost future profits are recoverable only to the extent their amount is proved with a fair degree of certainty rather than by speculation.

sections.Parties: Hendricks & Associates, Inc., a Massachusetts apparel-import consulting firm that bought garments from Daewoo Corporation and resold them to Champion Products, sued Daewoo, the manufacturer and seller, for damages caused by defective garments, including sums Champion charged back and future profits lost when Champion ended the relationship. Hendricks was the plaintiff and prevailed at trial; Daewoo, the defendant, appealed. Champion was not a party.
sections.Procedural History: Hendricks sought the entire debit-memorandum amount and $150,000 for anticipated future profits. The jury awarded $275,000 for the debit memoranda and $375,000 for future profits. The district court denied judgment notwithstanding the verdict and conditionally denied a new trial on the debit damages if Hendricks accepted a reduction to $21,614.73, which Hendricks accepted. The $375,000 future-profit award remained intact. Daewoo appealed. The First Circuit affirmed the future-profit award conditionally on remittitur of everything above $45,000, with a new trial on the amount of those damages otherwise, affirmed the judgment in all other respects, and remanded.
sections.Material Facts:
James Hendricks began advising Champion Products about overseas apparel production in December 1981. Two initial Daewoo orders had minor quality problems that Hendricks helped resolve. For Champion's 1984 Stripe Collection, Hendricks selected Daewoo and became an intervening buyer and seller: Champion ordered from Hendricks, which ordered from Daewoo and resold at a five-percent markup. No contract directly joined Champion and Daewoo. Champion funded irrevocable letters of credit, so Hendricks and Daewoo were paid in full before the quality dispute was resolved.

Daewoo shipped directly to Champion in three installments. The first contained serious defects; Daewoo promised conformity in later shipments. The second was also defective, and the entire third shipment was ultimately unacceptable, with pants whose seams opened after repeated washing.

Champion issued debit memoranda totaling $213,486.61 and actually withheld a $21,614.73 credit owed to Hendricks; the record did not show that Hendricks became accountable for the remainder. Champion ceased doing business with Hendricks. Its former purchasing manager, Donald Sullivan, testified that their business had been increasing and would have continued to increase. Champion revenues were $75,000 in fiscal 1983 and $170,000 in fiscal 1984, against total firm expenses of $188,000 and $350,000, and the firm's highest annual profit from all clients was $20,000.
sections.Issue: Whether the loss of Hendricks's continuing business with Champion was a foreseeable consequence of Daewoo's breach and caused by it, whether the withheld credit was recoverable, and whether the evidence proved lost future profits with enough certainty to support the $375,000 award.
sections.Holding: The First Circuit, in 1991, in an opinion by Judge Cyr for Chief Judge Breyer and Senior Judge Bownes, with no separate opinion, sustained liability for consequential loss caused by the defective garments. It held that loss of the Champion relationship was foreseeable and caused by the breach and affirmed the $21,614.73 withheld credit, but held that the evidence supported lost future profits only up to $45,000 for fiscal 1985, and required remittitur of the $375,000 award to that amount or a new trial on it.
sections.Reasoning:
Applying Massachusetts law, the court said that under UCC sections 2-714 and 2-715 lost prospective profits must be a natural and probable consequence of breach, reasonably foreseeable at contracting, and demonstrated with a fair degree of certainty.

Foreseeability is objective: what a reasonably prudent seller should contemplate at contracting. Daewoo needed no express notice. Earlier transactions had shown Champion's insistence on precise specifications, and Daewoo knew it was supplying Champion through Hendricks. A rational jury could find that another delivery of severely and pervasively defective goods would probably end that continuing relationship. The court relied on the magnitude of the defects, the prior dealings and the known relationship; it did not hold that every defective resale shipment makes all future customer business recoverable. Causation was supported by the collection's importance to Champion and by Sullivan's testimony. The withheld credit was a concrete, foreseeable loss with a firm basis in Hendricks's records; the balance of the debit memoranda was not shown to be an incurred loss.

Proving that the relationship would have continued did not establish the profit Hendricks would have earned. Allocating even half of operating costs to Champion left losses on that account in both prior years. A pre-breach fiscal 1985 forecast projected $220,000 in Champion revenues, including $50,000 from a contemplated polo-shirt order, yielding possible profit of $10,000 to $45,000. The court considered the issue close but found enough support for $45,000, since the polo-shirt work had already been priced and sampled. Nothing established profits beyond fiscal 1985: there were no later projections, no time horizon and no rational method, and general testimony that business would have grown did not let the jury guess at years of net profits.

The casebook uses the case twice, once on why future resale contracts were foreseeable and once for the certainty limitation and conditional remittitur.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-010.rule: A seller is liable for the buyer's losses on resale contracts only if circumstances known to the seller at contracting made it reasonably foreseeable that its breach would cause the buyer to breach them; mere knowledge that the buyer is a wholesaler or intends resale is not enough.

sections.Parties: Czarnikow-Rionda Company, a sugar wholesaler, was the buyer and plaintiff. It sued Federal Sugar Refining Company, the refiner and seller, to recover the sums it paid its own customers, and its litigation expenses, after Federal delivered discolored sugar. Czarnikow prevailed at trial and in the Appellate Division. Federal, the defendant, appealed to the New York Court of Appeals in these consolidated actions.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court awarded the customer payments and litigation expenses as the measure of Federal's breach damages, overruling Federal's objection that damages should be the difference between what Czarnikow should have received and what it actually received; Federal took an exception. Czarnikow recovered $442,484.03 from Federal including interest. The Appellate Division sustained the judgment. On November 18, 1930, the Court of Appeals reversed the judgments of both the Appellate Division and Trial Term and granted a new trial, with costs to abide the event. It did not fix a general-damage award or reject the existence of breach.
sections.Material Facts:
Czarnikow and Federal made contracts on September 15, 1919, March 8, 1920, and April 21, 1920, covering approximately 75,000 tons of fine granulated sugar to be delivered in installments from April through August 1920. The September contract required export, but Federal later offered to permit domestic sales; the March contract expressly permitted domestic shipments, and the April contract specified neither. Federal therefore contemplated possible domestic resales. The majority found, however, that it did not learn until May 18 that domestic resale contracts had actually been made and did not learn their precise terms until the litigation.

Beginning March 27, Czarnikow contracted with customers across the United States. All but one resale contract specified Eastern cane fine granulated sugar bearing Federal's brand rather than fine granulated sugar generically. Federal shipped directly to those customers under Czarnikow's directions. Of approximately 1,670,000 hundred-pound bags, 29,691 contained discolored sugar. Customers rescinded and demanded advance payments back or sought damages. Czarnikow ultimately paid or refunded more than $310,000 and incurred more than $30,000 defending suits.
sections.Issue: Whether a wholesaler that resold a standard commodity may recover from its seller, as special damages, the sums it paid to settle its customers' claims and its litigation expenses, where the seller knew resale was possible but did not know the terms of the resale contracts or of circumstances preventing substitute purchases.
sections.Holding: The New York Court of Appeals, in 1930, in an opinion by Judge Kellogg joined by Chief Judge Cardozo and Judges Pound, Lehman and O'Brien, with Judges Crane and Hubbs dissenting, held five to two that the proof did not justify passing the wholesaler's customer-settlement losses through to the refiner as special damages. Such losses are recoverable only when circumstances known at contracting made it reasonably foreseeable that the seller's breach would cause the buyer to breach a resale agreement; mere knowledge that the buyer was a wholesaler or intended resale does not suffice.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority treated replacement through the general market as central. Ordinarily a buyer that can obtain substitute goods can fulfil its resale obligations and recover general damages from the seller. A resale contract need not already exist; a contemplated resale could suffice if the seller also knew circumstances preventing substitute procurement. Notice after the original contract was made does not enlarge the seller's exposure. The majority did not resolve whether special-damage liability rests on an implied promise or is imposed by law, since either explanation required knowledge of the special circumstances. It contrasted cases where sellers knew why ordinary substitution would be unavailable.

Fine granulated sugar was a standard commodity, and the proof did not establish that Federal knew other conforming sugar would be unavailable or that the market lacked enough to replace the defective bags. Czarnikow's own undisclosed resale specifications narrowed replacement to Federal's brand, and the majority would not charge Federal with that added consequence without advance knowledge. The resale contracts also called for delivery by August although shipments to distant customers could take more than twenty-one days, so a late shipment might not be rejected until replacement within the agreed month was impossible; that was an undisclosed consequence of how Czarnikow framed its subcontracts. So either undisclosed special circumstances prevented replacement, and the resulting loss was not chargeable to Federal, or replacement was possible and the buyer was limited to general damages. Federal's later settlement negotiations did not establish liability; they occurred largely after the August replacement opportunity had expired.

Judge Crane, dissenting, thought Federal knew it was supplying immediate domestic resale customers directly, that the wholesaler had no opportunity to inspect, and that the conduct of Federal's agent Lowry in trying to replace sugar or settle claims estopped it; he would have affirmed. Judge Hubbs dissented without opinion.

The casebook uses the case in a problem asking whether undisclosed brand restrictions affect recovery, with simplified figures.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-011.rule: Under this district-court ruling, which the First Circuit later rejected, consequential contract damages for career harm that depends on others drawing a message from a cancellation require proof of an unprivileged, materially false communication, by analogy to defamation law.

sections.Parties: Vanessa Redgrave and Vanessa Redgrave Enterprises, Ltd., the plaintiffs, sued the Boston Symphony Orchestra, Inc. (BSO), the defendant, over its cancellation of Boston and New York performances of Stravinsky's Oedipus Rex in which Redgrave was to narrate. Both plaintiffs asserted breach of contract and sought the performance fee and damages for harm to Redgrave's career; Redgrave individually asserted a Massachusetts Civil Rights Act claim. Both sides moved for judgment notwithstanding the verdict.
sections.Procedural History: Several other theories were rejected before trial in a separate 1983 opinion. After a sixteen-day jury trial, the jury found that the cancellation was not caused by circumstances beyond BSO's reasonable control and that it caused foreseeable consequential harm to Redgrave's career, which it assessed at $100,000; it rejected the factual premises of her retaliatory-purpose theory. On cross-motions for judgment notwithstanding the verdict, Judge Keeton, in this post-trial opinion of February 13, 1985, directed judgment for the plaintiffs for $27,500 on the contract claim and for BSO on all other claims, rejecting the consequential-damage award. Costs were to be assessed under Rule 68, and the clerk was directed to withhold final judgment pending counsel's report. This is the district-court stage only; the later First Circuit decision is a separate stage.
sections.Material Facts:
Redgrave was engaged to narrate Oedipus Rex with BSO in Boston and New York, and BSO cancelled the performances. Redgrave alleged that BSO cancelled in retaliation for her public political statements, particularly her support for the Palestine Liberation Organization. BSO maintained that physical-security risks and possible disruption would impair the performances' artistic integrity. A contractual clause excused nonperformance caused by events beyond a party's reasonable control. The agreed performance fee was $31,000; after expenses Redgrave would have borne, the parties stipulated to $27,500.

The jury rejected the propositions that political disagreement was the primary or only reason for cancellation and that a BSO agent had urged cancellation out of personal disagreement with her views. It found that cancellation was not caused by circumstances beyond BSO's reasonable control, that it caused consequential harm to her career, and that such harm was foreseeable. It answered no to a question asking whether the cancellation and press release implied that BSO's agents held a specified opinion about the risks of presenting her. Theodore Mann testified that he decided against hiring Redgrave for Heartbreak House after BSO's cancellation, reasoning that if a leading arts institution could not take the perceived risk, his organization should not either. BSO had offered $31,000 under Rule 68 on November 16, 1982.
sections.Issue: Whether BSO was liable under the Massachusetts Civil Rights Act, whether its cancellation was excused under the contract, and whether Redgrave could recover the jury's $100,000 in consequential damages for career harm that depended on others learning of the cancellation and drawing a message from it.
sections.Holding: The United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts, in 1985, per Judge Robert E. Keeton, held that BSO breached the contract and owed the stipulated $27,500 fee, that BSO was entitled to judgment on the civil-rights claim, and that the $100,000 consequential-damage finding, although supported by sufficient evidence of foreseeability, causation and amount, could not be recovered because the plaintiffs had not identified an unprivileged, materially false factual communication in the causal chain, a requirement the court drew by analogy from defamation law.
sections.Reasoning:
Civil rights. The Massachusetts statute required interference or attempted interference with protected rights through threats, intimidation or coercion. The retaliatory-purpose theory failed because the jury rejected its factual premises, and merely acquiescing in others' public pressure, without the relevant conduct and intent, was not threats, intimidation or coercion. The judge did not decide whether a jury trial was required on this claim; he made the same findings independently.

Contract. The jury's answer defeated the excuse clause, and once it had contracted BSO could not invoke its freedom to choose artists to avoid the consequences of cancelling. The fee was recoverable regardless of the dispute over further damages.

Consequential damages. The instructions allowed recovery for harm sufficiently likely that a reasonably prudent party would have considered it in deciding whether to contract, an objective test, and required that the cancellation be a but-for cause of an incremental loss beyond what Redgrave's political views would independently have caused. Keeton found the evidence sufficient, though the amount issue was close, since Massachusetts law does not demand mathematical precision.

He nonetheless denied the award. The claimed loss depended on people learning of the cancellation, deriving a message from it, and declining to employ Redgrave because of it. He treated that communicative link as raising expression protections analogous to defamation law, reasoning that judicial enforcement of a state damages rule could be state action. He predicted that state and federal protections would require the plaintiff to identify an unprivileged communication, that truthful facts and genuinely held opinions could not supply it, and that a public figure such as Redgrave would have to show knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard. The plaintiffs' five proposed implied messages mixed opinion with fact and isolated no materially false fact. He framed these as unsettled predictions.

The casebook reproduces the foreseeability instruction and distinguishes the supported jury finding from the judge's legal restriction, reporting that the First Circuit later rejected that restriction.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-012.rule: Contract damages for specific, identifiable employment opportunities lost because of a breach are recoverable if they satisfy the ordinary requirements of natural consequence, foreseeability and reasonably certain proof, and are not barred as general reputation damages.

sections.Parties: Vanessa Redgrave, the plaintiff, sued the Boston Symphony Orchestra, Inc. (BSO), the defendant, for breach of contract and under the Massachusetts Civil Rights Act after BSO cancelled concerts she was to narrate. Her company joined only the contract claim. Redgrave appealed the district court's damages and civil-rights rulings; BSO cross-appealed the evidentiary sufficiency of the consequential damages.
sections.Procedural History: After a sixteen-day trial, the jury found that BSO's cancellation breached the contract and caused foreseeable career harm. The district court awarded the stipulated $27,500 net performance fee but set aside the jury's additional $100,000 consequential award under expression protections drawn by analogy to defamation law, and entered judgment for BSO on the civil-rights claim. On appeal, the First Circuit first certified state-law questions to the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court, then issued a divided panel decision, and then withdrew the panel opinion and dissent to reconsider the civil-rights issue en banc. The en banc court affirmed the judgment for BSO on the civil-rights claim and vacated and remanded the contract judgment for entry of consequential damages of $12,000 less performance expenses, with no appellate costs. The state certification decision and the withdrawn panel writings are procedural history rather than opinions separately briefed.
sections.Material Facts:
BSO engaged Redgrave in March 1982 to narrate a series of Oedipus Rex concerts in Boston and New York. Subscribers and others protested her support for the Palestine Liberation Organization and her positions concerning Israel. Around April 1, BSO cancelled both her engagement and the performances, asserting concerns about audience and performer safety, disruption and artistic integrity. Its press release did not name her. The jury, advisory on the civil-rights claim, found that BSO's own political disagreement did not motivate the cancellation.

On damages, Redgrave claimed a sharp loss of secure film offers during the fourteen months after cancellation. She accepted three offers that together would have produced $850,000 had the films been made, Annie's Coming Out at $250,000, No Alternatives at $350,000 and Track 39 at $250,000, but each failed or fell through, and nothing linked those failures to the cancellation. She had acknowledged losing work from political controversy before the BSO incident. No film producer attributed a lost opportunity to the cancellation. Theodore Mann testified that he decided against hiring her for Heartbreak House partly because a premier organization with similar financial support had cancelled its engagement; the contemplated fee was $12,000.
sections.Issue: Whether consequential contract damages for professional opportunities lost because of the cancellation were barred as reputation damages or by expression protections analogous to defamation law, how much of the $100,000 award the evidence supported, and whether BSO was liable under the Massachusetts Civil Rights Act for acquiescing in third-party pressure.
sections.Holding: The First Circuit, en banc, in 1988, in an opinion by Judge Coffin, unanimously as to the contract ruling among the five participating judges, held that Redgrave could recover consequential damages for identifiable lost engagements under ordinary contract-damage requirements, without the district court's added defamation-derived hurdle, but that the evidence supported only the Heartbreak House opportunity: $12,000 less the expenses she would have incurred. By three to two, with Judges Bownes and Selya dissenting, it affirmed judgment for BSO on the civil-rights claim as a matter of Massachusetts law.
sections.Reasoning:
BSO relied on decisions denying contract damages for reputational injury. The court explained that those decisions usually turned on remoteness, lack of foreseeability and speculative valuation. Redgrave's theory was narrower: identifiable movie or theater engagements that would otherwise have been offered were lost because of the breach. Such pecuniary losses can satisfy Massachusetts requirements of natural consequence, reasonable foreseeability and rational calculation on a firm factual basis.

The court rejected the district judge's communicative-link reasoning on these facts. BSO had not intended the cancellation as symbolic speech or a statement about Redgrave. Information being communicated about an act differs from the actor intentionally communicating a protected message through it; another employer could draw an inference from BSO's decision without the cancellation becoming protected speech. The court reserved whether an intentionally expressive cancellation might ever be protected.

Most of the $100,000 lacked support. Favorable review does not permit conjecture about causation or amount. The film and most theater evidence did not separate the cancellation's effect from producers' independent concerns about her politics, a change of agents, or production failures. Mann's testimony was different: one reasonably available inference was that BSO's example actually influenced his decision, and he supplied an ascertainable fee.

On civil rights, the Supreme Judicial Court had answered that acquiescing in third-party pressure could create liability, defeating the district court's ground. The majority nevertheless predicted, from the state plurality, concurrence and dissent, that a majority of that court would deny liability in this artistic setting on state statutory or constitutional grounds, and declined to decide any federal First Amendment defense.

Judge Bownes, joined by Judge Selya, agreed with the contract analysis but objected to assembling a state-law bar from separate minority positions; they would have reached the constitutional issues and rejected a broad artistic-integrity defense as permitting a heckler's veto.

The casebook cites this decision as the appellate correction of the district court and for the distinction between general reputation and specific employment losses.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-013.rule: Where a contract expressly leaves the time of performance to later mutual agreement, the foreseeability of damages from delay is judged by what the breaching party knew when that date was fixed; reasonable costs of mitigating foreseeable harm are recoverable.

sections.Parties: Spang Industries' Fort Pitt Bridge Division (Fort Pitt), a steel fabricator and subcontractor, sued Aetna Casualty & Surety Co., which had provided the labor-and-material bond of highway contractor Torrington, for the unpaid subcontract balance. Torrington separately sued Fort Pitt for damages caused by late steel delivery. Fort Pitt appealed, challenging the offset allowed to Torrington for delay expenses and seeking correction of interest on its unpaid balance.
sections.Procedural History: Fort Pitt's federal action against Aetna was transferred to the Northern District of New York. Torrington's state-court action against Fort Pitt for delay damages was removed to the same court, and the cases were consolidated. After a three-day bench trial, the court found Fort Pitt in breach and allowed Torrington a $7,653.57 offset against the amount due, reduced from an original claim of $23,290.81. Judgment for Fort Pitt against Torrington and Aetna followed; a later amendment left Aetna's obligation uncertain. Fort Pitt's third-party action against its erection subcontractor, Syracuse Rigging, ended in Syracuse's favor and was not appealed. Fort Pitt appealed. The Second Circuit affirmed the damage offset, reversed in part as to interest, and remanded for recomputation of interest and entry of amended, separate judgments against Torrington and Aetna, with no appellate costs.
sections.Material Facts:
Torrington won a New York highway reconstruction contract that included a 270-foot, two-span bridge over the Battenkill River near the Vermont border. Before bidding, Torrington obtained Fort Pitt's quotation to fabricate, supply and erect about 240 tons of structural steel at 27.5 cents per pound. A September 5, 1969 confirmation expressly left delivery to mutual agreement. Fort Pitt had specifications showing work would begin October 1, 1969, with overall completion by December 15, 1971.

On November 3, in response to Fort Pitt's inquiry, Torrington specified late June 1970 for delivery and erection, and on November 12 Fort Pitt said it was tentatively scheduling accordingly. On January 29, 1970, it announced that it could not meet that date. After Torrington threatened to cancel, Fort Pitt promised early August delivery, but heavy structural components were shipped only from August 24 through September 4. Fort Pitt also failed to notify Syracuse Rigging of the first shipment, so Torrington had to unload steel until Syracuse arrived September 8.

Erection finished October 8 and the bridge was ready for concrete October 28. With freezing weather imminent, and with special permission to pour at thirty-two degrees, Torrington completed a crash pour lasting until 1 a.m., incurring overtime, equipment and concrete-protection expenses.
sections.Issue: Whether Torrington's expenses caused by late steel delivery were recoverable under Hadley v. Baxendale when the original contract left the delivery date open and the supplier learned of the required date only later, and whether Fort Pitt was entitled to interest on the unpaid balance despite accepting partial payments.
sections.Holding: The Second Circuit, in 1975, in an opinion by Judge Mulligan for a panel of Judges Waterman, Hays and Mulligan, held that where an agreement expressly reserves the performance date for later mutual determination, knowledge of the consequences of delay is assessed when the parties agree on that date. Fort Pitt knew the required timing when it accepted the June 1970 date, and the unloading and accelerated-pour expenses were reasonably foreseeable mitigation costs properly offset. Fort Pitt remained entitled to statutory interest, which had to be recalculated. No separate opinion appears.
sections.Reasoning:
Fort Pitt did not contest the findings of fact or breach. It argued that the expenses were special damages outside the parties' contemplation in September 1969, because the project could run until December 1971 and later knowledge could not expand its liability. The court accepted the rule that breach damages must be reasonably anticipated at contracting and that notice of unusual circumstances ordinarily must precede or accompany the commitment, but rejected the application. Fort Pitt accepted a June 1970 requirement pursuant to the original agreement and could not then rely on a 1971 delivery date. The court left open whether the September contract was already valid or became valid only when the date was settled; either way Fort Pitt knew the timing when it became committed to it. This was not a unilateral expansion of liability by later notice.

Fixing the knowledge date did not by itself establish recovery. An experienced bridge fabricator would understand the sequence from steel erection to pouring a concrete deck, knew the northern location, and had the specifications. Delay beyond summer predictably jeopardized concrete work before freezing weather, which the trial court found would otherwise have forced postponement until June 1971. Torrington's response avoided a potentially much greater loss at modest cost. A footnote states that reasonable expenditures to avoid foreseeable harm from breach may be recovered whether the mitigation succeeds or fails. These were not the unusual, uncommunicated losses Hadley excludes.

On interest, Torrington's partial payments in 1972 did not extinguish the debt, and accepting them without protest did not waive interest that Fort Pitt had demanded. Payments were to be applied first to accrued interest, and the district court had to account for the statutory rate change from seven and one-half to six percent effective September 1, 1972.

The casebook uses the case as the basis for a problem isolating the September contract, the later June delivery agreement and the freezing-weather mitigation.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-014.rule: When lost property has neither a market value nor a means of replacement or reproduction, damages are measured by its actual or intrinsic value to the owner, which may reflect ordinary attachment but excludes unusual sentimental or fanciful value.

sections.Parties: The Mieskes, a married couple, were the plaintiffs. They sued Bartell Drug Company, the retailer to which they delivered their developed family movie films for splicing, GAF, the film processor to which Bartell sent the films, and a janitorial company, for loss of the films. Bartell and GAF, held liable by the jury, appealed, challenging the damages instructions and the treatment of an exclusionary clause on the receipt. The janitorial company was not a party to the appeal.
sections.Procedural History: The jury returned a $7,500 verdict against Bartell and GAF, but not against the janitorial company that apparently removed the package. Bartell and GAF appealed, admitting negligence for purposes of the appeal and challenging the damages instructions and the handling of the receipt's limitation clause. The Washington Supreme Court, en banc, affirmed the judgment on April 19, 1979, leaving the $7,500 verdict intact with no remand.
sections.Material Facts:
Over many years the Mieskes filmed their wedding, honeymoon, vacations, holidays, their son's activities, pets, the construction of their home, and relatives who had since died. They had thirty-two fifty-foot reels of developed film and wanted them spliced onto four larger reels. Mrs. Mieske, a customer of Bartell's camera department for at least ten years, was told the service was available. The couple arranged and marked the reels in order and delivered them.

Bartell's manager handed Mrs. Mieske a receipt stating that responsibility did not extend beyond retail film cost unless otherwise agreed in writing. They did not discuss the clause, and she had never read it. She specifically warned that the films represented her life and should not be lost. Nothing was said about who would do the splicing; she assumed Bartell would. Bartell sent the package to GAF, which intended to forward it to another lab. The films were present in GAF's lab one day and missing the next. The court described disposal through a dumpster and landfill as the best explanation, not as a proven chain of custody.
sections.Issue: How damages should be measured for the loss of irreplaceable developed family films, and whether a receipt clause limiting the processor's responsibility to the retail cost of film was effective by trade usage, course of dealing or otherwise, or was unconscionable.
sections.Holding: The Washington Supreme Court, en banc, in 1979, in an opinion by Justice Brachtenbach in which Chief Justice Utter and Justices Rosellini, Stafford, Wright, Horowitz, Dolliver and Hicks concurred, with no separate opinion, affirmed the $7,500 verdict. It upheld valuation of the lost films by their actual or intrinsic value to the owners and rejected the receipt clause purporting to limit responsibility to the film's retail cost.
sections.Reasoning:
Washington law has three measures: market value for property that has a market; replacement or reproduction cost when property without a market can be replaced or reproduced; and value to the owner when neither is available. Defendants wanted damages confined to the cost of blank film, but that confused the physical medium with what was lost, images of unrepeatable family events. The third category therefore applied, and difficulty in fixing that value was no reason to deny recovery.

The court clarified the exclusion of sentimental value. Intrinsic value necessarily includes a subjective element; what is excluded is unusual, unwarranted emotional indulgence or a fanciful price placed on an object for peculiar reasons, not every ordinary human attachment. The instruction given, which allowed fair compensation for actual or intrinsic value while excluding sentimental or fanciful value and speculation, was proper. Defendants' proposed instruction was not a correct alternative.

On the limitation clause, the court applied the UCC's policy on excluding consequential damages to this service bailment, at least by analogy, although no title passed. Trade usage and course of dealing require proof. Defendants proved a practice among film processors, not a usage that retail customers understood, and Mrs. Mieske's ten years as a customer did not establish a common understanding, since the record did not show what earlier receipts said. Unconscionability is a question of law for the court on all the circumstances, and the parties had been given the opportunity to present evidence. The instruction making the limitation ineffective absent a specific agreement was not ideal, but any error was harmless because the judge had considered the required circumstances. The court did not hold every unread receipt clause automatically unconscionable.

The casebook quotes the intrinsic-value discussion in a passage on sentimental value, with an editorial footnote explaining value to a reasonable owner.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-015.rule: Damages for mental suffering are recoverable for breach of a personal contract so closely connected with the promisee's sensibilities that anguish from its breach is reasonably foreseeable, such as a contract to conduct a burial, without proof of a willful tort.

sections.Parties: Blummer Waddell Lamm, a widow, was the plaintiff and appellant. She sued the defendants, who operated Hunt Funeral Home and included Shingleton, for breach of their agreement to conduct her husband's funeral and inter his body and for breach of warranty in the sale of a burial vault, seeking damages for the shock and nervous injury she suffered. The defendants prevailed at trial.
sections.Procedural History: Lamm pleaded two causes of action: breach of the agreement to conduct the funeral and inter the body, and breach of warranty in the sale of the vault. At the close of her evidence the trial court nonsuited the warranty claim but let the burial-contract claim proceed, and it again refused to dismiss that claim after the defendants' evidence. The first jury issue asked whether the defendants caused injury through unlawful, willful negligence and carelessness in the burial. The jury answered no, and judgment was entered that she take nothing. She appealed. The North Carolina Supreme Court sustained the nonsuit on the warranty claim and ordered a new trial on the burial-contract claim.
sections.Material Facts:
Lamm's husband, Larry Waddell, died on August 3, 1946. She employed the defendants to conduct the funeral and bought a casket and burial vault from them. The vault had a base and a metal cover secured by ratchet locks at each end, and the defendants represented and warranted that it was watertight and would protect the body from water for years.

During a rainy period on the Wednesday before Thanksgiving, she discovered that one end of the vault's top had risen about six inches above ground. The following Saturday, employees of the defendants and the cemetery met to move the vault to an adjoining grave while she was present. When it was raised, water and mud were found inside and the casket was wet.

The evidence conflicted. Hers tended to show that the cover had not been locked at the original burial; the defendants' tended to show that it had been locked but that a lever slipped during removal and dislodged the locks. They also offered evidence that cemetery rules reserved interment and removal to cemetery authorities. She testified that the sight shocked her, made her extremely nervous and impaired her condition, and that Shingleton refused to remove the mud and angrily disclaimed concern.
sections.Issue: Whether the plaintiff's proof supported the separately pleaded warranty claim, whether her remaining claim sounded in contract despite allegations of negligence, and whether she could recover for mental anguish from breach of the burial contract without proving unlawful, willful negligence.
sections.Holding: The North Carolina Supreme Court, in 1949, in an opinion by Justice Barnhill, with Justice Seawell writing a dissent that agreed a new trial was necessary, held that the remaining claim was contractual and that mental suffering could be compensable for breach of this personal burial contract without requiring the jury to find unlawful, willful negligence; the issue and charge imposing that requirement were error requiring a new trial. It sustained the nonsuit of the vault-warranty claim. It did not decide the amount of injury or that the funeral home caused the failure.
sections.Reasoning:
Warranty. The plaintiff's evidence attributed the water to failure to lock the vault, not to a defect making it non-waterproof when properly assembled and locked, so she had not proved breach of the product warranty. The defendants' later testimony could not help her, because review of a nonsuit entered when she rested depended on her evidence at that point.

Contract, not tort. Her remaining claim rested on an agreement to furnish the necessary articles, conduct the funeral and inter the body, breached by failing to secure the vault. Calling that failure negligent did not convert the action into tort. Undertakers who undertake this service impliedly promise to perform it in a good and workmanlike manner.

Mental suffering. Contract damages cover injuries naturally and proximately resulting from breach and reasonably within the parties' contemplation. In ordinary commercial agreements pecuniary interests predominate and anxiety over financial loss is generally too remote. But the court rejected an absolute prohibition: where a personal contract is closely connected with mental concern, solicitude or the promisee's sensibilities, and its nature makes resulting anguish reasonably foreseeable, that suffering may be compensated. It gave marriage promises and death-message contracts as examples. The burial agreement was such a contract. The defendants knew she was the widow; her concern for her husband's proper burial, not pecuniary gain, was the reason for contracting, and the agreement itself put the undertakers on notice. The court added that North Carolina treats impairment of health from shock or fright as physical injury, and reserved whether it might adopt a willful-or-independent-tort doctrine in a proper case. The cemetery-control evidence was a defense for the jury.

Justice Seawell agreed a new trial was needed but would have treated the vault as an accessory to a specific undertaking to bury the body in a watertight vault rather than a separate sale, and thought the majority's implied promise too narrow.

The casebook cites the case in its account of emotional-distress damages.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-017.rule: Contract damages are limited to probable consequences of breach that were reasonably foreseeable when the contract was made; proof that a discharge caused a continuing psychiatric disability does not show the employer should have foreseen it at hiring.

sections.Parties: Eugenia Saporoso sued her former employer, Aetna Life and Casualty Company, for intentional infliction of emotional distress and breach of her employment contract; her husband asserted derivative consortium counts. The defendants obtained a directed verdict at trial. Saporoso appealed, seeking among other things contract damages for earnings and benefits lost over the rest of her career.
sections.Procedural History: Saporoso withdrew statutory workers' compensation-discrimination and unfair-trade-practices counts before trial. After several weeks of trial, the court directed a verdict for the defendants on the remaining claims. On the contract count it assumed the termination might be a breach but found no recoverable loss. Saporoso appealed without first moving to set the verdict aside, so review was limited to plain error. The Connecticut Supreme Court affirmed the directed verdict in a decision released March 3, 1992.
sections.Material Facts:
These facts are stated as the court assumed them, viewing the evidence most favorably to Saporoso. She worked for Aetna from 1966 until 1974, left to give birth, and returned in September 1982. In 1984 she moved to a department supervised by Larese. After January 1985 Larese became unduly critical, required work through lunch, and blamed her for tasks assigned to others. After a written warning in February she sought help for nervousness, headaches, shaking and stomach problems, and physicians certified that she could not work. Larese continued calling and writing about her absence, sometimes accusing her of malingering. An Aetna-selected orthopedist found no orthopedic problem and referred her to a specialist, who recommended that she stay out until June 18. Relying on the orthopedist's report, Larese demanded that she return June 5, and Aetna terminated her when she did not appear.

Her condition worsened after discharge. A psychiatrist attributed her anxiety, depression and physical symptoms to her employment and termination and found her totally disabled. After a contested hearing, a workers' compensation commissioner awarded total-disability benefits from March 6, 1985. Under the sick-pay plan, benefits for the maximum twenty-six months and on disability termination would have totaled $23,107.73; she had received $63,132.75 in compensation after discharge, and the plan required compensation payments to be deducted from sick pay.
sections.Issue: Whether, on plain-error review, the trial court erred in directing a verdict for the defendants, and in particular whether Saporoso could recover as contract damages the career-long earnings and benefits lost because her termination prolonged her psychiatric disability.
sections.Holding: The Connecticut Supreme Court, in 1992, in an opinion by Justice Shea for himself and Justices Callahan and Glass, with Justice Berdon, joined by Justice Borden, concurring in the result, affirmed the directed verdict for the defendants, finding no plain error. On the contract claim it held that, although a jury could find the termination caused her continuing disability and lost earnings, nothing in the record supported a finding that Aetna should have foreseen, when she returned in 1982, a continuing disabling psychiatric disorder if her employment were later terminated.
sections.Reasoning:
Under the majority's reading of General Statutes section 52-228b and the practice rules, a motion to set aside the verdict was necessary for full appellate review of a monetary verdict, including a directed verdict. Because Saporoso conceded that plain error was the standard, the court asked whether an obvious error so affected fairness, integrity and public confidence that extraordinary review was warranted. None of her claims met that standard, which limits how broadly the affirmance should be read.

Her argument that a proposed July 1990 amendment had automatically superseded the complaint failed: she had submitted it for a ruling, acknowledged its denial, and never argued automatic adoption at trial. The operative emotional-distress count alleged acts from January through March 1985, before the discharge, and she conceded that the resulting distress was the injury for which she received compensation. The majority applied collateral estoppel and workers' compensation exclusivity to that claim. It noted that Larese was not a party to the compensation proceeding, but Saporoso made no separate appellate claim against her.

On the contract count, the promised sick-pay benefits yielded no unpaid net entitlement once compensation payments were deducted. Saporoso proposed instead that the termination prolonged her disability and cost her earnings for her remaining career. The court accepted that the evidence could support causation and greater earnings from resumed employment, but applied Restatement (Second) of Contracts section 351: probable consequences must have been reasonably foreseeable when the agreement was made. Causation after discharge did not establish that foreseeability. The decision does not hold that a wrongful discharge can never cause psychiatric injury.

Justice Berdon, concurring, agreed to affirm only because the plaintiff conceded the restrictive standard; he opposed requiring a post-trial motion for legal rulings the trial judge had already carefully considered.

The casebook quotes the foreseeability conclusion in its discussion of employment contracts.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-018.rule: Emotional-distress damages for breach of contract may be available when they are both foreseeable from breach and explicitly within the parties' contemplation at formation, judged by the agreement's nature and language and the parties' reasonable expectations.

sections.Parties: Kipp Cabaness worked for Bountiful Light & Power from March 1978 until January 2004 and was a line-working foreman from 1984. He sued his immediate supervisor, superintendent of operations Brent Thomas, and director Clifford Michaelis for intentional infliction of emotional distress, and sued the municipal employer for breach of obligations in its personnel manual and for wrongful termination. The defendants sought, and obtained, summary judgment.
sections.Procedural History:
The district court granted the defendants summary judgment, denied Cabaness's cross-motion on contract formation, and rejected his postjudgment motion, which was accompanied by two city employees' affidavits about intent to make the manual binding. The Utah Supreme Court reviewed the summary-judgment legal questions for correctness and the exclusion of evidence for abuse of discretion, and refused to strike Cabaness's appellate brief.

In an amended opinion dated April 23, 2010, the court affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded. The contract claim and the intentional-infliction claim against Thomas survived; dismissal of the tort claim against Michaelis and of the wrongful-constructive-termination claim was affirmed.
sections.Material Facts:
Thomas lacked firing authority; Michaelis had it. The city's personnel manual applied to regular employees, undisputedly including Cabaness. Its disclaimer excluded contractual obligations concerning salary, salary ranges, movement within those ranges, and employee benefits. Other provisions promised not to tolerate harassing, intimidating, offensive, or hostile workplace conduct, prohibited threats and violence, and barred retaliation against employees using the manual's procedures in good faith.

Viewing the facts favorably to Cabaness, employees described years of Thomas's profanity, humiliation, unnecessary changes to work arrangements, threats of dismissal, and disregard of electrical-safety concerns. In July 2003, while Cabaness was on medical leave, Thomas ordered another employee to use a jackhammer near live electrical equipment despite warnings. Cabaness was diagnosed with workplace-related depression in 1997 and again in 2003. After a medically supported absence in summer 2003, Thomas publicly singled him out and threatened dismissal despite knowing of his depression. Employees had repeatedly complained to Michaelis; a later investigation interviewed fifteen employees and produced a warning to Thomas. Cabaness resigned in January 2004 and sued in March 2004. These were allegations and supporting testimony, not findings of liability.
sections.Issue: Whether the personnel manual's protective provisions created an enforceable contract; whether governmental immunity barred the contract claim; whether emotional-distress damages could be recovered for its breach; and whether the intentional-infliction and wrongful-constructive-termination claims survived summary judgment.
sections.Holding: The Utah Supreme Court, in a 2010 amended opinion by Justice Parrish joined by Chief Justice Durham, Associate Chief Justice Durrant, and Justice Nehring, with Justice Wilkins dissenting, held that the relevant manual provisions created a contract as a matter of law carrying an implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, that governmental immunity did not bar that contract claim, and that emotional-distress damages remained potentially recoverable on the required proof. The intentional-infliction claim against Thomas survived summary judgment; the claim against Michaelis and the wrongful-constructive-termination claim remained dismissed. The court did not establish breach or award damages.
sections.Reasoning:
A government employer can voluntarily assume contractual duties, and a manual can supply definite communicated promises under unilateral-contract principles, with employee service as acceptance and consideration. Because the parties stipulated that no formation facts were disputed, the court decided formation as law. The disclaimer was limited to salary and benefits, unlike a blanket disclaimer, so the affirmative anti-harassment promises objectively manifested additional obligations.

The pre-July-2004 immunity statute waived immunity for any contractual obligations, and the court refused to import the emotional-anguish exception from the separate negligence waiver.

Ordinary commercial disappointment does not normally support emotional damages. Drawing on its insurance decision in Beck, the court held that such damages could be available when both foreseeable from breach and explicitly within the parties' contemplation at formation. Promises protecting employees from harassment, intimidation, and a hostile environment were directed toward mental concerns, which made contemplation possible and defeated summary judgment; whether the parties actually contemplated such damages was remanded.

For the tort, the court adopted a continuing-conduct limitations rule, excluded the jackhammer episode because conduct outside the plaintiff's presence counts only in particularly compelling circumstances, and found that Thomas's persistent course of conduct could reasonably be considered outrageous. It declined to extend liability to Michaelis for failing to curb another's conduct. The constructive-termination claim failed because the provisions did not restrict termination and no public-policy violation was pleaded.

Justice Wilkins would have affirmed every ruling, rejecting extension of Beck beyond insurance contracts and finding the manual insufficient to create a contract. The casebook cites the case in its employment-contract reference and compares it with Ward; the brief notes that the casebook's shorthand that damages were available must be read with the conditional posture.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-019.rule: A seller's factual assurance about goods that forms the basis of the bargain is an express warranty under UCC 2-313, and emotional or spiritual injury and foreseeable consequential costs from its breach may be pursued under UCC 2-715.

sections.Parties: Sixteen Hindu vegetarians, including Gupta and Agarwal, who placed the order, sued an Indian restaurant, Asha Enterprises, alleging it supplied meat-filled samosas after assuring them the order was vegetarian. They sought compensation for emotional distress and the cost of travelling to India for a purification ceremony. The restaurant sought dismissal of all claims. The plaintiffs appealed the dismissal.
sections.Procedural History:
The restaurant moved to dismiss for failure to state a claim. The motion judge considered certifications and other evidence, converted the application to summary judgment, concluded further discovery was unnecessary, and dismissed all claims. The plaintiffs appealed, arguing that discovery had not begun and that the judge misconstrued each theory.

The New Jersey Superior Court, Appellate Division, argued March 22 and decided July 18, 2011, affirmed dismissal of the product-liability, implied-warranty, consumer-fraud, and negligence theories, reversed summary judgment on the express-warranty claim, and remanded. It did not award damages.
sections.Material Facts:
Viewed favorably to the plaintiffs, Gupta and Agarwal ordered vegetarian samosas on August 10, 2009, explaining that the group was strictly vegetarian. An employee assured them the restaurant did not make meat samosas. When they returned thirty minutes later the tray was allegedly marked as vegetarian and the assurance was repeated. After beginning to eat, some plaintiffs questioned the filling; an employee again assured them by telephone that the restaurant did not make meat samosas. They continued eating for a time, then returned the remaining food and were told it contained meat. The menu listed vegetable samosas and no meat samosas.

The restaurant's partner said two nearly simultaneous orders, one vegetarian and one with meat, were accidentally exchanged. The restaurant then supplied a replacement vegetarian order without payment, which the plaintiffs accepted. The plaintiffs explained that their religious beliefs treated even accidental meat consumption as spiritually harmful and required a purification ceremony in India. Those beliefs and consequences were the plaintiffs' description of their injury, not judicial findings. Discovery had not begun.
sections.Issue: Whether Hindu vegetarians who were served meat samosas after assurances that their order was vegetarian could recover for emotional or spiritual injury and purification costs under product-liability, implied-warranty, consumer-fraud, negligence, or express-warranty theories.
sections.Holding: The New Jersey Superior Court, Appellate Division, in 2011, in an opinion by Judge Payne for a panel with Judges Wefing and Hayden and no separate writing, held that the plaintiffs presented prima facie evidence of an express warranty of vegetarian samosas, so summary judgment on that claim was reversed and the claim remanded for development of emotional or spiritual injury and possible consequential purification costs. Dismissal of the product-liability, implied-warranty, consumer-fraud, and negligence claims was affirmed. No damages were awarded.
sections.Reasoning:
The Products Liability Act unified recovery for harm caused by a defective product, except breach of express warranty. The plaintiffs did not allege the samosas were unsafe or unfit for human consumption; their complaint was that employees supplied the wrong order, not a defective product. That disposed of the product-liability and implied-warranty claims.

On consumer fraud, the repeated assurances and alleged tray label were prima facie evidence of an unlawful misrepresentation, but a private claim required an ascertainable loss of money or property. The free replacement undercut any unpaid value, and the purification trip was a cost of curing alleged spiritual injury, not of repairing lost property.

On negligence, the plaintiffs fit neither of New Jersey's recognized independent emotional-distress patterns, and they offered no evidence of substantial bodily injury or sickness or severe mental or emotional harm.

Express warranty was different. Under UCC 2-313, factual promises or descriptions forming the basis of the bargain warrant conformity without formal language or intent to warrant, and the alleged failure concerned exactly the promised characteristic. UCC 2-715 permits consequential loss from needs the seller had reason to know when contracting and injury to person proximately resulting from breach. The court found relevant its funeral-services precedent recognizing emotional distress from breach of a promise of religiously significant services; difficulty of calculation did not warrant dismissal. Purification costs had to be reasonably foreseeable when the order was placed and a reasonably certain consequence, which could not be decided without discovery.

The court left open whether liability extends beyond the person who placed the order and any question of religious entanglement. The casebook uses the case as an example of emotional damages under the UCC warranty provisions; the brief notes that the casebook's statement that such damages were awarded overstates the disposition.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-020.rule: Mental suffering caused by breach of contract is generally not recoverable; the few exceptions arise in fiduciary or quasi-fiduciary contractual relationships coupled with tortious conduct.

sections.Parties: Mrs. Myron Levin of Highland Park, Illinois, the purchaser of a custom-made dress, sued Halston Limited, the designer, for return of her deposit and for mental anguish. Halston moved to dismiss the mental-anguish cause of action for insufficiency.
sections.Procedural History: Levin sued in the Civil Court of the City of New York for return of the deposit and for mental suffering. Halston moved to dismiss the first cause of action, for mental-suffering damages. On October 3, 1977, Judge Burton S. Sherman, at Special Term, New York County, dismissed that cause of action and directed judgment accordingly. The report does not dispose of the separate request for return of the deposit. This is a trial-court ruling on the sufficiency of the damages claim, not an appellate decision.
sections.Material Facts:
Levin wanted a custom-made Halston dress to wear at her daughter's wedding. In February 1975 she visited the defendant's New York showroom, selected a dress as a possibility, had measurements taken, and received fabric samples. At the end of April she ordered it and sent a $335 deposit. She alleged that the defendant lost her measurements, requiring another flight to New York, and she returned a third time in June for a fitting. The dress arrived before June 20, as promised.

Her letter described an uneven hem, an ill-fitting neckline and capelet, and poor packing. With fewer than six weeks until the wedding she could not return to New York to have it remade. Payment of the remaining $345 was stopped. She hastily obtained another dress for the occasion and never wore the disputed one. These were her allegations, taken favorably for the motion; the court did not adjudicate each claimed defect.
sections.Issue: Whether a purchaser may recover damages for mental suffering caused by the alleged breach of a contract for a custom-made dress she intended to wear at her daughter's wedding.
sections.Holding: The Civil Court of the City of New York, in 1977, per Judge Burton S. Sherman, held that the claimed mental suffering was not recoverable for this alleged breach of contract and dismissed the first cause of action as a matter of law. The court did not direct repayment of the deposit, determine replacement-dress expenses, or decide whether the dress had been properly made.
sections.Reasoning:
The judge applied the general rule that mental suffering caused by breach of contract is not recoverable. He described the few exceptions recognized by the authorities he cited as arising in fiduciary or quasi-fiduciary contractual relationships, such as hotel and guest, common carrier and passenger, or amusement park and patron, coupled with tortious conduct. None applied to this transaction.

He also invoked Hadley's limitation of contract damages to natural and probable consequences reasonably foreseeable at formation, and concluded that the claimed mental suffering did not qualify here. The analysis is brief: it states that conclusion without detailed findings about what the designer knew. The purchaser's letter and the importance of the wedding made her disappointment understandable to the judge, but sympathy did not answer whether this contract claim supported that category of recovery.

The casebook uses the case as its designer-dress example of denied emotional-distress damages; the brief notes that the casebook describes the dress as one the purchaser's daughter could not wear, whereas the report identifies the purchaser herself as the intended wearer.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-021.rule: A recipient of federal funds under Spending Clause antidiscrimination statutes is on notice only of remedies traditionally available for breach of contract, and emotional-distress damages, generally unavailable in contract, are therefore not recoverable in the implied private action.

sections.Parties: Jane Cummings, who is deaf and legally blind and communicates primarily in American Sign Language, sued Premier Rehab Keller, a small physical-therapy business in the Dallas-Fort Worth area, under the Rehabilitation Act and the Affordable Care Act. She sought declaratory and injunctive relief and damages. Premier, subject to those statutes because it received Medicare and Medicaid reimbursements, prevailed below; Cummings sought review.
sections.Procedural History: The District Court dismissed the complaint, reasoning that Cummings's only alleged compensable injuries were humiliation, frustration, and other emotional distress, and that such damages were unavailable. The Fifth Circuit affirmed. The Supreme Court granted review of the remedial question and, on April 28, 2022, affirmed the Fifth Circuit's judgment.
sections.Material Facts: In October 2016 Cummings sought physical therapy from Premier and requested an interpreter at her appointments. Premier declined, explaining that written notes, lip reading, or gestures could be used instead. Cummings sought and obtained treatment elsewhere. Premier received Medicare and Medicaid reimbursements, which made it subject to the antidiscrimination provisions of the Rehabilitation Act and the Affordable Care Act. The statutes did not expressly supply the private causes of action at issue; the Court had recognized implied actions, later ratified by Congress. The alleged discriminatory refusal remained an allegation; the Court did not try the provider's liability.
sections.Issue: Whether emotional-distress damages are available in the implied private cause of action under the Spending Clause antidiscrimination statutes at issue, the Rehabilitation Act and the Affordable Care Act.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States, in 2022, in an opinion by Chief Justice Roberts joined by Justices Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, Kavanaugh, and Barrett, held that emotional-distress damages are not recoverable under the Spending Clause antidiscrimination statutes considered. Justice Kavanaugh, joined by Justice Gorsuch, concurred; Justice Breyer, joined by Justices Sotomayor and Kagan, dissented. The ruling does not bar other compensatory relief or address every civil-rights statute.
sections.Reasoning:
The controlling analogy treats a funding recipient as voluntarily agreeing to conditions in return for federal money. The recipient must have clear notice of the liability attached to violating a condition; where the statute does not identify remedies, it can expect those traditionally available for breach of contract. Barnes v. Gorman had excluded punitive damages on that basis because they are generally unavailable in contract. The same reasoning excluded emotional-distress damages.

Cummings relied on the exception, reflected in Restatement (Second) of Contracts section 353, for contracts in which serious emotional disturbance is a particularly likely result of breach. The majority gave two answers. First, Barnes looked to general contract rules, not to whether a transaction fits an exception; a recipient cannot be charged with notice of every exceptional rule. Second, even on Cummings's approach there was no sufficiently settled general rule: some jurisdictions rejected such recovery altogether, others confined it narrowly, and many historical examples involved conduct actionable in tort.

Justice Kavanaugh considered the contract analogy imperfect and would leave expansion of remedies in implied actions to Congress. Justice Breyer agreed that contract law supplies the analogy but argued that a promise not to discriminate, like other promises serving personal or dignitary interests, foreseeably protects against emotional harm, that such damages compensate and do not punish, and that victims without pecuniary injury could be left without a remedy. The casebook presents the case for its funding-contract approach and the resulting exclusion of emotional-distress damages.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-022.rule: Emotional-distress damages for breach of contract require both that emotional injury be foreseeable and that the contract's specific language and obligations show the parties explicitly contemplated such damages at formation; foreseeability alone is not enough.

sections.Parties: Sara Marie Ward sued Meredith Dwight McGarry, with whom she had been romantically involved for approximately two-and-a-half years and had a child. She pleaded intentional and negligent infliction of emotional distress, breach of contract, equitable estoppel, punitive damages, negligent misrepresentation, and fraud. McGarry moved to dismiss. Ward appealed the dismissal.
sections.Procedural History: McGarry moved to dismiss based on the economic loss rule, the absence of recoverable contract damages, and the inability to plead equitable estoppel or punitive damages as independent causes of action. The District Court dismissed the complaint. The fraud dismissal rested on limitations and was not challenged on appeal. The Utah Court of Appeals reviewed the dismissal for correctness and, on May 12, 2022, affirmed.
sections.Material Facts:
During their relationship Ward sent McGarry nude photographs of herself. After they separated and a custody dispute began, she asked him by text to delete the photographs, promising in exchange not to use them in that dispute. He agreed. The messages were not in the record, but both parties accepted that the complaint accurately reflected their contents.

Several years after the separation, McGarry's former wife told Ward that she and her son had seen the photographs. According to the former wife, McGarry had given his phone to the child to play with; the child brought it home and showed the photographs to his mother, who sent one to Ward as proof. These were the complaint's allegations, not trial findings.
sections.Issue: Whether emotional-distress damages were recoverable for breach of an agreement to delete intimate photographs; whether promissory estoppel could supply those damages; and whether Ward's tort claims survived the economic loss rule.
sections.Holding: The Utah Court of Appeals, in 2022, in an opinion by Judge Michele M. Christiansen Forster for a unanimous panel with Judges Gregory K. Orme and Jill M. Pohlman, held that emotional damages were unavailable because the agreement's language did not show that the parties explicitly contemplated them, that promissory estoppel could not supply damages excluded under an enforceable agreement, and that the tort claims and dependent punitive damages failed because the independent duty Ward asserted on appeal had not been preserved. The court did not hold that no independent tort duty concerning intimate photographs could exist.
sections.Reasoning:
Utah ordinarily denies mental-anguish damages for breach of contract. The exception requires both foreseeable emotional injury and explicit contemplation of emotional damages at formation, shown through the contract's specific language and obligations. These are separate requirements. The agreement was personal and the District Court accepted foreseeability, but the language promised only deletion in exchange for nonuse in custody litigation and said nothing about mental or emotional harm.

The court distinguished Cabaness, where promises prohibiting harassment and a hostile environment specifically concerned mental well-being and so created a factual question about contemplation; the court stressed that Cabaness had not conclusively established contemplation and that Kranendonk later clarified and disavowed portions of it.

On estoppel, the court distinguished a valid contract under which a loss is not compensable from an absent or unenforceable contract. The agreement's enforceability was undisputed, so failure to prove recoverable contract damages could not convert it into a quasi-contract.

On tort, the economic loss rule confines a contract-supplied duty to contract remedies. The deletion duty came from the agreement, and the independent duty Ward asserted on appeal, not to show her intimate photographs to others, had not been argued below. A footnote assumed without deciding that such a duty might exist.

The casebook contrasts Cabaness with this deletion agreement in its discussion of degrees of certainty.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-023.rule: Lost profits are recoverable only if the breach caused them, they are proved with reasonable certainty and are not speculative, and they were fairly within the parties' contemplation when contracting; a new enterprise faces stricter scrutiny.

sections.Parties: Kenford Company and Dome Stadium, Inc. (DSI) sued Erie County for breach of a contract for a domed stadium near Buffalo. DSI sought twenty years of prospective operating profits under a management agreement and argued in the Court of Appeals that its expert proof was legally sufficient. The county sought affirmance of the dismissal of that claim.
sections.Procedural History: Kenford and DSI sued in June 1971. Roughly a decade of preliminary proceedings ended in an affirmed summary judgment establishing county liability and directing a damages trial. That trial lasted about nine months and produced a multimillion-dollar verdict for the plaintiffs. The Appellate Division reversed the lost-profit and certain out-of-pocket awards and directed a new trial on other issues. Only the dismissal of DSI's claim for prospective profits under the twenty-year management contract was before the New York Court of Appeals. On May 6, 1986, it affirmed that portion of the order, with costs. This is the 1986 stage, distinct from the 1989 Kenford decision.
sections.Material Facts:
On August 8, 1969, Erie County contracted with Kenford and DSI for a domed stadium near Buffalo. County construction was to begin within twelve months. The parties were to negotiate a mutually acceptable forty-year operating lease within three months after the county received preliminary plans, drawings, and cost estimates. If no acceptable lease emerged, an appended management agreement would give DSI twenty years of operation after the stadium was completed and available. Extensive negotiations produced neither a lease nor construction.

At trial DSI's experts used contemporary economic methods, data from other domed stadiums and related facilities, and a detailed Buffalo-area market study to project twenty years of operating profits. At the time of breach, only the Houston Astrodome offered a comparable facility in the country. The casebook identifies the operating-profit award as $25.6 million; the opinion itself does not print that figure.
sections.Issue: Whether DSI could recover twenty years of prospective operating profits for the county's breach of the stadium contract, given the requirements that such profits be within the parties' contemplation and proved with reasonable certainty.
sections.Holding: The New York Court of Appeals, in 1986, in a per curiam opinion in which Chief Judge Wachtler and Judges Meyer, Alexander, Titone, and Kane concurred, with Judges Simons, Kaye, and Hancock taking no part, held that DSI could not recover the claimed lost profits. The proof did not establish that the parties contemplated county liability for twenty years of profits, and the projection was not reasonably certain. The court affirmed dismissal of that damages claim.
sections.Reasoning:
New York allows prospective profits when the claimant proves that breach caused the loss, that the loss is reasonably certain and directly traceable, not speculative or attributable to intervening causes, and that the particular damages were fairly within the parties' contemplation when contracting. A new enterprise faces stricter scrutiny because it has no operating history. The court did not announce an absolute bar on new-business profits or require mathematical certainty.

On contemplation, the contract's default remedies did not suggest the heavy responsibility of guaranteeing the operator's profits for twenty years. Absent a provision on point, the court asked what the parties would reasonably have concluded had they considered the issue, and the evidence did not establish contemplation of that liability.

On certainty, the court acknowledged the sophistication of DSI's proof and found it difficult to identify further evidence DSI could have supplied. But the forecasts assumed successful completion and operation for twenty years, hosting professional sports, entertainment, meetings, and conventions. The many assumptions about long-term success, economic conditions, popular demand, and public support for professional athletics undermined the model, and sophisticated procedures could not remove their speculative nature.

The court expressly rejected the "rational basis" test of the federal Perma Research decision that had been adopted below. The casebook introduces its treatment of certainty by recounting the 1989 opinion's discussion of this earlier judgment.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-024.rule: A contestant deprived of the chance to continue a winner-take-all contest cannot recover a share of the prize where it can be neither assumed nor proved that he would have won.

sections.Parties: Collatz, a contestant in a theater's promotional quiz, sued the theater, Fox Wisconsin Amusement Corporation, claiming that ending the contest early deprived him of an opportunity to win the prize automobile. He recovered half the car's value in the circuit court.
sections.Procedural History: The case was tried to a circuit judge, who found that ending the contest was a breach and awarded Collatz half the car's value. The case reached the Wisconsin Supreme Court without a bill of exceptions, so review rested on the trial judge's findings and admitted allegations. In an opinion filed October 7, 1941, the court reversed the circuit court and directed dismissal of the complaint. Rehearing was denied on December 2 with $25 costs.
sections.Material Facts:
