On unconscionability, the court assessed the bargain as of formation, not with hindsight. The estate had dictated the prices, there had been no negotiation, and Carl paid exactly what was asked. An unexpectedly bad bargain was insufficient on these facts to establish oppressive terms.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-043.rule: A sale may be annulled for mistake about a substantial quality when the sellers consented in the firm conviction that a painting could not be by a particular artist while that attribution in fact remained possible.

sections.Parties: The Saint-Arromans owned and sold the painting; by the Versailles hearing Monsieur Saint-Arroman had died, and Madame Saint-Arroman acted for herself and as his heir, seeking affirmance of the annulment and return of the painting. The Réunion des musées nationaux, the appellant, and the Minister of Culture, who had intervened, sought reversal and preservation of the sale. The auctioneers and the successors of the deceased expert, Lebel, asked that the judgment releasing them be upheld; Madame Saint-Arroman sought damages against them in the alternative.
sections.Procedural History:
The owners brought their action in 1971. On December 13, 1972, the Paris trial court annulled the sale under then-article 1110 of the Civil Code and put the auctioneers and expert out of the case. The museum appealed. The Court of Cassation remanded on December 13, 1983, and the final costs order covered appellate proceedings before Paris, Amiens and Versailles, including the quashed decisions. The brief treats those earlier decisions only as litigation history.

On January 7, 1987, the combined chambers of the Versailles Court of Appeal affirmed the trial judgment, extended its effects to the Minister of Culture, and ordered the painting returned to Madame Saint-Arroman.
sections.Material Facts:
The Saint-Arromans needed money and retained the auctioneer Rheims to sell their painting. A family tradition attributed it to Nicolas Poussin, but Lebel, the auctioneer's expert, classified it as an anonymous work of the Carracci school and estimated it at 1,500 francs. The catalogue offered it under that attribution, with no suggestion of Poussin. At the February 21, 1968, auction it fetched 2,200 francs; the administration exercised its statutory preemption right, and the painting went to the Louvre. The museum had authority to preempt up to 40,000 francs, more than twenty-five times the expert's estimate.

The Louvre displayed the painting as a Poussin. A 1969 article by the curator Rosenberg explained that attribution and reported supporting expert views. Other specialists later disputed the attribution, and the Versailles court did not finally determine the artist.
sections.Issue: Whether a sale at public auction may be annulled for mistake under article 1110 of the Civil Code when the sellers sold in the conviction that the painting was not by Poussin, although its true authorship remains uncertain, or whether such a mistake concerns only experts' opinions or monetary value.
sections.Holding: The Versailles Court of Appeal, sitting in combined chambers in 1987, confirmed the nullity of the sale under article 1110. The judgment as reproduced has no separate writing or numerical vote. The court affirmed the 1972 trial judgment in all its provisions, extended its effects to the Minister of Culture, ordered restitution of the painting to Madame Saint-Arroman, and recorded her undertaking to repay the 2,200-franc price. It did not rule on her subsidiary damages claim against the auctioneers and the expert's heirs, and it did not determine who painted the work.
sections.Reasoning:
For a public auction using an expert-certified catalogue, the attribution of an artwork was a substantial quality for both seller and buyer, and the catalogue's description evidenced the seller's understanding of the thing offered. This description named the Carracci school and made no reference to Poussin, his school, style or manner. Since Poussin did not belong to that school, the description excluded that attribution rather than presenting it as a possibility the sellers knowingly put at risk. The court found the sellers' conviction at contracting was that this was not a Poussin.

The family tradition did not change that inquiry. The owners were laypeople entitled to accept the categorical view of a reputable expert and auctioneer. The professionals' assertion that the owners had concealed the tradition lacked independent support, came from interested parties and was implausible, so the alleged inexcusable fault had no factual basis.

Conflicting expert opinions prevented the court from deciding whether Poussin painted the work, but that did not reduce the mistake to an error about other people's opinions. The inability to exclude an authentic Poussin demonstrated the error in the sellers' absolute conviction that it could not be one. The museum, meanwhile, had at least believed the origin differed from the catalogue, as its 40,000-franc preemption authority and the favorable article fifteen days after the sale suggested. The court distinguished a mistaken economic estimate based on accurate knowledge of an object's qualities from a mistake about a substantial quality that consequently affected value; the latter was the operative error. The owners would not have consented had they known the actual uncertainty.

The casebook presents the case as the Putative Poussin problem, giving the price as approximately $500 and retaining the uncertainty over authorship. The brief was prepared from a reproduction of the French judgment and an English translation; the Gazette report itself was not inspected.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-044.rule: Caveat emptor does not bind parties who were honestly mistaken, in the essence of their bargain, about the identity of its subject matter, and a description of the goods in signed sale papers may operate as a warranty in law.

sections.Parties: The seller, and plaintiff, was an eighty-six-year-old amateur collector of rare violins, not a dealer; the appellate caption identifies George H. Smith as administrator. The seller sued to collect the unpaid balance of the price for two violins and was the appellant. Efrem Zimbalist, an internationally prominent violinist who also owned and collected old instruments, was the buyer, defendant and respondent; his defense was mutual mistake.
sections.Procedural History: The seller sued for the unpaid purchase-price balance. The trial court concluded that mutual mistake defeated recovery and entered judgment for Zimbalist. The seller appealed, urging caveat emptor. On November 20, 1934, California's District Court of Appeal, Second Appellate District, Division One, affirmed the judgment for the buyer. The report notes that a hearing in the California Supreme Court was denied on January 17, 1935. The opinion does not report a judgment returning the down payment or adjudicate a buyer's counterclaim for it.
sections.Material Facts:
Zimbalist visited to see the collection at another person's suggestion; the collector had not invited him to buy. Zimbalist picked up a violin, called it a Stradivarius, and asked its price. The collector offered $5,000. Zimbalist then selected another violin, called it a Guarnerius, and was offered the pair for $8,000. He accepted, with $2,000 down and $1,000 monthly installments for the balance.

Both sides signed documents identifying one Joseph Guarnerius violin and one Stradivarius dated 1717. Zimbalist's receipt acknowledged the instruments and payment terms; the seller's bill of sale repeated their makers, price and installments. The trial findings stated that both parties fully believed the instruments were made by those masters, that before closing the seller had made no representations or warranties about the makers and had acted without fraud, and that a preponderance of the evidence showed the instruments were imitations worth no more than $300.
sections.Issue: Whether a seller may collect the unpaid balance of the price for two violins that both parties believed were made by Stradivarius and Guarnerius but that were imitations, or whether caveat emptor places the risk of the mistaken attribution on a buyer who examined the instruments himself.
sections.Holding: California's District Court of Appeal, in 1934, in an opinion by Justice Houser with Presiding Justice Conrey and Justice York concurring, affirmed the judgment against collection of the balance. It held that strict caveat emptor did not apply where the parties were honestly mistaken, in the essence of their bargain, about the identity of its subject matter, so that no enforceable sale had occurred. Alternatively, the documents and conduct established a warranty in law that the instruments corresponded to their description. The judgment was affirmed under either analysis.
sections.Reasoning:
The court first traced older authorities supporting the seller: decisions treating an artist's name in a catalogue as opinion rather than warranty and denying relief for incorrect descriptions absent an express warranty or fraud. It then examined criticism and qualification of those decisions. Written descriptions in sale papers could themselves warrant kind and quality, and a buyer's opportunity to examine did not necessarily waive that protection. The court described Sherwood as supporting avoidance for a shared error about the substance of the bargain, while acknowledging Wood's contrary treatment of a discovered diamond's value. It relied on Henshaw, where inspection did not defeat a buyer when an imitation would deceive a skilled dealer, and on the California case Flint, which treated a flour brand in a sale note as a warranty.

On these findings the court rejected strict caveat emptor. Both parties believed they were contracting for authentic instruments made by the named masters; the finding of good-faith belief therefore did not establish the seller's right to the balance.

Alternatively, if the transaction were treated as a sale subject to a voidable condition, a warranty arose in law despite the trial finding that the seller had made no representations or warranties. The seller acquiesced in the buyer's attribution and signed a bill of sale certifying the makers, and that description committed him to delivering instruments corresponding to it. Later authorities and Civil Code section 1734 supported that consequence without requiring a separately spoken warranty or fraudulent intent.

The casebook's Sham Stradivarius problem deliberately changes the transaction to one violin, a $9,000 price, $3,000 down, a value of at most $500, and a buyer's claim for repayment; no such repayment award was entered in the actual case.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-046.rule: Death excuses further performance of a personal-service contract but does not nullify the agreement, so a dispute over compensation for work already done arises under the contract and is within a broad arbitration clause that the personal representative may invoke.

sections.Parties: Flora Buccini, executrix of the decorator Alberto Buccini, was the petitioner; she demanded arbitration of the compensation due for work performed before his death. Paterno Construction Co., the other contracting party, resisted, arguing that the claim was outside the arbitration provision, that a progress-payment clause left valuation to the owner, and that an executrix could not elect arbitration.
sections.Procedural History: The executrix petitioned to compel arbitration. Special Term granted her petition, and the Appellate Division denied it. The New York Court of Appeals, after submission on February 10, decided the case on March 18, 1930. It reversed the Appellate Division and affirmed Special Term, with costs in both appellate courts. Its order compelled arbitration; it did not calculate or enter a monetary award.
sections.Material Facts: Alberto Buccini contracted to decorate the ballroom, banquet hall and swimming pool at Paterno's Castle, a residence on Riverside Drive in New York City. The work required artistic skill. The contract expressly required Buccini to do the decorative figured work personally while allowing mechanics to perform plain work. It required arbitration, at either party's election, of all questions arising under the contract and in performance of the work. It also required payments during progress at seventy-five percent of the installed work's value and permitted the owner to determine the amount when such payments were requested. Buccini died while work was in progress, and the parties disputed the value of the benefits already received.
sections.Issue: Whether, after a contractor's death has excused further personal performance, a dispute over compensation for the work already done arises under the contract so as to fall within its arbitration clause, and whether the contractor's executrix may elect arbitration.
sections.Holding: The New York Court of Appeals, in 1930, in an opinion by Chief Judge Cardozo for a unanimous court, held that the controversy over the value of work done before Buccini's death arose under the contract and its performance and was within the broad arbitration clause, that the progress-payment clause did not displace arbitration, and that the executrix could exercise the deceased's election to arbitrate. The court did not find a specific value, fraction completed, or balance due.
sections.Reasoning:
The law treats sickness or death as an implied excuse in a personal-service undertaking; Buccini's death excused the duty to continue but left the owner liable for benefits already received. Discharge of the future performance duty did not nullify the entire agreement or free a compensation claim from its conditions. The controversy arose under the contract whether compensation on excused interruption was fixed by the parties or supplied by quasi-contract and equitable principles. Cardozo compared it with completed work under an agreement silent about price, where reasonable value could still be a dispute originating in the contract.

The agreement remained important to the extent of recovery. An estate could not obtain compensation for a willful, unexcused substitution merely because the substitute work was better than the plans required, nor could recovery exceed the contract price or its rate for the part performed. The relevant benefit was advancement of the owner's contractual purposes, not the work's value viewed independently of the bargain.

The progress-payment provision addressed continuing performance and interim payment applications; it did not control compensation after death had ended performance without either party's fault. And absent contrary express words, contracting parties are presumed to bind their personal representatives as well as themselves, so succession to the dispute included succession to the agreed means of resolving it.

The casebook cites the case twice: first for death as an excuse for personal service, and again in its restitution discussion, where it characterizes the compensation discussion as dictum and notes that the estate sought arbitration.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-047.rule: A seller who promises delivery of a product it markets as a technological breakthrough assumes the risk that the breakthrough cannot be realized, and is not excused for impracticability under the standard of UCC section 2-615.

sections.Parties: The United States, on behalf of the Federal Reserve Board as buyer, was the plaintiff and appellee; it sought damages for the failure to deliver a computer system. Wegematic Corp., the manufacturer and seller, was the defendant and appellant; its sole appellate defense was that delivering the promised computer was practically impossible.
sections.Procedural History: The district court for the Southern District of New York entered judgment for the United States for $235,806, with six-percent interest from October 6, 1958. The award consisted of $46,300 in delay damages, $179,450 for the excess cost of the replacement IBM equipment, and $10,056 in preparatory expenses unusable with the IBM system. Wegematic appealed, asserting only practical impossibility. The Second Circuit, after argument on March 28, decided the case on May 5, 1966, and affirmed. It did not independently decide every possible dispute about the damages calculation.
sections.Material Facts:
In June 1956 the Federal Reserve Board invited five manufacturers to propose an intermediate, general-purpose electronic digital computing system, emphasizing early delivery. Wegematic offered a new ALWAC 800 as a revolutionary system incorporating the latest advances, with delivery within nine months after an order. In September the Board ordered components at an aggregate price of $231,800 for delivery June 30, 1957. The order imposed $100 a day in liquidated damages for delay and authorized substitute procurement with the contractor responsible for excess cost. Wegematic accepted.

In March 1957 Wegematic suggested postponement; in April it promised delivery by October 30, citing redesign; in August it projected delay possibly into 1959. In April and August it sought waiver of delay damages; the Board considered the requests but expressly reserved its rights. In mid-October Wegematic said engineering difficulties made delivery impracticable and sought cancellation without damages. The Board procured an IBM 650, delivered October 6, 1958, at annual rent of $102,000 with a $410,450 purchase option. Wegematic asserted that correcting the engineering problems would take one to two years and $1 million to $1.5 million, with success probable but uncertain; experts suggested that the magnetic cores lacked sufficient uniformity.
sections.Issue: Whether a manufacturer that contracted to deliver a new computer it had promoted as a revolutionary advance is excused from liability for nondelivery on the ground of practical impossibility when engineering difficulties prevented it from producing the machine.
sections.Holding: The Second Circuit, in 1966, in an opinion by Judge Friendly for a panel with Chief Judge Lumbard and Judge Anderson, with no separate writing reported, rejected the practical-impossibility defense and affirmed the judgment for the United States. It held that the manufacturer had assumed the risk that the promised technological advance could not be realized. The court expressly left open whether the government could refuse a chance to correct the design yet recover both delay and replacement costs.
sections.Reasoning:
Both parties accepted federal law as governing. Friendly first distinguished the government's precedents by the relief and posture involved; they did not mechanically resolve the appeal, but neither did that establish an excuse. The court accepted Wegematic's suggestion that the Uniform Commercial Code could guide federal sales law, citing its widespread adoption and the value of commercial uniformity, without finding that any state's enactment governed directly. Section 2-615 excuses nonperformance when an unforeseen contingency defeats a basic assumption and renders performance impracticable, except insofar as the seller has assumed a greater obligation. Friendly treated the basic-assumption inquiry as substantially a question of how much risk the promisor accepted.

Marketing the machine as a technological breakthrough did not place the risk of achieving that breakthrough on the buyer. The reasonable understanding was that it had already occurred, or that the manufacturer assured its realization. The Board solicited a computer, not proposals for a development program. Otherwise a manufacturer could bind the purchaser with an attractive promise, gamble on technical success, and escape liability if it failed while demanding the price if it succeeded. The express delay and replacement-cost provisions made that reading particularly implausible, and a seller wishing to exclude development risk could use exculpatory terms, which this contract lacked.

The evidence of prohibitive cost was also unpersuasive: the redesign expense had to be assessed against the whole contemplated ALWAC 800 program, not this sale alone. The court's twenty-five-machine illustration suggested possible gross revenues of approximately $10 million at the comparable IBM price.

The casebook's note on the case addresses the seller's assumption of a greater obligation and asks about mistake.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-048.rule: Foreseeability of a supervening event is not an absolute bar to the defense of impossibility; it is evidence bearing on whether the event was sufficiently likely that the promisor should have guarded against it or bore its risk.

sections.Parties: The Opera Company of Boston, the plaintiff and appellee, sued for the unpaid balance of the contract price, maintaining that it had been ready, willing and able to perform but was prevented by cancellation. The Wolf Trap Foundation for the Performing Arts, the defendant and appellant, had engaged the company and asserted impossibility. The federal National Park Service owned and controlled the park where the performances took place.
sections.Procedural History: Five years after the canceled performance the Opera Company sued Wolf Trap for the balance. The district court found a complete power failure, public-safety concerns and the company's readiness to perform, but rejected impossibility because prior outages made an interruption affecting a performance foreseeable, and entered judgment for the company. Wolf Trap appealed and did not pursue an Act of God defense. The Fourth Circuit, after argument on November 13, 1986, decided the appeal on May 4, 1987. Although the opinion also describes the judgment as reversed, its concluding disposition vacated and remanded with instructions for findings about the likelihood and allocation of the power-failure risk.
sections.Material Facts:
The Opera Company promised four fully staged performances on June 12 to 15, 1980, at the Filene Center in Wolf Trap National Park. Wolf Trap promised $272,000, with the balance payable in four equal installments before each curtain, and provided the venue and specified lighting equipment. The covered auditorium seated approximately 3,500 and the lawn another 3,000; audience members walked hundreds of yards from parking to the center.

The first three performances went ahead. On June 15 a severe thunderstorm around 6:00 to 6:30 p.m. interrupted electricity throughout the park, and the utility predicted that power could not resume until after eleven and possibly not until morning. Approximately 3,000 people had arrived and 3,500 more were expected before the eight o'clock performance. The Park Service recommended immediate cancellation and disclaimed responsibility for safety if the performance proceeded. Wolf Trap agreed. An Opera Company representative attended some discussions, did not participate in the decision, and voiced no objection. Wolf Trap withheld the final payment.
sections.Issue: Whether the district court applied the proper legal standard in rejecting the impossibility defense solely because a power interruption was foreseeable, or whether the defense turns on how likely the event was and on who bore its risk.
sections.Holding: The Fourth Circuit, in 1987, in an opinion by Judge Donald Russell joined by Judge Hall, with District Judge McMillan dissenting from the disposition, vacated the judgment for the Opera Company and remanded. It held that foreseeability alone does not defeat impossibility: the district court had to make findings, with reasons, on whether the power failure was sufficiently likely that Wolf Trap should have guarded against it or negotiated protection, and the parties could offer further evidence. The court did not finally hold that Wolf Trap owed nothing.
sections.Reasoning:
Russell traced the movement from strict enforcement despite unexpected impediments to relief when a necessary person or thing becomes unavailable, and treated modern impossibility or impracticability as an equitable doctrine concerned with a change so severe that enforcing the promise as written would be unreasonable. The court drew on Virginia decisions, federal precedents, the Restatement and the UCC as doctrinal support. The defense required an unexpected intervening event, whose nonoccurrence was a basic assumption of the agreement, making performance impracticable; a promisor could not rely merely on its personal inability.

The important distinction was between a contingency being conceivable and its risk having been assigned to the promisor. Even a reasonably foreseeable or foreseen event did not necessarily defeat discharge, because parties cannot always negotiate terms for every contingency; the event's degree of likelihood and commercial significance mattered. The court rejected an absolute foreseeability bar while preserving foreseeability as evidence bearing on reasonable risk allocation.

The majority agreed that electricity was necessary to a satisfactory performance and that the findings supported impracticability, subject to the unresolved risk issue. The district judge had stopped at foreseeability. Responding to the dissent, Russell stressed that the danger extended beyond a dark stage: auxiliary service would have delayed the start until ten or eleven without illuminating park roads and paths, leaving thousands in a wooded park during a lightning storm.

Judge McMillan accepted the doctrinal discussion but would have affirmed. Lighting was an essential, priced component of Wolf Trap's undertaking; a memorandum by Wolf Trap official Craig Hankenson described inexpensive backup arrangements, earlier outages, and his prior warning that a theater without emergency capacity was incomplete; and no power-failure exemption had been written into the contract.

The casebook presents the case in a note titled The Case of the Foreseeable Finale and summarizes the result as a reversal and remand.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-049.rule: Under Ohio law impossibility is an affirmative defense requiring an unforeseen event after contracting that makes performance impossible without the promisor's fault; reasonably foreseeable difficulties and mere difficulty or burden do not excuse performance.

sections.Parties: Brianna Belk and Tiffany Morris, workers at a childcare center, were the plaintiffs in a wage-and-hour suit, joined by thirty-five opt-in workers; they moved to enforce a settlement. Le Chaperon Rouge Co. and Stella Moga-Kennedy, its owner and operational manager, were the defendants, alleged to be joint employers. They resisted enforcement on the grounds that Moga-Kennedy had not individually agreed to the settlement and that pandemic-related financial hardship made payment impossible.
sections.Procedural History:
Belk and Morris sued on August 27, 2018, under the FLSA and Ohio law. The court conditionally certified an FLSA collective action in February 2019, and an amended complaint was filed January 31, 2020. Mediation on February 28, 2020, failed, but continued proceedings on March 12 produced a settlement recited on the record before a magistrate judge. Defendants did not execute the written draft, and plaintiffs moved on April 11 to enforce the agreement and obtain class certification and settlement approvals.

On July 6, 2020, the district court for the Northern District of Ohio granted the motion in part and denied it in part. It enforced the agreement against both defendants and certified the Rule 23 class, but withheld approval of the settlements, notice and a fairness hearing, ordering revised documents within thirty days.
sections.Material Facts:
The plaintiffs alleged unpaid work before and after scheduled shifts and uncompensated mandatory training; these were allegations, not adjudicated violations. On March 12, 2020, the material settlement terms were recited on the record: defendants would pay $200,000 forty days after court approval. Moga-Kennedy personally confirmed that she heard, understood and agreed to the terms.

Ohio had declared an emergency on March 9; the WHO declared a pandemic on March 11; and on March 12 Ohio ordered kindergarten-through-twelfth-grade schools closed and authorized emergency childcare rules. Later measures imposed a stay-at-home order and required childcare centers to close March 25 unless licensed for temporary pandemic care. Plaintiffs circulated a written draft on March 19. On March 31 counsel cited shutdown and financial repercussions, and the approval deadline passed.

Defendants described an enterprise with eleven childcare centers, a private school and approximately 1,174 enrolled children, and Moga-Kennedy declared that shutdown, layoffs and reduced attendance made payment impossible. Defendants deliberately omitted detailed evidence of her personal ability to pay.
sections.Issue: Whether an oral settlement recited on the record bound the individual owner as well as the company, and whether financial hardship caused by the COVID-19 pandemic and the resulting closure orders excused the defendants from the settlement under the doctrine of impossibility.
sections.Holding: The district court for the Northern District of Ohio, in 2020, in a memorandum opinion and order by Judge Pamela A. Barker, held that the March 12 oral agreement bound both the company and Moga-Kennedy individually, jointly and severally, and that pandemic-related financial hardship did not establish impossibility. It certified the Rule 23 class but withheld approval of the collective and class settlements until the parties corrected inconsistent financial provisions. The decision was neither a determination that the wage allegations were true nor final approval of the settlement.
sections.Reasoning:
Ohio contract law governed by agreement. Enforcing a settlement required assent to all material terms, assessed objectively, and the lack of a completed written memorial did not diminish an already binding oral agreement. The court did not infer contractual liability from possible statutory liability alone. The recorded terms repeatedly referred to the defendants without separating them, counsel represented both, Moga-Kennedy personally confirmed her agreement, and no one added a limitation. The later draft named both defendants with two signature lines. Against Ohio's presumption concerning multiple promisors, joint and several liability was the only reasonable reading of the objective assent; her private understanding could not make the agreement ambiguous.

Impossibility was an affirmative defense defendants had to prove: an unforeseen postcontract event must make performance impossible without their fault, and difficulty, danger or burden alone was insufficient. The defense failed for two independent reasons. First, by March 12 the emergency measures made significant business disruption reasonably foreseeable. Defendants knew schools had just been closed, directly affecting their private school and signaling possible effects on childcare. The court did not require foresight of each later restriction, and noted that defendants could have deferred settlement or negotiated force majeure protection but instead assented to payment. Second, even assuming the impact was unforeseeable, defendants did not prove that Moga-Kennedy personally could not pay; they supplied no sworn declaration or documentation of that inability.

Approval was deferred because the draft agreement, the proposed joint motion and the proposed order gave inconsistent allocations and fee and cost amounts.

The casebook's note, The Handwriting on the Wall, emphasizes the foreseeability reasoning. Its shorthand that the agreement was executed and defendants ceased paying differs from the actual chronology.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-050.rule: A force majeure clause excusing performance made inadvisable by a listed event is construed objectively in light of its risk-allocation function, and economic undesirability following such an event does not by itself excuse performance.

sections.Parties: The plaintiff was the resort, Outrigger Wailea Resort, which had contracted to host a conference; it sought liquidated damages for cancellation. The defendants were SFX, the contracting party that signed as Urban Network-SFX Multimedia Group and asserted force majeure, and Clear Channel Communications, Inc., which the resort characterized as the parent of the signatory organization and which denied being a contracting party.
sections.Procedural History: The resort sued on March 4, 2002, seeking $625,912.65 in liquidated damages after crediting a $10,000 deposit. The parties filed cross-motions, and the resort moved to strike evidence. On February 5, 2003, the district court for the District of Hawai'i granted the resort's motion rejecting SFX's force majeure defense and on the difficulty-of-proof component of liquidated damages, left reasonableness and the amount of damages unresolved, granted Clear Channel Communications' motion, denied SFX's motion, and denied the motion to strike as moot and, alternatively, on admissibility grounds. The decision was interlocutory and awarded no damages.
sections.Material Facts:
On November 19, 2000, the resort contracted with Urban Network-SFX Multimedia Group to host Power Jam 2002, a music-industry conference scheduled February 13 to 17, 2002. The resort drafted the agreement, which held 2,270 room nights at rates between $235 and $900. Cancellation zero to thirty days before arrival required one hundred percent of total guest-room revenue plus applicable taxes.

The force majeure provision identified acts of God, war, government regulation, terrorism, disaster, specified strikes, civil disorder, transportation curtailment and other emergencies beyond the parties' control, making performance inadvisable, illegal or impossible, and allowed either party to cancel for such reasons on written notice. Miller London's January 16, 2002, cancellation letter cited September 11 together with fragile consumer economies and withdrawn sponsor and participant commitments. SFX described only 150 of 500 rooms booked, three secured by credit card, and thirty-eight participating companies compared with 102 the previous year.
sections.Issue: Whether the September 11 attacks made holding a conference in Maui five months later inadvisable within the force majeure clause, so as to excuse cancellation; whether the named parent company was bound by the contract; and whether the liquidated damages clause was enforceable.
sections.Holding: The district court for the District of Hawai'i, in 2003, in a decision by District Judge Kay, held that SFX's force majeure defense failed because its evidence showed cancellation was economically sensible but not that travel to Maui was objectively inadvisable. It held that Clear Channel Communications was not a contracting party and was not bound through agency. On liquidated damages, the resort established difficulty of proof, but reasonableness remained genuinely disputed. The court did not award the damages sought or finally enforce the clause.
sections.Reasoning:
The parties agreed that the attacks were a force majeure event of a kind the clause described; they disagreed about their effect on this conference. Under Hawai'i law the court construed the language as a legal question using an objective standard. The word inadvisable could not be detached from the clause's risk-allocation function, and construing ambiguity against the drafter was inapplicable to equally sophisticated parties. The court used Restatement section 261 and impracticability decisions to inform construction, while acknowledging the Restatement did not specifically address force majeure clauses. Ordinary market shifts, financial inability or increased expense do not usually discharge a promise, and economic undesirability did not become an excuse merely because it followed a named event. The agreement did not allocate the risk of low attendance or withdrawn commitments to the resort.

The record contained no specific terrorism threat to Maui or relevant air travel, and substantial travel and convention attendance continued; general fear and tourism decline did not prove the necessary effect on performance. The court observed that an event scheduled immediately after September 11 would present a stronger excuse, without deciding such a case, and that a single attack could not excuse performance indefinitely.

On parent liability, a general-counsel declaration and Delaware formation documents showed SFX Multimedia was a separate entity, and there was neither actual nor apparent authority to bind Clear Channel Communications; the resort did not establish reliance on any representation of agency.

On liquidated damages, under Hawai'i law and Restatement section 356 the resort showed difficulty of proof because a conference generates uncertain ancillary profits. Reasonableness was disputed: the clause used revenue rather than profit, and the experts' loss estimates were at least $410,645 for the resort against $29,000 to $38,000 for defendants.

The casebook's account refers to the defendants as Clear Channel, whereas the opinion distinguishes the released parent from SFX.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-051.rule: A party asserting impossibility must show that it took virtually every action within its power to perform; an impediment the party itself procured is no excuse, and a force majeure catchall is read in light of the listed events and the clause's purpose.

sections.Parties: Kama Rippa Music, Inc., a music publisher, was the plaintiff and appellant; it sued for specific performance of an alleged obligation to release recordings and resisted reversion of rights. Melanie Schekeryk, a songwriter and performer, was the defendant, counterclaimant and appellee; she sought declaratory and injunctive relief establishing that rights in her compositions had reverted to her.
sections.Procedural History: Kama Rippa sued on August 31 for specific performance, and in mid-September repeated its claim in state court and obtained an attachment, which the state court later vacated on technical grounds. The district court granted Melanie partial summary judgment on two counterclaims, with declaratory and injunctive relief, reserved the complaint for an evidentiary hearing, and made express Rule 54(b) findings permitting an appeal. The Second Circuit, after argument on January 6, decided the appeal on February 10, 1975, and affirmed. Other claims remained pending below.
sections.Material Facts:
Melanie's May 1968 songwriter agreement required her to deliver compositions that Kama Rippa would publish, sharing royalties. A rider made timely royalty payment essential: failure to account and pay persisting after thirty days' written notice would terminate the agreement and return rights to her. The rider permitted suspension upon notice for delays, impossibility or impracticability caused by listed events such as fire, earthquake, strikes, government action, war or material shortages, followed by a general reference to similar or dissimilar reasons. An August 1971 letter agreement required her to deliver twenty compositions and record at least three within two years, with $25,000 liquidated damages per unfinished recording as the sole remedy.

In August 1973 Kama Rippa intentionally withheld royalties, claiming Melanie had recorded but not released the required songs. She gave written notice of default. The publisher then obtained a state-court attachment of almost all its debt to her and asserted that the order made paying her legally impossible. When the attachment was vacated the publisher sent a check, but the thirty-day cure period had long expired.
sections.Issue: Whether the publisher's failure to pay royalties within the cure period was excused because royalty payment depended on the songwriter's recording obligations, because of the rider's force majeure language, or because a court attachment the publisher itself obtained made payment impossible; and whether equity barred the reversion.
sections.Holding: The Second Circuit, in 1975, in an opinion by Judge J. Joseph Smith for Judges Oakes and Timbers, applying New York contract law, affirmed the partial summary judgment. Rights in the submitted compositions had reverted to Melanie because the publisher failed to pay royalties after notice and the contractual cure period, and the publisher could no longer claim an interest or collect royalties on them. The attachment did not excuse the default because the publisher procured it. The court did not decide the still-pending complaint.
sections.Reasoning:
Reading related documents together does not make every obligation mutually dependent. The letter agreement expressly made liquidated damages the sole remedy for failure to record while preserving rights and claims under the songwriter agreement, so a possible recording breach did not excuse timely royalty payment. The publisher identified no material ambiguity justifying custom-and-usage evidence; its evidence sought to vary the agreement, particularly the forfeiture rider. The publisher's own conduct in obtaining an attachment shortly before the cure period expired, then paying when it was lifted, suggested it understood payment to be independent of the recording dispute.

As to the phrase covering dissimilar reasons at the end of the force majeure list, the district court disregarded it to give effect to the rider's purpose, a method the appellate court found supported by New York law; alternatively, ejusdem generis could assimilate the generic language to the preceding specific events. Either approach produced the same construction.

The attachment was no excuse. A party asserting impossibility had to show that it took virtually every action within its power to perform, rather than deliberately incapacitating itself, and a lawful attachment procedure could not be exploited to defeat contractual duties.

The court rejected the argument that restitution required Melanie to compensate the publisher for development expenditures: the publisher had already received substantial sums rewarding its efforts, and the claimed uncompensated expenditures lacked record support. The general equitable aversion to forfeiture did not authorize erasing a reversion right deliberately included in the bargain, and the attachment maneuver implicated unclean hands.

The casebook uses the case twice: for the rider and the alternative ejusdem generis construction in its force majeure discussion, and in a note titled Promisor's Good Faith? for the rule against self-induced impossibility.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-052.rule: Where a lease's force majeure clause allocates the risk of a contingency and expressly preserves the duty to pay rent, common-law frustration, impossibility and failure of consideration do not supply discharge or abatement contrary to the agreed terms.

sections.Parties: 1600 Walnut Corp., the landlord and plaintiff, sought rent arrearages, additional rent, late fees, interest, attorneys' fees and costs, and moved to dismiss the tenant's counterclaims. Cole Haan Company Store, the tenant and counterclaimant, sought six declarations that its lease obligations were discharged, abated or terminated because of the COVID-19 closure.
sections.Procedural History: The landlord sued in the district court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, within diversity jurisdiction, and the tenant pleaded six amended counterclaims. The landlord moved under Rule 12(b)(6). By memorandum and order signed March 29, 2021, and filed March 30, the court granted the motion and dismissed all six amended counterclaims with prejudice. It did not then award rent or resolve the entire action: the order set deadlines for summary-judgment motions and responses.
sections.Material Facts:
Cole Haan entered a long-term commercial lease with 1600 Walnut in 2004, extended in 2014 through March 31, 2025. A force majeure clause excused delayed performance for strikes, labor trouble, material shortages, power failure, restrictive governmental laws or regulations, riots, insurrection, war, and other reasons not the delayed party's fault or beyond its reasonable control. The clause expressly preserved the tenant's duty to pay rent, apart from a delayed commencement date, and excluded lack of funds or financing as grounds for relief. The lease also provided automatic termination if the entire premises was taken by eminent domain.

Cole Haan permanently vacated in March 2020 and stopped paying rent. The governor's March 23 COVID-19 order prohibited operation of the store. Philadelphia retailers could reopen with restrictions after June 5, but Cole Haan did not reopen or resume payments. These were the tenant's pleaded facts, accepted as true at this stage.
sections.Issue: Whether a commercial tenant whose store was closed by COVID-19 government orders may obtain discharge or abatement of rent through frustration of purpose, impossibility or impracticability, or failure of consideration, or termination under the lease's eminent-domain provision, when the lease's force majeure clause expressly preserves the duty to pay rent.
sections.Holding: The district court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, in 2021, in a memorandum by Judge J. Curtis Joyner applying Pennsylvania law, dismissed all six counterclaims with prejudice. It held that the pandemic and the governor's orders fell within the force majeure clause, which expressly kept rent payable, so the contract's own allocation displaced the common-law doctrines. It also held that the restrictions were not a taking that triggered the eminent-domain termination provision. The ruling did not determine that government closures never frustrate commercial leases.
sections.Reasoning:
Pennsylvania parties may allocate contractual risks broadly, and a court turns to common-law impossibility and frustration to allocate risk only if the contract has not already done so. Here the force majeure clause specified both the excusing events and an exception keeping rent payable, and separately excluded lack of funds. The question was therefore whether the COVID-19 interruption fell within that agreed allocation.

The governor's restrictive retail orders were the most obvious proximate cause of nonperformance and were expressly covered as restrictive governmental laws or regulations. Cole Haan argued that the pandemic itself lay outside the clause because the listed events were manmade and short-lived while COVID-19 was naturally occurring. The court rejected that reading, regarding the pandemic as belonging with the listed life-altering national events such as war, riots and insurrection and thus within the broad catchall. The clause was unambiguous and construed as a matter of law. Coverage did not free the tenant from rent; it triggered the allocation expressly preserving that obligation. Because the contract allocated this contingency, frustration, impossibility or impracticability, and failure of consideration could not supply relief contrary to its terms.

On the sixth counterclaim, the court relied on the Pennsylvania Supreme Court's treatment of the governor's orders as a valid exercise of police power rather than eminent-domain power, and so rejected the asserted taking and the resulting termination claim.

The casebook reproduces the rent-preserving clause and uses the case to explain the allocated pandemic risk.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-053.rule: Where a lease's force majeure clause relieves a party from liability when a specified event prevents performance and contains no proviso preserving rent, the rent obligation is excused during the event rather than merely delayed.

sections.Parties: BP Prucenter Acquisition LLC and Saks Fifth Avenue LLC were parties to a lease under which Saks owed rent. Saks was excused from paying rent after a mandated COVID-19 closure; BP contested that result and moved to reconsider or clarify the court's decision.
sections.Procedural History: The Massachusetts Land Court issued its decision on December 15, 2022; the brief states that this complete opinion could not be obtained and describes it only through the casebook's account. In a March 20, 2023, order Judge Jennifer S.D. Roberts addressed BP's motion to reconsider or clarify, allowing it only to clarify that rent was excused rather than delayed and denying it in all other respects. A May 11, 2023, order then assessed monetary relief. These later orders are distinct stages.
sections.Material Facts: As the casebook reports the 2022 decision, the lease's force majeure clause lacked a proviso preserving the duty to pay rent, and Saks was subject to a mandated COVID-19 closure. The March 2023 order reproduced lease language relieving a party from liability when a specified event prevents performance. Payments were made under protest during the excused period; the May 2023 order used April and May 2020 and a specified June 2020 period. The brief does not have the full 2022 findings or clause.
sections.Issue: Whether a force majeure clause that lacked a rent-preserving proviso excused the tenant from paying rent during a mandated COVID-19 closure, and, on reconsideration, whether the rent duty was excused or merely postponed.
sections.Holding: The Massachusetts Land Court, in 2022, as the casebook reports it, held that the clause excused Saks from paying rent after the mandated COVID-19 closure. On reconsideration in March 2023, Judge Roberts clarified that the lease excused the rent obligation during the force majeure event rather than delaying payment until afterward. In May 2023 the court awarded $196,439.17 for payments made under protest during the excused period, plus $510,294.46 in fees and $17,946.82 in costs; those amounts belong to the later order, not the 2022 ruling.
sections.Reasoning:
The reasoning of the December 2022 opinion is not given in the brief beyond the casebook's summary, because the complete opinion could not be obtained.

In the March 2023 order the court rejected BP's challenge to the use of proximate causation, noting that BP itself had used that concept in its earlier argument. The newer authorities BP cited concerned either common-law excuses without a force majeure clause or clauses with materially different language, and did not show a demonstrable error. The court contrasted language relieving a party from liability when a specified event prevents performance with provisions that merely extend deadlines or suspend duties, and read this lease as excusing rent during the event. It explained that its equitable forfeiture discussion was an alternative in case an appellate court rejected the contractual ground; the two theories had not been applied simultaneously.

In the May 2023 order the court allowed fee recovery under the lease provision for reasonable expenses connected with obtaining a favorable final outcome, excluded unsuccessful or unrelated work, and after a further reasonableness assessment reduced the recoverable fees by 60 percent.

The casebook contrasts this lease with leases that expressly preserve the duty to pay rent during force majeure, to show why the language allocating risk matters.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-054.rule: Illness of an employee discharges a contractual duty only if the parties understood performance to depend on that particular person's services; if another can perform without violating the contract, the promisor's own inability or added cost is no excuse.

sections.Parties: George Seitz, the contractor on a theater renovation, was the plaintiff; he sought the difference between his sign subcontract price and the cost of a replacement. Mark-O-Lite Sign Contractors, Inc., the sign subcontractor, was the defendant; it relied on a force majeure clause and on impossibility after its only capable employee was hospitalized.
sections.Procedural History: The case was a contract action in the Law Division of the New Jersey Superior Court, Monmouth County, submitted at trial on stipulated facts. On January 31, 1986, the court rejected the subcontractor's defenses, held its refusal a material anticipatory breach, and directed entry of a $7,200 judgment for Seitz, requiring him to submit an appropriate judgment form. This was a trial-court determination; it did not affirm a lower-court judgment or remand for damages.
sections.Material Facts:
Seitz was the low bidder on renovations of the Strand Theater for the Ocean County Center for the Arts and signed the owner's $51,200 contract on December 26, 1983. On April 18, 1984, Seitz and Mark-O-Lite signed a subcontract for the sign work for $12,800, and Seitz gave a $3,200 deposit check. The subcontract excused failures resulting from labor strikes, fires, floods, earthquakes, acts of God, and other conditions or contingencies beyond the company's control.

Within days Mark-O-Lite discovered that Al Jorgenson, its only employee capable of the detailed sheet-metal work, had to enter the hospital for an unknown period. Jorgenson was diabetic, and progressive infection led to partial amputation of his foot. The company told Seitz by telephone and on May 3 returned the uncashed deposit with a letter offering whatever portion of the work it could perform. Other sign companies it contacted quoted $18,000 to $20,000, which would make subcontracting economically infeasible for it. Seitz contracted with City Sign Service for $20,000 and claimed the $7,200 difference. The stipulated replacement description identified added rail, neon and a neon border as extras beyond the original specifications.
sections.Issue: Whether the hospitalization of the subcontractor's only employee capable of the work excused its performance, either under a force majeure clause covering acts of God and other contingencies beyond its control or under the common-law doctrine of impossibility.
sections.Holding: The New Jersey Superior Court, Law Division, in 1986, in a decision by Acting Superior Court Judge Milberg, rejected both the force majeure and the impossibility defenses, held that Mark-O-Lite's May 3 letter and return of the deposit were a material anticipatory breach, and directed judgment for Seitz for $7,200, calculated as $20,000 less $12,800. The court used the full replacement price without explaining any separate adjustment for the stipulated extras.
sections.Reasoning:
On the clause, the court applied ejusdem generis: general language following listed events reaches contingencies of the same general nature, not every event outside the obligor's control. Jorgenson's illness was not in the class of the listed disasters. Nor did the progressive consequences of diabetes qualify as an act of God; his disability was not sudden and was reasonably foreseeable given his condition. The court's reference to a sudden stroke or heart attack identified circumstances that might be treated differently, without establishing an exemption for every sudden illness.

Failure under the clause did not itself eliminate common-law impossibility. The court examined the original Restatement's rule for death or illness of a necessary person and the Second Restatement's sections 261 and 262. Under either, the defense required that the parties understand performance to depend on a particular person's services; if another could perform without violating the contract, the expected employee's illness would not discharge it. The subcontract did not require Jorgenson personally, and his peculiar skill or discretion was not indispensable. Mark-O-Lite's own efforts to hire outside shops showed the work was delegable, and Seitz's replacement contract confirmed that it remained possible. The problem was that Mark-O-Lite could not perform with its existing staff at a satisfactory cost. The court distinguished subjective from objective impossibility and rejected marginal profit or a loss on replacement subcontracting as an excuse for a fixed-price obligation.

A definite, unconditional declaration that essential promised performance will not be rendered is a material anticipatory breach. The offer to perform some work did not oblige Seitz to accept a divided substitute, and given deadlines under the owner's contract, replacing the entire sign subcontract was reasonable.

The casebook adapts the case as its Hospital Case problem, renaming the parties Brighten and T-Square; the answer the actual judgment gives is that the employee's being uniquely capable within his employer did not make his services contractually nondelegable.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-055.rule: Impracticability excuses performance only when a supervening extreme event actually causes the inability to perform the promised obligation and the risk was not assigned to the promisor; frustration requires destruction of a principal purpose shared by both parties.

sections.Parties: Le Fort Enterprises, Inc., the seller of a cleaning franchise, was the plaintiff and appellee; it sued on a note for the remaining purchase price. Lantern 18, LLC, the purchaser, and Samuel and Marcia Bergman, individual co-obligors, were the defendants and appellants; they asserted pandemic impracticability and frustration and asked the court to amend the note in equity.
sections.Procedural History: The seller began the action on May 21, 2020, and moved for summary judgment in October. A counterclaim asserting failure to credit a price adjustment was dismissed by stipulation. The Superior Court granted summary judgment for the seller and denied reconsideration. The co-obligors appealed, and the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court transferred the appeal on its own initiative. On January 3, 2023, reviewing de novo, the court affirmed the judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
In May 2015 Lantern 18 bought a Merry Maids of Boston franchise from Le Fort, paying a deposit and a closing sum and promising monthly payments of the balance with a May 2018 balloon payment. The purchase agreement allowed a $15,000 principal reduction if sales fell below a threshold during the first six months; no other clause linked the price to business revenue, and there was no force majeure clause. An August 2018 amended note gave Lantern 18 and both Bergmans, individually and jointly and severally, four more years, with a May 2022 balloon payment. A November modification reduced monthly payments to $3,243. Failure to pay within ten days was a default permitting acceleration, and an adverse change in an obligor's financial condition that impaired the seller's security or increased its risk, if uncured thirty days after notice, was itself an event of default.

Massachusetts declared an emergency on March 10, 2020. Executive orders effectively shut the franchise down from March until June, and after reopening many customers declined cleaning crews. Samuel's affidavit described a precipitous revenue decline. The co-obligors missed the April 1 payment. On April 22 the seller declared default, accelerated, and requested financial records. By the October motion six installments had been missed.
sections.Issue: Whether the COVID-19 pandemic and resulting shutdown excused the buyers of a franchise and their individual co-obligors from paying the remaining purchase price, under impracticability or frustration of purpose, and whether equity warranted amending the note to permit cure.
sections.Holding: The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court, in 2023, in an opinion by Justice Wendlandt for the seven-member court with no separate writing, affirmed summary judgment for the seller. It held that on this record neither impracticability nor frustration excused the purchaser and its individual co-obligors from paying the remaining price, and that equity did not warrant rewriting the note. The court expressly left pandemic defenses available where other facts and contracts support them.
sections.Reasoning:
Although these defenses ordinarily raise factual questions, summary judgment was appropriate where no rational view of the evidence supported them. Impracticability required a supervening extreme event causing impracticability, nonoccurrence as a basic assumption with the risk not assigned to the promisor, and absence of fault. The pandemic was not the obligors' fault, so the first two elements controlled.

Causation was missing. The affidavit could support inability to fund payments from franchise revenues, but contained no evidence about the individual co-obligors' financial condition or their own ability to pay. The promise was repayment, not repayment exclusively from business proceeds. Mere financial difficulty ordinarily does not excuse payment, and juxtaposing a pandemic and payment problems was insufficient.

Even adequate causal evidence would not cure the risk-allocation problem. Stable franchise revenue after the first six months was not an essential contractual assumption. The extension, the personal joint liability, the limited six-month sales adjustment, and the default, financial-information and acceleration provisions assigned subsequent business risk to the buyers. The parties need not have contemplated COVID-19 specifically to allocate financial deterioration regardless of its source. The absence of a force majeure clause was additional context.

Frustration concerns destruction of a principal purpose understood by both parties, so foundational that the transaction otherwise makes little sense. Here the shared purpose was acquisition of the franchise and spreading its price over time; Le Fort had fully performed by delivering the business in 2015, and nothing supported a mutually understood purpose of funding repayment solely through later revenues.

On equity, the record showed no fraud, mistake, accident, illegality, predatory pricing, duress or inequitable acceleration clause. Acceleration collected the agreed remaining price of a business already received, and the missed payments, failure to cure and failure to provide records were material defaults.

The casebook cites the case in a note on subjective and objective impracticability.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-056.rule: Seven Justices, without a single majority rationale, held that when the Government contractually assumes the risk of a change in regulatory law, it is liable in damages if later legislation prevents the promised performance, and the special sovereign defenses do not excuse it.

sections.Parties: Three thrift acquirers, Winstar, Statesman and Glendale, were the plaintiffs; they sued the United States in contract, seeking compensation for the bargain lost when new banking legislation barred the accounting treatment promised to them. The United States was the defendant. It argued that the documents gave only existing accounting permissions and invoked four government-contract defenses: unmistakability, reserved sovereign powers, absence of express delegation, and the sovereign-acts doctrine.
sections.Procedural History: The Claims Court recognized Winstar's implied-in-fact contract in 1990 and determined liability in 1992, and granted corresponding liability rulings for Statesman and Glendale. On consolidated interlocutory appeals a Federal Circuit panel reversed, finding no unmistakable promise limiting future regulation. The en banc Federal Circuit vacated the panel result and affirmed the liability determinations. The Court, after argument on April 24, decided the case on July 1, 1996. It affirmed the Federal Circuit and remanded because the Court of Federal Claims had not yet determined the measure or amount of damages.
sections.Material Facts:
In the early 1980s rising interest rates left many thrifts insolvent, and the Federal Savings and Loan Insurance Corporation lacked reserves to close and liquidate them all. Federal regulators encouraged supervisory mergers in which private acquirers assumed failed thrifts' liabilities in exchange for financial assistance and favorable regulatory accounting. Regulators allowed supervisory goodwill to count toward required capital with long amortization periods, and other arrangements allowed capital credits tied to federal cash assistance.

Glendale's 1981 acquisition of Broward involved a roughly $734 million asset shortfall and forty-year goodwill amortization. Winstar's 1984 acquisition of Windom involved thirty-five-year amortization, and its documents gave the negotiated terms priority over conflicting regulatory changes. Statesman's 1988 transaction involved a $26 million capital credit and twenty-five-year amortization.

In 1989 Congress enacted the Financial Institutions Reform, Recovery, and Enforcement Act, FIRREA, imposing stricter capital requirements under which goodwill could not count as tangible capital. Winstar and Statesman were seized and liquidated after failing the new requirements; Glendale survived through private recapitalization.
sections.Issue: Whether the United States is liable for breach of contract when legislation bars the regulatory accounting treatment it promised to thrift acquirers, or whether the unmistakability doctrine, reserved sovereign powers, the lack of express delegation, or the sovereign-acts doctrine relieves it of liability.
sections.Holding: The Court, in 1996, in a judgment announced by Justice Souter, with seven Justices affirming, held the United States liable for breaching its accounting commitments to the three thrift acquirers and remanded for damages proceedings. Justices Stevens and Breyer joined Souter's entire opinion and Justice O'Connor joined all but Parts IV-A and IV-B; Justice Scalia, joined by Justices Kennedy and Thomas, concurred in the judgment on different reasoning; Chief Justice Rehnquist dissented, joined in part by Justice Ginsburg. The Court did not invalidate FIRREA or award a quantified recovery, and the seven votes for liability do not make every proposition in Souter's opinion a majority holding.
sections.Reasoning:
Souter's principal opinion treated the documents as contractual commitments, not statements of current policy: integration provisions incorporated the specific accounting promises, and the acquirers had accepted liabilities whose accounting treatment was essential to solvency. The promise allocated the risk of regulatory change to the Government without authorizing the thrifts to operate contrary to FIRREA.

The unmistakability doctrine requires unmistakable terms before a contract is read to surrender sovereign authority. Souter distinguished a contract that restricts sovereign power from one that leaves regulation effective while requiring compensation; the latter surrendered nothing, though he rejected a categorical rule that a damages claim always avoids the doctrine. The reserved-powers and express-delegation objections failed on the same understanding, and FSLIC had authority to make the promise.

On sovereign acts, Parts IV-A and IV-B, joined only by Souter, Stevens and Breyer, concluded that FIRREA lacked the required public and general character because its substantial effect included releasing the Government from its own commitments. This was the plurality's approach. Part IV-C, joined also by O'Connor, concluded that even assuming public and general action, ordinary impossibility did not excuse the Government: nonoccurrence of regulatory change was not a basic assumption, and the agreements assigned that risk to the Government.

Breyer, concurring, explained that language and circumstances can establish a binding promise to hold a counterparty harmless from legal change. Scalia, with Kennedy and Thomas, rejected the risk-shifting label but applied unmistakability and found it satisfied, since a promise lasting only as long as the Government chose would make the bargain illusory. Rehnquist, dissenting, maintained that unmistakability must guide interpretation and, in a part Ginsburg did not join, regarded FIRREA as satisfying the sovereign-acts doctrine.

The casebook cites the case in its account of governmental acts and quotes the principal opinion's economic discussion of honoring negotiated risk allocation; the brief notes that the casebook compresses the divided decision.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-057.rule: Government closure orders that bar a tenant's business but do not prevent the payment of rent do not excuse rent under force majeure or impossibility, and a temporary closure does not frustrate a long-term lease whose value is not destroyed.

sections.Parties: SVAP III Poway Crossings, LLC, the commercial landlord, was the plaintiff, cross-defendant and respondent; it sued for unpaid rent. Fitness International, LLC, the tenant operating a health club, was the defendant, cross-complainant and appellant; it raised thirty-seven defenses and cross-claimed for contract breach, breach of the good-faith covenant, declarations, specific performance and promissory estoppel, arguing that the pandemic closure excused rent or required abatement.
sections.Procedural History: SVAP sued in May 2020 after April and May rent went unpaid, and sought summary judgment on its claim and on the cross-complaint. The trial court found that possession had been provided, rent had been intermittently withheld, and no excuse applied. Fitness's January 2022 notice of appeal attached only the summary-judgment minute order; after the appellate court questioned appealability, the trial court entered a final judgment on April 13, 2022. On January 20, 2023, California's Fourth District Court of Appeal, Division One, reviewing de novo, affirmed the judgment for the landlord on its rent claim and the cross-complaint and awarded SVAP costs on appeal.
sections.Material Facts:
The parties' June 12, 2002, retail lease initially ran fifteen years with three five-year renewal options; amendments extended the initial term through October 31, 2025. Fitness occupied space in the Poway Shopping Center for its health club. The Initial Uses provision described a health club, but the opening obligation required that use for only one day, and Fitness could change to another lawful retail use within specified restrictions. The landlord's legality warranty was measured as of the lease's effective date. The force majeure clause covered restrictive laws and similar or dissimilar causes beyond reasonable control, but excluded financial inability and failures curable by paying money.

Pandemic orders made operation of gyms temporarily illegal, and Fitness could not operate during intermittent periods from March 2020 through March 2021. Fitness remained in possession. The undisputed unpaid rent was $520,361.29 as of October 2021. Fitness asserted no disputed material facts.
sections.Issue: Whether pandemic orders temporarily prohibiting gym operation excused a health-club tenant's obligation to pay rent, on the theory that the landlord breached a guarantee of continuous health-club use or under the lease's force majeure clause, impossibility or impracticability, Civil Code section 1511, or frustration of purpose.
sections.Holding: California's Fourth District Court of Appeal, Division One, in 2023, in an opinion by Justice Buchanan with Acting Presiding Justice Huffman and Justice O'Rourke concurring, affirmed judgment for the landlord. It held that the landlord had not guaranteed continuous health-club use and had not breached; that the closure orders did not prevent the performance Fitness owed, which was paying rent, so force majeure, impossibility and section 1511 did not apply; and that a temporary closure did not frustrate the lease.
sections.Reasoning:
Reading the lease as a whole, the court found no guarantee of continuous health-club use. The opening obligation required that use for one day, and the legality warranty was dated to June 12, 2002; reading another provision to guarantee legal operation throughout the term would make that dated warranty meaningless. The right to use the premises for permitted purposes bound the landlord not to restrict those uses; it did not insure against later governmental prohibitions. Fitness admitted continued possession and identified government interference, not restrictions imposed by SVAP.

The closure orders were restrictive laws within the force majeure clause, but they did not delay or prevent paying rent, and the clause's financial exclusions would independently defeat the argument. Impossibility or impracticability likewise focused on Fitness's own promised performance: the laws prohibited operating a gym, not paying rent, and the argument that the contractual object had become impossible confused that defense with frustration. Civil Code section 1511(1) and (2) failed for the same reason, since payment remained lawful and was not prevented.

Frustration required a mutually contemplated purpose, an unallocated and not reasonably foreseeable risk, and total or nearly total destruction of the value of counter-performance. The court assumed without deciding that operating a fitness facility was the lease's primary purpose and that the closure risk had not been allocated exclusively to Fitness. Even so, closure for months did not destroy the value of a lease already used for more than nineteen years and spanning more than twenty-three overall; possession remained valuable. The court also rejected a temporary frustration defense under the California cases it applied: commercial frustration terminates a contract rather than suspending it, and Fitness remained in possession and did not seek rescission.

The casebook cites the case in its discussion distinguishing frustration from impossibility, noting the fitness-center closure and the landlord's victory.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-058.rule: Impossibility excuses performance only when destruction of the subject matter or means of performance makes it objectively impossible through an event that could not have been foreseen or guarded against in the contract; a force majeure catchall reaches only events of the kind listed.

sections.Parties: Kel Kim Corporation, the tenant of a roller-skating rink, and its individual lease guarantors were the plaintiffs and appellants; they brought a declaratory action seeking to be excused from the tenant's liability-insurance obligation. The landlords, including Central Markets, Inc., were the defendants and respondents; they had issued a default notice requiring cure or surrender of the premises and obtained summary judgment.
sections.Procedural History: Kel Kim and the guarantors brought a declaratory action. Special Term granted the landlords summary judgment, nullified the lease, and directed the tenant to vacate. A divided Appellate Division affirmed. The New York Court of Appeals, after argument on November 18, decided the case on December 21, 1987, and in an unsigned memorandum affirmed the Appellate Division's order with costs.
sections.Material Facts:
In early 1980 Kel Kim leased a vacant supermarket in Clifton Park for ten years with two five-year renewals. Both parties understood it would become a public roller-skating rink, although the lease did not restrict use to that activity. The tenant promised to maintain public liability insurance in responsible solvent companies, covering at least $500,000 for one person and $1 million in the aggregate for a single accident. It obtained coverage and operated for six years without incident.

In November 1985 the insurer notified Kel Kim that its policy would expire January 6, 1986, and would not be renewed because of uncertainty about a reinsurer's financial condition. Kel Kim asserted that it made every effort to obtain replacement coverage but that the liability-insurance crisis prevented compliance. On January 7, 1986, with the tenant uninsured, the landlords issued a default notice requiring cure in thirty days or surrender. Kel Kim obtained a $500,000 aggregate policy effective March 1, 1986, and the specified coverage in August 1987. The lease's force majeure clause listed labor disputes, unavailable materials, failed utility service, restrictive laws or regulations, riots, insurrection, war, adverse weather, acts of God, or other similar causes beyond control.
sections.Issue: Whether a tenant's inability to obtain the liability insurance its lease required, because of a crisis in the insurance market, excused that obligation under the common-law doctrine of impossibility or under the lease's force majeure clause.
sections.Holding: The New York Court of Appeals, in 1987, in an unsigned memorandum in which all seven judges concurred, affirmed. It held that neither common-law impossibility nor the force majeure clause excused the tenant's failure to maintain the required coverage, so the lease could not be preserved without it. The court did not decide whether an expressly drafted insurance-market contingency would produce a different result.
sections.Reasoning:
The court began with the binding character of promises despite unforeseen burdens. Excuse doctrines are applied narrowly because contracts allocate performance risks. Impossibility requires objective impossibility from destruction of the subject matter or means of performance, produced by an unanticipated event that could neither be foreseen nor guarded against in the contract. Kel Kim specifically undertook to procure and continuously maintain stated insurance limits, and inability to obtain that coverage was a contingency the parties could have foreseen and addressed in the lease. The insurance-market crisis therefore did not excuse the undertaking.

On the clause, the court stated that force majeure ordinarily excuses performance only when the preventing event is specifically included, and insurance unavailability was not listed. The residual similar-causes language did not expand to every uncontrollable difficulty; general words were confined to the kind of events enumerated. Those events affected daily commercial operations, such as access to labor, materials and utilities. Liability insurance instead protected the landlord's separate economic interests when the tenant chose to continue operating a public skating rink. Kel Kim's argument that insurance also affected operation did not erase that distinction.

The casebook describes the case as a tenant seeking to retain its lease without maintaining the required insurance and the landlord's victory.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-059.rule: A tenant's loss of clients and inability to afford rent because of the pandemic neither frustrates the purpose of an office lease nor makes performance objectively impossible.

sections.Parties: 1140 Broadway LLC, the landlord, was the plaintiff and moved for summary judgment. Bold Food, LLC, the tenant, and KBFK Restaurant Corp., which had furnished a good-guy guaranty, were the defendants. They attributed the rent default to the pandemic, asserted objective impossibility and frustration of purpose, and alternatively demanded an inquest to establish damages.
sections.Procedural History: The landlord sued in the New York Supreme Court, New York County, and moved for summary judgment. On December 3, 2020, the court granted judgment as to liability only, ordered a trial to determine damages, and directed the landlord to file a note of issue by December 15. The decision is marked non-final; it did not determine a monetary award.
sections.Material Facts:
Bold Food leased part of the twelfth floor of a Manhattan office building. Its business provided management and consulting services to restaurants, including help with human resources, payroll and accounting. The landlord described the lease as running through February 2022 and alleged that rent payments stopped in February 2020, with the tenant remaining until June 30. The court treated the lease of office space and the cessation of payments as undisputed.
