The defendants said that restaurants' curtailed operations or closures during the pandemic eliminated demand for their services, making the consulting business unprofitable and unable to afford rent. The tenant was an office-based service provider, not itself shut down by the public-health directives. The lease had a casualty provision addressing physical damage, and the landlord had not made rent contingent on the tenant's ability to afford it. The landlord supplied neither a ledger nor documentation of how it calculated its damages, and defendants disputed whether the security deposit had been deducted.
sections.Issue: Whether a restaurant-consulting firm that lost its clients when the pandemic curtailed restaurant operations is excused from paying office rent, and its guarantor from liability, under frustration of purpose or impossibility, and whether the landlord had proved the amount of its damages.
sections.Holding: The New York Supreme Court, New York County, in 2020, in a decision by Justice Arlene P. Bluth, granted the landlord summary judgment on liability against the defendants, rejecting frustration of purpose and impossibility, and ordered a trial on damages because the landlord had not adequately documented the amount sought. The court expressly declined to decide whether an actual restaurant could succeed on impossibility or frustration, and reserved which other circumstances might support frustration under a generic office lease.
sections.Reasoning:
Frustration is narrow: the disappointed purpose must have been so completely the shared basis of the bargain that without it the transaction would make little sense, and the frustration must be substantial. Leasing office space while the tenant's industry later suffers a precipitous decline does not by itself satisfy that rule. The office had not been destroyed or lost a unique capacity for an agreed specific purpose; the consulting enterprise had lost clients and could not afford the rent. The court contrasted a condemned factory, or costumes rented for a particular performance in a theater that burns down.

For impossibility the court applied Kel Kim's requirement of objective impossibility through destruction of the subject matter or means of performance, caused by an unanticipated event that could not have been foreseen or guarded against in the agreement. The office space remained the subject of the contract, and lack of clients and funds did not destroy it or the means of performing. The consultant's indirect exposure to the restaurant orders was insufficient; restaurants themselves were restricted in activities such as indoor dining rather than uniformly forbidden to operate.

The casualty provision addressed physical damage, not the loss of clientele, and the court declined to revise the lease's allocation simply because both landlord and tenant faced hardship. The good-guy guaranty protected the guarantor if the business failed, provided its conditions were fulfilled; the court described the guarantor as responsible for rent while the tenant remained in possession, with power to return the space. Instead the tenant kept possession for five months after payments stopped.

Damages required a trial: the landlord conceded that any award should be reduced by the security deposit, and its agent's affidavit did not establish the arithmetic.

The casebook adapts the case as a problem about a consultant named Hannibal, adding an initial lack of workplace access and a two-year lease entered just before COVID-19; those added premises are the exercise's, not the court's findings.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-060.rule: Under Michigan law as the Sixth Circuit applied it, a market downturn and a party's own financial losses are not the failure of a basic assumption, so neither impracticability nor frustration excuses a manufacturer that ends a dealer agreement without following its agreed termination procedures.

sections.Parties: Karl Wendt Farm Equipment Co., an International Harvester (IH) dealer in Marlette, Michigan, sued IH for breach of its Dealer Sales and Service Agreement and on other theories; only the contract claim survived to trial. IH, the manufacturer, defended on impracticability, frustration and other grounds and counterclaimed for debts on equipment and parts it had supplied on credit. Both sides appealed the rulings that went against them.
sections.Procedural History:
In this diversity case the trial court submitted impracticability to the jury, which returned a verdict of no cause of action on Wendt's contract claim, and the court denied Wendt judgment notwithstanding the verdict or a new trial. It directed verdicts for Wendt against IH's frustration defense, its asserted authority to discontinue products, and its claimed implied limit on the contract's duration. On the counterclaim it initially found $253,839.69 owed to IH and ordered the equipment returned and sold; after the sale, judgment entered for a stipulated deficiency of $180,379.21.

The Sixth Circuit decided the appeal on April 26, 1991, and rehearing was denied May 21. It reversed the verdict on the contract claim and remanded for a new trial only on damages for IH's breach, and it affirmed every other challenged ruling, including the rejection of IH's alternative defenses and the deficiency judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
Wendt became an IH dealer under a fall 1974 Dealer Sales and Service Agreement that governed sales, purchase and servicing of equipment and operating requirements and set out specified termination procedures. Section 2 let IH add or eliminate listed products, including discontinuing a line or lines, without responsibility to the dealer.

A dramatic downturn in the farm-equipment market and substantial losses led IH to sell its farm-equipment assets to J.I. Case and Tenneco for a base consideration of $246.7 million in cash and $161.3 million in participating preferred stock. IH pointed to losses exceeding $2 million a day, a decline in its Fortune 500 standing, and evidence that it might have gone bankrupt without the sale.

The purchaser received access to IH dealers, not the franchise network itself. In roughly four hundred areas that had both an IH and a Case dealership, Case offered only one franchise. IH dealers received nearly two-thirds of those franchises, but Wendt did not receive one in its conflicted area. IH did not follow the agreement's termination procedures.
sections.Issue: Whether, under Michigan contract law, IH's defense of impracticability should have gone to the jury, and whether frustration of purpose, the contract's product-discontinuation clause, or an implied term ending dealerships when the manufacturer left the business excused IH from ending the dealership without following the agreed termination procedures.
sections.Holding: The Sixth Circuit, in 1991, in an opinion by Judge Nathaniel R. Jones joined by Judge Boggs, with Judge Ryan dissenting on impracticability, held that Wendt was entitled to a directed verdict on the impracticability defense. The court did not decide that Michigan would never recognize impracticability; it held that even if the doctrine were recognized, it would not excuse IH in these circumstances as a matter of law. It affirmed the directed verdicts rejecting frustration, the product-discontinuation argument and the implied-duration argument, and it affirmed the deficiency judgment because Wendt had not timely renewed its statutory repurchase-credit argument when the deficiency was calculated and the amount entered was the one Wendt itself proposed.
sections.Reasoning:
Michigan's highest court had not squarely addressed modern impracticability in this setting, so the majority looked to its impossibility decisions, an intermediate appellate decision broadening the doctrine, and Restatement section 261. The Restatement requires an event that defeats a basic assumption, without the obligor's fault and without a contrary allocation of the risk. Extreme shortages can qualify, but ordinary market conditions and a party's financial position generally are not basic assumptions. The scale of IH's losses did not change their legal character. The contract itself allocated termination through stated conditions and procedures, and IH could have sought mutual termination and shared the sale proceeds. IH did not necessarily cause the recession, but it chose the asset sale; excusing it would let it shed franchise obligations while the purchaser picked the dealers it wanted and the others bore the loss.

Frustration under Restatement section 265 failed because the agreement's stated purpose was to establish and govern the dealer relationship, not mutual profitability; treating profitability as every contract's principal purpose would empty the requirement of meaning. The frustrating event was also IH's own decision to sell. The power to drop some product lines did not create an alternative way to end the relationship when the contract had specific termination provisions, and Michigan precedent did not imply at-will termination where a contract specified termination for cause.

Judge Ryan, dissenting, thought Michigan would likely adopt Restatement impracticability and that reasonable people could disagree whether a sudden nationwide industry collapse, with over $2 billion in IH losses in four years, defeated a basic assumption; he would have left the jury's verdict undisturbed.

The casebook adapts the case as a problem on impracticability and frustration and states a $4 billion loss figure that is the casebook's, not the court's.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-061.rule: Under UCC section 2-207, a buyer's added form term is excluded where the seller's offer barred changes or the contract arose only from conduct, and a buyer whose seller was not told of the downstream use assumes the risk that its own customer cannot perform.

sections.Parties: Power Engineering & Manufacturing, Ltd., an Iowa manufacturer, sued Krug International, the buyer of a custom gearbox, for breach after Krug refused shipment. Krug defended on a force majeure clause in its purchase order and on statutory impracticability. Power Engineering won at trial, and Krug's defenses were rejected again in the Iowa Supreme Court.
sections.Procedural History: After a bench trial at law, the district court found that Power Engineering had fully performed and that Krug had breached, and entered judgment for the manufacturer for one-half the purchase price plus interest and costs. The opinion reports a $149,700 price and a $75,000 initial payment but does not state a precise judgment amount. The Iowa Supreme Court, treating factual findings as binding if supported by substantial evidence and reviewing legal conclusions for correction of errors, affirmed on June 16, 1993.
sections.Material Facts:
Tripod Laing promised Iraqi Airways an aeromedical laboratory in Iraq. It engaged Krug's U.K. subsidiary, which engaged Krug to make a human centrifuge for pilot training, and Krug ordered a custom gearbox from Power Engineering. The manufacturer did not know Krug's buyer or the ultimate consumer until the August 1990 stop-work order.

The parties negotiated orally and then exchanged a March 14 quotation, a March 16 purchase order and an April 26 acknowledgment. The manufacturer's quotation and acknowledgment said orders were noncancellable, and its quotation barred waiver, alteration or modification without written agreement, though Power Engineering conceded an oral understanding that Krug could cancel while paying for completed work. The reverse of Krug's purchase order contained a force majeure clause allowing termination or deferral without cost for causes beyond Krug's control that made acceptance unreasonable in Krug's judgment. Power Engineering at first received only an oral order and a fax of the front; the complete form arrived April 16, after manufacturing began.

Krug paid $75,000 during manufacturing. The gearbox was completed in late July, with a minor adjustment finished in early August, and Krug authorized shipment August 7, but routine matters delayed shipping. An embargo began around August 6, and an upstream directive of August 7 halted work and spending. On August 10 Krug orally told Power Engineering not to ship, and it gave written notice August 13. The gearbox remained in storage.
sections.Issue: Whether the force majeure clause on the reverse of Krug's purchase order became a term of the contract under Iowa Code section 554.2207, Iowa's UCC section 2-207, and, if not, whether the embargo on shipments to Iraq excused Krug under the impracticability provision, section 554.2615.
sections.Holding: The Iowa Supreme Court, in 1993, in an opinion by Justice Harris for the five-member court with no separate writing, held that the force majeure clause never became part of the contract and that statutory impracticability did not excuse Krug. Permission to cancel while paying for completed work was not agreement to cancellation without cost. Because the manufacturer had not been told the proposed use or destination, Krug assumed the risk that its own purchaser would not or could not perform. The court affirmed the judgment for the manufacturer without needing to decide how the force majeure clause would operate if it had been agreed.
sections.Reasoning:
Article 2 applied to the specially manufactured gearbox. Contract interpretation gives effect to intent and will not place one party at another's mercy without clear language. The restriction on changes in the manufacturer's quotation had two possible readings, and both excluded the clause. If it allowed a contract to form through Krug's acceptance while objecting to added terms, the force majeure provision was only a proposed addition, excluded by the offer's limitation and prior objection under subsections (2)(a) and (c). If instead acceptance had to contain neither additional nor different terms, the forms did not create a contract; the parties' conduct did so under subsection (3), which brings in the agreed written terms and statutory supplements but not the disputed clause.

On impracticability, Iowa precedent applied section 554.2615 to buyers as well as sellers. The court required commercially impracticable performance caused by an unforeseen contingency that defeated a basic assumption, or good-faith compliance with a governmental regulation, and no assumption of the risk. The embargo prohibited shipment to Iraq, not a domestic buyer's purchase from a domestic manufacturer, so Krug's own performance was not impracticable merely because its downstream transaction failed. The upstream stop order was not the failure of a shared basic assumption, because Power Engineering did not know the use or destination.

The casebook adapts the case as a problem on frustration that describes cancellation before completion and a later resale near the contract price; those are the casebook's added facts, and the court did not rest on resale or decide a separately framed frustration claim.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-062.rule: When a contract is frustrated, a party who paid in advance for future performance may recover the money in restitution if the consideration has wholly failed, that is, if the payer received none of the performance for which the payment was made.

sections.Parties: Fibrosa Spolka Akcyjna, a Polish buyer, sued Fairbairn Lawson Combe Barbour, Ltd., an English seller of machinery, for contractual relief including damages or specific performance and, in the alternative, repayment with interest of the advance it had paid. The seller resisted repayment, pointing to work it had already done. Fibrosa lost below and was the appellant in the House of Lords.
sections.Procedural History: Fibrosa issued its writ on May 1, 1940. Tucker J. dismissed the action on March 7, 1941, and the Court of Appeal affirmed on May 15. Both lower courts treated Chandler v. Webster as preventing restitution once a valid contract was later frustrated. A Board of Trade license obtained on April 17, 1942 permitted the appeal to proceed; by the time of the hearing in the House, Vilna itself was enemy territory. On June 15, 1942 the House of Lords allowed the appeal. The report does not print a separate quantified interest or costs order, and the House preserved whatever statutory restrictions applied to payment to an enemy.
sections.Material Facts:
On July 12, 1939, Fairbairn agreed to supply Fibrosa with flax-hackling machinery for a lump price of 4,800 pounds, c.i.f. Gdynia. One third, 1,600 pounds, was payable with the order and the 3,200 pound balance against shipping documents. Delivery was contemplated within three to four months after final details, and the price included a skilled installer. The machinery was intended for Fibrosa's factory at Vilna. Fibrosa paid 1,000 pounds on July 18 rather than the whole first installment. Clause 7 allowed a reasonable extension for delay beyond the seller's control, including war.

Germany invaded Poland on September 1, Britain entered the war on September 3, and Gdynia was occupied on September 23. Fibrosa's agents asked for repayment on September 7. The seller refused the next day, pointing to work already performed and suggesting the matter be reconsidered after the war. Fibrosa received neither machines nor shipping documents.
sections.Issue: Whether the contract was discharged by frustration despite the express war-delay clause, and, if so, whether a buyer who paid part of the price in advance and received none of the promised performance can recover the payment, notwithstanding the rule in Chandler v. Webster that payments made before frustration stay where they fall.
sections.Holding: The House of Lords, in 1942, unanimously held that the contract was frustrated and that the buyer could recover its 1,000 pound advance as money paid on a consideration that had wholly failed. Lord Simon L.C. and Lords Atkin, Russell of Killowen, Macmillan, Wright, Roche and Porter each delivered a speech supporting the result. The rule in Chandler v. Webster could not govern a total failure of consideration. The recovery was restitution, not damages for breach, and the contractual breach theory failed. The recovery was subject to the preserved restrictions on payment to an enemy.
sections.Reasoning:
The war-delay clause provided a reasonable extension, not indefinite suspension for the length of a war. Occupation of Gdynia made the contemplated British shipment there unlawful, manufacturing the machinery at Leeds did not satisfy an agreement for shipment c.i.f. Gdynia, and the House would not rewrite the destination. The contract was therefore discharged, which is different from treating it as void when made.

On restitution, money paid for future performance can become repayable when the whole relevant performance fails. The buyer's inability to claim damages for an excused failure did not extinguish the distinct claim for money had and received, and neither fault in the recipient nor invalidity of the original contract was essential. Lord Simon distinguished the promise that supplies consideration for forming a contract from the performance whose absence supports repayment; the advance was part of the price for that performance, and work done in the seller's own factory gave the buyer none of the promised benefit. Lord Atkin reached the same result while doubting that two meanings of consideration were needed.

The whole relevant consideration had to fail; the speeches did not authorize a proportional refund, and a payment made finally for a chance or a promise, or governed by a contrary custom such as prepaid freight, need not be refundable. The common law gave no general deduction for the seller's sunk costs. Lords Simon and Wright pointed to legislation as the route to a broader adjustment, and Lord Porter rejected judicial creation of an unspecified equitable fraction.

The casebook uses the case to contrast full restitution with protection of the seller's reliance interest; its 800 pound expense figure is the casebook's classroom assumption, and the Law Reform (Frustrated Contracts) Act 1943 it discusses came after this judgment.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-063.rule: Where an express contract makes a lump-sum payment conditional on complete performance, the law will not imply an inconsistent promise to pay proportionately for part performance, even when the performer's blameless death prevented completion.

sections.Parties: The administratrix of Thomas Cutter, a second mate who died at sea, sued the defendant, the master of the ship Governor Parry, in assumpsit for work and labor performed by Cutter. She sought a proportionate recovery on a quantum meruit. The defendant relied on the express written promise, which made payment conditional on Cutter serving through the whole voyage.
sections.Procedural History: The defendant pleaded the general issue. At Lancaster the jury returned a verdict for the plaintiff for 31 pounds 10 shillings, subject to the opinion of the Court of King's Bench on a stated case. The case was argued in the preceding term, and the court postponed its decision to inquire into commercial usage; on renewed argument no fixed and settled usage was established. On June 9, 1795 the court gave a postea to the defendant, unless further information about commercial usage was supplied before the end of the term. The case was not mentioned again.
sections.Material Facts:
At Kingston, Jamaica, on July 31, 1793, the defendant delivered a written promise to Cutter: ten days after the ship arrived at Liverpool he would pay Cutter thirty guineas, provided Cutter proceeded, continued and did his duty as second mate from Jamaica to Liverpool. Cutter boarded on July 31 and the vessel sailed on August 2. He performed his duty until his death on September 20, before the ship reached Liverpool on October 9. The report does not find desertion, misconduct or fault by Cutter.

The usual wage of a second mate hired by the month was 4 pounds per month. Sailors hired for the run from Jamaica to England ordinarily received a gross sum, and the usual voyage lasted about eight weeks. The thirty guineas, 31 pounds 10 shillings, was therefore substantially more than the roughly 8 pounds that two months' service at the monthly rate would yield.
sections.Issue: Whether the estate of a seaman who served until his death partway through the voyage can recover compensation for the service actually performed, on an implied promise, when the express promise made payment conditional on his continuing to do his duty for the whole voyage.
sections.Holding: The Court of King's Bench, in 1795, with Lord Kenyon, Chief Justice, and Justices Ashhurst, Grose and Lawrence each giving reasons, held for the defendant on the contract and the facts stated. The estate recovered neither the promised thirty guineas nor a proportionate quantum meruit in this proceeding. The express bargain was entire, and full performance was a condition of payment. The result was conditional: the postea went to the defendant unless further information about usage was supplied before term ended, and several judges said a proven usage could affect the construction of the bargain.
sections.Reasoning:
Lord Kenyon confined himself to this contract and these facts and avoided a general ruling on every marine contract. Where parties have expressly agreed on compensation, the law does not imply an inconsistent obligation. The nearly fourfold difference between thirty guineas and ordinary wages for two months supported an all-or-nothing bargain, which he described as a kind of insurance: Cutter would get the larger sum if he performed the whole duty and nothing under that bargain if he did not. The Liverpool examples of merchants' practice did not establish a usage, but he said a universal commercial understanding construing these notes differently would lead him to change his view.

Justice Ashhurst likewise treated full performance as a condition precedent. The estate could not abandon the express agreement because an implied one would give a better result, and Cutter's lack of fault did not fulfill the condition.

Justice Grose had looked at the laws of Oleron, merchant practice, and Chandler v. Greaves, and was cautious, but concluded that the large conditional sum meant thirty guineas for the entire duty or nothing. Justice Lawrence relied on a reported entire-service agreement for 100 pounds a year, distinguished ordinary hired service, where proportionate wages are understood, and said a proven usage of proportionate pay for a mate in Cutter's position could support the plaintiff; without it the express entire contract controlled.

The casebook uses the case to ask whether death can be an excuse while the agreement still determines compensation; its statement that the administratrix sued for the thirty guineas compresses the fuller report.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-064.rule: Where a contract to do work on a building presupposes the building's continued existence and the building is destroyed without the worker's fault, further performance is excused and the worker may recover the fair value of the work done before the destruction.

sections.Parties: The plaintiffs were building movers who sued the owner of the buildings on an account annexed for the fair value of the services they had rendered before a fire. The owner, the defendant, answered that the movers had not performed and that the fire was caused by their negligence, and brought the case up on exceptions after a jury verdict for the movers.
sections.Procedural History: At trial the judge refused the owner's requested ruling that no recovery was possible and instructed the jury to allow recovery if the fire was not attributable to the plaintiffs' negligence. The jury found for the movers; the report does not state the amount of the award. The owner took exceptions to the refusal to bar recovery and to the instructions. The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court heard argument November 23, 1899 and on June 20, 1900 overruled the exceptions.
sections.Material Facts: The movers agreed, for $840, to relocate the owner's large building from Third Street to First Street and to change the positions of two other buildings, one on each lot. They first moved the house on Third Street and then moved the large building across open lots toward First Street. When it had gone about halfway, fire entirely destroyed it during the night. With the owner's assent, no further moving work was done. The owner alleged that the movers' negligence caused the fire; that was not established, and the verdict was authorized only on the condition that the fire was not attributable to their negligence.
sections.Issue: Whether movers who had partly performed a contract to move a building, when the building was destroyed by fire without their fault, can recover the fair value of the work done before the fire even though the contract was never completed.
sections.Holding: The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court, in 1900, in an opinion by Justice Hammond with no separate writing, held that the movers could recover the fair value of the services they performed before the building was destroyed. The owner's exceptions were overruled. The recovery is compensation for proper partial work after the failure of an implied condition; it is not lost profits for a breach by the owner and not the full contract price.
sections.Reasoning:
The contract necessarily presupposed the continued existence of the building on which the work was to be done, and its destruction made completion of the undertaking impossible. Massachusetts precedent supplied an implied obligation to pay for what either party had properly done before the condition failed, treating the work as done at the other's request. Its value could be measured from the contract price, or by another method if that price could not appropriately be applied. Being excused from finishing the move did not erase liability for services already rendered.

The court stated the specific rule as allowing recovery where a person has contracted to repair or do other work on another's house and, without the worker's fault, the destruction of the house makes further performance impossible. The movers' situation fell within that rule.

The casebook presents the case as a note about a house moved halfway, leaving out the other building work and the $840 price, and later cites it as support for the related reliance analysis in Albre Marble.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-065.rule: After supervening impossibility, a subcontractor may recover the fair value of preparatory work the general contractor specifically requested under the contract, at least where the contractor contributed more to the impossibility and the work could not by its nature be wrought into the building.

sections.Parties: Albre Marble and Tile Company, a subcontractor, sued John Bowen Co., the general contractor on a public hospital project. Counts 1 and 2 alleged breach of two subcontracts for tile and marble work; counts 3 and 4 sought in quantum meruit the value of work and labor supplied at Bowen's request. Bowen defended on impossibility. Albre brought exceptions, and a separate appeal, to the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court.
sections.Procedural History: Bowen moved for immediate judgment under the then-existing Massachusetts summary-judgment statute, supported by an affidavit on impossibility, and the motion was granted. Albre's vice-president had opposed it with an affidavit on information and belief. The Supreme Judicial Court heard argument November 6, 1958 and decided the case January 15, 1959. It overruled Albre's exceptions on the two breach counts, sustained its exceptions on the two quantum-meruit counts and remanded those counts for further proceedings, and dismissed the separate appeal because every issue was available through the exceptions. No damages amount was fixed.
sections.Material Facts:
Albre agreed to provide tile and marble labor and materials to Bowen, general contractor for a public Chronic Disease Hospital and Nurses' Home in Boston. In earlier litigation the general contract with the Commonwealth was declared invalid, which made continued performance of the subcontracts impossible. According to earlier decisions, Bowen's involvement in causing the invalidity was greater than the subcontractors'.

Both subcontracts contained clauses, drafted by Bowen, requiring the subcontractor to submit samples, shop drawings, tests and affidavits for approval as ordered or specified, and Albre had supplied them. No tile or marble had been installed, and Albre conceded that no labor or materials were wrought into the structure.

Albre's vice-president asserted on information and belief that Bowen deliberately left subcontractor performance-bond costs out of its bid, procured the general contract by fraud, and fraudulently induced the subcontracts knowing of the defects. Those allegations were not treated as proven. Against quantum meruit, Bowen asserted the absence of an architect's certificate and that it need not pay before being paid by the Commonwealth.
sections.Issue: Whether Albre's information-and-belief affidavit was enough to keep its breach counts alive against Bowen's impossibility defense, and whether, after impossibility, a subcontractor can recover the fair value of preparatory work that was requested under the contract but never wrought into the building.
sections.Holding: The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court, in 1959, in an opinion by Justice Spalding for the four listed justices with no separate writing, held that judgment against the two breach counts was proper because Albre's affidavit did not meet the statute, and that Albre could recover on the quantum-meruit counts the fair value of work done in conformity with Bowen's specific contractual request after the contracts were executed. Precontract expenditures such as bid preparation were excluded. Bowen's argument that payment depended on receipt of Commonwealth funds had been rejected in related precedent and was no defense.
sections.Reasoning:
On the breach counts, the statute required affidavits made on personal knowledge of admissible facts by someone shown competent to testify, and allegations on information and belief did not qualify. A separate statutory route allowed an affidavit specifically identifying reasonable grounds to expect contradiction at trial, but Albre did not satisfy it: it showed no attempt to obtain interrogatory answers or admissions, and vague assertions of expected proof would defeat the statute's purpose of avoiding trials where there is no genuine factual issue.

On quantum meruit, Bowen argued that Young v. Chicopee limited recovery after impossibility to installed materials or work. The court recognized the conventional tendency to allow the fair value of actual performance and deny merely preparatory or reliance expenditures, often through benefit or wrought-in tests, but said a literal requirement of surviving benefit was unworkable. It did not adopt a rule compensating every preparatory expenditure whenever faultless impossibility intervened. Recovery rested on a combination of circumstances. Bowen's contribution to the invalidity was greater than the subcontractors', though short of culpability sufficient for breach liability. Bowen drafted the clause specifically requesting the submissions, so Albre did not control all the preparations on its own. And the requested drawings, tests and affidavits could not by their nature be wrought into a building. The house-moving recovery in Angus v. Scully was a closer analogy than Young, where recovery was denied for stored materials lost in a fire not attributable to either party.

The casebook discusses the case under reliance interests, stressing Bowen's comparative contribution to the event and the distinction from Young.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-066.rule: A court may equitably modify the price term of a long-term contract when a mutual mistake about the capacity of a negotiated price index, or resulting impracticability or frustration, causes severe loss beyond the bounded risk the disadvantaged party assumed.

sections.Parties: Aluminum Company of America (ALCOA), which converted alumina into molten aluminum for Essex Group, Inc. under a long-term agreement, sued Essex. Count one sought relief from the pricing formula; count two alleged an oral modification; count three sought termination under a side letter. Essex, the customer, opposed any adjustment and counterclaimed over reduced deliveries in 1977 and 1978 and in 1979.
sections.Procedural History: This was a diversity action in the Western District of Pennsylvania. Pennsylvania conflicts rules required enforcement of the parties' Indiana choice-of-law clause, and where Indiana authority did not settle an issue the district court predicted how Indiana courts would decide. After trial, on April 7, 1980, the court issued findings of fact and conclusions of law. It granted ALCOA equitable modification of the pricing formula on count one, rejected its oral-modification and termination claims, and dismissed both parts of Essex's counterclaim. The opinion ends by saying an appropriate order will issue. The casebook reports that the dispute settled while on appeal.
sections.Material Facts:
Essex wanted a secure long-term aluminum supply for its expansion into aluminum wire. After negotiations beginning in spring 1967, the parties made the Molten Metal Agreement on December 26. Essex would supply alumina, ALCOA would convert it at its Warrick, Indiana works, and Essex would collect the output. The agreement ran through 1983, and Essex could extend it through 1988.

The initial charge was fifteen cents per pound: five cents for a demand component tied to a construction-cost index, four cents fixed, three cents for non-labor production costs tied to the Wholesale Price Index for Industrial Commodities, and three cents for labor tied to ALCOA's local hourly labor costs. The price could not exceed sixty-five percent of a specified published market price. ALCOA devised the formula with economist Alan Greenspan's help and sought a stable return near four cents per pound; the court found both parties contemplated ordinary variation of roughly one to seven cents. Essex examined the indices' stability before accepting them.

Starting in 1973, oil-price increases associated with OPEC and unexpected pollution-control costs sharply raised electricity costs, the main non-labor input in smelting, and the index did not track the increase. By 1978 ALCOA was losing 10.484 cents per pound, while Essex could resell surplus metal at a substantial profit. The court projected losses exceeding $75 million over the remaining potential term. Essex noted that ALCOA had still earned about $9 million cumulatively by trial.
sections.Issue: Whether ALCOA was entitled to relief from the indexed price on the grounds of mutual mistake, impracticability or frustration, or had instead assumed the risk that the index would fail to track its costs, and, if relief was due, what remedy was appropriate.
sections.Holding: The United States District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania, in 1980, in findings and conclusions by Judge Teitelbaum, held that mutual mistake warranted a remedy and that ALCOA separately qualified for relief through impracticability and frustration. The court modified the price rather than rescinding. The price per pound became the lesser of A, the original contractual ceiling, and B, the greater of the original indexed price and a price calculated to yield ALCOA one cent per pound, computed quarterly. ALCOA's oral-modification and termination claims failed, and Essex's two counterclaims were dismissed.
sections.Reasoning:
Essex argued that the index's failure was an erroneous forecast of future events, that any mistake was ALCOA's alone, and that ALCOA accepted the risk by drafting an indexed price without a floor. The court characterized the parties' assumption as a present actuarial error: they chose an elaborate risk-limiting device believing it could track costs within a tolerable range, and they were mistaken about its capacity to do so. The mistake was mutual because Essex's chairman understood the index's function was to protect ALCOA against cost fluctuations, and it was basic to an unusually long agreement. On risk, the indexed price, ALCOA's sophistication, its drafting role and the missing floor made it bear ordinary variation, but the court refused to infer that it assumed every possible deviation; the indices, ceiling, and extensive negotiation showed an effort to limit risk, which differs from a limitless gamble in conscious ignorance.

Impracticability and frustration share mistake's concern with basic assumptions and risk allocation but focus on severe hardship. Increased cost is ordinarily a contractual risk, so the court required expense well beyond ordinary variation and found it in ALCOA's severe out-of-pocket losses, the extraordinary index divergence, and its lack of fault. Frustration addressed ALCOA's principal purpose of earning money rather than sustaining serious losses; the court cautioned that merely losing the chance to sell at a higher market price is ordinarily insufficient.

On remedy, the court acknowledged this was not traditional reformation and relied on equitable restitution and modification. Rescission would give ALCOA a market-price windfall and cost Essex its secure supply; full enforcement would put the extraordinary loss on ALCOA.

The casebook questions whether this was genuinely a present mistake rather than an erroneous prediction; that challenge is the editors', not the court's.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-067.rule: Frustration of purpose discharges a promisor only if the frustrating event was not reasonably foreseeable and totally or nearly totally destroyed the value of the counterperformance; a regulation that merely makes a business less profitable does not excuse.

sections.Parties: The landlords sued their tenant, Murphy, an automobile dealer, for declaratory relief and unpaid rent after he vacated the leased premises and repudiated the lease. Murphy defended on the ground that wartime restrictions on new-car sales had frustrated the purpose of the lease. He lost at trial and appealed.
sections.Procedural History: The landlords sued on May 11, 1942. The trial court ruled that wartime conditions had not discharged Murphy's obligations, declared the lease, as modified by the landlords' waiver, still in effect, and ordered him to pay unpaid rent with interest, less the sums received through reletting. Murphy appealed on frustration of purpose. The California Supreme Court affirmed on October 31, 1944, and rehearing was denied November 28. The opinion states no exact monetary award.
sections.Material Facts:
On August 4, 1941, the landlords leased Murphy premises at Almont Drive and Wilshire Boulevard in Beverly Hills for five years beginning September 15. The specified purpose was displaying and selling new automobiles, servicing and repairing them, and selling a major oil company's petroleum products, with occasional used-car sales allowed. Other uses, assignment and subletting required written consent. The property had gasoline pumps and a one-story storeroom adaptable to other commercial uses on a major traffic artery.

A federal order of January 1, 1942 stopped new-car sales; a January 8 modification allowed sales to persons engaged in military activities; and a January 20 priorities system permitted sales to persons with qualifying preference ratings. On March 10 Murphy explained the restrictions to a landlord authorized to act for the others. The landlords orally waived the use and subletting restrictions and offered a rent reduction if Murphy could not operate profitably. Murphy nevertheless vacated on March 15, repudiated orally, and gave written notice on March 24. The landlords confirmed their waiver in writing on March 26 and, after trying to persuade him to perform, relet to mitigate damages.

Murphy continued to sell and service cars at two other locations, one of which sold new cars exclusively.
sections.Issue: Whether federal wartime restrictions on the sale of new automobiles frustrated the purpose of a lease made for a new-car dealership and so discharged the tenant's obligation to pay rent.
sections.Holding: The California Supreme Court, in 1944, in an opinion by Justice Traynor in which Chief Justice Gibson and Justices Shenk, Curtis, Edmonds, Carter and Schauer concurred, with no dissent, held that the lease was not frustrated and affirmed the judgment. Frustration can apply to a lease in a proper case, but the promisor must establish that the risk of the event was not reasonably foreseeable and that the value of the counterperformance was totally or nearly totally destroyed. Murphy showed neither, and he remained bound by the lease as modified by the waiver.
sections.Reasoning:
The court refused the categorical view that a lease, as the conveyance of an estate, puts every risk on the tenant. Frustration differs from impossibility, including extreme impracticability: performance remains possible, but an unforeseen event destroys the expected value of the counterperformance to the party seeking discharge. The inquiry allocates risk by looking at the parties' relationship, the contract's terms and the circumstances of formation. Where a risk was foreseeable and the contract did not address it, the court inferred that the promisor assumed it. A regulation that makes a business less profitable, more difficult or more expensive does not by that fact excuse performance, and the court declined a looser standard of substantial frustration that would invite tenants to repudiate whenever emergency rules cut profits.

First, the restrictions were not wholly outside the parties' contemplation. The lease preceded the United States' entry into the war, but national-defense mobilization was under way, statutory authority to allocate materials had existed for more than a year, automobile production was converting to military needs, and an experienced dealer could foresee the effects. Second, the lease kept substantial value: new-car sales were restricted, not uniformly illegal, Murphy made such sales elsewhere, and gasoline could still be sold. In addition, the landlords' waiver opened the premises to other lawful commercial uses and responsible subtenants, and prompt reletting confirmed their value. The court distinguished premises usable only for an activity made wholly unlawful, such as a saloon after prohibition.

The casebook uses the case to distinguish frustration from impossibility and, in a second account, to highlight the landlords' concessions.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-068.rule: An unconditional sale of specific goods in a deliverable state passes title when the contract is made, but a mutual mistake about a collateral fact existing at formation that materially induced the sale, such as a fire already threatening the goods, can permit rescission.

sections.Parties: Richardson Lumber Co., the seller, sued in assumpsit for the price of cedar ties destroyed by fire. The defendants were the buyers, Western Cedar and Lumber, for which Hoey had accepted the offer. The buyers argued that title had not passed, that the seller concealed the fire danger, and that the sale rested on a mistake. They lost at trial and brought error.
sections.Procedural History: The case was tried to a jury in the Alpena circuit court, which gave the seller judgment for its full claim. The trial judge submitted the alleged oral agreement on title and the concealment defense to the jury but refused to submit mutual mistake. The buyers brought error. The Michigan Supreme Court decided the case on October 2, 1922 and denied rehearing on November 2. It reversed and granted a new trial, with costs to the buyers. It did not finally rescind the sale or decide that the alleged mistake had been proved.
sections.Material Facts:
On September 16, 1916, Richardson Lumber offered to sell Western Cedar all its cedar ties on the Boyce property at Essexville. The estimated quantity was 11,500, the price was forty-two cents per tie on the ground, the buyers could reject none, and cash payment would follow counting. Hoey accepted for Western Cedar.

The buyers also claimed an oral understanding, which was disputed, that title would stay with Richardson until the ties were counted and paid for.

The buyers began loading and removing ties on September 19. They had removed 1,721 when fire destroyed the uncounted remainder. They tendered payment for the 1,721 at the contract price as full settlement; Richardson refused and sued for the whole quantity. Some testimony supported the claim that an underground fire was already burning close to the pile when the contract was made and later consumed it.
sections.Issue: Whether title to the ties passed to the buyers when the contract was made although the ties had not been counted, and whether the buyers were entitled to have the jury consider a defense of mutual mistake about a fire danger already existing when the sale was made.
sections.Holding: The Michigan Supreme Court, in 1922, in an opinion by Justice McDonald in which Chief Justice Fellows and Justices Wiest, Clark, Bird, Sharpe, Moore and Steere concurred, held that the written contract passed title when made unless the jury found the later oral agreement reserving title, but that refusing to submit mutual mistake to the jury was error requiring a new trial. If both parties believed there was no imminent fire danger while such a danger in fact threatened destruction before the buyers could reasonably remove the ties, the buyers could rescind, and if there was no time to rescind they would be liable only for the ties actually delivered.
sections.Reasoning:
Intention controls the passing of title. Under the Uniform Sales Act, an unconditional sale of specific goods already in a deliverable state passes the property to the buyer when the agreement is made, even if payment or delivery is postponed; title waits only where the seller still has to put the goods into a deliverable state. Here the whole identified pile was sold and the seller had nothing left to do. Counting to calculate the price did not prevent title from passing, because measurement is needed to identify goods only when part of a larger mass is sold.

The circuit judge thought the alleged mistake insufficient because it did not concern the identity or existence of the ties. That was too narrow: a collateral fact that materially induced the sale can support relief when both parties are mistaken about it. The decisive distinction was one of time. A fire starting after the sale would be a later casualty and would not affect the buyers' liability. An underground fire already threatening the pile when the contract was made was a present fact, and a mistake about it could go to the entire consideration. The existence, timing and consequences of the fire remained for the factfinder. The court also approved the instructions on fraudulent concealment.

The casebook adapts the case as a problem asking whether the underground fire presents a mistake or an erroneous prediction; its premise that the buyer immediately assumed the risk of loss belongs to the casebook's problem, not the opinion.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-069.rule: Frustration of purpose requires complete destruction of the basis of the contract; a tenant that can still use leased premises for part of its intended business shows only partial frustration, which does not excuse rent.

sections.Parties: The parties are a commercial tenant that operated a café and its landlord; the brief refers to them only as tenant and landlord, and the caption names Dr. Smood New York LLC and Orchard Houston, LLC. The tenant moved for a preliminary injunction and temporary restraining order after the landlord served default notices for unpaid rent. The landlord cross-moved for monthly use and occupancy during the litigation and a $250,000 undertaking.
sections.Procedural History: After a first notice to cure, the tenant sought a Yellowstone injunction, which preserves an opportunity to cure a lease default; the parties withdrew that notice and application while attempting settlement. A second notice, covering April through September, prompted the present application. In reply the tenant withdrew its Yellowstone request and sought only a preliminary injunction and temporary restraining order. The court noted that the order to show cause had not been served timely but decided both applications on the merits. On November 2, 2020, the New York Supreme Court, New York County, denied the tenant's motion and the landlord's cross-motion in their entirety. The order is marked a non-final disposition.
sections.Material Facts:
On or about February 22, 2017 the parties entered a ten-year lease of ground-floor and basement space at 181-185 East Houston Street. Its agreed purpose was operation of a full-service café offering fresh and raw quick-service products, meals, beverages, juices, shakes, smoothies and related items.

The tenant last paid monthly rent in March 2020 and withheld later payments, claiming that the pandemic, executive orders and the lease excused them. After June negotiations about revising the rent, the landlord served a July 1 notice to cure the April through June defaults, warning that it would draw on the security deposit. The landlord claimed arrears of $198,764.31 for the six months of April through September.

Lease section 11.3 proportionately reduced rent, tax and operating payments when physical damage by fire or other casualty, or damage to the building affecting access, left space unusable or inaccessible. The tenant asserted that the virus and the March 16 restrictions were such a casualty. The landlord showed that the café had operated in the premises since at least July, offering counter service and collection of orders placed online; the executive orders prevented indoor dining.
sections.Issue: Whether the tenant showed a likelihood of success, as required for a preliminary injunction, on its claims that the lease's casualty provision or the doctrine of frustration of purpose excused its rent during the pandemic restrictions.
sections.Holding: The New York Supreme Court, New York County, in 2020, in a decision by Justice Laurence L. Love, held that the tenant had not shown a likelihood of success on either theory and denied the preliminary injunction. The court said the tenant's rent and tax obligations continue unabated. It also denied the landlord's cross-motion: no bond was required because no injunction was granted, and it did not order use and occupancy or award the claimed arrears. The decision is an interim ruling, not a final judgment for arrears.
sections.Reasoning:
A preliminary injunction requires a likelihood of ultimate success, irreparable injury without relief, and a favorable balance of the equities, and granting it is discretionary.

The court rejected the casualty theory because there had been no physical harm to the premises. It said the lease did not provide abatement in these circumstances and that the tenant had been required to obtain insurance to assure payment under them.

On frustration, the tenant invoked the principle that the disappointed purpose must have been so completely the shared basis of the bargain that the transaction would otherwise make little sense. The court applied the further requirement that the underlying basis be completely destroyed: diminished business is not enough where the tenant can still use the space for an intended purpose. The café had been operating with counter service and online-order collection, so the premises still served permitted parts of the business. The court treated the disruption as partial frustration and held that the tenant had not shown likely success on its claimed excuse. It did not calculate a percentage rent reduction. Because the likelihood-of-success showing failed, it did not separately analyze irreparable injury or the equities.

The brief notes that an original image of the decision's pages was not available for visual inspection and that it was read through an archived extraction of the official document.

The casebook contrasts this refusal to recognize partial frustration with the contractual force-majeure relief in Hitz and asks whether the presence of that clause explains the difference.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-070.rule: A child for whose benefit a promise was made to her father, on consideration the father supplied, may sue the promisor on it although she neither made the bargain nor furnished the consideration.

sections.Parties: The plaintiffs were Grizil, daughter of Sir Edward Pool, and her husband Ralph Dutton. They sued Nevil Pool, Sir Edward's heir, in assumpsit on his promise to Sir Edward to pay Grizil 1,000 pounds. The defendant objected that only the father or his executors could sue. After judgment for the plaintiffs he was plaintiff in error in the Exchequer Chamber.
sections.Procedural History: The defendant pleaded non assumpsit and the jury found for the plaintiffs; the error report records a verdict for 1,000 pounds damages. The defendant moved in arrest of judgment in the King's Bench. At the first argument the court divided, with Wylde and Jones inclined toward the defendant and Twysden and Rainsford against. After Scroggs replaced Rainsford as Chief Justice and Dolben replaced Twysden, the case was reargued and judgment was given for the plaintiffs in 1677 with the final agreement of all four judges. Error was brought at once, and in Trinity term 1679 the Exchequer Chamber affirmed the judgment.
sections.Material Facts: Sir Edward Pool intended to sell timber in Oaksey Park, Wiltshire, to raise portions for his younger children; the error report places that intention on May 1, 1674. His heir, the defendant, asked him to refrain and promised instead to pay the daughter 1,000 pounds. The request and undertaking were made at Sherborn, Gloucestershire. The declaration averred that the father did refrain. The promised payment was not made, either while Grizil was unmarried or after her marriage. The son obtained the preserved timber, while the daughter lost the portion its sale would otherwise have provided.
sections.Issue: Whether a daughter, who was not a party to her father's bargain with his heir and did not herself supply the consideration, can maintain an action on the heir's promise to the father to pay her money.
sections.Holding: The King's Bench, in 1677, ultimately with the agreement of all four judges, Scroggs, Dolben, Jones and Wylde, held that the daughter and her husband could maintain the action and gave judgment for the plaintiffs on the verdict. In 1679 all the justices and barons in the Exchequer Chamber agreed that either the promisee or the person for whose use the promise was made could maintain the action, and affirmed the existing 1,000 pound judgment. The report does not establish that any person incidentally benefited by another's contract can sue.
sections.Reasoning:
The defendant argued that the promise was made to the father, that the daughter was neither privy to it nor interested in the consideration, that no debt was already due to her, and that she could not release a promise made to someone else. He relied on decisions denying recovery by children on promises to pay them money in consideration of a marriage, including the recent Norris and Pine.

The plaintiffs compared the daughter to a person entitled to money or goods delivered through an intermediary for that person's benefit, and argued that natural affection obliged a father to provide for his children.

On reargument Scroggs reasoned that the father's natural obligation and affection toward his children allowed the consideration and the promise made to the father to extend to them, and he rejected the contrary resolution in Norris and Pine. Dolben agreed. Jones and Wylde hesitated at first and agreed the next day, Jones acknowledging doubts about Norris and Pine while explaining his reluctance to depart from a resolved case. The reference to natural affection does not mean the father supplied no consideration; his forbearance was pleaded and supported the verdict.

In the Exchequer Chamber, Holt renewed the objection for the defendant below, and Pollexfen answered that either the promisee or the person for whose use the promise was made could sue. The individual names of the justices and barons are not given. The brief covers the two preserved reports only; other parallel reports were not read.

The casebook uses the case as an early example of enforcement by a daughter who personally supplied no consideration, and then contrasts later English restrictions.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-071.rule: A business buyer's promise to the seller to pay the seller's listed debts makes each listed creditor an intended beneficiary of a new, separate obligation, and limitations on a debt not yet barred when assumed runs from the new undertaking, not the original maturity.

sections.Parties: Spiklevitz, a creditor who had lent money to Vincent P. and Geraldine B. Heron, sued the defendants, who had bought the Herons' business and promised the Herons to pay their listed debts. He claimed as a third-party beneficiary of that assumption agreement. The purchasers argued that the original note was time-barred and that he could not enforce their agreement. Spiklevitz was the appellant.
sections.Procedural History: Spiklevitz sued in district court on June 21, 1981. The district judge treated the original note as the source of the claim, reasoned that the assumption gave Spiklevitz no additional rights, and allowed the defendants the original obligors' limitations defense. The circuit court affirmed, treating the arrangement as an assignment and concluding that beneficiary status had not been intended. The Michigan Court of Appeals granted leave, noting that the disposition labeled summary judgment should have been called accelerated judgment. On August 7, 1984 it reversed and remanded to the district court, with costs to the appellant; it did not enter a damages award.
sections.Material Facts:
Spiklevitz lent money to the Herons in 1974. Their July 5 note promised $4,800 by January 15, 1975. On April 1, 1980 the Herons sold their business to the defendants; $3,510 remained unpaid, and the attached creditor schedule listed the debt as $3,510.07.

As part of the purchase price for the building, business and interest in the Class C license for Vince's Lounge in Detroit, the purchasers executed an assumption agreement. They agreed to pay the obligations on Exhibit A, to hold Vincent Heron harmless, and to indemnify him for liability on those obligations and related litigation expense. Exhibit A expressly listed Spiklevitz. The Herons remained obligated on the note.
sections.Issue: Whether a creditor listed in a business purchasers' assumption agreement is an intended third-party beneficiary who can enforce their promise to pay, and whether the limitations period on his claim runs from the original note's maturity or from the new undertaking.
sections.Holding: The Michigan Court of Appeals, in 1984, in a per curiam opinion by a unanimous panel of Shepherd, P.J., Allen, and assigned circuit judge A. E. Keyes, held that Spiklevitz was an intended third-party beneficiary of the purchasers' promise and that his claim on the April 1980 undertaking was timely. The limitations period began on the new contract, which the court fixed at April 1, 1980, its execution date, and did not run exclusively from the maturity of the sellers' original note.
sections.Reasoning:
The court began with the rule that applies when someone assumes another person's past-due debt before the debt is barred by limitations: as between the new promisor and the creditor, the period runs from the new undertaking, not the original maturity date, because the new agreement creates a separate obligation. That defeated the lower courts' view that the purchasers simply took the rights and defenses attached to the old note. The creditor was enforcing the promise the purchasers made in acquiring the business, and his claim did not depend on a release of the original borrowers, so continued recourse against the Herons did not show that no new obligation existed.

Michigan's beneficiary statute, MCL 600.1405, lets a person for whose benefit a contractual promise is made enforce it as if it had been made directly to that person, and treats a promise as benefiting a person when the promisor undertakes to give, do or refrain from doing something directly to or for that person. A business purchaser's promise to discharge specified debts to the seller's creditors is the ordinary creditor-beneficiary arrangement, and the express listing of Spiklevitz together with the promise to pay supplied it. The argument that he received no additional rights was circular: if the promise was enforceable it gave him additional security, and if not it did not.

The casebook's problem changes the facts so that the listed debt was already barred when the business was sold; the court's stated rule concerned a debt not yet barred, and it did not decide that a promise to assume an already-barred debt revives it.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-072.rule: The Contract Disputes Act governs only claims between the United States and its contractors, so it does not strip a district court of jurisdiction over an alleged third-party beneficiary's suit against a private supplier under a federal procurement contract.

sections.Parties: The United Kingdom Ministry of Defence sued Trimble Navigation Limited, a private supplier, for breach of procurement contracts between Trimble and the United States Department of Defense, claiming to be an intended beneficiary of those contracts. Trimble sought dismissal. The Ministry was the appellant; the United States, invited to participate as amicus, supported Trimble's reading of the statute.
sections.Procedural History: The Ministry invoked diversity jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. section 1332(a)(4). Trimble moved to dismiss on three grounds: the Contract Disputes Act (CDA) displaced district-court jurisdiction, the Ministry was not a third-party beneficiary, and the United States was an indispensable party that had not been joined. The district court reached only the first ground and dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, reasoning that rights derived from procurement contracts necessarily fell within the CDA scheme. The Ministry appealed. Reviewing the jurisdictional question de novo, the Fourth Circuit on September 6, 2005 reversed and remanded for further proceedings.
sections.Material Facts:
Under the Arms Export Control Act the United States may procure military goods for cash sale to foreign governments: the foreign government pays the United States in advance, the United States contracts with a supplier, and the supplier furnishes the goods to the foreign government. In July 1998 the Department of Defense agreed to procure for the Ministry, on a nonprofit basis, more than 2,000 auxiliary output chips made by approved supplier Trimble. It entered four procurement contracts with Trimble, which the parties agreed were covered by the CDA. The Ministry was not a party to those contracts.

Deliveries began in early 2000. According to the Ministry, about 95 percent of the initial chips failed military specifications and were returned, and about 20 percent of the repaired or replaced chips remained defective, which allegedly delayed a cruise-missile program and raised its cost. The Ministry asked the United States to help recover its costs. In January 2003 the Department of Defense released an Air Force legal opinion that did not recommend action against Trimble. These were the Ministry's allegations, not findings.
sections.Issue: Whether the Contract Disputes Act deprives a federal district court of subject-matter jurisdiction over a suit by a foreign government, claiming as a third-party beneficiary of federal procurement contracts, against the private supplier that was party to those contracts.
sections.Holding: The Fourth Circuit, in 2005, in a unanimous opinion by Judge Traxler for a panel with Judges Widener and Gregory, held that the CDA did not govern the Ministry's suit merely because the alleged beneficiary rights arose from federal procurement contracts. The Act's dispute procedures concern claims between the United States and its contractors, and neither side of this suit asserted such a claim. The court expressly declined to decide whether the Ministry actually had enforceable third-party-beneficiary rights, and the indispensable-party ground was not adjudicated.
sections.Reasoning:
The court separated the question of which contracts the Act covers from the question of whose claims its procedures cover. Section 602 applied to the procurement contracts, but section 605 supplied procedures only for a contractor's claim against the government or the government's claim against a contractor, and section 601 defined a contractor as a party to a government contract other than the government. The Ministry, claiming as a beneficiary and not a party, was not a contractor, and it sought relief from Trimble, not the United States. The review provisions pointed the same way: nothing provided a procedure for a foreign beneficiary to proceed against a private supplier, and the Court of Federal Claims could enter the relevant money judgments against the United States, not a private company, so Trimble's reading would send the Ministry to a forum that could not grant its relief.

The court found the statutory language and structure unambiguous, so arguments about the expertise of specialized procurement tribunals could not enlarge the Act; in the alternative, the legislative history showed concern with claims by or against the United States. Trimble also argued that a beneficiary cannot have greater rights than the contracting party through whom it claims, so the Ministry was bound to CDA procedures as the United States was. The court answered that Congress sets federal jurisdiction by statute; limits on derivative contract rights could matter on the merits but did not expand the Act. Beneficiary intent required a fact-sensitive inquiry best made first by the district court.

The casebook's problem asks whether the Ministry may act as a beneficiary when the Air Force will not sue; this decision settles only that the CDA does not close the district-court forum.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-073.rule: Under Florida's section 542.335, a third party may enforce a business restrictive covenant only if the covenant expressly identifies that person as a beneficiary and expressly states that it is for that person's benefit; a covenant in the claimant's own contract remains enforceable.

sections.Parties: Gaetano Tusa, a tenant operating Rocco's Pizza, sued his landlord, Ralph Roffe, and a competing tenant in the same building, KKA, Inc., which operated The Oasis. He sought injunctive relief, alleging breaches of the restrictive covenants in the two leases. Tusa appealed after the trial court dismissed all his claims and awarded Roffe attorney's fees.
sections.Procedural History: KKA moved for summary judgment on the ground that Tusa was not its contracting counterparty and could not meet the statutory conditions for third-party enforcement, and the trial court agreed. Tusa then tried to add a declaratory-relief count. KKA moved to strike or dismiss that amendment, and Roffe moved to strike Count II and for summary judgment, arguing he had not breached Tusa's lease. The trial court granted all three motions, entered a final order dismissing all claims, and awarded Roffe $11,075 in attorney's fees. On consolidated appeals, Florida's Fourth District on July 18, 2001 affirmed the dismissal of the claims against KKA and reversed so that the claim against Roffe could proceed. Rehearing was denied August 22, 2001.
sections.Material Facts:
In October 1997 Tusa entered a ten-year business lease, beginning in January 1998, to operate Rocco's Pizza in Hollywood, Florida. The lease allowed other restaurants on property owned or controlled by the landlord, with an exception prohibiting anyone other than Rocco's Pizza from selling pizza on the premises.

In December 1997 Roffe leased space in the same building to KKA for The Oasis. That separate lease prohibited KKA from making or selling specified foods, including pizza. The Oasis nevertheless sold pizza. Roffe knew of the sales and refused to act. KKA's covenant did not expressly identify Tusa as a beneficiary or state that it was for his benefit.

The Oasis apparently occupied two joined areas: its original premises, owned by KKA and outside Roffe's lease, and an adjoining 29-seat area in Roffe's shopping center that was subject to the lease.
sections.Issue: Whether a tenant can enforce, as a third-party beneficiary, a restrictive covenant in a competing tenant's lease that does not expressly name him, and whether the landlord breached the covenant in the tenant's own lease by knowingly allowing the competitor to sell pizza.
sections.Holding: The Florida Fourth District Court of Appeal, in 2001, in an opinion by Polen, C.J., for a unanimous panel with Stone and Gross, held that section 542.335 barred Tusa from enforcing KKA's lease because that covenant neither expressly identified him as a third-party beneficiary nor expressly stated that it was for his benefit. It also held that Roffe breached the covenant in Tusa's own lease by knowingly permitting the pizza sales without ordering KKA to stop or face eviction. The court directed that the case proceed against Roffe alone; it did not itself issue an injunction, order eviction or fix damages.
sections.Reasoning:
Section 542.335 governed business restrictive covenants entered after July 1, 1996. Subsection (1)(f)(1) required the covenant to identify the claimant expressly as a third-party beneficiary and to state expressly that it was intended for that person's benefit. KKA's prohibition on pizza sales did neither, and a practical benefit to Tusa could not substitute for the express identification the statute required. The court noted the awkward consequence that a later injunction against Roffe might require him to terminate KKA's lease even though KKA had left the litigation, possibly requiring a second suit, but that concern did not change KKA's entitlement to dismissal.

As to Roffe, the statute required a legitimate business interest and a restraint reasonably necessary to protect it. It was undisputed that the covenant in Tusa's lease aimed to prevent the loss of customers to another restaurant selling pizza on the same premises, and the court placed that interest in the statutory category of customer relationships. It read the covenant to prohibit Roffe from leasing space in the same building to another restaurant that sold pizza; a reading that let him authorize that competition would defeat the covenant's purpose, and contract terms should receive a reasonable construction, not one producing an absurd result. This claim enforced a promise in a lease to which Tusa and Roffe were both parties. Tusa's counsel agreed that relief would apply only to the 29-seat portion.

The casebook cites the case, in a problem on tenant mix, as an example where a statute defeated beneficiary enforcement.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.rule: Employees who work under a city service contract are intended third-party beneficiaries of the contractor's express promise to the city to comply with its living wage ordinance and may sue the contractor for breach of that promise.

sections.Parties: A certified class of production and stockroom employees at two Cintas plants sued Cintas Corporation No. 2, their employer, alleging violations of Hayward's living wage ordinance, the Labor Code and the unfair-competition law, and breach of contract; they later added penalty claims under PAGA. The City of Hayward intervened. Cintas appealed the judgment for the employees, and the employees cross-appealed for enhanced penalties and additional litigation expenses.
sections.Procedural History: The employees sued on June 23, 2003. The trial court rejected an early extraterritoriality challenge and on September 23, 2005, on cross-motions for summary judgment or adjudication, found the ordinance constitutional and enforceable, applicable to all hours of covered workers, and violated by Cintas. It awarded $790,489 in unpaid hourly wages, $14,254 in unpaid vacation benefits and $258,900 in Labor Code penalties, found no willfulness, and awarded $1,199,550 in attorney fees plus $60,611 for the fee motion. Both sides appealed, and the appeals were consolidated. On June 11, 2008 California's First District, Division Three, affirmed the entire judgment and all appealed postjudgment orders. Rehearing was denied July 2, 2008 and California Supreme Court review was denied September 10, 2008.
sections.Material Facts:
Between July 1999 and June 2003, Cintas leased uniforms and janitorial items to the City of Hayward, collected them weekly, and processed them at plants in Union City and San Leandro, outside Hayward. City items were commingled with other customers' items, and workers were not assigned City-only tasks. The City contract supplied less than one percent of the facilities' revenue.

Hayward adopted its living wage ordinance in April 1999 for service contracts entered from July 1, covering contracts above $25,000 for listed services including laundry. Covered workers were initially entitled to at least $8 an hour with health benefits or $9.25 without, plus compensated time off, and contractors had to accept civil enforcement by aggrieved employees.

Before renewal the City sent Cintas the complete ordinance and advised that its purchase order was subject to it. In June 1999 a Cintas manager signed a compliance certification without recalling that he had read the ordinance; another certification followed in 2000, and purchase orders incorporated the undertaking. Cintas did not pay the ordinance rates and sought no clarification. In 2003 another manager noticed the requirement, and Cintas terminated the contract by a July 3 letter.
sections.Issue: Whether employees working outside Hayward could enforce, as intended third-party beneficiaries, Cintas's contractual promise to the City to comply with the living wage ordinance, and whether the ordinance was a valid, sufficiently definite condition covering all hours of employees who did City work.
sections.Holding: The California Court of Appeal, First District, Division Three, in 2008, in an opinion by Presiding Justice McGuiness in which Pollak and Jenkins concurred, held that the employees were intended beneficiaries of the compliance provision incorporated in Cintas's contract with the City and could sue for its breach, even though their workplaces were outside Hayward. It upheld the ordinance against extraterritoriality and vagueness challenges, held that the ordinance rate applied to all hours of an employee who worked on or under the City contract, and affirmed the wage, vacation, penalty, fee and cost awards. It rejected the employees' cross-appeals.
sections.Reasoning:
Cintas argued that Hayward could not regulate work outside its boundaries. The court distinguished regulatory power from proprietary contracting power: the City chose the employers it would do business with and set conditions on its service contracts, and a company could avoid the ordinance by declining a City contract. The ordinance was not unconstitutionally vague, since reasonable certainty suffices and economic regulation permits more flexibility than penal regulation.

Once an employee worked on or under the City contract, the ordinance required its minimum rate for all that employee's hours; the text contained no limit to City hours and no de minimis exception, though a contractor could segregate City work to a subset of employees. Because Cintas commingled the work, kept no records of who handled City items and controlled the information, fairness required it to show which employees did no covered work.

The same reasonable certainty defeated the claim that the compliance promise was too indefinite to enforce. Civil Code section 1559 allows a nonparty to enforce a contract made expressly for that person's benefit when the intent appears in its terms, and prevailing-wage decisions had treated employees as beneficiaries of a contractor's express wage promise to a public agency. Requiring higher wages plainly benefited employees doing City work. The contractual right was distinct from statutory wage recovery and did not depend on the absence of a statutory private action.

The court also held that PAGA gave new standing to recover existing penalties without creating new liabilities, that Cintas's good-faith defenses negated willfulness, that base penalties were mandatory, and that the 1.65 fee multiplier was justified.

The casebook cites the case for the employees' status as intended beneficiaries.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-075.rule: Where a government form contract merely incorporates statutory obligations for which Congress provided no private right of action, the statute's intended recipients cannot enforce those same obligations by suing as third-party beneficiaries of the contract.
