CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-094.rule: A motorist's beneficiary rights under particular clauses of a roadside-service contract do not extend to consequential personal-injury and death damages that fall outside the responsibility the contracting parties contemplated.

sections.Parties: The appellant was the widow of a disabled motorist who died after receiving no roadside assistance. The respondents were Chevron and its roadside-service contractor. The widow sought to overturn the order dismissing her action; the respondents sought affirmance.
sections.Procedural History: A jury awarded the widow damages under a third-party-beneficiary contract theory. In 1978 the Appellate Division found the service evidence sufficient to support breach but held the personal-injury and death loss outside the contemplated contractual responsibility, reversed, and dismissed. The widow appealed. On November 27, 1979, the New York Court of Appeals affirmed the order, with costs. This brief covers only the Court of Appeals stage; the 1978 reversal is recorded separately.
sections.Material Facts: The 1979 memorandum makes no fresh findings; the facts come from the 1978 report. A disabled motorist received no contracted assistance after repeated reports and assurances, changed his tire in extreme summer heat, suffered a myocardial infarction, and died twenty-eight days later. As the dissent described it, the service arrangement was exclusive and promised a thirty-minute response; more than three hours passed without help.
sections.Issue: Should the dismissal of the widow's third-party-beneficiary contract action for her husband's injury and death, following the failure to provide contracted roadside service, be affirmed?
sections.Holding: The New York Court of Appeals, in 1979, by a vote of six to one, affirmed with costs for the reasons stated in Hopkins's Appellate Division opinion rather than issuing a new extended analysis. Cooke, Jasen, Gabrielli, Jones, Wachtler and Meyer concurred; Fuchsberg dissented and would have reversed and remitted to the Appellate Division for consideration of the facts. The court neither awarded damages nor ordered the remittal.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority adopted Hopkins's reasons. Those reasons recognized particular contractual benefits to motorists, including regulated charges and overcharge refunds, while rejecting recovery for consequential injury under the contractual foreseeability analysis. Martuscello's separate concurrence below was not the opinion adopted, so the court was not affirming on the ground that motorists lacked beneficiary rights under every clause.

Fuchsberg, dissenting, approached the case as an exclusive protective undertaking followed by a prolonged, knowing failure to respond. He invoked Restatement (Second) of Agency section 354, under which an agent undertaking action necessary to protect another could be liable for physical harm caused by reliance and an unexcused failure to act creating a foreseeable unreasonable risk. He examined five elements: necessary protective action, reliance, unexcused nonperformance, unreasonable risk and awareness of that risk. A stranded vehicle on a limited-access high-speed highway showed an evident need for protection; the exclusive arrangement and thirty-minute promise supported reliance; whether the failure was excusable was for the jury. He also challenged rigid reliance on Moch, distinguishing it because highway users received and paid for the roadside service themselves, whereas Moch concerned hydrant water furnished to the city. In his view contract, agency and tort principles were interrelated and the plaintiff had proved a prima facie case.

The casebook lists this stage as affirmed on the opinion below, without mentioning the dissent.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-095.rule: Persons expressly designated in a public contract as the consumers the promisor undertakes to serve are intended third-party beneficiaries, even though they buy from the promisee rather than directly from the promisor.

sections.Parties: The plaintiffs were New York City and fourteen public benefit corporations, which obtained their electricity from the Power Authority of the State of New York, or PASNY. The defendant was Consolidated Edison, whose facilities transmitted and delivered that power. The plaintiffs sought damages for losses from the 1977 blackout, alleging gross negligence and reckless and willful conduct. Con Edison appealed to the Court of Appeals; the plaintiffs cross-appealed.
sections.Procedural History: The plaintiffs sued on September 7, 1978. In separate litigation, Food Pageant had obtained a jury verdict, upheld on appeal, that Con Edison's gross negligence caused the blackout. The plaintiffs moved for partial summary judgment treating that determination as conclusive. Con Edison moved for partial summary judgment denying third-party-beneficiary status and excluding losses from criminal activity and governmental expenditures. Special Term granted the plaintiffs' motion and denied the relevant parts of Con Edison's. The Appellate Division affirmed without opinion and granted leave to appeal. On June 14, 1984, the Court of Appeals modified the order to dismiss the claims for additional governmental operating expenditures and for lost revenues or similar economic damage, affirmed as modified without costs, dismissed the plaintiffs' cross appeal, and answered the certified question in the negative.
sections.Material Facts:
Electrical service failed at about 9:36 p.m. on July 13, 1977, throughout New York City except an area of Queens supplied by another utility, and was not completely restored until about 10:40 p.m. the next day. The plaintiffs claimed physical injuries and property losses, looting and vandalism, additional police, fire, sanitation and hospital personnel costs, lost public revenues, and employee absenteeism or lost productivity.

Legislation enacted in 1974 authorized emergency measures to preserve reliable metropolitan electric service. PASNY acquired Con Edison's partially completed Astoria 6 and Indian Point 3 generating units in December 1974 and December 1975, with transmission and delivery to continue through Con Edison's facilities. A service agreement expressly provided that Con Edison would assist PASNY in serving the designated Astoria-Indian Point customers, deliver the same quality of service it supplied its own customers under its regular tariffs, and operate and maintain the necessary facilities according to good utility practice. A simultaneous power-sale contract required sufficient energy to meet those customers' requirements. The plaintiffs belonged to that customer group. In Food Pageant the jury had awarded $40,500 for a grocery chain's spoiled food and lost business.
sections.Issue: Was Con Edison precluded from relitigating the earlier finding that its gross negligence caused the blackout? Were PASNY's customers intended third-party beneficiaries of Con Edison's agreements with PASNY? And which categories of claimed loss, including looting, added governmental service costs and lost revenues, were recoverable?
sections.Holding: The New York Court of Appeals, in 1984, in an opinion by Judge Jones for all seven judges, upheld issue preclusion against Con Edison on gross negligence causing the blackout and held that the plaintiffs were intended third-party beneficiaries of the agreements with PASNY. Physical injury directly resulting from the interruption was compensable on proof, and whether looting and vandalism losses were contemplated or reasonably foreseeable required a trial. Claims for additional governmental operating expenditures and for lost revenues or similar economic damage were dismissed. The ruling defined liability issues and recoverable categories; it was not a final damages assessment.
sections.Reasoning:
On preclusion, an issue actually litigated, necessarily determined and established by a valid final judgment may bind the losing party against a different opponent, subject to a full and fair opportunity to litigate. Con Edison bore the burden of showing a reason to relitigate and did not carry it. The inconsistent decisions were small-claims judgments that by statute could not be treated as adjudications in other actions; the investigative reports had been offered and excluded in Food Pageant; the jury-compromise argument was speculative; and despite the small verdict Con Edison had defended vigorously, aware of possible future preclusion.

On beneficiary status, the contracts and legislation identified the plaintiffs as the very consumers they were designed to serve. Direct purchase from Con Edison was unnecessary: the promise ran to PASNY, but its explicit performance concerned the designated end users. The court contrasted Moch's public fire-hydrant arrangement and Kornblut's Thruway repair-service agreement with this express undertaking to supply these customers. The decisive distinction was the obligation's stated beneficiaries and purpose, not the mere existence of a public contract or a general benefit to society.

On damages, looting and vandalism were not automatically superseding causes. Additional public-service costs were barred by the general public-policy rule against recovering expenditures made in performing governmental functions. Lost taxes, fares, tolls, betting receipts and productivity were excluded because the proof depended speculatively on collateral transactions and policy opposed shifting losses from general economic disruption to the utility. The cross appeal failed because the plaintiffs had not appealed to the Appellate Division.

The casebook discusses the case in its treatment of government-contract beneficiaries.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-096.rule: Those who benefit from a government contract are presumed incidental beneficiaries and may enforce it only if the contract's precise language shows a clear intent to give them enforceable rights; explicit mention of their class is not by itself sufficient.

sections.Parties: The appellants were individual farmers, landowners and water users within Westlands Water District, who had intervened as plaintiffs. The defendant and appellee was the United States, which supplied water to Westlands from the San Luis Unit of the federal Central Valley Project under a 1963 contract. The farmers sought damages for a reduced water allocation, asserting appropriative water rights, trust law, challenges to project surcharges and breach of the 1963 contract. Westlands returned as an intervenor on appeal to protect its interests, and the Natural Resources Defense Council also filed an appellate brief.
sections.Procedural History: Westlands began the action in May 1993; the farmers and the Natural Resources Defense Council intervened. Westlands dismissed its complaint without prejudice in 1995, leaving the farmers to file a second amended complaint. On June 5, 1998, the district court dismissed statutory claims for lack of jurisdiction under the Tucker Act. It initially treated the farmers as a contracting entity covered by the waiver of sovereign immunity in 43 U.S.C. section 390uu, granted the government summary judgment on three of the four remaining claims, and found triable issues on the contract claim. On reconsideration on April 12, 2000, it concluded the farmers were merely incidental beneficiaries, found no waiver, and entered final judgment for the government on August 1, 2000. The Ninth Circuit affirmed the conclusion that immunity was not waived and vacated the earlier merits rulings, each party bearing its own costs. This brief covers only the 2004 Ninth Circuit stage.
sections.Material Facts:
Westlands received project water under a 1963 contract with the United States. A 1986 stipulated judgment in Barcellos upheld the contract and required federal performance. The individual landowners and water users within Westlands benefited from the deliveries but were not parties to the 1963 contract.

The Sacramento River winter-run chinook salmon was listed as threatened in 1990 and the delta smelt in 1993. The Bureau of Reclamation reduced Westlands' 1993 allocation to fifty percent of its contractual supply under the Endangered Species Act and the Central Valley Project Improvement Act.

Article 15 of the contract required payment of district assessments or charges before an individual water user could receive project water and required any district-user contracts to subject the user's supply to the federal contract. Article 11(b) made a payment adjustment the sole remedy for a shortage and referred to the district or anyone claiming water rights by, through or under it. The farmers also held recordable contracts with the government concerning excess-acreage lands. The Barcellos stipulated judgment provided that it was not a contract or amendment for purposes of section 390uu.
sections.Issue: Were the farmers intended third-party beneficiaries of the 1963 contract between Westlands and the United States, so as to qualify as a contracting entity under 43 U.S.C. section 390uu and bring their claims within that waiver of sovereign immunity?
sections.Holding: The Ninth Circuit, in 2004, in an opinion by Judge Clifton for a panel of Judges Noonan, Thomas and Clifton with no separate writing, held that the farmers were not intended third-party beneficiaries of the 1963 contract and so did not come within the section 390uu waiver; the United States had not waived immunity for their claims. Because the district court therefore lacked jurisdiction, its earlier merits rulings on appropriative water rights, trust obligations and surcharges were vacated. The court did not hold that the water reduction satisfied every contractual or statutory duty.
sections.Reasoning:
The United States cannot be sued without an express waiver, strictly construed in its favor. Barcellos did not preclude the immunity defense: it had involved alleged ultra vires agency action and the McCarran Amendment, and the 1993 allocation arose from a different nucleus of facts. The McCarran Amendment did not cover this private damages suit.

Section 390uu permits joining the United States to adjudicate the contractual rights of a contracting entity under federal reclamation contracts. Applying Klamath, the panel required clear contractual intent to give beneficiaries of a government contract enforceable rights. A beneficiary need not be individually named if within the intended class, but mention of the class is not itself enough; a project may knowingly benefit farmers without giving them a right to enforce the district's contract.

Article 15's references to individual users were conditions on obtaining water through Westlands and described a possible relationship between Westlands and its users, not between users and the United States. Article 11(b)'s language could sensibly refer to an assignee taking over the district's rights and duties, and the farmers had no such assignment. The panel acknowledged possible disagreement with the Federal Circuit's H.F. Allen Orchards decision, which as it understood that case had found beneficiary status from beneficial use and ultimate payment. The recordable contracts were separate agreements that the farmers were not suing to enforce, and the court did not decide whether Westlands was a trustee, since the conditions for suing in a trustee's place were not met. Without a waiver the district court lacked authority from the outset, so its merits rulings were nullities.

The casebook uses the case to show that an intended economic benefit and an enforceable third-party right are distinct.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-098.rule: A nonclient can enforce a lawyer's retainer as a third-party beneficiary only if the retainer was intended to benefit it and the benefit is immediate enough to show the contracting parties assumed a duty to compensate it; an indirect economic benefit is not enough.

sections.Parties: The plaintiff and appellant was the State of California Public Employees' Retirement System, or CalPERS, which bought commercial property loans originated for it by Equitable Real Estate Investment Management. The defendant and respondent was Shearman & Sterling, the law firm Equitable retained to negotiate and close one such loan. CalPERS sued for professional negligence and breach of contract, both directly, on a relationship approaching privity and as an intended third-party beneficiary, and as Equitable's assignee, seeking the shortfall in an acceleration fee. The firm sought dismissal.
sections.Procedural History: Supreme Court dismissed CalPERS's direct claims but allowed the assigned claims, reasoning that the original omnibus assignment was insufficient to transfer malpractice claims but the later settlement assignment expressly did so. The Appellate Division dismissed the entire complaint: it agreed the first assignment was too narrow and concluded the later one could not convey an actionable malpractice claim because Equitable had received the full benefit of its bargain and suffered no injury. On November 16, 2000, the New York Court of Appeals affirmed, with costs. This was a pleading-stage disposition.
sections.Material Facts:
In 1988 CalPERS and Equitable entered a correspondent agreement under which Equitable originated and closed commercial property loans for sale and assignment to CalPERS. The agreement treated Equitable's agents as independent, not CalPERS's agents, and required CalPERS's own counsel to approve closing documents. In August 1993 CalPERS approved purchase of a $23.3 million loan to Nathan Serota, whose commitment was later assigned to Sersons Corporation. Equitable retained Shearman & Sterling to negotiate and close it. CalPERS alleged that Equitable asked the firm to use a standard note with prepayment and acceleration provisions. The firm sent the draft to CalPERS and its counsel with a letter identifying black-lined changes, which included the acceleration clause. CalPERS did not object.

Sersons executed the note in November 1994, and the next month Equitable assigned its rights under the loan documents to CalPERS. After Sersons defaulted, CalPERS allegedly discovered that the note produced an acceleration fee of approximately $1.1 million instead of approximately $9.1 million under the standard form. Sersons paid $1.1 million in March 1997. CalPERS then settled with Equitable, which paid $400,000 and expressly assigned any malpractice and contract claims against the firm not previously transferred.
sections.Issue: Could CalPERS recover from the law firm retained by its commercial counterparty, either directly, on a relationship approaching privity or as an intended third-party beneficiary of the retainer, or as the assignee of the counterparty's claims against the firm?
sections.Holding: The New York Court of Appeals, in 2000, in an opinion by Judge Wesley in which Chief Judge Kaye and Judges Smith, Levine and Ciparick concurred, Judge Rosenblatt taking no part, held that it could not. CalPERS established neither a relationship with the firm approaching privity nor intended-beneficiary status under Equitable's retainer. The omnibus assignment of rights under the loan documents did not carry a malpractice claim, and the later express assignment could not transfer a claim Equitable did not possess because the reduced fee caused Equitable no injury. No damages were tried or awarded.
sections.Reasoning:
A tort claim for negligent misrepresentation causing pecuniary loss required actual privity or a relationship close to it: awareness that a statement would be used for a particular purpose, reliance by a known party, and conduct linking the maker to that party and showing an understanding of the reliance. The firm's only direct preclosing contact was its request that CalPERS and its counsel review and approve the marked-up documents. CalPERS had kept final approval for itself and its lawyers and received a version showing the changes, so its failure to object did not show the firm understood CalPERS would rely on the note without reviewing it.

Third-party enforcement required a valid contract between others, intent to benefit the claimant, and a benefit immediate enough to show the contracting parties assumed a duty to compensate the claimant if it was lost. The retainer was valid but was not intended to impose a legal-service duty to CalPERS. The parties did not invariably share interests: the firm represented Equitable in satisfying the correspondent agreement while protecting Equitable's interests, and CalPERS stood on the other side of that agreement. The indirect economic benefit of accurate documents was not enough.

The omnibus assignment covered Equitable's rights in and under the loan documents with Sersons, not a malpractice claim under the separate correspondent agreement. The settlement assignment was broader, but CalPERS had paid Equitable in full and Equitable had no remaining right to the acceleration payment, so it had no injury and no claim to assign.

The casebook cites the case for the point that a common transaction does not erase potential conflicts between a lawyer's client and a claimed beneficiary.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-099.rule: A lawyer retained to represent a client against an adverse party in litigation owes that party no ordinary negligence duty as an intended beneficiary of the retainer, and a promise to hold security as custodian creates duties only once the security is delivered.

sections.Parties: Janice Baker, the former wife of James Collins, was the plaintiff and appellant. Ronald Coombs, who had been Collins's attorney in the divorce and other matters, was the defendant and appellee. Baker sued Collins's estate, his surviving widow and Coombs; against Coombs she claimed professional negligence, charging that he failed to hold certificates securing her divorce settlement or to ensure payment when businesses were sold. Coombs sought to keep the summary judgment he had won.
sections.Procedural History: Baker filed a claim against the estate on November 30, 1999, and after the estate objected sued the estate, the widow and Coombs on December 22. She obtained a judgment against the estate on August 6, 2003. Following cross-motions, the circuit court entered summary judgment for Coombs on August 26, 2005, holding that he signed the settlement as counsel, not as a contracting party, and that the agreement did not oblige him to compel delivery of the certificates or notify Baker of nondelivery. Baker appealed. On March 23, 2007, the Kentucky Court of Appeals affirmed, reviewing de novo.
sections.Material Facts:
Baker filed for dissolution of her marriage to Collins in 1989. The decree entered December 11, 1990, incorporated a property settlement under which Collins agreed to pay $500,000: a $300,000 balloon payment due January 1, 2002, and $200,000 in ten annual $20,000 installments ending January 1, 2001. The agreement gave Baker liens on Collins's holdings in closely held corporations. Collins was to execute the necessary documents, and the certificates were to be held by Coombs.

Coombs testified that he requested the certificates during negotiation and after signing, but Collins never delivered them before his death on September 30, 1999. Shortly before the death, Baker discovered that Collins apparently had sold his interest in Advanced Care Medicine in 1992 without perfecting the lien or making the agreed transfer. She lacked documents showing perfected liens and could not recall inquiring about them or the certificates before Collins died. Baker had her own counsel, who also made no inquiry.
sections.Issue: Did the attorney for one spouse in a divorce, named in the property settlement as holder of the security for the other spouse, owe that other spouse a duty to obtain the certificates, force his client to deliver them or tell her they were missing, either as a fiduciary or because she was an intended third-party beneficiary of his retainer?
sections.Holding: The Kentucky Court of Appeals, in 2007, in an opinion by Chief Judge Combs in which Judge Moore and Senior Judge Henry concurred, held that the asserted duty did not arise on these facts and affirmed summary judgment for Coombs. The agreement obligated Coombs only to hold and secure the certificates if and when he received them, so his custodial duty was contingent on Collins's delivery and never arose. The retainer for adversarial divorce litigation was not primarily and directly intended to benefit Baker.
sections.Reasoning:
An attorney's required signature on a filed paper did not alone create a fiduciary duty. The designated-holder clause was a more serious matter, because Coombs had pledged a potential escrow role. But the court found the agreement unambiguous: it obligated Collins to deliver the certificates and Coombs to hold them once received, and no clause required Coombs to acquire the documents, coerce his client or notify anyone of nondelivery. The court adopted the reasoning of Muscara v. Lamberti, where a designated attorney who never received escrow funds never acquired the escrow duty, and Kentucky precedent likewise required delivery to the depositary to create an escrow. Because the certificates never reached Coombs, any fiduciary duty remained inchoate. The court recognized that actual receipt would have imposed the custodial duties to Baker.

On the beneficiary theory, which the court chose to consider although preservation was not established, it distinguished client malpractice claims from possible liability to nonclients, including negligent injury to an intended beneficiary. Collins retained Coombs to represent him against Baker, and their conflicting interests meant the retainer was not primarily and directly intended to benefit her. An ordinary negligence duty to the adverse party would chill representation. The court excepted willful and wanton conduct, fraud or malice, but Baker identified no facts supporting them. It closed with a warning about the divided loyalties created when adversarial counsel also accepts an escrow role.

The casebook compares the case with CalPERS to show that another party's economic interest does not automatically make it an intended beneficiary of a legal retainer.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-100.rule: A court-appointed guardian's responsibility for the ward does not end by informally delegating the work to an assistant, and a lawyer remains responsible for ensuring that delegated legal responsibilities are completed properly.

sections.Parties: Disciplinary Counsel brought the proceeding against James Cornell Young, an attorney admitted in 1980 and already under an indefinite suspension. Disciplinary Counsel charged Young with professional misconduct in his role as court-appointed guardian for Michael Gordon, whom the Department of Veterans Affairs had declared incompetent. Young contested the sanction, asking for a suspension concurrent with his existing one. This was attorney discipline, not an action awarding contract damages to the ward.
sections.Procedural History: The probate court removed Young as guardian on December 5, 2002, and a successor obtained an agreed surcharge judgment finding willful and wanton neglect. Disciplinary Counsel brought the guardianship charges on June 13, 2005. Young stipulated to three violations and initially denied a fourth. The panel and board found all four by clear and convincing evidence. The panel proposed a concurrent two-year suspension with a conditional stay; with the panel's approval, the board recommended a consecutive indefinite suspension. On the board's certified report, the Supreme Court of Ohio on March 21, 2007, overruled Young's objections and imposed a second indefinite suspension, consecutive to the one already in effect, with reinstatement and probation conditions and costs taxed to Young.
sections.Material Facts:
In May 1992 the probate court appointed Young guardian for Gordon. Young had to arrange medical care and use Gordon's monthly benefits for bills and necessities. He opened a guardianship checking account on which he alone was the authorized signatory. His secretary, LaTonya Jackson, at first handled many daily tasks; as Young grew impatient with the demands, he delegated all daily responsibilities to her and authorized her to sign his name, including on checks.

In January 1996 Young decided to relinquish the guardianship and Jackson agreed to succeed him, but the withdrawal motion was never signed or filed and Jackson was never formally appointed. Young later dismissed Gordon's concerns by saying Jackson was guardian and he was no longer responsible. Jackson continued submitting reports in his name, changed the account address so statements no longer reached his office, and eventually stopped telling him of probate notices. After Young's removal for failure to file an account, the sureties paid $40,000 for which he had failed to account and $4,101.06 for the successor's services, and took judgment against Young for $44,101.06, which he had not tried to satisfy.
sections.Issue: Did an attorney appointed as guardian commit professional misconduct, including intentional failure to carry out a contract for professional services, by handing the guardianship to his secretary without completing his withdrawal or supervising her, and what sanction was warranted given his existing indefinite suspension?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of Ohio, in 2007, in a per curiam decision in which six justices concurred in the judgment, found four violations, under DR 1-102(A)(6), 6-101(A)(3), 9-102(B)(3) and 7-101(A)(2), and imposed a second indefinite suspension consecutive to the existing one. Reinstatement was conditioned on successful completion of an approved substance-abuse program, a showing of ability to practice competently and ethically, and compliance with a monitor-approved plan to repay $44,101.06 to the insurers, followed by three years' probation. Justice Lundberg Stratton concurred in the findings and the indefinite suspension but would have made it concurrent.
sections.Reasoning:
The court accepted the findings, to which Young no longer objected, including intentional abandonment of his employment obligation: he knowingly handed control to his secretary, failed to verify that a successor was appointed, and disclaimed responsibility when Gordon sought help. Informal delegation and the purported succession did not end his court-appointed role, and the court emphasized a lawyer's duty to ensure that delegated legal responsibilities are completed properly.

On sanction, the board credited Young's disclosure, cooperation, character evidence and recovery, but did not treat chemical dependency as a mitigating cause, since Young's own testimony attributed the abandonment to not wanting the burdensome guardianship. Aggravating factors included prior discipline, a self-centered abandonment, repeated unsupervised delegation and multiple violations, harm to a particularly vulnerable client, and failure to repay the sureties. The court rejected Young's arguments that contemporaneous misconduct did not justify a consecutive suspension, that addiction caused the misconduct, and that the sureties' reimbursement removed the harm; a $40,000 estate loss harmed the ward despite later compensation. Each disciplinary action required an independently justified sanction, and concurrency was not automatic. Abandoning an incompetent ward, combined with a grave disciplinary history, outweighed cooperation and good character. Justice Lundberg Stratton considered consecutive time too severe because the misconduct occurred in the same period as the earlier misconduct.

The casebook uses the case as an example of a status-based duty that does not disappear upon delegation; the court's own reasoning concerned professional obligations and did not hold that every delegation of tasks is an offense.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-101.rule: Accepting an assignment of rights under a contract is analytically distinct from undertaking the assignor's existing duties under it, such as its unpaid debts to the other party.

sections.Parties: The claimant was a firm engaged by Walsh, a construction contractor, for structural steel and other work; the casebook calls it a subcontractor while noting that it apparently was a sub-subcontractor. It sought payment from Presbyterian Hospital, which had engaged Walsh for construction work and had taken an assignment of Walsh's contract with Metropolitan Steel.
sections.Procedural History: The casebook reports that the complaint was dismissed. The brief is limited to the casebook's account: the complete judicial opinion was not recovered, and the judgment, its scope, the procedural posture and any opportunity to amend have not been verified.
sections.Material Facts: A hospital engaged Walsh for construction work, and Walsh in turn engaged a firm for structural steel and other work. After Walsh defaulted, the hospital terminated the main construction agreement. The steel claimant alleged that it had performed work before termination and had not been paid. It sought payment from the hospital on the basis of a document assigning Walsh's contract with Metropolitan Steel to Presbyterian Hospital. The casebook says the court treated the issue on simplified facts, and it does not reproduce the full assignment.
sections.Issue: Did the hospital's acceptance of an assignment of the contractor's subcontract make the hospital responsible for the contractor's existing duty to pay for work already performed?
sections.Holding: A federal district court in New York, in 1989, dismissed the complaint, according to the casebook. The casebook does not reproduce the court's complete explanation, so the precise basis for the dismissal is not given.
sections.Reasoning:
The casebook does not reproduce the court's reasoning. The claimant's argument linked the hospital's acceptance of the assignment to responsibility for Walsh's existing payment duty, but receiving rights under a subcontract and undertaking the assignor's debts are analytically different steps.

The casebook editors use the case to introduce the rules on assignment and delegation. They say UCC section 2-210 did not govern the case, and they use that provision as an analogy for sales transactions assigned in general terms, comparing Restatement section 328's treatment of delegation and the recipient's undertaking. In the editors' framing, the question is whether general assignment language, its acceptance and the surrounding circumstances establish an undertaking to perform duties, including the particular unpaid obligations asserted. This is the casebook's comparison, not a finding that the court applied Article 2.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-102.rule: A sale of a contracting corporation's stock is not an assignment of the corporation's contract or a delegation of its duties where the corporation continues to exist and perform as a separate entity.

sections.Parties: Baxter Healthcare Corporation, a distributor of health-care products, was the plaintiff and appellant. O.R. Concepts, which manufactured and sold such products, was the defendant and appellee. Baxter sought a declaration that O.R. had breached their supply agreement, violated UCC section 2-210 and breached the implied covenant of good faith when O.R.'s shareholders sold its stock to a Baxter competitor. O.R. sought dismissal.
sections.Procedural History: Baxter filed a declaratory action on May 10, 1994, the day it terminated the agreement. The district court dismissed its claims for breach of contract, violation of UCC section 2-210 and breach of the implied covenant of good faith under Rule 12(b)(6). Baxter appealed. The Seventh Circuit reviewed de novo, accepting the pleaded facts and examining the sixteen-page agreement attached to the pleading. On November 2, 1995, it affirmed the dismissal, with costs against Baxter. Rehearing and rehearing en banc were denied on November 28.
sections.Material Facts:
In January 1992 Baxter agreed to buy at least $3 million of Thermadrape, a heat-retention surgical drape, from O.R. over twenty-seven months. Baxter knew O.R. already sold Thermadrape through other independent distributors. The agreement granted no exclusive rights to existing Thermadrape products and did not bar O.R. from competing with Baxter; a separate provision gave Baxter a right of first refusal for new Thermadrape products. O.R. had to obtain Baxter's prior written consent before transferring or assigning interests in the agreement. The agreement declared itself the entire agreement and chose Illinois law.

In November 1992 O.R.'s president and majority shareholder, Jim Elder, told Baxter that he and other shareholders were selling ninety-five percent of O.R.'s stock to Baxter's competitor, Vital Signs. Elder later advised that Vital Signs' 120-person sales force would sell Thermadrape alongside Baxter. O.R. remained a distinct, independent, functioning corporation and kept making and selling its products. Baxter's letter of June 18, 1993, claimed the stock sale was a prohibited assignment; its letter of May 10, 1994, terminated the agreement, refusing to buy the remaining $1 million of product.
sections.Issue: Did the sale of the supplier's stock to the buyer's competitor breach the agreement's clause requiring consent to any transfer or assignment of interests, breach an implied exclusivity or noncompetition term, amount to a prohibited assignment or delegation under UCC section 2-210, or breach the implied covenant of good faith?
sections.Holding: The Seventh Circuit, in 1995, in an opinion by Judge Cummings for a panel with Judges Manion and Kanne and no separate writing, held that it did none of these. Under Illinois law the anti-assignment clause did not prohibit shareholders from selling their stock, and because O.R. kept its separate identity its contractual interests and obligations remained its own. No exclusivity term could be supplied by interpretation, there was no assignment or delegation to trigger section 2-210, and good faith could not create unbargained duties. The holding concerns this stock sale and this nonexclusive agreement.
sections.Reasoning:
Changing O.R.'s owners did not transfer its contract interests to Vital Signs, and Baxter's own choice to sue O.R. rather than the shareholders reinforced the distinction between corporation and owners. Rural Electric concerned a merger and a specific statute. Sally Beauty involved an exclusive distributorship and a merger in which the contracting distributor lost its independent identity; here there was a stock sale, O.R. continued to exist and perform, and distribution of existing products was nonexclusive.

Baxter conceded there was no express exclusivity or noncompetition term for existing products but claimed ambiguity. Contextual evidence could not manufacture a conflict apart from the contract; there had to be ambiguous language or an omission genuinely calling for an implied term. The new-product right showed the parties knew how to distinguish the two categories. Favorable pricing, sales literature, samples and reports did not require exclusivity, and the contract worked as written. Sophisticated parties with counsel could have written broader exclusivity; the court distinguished Wood v. Duff-Gordon. The integration clause excluded the alleged negotiations about eventual exclusivity.

Under section 2-210 the predicate assignment or delegation was absent, since the same corporation remained the supplier on the agreed terms. The covenant of good faith guided interpretation of agreed terms rather than creating new duties, and other distributors' participation was known when the parties contracted.

The casebook contrasts the case with Sally Beauty.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-103.rule: Under the Michigan wine-distribution statute, a supplier may not withhold consent to a distributor's business transfer where the proposed transferee meets the supplier's material and reasonable qualifications and standards, and whether it does can be a question of fact.

sections.Parties: The plaintiff was Scher Enterprises, formerly Viviano Wine Importers, which had distributed several of the defendant's wine brands in Michigan. The defendant was Bronco Wine Company, a California-based supplier. Viviano claimed that Bronco unreasonably refused consent to the transfer of its business to J. Lewis Cooper Company, forcing a reduced-price sale, and that Bronco improperly withheld wine orders placed before the sale. Bronco moved for summary judgment.
sections.Procedural History: Viviano sued on November 2, 2000. Bronco moved for summary judgment. At the hearing the court invited supplemental evidence on the materiality and reasonableness of Bronco's stated qualifications and on Cooper's compliance. On December 11, 2001, District Judge Cohn of the Eastern District of Michigan issued a memorandum and order denying the motion, leaving the dispute for further proceedings. The order did not establish liability, fix damages or enter final judgment, and it did not decide the pending-deliveries claim. This was a trial-level ruling on a motion.
sections.Material Facts:
On July 26, 2000, J. Lewis Cooper Company signed a letter of intent to buy Viviano's business. They executed an asset-purchase agreement on September 29, amended October 5, with closing set for October 17. Viviano and Cooper met Bronco's chief financial officer, Fred Franzia, in California on October 12; Viviano asserted that Bronco then expressed no concerns and said it delivered written notice and an approval request on October 16. Bronco's refusal of October 25 cited insufficient notice and Cooper's distribution of Gallo wines, Bronco's largest competitor. Bronco said its national policy avoided distributors carrying its chief competitors where alternatives existed. At the hearing it also relied on Cooper's distribution of spirits. Bronco chose L & L as its Michigan distributor instead. Viviano alleged that losing the Bronco business forced a reduced-price sale to Cooper for $1.65 million.

Scher identified twenty-eight Bronco distributors that also carried Gallo, and three more learned of through contacts, and twenty-two outside Michigan that handled spirits. Franzia said the thirty-one were all outside Michigan and were only 7.5 percent of 413 national distributors. L & L did not itself distribute Gallo but used nineteen out-state jobbers, ten of whom did.
sections.Issue: Was Bronco entitled to summary judgment on the claim that it unreasonably withheld consent to the transfer of a distributor's business, or was there a genuine factual dispute whether the proposed transferee met Bronco's material and reasonable qualifications and standards under M.C.L. section 436.1305(15)?
sections.Holding: The United States District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan, in 2001, per District Judge Cohn, denied Bronco's motion for summary judgment because the evidence created a genuine factual dispute over whether it unreasonably withheld consent to the distributor's business transfer under the Michigan wine-distribution statute. The court did not find Bronco liable or award damages.
sections.Reasoning:
The statute forbade withholding consent where the proposed transferee met the supplier's material and reasonable qualifications and standards, required written notice, prohibited unreasonable delay and made unapproved transfers null and void. It defined reasonable qualifications by the average standard of the supplier's criteria for wholesalers entering or renewing agreements in the twenty-four months before the proposed transfer.

Bronco gave two apparently legitimate reasons: Cooper distributed competing Gallo wine and distributed spirits. On summary judgment the court could not choose between conflicting evidence, and inferences were drawn against the moving supplier. Bronco did not deny that other distributors carried Gallo; Franzia explained that many came with an acquired brand, resulted from distributor mergers or served markets with no other option. Those distinctions supported Bronco but did not conclusively remove the factual question, particularly since Bronco knew its replacement network also carried Gallo. On spirits, Scher pointed to Michigan's state-controlled system, the limited functions Cooper performed and its separate spirits sales force; Franzia pointed to the leverage concentrated in a few authorized agents. These competing explanations left factual questions about the supposedly national policies, their exceptions, the choice of L & L, and whether Cooper actually failed material and reasonable standards.

The court found Sally Beauty's UCC treatment of a competitor-controlled transferee factually and legally inapplicable to this statutory dispute, and noted a prior Sixth Circuit decision affirming a supplier's victory only after a full bench trial.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-104.rule: Under California Uniform Commercial Code section 9403, an assignee taking for value, in good faith and without notice of claims or defenses may enforce an account debtor's waiver of defenses, despite nondelivery of the goods and a later rescission between the original parties.

sections.Parties: Wells Fargo Bank Minnesota, acting as trustee of a securitized pool, was the assignee of an equipment lease and personal guaranty. It sued for breach of the lease and for declarations concerning the lease and guaranty, and was the respondent on appeal. B.C.B.U., which operated a Utah nursing home and in-home care service, was the lessee, and its president, Dee R. Bangerter, signed the guaranty; they asserted cancellation, failure of consideration and other defenses. Crocker Capital was the original lessor and assignor.
sections.Procedural History: Wells Fargo sued in January 2003. B.C.B.U. later dismissed its cross-complaint against Crocker. The case was tried on stipulated facts and declarations. The trial judge held the waiver of defenses enforceable under California Uniform Commercial Code section 9403, awarded $107,656.24 plus interest against the corporate lessee, and declared the president's guaranty enforceable. The Fourth District Court of Appeal, Division Three, filed its opinion on September 27, 2006. An October 27 modification added a footnote addressing a late argument about the statute's effective date, denied rehearing, and left the judgment unchanged. The judgment was affirmed, with appellate costs to Wells Fargo.
sections.Material Facts:
In October 2000 B.C.B.U. began negotiating with Crocker Capital to finance computer equipment. Crocker told Bangerter that signing documents before completion was customary and that it would hold them in escrow pending agreement. On November 22 Bangerter signed an undated lease, an equipment-acceptance certificate, Schedule A and a personal guaranty. The lease permitted assignment and waived, as against an assignee, defenses, counterclaims and setoffs the lessee might have against the lessor. The certificate stated that the equipment had been received and accepted unconditionally, although a warning beside the signature told the signer to wait until actual receipt and satisfaction.

On December 4 Crocker dated the documents without B.C.B.U.'s permission and assigned the lease and guaranty to a third party for approximately $99,000. The lease entered a securitized pool. Wells Fargo reviewed the pool on December 8, found nothing amiss, and received assignment on December 11. B.C.B.U. and Crocker never reached their deal; on January 30, 2001 they rescinded the lease and Crocker returned the first and last months' payments. No equipment was ever delivered or accepted. B.C.B.U. said it did not learn of the assignment until January 2003.
sections.Issue: Could a qualified assignee enforce the lease's contractual waiver of defenses despite nondelivery of the equipment and the original parties' later rescission? Related questions were whether section 10407, which makes finance-lease promises irrevocable upon acceptance of the goods, barred enforcement absent actual acceptance, and whether sections 9405 or 9406 gave effect to the rescission.
sections.Holding: The California Court of Appeal, Fourth District, Division Three, in 2006, in an opinion by Acting Presiding Justice Bedsworth in which Justices O'Leary and Ikola concurred, held that section 9403 protected Wells Fargo. The lease's waiver fell within the provision and Wells Fargo met all four conditions: it took for value, in good faith, without notice of a property or possessory claim, and without notice of the specified defenses or recoupment claims. Section 10407 did not erase the protections created by assignment to a qualified purchaser. The rescission was not a modification or substitution protected by section 9405, and section 9406 allows discharge by payment to the assignor, not by cancellation. The court expressly declined to decide a hypothetical forgery case.
sections.Reasoning:
The official comments to section 9403 contemplate enforcement by a qualified assignee even when other law would prevent the assignor from enforcing the underlying undertaking. The court declined to resolve the dispute by labeling one statute more specific; the transaction was an assignment of an account, and an account may be a payment right not yet earned by performance. Section 9403 places a qualifying assignee in a position analogous to a holder in due course; it does not make the lease a negotiable instrument.

The court allocated the loss to the party who could have kept misleading documents out of commerce. B.C.B.U. could have refused to sign an acceptance certificate contrary to the facts and its express warning; Wells Fargo could not discover that the apparently completed transaction was unfinished. Schedule A's not being physically attached was neither unusual nor notice of a defense. Failure of consideration was not a defense good against a protected holder, and asserted lack of mutual assent and material alteration supplied no available defense here; the court declined to decide a hypothetical forgery case, because Bangerter had knowingly signed. Calling an altered contract void did not make it illegal.

Section 9405 gives the assignee rights under a good-faith modified or substituted contract, but cancellation leaves no replacement rights. Under section 9406 an account debtor without authenticated notice may discharge its obligation by paying the assignor, not through all dealings with it. The acceptance certificate was properly admitted. The modification footnote noted that former section 9206 supplied the same relevant rule. The casebook's account emphasizes the court's distinction between modification and rescission.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-105.rule: A contract to sell all the cotton a farmer grows on specified acreage is a definite, mutual and enforceable output contract, and a later dramatic rise in the market price does not make it unconscionable.

sections.Parties: R. L. Kimsey Cotton Company, a cotton buyer, sued four farmers in one action; in a second action Kimsey and its own cotton buyer, W. B. Dunavant & Co., sued five farmers. The buyers sought specific performance of the farmers' contracts to sell their crops and an injunction preventing sale elsewhere. The farmers defended on indefiniteness, lack of consideration or mutuality, unconscionability and fraudulent procurement. The buyers were appellants in Cases 29541 and 29543; the farmers cross-appealed in Cases 29542 and 29544.
sections.Procedural History: A restraining order and interlocutory injunction first prevented violation of the contracts while allowing delivery and sale of cotton and requiring bonds to secure any damages pending final determination. After considering pleadings, depositions and affidavits, the trial judge denied the buyers' motions for summary judgment and to strike defenses, and denied the farmers' motions for judgment on the pleadings and dismissal. The judge certified immediate appeals and contemplated a jury trial on fraud. On March 17, 1975 the Georgia Supreme Court reversed the orders in the buyers' appeals, because their summary-judgment motions should have been granted, and dismissed the farmers' cross-appeals without deciding their issues. This was review of certified interlocutory rulings, not of a final decree or damages judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
In March 1973 the farmers contracted to sell their cotton crop to Kimsey. The contracts were materially alike except for names, some prices, farm locations and acreage. The reproduced Ferguson agreement covered all cotton produced during 1973 on approximately 230 acres in Bartow and Polk Counties, with identified farm numbers. It set 30 cents for the stated grades and staples and 24.5 cents for below-grade cotton, specified picking and ginning methods, and required delivery by December 20. The farmer promised normal good farming methods. The agreement declared integration and required written modifications.

The market later rose dramatically. The court read the depositions as showing dissatisfaction only after prices rose in August and September; the farmers first sought upward renegotiation and repudiated when that failed. At the hearing the parties stipulated execution, repudiation, uniqueness of the cotton and the propriety of injunctive relief. The farmers alleged that Kimsey falsely represented the price as fair, claimed other farmers had already signed, and predicted a lower fall price. Kimsey itself had sold most of the contracted cotton months later at prices below the eventual market peak.
sections.Issue: Were the cotton contracts unenforceable for indefiniteness, lack of consideration or mutuality, or unconscionability, or procured by actionable fraud, so that the buyers were not entitled to summary judgment on their claims for specific performance?
sections.Holding: The Georgia Supreme Court in 1975, in an opinion by Justice Jordan in which all justices concurred, held that the contracts were enforceable output contracts under Code section 109A-2-306(1), were not invalid or unenforceable on any asserted ground, and were not induced by actionable fraud. Specific performance was available under section 109A-2-716 because the parties had stipulated that the cotton was unique. The buyers were entitled to summary judgment. The court did not report a final amount of recovery and did not hold that every crop or fungible commodity is unique.
sections.Reasoning:
Quantity was defined by the farmer's crop on specified acreage rather than by an arbitrary later election. Following Harris v. Hine, the description was sufficiently definite as to quantity and subject matter and satisfied the UCC statute of frauds. Each side made a binding promise, the farmer to sell the output and the buyer to buy it, so the buyer's promise supplied consideration and mutuality was present.

On unconscionability, the farmers relied on Campbell Soup v. Wentz, but the objectionable provisions there, which could free the buyer from accepting goods while barring the producer from selling elsewhere, were absent. The court judged the contracts against the cotton trade's commercial background and the circumstances when made. A forward contract can benefit the producer by guaranteeing a market and a price; the March price was fair when agreed, and the later rise did not make the terms unconscionable.

On fraud, the buyers offered uncontradicted evidence, much of it the farmers' own testimony, that 30 cents was satisfactory and above or close to prevailing prices. March futures quotations of 36 to 38 cents did not contradict this because the local crop was valued about 10 cents below futures. Market information was public, and about 75 percent of the area's crop was under contract at similar prices. Predictions about fall prices were conjecture about future events. Under section 81A-156(e) the farmers could not rest on their pleadings. The casebook uses the stipulation of uniqueness to illustrate equitable relief.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-106.rule: A party who agreed to a broad arbitration clause is bound by the arbitrators' determination that a damages clause is enforceable rather than a penalty, unless a public-policy question of sufficient magnitude warrants judicial intrusion.

sections.Parties: Associated General Contractors, New York State Chapter, a multi-employer collective-bargaining association, demanded arbitration of its damages claim against a member, Savin Brothers, and moved to confirm the resulting award. Savin cross-moved to vacate, arguing that enforcing a penalty violated public policy.
sections.Procedural History: The arbitrators found a 58-day violation and awarded $104,400, expressly deeming the liquidated-damages clause reasonable, necessary and not a penalty. Special Term confirmed the award and refused vacatur. The Appellate Division affirmed, although its majority and dissenters agreed that the provision imposed a penalty; they disagreed about enforcement. On June 16, 1975 the New York Court of Appeals affirmed, with costs, the order confirming the award.
sections.Material Facts:
Each member of the association agreed to arbitrate the association's damage claims for alleged violations of membership obligations. The damage formula required an award of at least three times the daily liquidated damages specified in each of the member's heavy and highway construction contracts in the geographic area of the applicable labor contract, for each day of the violation.

Further chronology comes from the dissent. Savin had belonged since 1958 and appointed the association its exclusive bargaining agent. The designation allowed additional damages in the arbitrators' discretion. Withdrawal required notice at least 30 days before negotiations began and could not be given during negotiations. In 1972 Savin was building an arterial highway for the State in Albany. The Teamsters agreement expired March 31 and a strike began the next day, continuing until June 2. During the negotiations Savin independently signed a one-year union agreement on May 5. Associated demanded arbitration on May 15, and Savin announced an immediate resignation on May 17.
sections.Issue: Was the judicial policy against contractual penalties strong enough, in these circumstances, to overturn the arbitrators' determination that the damages clause was enforceable and not a penalty?
sections.Holding: The New York Court of Appeals in 1975, in a per curiam opinion joined by Judges Jones, Wachtler, Fuchsberg and Cooke, with Chief Judge Breitel dissenting joined by Judges Jasen and Gabrielli (4 to 3), held that Savin, having selected arbitration, was bound by the arbitrators' resolution of the legal issue presented to them, including their determination that the damage clause was enforceable. The court found no public-policy question of sufficient magnitude to warrant judicial intrusion. It did not itself recalculate probable loss or find that the association proved $104,400 of actual loss.
sections.Reasoning:
Ordinary questions of law submitted to arbitrators cannot be reopened simply because a court would reach another legal conclusion. The majority acknowledged both the policy favoring peaceful arbitration in collective bargaining and the policy disfavoring penalties. It emphasized the broad arbitration clause, the collective-bargaining context, and the absence of third-person interests transcending the parties' own concerns. The holding thus preserved a role for sufficiently weighty public-policy objections while rejecting this one.

Chief Judge Breitel would have reversed and vacated the award. In his view the provision was plainly a penalty: damage to the association from separate bargaining had no ascertainable relationship to damages Savin might owe owners under its construction contracts, and trebling, with additional damages available, intensified the discrepancy. He accepted that ordinary factual or legal error would not ordinarily invalidate an award, but reasoned that precisely because such errors are insulated from correction, arbitrators cannot be permitted to enforce an agreement violating strong public policy. A penalty is disproportionate by definition. He also discussed the risk of abusive or collusive relationships among trade associations, unions and arbitrators, without finding that these parties had any corrupt arrangement.

The casebook's note asks whether a penalty objection would defeat an arbitration award under a hypothetical lease clause and cites this case for the binding effect of the arbitrators' determination.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-107.rule: An innocent misrepresentation, made without any indication that the speaker knew it was inaccurate, can justify rescission of a transaction it induced.

sections.Parties: Freda Alibri, a property owner who had conveyed her land, sought rescission of the transaction. The defendant was the Detroit Wayne County Stadium Authority.
sections.Procedural History: On July 11, 2000 the Wayne Circuit Court granted partial summary disposition for Alibri and dismissed the remaining claims. The Michigan Supreme Court granted leave to appeal, considered briefs and oral argument, and on July 20, 2004 reversed the Court of Appeals and reinstated the circuit court's order, on a somewhat different basis from the circuit court's. No original filed or reporter scan of this short order was recovered; it was read in reproductions.
sections.Material Facts: The factual narrative comes from the casebook's note rather than the Supreme Court's two-paragraph order. A memorandum of understanding involving Detroit's Downtown Development Authority, Wayne County, and the Detroit Lions and Tigers provided for a downtown stadium project. Negotiations with Alibri began in 1996 because her property was represented as necessary for stadium parking. The authority threatened acquisition through eminent domain if necessary. She conveyed the property in January 1997 for $264,551.94. The stadium project and its parking requirements were later downsized. The order itself identifies the representation that all west-side properties, including Alibri's, were needed for project parking, and the later determination that this was incorrect.
sections.Issue: Could the property transaction be rescinded on the basis of an inaccurate representation of the project's need for Alibri's property, although nothing indicated that the defendant knew the representation was false?
sections.Holding: The Michigan Supreme Court in 2004, in a short order with no individually authored opinion, separate writing or voting division specified, held that innocent misrepresentation justified rescission. It expressly noted the absence of any indication that the defendant knew the representation was inaccurate, so lack of demonstrated knowledge did not defeat this ground. The order reinstated the circuit court's order, including its dismissal of the remaining claims; it specified no monetary award and did not describe the mechanics of reconveyance or repayment.
sections.Reasoning: The order cited United States Fidelity & Guaranty v. Black generally for innocent misrepresentation. It did not rest on proof of deliberate deceit, and it did not say that every later change in a development plan establishes an actionable false representation. The relevant facts were the particular representation of need and its established inaccuracy. The order does not set out a full elements test, detailed reliance findings, a risk-allocation clause or a damages measure. The remedy was rescission on that ground, not tort damages for intentional fraud. The casebook uses the case to illustrate the relationship between mistake and misrepresentation: one party's mistaken factual assertion can induce the other's transaction even without fraudulent knowledge.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-108.rule: A personal-service duty is discharged by operation of law when physical incapacity makes performance impossible or impracticable before it is due, and that excused nonperformance also discharges the other party's duties under the contract.

sections.Parties: Stanley Oneal, a teacher, appealed his discharge by Colton Consolidated School District No. 306 and sought damages including payment for accumulated sick leave. The school district had discharged him with notice of probable cause and refused the leave payment.
sections.Procedural History: Oneal appealed his discharge directly to superior court under the school-employment statute. That court upheld the district, concluding that Oneal breached and that probable cause justified his discharge, and required each side to bear its own fees and costs. On December 8, 1976 the Washington Court of Appeals, Division Three, reversed the approval of the discharge and ordered it expunged from his employment record, but affirmed the denial of accumulated sick-leave benefits. Each side bore its own costs and attorney fees on appeal.
sections.Material Facts:
In April 1974 Oneal signed a contract to teach during the 1974-75 school year beginning August 29. Diabetes had caused his eyesight to deteriorate over several years, and during the summer he realized he could no longer perform his teaching duties. On July 24 he asked to be released after using his 27 and one-half days of accumulated sick leave. He did not report for work at the start of the term, although the district had not accepted his conditional resignation. The district refused his offer on September 20, and he renewed his insistence on sick leave on September 25. On October 3 it discharged him with notice of probable cause and also accepted his resignation while refusing leave payment.

The trial court found actual physical incapacity. A retirement-system official testified that a medical report found Oneal disabled from teaching and eligible for disability benefits. A fellow teacher described his need to hold papers close, write large letters and use a more readable grade record. His wife corroborated his frustration trying to prepare summer lesson plans.
sections.Issue: How did the contractual relationship end: by resignation, by disciplinary discharge, or by operation of law through impossibility? And if the teacher's duty was discharged, was he still entitled to payment for accumulated sick leave?
sections.Holding: The Washington Court of Appeals, Division Three, in 1976, in an opinion by Chief Judge McInturff joined by Judges Green and Munson, held that Oneal's duty to teach was discharged by operation of law through impossibility before performance was due. His failure to teach was therefore not a breach, and the district lacked probable or sufficient cause under the school-employment statute for the discharge entry, which was ordered expunged. But his excused failure to perform also discharged the district's duties, including the sick-leave payment provision, so denial of the leave payment was affirmed. No damages were awarded.
sections.Reasoning:
General contract principles governed how the relationship ended. The court's conception of impossibility included impracticability from extreme and unreasonable difficulty, expense, injury or loss; it was not limited to acts no person could physically accomplish. The trial court's findings, read in light of its memorandum, showed actual physical incapacity rather than an unsupported preference to withdraw, and were substantially supported. The finding of greatly impaired eyesight satisfied the doctrine for this teacher's personal performance.

The superior court's conclusions of breach and probable cause could not survive discharge of the underlying duty: once the law excused the duty, failure to teach breached no enforceable obligation.

Excuse operated on both sides of the exchange. Because the contract was completely discharged before August 29, the employment relationship had ended before the period for which Oneal sought leave. The statute provided that accumulated leave not taken when a person retires or ceases school employment was not compensable, subject to specified retirement-service-credit treatment. The statutory fee award was discretionary, and each side prevailed on one major issue and lost another.

The casebook's Death and Illness note cites the deterioration of a teacher's vision as a basis for discharge of personal-service duties; the full decision adds the reciprocal-payment consequence.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-109.rule: A promise requiring a particular person's services is excused when, without the promisor's fault, existing grounds reasonably indicate that performing would seriously endanger that person's life or health, even if performance remained physically possible and the fear later proves unfounded.

sections.Parties: Wasserman Theatrical Enterprise, Inc., a theatrical promoter, sued Jed Harris for damages for its preparations and expected profit after Harris canceled a contracted performance. Harris, the defendant, pleaded the contract's illness exception and impossibility because the star, Walter Huston, was essential.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court entered judgment for the defendant. On December 26, 1950 the Connecticut Supreme Court of Errors, on the findings as corrected, found no error. The plaintiff received no compensation for its preparations or expected profit.
sections.Material Facts:
On October 30, 1946 Wasserman contracted with Harris for a performance of The Apple of His Eye starring Walter Huston in Worcester on December 16. The agreement made its obligations subject to customs governing uncontrollable circumstances, including illness of a chief artist, and barred compensation or damage claims by either side in that event. Wasserman had produced Worcester performances for about eleven years, expected a profit, incurred preparation expenses, and remained ready and able to perform. Huston was the leading man and had no understudy.

For about two weeks before December 12 Huston had recurring and worsening throat symptoms; his throat tightened two or three times during some performances, and medication gave only temporary relief. He feared he might be unable to finish and wanted a definite diagnosis. His physician friend, Dr. Loyal Davis, heard the symptoms without examining him and advised a thorough examination and treatment in Chicago. On December 12 Harris canceled Worcester on account of Huston's illness, along with the following bookings at Ithaca, Springfield and Rochester. Huston performed all four New Haven shows on December 12 to 14. In Chicago he underwent a minor throat operation and tissue sampling; a report finding no malignancy relieved his concern, and he performed the Chicago engagements beginning December 25.
sections.Issue: Did the actor's apprehension of serious harm to his health justify the producer's cancellation of the performance, where the actor performed immediately before and after the canceled date and probably could have completed the show?
sections.Holding: The Connecticut Supreme Court of Errors in 1950, in an opinion by Chief Justice Brown in which Justices Jennings, Baldwin, Inglis and O'Sullivan concurred, upheld the conclusion that Huston reasonably feared serious harm, especially to his voice, without prompt expert care. That reasonable apprehension justified Harris's cancellation and defeated the promoter's damage claim. The holding did not require a later finding of cancer or proof that performing one more show was literally impossible.
sections.Reasoning:
Unless a contrary intention or assumption of risk appears, a promise requiring a particular person's personal services depends on that person's physical ability to perform at the appointed time, and the principle applies when the promisor arranges for a third person to provide the services. The contract's express illness clause substantially reflected that implied condition.

The court also applied the Restatement's rule on reasonable apprehension of serious harm. A promisor without contributing fault or a contrary undertaking may decline to begin performance when existing grounds reasonably indicate serious danger to life or health. Reasonableness depends on the apparent probability and seriousness of the threatened harm compared with the consequences of nonperformance to the promisee. Actual physical ability to perform is not conclusive, and later discovery that no harm would have occurred does not make the apprehension unreasonable in retrospect. The apprehended harm must still be serious and the apprehension reasonable; ordinary reluctance or unsupported anxiety does not suffice.

Applying this, the court recognized that lozenges probably would have let Huston complete Worcester, but that did not remove the concern that delay in medical attention could seriously damage his health or voice. His forty-five-year theatrical history and sincere desire to fulfill obligations supported the assessment.

The casebook's Death and Illness note uses the decision to show that apprehension of illness can excuse performance and describes the ultimately minor ailment.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-110.rule: A c.i.f. sale that names no route is not frustrated when the customary route closes if a reasonable alternative route remains available at the time for shipment, even though it is longer and more expensive.

sections.Parties: Tsakiroglou & Co. Ltd. were the sellers of Sudanese groundnuts, who shipped no goods and treated the contract as canceled; they were the appellants, asserting an implied route obligation, frustration and the contract's force-majeure exception. Noblee Thorl G.m.b.H. were the buyers, who had obtained an arbitration award of damages.
sections.Procedural History: Under the incorporated London arbitration clause, the arbitrator awarded the buyers £5,625 damages and £79 15s. award costs. The association's appeal board upheld the award and stated a special case, finding that transport via the Cape was possible and that performance by that route was not commercially or fundamentally different. Diplock J. upheld the award and the Court of Appeal affirmed. The House of Lords, deciding on March 28, 1961, unanimously dismissed the sellers' appeal, affirmed the Court of Appeal, directed that the £5,625 deposited in court be paid to the buyers, and required the sellers to pay appellate costs. The proceeding reviewed an existing award on a case stated. The brief was prepared from a retypeset reproduction of the report; no original filed or reporter scan was recovered.
sections.Material Facts:
On October 4, 1956 the sellers agreed to sell approximately 300 tons of Sudanese groundnuts in shell at £50 per 1,000 kilos, including bags, c.i.f. Hamburg, for shipment in November or December. The contract incorporated the Oil Seed Association's form. The case stated found that the parties meant shipment from Port Sudan. The contract did not expressly prescribe passage through Suez. Clause 6 extended shipment for up to two months when specified events or force majeure prevented performance, and canceled the contract if the impediment continued.

The sellers held the goods in Port Sudan warehouses from November 1 and booked space on vessels due to call during the shipment period, but the bookings were canceled on November 4. The Suez Canal had been blocked on November 2 and remained closed until April 1957. A voyage round the Cape of Good Hope remained available during the shipment period; it was approximately 11,137 miles instead of 4,386. Freight, originally about £7 10s. per ton, carried a 25 percent surcharge from November 10 and a 100 percent surcharge from December 13.
sections.Issue: Was the c.i.f. contract subject to an implied term that shipment be via Suez, or frustrated by the canal's closure, or were the sellers excused by the force-majeure clause, where shipment round the Cape remained possible at greater length and cost?
sections.Holding: The House of Lords, deciding in 1961, with speeches by Viscount Simonds and Lords Reid, Radcliffe, Hodson and Guest, unanimously held that the sellers were not excused. No term requiring shipment via Suez was implied; the sellers had to ship by a reasonable route available when performance was called for. The change to the Cape route did not fundamentally alter the bargain, so the contract was not frustrated. Clause 6 did not apply because the closure prevented use of Suez, not shipment. Whether the combined facts frustrated the contract was a legal conclusion for the court, not concluded by the appeal board's general finding.
sections.Reasoning:
Viscount Simonds declined to imply either an exclusive Suez term or an unqualified obligation to use the route customary at formation. Customary performance is judged when performance is called for; if no customary route is then available, a reasonable route must be chosen under the Sale of Goods Act. The contract was a sale on c.i.f. terms with carriage only one component, and no evidence showed that the longer trip would damage the nuts, defeat a seasonal market or miss a material arrival requirement. Higher carriage and insurance expense, or lost profit, did not fundamentally alter the bargain. He rejected Carapanayoti's contrary approach.

Lord Reid compared the parties' rights and obligations after closure with what they would have been had Suez stayed open. The only identified change for the sellers was freight expense, and they did not argue that the increase alone sufficed; he left an astronomical cost increase for another case and expressed no opinion on a shipowner's separate carriage obligation. Lord Radcliffe reasoned that usual practice fills contractual gaps but cannot freeze an unavailable route into the contract, pointing to the flexible shipment window and the absence of a stipulated arrival date. Lord Hodson emphasized reasonable carriage under the Sale of Goods Act and declined to imply Suez exclusivity; Lord Guest judged the carriage obligation at the time of shipment and distinguished inability to use a contemplated route from a radically different obligation.

The casebook's Other Suez Cases note contrasts a seller's c.i.f. obligation with a carrier's possible excuse.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-111.rule: A seller that complies in good faith with informal governmental requirements barring performance establishes commercial impracticability under UCC section 2-615; it need not defy the government before claiming excuse.

sections.Parties: Harriscom Svenska, AB, a Swedish company and the exclusive distributor in Iran for Harris Corp.'s RF Systems division, sued its supplier on contract claims, claimed lost profits, and sought return of a deposit. Harris Corp. (RF Systems) defended on excuse and counterclaimed on an inventory-purchase agreement. Harriscom was the appellant.
sections.Procedural History: Harriscom sued in June 1988 and amended in September; negligence and fraud claims were dismissed that December. A December 1990 summary judgment disposed of the remaining complaint, but the district court revived the deposit claim, Count X, in February 1991 and left RF Systems' counterclaim for trial. The Second Circuit dismissed a first appeal for want of appellate jurisdiction because related claims remained unresolved. Harriscom filed a second action in November 1991. The district court granted summary judgment on Count X in May 1992 and stayed the second action on preclusion grounds in June. RF Systems voluntarily dismissed its counterclaim without prejudice on December 17, and final judgments were entered on December 18, 1992. On August 23, 1993 the Second Circuit affirmed both judgments.
sections.Material Facts:
RF Systems appointed Harriscom its exclusive distributor in Iran in 1983.
