On December 6, 1985 U.S. Customs detained a shipment of model 2301 radio spare parts, worth $663,869, destined for Iran through Sweden. The State Department began a commodity-jurisdiction proceeding to decide whether the radio belonged on the Munitions List. For more than six months RF Systems negotiated with Commerce, State and Defense officials; the problem that emerged was the Iranian destination. In July 1986 RF Systems agreed to withdraw from further Iranian sales, and in September the government determined that the radio was not a Munitions List product.

Only three of eight outstanding Harriscom orders were allowed to proceed. Harriscom, which had guaranteed performance to Iran in the amount of $550,000, lost $270,000 on the five unfilled orders. It argued that the supplier voluntarily sacrificed its contracts, should have supplied substitutes through its Indian licensee, and should have applied under a November 1987 regulation.

Under a related 1984 agreement Harriscom was to buy the entire model 301 inventory for $3 million and had paid a $150,000 deposit expressly characterized as nonrefundable.
sections.Issue: Was the supplier excused from filling the Iranian orders by commercial impracticability or the contracts' force-majeure provisions when it withdrew from Iranian sales under informal government pressure? Further, was the deposit refundable, and was the second action barred by claim preclusion?
sections.Holding: The Second Circuit in 1993, in an opinion by Judge Cardamone for a panel including Judges Lumbard and McLaughlin, held that RF Systems established commercial impracticability under New York UCC section 2-615 because it complied in good faith with informal governmental requirements, and that the express force-majeure provisions independently covered governmental interference beyond the parties' control. The deposit was an unambiguous nonrefundable first installment of the $3 million price. Claim preclusion supported dismissal of the second complaint. The court awarded no new damages.
sections.Reasoning:
Reviewing summary judgment de novo, the court found that describing the withdrawal as voluntary did not overcome overwhelming, uncontradicted evidence that the government would not permit continued sales to Iran and had power to compel compliance. Comment 10 recognizes such good-faith compliance; the seller need not adopt a foolhardy refusal to cooperate before claiming excuse.

Good faith did not automatically create a triable issue. Harriscom produced no evidence of bad faith, and speculation was insufficient. For substantially the same reasons, the covenant of good faith did not require the proposed Indian substitute. The November 1987 regulation did not help because it applied to existing contracts predating October 22, 1987, and performance had been excused in July 1986, with the unfilled orders treated as cancelled.

On the deposit, extrinsic evidence was unnecessary to establish its meaning, and calling the term unreasonable did not create ambiguity or a factual dispute. The challenged affidavits rested on personal knowledge and the supporting documents were admissible business records.

The second action repeated allegations already argued between the same parties and rejected on the merits by summary judgment; their absence from explicit discussion in an earlier district-court opinion did not mean they had escaped adjudication.

The casebook's governmental-acts note isolates the informal-pressure and force-majeure point.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-112.rule: Temporary impossibility suspends a duty unless performance after it ends would impose a substantially greater burden, in which event the discharge is permanent; a specific clause leaving wartime obligations to future agreement controls inconsistent general provisions.

sections.Parties: Gene Autry, an actor in western films, brought a declaratory action against his employer, Republic Productions, Inc., seeking a declaration that he was no longer bound by his prewar acting contracts, relying on frustration and impossibility. Republic relied on contractual suspension or extension provisions to require the remaining films after his military service. Autry was the appellant.
sections.Procedural History: Autry filed the declaratory action on June 27, 1944, while still in the Army. The trial court treated military service as temporary impossibility that suspended performance and declared the contracts still binding, requiring five films under the third option, eight under the fourth and eight under the additional option after discharge; it found that delayed performance would create no substantially greater burden. Its decision came in February 1945 and was entered March 20. On May 23, 1947 the California Supreme Court, sitting in bank, reversed the declaratory judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
The September 22, 1938 agreement covered ten pictures in an initial year, at $6,000 for each of the first two and $10,000 for the remaining eight, with four successive annual options for eight films a year at an annual increase of $1,000 per picture. The first three options were exercised, with the third to expire March 6, 1943.

After Autry was classified 1-A in April 1942, the parties made a May 11 agreement granting an additional annual option at $15,000 per film. Its paragraph 24 provided that if he was required to serve or volunteered for military service, they would agree upon their mutual rights and obligations in view of that service. Autry had sought automatic termination on military entry; Republic rejected that, and the future-agreement provision was their compromise. Autry enlisted on July 26, 1942, with five pictures unmade under the third option, and performed no further services. The remaining options were exercised, producing an ordinary termination date of March 6, 1945.

On March 3, 1944 Republic announced it would extend performance by the duration of military service. Autry gave notice of termination in June. Negotiations for pictures during service and for a replacement postwar contract failed. He was discharged in July 1945.
sections.Issue: After his discharge from military service, was Autry still obliged to make the films remaining under his prewar contracts, or had the contracts' provisions and the burden of delayed performance ended that duty absent a new agreement?
sections.Holding: The California Supreme Court in 1947, in an opinion by Justice Shenk in which Chief Justice Gibson and Justices Carter, Traynor and Schauer concurred, reversed and held that, absent a new agreement, Autry owed no post-discharge services under these contracts. Paragraph 24 controlled the military-service contingency and could not be ignored in favor of automatic postwar continuation. Alternatively, the finding that delayed performance imposed no substantially greater burden lacked support. The court did not decide whether military entry alone, under an unamended 1938 agreement, always permanently discharges employment obligations, and it awarded no damages.
sections.Reasoning:
Frustration and impossibility are related but distinct; frustration concerns destruction of the expected value of an otherwise possible performance, which was not strictly involved here.

The 1938 provisions did not authorize Republic's extension. Paragraph 12 covered events such as war that prevented film production but let Autry terminate after four weeks of unpaid suspension unless Republic paid a specified weekly amount, which it had not done. Paragraph 13 concerned illness or comparable impairment, and paragraph 14 voluntary refusal while capable of serving; wartime enlistment was neither.

The 1942 paragraph specifically governing military service controlled inconsistent general provisions. An agreement to agree cannot support enforcement of undefined future terms, and a court cannot supply them, but paragraph 24 was part of an existing agreement and still affected the allocation of rights. Either the contracts ran without suspension and expired March 6, 1945, or, if service suspended performance, paragraph 24 abrogated the old terms for that contingency and failure to agree on substitutes did not restore them.

Alternatively, Autry's career depended on physical agility, audience following and a limited period of peak performance; service consumed years of it, and wartime economic change reduced the real value of the agreed pay. Republic's annual options protected it, while the actor had no comparable protection. Whether the found facts supported the conclusion of no added burden was a legal question.

The casebook's temporary-impracticability account briefly describes this absence of breach.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-113.rule: As the casebook reports the interim Richmond ruling, a seller facing a steep market rise was not wholly excused from its uranium supply contracts, though the judge was willing to hear argument for limiting the remedy.

sections.Parties: Westinghouse had contracted to provide uranium oxide for utilities' nuclear-power plants and asserted commercial impracticability as an excuse. Several utilities sued it, and those suits were consolidated for trial in Richmond.
sections.Procedural History: The source is the casebook's account of an interim ruling; the actual ruling or hearing transcript for that stage was not recovered, and no report citation, date or court lineup is given. Westinghouse's assertion of excuse led to multiple suits and settlements, and several utility suits were consolidated for trial in Richmond. With court approval, Westinghouse arranged to deliver the uranium available to it, subject to later determination. After nine months of hearings the judge ruled that Westinghouse was not wholly excused. Submissions on damages and an equitable adjustment followed, and ultimately all claims settled on terms relatively favorable to Westinghouse.
sections.Material Facts: According to the casebook's account, the market price of uranium rose from about $6 per pound in 1972 to about $40 in 1976. Late in 1975 Westinghouse wrote seventeen utilities asserting commercial impracticability as an excuse from supplying approximately eighty million promised pounds. It proposed prorating the approximately fifteen million pounds it could command. These figures and the chronology are the textbook's account, not independently verified trial findings.
sections.Issue: Was Westinghouse excused by commercial impracticability from its contracts to supply uranium after the market price rose steeply?
sections.Holding: As the casebook reports it, the judge in the consolidated Richmond litigation ruled after nine months of hearings that Westinghouse was not wholly excused, and was willing to hear argument that judicial limitation of the remedy might be appropriate. This was not a holding that the utilities were entitled to no damages, that any particular amount was awarded, or that the court had rewritten the delivery obligations.
sections.Reasoning: The casebook's passage does not state the judge's exact legal test, causation findings, allocation of price risk, damages calculation or statutory interpretation. The denial of a complete excuse and the willingness to consider a remedy limitation are distinct points, and the later settlement does not establish an appellate affirmance of the interim reasoning. The casebook's footnote points to Florida Power & Light Co. v. Westinghouse Electric Corp., a later Fourth Circuit opinion, and briefly contrasts the parties' expertise in that dispute; that opinion is a distinct litigation stage and does not supply the missing Richmond ruling.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-114.rule: Performance is excused for impossibility or commercial impracticability when an unexpected intervening occurrence, whose nonoccurrence was a basic assumption of the agreement, makes performance impracticable without the promisor's fault and no reasonable alternative exists.

sections.Parties: Florida Power & Light Co., a utility operating two nuclear plants at Turkey Point, sued Westinghouse Electric Corp., its reactor supplier, for specific performance or damages on Westinghouse's contractual promise to remove and dispose of spent nuclear fuel. Westinghouse pleaded impossibility, force majeure, UCC section 2-615, frustration and mutual mistake. The appeal challenged the judgment charging Westinghouse with future permanent-storage costs.
sections.Procedural History: The district court issued three rulings. The first, on June 25, 1981, rejected Westinghouse's defenses but deferred a remedy and asked the parties to seek an equitable resolution. An unreported second opinion concluded that performance had become vitally different from what either party could anticipate, charging Westinghouse with reracking costs and leaving remaining disposal costs with Florida. On Florida's request for rehearing, the third opinion, of November 8, 1984, reaffirmed much of the original rejection of excuse, divided reracking costs, and placed future permanent-storage costs on Westinghouse. On August 12, 1987 the Fourth Circuit reversed the storage-cost portion and affirmed the division of interim reracking costs, which neither party appealed: affirmed in part and reversed in part.
sections.Material Facts:
Extended negotiations produced a 1966 contract covering construction, fixed-price uranium supply for the first ten operating years, and disposal options for spent fuel generated in that period. The two plants reached initial criticality in October 1972 and June 1973. Florida elected Option C, informally in 1970 and formally in 1972: Westinghouse would remove irradiated fuel from the site and dispose of it as it saw fit.

The federal government had promoted nuclear generation and regarded reprocessing as the practical means of disposing of spent fuel; in 1957 the AEC assured utilities it would provide reprocessing when private services were unavailable on reasonable terms. From 1969 Westinghouse negotiated with Allied General Nuclear Services for reprocessing at its proposed Barnwell facility. An agreement was drafted in 1974, but AGNS refused to sign as regulatory changes raised costs and uncertainty. When Florida requested disposal in 1975, Westinghouse said it could not remove the fuel.

Environmental proceedings, licensing obstacles and President Carter's indefinite deferral of commercial reprocessing then removed that disposal route. Neither President Reagan's lifting of the ban nor the Nuclear Waste Policy Act of 1982 supplied a licensed reprocessing facility or off-site repository when performance was required. Florida had been reracking fuel onsite.
sections.Issue: Was Westinghouse excused by impossibility or commercial impracticability from its obligation to remove and dispose of spent fuel after commercial reprocessing became unavailable, so that it could not be charged with the cost of future permanent storage?
sections.Holding: The Fourth Circuit in 1987, in an opinion by Judge Donald Russell joined by Judge Widener and Senior Judge Butzner, held that Westinghouse established impossibility or commercial impracticability excusing its spent-fuel disposal obligation. Florida could not recover from Westinghouse the cost of future federal storage for fuel discharged during the initial ten-year period. The existing allocation of reracking costs was affirmed because neither side challenged it. The court confined its decision to impossibility or commercial impracticability among the defenses pleaded.
sections.Reasoning:
Drawing on its Opera Company decision, the court required an unexpected intervening occurrence, whose nonoccurrence was a basic assumption of the agreement, and resulting impracticability. Because the doctrine is equitable, the absence of an express term specifying reprocessing did not dispose of the defense.

On this record reprocessing was a basic assumption, not a mere expectation. No permanent off-site storage alternative existed when the contract was made, and the negotiations, technical documents and the fuel-cycle price all assumed reprocessing. Even if private reprocessing failed, government assurance was the fallback; its abandonment was the unforeseen contingency. The district court had inconsistently recognized that failure for timing but not for the disposal duty.

Greater diligence would not have made performance possible: converting AGNS to storage required licensing, AGNS was not interested, and the obstacles that defeated governmental and commercial efforts were not avoidable by Westinghouse. Future federal storage was not a reasonable alternative like the Cape route in the Suez cases; it was unavailable when performance was due, and an anticipated reprocessing profit of about $18 to 20 million would become a loss exceeding $80 million. Under Hadley the loss was different in kind from what the parties contemplated. On the equities, Florida's ratepayers had enjoyed major savings and could fairly bear the unforeseen cost.

The casebook's footnote discusses the district finding that Florida's drafting expertise surpassed Westinghouse's nuclear expertise; the opinion called being out-negotiated irrelevant because the contract was freely executed.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-115.rule: A promise that can be performed by alternative methods is not discharged because one becomes impracticable while the other remains practicable; but a clause adjusting minimum purchases when the buyer is unable to receive is triggered by impracticability, not only absolute impossibility.

sections.Parties: International Minerals & Chemical Corp. (IMC), which operated a potash mine and refinery near Carlsbad, New Mexico, was the gas buyer; it sought a declaration that it was excused from paying for gas it did not take. Llano, Inc., the gas seller, counterclaimed for $3,564,617.12 under the contract's minimum-payment terms. IMC was the appellant.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court rejected the buyer's defenses and awarded Llano $3,441,869.79 for untaken gas. It read UCC section 2-615 primarily as a seller's defense, construed the contract clauses to require absolute impossibility or illegality of buying the gas, and treated IMC's early voluntary compliance and regulatory cooperation as failures to exhaust available means of performance. On August 9, 1985 the Tenth Circuit reversed and remanded with directions to enter the appropriate declaratory judgment. It considered only impracticability and paragraphs 15 and 16, and did not decide IMC's penalty, unconscionability or damages-computation arguments.
sections.Material Facts:
Under a 1972 contract running to June 30, 1982, Llano supplied the plant's fuel requirements, subject to a daily minimum of 4,800 million BTUs and an annual minimum of 355 times that figure; if IMC took less it had to pay for the deficiency. Paragraph 15 excused performance prevented by listed force-majeure events, including governmental interference, subject to notice and mitigation. Paragraph 16 required an appropriate adjustment of paragraph 7's minimum purchase requirements when the buyer could not receive gas for reasons beyond reasonable control or when paragraph 15 force majeure occurred.

Regulation 508, promulgated by the New Mexico Environmental Improvement Board in December 1978, limited emissions from IMC's nine gas-fired evaporators, with deadlines of December 31, 1982 and, for replacement technology, December 31, 1984. Scrubbers and a solar process proved infeasible; IMC developed a chemical salting-out process and in March 1981 reported that the old evaporators could be eliminated. The evaporators had used about 60 percent of plant gas, and their shutdown left IMC below its minimum from January 1981 through June 1982. IMC telephoned Llano in May and August 1980 about reduced consumption without explaining the environmental reasons or identifying force majeure. Llano sold the untaken gas elsewhere at a higher price.
sections.Issue: Did the contract's force-majeure clause or its minimum-purchase adjustment clause, read against the background of impracticability and UCC section 2-615, relieve the buyer of paying for gas it did not take after environmental regulation led it to shut down its gas-fired evaporators?
sections.Holding: The Tenth Circuit in 1985, in an opinion by Judge Barrett for a panel with Judges Doyle and McKay, held that paragraph 15 did not excuse the payment obligation, but that paragraph 16 was triggered for January 1, 1981 through June 30, 1982, so IMC should not have to pay for the gas it had not taken during that period. The court fixed no new monetary award and did not resolve the other asserted defenses.
sections.Reasoning:
The starting point was reasonable construction of the contract under New Mexico law, with impracticability and section 2-615 as commercial background; the holding rests on the buyer's contractual protection.

Paragraph 15 failed for two reasons. The telephone notice omitted the reasons for decreased consumption and did not trigger the clause. And even if the regulation prevented taking gas, it did not prevent paying: IMC could take and pay, or pay the minimum bill without taking, so the general clause at most excused taking.

Paragraph 16 explicitly adjusted paragraph 7's minimum requirements, and because the minimum bill depended on them, lowering them lowered the bill. The word 'unable' did not demand scientific impossibility; a buyer could physically receive and vent gas even after its facilities were destroyed, so a literal reading would be commercially absurd. Inability meant impracticability involving extreme or unreasonable difficulty, expense, injury or loss, measured against the parties' reasonable contemplation. The trial findings showed no technically suitable way to comply with Regulation 508 without shutting the evaporators.

The later final deadline did not require IMC to stall compliance. Cooperation with proper regulation deserves encouragement, and governmental policy need not take an explicitly mandatory form to create impracticability, though causing or collusively inducing governmental action to escape a contract would defeat excuse.

The casebook uses the decision in its take-or-pay reprise and notes that relief came through the adjustment clause.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-116.rule: A promisee who furnished consideration may sue in equity to enforce a promise to pay third-party beneficiaries, because his damages remedy at law is inadequate when nonpayment to them causes him no personal pecuniary loss.

sections.Parties: Richard Croker, Jr., the promisee, sued in equity to enforce his late father's alleged oral promise to pay sums to the son's brother Howard and sister Ethel. The defendant and appellant was the administrator of the father's estate; Howard and Ethel, the beneficiaries, were also before the court and defended the recovery.
sections.Procedural History: Special Term gave the son a total recovery of $229,174.58 for the two beneficiaries. The Appellate Division unanimously affirmed, so no factual question remained for the Court of Appeals. The administrator appealed by permission, challenging the promisee's right to maintain the equitable action and the competency of his testimony under Civil Practice Act section 347. On March 29, 1927 the New York Court of Appeals reversed the judgments and granted a new trial, with costs to abide the event.
sections.Material Facts: The son alleged an oral agreement with his father: in exchange for the son's promise to transfer his share of his mother's estate to his brother Howard, the father promised, after notice of its amount, to pay an equal sum to Howard and another equal sum to the son's sister Ethel. The son established that his one-fourth share was $76,191.15 and that he paid it to Howard. Each promised share, with interest, was computed at $114,587.29. The father's promise was established through the plaintiff son's own testimony about their transaction, the father having died.
sections.Issue: May a promisee maintain an action in equity to enforce a promise made for the benefit of third persons? And was the promisee a person interested in the event, and so incompetent under section 347 to testify to his personal transaction with the deceased promisor?
sections.Holding: The New York Court of Appeals in 1927, in an opinion by Judge Pound in which Chief Judge Cardozo and Judges Crane, Andrews, Kellogg and O'Brien concurred, Judge Lehman not voting, held that the promisee could resort to equity to enforce the promise for the beneficiaries. But the son was interested in the event, because he could be charged costs if his action failed, and so could not give the testimony establishing his transaction with his deceased father. The court did not hold that the promise could never be proved or enforced.
sections.Reasoning:
The administrator accepted that Howard and Ethel could potentially enforce a contract made for their benefit but denied that the promisee could enforce it in equity. The court rejected that restriction. The contract was with the son, who had parted with a substantial sum in reliance on his father's undertaking and had a legitimate interest in its fulfillment though payment was to go to others. His damages remedy was inadequate because nonpayment to the beneficiaries caused him no personal pecuniary loss; his own legal injury was merely technical. Equity could bring all interested parties before the court and enforce the promisor's obligation.

On the evidence point, section 347 kept a deceased-person exception to the abolition of witness disqualification, to prevent an interested survivor from establishing a personal transaction when death prevents the other participant from contradicting it. Being a named party or favoring a relative is not necessarily a disqualifying interest; the question is whether the witness could gain or lose by the outcome. The son's possible liability for costs was a sufficient financial interest, and the common-law rule did not treat costs in equity as too discretionary or contingent. The court surveyed, without resolving, whether the beneficiaries derived their interest from, through or under the son.

The casebook quotes the inadequate-remedy point in discussing enforcement by the promisee.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-117.rule: The beneficiary of a life insurance policy has the contractual and statutory relationship with the insurer needed to claim breach of the insurer's duty of good faith.

sections.Parties: Robert Roach, the named beneficiary of a life policy insuring his former wife Nadine, sued Atlas Life Insurance Co. for bad faith in handling the policy proceeds. Atlas, the insurer, obtained summary judgment and argued that its earlier interpleader discharge extinguished all liability. In an earlier action the administratrix of Nadine's estate had claimed the proceeds.
sections.Procedural History: The administratrix sued Atlas in February 1982. Atlas deposited the proceeds in interpleader in April; in June the court discharged Atlas and granted the administratrix summary judgment for the proceeds. Robert appealed the beneficiary determination but not Atlas's dismissal. In February 1984 the Court of Appeals reversed the beneficiary judgment; the administratrix then dismissed her action and no remand adjudication occurred. Robert filed this bad-faith action in July 1986. Atlas obtained summary judgment in November, and the Court of Appeals reversed. On certiorari, the Oklahoma Supreme Court on February 21, 1989 vacated the Court of Appeals' opinion and affirmed summary judgment for Atlas.
sections.Material Facts:
In 1970 Atlas issued a $35,000 life benefit through a University of Oklahoma group policy insuring Nadine Roach and naming her then-husband Robert as beneficiary. They later divorced without changing the beneficiary. Nadine died December 3, 1980. The policy required university notice and a death certificate before payment. Before Atlas received either, it was served with a December 30 court order prohibiting payment. The documents arrived March 10, 1981, with a comment questioning Robert's beneficiary status.

When the administratrix sued, claiming Robert was not the intended beneficiary, Atlas acknowledged the policy, expressed willingness to pay the proper claimant, and pointed to the outstanding prohibition. It then deposited the proceeds in court. While Robert's appeal was pending, the fund was paid to the estate and a requested stay was denied. After the reversal Robert sought redeposit of the proceeds, but his motion was dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.
sections.Issue: May the beneficiary of a life insurance policy sue the insurer for bad faith? Did the insurer's discharge in the interpleader action bar such a claim? And did this record raise a triable issue of bad faith?
sections.Holding: The Oklahoma Supreme Court in 1989, in a majority opinion by Justice Kauger joined by Chief Justice Hargrave and Justices Hodges, Lavender, Doolin, Alma Wilson and Summers, with Vice Chief Justice Opala concurring in the judgment and Justice Simms agreeing with affirmance but dissenting in part, held that a life-policy beneficiary may claim bad faith and that the interpleader discharge did not automatically immunize Atlas against a tort issue not determined there. Atlas nevertheless prevailed because, with a court order prohibiting payment, reasonable people would not disagree that it acted in good faith.
sections.Reasoning:
An insurer's good-faith duty applies across insurance types but not to every person entitled to payment from proceeds; a claimant needs a contractual or statutory relationship supporting the duty. A life-policy beneficiary has both: the policy expressly provides the benefit, and Oklahoma's third-party contract statute allows enforcement before rescission. Recognizing the claim serves the insured's purchase of security for the beneficiary after death.

Robert conceded that Atlas's discharge barred another contract action for the proceeds. The majority applied the interpleader statute then in force, former section 238, which limited discharge to liability respecting the subject of the action; the original proceeding concerned contractual responsibility for the fund, not bad faith. The former cross-claim statute was permissive, so Robert's failure to assert bad faith as a cross-claim did not necessarily bar a later suit.

Removing the preclusion barrier did not establish bad faith. Summary judgment is inappropriate if reasonable people could draw materially different inferences from undisputed facts, but here the outstanding order prevented Atlas from disbursing the proceeds.

Justice Simms concurred in affirmance but called the extension of a bad-faith cause of action to someone not a direct contracting party dicta, and thought the majority undermined the purpose of interpleader. Justice Opala gave no written explanation.

The casebook's third-party bad-faith account quotes the relationship requirement and the life-policy rationale.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-118.rule: An attorney who drafts an estate plan owes a duty of ordinary care to its intended beneficiaries, who may sue for negligent drafting despite lack of privity, on a third-party contract or negligence theory.

sections.Parties: The plaintiffs and appellants were the beneficiaries of an inter vivos trust created by George and his wife Ruby. They sued Livingston, the attorney who prepared the trust, for malpractice, alleging that a drafting error diminished the trust and estate assets they received. Livingston argued that he owed the beneficiaries no legally enforceable duty.
sections.Procedural History: The beneficiaries filed suit in August 1970. They stipulated to dismissal of the first five causes of action after it was determined that the nonmarital half would escape inclusion in Ruby's estate. The sixth through eighth amended causes remained. In November 1974 the trial court entered judgment on the pleadings for Livingston, relying on Ventura County Humane Society v. Holloway and the stipulation. On May 3, 1976 the California Court of Appeal, First District, Division Two, reversed. Rehearing was denied June 2 and a Supreme Court hearing was denied July 1, 1976.
sections.Material Facts:
These are allegations taken as true at the pleading stage. In July 1961 George engaged Livingston to plan his and Ruby's estates so as to minimize federal estate and California inheritance taxes. One-half of George's trust was to be available to Ruby with the marital deduction, and the other half available to her for life without inclusion in her taxable estate. Income would then pass to Barbara and, after her death, the corpus to her children following a $175,000 payment to her husband Howard.

Article IX, however, gave George and, after his death, Ruby the power to alter, revoke or terminate the agreement. The complaint alleged that this general power of appointment defeated the intended treatment of the nonmarital half. George died July 27, 1964. Livingston then represented Ruby and allegedly failed to explain the power's consequences or her ability to disclaim it. Ruby incurred California inheritance taxes on the nonmarital half. On March 21, 1969 she renounced the power and assigned her life estate; she died September 18. The renunciation was later held effective. The complaint alleged inheritance tax at George's death, approximately $50,000 in gift taxes from the remedial steps, and $3,750 in legal fees.
sections.Issue: Did the complaint state a cause of action for malpractice by the intended beneficiaries of an inter vivos trust against the drafting attorney, with whom they were not in privity, for a drafting error that allegedly reduced their shares?
sections.Holding: The California Court of Appeal, First District, Division Two, in 1976, in an opinion by Presiding Justice Taylor in which Justices Kane and Rouse concurred, held that the allegations stated a malpractice cause of action and reversed the judgment on the pleadings. It did not hold that negligence or damages had been proved. The court expressly reserved that trial might show no diminished trust assets, or that George and Ruby had been advised but deliberately preferred the provision for other family reasons.
sections.Reasoning:
Professional negligence requires duty, breach, proximate causation and actual loss. An attorney's undertaking to use ordinary care, skill, judgment and diligence can support rights of intended beneficiaries despite lack of privity, under a third-party contract or negligence theory, though liability is not automatic. The court applied the policy factors of intended effect, foreseeability, certainty of injury, causal connection, moral blame and prevention of future harm, and held that principles developed for wills apply equally to an inter vivos trust.

The tax consequences of a general power in a marital-deduction trust fell within reasonably competent estate practice: the device was familiar and the federal provisions predated the 1961 drafting. The engagement was directly intended to benefit these designated beneficiaries by preserving their inheritance, and the allegedly defective language foreseeably reduced it. Livingston's arguments that the ultimate tax-free passage fulfilled George's intent, and that Ruby rather than the trust bore the charges, could not be resolved against the plaintiffs on the pleadings.

Ventura was different: there the testamentary purpose could be carried out and no intended specific share was alleged. The court required neither litigation-proof documents nor a tax specialist in every estate plan, and noted the absence of alleged moral blame.

The casebook's Wanted: Enforcers note quotes the prevention-of-harm rationale: the estate itself ordinarily loses nothing but fees, so excluding the beneficiaries could leave the principal injury without an enforcer.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-119.rule: According to the 1997 Connecticut Appellate Court, a third party may enforce a contract as an intended beneficiary when the promisee's purpose was to fulfill its own obligation to that party; mere foreseeability is not enough.

sections.Parties: Grigerik, the buyer of a parcel of land, sued engineer Gary Sharpe and his firm in contract and negligence over site-plan, septic-design and soil-testing work they had done for the seller, Edward Lang. Grigerik claimed as a third-party beneficiary of the oral engineering contract between Lang and the defendants. The defendants appealed the jury judgment.
sections.Procedural History: Grigerik served Sharpe in September 1989 and joined the corporation in 1991. A jury found for him on the counts the opinion calls contract and negligence; the report prints the award including interest inconsistently as $44,024 and $44,074. On July 22, 1997 the Connecticut Appellate Court reversed, ordering a new trial on contract and judgment for the defendants on negligence. This brief covers only that intermediate stage; the casebook's introduction to the later 1998 Supreme Court opinion says the Supreme Court disagreed with the first ruling.
sections.Material Facts:
Lang owned undeveloped land in Killingworth within a watershed area. Grigerik offered $9,000 as is, or $16,000 if Lang obtained approval as a building lot, and Lang agreed. A sanitarian told them an engineer needed to prepare a drainage plan. Lang retained Sharpe and his firm for the site plan, septic design and soil testing. Evidence supported a finding that Lang told Sharpe the work was needed for a sale to a buyer, although Sharpe denied it.

The work was completed in October 1985 and the wetlands commission approved the plan. Grigerik bought the property on November 19 for $16,000. A new sanitarian denied his later building-permit application because of soil suitability and doubts about the original testing. Tests in March 1987 required a curtain drain; after it was installed, further tests still showed the land unsuitable, and state-supervised testing in 1989 again concluded minimum standards could not be met.

The trial court allowed recovery if Grigerik was an intended, contemplated or foreseeable beneficiary. The jurors answered no to intended and contemplated, but yes to foreseeable.
sections.Issue: Could the buyer enforce the seller's contract with the engineers as a third-party beneficiary on a finding that he was merely a foreseeable beneficiary, and what intent is required for beneficiary status? Separately, was the negligence claim time-barred?
sections.Holding: The Connecticut Appellate Court in 1997, in an opinion by Judge Shea in which Judges Landau and Heiman concurred, held that foreseeability alone does not make a third party a beneficiary entitled to enforce a contract, but also rejected the defendants' requirement of a shared conscious intent; the focus is the paying promisee's purpose. Because the charge was defective, the jurors' negative answers did not warrant final judgment for the defense, and a new contract trial was required. The negligence claim was barred by former section 52-584, requiring judgment for the defendants.
sections.Reasoning:
Examining the first Restatement's donee, creditor and incidental categories and the second's intended and incidental distinction, the court reasoned that if Lang retained the engineers to fulfill his commitment to convey an approved building lot, the buyer could be a creditor beneficiary under the former and an intended beneficiary under section 302(1)(b), which includes nonmonetary performance of the promisee's obligation.

Earlier Connecticut cases spoke of both parties' intent to create a direct obligation. The court read Stowe v. Smith as changing that mutual-intent requirement in line with Williston, Corbin and the Restatement. The promisor need not consciously intend a beneficiary's later suit, the beneficiary need not be identified when the contract is made, and intent is derived objectively from language, acts and circumstances.

Foreseeability was insufficient because it could describe an incidental beneficiary with no contract right; it is a tort-duty concept. The defective charge may also have influenced the negative answers, since jurors told that any of three categories sufficed could pick the easiest, and it omitted the relevance of Lang's purpose.

On negligence, section 52-584 required suit within two years of discovery and three years of the act; the work ended in October 1985 and suit began in September 1989. Section 52-584a's seven-year period was additional repose protection, not an extension, and an unbuilt septic design was not the contemplated improvement. The court also upheld the admission of expert testimony.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-120.rule: Travelers for whom a group proposed to contract for lodging may assert rights as intended third-party beneficiaries under section 1981, and their common beneficiary position can support class certification under Rule 23(b)(3).

sections.Parties: The plaintiffs were Macedonia Church, a predominantly African-American congregation in South Norwalk, Connecticut, and congregants and affiliates who took part in a church trip. They alleged that the defendants, Lancaster Hotel Limited Partnership, MASSPA Realty Corporation and Fine Hotels Corporation, denied the group lodging at Lancaster Host because of race, in violation of section 1981, and moved for class certification. The defendants opposed certification.
sections.Procedural History: This is the District of Connecticut's ruling of September 30, 2010 on the plaintiffs' renewed motion for class certification; an earlier 2008 standing decision in the same case is a separate stage not covered here. The judge granted certification under Rule 23(b)(3), rejected mandatory limited-fund certification under Rule 23(b)(1)(B), and certified no punitive-damages class. The order determined how the action could proceed; it neither adjudicated racial discrimination nor awarded damages.
sections.Material Facts:
In April 2004 Reverend Dewitt Stevens, his wife Addie, and Merle and assistant pastor Michael Rumble, all African-American, inspected Lancaster Host for a proposed church excursion and discussed approximately forty rooms with sales representative Bonnie Skagen, who said a signed contract was necessary to confirm a reservation. Participants would pay the church, which would pay the hotel. Skagen's April 21 document was characterized by the defendants as promotional information and by the plaintiffs as a written proposal. A revised proposal after a May 10 request said no space was being held because the function remained tentative. On May 17 Rumble requested corrected dates and forty rooms. On June 3 Skagen said forty rooms were unavailable.

Stevens enlisted Judith Addington, a Caucasian church friend. On June 11 she requested thirty rooms for the same weekend for Connecticut church members; Skagen confirmed availability and sent a tentative contract quoting thirty-five rooms, and on June 21 indicated fifteen more were available. The group stayed instead at a Ramada Inn, reporting fewer amenities. The defendants maintained that the hotel had no vacancies and that tentative bookings could exceed capacity. The proposed class contained approximately 112 people.
sections.Issue: Did the proposed class of trip participants denied accommodations satisfy Rule 23(a) and a Rule 23(b) category, given that the church was the proposed contracting party and the individual travelers claimed as intended third-party beneficiaries?
sections.Holding: The District of Connecticut in 2010, per District Judge Alvin W. Thompson, certified under Rule 23(b)(3) a class of Macedonia Church, its members, and members' relatives or friends who participated in the July 9-10, 2004 church trip to Lancaster, Pennsylvania and were denied accommodations at Lancaster Host. The individual travelers were treated as intended third-party beneficiaries sharing a common position. Mandatory limited-fund certification was refused, as was a punitive-damages class. No finding of discrimination, executed contract, individual injury or damages was made.
sections.Reasoning:
The plaintiffs had to establish numerosity, commonality, typicality and adequate representation, plus a Rule 23(b) category, with factual disputes relevant to those requirements resolved by a preponderance.

The church was the proposed contracting party and the travelers intended third-party beneficiaries. Connecticut law asks whether the contracting parties intended the promisor to assume a direct obligation to the beneficiary, and providing accommodations to the group's travelers supplied that obligation. The judge relied on the earlier ruling and on Second Circuit recognition of beneficiary rights under section 1981, and treated Domino's Pizza as having reserved the question. The theory did not require each traveler to negotiate or have contractual capacity; differences in when they signed up or whether they knew the hotel's identity did not alter their common position.

A class of about 112 was numerous and identifiable. All alleged injuries arose from one group denial at one time, supporting commonality and typicality; white or Hispanic friends could pursue discrimination suffered through association. Counsel and the representatives were adequate.

A $5 million insurance policy did not prove a limited fund under Ortiz, since insurance did not show the defendants lacked other assets. Predominance was met because liability concerned one alleged discriminatory event, and individualized damages could be managed by devices such as bifurcation or subclasses. A class action was superior.

The casebook places background from this 2010 decision beneath the caption and analysis of the separate 2008 standing decision.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-121.rule: Dissolution of a partnership by one partner's withdrawal does not by itself terminate the firm's existing service contract where the firm's critical engineers remain available and able to perform.

sections.Parties: P. Clifford Sharp, an engineer and continuing partner in the firm Haskins, Riddle and Sharp, sued the City of North Kansas City for breach of a professional-engineering contract, seeking lost profits. The City, the defendant and appellant, contended that the contract was not properly authorized, that it ended when a partner withdrew, and that it could terminate after the preliminary phase.
sections.Procedural History: After a bench trial, judgment was entered awarding Sharp $131,262 plus interest for the City's breach. On August 8, 1969 the Eighth Circuit affirmed in full, rejecting challenges to municipal authorization, continued performance after a partner's withdrawal, the asserted right to terminate after the preliminary phase, and damages, costs and interest. Rehearing was denied September 10, 1969.
sections.Material Facts:
Riddle and Sharp, continuing under the firm name after Haskins died in 1956, entered a written engineering agreement with the City on November 12, 1957. Preliminary services covered sanitary-sewage studies, a report, bond-election assistance and a federal grant; a second phase required design, bidding and construction supervision, with detailed documents to be prepared when the engineers were so instructed by the City. The preliminary services were performed and paid for, the 1960 bond election succeeded, and the grant was obtained. According to testimony, Ordelheide joined the firm in 1958.

In January 1961 the partners executed an agreement, effective December 31, 1960, for Riddle's withdrawal. It did not mention or assign the City contract, and Riddle remained available to complete outstanding contracts. On January 27 Sharp and Ordelheide told clients the firm would continue the City work. On February 1 the city attorney said dissolution terminated the agreement, and on February 21 the council resolved that it had ended and authorized negotiations with other engineers. Sharp repeatedly offered performance. The trial judge found that the mayor favored another firm that would admit Riddle, at a higher fee. The City ultimately employed Black & Veatch to complete the work.
sections.Issue: Did a partner's withdrawal from the engineering firm entitle the City to treat its contract with the firm as ended? Further, was the contract shown to be properly authorized, could the City end it after the preliminary phase, and were lost-profit damages properly computed?
sections.Holding: The Eighth Circuit in 1969, in an opinion by Judge Blackmun for a panel of Judges Blackmun, Gibson and Heaney, held that the City breached the contract. Assuming without deciding that professional engineering is a personal service, the partner's withdrawal did not terminate the contract where the critical engineers remained available and capable of working collectively. The words 'when so instructed' fixed the timing of design work and gave no power to substitute another engineer once the City proceeded. The damages award was affirmed. The court left open whether the City was required to proceed with the project at all.
sections.Reasoning:
On authorization, Missouri's mandatory requirements for municipal contracts were not dispensed with, but Sharp made a prima facie showing from the contract's facial regularity, the clerk's contemporaneous letter stating approval by mayor and council, pretrial admissions and the City's later resolution recognizing the contract. That shifted to the City the burden of coming forward with evidence, and it offered none.

On the personal-service argument, the trial judge found neither principal reliance on Riddle nor inability of Sharp to perform. Under Missouri's Uniform Partnership Act, dissolution changes the partners' relation but does not terminate the partnership until winding up; existing contracts ordinarily survive. The engineers remained available and able to work collectively, the withdrawal agreement did not assign the contract, Riddle functioned collectively into 1963, and the City itself solicited the continuing firm for a new bid. The holding depended on continued availability and capacity, not an unrestricted right to replace personally selected professionals.

On severability, a single agreement covered a single project; the instruction language protected the City from ordering plans before the bond vote and grant, both of which had occurred.

On damages, lost profits were the agreed measure. Black & Veatch's gross profit was $168,038.69; declining to deduct its $12,535.75 project-manager salary, because Sharp would do that work himself, and the 27 percent expense allocation were not clearly erroneous. A verified-claims statute did not defeat costs or interest.

The casebook's account emphasizes the qualification about continued availability and capacity.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-122.rule: An assignment is effective when the assignor manifests intent to transfer the right and relinquishes control and power of revocation; an obligor with notice who pays the assignor instead is liable to the assignee.

sections.Parties: Dr. Herzog, a doctor and the assignee, sued attorneys Irace and Lowry to enforce their client's assignment to him of settlement proceeds they had received and distributed. The attorneys, who were the appellants, challenged the assignment's validity and argued that honoring it conflicted with their professional duties to their client, Gary Jones.
sections.Procedural History: The case was tried in the District Court on stipulated facts, and that court found a valid assignment enforceable against the attorneys. The attorneys' appeal to the Superior Court was unsuccessful. Because the Superior Court acted as an intermediate appellate court, the Maine Supreme Judicial Court reviewed the District Court's decision directly, for clear error, and on August 6, 1991 affirmed the judgment for Herzog.
sections.Material Facts:
Gary Jones retained Irace and Lowry for a motorcycle personal-injury claim. He later dislocated his shoulder twice in unrelated incidents. Dr. Herzog determined that surgery was needed, but Jones could not pay. In exchange for the surgery, Jones signed a June 14, 1988 letter on the doctor's letterhead requesting direct payment to Herzog from the settlement of the pending claim. It referred to treatment of the shoulder injury and specified no dollar amount. Herzog notified the firm, and a firm employee said the letter was sufficient for payment of the bills at the case's conclusion. The doctor performed the surgery and treated Jones for about a year.

The motorcycle case settled for $20,000 in May 1989. Jones told the attorneys not to pay Herzog, saying he would handle payment himself. The attorneys told the doctor their client had revoked his permission and that they would follow his instruction. They paid Jones $10,027 and distributed the rest to other creditors. Jones's later check to Herzog was dishonored for insufficient funds, and the doctor remained unpaid.
sections.Issue: Did the client's letter 'requesting' payment to the doctor from settlement proceeds effect a valid, irrevocable assignment enforceable against the attorneys holding the fund, and did the attorneys' professional duties to their client permit them to disregard it on his instruction?
sections.Holding: The Maine Supreme Judicial Court in 1991, in an opinion by Justice Brody in which Chief Justice McKusick and Justices Roberts, Wathen, Glassman, Clifford and Collins all concurred, affirmed the finding of a valid assignment enforceable against the attorneys. A later attempted withdrawal of payment permission could not revoke a completed assignment, and honoring the assignment conflicted with neither bar rule the attorneys invoked. The opinion states no new damages amount.
sections.Reasoning:
An assignment manifests the right-holder's intent to transfer the right; to be effective, the assignor must relinquish control and power of revocation. The obligor's acceptance is unnecessary. Once notified, the holder must preserve the assigned fund for the assignee, and paying the assignor or another creditor exposes the holder to direct enforcement. Maine recognized equitable assignments of future litigation proceeds, including partial assignments, as distinct from assignment of the personal-injury cause of action itself.

The attorneys argued that the word 'request' merely authorized payment. Context supported the trial finding instead: the letter reserved no control, the surgery furnished consideration, and the necessary services and reasonable charges were undisputed. The absence of a fixed sum did not make the treatment-related assignment unenforceable here. The attorneys had ample notice and enough settlement funds to satisfy all creditors, including Herzog, and still pay Jones.

The then-applicable bar rules required prompt delivery of funds the client was entitled to receive and generally barred an attorney from placing a third-party lien on a client's file. After the transfer Jones was no longer entitled to the assigned portion, and he, not the lawyers, had placed the encumbrance on the funds. The record showed no contractual obligation requiring the lawyers to honor his contrary instruction.

The casebook presents the actual letter in its Means of Assignment discussion and questions its less customary wording.

CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-001.rule: A preliminary injunction requires both a likelihood of success and likely immediate, irreparable injury; ordinary unrecoverable compliance costs and speculative employee departures are not irreparable harm.

sections.Parties: ATS Tree Services, LLC, a tree-care business in Bucks County, Pennsylvania with twelve employees that required employee noncompete agreements, sued the Federal Trade Commission to challenge the FTC's rule prohibiting most employment noncompetes. ATS moved for a stay of the rule's effective date and a preliminary injunction.
sections.Procedural History: The FTC adopted the rule on April 23, 2024, to take effect September 4. ATS sued two days later, asserting lack of substantive rulemaking authority, excess of any such authority, arbitrary and capricious treatment of existing agreements, and unconstitutional delegation. Its May 14 motion for a stay and preliminary injunction excluded the arbitrary-and-capricious count. The July 10 hearing was oral argument on a stipulated written record, and the court later denied a motion to supplement the record. On July 23, 2024 the Eastern District of Pennsylvania denied the motion. This was an interim ruling, not a final judgment on the complaint.
sections.Material Facts:
ATS asserted that its noncompetes protected its investment in specialized training. It described a one-year restriction on doing the same work for nearby direct competitors, but did not submit the actual contract or noncompete language, and the court declined to decide whether the restrictions were enforceable under Pennsylvania law.

The rule would have barred new noncompetes, made existing agreements unenforceable except for qualifying senior executives, and required covered employers to notify affected current and former workers. ATS claimed unrecoverable compliance costs: notifying its twelve employees, changing contracts and business plans, and revising training practices. It conceded that the estimated one-time notice expense of $27.78 was de minimis; the cited contract-revision estimate was up to $1,211.58. ATS also feared that employees freed from the covenants would immediately join competitors, prompting it to scale back training, but identified no employee who had left, planned to leave or was likely to leave because of the rule.
sections.Issue: Did ATS show likely immediate, irreparable injury and a likelihood of success on its claims that the FTC lacks authority to issue substantive unfair-methods-of-competition rules, exceeded that authority, or acted under an unconstitutional delegation, so as to justify staying the noncompete rule?
sections.Holding: The Eastern District of Pennsylvania in 2024, per Judge Kelley B. Hodge, denied ATS's motion for a stay of the effective date and a preliminary injunction. ATS failed to show irreparable harm, which alone was enough to deny relief, and also failed to show the requisite likelihood of success on the claims in its motion. Because both threshold factors failed, the court did not analyze the balance of equities or the public interest. It did not adjudicate the omitted arbitrary-and-capricious claim.
sections.Reasoning:
On irreparable harm, neither speculative risk nor loss remediable by damages suffices, and a constitutional label does not establish it. Applying the Third Circuit's A.O. Smith decision, the court held that ordinary mandated business expenses are not irreparable merely because they cannot be recovered from the government; ATS's estimate was under $1,250. The feared loss of training investment rested on contingencies, and loss of contractual rights did not by itself show immediate injury. Tailored nondisclosure agreements offered another way to protect confidential information.

On the merits, the court interpreted the FTC Act independently, acknowledging Loper Bright. Section 5 directs the FTC to prevent unfair methods of competition and section 6(g) authorizes rules carrying out the subchapter; read together they permit substantive as well as procedural competition rules, and adjudication is not the exclusive means of enforcement. The preventive mandate, National Petroleum Refiners, and the 1975 amendments, which preserved any authority for unfair-methods rules, supported that reading.

The court rejected, for purposes of interim relief, the arguments that noncompetes require rule-of-reason treatment, that the field belongs to the states, and that the major questions doctrine applied, since competition regulation is within the FTC's core mission. The mandate to prevent unfair competition supplied an intelligible principle.

The assigned Federal Register account identifies this denial alongside the Properties of the Villages and Ryan decisions and reports that the FTC voted in September 2025 to accede to the rule's vacatur, with the regulatory provisions removed in a February 2026 notice.

CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-002.rule: Under the major questions doctrine, an agency's extraordinary assertion of economic and political power needs clear congressional authorization, which the general rulemaking language of FTC Act sections 5 and 6(g) likely did not supply for a near-total noncompete ban.

sections.Parties: Properties of the Villages, a real-estate broker in The Villages whose agents were subject to noncompete clauses, sued the Federal Trade Commission to challenge the FTC's 2024 Non-Compete Clause Rule. The broker, as plaintiff, sought a preliminary injunction and a stay before the rule took effect. The FTC, as defendant, opposed interim relief.
sections.Procedural History:
The broker filed suit on June 21 in the federal district court for the Middle District of Florida and moved for a preliminary injunction and stay on July 2. Its four counts asserted no substantive rulemaking authority over unfair competition, an excessive exercise of any such authority, impermissible retroactivity, and a Commerce Clause violation; the complaint did not allege arbitrary and capricious rulemaking. After briefing and amici submissions, Judge Timothy J. Corrigan announced his reasons from the bench, and a written order of August 15, 2024 incorporated that ruling and attached the transcript. The written order refers to an August 13 hearing while the transcript gives August 14.

The court granted the motion only in part: the FTC and its agents were enjoined from implementing or enforcing the rule against Properties of the Villages until further order, with no bond, and a general stay or nationwide injunction was refused. The assigned Federal Register account separately reports that in September 2025 the FTC decided to dismiss its Properties and Ryan appeals and accede to the rule's vacatur, followed by removal of the regulation in February 2026.
sections.Material Facts:
The FTC's 2024 Non-Compete Clause Rule would have prohibited nearly all existing and future employment noncompetes and was scheduled to take effect on September 4. The broker's agents were subject to noncompete clauses, so the broker was subject to the rule.

By the FTC's own estimates, approximately thirty million workers, about one fifth of the workforce, had affected noncompetes, and anticipated increased wages alone ranged from $400 billion to $488 billion over ten years, with aggregate compliance costs and other large financial effects besides. Noncompetes had long been governed by common-law contract and state legislation; states had adopted varying restrictions, including outright bans in some, while attempts at federal legislation had not produced comparable regulation. The FTC had not previously attempted competition rulemaking of this magnitude, and its recent noncompete consent decrees were announced immediately before the proposed rule.

Compliance would require the broker to review contracts, decide how to revise agreements, and adjust business arrangements.
sections.Issue: Whether the broker clearly established the requirements for a preliminary injunction against the Non-Compete Clause Rule, and in particular whether it was substantially likely to succeed in showing that the FTC lacked any substantive competition-rulemaking power or, if it had some, that this rule exceeded it because it presented a major question lacking clear congressional authorization.
sections.Holding: The federal district court for the Middle District of Florida, in 2024, Judge Timothy J. Corrigan deciding alone, held that the broker had shown a substantial likelihood of success only on Count II, the excess-of-authority claim: the rule likely presented a major question, and sections 5 and 6(g) of the FTC Act did not clearly authorize it. The broker had not shown likely success on its contention that the FTC lacked any substantive competition-rulemaking power, or on its standalone interstate-commerce, separation-of-powers, nondelegation and retroactivity theories. Irreparable harm and the merged equities and public interest also favored relief, so the FTC was enjoined from enforcing the rule against this plaintiff only. These were preliminary assessments, not a final merits judgment, and the rule was not set aside for everyone.
sections.Reasoning:
The broker had to clearly establish a substantial likelihood of success, imminent irreparable injury, a favorable balance of harms and consistency with the public interest; with the government opposing, the last two merged. Applying independent statutory judgment under Loper Bright, the court first found that sections 5 and 6(g), read together, coupled the directive to prevent unfair methods of competition with rulemaking authority. The broker's points about section 6(g)'s placement among ministerial powers, the lack of penalty provisions and fifty years without comparable rulemaking had some force but did not show likely success; nothing limited section 6 to procedural rules, the 1975 and 1980 amendments pointed the other way, and National Petroleum Refiners and JS&A had upheld substantive authority.

The decisive distinction was between some rulemaking authority and authority for this rule. Major questions decisions require clear congressional authorization for extraordinary assertions of economic and political power. The rule's economic scale, its displacement of a politically contested field long governed by common-law contracts and state legislation, its breadth and its reach to existing agreements made a major question substantially likely, even though competition is within the FTC's mission. General rulemaking language, in its text, placement, context and history, fell short of clear authorization. The court did not decide the limits of narrower FTC competition rules or the policy merits of noncompetes.

On irreparable harm, the broker had not forfeited the claim by delay, and compliance costs that were more than de minimis and not readily recoverable from the government sufficed under Eleventh Circuit authority. The FTC would not be substantially harmed by nonenforcement against one plaintiff.

The assigned Federal Register account cites the decision for its plaintiff-limited preliminary relief.

CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-003.rule: Section 6(g) of the FTC Act is a housekeeping provision that does not authorize substantive legislative rules on unfair methods of competition, and a categorical nationwide noncompete ban lacking a reasoned explanation is arbitrary and capricious and must be set aside.

sections.Parties: Ryan, LLC, the plaintiff, challenged the FTC's April 2024 Non-Compete Clause Rule under the APA and the Declaratory Judgment Act. The Chamber of Commerce of the United States, Business Roundtable, Texas Association of Business and Longview Chamber of Commerce intervened on the plaintiff's side. The Federal Trade Commission, the defendant, defended the rule and, failing that, asked that any relief be restricted to the parties.
sections.Procedural History:
Ryan sued on April 23 in the federal district court for the Northern District of Texas and amended its complaint on May 1. On July 3, Judge Ada E. Brown granted preliminary protection limited to Ryan and the named intervenors, based on a likely statutory-authority violation, likely arbitrary and capricious action, and irreparable injury. The plaintiffs moved for summary judgment on July 19 and the FTC cross-moved on August 2, putting the rule's validity and the final remedy before the court.

On August 20, 2024 the court granted Ryan's and the intervenors' motions, denied the FTC's cross-motion, held the rule unlawful and set it aside under APA section 706(2) with nationwide effect. The assigned Federal Register account reports that in September 2025 the FTC decided to dismiss its appeal and accede to the vacatur, and that the regulation was removed in a February 2026 notice.
sections.Material Facts:
The FTC's April 2024 Non-Compete Clause Rule treated entering or enforcing most employment noncompetes as an unfair method of competition. It barred new agreements even for qualifying senior executives while allowing their existing agreements to remain enforceable; for other covered workers it also reached existing restrictions. It contained exceptions for bona fide business sales, previously accrued causes of action, and certain good-faith beliefs about inapplicability. It displaced state permission for prohibited agreements while preserving parallel state restrictions and enforcement authority. Its scheduled effective date was September 4, 2024.

The FTC had disclaimed substantive rulemaking for its first forty-eight years, asserted it in 1962, and gained the D.C. Circuit's approval in National Petroleum Refiners. Congress later expressly granted binding rulemaking power for specific subjects and, in the 1975 Magnuson-Moss amendments, for unfair or deceptive acts or practices.

The prohibition was nearly universal and of indefinite duration, broader than the state approaches addressed by the studies on which the FTC relied.
sections.Issue: Whether the FTC had statutory authority under sections 5 and 6(g) of the FTC Act to issue a substantive rule banning most employment noncompetes, whether the rule was arbitrary and capricious under the APA, and whether relief should be limited to the parties or should set the rule aside generally.
sections.Holding: The federal district court for the Northern District of Texas, in 2024, Judge Ada E. Brown, held that the FTC exceeded its statutory authority because section 6(g) did not confer substantive legislative rulemaking of the kind exercised, and independently that the rule was arbitrary and capricious. It granted summary judgment for Ryan and the intervenors, denied the FTC's cross-motion, and set the rule aside under APA section 706(2) with nationwide effect, so that it could not be enforced or take effect on September 4 or thereafter. Having found those two grounds sufficient, the court declined to reach the remaining arguments, so it did not hold the Commission's removal protections or congressional delegations to it invalid.
sections.Reasoning:
Citing Loper Bright's rejection of Chevron deference, the court resolved statutory authority independently. Section 5 created a scheme for preventing unfair competition through administrative proceedings and cease-and-desist orders. Section 6 listed mostly investigative or ministerial powers, and subsection (g) allowed the Commission to classify corporations and make rules carrying out the subchapter. The court accepted that the FTC had some rulemaking authority but distinguished procedural rules from rules imposing binding duties on regulated parties. The claimed authority sat in the seventh of twelve predominantly investigative powers, shared a provision with corporate classification, did not expressly refer to section 5's substantive standards, and carried no penalty, contrary to the historical convention of pairing legislative rulemaking grants with sanctions. It was a housekeeping authorization.

History did not show a grant either. The court acknowledged National Petroleum Refiners but did not adopt it. Section 18's preservation of any competition-rulemaking authority did not itself create such power, and the 1980 amendments did not ratify it; Congress had to delegate the power affirmatively.

Separately, although arbitrary-and-capricious review is deferential, the FTC had to connect its evidence to its chosen policy. The court found no adequately explained bridge from studies of varied state approaches to a categorical nationwide rule, found the record relied on inconsistent and flawed evidence and overlooked benefits of noncompetes, and found that the FTC had not adequately justified rejecting alternatives or its treatment of reliance interests.

On remedy, under the Fifth Circuit authorities the court applied, setting aside agency action had nationwide effect.

The assigned Federal Register account cites the decision for its nationwide consequence, in contrast to the narrower preliminary relief in Properties of the Villages and the denial in ATS.

CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-004.rule: A creditor of an unpaid contractual money obligation may choose payment of the price rather than damages or dissolution, and a court that has rejected every ground for undoing the contract may not substitute damages for the price.

sections.Parties: M. X, the seller of a dental practice, sued the buyer, M. Y, for the agreed price. Before the Cour de cassation the seller brought the principal appeal, seeking confirmation of the trial judgment awarding the price; the buyer brought an incidental appeal disputing the validity of the transfer.
sections.Procedural History: The seller sued for the agreed sum, and the trial judgment awarded the principal amount of 225,000 francs. On September 13, 2000, the Court of Appeal of Pau instead ordered payment of only 20,000 francs. Both parties went to the Cour de cassation, the seller by principal appeal and the buyer by incidental appeal. On July 9, 2003, the First Civil Chamber rejected the buyer's incidental appeal, quashed the Pau judgment only insofar as it had dismissed M. X's claim, and remanded to the Court of Appeal of Agen. It charged M. Y with costs and did not enter its own 225,000-franc award.
sections.Material Facts: By an instrument and amendment dated December 30, 1994 and January 24, 1995, M. X transferred his dental practice to M. Y for 225,000 francs. The buyer did not pay. The Court of Appeal of Pau reasoned that neither party intended to execute the reciprocal commitments and that the seller's compensable loss was limited to a delay in transferring his practice, so it awarded 20,000 francs. That court had nonetheless rejected every cause for undoing the agreement and had acknowledged the seller's demand for confirmation of the price judgment. It had also found that the lease of the premises already permitted assignment to a successor in dental surgery.
sections.Issue: Whether a court that has rejected every ground for undoing a contract may award the unpaid seller damages in place of the agreed price he claims, and, on the buyer's incidental appeal, whether the transfer was invalid for want of the landlord's written agreement to assignment of a lease of mixed professional and residential premises.
sections.Holding: The First Civil Chamber of the Cour de cassation, in 2003, with Lemontey presiding, held that a creditor of an unpaid contractual money obligation could elect payment of the price instead of damages or dissolution of the agreement. Replacing the price with damages refused application of former Civil Code article 1134 and wrongly applied articles 1142 and 1184. The court rejected the buyer's challenge to the transfer's validity. The judgment records no numerical vote or separate opinion.
sections.Reasoning:
On the incidental appeal, the court reasoned that the landlord's written permission could be given in advance, and the lower court had found the lease already permitted assignment to a successor in dental surgery. The absence of a new permission at the transfer therefore did not invalidate it on the theory argued.

On the seller's principal appeal, the court applied former Civil Code articles 1134, 1142 and 1184. An unpaid contractual creditor remained entitled to prefer payment of the price to damages or dissolution. The Court of Appeal had rejected every cause for undoing the agreement and had acknowledged the seller's demand for confirmation of the price judgment, so substituting damages failed to respect its own findings. The lower court's view that the parties did not intend actual reciprocal performance was not enough to deprive the creditor of his chosen remedy. The court did not need to decide the first branch of the seller's ground.

The decisive distinction is between a valid contract still giving rise to the price obligation and one that has been legally undone; the judgment does not establish that every price is payable regardless of termination, validity or the creditor's own obligations.

The assigned reading quotes the creditor-choice principle and cites this decision for it; the student correspondence-course example printed beside the citation is not from this case.

CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-005.rule: As the assigned chapter reports it, a seller who supplies goods that do not conform to the contractual specification may be ordered to perform the sale contract by replacing them.

sections.Parties: Not given in the brief.
sections.Procedural History: The Court of Appeal of Dijon decided the case on 19 September 1989 and, as the assigned comparative-law chapter reports, ordered replacement of the nonconforming equipment. The brief rests only on that short secondary description because the full French judgment has not been recovered; the trial decision, the precise procedural result and any further disposition are not verified.
sections.Material Facts: The assigned chapter says a vendor originally supplied computer equipment that failed to conform to the contractual specification. It does not identify the equipment model, the contractual terms, the defect, the price, or whether replacement equipment was available. No additional damages, rescission, costs or timetable can be verified from it.
sections.Issue: Not given in the brief.
sections.Holding: The Court of Appeal of Dijon, in 1989, as reported by the assigned chapter, ordered performance of the sale contract by requiring the vendor to replace the nonconforming computer equipment. That replacement order is the only result the chapter reports.
sections.Reasoning:
The court's own reasons are not available; the full judgment has not been recovered, and the judicial reasons remain unverified. Without it, the brief cannot say that the Dijon court expressly considered and rejected a mitigation argument, an impossibility defense, a supervision objection or a proportionality test. The 1989 decision is also not an application of the later 2016 Code reforms the chapter discusses.

The chapter's author uses the decision to illustrate specific enforcement of obligations to deliver goods, contrasting enforcement of the promised performance with an award that merely pays for substitute performance; that framing is the author's, not the court's.

CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-006.rule: Under the binding force of agreements, a court that has found an express contractual commitment to construct, and a clause giving that contract priority over other documents, may not rely on subordinate documents to deny performance of the construction obligation.

sections.Parties: The owner of a parcel of land sued Etablissements Léon Cuny, which had contracted with him for a solid-wood chalet, for performance of an obligation to assemble the chalet. The owner brought the appeal to the Cour de cassation after the Court of Appeal rejected his demand.
sections.Procedural History: After an expert investigation, the owner sued for performance of the obligation to assemble. The Nancy Court of Appeal rejected his demand on October 19, 1998. On May 3, 2001, the Third Civil Chamber of the Cour de cassation quashed the Nancy judgment in all its provisions, restored the parties to their prior position, and remanded to the Colmar Court of Appeal. It did not itself order how or when Cuny must assemble the chalet, calculate damages or impose an astreinte.
sections.Material Facts:
On March 23, 1992, the owner entered into a document styled a sale contract with Etablissements Léon Cuny for a particular model of solid-wood chalet. Cuny delivered wooden components.
