The owner maintained that the agreement was an individual-house construction contract requiring Cuny to assemble them.

The Court of Appeal relied on article 1's reference to an attached descriptive specification and on the descriptive and price estimates, which, subject to certain structural and finishing works, described a ready-to-assemble chalet whose components would be delivered to the owner's land. Later correspondence and the expert's report also led it to conclude that the parties intended a kit sale; Cuny had supplied assembly plans and help with administrative arrangements but, in that court's view, had not undertaken assembly.

By adopted reasons, however, the same court had found a contractual commitment to construct a chalet for an identified price under a document corresponding to an individual-house construction agreement. Article 2.2 of that contract specified that its indications and stipulations prevailed over every other contractual document.
sections.Issue: Whether descriptive specifications, estimates, later correspondence and an expert's report could justify denying the owner's demand for construction when the lower court had also recognized an express construction undertaking and a contractual clause giving the contract priority over every other contractual document.
sections.Holding: The Third Civil Chamber of the Cour de cassation, in 2001, with M. Beauvois presiding and Mme Lardet as rapporteur, held that the Court of Appeal violated former Civil Code article 1134 by rejecting the owner's performance demand. Having found a commitment to construct and a priority clause, it could not rely on subordinate documents to defeat the undertaking to construct. No individual vote or separate writing appears.
sections.Reasoning:
The court applied former Civil Code article 1134, the provision governing the binding force of agreements, and rested its analysis on the lower court's own findings. That court had found, by adopted reasons, a contractual commitment to construct a chalet for an identified price under a document corresponding to an individual-house construction agreement, and article 2.2 made the contract's stipulations prevail over every other contractual document. The appellate reasons did not reconcile the kit-sale conclusion with the recognized construction promise and the agreed hierarchy of documents. Having made those findings, the Court of Appeal could not use subordinate documents to defeat the undertaking to construct.

The opinion turns on an express obligation and the priority provision. It does not hold that every delivery of a wooden chalet kit includes an assembly service, and it does not prescribe a rule disregarding all specifications in construction disputes. The result was cassation and remand, not a direct final construction order; further adjudication belongs to the remand court.

The assigned reading cites the judgment as a chalet-construction example supporting specific enforceability of building contracts.

CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-007.rule: Under former Civil Code article 1184, a party whose counterparty has not performed may compel performance when it is possible, so a proven departure from contractual specifications cannot be left uncorrected merely because the building is usable and the term nonessential.

sections.Parties: The homeowners, anonymized as M. and Mme X... Y..., sued their builder, Les Bâtisseurs du Grand Delta, seeking an order that it demolish and reconstruct their house or, alternatively, pay the equivalent cost of those operations. The homeowners appealed to the Cour de cassation after the Court of Appeal rejected their demand.
sections.Procedural History: The homeowners sued for demolition and reconstruction or its cost equivalent. The Court of Appeal of Aix-en-Provence rejected their demand on September 23, 2003. On May 11, 2005, the Third Civil Chamber of the Cour de cassation quashed and annulled that judgment in all its provisions, restored the parties to their prior position, and remanded to the Court of Appeal of Grenoble. It ordered the builder to bear costs and pay the homeowners 2,000 euros under article 700 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It did not itself enter a reconstruction order.
sections.Material Facts: The homeowners entered a single-family-house construction contract with Les Bâtisseurs du Grand Delta. They paid the entire price but refused to sign the acceptance record because the construction level failed to comply with the contract. The Court of Appeal found a 0.33-meter shortfall in the level of construction compared with the contractual specification. It nevertheless reasoned that the nonconformity did not make the house unfit for its destination or use and did not concern essential and determining elements of the agreement. The judgment does not state the total contract price, the estimated rebuilding cost, or how the owners intended to spend a substitute monetary award.
sections.Issue: Whether a court that has found a departure from the contractual specification may refuse the owners' demand for demolition and reconstruction, or its cost, on the grounds that the house remains fit for use and the nonconformity does not concern an essential and determining element of the agreement.
sections.Holding: The Third Civil Chamber of the Cour de cassation, in 2005, with Weber presiding and Paloque reporting, held that the Court of Appeal violated former Civil Code article 1184 by refusing the owners' demand on usability and nonessentiality grounds after finding a 0.33-meter departure from the contract. The judgment records no numerical vote or separate opinion. The result was cassation with remand, not a reconstruction order entered by the Cour de cassation itself.
sections.Reasoning:
The court began from article 1184: a party whose counterparty had not performed its commitment could compel performance when performance was possible. The Court of Appeal had itself found a 0.33-meter shortfall in the construction level, yet it denied the corrective remedy because the house remained usable and the departure was not essential. In doing so it failed to draw the legal consequences of its own finding. The claim concerned promised conformity, not merely whether the resulting structure had some useful value.

The judgment does not conduct a separate proportionality calculation, identify a bad-faith motive or make impossibility findings, and it does not hold that the owners had proved every element of a cost award. Its reasoning rejects the lower court's grounds for denying enforcement within the historical statutory framework and should not be read as an unqualified description of the post-reform law.

The assigned reading cites the decision twice, as a building-contract claim for demolition and reconstruction and as a house built approximately thirteen inches below the agreed height.

CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-008.rule: A judge in urgent proceedings may order continued performance of a contract, backed by a daily coercive penalty, where a cost increase has not made performance materially impossible and the obligation continues through the contractual termination notice period.

sections.Parties: The Chambre de commerce et d'industrie du Jura sued the airline Air Alpes in urgent proceedings for an order restoring a daily flight the airline had dropped from a contracted Dole–Paris service. Air Alpes, having lost before the urgent judge and the Court of Appeal, brought the cassation challenge seeking to undo that order.
sections.Procedural History: The Chamber sued before the juge des référés of the Dole commercial court, which ordered performance backed by an astreinte of 2,000 francs per day of noncompliance. The Besançon Court of Appeal affirmed the urgent order on July 2, 1975. Air Alpes brought a cassation challenge with a single ground in five branches. On May 31, 1976, the Commercial Chamber of the Cour de cassation rejected the pourvoi, so the urgent performance order and its time-limited coercive sanction stood.
sections.Material Facts:
Agreements made in January 1972 committed Air Alpes to operate a Dole–Paris air service for four years, ending April 10, 1976, with at least two daily flights in each direction. On February 17, 1975, invoking economic conditions arising from the fuel crisis, the airline removed one of the two services; it did not abandon the route. The Chamber then invoked the contractual three-month termination notice and sought an urgent order restoring the omitted service. The airline's challenge referred to a termination letter from the Chamber dated April 5, and the adopted reasons treated July 15, 1975 as the effective termination date. The lower court found that rising fuel prices did not make the promised service materially impossible.

The official text is internally inconsistent about who terminated: its opening says the Chamber did, while its final reasoning refers to termination by Air Alpes.
sections.Issue: Whether a judge in urgent proceedings could order the airline to restore the omitted service under a daily astreinte despite its claims that the fuel crisis raised a force-majeure question for the merits court, that urgency was not shown, that termination of the agreement defeated the demand for continued performance, and that the astreinte had no stated time limit.
sections.Holding: The Commercial Chamber of the Cour de cassation, in 1976, with M. Lancien presiding and M. Larere as rapporteur, rejected Air Alpes's pourvoi. The référé judge could order the measure because the claimed force majeure raised no serious contestation, urgency was for the appellate court to assess, and the obligation and the astreinte ran until termination took effect at the end of the notice period. The judgment gives no voting count or separate opinions.
sections.Reasoning:
The court applied article 73 of the decree of September 9, 1971, which in an urgent case let the référé judge order measures facing no serious contestation or justified by the existence of a dispute. The dispute concerned the immediate cessation of part of an existing contractual service. Because the lower court had found that rising fuel prices did not make the promised service materially impossible, it could reject the claimed force majeure and find no serious contestation. That establishes only that this price increase did not satisfy the defense on these findings, not a general rule for hardship claims. The appellate court also had sovereign authority to assess the urgency of ending the situation created by the unilateral reduction.

Termination did not erase obligations during the notice period. Air Alpes had to perform until July 15, 1975, and the astreinte necessarily had the same temporal limit even without an express cap. The lower court had not required a judicial decree before termination. The first two branches were unfounded and the other three lacked a factual basis in the challenged decision.

The court did not order indefinite operation, extend performance to April 1976, or award damages; it preserved a référé measure rather than a merits judgment.

The assigned reading uses the case to illustrate that increased cost and possible supervision do not necessarily prevent specific performance.

CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-009.rule: Under former Civil Code article 1143, a creditor of a contractual obligation may demand destruction of what was done in breach of the commitment, and the absence of demonstrated prejudice does not justify refusing restoration.

sections.Parties: Two condominium associations, for two buildings in a group of buildings, sued SCI du 12, place des Terreaux, the owner of ground-floor lots bordering a passage, seeking restoration of the passage to its earlier state after the SCI altered it to create a shopping gallery. The associations brought the appeal to the Cour de cassation after losing in the Court of Appeal.
sections.Procedural History: The associations sought restoration of the premises to their earlier state. The Court of Appeal of Lyon rejected that demand on June 4, 1992. On January 25, 1995, the Third Civil Chamber of the Cour de cassation quashed and annulled the Lyon judgment in all its provisions, restored the parties to their prior position, and remanded to the Court of Appeal of Dijon. It did not itself specify restoration measures, fix an astreinte or award damages.
sections.Material Facts:
The condominium regulations gave the owners of ground-floor lots bordering a passage an exclusive and particular right to enjoy its ground surface. The passage lay inside a group of buildings, depended on each of them, and was open to public circulation. The enjoyment right was attached directly to the bordering premises and could neither be sold independently of them nor rented to a third party. SCI du 12, place des Terreaux owned the relevant lots and carried out a shopping-gallery project affecting the passage.

The conseils syndicaux of the associations had agreed to endorse both the completed works and breaches of the regulations, but the general assemblies had not given that agreement. The Court of Appeal found that the works had improved the building and that the associations had shown no injury. The report gives no project budget, engineering description or damages amount.
sections.Issue: Whether an exclusive right to enjoy the passage made it a private portion under article 2 of the July 10, 1965 law; whether endorsement by the conseils syndicaux could stand in for the authorization articles 25 and 30 require; and whether improvement of the building and absence of proven injury could defeat a demand to undo work done in breach of the regulations.
sections.Holding: The Third Civil Chamber of the Cour de cassation, in 1995, with Beauvois presiding and Capoulade reporting, quashed the judgment on three grounds. The exclusive enjoyment right did not make the passage a private portion; approval from the conseils syndicaux could not replace the legally required authorization; and under former Civil Code article 1143 the absence of demonstrated prejudice did not support rejecting the restoration claim. The published text contains no numerical vote or separate writing.
sections.Reasoning:
First, article 2 of the 1965 law defines private portions as those reserved for the exclusive use of a particular co-owner. The regulations had created only an exclusive enjoyment right attached to the bordering premises, which could not be sold separately or rented to a third party. Treating that as a private portion violated article 2; a special right to use common property did not take the passage outside the rules for common areas.

Second, articles 25 and 30 required the votes of a majority of all co-owners to permit work, at the interested owners' expense, affecting common areas or the building's external appearance, with the tribunal de grande instance able to authorize qualifying improvements if the general assembly refused. The Court of Appeal said the associations wrongly withheld permission because their councils had agreed to endorse the works, while acknowledging that the general assemblies had not agreed. Relying on a different body's approval violated the statute. This was not a ruling that the improvements could never be approved or judicially authorized.

Third, under former article 1143 a creditor of a contractual obligation could request destruction of what had been done contrary to the commitment. Enforcing the obligation by undoing the work is distinct from compensation measured by an established loss, so neither the lack of injury nor the claimed benefit to the building excused compliance.

The assigned reading cites the decision for enforcement of negative promises, with an illustration of a tenant modifying leased premises; the no-prejudice principle is supported by the judgment, but the lease, tenant and landlord are not its facts.

CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-012.rule: Under former Civil Code article 1184, a party whose counterparty has not performed may compel performance when it is possible, so a court may not refuse conformity with a contractual specification without investigating whether restoring conformity is impossible.

sections.Parties: M. Abou, the owner of a swimming pool, sought useful works and conformity of the pool and its accessories from M. Alessandra. Abou challenged before the Cour de cassation the Court of Appeal's refusal of that request.
sections.Procedural History: The Aix-en-Provence decision of May 13, 1982 rejected the owner's request for conformity. On January 17, 1984, the Third Civil Chamber of the Cour de cassation quashed and annulled that decision within the limits of the first ground of appeal. The brief rests on a partial judicial excerpt that omits material before the first-ground discussion and after the operative cassation language; the remand designation, costs ruling and resolution of the other grounds are not available.
sections.Material Facts: A contractual estimate dated December 26, 1977 specified an access stairway with four steps, each 0.20 metres high. The stairway actually built had three steps instead of the four required by the agreement. The Aix-en-Provence court rejected the owner's request for conformity because he had not proved that the modification made access to the pool more difficult. The contract price, construction chronology, other defects and other claims are not supplied.
sections.Issue: Whether a court may reject an owner's request that a pool stairway be brought into conformity with the contractual specification on the ground that he had not proved the departure made access more difficult, without investigating whether restoring conformity was impossible.
sections.Holding: The Third Civil Chamber of the Cour de cassation, in 1984, held that the lower decision lacked a legal basis because it rejected the request on the access-difficulty rationale without investigating whether restoring conformity was impossible. It quashed the Aix-en-Provence decision within the limits of the first ground. The excerpt does not show that the Cour de cassation itself ordered a construction modification or awarded a sum.
sections.Reasoning:
Invoking former article 1184 of the Civil Code, the court stated that a party whose undertaking had not been performed could compel performance when performance was possible. The lower court had refused conformity because the owner had not shown that three steps rather than four made access to the pool more difficult. The Cour de cassation faulted it for deciding on that rationale without investigating whether restoring conformity was impossible, and held that the omission deprived the decision of a legal basis. The reasoning thus focuses on the proper inquiry into possible performance rather than making reduced usability the prerequisite for enforcing the agreed specification.

The assigned chapter summarizes the case as error in refusing to order modification of a pool built with three rather than the specified four steps despite the absence of impaired access, and uses it as a historical illustration of strong specific enforcement.

CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-013.rule: As the assigned chapter reports it, the minimal nature of the difference between the work promised and the work done is irrelevant to whether the builder can be compelled to correct a departure from contractual specifications.

sections.Parties: The dispute was between a homeowner and a builder over a house; the assigned chapter does not name either of them.
sections.Procedural History: As the assigned chapter reports, a lower decision refused to compel corrective modifications and the Cour de cassation quashed that decision; the chapter attributes this to the Third Civil Chamber on November 17, 1977. The complete judgment has not been recovered and the citation has not been independently confirmed, so the lower court's date, the scope of cassation and any remand designation are unresolved.
sections.Material Facts: The assigned chapter describes a house built slightly out of alignment with the contractually specified dimensions. It does not quantify the discrepancy, reproduce the contract, or identify the corrective modifications sought. The brief stresses that this is a developed illustration with limited facts rather than a complete case report.
sections.Issue: Whether a court may refuse to compel a builder to make corrective modifications to a house built slightly out of alignment with the contractually specified dimensions because the departure is small.
sections.Holding: The Cour de cassation, Third Civil Chamber, in 1977, as reported by the assigned chapter, quashed the lower decision that had refused to compel corrective modifications. Quashing that refusal does not establish that a particular reconstruction order was ultimately entered on remand.
sections.Reasoning:
The court's own reasons are not available because the judgment has not been recovered. The chapter's author says the court treated the minimal nature of the difference between promised and actual work as irrelevant. The Code text the court relied on is unresolved. The chapter's later discussion of an exception and of commentators' views on proportionality, abuse of right and the binding force of contract is editorial material, not part of the 1977 case.

The assigned chapter uses the decision to show the historical strength of enforcement of contractual specifications, even where the defect appeared small.

CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-014.rule: Under the 1993 approach, later reversed, a promisor under a unilateral promise of sale owes only an obligation to act until the option is exercised, so withdrawal before exercise prevents the sale from forming and bars compelled completion.

sections.Parties: The consorts X, beneficiaries of a unilateral promise to sell an immovable property, sued the promisor, Mme Y, to compel completion of the sale. Having lost in the Court of Appeal, the beneficiaries brought the pourvoi; Mme Y resisted compelled sale on the ground that she had withdrawn her promise.
sections.Procedural History: The beneficiaries sued to compel completion of the sale. The Court of Appeal of Paris rejected their demand on November 8, 1990. On December 15, 1993, the Third Civil Chamber of the Cour de cassation rejected their pourvoi. It did not order a transfer, award compensation or remand for a damages determination.
sections.Material Facts: On May 22, 1987, Mme Y gave the consorts X a promise to sell an immovable property, valid until September 1, 1987. On May 26, she notified the beneficiaries that she no longer wished to sell. They exercised the option on June 10, within the stated option period but after the seller's withdrawal, and sued to compel completion. The published judgment gives neither the price nor a detailed description of the property, and does not identify a third-party purchaser or a damages award.
sections.Issue: Whether the beneficiaries' exercise of an option within its agreed period could produce an enforceable sale when the promisor had already withdrawn, which turned on whether the promisor's commitment was an obligation to transfer (obligation de donner), as the beneficiaries argued under former Civil Code articles 1134 and 1589, or only an obligation to act (obligation de faire).
sections.Holding: The Third Civil Chamber of the Cour de cassation, in 1993, with President Beauvois presiding and Cathala reporting, held that until the beneficiaries declared that they would purchase, the promisor's obligation was only an obligation de faire, and that her withdrawal prevented the later exercise of the option from bringing together reciprocal intentions to sell and to buy. The pourvoi was rejected. The judgment gives no numerical vote or separate opinion.
sections.Reasoning:
The court accepted the Court of Appeal's classification of the promisor's commitment before exercise of the option as an obligation to act. It then treated the withdrawal as preventing the later option exercise from producing a meeting of reciprocal intentions to sell and to buy. Timely exercise was therefore insufficient because the withdrawal had come first. Under this approach the promise did not establish an irrevocable consent to the eventual sale sufficient to support compelled completion. The brief reasoning does not discuss consideration, an option fee, impossibility or the adequacy of a monetary remedy.

The brief also records a later change. On June 23, 2021, the same chamber expressly identified the 1993 rule and adopted a different interpretation under the pre-2016 law: a unilateral promise already contains the seller's consent and the essential terms, and unless the parties stipulate otherwise the promisor commits definitively to sell when making it, so withdrawal does not prevent a sale from forming on timely exercise. The 1993 formation rule is therefore historical.

The assigned reading uses the decision to explain the former limitation on specific enforcement of unilateral promises and the reforms removing it, including article 1124; its illustration of a sale to a third party and a beneficiary confined to damages is the reading's general explanation, not a finding in this judgment.

CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-015.rule: A contract price is due only upon performance, even if fixed as a lump sum, so once termination of the contract is recognized the other party recovers damages, absent a penalty clause, rather than the full agreed price.

sections.Parties: Approchim, a customer, had entrusted the carrier Eurocollect with transporting its products and terminated their transport contract after five trips. The Court of Appeal ordered Approchim to pay Eurocollect the full annual contract price less payments already made, and Approchim brought the challenge to the Cour de cassation.
sections.Procedural History: On September 21, 1993, the Court of Appeal of Paris ordered Approchim to pay the principal sum of 892,500 francs, less what it had already paid for the five completed trips. Approchim challenged that judgment on a single ground. On October 22, 1996, the Commercial Chamber of the Cour de cassation quashed and annulled the Paris judgment in all its provisions, restored the parties to their prior position, and referred the matter to the Court of Appeal of Orléans.
sections.Material Facts: By a contract of February 22, 1990, Approchim entrusted Eurocollect with transporting dangerous products. The agreement lasted one year and renewed tacitly. It provided for fifty trips each year at a fixed price of 892,500 francs, although payment was to occur on each trip. After having five trips performed, Approchim terminated the contract on August 17, 1990. The Court of Appeal itself found that Approchim had terminated the agreement, and reasoned that the obligation to pay the agreed price could not be treated as merely an obligation to act giving rise only to damages. The published account does not give the reasons for termination or the costs the carrier saved on the remaining trips.
sections.Issue: Whether, after a customer has terminated a transport contract with a fixed annual price, the carrier may recover the entire agreed price for the unperformed balance, or only damages for the termination.
sections.Holding: The Commercial Chamber of the Cour de cassation, in 1996, with President Bézard presiding and Grimaldi reporting, held that the agreed price was due only upon performance of the contract, even though fixed as a lump sum. Since the Court of Appeal had found that Approchim terminated the agreement, it had, absent a penalty clause, to determine the damages owed to Eurocollect rather than award the full price; its judgment violated former Civil Code article 1184. No numerical vote or separate writing is given.
sections.Reasoning:
The court separated two bases for recovery. A price claim enforces the payment required for contractual performance; damages compensate the consequences of ending the agreement. Fixing the price in advance as a lump sum did not make it automatically payable for the unperformed balance after the termination the lower court had recognized. On that premise, and absent a penalty clause, the Court of Appeal had to assess damages rather than award the contract price as such.

The court did not itself calculate the carrier's loss, find a penalty clause, or decide that the carrier suffered no recoverable loss, and it did not decide that a promisor may generally terminate every fixed-term contract at will. The result was cassation with remand, not a judgment that Approchim owed nothing.

The assigned reading, which mainly explains the creditor's right to seek payment of a monetary obligation rather than termination or damages, cites this decision as a qualification and reports the explanation that the lower court had accepted unilateral termination, even if wrongly; the judgment itself does not say that accepting termination was erroneous.

CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-STUDENT-COURSE.skip: It is an assigned chapter's illustration of an unidentified Cour de cassation ruling on unpaid correspondence-course fees, with no caption, date or citation, and the judgment has not been identified or recovered.

CT-ATLAS-KLAR.rule: A bailee for hire relying on a liability limitation printed on a claim check must show reasonable notice of its terms and the bailor's assent; accepting a ticket issued to identify property does not establish that assent as a matter of law.

sections.Parties: The plaintiffs sued over a lost package of valuable furs; Ellis acted for them in checking it, and Sidney R. Klar later presented the claim check. The defendant, H. & M. Parcel Room, Inc., operated a parcel room on the concourse of the Hudson & Manhattan Railroad's 33rd Street station in New York City. The plaintiffs wanted $1,000, the alleged value of the package. The parcel room, with ordinary negligence conceded, wanted its responsibility reduced to $25 under the terms printed on the check. The plaintiffs were the appellants in the Appellate Division.
sections.Procedural History: The plaintiffs sued in Municipal Court for $1,000. After a trial without a jury they obtained a judgment of $939.50. The Appellate Term reduced the recovery to $25 because it regarded the printed limitation as sufficiently communicated to form a contract. The plaintiffs then appealed by permission to the Appellate Division, First Department. On April 5, 1946, by a vote of three to two, that court reversed the Appellate Term's determination and affirmed the Municipal Court's $939.50 judgment, awarding the plaintiffs costs in both appellate courts. The Court of Appeals later affirmed with costs and without opinion, so it supplied no further written rationale.
sections.Material Facts:
Ellis, acting for the plaintiffs, deposited a brown-paper package containing valuable furs at the parcel room and received claim check 34-971. The cardboard check measured three inches by two and a half inches. Its identifying number appeared prominently in red, and the word CONTRACT also appeared in red near the top. Beneath that word, finer print stated that acceptance bound both parties, that checking cost ten cents per twenty-four hours or fraction, and that no claim exceeding $25 could be made for loss or damage to any piece. The limitation was on the face of the check, not hidden on its reverse.

Ellis testified that he neither read the check nor was asked to read it, and thought it was simply a receipt. No evidence showed any further notice or explanation of the limitation. When Sidney R. Klar presented the check two days later, an employee admitted that the parcel had mistakenly been delivered to someone presenting a differently numbered receipt. Ordinary negligence was conceded.
sections.Issue: Whether a limitation of liability to $25, printed on the face of a parcel-room claim check that the bailor accepted without reading, had become part of the parties' agreement, and in particular whether acceptance of the check established assent to the limitation as a matter of law.
sections.Holding: The New York Appellate Division, First Department, in 1946, in an opinion by Justice Cohn joined by Justices Townley and Glennon, with two justices dissenting, held that printing the limitation on the face of the ticket, followed by its acceptance, did not compel a finding of agreement as a matter of law. Whether acceptance of this check constituted assent was a question for the trial judge, and the finding that no such agreement existed had ample evidentiary support. The Appellate Term erred by treating acceptance as establishing the limitation. The majority did not hold that every unsigned ticket is unenforceable, that failure to read always excuses assent, or that every liability limitation is contrary to public policy.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority accepted that a bailee for hire owes ordinary care and, absent an effective special agreement, answers for the reasonable value of property lost through negligence. It also accepted that parties may contract to reduce that obligation within the limits of law and public policy. To establish the limitation, however, the bailee had to show reasonable notice of its terms and the bailor's assent. A ticket issued as a means of identifying property does not necessarily communicate that it also changes substantive rights. The record contained no conspicuous signs, placards, other notice of special terms, or evidence that the plaintiffs were given an opportunity to assent or dissent. Relying on Madan and Healy, the majority said an omission to read a parcel receipt is not invariably negligence or assent. Healy involved fine print on the reverse of a check, but its reasoning applied: the customer could reasonably regard the paper as identification rather than an agreement limiting recovery.

Justice Dore, joined by Presiding Justice Martin, dissented and would have affirmed the $25 recovery. He viewed the conspicuous word CONTRACT, the brief text beneath it, the time available to read and the ten-cent charge as adequate notice of a reasonable limitation, and treated the failure to read as inexcusable. He also questioned the credibility of the account of how the furs came to the parcel room.

The assigned reading is a casebook account rather than a reproduced opinion. Its comparison with Restatement section 211(3) is the casebook's editorial point, not a rule announced by this court.

CT-ATLAS-TOLOSA.rule: Under Texas law, a loan agreement over $50,000, including a financial institution's promise to delay repayment or make a financial accommodation, must be in a signed writing, and promissory estoppel avoids that requirement only if the promisor promised to sign a complying written document.

sections.Parties: The plaintiffs were borrowers who had obtained a loan to buy property in Sugar Land, Texas, and who sued after a completed foreclosure sale in order to delay eviction. The defendant was HSBC Bank USA, N.A. The plaintiffs wanted an injunction and relief on several claims, including promissory estoppel based on an alleged promise not to foreclose while a loan modification was under review. The defendant wanted the suit dismissed, arguing among other things that the statute of frauds barred all the claims.
sections.Procedural History:
In September 2011 the plaintiffs filed suit in state court. They said the state court issued a temporary restraining order before removal. The defendant removed the suit to federal court on diversity grounds and moved to dismiss. The federal district court, Judge Nancy F. Atlas, granted the motion to dismiss and dismissed the case; the reproduced order does not state whether the dismissal was with or without prejudice.

This account covers only the abridged text printed in the casebook. The excerpt jumps from section I to section III.B, and the complete opinion has not been recovered, so the court's other grounds for dismissal and its treatment of the restraining-order argument cannot be given.
sections.Material Facts:
The plaintiffs obtained a $276,000 loan to buy property in Sugar Land, Texas. A promissory note evidenced the debt and a deed of trust secured it. They defaulted on their payment obligations, and the property was sold at a foreclosure sale in April 2011. In September 2011 they sued to delay eviction following the completed foreclosure; the action followed the sale and did not prevent it.

Besides an injunction, they sought relief for fraud, wrongful foreclosure due to fraud, slander of title, promissory estoppel, unreasonable collection, and an accounting. Their relevant allegation was that the defendant had promised not to foreclose while reviewing a loan modification. That promise is an allegation recorded by the court, not a finding that the bank made it. The excerpt does not give the promise's wording, speaker or date, or a detailed account of reliance. The plaintiffs did not allege that the defendant promised to sign a written agreement embodying the postponement.
sections.Issue: Whether an alleged oral agreement to delay foreclosure on a $276,000 loan could be enforced notwithstanding the writing requirement of section 26.02(b) of the Texas Business and Commerce Code, and whether promissory estoppel supplied a route around that requirement.
sections.Holding: The United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas, in 2011, Judge Nancy F. Atlas, held in the reproduced portion of its opinion that the alleged foreclosure delay was a financial accommodation covered by the statute of frauds and could not be enforced on the pleaded basis because it lacked the required statutory form. The promissory-estoppel theory failed because the plaintiffs had not alleged a promise to sign a written agreement that would satisfy the statute. The defendant was therefore entitled to dismissal of the promissory-estoppel claim. The court granted the motion to dismiss and dismissed the case.
sections.Reasoning:
Section 26.02(b) required a loan agreement involving more than $50,000 to be in writing and signed by the party to be bound or its authorized representative. The $276,000 loan exceeded that threshold. The statutory definition of a loan agreement included a financial institution's promise to delay repayment or make a financial accommodation, so the court did not treat the alleged postponement as a separate undertaking outside the statute merely because it concerned the timing of foreclosure.

The court then stated a further requirement for promissory estoppel in this setting: the promisor must have promised to sign a written document that would satisfy the statute of frauds. It applied that requirement both to estoppel as an affirmative claim and to estoppel used to oppose the statute-of-frauds defense, citing Burnette v. Wells Fargo Bank and Ford v. City State Bank of Palacios. Alleging the underlying oral accommodation did not itself allege that additional promise.

The ruling concerns enforceability and pleading on a motion to dismiss. It is not a finding that the promise was never made, and it does not establish that a bank may always disregard a loan-modification agreement or that every foreclosure-related tort claim fails.

The casebook editors, not the court, go on to ask whether an accurately remembered oral promise ought to be enforceable, to distinguish estoppel as a source of obligation from estoppel as a way to enforce an otherwise unenforceable agreement, and to discuss the statute's notice provisions. Because only the excerpt was available, the reasoning on the other claims cannot be supplied.

CT-CB-0002.rule: When a physician guarantees a specified result, damages for breach are the difference between the value of the promised condition and the value of the actual condition, plus incidental consequences within the parties' contemplation, and not the pain ordinarily incident to the agreed operation.

sections.Parties: Hawkins was the patient, who sought contractual compensation for a surgeon's allegedly guaranteed result. McGee was the defendant physician. Hawkins's theory depended on proving an undertaking to produce a specified condition of his hand. McGee disputed whether his words could create that obligation and challenged the jury instructions governing both contract formation and damages.
sections.Procedural History: The formation question was submitted to a jury. On damages, the trial judge instructed the jury to consider the patient's operative pain and suffering and injury beyond the preexisting condition, and McGee objected. The trial court later set aside the verdict under its own assessment of damages, regarding an award exceeding $500 as excessive. McGee had also requested instructions that would have required an identical subjective understanding by physician and patient and barred liability unless a further operation could not correct the condition. The Supreme Court of New Hampshire, deciding the case on June 4, 1929, rejected the damages instruction and ordered a new trial.
sections.Material Facts:
An electric-wire burn about nine years before the treatment had left scar tissue on the palm of Hawkins's right hand. McGee operated by removing a substantial quantity of scar tissue and grafting skin from Hawkins's chest.

The evidence included two kinds of statements. Asked about hospitalization, McGee predicted three or four days in the hospital and a return to work a few days later. Separately, witnesses attributed to him a guarantee of a completely good or perfect hand, made before the decision to operate and in Hawkins's presence; this alleged guarantee was the substantial basis of the contract claim.

There was evidence that McGee had repeatedly solicited the opportunity to perform the operation, and Hawkins's counsel suggested in cross-examination that McGee wanted experience in skin grafting. The court treated that as a theory the jury could accept, not as an established fact. The evidence also permitted the conclusion that Hawkins and his father took the alleged guarantee seriously. There was evidence that McGee had refused to perform another operation.
sections.Issue: Whether the evidence of the physician's words and surrounding conduct could support a finding that he undertook a contractual obligation to achieve a specified result; and, if so, whether damages should restore the patient's preoperative position, reimburse the burden of undergoing treatment, or compensate for the difference between the promised result and the actual result.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of New Hampshire, in 1929, in an opinion by Justice Branch in which the participating judges concurred, Justice Marble not sitting, held that the alleged guarantee could create a contractual undertaking and that the evidence justified submitting that question to the jury, while the estimates of hospitalization and recovery time were predictions rather than promises on this record. If a good or perfect hand was promised, the measure of damages is the difference between the value to the patient of the promised hand and the value of the actual hand, together with incidental consequences within the parties' contemplation. Pain necessarily incident to the agreed operation is not a separate item. The court ordered a new trial.
sections.Reasoning:
The court first separated statements that could reasonably bear a promissory meaning from ordinary medical forecasts. Whether language is capable of the asserted contractual meaning is initially a question of law for the judge; once that threshold is met, the jury decides whether the words were spoken and what the circumstances establish. The alleged explicit guarantee cleared the threshold and the recovery predictions did not. McGee argued that, given the uncertainty of surgery, no reasonable person would take a guarantee literally. The court did not decide whether that argument would be conclusive in every case; here the alleged solicitation and possible wish for experience, if the jury accepted them, made a result warranty plausible.

On damages, the promised improvement defines the protected interest. A comparison of the hand before and after the operation would miss the loss where an operation fails to improve the hand without making it worse, and where the hand is worsened the promised-versus-actual measure already captures the deterioration, so adding it again would count harm twice. The court drew an analogy to a machine warranted to perform a specified function. Ordinary pain of the operation would have been suffered even with the promised result and was part of what the patient agreed to bear.

The rejected instructions were wrong. Assent is judged by an external standard, so an undisclosed mental reservation does not undo an objectively manifested guarantee. The corrective-surgery request was inconsistent with evidence that McGee had refused another operation. The court did not decide whether the evidence otherwise supported the $500 assessment. There was no separate opinion.

CT-CB-0004.rule: A seller's statement creates an express warranty only if it is an affirmation, promise or description relating to the goods actually sold that forms part of the basis of the bargain; statements about differently configured goods and general commendation do not.

sections.Parties: John R. Crow bought a sport-fishing boat and was the prevailing plaintiff at trial. Bayliner Marine Corporation manufactured the boat and appealed the warranty judgment against it. Tidewater Yacht Agency was the authorized local dealer; Crow nonsuited his claim against it before trial. Brunswick, the diesel-engine manufacturer, had also been sued, but the final trial order dismissed the negligence claim against it. Bayliner challenged both liability and damages.
sections.Procedural History: After a bench trial, the circuit court found that Bayliner had breached an express warranty, the implied warranty of merchantability, and the implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose. It awarded $135,000 plus prejudgment interest, consisting of the $120,000 purchase price and approximately $15,000 toward the claimed costs of storing, maintaining, insuring and financing the boat. Bayliner appealed. The Supreme Court of Virginia, deciding the case on January 8, 1999, viewed the evidence in the light most favorable to Crow, held it insufficient to support any of the three warranty findings, reversed, and entered final judgment for Bayliner without a remand. It did not reach the damages assignments.
sections.Material Facts:
In the summer of 1989 Crow took a short ride on a Bayliner 3486 Trophy Convertible offered through Tidewater and asked the dealer's representative, John Atherton, about maximum speed. Atherton could not answer from his own experience, so he gave Crow two manufacturer 'prop matrixes' from the dealer's manual. The thirty-mile-per-hour figures in them concerned boats with propellers different from the 20-by-17 propeller on Crow's boat, and the data specified testing with approximately 600 pounds of passengers and gear. Atherton also showed a sales brochure promoting the model's performance for reaching offshore fishing grounds.

Crow bought the boat for $120,000 before taxes, with about 2,000 pounds of added equipment, and did not test it again before delivery. On delivery in September 1989 its maximum speed was thirteen miles per hour; after repeated repairs it generally reached seventeen, and briefly about twenty-four. In July 1990 Bayliner wrote that the performance representations at purchase had been incorrect and that twenty-three to twenty-five miles per hour was the boat's maximum capability. Crow testified that he would not have bought it even at that speed. The boat logged approximately 850 engine hours over five years, and Crow had used it for offshore fishing in the first years.
sections.Issue: Whether the numerical matrices or the brochure's general language created a thirty-mile-per-hour express warranty for Crow's boat; whether failure to reach that speed established unmerchantability in the trade or unfitness for the boat's ordinary purpose; and whether the seller knew of Crow's particular thirty-mile-per-hour requirement so as to support an implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia, in 1999, in an opinion by Justice Barbara Milano Keenan with no separate opinion, held that the evidence did not support any of the three warranty findings. Under Virginia's version of UCC section 2-313, the matrices did not warrant the performance of Crow's differently configured boat, and the brochure's general praise was commendation and opinion rather than a description promising a specific speed. Under section 2-314, Crow did not establish a relevant trade standard or show the boat was generally unacceptable or unfit for ordinary offshore fishing. Under section 2-315, he did not show that the seller had reason to know of his precise speed requirement. The court reversed and entered final judgment for Bayliner.
sections.Reasoning:
The court began with express warranty. The thirty-mile-per-hour figures were definite numbers, so the problem was not puffery but what they referred to: boats with different propellers and materially different equipment weight. A precise statement about a differently configured product does not automatically become a warranty about the buyer's actual boat. The court contrasted an earlier jewelry case in which an appraisal described the very diamonds being sold. The brochure, by contrast, identified no specific speed or other measurable characteristic; section 2-313(2) preserves the distinction between an affirmation or description and an opinion commending the goods, and on this record the sentence was commendation.

On merchantability, the court considered two statutory aspects separately. For acceptance in the trade, Crow offered no evidence of the offshore-boat trade's standard or that a substantial segment of buyers would reject a boat of this capability; his testimony that travel to the Gulf Stream took too long described his own preferences. For fitness for ordinary purposes, the evidence of actual offshore fishing and substantial engine hours undermined any inference of general unfitness, and his explanation that many hours were spent on repairs did not prove otherwise.

On fitness for a particular purpose, Crow identified the purpose as offshore fishing in a boat capable of thirty miles per hour. He had discussed fishing and speed, but the record did not show that Atherton knew a slower boat was unacceptable to him, and that failure defeated the claim. Because every ground of liability failed, the court did not decide the damages questions. The casebook excerpt omits the implied-warranty discussion.

CT-CB-0013.rule: A patient may recover on a physician's clearly proved promise of a specific result even without negligence, and the damages may include out-of-pocket expenses, the worsening of the patient's condition, and pain and mental distress beyond what the promised treatment would have entailed.

sections.Parties: Alice Sullivan, the patient, sued physician James H. O'Connor for breach of a promise concerning the result of cosmetic surgery and, separately, for negligent treatment. On appeal O'Connor sought to confine her compensation to her out-of-pocket expenses. Sullivan had objected that the instructions did not grant full compensation for the promised result, but she offered to abandon those objections if the verdict in her favor stood.
sections.Procedural History: The case was tried to a jury. The jury found for Sullivan on the contract count and for O'Connor on the negligence count. The damages instructions then allowed out-of-pocket expenses, the worsening of her appearance and associated mental distress, and pain and suffering from the third operation, and excluded pain from the first two operations and unproved lost earnings. The jury awarded $13,500. O'Connor excepted to the refusal to restrict recovery to expenditures and to the inclusion of disfigurement and third-operation suffering. Sullivan conditionally waived her own exceptions. The Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts, on May 9, 1973, overruled the defendant's exceptions and treated the plaintiff's as waived, so the verdict stood and no new trial was ordered.
sections.Material Facts:
Sullivan was a professional entertainer, as O'Connor knew. The jury could find that he undertook to improve her appearance by making her relatively long, prominent nose shorter and more pleasing in relation to her other features. The contemplated treatment was two operations. He performed three, and the result worsened her appearance: the opinion describes a concave upper line, a bulbous lower portion, flattening and broadening, and an asymmetrical tip. Further surgery evidently could not improve it.

Sullivan incurred stipulated physician and hospital expenses totaling $622.65. She did not prove lost employment or earnings attributable to the changed nose, and the trial judge excluded lost earnings from the damages calculation. The two contemplated operations already entailed some pain and distress; the third operation was additional. She no longer sought on appeal the improvement above her preoperative condition, and she waived any claim for suffering from the first two operations.
sections.Issue: Whether damages for breach of a physician's promise of a result may include physical deterioration, mental distress and the pain of an additional operation when the physician was not negligent, or are limited to a refund of expenditures; and whether the case required a choice between expectation damages and reliance damages.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts, in 1973, in an opinion by Justice Kaplan with no separate opinion reported, held that Massachusetts recognizes an action on a physician's promise of a specified result, on clear proof that the promise was made, and that the jury's rejection of negligence does not defeat it. The award could include Sullivan's expenditures, the worsening of her condition, and the suffering and distress associated with the third operation. Those items were recoverable under either an expectation or a reliance approach, and because Sullivan waived the claims that would distinguish the two measures, the court did not select one as the exclusive formula. It overruled the defendant's exceptions, and the $13,500 verdict stood.
sections.Reasoning:
Justice Kaplan first addressed whether such promises should be enforced at all. Medical results are uncertain, disappointed patients may recast optimistic reassurance as a guarantee, and broad liability could encourage defensive practice; yet refusing to enforce genuine promises would let practitioners induce patients with commitments they never intend to honor. Massachusetts takes an intermediate position: the action exists, but the jury should scrutinize whether an actual undertaking, rather than an opinion or therapeutic assurance, was proved. Absence of negligence goes to the quality of treatment; the contract count goes to the content of the undertaking.

The court then distinguished three interests. Restitution returns the benefit conferred on the physician, most obviously the fee. Reliance reverses detrimental changes incurred because of the agreement, including payments to third parties and a worsened condition. Expectation compares the actual result with the promised one; on the Hawkins model it captures failure to improve and deterioration but ordinarily excludes pain the patient would have endured in any event. A fee-only recovery might protect too little, while the full value of the promised appearance might be hard to estimate and disproportionate to the fee, so the court spoke favorably of reliance without holding that it excludes expectation in every medical case.

The deterioration and the extra operation were compensable on either view. Mental distress was recoverable because an agreement to operate on a person's body, unlike an ordinary merchandise transaction, makes bodily change and the attending distress central to what the parties contemplate; her known professional circumstances were relevant to that appraisal. The footnotes warn against double recovery.

CT-CB-0021.rule: Contract damages ordinarily compensate the injured party's own loss; the breaching party's gains can sometimes help measure that loss, but gains that do not correspond to it are not automatically recoverable in an ordinary contract action, and a supported estimate of the loss suffices despite uncertainty.

sections.Parties: The United States Naval Institute held the author's copyright in The Hunt for Red October and marketed the hardcover edition. It licensed paperback rights to Charter Communications and Berkley Publishing Group, treated collectively as Berkley. Naval was the plaintiff and appellant; Berkley was the defendant and cross-appellant. Naval sought relief for premature paperback retail sales and, on this appeal, wanted a larger recovery of Berkley's profits, additional interest and attorney's fees. Berkley wanted the judgment eliminated or reduced.
sections.Procedural History: Naval unsuccessfully sought preliminary relief, and the district court initially entered judgment against it after trial. In 1989 the Second Circuit, in Naval I, reversed on contract liability and remanded for appropriate relief. On remand the district court treated the conduct as copyright infringement and awarded $35,380.50 in lost hardcover profits, $7,760.12 of Berkley's profits, and $15,319.27 in prejudgment interest on the compensatory award, plus costs; it denied attorney's fees and interest on the profit award. Naval appealed and Berkley cross-appealed. On June 18, 1991, the Second Circuit reversed the $7,760.12 profits award and affirmed the judgment in all other respects.
sections.Material Facts:
The parties made their licensing agreement in September 1984. One provision conveyed an exclusive right to publish and sell paperback editions, and another made the license term begin on the date of the agreement. A separate provision prohibited publication before October 1985.

Berkley shipped paperbacks to outlets early, and retail sales began on September 15, 1985. Sales were extensive enough for the book to approach the top of the paperback bestseller lists before the end of September. The earlier appellate decision had held that causing such substantial early retail sales breached the timing provision.

Some buyers of the cheaper paperback in September would otherwise have bought the hardcover, but others would have waited for the paperback and never bought the hardcover. Hardcover sales had been declining before the premature release. Naval proposed $724,300 as the measure of Berkley's profits. The district court estimated Naval's lost September hardcover sales by reference to August hardcover sales. Naval had accepted substantial royalties and renounced rescission.
sections.Issue: Whether Berkley's early retail publication infringed a copyright interest owned by Naval or only breached a covenant governing rights already licensed to Berkley; whether, without copyright remedies, Naval could still recover contract damages and could recover Berkley's profits; and whether the comparison with August hardcover sales was a permissible estimate of Naval's loss.
sections.Holding: The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, in 1991, in an opinion by Judge Kearse for a panel with Judges Winter and Altimari and no separate opinion, held that an exclusive license transfers ownership of the rights conveyed, so Berkley's premature publication breached the agreement without infringing copyright, and the Copyright Act supplied no basis for the profits award or attorney's fees. Naval could still recover contract damages. Berkley's paperback profits did not measure Naval's lost hardcover profit and were not recoverable. The $35,380.50 estimate based on the prior month's hardcover sales was not clearly erroneous, and prejudgment interest followed under New York law. The court reversed the $7,760.12 award and otherwise affirmed.
sections.Reasoning:
The district court had treated October 1985 as the date the license took effect, but the agreement tied its beginning to the September 1984 agreement date and referred to first publication elsewhere. Berkley therefore owned the paperback rights when the early sales occurred, and the publication restriction was a contractual covenant; a licensee does not infringe rights already conveyed to it. Since the Copyright Act's route to an infringer's profits depended on infringement, it was unavailable, but the license did not free Berkley from its contractual restriction.

Berkley argued that Naval had abandoned its monetary contract claim. The court answered that Naval I had held Naval entitled to relief for the breach, which was the law of the case, and that Naval had asked for other just and proper relief and Rule 54(c) directs a judgment to grant the relief warranted.

On measure, Naval's proposed figure included profits on sales to buyers who would never have bought the hardcover; those sales enriched Berkley without depriving Naval of corresponding hardcover sales, and awarding them would detach damages from the injury. The court recognized that a defendant's profit can sometimes help define the plaintiff's loss, but that relationship was absent here. The $7,760.12 award rested on the rejected copyright theory, while the separate lost-profit estimate could stand under contract law.

On certainty, there was evidence of actual lost sales, and only the amount was uncertain. Nothing showed purchases were even throughout September, so Berkley's alternative projection was not compelled, and uncertainty caused by the wrongdoer could be resolved against it. An ordinary contract claim gave no basis for attorney's fees.

CT-CB-0026.rule: Although specific performance is ordinarily not the remedy for an agreement to sell personal property, equity may order delivery of a specific chattel when special circumstances give it a peculiar and unique value that makes damages inadequate.

sections.Parties: Archie Sparrow, a cowboy and experienced horse trainer, was the plaintiff and sought delivery of a particular horse, Keno, as promised compensation for ranch work. C. L. 'Chip' Morris, who owned the ranch and the horse, was the defendant and the appellant. Morris argued that Sparrow had not satisfied a condition about the quality of his work, that money rather than delivery was the proper remedy for personal property, and that a final wage check had settled everything between them.
sections.Procedural History: Sparrow brought an action in chancery for specific performance. After hearing testimony from both parties, the chancellor ordered Morris to deliver the horse. Morris appealed the decree to the Supreme Court of Arkansas. That court, deferring to the chancellor's superior opportunity to evaluate the witnesses, found no basis for saying the finding for Sparrow was against the preponderance of the evidence. On February 20, 1956, it affirmed the decree requiring delivery of Keno. Rehearing was denied on March 26.
sections.Material Facts:
The parties met in Florida through rodeo activities. They arranged that Morris would go to Canada while Sparrow stayed at Morris's Arkansas ranch to do the necessary work. They agreed on sixteen weeks of work for $400 in cash. Sparrow maintained that the compensation also included the brown horse Keno. Morris acknowledged a possible transfer but said it depended on satisfactory ranch work, which he said Sparrow had not done.

Keno was essentially unbroken when Sparrow arrived. In his spare time Sparrow trained the horse so that, with a little further training, it would be a first-class roping horse.

After the sixteen weeks, the parties agreed that $167 of the cash remained owing. At a bank, Morris gave Sparrow a check for exactly that amount with a notation that labor had been paid in full. Sparrow cashed it while continuing to claim the horse. During the same encounter Morris was willing to turn over Keno on a new condition that Sparrow not sell or dispose of him, and Sparrow refused that restriction.
sections.Issue: Whether equity may require delivery of a specific item of personal property that has acquired a peculiar value through the promised recipient's training; whether the evidence required rejecting Sparrow's claim because his work was unsatisfactory; and whether cashing a final wage check marked paid in full discharged the separate obligation concerning the horse.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of Arkansas, in 1956, in an opinion by Justice Robinson with no separate opinion, held that although specific performance ordinarily is not the remedy for an agreement to sell personal property, equity may grant it when special circumstances make damages inadequate, and Sparrow's training of this particular horse created the requisite peculiar and unique value. The court also relied on an Arkansas statute authorizing a court of equity, when appropriate, to order specific delivery of specific or ascertained goods. The chancellor's finding for Sparrow on the asserted condition of satisfactory work stood, and acceptance of the check for the undisputed cash balance was not an accord and satisfaction of the horse claim. The decree was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning:
The court accepted the ordinary preference for damages in transactions involving chattels but found special circumstances. Sparrow had turned a green horse into a trained roping prospect through his own time and skill, which gave this animal a distinctive value to him. A payment of market value would not supply the promised performance in an adequate form, so he was entitled to Keno himself. The court did not find that all horses are irreplaceable for every buyer.

The court quoted Arkansas Statutes section 68-1468, which authorized specific performance of a seller's broken undertaking to deliver specific or ascertained goods when a court of equity thought the remedy appropriate, as an additional basis for relief. The statute did not make the remedy automatic; the inquiry into why damages were insufficient remained necessary. This statutory discussion is in the full opinion but not in the casebook excerpt.

Morris's objection that delivery was conditional on a good job turned on disputed testimony. Both parties had testified before the chancellor, and the court sustained his finding for Sparrow. It announced no general test for satisfaction conditions.

On accord and satisfaction, the check paid precisely the cash balance both sides acknowledged, Sparrow never abandoned his claim to Keno, and Morris himself was still discussing delivery of the horse at the bank. There was thus no clear basis for reading the check as an agreed replacement for the whole compensation package. The words paid in full must be read in their setting. The court recognized that a disputed money amount, knowingly accepted in full settlement, might have a different consequence, but did not decide that case.

CT-CB-0030.rule: Punitive damages are not available for breach of contract, even a willful and malicious one, where no tort is pleaded or proved; and actual damages need not be proved with mathematical precision to support a modest compensatory award.

sections.Parties: Virgil and Gwynneth White were homeowners entitled under an agreement to receive water from a well on their neighbors' property. Paul and Ruth Benkowski, the defendants, controlled the well. The Whites, the plaintiffs, sought compensation for interruptions of the promised supply and punitive damages based on the jury's finding that the interruptions were malicious. After the trial court reduced the verdict, the Whites appealed to restore both components.
sections.Procedural History: The action was tried to a jury. The trial court instructed that compensatory damages could include pecuniary loss and inconvenience naturally resulting from the breach, and that unproved actual damages could produce a nominal recovery; the Whites did not object. The jury awarded $10 in compensatory damages and $2,000 in punitive damages. The trial court then reduced the compensatory award to $1 and struck the punitive damages, valuing the undelivered service at about twenty-five cents and treating the injury as nominal. The Whites appealed. On December 22, 1967, the Supreme Court of Wisconsin reversed in part, reinstating the $10 compensatory award, and otherwise affirmed, leaving the punitive award eliminated. It awarded costs to the appellants.
sections.Material Facts:
The Whites' home lacked its own water supply but was connected to the Benkowskis' well. According to the casebook's bracketed account of the facts, a written agreement provided water for ten years, subject to contingencies such as municipal supply, an inadequate well, or the Whites' acquiring their own well, and the Whites agreed to pay $3 monthly and share future repair and maintenance costs. The initially friendly relationship deteriorated, and the water was shut off on several occasions. The casebook identifies nine interruptions of less than an hour and reports the Benkowskis' explanations involving sand in the pipes and excessive use.

The opinion identifies three concrete inconveniences. Once, lack of water in the bathroom produced an odor. Twice, Mrs. White had to take her children to a neighbor's home for bathing. The plaintiffs supplied no precise calculation of the value of these inconveniences. The jury found that the shutoffs had been imposed maliciously to harass the Whites. The action was pleaded and proved in contract; no tort was pleaded or proved.
sections.Issue: Whether the trial court was entitled to reduce a modest jury award of compensatory damages to a nominal sum despite evidence of inconvenience from the interrupted water supply; and whether a malicious, willful breach justified punitive damages in an action where no tort was pleaded or proved.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of Wisconsin, in 1967, in an opinion by Justice Wilkie with no separate opinion, held that the evidence of inconvenience established actual injury and that damages did not have to be proved with mathematical precision before the jury could assign a reasonable compensatory amount. The $10 award was actual compensation despite its small size, and the trial court erred in replacing it with $1. Punitive damages were unavailable on the contract claim presented, even though the breach was willful, because no tort was pleaded or proved. The court reversed in part to reinstate the $10 award and otherwise affirmed.
sections.Reasoning:
On compensation, the value of the interrupted water was not exhausted by prorating the monthly charge. The agreement supplied a household necessity, and the interruptions disrupted bathing and sanitation. The trial judge's arithmetic overlooked the testimony describing those effects. The jury could attach a modest reasonable amount to them without receipts or an exact price. A small award can compensate a real injury, whereas a nominal award recognizes a violation without measuring a demonstrated loss; the court contrasted a prior wrongful-entry case in which no actual injury had been shown.

On punishment, punitive damages serve to punish and deter wrongdoing beyond making the injured party whole. The court reviewed the general availability of that remedy in tort and the separate tradition limiting recovery for ordinary breach of contract to compensation. It found the overwhelming weight of authority against punitive damages for breach of contract and regarded willfulness as insufficient to change that result. The finding of malice described motive; it did not create a new cause of action. The authorities reviewed included historical discussion of actions for breach of promise to marry.

The court acknowledged that a contract can create a relationship out of which a duty of care arises, and that breach of that duty might support tort liability in an appropriate case. But the Whites had not pleaded or proved such a tort, and the court would not convert evidence of a malicious breach into a tort judgment to preserve the punitive award. The two questions were independent: proof of actual injury defeated the reduction to nominal damages but did not make punishment legally available.

CT-CB-0074.rule: A moral obligation or gratitude for a benefit already conferred, without a prior request or an existing legal obligation of the promisor, is not consideration for a later express promise to pay.

sections.Parties: Daniel Mills, the plaintiff, sued Seth Wyman, the defendant, on Wyman's written promise to reimburse Mills for sheltering and caring for Wyman's adult son, Levi. Mills took exceptions to a nonsuit and sought recovery on the promise; Wyman resisted payment.
sections.Procedural History: Mills sued to recover compensation for the services on the father's promise. The Court of Common Pleas directed a nonsuit because the family relationship and subsequent promise supplied no sufficient consideration. Mills took exceptions. The Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts sustained the nonsuit and directed entry of judgment for the defendant, with costs.
sections.Material Facts:
Daniel Mills supplied shelter and care to Levi Wyman, the twenty-five-year-old son of Seth Wyman. Levi had long since left his father's household and was returning from a voyage when he became ill among strangers. The care was supplied without a request from Seth, and the opinion describes Mills as caring for Levi until his death. After the services and expenses had already been incurred, Seth wrote promising reimbursement and subsequently refused to pay.

The father had neither engaged Mills nor been shown to bear an existing legal responsibility for the expense. The record did not establish the triggering facts or the adjudication required by the Massachusetts statute obliging certain relatives to support impoverished family members. The casebook's notes raise historical questions about the underlying events; these facts are those on which the opinion proceeds.
sections.Issue: Whether a father's moral obligation or gratitude for care already given to his adult son can support his later express promise to reimburse the caregiver, absent a prior request or established legal obligation; whether the cases enforcing new promises to pay old debts support that result; and whether the family-support statute supplied the necessary obligation.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts, in 1825, in an opinion by Chief Justice Parker in which he said all members of the court agreed the nonsuit was proper, held the promise unenforceable. Moral obligation, understood as a conscientious reason to pay, does not itself furnish consideration. The cases sustaining a new promise after an earlier obligation became legally unenforceable depend on a valuable consideration or obligation in the underlying transaction. The statutory support argument failed because the facts and adjudicative prerequisites for liability had not been established.
sections.Reasoning:
Parker first identified what was missing: the services were not given at the father's request, and the adult son was no longer under his care. The later writing could acknowledge gratitude but could not show that the earlier care was rendered as the price of it, and kinship did not make an independent adult's expenses the father's debts. The court recognized the humane value of the services; the difficulty was whether they supported this defendant's promise.

Mills relied on the proposition that moral obligation can support an express promise. Parker examined the usual illustrations: a debt barred by limitations, an obligation incurred during infancy, and a debt discharged in bankruptcy. In each there was an original transaction with a quid pro quo, and the later promise removes or waives a legal impediment to an obligation with that antecedent basis. The father's promise instead sought to create an obligation from gratitude where none had existed.

Parker accepted that breaking a deliberate promise can be morally wrong but reasoned that society leaves many family and benevolent duties to conscience. If moral obligation alone created a legal duty, it would be hard to explain why a later express promise was needed at all. That the promise was written did not help: instruments under seal and certain negotiable commercial instruments have their own legal treatment, which an ordinary reimbursement letter does not share.

Finally, the family-support statute could not apply because the record did not establish its triggering facts or the required judgment after an opportunity to be heard.

The brief's own study analysis, not the court's, treats Mills as the restrictive position against which Webb v. McGowin's later material-benefit reasoning is studied.

CT-CB-0076.rule: A moral obligation coupled with a material benefit actually received by the promisor, such as having his life saved, can support his later express promise to pay, even without a prior bargain or an original duty to pay.

sections.Parties: Joe Webb, the plaintiff and appellant, sued the executors of J. Greeley McGowin's estate, the defendants, to recover installments allegedly due under McGowin's promise to support Webb for life. The executors demurred, contending among other things that the promise lacked consideration.
sections.Procedural History: Webb filed an action in assumpsit and amended his complaint. The trial court sustained demurrers, whose grounds included failure to state a cause of action, absence of consideration, absence of an agreement to pay before the rescue, and the Statute of Frauds. Webb took a nonsuit because of that ruling and appealed. The Alabama Court of Appeals reversed and remanded on November 12, 1935; rehearing was denied on February 18, 1936. The Alabama Supreme Court denied certiorari on May 14, 1936, in an opinion by Justice Foster. The decision tests the legal sufficiency of the pleaded facts, not facts found at trial.
sections.Material Facts:
On August 3, 1925, Webb was working for the W. T. Smith Lumber Company, clearing an upper mill floor by dropping waste material to the ground. While preparing to drop a pine block weighing about seventy-five pounds, he saw McGowin directly below; as pleaded, releasing it would probably have killed or seriously injured McGowin. Webb could have stayed safe by releasing the block. Instead he held on and fell with it, diverting its path. McGowin escaped injury, but Webb suffered severe injuries to his right leg, right heel and right arm and was permanently disabled, described as unable to do physical or mental labor.

On September 1, 1925, McGowin allegedly agreed to pay Webb fifteen dollars every two weeks for the rest of Webb's life, in recognition of the rescue and the injuries. Payments continued for more than eight years until McGowin died on January 1, 1934, and afterward through January 27, 1934, and then stopped. Webb sought the unpaid installments accruing after that date through commencement of suit.
sections.Issue: Whether a person's later express promise to compensate another for saving his life and suffering permanent injury in the rescue is enforceable although there was no preceding bargain or legal obligation to pay, whether the material benefit to the promisor distinguishes it from a promise resting only on gratitude, and whether the Statute of Frauds defeats it.
