The memorandum was an offer. The promise of a deadline, unsupported by consideration, created no enforceable obligation to keep the offer open, so Dodds remained free to withdraw before acceptance. No particular formula of express withdrawal was necessary on these facts: once Dickinson knew that Dodds had agreed to sell to someone else, he could not form a contract by purporting to accept the earlier proposal.
sections.Reasoning:
James distinguished an unaccepted proposal from a binding agreement. Dickinson's wish to keep a choice until Friday showed that he had not yet accepted, and the promise of time was unsupported because he gave nothing for it. Mellish added that a signed writing sufficient under the Statute of Frauds does not establish that acceptance occurred while the offer was still available.

James rejected the proposition that Dodds had to say expressly that he withdrew. The question was whether Dickinson had information equivalent to that message before trying to accept, and on the court's view of his own allegations he did: his hurried attempts followed his knowledge of the sale to Allan. The status of the messenger was not decisive once the offeree actually knew of the inconsistent transaction. Mellish framed the point as knowledge of a completed agreement with a third person: a purchaser who knows the property has been sold cannot afterward create the earlier bargain by accepting its old terms. His application repeatedly included the offeree's knowledge.

Without a binding option, the deadline set an outside period for acceptance only while the offer remained open. Because Dickinson had no contract, the court did not decide priority between two binding contracts; Mellish expressly declined to resolve it, and assumed for analysis that Allan knew of the earlier proposal.

The reporter's headnote adds a tentative proposition that a sale alone might withdraw an offer without the offeree's knowledge; the brief treats that as broader than the holding the appellate judgments support.

CT-CB-0263.rule: Where a policy lets the insured reinstate lapsed coverage by payment alone, payment by an authorized mailed check is effective under the mailbox rule when the check is dispatched to the insurer, not when it is received or negotiated.

sections.Parties: Elizabeth Wilson, the plaintiff and appellee, was the primary beneficiary of a life policy on her husband, Dr. John G. Griffith. US Life underwrote the policy and promised its death benefits. AMA Insurance Agency, Inc. (AMAIA) administered the policy, billed and collected premiums, and was authorized to receive payments for US Life. Wilson sought $400,000 in ordinary death benefits plus $250,000 in accidental-death benefits after both companies, the defendants and appellants, denied payment.
sections.Procedural History: The parties filed cross-motions for summary judgment. The circuit court ruled that the policy had been reinstated and entered judgment against both defendants for $650,000; on postjudgment motions it added prejudgment interest at six percent from the date of death. Both defendants appealed. The Court of Special Appeals of Maryland reviewed the legal determinations de novo and, by agreement of the parties, applied Illinois substantive law. It affirmed the judgment against US Life, including the benefits and prejudgment interest, reversed the judgment against AMAIA, and remanded with instructions to enter judgment for AMAIA.
sections.Material Facts:
The ten-year policy became effective November 15, 1998, with premiums due May 15 and November 15 and paid through AMAIA's Chicago office. It allowed a 31-day grace period, which US Life could extend by written notice stating when coverage would end. A reinstatement clause permitted reinstatement within 90 days after the first unpaid premium's due date; evidence of insurability was not required within 31 days after the grace period ended.

Griffith missed the May 15, 2007 payment. A reminder notice said payment must be received within sixty days of that due date to assure active coverage. A later lapse notice referred to a 31-day grace period and told him to submit a good-health application.

On Monday, July 23, Griffith electronically instructed his bank to pay $369.46 to AMAIA. The bank generated a paper check, dated July 30, and its records showed dispatch on Wednesday, July 25, and delivery on Monday, July 30. Griffith died in a bicycle-related automobile accident on Saturday, July 28. He had not supplied a good-health application. AMAIA returned the check on August 2, before learning of his death.
sections.Issue: Did the reminder extend the grace period? Did the policy permit reinstatement through payment alone in the extended window? Was payment made when Griffith instructed his bank, when the bank dispatched the check, when AMAIA received it, or when it could negotiate it, and did the check's future date matter? Was AMAIA liable for the insurer's contractual benefits?
sections.Holding: Court of Special Appeals of Maryland, 2011, in an opinion by Judge Deborah S. Eyler for a panel with Judges Kehoe and Sharer, with no separate opinion. The reminder was an effective written extension, so the policy allowed reinstatement without new evidence of insurability within the relevant period. Payment did not require the insurer's receipt or negotiation of a check. Applying the mailbox rule to an authorized mailed payment, the court held that reinstatement occurred July 25, when the bank dispatched the paper check; the postdating did not delay payment. AMAIA, an agent for a disclosed principal, had no independent contractual duty to pay the benefits.
sections.Reasoning:
The insurer had reserved power to extend the grace period by written notice and exercised it in ordinary language; a reasonable insured could calculate July 14 from the reminder. Coverage lapsed July 15, and the last permissible reinstatement date was August 13, the ninety-day limit measured from May 15. The later notice could not add a receipt condition or demand a health application where the policy excused one.

US Life argued that payment meant negotiation of the check. The court rejected that reading as unreasonable: the policy described payment as something the insured makes, while negotiating a check is the payee's act, and coverage would otherwise depend on when the administrator happened to deposit it. The court did not need contra proferentem.

The court predicted that Illinois would follow the majority approach treating reinstatement as revival of the existing policy, particularly where timely payment alone satisfies the clause, and used unilateral-contract analysis to explain the offer and performance. It left room for a different analysis where reinstatement requires evidence of insurability and insurer approval.

The mailbox rule can apply to performance consisting of an authorized remittance, but it requires dispatch. The July 23 instruction went to Griffith's own agent and could still have been countermanded. On July 25 the bank sent the paper check. Under UCC §§ 3-113 and 4-401(c), with no notice of postdating in the record, the check was properly payable on July 25. US Life's claim of a factual dispute, first raised in its appellate reply, was not entertained.

The casebook excerpt focuses on the mailbox rule and reinstatement.

CT-CB-0285.rule: Between merchants under UCC section 2-207(2), additional terms in an acceptance become part of the contract unless an exception applies, and the party opposing inclusion bears the burden of proving that the term materially alters the contract.

sections.Parties: Bayway Refining Co., a petroleum seller, was the plaintiff and the appellee. Oxygenated Marketing and Trading A.G. (OMT), its buyer, was the defendant and the appellant. Bayway sought reimbursement of $464,035.12 in federal excise taxes, which the government had imposed on Bayway because OMT lacked the relevant tax registration, asserting that the parties' contract shifted that burden to OMT. OMT refused, claiming it had never agreed to bear the tax.
sections.Procedural History: Bayway sued in the Southern District of New York, which granted it summary judgment. The district court held that incorporation of Bayway's general terms by reference was effective even though they were not attached, because OMT could have obtained them on request, and that OMT had not established material alteration. OMT appealed the materiality determination and the district court's use of trade-practice evidence that Bayway submitted with its reply. The Second Circuit reviewed summary judgment de novo and the decision to receive the reply evidence for abuse of discretion. It declined two arguments OMT raised for the first time on appeal. On June 8, 2000, it affirmed the judgment for Bayway.
sections.Material Facts:
The transaction involved 60,000 barrels of methyl tertiary butyl ether, a gasoline blendstock. On February 12, 1998, OMT faxed a confirmation describing its purchase, stating that the confirmation constituted the entire contract, and asking that discrepancies or omissions be raised within two working days. The litigation treated this document as the offer. Bayway responded the next day with its own confirmation, which stated the commercial particulars and incorporated its March 1994 general terms by reference. Those terms were not attached to the fax.

The incorporated Tax Clause required the buyer to reimburse the seller for enumerated federal, state and local taxes connected to the product or its value, excluding taxes on income. OMT made no objection and accepted delivery on March 22. Bayway later learned that OMT lacked the registration that would avoid the federal excise tax, paid $464,035.12, and demanded reimbursement. The parties had no contrary prior course of dealing. OMT's executives called the clause an unwelcome surprise but offered no evidence that a reasonable petroleum merchant would have been surprised. Bayway produced industry affidavits and standard forms from five petroleum firms showing that buyers ordinarily bore the taxes on their purchases.
sections.Issue: Who bears the burden of showing material alteration when an additional term appears in a merchant's acceptance under UCC section 2-207(2); whether the Tax Clause materially altered this contract because of its character, the buyer's surprise, or hardship; and whether the court could consider trade-practice affidavits first offered with Bayway's reply.
sections.Holding: The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, in 2000, in an opinion by Judge Jacobs for a panel with Chief Judge Winter and Judge Calabresi and no separate opinion, held that the party opposing inclusion of an additional term bears the burden of proving material alteration under section 2-207(2)(b). OMT did not establish that the Tax Clause was material per se or raise a genuine factual issue of surprise or hardship. Subjective surprise did not establish objective surprise where the term reflected unrebutted industry practice. The court expressly declined to decide whether hardship is an independent basis of material alteration. Receiving Bayway's reply evidence was within the district court's discretion. The judgment for Bayway was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning:
For purposes of the appeal, Bayway's fax was an effective acceptance under section 2-207(1), not one expressly conditioned on assent to its new terms, so the contract existed and section 2-207(2) governed which additional terms entered it. Both parties were merchants, and the only preserved exception was material alteration. Because the statute presumptively includes additional terms between merchants, the court reasoned that the party seeking an exception must show why that result should not follow; it treated this allocation as a substantive question of New York law in the diversity case. A footnote adds that Bayway still had to prove any trade usage on which it relied.

The court rejected the argument that the clause was inherently material as a broad indemnity. The duty concerned taxes on an identified sale, not a prolonged, unpredictable allocation of unrelated liabilities.

Surprise has an objective component. OMT's executives showed their personal surprise but offered nothing showing that the clause lay outside what a reasonable merchant in the trade should anticipate. Bayway's evidence positively showed the opposite: three comparison contracts allocated taxes like the clause, Chevron's form built the tax into the price, and Texaco's silence did not contradict the unrebutted affidavits. The buyer's ability to obtain the registration that avoided the tax supplied a practical reason for the allocation.

On hardship, OMT argued that it operated on thin margins. Even assuming hardship independently qualified, this liability was limited to one sale, commercially ordinary, and avoidable through registration.

On the reply evidence, OMT first raised material alteration in its opposition and criticized the lack of industry evidence; it requested no sur-reply and identified no contrary evidence it could have offered.

CT-CB-0290.rule: Under the majority knockout rule, which the court predicted Illinois would adopt for UCC section 2-207, conflicting terms in an offer and an acceptance that is not expressly conditional cancel each other out, and the Code's gap-filling provisions supply the term.

sections.Parties: Northrop, a defense manufacturer, bought electronic boards from Litronic for use in weapon systems and was the plaintiff. It sued to recover amounts paid for allegedly defective boards of two different specifications. Litronic, the seller and defendant, defended the claim concerning the No. 1714 boards on the ground that its ninety-day warranty had expired. Both sides appealed; Northrop's own appeal concerned a separate group of boards for which recovery had been denied.
sections.Procedural History: A magistrate judge awarded Northrop $58,000 for the delivered No. 1714 boards but denied recovery for a separate group of boards that the factfinder determined Northrop had not returned. Both sides appealed to the Seventh Circuit. The parties agreed that Illinois substantive law governed, and because Illinois courts had not chosen among the competing interpretations of different terms in section 2-207, the federal court had to predict Illinois law. It reviewed the finding that Northrop had not returned the other boards for clear error and found none. On July 18, 1994, the court affirmed the judgment on both appeals.
sections.Material Facts:
In 1987 Northrop requested bids for customized No. 1714 printed wire boards, stating that any purchase would use a Northrop purchase order whose terms would override inconsistent seller terms. Litronic offered four boards at $19,000 each with delivery in six weeks. Its form contained a ninety-day warranty in lieu of other warranties and a clause giving its terms priority over the buyer's unless separately negotiated.

Northrop's purchasing officer, Lynch, telephoned Litronic's representative, Lair, and accepted up to Lynch's $24,999 authority, indicating that a formal order for all four boards would follow. Litronic began manufacturing. A month later Northrop sent a 'turn on' letter authorizing all four boards. The formal order, which may not have been mailed until several months after the call, contained a warranty without a time limit and requested written acknowledgment. Litronic never signed and returned the acknowledgment, and Northrop did not pursue it.

Litronic delivered the first three boards in July 1988. Testing took months, and Northrop returned the three boards in December and January as defective. Litronic invoked its ninety-day limit; Northrop pointed to its unlimited warranty. The parties treated the warranty dispute as controlling the time allowed for rejection.
sections.Issue: Whether Northrop's oral acceptance, referring to its forthcoming form, created a contract while stating a warranty inconsistent with Litronic's offer; whether under the Illinois rule the court predicted, conflicting terms drop out, the offeror's terms prevail, or different terms are treated like additional terms; and whether Northrop could recover for boards it did not return without accounting for them.
sections.Holding: The United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit, in 1994, in a principal opinion by Chief Judge Posner with Judge Ripple writing separately, held that a contract existed and that Northrop's acceptance contained a different warranty term without being expressly conditioned on Litronic's agreement to it. The court predicted that Illinois would adopt the majority knockout approach, so the ninety-day and unlimited warranty provisions both dropped out, leaving a reasonable period supplied through the Code. Northrop's separate appeal failed because a buyer retaining rejected goods under a security interest must account for them. The judgment was affirmed on both appeals, leaving Northrop its $58,000 recovery.
sections.Reasoning:
Lynch's reference to the forthcoming Northrop form mattered because both parties knew, or should have known from prior dealings, that it contained a different warranty. But he did not make agreement contingent on Litronic's acceptance of that warranty, so a contract was formed under section 2-207(1) and the question of terms remained.

Subsection (1) mentions terms that are additional or different, while subsection (2) speaks only of additional terms. The court set out three responses: the knockout view, which removes the conflicting terms and uses a neutral Code rule; the view that the offeror's terms win; and a third view treating different terms like additional terms, so that materiality decides. Chief Judge Posner preferred the third, which here would have preserved Litronic's ninety-day limit, but that preference was not the holding. Illinois had followed majority approaches in other UCC disputes, and uniformity is a Code objective, so the court predicted it would adopt the prevalent knockout rule. The result gave Northrop only a reasonable period, and the complicated testing supported the six-month rejection period found reasonable below.

Litronic did not argue that its priority clause conditioned formation on acceptance of its warranty, so that argument was waived. The court added that treating the contract as formed by conduct under subsection (3) would lead to the same result.

As to the other boards, section 2-711(3) gave a security interest, but Northrop did not show what had happened to them, and recovering full payment without accounting risked double recovery.

Judge Ripple concurred in the judgment and in the prediction of Illinois law but declined to endorse an institutional view on which interpretation was best.

CT-CB-0294.rule: A seller may propose a contract whose written terms arrive with the product and invite acceptance by retention; a buyer who keeps the product beyond the stated return period after an opportunity to read the terms accepts them, including an arbitration clause.

sections.Parties: Rich and Enza Hill, the plaintiffs, bought a computer directly from Gateway 2000, Inc. They sued over its components and performance, alleging among other things mail and wire fraud as predicates for a RICO claim, and sought relief for themselves and a proposed class, including treble damages. Gateway, the defendant and the appellant, sought enforcement of the arbitration clause included in the documents shipped with the computer.
sections.Procedural History: The district court refused to enforce the arbitration clause because it considered the record insufficient to establish a valid agreement or adequate notice. Gateway immediately appealed under 9 U.S.C. section 16(a)(1)(A), which permits an appeal from denial of the specified arbitration relief; this was not review of a final adjudication of the product claims. On January 6, 1997, the Seventh Circuit vacated the district court's decision and remanded with instructions to compel the Hills to submit their dispute to arbitration. Rehearing was denied on February 3.
sections.Material Facts:
The Hills ordered the computer by telephone and gave a credit-card number. The computer arrived with a written statement of terms. The terms said they governed unless the buyer returned the computer within thirty days, and one term required arbitration. The Hills kept the computer for more than thirty days before complaining about its performance. They acknowledged noticing the statement of terms but said they had not read it closely enough to discover the arbitration clause.

Gateway also offered warranties, support and service, including a telephone hotline and advertised lifetime support. The Hills relied on the warranty in seeking a remedy and were dissatisfied with Gateway's response. Gateway's shipping carton did not display a notice of enclosed legal terms like the one on the retail software packaging in ProCD. The Hills nevertheless knew before ordering that important terms would accompany the product, because Gateway advertised limited warranties and lifetime support without stating every detail.
sections.Issue: Whether Gateway could propose a contract whose written terms were delivered with the computer and accepted by retention beyond a stated return period; whether the absence of oral recitation, actual reading, special prominence for arbitration, or notice on the carton defeated the agreement; and whether section 2-207 or the buyers' consumer status changed the result.
sections.Holding: The United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit, in 1997, in an opinion by Judge Easterbrook for a panel with Judges Cummings and Wood, Jr., and no separate opinion, held that a seller may make an accept-or-return proposal, provide terms with the product, and invite acceptance by keeping the product after an opportunity to read and reject them. The Hills' retention of the computer beyond thirty days was acceptance of Gateway's offer, including the arbitration clause. They could not invalidate the clause because it was not specially prominent or because they failed to read it, and the court treated section 2-207 as inapplicable to this one-form arrangement. The court vacated and remanded with instructions to compel arbitration.
sections.Reasoning:
The court applied its formation analysis from ProCD: commercial actors may design the mode of acceptance, and a buyer's initial payment can begin the transaction without foreclosing a later opportunity to accept or reject the full proposal. The enclosed terms were therefore not analyzed as an attempted modification of an existing bargain.

Practical considerations supported this. Requiring a telephone operator to read every term before taking an order would consume time without reliably communicating the content. ProCD was not limited to software; it concerned contract formation, and Gateway's computer in any event contained software.

The Hills admitted noticing the statement of terms, and a person who accepts a contractual document bears the risk of not reading it. Their demand that arbitration stand out sought special treatment for that kind of term, which the court rejected under section 2 of the FAA and Doctor's Associates v. Casarotto.

The buyers argued that their purchase, unlike the license in ProCD, was complete when the box arrived. The court distinguished formation from performance and noted that Gateway still owed warranty and support duties, which the Hills themselves invoked. To the argument that as consumers they were not bound by additional terms under section 2-207(2), the court answered that ProCD had not depended on merchant status and had declared section 2-207 irrelevant where there is only one form. The full brief notes this point is contested and was later challenged in Klocek.

A shipping carton, unlike retail packaging, generally addresses handlers after the order has been placed, so the lack of outside notice did not by itself distinguish the case; the court relied on the Hills' prior awareness that important terms would accompany the product. The court raised but did not decide the problem of return shipping expense. It cited Prima Paint and McMahon in rejecting the fraud and RICO objections to arbitration.

CT-CB-0298.rule: UCC section 2-207 applies even when only one written form is exchanged; where the buyer is the offeror and is not a merchant, terms enclosed with the goods are proposals for additional terms that bind the buyer only on express assent, not on mere retention.

sections.Parties: William S. Klocek, an unrepresented plaintiff, sued Gateway, Inc. over a computer and technical-support package and Hewlett-Packard over a scanner. He alleged that Gateway made false technical-support promises and breached contract and warranty duties, and that Hewlett-Packard failed to warn that its scanner was incompatible with Gateway computers. He sought to proceed individually and for a class. Gateway, a defendant, sought dismissal based on an arbitration provision; Hewlett-Packard separately challenged subject-matter jurisdiction.
sections.Procedural History: Klocek sued in the United States District Court for the District of Kansas, a diversity action. Gateway moved to dismiss the claims as arbitrable, Hewlett-Packard moved to dismiss for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, and Klocek filed motions for class certification and other relief. On June 15, 2000, Judge Kathryn H. Vratil denied Gateway's motion to dismiss, allowing Gateway to submit a factually supported supplemental motion if it contended that another state's law controlled. The court granted Hewlett-Packard's motion and denied Klocek's motions for class certification, sanctions and related relief, a writ of certiorari, and verification concerning a disciplinary complaint. This is a district court order; it did not decide the merits of Klocek's claims.
sections.Material Facts:
Gateway routinely enclosed four pages of Standard Terms with its computers. A prominently boxed notice stated that retaining the computer more than five days after delivery constituted acceptance. Paragraph ten required binding arbitration in Chicago before a single arbitrator under International Chamber of Commerce rules. Gateway relied on Klocek's continued possession of the computer as his assent.

The record did not reliably establish how or where the sale occurred. Gateway submitted an affidavit saying it shipped a computer to Klocek on or about August 31, 1997, with few details. Klocek said he bought the computer in person at the Gateway store in Overland Park, Kansas, on August 27 and took it with him. He lived in Missouri. The court did not select either account as proven.

Gateway produced no evidence that, at the time of sale, it told Klocek the transaction was conditioned on the enclosed terms, that he agreed to a five-day review-and-return mechanism, or that the parties contemplated later-supplied terms. The court had proof of a sale through payment and receipt.
sections.Issue: Whether shipment and retention of a computer established assent to an arbitration term enclosed with it; whether section 2-207 was inapplicable because there was only one written form; whether Gateway could be presumed the offeror with power to postpone formation until the review period expired; and whether its insert made acceptance expressly conditional on the buyer's assent.
sections.Holding: The United States District Court for the District of Kansas, in 2000, Judge Kathryn H. Vratil, held that Gateway had not shown that the parties agreed to arbitrate. On the assumed Kansas or Missouri analysis, the purchaser ordinarily makes the offer and the seller accepts by completing the sale, agreeing to ship, or shipping. The enclosed terms were an acceptance or confirmation containing additional terms governed by section 2-207, which does not require two competing forms. Gateway did not establish an expressly conditional acceptance, and because Klocek was not a merchant the additional terms required his express assent, which keeping the computer beyond five days did not supply. Gateway's motion to dismiss was denied.
sections.Reasoning:
The FAA enforces agreements; it does not create them. The court first had to decide, under ordinary state-law principles, whether an arbitration agreement was formed, and Gateway bore an initial burden, similar to that on summary judgment, of presenting evidence of one. Because Gateway did not establish where the contract was formed, a definitive choice of law was impossible, but Kansas and Missouri both applied Article 2 and appeared not to differ materially.

Klocek paid for and received a computer, which showed a sale. Gateway could not simply label its later insert the offer and assume no contract existed until five days passed. A seller is sometimes the offeror, but not automatically; ordinary purchase orders are offers that a vendor accepts by agreeing to ship or shipping.

Hill and ProCD had called section 2-207 irrelevant where only one form is exchanged. Judge Vratil rejected that reading: the statute expressly includes a written confirmation, and its commentary describes an oral agreement followed by one or both parties' written memoranda adding previously undiscussed terms.

The proviso in section 2-207(1) requires a seller to communicate clearly that it is unwilling to proceed without assent to its additional terms. Gateway offered no evidence of such a communication at the sale, and shipping the product with a statement of conditions did not suffice. Under section 2-207(2), additional terms are not automatically included against a nonmerchant, and Gateway could not prove acceptance by relying on a provision in the same unaccepted document saying retention would count.

Separately, Klocek had not shown the jurisdictional amount against Hewlett-Packard, and as a nonlawyer proceeding pro se he could not represent a class.

CT-CB-0304.rule: An online contract requires reasonable notice of the terms and a reasonable manifestation of assent to them, and the party seeking to enforce the contract bears the burden of showing both.

sections.Parties: Christopher and Hannah Kauders, the plaintiffs, sued Uber Technologies and its wholly owned subsidiary Rasier, alleging that three Uber drivers refused Christopher rides because of his disability and guide dog. Uber, the appellant, sought to enforce an arbitration clause in the terms linked from its rider registration process. The plaintiffs objected that no agreement had formed.
sections.Procedural History: The plaintiffs filed in Superior Court in July 2016. Uber moved to compel arbitration in June 2017, and the judge compelled it without analyzing formation. Arbitration ended with an award for Uber on June 4, 2018. Three weeks later the First Circuit held in Cullinane that the same registration process did not give adequate notice under Massachusetts law. Uber moved to confirm in September; the plaintiffs moved for reconsideration in November. On January 2, 2019, the judge vacated his original order, denied arbitration, and denied confirmation. Uber appealed, and the Supreme Judicial Court transferred the appeal to itself. It concluded that no enforceable agreement existed and that the dispute was not arbitrable, and remanded for further proceedings.
sections.Material Facts:
Christopher Kauders was blind and used a guide dog. He registered on June 27, 2014; Hannah registered around October 2015. Christopher's mobile registration involved three dark-background screens. The first, CREATE AN ACCOUNT, and the second, CREATE A PROFILE, requested contact and identifying information and used a NEXT button; neither directed the user to contractual terms.

The third screen, LINK PAYMENT, had a white credit-card field at the top, scan-your-card and promo-code options below it, and a prominent PayPal button in the middle. At the bottom was a sentence stating that creating an account meant agreeing to the Terms & Conditions and Privacy Policy; the words explaining the legal significance were less prominent than the linked terms. Reaching the terms required clicking the link and then clicking again. Entering a credit-card number brought up a keypad that moved the notice toward the middle. The final button said DONE.

The terms purported to permit amendment without notice, disclaim liability and warranties, require indemnification, permit extensive collection of user information, and require arbitration. In the compelled arbitration, the arbitrator found discriminatory acts by drivers but ruled for Uber because the drivers were independent contractors.
sections.Issue: Did Uber's rider registration interface give reasonable notice of its terms and obtain a reasonable manifestation of assent, so as to form a contract containing an arbitration agreement? Separately, could the trial judge reconsider his order compelling arbitration after the arbitration was complete and the period for challenging the award had expired?
sections.Holding: Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court, 2021, in an opinion by Justice Kafker, with no separate writing. Uber's rider registration interface did not create an enforceable agreement with the Kauderses: there was neither reasonable notice of the terms nor a reasonable manifestation of assent. The dispute therefore was not arbitrable. The court also held that the trial judge should have confirmed the award and that allowing reconsideration in these circumstances was an abuse of discretion, but it reached the preserved formation question itself for judicial economy.
sections.Reasoning:
On procedure, the court explained that under the Massachusetts Arbitration Act an order compelling arbitration is not immediately appealable; a resisting party preserves its objection and obtains review after confirmation. Vacatur for lack of agreement is unavailable when the issue was already decided adversely in the proceedings to compel. After completed arbitration and expiration of the thirty-day challenge period, the statutory scheme constrained the judge's ordinary authority to correct interlocutory rulings. Because a remand to confirm would simply bring the same briefed issue back, the court decided formation at once.

Arbitration policy cannot supply missing consent; ordinary state contract principles decide whether a contract exists. The court adopted two requirements for online agreements, reasonable notice and reasonable manifestation of assent, with the burden on Uber. It did not impose a separate requirement that notice be conspicuous. Actual notice suffices; otherwise the court looks to the totality of the circumstances, including the kind and size of transaction, whether the interface looks contractual, the placement of terms, the steps needed to reach them, and clarity about the consequences of the user's action. An I agree button is a strong signal of assent but not indispensable.

Both requirements failed. Registration described arrangements for future small ride transactions and did not alert users to sweeping liability, data, indemnity, and arbitration terms. The screen steered attention to the payment field and other prominent features. DONE signaled completion of payment information, and a user could finish without opening or acknowledging the terms. Uber's driver interfaces, which required affirmative acceptance and a second confirmation, showed that clear assent was achievable.

CT-CB-0314.rule: A user who lacks actual notice of online terms is bound if a reasonably prudent user would be on inquiry notice of them through reasonably conspicuous notice and the user unambiguously manifests assent, even without clicking a button labeled I agree.

sections.Parties: Spencer Meyer, the plaintiff and appellee, brought a putative class action against Travis Kalanick, Uber's cofounder and former chief executive, alleging that the Uber application enabled drivers to fix prices in violation of federal and New York antitrust statutes. Uber Technologies was later joined as a necessary party. Kalanick and Uber, the appellants, sought to compel arbitration under Uber's terms.
sections.Procedural History: Meyer sued in December 2015. The district court denied Kalanick's dismissal motion and joined Uber. After discovery began, both defendants moved to compel arbitration. The district court denied the motions, finding insufficient notice and assent, and did not reach waiver or Kalanick's ability to enforce terms he had not signed. The defendants took an interlocutory appeal under 9 U.S.C. § 16. The Second Circuit vacated the denial and remanded for the district court to decide whether the defendants' litigation conduct waived arbitration.
sections.Material Facts:
On October 18, 2014, Meyer registered for Uber on a Samsung Galaxy S5 running Android and later took ten rides. The first registration screen requested name, email, telephone number, and password; he entered them and clicked Next. The second screen, Payment, requested credit-card details or permitted PayPal or Google Wallet. He entered his credit card and clicked REGISTER in the middle of the screen.

Directly below the registration controls was a statement that creating an Uber account meant agreeing to the TERMS OF SERVICE & PRIVACY POLICY. That phrase was bright blue and underlined, linking to another screen with a button through which the terms could be opened. The whole payment screen was visible without scrolling, with a white background, dark text, and few items.

The terms called for binding arbitration of disputes relating to the agreement or service and waived jury trial and class participation. Meyer did not recall seeing the link and declared that he had not read the terms. The material facts, drawn from an Uber engineer's declaration and screenshots, were undisputed.
sections.Issue: Under California contract law, did the registration interface give Meyer reasonably conspicuous notice of Uber's terms, and did his clicking REGISTER objectively manifest assent to them, so that an agreement to arbitrate was formed even though he had no actual awareness of the terms?
sections.Holding: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, 2017, in an opinion by Judge Chin for a panel of Judges Raggi, Chin, and Carney, with no concurrence or dissent. The interface gave reasonably conspicuous notice of the terms, and registering objectively manifested assent under California law. Formation was established as a matter of law on the undisputed record. The court vacated the denial of the motions to compel arbitration and remanded for the district court to decide waiver. In a footnote it also held that Kalanick could rely on the agreement although he was a nonsignatory.
sections.Reasoning:
The Federal Arbitration Act puts arbitration agreements on the same footing as other contracts but does not force arbitration without agreement, and state contract law decides whether an agreement exists. Mutual assent is objective. An offeree without actual awareness can be bound if a reasonably prudent user would be on inquiry notice and unambiguously manifests assent; for apps this depends on the design and content of the interface. Because the screenshots and registration evidence were undisputed and no trial had been held, review was de novo.

The court rejected the argument that a general allegation in Meyer's complaint conceded his consent. It took the perspective of a reasonably prudent smartphone user, who is not assumed to be unfamiliar with apps or blue underlined hyperlinks. The notice sat directly below the registration button, its dark text contrasted with the white background, the hyperlink was distinct, and no scrolling was needed. The court contrasted the cluttered Amazon page in Nicosia and emphasized the spatial and temporal connection between notice and registration. Access by hyperlink did not defeat notice, and the arbitration clause's place within lengthy terms did not defeat formation; the court distinguished Sgouros.

Express assent was unnecessary because the interface unambiguously connected REGISTER to the terms, and the difference between the words creating and register did not obscure that. Kalanick could rely on the agreement under authority protecting employees or disclosed agents of a contracting entity. Waiver founded on litigation conduct can be decided by the district judge, so the court remanded that question without deciding it.

CT-CB-0328.rule: Under Restatement (First) of Contracts § 90, a promise that foreseeably and actually induces definite and substantial reliance supports relief where injustice requires it, even if the promise lacks the terms needed for an enforceable contract.

sections.Parties: Joseph Hoffman and his wife, the plaintiffs, operated a bakery in Wautoma, Wisconsin, and sought a Red Owl grocery franchise. They sued Red Owl Stores, Inc. and its representative, Lukowitz, for losses incurred in reliance on assurances made during franchise negotiations. Red Owl appealed liability and all damage items; the Hoffmans cross-appealed the order for a partial new trial.
sections.Procedural History: A special verdict found the necessary representations, reliance in the exercise of ordinary care, and fulfillment of the conditions demanded of Hoffman. The jury assessed $16,735 for the grocery sale, $2,000 for the bakery loss, $1,000 for the lot payment, $140 in moving expenses, and $125 in rent. The trial court upheld the latter four items but ordered a new trial on the grocery-sale damages. Red Owl appealed and the Hoffmans cross-appealed. The Wisconsin Supreme Court affirmed the order, leaving the four amounts intact and the grocery-sale damages for a new trial.
sections.Material Facts:
The brief takes the detailed chronology from the casebook's editorial introduction. Beginning in 1959, Hoffman discussed a Red Owl franchise and explained that he had only $18,000 to invest; Lukowitz repeatedly assured him that this would suffice. In February 1961 Hoffman bought a small grocery store to gain experience. In June, on Lukowitz's advice, he sold it, having been told that Red Owl would establish him in a larger store.

In September, on Red Owl's advice, he paid $1,000 toward a lot in Chilton. Red Owl then urged sale of the bakery building as the last necessary step; it sold in November at a $2,000 loss. Hoffman rented a home in Chilton for one month at $125, and the family moved to Neenah at a cost of $140.

Red Owl's financing requirements kept increasing, from $18,000 to $24,100 and, in a final proposed statement, to $34,000, including $13,000 from his father-in-law as a gift, which Hoffman refused. Talks collapsed without agreement on the building's size, cost, design, and layout or on lease terms.
sections.Issue: Should Wisconsin recognize Restatement § 90 promissory estoppel as an affirmative basis for relief? Can it apply although negotiations were incomplete and the promises were not definite enough to form a contract? Were the damage awards supported?
sections.Holding: Wisconsin Supreme Court, 1965, in an opinion by Chief Justice Currie, with no concurrence or dissent reproduced. The court recognized promissory estoppel under Restatement (First) of Contracts § 90 and sustained liability for promises that induced substantial detrimental reliance during franchise negotiations. The promises did not need to contain every term necessary for an enforceable franchise agreement. Relief is shaped to prevent injustice rather than to give the value of a completed bargain. The court affirmed the order, including a new trial confined to damages from the sale of the grocery inventory and fixtures.
sections.Reasoning:
Wisconsin had approached § 90 in earlier cases without squarely adopting it, and the court now endorsed it as a needed means of preventing injustice from induced reliance. Fraud was not an adequate alternative, because a promise of future performance supports fraud only if made with a present intention not to perform, and the record did not show that.

Under § 90 as adopted, the promise must foreseeably induce action or forbearance of a definite and substantial character, must actually induce it, and enforcement must be needed to prevent injustice. The first two questions ordinarily belong to the jury; the third is a judicial policy judgment that includes discretion about remedy. The court rejected the argument that the promise must be as comprehensive as an offer. Earlier uses of promissory estoppel often supplied consideration for an otherwise complete gratuitous promise, but § 90 is not so limited, and treating it as identical to breach of contract would deny relief precisely because details remained unresolved.

On damages, the bakery loss was supported, including the wife's half, because Red Owl had foreseen and requested sale of her jointly owned interest. The $1,000 was paid toward the lot's price, the record showed no foreclosure of Hoffman's equity, and avoiding the loss did not reasonably require paying another $5,000. The rent and moving costs were proper reliance losses. The grocery-sale award lacked proof of fair market value, and anticipated profits were not recoverable as though a franchise contract had been breached; the appropriate loss was the proven fair-market-value shortfall from the induced sale.

CT-CB-0333.rule: As a federal court predicted Massachusetts law, a lender's promise to consider a borrower for a loan modification that induces the borrower to default can support a promissory-estoppel claim despite indefinite modification terms, with relief aimed at restoring the position lost through reliance.

sections.Parties: Frank and Deana Dixon, the plaintiffs, owned and lived in a mortgaged home in Scituate, Massachusetts. The defendant was Wells Fargo Bank, N.A.; the alleged conduct involved its predecessor Wachovia Mortgage, a federal savings bank. The Dixons sought an injunction against foreclosure, specific performance, and damages. The bank sought dismissal, arguing that an indefinite agreement to agree creates no legal obligation and that federal banking law preempted the state claim.
sections.Procedural History: The Dixons sued in Massachusetts Superior Court on January 6, 2011. The state court issued a preliminary injunction on February 14. The bank removed the case to federal court on March 4 and moved to dismiss on April 11. At a May 9 hearing, Judge William G. Young denied the Dixons' motion to remand and dismissed their ordinary contract claim as insufficiently pleaded, reserving the sufficiency of their reliance theory and the bank's preemption defense under the Home Owners' Loan Act (HOLA) for supplemental briefing. The July 22, 2011 opinion decided those remaining issues: the court denied the bank's remaining request for dismissal and placed the case on the September trial list.
sections.Material Facts:
The facts are the complaint's allegations, which the court assumed true for the motion to dismiss. On or about June 8, 2009, the Dixons and the bank orally agreed to take the steps necessary for a mortgage modification. The bank told them to stop making payments and to submit financial information. They promptly supplied the information and stopped paying, understanding that the missed installments would be added to the modified loan. The bank then failed or effectively refused to follow through and instead proceeded toward foreclosure. On December 8, 2010, the Dixons received notice of a Land Court foreclosure proceeding with a January 10, 2011 return date. They alleged on information and belief that their home's value exceeded the balance and arrears.

In opposing dismissal the Dixons clarified that the promise they sought to enforce was a promise to consider them for a modification and to engage in negotiations after they took the requested steps, not a promise of a completed new loan.
sections.Issue: Whether reliance on a bank's promise to consider or negotiate a mortgage modification could be actionable under Massachusetts law even though the parties had not specified the essential terms of a new loan; and whether enforcing that voluntarily made promise imposed a state lending regulation preempted by HOLA.
sections.Holding: The United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts, in 2011, Judge William G. Young, held that the complaint plausibly stated a promissory-estoppel claim and that this particular claim was not preempted by HOLA. The court denied the bank's remaining request for dismissal and placed the case on the September trial list. It awarded no damages and made no finding that the bank was liable; whether the promise, reasonable reliance and injury could be proved remained for trial. The opinion did not reinstate the previously dismissed contract claim, and it is a federal district court's application and prediction of state law.
sections.Reasoning:
Massachusetts treats a promise enforceable because of reliance as contractual in character, requiring the elements of a contract other than consideration, including a genuine commitment. Courts generally will not enforce an agreement whose essential terms are left for future agreement, and Judge Young acknowledged that a promise of a completed modification would ordinarily fail on that ground.

The clarified claim was narrower. The bank allegedly induced the Dixons to stop paying and then took advantage of the resulting default without honestly considering the promised modification. Enforcing a duty to deal honestly after inducing that change of position does not compel either side to accept unspecified loan terms. The court drew on Massachusetts cases, including Greenstein, McLearn and Cohoon, for the concern that a party should not induce a predictable loss of position and then exploit it by disavowing its undertaking. It did not recognize a general duty to negotiate in good faith whenever negotiations begin, and it did not require proof of fraudulent intent. It acknowledged uncertainty in Massachusetts precedent and said it would entertain a request for certification.

Remedy was part of the answer to indefiniteness: relief would protect the position the borrowers lost by following the bank's instructions, not give them the benefit of an unformed agreement. A footnote illustrated, without ordering, restoring the loan to nondefault status by amortizing the missed payments.

On preemption, under 12 C.F.R. section 560.2 state contract and tort laws survive when they only incidentally affect lending. The claim held the bank to its own voluntary undertaking rather than prescribing loan terms or requiring modifications generally, so it affected lending only incidentally.

CT-CB-0340.rule: Under New York law, promissory estoppel requires a clear and unambiguous promise, reasonable and foreseeable reliance, and injury from that reliance, and it can support reliance damages, including properly attributable overhead, even though the parties never formed the contemplated contract.

sections.Parties: Cyberchron Corp., the plaintiff, made specialized computer equipment. Calldata Systems Development, Inc., the defendant, was a Grumman subsidiary developing a system for the Marine Corps and wanted Cyberchron to supply workstation components. Cyberchron appealed to seek recovery under a termination-liability provision and fuller reliance damages. Calldata cross-appealed, challenging the availability and scope of promissory estoppel.
sections.Procedural History: After a bench trial in the Eastern District of New York, Judge Arthur Spatt rejected Cyberchron's contract claim, Calldata's contractual counterclaim, and Cyberchron's quantum-meruit claim; neither side appealed those rulings. The trial court awarded Cyberchron reliance damages on promissory estoppel for materials and direct labor from July 15 to September 25, 1990. The September 1, 1993 judgment was $162,824.19, with prejudgment interest from December 18, 1990. It excluded overhead and lost profits and did not address shutdown expenses. Both sides appealed. In 1995 the Second Circuit affirmed the determination that Cyberchron could recover on promissory estoppel, rejected independent recovery under the termination-liability provision, and vacated the judgment and remanded for a redetermination of damages.
sections.Material Facts:
The proposed transaction involved three components with a maximum combined weight of 145 pounds and penalties for excess weight. The weight specification and penalties were disputed throughout; Cyberchron never accepted them, no purchase contract was formed, and no equipment was delivered or paid for.

A May 15, 1990 purchase order included a termination-liability provision limiting Calldata's exposure to $200,000; a June modification raised the limit to $700,000. The provision reserved to Grumman the power to delete it unilaterally.

Beginning in mid-July 1990, Grumman's Wilhelm told Cyberchron to proceed as if the weights were approved and that the differences would be resolved later, and repeatedly pressed it to continue and meet the delivery deadline. Cyberchron asked for written confirmation and did not get it, but received further directions to proceed. Cyberchron requested a progress payment on July 30 and received none. During August Calldata explored an alternative supplier, Codar, while still pressing Cyberchron to perform. Calldata issued a show-cause notice on September 6, terminated for asserted default on September 25, and contracted with Codar the next day. The record indicated that Codar's equipment was heavier and inferior.
sections.Issue: Whether Cyberchron could recover independently under the termination-liability provision; whether, although no contract was formed, Calldata's assurances supported recovery under New York promissory estoppel and for what period; and whether reliance damages could include overhead and shutdown expenses.
sections.Holding: The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, in 1995, in an opinion by Judge Mahoney for a panel with Judges Walker and Sprouse and no separate opinion, held that Cyberchron was entitled to recover on promissory estoppel for the period from July 15 to September 25, 1990, and that the termination-liability provision supplied no independent recovery. It rejected the trial court's categorical exclusion of overhead and directed consideration of shutdown expenses caused by the reliance. The court affirmed liability and vacated the judgment for a redetermination of damages, which the district court could make on additional evidence or the existing record. It set no replacement dollar amount.
sections.Reasoning:
The court first rejected Calldata's argument that the claim under the termination-liability provision had been abandoned, but rejected the claim on the merits. The provision contemplated termination of a valid purchase order, and none existed because essential terms were unsettled. Grumman's reserved power to delete the clause also prevented treating it as a clear promise on which Cyberchron reasonably relied.

The court stated New York's requirements as a clear and unambiguous promise, reasonable and foreseeable reliance, and injury caused by the reliance, and noted authorities also requiring unconscionable injury. Without resolving the differences among those formulations, it concluded the trial findings satisfied both. The directions to proceed as though the weight issue were resolved, with repeated pressure to meet the deadline, supported a clear promise. Calldata's continued pressure while seeking another supplier, followed by termination, supported the finding of unconscionable injury. July 15 was properly the start of the reliance period, since earlier expenses could not be attributed to the assurances.

Calldata urged a reading of Swerdloff confining promissory estoppel to categories such as charitable contributions and marriage settlements. The court treated that formulation as dictum inconsistent with later New York authority. It also refused to end the damages period at the August 28 delivery date.

On damages, the court agreed with a reliance measure but held that overhead is a real cost. If Cyberchron could establish an appropriate share of actual overhead attributable to the induced work, by operating history and normal allocation methods, it could be recovered without proof of a particular lost alternative project. Shutdown costs after September 25 were recoverable only so far as caused by the reliance beginning in July. Lost profits were not the basis of the relief.

CT-CB-0345.rule: An express agreement to negotiate in good faith is enforceable, even though the ultimate contract is unfinished, if the parties manifested an intent to be bound by it, its terms are sufficiently definite, and it is supported by consideration.

sections.Parties: Channel Home Centers, a division of Grace Retail Corp. that operated home-improvement stores, was the plaintiff and the appellant. It sued for breach of a signed letter of intent and sought preliminary relief. The defendant side was developer Frank Grossman, who with his sons controlled the entities acquiring and leasing Cedarbrook Mall in Cheltenham Township, near Philadelphia. Grossman maintained that an agreement to negotiate was unenforceable without agreement on the underlying transaction and that Channel had supplied no consideration.
sections.Procedural History: Channel filed a diversity action on February 15, 1985 in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania. A temporary restraining order protected its position pending a February 25 preliminary-injunction hearing, which lasted about ten minutes. Without advance notice, the district court treated that hearing as a trial on the merits under Rule 65(a)(2), denied relief, and entered judgment against Channel on March 26, concluding that the letter lacked binding intent and consideration and did not satisfy the statute of frauds for a lease. On reconsideration, on May 7, the court adhered to its judgment but offered another evidentiary hearing if Channel requested it within fifteen days; Channel did not. Channel appealed. The Third Circuit reversed the judgment and remanded for a full trial.
sections.Material Facts:
After a November 28, 1984 tour, Channel's officers indicated interest in leasing space in Cedarbrook Mall, where Channel would be a fourth anchor store. Grossman requested a letter of intent that he could show banks or others. Channel prepared and signed a detailed letter dated December 11, which Grossman promptly signed and returned. It described approximately 70,400 square feet, a twenty-five-year term, rents and other terms; execution of a mutually satisfactory lease remained subject to approval by Channel's corporate parent, satisfactory title, and sign permits or variances. The letter stated that, to induce Channel to proceed, Grossman would withdraw the store from the rental market and negotiate only the described transaction to completion.

Channel had its parent's legal department prepare the lease, obtained its real-estate committee's approval, and indicated expenditures of about $25,000. On January 11, 1985 its lawyer sent a forty-one-page draft lease. Mr. Good Buys, a direct competitor of Channel, contacted Grossman around January 22 and toured the space on January 25. On February 6 Grossman announced that negotiations had terminated because Channel had not submitted a signed, mutually acceptable lease within thirty days of the letter. The letter contained no thirty-day deadline, and Channel's officers denied orally agreeing to one. On February 7 Grossman executed a lease with Mr. Good Buys at substantially higher base rents.
sections.Issue: Whether, under Pennsylvania law, a signed letter of intent in which a developer promised to withdraw premises from the rental market and negotiate only the described lease to completion can be an enforceable agreement to negotiate in good faith, although it does not bind the parties to the final lease, and whether the prospective tenant supplied consideration for that promise.
sections.Holding: The Third Circuit in 1986, in an opinion by Judge Becker for himself and Judges Weis and Higginbotham, held that the record could support a binding agreement to negotiate in good faith, that the described negotiation promise was sufficiently definite, and that the asserted exchange supplied consideration. It predicted that Pennsylvania would enforce such an agreement if it otherwise satisfied the requirements for a contract. It reversed and remanded for a full trial. At least two issues remained for the factfinder: whether the parties actually intended to bind themselves to the preliminary agreement, and whether they agreed to a thirty-day time limit. The court did not award possession, damages, or specific performance of a lease.
sections.Reasoning:
No Pennsylvania court had squarely considered an agreement to negotiate, so the court looked to contract principles and decisions from other jurisdictions and predicted that Pennsylvania would enforce one that showed manifested intent to be bound, sufficiently definite terms, and consideration. The holding concerns an expressly undertaken negotiation obligation, not a universal duty of good faith at every precontractual stage.

The district court had focused on the wrong potential contract. Channel conceded the letter was not a completed lease, so the statute of frauds governing leases and the final transaction's contingencies did not defeat the narrower promise to withdraw the premises from the market and negotiate exclusively. On intent, the explicit exclusivity language, the parties' reciprocal efforts to satisfy contingencies, and the letter's detail could support a finding that the preliminary commitment was meant to bind; the court did not hold that the evidence compelled that finding. On consideration, a bargained-for benefit need not be a cash payment. Grossman wanted a signed letter to help obtain financing, and Channel executed and delivered it in return for his promise.

The court did not reach the alternative unilateral-contract and promissory-estoppel theories. It strongly disapproved of converting the preliminary hearing into a trial without notice, but held that Channel waived that objection by not using the later offered hearing or asking for discovery. If there was no fixed deadline, a reasonable time would apply.

CT-CB-0353.rule: Where parties leave for future agreement both a price and the length of time that price will govern, a price ceiling alone does not complete the bargain; the court will not supply the missing duration, and the arrangement is an unenforceable agreement to agree.

sections.Parties: Sun Printing & Publishing Association, the buyer of newsprint, was the plaintiff; it sued for the damage caused by nondelivery and moved for judgment on the pleadings. Remington Paper & Power Co., the seller, was the defendant and the appellant in the Court of Appeals. Remington argued that neither the price nor the term for which a price would govern had been settled and that the court could not make those agreements for the parties.
sections.Procedural History: The case arose on the complaint and the buyer's motion for judgment on the pleadings, not on trial findings. Special Term denied the buyer's motion. The Appellate Division reversed and granted it. The seller took a permitted appeal to the New York Court of Appeals on the certified question whether the complaint stated facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action. The Court of Appeals reversed the Appellate Division, affirmed Special Term's denial of the buyer's motion, awarded the stated appellate costs, and answered the certified question in the negative.
sections.Material Facts:
Sun Printing agreed to buy, and Remington agreed to sell, 1,000 tons of newsprint each month from September 1919 through December 1920, a total of 16,000 tons. The writing specified the paper's sizes and quality and payment terms. The price for September was $3.73 3/4 per hundred pounds and for October through December 1919 was $4. Those four months were performed and paid for.

For the remaining twelve months, the parties agreed to fix both the price and the length of time for which that price would apply, fifteen days before each previously established period expired. The new price could never exceed the contract price charged to large consumers by the Canadian Export Paper Company, adjusted for freight differentials. The benchmark limited price but did not specify the duration of each pricing period.

Before the time for the next agreement arrived, Remington announced that the arrangement was incomplete and disclaimed an obligation to deliver more paper. Sun Printing demanded 1,000 tons during each month of 1920 at the Canadian company's then-current contract price, adjusted for freight, renewed the demand month by month until the year ended, and sued. Market prices rose during 1920.
sections.Issue: Whether a complaint states a cause of action for nondelivery where the contract left both the price and the length of time that price would govern to be fixed by later agreement, subject only to a maximum price tied to another company's contract price, and the buyer demanded delivery at that maximum.
sections.Holding: The New York Court of Appeals in 1923, in an opinion by Judge Cardozo joined by Chief Judge Hiscock and Judges Pound, McLaughlin, and Andrews, with Judges Crane and Hogan dissenting, a five-to-two decision, held that the complaint did not state a cause of action. On the complaint before the court, the arrangement for the remaining twelve months was an agreement to agree, because the parties had named a maximum price but had not agreed on how long a fixed price would last. The decision concerns the complaint actually presented; the buyer could amend its pleading.
sections.Reasoning:
Cardozo distinguished two subjects reserved for future agreement: the price and the interval during which it would remain fixed. If price alone had remained open, the ceiling might have supported treating the buyer as having an option to demand delivery at the maximum. But determining a price at one point does not decide how long it will govern, and the length of the period allocates market risk: if the Canadian price rose after a period began the seller stayed bound to the lower price, and if it fell the buyer stayed bound to the higher one.

The buyer asserted an option, not an obligation to take the Canadian price for the year. Without agreed periods, its reading would give it successive monthly choices, and nothing showed Remington had agreed to that. Adding monthly terms, a reasonable term from trade practice, or a fluctuating price would revise the bargain rather than interpret it.

The majority left open two points. The buyer had not pleaded that the Canadian price was itself fixed for the whole year and could amend. The court also did not decide whether an arbitrary refusal to agree on duration might breach a duty had the buyer offered to let the seller divide the terms as it chose.

Judge Crane, dissenting, would have given effect to the evident intention to make a binding agreement. He treated the Canadian contract price as an intelligible standard and proposed several ways to resolve duration, including monthly periods or a reasonable period.

CT-CB-0366.rule: When parties intend to remain bound by a long-term contract and the agreed mechanisms for setting the price fail, a court may supply a reasonable price supported by the evidence and may order continued performance where future damages would be too speculative.

sections.Parties: Oglebay Norton Co., which maintained shipping capacity to carry Armco's iron ore on the Great Lakes, sought declaratory relief when the parties could no longer agree on a shipping rate. Armco, Inc., the customer obliged to use that capacity, counterclaimed for a declaration that the agreement was unenforceable. In the Ohio Supreme Court, Armco challenged the judgment in Oglebay's favor.
sections.Procedural History: Oglebay sought declaratory relief in April 1986, and Armco eventually counterclaimed for a declaration that the agreement was unenforceable; the parties continued to perform while the dispute was pending. After trial, the court fixed a rate of $6.25 per gross ton for the 1986 season. For future seasons it required the parties to notify it if they could not agree, in which case it would appoint a mediator and require the chief executives to meet to establish a rate. The court of appeals affirmed. Armco challenged the finding of continuing contractual intent, the authority and evidentiary basis for the 1986 price, and the continuing equitable arrangement through 2010. The Ohio Supreme Court affirmed on all three questions.
sections.Material Facts:
A 1957 agreement required Oglebay to maintain shipping capacity for Armco's iron ore on the Great Lakes and required Armco to use it. The price was first to be the regular seasonal net contract rate recognized by leading iron ore shippers. If no such rate existed, the parties were to agree on a rate, taking into account rates charged for similar transportation by leading independent vessel operators.

According to the casebook's introductory account, the agreement was modified four times over the next twenty-three years, each time extending the relationship and requiring substantial investment by Oglebay. After the fourth extension, which ran through 2010, Oglebay began a $95 million capital-improvement program. Through 1983 the parties used a rate published in Skillings Mining Review. After an industry downturn they negotiated a 1984 rate, but later could not agree.

By the relevant period no new published benchmark was available, and Armco maintained that independent operators' rates were no longer publicly available; the trial court had quashed subpoenas seeking that information from nonparties. The parties had a long and close relationship, including joint ventures, interlocking directorates, and Armco's stock ownership in Oglebay.
sections.Issue: Whether the parties intended to remain bound when both agreed pricing mechanisms failed; whether the trial court had authority to set a reasonable shipping rate outside those mechanisms and whether its 1986 rate was supported; and whether the court could retain equitable jurisdiction and order negotiation and mediation over future seasons' rates.
sections.Holding: The Ohio Supreme Court in 1990, in a per curiam opinion joined by all seven justices with no separate opinion, affirmed. It held that competent, credible evidence supported the finding that the parties intended to remain bound despite the failure of the pricing mechanisms; that the trial court could fill the price gap with a reasonable rate and that $6.25 per gross ton for 1986 was a reasonable rate supported by the evidence; and that the trial court properly retained continuing equitable jurisdiction, ordering negotiation and mediation when the parties could not agree on future rates.
sections.Reasoning:
The court treated these as mixed questions of fact and law and asked whether competent, credible evidence supported the critical findings. Intent to remain bound was a factual question. The long and close relationship, and the agreement's recognition of Armco's vital and unique interest in having Oglebay's bulk fleet dedicated to its needs, supported the finding that the dedicated capacity and ongoing relationship were the central undertaking and that the pricing provisions served it. The court did not announce that a failed benchmark always permits judicial substitution regardless of intent.

On authority to set a price, the court approved use of Restatement (Second) of Contracts section 33 and its comments, under which a binding bargain can be made definite through usage, course of dealing, or a term supplied by law; it noted the parallel to UCC section 2-305 and Ohio authority applying the open-price principle by analogy to service contracts. The trial court's rate of $6 plus twenty-five cents for self-unloading vessels fell within a range of evidence running from $5 to $7.44.

On the equitable order, Restatement section 362 requires sufficiently certain terms but directs courts to use supplied terms first. Specific performance was justified because market changes and the agreement's long duration made future damages too speculative, and a 1962 amendment had given Armco itself a right to specific performance. Negotiation and mediation neither added to nor subtracted from the parties' obligations.

CT-CB-0385.rule: Under Connecticut's one-year statute of frauds provision, an oral contract that does not expressly prescribe a duration beyond one year is treated as of indefinite duration and falls outside the provision, however long performance will actually take.

sections.Parties: C. R. Klewin, Inc., a provider of general construction and construction-management services, sued Flagship Properties and DKM Properties, which did business together as Conn-Tech and were developing a project near the University of Connecticut's Mansfield campus. Klewin claimed that an oral agreement gave it construction-management work on the entire development. Flagship sought summary judgment on the ground, among others, that the one-year statute of frauds barred the alleged oral agreement.
sections.Procedural History: Klewin sued in the District of Connecticut for breach of the project-wide oral agreement, quantum meruit for services anticipating later phases, and detrimental reliance on a promise to pay for preconstruction services. The district court agreed with Flagship that the one-year statute of frauds barred the oral agreement, reasoning that the undertaking was not indefinite because it would end on completion of the project and that a project of this scope could not possibly be completed within one year. The Second Circuit, finding no clear controlling precedent, certified two questions of Connecticut law. The Connecticut Supreme Court accepted them under its statutory certification jurisdiction, answered the first yes and the second no, and taxed no costs to either party. It supplied state-law answers only: it did not enter a judgment, resolve every claim, or decide whether the parties had made a sufficiently definite contract, a question a footnote expressly reserved.
sections.Material Facts:
Conn-Tech's master plan included twenty industrial buildings, a 280-room hotel and convention center, and housing for 592 graduate students and professors, at an estimated total cost of $120 million. At a March 1986 dinner the parties' representatives discussed Klewin becoming construction manager for the project. Klewin proposed a fee of four percent of construction cost plus four percent for overhead and profit, subject to adjustment according to the timing of different phases. Flagship's representative ended the meeting with a handshake and the assurance that Klewin had the job and they had a deal. The parties publicized their agreement, held a videotaped press conference, and ceremonially signed an American Institute of Architects form without filling in its blanks. No express time for completion was stated; Klewin acknowledged an intended construction period of three to ten years.

The parties separately entered a written agreement for the first phase, Celeron Square. Construction began May 4, 1987 and was completed by mid-October. By then Flagship was dissatisfied with Klewin's work and was negotiating with other contractors, and in March 1988 it retained another contractor for sitework on the next phase, Celeron Square II.
sections.Issue: Under General Statutes § 52-550(a)(5), which required a signed writing for an agreement not to be performed within one year from its making, is an oral agreement that does not explicitly state a time for performance of indefinite duration and outside the provision, and is an oral agreement unenforceable when its method of performance contemplates more than a year but its terms do not expressly exclude completion within a year?
sections.Holding: The Connecticut Supreme Court, in 1991, in an opinion by Chief Justice Peters for a unanimous five-member court, answered the first certified question yes and the second no. For the one-year provision, an oral contract that does not expressly prescribe a specific duration beyond one year is the functional equivalent of an indefinite-duration agreement and lies outside the provision regardless of how long performance will actually take. The court did not hold that the handshake created an enforceable contract on every necessary term, that the blank signed form satisfied all writing requirements, or that Flagship owed the contemplated fee; those questions exceeded the certification.
sections.Reasoning:
The court began with the statute's origins in the 1677 English law aimed at fraud and perjury and found the one-year clause especially difficult to justify on modern policy grounds. It does not measure the time between agreement and litigation, and it does not reliably distinguish substantial undertakings from minor ones: a single day's work scheduled thirteen months after formation may fall within it, while a year's work beginning immediately may not. These criticisms did not repeal the statute or permit the court to disregard an express multi-year term, but they explained why it declined to extend the statute beyond a narrow reading.

Connecticut precedent was consistently restrictive. Russell v. Slade required the inability to perform within a year to appear from the agreement itself, and Clark v. Pendleton distinguished the parties' expectation that a voyage would last eighteen months from a contractual term requiring that duration. The legislature's repeated reenactment of similar wording against that background supported retaining the restrictive interpretation. The test is whether completion within a year conflicts with the contract's terms, not whether it is realistically possible; a finite objective such as completing a development differs from an express contractual duration beyond one year.

The court distinguished Burkle as involving perpetual rather than indefinite obligations, relied on Warner v. Texas & Pacific Railway, and acknowledged but did not adopt a contrary Restatement illustration treating an oral promise to sell five crops of potatoes as within the statute. It also rejected collateral litigation over whether an unspecified completion period was realistically feasible, an issue unrelated to breach, formation or the merits.

CT-CB-0400.rule: A grantee who accepts a deed is bound by its mortgage-assumption clause even without signing it, and that promise to the grantor is an original undertaking, not a promise to answer for another's debt within the suretyship statute of frauds.

sections.Parties: Dr. Margaretha Langman, one of two grantors of a mortgaged commercial property, sued the Alumni Association of the University of Virginia, the grantee, for a declaration of the obligations under the deed after she cured a mortgage default under a reservation of rights. She was the appellant. The Association disclaimed responsibility for the mortgage and, by cross-error, asserted the absence of its signature, the suretyship statute of frauds, fraud, mutual mistake, inequitable conduct inducing unilateral mistake, and failure of consideration.
sections.Procedural History: After a three-day hearing, the trial court found that the Association had not knowingly accepted contractual conditions, that an unknown draftsman mistakenly inserted the assumption clause, and that the Association had sufficiently repudiated the gift.
