On warnings, the court rejected the district court's suggestion that experienced welders' general knowledge of fire risks eliminated any duty to warn of a particular limitation. Each proposed warning still failed. A vertical-use-only warning concerned light-duty blankets. A prohibition on cutting operations rested on expert Robert Waite's opinion, properly excluded for lack of methodology. As to a temperature-rating warning, Austin said he would have consulted his foreman, and nothing showed what the foreman would have done differently. As to concentrated spatter, the record described molten slag without equating it with spatter or red-hot cut pieces, so the read-and-heed presumption could not show the warning addressed the hazard encountered.

The casebook selects the merchantability discussion.

CT-NEXT-CM-0093.rule: Under UCC §2-315, an implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose arises when the seller has reason to know the buyer's particular purpose and that the buyer is relying on the seller's skill or judgment to select suitable goods.

sections.Parties: Lewis, who had operated an Arkansas sawmill since 1956, sued Mobil Oil Corporation in a diversity action for breach of warranty, claiming that the oil Mobil recommended for his hydraulic system was unsuitable and caused repair expenses and lost profits. Mobil, the defendant and appellant, denied a particular-purpose warranty, blamed filtration and air entrainment, challenged consequential damages and their proof, and asserted inadequate notice and mitigation.
sections.Procedural History: A jury awarded Lewis $89,250, and Mobil appealed the judgment. On January 7, 1971 the Eighth Circuit upheld Mobil's liability but found the lump-sum award excessive, and it reversed and remanded for a new trial on damages only. Both parties petitioned for rehearing. A February 16 memorandum denied both petitions and clarified why the award remained excessive, leaving the direction for a damages-only new trial in place.
sections.Material Facts:
Lewis bought a functioning used hydraulic system in May 1963 and installed it in a new building in November 1964. A longtime Mobil customer, he asked its local dealer, Frank Rowe, to provide the proper hydraulic fluid, supplied the pump type and made clear that he did not know the system's lubricant requirements. Rowe did not know either; he relayed the request within Mobil and supplied the recommended Ambrex 810, a straight mineral oil without chemical additives. Mobil did not dispute Rowe's authority.

Within days the oil discolored, foamed and became hot, and repeated oil changes did not help. By April 1965 the system failed and was replaced. Lewis asked Rowe to verify the oil, but Mobil kept recommending Ambrex. Over the next two years six Commercial-brand pumps failed. In April 1967 Lewis switched to a Tyrone pump with an additional disposable filter; Mobil engineer Ted Klock again recommended Ambrex and that pump failed after three weeks. On May 9, 1967 Mobil and Tyrone representatives flushed and cleaned the system, installed a new Tyrone pump and recommended DTE-23 with additives including a defoamant. The system then ran satisfactorily through trial, although from July 25, 1967 Lewis used another company's additive-containing oil.
sections.Issue: Did an implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose arise under Arkansas's version of UCC §2-315 when a sawmill operator asked the oil seller to select the proper fluid for his hydraulic system, and did the evidence support causation and the amount of the lost-profits award?
sections.Holding: Eighth Circuit, 1971, Judge Gibson for a panel with Chief Judge Matthes and Judge Mehaffy, with no separate opinion. An implied warranty of fitness arose because Mobil knew the oil was being selected for Lewis's actual sawmill system and knew he depended on its recommendation, so the court did not need to decide whether Ambrex also breached the warranty of merchantability. The evidence supported the jury's finding that the unsuitable oil caused the failures, and notice and mitigation were properly left to the jury. Lost profits were recoverable as consequential damages, but the $89,250 award was excessive, requiring a new trial on damages only.
sections.Reasoning:
Section 2-315 requires that the seller have reason to know the buyer's particular purpose and the buyer's reliance on the seller's skill or judgment, and both had substantial evidentiary support. Comment 1 explains that the buyer need not communicate every detail if the circumstances give the seller reason to realize the purpose and reliance. Mobil's argument that Lewis never specified additive oil or gave enough technical information inverted the transaction: Lewis asked Mobil to choose because he could not. If Mobil needed more information it should have obtained it, as its later inspection showed was feasible. Its claims of abnormal filtration or air entrainment went mainly to causation.

On causation, Lewis's expert Edwards explained that oil without appropriate additives permitted cavitation, with air bubbles interrupting lubrication and metal particles spreading through the system. Mobil's tests on new oil and its filtration theory did not compel a verdict in its favor.

On damages, suspicion of the oil was not established knowledge of its unsuitability, and Lewis's repeated communications gave sufficient notice under §2-607. Arkansas's older tacit-agreement approach did not defeat consequential damages under §2-715; Mobil knew it was supplying a productive sawmill, so lost production was foreseeable. The original opinion read the lump-sum verdict as including later losses caused by Lewis's undercapitalization, which could not be charged to Mobil. On rehearing the court accepted that the claimed $80,000 in lost profits covered only the thirty months of Ambrex use but still found it excessive, because it implied annual profits of roughly $37,000 that the record did not support.

The casebook prints the facts and the warranty-of-fitness discussion, ending before the causation and damages analysis.

CT-NEXT-CM-0094.rule: Under New York UCC §2-316(2) and §1-201(b)(10), a written disclaimer of implied warranties is conspicuous if a reasonable person ought to notice it from its overall presentation, and the statute sets no absolute rule that it must appear before the signature.

sections.Parties: NY Drilling, Inc., a Queens construction company, sued TJM, Inc., a Pennsylvania distributor alleged to have the exclusive right to distribute HD Engineering drilling rigs in the United States. NY Drilling alleged breach of the implied warranties of merchantability and fitness, sought $93,000 in repair and replacement costs, and claimed $369,155 as a third-party beneficiary of the manufacturer's warranty. TJM moved to dismiss.
sections.Procedural History: NY Drilling sued in July 2020 in a diversity action in the Eastern District of New York and twice amended its complaint in response to identified deficiencies. TJM moved under Rule 12(b)(6) to dismiss the second amended complaint. The court took the alleged equipment failures as true for the motion and ordered clearer copies of the attached contracts, which had initially looked faded. On November 30, 2021 it granted the motion, dismissed the entire complaint, and directed entry of judgment and closure of the case, without granting another opportunity to amend.
sections.Material Facts:
HD Engineering of Hong Kong manufactured the rigs, and NY Drilling bought through TJM rather than directly. HDE and TJM had a one-year warranty agreement that did not name NY Drilling. In July 2018 NY Drilling signed a "Final Revised & Updated Quotation" for an HD110-4T rig at $482,137. Immediately below the signature block of its representative, Wayne Fried, an all-capitals paragraph excluded express and implied warranties and specifically named merchantability and fitness for a particular purpose.

According to the complaint, the rig's front collapsed shortly after delivery, TJM repaired it, and it failed again a few months later. TJM replaced it with an HD200A under a separate November 28 contract with the same disclaimer in the same location; that contract listed $568,614, but the amount actually paid was unclear. The HD200A allegedly malfunctioned repeatedly and TJM made at least two repairs. In July 2019 NY Drilling reported a failing mast section. TJM collected the machine at the end of August and allegedly had not repaired or returned it by September 2021.
sections.Issue: Were disclaimers of the implied warranties of merchantability and fitness conspicuous under New York UCC §2-316(2) when they appeared in a capitalized paragraph below the signature blocks, and could the buyer recover from the distributor on an agency theory or as a third-party beneficiary of the manufacturer's warranty?
sections.Holding: Eastern District of New York, 2021, Judge Komitee. Viewed as a whole, both sale contracts effectively excluded the implied warranties, so the merchantability and fitness counts were dismissed; the statutory standard imposes no absolute rule that a disclaimer precede the signature. The related damages count fell with the dismissed warranties, and the third-party-beneficiary count failed on four cumulative grounds. The ruling resolved exclusion only; it did not decide whether the alleged defects would have breached a warranty.
sections.Reasoning:
Section 2-316(2) requires a written merchantability exclusion to mention merchantability and be conspicuous, and a fitness exclusion to be written and conspicuous. Under §1-201(b)(10) the court decides whether a term is presented so that a reasonable person against whom it operates ought to notice it. The words named both warranties, so only presentation was disputed.

Location counted against enforcement: a reader should understand the agreement by the signature stage, the disclaimers followed the signature blocks, they sat with material apparently outside the contract including a Facebook invitation, and nothing above the signature pointed to them. Other features overcame that problem: the text was entirely capitalized, clear about the warranties excluded, set off by blank space, and a discrete paragraph in a different font and type size. New York authority on below-signature placement was sparse, so the court considered the Justice Court decision in Ireland and out-of-state decisions including Vision Graphics and Fleming Farms. It also noted that the legislature removed the statutory examples of conspicuous formatting in 2014, inferring that no one form of emphasis is required.

Count Three, recast in opposition as an agency claim, rested on allegations absent from the complaint and depended on the dismissed warranties. Count Four failed because the pleading showed no clear intent to let NY Drilling enforce the HDE-TJM warranty, whose buyer was TJM; because the promisor, HDE, was not a party; because the agreement chose Hong Kong law, which NY Drilling did not address; and because it required Hong Kong arbitration, which binds a nonsignatory claiming beneficiary rights.

The casebook extracts the implied-warranty disclaimer analysis.

CT-NEXT-CM-0095.rule: A written "as is" exclusion of implied warranties under UCC §2-316(3)(a) satisfies the language requirement through commonly understood words but must still be conspicuous within the meaning of §2-316(2).

sections.Parties: Maritime Air Service, Ltd., which had leased and then bought a helicopter from Fairchild Industries, sued Fairchild for alleged breaches of express warranty and the implied warranties of merchantability and fitness for a particular purpose. Fairchild, the seller, moved to dismiss on the strength of an "as is" exclusion in the purchase document.
sections.Procedural History: Maritime sued in Baltimore's Superior Court, and the case was removed to federal court. Fairchild's motion to dismiss invoked the contractual exclusion, and the federal district court certified two questions of state law to the Maryland Court of Appeals. On March 10, 1975 that court answered the first question affirmatively, declined the second as unnecessary, and directed that costs abide the ultimate result. It did not grant or deny the dismissal motion, decide whether the helicopter was defective, or expressly find the clause inconspicuous; the federal court still had to apply the answer.
sections.Material Facts:
Fairchild leased a helicopter to Maritime on May 9, 1969 for one year, with options to extend the lease for two more years and to purchase during the lease. Maritime exercised the purchase option. On March 19, 1970 the parties signed a Fairchild printed form containing typewritten additions. One addition sold the aircraft as is, denied express and implied warranties except title, and acknowledged that the buyer had examined the aircraft as fully as desired.

The first certified question asked whether the requirement in §2-316(2) that written exclusions be conspicuous applies to §2-316(3)(a). The second, contingent on conspicuousness being required sometimes but not always, asked whether business dealings, the circumstances of the transaction, prior examination or use, and relative commercial skill determine its necessity.
sections.Issue: Does the conspicuousness requirement that UCC §2-316(2) imposes on written exclusions of implied warranties also apply to an "as is" exclusion under §2-316(3)(a)?
sections.Holding: Maryland Court of Appeals, 1975, Judge Levine for a four-to-three majority; Judge Singley dissented, joined by Judges Smith and O'Donnell. A written "as is" exclusion under §2-316(3)(a) must satisfy the conspicuousness requirement of subsection (2). Such words meet the language requirement because they are commonly understood, but they must still be conspicuous. The majority did not decide the examination or usage routes under subsection (3)(b) and (c), and the second certified question became unnecessary.
sections.Reasoning:
Fairchild read subsection (3), which operates "notwithstanding" subsection (2), as an independent alternative under which an as-is provision excludes implied warranties without conspicuousness. The majority agreed that the as-is route is an exception to some requirements but found its extent ambiguous: using those words can dispense with naming merchantability without necessarily dispensing with conspicuousness in a written disclaimer. It therefore looked to purpose, context and consequences.

Official Comment 1 identifies protection against unexpected, unbargained disclaimer language as a central purpose, and Comment 6 describes the subsection (3) exceptions as situations in which the circumstances themselves alert the buyer. Comprehensible language is useful only when the buyer's attention is called to it. Otherwise an as-is expression buried in a lengthy document would escape protection that an explicit merchantability exclusion in the same place would have to satisfy, an anomalous result. That the Code prints its as-is examples in lowercase proved nothing, since the subsection (2) examples are also lowercase, and Comment 7 explained the expression's commercial meaning without licensing hidden terms. The majority found Gindy Manufacturing particularly persuasive, cited Woodruff and Osborne, distinguished Smith v. Sharpensteen, and noted Professor Hawkland's view that these expressions should be conspicuous.

Judge Singley's dissent saw no ambiguity: "notwithstanding" meant the subsection (3) alternatives operate despite subsection (2), and the court should not supply a requirement the drafters could easily have stated. He would have answered the first question negatively.

CT-NEXT-CM-0096.rule: Under UCC §2-313, a seller's affirmation of fact or description creates an express warranty without formal words or intent to warrant, and it is presumed to be part of the basis of the bargain unless the seller proves otherwise.

sections.Parties: Keith, the buyer of an Island Trader 41 boat, sued the sellers for breach of express warranty and of the implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose. Keith was the plaintiff and appellant; the sellers were defendants and respondents, defending the judgment entered for them at trial.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court entered judgment for the sellers under Code of Civil Procedure §631.8 at the close of Keith's case. It reasoned that no defendant had made a written undertaking to preserve performance or compensate for its failure, classified the brochures as opinions or commendations, and found that Keith had not relied on the sellers' judgment in selecting the boat. Keith appealed. On October 9, 1985 the Court of Appeal reversed the determination that no Commercial Code express warranty existed, affirmed the remaining determinations, and remanded because the trial court had made no finding on breach. Each party bore its own appellate costs.
sections.Material Facts:
In October 1978 Keith visited a Long Beach boat show, examined several vessels, spoke with sales representatives and collected advertising brochures. He had attended sailing school, belonged to a yacht club and the Coast Guard Auxiliary, and had sailed on many yachts, although he had never owned one. The sellers' Island Trader 41 brochures described a seaworthy live-aboard vessel. Keith discussed his desire for long-distance ocean cruising with a sales representative and testified that he relied on the brochure representations.

He asked his friend Buddy Ebsen, who was involved in boatbuilding, and another experienced person to look at the boat; they observed it without testing it in the water and advised that it would suit his needs. He paid a deposit, contracted, ordered accessories and bought the vessel in November for $75,610. After delivery its seaworthiness became disputed.
sections.Issue: Did the sellers' brochure descriptions of the boat as seaworthy create an express warranty under California Commercial Code §2313 even though the buyer had friends inspect the boat, and did an implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose arise under §2315?
sections.Holding: California Court of Appeal, Second District, Division Six, 1985, Justice Ochoa, with Presiding Justice Stone and Justice Gilbert concurring. The brochures' definite, unequivocal representations of seaworthiness were affirmations of fact rather than opinion, and the sellers did not rebut the presumption that they formed part of the basis of the bargain, so an express warranty existed under §2313. The implied fitness claim failed because substantial evidence supported the finding that Keith relied on his own experience and advisers to select the vessel. The trial court's ruling under the Song-Beverly Consumer Warranty Act was also affirmed. Breach remained undecided.
sections.Reasoning:
The Song-Beverly Act defines an express warranty as a written undertaking to maintain a consumer good's utility or performance or compensate for a failure, and the trial court correctly found none. But that Act does not displace the buyer's independent Commercial Code rights, which the trial court had not properly analyzed.

Section 2313 asks whether the seller made an affirmation of fact, promise or description rather than mere opinion or commendation; whether it became part of the basis of the bargain; and whether the goods breached the warranty. Formal warranty language and intent to warrant are unnecessary. Whether sales language is fact or opinion depends on context. Here the advertisements were definite and unequivocal, the representative knew Keith wanted a boat for long-distance ocean travel, the literature described production after careful testing, and nothing suggested an experimental vessel.

Former law demanded proof of reliance. The basis-of-the-bargain language and Official Comment 3 changed that: the buyer need not show the statement was the dominant reason for buying. A seller's representation is presumptively a factor inducing the bargain, and the seller must show the bargain did not rest on it at all. Actual knowledge of the goods' true condition before contracting could do so, but inspection does not erase an express warranty when the defect was not discovered and waived. The friends' observation without a water test could not establish seaworthiness. An inspection after contracting but before delivery was irrelevant to formation of the warranty.

The implied warranty of fitness under §2315 instead requires the buyer's actual reliance on the seller's skill or judgment to select suitable goods. Keith's sailing experience, precise specifications, comparisons among boats and use of his friends' expertise supported the finding that he did not so rely.

CT-NEXT-CM-0097.rule: Equity may refuse specific enforcement of a contract, though no sharp practice is shown, where the consideration is grossly inadequate and enforcement would impose oppressive hardship on the defendant out of proportion to the benefit to the plaintiff.

sections.Parties: The McKinnons, seasonal residents who owned an approximately 1,170-acre tract on Mamie Lake, sued the Benedicts, who had bought the roughly eighty-acre resort called Bent's Camp that the tract surrounded. The McKinnons sought an injunction enforcing a letter agreement restricting the Benedicts' use of the resort and also claimed trespass. The Benedicts, defendants below, appealed the injunction.
sections.Procedural History: After a bench trial the county court restrained further grading and trailer or camper rentals, limited resort use through August 31, 1985, and purported to bind subsequent purchasers. The Benedicts appealed to the Wisconsin Supreme Court. On April 9, 1968 that court affirmed in part, reversed in part and remanded: it refused equitable enforcement of the resort-use agreement, preserved the damages and injunction for trespass on the McKinnons' land, and sent back questions of costs and any damages from the improvident injunction. Rehearing was denied with costs on June 4. The casebook's abbreviated "Reversed" disposition concerns only the contractual restriction.
sections.Material Facts:
The financially constrained Benedicts were referred to McKinnon, who lent $5,000 toward their $60,000 land-contract purchase of Bent's Camp, which had fourteen cabins and a lodge. His August 31, 1960 letter required an interest-free note secured by a first mortgage on the buyers' Michigan cottage and contemplated an agreement that for twenty-five years no trees would be cut in specified areas and no improvements built closer to his property than the existing buildings. The letter also offered help: trees for planting, free firewood, an attempt to solve a fifty-year cabin lease at $5 annually, efforts to generate customers, and help organizing the operation.

The Benedicts signed, received the advance and repaid it in spring 1961 after about seven months. McKinnon's effort on the lease failed, and the record showed almost no generated business. Between 1961 and 1964 the Benedicts spent $20,000 improving cabins, but income declined. In fall 1964 they developed eighteen trailer spaces at approximately $8,000 and the next spring a tent campsite at approximately $1,200. The McKinnons sued in June 1965.
sections.Issue: Should a court of equity enforce by injunction, against the original contracting parties, a twenty-five-year restriction on the development of resort land that was given in exchange for a short-term interest-free loan and promises of assistance?
sections.Holding: Wisconsin Supreme Court, 1968, Justice Heffernan, with no separate opinion. The court refused to enforce the restriction by injunction. Grossly inadequate consideration, a small benefit to the McKinnons, oppressive restrictions on the Benedicts and the circumstances of the bargaining together made equitable enforcement unfair, even viewed at the agreement's inception and even though the record showed no sharp practice, dishonesty or overreaching by McKinnon. The court did not hold the agreement unenforceable at law. It also held that the decree could not bind subsequent purchasers and affirmed relief for the separate trespass.
sections.Reasoning:
The respondents conceded this was a simple contract action between the original parties, so binding later purchasers was error. They had brought no action at law for damages, and asserting that damages were inadequate did not automatically entitle them to an injunction. Equitable remedies are discretionary. Restatement (First) of Contracts §367 lists grossly inadequate consideration or unfair terms, disproportionate hardship, and sharp practice, misrepresentation or mistake as alternative grounds for refusing specific performance, so deliberate misconduct need not be shown.

Literal enforcement would freeze the resort in its 1960 state for twenty-five years, confining even ordinary new cottages to a narrow area, while the unrestricted land across the road was farthest from the lake and least useful. The consideration was not a $5,000 gift but seven months' interest-free use of secured money, which the court valued at about $145 at the land contract's 5% rate; the other assistance produced only a failed attempt on the lease and a small group's brief stay. That the buyers could not have purchased without the advance showed their inability to bargain at arm's length. The benefit to the McKinnons was small: the trailer park could not be seen from their house and summer foliage hid the campsite, and McKinnon's $50,000 depreciation testimony had slight probative force. McKinnon's legal, investment, corporate and governmental experience far exceeded that of the retail jeweler buyer.

The court also rejected the neighbors' attacks on the town trailer-park ordinance and permits. It upheld the trespass relief, including a $750 tree-planting item, but held that a $1,355.70 counsel-fee item could not stand in the amount awarded.

The casebook's editors note that a free-use-of-land passage the opinion attributed to Stein came from that decision's dissent.

CT-NEXT-CM-0098.rule: The fairness of a contract and the adequacy of its consideration, for purposes of specific performance, are judged prospectively as of the time the contract was made, and a fair written contract to devise land is ordinarily specifically enforced.

sections.Parties: Ruby Tuckwiller sought specific performance of a written agreement in which Flora Metta Morrison promised to devise her farm to Ruby in exchange for lifetime care. The defendants were Morrison's executor and Davidson College, the residuary beneficiary under Morrison's will; they appealed, arguing that the bargain was inequitable and that Ruby should receive only the reasonable monetary value of her services.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court found that when the agreement was made the kind and duration of care were too uncertain to measure by a monetary standard, that the contract was then equitable, and that Ruby had performed, and it decreed specific performance. The executor and the college appealed; their sole contention concerned equitable fairness and the adequacy of monetary compensation. Division One of the Missouri Supreme Court affirmed on March 13, 1967. On April 10 rehearing or transfer to the full court was denied, with the opinion modified on the court's own motion; the brief reflects the modified report.
sections.Material Facts:
Morrison owned a 160-acre Saline County farm valued in the estate inventory at $34,400. Her nephew John Tuckwiller and Ruby Tuckwiller lived on the nearby family home place and operated the farms. By early 1963 Morrison's Parkinson's disease had worsened. Ruby worked in food service at the State School for $206 monthly, and Morrison wanted her to resign and care for her for life rather than leave her dependent on a nursing home. Morrison suffered an apparent stroke in April, but her physician and a longtime friend found her mentally clear on May 2 and 3.

On May 3 they agreed in writing: Ruby undertook lifetime care, and Morrison agreed to devise her farm to Ruby while keeping its income for life and paying for medication. Ruby wrote the terms, Morrison signed, and Ruby resigned her job on May 6. Morrison made a May 7 appointment with her lawyer to change her will, but she fell and was taken by ambulance to hospital; before leaving she asked that the agreement be witnessed and dated. She died on June 14 at seventy-three with her 1961 will unchanged. That will directed sale of the farm for a Davidson student loan fund.
sections.Issue: Should equity refuse specific performance of a written contract to devise a farm in exchange for lifetime care, and award only the monetary value of the services, where the promisor died shortly after the agreement and the care actually given lasted only a short time?
sections.Holding: Missouri Supreme Court, Division One, 1967, in an opinion by Commissioner Welborn adopted per curiam, with Commissioners Houser and Higgins and all judges concurring. The decree of specific performance was affirmed. Fairness and adequacy of consideration are examined prospectively, as of the making of the contract, and so judged this agreement was fair. The short period of actual services did not make the bargain unconscionable or entitle the estate to substitute a reasonable-value payment for the promised land.
sections.Reasoning:
The court accepted that specific performance can be withheld from written as well as oral contracts that are inequitable, unconscionable, supported by shockingly inadequate consideration, or adequately remedied at law. But many of the defense's precedents involved oral promises to devise land, where equity must first decide whether avoiding fraud justifies an exception to the statute of frauds; this written agreement did not raise that threshold problem.

Viewed prospectively, Ruby gave up employment she liked and undertook care of uncertain duration that, given the course of Parkinson's, could become increasingly onerous. The evidence did not show that she knew Morrison would die soon; a seventy-three-year-old's life expectancy was measured in years. From Morrison's side, personal attention from a compatible, trusted caregiver had value beyond routine institutional care, she kept the farm's income, and she had no immediate family dependent on the property. Her effort to change her will and her demand that the terms be witnessed showed satisfaction with the arrangement. Hints of exploitation based on confusion in hospital did not overcome consistent evidence of mental alertness when the agreement was reached.

Once the agreement was found fair, its subject was real estate, and specific performance of an unobjectionable written contract to convey or devise land is the ordinary remedy; the ability to price services already rendered did not replace the promised land with their smaller retrospective value. The appellants had suggested $133 for seven days' services. The court acknowledged that no prior Missouri decision had enforced a devise agreement after so brief a service period, but held that the case must stand on its own merits.

CT-NEXT-CM-0099.rule: A contract freely made at arm's length without fraud is not void as against public policy merely because one party's return is large or the goods will ultimately be sold to the government; public policy must rest on identifiable law and precedent.

sections.Parties: Black Industries, Inc., an Ohio manufacturer and purchaser of subcontract work, sued Bush, a New Jersey supplier, for breach of two agreements to supply component parts, claiming $14,625 and $4,460.95 plus interest. Bush, the defendant, moved for summary judgment on the ground that the agreements were void as against public policy.
sections.Procedural History: Black sued in the federal District of New Jersey. Bush's answer also raised the statute of frauds, vagueness, an alleged limitation of compensation to money actually collected, and impossibility, and he disputed that the second agreement existed. He moved for summary judgment on the public-policy defense to both agreements. On March 13, 1953 the court denied the motion, even assuming Bush's asserted facts, and called for an order implementing its opinion. It entered no judgment on breach, and the other defenses remained unresolved.
sections.Material Facts:
Black obtained an invitation to bid on components for Hoover. It alleged that around March 22, 1951 Bush agreed to make 1.3 million anvils at $4.40 per thousand, 750,000 holder primers at $11.50 per thousand and 700,000 plunger supports at $12 per thousand, to government specifications and drawings. Hoover agreed to pay $8.10, $16 and $21.20 per thousand respectively. An April 13 letter, signed as agreed by Bush on April 19, made Black's compensation the spread between Bush's fixed price and Hoover's purchase-order price: the order would run to Bush, who would manufacture and ship directly, while Black would service it, bill on Bush's forms, cash checks payable to Bush, remit Bush's price and keep the balance.

A second alleged agreement covered 525,000 plunger supports at $13.20 and 969,500 anvils at $4.40 per thousand, against a Standby Products order at $23.20 and $8.10. The customers would use the components in products fulfilling government defense contracts. Black alleged that Bush began but failed to complete performance. Bush calculated Black's spreads at about 84%, 39% and 68% and asserted that the billing structure concealed them.
sections.Issue: Are agreements under which an intermediary keeps a large spread between its supplier's price and its customer's price void as against public policy because the components will ultimately go into products sold to the government under defense contracts?
sections.Holding: District of New Jersey, 1953, Chief Judge Forman. The summary-judgment motion was denied. The agreements were not void as against public policy: Black was not paid to influence a public official, to perform an illegal act or to suppress competitive public bidding, and neither party dealt with the United States on account of the agreements. High intermediary compensation combined with eventual government purchase does not by itself invalidate a bargain between businesspeople dealing at arm's length without fraud.
sections.Reasoning:
Bush invoked the Renegotiation Act's policy of eliminating excessive profits in defense contracts and related subcontracts, and statutory prohibitions on subcontractor fees or kickbacks in certain reimbursable arrangements. Drawing on Muschany, the court required a legally recognized basis for invalidity: public policy comes from law and precedent, supported by definite indications of a dominant policy, not from a judge's general view of the public interest, and preserving freely made good-faith agreements is itself significant.

The cited precedents fell largely into three categories: compensation for inducing public officials to exercise discretion, as in Tool Company v. Norris; agreements to commit an illegal act or resting on illegal consideration, such as a lease for unlawful dog racing; and collusive restraints on government bidding, as in Gulick. Neither supply agreement fit. Their only connection to government was that the components would eventually enter products sold to it.

The spread might reflect a generous customer price, a low supplier quotation or other circumstances requiring proof. Even if Black stood to earn much more for a smaller contribution, relative values of consideration alone do not invalidate an arm's-length bargain without fraud. A contrary rule would require either invalidating all compensated intermediaries in the chain of government supply, which lacked precedent and ignored commercial realities, or having courts decide the reasonableness of each intermediary's return, a price-regulation function unsuited to a contract suit. Competitive purchasing procedures, the prime contractor's commercial incentives and any applicable statutory renegotiation were better protections. The court did not rule that fraud, kickbacks, collusion or an applicable statute could never invalidate a private agreement, and it did not find that concealment actually occurred.

CT-NEXT-CM-0100.rule: Exculpatory clauses are enforced unless settled public policy or the relationship of the parties counsels otherwise, and in 1958 Illinois applied that rule to uphold a residential lease clause relieving the landlord of liability for its own negligence.

sections.Parties: Ella O'Callaghan, a residential tenant, sued her landlord, Waller & Beckwith Realty Co., for injuries from a fall she attributed to defective pavement and negligent maintenance. She died before trial and her administratrix was substituted as plaintiff. The landlord defended on an exculpatory clause in the signed lease. The plaintiff obtained leave to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court after the appellate court directed judgment for the landlord.
sections.Procedural History: A jury returned a $14,000 verdict for the plaintiff. The appellate court reversed and instructed entry of judgment for the defendant, reasoning that the signed lease required a directed verdict on the exculpatory defense. The Illinois Supreme Court granted leave to appeal and on November 26, 1958 affirmed the appellate court's judgment, so the verdict was not reinstated. Rehearing was denied on January 22, 1959.
sections.Material Facts:
Ella O'Callaghan fell while crossing the paved courtyard between her garage and her apartment. She alleged that defective pavement and the defendant's negligent maintenance and operation caused her injuries. Her lease contained a clause expressly relieving the landlord and its agents from liability to the tenant for injuries or property damage caused by their acts or neglect, and the plaintiff conceded that the clause covered this claim if it was valid.

There was a housing shortage, but the majority noted no trial evidence that this tenant objected to the clause, tried to negotiate it away, or sought another apartment. The dissent described a 1947 metropolitan lease signed amid acute shortages and waiting lists, and uncontroverted testimony that the landlord would not rent to anyone who refused to sign the form as offered.
sections.Issue: May a residential landlord, consistently with public policy and the relationship between landlord and tenant, rely on a lease clause that exempts it from liability to the tenant for injuries caused by its own negligence?
sections.Holding: Illinois Supreme Court, 1958, Justice Schaefer; Justice Bristow and Chief Justice Daily jointly dissented. The exculpatory clause in the residential lease was valid and barred the tenant's negligence claim, so judgment for the landlord was affirmed. Such agreements are enforced unless settled public policy or the parties' relationship counsels otherwise, and the majority found neither ground here, regarding the question as one suited to the legislature. The brief notes that this is a historical holding, not a statement of current Illinois landlord-tenant law.
sections.Reasoning:
Jackson had sustained an exculpatory clause in a commercial lease under the general rule, and the majority applied that framework to residential leasing. It acknowledged that contracting out of the consequences of negligence can dilute standards of care, but treated freedom of contract and the allocation of liability risks as substantial competing considerations. Illinois had invalidated or limited negligence exemptions for common carriers, telegraph companies and employers; the majority attributed those decisions to public interests and dominant bargaining positions and regarded ordinary leasing as a private matter. It saw little highest-court authority invalidating residential clauses absent legislation. Risk-shifting agreements could also benefit tenants, and accepted liability insurance similarly reduces the financial consequences that encourage care.

On housing scarcity, the majority accepted that a shortage existed but pointed to the lack of evidence that this tenant objected or looked elsewhere, to the many competing landlords and housing types, and to the insufficiency of a form contract alone to show bargaining disparity. It resisted grounding enduring judicial public policy in housing conditions that vary over time and place, and thought legislative attention to the shortage suggested the legislature had taken the remedies it thought appropriate.

The dissent argued that freedom of contract is not absolute, that exculpatory terms were widespread in urban form leases so that changing landlords offered no real choice, and that negligence exemptions in housing defeat rather than dilute standards of care. It asked why safety in a dwelling deserved less protection than workplace safety, distinguished Jackson as an arm's-length commercial lease, and defended the court's authority to update the common law rather than wait for legislation.

The casebook separately discusses later statutory restrictions.

CT-NEXT-CM-0101.rule: A contract of adhesion is enforceable unless a term falls outside the adherent's reasonable expectations or is unduly oppressive or unconscionable; an arbitration clause naming a body whose interests are effectively identical to one party's as sole arbitrator will not be enforced.

sections.Parties: Bill Graham, an experienced concert promoter, was the plaintiff; he sued for breach, declaratory relief, and rescission and appealed the judgment confirming an arbitration award against him. Scissor-Tail, Inc., the corporation wholly owned by performer Leon Russell that marketed his group's services, was the defendant; it obtained an order compelling arbitration before the musicians' union and appealed a later order striking its claimed attorney fees from costs.
sections.Procedural History: Graham sued in October 1973. After an initial arbitration order and reconsideration allowing discovery, the trial court compelled arbitration in March 1976. The union first awarded the full claim of about $53,000 without a hearing, reopened the matter after Graham protested, and issued the same award in February 1977. The superior court confirmed the award and later struck an attorney-fee cost item of about $16,000. Graham appealed the confirmation, and Scissor-Tail appealed the fee order. On February 5, 1981 the California Supreme Court reversed the confirmation judgment, directed that the order compelling arbitration be vacated, provided for further proceedings before a suitable substitute arbitrator, and dismissed the fee appeal as moot.
sections.Material Facts:
In 1973 Russell's manager arranged four concerts with Graham as part of a larger tour. All four used the American Federation of Musicians' Form B. Graham signed all four; Scissor-Tail signed only those for Ontario and Oakland, scheduled July 29 and August 5, 1973. The form paid the musicians the greater of union scale or a stated percentage of receipts after specified expenses, 85% for three venues. The contracts did not expressly allocate net losses. They required disputes to be decided finally by the union's executive board or an appropriate local board. Significant artists belonged to the union, and its rules required its forms.

The Ontario concert lost roughly $63,000, while Oakland produced about $98,000 in net profit. Scissor-Tail claimed that Graham bore the loss without offset. Graham invoked an industry understanding that a promoter taking only a 10% or 15% profit share bore no risk of loss. Scissor-Tail refused to execute the other two contracts.

Graham had signed thousands of similar contracts, had promoted at least fifteen Russell concerts under similar provisions in the preceding three years, had taken part in prior union proceedings, and had threatened to file union charges in this dispute.
sections.Issue: Whether a standard-form union contract was a contract of adhesion as to an experienced promoter, and whether its clause requiring disputes to be arbitrated by the musicians' union, of which one party's principal was a member, was enforceable.
sections.Holding: The California Supreme Court in 1981, in an opinion by the court with Justice Mosk not participating and no separate opinion, held that the contract was one of adhesion and that the arbitration clause, although within Graham's reasonable expectations, could not be enforced because it designated the union, a body whose interests were allied with one party, as sole arbitrator and so failed the minimum level of integrity required of a contractual substitute for the courts. Because the parties had agreed to arbitrate, they were to have an opportunity to agree on a suitable arbitrator, failing which either could petition the court to appoint one.
sections.Reasoning:
The court separated two inquiries: whether the contract was adhesive and whether its terms were enforceable. Adhesion describes a standardized agreement imposed by a party of superior bargaining strength on a take-it-or-leave-it basis, and it can arise in business dealings. Graham's prominence gave him no practical freedom to remove the clause, because significant artists belonged to the union and its rules required its forms; the terms that were negotiable were minor.

Adhesion is only a starting point. Such a contract is enforced unless a provision falls outside the adherent's reasonable expectations or is unduly oppressive or unconscionable in context. The union forum was within Graham's reasonable expectations, given his long familiarity with the clause.

The term nonetheless failed. The Arbitration Act leaves parties wide freedom in choosing arbitrators, including nonneutral ones, but naming a party, or a body whose interests are effectively identical to a party's, as sole adjudicator yields the power of decision to the adverse interest and is an illusory substitute for adjudication. A union seeks favorable wages and conditions for its members and naturally shares their interest in a compensation dispute with a third party. The court treated this defect as a ground for denial even apart from adhesion, and disapproved a contrary earlier decision, Federico, to the extent inconsistent. It did not find that the union's procedures denied a fair hearing.

The court doubted that the form was a collective bargaining agreement under section 301 of the Labor Management Relations Act and found no controlling federal rule requiring this forum.

CT-NEXT-CM-0102.rule: Under New York General Business Law § 394-c as applied in 2005, a dating-service contract that does not promise a specified number of referrals per month may charge at most $25, and an injured consumer may recover actual damages or $50, whichever is greater.

sections.Parties: Jennifer Doe and Debra Roe were consumers who had bought memberships from Great Expectations, a dating service. Each brought her own small-claims action as claimant against the company to recover the price she had paid, $1,000 for Doe and $3,790 for Roe. Great Expectations was the defendant; before entering judgment the court amended the defendant's name to include GE Management Group of NY, Inc.
sections.Procedural History:
Doe and Roe filed separate small-claims actions in the New York City Civil Court. Judge Lebedeff heard testimony and issued a consolidated decision on October 31, 2005, so the findings rest on testimony rather than on allegations resolved on a motion. No separate opinion appears.

The court awarded Doe $1,000 and Roe $3,790, with interest running from their respective contract-payment dates. Doe's membership had expired; the judgment terminated Roe's. The court amended the defendant's name before entering judgment. The judge also exercised discretion to send the decision to the New York Attorney General's Consumer Fraud Unit and the New York City Department of Consumer Affairs.
sections.Material Facts:
Doe paid $1,000 for six months of service. Roe paid $3,790 for thirty-six months, later extended to fifty-four. The printed contracts offered photographs, video, a dating workbook, counseling, background checks and dating etiquette, but expressly promised zero social referrals and declared that members neither desired nor expected referrals. Members could view other members' Internet profiles and approach one another. Roe's handwritten "Marriage Program" and "Platinum Shopper" terms came with an oral assurance of twelve introductions during the program, rather than a specified monthly number. Roe testified that the service introduced her to nobody, although one person contacted her after seeing her information. Doe met nobody and eventually stopped checking for contacts.

The forms omitted the refund option when promised referrals were not made, restrictions on disclosing personal information without written consent, the unilateral right to suspend membership for up to a year, return of personal materials by certified mail after termination, the maximum distance for face-to-face meetings, the policy for a member who moved outside the service area, and the separate Dating Service Consumer Bill of Rights. Only the three-day cooling-off cancellation notice complied.
sections.Issue: Whether an Internet-based service that lets members view profiles and approach one another, without itself matching them, is covered by New York General Business Law § 394-c; whether these contracts violated the statute; and what a consumer may recover as actual damages under § 394-c(9)(b).
sections.Holding: The New York City Civil Court in 2005, in a consolidated small-claims decision by Judge Lebedeff, held that the service fell within § 394-c because supplying the place and mechanism for members to assess and approach one another sufficed. Because neither contract promised a specified number of referrals per month, $25 was the maximum charge for each contract, not a monthly allowance, and the forms omitted most of the required terms. Each claimant recovered her entire price as actual damages: $1,000 to Doe and $3,790 to Roe, with interest.
sections.Reasoning:
The statute covered paid social matching by computer or other means, and earlier litigation involving Great Expectations had established that a service need not itself match particular people, so the company's Internet method did not avoid the Dating Services Law. Under the statute as applied in this decision, a contract charging more than $25 had to promise a specified certain number of referrals per month; neither contract did.

Section 394-c(9)(b) allowed an injured consumer actual damages or $50, whichever was greater. The court found that actual damages included the contract price minus the lawful $25 maximum. Recovering the remaining $25 required a further finding: having observed their testimony, the judge found that both claimants carefully negotiated the services and would not have signed contracts with unlawful terms if the mandatory notice had told them of their statutory rights. That justified returning the whole price as restitutionary actual damages and achieved substantial justice in the small-claims proceedings.

The court grounded the awards in statutory injury and actual damages rather than simply treating every noncompliant dating contract as void on public-policy grounds. It read a 1992 amendment, which supplied an individual actual-damages remedy and authorized Attorney General enforcement with civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation, as giving consumers alternate routes to restitution. Relief did not rest on the statutory refund calculation for missed monthly referrals. The court's suggestion that the company should return the claimants' personal materials was a warning, not an order, and the referral to regulators was not a finding of criminal guilt or an award of civil penalties. The full brief explains the law as applied in 2005 and does not certify present statutory requirements.

CT-NEXT-CM-0103.rule: A court may refuse to enforce a contract that was unconscionable when made, meaning that one party lacked meaningful choice and the terms unreasonably favored the other party.

sections.Parties: Walker-Thomas Furniture Co. sold household goods on installment contracts and pursued replevin of goods from two customers who had defaulted, William Thorne and Ora Lee Williams. The seller won in the trial court and in the first appellate court. The customers challenged the operation of the contract's payment-allocation clause, and their cases reached the federal circuit court after that court granted leave to appeal.
sections.Procedural History: The Court of General Sessions entered judgment for the seller. The District of Columbia Court of Appeals affirmed because it believed existing District law gave it no authority to refuse enforcement on unconscionability grounds, although it criticized the transaction and called for legislation. The federal circuit court granted leave to appeal and decided the case on August 11, 1965. It remanded both cases for further proceedings, because the courts below, thinking themselves powerless to refuse enforcement, had made no findings on unconscionability and the appellate record did not permit deciding that issue as a matter of law.
sections.Material Facts:
Walker-Thomas's installment contracts called the transactions leases, reserved title until the stated price was paid, and allowed repossession after a missed payment. A further printed provision allocated each payment proportionally across every outstanding purchase, which kept a small balance owing on each older item until the customer paid off the whole account. Each new purchase therefore exposed previously acquired goods to repossession, and the new item also secured prior indebtedness. The court described this effect as obscured by the contractual wording.

William Thorne bought a Daveno, three tables and two lamps for $391.10 in May 1962, defaulted soon afterward, and faced replevin of goods acquired since 1958. Ora Lee Williams bought a $514.95 stereo in April 1962, soon defaulted, and faced replevin of goods bought since December 1957. At the stereo purchase her older balance was $164. The opinion's first footnote reports approximately $1,800 in aggregate purchases and $1,400 in payments. The quoted lower-court account says the seller knew that Williams supported herself and seven children on a $218 monthly government stipend; the contract identified her social worker and income.
sections.Issue: Whether the absence of a prior District of Columbia decision foreclosed a common-law defense of unconscionability, or whether courts had authority to withhold enforcement of a contract that was unconscionable when made, and how such a claim is to be examined.
sections.Holding: The D.C. Circuit in 1965, in an opinion by Judge J. Skelly Wright joined by Chief Judge Bazelon, with Judge Danaher dissenting, held that courts have authority to withhold enforcement of a contract unconscionable when made. Unconscionability is the absence of meaningful choice together with terms unreasonably favorable to the other party. The court established an available defense and a framework for examining it and remanded both cases; it did not itself find the contracts unconscionable, invalidate them, discharge the debt, or prescribe a new payment-allocation schedule.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority reasoned that decisions from other jurisdictions and the Supreme Court's treatment of unconscionable bargains showed the principle was not a novel legislative invention. The District had neither adopted nor rejected it, so the case was one of first impression. Congress's later enactment of UCC § 2-302 did not show that earlier common law required enforcement; although the enactment postdated these purchases, the majority treated its rationale as persuasive support for developing District common law rather than applying the statute retroactively.

Meaningful choice is assessed from all the circumstances, including bargaining power, the buyer's education, a reasonable opportunity to understand the writing, fine print, and deceptive presentation. A signature ordinarily exposes a party to unfavorable terms, but that rule loses force when a party with little bargaining power and little real choice accepts commercially unreasonable terms without meaningful knowledge of them. Fairness is judged at formation against the trade's commercial background and the business practices of the time and place, asking whether the terms were extreme in that setting, not by a mechanical test or a rule that every unequal exchange is invalid. Substantive one-sidedness can shed light on bargaining inequality, but neither poverty nor inequality alone was announced as an automatic defense.

Judge Danaher, dissenting, would have kept the lower court's disposition. He thought Williams appeared to understand her position, stressed the risks of judicial intervention in consumer credit and the uncertain effects on thousands of installment transactions, and said legislation or existing loan-shark law might supply a remedy. His footnote stressed that the new UCC provision did not take effect until January 1, 1965.

CT-NEXT-CM-0104.rule: A contract term is unconscionable and unenforceable when, judged at formation, an absence of meaningful choice combines with terms so one-sided that they oppress or unfairly surprise a party; the question is one of law for the court.

sections.Parties: Ronald Stoll, the seller of sixty acres in Delaware County, Oklahoma, was the plaintiff and the appellant. He sued the buyers, Chong Lor Xiong and Mee Yang, a married couple who operated six poultry houses, seeking specific performance of a chicken-litter provision, a temporary injunction against third-party litter sales, and immediate possession of the litter. The buyers asserted unconscionability among other defenses and counterclaims and requested reformation or invalidation.
sections.Procedural History: Stoll sued the day after the date on which he alleged the buyers' litter shed was empty. The buyers pleaded unconscionability, fraud, merger into a deed that omitted the litter provision, impossibility based on alleged statutory violations, trespass, and damage to the shed; these were pleaded positions, not findings. Both sides moved for summary judgment. The trial court held the litter clause unconscionable, granted the buyers' motion, denied Stoll's, and entered judgment against his petition. Stoll appealed. Reviewing de novo, with inferences drawn in Stoll's favor, the Oklahoma Court of Civil Appeals found no material factual dispute requiring a trial and on September 17, 2010 affirmed the judgment for the buyers on Stoll's petition.
sections.Material Facts:
The January 1, 2005 agreement described a price of $2,000 per acre plus $10,000 for an access road; its words said "One Hundred Twenty Thousand Dollars" while its figure said $130,000. A separate provision required the buyers to build a concrete-floor litter shed at least forty-three by eighty feet, deposit poultry litter there after growing cycles, and give Stoll all rights to that litter for thirty years. Stoll had to empty the shed between cycles, and he acknowledged that he had devised the provision.

Xiong had three years of schooling in Laos, understood some spoken English, and could read only a few English words. Yang, a Hmong immigrant from Laos, had no schooling there and only six months of adult education in the United States; the relative who interpreted for her did not understand the litter term. Stoll argued that the buyers had signed a preliminary version in November 2004 and had time to obtain an explanation.

After an initial cycle the buyers paid $900 to remove the upper layer of bedding; Yang asked Stoll to pay half and he refused. In February 2009 Xiong traded litter from a complete cleanout for replacement shavings. Stoll alleged that the buyers were selling litter to others.
sections.Issue: Whether a court may judge the fairness of a contract term independently, rather than only on traditional grounds such as fraud, duress, undue influence, mistake or illegality, and whether the thirty-year chicken-litter provision in this land sale was unconscionable as a matter of law on the summary-judgment record.
sections.Holding: The Oklahoma Court of Civil Appeals in 2010, in an opinion by Judge Hetherington joined by Presiding Judge Buettner and Judge Hansen, affirmed the judgment for the buyers on Stoll's petition, holding the chicken-litter paragraph unconscionable. The combination of an extreme hidden burden and the buyers' inability to understand it shocked the conscience. The holding invalidated the litter paragraph supporting Stoll's enforcement claim; it did not award the buyers $216,000, cancel their land purchase, or separately resolve every counterclaim.
sections.Reasoning:
Oklahoma precedent assesses unconscionability at formation against the commercial setting, asking whether onerous inequality, deception or oppression produced terms so one-sided as to oppress or unfairly surprise a party, and links the absence of meaningful choice to terms unreasonably favorable to the other side. It is a legal issue for the court. UCC § 2-302 directly addresses sales of goods, but the court used its principle by analogy in this land transaction, consistent with Restatement § 208. Both parties had supplied evidence of the transaction's setting.

The court then looked at the economics. Stoll's testimony supplied a yield of about twenty tons per house from each de-caking, a pre-2008 price of up to $12 per ton, and the buyers' five annual flocks in six houses, producing approximately $7,200 a year and $216,000 over thirty years from de-caking alone. The $25 figure Yang attributed to Stoll produced approximately $15,000 annually, and complete cleanouts would add more. These were estimates derived from testimony, not a damages award. The court saw the clause as making the buyers' independently funded business generate another major stream of payment for Stoll while they paid the costs of producing the litter.

The court analogized to deed-cancellation cases in which grossly inadequate consideration and inability to understand the transaction could support a presumption of fraud. Here the inequality ran the other way: the buyers' real burden far exceeded the stated price. Ordinary price inadequacy alone would not suffice. Stoll's claim that cleared and leveled land deserved a premium over nearby land did not justify the separate thirty-year litter burden.

CT-NEXT-CM-0105.rule: Under California law an arbitration agreement is unenforceable only if both procedurally and substantively unconscionable on a sliding scale, and a court may sever unconscionable terms that are collateral to the agreement's lawful central purpose and enforce the rest.

sections.Parties: Stephanie Prasad, a former property manager, sued her employer, Pinnacle Property Management Services, LLC, on eleven claims: seven wage-and-hour, penalty and unfair-business-practice claims pursued on class, collective or representative bases, and four individual disability, accommodation, interactive-process and emotional-distress claims. Pinnacle moved to compel arbitration under its Issue Resolution Agreement; Prasad opposed the motion as unconscionable.
sections.Procedural History: Pinnacle moved in the Northern District of California to enforce the arbitration agreement. Prasad at first denied signing it, but an earlier order found that she had entered it. The court deferred the remaining enforceability issues while the Supreme Court reviewed the Ninth Circuit's Morris decision; after Epic Systems reversed Morris in May 2018, the stay was lifted for supplemental briefing. On September 25, 2018 the court severed four provisions, compelled arbitration of Prasad's individual claims, held that she could not maintain the class, collective and representative claims, stayed the action and directed administrative closure. A concurrent separate order allowed amendment to assert a PAGA claim, to remain stayed pending individual arbitration.
sections.Material Facts:
Prasad applied online and was hired in May 2016 as a property manager at a Mountain View apartment complex; her employment ended less than a year later. She alleged that her type I diabetes sometimes required accommodations and that after a two-week medical leave she returned to find another employee in her position and was reassigned as a lower-paid temporary roving manager. These allegations had not been adjudicated.

Applicants could not submit an application without agreeing to the Issue Resolution Agreement, which required final binding arbitration of disputes arising from applications, employment or termination. Withdrawal was permitted within three days but ended consideration for employment. The rules allowed only one employee's claims per proceeding; set a one-year deadline for employee claims only; required the employee to send a $50 filing fee to "American Management Services", which counsel acknowledged was Pinnacle; divided arbitration costs equally with the employee's share capped at $100 apart from the filing fee; let Pinnacle amend or terminate the rules each December 31 on thirty days' written notice; and made the arbitration and its record confidential, subject to exceptions.
sections.Issue: Does California's generally applicable unconscionability doctrine defeat enforcement of the employer's arbitration agreement or require narrower relief, and if some of its provisions are unconscionable, can they be severed so that the remainder is enforced?
sections.Holding: Northern District of California, 2018, Magistrate Judge DeMarchi, deciding with the parties' consent. The agreement showed some procedural unconscionability, and four provisions were substantively unconscionable: the employee-only one-year deadline, the $50 filing fee payable to the employer, the equal division of arbitration costs, and the employer's unilateral power to amend or terminate the rules. The class waiver and the confidentiality clause survived. Because the defective terms were collateral to a lawful agreement to arbitrate, the court severed them and enforced the remainder, compelling arbitration of the individual claims.
sections.Reasoning:
California law requires both procedural and substantive unconscionability, with more of one permitting less of the other. Adhesion begins the inquiry but does not itself invalidate an agreement. Procedural unconscionability was present: applicants had to agree in order to apply, withdrawal meant giving up the job opportunity, the employer had superior bargaining power, and the form presented arbitration without its potential disadvantages. The consequence was closer scrutiny of the terms, not automatic nonenforcement.

The class-waiver challenge failed after Prasad's concession following Epic Systems. The one-year deadline shortened potentially longer statutory periods for the employee alone without justification, and fairness is assessed when the agreement was made, so her own timely filing was irrelevant. The $50 fee was a payment to the very opponent against whom the employee sought relief, an expense she would not bear in court. Applying Ingle strictly, the court found the cost division unconscionable even though the $100 cap left only a modicum of unfairness, and it followed Ingle over contrary district-court reasoning in holding that unilateral control over the rules in an adhesive agreement deprived employees of bargaining power, despite the notice requirement and the protection against retroactive change. The confidentiality clause was narrower than those in Davis and Pokorny, and Poublon, relying on California appellate authority on substantially identical language, supplied the closer comparison.

On severance, the question was whether the agreement's central purpose remained lawful and whether the defects could be removed without adding contractual promises. Unlike Armendariz, both employer and employee claims were subject to arbitration, no improper restriction on available relief had been presented, and the four invalid provisions were collateral to a lawful alternate forum before AAA or JAMS.

CT-NEXT-CM-0106.rule: The implied covenant of good faith requires a party to actually exercise discretion it has promised to exercise and to do so neither arbitrarily nor irrationally, but it cannot create obligations inconsistent with the contract's terms.

sections.Parties: Brian Dalton, a high-school student who took the SAT, was the plaintiff; the proceeding was filed by his father. The defendant was Educational Testing Service (ETS), whose registration contract governed the test and which questioned Dalton's November 1991 score. Dalton sought to prohibit cancellation of the score and to compel its release. ETS lost at trial and in the Appellate Division before the case reached the Court of Appeals.
sections.Procedural History: Dalton's father filed an article 78 proceeding, which was converted to an action at law. After a twelve-day nonjury trial, the judge found that ETS had failed even to evaluate or investigate the submitted information and ordered the score released. The Appellate Division affirmed. The New York Court of Appeals accepted the supported, affirmed finding that relevant information had not been evaluated, which it could not reweigh, but rejected any duty to conduct an external investigation. On December 7, 1995 it modified the Appellate Division order to require good-faith consideration of Dalton's material rather than immediate release, and affirmed as modified without costs.
sections.Material Facts:
Dalton took the SAT as a junior in May 1991 and again as a senior that November. His combined score rose 410 points, crossing ETS's 350-point threshold for security review. Staff compared the answer sheets, saw handwriting disparities, and obtained an examiner's opinion that different individuals had completed them. The Board of Review preliminarily found substantial evidence for cancelling the November score.

The registration contract reserved ETS's right to cancel a score when it had reason to question validity, but promised notice and five options: submit additional relevant information, take a free retest, accept cancellation and a fee refund, obtain review by a score-receiving institution, or arbitrate. ETS's notice identified suspected impersonation as the concern.

Dalton submitted medical verification of mononucleosis during the first examination, preparatory-course diagnostic scores consistent with the later improvement, statements from a proctor and two students confirming his presence at the November test, and a family-retained examiner's opinion that he wrote both answer sheets. ETS held several meetings, obtained a second examiner's opinion supporting its original conclusion, and continued to question the score. Board members regarded presence at the examination as irrelevant to handwriting and believed only a retest could validate the score.
sections.Issue: Whether ETS breached its contract with Dalton, including the implied covenant of good faith, by failing to consider the relevant information he submitted under the option the contract gave him, and if so whether the proper remedy is release of the questioned score or good-faith reconsideration.
sections.Holding: The New York Court of Appeals in 1995, in an opinion by Chief Judge Kaye for five judges (joined by Titone, Bellacosa, Smith and Ciparick), with Judge Levine dissenting joined by Simons, held on the binding findings that ETS breached its contract by refusing to exercise the discretion it had promised, because it did not consider the relevant material Dalton submitted. ETS had no duty to investigate or to prove cheating. The remedy was specific performance in the form of good-faith reconsideration, not release of the score; the court did not validate the score or award damages.
sections.Reasoning:
Every contract includes a covenant of good faith in performance: neither party may destroy the other's entitlement to the benefits of the bargain, and promised discretion may not be exercised arbitrarily or irrationally. But the covenant cannot imply an obligation inconsistent with the agreed terms. ETS had not promised to prove cheating before withholding a score, to gather independent evidence, or to interview everyone whose statement a student supplied; such duties would contradict the allocation of the burden to the test-taker to address the security concern.

ETS did promise an opportunity to submit relevant information, and that option would be empty unless ETS genuinely considered what was submitted. Presence at the examination, illness during the lower-scoring sitting, and later diagnostic performance were relevant to the impersonation question ETS itself had posed, and its internal manual recognized medical information and other test results as pertinent. ETS could not narrow the issue to handwriting alone.

The court distinguished two stages. Once ETS considers relevant material in good faith, it ordinarily controls evidentiary weight and score validity, subject to review for arbitrary or irrational action. Refusing to exercise the promised discretion at all raises the direct question whether a contractual obligation was breached. Specific performance had to supply what performance would have supplied; ETS never promised to release an invalid or still-questioned score, and certifying it automatically would exceed the bargain and undermine the credentials on which colleges, students and others relied.

Judge Levine, dissenting, agreed that no investigative duty existed but would ultimately have dismissed the complaint, viewing the additional examiner and resubmitted handwriting samples as evidence of consideration and the board's focus on handwriting as a rational exercise of reserved discretion.

CT-NEXT-CM-0107.rule: The Airline Deregulation Act preempts a state-law implied covenant of good faith claim that relates to airline prices, routes or services when the covenant is a state-imposed obligation that enlarges the airline's voluntarily adopted contractual undertakings.

sections.Parties: Ginsberg, a member of Northwest's WorldPerks frequent-flyer program, was the plaintiff in a proposed class action against the airline Northwest, Inc. He asserted breach of contract, breach of the implied covenant of good faith, and negligent and intentional misrepresentation, and sought more than $5 million and restoration of his membership. Northwest, the defendant, had lost on the implied-covenant claim in the Ninth Circuit before the case reached the Court.
sections.Procedural History: The district court dismissed the covenant and misrepresentation claims as preempted by the Airline Deregulation Act, and dismissed the express-contract claim without prejudice for failure to identify a material breach, reasoning that the agreement reserved sole discretion over abuse. Ginsberg appealed only the implied-covenant dismissal. The Ninth Circuit reinstated that claim as insufficiently connected to rates or services to trigger preemption. The Court therefore reviewed the covenant theory and did not adjudicate the merits of the abandoned express-contract claim. On April 2, 2014 it reversed the Ninth Circuit and remanded for proceedings consistent with its holding.
sections.Material Facts:
Ginsberg joined WorldPerks in 1999 and reached its highest status, Platinum Elite, in 2005 through extensive travel. Members earned miles on Northwest and partner flights and redeemed them for tickets and upgrades. In 2008 Northwest terminated his membership, apparently invoking a clause allowing cancellation for program abuse, including improper conduct determined in its sole judgment. Its letter reported twenty-four complaints since December 2007, including nine about baggage reaching the carousel late, and listed $1,925 in travel vouchers, 78,500 bonus miles, a voucher extension, and $491 in reimbursements. The company said it would stop granting compensation with every contact.

Ginsberg alleged that the termination instead served cost cutting connected to Northwest's merger with Delta. That ulterior motive was an allegation, not a judicial finding about the airline's actual intent. He alleged only flight-earned miles and ticket or upgrade redemptions. Minnesota law controlled under an unchallenged choice-of-law determination, and Minnesota did not permit parties to disclaim its implied covenant.
sections.Issue: Whether the Airline Deregulation Act's bar on state enactment or enforcement of provisions having the force of law related to airline prices, routes and services preempts a claim under Minnesota law for breach of the implied covenant of good faith arising from termination of a frequent-flyer membership.
sections.Holding: The Court in 2014, in a unanimous opinion by Justice Alito, held that the Airline Deregulation Act preempted Ginsberg's Minnesota implied-covenant claim because that claim related to airline prices and services and enlarged the airline's voluntarily adopted obligations. The Court reversed the Ninth Circuit and remanded. It did not announce that every airline contract or every implied-covenant claim is unenforceable, and it did not decide whether the agreement permitted termination for an ulterior cost-cutting purpose.
sections.Reasoning:
The Act sought to let competitive markets set airline prices, routes and services. Morales gave "related to" a broad connection-or-reference meaning, and Wolens distinguished state consumer regulation from enforcement of the airline's own voluntarily accepted promises, which can be enforced without imposing additional state standards. That distinction, not the contractual label on a pleading, controlled.

Common-law rules qualify as provisions having the force of law. The statutory language, its earlier references to rules and standards, the nonsubstantive 1994 recodification, and the deregulatory purpose all rejected the idea that only statutes and administrative regulations can be preempted. Sprietsma, on a differently worded boat-safety statute, did not compel another answer, and the older general aviation saving clause could not override the later specific preemption rule.

The claim related to prices and services because reinstatement would restore miles redeemable for cheaper tickets and access to flights and upgrades. The Court left open whether programs that earned or redeemed miles outside aviation might matter in another case.

The Court rejected both categorical positions, that all good-faith claims are preempted and that all survive. States use the covenant differently: some implement implicit contractual intentions, others impose community standards independent of assent. Minnesota did not permit parties to disclaim its covenant, making it a state-imposed obligation, and its general application except to employment contracts for policy reasons showed that state policy determined its reach.

Answering Northwest's concern about a regulatory patchwork, the Court said airlines could contract around the covenant where the relevant state allowed it, and identified market reputation and federal DOT enforcement as protections for passengers. An express-contract claim might have tested whether discretion to determine abuse authorized this termination, but Ginsberg chose not to pursue it.

CT-NEXT-CM-0108.rule: The duty of good faith in performance does not require altruism or general candor, but it forbids deliberately exploiting the other party's oversight about its rights under the existing contract.

sections.Parties: Market Street Associates Limited Partnership, which in 1987 acquired J.C.
