The absence of proven nutritional superiority, or of a precise breakdown between soup stock and visible ingredient, did not defeat Campbell's commercial interest in them. Personal or commercially distinctive value could matter even without an objectively incomparable object: Campbell had contracted well ahead for a special type and built a reputation partly dependent on product uniformity. An order would not require difficult continuing supervision.

The contract nevertheless barred relief. Campbell's unilateral right to determine conformity was not independently unconscionable, since by analogy to satisfaction clauses it could be liable for refusing carrots that met specifications. But the other clauses, and above all paragraph 9, drove the buyer's protections too far: carrots the grower could not deliver to Campbell could not be disposed of otherwise.

The individual provisions were separable, but severing illegal terms was beside the point, because illegality was not the holding. The sum of the provisions led the court to deny the additional assistance of a court of conscience to the party that secured that bargain.

CT-NEXT-CM-0140.rule: Specific performance rests in judicial discretion; physical uniqueness does not compel it, because the question is whether the promised interest can be valued reliably enough for damages to be adequate, and relief may also be denied where it would impose disproportionate hardship.

sections.Parties: Van Wagner Advertising Corp., which leased a building's exterior wall for a billboard, was the plaintiff; it sued for declarations, specific performance and damages after its lease was cancelled. S & M Enterprises, which bought the building from the original lessor, Michaels, and purported to cancel the lease, was the defendant. Both sides appealed to the Appellate Division and then to the Court of Appeals.
sections.Procedural History: A preliminary injunction was denied on S & M's reading of the cancellation clause. After a nonjury trial, Trial Term found Van Wagner's interpretation correct, either from the text or from the parties' negotiations, and declared the lease valid. It denied specific performance, finding damages adequate and compelled performance disproportionately harmful to S & M, and awarded lost revenues only through trial, permitting later suits for the continuing exclusion. The Appellate Division affirmed without opinion, and both parties obtained leave to appeal. The New York Court of Appeals modified, with costs to Van Wagner, remitted to Supreme Court, New York County, for further damages proceedings, and otherwise affirmed.
sections.Material Facts:
In December 1981 Michaels leased Van Wagner the eastern exterior wall of a Manhattan building facing the Midtown Tunnel exit. The term was three years, with options adding seven more. Van Wagner erected an illuminated billboard and subleased it to Asch for three years beginning March 1, 1982.

Michaels agreed in January to sell the building to S & M. In August S & M purported to cancel the billboard lease effective October 18, relying on a clause permitting the lessor or its successor to terminate on sixty days' notice in the event of a bona fide sale to an unrelated third party. Van Wagner read the clause as giving the right to an owner making a sale, to enable an unencumbered conveyance; S & M read it as giving the new owner a cancellation right. Van Wagner left under protest and sued in November.

At trial S & M proved plans to demolish the existing buildings and develop a mixed residential and commercial project when another lease expired in 1987, or sooner. The building had been sold only once in forty years. Van Wagner itself held more than four hundred billboard leases.
sections.Issue: Whether S & M's cancellation breached the lease, and, if so, whether Van Wagner was entitled to specific performance because the billboard location was unique, or was properly limited to damages, and for what period those damages should be awarded.
sections.Holding: The New York Court of Appeals (1986), in an opinion by Kaye in which Wachtler, Meyer, Simons, Titone and Hancock concurred and Alexander took no part, held that S & M's cancellation was a breach but that specific performance was properly denied. The finding that the location was unique did not dictate relief, because the value of the leasehold could be fixed with reasonable certainty, and the denial was independently justified by disproportionate harm to S & M. The trial court erred in stopping damages at November 23, 1983 and requiring successive suits; damages should cover the entire Van Wagner term in this action.
sections.Reasoning:
On breach, the court held the clause ambiguous as a matter of law, since reasonable readers could differ on whether a purchaser could cancel merely on acquiring the building. But the alternative finding from parol evidence was factual, supported by the record, affirmed below, and so outside the court's review. Denial of the preliminary injunction did not fix the law of the case.

Specific performance lies in sound judicial discretion. The traditional treatment of sales of real property did not make every lease of real property specifically enforceable as a matter of course. Every parcel may differ physically; what matters to the adequacy of damages is whether the promised interest can be valued reliably. Sparse or unreliable information about substitutes creates a substantial risk of undercompensation and favors performance, while abundant dependable comparisons can support a sufficiently certain award even for a physically singular object.

Here the Asch contract fixed value for its own term, and comparison with similar commercial billboard leases could establish later value. Projecting damages beyond Asch's February 1985 expiration through Van Wagner's 1992 term was not inherently speculative. S & M could not claim that damages were adequate while insisting that damages beyond sixty days were too conjectural. Possible termination on a future sale did not change this, because that contingency was outside Van Wagner's control and served S & M's interests.

Equitable relief should not itself create inequity or undue hardship, and given S & M's development plans there was no abuse of discretion. Each side's attempt to revise the Asch-period valuation failed for want of proof offered at trial.

The casebook excerpt cuts off before the judgment and the correction of the damages period.

CT-NEXT-CM-0141.rule: Under the prevention doctrine, a party whose breach of contract materially contributes to the nonoccurrence of a condition cannot rely on that nonoccurrence, so a buyer who breaches its financing-efforts covenant cannot invoke the unfunded-debt condition to avoid specific performance.

sections.Parties: The plaintiffs were on the seller's side of the sale of DecoPac, a supplier of cake-decorating products and technology to supermarket bakeries that Snow Phipps had acquired in 2017 and decided to sell in 2019; they sought specific performance of the stock purchase agreement. The defendants were the buyer, KCAKE Acquisition, Inc., and related Kohlberg funds, which had refused to close and purported to terminate the agreement.
sections.Procedural History: Plaintiffs sued on April 14, 2020. The court initially declined an extremely compressed trial schedule and later expedited the matter. An October ruling on a motion to dismiss rejected a duplicative implied-covenant count and addressed contractual remedy limits. After a five-day trial, Vice Chancellor McCormick entered judgment for the plaintiffs on specific performance, obligating the buyers to close. The court requested supplemental submissions within five business days on the closing deadline and entitlement to prejudgment interest; it did not adopt plaintiffs' proposed fifteen-day deadline or finally award interest. This is a single-judge trial decision.
sections.Material Facts:
Kohlberg proposed $580 million in February 2020, raised its offer to $600 million, and before signing demanded a reduction to $550 million. The parties signed March 6, 2020, as COVID-19 spread. Plaintiffs sought an express pandemic exclusion from the material-adverse-effect (MAE) definition and Kohlberg rejected it, but the definition kept broad exceptions, including effects arising from or related to changes in government laws and orders, unless materially disproportionate to comparable businesses.

The buyer promised reasonable best efforts to obtain financing on terms no less favorable than its debt commitment letter (DCL), under which lenders committed $365 million and which expired May 12, 2020. Debt financing was not a closing condition, but the specific-performance provision conditioned that remedy on the debt being funded. A $33 million termination fee was the exclusive monetary remedy.

DecoPac's regular sales fell sharply as shutdown orders spread. Kohlberg's senior personnel developed buyer's remorse. After consulting litigation counsel, Kohlberg produced progressively pessimistic forecasts without meaningful management input, dismissed management's detailed forecast seventeen minutes after receiving it, and did not send it to lenders. With its own March 26 model it demanded a larger revolver, extraordinary EBITDA addbacks and a covenant-testing holiday. The lenders refused the new terms but remained willing to fund under the DCL. Kohlberg reported financing unavailable, looked for alternatives for four days, rejected the seller's offer of financing assistance, refused to close April 8, and purported to terminate April 20. DecoPac's sales recovered; its 2020 results showed a fourteen-percent revenue decline and a twenty-five-percent adjusted-EBITDA decline from 2019.
sections.Issue: Whether the buyer was excused from closing because of a material adverse effect or a breach of the ordinary-course covenant; whether the buyer breached its obligation to use reasonable best efforts to obtain debt financing; and whether the seller could obtain specific performance although the debt financing, a condition of that remedy, had not funded.
sections.Holding: The Delaware Court of Chancery (2021), Vice Chancellor McCormick, ordered the buyers to close. The buyer did not prove an MAE, and even assuming one, the government-order exception applied. The ordinary-course defense also failed: the revolver draw was not a material deviation in the contractual sense, and the cost reductions followed historical practice. The buyer breached its financing-efforts obligation in Section 6.15(a). Under the prevention doctrine that breach, which materially contributed to the absence of debt funding, excused the debt-funding condition on specific performance. Prejudgment interest and the exact closing deadline were left for further submissions.
sections.Reasoning:
On the MAE, the buyer had to show a qualifying effect, the seller an exclusion, and the buyer then a materially disproportionate effect. An effect must be durationally significant, ordinarily measured in years rather than a short earnings interruption. The sharp weekly decline did not qualify: recovery had begun before termination, credible contemporaneous forecasts projected a rebound, and the court rejected the March 26 model as a reliable forecast. Even assuming an MAE, the government-order exception's broad relation language did not require the orders to be the exclusive cause, regression evidence tied most of the decline to them, and Kohlberg did not show disproportionate harm against appropriate comparisons.

The ordinary-course inquiry was separate and less demanding, but DecoPac's $15 million revolver draw followed prior draws, was disclosed, was never used, and was repaid; Kohlberg also failed to honor the contractual notice and cure protection. The cost reductions followed historical practice, and that theory was waived by being raised late.

On financing, the court read the provisions together: the DCL was a floor, and the buyer could seek better terms but could not insist on new ones and refuse the agreed financing when they were unavailable. Language making terms acceptable to the buyer did not give it unlimited discretion. Its reliance on an unsupported model, disregard of management's forecast and of improving sales, and failure to work constructively with counterparties breached its efforts duties.

On the remedy, a party's breach that materially contributes to a condition's nonoccurrence excuses it. Plaintiffs did not have to prove strict but-for inevitability; the buyer bore the burden of showing the condition would have failed regardless. Letting the DCL expire did not cleanse the breach, and no separate showing of subjective bad faith was needed because express financing duties supplied the wrongful conduct.

CT-NEXT-CM-0142.rule: A permanent injunction against breach of contract is proper when the plaintiff shows that damages are an inadequate remedy, which the court decides by comparing the costs and benefits of damages and injunctive relief in the particular case.

sections.Parties: Walgreen Co., which operated a pharmacy in Milwaukee's Southgate Mall under a lease containing an exclusivity promise, was the plaintiff; it sued to stop the mall from leasing space to a competing pharmacy. The defendants were its landlord, Sara Creek Property Co., and Phar-Mor, the deep discount store Sara Creek proposed to bring in. Sara Creek appealed, arguing that money damages rather than an injunction were the proper remedy.
sections.Procedural History: Walgreen sued both Sara Creek and Phar-Mor in federal court under diversity jurisdiction. Following an evidentiary hearing, the district court found a breach and permanently enjoined Sara Creek from leasing the anchor premises to Phar-Mor until Walgreen's lease expired. On appeal, Sara Creek challenged the choice of remedy; its antitrust objection to the exclusivity clause, raised below, was not pressed, so the Seventh Circuit did not resolve it. Asking whether the district judge had exceeded the range of permissible choices, the Seventh Circuit affirmed the permanent injunction.
sections.Material Facts:
Walgreen had operated a pharmacy in Southgate Mall from the mall's opening in 1951. Its 1971 lease ran for thirty years and six months and promised that the landlord, Sara Creek, would not lease mall space to another pharmacy or a store containing one. In 1990 the mall's largest tenant had become insolvent and threatened to close. Sara Creek proposed buying out that tenant and replacing it with Phar-Mor, which would occupy 100,000 square feet, including a 12,000-square-foot pharmacy equal in size to Walgreen's. The entrances would be only a few hundred feet apart.

Walgreen's lease still had ten years to run. Sara Creek's expert considered Walgreen's loss readily estimable; Walgreen's employees disputed that and emphasized difficult-to-value goodwill. Sara Creek offered evidence that Phar-Mor had caused little harm to Walgreen in other malls, but the comparability of those malls to Southgate was seriously disputed. Sara Creek did not claim that excluding Phar-Mor would force the mall to close, and Phar-Mor was not the only possible anchor tenant.
sections.Issue: Whether the district court permissibly granted a permanent injunction, rather than leaving Walgreen to money damages, to enforce the landlord's promise not to lease mall space to a competing pharmacy.
sections.Holding: The Seventh Circuit in 1992, in an opinion by Judge Posner joined by Judge Kanne, with Senior Judge Harlington Wood, Jr. separately concurring and joining the affirmance and Posner's analysis, affirmed the permanent injunction. The plaintiff bears the burden of showing that damages are inadequate, and the district judge did not exceed the range of permissible choices in granting the injunction. The holding sustained a fact-specific exercise of remedial discretion; it did not make every real-estate promise specifically enforceable or declare injunctions presumptively mandatory for shopping-center exclusivity clauses.
sections.Reasoning:
Posner accepted much of Sara Creek's efficient-breach reasoning but rejected its conclusion. Decisions awarding damages for exclusivity breaches did not establish a categorical prohibition on injunctions. The choice requires comparing the costs and benefits of the available remedies in the particular circumstances; if the balance is even, the injunction should be withheld. For a permanent injunction the relevant burden is inadequacy of damages, which the court distinguished from irreparable injury in the preliminary setting.

An injunction has two possible benefits. It lets the parties price the protected right themselves, since if Sara Creek gains more from Phar-Mor than Walgreen loses they can negotiate a payment for surrendering the injunction, and bargaining may reveal actual valuations more accurately than a battle of damages experts. It also has costs: some injunctions demand continuing judicial supervision or harm third parties, and an injunction can create a bilateral monopoly in which negotiations consume resources or collapse. The court's figures of a $1 million loss and a $2 million gain were a hypothetical, not findings. Damages avoid those costs but require litigation to estimate value and risk getting it wrong.

Here the balance favored Walgreen. Damages would require forecasting revenues and costs over ten years, isolating Phar-Mor's competitive effect, and discounting to present value, steps that apart from discounting were deeply uncertain; the disputed comparison to other malls did not resolve that, and the discovery burdens themselves illustrated costs of the damages remedy. The injunction imposed a simple negative obligation needing little supervision, Phar-Mor was already a party, and the relatively modest expected bargaining costs did not outweigh the expense and uncertainty of valuation. The court recognized a possible argument for a presumption favoring injunctions for exclusivity clauses but left its strength undecided.

CT-NEXT-CM-0143.rule: Under the UCC, specific performance is available when goods are unique or in other proper circumstances, such as when a substitute cannot readily be obtained; and an accepted part payment satisfies the statute of frauds for an oral sale of one indivisible item.

sections.Parties: Dr. Joseph and Linda Sedmak, automobile enthusiasts, were the plaintiffs; they sued for specific performance of an oral agreement to sell them a limited-edition Corvette. Charlie's Chevrolet, Inc., the dealership, was the defendant and the appellant. It challenged the evidentiary basis for the contract, its enforceability without a writing, and the propriety of specific performance.
sections.Procedural History: The case was tried to the court. The trial judge credited the Sedmaks, found an oral purchase contract excepted from the statute of frauds, and ordered Charlie's to make the car available for delivery. The dealership appealed. Under Murphy v. Carron the appellate court would sustain a court-tried judgment unless it was unsupported by substantial evidence, against the weight of the evidence, or based on an erroneous declaration or application of law, with witness credibility left to the trial judge. The Missouri Court of Appeals affirmed the specific-performance decree.
sections.Material Facts:
Chevrolet announced a limited edition of approximately 6,000 Corvettes commemorating the car's selection as the Indianapolis 500 Pace Car. In November 1977 the Sedmaks, who already owned six Corvettes, asked the dealership's sales manager, Tom Kells, about obtaining one; he said that if the dealership received a car they could purchase it.

On January 9, 1978, Kells required a deposit and Mrs. Sedmak delivered a $500 check. Before paying she asked whether they would definitely own the car; by her testimony Kells said yes. She then requested an L82 engine, a four-speed standard transmission, and an AM/FM radio with a tape deck, and the car arrived with those options. As the trial court found, the price was to be the manufacturer's suggested retail price at delivery, estimated at approximately $15,000. Kells promised to mail a retail order form but none was sent.

On April 3 Kells told the Sedmaks that because of rising demand they could no longer buy at the suggested retail price but could bid. They declined and sued. Kells denied discussing a price, and his explanation of the $500 shifted.

Each dealership received only one Pace Car, and only some had these options. The sticker price was $14,284.21; buyers in Hawaii and Florida offered $24,000 and $28,000.
sections.Issue: Whether the evidence supported an oral contract with a sufficiently definite price; whether a $500 deposit took an oral contract for one car out of the statute of frauds; and whether specific performance was proper for a car that was not one of a kind.
sections.Holding: The Missouri Court of Appeals (1981), in an opinion by Judge Satz in which Presiding Judge Smith and Judge Weier concurred, affirmed. The parties agreed on an ascertainable price, the manufacturer's suggested retail price at delivery. The accepted deposit satisfied the statute of frauds; that holding was expressly limited to partial payment for a single indivisible commercial unit with no quantity dispute. Practical difficulty of replacement was an 'other proper circumstance' supporting specific performance even without traditional uniqueness.
sections.Reasoning:
On the existence of a contract, the court found the supposed conflicts in the Sedmaks' testimony reconcilable and accepted the trial judge's credibility determination. A price need not be stated in dollars and cents at formation when the parties choose a method that will fix it, and the later rise in market value did not undo the bargain.

On the statute of frauds, the court relied only on partial payment and did not decide whether the memoranda sufficed. Historically, partial payment could validate an entire oral contract for goods. The UCC narrowed that to goods for which payment had been made and accepted, to prevent a small payment for one item being used to fabricate a larger quantity; for divisible goods the payment validates only the quantity to which it can fairly be apportioned. Charlie's argued that partial payment could therefore never validate a sale of one indivisible object. The court disagreed: the Code's concern was uncertain quantity, and here the dispute was whether there was a sale or only an opportunity to bid, not how many cars. The deposit evidenced a purchase, identified Charlie's, and concerned one car. Denying enforcement would permit repudiation of a promise actually made rather than prevent fabrication.

On the remedy, Missouri's UCC permitted specific performance when goods were unique or in other proper circumstances. Missouri had long asked practically whether replacement was feasible, as in Boeving v. Vandover. The trial court found that a car of the same mileage, condition, ownership and appearance could not readily be obtained, and the distant, high offers supported an inference of scarce supply and substantial demand. The holding does not make every limited-production car sale specifically enforceable.

The casebook excerpt omits most of the contract and statute-of-frauds analysis.

CT-NEXT-CM-0144.rule: In computing lost profits for breach of contract, fixed overhead that the plaintiff would have borne whether or not the contract was performed is normally not deducted, because the breach did not save it.

sections.Parties: Vitex Manufacturing Corp., which chemically shower-proofed imported wool in the Virgin Islands, was the plaintiff and appellee; it sued for the profits it lost when its customer supplied no cloth to process. Caribtex Corp., which imported cloth, arranged for its processing, and exported the finished goods, was the defendant and the appellant.
sections.Procedural History: The district court, sitting without a jury, found an agreement to process 125,000 yards despite conflicting accounts of the negotiations and awarded Vitex $21,114 plus interest. Caribtex appealed, attacking several components of the estimated costs, arguing that the agreement was unconscionable, and, for the first time at appellate oral argument, objecting that overhead had not been deducted. The Third Circuit affirmed the $21,114 judgment plus interest.
sections.Material Facts:
Foreign goods sufficiently increased in value through processing in the Virgin Islands could enter the continental United States without otherwise substantial tariffs, and local quotas limited each processor's output. In autumn 1963 Vitex had unused quota but no customers and had closed its plant. Caribtex then acquired Italian wool and negotiated with Vitex in New York for processing.

Vitex reopened its plant, recalled workers, ordered chemicals, and prepared to perform. Caribtex supplied no cloth despite repeated demands, apparently because it doubted that customs officials would give the processed wool duty-free treatment.

The trial court deducted $10,136 in costs from a gross amount of $31,250 to reach the $21,114 award, charging all expenses directly associated with reactivating the plant and processing. The opinion states a price of twenty-six cents per yard, which for 125,000 yards would give $32,500; $31,250 corresponds to twenty-five cents. The source leaves that inconsistency unresolved.

Overhead, meaning continuing business expenses such as executive and clerical salaries, property taxes and administration, was not deducted.
sections.Issue: Whether, in calculating the profits a processor lost when its customer repudiated, a pro rata share of the processor's fixed overhead must be deducted as a cost of the contract; and whether the agreement was unconscionable.
sections.Holding: The Third Circuit (1967), in an opinion by Chief Judge Staley for a panel also including Judges Maris and Coffin, the latter sitting by designation, affirmed. Adopting what it called the better view while acknowledging contrary authority, the court held that fixed overhead normally need not be deducted in calculating profits lost on a particular contract. The damages findings had substantial support in the record, and the agreement was not unconscionable.
sections.Reasoning:
On proof, exact costs were hard to establish because Caribtex repudiated before any processing occurred, and the breaching party could not benefit from uncertainty it had caused; the court nonetheless found a sufficient evidentiary basis.

On overhead, the compensatory principle allows losses incurred and gains prevented, less savings made possible by the breach. Nonperformance did not save these expenses, so subtracting them would undercompensate Vitex. The closed plant made the point concrete: without the Caribtex contract Vitex would still have borne its existing overhead, while reopening and processing would add labor, chemicals, fuel and other direct expenses, which were properly deducted.

The court agreed that allocating overhead to transactions is useful for pricing and planning, but denied that such an allocation identifies a cost saved by breach. Expenses paid from overall receipts do not become causally tied to each transaction because an accountant spreads them across the year's output.

Alternatively, even if allocation were accepted, losing the contract's contribution leaves the remaining business to bear more of the fixed expense. In the court's illustration, a business with $10,000 of overhead and five transactions contributing $2,000 each would, on losing one, carry $2,500 on each of the other four. Commercial parties could foresee that loss.

The UCC's seller's lost-profit provision, which expressly includes reasonable overhead, reinforced the conclusion as persuasive authority, though the Code did not govern this processing agreement.

Unconscionability failed because negotiations were extensive, the parties apparently had equal strength, Vitex was not the only island processor, and Caribtex had obtained successive substantial price reductions.

CT-NEXT-CM-0145.rule: A buyer faced with the seller's repudiation may cover by reasonable substitute purchases made in good faith and without unreasonable delay and recover the difference between cover cost and contract price plus incidental damages, without also proving market price.

sections.Parties: Laredo Hides Company, Inc., which bought hides from American meatpackers for resale to Mexican tanneries, was the plaintiff and the appellant. H & H Meat Products Company, Inc., which operated a meatpacking plant in Mercedes, Texas, and had contracted to sell Laredo its entire hide production, was the defendant and appellee. Laredo sought damages for H & H's refusal to make further deliveries.
sections.Procedural History: After a bench trial the trial court entered a take-nothing judgment. Its findings treated time as essential, the absence of payment on March 18 as a breach, and the March 21 deadline as an agreed extension that Laredo failed to satisfy. Laredo appealed both the seller's asserted right to terminate and the denial of damages. The Texas Court of Civil Appeals at Corpus Christi reversed and rendered judgment for Laredo for $152,960.04, with six percent interest from August 6, 1973, the date of the trial judgment. Rehearing was denied August 29, 1974, and a second motion on September 23, 1974.
sections.Material Facts:
The written contract of February 29, 1972 covered H & H's entire hide production from March through December, with deliveries at least twice monthly and payment in cash on delivery. In practice Laredo paid by check, including for the first March delivery.

On March 17 Laredo issued a $9,000 check and left it with its trucking agent for the next day's pickup, but the driver departed without it. The agent telephoned H & H's manager, Hinojosa, who authorized mailing the check, and H & H released the hides. The check was mailed March 18. On March 21 Hinojosa demanded that money actually reach him by 4:30 that afternoon or H & H would deliver no more hides. Laredo arranged a bank transfer, but the correspondent bank had closed before it could be completed. Two telegrams reached H & H after the deadline, announcing the transfer and that payment on the mailed check had been stopped. H & H's account was credited March 23. On March 30 H & H unequivocally refused future deliveries.

Laredo, which already had a resale commitment to a Mexican tannery, bought replacement hides periodically through the rest of the contract term because hides could not practically be stored for long. Prices rose sharply. H & H actually produced 17,218 hides from April through December. The price differences were $134,252.82 for steer hides and $8,001.66 for bull hides, and added transportation and handling came to $3,448.95.
sections.Issue: Whether the late payment for one delivery, after the seller had authorized payment by mail and released the hides, entitled the seller to terminate all remaining installments, and whether the buyer's periodic replacement purchases established recoverable cover damages without proof of market price.
sections.Holding: The Texas Court of Civil Appeals at Corpus Christi (1974), in a majority opinion by Bissett with Chief Justice Nye dissenting, reversed and rendered judgment for Laredo. H & H had waived strict concurrent payment, its few-hours demand was not reasonable notice restoring strict performance, and its March 30 refusal to deliver was an anticipatory repudiation. Laredo was entitled under sections 2.711 and 2.712 to the difference between its cover cost and the contract price plus incidental damages; the $152,960.04 included the cover and incidental sums and prejudgment interest.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority rejected the premise that every delay in payment made time essential or justified forfeiting the whole contract; the agreement had no termination provision tied to punctual payment. Because H & H authorized payment by mail, proper mailing was payment for this purpose and H & H bore the risk of postal delay. Releasing the hides without the check also waived simultaneous payment. A party that has waived strict performance must give reasonable notice and an opportunity to comply before restoring it, and a demand for money within a few hours, between parties about 165 miles apart, was unreasonable. Nor did Laredo's attempt to avoid termination by a bank transfer turn the demand into an agreed modification; on rehearing the majority stressed that no actual agreement was pleaded or proved.

H & H's refusal was an anticipatory repudiation, and section 2.610 excused Laredo from futile tenders. Under sections 2.703 and 2.612, a right to insist on payment before releasing one delivery did not establish a right to cancel all future installments without substantial impairment of the whole contract.

Cover and section 2.713 market damages are alternatives, so a buyer who proves proper cover need not prove market price when it learned of the breach. Laredo's documented purchases were presumptively proper, H & H offered nothing to rebut their reasonableness or to show expenses saved, and periodic purchases matched the perishable goods and the delivery pattern. A prayer for at least $100,000 with general relief did not cap recovery.

Chief Justice Nye first would have remanded on damages; on rehearing he withdrew that dissent and would have affirmed, reading the buyer's conduct as assent to a modification needing no consideration under section 2.209, and relying on earlier dishonored checks as substantial impairment.

CT-NEXT-CM-0146.rule: A builder who substantially performs, judged by the essential purpose of the contract, recovers the contract price less damages for defects, measured by cost of repair for defects that can reasonably be corrected and by diminution in value where correction would cause unreasonable economic waste.

sections.Parties: Eugene Plante, the builder, was the plaintiff; he sought a lien to recover the unpaid balance of the price of a house and claimed extras. Frank and Carol Jacobs, the owners and defendants, asserted deficient and incomplete construction and argued that Plante had not substantially performed. The owners appealed, and Plante also sought review of the denial of his claimed extras and the allowance for rebuilding a patio wall.
sections.Procedural History: Plante sought a lien for the unpaid balance and claimed extras. The trial court found substantial performance, allowed the owners $1,601.95 for conceded omissions, deducted compensation for established defects from the builder's recovery, rejected unproved items, and denied Plante's claimed extras. The owners appealed, and Plante sought review of the denial of extras and the patio-wall allowance. Both sides challenged the damage methodology, the owners arguing for $10,000 in damages and Plante for only $650. The Wisconsin Supreme Court affirmed the judgment rather than accepting either proposed total. The report records denial of rehearing on October 4, 1960, with $25 costs.
sections.Material Facts:
According to the casebook's editorial introduction, Plante agreed to provide materials and build a house for the Jacobses on their Brookfield lot for $26,765; they paid $20,000 before disputes about workmanship and completion led them to stop further payment, and Plante did not finish. The judicial opinion itself begins with the parties' appellate arguments about substantial performance.

Plante conceded omissions of kitchen cabinets, gutters and downspouts, a sidewalk, closet clothes poles and an entrance seat, totaling $1,601.95. The owners asserted about twenty additional defects and argued that full correction would cost 25 to 30 percent of the contract price. Their principal objection was a misplaced interior wall that narrowed the living room by more than a foot. Moving it would cost approximately $4,000. The house was finished and decorated around the wall, and the owners occupied it. Experts for both sides agreed that the narrower room did not reduce the house's market price. The plan was a stock floor plan, not detailed blueprints, and the specifications were standard forms with modifications and additions. Nothing showed that the owners demanded the wall's relocation while construction was underway. The contract required written agreement for extras, and none existed.
sections.Issue: Whether the defects and omissions prevented the builder from recovering on the contract, leaving him at most a claim in quantum meruit, and, if performance was substantial, whether the owners' damages for each defect are measured by cost of repair or by diminution in value.
sections.Holding: The Wisconsin Supreme Court in 1960, in an opinion by Hallows with no separate writing reported, affirmed. Plante substantially performed, so he recovered the contract price less damages attributable to incomplete or defective work. The trial court's differentiated treatment of the proven defects stood: repair cost for the plaster cracks, patio floor and patio wall, and no award for relocating the living-room wall, because moving it would substantially destroy completed work and both sides' experts agreed it did not affect market price. Denial of the builder's disputed extras was also affirmed.
sections.Reasoning:
Contract recovery requires substantial performance, which the court defined by the essential purpose of the promised performance rather than a mathematical percentage of completion or repair cost. A building need not comply perfectly with every specification unless the parties make particular details essential, although a feature of special or great personal importance could defeat substantial performance if left unperformed. Prior decisions, such as those involving a grossly inadequate boiler or a practically useless boathouse, illustrated failures to accomplish a contract's essential purpose. Here the owners received a usable house built from a stock plan and standard-form specifications, and the record did not show that every detail was essential to their agreement.

On damages, diminution in value compares the building as delivered with the building as properly promised. Small, separable defects that can reasonably be corrected without destroying substantial completed work may be measured by correction cost, with unreasonable economic waste limiting destructive reconstruction. The defects here could be separated without confusion. Correcting ceiling plaster cracks, mud jacking and repairing the patio floor, and reconstructing a nonstructural patio wall did not involve unreasonable waste, so those repair allowances stood.

Moving the living-room wall was different. It would substantially destroy completed work, damage other portions of the house, and require replastering and redecorating walls and ceilings in at least two rooms. The court treated the diminution measure as contemplating that the wall would remain, and because both sides' experts agreed it did not affect market price, the owners established no recoverable loss for it. That conclusion depended on these facts.

Plante's claimed extras failed because the contract required written agreement, none existed, the evidence about waiver conflicted, and he carried the burden.

CT-NEXT-CM-0147.rule: When a contractor deliberately fails to perform a construction obligation, the owner's damages are the reasonable cost of performing the promised work, even if that cost exceeds the value of the completed land; economic waste concerns only destroying a completed or substantially completed structure.

sections.Parties: Frank Groves was the plaintiff and the appellant. He sued as assignee and successor to the rights of S. J. Groves & Sons, the landowner and lessor, and sought damages measured by the cost of completing the grading that had been promised. John Wunder Co., the lessee that had promised to grade the site, was the defendant. Liability for breach was not the disputed question on appeal; the dispute was the measure of damages.
sections.Procedural History:
The trial findings established that Wunder failed to perform the grading covenant. The trial court applied a market-value measure and entered judgment of slightly more than $15,000 including interest, rather than awarding the cost of completion. The plaintiff appealed the measure of damages.

The Minnesota court reversed and ordered a new trial. It did not render a fixed award above $60,000. The first question on remand was what the grading language actually demanded, an interpretation the court expressly withheld because the issue had not been argued on appeal. Justice Olson, joined by Justice Holt, dissented and would have affirmed the existing judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
S. J. Groves & Sons owned twenty-four acres of suburban Minneapolis land zoned for heavy industry, with existing or readily available railroad access. Limited development in the neighborhood made the sand and gravel deposit the property's principal immediate asset. Groves operated an excavating and screening plant there, and Wunder operated a nearby competing plant.

In August 1927 the parties' transaction gave Wunder a seven-year lease, the screening plant and rights to remove sand and gravel, and eliminated Groves as a competitor. Wunder paid $105,000 and promised to leave the site at a uniform grade substantially matching the existing roadway, using stripped overburden to establish and maintain that grade.

Wunder removed the richest gravel and left the land broken, rugged and uneven. Under the interpretation used at trial, completion required moving 288,495 cubic yards of overburden off the property at a reasonable cost above $60,000. The land's value if properly graded was only $12,160.
sections.Issue: Whether the promised grading was compensable at its reasonable completion cost even though that cost exceeded the value of the completed land, or whether recovery was limited to a market-value measure.
sections.Holding: The Minnesota court, 1939, in a prevailing opinion by Stone, with Olson and Holt dissenting and Hilton and Loring not participating, held that cost of performance was the appropriate measure for this deliberate failure to perform a construction obligation, subject to determining on remand exactly what work the contract required. The prevailing opinion represented a majority of the sitting quorum, although a minority of the full membership. The judgment was reversed and a new trial ordered. The court did not fix an award; whether every point had to be lowered to roadway level, even if that required hauling material away, remained for initial determination below.
sections.Reasoning:
The aim was to give the promisee, so far as money could do so, the promised accomplishment. A landowner may purchase an improvement for reasons not exhausted by current market value, including future development or personal preferences, and a contractor who has received the agreed consideration cannot escape the cost of the promised work simply because the land is worth little. Stone characterized the breach as willful and in bad faith and distinguished cases of good-faith substantial performance.

The opinion separated contractual loss from tort valuation. Tort generally compensates the decrease in an asset's money value, but this contract entitled the owner to a specified alteration of the property, so the loss was the promised work. Drawing on grading and farm-improvement precedents, the court treated reasonable performance cost as the value of that lost accomplishment and refused to confine that treatment to municipal construction agreements. Its illustration of a monument to an owner's taste showed why the promisor's opinion of economic benefit did not replace the bargain.

The court acknowledged the Restatement's economic-waste limitation but construed it narrowly, as addressing destruction of a completed or substantially completed structure to cure a defect. Here the grading had not been performed, and a large gap between completion cost and land value did not itself establish that kind of waste.

Olson, dissenting, regarded damages as compensation for actual loss, not punishment for motive. He disputed the majority's use of willfulness, saw no showing of a unique personal use, and favored diminution in value when reconstruction expense was disproportionate to its benefit.

CT-NEXT-CM-0148.rule: Reasonable cost of performance ordinarily measures damages for omitted remedial work under a coal lease, but where the breached provision is merely incidental to the main purpose and the economic benefit of performance is grossly disproportionate to its cost, recovery is limited to diminution in value.

sections.Parties: Willie and Lucille Peevyhouse, owners of coal-bearing farm property, were the plaintiffs and lessors. Garland Coal & Mining Co., the strip-mining lessee, was the defendant. Both sides appealed the jury's award. The owners sought the cost-of-performance measure for the restoration work Garland omitted, while Garland sought to limit recovery to the value the restoration would add to the farm.
sections.Procedural History:
The owners sued for $25,000. Over their objection, Garland introduced testimony on the difference between the farm's value without restoration and its value if restoration occurred. The trial judge required a verdict for the owners but let the jury consider both performance cost and the other evidence in fixing the amount. The jury awarded $5,000, and both sides appealed.

The Oklahoma court modified the judgment to $300 and affirmed it as modified; it did not remand for a new damages trial. The original judgment was issued December 11, 1962. The report records modification and denial of rehearing on March 26, 1963, with a supplemental opinion by Jackson and the same five-to-four grouping, and denial of a second rehearing on May 28.
sections.Material Facts:
In November 1954 the Peevyhouses leased their farm to Garland for a five-year strip-mining operation. The agreement permitted use of the surface necessary for mining and payment of royalties, and it also imposed specific restoration obligations, including filling pits at property lines to permit fences and access, smoothing the tops of the spoil banks, and leaving no shale or dirt on the high wall of the pits.

The parties stipulated that every contractual obligation had been performed except the remedial work, and Garland conceded that omission. Experts estimated that the omitted work, involving many thousands of cubic yards of dirt, would cost about $29,000. The court found no evidence supporting more than $300 as the increase in value attributable to the restoration, and the owners did not argue for a higher figure under that measure. The owners had tried the claim on the premise that only performance cost mattered: they objected to the valuation testimony, did not cross-examine Garland's valuation witnesses and offered no rebuttal.
sections.Issue: What is the proper measure of damages for a lessee's failure to do promised restoration work under a coal lease when the cost of the work greatly exceeds the increase in the property's market value that the work would produce?
sections.Holding: The Oklahoma court, 1962, in an opinion by Jackson joined by Welch, Davison, Halley and Johnson, with Williams, Blackbird, Irwin and Berry dissenting, a five-to-four division, held that reasonable cost of performance ordinarily measures a lessor's loss from omitted remedial work under a coal lease. Where, however, the breached provision is merely incidental to the agreement's main purpose and the economic benefit of performance to the lessor is grossly disproportionate to its cost, recovery is limited to the diminution in value caused by the omitted work. The $5,000 judgment was modified to $300 and affirmed as modified. The full brief notes that the casebook's bracketed 4-3 disposition conflicts with the actual report.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority characterized the principal bargain as the economical extraction and sale of coal for the parties' profit and treated the restoration provisions as incidental. It thought it unrealistic that an ordinary owner would spend $29,000 for a $300 increase in value. It distinguished the Restatement's concern about destroying a substantially completed structure from a broader inquiry into expense disproportionate to the end attained, and regarded relative economic benefit as an appropriate consideration even though no completed building needed destruction. It compared Groves with decisions applying diminution in value to similar grading arrangements.

Its governing grounds were Oklahoma statutes barring damages greater than the benefit of full performance and requiring reasonable rather than unconscionable, grossly oppressive damages, which it analogized to restrictions on contractual penalties. On its valuation premise, performance-cost recovery would give the owners more economic benefit than completed restoration. Both qualifications matter: the court acknowledged that where a principal contractual purpose is an improvement that reduces resale value, performance cost would ordinarily govern.

Irwin, dissenting, disputed the incidental-purpose characterization: Garland admitted the owners insisted on restoration and would not lease without it, the cost was reasonably predictable when the contract was made, and he considered the breach willful and without good faith. He would have enforced the unambiguous obligations as written and favored the Groves performance-cost approach.

On rehearing the court refused to let the owners change their theory of the case to develop a valuation claim, and it rejected a federal Contract Clause argument raised by amici because the damage statutes predated the 1954 agreement.

CT-NEXT-CM-0149.rule: A seller who resells is not confined to UCC section 2-706 and may recover lost profit under section 2-708(2) by proving it is a lost-volume seller: it had capacity for both sales, both would have been profitable, and it probably would have made the second sale anyway.

sections.Parties: R. E. Davis Chemical Corp., the buyer of medical diagnostic equipment, was the plaintiff; it sought restitution of its $300,000 deposit under Illinois UCC section 2-718 after refusing delivery. Diasonics, Inc., the seller, was the defendant and the appellant; it claimed an offset for lost-volume profits under section 2-708(2). Diasonics also filed a third-party complaint against the physicians Dobbin and Valvassori, whose breach of their own agreement with Davis preceded Davis's breach.
sections.Procedural History: The district court held that a seller who resells is limited to section 2-706 and entered summary judgment for Davis for $322,656, described as the deposit plus prejudgment interest less incidental damages. By an earlier order it dismissed the third-party complaint because it did not allege intentional inducement of Davis's breach of the equipment contract. Diasonics appealed both rulings. Because Illinois courts had not resolved the remedy questions, the Seventh Circuit predicted how the Illinois Supreme Court would decide them. It affirmed dismissal of the third-party complaint, reversed the summary judgment for Davis, and remanded. Rehearing and rehearing en banc were denied September 10, 1987.
sections.Material Facts:
In February 1984 Davis agreed to buy medical diagnostic equipment from Diasonics and paid a $300,000 deposit. Davis planned to use the equipment at a facility it would establish with the physicians Dobbin and Valvassori. After the physicians breached their agreement with Davis, Davis refused delivery and refused to pay the rest of the price.

Diasonics resold the equipment to another customer at the same price. The resale therefore left no difference between contract price and resale price, but Diasonics maintained that it had lost the profit on an additional sale. Diasonics accepted that the statutory deposit rule allowed Davis restitution less $500, subject to an offset for whatever damages it could establish under Article 2.

In its third-party complaint Diasonics alleged that the physicians knew their own breach would leave Davis unable to use the equipment and was reasonably certain to cause Davis's breach. Those were allegations tested on a motion to dismiss, not findings.
sections.Issue: Whether a seller that resold the goods in a commercially reasonable resale is barred from seeking lost profits under section 2-708(2); what a seller must prove to recover as a lost-volume seller; and whether the resale proceeds must be credited against that profit.
sections.Holding: The Seventh Circuit (1987), in an opinion by Cudahy for a panel with Chief Judge Bauer and Flaum and no separate writing, held that a reselling seller is not confined to section 2-706 and may seek damages under section 2-708. To recover lost-volume profit under subsection (2), Diasonics must prove on remand its capacity to supply both Davis and the resale buyer, that both sales would have been profitable, and that it probably would have made the second sale absent the breach. The resale-proceeds credit does not apply to such a sale. Dismissal of the third-party complaint was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning:
The court rejected a compulsory hierarchy sending every commercially reasonable reseller to section 2-706. Article 2's seller remedies are generally cumulative, subject to the facts and the bar on duplicate compensation. The court did not decide whether a reseller could elect the contract-market differential of subsection (1), because Diasonics sought only the profit measure; an action for the price under section 2-709 was unavailable after resale.

Subsection (2) applies only when subsection (1) is inadequate to put the seller in as good a position as performance. For a seller with limited demand or capacity, a resale may replace the lost transaction. For a lost-volume seller the second purchaser would have bought anyway, so the breach reduces total sales and profit despite a resale at the same price. Calling oneself a manufacturer or proving a resale does not establish that status. Capacity alone is not enough, because rising marginal costs could make the additional sale unprofitable. Diasonics bore the burden because it claimed the damages and had the production and cost information. The court did not find the elements proved or award a sum.

On the credit, subsection (2) calls for credit for payments or resale proceeds, but crediting the full replacement price against genuine lost-volume profit would ordinarily erase the recovery. The court predicted that Illinois would confine that language to situations such as unfinished goods sold for scrap. Davis's restitution of the deposit remained subject to the damages offset.

On the third-party claim, Illinois law required more than knowledge that the physicians' own default was substantially certain to interfere with another contract; Diasonics did not allege that they desired to induce Davis's breach. The court also rejected an objection to the notice of appeal and declined to direct sanctions.

The casebook excerpt omits the third-party and appellate-procedure sections.

CT-NEXT-CM-0150.rule: A subcontractor who justifiably stops work after the other party's material breach may elect restitution for the reasonable value of the performance conferred, less payments received, without deduction for the loss it would have suffered by completing and without the contract price as a ceiling.

sections.Parties: Coastal Steel Erectors, Inc., a steel-erection subcontractor, was the plaintiff and the appellant. It sued in the name of the United States under the Miller Act to recover for labor and equipment it had already supplied. The defendants were Algernon Blair, Inc., the prime contractor on a naval hospital, and its payment-bond surety, United States Fidelity and Guaranty. Blair maintained that the subcontract did not require it to pay crane rental.
sections.Procedural History:
The district court found that the subcontract required payment for crane use and that Blair's refusal to pay was a material breach justifying Coastal's termination; those findings were not challenged on appeal. It estimated that approximately $37,000 remained payable for Coastal's performance under the contract after payments received, but it also found that Coastal would have lost more than $37,000 had it finished. Treating that expected loss as a deduction from contract damages, it denied recovery.

The Fourth Circuit reversed and remanded with instructions to determine accurately the reasonable value of the labor and equipment use Coastal furnished and then enter judgment for Coastal after subtracting prior contractual payments.
sections.Material Facts:
Algernon Blair contracted with the United States to build a naval hospital in Charleston County, South Carolina. It subcontracted steel erection and the supply of associated equipment to Coastal Steel Erectors. Coastal used its own cranes to handle and place the steel. Blair refused to pay crane rental, maintaining that the subcontract did not require payment.

Coastal stopped work after completing approximately twenty-eight percent of its obligations, and Blair hired another subcontractor to finish. The district court estimated that approximately $37,000 remained payable for Coastal's performance under the contract after payments received, and it found that Coastal would have lost more than $37,000 if it had finished the job. The appeal therefore concerned an alternative remedy for a justified cessation after the other party's breach, not whether Coastal itself wrongfully abandoned the project.
sections.Issue: Whether a partly performing subcontractor may elect quantum meruit recovery for the labor and equipment it has already supplied even though completing the contract would have been unprofitable and contract damages would yield no award.
sections.Holding: The Fourth Circuit, 1973, in an opinion by Craven for a panel of Chief Judge Haynsworth, Senior Judge Bryan and Craven, with no separate writing, held that it could. Restitution measures the reasonable value of the performance conferred on Blair, without deducting the loss Coastal would have incurred on the unperformed balance. The contract price may be evidence of reasonable value but neither sets the measure nor caps recovery. Amounts already paid remain deductible. The court reversed and remanded for an accurate finding of reasonable value; it did not award $37,000 as the final restitution figure.
sections.Reasoning:
The court distinguished the expectation question, what financial position completion of this bargain would have produced, from the restitution question, what reasonable value Coastal had already supplied at its own expense and Blair retained without full payment. Blair's material breach entitled Coastal to stop and elect recovery of that value. The anticipated loss on the remaining work did not turn the completed labor and equipment use into a benefit Blair could keep unpaid.

The opinion relied on Miller Act and construction precedents recognizing a promisee's option to forgo contract damages and seek reasonable value after the other party's breach. That remedy could be pursued against the payment-bond surety as well as the prime contractor. Imprecision in the complaint's theory did not preclude quantum meruit, which could be pleaded alongside contract damages, though not to collect duplicative awards.

The relevant value was the amount for which the services could have been purchased from someone in Coastal's position at the time and place of performance. The restitution rationale rested on both Coastal's expenditure and Blair's retained gain, but it did not make every expense automatically recoverable. A footnote acknowledged that restitution could exceed the value of the promised return, consistent with refusing to make the contract price a ceiling.

A footnote stated that federal substantive law controls a Miller Act action when federal and state law differ, while the court believed the outcome would be the same under the pertinent state law. The opinion did not decide the separate case of a claimant who has fully performed. The district court's $37,000 approximation was not a precise reasonable-value finding.

CT-NEXT-CM-0151.rule: After receiving an absolute repudiation, a contractor may not continue performing and charge the avoidable cost to the repudiating party; recovery is limited to labor, materials and expenses in partial performance before repudiation plus the profit the contract would have produced.

sections.Parties: Luten Bridge Co., a bridge builder, was the plaintiff. It sued Rockingham County for $18,301.07 allegedly earned under a bridge-building contract through November 3. Rockingham County was the defendant and the appellant. The county initially contested the contract's validity, but on appeal it admitted execution, validity and its own breach, so the ultimate dispute was the amount Luten could recover.
sections.Procedural History:
Three of the original commissioners met privately with an attorney and filed an answer admitting the complaint. After a new board took office, the county sought to strike that answer and filed its own defense. The trial judge treated the commissioners' answer as the county's admission, admitted it in evidence, excluded the county's proffered resignation and cancellation evidence, and directed a verdict for Luten's full claim. The county appealed.

The Fourth Circuit reversed and remanded for a new trial because the unauthorized answer should have been stricken, the county's evidence should have been admitted, and the directed verdict for the full claim was erroneous. It did not finally calculate the county's liability.
sections.Material Facts:
On January 7, 1924 the county's five-member board awarded Luten the bridge contract by a three-to-two division, and public controversy followed. Pruitt, one of the supporters, submitted his resignation to the superior-court clerk on February 11. The county offered evidence that the clerk accepted it before Pruitt tried to withdraw it and appointed Hampton as successor. Hampton took the oath and thereafter regularly conducted county business with Martin and Barber, while the three original supporters attended no further meetings. These details reached the appellate court through affidavits and offers of proof, much of which the trial court excluded.

At a regularly advertised February 21 meeting the functioning board declared the contract invalid, instructed Luten to proceed no further, and abandoned the road for which the bridge was to be a connecting link. The resolution was sent to Luten. Resolutions in March and April warned that construction would be at Luten's risk, and a September resolution refused payment of bridge bills. When the first notice issued, labor and materials on site amounted to about $1,900. Luten nevertheless continued building.
sections.Issue: Whether an answer filed privately by three commissioners bound the county; whether the functioning board's notices were county action; and whether Luten could recover for construction it continued after receiving an effective repudiation. The assigned casebook excerpt concentrates on the third question.
sections.Holding: The Fourth Circuit, 1929, in an opinion by Parker for a panel with District Judges McClintic and Soper and with no separate writing, held that once Luten received the county's repudiation it could not continue building a bridge the county no longer wanted and charge the avoidable expenditure to the county. On proof of duly given notice, the measure is compensation for labor and materials expended and expenses incurred in partial performance before repudiation, plus the profit the contract would have produced. The privately filed answer was unauthorized and should have been stricken, and the county's resolutions and notices could not be excluded for want of authority. The judgment was reversed and remanded for a new trial.
sections.Reasoning:
A county board exercises its corporate powers as a body in a legally convened meeting. Even assuming the three original commissioners were still a numerical majority, their private conference met none of the statutory requirements for a meeting, so their answer was unauthorized as the county's pleading and could not be evidence of a county admission.

The proffered resignation evidence was relevant. If the offered facts were true, acceptance by the proper authority ended Pruitt's ability to withdraw and permitted Hampton's appointment, giving the three acting members a quorum. Independently, Hampton's appointment by the proper official, his oath and his unchallenged exercise of the office made him a de facto commissioner, so acts at lawful meetings were valid for the county and those dealing with it.

The county had no right to rescind the valid bargain without compensation; its notice was a breach. But after receiving the repudiation Luten could not go on building and charge the avoidable expenditure to the county. The abandoned road left the bridge useless to the county, and Luten's compensable interest was its loss from being stopped, including anticipated profit, which did not require completing unwanted work.

The court applied the American rule against increasing damages through continued performance after absolute repudiation, and distinguished authorities allowing an immediate suit for anticipatory breach. The measure did not confine Luten to $1,900 or eliminate its lost profit, and it did not entitle Luten to the $18,301.07 claimed. The opinion spoke of a duty to mitigate; its consequence here was a limit on recoverable damages.

CT-NEXT-CM-0152.rule: When a seller anticipatorily repudiates, the buyer's market-price damages under UCC section 2-713 are measured at the date of repudiation if cover then would be commercially reasonable; otherwise the buyer may wait a commercially reasonable time, and bears the burden of showing why immediate cover was unreasonable.

sections.Parties: Trinidad Bean & Elevator Co., which operated a grain elevator in Imperial, Nebraska, was the buyer, the plaintiff and the appellant; it claimed the difference between market and contract price under section 2-713 for beans that were never delivered. Elmo Frosh, a farmer who had contracted to sell his navy beans to Trinidad, was the defendant and appellee.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court instructed the jury that a contract existed and measured market damages at harvest, while also submitting as defenses common-law mitigation and unreasonable delay after anticipatory repudiation. The jury returned a general verdict for Frosh. Trinidad unsuccessfully sought a directed verdict, judgment notwithstanding the verdict, and a new trial, and then appealed, contending that October market prices of $37 to $38 established substantial damages and that the mitigation instruction was improper. The Nebraska Court of Appeals affirmed the judgment for Frosh.
sections.Material Facts:
On April 26, 1988, Frosh contracted to sell Trinidad 1,875 hundredweight of edible navy beans after the year's harvest. An inexperienced employee mistakenly completed both alternative payment options: $16.25 per hundredweight deferred until January 15, 1989, and $16 per hundredweight paid in halves at harvest and on December 1. A replacement page identifying one option was prepared, but no corrected contract was signed.

Frosh testified that around May 1 he told the elevator manager to tear up the contract; the manager denied that conversation. Contract and market prices were equal around that date. Frosh asked again in August whether the contract had been destroyed and sent a September letter saying he considered it void. He delivered no beans after the October harvest.

Drought drove prices from approximately $16 in April to $32 in late August or early September and $36 in late September, when Trinidad bought beans elsewhere. The opinion nonetheless characterizes Trinidad's claim as one for the market differential under section 2-713, not for cover damages under section 2-712.
sections.Issue: When a buyer's market-price damages under section 2-713 are to be measured after the seller's anticipatory repudiation: when the buyer learns of the repudiation, or when delivery becomes due.
sections.Holding: The Nebraska Court of Appeals (1992), in an opinion by Connolly for a panel with Chief Judge Sievers and Miller-Lerman and no separate writing, held that the relevant date is the date of repudiation, provided cover on that date would be commercially reasonable. If immediate cover would be commercially unreasonable, the buyer may wait a commercially reasonable period, and the buyer claiming that qualification bears the burden of showing why. The evidence could support an early-May repudiation, when no market-contract differential existed, so the verdict for Frosh was not clearly wrong. The common-law mitigation instruction was erroneous but not prejudicial.
sections.Reasoning:
The court recognized plausible textual arguments for each date. Valuing at the performance date could align the buyer's remedy with the seller's under section 2-708 and draw support from section 2-723's express reference to learning of repudiation for an action tried before the performance date. Earlier Nebraska precedent did not settle the point because there the repudiation and nondelivery dates had coincided.

The court preferred the repudiation date because otherwise section 2-610's limit of a commercially reasonable time to await performance, and section 2-712's bar on unreasonable delay in covering, would have little practical effect. A buyer in a rising market could postpone its substitute transaction while charging the seller the higher later price, and if the market fell could buy more cheaply. The court considered that speculation inconsistent with compensation. This is a valuation rule, not a command that the buyer actually cover: section 2-712(3) preserves other remedies despite a failure to cover.

Applying the rule, the disputed May conversation prevented a directed verdict for Trinidad; if Frosh's testimony was credited, his instruction to tear up the contract communicated a clear determination not to perform. Trinidad's argument that fluctuating futures prices made a four-month wait reasonable did not show a lack of access to the bean futures market or another concrete reason why prompt cover was unreasonable.

The mitigation instruction was error because under section 1-103 common-law principles supplement the Code only where its particular provisions do not displace them, and the timing, cover and market rules already supplied the system for preventing avoidable loss. The error was harmless because the jury could reach the same result under the anticipatory-repudiation instruction.

The casebook excerpt omits the mitigation analysis.

CT-NEXT-CM-0153.rule: When a seller repudiates and the buyer does not cover, the buyer may recover the market-price/contract-price difference under UCC section 2-713 even if that exceeds the buyer's actual lost profit; the specific damages provision controls over the Code's general compensatory principle in section 1-106.

sections.Parties: Denis Tongish, a grower of sunflower seeds, began the case by suing Thomas, to whom he had sold seeds, for the unpaid balance of the price. Thomas deposited $7,359.61 in court and was dismissed. Decatur Coop, which had contracted to buy Tongish's crop, intervened with a claim against Tongish for breach of that contract. In the Kansas Supreme Court Tongish was the party seeking review of the damages ruling.
sections.Procedural History: After a bench trial the district court found that Tongish breached without a valid basis but awarded Coop only $455.51 in lost handling charges. The Court of Appeals reversed and remanded for calculation of damages under the UCC market-price formula. Tongish obtained review in the Kansas Supreme Court of that damages ruling. The Supreme Court adopted the Court of Appeals' analysis, affirmed its reversal and remand for determining and awarding section 2-713 damages, and reversed the district court's judgment. It did not itself enter a calculated award.
sections.Material Facts:
In April 1988 Tongish agreed to grow sunflower seeds for Decatur Coop; the acreage was reduced by agreement from 160 to 116.8 acres. Coop promised $13 per hundredweight for large seeds and $8 for small seeds, with deliveries in thirds by December 31, March 31 and May 31. Coop separately arranged to transfer the seeds to Bambino Bean & Seed, passing the purchase price through and anticipating only a handling return of fifty-five cents per hundredweight.

Tongish delivered some seeds in October and November. A dispute about dockage was resolved by an additional payment from Coop. By January a short crop, weather and other factors had doubled the market price. On January 13 Tongish notified Coop that he would deliver no more. In May he sold 82,820 pounds to Thomas for $14,714.89, approximately $5,153.13 more than the Coop agreement would have yielded.

Tongish knew the seeds ultimately went to Bambino, although he may not have known the details of that arrangement.
sections.Issue: Whether the general compensatory objective of K.S.A. 84-1-106 limited Coop's recovery to its actual lost handling profit, despite the specific measure in K.S.A. 84-2-713 of market price less contract price for nondelivery or repudiation.
sections.Holding: The Kansas Supreme Court (1992), in an opinion by McFarland with no separate writing, upheld the specific statutory market remedy. Coop was entitled to damages measured under section 2-713 by the market price when it learned of the breach less the contract price, not merely to its lost handling charges. The court also rejected Tongish's argument that the larger award would unjustly enrich Coop. It did not treat the $5,153.13 resale gain as automatically the damage figure.
sections.Reasoning:
Section 2-713 permits the market price when the buyer learned of the breach, less the contract price, with applicable incidental and consequential damages and less expenses saved, and a buyer who does not cover may pursue it. General and specific statutes should be harmonized where possible, but the specific provision controls an irreconcilable conflict unless the legislature indicates otherwise. Limiting this buyer to its handling profit could not be reconciled with the specific measure on these facts.

The court considered whether Coop's protection against price fluctuations warranted an exception. It examined Allied Canners, where heavy rains prevented a supplier from delivering raisins, the downstream buyers released the middleman, and a California court limited recovery to the middleman's actual expected profit; that court's concerns included the seller's knowledge of the resale contract and whether the breach was in bad faith. Tongish's case differed: he knew of the resale, his crop was available, and he sold it elsewhere after prices rose. The district court made no separate express finding of bad faith but found no valid reason for the breach.

The court stressed that Coop remained bound to buy at the agreed price even if it lacked a buyer or prices fell. If Tongish owed only the small handling return when prices rose, the contract would be a floor protecting him against declines while leaving him the profit from repudiating on increases. Market damages preserved the reciprocal allocation of price risk and encouraged contractual stability, even though the result might exceed the middleman's realized loss.

The unjust-enrichment argument had not been presented below and also failed on the merits, since the dispute concerned which statutory measure applied rather than a restitution claim. The casebook excerpt omits that holding.

CT-NEXT-CM-0154.rule: A wrongfully discharged employee recovers the agreed compensation less what the employer proves was or could reasonably have been earned in other employment, but only comparable or substantially similar work counts; different or inferior work need not be accepted.

sections.Parties: Shirley MacLaine Parker, who had contracted to play the female lead in a Fox film, was the plaintiff and the respondent on appeal. She sued Twentieth Century-Fox Film Corp. for the compensation due under her contract and, alternatively, for breach damages. Fox, the defendant and appellant, admitted the agreement's validity, Parker's compliance and readiness to perform, and its own anticipatory repudiation. Its sole defense was that by rejecting a substitute role she unreasonably failed to mitigate her loss.
sections.Procedural History:
Parker sued for compensation due and, alternatively, breach damages, and obtained summary judgment for $750,000 plus interest. Although she had not started performing, the parties stipulated for the motion that she had been discharged, allowing wrongful-discharge damage principles to apply. Fox appealed.

The California court affirmed the judgment for $750,000 plus interest by a six-to-one division, with Acting Chief Justice Sullivan dissenting. Rehearing was denied October 28, 1970; Mosk did not participate in that denial and Sullivan favored granting it.
sections.Material Facts:
In August 1965 Parker contracted to play the female lead in Fox's proposed musical Bloomer Girl. The agreement guaranteed $750,000 for fourteen weeks beginning May 23, 1966, expressed as $53,571.42 weekly. Bloomer Girl was to be produced in California and would use her dancing as well as her acting talents.

Fox decided not to make the film and notified Parker on April 4 that it would not fulfill its obligations. In the same letter it offered her the lead in Big Country, Big Man, a dramatic western to be filmed in Australia. Fox offered the same compensation and thirty-one of the original agreement's thirty-four numbered provisions, but it removed dance-director approval because the replacement was not a musical and replaced her director and screenplay approvals with consultation subject to Fox's final decision. Parker had one week to accept and did not do so.

The original agreement also stated that Fox need not use Parker's services and that its obligation was to pay the guaranteed compensation, subject to the agreement's terms.
sections.Issue: Whether Fox's substitute offer raised a triable mitigation defense that barred summary judgment, or whether the different and inferior character of the substitute employment could be decided as a matter of law.
sections.Holding: The California court, 1970, in a majority opinion by Burke joined by McComb, Peters, Tobriner and assigned Justices Kaus and Roth, with Sullivan dissenting, six to one, held that the musical lead in Los Angeles and the straight dramatic western lead in Australia were different kinds of employment and that, independently, eliminating contractual approval rights made the substitute inferior. Fox's offer therefore could not support its mitigation defense, and summary judgment for $750,000 plus interest was affirmed. The majority expressly did not decide Parker's separate argument that the guaranteed-pay clause and other grounds excused mitigation altogether.
sections.Reasoning:
Normally an employee recovers agreed compensation less earnings the employer affirmatively proves were received or could reasonably have been received from other employment.
