Each required arbitration in Wall Township, New Jersey of disputes relating to the agreement or its breach, under AAA rules and New Jersey law, and each said that rights and obligations would not be assignable without written consent. The agreements did not state that a nonconforming transfer would be void or ineffective. After first representing that it had changed its name, Chemrite sold its lubricant business and expressly transferred the Trade Agreements to newly formed Lubritene in October 1996, then entered liquidation. Lubritene continued the business at the same location with the same personnel and management. Bel-Ray was sent the asset-sale documents and the parties kept trading under the agreements. Bel-Ray later obtained board minutes describing a plan to keep trading without alerting it, leave Lubritene without recoverable assets, and later deny the agreements' validity. Bel-Ray alleged unfair competition, fraud, misappropriation, breach and deceptive labeling; the appeal did not decide those merits.
sections.Issue: Whether Chemrite's assignment of the Trade Agreements to Lubritene without Bel-Ray's written consent was effective, so that Lubritene was bound by the arbitration clauses; and whether the four individuals were subject to personal jurisdiction and could be compelled to arbitrate.
sections.Holding: The Third Circuit in 1999, in an opinion by Judge Stapleton for a panel with Rendell and Aldisert and no separate writing, held that the consent clause did not negate Chemrite's power to assign, so the assignment bound Lubritene to the agreements and their arbitration clauses. The individuals had waived their personal-jurisdiction defense by their conduct, but they had not agreed to arbitrate and could not be compelled to.
sections.Reasoning:
The court applied New Jersey contract law because Lubritene had neither adequately raised South African contract law nor supplied its content; Rule 44.1 permits but does not require independent judicial research.

New Jersey's highest court had not decided the anti-assignment question. Following the intermediate appellate court's Garden State decision and Restatement § 322(2)(b), the court distinguished a restriction on the right to assign from a restriction on the power to assign. A covenant requiring consent ordinarily makes an unauthorized assignment a breach, possibly supporting damages, while leaving the transfer effective. To negate the power the agreement must say so clearly, for example by declaring a nonconforming assignment void or invalid, denying the assignee rights, or stating that the other party will not recognize it. These agreements had no such language. The court did not decide whether Chemrite owed damages for breaching the covenant.

The individuals preserved their jurisdictional defense in their answer but waived it by seeking and litigating summary judgment for affirmative injunctive relief on the same dispute before getting a jurisdictional ruling. Jurisdiction did not establish consent to arbitrate. An agent for a disclosed principal ordinarily does not become a party, and none of the usual nonsignatory theories, incorporation, assumption, agency, veil piercing or alter ego, and estoppel, was supported by the record. Bel-Ray could ask the district court to stay the litigation against them during arbitration. The casebook excerpt selects the assignment discussion and omits the rulings on the individuals.

CT-NEXT-CM-0190.rule: Under UCC § 9-404(a)(1), an assignee's rights are subject to all terms of the agreement between the account debtor and the assignor and to defenses arising from that transaction, regardless of when the account debtor received notice of the assignment.

sections.Parties: Delacy Investments, Inc., doing business as Commission Express (CE), factored real-estate agents' future commissions and was the plaintiff and appellant; it sought payment of a commission that agent Steven Thurman had assigned to it. Re/Max Real Estate Guide, Inc., Thurman's broker and the account debtor, was the defendant and had applied the commission to Thurman's overhead arrears. Thurman defaulted and was not a party to the appeal.
sections.Procedural History: CE sued, and Re/Max counterclaimed against Thurman. The district court entered summary judgment for Re/Max because Thurman had no payable commission once the arrears limitation was applied, and his assignee could not obtain greater rights. An earlier appeal was dismissed because the purported final judgment left claims unresolved. After final disposition of all claims in July 2004, the Minnesota Court of Appeals accepted the present appeal and affirmed summary judgment for Re/Max.
sections.Material Facts: In November 2001 Thurman granted CE a security interest in his present and future accounts receivable under a master repurchase and security agreement, and CE filed a financing statement. In February 2003 Thurman entered an independent-contractor agreement with Re/Max requiring him to pay overhead expenses. Under it he was entitled only to commissions exceeding his past-due obligations; the portion needed to satisfy arrearages belonged to Re/Max. On April 22, 2003, CE purchased Thurman's $10,000 receivable from a sale at Keller Lake Drive, paying $8,000 immediately and promising $1,000 more on collection. Re/Max terminated Thurman on June 7 for performance problems, delayed earnest-money deposits and customer complaints. His overhead arrears were $11,126.38, more than the commission. Re/Max applied the commission to the arrears and refused CE's demand for payment. CE pointed to three notices: its 2001 financing statement, a March 2003 default notice about a different commission, and the April 2003 Keller Lake assignment.
sections.Issue: Whether CE, as assignee of Thurman's commission, took subject to the term of the Re/Max agreement limiting Thurman to commissions exceeding his arrears, even if Re/Max had notice of CE's assignment before that agreement was made.
sections.Holding: The Minnesota Court of Appeals in 2005, in an opinion by Judge Halbrooks for a panel with Huspeni and Crippen and no separate opinion, held that CE's claim fell under Minn. Stat. § 336.9-404(a)(1). Because CE's rights were subject to the Re/Max agreement and Thurman's arrears exceeded the commission, CE had nothing to collect from Re/Max.
sections.Reasoning:
Section 9-404(a) separates two kinds of limits on an assignee. Under (a)(1), assigned rights are subject to all terms of the agreement between account debtor and assignor and to defenses or recoupment arising from the transaction that gave rise to the contract. Under (a)(2), other defenses or claims are available only if they accrued before the debtor received authenticated notification of the assignment. The official comment explains that notice timing does not affect an (a)(1) defense.

The Re/Max agreement defined Thurman's entitlement as what remained after overhead arrears, and at closing nothing remained. The rule that an assignee gets no greater rights than the assignor was consistent with Article 9, not a competing common-law doctrine as CE argued. A perfected assignment of future receivables does not create a payment entitlement greater than the contract that creates the receivable. The court distinguished recoupment arising from the same transaction from setoff based on an independent demand.

On notice, the court said Re/Max apparently had notice before the independent-contractor agreement but did not make chronology decisive. Section 9-201 makes a security agreement effective subject to other UCC provisions, and § 9-404(a)(1) is such a limit; the (a)(2) cutoff did not govern this contract-based defense. CE could have arranged contractual protection against unfavorable terms. CE's undeveloped attack on the summary-judgment procedure could not be revived in reply. The casebook excerpt omits the full notice analysis, and the editors' criticism of the timing is their own.

CT-SUP-0011.rule: An ordinary domestic arrangement between spouses living in amity, such as a promised allowance during a temporary absence, is not an enforceable contract unless the party asserting it proves a contract, expressly or by necessary implication, intended to have legal consequences.

sections.Parties: Mrs. Balfour, the wife, was the plaintiff at trial and the respondent on appeal. She sued her husband, a civil engineer and Director of Irrigation for the government of Ceylon, to enforce his August 1916 promise to pay her £30 a month. Mr. Balfour was the defendant and the appellant. He argued that the arrangement was domestic and temporary, was not intended to have contractual effect, and lacked consideration. She argued that spouses could contract and that she had given up the ability to pledge his credit for necessaries in exchange for the allowance.
sections.Procedural History: The wife sued to enforce the allowance promise. Sargant J., sitting as an additional King's Bench judge, entered judgment for her. He reasoned that the husband already owed a duty to support her, that the parties had contracted to define the amount of that obligation, and that her consent to the arrangement was sufficient consideration. The husband appealed. Separately, in March 1918 the wife had begun proceedings for restitution of conjugal rights, obtaining a decree nisi on July 30 and an alimony order on December 16, 1918; those proceedings were not the contract action. The Court of Appeal unanimously allowed the husband's appeal, and Warrington L.J. expressly directed that judgment be entered for the defendant husband.
sections.Material Facts:
The Balfours married in August 1900 and ordinarily lived together in Ceylon. They returned to England in November 1915 while the husband was on leave. When his leave expired in August 1916 he had to return to Ceylon; the wife stayed in England on medical advice because she suffered from rheumatic arthritis.

According to the wife's evidence, on August 8, 1916, the day he sailed, the husband gave her a £24 cheque covering the rest of August and promised £30 a month until she returned. They had discussed her expenses and considered figures together, and she expected him to return to England within a few months. She acknowledged that they had not then agreed to live apart; differences developed afterward, and the husband later wrote suggesting that they should remain apart. The promise was therefore made during an amicable, medically necessary absence with reunion anticipated, not as part of a negotiated separation.
sections.Issue: Whether the discussion and promise concerning a wife's allowance during a temporary absence, made while the spouses were living in amity, established an enforceable contract, either expressly or by necessary implication.
sections.Holding: The Court of Appeal in 1919, in separate judgments by Warrington, Duke and Atkin L.JJ. with no dissent, held that the wife had not established the contract on which she sued. The allowance promise was an ordinary domestic arrangement, not an enforceable bargain, so Sargant J.'s judgment could not stand. The court did not hold that spouses can never contract; Warrington and Duke both accepted that they can. Nor did it decide the wife's rights of maintenance through other legal proceedings, or the separate alimony proceedings.
sections.Reasoning:
Each Lord Justice gave separate reasons. Warrington L.J. said a contract required either express terms or circumstances necessarily implying one. The wife had made no express bargain; the couple had amicably estimated what would maintain her, but she never promised to accept £30 as satisfaction of his maintenance obligation in every circumstance. Implying the contract would bind her to £30 however her needs changed and bind him to pay indefinitely however his circumstances changed, and neither implication followed from the domestic discussion. The husband had undertaken an obligation of honour only.

Duke L.J. focused on consideration. The communications were grounded in the relationship of spouses living in amity, and no separation agreement existed. He rejected the argument that the wife surrendered a right to pledge her husband's credit: the authorities described that power as an agency, not an independent, irrevocable right, and giving up something that was not a right furnished no consideration. He also feared unlimited litigation.

Atkin L.J. distinguished agreement from contract. Domestic allowances may involve reciprocal promises and something that would be consideration between other parties, yet lack contractual force because the spouses never intended legal consequences. Spouses vary, renew or abandon such arrangements, and enforcing them would multiply litigation over matters they never meant courts to regulate. The wife bore the burden of proving a contract, and neither her oral evidence nor the letters sufficed.

CT-SUP-0022-PSENICSKA-DISTRICT.rule: Under New York law, a contractual disclaimer of reliance that specifically addresses the subject of the alleged misrepresentations defeats the reasonable-reliance element of fraudulent inducement, so a release containing it can be enforced on a motion to dismiss.

sections.Parties: The plaintiffs in three related suits were people who appeared in the 2006 film Borat: driving-school operator Michael Psenicska; etiquette-business owner Cindy Streit and dinner guests including Sarah Moseley, Ben McKinnon, Michael Jared and Lynn Jared; and etiquette-school operator Kathie Martin. They sued over the use of their images, alleging they were misled into participating. The defendants, including Twentieth Century Fox Film Corp., moved to dismiss on the signed consent agreements.
sections.Procedural History: Psenicska filed suit on December 3, 2007. The Streit plaintiffs sued in Alabama, and their action was transferred to the Southern District of New York in February 2008. Martin filed suit in February 2008. The defendants moved to dismiss all three under Rule 12(b)(6). The district court granted all three motions, directed the clerk to close each action and denied all pending motions as moot. This brief covers the district-court decision only; the later appellate decision is briefed separately.
sections.Material Facts:
According to the complaints, Todd Lewis Schulman recruited each plaintiff with a false description of the project. Psenicska was told in May 2005 of a documentary about the integration of foreign people into American life; on June 13 the crew allegedly arrived ninety minutes late with $500 and papers, he was rushed and without his reading glasses, and he signed the Standard Consent Agreement without reading it. Streit was allegedly asked to train a Belarus dignitary and arrange a dinner party for an educational documentary for Belarus television; the guests were allegedly handed consent forms just before Borat arrived and rushed, and each signed. Martin was allegedly told she would give dining instruction to a foreign reporter filmed for Belarus television; she received $350 and signed what Schulman called a standard filming release. Sacha Baron Cohen, as Borat, allegedly drove erratically and made derogatory, sexist and anti-Semitic remarks.

The agreements were materially identical. They consented to participation in a documentary-style motion picture, waived listed categories of claims including fraud involving deception or surprise about the film, and in paragraph 5 stated that the participant was not relying on promises or statements about the nature of the film or the identities of other participants or people involved.
sections.Issue: Whether the term documentary-style film was ambiguous or failed to describe Borat, and whether the plaintiffs could avoid the consent agreements' waivers by alleging fraudulent inducement or a failure to disclose despite the agreements' disclaimer of reliance.
sections.Holding: The district court for the Southern District of New York in 2008, Judge Loretta A. Preska, held that the consent agreements were unambiguous and covered Borat, and that paragraph 5's specific disclaimer of reliance defeated the fraudulent-inducement claims, whether framed as misrepresentation or as nondisclosure. It dismissed all three suits. The ruling enforced these agreements; it did not find that the plaintiffs' accounts of deception were false.
sections.Reasoning:
On a motion to dismiss the court accepted the factual allegations as true but could consider the agreements as documents incorporated in or relied on by the complaints.

Ambiguity, under the undisputed New York choice-of-law provision, was a threshold question of law; a party cannot create it by urging a strained reading. Psenicska supplied a definition the other parties accepted: documentary-style describes a work displaying the characteristics of a film that provides a factual record or report. The operative word was style. A fictional character's story could be told with real interviews and events in the manner of a documentary, and Borat fit because it depicted real people and events as part of the protagonist's journey. Humor did not disqualify it.

On fraud, New York law requires reasonable reliance, and a sufficiently specific disclaimer can defeat reliance on the subject it addresses. The alleged deception concerned exactly the nature of the film and the identities of those involved, and paragraph 5 disclaimed reliance on statements about those subjects. The court treated it as specific enough under Danann, not as a boilerplate integration clause. The waiver released the claims; the nonreliance language defeated the fraud-based escape from the waiver.

The plaintiffs also invoked a duty to disclose based on superior knowledge. The court rejected the attempt to recast the same representations as omissions, which did not supply the reliance the disclaimer negated. It did not say superior knowledge can never matter, and it declined to reach the defendants' other arguments.

CT-SUP-0032-PSENICSKA-APPEAL.rule: Under New York law, a specific disclaimer of reliance on representations about the very subject of the alleged fraud ordinarily bars a fraudulent-inducement claim, and the peculiar-knowledge exception does not ordinarily protect someone who could have insisted on a written assurance.

sections.Parties: The plaintiffs and appellants were people who appeared in the film Borat, among them Psenicska; their participation involved a driving lesson, an etiquette dinner and etiquette instruction. The defendants and appellees were the filmmakers. The plaintiffs sued for claims including fraud, unjust enrichment and infliction of emotional distress, and on appeal sought to revive complaints that had been dismissed. The filmmakers relied on the Standard Consent Agreements the plaintiffs had signed.
sections.Procedural History: Three related actions were brought against the filmmakers. The district court dismissed the complaints under Rule 12(b)(6); Judge Preska's September 3 memorandum and order is a separate judicial decision from the one briefed here, and the judgment dismissing all three actions is dated September 24, 2008. The plaintiffs appealed. The Second Circuit, in a summary disposition issued on November 17, 2009 by Judges Roger J. Miner, John M. Walker Jr. and Reena Raggi with no separate writing, reviewed the dismissals de novo, accepting the allegations as true and drawing reasonable inferences for the plaintiffs. It affirmed the judgment dismissing all three complaints.
sections.Material Facts:
The plaintiffs alleged that the production had been represented to them as a documentary about a foreign visitor's experiences in the United States, intended for Belarus television; Psenicska's account described a documentary about the integration of foreign people into American life.

Each plaintiff signed a Standard Consent Agreement, which described a documentary-style film. Its Paragraph 5 expressly disclaimed reliance on statements about the film's nature or the identities of its participants and creators, and its release provisions waived claims arising from participation. Nothing in the agreements affirmatively represented that the film was a documentary about a foreign traveler for Belarus television; that understanding could come only from the alleged oral statements. The plaintiffs apparently took no steps to confirm the representations, including inexpensive ones such as requesting the reporter's name or asking to meet him.

Borat's central character was fictional, but the film told his story in the style of a traditional factual documentary. The appellate decision assumes familiarity with the record; the detailed chronology and the differences between the releases belong to the separate brief of the district court's decision.
sections.Issue: Whether a consent agreement limited to a documentary-style film was ambiguous as applied to Borat, and whether plaintiffs who signed a specific disclaimer of reliance could nonetheless plead fraudulent inducement or fraudulent concealment under New York law, including through the exception for facts peculiarly within the defendant's knowledge.
sections.Holding: The Second Circuit in 2009, in a summary disposition by Judges Miner, Walker and Raggi, held that no reasonable trier of fact could find that Borat fell outside the documentary style described in the agreements, so the releases were not ambiguous. It held that Paragraph 5's specific disclaimer defeated the reasonable reliance required for fraudulent inducement, that the peculiar-knowledge exception did not apply, and that the concealment theory failed for the same lack of reliance. The remaining arguments were meritless, and the judgment dismissing all three complaints was affirmed. The panel did not determine that the alleged misrepresentations never occurred.
sections.Reasoning:
Contract ambiguity was a legal question construed de novo. Although Borat's central character was fictional, the film unmistakably told his story in the style of a traditional factual documentary, and that resemblance was one of its comedic devices. The panel distinguished the truth of the story from the manner of presentation. Whatever uncertainty exists at the outer boundaries of the genre, Borat fell comfortably within the contractual description.

Reasonable reliance is an essential element of fraudulent inducement under New York law. Under Danann and related authority, a party that expressly disclaims reliance on representations concerning the very subject of the alleged fraud ordinarily cannot base an inducement claim on them, and Paragraph 5 referred specifically to the film's nature and participants. The peculiar-knowledge exception protects a party facing high costs in determining whether an oral representation is true; it does not ordinarily protect someone who could insist that a deal-breaking assurance be written into the bargain. The plaintiffs took no steps to confirm the representations and could have walked away without collateral harm if the filmmakers refused written terms.

The disclosure theory also required reasonable reliance. Because the agreements made no affirmative representation, the claimed understanding came only from oral statements on which reliance was disclaimed; restyling misrepresentation as omission did not cure the defect. This was not a finding that the filmmakers acted honestly; the panel expressly declined to credit the alleged conduct if true.

CT-SUP-0037.rule: When a writing is the complete agreement on a subject, an alleged prior or contemporaneous oral term that parties would naturally and normally include in that writing is barred by the parol evidence rule, even if sued on as a separate contract.

sections.Parties: Gianni, the plaintiff at trial and appellee, was a tenant who ran a small store in a Pittsburgh office building. R. Russel & Co., the defendant at trial and appellant, was the landlord that had acquired the building. Gianni sought damages for breach of an alleged oral promise giving him the exclusive right to sell soft drinks in the building. The landlord's agent denied the promise, and the landlord relied on the parol evidence rule and sought judgment in its favor notwithstanding the verdict.
sections.Procedural History: Gianni sued in the Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas for damages for breach of the alleged oral agreement. The reporter's procedural statement records a jury verdict and judgment for him for $3,694. The landlord appealed to the Pennsylvania Supreme Court, challenging among other things the refusal to enter judgment in its favor notwithstanding the verdict. Gianni's lawyer expressly rejected reformation based on fraud, accident or mistake and argued instead that the oral undertaking was an independent agreement. The Supreme Court decided the appeal on November 24, 1924. It reversed the tenant's judgment and entered judgment for the landlord, without ordering another trial.
sections.Material Facts:
Gianni sold tobacco, fruit, candy and soft drinks from his store. After acquiring the property, R. Russel & Co. negotiated a new three-year lease with him. The written lease described the permitted merchandise, including fruit, candy and soda water, and expressly prohibited selling tobacco under penalty of immediate forfeiture. It was prepared after the negotiations, left in Gianni's possession, and read to him by two people, including his daughter, before he signed. It contained no exclusivity term.

Gianni claimed that the landlord's agent had promised him the exclusive right to sell soft drinks in the building, as consideration for accepting a higher rent, giving up tobacco sales and entering the lease. He testified that the promise was made at least two days before signing and repeated at signing. One witness corroborated a conversation several days before execution, but no witness present at the signing corroborated the repetition, and the agent denied making the promise at either stage.

Shortly afterward the landlord leased the adjoining room to a drug company without restricting its right to sell soda water and other soft drinks. Gianni alleged that the competition substantially reduced his receipts and profits.
sections.Issue: Whether a tenant could enforce an alleged prior or contemporaneous oral promise of exclusive soft-drink sales when the written lease regulated what he could sell but omitted exclusivity, and whether he could avoid the parol evidence rule by treating the promise as an independent agreement.
sections.Holding: The Pennsylvania Supreme Court in 1924, in an opinion by Justice Schaffer with no separate opinion, held that he could not. The lease was the complete agreement on the subject of what the tenant could sell, so evidence of the alleged oral undertaking was inadmissible, and the undertaking could not be enforced by relabeling it a separate contract. The court reversed the judgment for Gianni and entered judgment for the landlord. It did not resolve the credibility dispute over whether the promise was made, and it did not decide that every oral promise by a landlord is unenforceable.
sections.Reasoning:
The court did not start from a rule that every signed writing contains every agreement between its signers. It first required that the writing be the entire contract and then compared the written and oral arrangements, asking whether similarly situated parties would naturally and normally include the alleged oral term in the same written transaction. If the terms concern the same subject and are sufficiently interrelated to be executed together, the writing embraces the subsidiary agreement. The court, not the jury, decides that question of scope.

Here the lease already addressed the store's permitted uses and merchandise, and exclusivity concerned that same commercial arrangement. Gianni himself said his written promise not to sell tobacco was part of the consideration for the unwritten exclusivity promise, which made inclusion in one writing especially natural; the court thought the claimed benefit more pertinent to the written provisions than almost any other term could be. Mere consistency with the lease was not enough, because the rule bars adding related terms to a complete agreement as well as contradicting it. A subject entirely absent from a writing may stand on a different footing, but sales restrictions were expressly present.

Suing on the promise separately could not validate it; otherwise a party could evade integration by dividing one transaction into written and oral causes of action. Fraud, accident or mistake could support reformation, but Gianni expressly disavowed that route.

CT-SUP-0040.rule: Under the CISG, which has no parol evidence rule, a merger clause bars evidence of prior oral understandings only if both parties shared the intention to be bound by it, so negotiations must be considered under Article 8 even when they contradict the writing.

sections.Parties: TeeVee Toons, Inc. (TVT), a record company founded and headed by Steve Gottlieb, and its affiliate Steve Gottlieb, Inc. (SGI) were the plaintiffs. Gerhard Schubert GmbH, a German manufacturer that marketed in the United States through its exclusive agent Rodico, was the defendant. The plaintiffs sought recovery for a failed packaging machine, repair and support expenses, facility costs, project administration and lost profits, and also pleaded common-law fraud and negligence. Schubert moved for summary judgment, relying on warranty disclaimers and a merger clause in its Terms and Conditions.
sections.Procedural History: TVT and SGI sued in the Southern District of New York in July 2000. A motion to dismiss was denied in 2002. Schubert later moved for summary judgment, and this memorandum and order by Judge Richard Casey, which the assigned source dates August 23, 2006, decided that motion; it did not review a verdict after trial. The court granted summary judgment to Schubert against SGI on all claims, against TVT on fraud and negligence, and against TVT's CISG claims insofar as they sought Cinram facility and service or replacement-facility damages. It denied summary judgment on TVT's remaining CISG claims and four other damages measures, and scheduled a conference to arrange trial. The casebook excerpt concentrates on contract interpretation; the other rulings come from the full opinion.
sections.Material Facts:
Gottlieb invented and patented the Biobox, a biodegradable cardboard package for audio and video cassettes, and in 1994 sought a company to develop a mass-production system. He chose Schubert. TVT and Schubert entered a written quotation contract in February 1995: a February 3 quotation, accepted February 13. The attached Terms and Conditions gave a six-month replacement warranty for defective materials or workmanship, excluded other express or implied warranties, disclaimed merchantability and fitness, and stated that the quotation and incorporated writings exhausted the agreement. Schubert also invoked a cap at the quoted $862,160 machinery price.

TVT said that between quotation and acceptance Rodico's agent Neuber expressly told Gottlieb that the fine print did not apply to this particular deal. Neuber admitted telling TVT not to worry about or overemphasize it but denied saying to ignore it.

Delays extended the project by nearly two years. The system arrived at TVT's contracted production facility, Cinram in Richmond, Indiana, in late August 1997 with serious speed and quality failures, and TVT began notifying Schubert of the defects by October 1997. SGI was incorporated in 1997. TVT had retained a certified packaging consultant, Kelsey, who took part in technical discussions, received specifications and recommended the manufacturer.
sections.Issue: Whether, in a sale governed by the CISG, a written merger clause and warranty disclaimers conclusively defeat the buyer's Convention warranty claims on summary judgment when the buyer offers evidence that the seller's agent orally said the fine print did not apply. The full opinion also addressed SGI's standing, recoverable damages, and the fraud and negligence claims.
sections.Holding: The United States District Court for the Southern District of New York in 2006, per Judge Richard Casey, held that the CISG governed the sale and that the merger clause would be operative only if both parties shared the intention to be bound by it. TVT's evidence did not conclusively establish exclusion of the fine print but raised a genuine question, so incorporation of the disclaimers could not be decided against TVT on summary judgment. The court did not hold that oral statements automatically trump every CISG merger clause. It dismissed SGI for lack of standing, rejected TVT's fraud and negligence claims and two damages measures, and left TVT's remaining CISG claims for trial.
sections.Reasoning:
The United States and Germany were Contracting States and the parties' places of business were there, so the Convention applied under Article 1(1)(a). Manufacturing was the preponderant obligation, so Article 3 did not remove the transaction, and neither party had expressly opted out. The record left no genuine dispute that the machine failed to produce at the proper speed and quality, and notice was reasonable under Article 39, but the contract might have varied the Convention's protections.

Article 11 permits proof of a sales contract without a writing. Article 8 looks to a party's intent when the other knew or could not have been unaware of it, otherwise to a reasonable person's understanding, and Article 8(3) directs attention to all relevant circumstances, including negotiations. The Convention therefore lacks the domestic parol-evidence exclusion. The court regarded the interaction with a merger clause as apparently novel in American CISG cases; MCC-Marble had not resolved it. It consulted CISG Advisory Council Opinion No. 3, which treats a merger clause's evidentiary effect as dependent on the parties' actual intention. Whether Neuber could not have been unaware of Gottlieb's interpretation was a genuine question for trial. If the parties intended the writing to govern, Article 6 allowed the disclaimers to undermine the warranty claims; if not, Article 35 protections remained available.

In the full opinion, SGI lacked standing because it was incorporated after the 1995 agreement and was neither a contracting party nor an intended beneficiary. Fraud failed for lack of justifiable reliance under New York law given the consultant; negligence failed because it sought economic loss without a sufficiently alleged duty independent of the contract.

CT-SUP-0076-CARNIVAL.rule: A forum-selection clause in a non-negotiated form passage contract is enforceable under federal admiralty law if it is reasonable and survives judicial scrutiny for fundamental fairness; lack of negotiation alone does not make it unenforceable.

sections.Parties: Eulala and Russel Shute, who bought their cruise tickets in Washington State, were the plaintiffs. Carnival Cruise Lines, Inc., the cruise line, was the defendant; it lost in the Ninth Circuit and obtained reversal in the Court. The Shutes sued for negligence by Carnival and its employees after Mrs. Shute was injured aboard ship, and brought the suit in Washington. Carnival sought summary judgment on two grounds: that the ticket required suit in Florida, and that it lacked constitutionally sufficient contacts with Washington.
sections.Procedural History: The Shutes sued in the Western District of Washington. Carnival moved for summary judgment, and the District Court granted the motion on personal-jurisdiction grounds. The Ninth Circuit reversed, reasoning that Carnival's solicitation in Washington supplied sufficient contacts, and refused to enforce the forum term because it had not been freely negotiated and because, in its view, the record showed the Shutes could not physically and financially pursue suit in Florida. An earlier 1988 Ninth Circuit opinion had been withdrawn while a Washington long-arm question was certified to the Washington Supreme Court, which answered affirmatively; the Ninth Circuit refiled its opinion with modifications in 1990, and that later judgment was the one reviewed. The Court reversed.
sections.Material Facts:
The Shutes bought a seven-day cruise on Carnival's Tropicale through a travel agent in Arlington, Washington. The agent forwarded their payment to Carnival's headquarters in Miami, and Carnival then prepared and sent the tickets to the Shutes in Washington, so they paid before receiving the detailed terms. The ticket face directed passengers to read three contract pages. Paragraph 3(a) treated acceptance of the ticket as agreement to its terms. Paragraph 8 required disputes arising under, connected with, or incident to the passage contract to be litigated exclusively in a court in Florida. Paragraph 16(a) disclaimed refunds for wholly or partly unused tickets.

The Shutes boarded in Los Angeles, and the ship traveled to Puerto Vallarta, Mexico, and back. While the ship was in international waters off Mexico, Mrs. Shute slipped on a deck mat during a guided galley tour.

Carnival's principal place of business was in Florida, and many of its cruises began and ended at Florida ports. The Shutes essentially conceded that the forum term had been reasonably communicated to them.
sections.Issue: Whether, under federal admiralty law, a forum-selection clause printed in a standardized cruise ticket that the passenger did not negotiate is enforceable, and whether former 46 U.S.C. App. § 183c prohibits it. The Court did not decide the constitutional personal-jurisdiction question or whether the Shutes had received sufficient notice before contracting.
sections.Holding: The Court in 1991, in an opinion by Justice Blackmun for seven Justices, with Justice Stevens dissenting joined by Justice Marshall, held the Florida forum clause enforceable and reversed the Ninth Circuit. A forum term in a form passage contract is not unenforceable merely because it was not negotiated; it is assessed for reasonableness and remains subject to judicial scrutiny for fundamental fairness. The Shutes had not carried the heavy burden required to set the clause aside for inconvenience, and § 183c did not prohibit forum selection. The Court did not rule on the negligence merits or approve every other term printed on the ticket.
sections.Reasoning:
The Bremen had enforced a forum clause in a carefully negotiated international towage agreement between corporations, and neither side could transplant its language without accounting for the different transaction. The majority acknowledged that a cruise passenger ordinarily cannot negotiate standardized terms and lacks bargaining parity, but rejected the inference that this alone makes the term unenforceable. It gave three reasons a reasonable clause is useful: a ship carries passengers from many places and could face suit in numerous forums; fixing the forum in advance reduces uncertainty and litigation over venue; and passengers might benefit from lower fares, which was an economic inference rather than a finding.

On fairness, nothing indicated that Carnival chose Florida to discourage legitimate claims, there was no evidence of fraud or overreaching, and given the notice concession the majority presumed the Shutes could have rejected the contract. The Ninth Circuit's inconvenience conclusion rested on no District Court findings; Florida was not a remote foreign forum, and an accident off Mexico was not inherently a local Washington dispute. Section 183c barred terms relieving a shipowner of negligence liability or weakening the right to trial in a competent court, and the clause preserved judicial resolution in a competent Florida court.

Justice Stevens, dissenting, emphasized that passengers often received the small-print terms only after paying and that the ticket disclaimed refunds, invoked traditional scrutiny of adhesion contracts and the rule against restricting the place of suit, and would have invalidated the clause under the statute and, independently, under the traditional admiralty rule.

CT-SUP-0094.rule: Under ordinary state contract-formation principles, an online amendment adding an arbitration clause binds existing users only with actual or constructive notice, and a unilateral modification clause silent about accrued claims does not reach claims that accrued before the amendment.

sections.Parties: Five named plaintiffs, including Anderson and Williams, lived in California, Nevada and Texas and opened Binance accounts between September 27, 2017 and April 15, 2018. They brought a class action alleging that Binance offered and sold digital tokens without complying with federal and state securities-registration requirements. Binance, the defendant and moving party, sought to compel arbitration under its 2019 terms and, separately, to bar class relief in court. The plaintiffs contested adequate notice, the purported waiver, and retroactive application to earlier claims.
sections.Procedural History: The original complaint was filed in April 2020. After a March 2022 dismissal, the Second Circuit reversed in March 2024, and the plaintiffs filed a third amended complaint that the opinion dates May 10, 2024. Binance moved to compel arbitration in July 2024. A March 28, 2025 district-court opinion denied arbitration for pre-amendment claims but left two issues unresolved; at all parties' request the court vacated it on April 16 and ordered supplemental briefing. Before the November 2025 argument the plaintiffs dismissed their claims on or after the effective date, and the court signed a joint stipulation on November 25, mooting that issue. On February 26, 2026 the court denied the motion to compel arbitration of the remaining claims predating February 20, 2019 and held the purported class-action waiver unenforceable in federal court for those claims.
sections.Material Facts:
Each plaintiff agreed through the registration process to the July 6, 2017 Terms of Use, and assent to that clickwrap contract was undisputed. Those terms had no arbitration clause, choice-of-law clause or class-action waiver. They permitted Binance to announce amendments on its website without individual notice, made amendments effective upon announcement, and treated continued use as acceptance unless users stopped using the service.

On February 20, 2019 Binance posted revised terms introducing arbitration, Singapore law and prominent references to a class-action waiver. The arbitration clause covered claims relating to the agreement, including its existence and validity, and incorporated Singapore International Arbitration Centre rules with a single arbitrator, English proceedings and a Singapore seat. A heading and warning mentioned waiver of class proceedings, but no operative provision detailed such a waiver.

Several plaintiffs traded after the revised terms were posted, and Anderson still held assets in his account in July 2024. Binance supplied no contemporaneous individual communication about the change, and the record lacked evidence that the arbitration provision was announced as the 2017 contract prescribed or that users were told where to look for amendments. The original complaint itself identified the date Binance imposed arbitration.
sections.Issue: Whether users who assented to the 2017 terms were bound by an arbitration clause Binance later posted on its website, which law governed that formation question, whether the clause reached claims accruing before February 20, 2019, and whether the 2019 class-action language barred class proceedings in federal court.
sections.Holding: The United States District Court for the Southern District of New York in 2026, per Judge Andrew Carter, held that the laws of the plaintiffs' home states, not the unaccepted Singapore-law clause, governed formation; that merely posting the 2019 terms did not give sufficient constructive notice, although all five plaintiffs had actual notice through the litigation by April 3 or June 8, 2020; and, alternatively, that the arbitration amendment did not apply to claims accruing before its effective date. The class-action language was ambiguous, was construed against Binance as drafter, and did not waive class proceedings in federal court. The motion to compel arbitration of the remaining pre-February 20, 2019 claims was denied.
sections.Reasoning:
The FAA favors enforcement of arbitration agreements, but the obligation is contractual and ordinary state formation principles decide whether the parties agreed. Applying the 2019 Singapore-law clause to decide whether it was adopted would assume the disputed fact, so the court used an interest analysis. The transaction was online and unnegotiated, Binance described itself as decentralized without headquarters, and the plaintiffs' states' laws governed and were treated as substantively similar.

For passive assent through website use, the question was whether a reasonably prudent user had actual or constructive notice. Binance relied on Needleman, where a bank sent individual communications through an agreed channel, prominently linked an arbitration notice and offered an opt-out. Binance had nothing comparable, and the amendment clause did not oblige customers to inspect the website periodically; allowing unlimited unnoticed amendments would undermine mutual assent. Actual notice arose later through the litigation, but that did not settle retroactive coverage.

Alternatively, even assuming constructive notice, California's implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing restricted a unilateral modification clause silent about known or accrued claims, and the phrase covering any claims supplied no temporal information.

On the class waiver, a heading and warning without an operative clause were ambiguous. The terms were a contract of adhesion, and ambiguity was construed against the drafter, so at best the language concerned disputes in arbitration. The same retroactivity analysis gave an additional reason to reject it. The court did not decide the securities merits or certify a class.

CT-SUP-0108.rule: Under UCC § 2-716, specific performance is available for unique goods or in other proper circumstances, but it remains inappropriate where money damages are available and adequate; a higher replacement price alone does not justify it.

sections.Parties: Eugene Klein wanted to buy a used Gulfstream G-II corporate jet and engaged Universal Jet Sales, Inc. (UJS), whose president was Patrick Janas, to find one. UJS negotiated to buy PepsiCo's aircraft and resell it to Klein; those were related but distinct transactions. PepsiCo, the seller, withdrew the aircraft, and delivery was demanded. PepsiCo challenged both the finding that a contract had been formed and the order requiring it to transfer the aircraft. The appellate caption reflects appeals involving PepsiCo, UJS and Klein.
sections.Procedural History: After extensive factual findings, the district court concluded that UJS and PepsiCo had formed a contract for the $4.6 million sale and ordered specific performance. It also rejected PepsiCo's arguments that Klein could not sue because the underlying contract failed the statute of frauds, because he was not an intended beneficiary, or because the Klein-UJS contract had been rescinded. On appeal the Fourth Circuit, deciding on April 25, 1988, reviewed the factual findings for clear error and the grant of specific performance for abuse of discretion. It affirmed in part, reversed in part and remanded: the determination that a contract existed stood, the specific-performance order was reversed, and the case was returned for a trial on damages.
sections.Material Facts:
Klein's pilot and mechanic inspected PepsiCo's jet in New York, and Klein inspected it in Arkansas on March 29, 1986. He gave Janas a $200,000 deposit and authorized a $4.4 million offer, which Janas sent by telex on March 31 to PepsiCo's broker, Welsch, referring to a satisfactory factory inspection and a definitive contract. PepsiCo countered at $4.7 million; negotiations reached $4.6 million, which Janas accepted by telex on April 3, referring to a $100,000 down payment. UJS planned to resell to Klein for $4.75 million.

Janas circulated agreements and sent PepsiCo a bill of sale, which PepsiCo executed and sent to the escrow agent. PepsiCo's counsel called the proposed agreement acceptable apart from the delivery date. The plane went to Savannah on April 7 for inspection; cracked turbine blades were found, with repairs estimated at $25,000 to $28,000, and the district court found that PepsiCo agreed to pay for them. On April 10 PepsiCo chairman Donald Kendall asked that the aircraft be removed from the market, and on April 11, the scheduled closing date, Janas told Klein that PepsiCo would not tender it.

Klein's expert described twenty-one G-II aircraft on the market, three roughly comparable. UJS later acquired two and offered them to Klein, and Klein bid on two others himself before deciding to buy a G-III.
sections.Issue: Whether PepsiCo and UJS formed a binding contract even though PepsiCo never signed the circulated written agreement, whether the satisfactory-inspection condition was met, and whether specific performance of the aircraft sale was proper under Virginia's version of UCC § 2-716.
sections.Holding: The Fourth Circuit in 1988, in an opinion by Judge Ervin for a panel including Judge Sprouse and Chief District Judge Britt, with no separate opinion, upheld the finding that a contract arose from the April 3 confirming telex and the parties' subsequent conduct, and relied on the supported finding that PepsiCo's agreement to make the repairs satisfied the inspection condition. It held, however, that the record supported neither the district court's view that the jet was unique nor its view that Klein's inability to cover was another proper circumstance for specific performance. It affirmed in part, reversed in part and remanded for a trial on damages.
sections.Reasoning:
PepsiCo argued that the parties did not intend to be bound until a final written agreement was signed. The evidence went well beyond an unresolved price discussion: PepsiCo received the $100,000 down payment, raised no objection to the confirming telex, said the memorializing agreement was acceptable, executed and deposited a bill of sale, sent the plane for the agreed inspection, and made admissions about accepting the offer. Those acts supported the finding that the later writing was meant to memorialize a transaction already agreed. PepsiCo did not show clear error; this was an application to a particular record, not a holding that an unsigned document can never prevent formation.

On the inspection condition, the court relied on the finding that PepsiCo had agreed to perform the repairs and did not need the alternative ground that refusal to tender excused the condition. In a footnote it affirmed, on the district court's reasoning, the rejection of PepsiCo's statute-of-frauds, intended-beneficiary and rescission arguments.

On remedy, Virginia's adoption of UCC § 2-716 had not displaced the equitable principle that specific performance is inappropriate where money damages are available and adequate. Other G-IIs were on the market, Klein's chief pilot acknowledged that others could be purchased, UJS offered him two, and he bid on two more. He did not buy another because prices were rising, but increased replacement expense alone does not establish entitlement to specific performance and can be addressed through damages. The district judge had repeatedly said damages would make Klein whole, and Klein had described a resale-for-profit objective.

CTR-017.rule: A promisee's surrender of a legal right at the promisor's request is sufficient consideration, even if the forbearance benefits the promisee and no benefit to the promisor is shown.

sections.Parties: Louisa W. Hamer was the plaintiff and appellant. She held the claim through assignments from William E. Story II, the nephew and promisee, and from his wife. Franklin Sidway, the executor of the estate of William E. Story Sr., the uncle who made the promise, was the defendant and respondent. Hamer's claim rested on the uncle's promise of $5,000; the executor argued that the abstinence benefited the nephew and that the uncle received no benefit.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court entered judgment for Hamer. The General Term reversed. The case then went to the New York Court of Appeals, which decided it on April 14, 1891. Because the General Term's order did not state that its reversal rested on the facts, the Court of Appeals treated the trial court's findings as controlling. It reversed the General Term and reinstated the trial court's judgment for Hamer.
sections.Material Facts:
On March 20, 1869, the uncle promised to pay his nephew $5,000 if the nephew refrained from drinking liquor, using tobacco, swearing, and playing cards or billiards for money until age twenty-one. The nephew agreed and fully performed, so the agreement required nearly six years of forbearance. The 1869 agreement was oral.

On January 31, 1875, the nephew wrote that he had turned twenty-one and had performed the agreement. On February 6, 1875, the uncle answered that the nephew 'shall have $5,000 as I promised you,' that the money was certain, that the uncle would not interfere with it until the nephew could care for it, and that the nephew could consider the money on interest. The uncle identified money in the bank and said it was intended for the nephew. The nephew consented to leave the money with the uncle on those terms.
sections.Issue: The principal question was whether the nephew's requested forbearance from lawful conduct supplied consideration even though the conduct may have benefited the nephew and no material benefit to the uncle was shown. The court also had to address the one-year Statute of Frauds and the statute of limitations.
sections.Holding: The New York Court of Appeals in 1891, in an opinion by Judge Parker for a unanimous court, held that the nephew's forbearance supplied consideration because he restricted his lawful freedom of action at his uncle's request and on the faith of the promise. The oral agreement fell within the one-year Statute of Frauds, but the defense was unavailable because it was not pleaded, and the court also treated the uncle's later letter and statements as a waiver. An action based solely on the 1869 contract would have been time-barred, but the 1875 correspondence and the nephew's assent created a trust relationship, which produced a different limitations result.
sections.Reasoning:
The executor argued that abstinence benefited the nephew and that the uncle received no benefit. The court rejected that framing because it would require courts to litigate in every case whether promised conduct was good for the promisee. The legally relevant fact was that the nephew had a lawful choice and surrendered it for years in response to the uncle's promise. Using the nineteenth-century language of legal detriment, the court explained that the waiver of a legal right at another person's request is sufficient consideration. It added that, even if benefit to the uncle were relevant, the record did not permit a finding that the uncle received no legal benefit.

On the Statute of Frauds, the opinion expressly states that the 1869 oral agreement was within the one-year provision. The court refused the defense for procedural and waiver reasons; it did not hold that the agreement fell outside the statute.

On limitations, the court accepted that the original contract claim would have been barred and asked whether the 1875 exchange left the parties as debtor and creditor or made the uncle a trustee. The uncle identified money in the bank, said it was intended for the nephew, promised not to interfere with it, offered interest, and received the nephew's assent; the court held that those circumstances created a trust. The opinion announces no general rule about when every claim against a trustee accrues.

The full brief adds, as a modern translation and not the 1891 court's language, that the facts fit Restatement (Second) § 71 and that § 79 explains why no additional showing of benefit, detriment, equivalent value or mutuality of obligation is required once consideration exists.

CTR-018.rule: Good-faith forbearance from asserting a claim that later proves invalid can be consideration if the claim was objectively doubtful or the surrendering party honestly believed it might fairly be determined valid.

sections.Parties: Dale Warren Dyer, an employee who lost his right foot in a job-related accident, was the plaintiff and appellant. National By-Products, Inc., his employer, was the defendant and appellee. Dyer alleged breach of an oral contract for lifetime employment, which he said he received in exchange for surrendering a personal-injury claim against the employer. The employer denied making that promise and obtained summary judgment.
sections.Procedural History: Dyer sued for breach of an oral contract for lifetime employment. The district court granted the employer summary judgment for two reasons: Dyer had made no reciprocal promise to work for life, and he had surrendered no viable claim because workers' compensation was apparently his exclusive remedy. Dyer confined his appeal to the second rationale. The Iowa Supreme Court, deciding the case on January 15, 1986, held that invalidity of the surrendered claim did not establish lack of consideration as a matter of law, and it reversed and remanded. It did not decide the district court's separate reciprocal-promise rationale.
sections.Material Facts:
Dyer lost his right foot in a job-related accident on October 29, 1981. The employer kept him on leave at full pay until August 16, 1982, when he returned to his former position as a foreman. The employer laid him off indefinitely on March 11, 1983.

Dyer alleged that he believed in good faith that he had a personal-injury claim against the employer and that he surrendered the claim in exchange for lifetime employment. The employer specifically denied offering a lifetime job. For purposes of analyzing the consideration issue, the court assumed that the tort claims against the employer and coemployees were clearly invalid. It did not decide whether Dyer actually held an honest belief in their possible validity, whether the employer promised lifetime employment, or whether an enforceable contract ultimately existed.
sections.Issue: Whether good-faith forbearance from asserting a claim that later proves invalid and unfounded can constitute consideration, so that the invalidity of Dyer's tort claim did not by itself entitle the employer to summary judgment.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of Iowa in 1986, in an opinion by Justice Schultz, answered yes. Under the approach stated in Restatement (Second) § 74(1), an invalid claim can support a settlement when the claim was objectively doubtful because of uncertainty about law or fact, or when the surrendering party honestly believed the claim might fairly be determined valid. Because a genuine factual dispute remained about Dyer's good faith, the invalidity of the tort claim did not entitle the employer to summary judgment on the consideration issue. The court reversed and remanded; it did not enforce lifetime employment.
sections.Reasoning:
Section 74(1) offers two routes. Under the first, the claim was genuinely doubtful because the facts or governing law were uncertain when it was surrendered, so the parties exchanged certainty and peace for the risk of litigating an uncertain claim. Under the second, the surrendering party honestly believed the claim might fairly be determined valid even though it was actually invalid; the policy favoring good-faith settlement permits the surrender to count, subject to proof that the asserted belief was genuine.

Objective weakness still matters, but as evidence. A bare assertion of belief is not sufficient; if invalidity was obvious, that obviousness can show that the claimant knew the claim was baseless. The court quoted the proposition that reasonable grounds are generally needed before a fact finder will be persuaded that the belief was honestly held. Reasonable grounds therefore help prove or disprove good faith; the court expressly rejected a stricter rule that every surrendered claim must possess objective merit.

The court favored settlements because parties should be able to trade uncertain claims for negotiated peace. If a party could reopen every settlement by litigating the merits of the surrendered claim, settlement would lose much of its value, while the good-faith requirement prevents parties from manufacturing nuisance claims solely to extract concessions. Dyer's good faith was a disputed fact left for later proceedings.

CTR-019.rule: A promise conditioned on the promisor's own satisfaction is not illusory, because the promisor must judge satisfaction honestly and in good faith, and that enforceable duty supplies consideration.

sections.Parties: Peter O. Mattei, a real-estate developer assembling land for a shopping center, was the plaintiff and appellant. He signed the buyer's side of a deposit receipt, paid the deposit, pursued leases, and sought damages after the conveyance failed. Amelia F. Hopper, owner of the adjacent parcel, was the defendant and respondent; she offered to sell the property, later repudiated through counsel, and obtained judgment at trial. Coldwell Banker & Company was the real-estate intermediary charged with obtaining leases satisfactory to Mattei.
sections.Procedural History: Mattei filed an action for damages, alleging that Hopper breached the parties' written land-sale agreement by failing to convey the parcel. The case was tried to the court without a jury. The trial court treated Mattei's satisfaction clause as leaving performance within his unrestricted choice, characterized the agreement as illusory and lacking mutuality, and entered judgment for Hopper. Mattei appealed. The California Supreme Court, in bank, decided the case on October 24, 1958, and reversed the judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
Mattei planned a shopping center on a tract beside Hopper's land. A real-estate agent negotiated with Hopper for several months, and she rejected several proposals because the price was inadequate. She then submitted an offer, and Mattei accepted it the same day, using the agent's deposit-receipt form.

The purchase price was $57,500. Mattei had to deposit $1,000 with the agent. The agreement gave him 120 days to examine title and consummate the transaction; at the end of that period the balance became payable when Hopper tendered a good and sufficient deed. The concluding provision stated that the transaction was subject to Coldwell Banker obtaining leases satisfactory to the purchaser. Mattei wanted time to secure tenant commitments before paying the balance and taking title.

Mattei paid the $1,000 deposit and worked to obtain leases. Before the 120-day period expired, Hopper's attorney informed him that Hopper would decline to sell on the deposit receipt's terms. Hopper later received notice that satisfactory leases had been obtained and that Mattei offered the unpaid purchase price. She withheld the deed.
sections.Issue: Whether the signed deposit receipt created an immediate contract whose performance was conditioned on Mattei's obtaining satisfactory leases, and whether the satisfaction provision imposed a legally enforceable standard on Mattei's judgment and thereby preserved consideration for Hopper's promise to convey.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of California in 1958, in an opinion by Justice Spence joined by Chief Justice Gibson and Justices Shenk, Carter, Traynor and Schauer, with Justice McComb dissenting without an opinion, held that the deposit receipt created a binding contract when the parties signed it. The lease clause made Mattei's duty to complete the purchase conditional on obtaining leases satisfactory to him and gave him a contractual power to terminate if that condition failed. Mattei had to evaluate the leases through honest, good-faith judgment; that legal duty restricted his discretion and made his promise sufficient consideration. The judgment for Hopper was reversed.
sections.Reasoning:
The court read the entire deposit receipt as one transaction stating the property, price, deposit, performance period, deed tender and lease condition. That structure formed a present agreement and located the satisfaction event within performance.

In a bilateral contract each exchanged promise must impose a legal obligation, and a promise is illusory when its maker retains unrestricted freedom to perform or withdraw; 'illusory promise' and 'lack of mutuality' identify the same inquiry, whether the exchange contains consideration. Satisfaction conditions fall into two classes. A condition concerning commercial value, quality, operative fitness or mechanical utility ordinarily uses an objective reasonable-person standard. A condition concerning taste, fancy or judgment uses the promisor's actual judgment, governed by honesty and good faith.

Shopping-center leases required evaluating duration, renewal options, covenants, restrictions, rent, financial responsibility and business mix, which called for business judgment. Mattei therefore had subjective evaluative authority coupled with a duty to exercise it honestly and in good faith. Genuine dissatisfaction could excuse his performance; a strategic or fabricated claim of dissatisfaction would breach the agreement. Because Hopper could challenge a refusal by proving that the stated dissatisfaction was not genuine, Mattei's promise carried a real legal detriment that supported her promise to convey. The same standard applied even though the leases came from third-party tenants.

The approach followed First Restatement § 265 and the Williston and Corbin treatises. The court disapproved dicta in Lawrence Block Co. v. Palston and Pruitt v. Fontana to the extent they treated objective reasonableness as the only enforceable standard.

CTR-020.rule: A requirements contract is supported by consideration even if the buyer has no requirements at formation, because UCC § 2-306 obligates the buyer to order its actual good-faith requirements from the seller.

sections.Parties: Structural Polymer Group, Ltd. and Structural Polymer Systems, Ltd., British corporations together called SP, manufactured prepreg and bought carbon fiber. They were the plaintiffs, appellees and cross-appellants; they obtained a jury verdict for lost profits and sought restoration of a vacated alternative award. Zoltek Corporation, a Missouri corporation that manufactured carbon fiber, was the defendant, appellant and cross-appellee. It supplied SP under a 2000 Supply Agreement, left the 2005 and 2006 orders unfilled, and challenged liability and damages after trial.
sections.Procedural History: On February 22, 2005, SP sued Zoltek in the Eastern District of Missouri for breach of the 2000 Supply Agreement, pleading alternative counts tied to Panex 35 and Panex 33. During trial District Judge Carol E. Jackson classified Zoltek's lack-of-mutuality contention as an affirmative defense omitted from its answer, denied a late amendment, and independently held that the writing contained consideration as a matter of law; she also refused an abandonment instruction. On November 29, 2006, the jury awarded $21,138,518 on the Panex 35 calculation and $14,906,377 on the alternative Panex 33 calculation and declined future lost profits. Under Rule 59(e) the court vacated the $14,906,377 component as duplicative and entered a $21,138,518 judgment, then denied Zoltek's Rule 50(b) and Rule 59(a) motions. Zoltek appealed and SP cross-appealed the reduction; SP withdrew its specific-performance challenge after terminating the agreement effective February 29, 2008. The Eighth Circuit affirmed the judgment in full.
sections.Material Facts:
SP wove carbon fiber into sheets and impregnated them with resin to make prepreg, used in products such as wind-turbine blades. 'Large-tow' fiber had bundles of at least 48,000 filaments; 'small-tow' fiber commonly had 24,000 or fewer, cost more to make and offered superior quality.

In November 2000 the parties entered a Supply Agreement running from November 6, 2000 through December 31, 2010. Zoltek promised to manufacture and sell all of SP's requirements for Large Filament Count Carbon Fibers meeting the Panex 33 specifications at the then-current market price. SP promised to obtain from Zoltek its total requirements for carbon fiber of suitable quality in SP's reasonable opinion. Annual volume could reach the quantity SP bought in the preceding contract year plus one million pounds. If another supplier offered large-tow fiber at a lower market price, Zoltek had a right of first refusal: if it matched, SP had to buy from Zoltek; if not, SP could buy from the competing source.

SP bought 28,219.17 pounds in 2000 and 20,943.91 pounds in 2001, and returned a 1,763.70-pound order in 2002 for asserted quality defects. In April 2002 Zoltek ended Panex 33 production and introduced Panex 35. SP placed no orders in 2003 and received 548,935 pounds of Panex 35 in 2004. Its 1,480,138-pound order in 2005 and its claimed entitlement to 2,480,138 pounds in 2006 went unfilled. SP also bought small-tow fiber from other sellers.
sections.Issue: Whether SP's promise to buy its total good-faith requirements of suitable large-tow carbon fiber from Zoltek, subject to an annual quantity cap and Zoltek's price-matching right, supplied consideration even assuming SP had zero large-tow requirements at formation and retained judgment about quality. Additional questions concerned abandonment, evidentiary rulings, proof and instruction of lost profits, the Gamesa shipment, and duplication of the alternative verdicts.
sections.Holding: The Eighth Circuit in 2008, in an opinion by Judge Colloton joined by Judge Shepherd and District Judge Erickson sitting by designation, held that the Supply Agreement contained mutuality and consideration as a matter of Missouri law. UCC § 2-306 imposed good faith on SP's requirements, the quality phrase used SP's reasonable opinion, the annual cap constrained expansion, and Zoltek's right to match a competing price preserved the purchase obligation. The court also held that the abandonment instruction was properly withheld, the curative directions resolved the evidentiary concern, sufficient evidence and a proper Missouri instruction supported the past lost-profit award, the Gamesa transaction fell outside the offset calculation, and the second alternative award duplicated the first. It affirmed on Zoltek's appeal and SP's cross-appeal.
sections.Reasoning:
Zoltek's mutuality argument was that SP's side of the exchange imposed no legal detriment. Invoking Restatement (Second) § 79 and Missouri decisions, the court said that satisfying the consideration requirement completes the formation inquiry and mutuality is no separate element; sufficiency of consideration in a written agreement is ordinarily a question of law for the court.

Missouri's UCC § 2-306(1) measures quantity by the buyer's actual requirements occurring in good faith. SP therefore promised to order its genuine large-tow needs from Zoltek. A zero level could result from good-faith operation of SP's business, while a zero level chosen to divert covered demand or escape the bargain could support a breach claim. That enforceable standard supplied consideration from the outset. SP's actual order pattern went to performance, and alleged manipulation was a breach theory for the jury, which found that SP performed. The right of first refusal also preserved a real obligation, because a match by Zoltek bound SP to buy. Buying small-tow fiber elsewhere could be a breach if SP used an interchangeable product in bad faith to divert a covered large-tow requirement.

On abandonment, a buyer's requirements may reach zero in good faith, so the two-year order gap fell short of the positive and unequivocal conduct that mutual abandonment requires; a theory based on the April 2004 Panex 35 agreement came after the verdict and was unpreserved. The lost-profit award rested on expert Donna Smith's calculation of $21,138,518 on 3,960,276 pounds of unfilled Panex 35 demand, which the jury could find reasonably certain. Adding both alternative awards exceeded that 3,960,276-pound ceiling under the annual formula, so Rule 59(e) permitted removing the duplicate.

CTR-021.rule: A promise to use reasonable efforts may be implied from an exclusive agency agreement read as a whole in its commercial setting, and that implied promise supplies consideration for the grant of exclusivity.

sections.Parties: Otis F. Wood, a marketer with a business organization suited to placing commercial endorsements, was the plaintiff and the appellant in the Court of Appeals. The agreement gave him exclusive marketing and licensing authority, and he sued for the share of revenues lost through independent endorsements. Lucy, Lady Duff-Gordon, a prominent fashion creator whose personal approval increased the market value of designs and products, was the defendant and respondent. She granted the exclusive rights, later made endorsements independently, and attacked the agreement's consideration on the pleadings.
sections.Procedural History: Wood filed a contract action; the complaint set out the signed written agreement in full. Lady Duff-Gordon challenged it through the New York code-pleading procedure described in the reports as a demurrer and as a motion for judgment on the pleadings, which accepted the well-pleaded facts. Special Term denied her motion. The Appellate Division, First Department, unanimously reversed on April 20, 1917; Justice Davis read the writing as stating no express undertaking by Wood to generate transactions, so his promises supplied neither mutuality nor consideration. Wood appealed. The Court of Appeals, on December 4, 1917, reversed the Appellate Division and affirmed Special Term, with costs in both appellate courts. Performance, breach and damages remained for later adjudication.
sections.Material Facts:
Lady Duff-Gordon's approval and name carried commercial value in fashion markets. Manufacturers paid for her endorsement, and her own fabrics, garments, parasols and related designs gained value when marketed under her name. She retained Wood to convert that influence into licensing and sales revenue.

The signed agreement gave Wood, subject to her approval, the exclusive right to place her endorsement on other creators' designs, and the exclusive right to sell her own designs or license others to manufacture and market them. It began April 1, 1915, ran for at least one year, and continued from year to year unless terminated by ninety days' notice. She was to receive one-half of all profits and revenues generated by contracts Wood made. Wood promised to collect the revenues, remit her share, account monthly for all money received, and obtain patents, copyrights and trademarks when his judgment found them useful. The writing recited that Wood possessed a business organization adapted to placing the endorsements she approved.

Wood alleged full performance on his side. He alleged that Lady Duff-Gordon independently endorsed fabrics, dresses and millinery for valuable consideration, excluded him from the transactions, and retained the revenues.
sections.Issue: Whether a signed exclusive marketing agreement with a revenue-sharing structure, monthly accounting duties, intellectual-property duties and a recital of the marketer's specialized organization implies a promise that the marketer will use reasonable efforts, thereby supplying consideration for the fashion creator's exclusive grant.
sections.Holding: The New York Court of Appeals in 1917, in an opinion by Judge Cardozo for a four-judge majority joined by Judges Cuddeback, McLaughlin and Andrews, with Chief Judge Hiscock and Judges Chase and Crane dissenting without separate opinions, answered yes. Reading the complete writing in its commercial setting, Wood assumed a duty to use reasonable efforts to place Lady Duff-Gordon's endorsements and market her designs. That implied promise supplied consideration and made her exclusivity promise enforceable, so the complaint stated a contract claim. The court reversed the Appellate Division and affirmed Special Term's denial of judgment on the pleadings.
sections.Reasoning:
Cardozo drew the obligation from the agreement's recitals, grants, compensation formula, duration and express administrative duties, read together in the parties' planned business.

For at least one year Lady Duff-Gordon placed her endorsement and designs within Wood's sole commercial channel, and his acceptance of that exclusive agency carried the duty to operate it. The recital that his business organization was adapted to placing approved endorsements linked the grant to his existing capacity and supported an undertaking to deploy it. Her compensation was half the revenue produced through his contracts, so her return depended directly on his efforts; a reasonable-efforts duty gave the revenue-sharing formula the business efficacy the parties assigned to it. Wood's express duties to collect and divide money, account monthly, and secure intellectual-property protection presupposed commercial activity and reinforced the implication.

The implied term exposed Wood to breach liability for an unreasonable failure to develop the business, and that legal commitment was the bargained-for obligation supporting her promise. The Appellate Division had focused on the absence of an express sentence compelling Wood to procure deals; Cardozo relied instead on The Moorcock's business-efficacy reasoning and New York exclusive-agency authorities.

The ruling addressed the pleadings only: Wood would still bear the burden of proving his own performance, her breach, causation and damages. The three dissenters wrote no opinions. The full brief adds, as later context, that UCC § 2-306(2) states a parallel rule for exclusive dealing in goods.

CTR-022.rule: A promise that the promisor should reasonably expect to induce definite and substantial action or forbearance, and that does induce it, is binding under Restatement (First) § 90 when injustice can be avoided only by enforcement, even without bargained-for consideration.

sections.Parties: Anna Sacks Feinberg, a former Pfeiffer employee who retired in reliance on the corporation's promise of $200 per month for life, was the plaintiff and respondent. Pfeiffer Company, formerly S. Pfeiffer Manufacturing Company, a pharmaceutical manufacturer whose board adopted the pension resolution and whose later management reduced the payments, was the defendant and appellant. Feinberg sought the accrued pension installments; Pfeiffer challenged evidentiary rulings, the factual findings on reliance, and the legal sufficiency of the pension promise.
sections.Procedural History: Feinberg sued in the Circuit Court of the City of St. Louis on the corporation's alleged obligation to pay $200 per month for life after retirement. The parties waived a jury, and the court tried the case and entered judgment for Feinberg for $5,100 in accrued pension installments through trial, plus interest. Pfeiffer appealed to the St. Louis Court of Appeals. Missouri statutes required the appellate court to review the law and the evidence and enter the judgment the trial court should have entered.
