They had not linked the harm to any possible federal enforcement of § 5000A(a), and they had not shown that the now-unenforceable provision caused residents to enroll in benefit programs they would otherwise decline. A causal chain running through independent third parties is not categorically barred but needs evidence that they will respond predictably. The States' direct costs came from other provisions operating independently of § 5000A(a), so they were not connected to enforcement of the challenged provision under the theories presented. The Court declined to consider inseverability-based standing theories raised by the federal respondents in their merits brief and by the dissent, because they had not been argued below or presented at the certiorari stage.

Justice Thomas, concurring, acknowledged that a properly framed theory of standing through inseverability might sometimes be supported but would not decide it here. Justice Alito would have found state standing because the States faced actual costs under enforceable provisions they claimed were inseverable from an unconstitutional mandate, and he would have reached the merits.

The casebook paragraph uses the case as a causation example.

LRS-ATLAS-N-STANDING-HAVENS.rule: A tester given racially discriminatory false information about housing availability suffers injury to a statutory right and has standing even without intent to rent, and an organization has standing when a defendant's practices perceptibly impair its services and drain its resources.

sections.Parties: Havens Realty Corp., which owned and operated two apartment complexes near Richmond, Virginia, and its employee Rose Jones were the defendants. The plaintiffs were Paul Coles, a Black prospective renter; Sylvia Coleman, a Black tester; R. Kent Willis, a white tester; and Housing Opportunities Made Equal, or HOME, a housing organization that employed the testers. They alleged racial steering in violation of the Fair Housing Act and sought damages and injunctive relief.
sections.Procedural History: The complaint was filed in January 1979. Before discovery or evidence, the district court dismissed Coleman, Willis, and HOME for lack of standing and expiration of the then-applicable 180-day limitations period. Coles's claims went to trial and produced a finding of unlawful steering, followed by a consent order awarding monetary and injunctive relief to him and his class. The Fourth Circuit reversed the other plaintiffs' dismissals, accepting their standing allegations and treating the alleged practice as a continuing violation extending through the timely Coles incident. On February 24, 1982, the Supreme Court affirmed insofar as the Fourth Circuit reinstated the neighborhood claims and HOME's own organizational claim, reversed insofar as it permitted the two tester claims to proceed, and directed further proceedings on remand.
sections.Material Facts:
Havens owned Camelot Townhouses and Colonial Court Apartments in Henrico County. The complaint alleged racial steering, meaning directing applicants toward or away from housing according to race to preserve segregation. Coles alleged that on July 13, 1978, he was falsely told Camelot had no apartments while being directed toward integrated Colonial Court.

Coleman and Willis posed as prospective renters to discover discriminatory practices, not to obtain housing. On three dates in March 1978 Coleman allegedly received no-vacancy answers while Willis was told vacancies existed. Coleman inquired again on July 6 and was again told Camelot had none, while a different white tester received contrary information. HOME provided housing counseling and investigated and referred discrimination complaints; it alleged that the steering impaired those services and drained its resources. The individual plaintiffs also claimed loss of the benefits of living in integrated communities.

The dismissed plaintiffs reached a conditional agreement with the defendants under which, if the district court approved, each would receive $400 if certiorari was denied or the judgment affirmed, but nothing if the Court reversed.
sections.Issue: Whether housing testers who did not intend to rent, residents claiming loss of the benefits of an integrated neighborhood, and a fair-housing organization alleging impairment of its services have standing to sue under the Fair Housing Act, and whether their claims were timely under the Act's 180-day limitations period.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court, in 1982, in a unanimous opinion by Justice Brennan, held that Coleman, who received discriminatory false information, alleged injury to a statutory right although she did not intend to rent, while Willis, who received accurate information, did not. Both could attempt to establish neighborhood injury on more definite allegations, and HOME adequately alleged injury to its counseling and referral work. The neighborhood and organizational claims were timely as part of a continuing practice, but Coleman's individual misinformation claims were time-barred. The conditional settlement did not moot the case. No damages were awarded. Justice Powell also concurred separately.
sections.Reasoning:
Under Gladstone, Congress intended the Fair Housing Act's private enforcement provision to reach Article III's limits, leaving no additional prudential barrier, though a plaintiff still must allege a distinct and palpable injury caused by the defendant. Section 804(d) prohibited racially discriminatory representations to any person that an available dwelling was unavailable. Coleman alleged exactly that misinformation; expecting discrimination and approaching the agent only to test compliance did not erase injury to her own right to truthful housing information. Unlike the provision on refusals to rent, this provision did not require a bona fide offer. Willis alleged accurate information and so identified no injury to that right.

The testers' claimed loss of the benefits of integrated neighborhoods was a personal injury even though the steering targeted others. Their pleading was strikingly vague, and the Court thought metropolitan-wide effects implausible, but it could not rule out an appreciable local effect; the district court was to permit more definite allegations and dismiss if standing was still not shown. HOME alleged perceptible impairment of its counseling and referral services with a consequent drain on resources, a concrete injury beyond frustration of an abstract social mission, which it would have to prove. Associational standing was left undecided.

On limitations, a continuing unlawful practice extending into the 180-day period differs from a stale isolated act. The neighborhood and organizational injuries were allegedly caused by a continuing pattern that included Coles's July 13 incident. Coleman's tester injury arose on four isolated occasions, all more than 180 days before filing.

Justice Powell criticized the vague neighborhood allegations and the expense of nearly four years of litigation without meaningful jurisdictional facts.

The casebook discussion highlights statutory information rights and organizational injury.

LRS-ATLAS-N-STANDING-MARITIME.rule: Conflicting interests among an association's members do not by themselves defeat associational standing, but the association may sue only if the members it represents themselves have standing, including a traceable and redressable injury.

sections.Parties: Three unions representing civil-service mariners and employees of Marine Transport Lines, but not employees of Lavino Shipping Company, sued over the Navy's Military Sealift Command's contracting-out of twelve oceanographic ships. They were plaintiffs below and appellants. They wanted performance enjoined, the Lavino award vacated and a new solicitation after a wage determination, or alternatively an administrative appeal and first-refusal rights for temporary mariners. Other unions intervened for the defendants.
sections.Procedural History: After the first tentative award, to Marine Transport Lines, affected employees and their representatives had an opportunity to appeal administratively, and the appeals were denied. After the later award to Lavino, the Command refused another administrative appeal. On cross-motions for summary judgment, the District Court dismissed for lack of standing. It concluded that the unions were outside the Service Contract Act's zone of interests because they did not represent the successful contractor's employees, and it regarded OMB Circular A-76 as an internal management instrument without protected private interests. The unions appealed. The D.C. Circuit affirmed judgment for the defendants, without deciding the zone-of-interests issue on which the District Court had relied.
sections.Material Facts:
The Military Sealift Command operated twelve government-owned oceanographic ships using permanent and temporary civil-service mariners. Under procedures implementing OMB Circular A-76, it compared continued government operation with private bids. The initial solicitation omitted Service Contract Act wage requirements, and Marine Transport Lines received the tentative award. The government then concluded that the Act applied, rescinded the tentative award, and requested new offers and a revised government cost estimate. The amended solicitation required the successful contractor to pay wages and benefits determined by the Labor Department, retroactively from the award date. The Department lacked a database permitting a timely wage schedule, so neither the solicitation nor the contract contained the actual schedule. Lavino Shipping Company was the lowest bidder and won.

The Command refused a second administrative appeal because the appealable issues could and should have been raised after the original tentative award. It limited contractual first-refusal employment rights to displaced permanent mariners, whom it considered particularly difficult to place in a tight labor market. The unions' demand for first-refusal rights for temporary mariners might therefore benefit temporary members at the expense of permanent members represented by the same organizations.
sections.Issue: Whether conflicting interests among a union's members defeat its associational standing under the Hunt conditions; whether the unions' members had Article III standing to attack the missing Service Contract Act wage determination; and whether the Command lawfully refused a second administrative appeal and first-refusal rights for temporary mariners.
sections.Holding: The D.C. Circuit in 1987, in an opinion by Judge Bork for a panel with Judges Starr and D.H. Ginsburg and no separate opinions, held that internal disagreement among members did not by itself defeat associational standing: the unions could represent some members despite conflicting interests if those members themselves had standing. The wage-determination claim failed for lack of Article III causation and redressability. The court accepted Article III standing for the administrative-appeal and first-refusal claims but rejected both on the merits. It affirmed judgment for the defendants.
sections.Reasoning:
The court applied the three Hunt conditions: individual member standing, germaneness to organizational purposes, and no need for individual participation. Germaneness was satisfied because the unions sought employment opportunities for members. The first-refusal demand presented a genuine conflict, but the court read UAW v. Brock as suggesting that such conflicts should not automatically destroy associational standing, while acknowledging that the Supreme Court's treatment was not entirely clear. Independently, associations routinely resolve internal policy disputes through their own procedures, and accepting the benefits of association often involves accepting a collective position unfavorable to some members. The court did not declare dissenting members individually bound; it discussed intervention, organizational procedural challenges and a possible duty-of-fair-representation problem.

On the wage claim, the Act's duties ran to the successful contractor's employees, not the unions' members. The lost jobs were real economic injuries, but nothing established that inserting a wage schedule would change the winner: the contract already required retroactive payment of prevailing wages, Marine Transport was not a party and might not bid again, and the government's cost estimate did not turn on the Act's wage requirements. A disappointed bidder could assert its own right to a fair procurement process, but that right belonged to Marine Transport.

On the remaining claims, the court assumed without deciding the zone, cause-of-action and justiciability questions. The regulations did not require a second futile appeal, and the court distinguished eligibility for first refusal from an unconditional entitlement and deferred to the Command's interpretation.

The full brief notes that the casebook's quotations emphasize internal organizational decisionmaking but omit the later analysis and the unfavorable disposition.

LRS-ATLAS-N-STANDING-NEWPORT.rule: An agency's regulatory or policy interest does not ordinarily make it a person adversely affected or aggrieved who may seek judicial review; the Longshore Act's silence about the Director's authority to appeal was read as withholding it, absent an extraordinary basis in the statutory scheme.

sections.Parties: The Director of the Labor Department's Office of Workers' Compensation Programs petitioned for judicial review of a Benefits Review Board order on a Longshore and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act claim brought by Jackie Harcum against his employer, Newport News Shipbuilding & Dry Dock Co. The Director considered Harcum's award inadequate. Harcum did not seek review himself and, though not opposing her petition, expressly declined the court's invitation to intervene.
sections.Procedural History: Harcum sought additional compensation, and an administrative law judge found partial rather than total disability. The Benefits Review Board affirmed and also held that the company could stop payments after 104 weeks, when a statutory special fund would assume responsibility. The Director petitioned the Fourth Circuit to review both rulings. The Fourth Circuit raised standing on its own initiative and held that the Director was not adversely affected or aggrieved by denial of the full-disability claim, while separately permitting her challenge concerning the special fund she administered. The Court reviewed only the former holding, expressly leaving the fund-related ruling unresolved, and affirmed the Fourth Circuit.
sections.Material Facts:
On October 24, 1984, metal grating fell on Newport News employee Jackie Harcum while he worked in a steam barge's bilge, injuring his lower back. Surgery removed a herniated disc, and the employer paid benefits until he returned to light duty in April 1987. He returned to his regular department under medical restrictions that November but could not perform essential tasks. The company terminated his employment in May 1988, and he obtained other work beginning February 1989. He sought additional compensation for the interval between jobs.

Section 21(c), 33 U.S.C. §921(c), allowed a person adversely affected or aggrieved by a Board order to petition for court-of-appeals review. The statute did not expressly make the Director a party or authorize her appeals. She argued that an erroneous benefits determination frustrated her responsibilities to secure proper compensation, administer the Act uniformly, and promote effective informal settlements.
sections.Issue: Whether the Director of the Office of Workers' Compensation Programs is a person adversely affected or aggrieved under section 21(c) of the Longshore and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act, so that she may petition for review of a Board order denying a claimant fuller benefits when the claimant himself does not seek review.
sections.Holding: The Court in 1995, in an opinion by Justice Scalia for eight Justices with Justice Ginsburg concurring in the judgment, held that the Director could not invoke the Act's general judicial-review provision simply because she considered a worker's award inadequate. An agency's regulatory or policy interest did not ordinarily make it a person adversely affected or aggrieved. The decision concerned statutory authorization, not an Article III prohibition on Congress authorizing agency appeals. The Court did not resolve the merits of Harcum's disability classification, fund-related standing, or whether the Director was a proper respondent to someone else's appeal.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court distinguished private or market interests from governmental policy interests. The United States could qualify as an injured shipper contesting an unlawful railroad rate, but an administrator's disagreement with a decision because it frustrated governmental policy was different, and recognizing it would put courts into recurring intrabranch and intraagency policy disputes. The phrase had an established history: the APA's definition of person excluded agencies, and statutes granting an administrator authority to seek review commonly said so expressly, as OSHA did in separately authorizing the Secretary to petition; the Black Lung Benefits Act likewise expressly made the Secretary a party to benefits proceedings. Those examples supported reading the Longshore Act's silence as withholding authority absent an extraordinary basis in the statutory scheme.

The Director's interests were insufficient. The Act embodied a compromise between employers and workers rather than a guarantee of the greatest possible compensation. Cases on federal representation of Indians and civil-rights decisions resting on express grants showed Congress could authorize such litigation, not that this statute did. An erroneous adjudication would not prevent her from processing claims, providing assistance, or enforcing final awards, and the 1972 amendments had deliberately separated administration from adjudication. The settlement concern was speculative, and liberal construction of a remedial statute could not add powers.

Justice Ginsburg accepted the statutory result but considered it an unintended consequence of the 1972 restructuring and an apparent congressional oversight that Congress, not the Court, had to repair.

The full brief notes that the casebook refers to the claimant as 'herself' and to 'inter-branch' disputes, whereas the report identifies Harcum as a man and speaks of intrabranch disputes.

LRS-ATLAS-N-STANDING-PATCHAK.rule: A plaintiff claiming no competing property interest may challenge a federal trust acquisition under the APA despite the Quiet Title Act's Indian-lands exception, and the APA zone-of-interests test requires only that the interest arguably fall within what the statute protects or regulates.

sections.Parties: David Patchak, a resident living near the Bradley Property in Wayland Township, Michigan, sued under the APA to challenge the Interior Secretary's decision to acquire that land in trust for the Match-E-Be-Nash-She-Wish Band of Pottawatomi Indians, which planned a casino there. He sought a declaration and an injunction. The Band intervened to defend the decision. The Secretary and the Band were the petitioners in the Supreme Court.
sections.Procedural History: An earlier suit by Michigan Gambling Opposition under environmental and gaming statutes failed in the District Court and the D.C. Circuit, and the Court denied review in January 2009. Patchak filed his separate APA challenge after the circuit ruling but before acquisition. The District Court dismissed without deciding the merits because Patchak's interests were outside the statute's zone. The D.C. Circuit reversed and also rejected the Secretary and Band's alternative sovereign-immunity argument. The Court granted their two certiorari petitions, in this case and in Salazar v. Patchak, to consider both threshold issues. It affirmed the D.C. Circuit and remanded for further proceedings.
sections.Material Facts:
The Band received formal federal recognition in 1999. In 2001 it asked the Secretary to acquire the Bradley Property in trust under section 5 of the Indian Reorganization Act, then codified at 25 U.S.C. §465, planning gaming operations to finance economic development, self-sufficiency, government, and social and educational programs. The Secretary announced approval in 2005 and allowed a thirty-day period before acquisition for judicial challenges, then delayed taking title while the Michigan Gambling Opposition litigation proceeded.

Patchak alleged that the Secretary could not acquire land for this Band because it had not been federally recognized when the Act was enacted in 1934. He alleged that the casino would increase traffic and crime, reduce property values, and permanently alter the area's rural character. He asserted no ownership or other competing interest in the Bradley Property. After the Court denied review in the earlier litigation, the Secretary took title; all parties agreed the continuing suit effectively sought to divest the government of title.
sections.Issue: Whether the Quiet Title Act's exception for trust or restricted Indian lands withholds the APA's waiver of sovereign immunity from a suit by a plaintiff who claims no interest in the land, and whether a neighbor's economic, environmental and aesthetic interests fall within the zone of interests of the Indian Reorganization Act's land-acquisition provision.
sections.Holding: The Court in 2012, in an opinion by Justice Kagan for eight Justices with Justice Sotomayor dissenting alone, held that the Quiet Title Act's Indian-lands exception did not govern Patchak's suit because he claimed no competing property interest, so the APA's general immunity waiver applied. It also held that his economic, environmental and aesthetic interests fell within the acquisition statute's zone. Those threshold holdings allowed the litigation to continue; they did not establish that the Secretary lacked authority to acquire the land, and the Court expressly reserved whether the Band was under federal jurisdiction in 1934.
sections.Reasoning:
APA section 702 waives immunity for nonmonetary relief unless another consent-to-suit statute expressly or impliedly forbids the relief. The Court focused on the kind of claim the Quiet Title Act addressed rather than only the practical effect of relief. An adverse owner could not relabel a quiet-title action as an APA case, but Patchak was not an adverse claimant: he wanted the government stripped of title because the Secretary allegedly exceeded statutory authority, not because the land was his. The Act's title, its jurisdiction and venue provisions, its requirement that plaintiffs plead their own right, title or interest, and its option to retain property by paying a successful claimant all presupposed a competing property claim. Shared subject matter alone did not make his different claim a quiet-title action; extending the Act's limits was for Congress.

On the zone of interests, the Court described the APA test as relatively undemanding: an interest need only arguably fall within what the statute protected or regulated, and intended benefit to the plaintiff was unnecessary. The acquisition provision was closely connected to land use. The Department's regulations required consideration of intended uses and potential land-use conflicts, and the Band's application and the Secretary's notice identified a gaming facility. A neighbor foreseeably affected by that use was a reasonable challenger.

Justice Sotomayor would have held the suit barred by sovereign immunity and did not reach standing. She read section 702's exception as focusing on the forbidden relief, divesting the government of Indian trust land, and warned that property claimants could recruit nonclaimants and that delayed challenges could undermine tribal investment.

LRS-ATLAS-N-STANDING-RAINES.rule: Individual legislators lack Article III standing to challenge a statute based on an abstract institutional dilution of legislative power shared by all members, and a congressional authorization to sue cannot supply the missing constitutional injury.

sections.Parties: Four Senators and two House members who had voted against the Line Item Veto Act in the 104th Congress sued the Treasury Secretary and the OMB Director, seeking a ruling that the Act was unconstitutional. The Executive officials, defendants below, appealed directly to the Supreme Court. One plaintiff, Senator Hatfield, had retired at the end of the previous Congress.
sections.Procedural History: The Act took effect January 1, 1997, and the legislators sued on January 2 under a provision permitting any member of Congress or adversely affected individual to challenge its constitutionality in the District of Columbia, with expedited direct Supreme Court review. The district court denied dismissal, found standing and ripeness even before the President had used the power, and granted the legislators summary judgment, holding that the Act violated the Presentment Clause and unconstitutionally delegated legislative power. The Executive officials appealed directly. The Court vacated the district court's judgment and remanded with instructions to dismiss the complaint for lack of jurisdiction.
sections.Material Facts:
The Senate passed the Act 69-31 on March 27, 1996, the House passed the identical bill 232-177 the next day, and President Clinton signed it April 4. The Act allowed the President, after signing a bill into law, to cancel specified discretionary budget authority, new direct spending, or limited tax benefits. He had to determine that cancellation would reduce the deficit without impairing essential governmental functions or harming the national interest, and transmit a timely special message to Congress. Congress could enact a disapproval bill to nullify a cancellation, but it would pass through the ordinary presentment process and face a possible veto.

The legislators alleged that this arrangement changed the effect of their future votes, removed their role in repealing legislation, and shifted the constitutional balance toward the Executive: a vote for a package of appropriations no longer ensured that the entire package would become effective. The President had not yet used the cancellation power. The legislators had no authority to represent either House, and congressional amici opposed their suit on the merits while taking no position on standing.
sections.Issue: Whether individual members of Congress have Article III standing to challenge the Line Item Veto Act on the ground that it diluted their legislative power, where the Act expressly authorized members of Congress to sue and the President had not yet exercised the cancellation authority.
sections.Holding: The Court in 1997, in an opinion by Chief Justice Rehnquist for six Justices, with Justice Souter concurring in the judgment joined by Justice Ginsburg, and Justices Stevens and Breyer dissenting, held 7-2 that the six legislators lacked Article III standing. They alleged an abstract institutional injury rather than deprivation of a personal entitlement or complete nullification of decisive votes. The Act's authorization for congressional plaintiffs removed prudential obstacles but could not supply the missing constitutional injury. The Court did not decide the Act's constitutionality, and reserved whether different circumstances would alter the outcome.
sections.Reasoning:
Standing requires a personal, particularized, concrete and judicially cognizable injury, fairly traceable and likely redressable, and the Court said rigorous enforcement matters especially when a suit asks whether another branch acted unconstitutionally. The legislators' claimed loss was institutional political power shared equally by all members. Unlike the member in Powell v. McCormack, who was excluded from his seat and salary, they had been deprived of no private entitlement; the injury attached to the office rather than the individual.

Coleman v. Miller did not control. As the Court read it, Coleman at most allowed legislators whose votes were sufficient to enact or defeat a specific measure to challenge complete nullification of those votes. Here the plaintiffs' votes against the Act were fully counted and they simply lost; they remained able, with enough colleagues, to repeal the Act or exempt legislation from it. Historical practice reinforced restraint: past disputes over removal authority, the legislative veto, appointments and pocket vetoes reached courts through plaintiffs with traditional injuries. Political remedies remained, and someone personally harmed by an actual cancellation could still sue.

Justice Souter, joined by Justice Ginsburg, thought the personal-official and abstract-concrete distinctions debatable but found the claim insufficient in light of separation of powers, preferring to await a private party deprived of money by a cancellation. Justice Stevens would have found standing, because each legislator lost the chance to vote on the precise law that survived cancellation, and would have affirmed. Justice Breyer also found standing, viewing the threat as at least as serious as in Coleman, but reserved the merits.

The full brief notes that the casebook reports five majority votes and describes the Coleman senators as voting to ratify; the report shows six, and votes against ratification.

LRS-ATLAS-N-STANDING-SFFA.rule: A voluntary membership organization with identifiable members that satisfies Hunt's three-part test has associational standing; Hunt does not additionally require that the members control and fund the organization.

sections.Parties: Students for Fair Admissions, a nonprofit founded in 2014 to defend civil rights and equal protection, sued Harvard, a private college receiving federal funds, and the University of North Carolina, a public university, challenging their race-conscious undergraduate admissions programs. It sought abandonment of the precedents permitting race-conscious admissions and alternatively disputed narrow tailoring. The schools defended individualized, holistic review and the educational benefits of diversity.
sections.Procedural History: SFFA sued both institutions in November 2014, invoking Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 against Harvard and including the Fourteenth Amendment against UNC. The Harvard trial lasted fifteen days with thirty witnesses; UNC's lasted eight days. Both district courts upheld the programs under the Court's admissions precedents, and the First Circuit affirmed Harvard's judgment. The Court granted ordinary certiorari in Harvard and certiorari before judgment in UNC, so there was no Fourth Circuit merits judgment. In one opinion resolving two distinct judgments, the Court reversed both the First Circuit and the Middle District of North Carolina.
sections.Material Facts:
At Harvard, first readers scored academic, extracurricular, athletic, school-support, personal and overall qualities, and race could affect the overall rating. Regional subcommittees made recommendations to a full committee of approximately forty members, which discussed racial composition. Tentative admissions were reduced through a final process called the lop, whose list identified legacy status, recruited-athlete status, financial-aid eligibility and race. The trial court found that race provided a determinative tip for a significant share of admitted African-American and Hispanic applicants. At UNC, readers rated multiple dimensions; race was one factor and could provide a substantial plus in individual cases, and a review committee examining every initial decision could also consider race. The Court and the dissents drew different inferences from the trial findings.

On standing, UNC argued that SFFA was not a genuine membership organization when it filed suit. At filing, the Harvard litigation involved an incorporated nonprofit with forty-seven voluntary members. The UNC record identified four rejected applicants who had joined, supported SFFA's mission, received updates, and had opportunities to provide input. Respondents did not contest that SFFA satisfied Hunt's three-part test.
sections.Issue: Whether associational standing under Hunt requires, in addition to its three conditions, that an organization's members control and fund it; and, on the merits, whether Harvard's and UNC's race-conscious admissions programs satisfied strict scrutiny under the Equal Protection Clause, which the Court applied to Harvard through Title VI.
sections.Holding: The Court in 2023, in an opinion by Chief Justice Roberts for six Justices, 6-2 in Harvard and 6-3 in UNC with Justice Jackson taking no part in Harvard, held that SFFA had associational standing: Hunt imposes no further control-and-funding requirement on a genuine voluntary membership organization with identifiable members that it represents in good faith. On the merits it invalidated both programs under strict scrutiny, the restrictions against racial negatives and stereotypes, and the requirement that racial preferences end. Military academies were expressly not decided.
sections.Reasoning:
Under Hunt, representative standing requires that members could sue in their own right, that the interests are germane to the organization's purpose, and that neither the claim nor the relief requires members' participation. Hunt involved a state apple commission with no conventional members; the growers' and dealers' control, service and financing showed they were effectively members. That analysis supplied a functional substitute for membership and did not impose governance requirements on every voluntary association, so no additional scrutiny of SFFA's operation was needed.

On the merits, the Court treated three conditions from its precedents as indispensable. First, objectives such as leadership, citizenship and exchange of ideas were commendable but not focused and measurable enough for strict scrutiny, and the racial categories were overbroad, undefined or underinclusive. Second, admissions were zero-sum, so a racial advantage disadvantaged others, and preferences grounded in race relied on stereotypes. Third, neither program had a meaningful end point. Universities may consider an applicant's account of how race affected their individual life, but not as a device to re-create the preference system.

Justice Thomas concurred with an originalist, colorblind account. Justice Gorsuch, joined by Justice Thomas, read Title VI as independently prohibiting the programs. Justice Kavanaugh emphasized the temporal limit on racial classifications. Justice Sotomayor, joined by Justice Kagan and by Justice Jackson only for UNC, dissented, arguing that the precedents permit limited race-conscious measures and that the Court displaced them without stare decisis justification. Justice Jackson, joined by Justices Sotomayor and Kagan in UNC only, dissented on the history of race-linked disparities.

The full brief notes that the casebook's surrounding discussion of Brown Group, Flyers Rights and American Physicians concerns other decisions.

LRS-ATLAS-N-STANDING-SPOKEO.rule: Article III injury in fact must be both particularized and concrete; violation of a statutory requirement does not automatically supply concrete injury, although a statutory procedural violation can do so in some circumstances, including through intangible harm or a material risk of harm.

sections.Parties: Thomas Robins filed a class-action complaint against Spokeo, Inc., the operator of a people-search website, alleging willful violations of the Fair Credit Reporting Act in a profile it assembled about him. Robins was the plaintiff and proposed class representative; Spokeo was the defendant. The dispute in the Supreme Court was whether Robins had Article III standing to pursue the statutory claim.
sections.Procedural History: Robins sued in the Central District of California. The District Court initially denied a jurisdictional dismissal motion, then reconsidered and dismissed with prejudice because Robins had not adequately pleaded injury in fact. The Ninth Circuit reversed, relying on circuit precedent that violation of a statutory right was usually enough and emphasizing that Spokeo allegedly violated Robins' own rights concerning his individualized information. The Court vacated the Ninth Circuit's judgment and remanded for proceedings consistent with its opinion. It did not affirm the District Court's dismissal, decide the merits, certify a class, or award damages.
sections.Material Facts:
Spokeo operated a people-search website: a user could enter a name, telephone number or email address, and Spokeo would search databases and assemble information about the individual. Its services could be used by employers evaluating applicants. The complaint did not identify who requested Robins' profile or explain exactly how he learned about it.

Robins alleged that the profile falsely described him as married with children, in his fifties, employed, affluent, and holding a graduate degree. The dissent further described his allegation that he was unemployed and seeking work, that the report used someone else's photograph, and that its misinformation threatened his employment prospects. These were asserted harms, not adjudicated facts.

The Fair Credit Reporting Act required consumer reporting agencies to follow reasonable procedures to ensure maximum possible accuracy and, for willful noncompliance, allowed actual damages or statutory damages of $100 to $1,000 per violation, costs and fees, and potentially punitive damages. The Court assumed, without deciding, that Spokeo was a consumer reporting agency.
sections.Issue: Whether the Ninth Circuit's reasoning, that Spokeo allegedly violated Robins' own statutory rights concerning his individualized information, was enough to establish the injury in fact that Article III requires, or whether the court also had to ask separately whether the alleged injury was concrete.
sections.Holding: The Court in 2016, in an opinion by Justice Alito for six Justices, with Justice Thomas also concurring separately and Justice Ginsburg dissenting joined by Justice Sotomayor, held that the Ninth Circuit had considered whether the alleged injury was particularized without adequately considering whether it was concrete. A statutory procedural violation can sometimes supply concrete injury, but violation of a statutory requirement alone does not automatically do so. The Court took no position on whether Robins had adequately alleged injury in fact.
sections.Reasoning:
Injury must be both particularized and concrete, as well as actual or imminent. Particularization asks whether the harm affects the plaintiff personally and individually; the Ninth Circuit's observations addressed only that. Concreteness asks whether the injury is real rather than abstract. It need not be tangible. For a statutory intangible injury the Court identified two guides: a close relationship to harms traditionally supporting suits in English or American courts, and Congress's judgment about which harms warrant protection. Congress can recognize previously inadequate injuries but cannot eliminate the requirement of an actual concrete injury, so a procedural defect entirely disconnected from concrete harm does not suffice merely because a statute authorizes suit. Yet a procedural violation can constitute injury in some circumstances without additional harm beyond what Congress identified.

Applying this, the Court noted that Congress designed the Act's procedures to reduce dissemination of false information, but some violations cause no harm or material risk of harm, such as a missed notice where the information is accurate or an incorrect ZIP code without more. The Ninth Circuit needed to ask whether the particular violations alleged entailed a sufficient degree of risk.

Justice Thomas explained standing through the distinction between private rights, whose invasion alone can support suit, and public rights, which require individualized injury; on remand the circuit could determine whether the accuracy provision created a private duty owed to Robins. Justice Ginsburg agreed with much of the general discussion but saw no need for remand: the alleged misinformation about Robins and its consequences for his job search differed materially from a wrong ZIP code, and she would have affirmed.

The full brief notes that the casebook's later reference to TransUnion is context only.

LRS-ATLAS-N-STANDING-THOMPSON.rule: Title VII's person-aggrieved language authorizes suit by a plaintiff within the zone of interests the statute protects, which includes an employee fired as the means of retaliating against another employee who filed a discrimination charge.

sections.Parties: Eric Thompson sued his former employer, North American Stainless, LP, under Title VII, alleging that the company fired him to retaliate against his fiancee and coworker, Miriam Regalado, for filing a sex-discrimination charge with the EEOC. Thompson was the plaintiff and lost in the en banc Sixth Circuit. The company, the defendant, argued that Title VII did not permit such third-party retaliation claims.
sections.Procedural History: Thompson filed his own EEOC charge and, after unsuccessful conciliation, sued in the Eastern District of Kentucky. The district court granted summary judgment to the employer on the ground that Title VII did not permit third-party retaliation claims. A Sixth Circuit panel reversed, but the en banc court affirmed the district court by 10-6, reasoning that Thompson had not himself engaged in protected activity and so belonged to no class of persons Congress authorized to sue for retaliation. The Court reversed the Sixth Circuit and remanded for further proceedings.
sections.Material Facts:
Eric Thompson and his fiancee, Miriam Regalado, both worked for North American Stainless. In February 2003, the EEOC notified the company that Regalado had filed a sex-discrimination charge. Three weeks later, the company fired Thompson. He alleged that his firing was intended to retaliate against her for filing that charge.

Because of the procedural posture, the Court was required to assume the alleged retaliatory motive; it did not independently find that motive proved, and the assumed facts remained allegations to be addressed in further proceedings. The company did not dispute that the alleged firing met the deterrence standard for retaliation. Thompson had not himself engaged in protected activity, whether for himself or for Regalado, which was the basis on which the en banc Sixth Circuit rejected his claim. No damages were awarded.
sections.Issue: Whether firing an employee in order to punish his fiancee for filing a discrimination charge is unlawful retaliation under Title VII, and if so, whether the fired employee, who did not himself engage in protected activity, is a person aggrieved with a cause of action under the statute.
sections.Holding: The Court in 2011, in an opinion by Justice Scalia for all eight participating Justices, with Justice Kagan not participating and Justice Ginsburg concurring separately joined by Justice Breyer, held that, assuming Thompson's allegations were true, firing him to punish his fiancee violated Title VII's antiretaliation prohibition. It further held that Thompson could sue as a person aggrieved: adopting the zone-of-interests approach for the statutory cause of action, he was an employee deliberately injured as the means of retaliation against another employee and so fell within the interests Title VII sought to protect.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court relied on Burlington Northern: the antiretaliation prohibition is not limited to conduct altering terms or conditions of employment, but covers employer conduct that could dissuade a reasonable worker from making or supporting a discrimination charge. Firing a worker's fiance plainly could do so, and nothing in that framework excluded injury inflicted through a third party. The employer objected that this created line-drawing uncertainty about girlfriends, close friends and trusted coworkers. The Court acknowledged the problem but found no textual basis for a categorical exemption and declined to fix a list of protected relationships: firing a close family member would almost always meet the standard, a mild reprisal against a mere acquaintance almost never would, and other cases depended on their circumstances, assessed objectively.

On the cause of action, the Court regarded Thompson's Article III injury, causation and redressability as clear but distinguished them from statutory authorization. It declined to follow Trafficante dictum equating person aggrieved with Article III; a shareholder whose shares lost value because a company unlawfully fired a valuable worker would have constitutional injury yet fall outside Title VII. The employer's reading, limiting the phrase to the employee who engaged in protected activity, was too narrow. Borrowing from the APA, the zone-of-interests test excludes only interests so marginally related to or inconsistent with statutory purposes that Congress could not reasonably be understood to permit suit. Thompson qualified not merely because harm to him was foreseeable, but because injuring him was the very device by which the employer punished Regalado.

Justice Ginsburg, joined by Justice Breyer, joined the opinion in full and added that the result accorded with the EEOC's longstanding Compliance Manual interpretation, which she considered worthy of Skidmore respect.

LRS-ATLAS-N-STANDING-TWIN-RIVERS.rule: An organization seeking direct review of agency action must, when standing is not apparent from the record, support members' standing with evidence in its opening brief, and a challenger whose interests align with a statute's intended beneficiaries only by accident, not systematically, falls outside the zone of interests.

sections.Parties: Consumer Action, a nonprofit membership organization, together with Twin Rivers Paper Company and three industry organizations, petitioned for direct appellate review of a Securities and Exchange Commission rule. The petitioners alleged violations of the Securities Act of 1933, the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, the Investment Company Act of 1940 and the APA. The industry petitioners alleged reduced demand for paper; Consumer Action claimed to represent members harmed by the rule. The SEC was the respondent.
sections.Procedural History: The SEC adopted Rule 30e-3, changing the default for delivery of investment-company shareholder reports. The petitioners sought direct appellate review in the D.C. Circuit. Consumer Action supplied an organizational affidavit with its opening brief and individual member affidavits only with its reply. In a 2019 opinion by Judge Katsas for a panel with Judges Henderson and Rogers and no separate opinions, the court denied the petition for review. It did not decide whether the rule was substantively valid, and there was no vacatur of the rule or remand to the SEC.
sections.Material Facts:
Investment companies, including mutual funds, had generally been required to mail shareholder reports unless an investor selected electronic delivery. Rule 30e-3 changed that default: a company could post reports online and mail notice of their availability, but still had to provide paper copies to investors who requested them. The SEC expected approximately $140 million in annual savings, ordinarily benefiting investors because printing expenses came out of fund assets, and found that many shareholders preferred internet access. Paper delivery had to continue through a transition, no earlier than January 1, 2021. Afterward, each online report required a mailed notice with a toll-free number for requesting paper, and a requested copy had to be mailed within three business days without charge.

Consumer Action's opening affidavit referred broadly to members, followers, supporters, retirees and community organizations without identifying a particular injured member. Its reply affidavits introduced a different injury theory: some members objected ideologically to the change and others complained of time spent making a free telephone call. No reply affiant alleged the originally suggested problem of access to or understanding of financial information.
sections.Issue: Whether Consumer Action established its members' Article III standing when it offered member affidavits only with its reply brief, and whether paper-industry petitioners' interest in selling paper falls within the zone of interests of the securities statutes under which they challenged the SEC's rule.
sections.Holding: The D.C. Circuit in 2019, in an opinion by Judge Katsas for a unanimous panel, denied the petition. Consumer Action failed to establish timely evidentiary support for its members' Article III standing, and the court could not find standing from its late submissions. The paper-industry petitioners' interest in selling paper was outside the zone of interests of the securities statutes: investors, not paper suppliers, were the intended beneficiaries, and the suppliers' interests did not align systematically with investors'. The court did not decide the rule's substantive validity.
sections.Reasoning:
An organization relying on its members' standing must show that at least one member could sue individually. On direct review of agency action, the court required evidence in the administrative record or supplementary material, and when standing was not apparent from the record the opening brief needed both the argument and the supporting evidence, so the adversary could respond. Consumer Action's organizational affidavit identified no particular injured member, and statements in a brief are not evidence. Failure to present standing evidence on time is not a jurisdictional bar and can be excused for good cause, where a party reasonably believed its initial evidence sufficient or standing apparent, but neither explanation fit these vague submissions. The reply affidavits also raised a new theory. An ideological objection was not concrete injury. The lost-time theory was a closer question, which the court did not categorically reject, but Consumer Action had identified neither a relevant statutory protection nor a traditional analogue, and raising it only in reply frustrated the adversarial process.

For the industry petitioners, the court explained that Lexmark recast the zone inquiry from prudential standing into identifying who may invoke a cause of action, and that it applies on direct review. A challenger may be an intended beneficiary or another suitable challenger whose interests align systematically, rather than by accident, with the beneficiaries. Paper companies' unconditional preference for more paper did not reliably promote investors' interests, given the SEC's findings that many investors preferred online reports and would benefit from lower printing costs. Cases letting competitors enforce statutory entry restrictions were distinguished, because general directions to consider the public interest, investor protection, efficiency, competition and capital formation did not similarly channel the industry's incentives.

LRS-ATLAS-N-STANDING-US-TEXAS.rule: A State's indirect costs from federal enforcement choices do not give it a judicially cognizable interest in a suit asking a federal court to require the Executive to make more arrests of third parties.

sections.Parties: Texas and Louisiana sued to challenge immigration-enforcement guidelines issued in 2021 by Secretary of Homeland Security Alejandro Mayorkas. The States, plaintiffs below, argued that the guidelines produced fewer arrests and detentions than federal statutes required and sought to have them set aside. The United States was the opposing party and the party named first in the Supreme Court, which reviewed the district court's judgment before any court of appeals judgment.
sections.Procedural History: After a trial, the district court found that the States incurred costs, held that they had standing, ruled the guidelines unlawful, and vacated them. The Fifth Circuit declined to stay that judgment. The Court granted certiorari before judgment in the court of appeals. It accepted that the district court had found costs but held that the States lacked the kind of judicially cognizable interest needed for this suit, and it reversed the district court's judgment. The Court decided only standing and expressly did not decide whether the guidelines complied with the immigration statutes.
sections.Material Facts:
Federal immigration laws direct detention of specified noncitizens. Section 1226(c) provides for custody of certain noncitizens after release from criminal custody, and section 1231(a)(2) provides for detention during the removal period after a final removal order. In 2021, Secretary Mayorkas issued enforcement guidelines prioritizing noncitizens who presented national-security or public-safety threats or had recently entered unlawfully. The guidelines called for an assessment of individual circumstances rather than treating every statutory category as an automatic enforcement priority.

Texas and Louisiana argued that this policy produced fewer arrests and detentions than the statutes required. They claimed resulting expenditures for incarceration, health care and education, and the district court found such costs after trial. The majority relied on the Government's representation that the guidelines concerned apprehension and removal rather than the duration of detention after custody had begun, and understood the States not to have argued that the Executive had completely abandoned its statutory responsibilities.
sections.Issue: Whether States that incur downstream costs from a federal immigration-enforcement policy have Article III standing to obtain a federal court order that would require the Executive to arrest and detain more noncitizens than its enforcement guidelines prioritize.
sections.Holding: The Court in 2023, in an opinion by Justice Kavanaugh for Chief Justice Roberts and Justices Sotomayor, Kagan and Jackson, held that Texas and Louisiana lacked standing to challenge the enforcement guidelines. Three Justices concurred in the judgment on redressability grounds and Justice Alito dissented, making the judgment 8-1. An expense does not automatically create a judicially cognizable injury; these States could not maintain a suit asking a federal court to require more arrests. Statutory compliance, universal APA vacatur, and several reserved categories of enforcement suits remained undecided.
sections.Reasoning:
Standing requires injury, causation and redressability, but history and the judicial role inform which injuries are judicially cognizable. The States asked a court to make the Executive arrest more third parties. The Court found no tradition of such suits and read Linda R. S. v. Richard D. as establishing that a person ordinarily lacks a judicially cognizable interest in the prosecution of someone else. The Executive must choose enforcement priorities when resources cannot reach every violator, a choice involving public safety, resources and foreign relations, and courts lack manageable standards for supervising overall arrest priorities. Indirect effects on state budgets are a common result of federal policy and could not justify this kind of suit. The Court did not say the losses were too small or that financial injury can never support state standing.

It reserved selective-prosecution claims, congressionally authorized enforcement suits, complete abdication of statutory responsibilities, policies combining nonenforcement with legal status or benefits, and continued detention of those already arrested. It distinguished Massachusetts v. EPA as involving denial of a statutorily authorized rulemaking petition, without overruling it.

Justice Gorsuch, joined by Justices Thomas and Barrett, concurred in the judgment on redressability, citing section 1252(f)(1) and officials' retained discretion; he questioned the continued significance of special solicitude and universal vacatur under the APA. Justice Barrett, joined by Justice Gorsuch, also relied on redressability and read Linda R. S. more narrowly. Justice Alito dissented, finding Texas's standing established and arguing that the majority moved reviewability and executive-power questions into Article III.

The full brief notes that the casebook's quotation about leaving special solicitude on the shelf comes from the three-Justice concurrence, not the Court's opinion.

LRS-ATLAS-N-STATE-FARM-DOLE.rule: Under Abbott Laboratories, a challenge to a contingent future agency action that may never occur is unripe absent immediate, direct and significant hardship, while an agency's immediately operative choices are reviewable and may be upheld under arbitrary-and-capricious review if the agency's path is reasonably discernible.

sections.Parties: Insurers, insurance-industry organizations, insurance commissioners, New York officials and two individuals petitioned for review of Secretary Dole's 1984 final rule on automobile passive restraints under Standard 208. They argued that the rule's automatic-rescission provision lacked a rational basis and conflicted with the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act. New York additionally challenged the rule's choices among protective devices. The Secretary defended the rule.
sections.Procedural History: The Department's 1981 rescission of its passive-restraint requirement was the subject of the Supreme Court's 1983 Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Association v. State Farm decision, which found the agency's explanation inadequate and required further consideration. After a proposed rule and supplemental comment proceedings, Secretary Dole published a new final rule on July 17, 1984. The petitioners sought direct review of that rule in the D.C. Circuit; this was not an appeal from a trial judgment. The court denied New York's petition insofar as it challenged the failure to require airbags or nondetachable belts, and dismissed every other petition and the remainder of New York's petition as unripe.
sections.Material Facts:
The 1984 rule allowed manufacturers to satisfy the passive-restraint requirement through airbags, padded interiors, or detachable or nondetachable automatic belts. It phased in: ten percent of cars manufactured after September 1, 1986, twenty-five percent after September 1, 1987, forty percent after September 1, 1988, and all cars after September 1, 1989. In the initial years a car using an airbag or passive interior earned an additional half-car credit.

The controversial feature was the trap door. The requirement would be rescinded if, by April 1, 1989, states containing two-thirds of the national population had enacted qualifying mandatory seatbelt-usage laws. Qualifying laws had to meet specified conditions, including a minimum $25 penalty, and the Secretary could consider waiving requirements for substantially complying laws adopted before August 1, 1984.

Twenty states covering approximately sixty percent of the population had such laws, yet apparently none satisfied the rule's requirements. Even assuming New York's earlier law counted under the waiver, additional states covering at least fifty-nine percent of the population would have to adopt complying laws, and some states were deliberately adopting laws that would not count toward rescission.
sections.Issue: Whether challenges to the rule's contingent future rescission of the passive-restraint requirement were ripe for review, and whether the Secretary acted arbitrarily and capriciously by permitting detachable automatic belts, declining to require airbags in every car, and declining to require airbags together with nondetachable belts.
sections.Holding: The D.C. Circuit in 1986, in an opinion by Judge Starr joined by Judge Scalia, with Judge Mikva concurring in part and dissenting in part, held the challenges to the contingent rescission provision unripe and dismissed them, without holding that the provision was lawful. It held New York's challenges to the immediately operative choice of permissible devices ripe and rejected them on the merits: the Secretary reasonably allowed detachable belts, reasonably chose incentives over an airbag mandate, and had considered requiring airbags together with nondetachable belts.
sections.Reasoning:
The court applied Abbott Laboratories' two-part inquiry: fitness of the issues for decision and hardship from withholding review. The record was developed, but actual rescission appeared unlikely, a contingency that might never arise and so might make adjudication unnecessary. The asserted hardships did not outweigh that. Additional deaths depended on rescission occurring, and petitioners could seek review and a stay if it became imminent. The claim that uncertainty would deter manufacturers lacked evidence and overlooked the near-term installation obligation and the extra-credit incentive. Effects on state legislatures were remote or hypothetical, and insurers' lobbying uncertainty was insufficient. The sixty-day filing period did not compel immediate adjudication.

The device choices were final and affected cars being produced immediately, so they were ripe. Under arbitrary-and-capricious review, the Secretary reasonably relied on adverse public reaction to nondetachable belts, including surveys suggesting ten to twenty percent might cut them, and on center-seat access. On airbags, she estimated $320 more per car and an $800 replacement cost and considered public fears; the Act let cost, practicability and public acceptance enter the safety judgment. On the combination, the explanation lacked ideal clarity but the agency's path was discernible.

Judge Mikva agreed most challenges to the Secretary's authority were unripe but thought New York's argument for combining seatbelt laws with passive restraints was a ripe challenge to the rule's present design that the agency had inadequately evaluated, and he would have found the device decisions arbitrary and capricious.

The full brief notes that the casebook excerpt omits the full ripeness analysis and the Mikva opinion, and that its statement that the trap door was never triggered is later editorial history.

LRS-ATLAS-O-AMERICAN-RADIO.rule: In notice-and-comment rulemaking an agency must disclose the technical studies and staff reports on which it relies, including intertwined portions, so that parties can comment meaningfully, and it must give a reasoned explanation for its technical choices.

sections.Parties: The American Radio Relay League, which represents amateur radio operators, petitioned for judicial review of FCC orders adopting technical rules for Access Broadband over Power Line. The League sought vacatur of the rule on four grounds. The FCC, the respondent agency, opposed all four and defended both its original order and its order on reconsideration.
sections.Procedural History: The FCC adopted the rules through notice-and-comment rulemaking. After one unsuccessful disclosure request and a later request following the final rule, it released five staff studies in partially redacted form and added them to the rulemaking record in December 2004, after promulgation. The League sought reconsideration, then petitioned the D.C. Circuit for review of the original and reconsideration orders. The court granted the petition in part and remanded the rule to the FCC with specified instructions, without ordering vacatur.
sections.Material Facts:
Access Broadband over Power Line transmits communications through electrical lines but also emits radio-frequency energy that could interfere with licensed radio users, including amateur operators. The FCC's longstanding Part 15 rules permitted certain unlicensed devices if their emissions lacked significant potential for harmful interference, and required operation to stop when harmful interference occurred. The new rules added certification, emission limits, a nationwide database, frequency and geographical exclusions, and mechanisms to lower power, change frequencies or stop system segments.

For mobile users, the FCC concluded that lowering power twenty decibels below the emission limit would leave only interference comparable to background noise, and on reconsideration said operators complying with that reduction need take no further action on mobile-interference complaints. It retained an extrapolation factor of forty decibels per decade for frequencies below thirty megahertz, which estimates how quickly signal strength falls with distance.

The FCC relied on its own field investigations in finding the interference risk low and manageable. The five staff studies it released covered particular companies and locations in New York, North Carolina and Pennsylvania. It withheld passages it characterized as preliminary results or deliberative staff opinions and asserted it had not relied on them.
sections.Issue: Whether the FCC unlawfully departed from its shutdown protection against harmful interference, failed to disclose relied-on studies for meaningful comment under section 553, failed to justify the forty-decibel extrapolation factor, and failed adequately to consider restricting the technology to the thirty-to-fifty-megahertz band.
sections.Holding: The D.C. Circuit in 2008, in an opinion by Judge Rogers joined by Judge Tatel, who also wrote separately, with Judge Kavanaugh concurring in part, concurring in the judgment on disclosure and dissenting on the extrapolation factor, held that the FCC had to disclose the unredacted studies on which it relied and allow comment, and had to supply a reasoned explanation for the extrapolation factor. It rejected the shutdown-protection and alternative-frequency challenges. The disclosure remand had all three judges' support; the extrapolation remand rested on Judges Rogers and Tatel.
sections.Reasoning:
The court rejected the shutdown challenge because the FCC did not redefine harmful interference; it found that after the required power reduction the remaining emissions would not meet the existing definition for mobile communications. The alternative-frequency proposal deserved a response and received one: the restriction would reduce capacity and flexibility and raise costs without corresponding need.

On disclosure, section 553 must permit useful participation, including evaluation of technical material on which a rule rests. Applying Portland Cement and related precedents, and after examining the unredacted pages in camera, the court found summaries of test data, scientific recommendations and analysis of methodology. An agency cannot make a study central factual support while preventing scrutiny of intertwined portions. The error was prejudicial because the League identified something useful it could say; it did not have to show its comments would certainly change the rule. FOIA's deliberative-process privilege did not justify secrecy for factual studies the agency had adopted, and the order enforced the agency's chosen process rather than adding procedures forbidden by Vermont Yankee.

On extrapolation, technical deference did not cure an unexplained choice. The FCC did not explain why uncertainty justified a factor designed for different technologies, and its conclusory statement did not engage with three 2005 British studies favoring twenty decibels. The remand required a reasoned justification or another factor; the court did not itself select twenty decibels.

Judge Tatel added that section 706's whole-record requirement independently supported complete disclosure. Judge Kavanaugh accepted that circuit precedent compelled disclosure but thought Portland Cement lacked support in section 553's text and conflicted with Vermont Yankee, and he found the extrapolation explanation adequate.

The casebook excerpt consists of editorial framing and passages from Judge Kavanaugh's separate opinion, which are not the majority holding.

LRS-ATLAS-O-ARNETT.rule: A nonprobationary federal employee removable only for cause may be discharged without a prior trial-type hearing where notice, a chance to respond and a full post-removal hearing are provided; no majority held that Congress may define the process along with the benefit.

sections.Parties: Wayne Kennedy, a nonprobationary competitive-service employee of the Office of Economic Opportunity, sued for declaratory and injunctive relief on March 27, 1972, the day his removal was to take effect, seeking a full hearing before removal and challenging the removal standard as a regulation of speech. Eighteen further plaintiffs, whose participation was largely nominal, were added by amendment. The government, the defendant below, took a direct appeal to the Supreme Court.
sections.Procedural History: Kennedy sued on March 27, 1972. A single district judge referred the procedural constitutional question to a three-judge court and dismissed the individual speech claim pending administrative exhaustion. Kennedy amended to add a facial vagueness and overbreadth challenge. The three-judge court granted him summary judgment, ordered reinstatement with backpay, required constitutionally sufficient proceedings for any future removal, and enjoined enforcement of the Act and rules as regulations of competitive employees' speech. Kennedy's Civil Service Commission appeal was delayed by the litigation and then terminated after his reinstatement. On the government's direct appeal, the Court reversed and remanded for further proceedings on April 16, 1974.
sections.Material Facts:
Kennedy was a field representative in the Office of Economic Opportunity's Chicago Regional Office. On February 18, 1972, Regional Director Wendell Verduin issued a proposed adverse-action notice charging misconduct in five incidents. The central allegation was that Kennedy had publicly accused Verduin and an assistant of offering a community-action representative a $100,000 grant in exchange for a statement against Kennedy and another employee, without proof and with reckless disregard of the facts. These matters were disputed; because Kennedy won summary judgment, the government's version was assumed, not found.

Kennedy was told he could answer orally and in writing, submit affidavits and inspect the supporting material. His lawyer instead demanded an impartial trial-type proceeding and asserted the conversations were protected speech. On March 20, Verduin sustained the charges, with removal effective March 27.

The Lloyd-La Follette Act, then 5 U.S.C. § 7501, permitted removal only for cause promoting the efficiency of the service and left a hearing to the removing official's discretion. Regulations added thirty days' notice, access to evidence, oral and written response, and an appeal with a full evidentiary hearing, typically held after removal, with backpay on reinstatement.
sections.Issue: Whether due process required a trial-type hearing before a nonprobationary federal employee removable only for cause could be discharged, and whether the Lloyd-La Follette Act's standard permitting removal only for cause promoting the efficiency of the service was unconstitutionally vague or overbroad as a regulation of employee speech.
sections.Holding: The Court in 1974, in a judgment announced by Justice Rehnquist joined by Chief Justice Burger and Justice Stewart, reversed the three-judge court. Five Justices sustained the discharge procedures, with Justice Powell, joined by Justice Blackmun, concurring in that result through independent constitutional balancing. Six Justices, including Justice White, rejected the facial vagueness and overbreadth challenge. Rehnquist's theory that the statutory benefit and its procedural limitations were inseparable had only three votes and was rejected by six Justices, so it is not a majority rule.
sections.Reasoning:
Justice Rehnquist's plurality reasoned that, under Roth, independent law defines property interests. The employee had a statutory expectancy of continued employment absent cause, but its dimensions included Congress's prescribed method for determining cause, so he had to accept the limited procedure along with the benefit. Any liberty interest in clearing his name could be served by the post-removal appeal.

Justice Powell, joined by Justice Blackmun, rejected that premise: once the legislature confers such an interest, it cannot define away constitutionally necessary safeguards. He nonetheless sustained the procedures by balancing the government's need for efficiency and discipline against the employee's interruption of income, noting reinstatement and backpay, and distinguishing the subsistence threat in Goldberg. An impartial decisionmaker at the post-removal hearing sufficed.

Justice White agreed that property and procedure were distinct and that notice and an opportunity for written presentation met minimum preliminary requirements. But because Verduin's own reputation was at issue, he would have read the statute to require an impartial initial decisionmaker and would have affirmed reinstatement and backpay, while reversing the speech injunction.

On speech, Rehnquist, with Powell, Blackmun and White, held the efficiency standard was a general employment protection, not a criminal code, and construed cause to exclude constitutionally protected speech.

Justice Douglas dissented, viewing Kennedy as punished for speech on a public issue. Justice Marshall, joined by Justices Douglas and Brennan, would have affirmed on both grounds: disputed accusations required a prior hearing with confrontation and an independent decisionmaker, and the efficiency formula chilled speech.

The casebook excerpts only the conflicting Rehnquist and Powell theories; the full brief notes that its description of an informal appeal before removal compresses a statutory right of reply.

LRS-ATLAS-O-ASHBACKER.rule: When two bona fide broadcast applications under the Communications Act are mutually exclusive, the Commission may not grant one without hearing both, because the grant substantially nullifies the other applicant's statutory opportunity to be heard.

sections.Parties: Ashbacker Radio Corporation, which operated station WKBZ in Muskegon, Michigan, appealed from the Federal Communications Commission's grant of a construction permit to a competing applicant, Fetzer Broadcasting Company. Ashbacker claimed to be a person aggrieved or adversely affected and sought a hearing on its own application before the facility was granted. The Commission moved to dismiss the appeal and defended its power to grant Fetzer's application without a hearing.
sections.Procedural History: The Commission granted Fetzer's application without a hearing and on the same day designated Ashbacker's application for hearing. Ashbacker petitioned for a hearing, rehearing and other relief against the Fetzer grant, and the Commission denied the petition. Ashbacker filed a notice of appeal from the Fetzer permit grant under section 402(b)(2). The Commission moved to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction, and the D.C. Court of Appeals granted the motion without an opinion. The Court granted certiorari and, on December 3, 1945, reversed the dismissal of Ashbacker's appeal. It did not select the superior broadcaster or decide the licensing merits.
sections.Material Facts:
In March 1944, Fetzer Broadcasting Company applied for permission to construct a station in Grand Rapids, Michigan, operating on 1230 kilocycles with 250 watts and unlimited time. In May, before that application was decided, Ashbacker applied to move its existing WKBZ station in Muskegon from 1490 to 1230 kilocycles, likewise with 250 watts and unlimited time. The Commission itself found that simultaneous operation at 1230 would create intolerable interference and that the applications were actually exclusive.

In June the Commission granted Fetzer's application without a hearing and designated Ashbacker's for a hearing. In denying Ashbacker's petition, it stressed that it had not denied Ashbacker's application, that Ashbacker could later show its proposal better served the public interest, and that the Fetzer grant did not foreclose later action. Yet the hearing notice required Ashbacker to establish, among other matters, the extent of interference with Fetzer's already authorized station, and its application would not be granted unless those issues were resolved in its favor. A requested stay of Fetzer's authorization had been denied.
sections.Issue: Whether, under section 309(a) of the Communications Act, the Commission may grant one of two bona fide, mutually exclusive applications without a hearing while setting the other for a later hearing, and whether the applicant so treated may appeal the grant as a person aggrieved or adversely affected.
sections.Holding: The Court in 1945, in an opinion by Justice Douglas, with Justice Frankfurter dissenting joined by Justice Rutledge and Justices Black and Jackson taking no part, held five to two that when two bona fide applications are mutually exclusive, granting one without hearing both substantially nullifies the other applicant's statutory opportunity to be heard. Scheduling the loser for a later hearing did not cure that deprivation once the facility had been granted to its competitor. The holding was confined to bona fide, mutually exclusive applications and the statutory hearing right.
sections.Reasoning:
Section 309(a) allowed a grant on examination when the public-interest finding could be made and otherwise required notice and an opportunity to be heard. Justice Douglas read the two directions together: a grant to one applicant that effectively foreclosed the other could not be justified by looking only at the power to approve the winner, because that would reduce the loser's hearing to an empty procedure. The Commission's own interference finding made Ashbacker's burden impossible, turning a hearing on its application into a rehearing of its competitor's grant. The Commission's own regulations favored consolidating conflicting applications.

The Commission's continuing authority to revoke or modify licenses did not remove the injury. Licensees had no vested property right in a frequency, but those procedures gave the incumbent a hearing, so Ashbacker was placed in the position of a newcomer seeking to displace an established broadcaster rather than an applicant competing for an unassigned facility. Nothing suggested workable adjustments, a disqualifying filing deadline, bad faith, or an urgent public need to act before a hearing. As to the appeal, earlier decisions allowed economically injured competitors and licensees facing interference to appeal grants, and Ashbacker was at least as adversely affected.

Justice Frankfurter, joined by Justice Rutledge, agreed the particular hearing order was defective because it required Ashbacker to negate interference already found, but thought the Commission could treat Fetzer's grant as conditional and modify it later. He would have returned the matter to the Commission to modify the hearing order.

The full brief notes that the casebook cites the later section 309(e) and describes a proximity rule applied at Ashbacker's hearing, whereas the opinion reports no completed hearing; the casebook's later discussion of auctions is editorial context.

LRS-ATLAS-O-BAILEY.rule: In the D.C.
