The $8,504 award stood.
sections.Reasoning:
Marshall distinguished section 1's general forfeiture language, which contemplated seizure within the United States, from section 5, which supplied the special authority for seizure at sea and limited it to covered vessels bound to a French port. Congress had thus prescribed a method of executing the law that excluded this seizure. Suspicion that the neutral ship was secretly American could not cure the defect, because even a genuinely American ship on this voyage out of a French port would not have been subject to high-seas seizure.

Marshall acknowledged that limiting seizure to vessels bound to French ports made evasion easier and that the executive's broader construction better served the law's practical objective. That assessment of usefulness could not substitute for the authority Congress enacted. He left open whether the President's faithful-execution and commander-in-chief responsibilities, without the particular statutory restriction, might have supported seizure of American vessels engaged in the illicit commerce.

On liability, Marshall stated that he had first inclined to think that a military officer acting in good faith under superior orders should be excused, given that military obedience is indispensable, with redress sought from the government through negotiation. He expressly abandoned that view and adopted the position of his brethren: instructions cannot change the nature of the transaction or legalize an act that would otherwise be a trespass. Little therefore remained answerable to the neutral owner. The Court also refused an objection to the damages account, since nothing objectionable appeared on its face and counsel had not excepted to it below.

LRS-ATLAS-O-MARBURY.rule: Courts may enforce a specific legal duty on which individual rights depend but cannot direct an executive officer's political discretion, and when a statute conflicts with the Constitution a court deciding the case must give effect to the Constitution.

sections.Parties: William Marbury, together with Dennis Ramsay, Robert Townsend Hooe and William Harper, applied to the Court for a writ of mandamus; they were represented by Charles Lee, formerly Attorney General. They stated that President John Adams had nominated them to be justices of the peace for the District of Columbia, that the Senate had consented, and that their commissions had been signed and sealed. The respondent was Secretary of State James Madison, from whom they sought their commissions after the change of administration. Madison showed no cause in response to the Court's rule.
sections.Procedural History: This was an original application to the Court, not an appeal from a lower court. The applications were brought in December 1801. The Court issued and served a rule requiring Madison to show cause why a writ of mandamus should not issue; Madison showed no cause. The Court took evidence, ordering State Department clerks Jacob Wagner and Daniel Brent sworn over their objection and hearing from former acting Secretary of State Levi Lincoln. On February 24, 1803 the Court discharged the rule. It issued no writ and did not order Madison to deliver the commission.
sections.Material Facts:
The applicants' affidavits stated that Adams nominated them, the Senate consented, Adams signed their commissions, and the Secretary of State affixed the seal of the United States. After the change of administration the commissions were withheld, and requests for information from the State Department and for Senate documentation failed.

Because the applicants could not obtain voluntary official affidavits, the Court ordered the clerks sworn while allowing objections to particular questions. Wagner could not remember seeing these particular commissions. Brent gave more direct evidence that commissions had been signed and sealed, including Marbury's and Hooe's. Lincoln was allowed to decline questions implicating confidential communications or self-incrimination, but the existence of the commissions in the office was treated as a public matter; he could not say that the commissions reached Madison. An affidavit by Hazen Kimball stated that he had seen Marbury's and Hooe's commissions signed on March 3.

Section 13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789 authorized the Court to issue writs of mandamus to persons holding office under the authority of the United States. Article III specifies the Court's original jurisdiction in cases affecting ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls, and those in which a state is a party. The office was held for a term of five years.
sections.Issue: Whether Marbury had a right to the commission he demanded; whether, if that right was violated, the law afforded him a remedy; and whether that remedy was a writ of mandamus issuing from the Court in an original proceeding.
sections.Holding: The Court in 1803, in an opinion by Chief Justice Marshall with no separate writing reported, discharged the rule and issued no writ. Marbury had a completed appointment and a vested legal right to his commission, and withholding it violated that right. But the Court could not entertain this original mandamus proceeding: section 13 of the Judiciary Act, insofar as it authorized this exercise of original jurisdiction, exceeded Article III's allocation and was incompatible with the Constitution. The full brief records that the casebook editors characterize the opinion's earlier discussion of ministerial duty as technically dicta, given the absence of jurisdiction.
sections.Reasoning:
On the right, the Court distinguished nomination, appointment and commission. Signing the commission is the President's last act, and the seal conclusively evidences the appointment. Delivery was a matter of convenience and could not undo a completed appointment. Marbury had been appointed to an office held for five years and not removable at executive will, so his right had vested.

On remedy, civil liberty includes the protection of the laws when a person is injured, and a government of laws must supply a remedy for the violation of a vested right. Where the Constitution entrusts political duties to the President and his officers act as his agents, their discretion is not judicially controllable. Where law imposes a specific duty on which individual rights depend, the character of the act, not the officer's rank, determines whether relief is proper. Providing the commission or a copy was ministerial, and an action of detinue was inadequate because the value of a public office cannot be ascertained.

On jurisdiction, Article III's division between original and appellate jurisdiction is an operative limit that Congress cannot enlarge; otherwise the enumeration would have no effect. Marbury's demand originated a new proceeding and was not appellate.

The Constitution establishes limited powers and is superior to ordinary legislation; if a statute could alter it, the distinction between limited and unlimited government would disappear. A court deciding a case must identify the governing law and, when two rules conflict, cannot apply both. Marshall reinforced this with Article III's extension to cases arising under the Constitution, the judicial oath, and the Supremacy Clause.

LRS-ATLAS-O-MEMPHIS-LIGHT.rule: Where state law permits a municipal utility to terminate service only for cause, the customer has a protected property interest, and due process requires notice explaining how to dispute a bill and a timely opportunity to present the complaint to an employee authorized to correct errors.

sections.Parties: Willie S. and Mary Craft, customers of Memphis Light, Gas and Water Division, sued the utility and its officials and employees under 42 U.S.C. section 1983, seeking declaratory and injunctive relief and actual and punitive damages for terminations of their service during a billing dispute. The utility, a municipal division directed by commissioners appointed by the City Council, and the individual officials were the defendants and the petitioners in the Court. They contested whether continued service was protected property and whether the procedures afforded were adequate, having abandoned their state-action contention.
sections.Procedural History: The Crafts and other customers sued in February 1974. After trial, the District Court denied class certification and entered judgment for the defendants, doubting that continued service during disputed nonpayment was protected property and rejecting the due-process claim, though it recommended a $35 credit and clearer termination notices. The Sixth Circuit affirmed the denial of class certification but held that the process afforded the Crafts violated due process. On May 1, 1978 the Court affirmed the Sixth Circuit's judgment, leaving the validity of the damages claim for initial determination below.
sections.Material Facts:
When the Crafts moved into a former duplex in October 1972, the house had two gas meters, two electric meters and one water meter. Relying on the seller, they believed the second gas and electric meters were inactive. In 1973 they began receiving two separate monthly bills, one in the name of Willie S. Craft and one of Willie C. Craft, each including a city service fee. In October a meter reader explained that both sets of meters were running. A plumber and an electrical contractor tried to consolidate them but did not do so correctly. The Crafts kept receiving two bills through January 1974 and suffered five service terminations.

Mrs. Craft repeatedly missed work to seek an explanation at the utility's offices. The District Court found her efforts were in good faith, but she obtained no satisfactory explanation or instructions for further recourse, and the opportunity to discuss the problem with management was not adequately explained to her. The litigation later disclosed that the accounts had not been properly combined in the utility's computer billing and that gas charges and city service fees included overcharges.

The utility's final notice stated the payment deadline and threatened cutoff. One flyer, sent in areas covering about 40 percent of customers, offered credit assistance without mentioning disputes; another referred to disputes, but there was no assurance the Crafts received it.
sections.Issue: Whether a customer of a municipal utility has a property interest in continued service protected by the Due Process Clause, and, if so, whether the utility's notice and complaint procedures before terminating service for nonpayment of a disputed bill were constitutionally adequate. A threshold question was whether the case was moot.
sections.Holding: The Court in 1978, in an opinion by Justice Powell for six Justices, affirmed. Tennessee law permitted termination only for cause and protected a customer's bona fide billing dispute, giving the Crafts a protected property interest in continued service. Due process required notice explaining an available means of disputing the bill and a timely opportunity to present the complaint to personnel authorized to correct errors; an informal conference could suffice. The process afforded the Crafts was inadequate. The Court did not award damages and left unresolved whether other circumstances would require an impartial decisionmaker or a written decision. Justice Stevens dissented, joined by Chief Justice Burger and Justice Rehnquist.
sections.Reasoning:
The case was not moot because the Crafts' claim for actual and punitive damages remained; the $35 credit was not an adjudicated award.

The substantive interest arose from Tennessee law, and federal law determined whether it was protected property. Tennessee decisions allowed cutoff for nonpayment of just charges but only at the utility's peril when disputed charges were wrong, and service could be denied only for good and sufficient cause. An entitlement does not cease to be property because it is disputed.

The final notice conveyed the threatened loss but did not adequately describe how to challenge the amount. Notice and hearing are connected: for customers of varied education and resources, being told merely to pay or lose an essential service does not make the chance to object effective. The lower courts had found that the opportunity to meet an employee empowered to resolve the dispute was not made available to Mrs. Craft.

Applying Mathews v. Eldridge, the Court noted that electricity, gas and water are necessities whose interruption can threaten health and safety, that computer billing carries a meaningful risk of error, and that an informal meeting before cutoff would serve the utility's own interest in accuracy without materially delaying collection. A pretermination injunction, damages after cutoff, or payment followed by a refund suit did not cure the defect, since restoration cannot undo the loss and the amounts are too small to justify litigation. The Court distinguished Ingraham.

Justice Stevens, dissenting, considered notice of the threatened loss and time to respond sufficient, thought Mrs. Craft had been heard by officials with adequate authority, and regarded judicial remedies and potential damages as adequate protection.

LRS-ATLAS-O-MIDWEST-OIL.rule: A long-continued executive practice, known to Congress and acquiesced in by it, raises a presumption of congressional consent that can authorize the President to withdraw public lands from private acquisition, although executive practice alone cannot create power.

sections.Parties: The United States sued in equity to recover a quarter section of withdrawn Wyoming public land and to obtain an accounting for 50,000 barrels of oil alleged to have been illegally extracted. The defendants and appellees were Midwest Oil Company and others, assignees of William T. Henshaw and others who had entered the land after the withdrawal. The government argued that the President's responsibilities and Congress's tacit consent authorized the withdrawal; the appellees answered that Congress had opened the land to acquisition and that the President had no dispensing power to suspend that law.
sections.Procedural History: The federal District Court for Wyoming sustained the defendants' demurrer and dismissed the government's bill. The Eighth Circuit rendered no decision on the merits; it certified questions to the Court, which called for the entire record. After argument and reargument, on February 23, 1915 the Court sustained the withdrawal and remanded to the District Court with directions that its decree dismissing the bill be reversed. The Court did not award a final accounting or determine how much oil had been extracted.
sections.Material Facts:
A statute of February 11, 1897 allowed qualified persons to acquire public land containing petroleum under the placer-mining laws. Oil beneath adjoining parcels could be drained by competing wells, and public reserves were disappearing through private acquisition; officials feared the government would have to buy back oil needed for naval fuel.

On September 17, 1909 the director of the Geological Survey warned the Secretary of the Interior that the remaining public petroleum lands might soon pass from government control and recommended suspending new claims pending legislation. On September 27, 1909, acting under President Taft's direction, the department issued Temporary Petroleum Withdrawal No. 5. It temporarily barred location, settlement, selection, filing, entry or disposal under the mineral and nonmineral public-land laws within listed areas totaling 3,041,000 acres in California and Wyoming, in aid of proposed legislation. Existing valid claims could proceed.

On March 27, 1910 Henshaw and others entered a quarter section of the withdrawn Wyoming land, drilled a well, discovered oil, and assigned their interests to the appellees, who took possession and extracted petroleum. A location certificate was filed on May 4. On June 25, 1910 Congress expressly authorized temporary withdrawals, providing that the statute should not be construed as recognizing, abridging or enlarging claims initiated on oil lands after earlier withdrawals.

The full brief notes that the casebook calls the withdrawal a 1910 order; the controlling order was dated September 27, 1909.
sections.Issue: Whether the President, without express statutory authority, could validly withdraw public petroleum lands that Congress had opened to private acquisition, pending proposed legislation, so that persons who entered the land after the withdrawal acquired no rights.
sections.Holding: The Court in 1915, in an opinion by Justice Lamar, sustained the September 27, 1909 withdrawal by a vote of 5 to 3 and directed reversal of the dismissal of the government's bill. The withdrawal was authorized by a long-standing executive practice known to and acquiesced in by Congress, understood as implied congressional consent to this manner of administering the public lands, so the appellees acquired no rights by their later entry. The Court expressly reserved whether, as an original question before any practice existed, a President could withdraw land Congress had opened, and it denied that executive conduct alone could create power. Justice Day dissented, joined by Justices McKenna and Van Devanter; Justice McReynolds did not participate.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court began with roughly eighty years of practice. Apart from orders resting on special statutory authority, Presidents had repeatedly withdrawn public lands, including 99 orders for Indian reservations, 109 for military reservations and 44 for bird reserves before 1910, and Congress had accepted this practice without repudiating it. Before a person initiated a legally protected claim, the land statutes gave no enforceable private interest in a particular parcel, so reserving unappropriated land defeated no existing right.

Settled governmental usage is relevant in construing a statute or identifying a power. Practice does not itself create authority, but practice known to Congress and left undisturbed supports a presumption of congressional consent. Congress's role as proprietor strengthened the inference: an owner may authorize its agent, without writing, to retain property temporarily when conditions change.

The Court rejected a categorical distinction between reserving land for a public use and withholding it pending legislation; temporary withdrawal was the lesser step, and the Des Moines River cases supplied direct precedent. In 1902 the Senate had asked what authority supported administrative withdrawals, received the Interior Department's assertion of a long-recognized power, and did not repudiate it. The June 25, 1910 statute left rights to the law existing when the order issued, so ratification was unnecessary.

Justice Day, dissenting, agreed that express or clear implied congressional authority could support a withdrawal, but argued that Article IV vests control of federal property in Congress and that the President cannot suspend its laws to await a preferable policy. He read the precedents as involving uses Congress had authorized, and treated Congress's refusal to ratify in 1910 as defeating implied consent.

LRS-ATLAS-O-MOBIL-OIL.rule: The Natural Gas Act gives the Federal Power Commission no jurisdiction over liquid petroleum, and rates subject to the Act's substantial-evidence review need a record whose factual premises parties could meaningfully test, though full formal APA procedures are not required.

sections.Parties: Mobil Oil Corp. petitioned the D.C. Circuit for review of Federal Power Commission orders fixing nationwide minimum charges for pipeline transportation of producers' liquid hydrocarbons and liquefiables. Mobil challenged the Commission's statutory power, its use of privileged settlement material, the adequacy of its procedure, the substantial evidentiary support for the rates, and discrimination or preference. The Commission argued that the liquids were involved in a larger transaction within its jurisdiction and that minimum liquid transportation charges protected gas consumers from subsidizing producers.
sections.Procedural History: Between 1954 and 1968 the Commission addressed the problem through cost allocation in individual certificate and rate proceedings. In February 1968 it proposed a general cost-allocation policy, received comments, and held conferences in September and October 1970. Without another notice or conference, it issued Order 449 on January 31, 1972, adopting national minimum transportation charges for liquids and liquefiables. Mobil unsuccessfully sought rehearing and petitioned for review. In an opinion decided July 11, 1973 and amended July 26, the D.C. Circuit vacated the challenged orders and remanded to the Commission, which first had to explain why mandatory liquefiables charges were needed instead of its former cost-allocation method and then develop a record adequate to justify any lawful rates.
sections.Material Facts:
Production from natural-gas wells could include liquid petroleum, liquefiables (gaseous when produced but later liquefied), and gas. Producers selling gas sometimes kept ownership of the liquids and liquefiables while sending them through the pipeline with the gas. Carrying them occupied capacity and incurred costs, and insufficient payment could shift costs to gas consumers.

The Commission's February 1968 notice proposed a general cost-allocation policy and did not announce the nationwide minimum rates eventually adopted. Fifteen producers, eleven pipelines and two state agencies commented; only the state agencies supported the proposal, and the comments did not provide the cost data later used. A September 29, 1970 conference was conducted by a Commission attorney with no transcript, only paraphrased minutes. At an October conference pipeline counsel supplied nine sheets of cost-of-service figures prepared for a Southern Louisiana settlement. The figures had not been sponsored as evidence, cross-examined, or confronted with opposing evidence; they covered ten of 116 pipelines and used different test years.

Order 449 set minimum charges of two cents per Mcf per hundred miles for liquefiables and twenty cents per barrel for liquids, stating that cost allocation was inadequate without explaining why. At argument the Commission acknowledged that nine of the ten pipelines' cost data had been found too high in later individual proceedings.
sections.Issue: Whether the Natural Gas Act gave the Commission jurisdiction to fix transportation charges for liquid petroleum, and whether, for liquefiables over which jurisdiction was uncontested, the Commission could adopt nationwide minimum rates on informal comments and untested settlement figures consistently with the Act's substantial-evidence review requirement.
sections.Holding: The D.C. Circuit, in 1973, in an opinion by Judge Wilkey for a panel that included Judge Leventhal and Senior District Judge Jameson, with no separate writing, held that the Commission had no statutory jurisdiction over liquid petroleum and set aside the liquid-price provisions. Independently, it held that the agency had inadequately exposed and tested the factual basis for its rates. Full trial-type rulemaking under APA sections 556 and 557 was not required, but the Act still required meaningful development and testing of the factual premises essential to the rates. The court rejected Mobil's settlement-privilege objection, did not separately resolve the discrimination issue, and did not adjudicate an appropriate rate amount.
sections.Reasoning:
On jurisdiction, the Natural Gas Act conferred power over natural gas, not liquid petroleum. The Commission's arguments that the liquids were involved in a larger jurisdictional transaction and that minimum charges protected gas consumers could not authorize regulating an excluded product; Congress, rather than an administrative assertion of necessity, had to supply added power. The former cost-allocation method also weakened the claimed necessity, because nongas costs could be withheld from gas charges without directly regulating the nongas service.

On procedure, the Act did not contain the required "on the record" direction, so under United States v. Florida East Coast Railway Mobil could not demand all formal APA hearing incidents. The court nevertheless treated the choice as more flexible than full formal procedure or untested written comments, describing intermediate devices such as written questions, prescreening and limited cross-examination. Section 16 implemented substantive statutory powers and conferred neither independent jurisdiction nor permission to avoid their safeguards. The substantial-evidence requirement, then at 15 U.S.C. § 717r(b), meant findings had to withstand examination of the whole record. This record failed: the Commission relied on material never introduced with notice that it would be the rule's foundation, parties had no adequate chance to rebut it, and the untested settlement figures covered ten of 116 pipelines without a demonstration of representativeness. Florida East Coast did not resolve this point because the proceeding there lacked the same review requirement. Even if the jurisdictional and broader procedural conclusions were rejected, the absence of fair notice and an adequate record independently required remand. Evidence from another proceeding could be used only if it had been tested, with notice and an opportunity to comment.

The casebook's discussion of the practical effects of hybrid-rulemaking decisions and the later Vermont Yankee response is editorial history, not the court's reasoning.

LRS-ATLAS-O-MOCK.rule: A rule that carries legal force is legislative and must go through APA notice and comment, and the proposal must adequately frame the issues so affected persons could reasonably anticipate the final rule's eventual course and comment meaningfully.

sections.Parties: Texas residents William Mock and Christopher Lewis owned braced pistols and wanted to buy more. Maxim Defense manufactured and sold braces and braced pistols. Firearms Policy Coalition represented gun owners and businesses, and the other three plaintiffs were its members. They challenged ATF's 2023 stabilizing-brace rule and sought injunctive relief; they were the plaintiffs below and the appellants. The government defended the rule as interpretive and exempt from notice and comment and, alternatively, as adequately noticed, and asserted harmless error.
sections.Procedural History: The Northern District of Texas denied a preliminary injunction. It considered ATF likely authorized to issue the rule, rejected lenity and vagueness arguments, treated the rule as interpretive, alternatively found adequate logical outgrowth, and rejected the preliminary First and Second Amendment claims. A Fifth Circuit motions panel granted an injunction pending appeal on May 23, and the merits panel clarified its coverage on May 26. On this interlocutory appeal under 28 U.S.C. § 1292(a)(1), a divided Fifth Circuit on August 1, 2023 reversed the denial and remanded for the district court to consider the remaining injunction factors and the appropriate scope, continuing its existing injunction until the district court ruled or sixty days elapsed, whichever came first. This brief covers only that interlocutory decision, not later merits proceedings.
sections.Material Facts:
The National Firearms Act covers short-barreled rifles but generally excludes ordinary pistols; a rifle must be designed, made and intended to be fired from the shoulder. Classification as a short-barreled rifle entails registration, ordinarily a $200 transfer tax, and potential felony consequences. A stabilizing brace attaches behind a handgun and supports or attaches to the forearm. In 2012 ATF concluded that a submitted brace did not convert a pistol into a shoulder-fired rifle; its later letters fluctuated.

ATF published a proposal on June 10, 2021. Proposed Worksheet 4999 assigned points to design characteristics, with a score of at least four in either of two sections indicating a rifle, and gave three worked examples. Approximately 217,000 of 237,000 comments opposed it. The January 31, 2023 final rule abandoned the worksheet. It asked whether a rearward accessory supplied surface area permitting shoulder firing and then considered six factors, including manufacturer marketing and evidence of likely community use. ATF's estimate suggested about 99% of brace-equipped pistols would be classified as rifles, and about sixty accompanying classifications gave results without explanations. The compliance deadline was May 31; options included replacing the barrel, permanently removing or altering the brace, surrendering or destroying the firearm, or registering it.
sections.Issue: Whether the plaintiffs were substantially likely to succeed on their claim that ATF's final stabilizing-brace rule was a legislative rule subject to APA § 553 notice and comment and that the proposal failed to give adequate notice of the final rule's approach, so that the denial of a preliminary injunction should be reversed.
sections.Holding: The Fifth Circuit, in 2023, in an opinion by Judge Jerry Smith joined fully by Judge Willett, with Judge Higginson dissenting, held that the plaintiffs were substantially likely to succeed on their APA notice-and-comment challenge: the final rule was legislative, and the proposal did not give adequate notice of its eventual approach. The court reversed the denial of a preliminary injunction and remanded for the remaining injunction factors and scope, declining to issue nationwide relief itself. It found the statutory-authority, lenity and nondelegation arguments unnecessary to decide, left the constitutional claims for later, and treated a distinct arbitrary-and-capricious challenge as forfeited on appeal.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority distinguished rules carrying legal force from interpretations advising the public how an agency understands existing law, and adopted the five-factor approach from Cargill: intended legal force, CFR publication, invocation of legislative authority, a claim to Chevron deference, and significant effects on private interests. ATF's disclaimer of Chevron deference weighed against legislative status, but the rule amended two CFR definitions, invoked delegated authority, used prospective compliance language with a deadline, and by ATF's own low estimate cost over $245 million annually. Taken together, the factors made the rule legislative.

On notice, an agency need not announce every final provision but must adequately frame the issues so affected persons could reasonably anticipate the eventual course. The majority read that as requiring sufficient similarity in regulatory kind. The worksheet was the proposal's organizing method, and requests for better criteria did not announce its replacement with an unweighted six-factor balancing test; marketing and community use were new features. Prejudice lay in the plaintiffs' inability to comment on the changed method. Likelihood of success satisfied only one of four requirements, so the district court had to address the rest.

Judge Willett's concurrence suggested the Second Amendment might protect such accessories; that was not the panel's holding. Judge Higginson would affirm: substantial impact distinguishes substantive from procedural rules, not legislative from interpretive ones; replacing a heavily criticized worksheet was a foreseeable response to comments; and any defect was harmless.

The casebook account retains selected logical-outgrowth passages and Higginson's competing account, omitting most of the legislative-character dispute and remedy discussion.

LRS-ATLAS-O-NEAGLE.rule: A federal officer held by a State for an act done in performing a duty under federal law, including a duty inferred from the Constitution or a marshal's general statutory responsibilities, may be discharged on federal habeas if he did no more than was necessary and proper.

sections.Parties: Thomas Cunningham, Sheriff of San Joaquin County, California, held Deputy U.S. Marshal David Neagle under a state murder warrant and was the appellant, challenging the grant of habeas corpus. Neagle was the successful habeas petitioner below and the appellee; he sought discharge from state custody for killing David S. Terry while protecting Justice Stephen Field. The sheriff's lawyers argued the defense should be tried in California's courts; the United States and Neagle argued he acted under federal authority.
sections.Procedural History: A Stockton magistrate issued a murder warrant naming both Field and Neagle on August 14, 1889, and Neagle was committed for examination. The charge against Field was dismissed. On August 16, fellow deputy A. L. Farrish applied for federal habeas relief on Neagle's behalf, and Sheriff Cunningham produced him and relied on the state warrant. Judges Sawyer and Sabin of the federal Circuit Court received a substantial documentary and testimonial record, found the petitioner's allegations true and his detention contrary to federal law, and discharged him. Cunningham appealed to the Supreme Court, which reexamined the record on facts as well as law and, on April 14, 1890, affirmed the discharge.
sections.Material Facts:
In federal litigation in California, a decree declared Sarah Althea Hill's alleged marriage declaration to William Sharon fraudulent and void. On September 3, 1888, Field delivered the decision reviving that decree against Hill and her husband, David Terry. Hill interrupted and accused Field of having been bought; when Marshal Franks tried to remove her, Terry struck him and reached for a bowie knife, which Neagle played the principal role in taking away. Both were jailed for contempt, and both continued threatening Field.

Attorney General Miller's letters of April 27 and May 27 directed unusual caution in protecting the judges and authorized special deputies. Franks appointed Neagle and instructed him to accompany Field in court and while traveling between courts. Returning from holding court in Los Angeles toward San Francisco, Field and Neagle stopped for breakfast at the Lathrop station dining room. Terry approached Field from behind, struck both sides of his face, and appeared ready to strike again. Neagle rose, identified himself as an officer, and told Terry to stop. Terry turned and thrust his hand into his clothing; Neagle, believing he was reaching for a bowie knife, fired twice, and Terry died within minutes.
sections.Issue: Whether Neagle, in killing Terry while guarding Justice Field, was in custody for an act done pursuant to a "law of the United States" within Revised Statutes § 753, although no statute specifically assigned marshals to protect a traveling judge, so that a federal court could discharge him on habeas before any state trial.
sections.Holding: The Court, in 1890, in an opinion by Justice Miller, decided six to two with Justice Field not participating and Justice Lamar dissenting joined by Chief Justice Fuller, held that Neagle acted under federal authority, did no more than was necessary and proper to protect Field, and could not be held for that act under California law. It affirmed his discharge, concluding he need not answer in California's courts for the transaction. The holding rested on constitutional protective authority together with the statutes governing marshals and federal habeas, not on a rule that a presidential directive immunizes any federal employee from state criminal law.
sections.Reasoning:
Under § 753, federal habeas extended to custody for an act performed pursuant to federal law, and § 761 required the judge to determine the facts summarily. Field was performing a federal duty: Revised Statutes §§ 606 and 610 assigned Justices to circuits, and necessary travel between places of holding court belonged to that duty.

The Court rejected reading "law" as confined to a congressional enactment naming this protective service. An obligation properly inferred from the Constitution, or a duty derived from a marshal's general statutory responsibilities, could qualify. Quoting Ex parte Siebold and Tennessee v. Davis, it explained that the federal government must be able to enforce its functions physically. The President's duty to see the laws faithfully executed embraced rights and duties arising from the Constitution and the protections implicit in the government's nature, not only the express terms of statutes and treaties; the Court illustrated this with the Koszta incident and other examples. Section 788 also gave marshals and deputies the powers of state sheriffs, and California sheriffs had to preserve the peace. An attack on Field breached the peace of the United States.

California's objection that a jury must try the charge failed: if a federal court properly established that an officer performed an authorized duty and did no more than necessary and proper, the act could not be a state crime.

Justice Lamar's dissent accepted that the killing could be justified for an ordinary bystander but denied that the justification derived from federal law. Implied powers had to be exercised through Congress under the Necessary and Proper Clause; the Take Care duty did not let the President create the missing rule, and the marshal statutes did not supply it. He would have remanded Neagle to Cunningham's custody.

LRS-ATLAS-O-NOEL-CANNING.rule: The Recess Appointments Clause covers intersession and intrasession recesses of sufficient length and vacancies that predate the recess, but a three-day recess is too short, one under ten days is presumptively too short, and the Senate is in session when it says so if it can conduct business.

sections.Parties: Noel Canning, a Pepsi-Cola bottler and distributor, petitioned the D.C. Circuit for review of a National Labor Relations Board order requiring it to execute a collective-bargaining agreement and make employees whole. The Board sought enforcement and, after losing, petitioned the Supreme Court. The company argued that the Board lacked a quorum because three members had been invalidly appointed under the Recess Appointments Clause; the administration argued that the Senate's pro forma sessions did not interrupt a longer recess.
sections.Procedural History: After a two-day hearing, an administrative law judge credited the union's account, and the Board issued its order on February 8, 2012. The company petitioned for review and the Board sought enforcement. On January 25, 2013, the D.C. Circuit, through Chief Judge Sentelle, rejected the company's nonconstitutional objections but held the appointments invalid, granted the petition, vacated the Board's order and denied enforcement. All three judges agreed that recess appointments are permitted only between formal Senate sessions; Sentelle and Judge Henderson also held that the vacancy must first arise during that recess, a ground Judge Griffith did not join. On the Board's petition, the Supreme Court on June 26, 2014 rejected both of those categorical interpretations but affirmed.
sections.Material Facts:
Noel Canning negotiated a replacement collective-bargaining agreement after its prior one expired in April 2010. At the final meeting on December 8, 2010, the parties discussed how to allocate a forty-cent hourly increase between wages and pensions. After a handshake and an understanding that the proposal would go to a ratification vote, the company sent an email imposing a ten-cent pension ceiling. Employees ratified a proposal assigning all forty cents to pensions; the company declared impasse and refused to execute the agreement.

The Board needed three lawfully appointed members to act. The deciding panel was Brian Hayes, Terence Flynn and Sharon Block. President Obama had appointed Block, Flynn and Richard Griffin on January 4, 2012, invoking the Recess Appointments Clause. The vacancies originated on August 27, 2010, August 27, 2011, and January 3, 2012. On December 17, 2011, the Senate had unanimously arranged brief pro forma sessions every Tuesday and Friday through January 20, contemplating that no business would be transacted, although it passed a payroll-tax extension by unanimous consent on December 23. The appointments fell between the January 3 and January 6 pro forma meetings.
sections.Issue: Whether "the Recess" in the Recess Appointments Clause includes intrasession as well as intersession recesses; whether vacancies that "may happen during the Recess" include vacancies that arose earlier and continue to exist; and whether the Senate's pro forma sessions prevented a recess long enough to support the January 4, 2012 appointments.
sections.Holding: The Court, in 2014, in an opinion by Justice Breyer joined by Justices Kennedy, Ginsburg, Sotomayor and Kagan, held that the Clause reaches both intersession and intrasession recesses of sufficient length and both vacancies arising during a recess and earlier vacancies remaining open during it. A recess of three days is too short, and one of more than three but fewer than ten days is presumptively too short. For this purpose the Senate is in session when it says it is, provided its own rules leave it capable of conducting business. The pro forma sessions counted, leaving only a three-day recess, so the appointments were invalid and the Board lacked a quorum. The judgment was affirmed unanimously; Justice Scalia, joined by Chief Justice Roberts and Justices Thomas and Alito, concurred only in the judgment.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority began from two commitments: the Clause is a subsidiary mechanism preserving continuity when the Senate is unavailable without routinely bypassing confirmation, and longstanding practice carries significant weight in resolving ambiguous allocations of power between the elected branches.

The text did not compel reading "the Recess" as one formal intersession interval, since a definite article may describe a class of recurring periods, and the Senate's practical availability matters in either kind of break. The Court relied on nineteenth- and twentieth-century practice and the Senate's lack of formal opposition. The three-day limit was informed by the Adjournments Clause. The ten-day presumption, which applies to both kinds of recess, yields to highly unusual emergencies such as a national catastrophe, but political opposition in the Senate is not one.

"May happen" could describe a vacancy that happens to exist; the narrower reading would frustrate the Clause's purpose, and the broader one became established through attorney-general opinions beginning with Wirt in 1823 and later practice.

Respect for the Senate's authority over its proceedings required deference to its own account. The pro forma sessions qualified because the Senate retained the capacity to act by unanimous consent, as the December 23 legislation showed.

Justice Scalia would have adopted readings substantially matching the D.C. Circuit's: "Recess" means the formal period between sessions, and vacancies must first arise then. He regarded the majority's time lines as judicially invented and disputed its reliance on practice.

The brief notes that the casebook's editorial account needs two corrections: the Court expressly applied the short-recess analysis to intersession recesses, and successors were already confirmed when the Court decided.

LRS-ATLAS-O-WEST-COVINA.rule: When officers lawfully seize property for a criminal investigation, due process requires reasonable steps to notify the owner of the seizure but not individualized notice of return remedies that are established in published, generally available statutes and case law.

sections.Parties: Lawrence Perkins and his family, whose home was searched and whose property was seized, sued the City of West Covina and its officers in federal court. They were the plaintiffs and prevailed in the Ninth Circuit; they claimed the City had to tell them how to seek return of the property and give them the information needed to do so. The City and officers were the defendants and asked the Court to reject that expanded notice requirement.
sections.Procedural History: The original complaint alleged a search without probable cause, action outside the warrant's scope, and a municipal policy allowing unlawful searches. The District Court granted summary judgment to the City and officers but invited briefing on a due-process issue the plaintiffs had not raised, the adequacy of remedies for return of seized property, without initially deciding it. On appeal the Ninth Circuit remanded for resolution of that issue. The District Court found California's remedies adequate and again entered summary judgment for the City. The Ninth Circuit reversed, holding that officials must give notice of the return procedures and the information needed to use them. On January 13, 1999, the Supreme Court reversed the Ninth Circuit and remanded for further proceedings.
sections.Material Facts:
On May 21, 1993, police searched Lawrence Perkins's home under a valid warrant in a homicide investigation of a former boarder, Marcus Marsh. Neither Perkins nor his family was a suspect. Officers seized photographs of Marsh, an address book, a shotgun, a starter pistol, ammunition and $2,629. They left an itemized inventory and a notice identifying the search date, the agency, the date of the warrant, the issuing judge and court, and officers to contact with telephone numbers. They omitted the warrant number because the warrant was sealed to protect the continuing investigation, though a public court index recorded its issuance by the address searched and the warrant number.

Perkins contacted one of the listed detectives and was told that return of the property required a court order. About a month after the search he went to the issuing court, where the judge was on vacation, and another judge could not locate a matter under Perkins's name. Rather than filing a written request, pursuing further inquiries or returning later, the family brought a federal suit. California law allowed a motion for return under Penal Code section 1536 or section 1540.
sections.Issue: Whether due process requires officers who lawfully seize property under a warrant for a criminal investigation to give the owner, in addition to notice of the seizure, individualized notice of the state-law procedures for seeking its return and the information needed to invoke them.
sections.Holding: The Court, in 1999, in an opinion by Justice Kennedy for seven Justices, with Justice Thomas joined by Justice Scalia concurring in the judgment, held that officers lawfully seizing property for a criminal investigation need not provide individualized advice about remedies for its return when those remedies are established in published, generally available statutes and decisions. Notice that a seizure has occurred is distinct from notice explaining the legal procedures available afterward. The Court did not decide the legality of the search, whether the State could keep the property, the adequacy of California's remedies as such, or precisely how detailed seizure notice must be.
sections.Reasoning:
A meaningful opportunity to be heard generally requires knowing that a matter affecting one's property is pending. Reasonable steps to tell an owner that officers have taken property are necessary because the owner otherwise may have no reasonable way to learn who caused the loss. The family conceded receiving the notice and inventory.

That rationale did not extend to individualized legal advice about procedures already publicly accessible. Once the owner knows the government has the property, public statutes and case law permit inquiry into remedies, and the owners raised no independent challenge to the adequacy of California's.

Memphis Light was different. There a utility customer had to be told of an internal billing-review procedure not described in publicly available documents, so the opportunity depended on word-of-mouth referral. It did not impose a general duty to advise people of published remedies. The Court distinguished Memphis Light rather than overruling it.

Settled practice pointed the same way: Federal Criminal Rule 41(d) required a warrant copy and receipt but no instruction on seeking return, and the federal and state laws collected in the Appendix did not support the Ninth Circuit's rule.

The owners' narrower argument that the City should have supplied the warrant number failed on the facts, because the District Court had found no evidence that the number was indispensable. The Court therefore did not decide that narrower constitutional question.

Justice Thomas agreed that detailed notice of remedies was unnecessary but rejected, as dictum, the suggestion that procedural due process requires notice of a seizure under a criminal warrant; any such requirement would belong to Fourth Amendment reasonableness, a question he left open.

The casebook's use of West Covina to reconsider the characterization of Memphis Light is editorial commentary.

LRS-ATLAS-O-WESTON.rule: Qualified participants already receiving available welfare funds have a conditional property interest in continued benefits, protected by due process despite statutory no-entitlement provisions, where officials have no discretion to deny funded benefits to eligible recipients for reasons outside the statutory standards.

sections.Parties: Frances Weston, Christine Kneubehl and Shauna Disher represented a class of Adams County welfare recipients who had been sanctioned under the Colorado Works Program. They sued the county department director and the social-services board, seeking declaratory and injunctive relief, reversal of sanctions, restoration of withheld benefits, and attorney fees under § 1988. The county defendants appealed the judgment against them. Denver defendants settled before trial, and the state defendants were not parties to the appeal.
sections.Procedural History: The plaintiffs sued under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, Colorado's Administrative Procedure Act and its declaratory-judgments law. After a bench trial, the trial court found that none of the five versions of sanction notices used between July 1997 and November 1999 complied with statutory or regulatory requirements. It declared the notices inadequate, enjoined their further use, ordered reversal and removal of records of prior sanctions based on them, and directed equitable restoration of cash assistance improperly withheld. On July 5, 2001, the Colorado Court of Appeals, reviewing statutory construction de novo, affirmed.
sections.Material Facts:
The federal Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996 replaced AFDC with TANF, funded by block grants conditioned on state implementation. Colorado enacted its Works Program in 1997. Participants entered individual responsibility contracts and could lose part of their cash assistance for noncompliance. Before sanctioning a participant, the county had to send notice describing the basis for the action, the available county conference and state-level appeal, and how to pursue review. The state department developed standardized forms; counties administered the program, completed the forms and gave the notices.

Federal law declared that TANF did not entitle any individual or family to assistance, and Colorado law said the Works Program created no legal entitlement. But Colorado's scheme also provided that, subject to available appropriations, a participant shall receive a basic grant, and that participants shall continue receiving cash assistance during an appeal.

All five versions of Adams County's notices failed to state the sanction amount and a sufficiently specific reason. Early notices also failed to explain effects on later benefits, cite the governing rule, or state the correct review period, giving twenty-six days where ninety were permitted. The county routinely restored benefits when sanctioned recipients appealed while continuing to use the defective notices, even after administrative findings of inadequacy.
sections.Issue: Whether welfare recipients had a protected property interest in continued benefits despite federal and state "no entitlement" provisions; whether the county's sanction notices satisfied due process; whether the county defendants were proper § 1983 defendants; and whether failure to exhaust administrative review barred the state-law claims.
sections.Holding: The Colorado Court of Appeals, in 2001, in an opinion by Judge Davidson in which Judges Metzger and Roy concurred, held that qualified participants already receiving available welfare funds had a conditional property interest in continued benefits despite the no-entitlement provisions. It sustained the conclusion that the county's notices denied due process, held the county defendants proper defendants for prospective declaratory and injunctive relief, and rejected the exhaustion defense on this record. The court did not hold that a no-entitlement clause can never matter, that appropriations limits disappear, or that exhaustion is excused in every benefits dispute.
sections.Reasoning:
Following Roth, a property interest requires a legitimate claim of entitlement grounded in an independent legal source. Welfare reform modified the former entitlement framework, but the disclaimers did not eliminate every protected interest; they had to be read with the scheme's mandatory directions on grants, continued assistance during appeal, and written notice.

The court distinguished an enforceable absolute benefit claim and the obligation to fund an entitlement program from a protected interest arising from standards that constrain discretion. Government kept discretion over funding, and before funds were available no personal entitlement had matured. But once the state received money and recipients met the eligibility requirements and had begun receiving benefits, the county had no discretion to deny them for reasons outside the statutory standards; officials conceded the obligation to pay eligible recipients when funds were available. Barry was distinguished because officials there chose among eligible families for scarce shelter. Under Loudermill, the legislature could not confer the interest and then eliminate appropriate procedural safeguards.

On notice, the court applied the regulatory minimum requirements; substantial failure to meet them could not support a deprivation, and the record supported the defects the trial court found in each of the five phases.

On § 1983, the rule excluding the state and certain official-capacity defendants from damages actions did not bar official-capacity suits for prospective relief against those who implemented the program.

On exhaustion, the court recognized exceptions for futility and practices avoiding judicial review. Restoring benefits on appeal resolved individual disputes without review of the recurring notice system, and the administrative framework could not provide classwide correction.

The casebook presents the property-interest reasoning alongside Barry.

LRS-ATLAS-O-WIRTZ.rule: Where a statute requires rulemaking on the record under the APA, statistical summaries may be admitted, but opposing parties must have adequate access to the underlying material to test them; an agency that withholds it risks failing the substantial-evidence requirement.

sections.Parties: Electric-motor and generator manufacturers, including Baldor, Holtzer-Cabot, Westinghouse, Louis Allis and Northwestern Electric, were the plaintiffs challenging a prevailing minimum-wage determination for their industry under the Walsh-Healey Public Contracts Act. Their trade association, NEMA, had contested the determination at the administrative hearing. The Secretary of Labor, who made the determination, defended it and the confidentiality of the survey responses on which it rested, and disputed the plaintiffs' standing.
sections.Procedural History: In the administrative proceeding, the examiner denied NEMA access to the survey's underlying responses, and Secretary Goldberg sustained the procedural rulings and issued the wage determination. The dispute then went to the District Court and to the D.C. Circuit. On December 31, 1963, the D.C. Circuit found substantive-evidence and procedural defects but remanded the record for the District Court to determine which plaintiffs had standing, retaining appellate jurisdiction and keeping the existing stay in force. On June 29, 1964, in a per curiam supplemental opinion after remand, it accepted standing for five companies, rejected the Secretary's proposals to rehabilitate the determination, and ordered it struck down, continuing the injunction's stay for sixty days to allow Supreme Court review. The source does not establish what later review occurred.
sections.Material Facts:
The Walsh-Healey Act required specified government contracts to include minimum wages the Labor Secretary determined to prevail in the industry. The 1952 Fulbright Amendment made the APA applicable and required wage determinations on the record after an opportunity for a hearing.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics sent questionnaires to 775 establishments seeking covered-worker and wage data for the payroll period nearest October 15, 1960, pledging not to disclose information identified by company name. Six wage tables summarized 216 firms. NEMA received the tables about five weeks before the hearing, obtained copies of responses from seventy-two establishments, and reported discrepancies, two of which BLS accepted. The day before the hearing NEMA sought a subpoena for the completed questionnaires and related material, having offered confidential treatment of anything inspected by counsel. The examiner denied access because of the confidentiality pledge. At the hearing the BLS supervisor could not answer some questions without consulting the underlying responses, and government counsel successfully objected to that consultation. Company affidavits identifying errors were eventually admitted and produced further revisions. Neither the Secretary nor the examiner consulted the underlying responses. The determination set prevailing hourly wages of $1.45 and $1.70 for the two branches, increased by three cents for intervening wage changes.
sections.Issue: Whether a wage determination required to be made on the record under the APA could rest on survey tables when the challengers were denied access to the underlying confidential responses needed to test them; which manufacturers had standing to sue; and whether relief should reach the entire industry determination.
sections.Holding: The D.C. Circuit, in a 1963 opinion by Judge Washington for a panel with Chief Judge Bazelon and Judge Wright and a 1964 per curiam supplement, with no dissent or separate concurrence, held that the tables could be admitted but that the denial of access to underlying material defeated the statutory rebuttal and cross-examination safeguards, and that the impeached tables standing alone failed the substantial-evidence requirement. Manufacturers actually paying covered workers less than the prescribed minimum had standing, and if at least one plaintiff had standing the entire industry determination should be enjoined. The court declined to compel production of the confidential files and struck down the determination.
sections.Reasoning:
Because Congress expressly required on-the-record rulemaking, the then-numbered APA § 7(c) applied: the proponent bore the burden, the evidence had to be reliable, probative and substantial, and parties were entitled to rebuttal and the cross-examination needed for full and true disclosure. The court applied those statutory requirements rather than declaring that all informal rulemaking must use trial procedures.

Statistical summaries were admissible, but only subject to adequate opportunity to test their authenticity, accuracy and meaning. Access had been denied even under NEMA's offered confidentiality arrangement. The Secretary's concern about future voluntary surveys could be substantial but did not authorize disregarding the hearing safeguards. The government could withhold the information and risk failing to prove its position, or disclose it and permit testing.

The evidence was also seriously impeached: eight accepted corrections reduced the estimated rates by three and four cents, and the covered-worker definition may have been widely misunderstood, with no adequate corroboration offered. The court reserved what might follow without impeachment or with different disclosure, and did not decide whether disclosure would violate the Federal Reports Act.

On standing, the Fulbright Amendment displaced Perkins v. Lukens Steel's denial of litigable rights but still required injury; firms paying at or above the minimum showed none. Industrywide relief was needed because relief confined to the suing firms would give them an inequitable competitive advantage in government bidding and undermine the uniform wage rule.

In 1964 the court rejected the Secretary's proposals because 1964 wage information could not prove what wages prevailed in 1960 and the proposed disclosure still allowed no meaningful testing. The Secretary could begin a lawful new determination.

The casebook's description of the Department's later implementation difficulties is editorial history.

LRS-ATLAS-O-WYMAN-GORDON.rule: A specific agency order directed to a party in an adjudication is enforceable even though it rests on a general prospective requirement announced in an earlier adjudication without APA rulemaking, though no majority agreed on whether that earlier requirement was validly adopted.

sections.Parties: The National Labor Relations Board sought judicial enforcement of its subpoena, or a mandatory injunction, requiring Wyman-Gordon Co. to supply the names and addresses of employees eligible to vote in a representation election. Wyman-Gordon, the employer, refused, arguing that the requirement rested on an invalidly adopted rule, was invalid on its merits, and sought material that was not evidence subject to subpoena. The Board prevailed in the district court, lost in the First Circuit, and prevailed in the Supreme Court.
sections.Procedural History: The Board directed an election, ordered the employer to provide the list, and, after the unions lost and Wyman-Gordon refused the list for a second election, subpoenaed it. The Board sought enforcement in the District of Massachusetts, which ordered compliance in 1967. The First Circuit reversed in 1968, reasoning that the order rested on an invalidly adopted general rule; it did not reach the subpoena objection. The Supreme Court granted review amid a circuit conflict and, on April 23, 1969, reversed the First Circuit and remanded to the district court with directions to reinstate its judgment compelling disclosure. This brief covers only the 1969 Supreme Court stage.
sections.Material Facts:
In Excelsior Underwear Inc. (1966), the Board considered losing unions' objections to elections at two companies that had refused to provide voter lists. It invited selected employer organizations and trade unions to brief and argue the general disclosure issue. It announced that employers would file eligible employees' names and addresses with the regional director within seven days after approval of an election agreement or direction of an election, and that failure to comply could justify setting aside an election. The Board declined to apply the requirement to the original parties; it applied only to elections directed or consented to more than thirty days after the decision. The requirement was not published in the Federal Register.

Later, on a Boilermakers petition, the Board directed an election among Wyman-Gordon's production and maintenance employees, who could choose either of two unions or no union, and ordered the employer to provide the names and addresses of eligible voters. Wyman-Gordon refused. Both unions lost; the Board sustained their objections based on the missing list and ordered a new election. Wyman-Gordon again refused, and the Board subpoenaed the list or the personnel and payroll records containing the information.
sections.Issue: Whether the Board's order requiring Wyman-Gordon to furnish a list of employee names and addresses was enforceable when it relied on the Excelsior requirement, which had been announced prospectively in an adjudication without APA rulemaking; and whether the disclosure requirement was valid on its merits and the list was evidence subject to subpoena under NLRA § 11.
sections.Holding: The Court, in 1969, reversed the First Circuit and directed reinstatement of the district court's enforcement judgment, with no majority rationale on Excelsior. Justice Fortas's plurality, joined by Chief Justice Warren and Justices Stewart and White, regarded Excelsior's general prospective command as improperly adopted without APA rulemaking but sustained the specific order addressed to Wyman-Gordon as a valid adjudicatory order. Justice Black, joined by Justices Brennan and Marshall, concurred in the result, considering Excelsior a valid adjudication. Seven Justices agreed that the disclosure requirement was valid on its merits and that the list was subpoenable. Justices Douglas and Harlan dissented separately and would have affirmed.
sections.Reasoning:
The plurality reasoned that NLRA § 6 authorized rules in the manner the APA prescribes, and the APA defines a rule as an agency statement of general or particular applicability and future effect. Briefing by selected amici did not substitute for Federal Register notice to all interested persons, and the disclosure requirement was substantive. Excelsior had not imposed the duty on its own parties but purported to create a general future command; adjudications can announce policies and serve as precedents, but that does not make those policies legislative rules binding the public. Wyman-Gordon, however, received its own express direction in the order for this election, which was a valid adjudicatory order despite its citation to Excelsior. A Chenery remand would be a useless formality because the result on remand was certain.

On the merits, the Board's broad authority to ensure fair and free elections supported disclosure, which promotes an informed electorate; and "evidence" under § 11 includes records assisting the Board's investigation. Black expressly agreed with these parts.

Justice Black thought no adoption violation occurred: Excelsior genuinely adjudicated a controversy, prospectivity did not erase its adjudicatory character, and the choice between rulemaking and adjudication lay primarily within the agency's informed discretion, as Chenery II explained. He objected to enforcing a requirement the plurality itself considered illegally adopted.

Justice Douglas thought the Board had chosen a general policy for all future elections and was bound to follow rulemaking procedures. Justice Harlan agreed and added that under Chenery I a court could not substitute its confidence that the agency would reach the same result once its stated ground was rejected.

The four-Justice plurality and the two dissenters shared the criticism of Excelsior's adoption but disagreed on its consequences.

LRS-ATLAS-O-YOUNGSTOWN.rule: Presidential authority to act must come from Congress or the Constitution, and neither the Commander in Chief power nor the Take Care duty authorizes the President to seize private businesses to avert a strike without statutory authorization.

sections.Parties: The steel companies sued Secretary of Commerce Charles Sawyer, who had taken possession of most steel mills under President Truman's Executive Order 10340. The companies sought declarations that the orders were invalid and preliminary and permanent injunctions, characterizing the seizure as lawmaking entrusted to Congress. The Government asserted inherent presidential authority, historical practice, and the combined executive, Take Care and Commander in Chief powers, and argued that a preliminary injunction was improper because the companies could obtain compensation.
sections.Procedural History: The District Court rejected the Government's arguments and issued a preliminary injunction on April 30, 1952. The D.C. Circuit stayed it the same day. The Supreme Court granted certiorari on May 3, on the companies' petition and Sawyer's cross-petition, and heard argument May 12 and 13. On June 2, 1952, the Court held the constitutional issue ripe at this preliminary stage, held the seizure unauthorized, and affirmed the District Court's judgment, sustaining the preliminary injunction.
sections.Material Facts:
During the Korean conflict, the steel companies and the United Steelworkers were negotiating new collective bargaining agreements; the existing ones expired December 31, 1951. The union announced a strike, federal mediation failed, and President Truman referred the dispute to the Wage Stabilization Board on December 22. The Board recommended a settlement, but the parties did not settle. The union then announced an industry-wide strike beginning at 12:01 a.m. on April 9, 1952.

Truman regarded uninterrupted steel production as indispensable to weapons, other defense materials and national security. On April 8 he issued Executive Order 10340, directing Secretary Sawyer to take possession of most steel mills and operate them. The order rested on the President's constitutional and statutory powers in the aggregate rather than a particular seizure statute. Sawyer ordered the companies' presidents to act as operating managers for the United States, and they complied under protest. Truman reported the seizure to Congress on April 9 and April 21; Congress had not acted on those reports when the Court decided the case. Existing statutes prescribed ways to address defense procurement and labor emergencies, and Congress had rejected a general plant-seizure proposal when adopting Taft-Hartley.
sections.Issue: Whether the President had authority, under any statute or under the Constitution's executive, Take Care and Commander in Chief provisions, to order the Secretary of Commerce to seize and operate the steel mills to avert a strike, and whether the question could be decided on a preliminary injunction.
sections.Holding: The Court, in 1952, in an opinion by Justice Black, decided six to three, held that the seizure was unauthorized and affirmed the District Court's preliminary injunction. Justices Frankfurter, Douglas, Jackson and Burton joined the opinion while writing separately; Justice Clark concurred in the judgment alone; Chief Justice Vinson dissented, joined by Justices Reed and Minton. No statute expressly or impliedly authorized the seizure, and the Constitution did not give the President this power. The decision establishes the invalidity of this seizure; it does not decide every future emergency seizure or treat each separate Justice's reasoning as a holding.
sections.Reasoning:
Black first held that equity did not require postponing the question: it was doubtful the Court of Claims could compensate an unlawful taking, and seizure of ongoing businesses would cause injuries difficult to measure. Presidential authority had to come from Congress or the Constitution. The Selective Service Act and Defense Production Act permitted acquisition only under conditions admittedly unmet, and Congress had rejected seizure authority in Taft-Hartley. The Commander in Chief power did not reach domestic seizure of private property in a labor dispute, and the Take Care duty presupposed laws to execute; the order made policy rather than executing Congress's.

Frankfurter found an affirmative congressional choice against general seizure authority. A systematic, unbroken practice known to Congress could gloss executive power, but the comparable seizures were too isolated. Douglas reasoned that a seizure was a taking requiring compensation, which only Congress could authorize. Jackson described three situations: presidential power is strongest with congressional authorization, uncertain where Congress has neither granted nor denied authority, and at its lowest against Congress's expressed or implied will; this seizure fell in the third. Burton said Congress had prescribed mechanisms for this emergency and reserved seizure to itself. Clark accepted extensive independent presidential authority in grave emergencies but concluded that Congress's specified procedures controlled.

Vinson's dissent characterized the seizure as temporary execution of Congress's defense procurement and anti-inflation programs pending legislative action, supported by history, and read Taft-Hartley as not exclusive.

The assigned casebook passage is an editorial account; the brief notes that it groups Burton with Clark as receptive to independent emergency authority, though Burton only reserved catastrophic situations.

LRS-ATLAS-S-AMALGAMATED.rule: A broad delegation is constitutional when Congress determines the basic policy and the statute's text, purpose, history, duration and implied constraints supply standards by which Congress, courts and the public can assess compliance; breadth alone does not make it invalid.

sections.Parties: The Amalgamated Meat Cutters union and its affiliated locals sued Treasury Secretary Connally and other Cost of Living Council officials for a declaration that the Economic Stabilization Act of 1970 and Executive Order 11615 were invalid and for an injunction against administering the stabilization program. A second count sought enforcement of the meat-packer employers' obligation to pay a scheduled wage increase. The government defended the statute and order; the employers contended that paying the increase would violate the order.
sections.Procedural History: The Union filed a two-count complaint. Count I sought a declaration of invalidity and an injunction against Council officials; Count II sought enforcement of the employers' wage obligations. A three-judge district court was convened on October 3, 1971 under the then-applicable statutes and heard argument on the preliminary-injunction motion on October 8. Because the parties' presentation contemplated no further evidentiary stage, the court treated the legal issues as calling for a determinative ruling. On October 22, 1971, it rejected the facial constitutional and statutory challenges and denied the Union's motion for injunctive relief. The reported order does not award unpaid wages or damages or separately announce dismissal of every claim.
sections.Material Facts:
In April 1970 the Union and its locals negotiated collective bargaining agreements with major meat packers. A general wage increase of twenty-five cents an hour was scheduled for September 6, 1971; the Union alleged this concession was decisive to accepting the agreements.

The Economic Stabilization Act of 1970, as amended, authorized the President in section 202 to stabilize prices, rents, wages and salaries at levels no lower than those prevailing on May 25, 1970, and permitted adjustments to prevent gross inequities. A 1971 amendment restricted controls aimed at a particular industry unless the President determined its prices or wages had increased disproportionately. Section 203 permitted delegation, sections 204 and 205 provided fines and injunctions, and the authority expired on April 30, 1972.

On August 15, 1971, President Nixon issued Executive Order 11615, imposing a ninety-day freeze on prices, rents, wages and salaries, generally at the highest rates applicable to a substantial volume of transactions during the thirty days ending August 14. The order created the Cost of Living Council, chaired by Secretary Connally, and delegated the President's statutory powers to it. The freeze intervened before the scheduled increase took effect. More than 150,000 employees were allegedly affected across numerous industries.
sections.Issue: Whether the Economic Stabilization Act of 1970 unconstitutionally delegated legislative power by giving the President discretion over whether, when and how broadly to stabilize prices and wages without adequate standards, and whether the freeze could lawfully reach wage increases promised in existing contracts and fringe benefits.
sections.Holding: A three-judge District Court for the District of Columbia, in 1971, in an opinion by Circuit Judge Leventhal for a panel with District Judges Robinson and Richey and no separate writing, held that Congress could delegate this stabilization authority because the Act's text, purpose, historical setting, duration, and implied procedural and substantive constraints supplied an ascertainable legislative policy. The court construed the Act to require broad fairness and avoidance of gross inequity for controls following the initial freeze, ongoing administrative standards, and meaningful review under the APA, and sustained the delegation on that construction rather than accepting unlimited presidential discretion. It rejected the contract and fringe-benefit objections and denied injunctive relief.
sections.Reasoning:
The court first held it had equity jurisdiction: individual wage suits would multiply litigation, and later recovery was not the same as receiving scheduled increases on time.

On delegation, the question was accountability to legislative will, not breadth. Under Yakus and Hampton, Congress had to determine the basic policy and identify the field of action so that Congress, courts and the public could assess compliance, and standards could draw meaning from purpose, history and administrative experience. The statutory floor and the limits on sector-specific controls confined presidential choice; earlier wartime stabilization programs supplied a recognizable context; and the House committee report contemplated a short general freeze. Congress had reasons to leave timing to the President, since advance proceedings might encourage anticipatory increases. Limited duration mattered because expiration forced Congress to revisit the delegation, but the court rejected the government's suggestion that a sunset and open courthouse doors sufficed if judges lacked standards to apply.

The court therefore read section 202 and the Act's purpose to imply a duty of broad fairness and avoidance of gross inequity. A general freeze's arbitrariness could be tolerated for a short opening period, but follow-on controls required more refined standards, and subsidiary administrative policies, once developed, would limit executive latitude. APA sections 701 through 706 permitted review, including pre-enforcement review when requirements were met; the Council was subject to the APA, and the court did not decide whether the President could be sued by name.

Schechter was distinguished as involving comprehensive industrial codes and delegation to private groups, and Youngstown as a seizure without statutory authorization. The Contracts Clause applies to states; the order operated prospectively; and wages and salaries covered fringe benefits.

The casebook's discussion of later amendments and practical limits on review is editorial.

LRS-ATLAS-S-BOWSHER.rule: Congress may not reserve to itself the power to remove, other than by impeachment, an officer charged with executing the laws, because removal power gives it practical control over execution.

sections.Parties: Congressman Synar, joined by eleven other Members of Congress, and the National Treasury Employees Union, with an individual union member later added, challenged the automatic deficit-reduction mechanism of the Balanced Budget and Emergency Deficit Control Act of 1985.
