Civil penalties can redress ongoing or threatened injury by deterring future violations even though the money is paid to the government. A defendant's voluntary cessation does not moot a case unless it is absolutely clear the challenged conduct cannot reasonably be expected to recur, and the defendant bears that formidable burden. Laidlaw's compliance did not automatically moot the controversy, and the effect of the closure required factual consideration on remand.
sections.Reasoning:
Members described specific uses of the North Tyger River and specific ways their reasonable concerns about concededly ongoing illegal discharges curtailed those uses. That differed materially from the indefinite 'some day' intentions in Lujan. Requiring proof of actual environmental degradation would make standing harder to establish than some merits violations of the Clean Water Act.

Standing must be shown separately for each form of relief. A substantial penalty makes future noncompliance less attractive and so reduces the threat that caused members to avoid the river; the remedy need not transfer money to the plaintiff. Steel Co. did not control because it involved wholly past violations, whereas these were ongoing when the complaint was filed. The Court acknowledged that deterrence can become too insubstantial or remote and declined to define those limits.

Standing is measured when the complaint is filed; mootness asks whether later events eliminated the live controversy. If stopping the challenged conduct automatically mooted a case, a defendant could stop during litigation and resume after dismissal. The record did not permit the Court to decide whether recurrence was impossible, especially because Laidlaw retained its permit. The Court also reserved whether the catalyst theory remained available for fees.

Justice Stevens, concurring alone, would treat the penalty claim as surviving post-filing compliance. Justice Kennedy, concurring alone, reserved Article II questions about private suits for public penalties. Justice Scalia's dissent disputed injury, given the finding of no environmental harm, and rejected general deterrence from Treasury penalties as redress. The brief notes that one page of the casebook's editorial note on mootness was missing, so that note could not be fully checked.

LRS-CB-1250.rule: Under the APA zone-of-interests test, a plaintiff need not show that Congress specifically intended to benefit it; the plaintiff's affected interest need only be arguably among the interests protected or regulated by the statutory provision at issue.

sections.Parties: The National Credit Union Administration (NCUA) and AT&T Family Federal Credit Union were petitioners in the consolidated matters; the Credit Union National Association intervened on the agency's side in the District Court and was also a petitioner. Five commercial banks and the American Bankers Association, the plaintiffs, were respondents. The banks challenged NCUA charter amendments under APA section 702, arguing that section 109 of the Federal Credit Union Act required a single common occupational bond across a credit union's membership.
sections.Procedural History: The District Court initially dismissed for lack of prudential standing, reasoning that Congress had not enacted section 109 to protect banks. The D.C. Circuit reversed, relying on financial-industry competitor-standing cases. On remand the District Court found the statutory language ambiguous at Chevron step one; it did not proceed to step two because the banks had not seriously argued that the agency's construction was unreasonable. The D.C. Circuit again reversed, holding at Chevron step one that Congress unambiguously required a single common bond. The Supreme Court granted review and affirmed.
sections.Material Facts:
Section 109 of the Federal Credit Union Act limited federal credit-union membership to groups having a common bond of occupation or association, or to groups within a defined geographic community. Before 1982, the agency required one occupational common bond across an occupational credit union. In 1982 it changed course, allowing multiple unrelated employer groups, each with its own occupational bond, to join the same federal credit union.

AT&T Family Federal Credit Union then expanded dramatically. Only about 35% of its roughly 110,000 members were AT&T employees or affiliates, while other members worked for unrelated companies.

The banks alleged competitive injury because the expanded credit union could serve people who otherwise might become bank customers. The Article III competitive injury was not disputed; the question was the additional statutory relationship required under APA section 702. Petitioners argued that Congress enacted the Act to promote credit unions, not to shield banks.
sections.Issue: Were commercial-bank competitors within the APA zone of interests protected or regulated by section 109 even if Congress did not specifically intend to benefit banks? On the merits, did section 109 unambiguously require one common occupational bond across all members, making NCUA's multiple-group interpretation unlawful under then-governing Chevron step one?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States, 1998, Justice Thomas writing for a five-Justice majority except as to footnote 6, which Justice Scalia did not join; Justice O'Connor dissented, joined by Stevens, Souter, and Breyer. The banks satisfied the zone-of-interests test: a plaintiff need not show that Congress specifically intended to benefit it, only that its affected interest is arguably among those protected or regulated by the provision. On the merits, section 109 is unambiguous: the same common bond of occupation must unite the members of an occupationally defined federal credit union, so NCUA's interpretation failed at Chevron step one.
sections.Reasoning:
Justice Thomas relied on Data Processing, Arnold Tours, Investment Company Institute, and Clarke, which allowed competitors of regulated financial institutions to challenge agency relaxation of statutory limits. The question was whether the competitors' interest bore the required relationship to interests protected or regulated by the statute, not whether legislative history showed a purpose to protect them.

Federal credit unions generally serve members, so limiting membership limits the potential customer market. NCUA's interpretation enlarged that customer base and affected the banks' competitive interest, which was at least arguably within section 109's zone. Commercial motives did not disqualify the banks. The majority distinguished Air Courier because the postal statutes there protected public service and postal revenue, not employees' job opportunities; competitive injury alone is not the complete test, and not every plaintiff with an interest in enforcement automatically qualifies.

On the merits, reading 'groups having a common bond of occupation' to require only the bond inherent in each unrelated employer group would make 'common bond' largely surplusage. The parallel geographic clause supported a unitary limit, and permitting unlimited employer groups would drain 'shall be limited' of practical force.

Justice O'Connor's dissent accepted the banks' Article III injury but argued the majority effectively equated injury from statutory noncompliance with a protected interest. She read the earlier cases as involving anti-competition restrictions, whereas section 109 governed each credit union's internal cooperative membership, and she would have vacated and remanded with instructions to dismiss.

The brief reports the case historically and does not treat Chevron as current doctrine.

LRS-CLOSURE-001.rule: Placing congressional agents on an executive agency as nonvoting members violates separation of powers (D.C. Circuit), and the Solicitor General's authorization after the filing deadline cannot ratify a certiorari petition an agency lacked statutory authority to file (Supreme Court).

sections.Parties: The Federal Election Commission (FEC) sued the National Rifle Association Institute for Legislative Action for making a prohibited corporate contribution, the NRA Political Victory Fund for accepting it, and the Fund's treasurer, Grant Wills, for facilitating it. The FEC sought enforcement of the Federal Election Campaign Act (FECA); the defendants raised statutory, First Amendment, and separation-of-powers objections and renewed them on appeal to the D.C. Circuit. The FEC then petitioned the Court for certiorari in its own name.
sections.Procedural History: After unsuccessful statutory negotiations the FEC sued, and both sides sought summary judgment. The district court held that the October transfer violated the statute, deemed the structural objections nonjusticiable, rejected the First Amendment defense, imposed a civil penalty measured by investigation and litigation costs, and enjoined similar transfers. On October 22, 1993 the D.C. Circuit reversed the enforcement judgment on the separation-of-powers ground, without deciding whether the contribution was prohibited or constitutionally protected. The FEC filed a certiorari petition on January 18, 1994. The Court granted review but on December 6, 1994 dismissed the petition for want of jurisdiction, leaving the D.C. Circuit's judgment in place without passing on its constitutional merits.
sections.Material Facts:
In March and July 1988 the NRA Political Victory Fund sent fundraising letters to NRA members. The mailings cost $415,744.72, paid by the Institute for Legislative Action. The Fund reimbursed that amount on August 1 but then faced a shortfall, and on October 20 the Institute returned the reimbursement to the Fund. The Fund's resources, including those funds, financed independent expenditures and direct campaign contributions before the November elections. The FEC accepted the first two transactions as lawful and treated the third transfer as a prohibited corporate contribution.

After Buckley v. Valeo, Congress provided for six voting FEC members appointed by the President with Senate consent, no more than three from one party; the Secretary of the Senate and the Clerk of the House, or their designees, remained nonvoting ex officio members.

The FEC filed its certiorari petition two days before the ninety-day period expired, without seeking or obtaining the Solicitor General's approval. After the Court asked for the United States' views, the Solicitor General authorized the petition by a May 26 letter, more than 120 days after the January 20 deadline.
sections.Issue: In the D.C. Circuit, whether the FEC's composition, including nonvoting congressional agents, violated separation of powers so as to defeat this enforcement action. In the Court, whether the FEC had statutory authority to petition for certiorari on its own, and if not, whether the Solicitor General's late authorization could ratify the filing.
sections.Holding:
The D.C. Circuit in 1993, in an opinion by Judge Silberman with no dissent, held that the FEC's composition violated separation of powers because congressional agents served as nonvoting members, and it reversed the district court's enforcement judgment. It found the partisan-limit challenge nonjusticiable and rejected the objection to independent enforcement. Judge Wald participated; Judge Ruth Bader Ginsburg did not participate in the decision.

The Court in 1994, in an opinion by Chief Justice Rehnquist (7-1, Justice Stevens dissenting, Justice Ginsburg not participating), held that the FEC lacked statutory authority to petition for certiorari independently and that the Solicitor General's late approval could not relate back. It dismissed for want of jurisdiction and did not affirm the constitutional reasoning on its merits.
sections.Reasoning:
The D.C. Circuit held that defendants facing civil sanctions could raise the independence and congressional-agent challenges without proving that a differently constituted Commission would have treated them better. It rejected the independent-enforcement objection under Morrison v. Olson and Humphrey's Executor, assuming that good-cause removal was available at minimum. Congressional membership was the decisive defect. Although the nonvoting officials could not chair, convene or adjourn meetings, or count toward a quorum, their membership could influence deliberations, and even silent congressional agents could convey a tacit message, much as nonvoting alternate jurors could improperly affect deliberations. Applying the anti-encroachment reasoning of Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority and Bowsher, the court held that placing congressional agents on an executive entity crossed the legislative boundary. FECA's severability clause allowed removing the ex officio provision, and the court rejected the de facto officer argument for leaving these defendants' sanctions intact.

In the Court, the majority reasoned that under 28 U.S.C. § 518(a) the Solicitor General ordinarily controls Supreme Court litigation involving the United States unless Congress supplies an exemption. The FEC's general power to initiate, defend, or "appeal" civil enforcement actions did not expressly authorize certiorari, whereas the presidential public-funding statutes expressly authorized both appeals and certiorari petitions; the majority treated the contrast as intentional. Under agency-law principles, ratification requires that the principal be able to perform the act both when done and when ratified, and by May 26 the Solicitor General could no longer file a timely petition; relation back would let him extend the mandatory ninety-day period.

Justice Stevens, dissenting, read "appeal" in its broader sense to include discretionary appellate review. The casebook cites the case in an editorial note following Buckley for the congressional-membership ruling and separately notes the Court's jurisdictional dismissal.

LRS-CLOSURE-002.rule: Congress may not hand the President the legislative choice whether to prohibit conduct without declaring a policy, setting a standard, or specifying the circumstances and findings on which he is to act.

sections.Parties: Panama Refining Co., owner of a Texas refining plant, and its coplaintiff, a holder of Texas oil and gas leases, and separately Amazon Petroleum Corp. and other Texas producers, brought civil suits to restrain federal officials from enforcing the petroleum transportation provision of the National Industrial Recovery Act and the orders and regulations under it. The plaintiffs challenged the delegation under nondelegation and commerce principles and attacked enforcement practices under the Fourth and Fifth Amendments; the Amazon plaintiffs also challenged state production limits and the federal Petroleum Code's quota restrictions.
sections.Procedural History: In Amazon, a three-judge district court considered the challenge to the state orders; by agreement the claims against federal officials were severed for decision by the district judge. The three-judge court upheld the state orders and dismissed that branch. The district judge permanently enjoined federal enforcement in both cases and specifically enjoined the Code quota provision in Amazon, unaware that it no longer existed. The Fifth Circuit reversed the federal decrees and ordered dismissal. The Court reviewed those federal judgments, not the distinct state-law branch. It reversed and remanded to the district court to modify its decrees and permanently enjoin enforcement of the July 11 and July 14, 1933 executive orders and the implementing Interior Department regulations.
sections.Material Facts:
Section 9(c) of the National Industrial Recovery Act authorized the President to prohibit interstate and foreign transportation of petroleum and petroleum products produced or withdrawn from storage in excess of amounts permitted by state law or valid state regulations. Violating a presidential order could bring a fine up to $1,000, imprisonment up to six months, or both. The statute did not itself impose the prohibition.

The President imposed the prohibition on July 11, 1933, in an order that stated no findings or grounds. Three days later, invoking § 10(a), he authorized the Interior Secretary to exercise enforcement powers and promulgate regulations. Interior's Regulations IV and V required sworn monthly information from producers, purchasers, shippers, refiners, and processors, and Regulation VII required accessible transaction records.

A separate Petroleum Code approved in August treated excess quota production as an unfair trade practice, but that provision was eliminated on September 13, 1933, before these October suits, and restored in September 1934. The litigants and lower courts initially proceeded unaware that it had been withdrawn.
sections.Issue: Whether § 9(c) of the National Industrial Recovery Act unconstitutionally delegated legislative power to the President by authorizing him to prohibit transportation of petroleum exceeding state allowances without a governing policy or standard, and whether the executive orders and regulations issued under it could be enforced.
sections.Holding: The Court in 1935, in an opinion by Chief Justice Hughes with only Justice Cardozo dissenting (8-1), held the § 9(c) delegation unconstitutional and invalidated the July 11 and July 14, 1933 executive orders and the Interior Department regulations implementing it. The majority assumed, without deciding, that Congress itself could prohibit the transportation; the question was who made that policy choice. The Court declined to decide the removed Petroleum Code quota provision, expressly reserving the Code's interpretation and validity, and it did not invalidate every part of the Recovery Act.
sections.Reasoning:
Section 9(c) neither directed prohibition nor specified when, under what circumstances, or on what findings the President should act. State production limits defined the oil eligible for prohibition but supplied no federal criterion for deciding whether to prohibit its transportation, and disobedience was a crime. Looking beyond § 9(c), the Court found that other § 9 provisions did not constrain the transportation power and that § 1's declaration of policy listed wide-ranging objectives that supplied no governing policy for excess-oil transportation. Treating a general menu of objectives as a sufficient criterion would leave the President choosing legislative policy rather than executing it.

Hughes acknowledged that Congress may set policies and primary standards, authorize subordinate rules within limits, and make legislation operative upon specified contingencies, but it may not abdicate the essential legislative choice. The Court distinguished precedents such as the Brig Aurora, Field v. Clark, and Hampton, which involved ascertainment of contingencies implementing legislative will or tariff adjustments under an intelligible principle. As an additional defect, the July 11 order stated no findings; for delegated legislative orders carrying criminal punishment, the order must appear within the delegated authority and the factual determinations conditioning that authority must be shown. The opinion distinguished actions properly belonging to the executive sphere, so this is not a rule that every presidential action requires formal findings.

Justice Cardozo, dissenting, read the statute as a whole: the President could act only on one commodity, unlawfully produced or withdrawn under state quotas, through the specified prohibition, and § 1 implicitly required action advancing Congress's declared recovery policies. He saw no constitutional demand for recited findings and would have affirmed. The casebook presents the case through a scholarly excerpt, Cary Coglianese's Dimensions of Delegation, which treats Panama Refining as a difficulty for a theory emphasizing the dimensions of delegated power and criticizes its reconciliation with other cases; that assessment is the scholar's, not the Court's.

LRS-CLOSURE-003.rule: As the Third Circuit held in 2013, the Recess Appointments Clause permits appointments only during breaks between Senate sessions, so an intrasession recess appointee does not count toward the three members an NLRB group needs to act.

sections.Parties: The National Labor Relations Board applied for enforcement of its order against New Vista Nursing and Rehabilitation, which operated a nursing and rehabilitation center in Newark and had refused to bargain with a healthcare workers' union that won an election to represent its licensed practical nurses. New Vista sought review, maintaining that the nurses were supervisors excluded from the NLRA's protected employee category and objecting to the makeup of the Board groups that acted in its case.
sections.Procedural History: A union petitioned in January 2011 to represent the nurses. The regional director rejected New Vista's supervisor argument, the Board upheld the representation determination, and the union won the election. New Vista refused to bargain, prompting an unfair-labor-practice charge and a motion for summary judgment; this refusal was the ordinary route to judicial review of a representation determination. The Board's unanimous decision and order was dated August 26, 2011. New Vista sought reconsideration in September while the Board applied for enforcement; the Board denied reconsideration on December 30 and denied further motions on March 15 and March 27, New Vista sought review in January 2012, and an April petition joined the earlier review and enforcement proceedings. On May 16, 2013 a divided Third Circuit panel vacated the Board's original and reconsideration orders.
sections.Material Facts: The NLRA allowed the five-member Board to delegate its powers to a group of three or more members, and New Process Steel required that group to maintain three members. The group that decided New Vista's case comprised Chairman Wilma Liebman and Members Becker and Hayes. Liebman left the Board the day after the August 26, 2011 order, and New Vista argued that the later mailing meant the order actually issued after her departure. Craig Becker had been appointed on March 27, 2010 during a seventeen-day Senate break beginning March 26 and ending April 12, an intrasession adjournment during which the Senate indisputably was not conducting business. The parties' initial recess arguments concerned later Board members appointed in January 2012, when the Senate was holding pro forma meetings; the court examined the original group's membership sua sponte.
sections.Issue: Whether the three-member Board group that decided New Vista's case had the lawful membership required to act, which turned on whether the Recess Appointments Clause permits an appointment made during an intrasession break of the Senate.
sections.Holding: The Third Circuit in 2013, in an opinion by Judge Smith joined by Judge Van Antwerpen with Judge Greenaway dissenting, held that the Recess Appointments Clause permitted appointments only during breaks between Senate sessions. Because Becker was appointed during an intrasession break, his appointment was invalid, the original group lacked three lawful members, and the court vacated the Board's orders. It did not decide the nurses' supervisory status, the meaning of vacancies that "happen," or the validity of the later groups' appointments.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority treated the three-member composition requirement, as distinct from a quorum, as a jurisdictional limit on the Board's adjudicatory authority that could be raised at any stage. To avoid an unnecessary constitutional decision it first rejected the argument about Liebman's departure: the order's face and docket showed August 26, and service by mail was ministerial. It also rejected an amicus's political-question objection.

The majority considered three definitions of recess: intersession breaks only; intersession breaks plus sufficiently long intrasession breaks; and any period when the Senate was unavailable to conduct business. It acknowledged that dictionary usage, parliamentary practice, state constitutions, and early executive actions were ambiguous. A bare unavailability test was broad enough to permit appointments during lunch, evenings, or weekends, and the majority found no constitutional basis for choosing a ten-day or three-day minimum. Its decisive inference came from the commission's expiration at the end of the Senate's "next Session": an intersession appointment lasts through one ensuing session, while an intrasession appointment could survive the rest of the current session plus the next, changing an auxiliary power into an additional route after an opportunity for the ordinary process had passed. It viewed modern intrasession practice as comparatively recent and disputed, and acknowledged that its rule left room for manipulation of timing.

Judge Greenaway, dissenting, would include both intersession and intrasession recesses because the Senate could be unavailable to consent in either, relied on longstanding intrasession practice, and rejected the majority's jurisdictional characterization. The casebook recounts Becker's appointment and the divided Third Circuit result alongside other circuits' cases and the Court's later Noel Canning decision, which the casebook describes as permitting intrasession appointments.

LRS-CLOSURE-005.rule: On a preliminary-injunction motion, the court concluded that Dodd-Frank's deputy-succession provision does not displace the Federal Vacancies Reform Act, which remains an available, nonexclusive means for the President to designate an acting CFPB Director.

sections.Parties: Leandra English, appointed Deputy Director of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) by outgoing Director Richard Cordray, sued President Trump and Mick Mulvaney, the Senate-confirmed Director of the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) whom the President designated to perform the CFPB Director's functions. English sought declaratory and injunctive relief restraining the President from appointing anyone other than her, requiring withdrawal of Mulvaney's designation, and prohibiting his acting service. Defendants maintained that the two statutes provided compatible alternatives and that neither prohibited Mulvaney's selection.
sections.Procedural History: English sued on November 26, 2017. After hearings on November 27 and 28, Judge Timothy Kelly denied a temporary restraining order. She amended her complaint and moved for a preliminary injunction on December 6; the court heard the motion on December 22 and decided it on January 10, 2018. This reported decision denies the preliminary injunction; it is not the earlier TRO ruling or a final dismissal of every claim. The casebook's account also reports a later appeal dismissal on July 13, 2018.
sections.Material Facts: Cordray resigned as CFPB Director effective at midnight on November 24, 2017, before completing his statutory five-year term. Earlier that day he appointed his chief of staff, English, Deputy Director effective at noon, publicly explaining that the appointment would provide an orderly succession. Dodd-Frank provided that the Deputy Director should serve as acting Director during the Director's absence or unavailability. President Trump instead designated Mulvaney under the Federal Vacancies Reform Act (FVRA), by a memorandum effective at 12:01 a.m. on November 26. The Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel and the CFPB's General Counsel concluded that the FVRA remained available, and senior CFPB management agreed to recognize Mulvaney. On November 27 he began working at the Bureau and issuing directives that staff followed, while continuing to serve at OMB. English continued working as Deputy Director and held herself out as acting Director in emails and meetings. Mulvaney asked her to stop and publicly stated that he was not considering terminating her.
sections.Issue: Whether English was entitled to a preliminary injunction, which turned on whether Dodd-Frank's provision making the Deputy Director acting Director displaced the President's FVRA authority to designate an acting CFPB Director, whether a still-serving OMB Director could be designated, and whether English showed irreparable injury.
sections.Holding: The U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia in 2018, per Judge Timothy Kelly sitting alone, denied the preliminary injunction. It concluded that English was unlikely to succeed because the FVRA remained an available, nonexclusive means of filling the vacancy and Dodd-Frank did not expressly exclude it, and because Mulvaney's Senate-confirmed OMB position qualified him under § 3345(a)(2). It also found that she had not shown irreparable injury and that the equities and public interest favored denial. Lack of likely success and lack of irreparable injury each independently supported denial. The court did not decide whether English's theory would violate the Constitution, and it reserved defendants' de facto officer and quo warranto objection.
sections.Reasoning:
The FVRA covered the vacancy on its own terms: the CFPB was an executive agency, its Director a Senate-confirmed officer, and Cordray had resigned. The exception for appointed members of multimember bodies did not apply merely because the CFPB Director sat ex officio on the FDIC board. Section 3347, which removes FVRA exclusivity where another statute supplies an acting-officer mechanism, made the FVRA nonexclusive, not unavailable; Hooks supplied an analogy. Dodd-Frank's own § 5491(a) applied federal laws dealing with federal officers to the CFPB unless otherwise expressly provided by law, and no provision expressly prohibited use of the FVRA. The court questioned, without deciding, whether absence or unavailability covers a permanent resignation.

Nor did "shall" end the inquiry: read in context, the deputy's service was a default qualified by the President's FVRA choice, and harmonious reading and the presumption against implied repeal favored giving both statutes effect. That reading did not make the deputy provision superfluous. Constitutional avoidance supplied additional confirmation, because English's theory could let an outgoing, removal-protected Director choose a successor insulated from presidential control, creating serious Take Care Clause concerns. Agency independence did not override the enacted mechanisms, and legislative history added little. Dodd-Frank barred the Director from holding positions in specified financial institutions and regulated entities but did not include OMB.

On irreparable injury, English remained employed, faced no identified imminent termination, and had never been the uncontested acting Director, so an injunction would not merely preserve the status quo. The casebook gives an editorial account of the competing appointments and this denial; its reference to a seven-year directorial term conflicts with the five-year term stated in the opinion.

LRS-CLOSURE-006.rule: In denying a preliminary injunction, the court held that ATF reasonably read ambiguous statutory terms to classify bump stocks as machine guns, and that the Federal Vacancies Reform Act allowed temporary designation of an acting Attorney General despite the succession statute.

sections.Parties: Damien Guedes and associated organizations, the Firearms Policy Coalition, and David Codrea, in three actions, challenged a rule of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) classifying bump-stock-type devices as machine guns. Each moved for a preliminary injunction against the rule. The Coalition principally attacked Acting Attorney General Matthew Whitaker's authority, and Codrea added a Takings Clause claim. William Barr, who had replaced Whitaker, was automatically substituted as a defendant under Rule 25(d).
sections.Procedural History: Guedes and associated organizations sued on December 18, 2018. The Firearms Policy Coalition then dismissed its claims from that suit and brought a separate action, later consolidated with Guedes. Codrea's separate action was transferred as related but, at the parties' request, not consolidated. After government-shutdown stays were lifted and hearings held, Judge Dabney Friedrich, the sole deciding district judge, denied all three preliminary-injunction motions on February 25, 2019. This is the district court's preliminary-relief decision; it did not finally dismiss the complaints or decide the takings merits, and later appellate dispositions are separate.
sections.Material Facts:
Following the October 2017 Las Vegas mass shooting, ATF reconsidered its treatment of bump stocks. A standard bump stock replaced a semiautomatic rifle's stock and allowed recoil to move the weapon back and forth against a maintained trigger finger. ATF had classified the spring-equipped Akins Accelerator as a machine gun in 2006 but had excluded standard versions as insufficiently automatic. The National Firearms Act defined "machinegun" as a weapon firing automatically more than one shot, without manual reloading, by a single function of the trigger. ATF's December 26, 2018 rule defined a single trigger function as a single pull and analogous motions, defined automatic operation as a self-acting or self-regulating mechanism permitting multiple rounds through such a function, and expressly classified bump-stock-type devices as machine guns. Existing owners would have to destroy or abandon them when the rule took effect on March 26, 2019.

Attorney General Sessions resigned in November 2018, and the President selected his chief of staff, Whitaker, to exercise the Attorney General's duties under the Federal Vacancies Reform Act (FVRA). Whitaker's acting service, which the court described as one hundred days, ended when Barr became Attorney General in February 2019.
sections.Issue: Whether plaintiffs were likely to succeed in showing that ATF's bump-stock rule violated the Administrative Procedure Act or the statutory hearing and comment requirements, whether a takings claim justified an injunction, and whether Whitaker's designation as Acting Attorney General violated 28 U.S.C. § 508 or the Appointments Clause.
sections.Holding: The U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia in 2019, per Judge Friedrich, denied all three preliminary-injunction motions because plaintiffs had not established likely success. Applying the then-governing Chevron framework, it found ambiguity in both the single-trigger-function and automatic-operation terms and accepted ATF's construction as reasonable, without holding it the only textually possible reading. It found the changed position sufficiently explained and the comment and hearing procedures adequate, and held that the takings theory did not justify an injunction. It held that § 508 did not displace the President's FVRA choice and that Whitaker's temporary service did not make him a principal officer requiring a new Senate-confirmed appointment.
sections.Reasoning:
Dictionaries did not resolve whether a single trigger function meant each mechanical resetting of the trigger or the shooter's single initiating pull, and ATF's shooter-centered reading drew support from decisions including Staples and Akins. Definitions of automatic did not say how much manual input remained permissible. ATF could therefore treat maintained pressure and recoil-directed operation as a single pull followed by automatic firing; whether bump stocks were automatic was the closer question. ATF acknowledged and explained its departure from earlier classifications and addressed the central operational objections. Section 926(b) did not compel an oral hearing, and any failure to extend the comment period after technical problems was harmless. The Takings Clause generally secures compensation rather than barring an authorized taking, and plaintiffs had not shown Tucker Act compensation inadequate.

On Whitaker, the court rejected the Coalition's argument that § 508's succession sequence had to be exhausted first. Section 3347 made the FVRA nonexclusive when another succession statute applied, not unavailable; Hooks and English supported compatible alternatives; and § 508 itself identified the Deputy Attorney General as first assistant for purposes of § 3345. The court rejected the government's separate congressional-acquiescence argument.

On the Appointments Clause, the court relied on Eaton: performing a superior's duties for a limited time under special, temporary conditions does not make a subordinate a permanent principal officer. It considered the historical justification to be temporary service rather than a preexisting first-assistant relationship. Courts could still police effectively permanent appointments, but plaintiffs did not contend Whitaker's service was such a pretext. Assuming without deciding that Whitaker had been an employee who needed an appointment, presidential direction under the FVRA was constitutionally an appointment. The casebook cites the decision in its account of the Whitaker appointment, with the shorthand that trial courts treated Whitaker as an inferior officer.

LRS-CLOSURE-007.rule: When a statute requires a hearing without specifying its form, there is no presumption for or against formal adjudication; the agency resolves the ambiguity in the first instance, subject to review for reasonableness under Chevron.

sections.Parties: Chemical Waste Management and Waste Management of North America petitioned directly for review of EPA's Part 24 procedural regulations governing hearings on certain corrective-action orders under the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA). The petitioners asserted that the statute required formal adjudication, that EPA had inadequately justified its contrary interpretation, and that the rules facially violated due process.
sections.Procedural History: The petitioners sought review of the rules themselves in the D.C. Circuit, not review of an individual corrective-action order. On May 5, 1989 the court, in an opinion by Judge D.H. Ginsburg for Chief Judge Wald and Judge Starr with no dissent or concurrence, denied the petition for review. The court's rejection of an earlier presumption about hearings had been circulated to and approved by the entire court, though the judgment was that of a unanimous panel, not an en banc judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
RCRA required hazardous-waste treatment, storage, and disposal facilities to obtain permits, while certain existing facilities could operate on interim status. Section 3008(a) authorized EPA enforcement orders, including civil penalties and permit suspension or revocation, and § 3008(b) required a public hearing upon a timely request. EPA's Part 22 regulations used APA formal adjudication for those hearings. The 1984 amendments added § 3008(h), allowing corrective-action orders when hazardous waste had been released from an interim facility, and extended the public-hearing right to those orders; noncompliance could trigger penalties of up to $25,000 per day.

EPA's Part 24 rules kept formal Part 22 procedures for orders suspending or revoking interim status or assessing noncompliance penalties. For other investigative and corrective orders they provided informal procedures: operators could submit written evidence and argument, make oral presentations, and receive assistance from legal and technical advisers. Direct and cross-examination were barred, but the presiding officer could question either party. The officer had to be a Regional Judicial Officer or another agency attorney without prior connection to the case. The officer recommended a decision and the Regional Administrator decided.
sections.Issue: Whether RCRA's requirement of a public hearing on corrective-action orders unambiguously demands formal adjudication, whether EPA's choice of informal procedures was a reasonable and adequately explained interpretation, and whether the Part 24 rules violate due process on their face.
sections.Holding: The D.C. Circuit in 1989, per Judge D.H. Ginsburg for a unanimous panel, denied the petition. It held that the statute's public-hearing language did not specify formal rather than informal proceedings, that Part 24 reasonably interpreted that ambiguous mandate, and that the rules survived the facial due-process challenge. It announced neither a presumption favoring formal hearings nor one favoring informal hearings: the agency initially resolves the ambiguity, subject to reasonableness review. The court did not preclude all as-applied challenges or hold that the APA never requires formal adjudication without particular words.
sections.Reasoning:
Applying the then-governing Chevron framework, the court found that the public-hearing language did not specify formal or informal proceedings, and that EPA's discretionary authority to issue discovery rules did not require otherwise. EPA's 1978 choice of formal process for subsection (a) orders did not lock it into a universal interpretation, and the 1984 amendments did not incorporate Part 22 into the statute. Union of Concerned Scientists had stated a presumption that a hearing requirement in adjudication means an on-the-record hearing; the court treated that statement as dictum and reasoned that such a presumption prematurely converts ambiguous language into an unambiguous limit and displaces the agency's interpretive role under Chevron.

On reasonableness, EPA expected corrective-action cases to raise fewer historical factual disputes than sanction cases, turning largely on technical data or policy rather than demeanor and credibility, which written submissions, oral statements, and officer-directed questions could resolve. That explanation sufficed. The court rejected EPA's additional reliance on a congressional desire for speed, so the result is not acceptance of both rationales.

Under Mathews v. Eldridge, corrective measures could have multimillion-dollar consequences, but the possibility of unusually expensive individual orders did not make the scheme facially unconstitutional. Petitioners did not show that trial-type hearings would substantially improve decisions. Due process does not categorically require an ALJ, and under Withrow a challenger must show intolerable unfairness or probable actual bias. EPA estimated that informal hearings would save roughly half its participation costs. The court contemplated possible trouble in a particular case combining high stakes with issues benefiting substantially from trial-type procedures or an actually biased officer. The casebook's editorial note critiques a deference-based approach to the organic statute and the consequent treatment of the APA; that criticism is the note's, not the court's.

LRS-CLOSURE-008.rule: Under the plurality's reasoning, the AUMF authorizes detaining a citizen who fought with hostile forces in Afghanistan, but a citizen-detainee must receive notice of the factual basis for the classification and a fair chance to rebut it before a neutral decisionmaker.

sections.Parties: Yaser Esam Hamdi, an American citizen held by the military as an enemy combatant, challenged his detention through a habeas petition filed by his father as next friend under 28 U.S.C. § 2241 in June 2002. The government claimed authority to hold him without criminal charges or ordinary judicial proceedings. Hamdi's father disputed the government's account of his son's conduct.
sections.Procedural History: The district court appointed counsel and ordered access, but the Fourth Circuit reversed the access order and instructed the court to begin with cautious, deferential procedures. The government then supplied the declaration of Michael Mobbs as its evidentiary support. The district court considered the declaration generic hearsay insufficient to support the detention, ordered extensive material for in camera review, and certified whether the declaration alone permitted meaningful judicial review. The Fourth Circuit reversed and ordered dismissal, reasoning that capture in an active foreign combat zone was undisputed and that separation of powers barred further factual inquiry; it also treated the Authorization for Use of Military Force (AUMF) as authority for detention. The Court vacated that judgment and remanded.
sections.Material Facts:
Hamdi was born in Louisiana and moved to Saudi Arabia as a child. In 2001 he was in Afghanistan, where Northern Alliance forces seized him and eventually transferred him to the United States military. The government held him in Afghanistan, then at Guantanamo Bay, and, on learning he was an American citizen, moved him in April 2002 to a naval brig in Norfolk and later to Charleston. It classified him as an enemy combatant. His father asserted that Hamdi had gone to Afghanistan for relief work and became trapped there when the military campaign began.

Mobbs, a Defense Department policy adviser reporting from records and reports, asserted that Hamdi affiliated with a Taliban unit, received weapons training, remained with the unit after September 11, and surrendered a rifle when the unit surrendered to Northern Alliance forces. Hamdi had not been able to speak through counsel to contest those assertions, and the competing accounts had not been adjudicated. The September 2001 AUMF authorized necessary and appropriate force against those responsible for the attacks or harboring those responsible.
sections.Issue: Whether the Executive had authority to detain a citizen as an enemy combatant, and if so, what process a citizen held in the United States is due to challenge that classification.
sections.Holding: The Court in 2004 vacated the Fourth Circuit's dismissal and remanded; six Justices supported that judgment, with no majority opinion. Justice O'Connor's plurality, joined by Chief Justice Rehnquist and Justices Kennedy and Breyer, concluded that the AUMF authorized detention of the narrow category alleged, a person part of or supporting hostile forces in Afghanistan who engaged in armed conflict against the United States, tied to the relevant active hostilities, and that a citizen challenging that classification must receive notice of its factual basis and a fair opportunity to rebut the government before a neutral decisionmaker. Justice Souter, joined by Justice Ginsburg, concurred in the judgment with express qualifications. The Court neither found Hamdi an enemy combatant nor ordered his release.
sections.Reasoning:
The plurality reasoned that detaining combatants to prevent their return to battle is a fundamental incident of war included in Congress's authorization even without the word detention, and that citizenship does not exempt an otherwise qualifying combatant, as it read Quirin. It did not reach any independent Article II detention power or decide whether the Non-Detention Act, 18 U.S.C. § 4001(a), applied to military detention; assuming those predicates, the AUMF supplied the authorization. It tied detention to active hostilities, not a perpetual global war or interrogation alone.

On process, all parties agreed habeas remained available because Congress had not suspended it. Applying Mathews, the plurality weighed the liberty interest of a possibly erroneously detained person against the interest in keeping actual combatants from returning to battle and the military burdens of greater process. Neither the government's some-evidence review of its own account nor the district court's apparent trial-like model struck the balance. Hearsay might be accepted and credible government evidence could carry a rebuttable presumption, provided a fair rebuttal opportunity remained; a properly authorized and constituted military tribunal might satisfy the standards; and Hamdi had a right to counsel on remand.

Justice Souter, with Justice Ginsburg, read § 4001(a) to require clear congressional authority that the AUMF did not supply, but joined the remand so Hamdi could contest his status, without agreeing to an evidentiary presumption or to military adjudication curtailing habeas inquiry. Justice Scalia, joined by Justice Stevens, dissented: a citizen must be prosecuted or the writ lawfully suspended, and he would have directed release unless one or the other occurred. Justice Thomas dissented and would have affirmed, deferring to the wartime executive determination. The casebook frames the case in an editorial note about balancing liberty and national security.

LRS-CLOSURE-009.rule: Foreign nationals detained as enemy combatants at Guantanamo Bay may invoke the Suspension Clause, and a statute withdrawing habeas jurisdiction without providing an adequate substitute is an unconstitutional suspension of the writ.

sections.Parties: Foreign nationals detained as enemy combatants at Guantanamo Bay, in Boumediene and the consolidated Al Odah case, sought habeas corpus to challenge their detention. None was a citizen of a country then at war with the United States, and each denied membership in al Qaeda or the Taliban. The Executive relied on the 2001 Authorization for Use of Military Force to detain them. The petitioners argued that the Military Commissions Act did not reach their pending habeas applications and invoked the Suspension Clause.
sections.Procedural History: Habeas actions began in February 2002. The district court and D.C. Circuit initially dismissed because Guantanamo lay outside U.S. sovereign territory. In Rasul in 2004 the Court held that statutory habeas jurisdiction extended to the base. On return, Judge Leon dismissed one group of cases for lack of enforceable rights, while Judge Green held in the other that the Fifth Amendment protected the detainees. During those appeals Congress enacted the Detainee Treatment Act of 2005 (DTA), withdrawing habeas jurisdiction over Guantanamo aliens and providing exclusive D.C. Circuit review of final Combatant Status Review Tribunal determinations. After Hamdan held that the withdrawal did not reach pending cases, Congress in 2006 passed the Military Commissions Act (MCA), expressly applying its withdrawal to pending cases. The D.C. Circuit held that the MCA removed jurisdiction and that the Suspension Clause did not protect petitioners. The Court reversed and instructed the D.C. Circuit to remand to the district court.
sections.Material Facts: Some petitioners were apprehended in Afghanistan, others as far away as Bosnia and Gambia. After Hamdi, the Defense Department established Combatant Status Review Tribunals (CSRTs) to decide whether detainees were enemy combatants under the Department's definition. Each petitioner appeared before a separate CSRT and received an adverse status determination, which remained contested. In a CSRT the detainee's personal representative was expressly neither a lawyer nor an advocate, government evidence carried a presumption of validity, and the confined detainee could present only reasonably available evidence. Cuba retained de jure sovereignty over Guantanamo under the lease and treaties, but the United States exercised complete, uninterrupted jurisdiction and control. Some petitioners had been held for six years, and DTA applications had been pending for over two years without merits decisions. One petitioner, Nechla, had asked the CSRT to contact an employer who could corroborate his denial of an al Qaeda affiliation; the tribunal found the witness relevant but unavailable, while counsel now represented that he could be heard.
sections.Issue: Whether foreign nationals detained as enemy combatants at Guantanamo Bay may invoke the Suspension Clause's protection of habeas corpus, and if so, whether the DTA's review in the D.C. Circuit is an adequate substitute for habeas or instead § 7 of the MCA is an unconstitutional suspension of the writ.
sections.Holding: The Court on June 12, 2008, in an opinion by Justice Kennedy joined by Justices Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer (5-4), held that the petitioners could invoke the Suspension Clause, which has full effect at Guantanamo. It held that the DTA's appellate review was an inadequate substitute for habeas, making § 7 of the MCA an unconstitutional suspension of the writ, while the DTA and CSRT process themselves remained intact. Petitioners need not complete DTA review before seeking district-court habeas. The Court decided neither the President's substantive authority to detain these petitioners nor that any petitioner must be released, and it made no judgment whether the CSRTs met due-process standards.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court first held that the MCA did withdraw jurisdiction over pending habeas cases, so the constitutional question could not be avoided by statutory construction. It treated habeas as both an individual protection and an instrument restraining executive power. Founding-era authorities did not conclusively answer the precise question, and the Court declined to turn the absence of precedent into proof for either side. Although Cuba kept de jure sovereignty, the United States had de facto sovereignty, and the Insular Cases, Reid, and Eisentrager showed that constitutional application can depend on local conditions and practical considerations; otherwise the political branches could switch constitutional constraints off. The Court considered at least three factors: citizenship and status, including the adequacy of the process establishing status; the nature of the places of capture and detention; and practical obstacles to resolving entitlement to the writ. Petitioners disputed their status, had not received a rigorous military trial, and were held where U.S. control was absolute and indefinite.

On adequacy, a substitute must provide a meaningful opportunity to show that detention rests on erroneous law and empower the court to order conditional release when necessary. The CSRT's limits created a substantial risk of factual error, and even on generous assumptions DTA review could not consider evidence that became available after the CSRT. Kennedy noted that this accords with Mathews but did not make a due-process holding.

Justice Souter, joined by Justices Ginsburg and Breyer, concurred. Roberts, joined by Justices Scalia, Thomas, and Alito, dissented on the ground that the statutory system adequately protected whatever rights the detainees had; Justice Scalia, joined by the same three, would have affirmed because the Suspension Clause did not reach aliens abroad. The casebook's account says the Court held CSRT procedures constitutionally inadequate by applying Mathews, which overstates the decision.

LRS-CLOSURE-010.rule: A document labeled a notice to appear that does not specify the time or place of removal proceedings is not a notice to appear under § 1229(a) and does not trigger the stop-time rule for cancellation of removal.

sections.Parties: Wescley Fonseca Pereira, a Brazilian citizen charged as removable for overstaying a temporary visitor visa, sought cancellation of removal, asserting more than ten years of continuous physical presence in the United States. The government's position was that the document the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) served on him in 2006 had triggered the stop-time rule, ending that period and making him ineligible.
sections.Procedural History: After Pereira's in absentia removal order was reopened, the immigration judge held that the 2006 document had stopped the clock, making him ineligible for cancellation. The Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA) dismissed his appeal under Matter of Camarillo, which treated the statutory reference to a notice under § 1229(a) as identifying a document without importing substantive notice requirements. The First Circuit denied review, finding ambiguity and deferring under Chevron to the BIA's interpretation. The Court took the case to resolve a circuit conflict, narrowing the question to the time-and-place defect actually presented. It reversed the First Circuit and remanded.
sections.Material Facts: Pereira entered the United States in 2000 at age 19 on a temporary visitor visa and remained after it expired. After a 2006 arrest in Massachusetts for operating a vehicle under the influence of alcohol, DHS personally served him on May 31 with a document charging him as removable for overstaying. It described the proceedings, his rights, and the consequences of failing to appear and directed him to an immigration judge in Boston, but supplied no hearing date or time. DHS filed the document with the immigration court on August 9, 2007. The court then mailed a separate notice setting a hearing for October 31 at 9:30 a.m., using his street address rather than the post-office box he had given DHS; it was returned undeliverable. He did not attend, was ordered removed in absentia, and remained unaware of the order. After a 2013 arrest for driving without headlights, the court reopened proceedings because he had not received the 2007 notice, and he sought cancellation of removal. The government represented at oral argument that almost all notices over the preceding three years omitted time and date.
sections.Issue: Whether a document styled a notice to appear that does not specify the time or place of the removal proceedings is a notice to appear under § 1229(a) that triggers the stop-time rule of § 1229b(d)(1)(A), ending the period of continuous physical presence required for cancellation of removal.
sections.Holding: The Court on June 21, 2018, in an opinion by Justice Sotomayor joined by Roberts, Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer, Kagan, and Gorsuch (8-1), held that a document styled as a notice to appear that does not specify the time or place of removal proceedings is not the statutory notice that triggers the stop-time rule. Because the statutory answer was clear, the majority did not proceed to Chevron deference. The Court did not itself grant cancellation, settle the consequences of every possible notice defect, or announce a constitutional due-process holding.
sections.Reasoning:
The stop-time rule refers to a notice to appear under § 1229(a), and paragraph (1) of that section describes a written notice specifying, among other things, the time and place of proceedings. That language is definitional, so those particulars are essential to the stop-time trigger. Paragraph (2), which requires notice of a new time or place when a hearing is changed or postponed, presupposes that hearing information was supplied earlier. Section 1229(b)(1) generally requires at least ten days between service of the notice and the first hearing to allow an opportunity to secure counsel, and a document with no hearing details would undermine meaningful preparation. Common sense pointed the same way: notice of where and when to appear performs an essential function, and the government conceded that a blank sheet would not stop the clock.

The majority rejected the argument that "under" meant only authorized by; here it meant in accordance with § 1229(a)'s substantive criteria. Administrative difficulties did not justify ignoring clear text, since Congress expressly allowed rescheduling with new notice and DHS and the immigration courts had previously coordinated scheduling. Requiring a compliant notice was also consistent with the rule's purpose of preventing noncitizens from exploiting administrative delay.

Justice Kennedy concurred, joining the opinion in full but criticizing reflexive deference and suggesting that Chevron's premises be reconsidered in an appropriate case. Justice Alito dissented: he would defer to the BIA under Chevron, reading "under" as reasonably meaning authorized by and distinguishing a document's required contents from whether a defective document still stops time. The casebook uses the case in a discussion of notices missing required information; the holding is specifically about the statutory stop-time rule.

LRS-CLOSURE-011.rule: A noncitizen who received a proper paragraph (2) notice of the hearing he missed cannot obtain rescission of an in absentia removal order for lack of notice, even if the initial notice to appear omitted the hearing date and time.

sections.Parties: Campos-Chaves, an El Salvador national; Singh, an Indian national; and Mendez-Colín, a Mexican national, were each ordered removed in absentia and later sought relief from those orders because their initial notices to appear lacked a hearing date and time. The government conceded that none of the initial notices complied with paragraph (1) of § 1229(a) but argued that each noncitizen later received a proper paragraph (2) notice for the missed hearing.
sections.Procedural History: In Campos-Chaves, the immigration judge and the BIA rejected the motion to reopen, and the Fifth Circuit denied review because he did not dispute receipt of the later hearing notice. In Singh, the judge and BIA rejected the motion, but the Ninth Circuit held that the absence of a single-document notice to appear was enough to permit rescission; rehearing en banc was denied over a twelve-judge dissent. In Mendez-Colín, the BIA refused reinstatement and the Ninth Circuit granted review in an unpublished decision alongside Singh. In the consolidated cases the Court affirmed the Fifth Circuit, reversed the Ninth Circuit in Mendez-Colín, and vacated and remanded in Singh because the Ninth Circuit had not reached his separate exceptional-circumstances argument.
sections.Material Facts:
Campos-Chaves entered without inspection near Laredo in 2005. Three days later the government served a notice to appear charging removability and naming the immigration court's address but leaving the date and time to be set. A notice of hearing sent a few months later specified September 20, 2005, at 9 a.m. He did not attend and was ordered removed in absentia; thirteen years later he sought reopening based on Pereira.

Singh entered in 2016 and received a notice listing the hearing date and time as TBD. Five days afterward the government sent a specific hearing notice to his supplied address. In October 2018 the court sent another notice setting November 26 at 1 p.m.; he did not attend, but the government lacked his file, so the court rescheduled to December 12 at 9 a.m. and again sent notice. He missed that hearing too and was ordered removed in absentia, and in April 2019 he sought rescission.

Mendez-Colín attempted entry at San Luis in 2001. His notice to appear named the court but left the time and date to be set. He attended the hearing scheduled by a later notice and further hearings in 2002. The judge then set September 15, 2003, at 9 a.m. for his intended cancellation application, sending notice to counsel. He was ordered removed in absentia, and about fifteen years later he sought reinstatement based on the defective initial notice.
sections.Issue: Whether a noncitizen ordered removed in absentia may obtain rescission under § 1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii), for not receiving notice in accordance with paragraph (1) or (2) of § 1229(a), when the initial notice to appear lacked a hearing date and time but he later received a paragraph (2) notice specifying the time of the hearing he missed.
sections.Holding: The Court on June 14, 2024, in an opinion by Justice Alito joined by Roberts, Thomas, Kavanaugh, and Barrett (5-4), held that a noncitizen who received a proper paragraph (2) notice for the hearing he missed cannot obtain rescission of an in absentia removal order on the notice ground, even though the initial notice to appear lacked a hearing date and time. The relevant notice is the one for the missed hearing at which removal was ordered. The decision does not hold that separate documents combine into a compliant paragraph (1) notice, and neither Pereira nor Niz-Chavez was overruled as to the initial notice or the stop-time rule.
sections.Reasoning:
The rescission ground applies when the noncitizen did not receive notice in accordance with paragraph (1) or (2). Giving "or" its ordinary disjunctive meaning, either type of notice can satisfy the notice condition. The nearby provision authorizing in absentia removal also refers to paragraph (1) or (2) and requires proof of "the written notice," singular; reading rescission to require both notices would let an order be validly obtained on one notice yet undone for failure to supply both. That did not mean any notice of any hearing suffices: the notice that matters is the one for the missed hearing, so a noncitizen who received a compliant initial notice could still obtain rescission if the government later changed the date without telling him.

The majority rejected the argument that a paragraph (2) notice of a change or new time requires an earlier specific time. A notice can change a TBD designation to an actual hearing time, Congress referred to any change, and a new time need not replace an old one, just as a new baby need not replace an old baby. Pereira's observation that paragraph (2) presupposed a prior time-and-place notice was supplementary dicta in a case about the stop-time trigger. The government must still issue a proper notice to appear, and a recipient of a later hearing notice must attend and can raise the initial notice's defects there.

Justice Jackson, joined by Justices Sotomayor, Kagan, and Gorsuch, dissented. She treated the paragraph (1) notice as indispensable and paragraph (2) as supplementary, so that a change notice presupposes a previously set time, and she objected that the majority shifted onto noncitizens a burden Congress placed on the government. The casebook describes the case as holding that a single-document notice is not required because an incomplete notice and a later amendment together provide it; that statement needs a narrower formulation, since the decision accepts a compliant later hearing notice only for the specific rescission ground.

LRS-CLOSURE-012.rule: An agency that adopts a new statutory interpretation in adjudication may ordinarily apply it in the case before it unless that would cause manifest injustice, assessed under the five Retail, Wholesale factors.

sections.Parties: Clark-Cowlitz Joint Operating Agency, formed by public utility districts, competed with incumbent licensee Pacific Power & Light for a new license for the Merwin hydroelectric project and claimed the Federal Power Act's preference for state and municipal applicants. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) abandoned its earlier interpretation of that preference and awarded the license to Pacific Power. Clark-Cowlitz argued that FERC was barred from reinterpreting the preference as to the participants.
sections.Procedural History: FERC held in a declaratory proceeding, City of Bountiful in 1980, that the municipal preference applied when an incumbent sought relicensing, and the Eleventh Circuit upheld that interpretation in Alabama Power in 1982 under a deferential standard. In the Merwin proceeding an ALJ found the competitors equally well adapted and ruled for Clark-Cowlitz. In 1983 the Commission overruled Bountiful and awarded the license to Pacific Power, alternatively finding the plans not equally well adapted. While judicial review was pending, Congress in 1986 eliminated the municipal preference for relicensing but expressly excluded the Merwin proceeding. On August 11, 1987 the en banc D.C. Circuit remanded FERC's economic justification for the award as insufficiently reasoned and affirmed the order in all other respects.
sections.Material Facts: Pacific Power & Light owned and operated the Merwin hydroelectric project on Washington's Lewis River. The original fifty-year license was issued in 1929 and transferred to Pacific Power in 1941. Pacific Power applied for a new license in 1976. Public utility districts then formed Clark-Cowlitz to compete, and it applied in 1977, claiming the statutory preference for state and municipal applicants whose plans were equally well adapted. Both competitors took part in the Bountiful declaratory proceeding. FERC later reconsidered; the Solicitor General disclosed the Commission's changed view in a Supreme Court certiorari brief, and certiorari was denied. Merwin became the first relicensing hearing after Bountiful. In overruling Bountiful there, FERC alternatively reasoned that Pacific Power's customers would face greater replacement-power costs if it lost the project than Clark-Cowlitz's customers would if its application failed: Pacific Power would need expensive thermal or Bonneville new-resources power, while Clark-Cowlitz could continue buying lower-priced Bonneville priority-firm power.
sections.Issue: Whether FERC was precluded from abandoning its Bountiful interpretation as to these parties, whether it could apply its new interpretation in the Merwin adjudication itself, whether the new reading of the municipal preference was permissible, and whether its economic ground for the award was adequately reasoned.
sections.Holding: The en banc D.C. Circuit in 1987, in an opinion by Judge Starr for a 4-3 majority of participating judges that also included Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Bork, and Buckley, upheld FERC's authority to abandon its earlier interpretation of the municipal preference and apply the new reading in this contest, and held the new reading permissible. It held that FERC could consider economic consequences beyond the applicants' technical plans but had not adequately explained its economic justification, and it remanded on that point while affirming in all other respects. It did not direct the license to Clark-Cowlitz. Judge Mikva dissented with Robinson and Edwards.
sections.Reasoning:
On preclusion, the majority distinguished the issue resolved earlier, whether Bountiful's interpretation was reasonable, from whether FERC's later contrary reading was also reasonable; an ambiguous statute might admit both, and Clark-Cowlitz and FERC had supported the same position in the earlier litigation.

On retroactivity, the majority started from the general rule that an agency interpreting law in adjudication may apply its new interpretation in the proceeding before it, with an exception to prevent manifest injustice. It weighed the five nonexclusive Retail, Wholesale considerations: whether the case is one of first impression; whether the rule is an abrupt departure from established practice or fills an unsettled area; actual reliance; the burden imposed; and the statutory interest in applying the new rule despite reliance. Merwin was the proceeding announcing the change; Bountiful was a single recent pronouncement; reasonable reliance lasted no more than six months before the Solicitor General's disclosure; Clark-Cowlitz lost an attractive competitive preference but faced no new liability for past conduct, fine, or damages and had never received a final license; and the statutory interest in a best-qualified applicant outweighed the brief reliance.

Under the then-governing Chevron framework, Congress had not clearly answered whether the preference applied when an incumbent sought renewal, and FERC reasonably treated an incumbent as an original licensee and applied the preference only where an incumbent was not competing. But FERC's customer-only cost balance risked creating an effective incumbent preference and ignored regional effects, so the court required further explanation.

Judge Mikva, dissenting, rejected the presumption favoring retroactivity, emphasized Clark-Cowlitz's concrete reliance, and concluded that the reversal was preclusively barred and rested in part on an unreasonable statutory interpretation. The casebook's editorial note quotes the five factors and emphasizes burdens involving liability for past conduct, fines, or damages.

LRS-CLOSURE-013.rule: An agency may issue binding substantive regulations under a general rulemaking grant through notice and comment, reviewed under the arbitrary-and-capricious standard on the administrative record, but it must supply an explanation adequate for that review.

sections.Parties: The National Nutritional Foods Association and Solgar, the plaintiffs and appellants, challenged FDA regulations classifying higher-dose vitamin A and vitamin D preparations as prescription drugs. The government, through the Commissioner who issued the regulations, was the defendant and had won summary judgment. The challengers wanted the regulations denied binding effect and sought a de novo trial and discovery; the government defended the district court's judgment.
sections.Procedural History:
The Commissioner proposed the rules on December 14, 1972 and announced the final rules on August 2, 1973, effective October 1. The plaintiffs sued on August 6. Judge Frankel denied preliminary relief, and the Second Circuit affirmed that earlier ruling. On April 5, 1974, after the rules took effect, Frankel granted summary judgment dismissing the complaint. He upheld the notice-and-comment procedure, applied arbitrary-and-capricious review rather than allowing a new evidentiary trial, and vacated the notice to depose the Commissioner. The court separately dismissed a direct petition for review for lack of jurisdiction.

On the appeal from the final summary judgment, the Second Circuit on February 3, 1975 remanded to the district court for proceedings consistent with its directions. It neither affirmed unconditionally nor invalidated the regulations.
sections.Material Facts:
The regulations classified vitamin A preparations containing more than 10,000 international units per dosage form, and vitamin D preparations containing more than 400 IU per dosage form, as prescription drugs. The Commissioner proceeded under § 701(a) of the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, which authorized regulations for efficient enforcement of the Act, rather than under § 701(e), which required notice, objections, an evidentiary hearing on request and appellate review for specified subjects.

The proposal described toxicity from prolonged excessive intake, sometimes causing death, and widespread promotion of high doses for disease prevention and treatment. The agency made its medical bibliography available and invited comments for sixty days. More than 2,500 comments arrived, collected in roughly forty-six folders; both plaintiffs submitted extensive opposition. In the final rules the Commissioner reasoned that amounts within the existing nutritional ranges met normal needs and that higher amounts were appropriate only for therapeutic use, with one exception permitting vitamin D up to 1,000 IU under medical supervision for people with poor absorption. He acknowledged that consumers could take many weaker tablets but believed convenient single high-dose units increased the risk of excessive consumption. The final explanation and the record supplied to the court were incomplete on why the preparations were drugs.
sections.Issue: Could the FDA issue regulations binding on private parties under the general rulemaking grant in § 701(a), using notice and comment, or only under § 701(e)'s hearing procedure? What standard of review governed, was a de novo trial available, and had the agency adequately explained why the preparations were drugs under § 201(g) and properly subject to prescription status?
sections.Holding: The Second Circuit in 1975, in an opinion by Mansfield joined by Waterman, with Lumbard concurring separately and all three agreeing to remand, held that the FDA could issue binding substantive regulations under § 701(a) using APA notice and comment, that no evidentiary hearing was required, and that § 706(2)(A)'s arbitrary-and-capricious standard governed. But the agency had not sufficiently explained why these preparations were drugs. The district court had to conduct an Overton Park-type inquiry into the entire administrative record, with explanatory affidavits or testimony as necessary. If classification as drugs was rational, the regulations could be upheld and summary judgment should stand; if it was irrational, summary judgment had to be vacated. The court did not grant a de novo trial.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority acknowledged that the statute did not explicitly identify the authoritative effect of each kind of regulation, but it rejected a rigid classification denying binding force to every § 701(a) rule. General delegations could support substantive rules, especially where agency scientific expertise made industry-wide regulation more useful than repeated enforcement suits. The Supreme Court's Hynson, Ciba, Bentex and USV decisions recognized FDA authority to decide new-drug status administratively, and § 701(e) supplemented the general grant rather than confining it to advisory statements. Rules meant to have legal force still required notice and comment. The court also rejected the argument that the 1951 Durham-Humphrey amendment withheld rulemaking power over prescription classifications.

Notice and comment was adequate because the decision turned on appraising scientific information and toxicity risks, not witness credibility. Arbitrary-and-capricious review still required an explanation adequate for review, and under Camp and Overton Park the focus remained the administrative record; an inadequate explanation did not authorize a new merits record, and a finding lacking support required vacatur and remand rather than the court's own scientific judgment.

On the drug definition, intent to treat or prevent disease could not be shown merely by proving that higher doses were nutritionally useless for most people, as the circuit had held in the 1974 NNFA v. FDA proceeding. Evidence of therapeutic promotion might establish objective intent, but the court could not assume that was the agency's supported reason. If the preparations were rationally drugs, the prescription restriction was defensible under § 503(b)(1)(B).

Lumbard, concurring, thought arbitrary-and-capricious review should closely examine the information before the agency, and that unsupported substantive rules abused discretion if they lacked substantial evidentiary support.

The casebook uses Mansfield's statement about accepting general delegations in areas of expertise to illustrate the historical expansion of rulemaking.

LRS-CLOSURE-014.rule: In formal rulemaking, an agency may control repetitive questioning but may not wholly deny cross-examination necessary for full and true disclosure; and broad authority to set food identity standards still requires a meaningful exceptions procedure and adequately supported restrictions.

sections.Parties: Fifteen petitions for review challenged FDA regulations for vitamin and mineral supplements sold as foods; the petitioners included Sunkist, which sought protection for fresh produce. The FDA was the respondent and defended its standards of identity and labeling rules. The petitioners attacked the agency's authority, particular restrictions, and the conduct of the hearing, including the denial of cross-examination to National Health Federation representative Dr. Miles Robinson.
sections.Procedural History:
The proceeding began with a June 1962 proposal. Revisions drew objections and requests for an evidentiary hearing under § 701(e); the hearing lasted more than twenty-two months and produced 32,405 transcript pages and hundreds of exhibits. Proposed findings and tentative regulations appeared in January 1973, and after a final round of exceptions the FDA published final rules on August 2, 1973 for full implementation on January 1, 1975. Fifteen petitions sought review in the Second Circuit under § 701(f).

On August 15, 1974 the court granted the petitions in part and denied them in part, stayed enforcement of the entire scheme until six months after its judgment became final or June 30, 1975, whichever was later, remanded to the FDA, and awarded no costs.
sections.Material Facts:
Part 80 set definitions and standards of identity for supplements.
