It permitted specified combinations of vitamins and minerals and single nutrients, defined mandatory and optional ingredients, and imposed minimum and maximum quantities, the maxima generally 150 percent of U.S. Recommended Daily Allowances derived from National Academy of Sciences recommendations. Part 125 governed label statements for special dietary uses but also contained substantive prohibitions: § 125.1(c) barred specified essential nutrients lacking an established allowance from general-purpose foods and supplements, and § 125.1(h) treated preparations above the maximum allowance as drugs. Other provisions prohibited misleading claims about therapeutic efficacy, the adequacy of ordinary diets, soil and processing effects, unnecessary ingredients, and the superiority of natural vitamins.

Dr. Sebrell, former chair of the committee that produced the 1968 allowances, was the critical witness. The FDA initially listed him, and its representations led participants to defer questions to him; it later did not call him because he disagreed with some proposals. When the American Medical Association called him, the examiner refused Robinson permission to cross-examine and denied an interlocutory appeal. The examiner had treated all nongovernmental participants as sharing an interest, although the National Health Federation opposed virtually the whole program while the AMA generally supported it.
sections.Issue: Could the court review the whole integrated scheme, and did the FDA have authority under §§ 401 and 403(j) to prescribe identity standards and labeling rules for dietary supplements, including maximum quantities? Were the all-or-nothing combinations and maxima, the ban on essential nutrients without allowances, and the blanket drug classification valid, and did the denial of cross-examination of Sebrell require reopening the record?
sections.Holding: The Second Circuit in 1974, in a unanimous opinion by Friendly for a panel with Smith and District Judge Bartels, broadly sustained the FDA's power to prescribe standards of identity and much of the labeling scheme, and held that it could decide every issue tendered. It required a broadened exceptions procedure allowing applications for other combinations and higher dosages, enjoined the restrictions on § 125.1(c)'s essential nutrients, invalidated § 125.1(h)'s drug designation, required further evidence or qualification of the iron-related prohibition, and enjoined enforcement against natural fresh produce. It required the record reopened for reasonable cross-examination by Robinson or a similarly interested representative. The maxima were substantively sustainable subject to that procedural defect.
sections.Reasoning:
An arguable invocation of §§ 401 and 403(j) supplied jurisdiction, and judicial economy supported reviewing the drug-classification provision as an integral part of the program. On authority, § 403(j) did not exclude standardized foods, and dietary supplement had become a common market designation. The FDA had substantial evidence of bewildering variation in ingredients and dosages, and Quaker Oats established that identity standards could exclude beneficial ingredients; weighing costs to sophisticated consumers against benefits to ordinary ones belonged primarily to the FDA.

Broad authority did not justify an all-or-nothing approach. The existing exceptions mechanism did not assure that the FDA would balance lost freedom against actual added confusion, and it did not permit requests to raise maxima. The absence of an established allowance did not itself justify banning an acknowledged essential nutrient. The drug designation failed because pharmacopoeia listing was counsel's post hoc justification, and the agency's actual rationale, that high doses had no nutritional use, mischaracterized the record; § 201(g)(1)(B) turned on therapeutic intent, which nutritional uselessness for most people did not alone establish.

On procedure, this was formal rulemaking under § 556, whose subsection (d) protected cross-examination necessary for full and true disclosure but not unlimited questioning. Robinson's persistence could have been controlled by limits rather than total exclusion. Sebrell's testimony uniquely supported key findings, other questioners did not cure the exclusion, and the court could not rule out a significant probability that vigorous examination would change the decision or the record. The remand was limited, not a fresh unrestricted hearing. Other procedural objections were rejected.

The casebook recounts the long nutritional-supplement proceeding and the cross-examination remand.

LRS-CLOSURE-015.rule: An agency may not dispense with notice and comment under the good-cause exception merely by characterizing its revised rules as compliance with new legislation, when the legislation leaves it new regulatory judgments to make.

sections.Parties: Manufacturers and trade associations petitioned for review of the FDA's reissued vitamin-and-mineral regulations, as did Dr. Miles Robinson, who appeared pro se. The FDA, through its Commissioner, was the respondent. The petitioners wanted the rules withdrawn and a new proceeding allowing participation, and raised further objections to particular provisions; the FDA defended its decision to issue final rules without further public participation.
sections.Procedural History:
In 1974 the Second Circuit broadly sustained the FDA's identity standards but stayed enforcement and remanded for particular corrections, including reopened cross-examination. In May 1975 the FDA announced opportunities to apply for additional formulations, proposed amendments, and a reopened hearing, which was held in November 1975; the ALJ concluded the questioning did not require different rules. Congress enacted Public Law 94-278 on April 22, 1976. The FDA issued final rules on October 19, 1976 without further participation concerning that legislation. The manufacturers' November 30 urgent petition sought withdrawal and a new proposed order; the FDA answered only in April 1977, invoking good cause. The rules were later postponed until July 1, 1979.

On petitions for review, the Second Circuit on February 16, 1978 vacated the regulations and remanded to the Commissioner.
sections.Material Facts:
The FDA's supplement-regulation effort began in 1962 and generated twenty-two months of hearings. After the 1974 remand, because Dr. Sebrell was no longer a Food and Nutrition Board member, the FDA tendered his successor as chair, Dr. Alfred Harper, at a six-day hearing that added 1,119 transcript pages.

Public Law 94-278 then added § 411. For covered special-dietary foods it generally barred maximum-potency limits, drug classification based solely on allegedly irrational or useless potency, and limits on ingredient combinations or numbers, with exceptions for products represented for disease treatment or management, children under twelve, and pregnant or lactating women. Section 501(b) directed that amendments implementing § 411 be promulgated under APA § 553.

The October 1976 final rules largely readopted the earlier scheme with revised organization, corrections, and an exemption from the restrictions Congress had forbidden. The FDA treated almost all formulation applications as moot and added a food-additive provision. The original final rule said only that the FDA had revised the rules in recognition of Congress's action. In April 1977 the agency invoked good cause to dispense with participation on the ground that Congress had already determined the changes, and it rejected renewed trial-type hearings.
sections.Issue: Could the FDA reissue its supplement regulations after the 1976 amendment without notice and comment, relying on § 553's good-cause exception because the revisions merely complied with Congress? The court also addressed, to guide further proceedings, objections concerning the recommended allowances, minimum potency limits, essential nutrients, the variance standard, iron labeling, and the food-additive provision.
sections.Holding: The Second Circuit in 1978, in a unanimous opinion by Friendly for a panel with Smith and Meskill, held that the FDA could not bypass notice and comment merely because it characterized the revisions as compliance with Congress. Notice and comment under § 553 was required, though renewed trial-type proceedings were not. The court vacated the regulations and remanded to the Commissioner. To guide further proceedings it upheld the minimum potency limits and found no infirmity in the food-additive provision, § 105.85(f), but found the continued exclusion of essential nutrients lacking allowances inadequately justified, the variance standard in need of correction, and the iron proviso inconsistent with its prior ruling.
sections.Reasoning:
Section 501(b) plainly reached these rules even though the earlier court had stayed them. The court accepted that § 553's exceptions came along with Congress's reference to that section, but they did not apply. The original final rule contained no proper good-cause finding; saying the FDA had revised the rules in recognition of Congress described what it did, not why participation should be omitted. The court considered the belated justification suspect and left open whether such a finding could ever be supplied on reconsideration.

The reasons would fail anyway. The exceptions were narrow. Fourteen years of proceedings followed by the agency's own extended stay showed no emergency, and this was no minor technical adjustment: Congress removed old powers, imposed new labeling duties, and left the FDA choices about whether and how to regulate the remaining protected groups. A record supporting an all-consumer scheme might not support narrower rules for those groups. The task was a new regulatory judgment, not simply cutting forbidden provisions from a completed rule. Because Congress chose § 553, formal proceedings were not required, and the agency need not reopen objections previously available or resolved unless the legislation gave them a significantly new aspect.

On the remaining objections, Robinson's renewed bias and methodology challenges were meritless, but the new proceeding had to address whether the allowances suited the three remaining categories. The conference report preserved minimum potency limits. A variance proponent need only show the change achieved the agency's objectives to the same extent. A food could also be a food additive, and the 1976 legislative materials preserved additive regulation for potentially toxic ingredients.

The casebook places Kennedy at the end of the nutrition-rulemaking chronology and notes the failure to invite participation on Congress's intervention.

LRS-CLOSURE-016.rule: A rule is arbitrary and capricious when the agency wholly fails to consider a factor that its governing statute makes mandatory, because such a factor is necessarily an important aspect of the problem.

sections.Parties: Public Citizen and other public-interest groups petitioned for review of the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration's 2003 revisions to the hours-of-service rules for commercial drivers. FMCSA was the respondent and defended the rule. The petitioners wanted the rule set aside.
sections.Procedural History: Congress had directed revision of the hours-of-service rules. FMCSA, which took responsibility after its creation in 1999, proposed changes in May 2000 and issued a materially different final rule in April 2003. Public Citizen and the other groups petitioned for review in the D.C. Circuit. On July 16, 2004, the court granted the petition, vacated the rule in its entirety, and remanded for proceedings consistent with its opinion.
sections.Material Facts:
The prior rules allowed ten hours of driving following eight hours off, barred driving after fifteen hours on duty, and barred driving after sixty on-duty hours in seven consecutive days or seventy in eight. A sleeper-berth exception let rest be split into two periods. The governing law required the agency to consider safe vehicle operation, drivers' fitness, the effects of operation on drivers' physical condition, and regulatory costs and benefits.

The 2000 proposal relied on regular twenty-four-hour schedules and uninterrupted sleep. It would have eliminated split sleeper-berth rest for solo drivers, required a weekly weekend covering two nighttime periods, and replaced logbooks with electronic on-board recorders. The April 2003 final rule instead permitted eleven driving hours, required ten hours off, and barred driving fourteen hours after work began. It kept the weekly limits but added a thirty-four-hour rest period that restarted the weekly calculation, allowing more work in an actual week; the opinion illustrates seventy-seven hours in seven days. It retained split sleeper-berth rest and declined to mandate recorders. The record disclosed no consideration of the rule's effects on drivers' physical health, which § 31136(a)(4) expressly required the agency to protect.
sections.Issue: Was the 2003 hours-of-service rule arbitrary and capricious because FMCSA failed to consider the rule's effects on drivers' physical condition, a factor its governing statute required it to consider?
sections.Holding: The D.C. Circuit in 2004, in a unanimous opinion by Sentelle for a panel with Edwards and Tatel, held that the agency wholly failed to consider the rule's effects on drivers' physical health, a statutorily required factor, and that this omission alone required vacatur. It vacated the entire rule and remanded. The court discussed other serious defects, concerning the eleven-hour driving limit, split sleeper-berth rest, electronic recorders, and the weekly restart, but expressly withheld final judgment on them. It did not mandate recorders or prescribe a replacement schedule.
sections.Reasoning:
Under State Farm, the agency had to connect its findings rationally to its choice and consider important aspects of the problem. A factor Congress makes mandatory is necessarily important to the agency's mission, and the record showed no consideration of the distinct health question.

FMCSA argued that driver health permeated its safety analysis and need not override costs and benefits. The court did not demand priority for health; it demanded consideration. Whether an overworked driver causes crashes differs from whether prolonged driving and lost sleep damage that driver's physical condition, and the two are not interchangeable. The agency could conclude that particular health effects were unproblematic or outweighed, but it had to explain that conclusion. Silence could not satisfy Congress's direction.

The court then voiced doubts without deciding them. FMCSA identified no studies explaining why a shorter workday compensated for an eleventh driving hour, and counsel's citations on appeal could not substitute for the agency's explanation. The cost-benefit model excluded time-on-task effects because their magnitude was uncertain, effectively assuming away a conceded effect. The sleeper-berth evidence did not show split rest was safe. Congress's direction on recorders required serious analysis of costs and benefits, though not necessarily adoption, and uncertainty was not a reason to disregard a congressional command. The restart explanation did not acknowledge the increase in maximum weekly work. Because the agency could reconsider these interrelated matters after assessing health, the court declined to decide them.

The casebook uses the case as an example of APA review enforcing analytical requirements found in an agency's authorizing legislation.

LRS-CLOSURE-017.rule: An agency under a statutory duty to consider a rule's economic effects must estimate costs as best it can despite uncertainty, and must consider a serious, familiar alternative or explain why it declined it.

sections.Parties: The Chamber of Commerce petitioned for review of SEC conditions on mutual funds. It claimed interests both as an investor and as an association whose members included advisers. The SEC was the respondent. The Chamber wanted the two governance conditions set aside as beyond the agency's authority and inadequately justified; the SEC defended them.
sections.Procedural History: In 2001 the SEC had required a majority of independent directors as a condition of ten exemptions. In early 2004 it proposed five new or revised conditions. After comment and a public meeting, it unanimously approved three, and approved the seventy-five-percent independence and independent-chairman conditions by a three-to-two agency vote, the dissenting Commissioners questioning costs, justification, and alternatives. The Chamber petitioned for review in the D.C. Circuit. On June 21, 2005, the court granted the petition in part and remanded the two conditions to the SEC for further consideration, without vacating them.
sections.Material Facts:
Mutual-fund shareholders elect a board that usually delegates management to a separate adviser whose interests can conflict with shareholders' returns. The Investment Company Act prohibits certain transactions benefiting advisers at funds' expense, and longstanding SEC exemptive rules permit some of them if specified safeguards are met.

Reports of late trading, market timing, and misuse of nonpublic portfolio information convinced the SEC that management controls had broken down. The two challenged conditions required funds using specified exemptions to have at least seventy-five percent independent directors and an independent board chairman. The agency majority sought stronger independent control of board agendas and better oversight of advisers.

On costs, the SEC described three possible ways to comply with the seventy-five-percent condition but said it lacked reliable knowledge of which funds would choose. For independent chairmen it acknowledged possible additional staffing costs but stopped because it could not reliably estimate them. The dissenting Commissioners had proposed instead prominently disclosing whether a chairman was inside or independent so investors could choose, and commenters urged leaving selection to market forces. The Act required the SEC to consider whether public-interest rulemaking promoted efficiency, competition, and capital formation.
sections.Issue: Did the SEC have statutory authority to impose the two governance conditions on funds relying on the exemptive rules, and did it satisfy the APA and its statutory duty to consider efficiency, competition, and capital formation, given its treatment of the conditions' costs, the empirical evidence, and the disclosure alternative?
sections.Holding: The D.C. Circuit in 2005, in a unanimous opinion by Chief Judge Douglas Ginsburg joined by Rogers and Tatel, held that the Chamber had standing as an investor, that the SEC had authority to impose the conditions on the specified exemptions, and that its preventive rationales satisfied the APA. But the SEC violated § 80a-2(c), and consequently the APA, by inadequately considering both conditions' costs, and it failed to consider disclosure, a serious alternative. The court granted the petition in part and remanded without vacatur. It did not mandate the disclosure alternative or decide the outcome of the corrected analysis.
sections.Reasoning:
Standing rested on the Chamber's wish to invest in funds undertaking exemptive transactions without the governance restrictions; losing the opportunity to buy that product was a concrete injury.

On authority, § 6(c) gave the SEC broad conditional exemption authority, and the Investment Company Act itself addressed internal fund management and used independent directors to check advisers' conflicts. The statutory forty-percent figure was a minimum, and the conditions applied only to funds electing exemptive transactions.

On the merits, the court accepted that abuses outside exemptive transactions exposed broader governance weaknesses justifying preventive safeguards, and that more independent directors and an independent chairman could reasonably strengthen oversight. Agencies cannot base every policy judgment on conclusive empirical evidence, so the SEC need not have commissioned its own study, and it gave adequate reasons for finding a Fidelity-sponsored study unpersuasive.

The cost analysis failed. Uncertainty about which compliance methods funds would choose could limit the SEC to a cost range but did not excuse doing the best analysis possible. Even if it could not aggregate chairman costs across the industry, it could estimate them for an individual fund, and counsel's rationalization on appeal could not supply the missing analysis. Uncertainty narrowed the feasible analysis; it did not erase the duty.

Disclosure was a familiar, significant option, not a remote alternative the agency could ignore. That the Act did more than require disclosure did not make disclosure unsuitable for every issue. The SEC could ultimately find it inadequate, but it had to consider it or give a reason for declining.

The casebook emphasizes how APA review enforces the SEC statute's economic-analysis obligation.

LRS-CLOSURE-018.rule: Whether to vacate an inadequately explained rule depends on the seriousness of its deficiencies, including doubt whether the agency chose correctly, and the disruptive consequences of an interim change that may itself be changed.

sections.Parties: Allied-Signal, a converter of uranium hexafluoride, and Combustion Engineering, which operated two separately licensed low-enriched-uranium facilities, petitioned for review of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's rule allocating generic fees among licensees and of its denials of exemptions. The NRC was the respondent. The petitioners wanted relief from fees they said they could not pass on to customers or that were disproportionate; the NRC defended its allocation.
sections.Procedural History: The 1990 legislation required the NRC to recover one hundred percent of its budget for 1991 through 1995. After notice and comment, the NRC issued its 1991 rule charging virtually all licensees, and it denied exemption requests. Allied-Signal and Combustion petitioned for review in the D.C. Circuit in four consolidated cases. On March 16, 1993, the court remanded two allocation issues for a reasoned explanation without vacating the rule, rejected another allocation challenge, and directed the NRC to grant Combustion an exemption for fees attributable to double licensing.
sections.Material Facts:
Congress directed fair and equitable allocation of fees among licensees and, to the maximum practicable extent, a reasonable relationship to regulatory costs. Allied competed with foreign converters outside the NRC's fee regime and alleged that bids could turn on one cent per pound while the new fees added nearly five cents, making price increases commercially impossible. Combustion faced a related inability to recoup the expense because of long-term fixed-price contracts. The agency did not dispute those assertions, yet it exempted nonprofit educational institutions after finding them unable to pass costs through.

The NRC assigned forty percent of its low-level-waste costs to materials licensees based on their share of waste output, then charged each large fuel facility $143,500 without a rationale beyond its belief that the charges should be identical. Output data apparently already existed.

Combustion asserted, without dispute, that its two licensed facilities together were operationally equivalent to other firms' single facilities and that historical acquisition explained the extra license. The second license added $836,500, while the NRC identified only minimal additional burdens: mailing a second set of materials and two regional offices handling allegations.
sections.Issue: Was the NRC's refusal to account for licensees' inability to pass fees through, its equal allocation of generic and waste-disposal costs within a class, and its denial of an exemption for Combustion's second license reasoned? Where the explanation was inadequate, should the rule be vacated or remanded without vacatur?
sections.Holding: The D.C. Circuit in 1993, in a unanimous opinion by Stephen F. Williams joined by Silberman and Douglas Ginsburg, held that the NRC's treatment of pass-through claims and its within-class allocation of low-level-waste costs were inadequately explained, and remanded both for reasoned, coherent treatment without vacating the rule. It rejected Allied's demand that generic fees track each converter's individual regulatory demands. It held the denial of Combustion's double-licensing exemption arbitrary and capricious and directed the NRC to grant that exemption. It did not grant Allied an exemption or accept the NRC's current explanation.
sections.Reasoning:
The statute contained no unambiguous command to exempt every firm unable to pass fees on, so under the then-governing Chevron analysis the question was whether the NRC's approach was reasonable. Its first rationale, that reducing one group's fees would shift expenses to others, conflicted with its exemption for educational institutions. Its second, the difficulty of assessing price elasticities for nine thousand licensees, justified rejecting a universal duty but not declining a reasonably accurate and economical inquiry for particular classes. The inconsistent handling made the denial unreasoned.

An inadequately supported rule need not invariably be vacated. The choice depends on the seriousness of the deficiencies, including doubt whether the agency chose correctly, and the disruptive consequences of an interim change that might itself later change. For pass-through, the NRC might supply a coherent distinction based on education's unusually large external benefits, and vacatur would require refunding fees the NRC apparently could not recover under a later retroactive rule.

Group-level allocation of generic costs was defensible because effort prompted by one firm could benefit its whole class and finer allocation raised measurement difficulties. The waste allocation was not: if benefits depended on output between classes, that seemed relevant within the class too. The court gave little weight to the prospect of a persuasive explanation but still declined vacatur, because total refunds would be a windfall and the $3.8 million apparently could be recovered from no one; firms whose correct liability was lower should receive only the difference.

The double-licensing denial failed the NRC's own exemption criteria for significantly disproportionate allocations.

The casebook presents the case for the court's two-part remedial test for remand without vacatur; the brief notes that the scholarly discussion of health-and-safety regimes there does not describe this case, which concerned fee allocation.

LRS-CLOSURE-019.rule: A court may issue mandamus to enforce its own remand when an agency egregiously delays responding, including by setting a firm deadline after which rules left in place without vacatur will be vacated.

sections.Parties: Core Communications, a competitive local exchange carrier serving internet service providers, petitioned the D.C. Circuit for mandamus against the FCC. Core sought an order requiring the FCC to explain within sixty days its legal authority for the interim compensation rules, followed by vacatur if it failed. The FCC opposed, urging patience while it pursued comprehensive intercarrier-compensation reform.
sections.Procedural History: The FCC's 1999 declaratory ruling was vacated and remanded in Bell Atlantic in 2000 for insufficient explanation. Its 2001 response relied on § 251(g) and adopted an interim regime. In WorldCom in May 2002 the court rejected § 251(g) as authority but remanded without vacatur because another lawful basis might exist. Core first sought mandamus in 2004; after FCC representations the court deferred, required ninety-day reports, and following a 2005 rulemaking notice denied relief without prejudice. Core filed this second mandamus petition in October 2007. On July 8, 2008, the court granted the petition, ordered a final, appealable order by November 5, 2008, provided for vacatur on November 6 absent notice of compliance, and retained jurisdiction.
sections.Material Facts:
A dial-up user usually called through an incumbent local exchange carrier to a competing carrier, such as Core, which delivered the call to the internet service provider. Section 251(b)(5) generally required reciprocal compensation, with the originating carrier paying the terminating carrier. Because ISP-bound calls tended to flow one way, the FCC believed the system encouraged arbitrage.

The 2001 interim regime imposed declining rate caps on what terminating carriers could collect, a mirroring requirement, growth caps, and a new-markets rule, and the FCC described it as a three-year interim solution. After WorldCom the rules stayed in force while the FCC was supposed to explain its authority. In separate forbearance proceedings the FCC stopped applying growth caps and the new-markets rule but kept rate caps and mirroring.

No remand explanation followed despite a 2004 draft order forwarded to the chairman and later notices. By 2008 the interim rules had operated for seven years and the legal explanation had been missing for six years after WorldCom. Core estimated that capped compensation was three to four hundred percent lower than other reciprocal-compensation rates. On the day of oral argument, counsel said the chairman intended to do everything possible to respond within six months.
sections.Issue: Was the FCC's six-year failure to respond to the court's remand by explaining its legal authority for the interim compensation rules so egregious as to warrant mandamus, and did Core's pending forbearance appeal supply an adequate alternative remedy that defeated the writ?
sections.Holding: The D.C. Circuit in 2008, in a unanimous opinion by Garland joined by Tatel and Griffith, with Griffith also concurring separately, held the unexplained delay egregious and granted mandamus. The FCC had to issue a final, appealable order explaining its legal authority by November 5, 2008, with no extensions; the rules would be vacated on November 6 unless the court received notice of compliance. The forbearance appeal was not an adequate alternative remedy. This was a conditional future vacatur, not immediate invalidation or a direction to choose particular compensation rates.
sections.Reasoning:
The All Writs Act and APA § 706(1) supported relief for unreasonably delayed action. Mandamus was extraordinary and required a clear duty and egregious delay, but the FCC's duty to respond to the remand was undisputed. TRAC supplied six guiding factors, and no fixed number of years controlled.

This differed from ordinary delay in an agency's own proceeding. By leaving the rules in place without explaining them, the FCC effectively nullified the court's prior determination and prevented Core from challenging a new final explanation. Mandamus could prevent frustration of an earlier order and protect the court's future jurisdiction, and timeliness was implicit in the remand.

The rule-of-reason factor was decisive: rules intended for three years had run seven, and Core was prejudiced by capped compensation, including as to past compensation. The court respected the choice to pursue comprehensive reform but found no technical reason why stating existing legal authority required years more. A chairman's intentions did not assure Commission action, so an enforceable order was necessary.

Forbearance addressed only future application and different statutory questions, whereas an explanation, followed if appropriate by vacatur, might permit a challenge to the lawful basis of past caps. The court did not decide that Core was entitled to retroactive payment. It gave the six months from oral argument the chairman had promised rather than Core's sixty days.

Griffith, concurring, questioned the prudence of open-ended remands without vacatur, which could invite agency indifference, and urged future panels to consider deadlines with automatic vacatur or similar devices; he did not decide the legality of remand without vacatur.

The casebook recounts the six-year delay and Griffith's concern; the brief notes that its shorthand of vacatur three months hence should yield to the judgment's exact dates.

LRS-CLOSURE-020.rule: Where two statutory regimes cover intersecting subjects and a saving clause preserves the agency's general authority, the agency may reasonably rely on that general authority, and a remand for an explanation does not dictate a particular analytical route.

sections.Parties: Core Communications and state regulators petitioned for review of the FCC's November 5, 2008 order supplying the statutory basis for its rate caps on intercarrier compensation for ISP-bound traffic. Core also intervened in the state petitions. The FCC was the respondent. The petitioners wanted the order set aside as beyond the FCC's authority, irrationally discriminatory, and contrary to the court's earlier mandate.
sections.Procedural History: The FCC's initial jurisdictional explanation for its treatment of ISP-bound traffic failed judicial review in 2000. Its second explanation, relying on § 251(g), failed in WorldCom in 2002, which remanded without vacating. Separate forbearance litigation followed, and the FCC's continuing silence led to the 2008 mandamus deadline. The FCC issued its new order on November 5, 2008, the last day allowed. Core and state regulators petitioned for review in four consolidated cases. On January 12, 2010, the D.C. Circuit denied all the petitions.
sections.Material Facts:
Dial-up internet access involved a call carried by an originating local exchange carrier to another local carrier serving an internet service provider, which connected the caller to the internet. Section 251(b)(5)'s reciprocal-compensation regime ordinarily required originating carriers to pay terminating carriers for their facilities.

The FCC believed the one-way pattern of ISP calls created excessive reciprocal payments, attracted competitive carriers primarily serving ISPs rather than providing broader local competition, and enabled them to pay ISPs to become customers. It adopted rate caps below previous compensation levels. Its 2008 order relied principally on § 201, which required just and reasonable charges for interstate communications and authorized implementing rules, rather than on the rejected transitional provision; § 251(i) expressly preserved that authority. The order acknowledged that ISP traffic was subject to the reciprocal-compensation provisions even while applying § 201 rate caps.
sections.Issue: Did § 201 authorize the FCC's rate caps for ISP-bound traffic notwithstanding the intercarrier provisions of §§ 251 and 252, was the different treatment of ISP-bound and ordinary traffic adequately explained, and did the FCC's explanation comply with the court's 2008 mandate?
sections.Holding: The D.C. Circuit in 2010, in a unanimous opinion by Senior Judge Stephen F. Williams joined by Chief Judge Sentelle and Senior Judge Randolph, found no legal error in the FCC's analysis and denied the petitions. The FCC's reliance on § 201 was at least a reasonable construction, the different rate treatment of ISP-bound traffic was adequately explained, and the explanation did not evade the 2008 mandate. The court declined to consider issues Core raised only as an intervenor or first in reply. It did not revive the rejected § 251(g) theory or calculate a new rate.
sections.Reasoning:
The parties agreed that Chevron's then-governing framework applied. Petitioners argued that the specific intercarrier provisions displaced general § 201 authority. The court rejected that characterization because the two regimes covered intersecting sets rather than one being a narrow subset of the other: interstate communications need not involve two connecting local carriers, and local intercarrier calls need not be interstate. Dial-up traffic fell in the intersection because it used local calls to deliver interstate communication. With § 251(i)'s saving clause, the FCC's construction was at least reasonable.

State petitioners argued that a call terminated locally at the ISP. That implicitly rejected the end-to-end analysis the FCC consistently used under § 201, which they had not challenged; they did not dispute that the communication traced through the ISP to the internet was interstate.

On differentiated rates, the court assumed without deciding that discrimination concepts applied across the two regimes. On narrow arbitrary-and-capricious review the FCC had a solid basis: ordinary reciprocal traffic was relatively balanced while ISP traffic was overwhelmingly one-way, and distorted payments encouraged arbitrage and cross-subsidies.

The 2008 order required an explanation of authority for the existing rules, not a preselected analytical path excluding § 251(b)(5). Finally, intervenors generally may join only issues another party has properly raised, and the prudential exception did not fit Core, which had itself petitioned; arguments first raised in reply would deprive respondents of a fair chance to answer.

The casebook mentions the decision in a short parenthetical confirming that the FCC issued its explanation on the deadline and that the court later upheld it.

LRS-CLOSURE-021.rule: An agency guidance document that states a settled position and is binding in practice is reviewable final agency action, and it cannot substantively expand a legislative rule without the required rulemaking procedures.

sections.Parties: Electric utilities and chemical- and petroleum-industry associations petitioned for review of the EPA's September 1998 Periodic Monitoring Guidance. Alternatively, they challenged the 1992 Title V permit rule if it already authorized the guidance's requirements. The EPA was the respondent and argued that the guidance was neither binding nor final and that the challenge was unripe.
sections.Procedural History: The EPA issued its Title V permit rule in 1992. Drafts of the guidance circulated in 1994 and May 1998 before the September 1998 version. The utilities and industry associations challenged the guidance directly in the D.C. Circuit in consolidated cases. On April 14, 2000, the court found reviewable final agency action, held that the challenged instructions expanded the rule without the required rulemaking, and set aside the entire guidance. It did not reach the petitioners' separate Compliance Assurance Monitoring challenge or the alternative attack on the original rule.
sections.Material Facts:
Title V of the 1990 Clean Air Act amendments required stationary sources to obtain operating permits under EPA-approved state or local programs, and existing federal and state emission standards became permit terms. Those standards often already specified testing or monitoring. The EPA's 1992 rule, 40 C.F.R. § 70.6(a)(3)(i)(B), required periodic monitoring where the applicable requirement lacked periodic testing or instrumental or noninstrumental monitoring. The parties agreed that a standard with no monitoring, an unspecified testing frequency, or only a one-time startup test needed supplementation.

The 19-page 1998 guidance required permit authorities to review whether existing monitoring adequately assured compliance and to add requirements when it did not, calling for an assessment of adequacy rather than merely the presence of testing at regular intervals. The EPA conceded that its position requiring sufficiency review was settled. A closing disclaimer denied that the document was final agency action or created enforceable rights. Petitioners reported, without dispute from the EPA, that state permit negotiations were producing continuous-opacity-monitor requirements even where existing standards specified visual observation.
sections.Issue: Was the Periodic Monitoring Guidance final agency action ripe for review despite its disclaimer, and did it merely interpret the 1992 rule's periodic-monitoring provision or substantively amend it without the required rulemaking procedures?
sections.Holding: The D.C. Circuit in 2000, in a unanimous opinion by Judge Randolph joined by Judges Williams and Henderson, held that the guidance was reviewable final agency action and that the challenge was ripe. The challenged instructions substantively expanded the 1992 rule and effectively amended subsection (i)(B) without the rulemaking required by 42 U.S.C. § 7607(d). Because the document's parts were intertwined, the court set aside the entire guidance. State permitting authorities could not use the guidance or subsection (i)(B) to demand more frequent monitoring than an applicable standard already provided, except where the standard lacked periodic testing, omitted a frequency, or required only a one-time test.
sections.Reasoning:
The court distinguished the legal force of a properly promulgated legislative rule from the practical binding effect of other agency documents. Headquarters instructions could bind in practice if field staff treated them as controlling, enforcement rested on them, or permit authorities understood that noncompliant permits would be invalid. Both Bennett finality requirements were met: the September version stated the EPA's unequivocal position, and legal consequences followed because the EPA expected permit authorities and sources to comply. Possible future revision did not make the position tentative. The closing disclaimer did not undo mandatory instructions throughout the document. The challenge was ripe because the legality of directing sufficiency review did not depend on a particular permit's details.

On the merits, the court read periodic testing in its ordinary sense, as testing at regular intervals. Where a standard already required such testing, the rule's supplementary authority was not triggered, so requiring adequacy review and added testing anyway was a substantial expansion. The 1992 preamble was consistent with filling missing frequencies, and the EPA had then promised to amend insufficient federal monitoring requirements through rulemaking, which conflicted with having states revise them through permits. Calling the changes monitoring did not make them insubstantial: a different measurement method could change a limit's stringency, and more frequent testing imposed costs.

Under the circuit's then-governing doctrine, a substantive addition or amendment could not avoid required notice and comment by being called an interpretation. The whole guidance fell because there was substantial doubt the EPA would adopt the unchallenged portions independently.

The casebook's note is an editorial account quoting the court's treatment of mandatory instructions and the disclaimer.

LRS-CLOSURE-022.rule: A guidance document that imposes no obligations, creates no basis for liability, and may be ignored without legal consequence is a general policy statement, not final agency action subject to pre-enforcement review.

sections.Parties: West Virginia, Kentucky, mining companies, and trade associations were the plaintiffs and, on appeal, the appellees. They challenged two measures affecting Appalachian surface-coal-mining permits: the Enhanced Coordination Process and the EPA's Final Guidance. The EPA and the Army Corps of Engineers, the defendants, and intervening environmental organizations were the appellants. The plaintiffs wanted both measures invalidated; the defendants defended them.
sections.Procedural History: In June 2009 the EPA and the Corps adopted the Enhanced Coordination Process, and in 2011 the EPA issued its Final Guidance. The plaintiffs challenged both, and the district court granted summary judgment invalidating both measures. The EPA, the Corps, and the environmental intervenors appealed. On July 11, 2014, the D.C. Circuit, reviewing de novo, reversed and remanded with instructions to enter judgment for the defendants on the Enhanced Coordination Process and to dismiss the challenge to the Final Guidance.
sections.Material Facts:
Clean Water Act projects discharging material into navigable waters needed two permits. The Corps issued § 404 dredged-or-fill permits, while the EPA could disallow disposal sites having specified unacceptable adverse effects. State authorities issued the relevant § 402 NPDES permits, with the EPA reviewing them for compliance with state water-quality standards and other Clean Water Act requirements.

The Enhanced Coordination Process covered 108 § 404 applications stalled by litigation. The EPA screened application information against the guidelines governing Corps permits, flagged potential problems, and discussed them with the Corps and interested parties over a 60-day period subject to extensions. The Corps retained the final permitting decision.

The 2011 guidance responded to peer-reviewed studies that mining increased water salinity and conductivity, threatening aquatic life. It recommended that Appalachian conductivity levels not exceed 300 to 500 microSiemens per centimeter and advised EPA staff to ask state permitting authorities to evaluate the issue. The guidance repeated nonbinding caveats throughout, and the EPA conceded that it had no legal impact.
sections.Issue: Did the Enhanced Coordination Process exceed the EPA's statutory authority or require notice and comment as a legislative rule? And was the EPA's Final Guidance final agency action subject to pre-enforcement review, or a nonbinding general policy statement?
sections.Holding: The D.C. Circuit in 2014, in a unanimous opinion by Judge Kavanaugh joined by Judges Griffith and Srinivasan, held that the Enhanced Coordination Process was lawful: no statute prohibited consultation between the EPA and the Corps, and the process was a procedural rule exempt from APA notice and comment. It held the Final Guidance presently unreviewable because it was not final agency action, and did not decide the guidance's statutory merits. The court reversed and remanded with instructions to enter judgment for the defendants on the coordination-process claim and to dismiss the guidance challenge.
sections.Reasoning:
The plaintiffs argued that Congress's express assignment of EPA participation at specified § 404 stages implicitly excluded participation elsewhere. But the process changed neither the statutory criteria nor either agency's responsibilities: the Corps still decided whether to issue permits. The court declined to infer a consultation ban from silence. Coordination among executive agencies was ordinary and desirable, and a prohibition would raise significant concerns under the President's executive and Take Care responsibilities; the court put independent agencies aside. The process was procedural because it changed the way agency consideration occurred without altering private rights or interests.

On the guidance, the EPA conceded that it consummated its decisionmaking, satisfying Bennett's first condition, so the question was whether it determined rights or obligations or produced legal consequences. Under circuit precedent a genuine general policy statement was not subject to pre-enforcement review. Actual legal effect was the most important factor. The guidance imposed no obligations, prohibitions, or permit requirements and no enforceable basis for liability; state authorities and applicants could ignore it without legal consequences, and the EPA could not rely on it to defend a later permit denial. Its wording also mattered: unlike Appalachian Power's mandatory instructions with one closing disclaimer, it repeated nonbinding caveats and lacked relevant commands. Practical pressure on applicants, without an order compelling compliance or a legal penalty, did not supply finality on this record. If the EPA later denied a permit, the applicant could challenge that denial, and the EPA would have to justify its policy as though the statement had never been issued.

The casebook uses the case for its finality account and contrasts its nonbinding caveats and lack of legal effect with Appalachian Power.

LRS-CLOSURE-023.rule: As this district court held before being reversed, a Secretary who rejects a parkland highway route under § 4(f) must affirmatively find that a feasible and prudent alternative exists and designate it so that the decision can be reviewed.

sections.Parties: Citizens to Preserve Overton Park, the plaintiffs, originally sued to prevent release of federal construction funds for Interstate 40 through Overton Park. Secretary Volpe and Tennessee's highway commissioner were defendants. At this stage the commissioner sought another remand after Volpe refused to approve the park route, while the plaintiffs and the Secretary defended that refusal.
sections.Procedural History:
The district court granted the defendants summary judgment in 1970, the Sixth Circuit affirmed, and the Supreme Court reversed for plenary review of the Secretary's November 1969 approval. After an evidentiary hearing, the district court on January 5, 1972 found that Volpe had not actually made the required route determination and alternatively had relied on an incorrect view of the law, and it remanded for a lawful route decision while leaving the design approval standing. No party appealed. On January 18, 1973 Volpe refused approval, and Tennessee's commissioner sought another remand.

In this memorandum decision of April 19, 1973, the district court directed preparation of a remand order requiring a decision within 45 days. This brief covers only that district-court stage, which the Sixth Circuit later reversed.
sections.Material Facts:
After the 1972 remand, Volpe requested a complete analysis in the context of an environmental impact statement and ordered additional route and design hearings, held in Memphis on September 14 and 15, 1972. On January 12, 1973, the Acting Federal Highway Administrator submitted a 457-page final environmental impact statement and recommended a finding that no feasible and prudent alternative existed and that the proposed design minimized harm. The Secretary did not claim the record was incomplete.

On January 18 Volpe nevertheless refused approval. In light of the Supreme Court's park-protection standard and intervening environmental legislation and noise requirements, he said he could not find that there were no feasible and prudent alternatives or that the environmental and noise requirements were satisfied. He suggested possible use of the I-240 circumferential with arterial improvements, the L & N Railroad corridor, public transportation, or combinations, and preferred a tunnel design's lesser harm to the park. He expressly did not endorse any particular alternative, exclude unmentioned ones, or reject the no-build alternative.
sections.Issue: When the Secretary refuses to approve a highway route through parkland, is it enough that he cannot find an absence of feasible and prudent alternatives, or must he affirmatively find that such an alternative exists and identify it, and identify any environmental or noise violations?
sections.Holding: The District Court for the Western District of Tennessee in 1973, in a memorandum decision by Chief Judge Bailey Brown, held that the Secretary had not made the necessary determinations. Rejection on the alternatives ground required an affirmative finding that a feasible and prudent alternative existed, and the Secretary had to designate that alternative. He also had to find affirmatively that the proposed route or design violated NEPA, the Federal-Aid Highway Act, or federal noise standards and identify in what respects. The court directed a remand order requiring a decision within 45 days. It did not approve the highway or select a route.
sections.Reasoning:
The court treated the federal-highway statutes as a cooperative scheme in which states proposed programs and project plans and the Secretary reviewed and approved them for federal funding. Section 4(f) did not shift highway planning to the federal department, but in the court's view it required the Secretary to determine whether a feasible and prudent alternative existed when the proposed route used parkland. Approval required finding no such alternative; rejection on that ground required an affirmative finding that one existed. With a complete record, the Secretary had to decide rather than stop at an inability to make the approval finding, and APA § 706(1) allowed the court to compel that decision.

The court went further and required the Secretary to designate the alternative so that Tennessee could obtain effective review. It acknowledged that the Supreme Court did not require formal findings, so the Secretary need not explain why the designated route was feasible and prudent, but a court could not review an unidentified alternative. Disapproval was reviewable under APA § 701, paralleling review of the earlier approval. The existing design approval need not be reconsidered, though the successor Secretary could reconsider design in his discretion. The 45-day deadline rested on the long delay and the department's familiarity with the record.

The affirmative-alternative requirement was later rejected by the Sixth Circuit in Citizens to Preserve Overton Park v. Brinegar. The casebook recounts this district stage and then the appellate reversal.

LRS-CLOSURE-024.rule: Section 4(f) prohibits approving a highway through parkland unless no feasible and prudent alternative exists, but it does not require the Secretary to identify a particular alternative route when he refuses approval.

sections.Parties: Citizens to Preserve Overton Park and the Secretary of Transportation, by then Brinegar, separately appealed a district-court order requiring another administrative decision after Secretary Volpe rejected the Interstate 40 route through Overton Park. Tennessee's highway commissioner, who had petitioned for that order, defended it as appellee. The appellants wanted the further remand set aside; the state wanted either approval of the park route or identification of a feasible and prudent alternative.
sections.Procedural History: District and appellate judgments initially sustained the 1969 approval; the Supreme Court reversed in 1971. After a full district hearing the case returned to the Secretary, with the design approval left standing and construction activity enjoined. Volpe refused approval on January 18, 1973. The commissioner petitioned on February 1, 1973 to compel compliance with the remand or dissolve the injunction against the state. The district court's May 1, 1973 order required the Secretary to make specified findings within 45 days. The Secretary and the park-protection plaintiffs appealed in consolidated cases. On April 3, 1974, the Sixth Circuit reversed the district court's remand order.
sections.Material Facts:
The original 1969 approval concerned a 3.7-mile Interstate 40 extension through Memphis, including 4,000 feet through publicly wooded Overton Park. Section 4(f) prohibited approval of a project using public parkland unless no feasible and prudent alternative existed and all possible planning minimized harm.

On remand Volpe undertook a broader review, including an environmental impact statement and public hearing under intervening legislation and regulations. He refused approval because he could not make the required no-alternative finding or find compliance with broader environmental and noise requirements. He suggested possible alternatives but endorsed none and did not reject the no-build option.

The district court's order required the successor Secretary to find either that no feasible and prudent alternative existed or that at least one did and to specify it, and to identify any environmental or noise violations. It allowed reconsideration of design, assigned the Secretary responsibility for obtaining any additional information, and discharged the state from further production obligations. The state feared being left without an obvious proposal assured of federal funding.
sections.Issue: When the Secretary of Transportation rejects a proposed highway route through parkland under § 4(f), must he affirmatively find that a feasible and prudent alternative exists and specify it, or is it enough that he is not convinced that no such alternative exists?
sections.Holding: The Sixth Circuit in 1974, in a unanimous opinion by Judge Celebrezze joined by Judges Weick and Peck, held that the Secretary had, at this point, complied with his statutory duties and reversed the district court's order remanding to him. Section 4(f) imposed no affirmative obligation to specify a particular alternative before rejecting a proposal. The court did not order construction through the park, resurrect approval of the park route, or choose another route.
sections.Reasoning:
The court agreed with the Secretary that § 4(f) scrutinized highway proposals to protect parkland and imposed no duty to specify an alternative. The statute was framed negatively: approval was prohibited absent the necessary finding. Congress could have expressly required identification of another route but did not. The statute's primary purpose was protecting parklands and analogous sites, not guaranteeing a substitute federally funded project.

The court also rejected the state's argument that identifying an alternative was necessary for adequate review. Neither the transportation statute nor the highway statute required formal findings. Volpe had suggested alternatives, and a definite finding selecting one was unnecessary to make his explanation reviewable; the validity of his action would stand or fall under the appropriate review standard applied to that explanation. The court did not hold that every unexplained rejection was adequate or that a refusal to approve escaped judicial review.

Finally, the broader federal-highway scheme assigned route selection and proposals to the state, subject to federal approval. States submitted programs and then surveys, plans, specifications, and estimates; the Secretary approved or disapproved what the state proposed and did not undertake the state's planning task. After disapproval the state had to submit another proposal, on which the Secretary would again have to act. That allocation answered the state's fear of being left without a federally guaranteed alternative.

The casebook recounts this appellate result after describing the district court's decision.

LRS-CLOSURE-025.rule: As the Second Circuit held in 2010 before the Supreme Court vacated its judgment, a broadcast indecency policy that gives broadcasters no discernible standard is impermissibly vague under the First Amendment because it chills protected speech.

sections.Parties: Fox Television Stations and other broadcast networks petitioned for review of an FCC order finding broadcasts indecent under the agency's indecency policy. The FCC was the respondent. The networks challenged the policy as unconstitutional and also urged that broadcasting's distinctive treatment be abandoned; the FCC defended the policy and its authority under Pacifica.
sections.Procedural History: The FCC's 2006 omnibus order applied its new fleeting-expletive approach to several broadcasts. After petitions for review and a voluntary remand, its November 6, 2006 order reaffirmed the two Billboard Music Awards findings, reversed the Early Show finding, and dismissed the NYPD Blue complaint on a procedural ground. The Second Circuit's 2007 majority found the policy change inadequately explained and did not reach constitutionality. The Supreme Court reversed in 2009, holding the change sufficiently justified under the APA, and remanded for the constitutional questions. On July 13, 2010, the Second Circuit granted the petition and vacated the order and the underlying policy. The Supreme Court vacated that judgment in 2012 with a narrower fair-notice ruling, so this brief describes only the 2010 stage.
sections.Material Facts:
Section 1464 prohibited obscene, indecent, or profane broadcast language. After Pacifica the FCC long focused on Carlin's seven words and kept a restrained policy toward single, nonliteral expletives. Its 2001 guidance asked whether material described sexual or excretory organs or activities and was patently offensive, considering explicitness, repetition or dwelling, and pandering, titillation, or shock value. After Bono's fleeting expletive at the 2003 Golden Globes, the FCC's 2004 order held that the F-word inherently had sexual connotations and that fleeting use no longer insulated a broadcast. Congress raised maximum fines tenfold, from $32,500 to $325,000.

The order under review concerned Fox's 2002 and 2003 Billboard Music Awards, where Cher used an unscripted F-word in an acceptance speech and Nicole Richie used expletives while presenting an award. The FCC treated variants of the F-word and S-word as presumptively indecent, with exceptions for bona fide news and artistic or educational necessity. It found repeated expletives in Saving Private Ryan permissible but real musicians' language in The Blues not necessary to its educational purpose, and it first found an Early Show remark indecent and then excused it as a bona fide news interview. The record showed stations declining or restricting a September 11 documentary, a novel reading, a local debate, and live news.
sections.Issue: On remand from the Supreme Court's APA ruling, is the FCC's indecency policy, including its treatment of fleeting expletives and its exceptions, unconstitutionally vague under the First Amendment?
sections.Holding: The Second Circuit in 2010, in a unanimous opinion by Judge Pooler joined by Judges Leval and Hall, held the FCC's indecency policy impermissibly vague under the First Amendment, granted the petition for review, and vacated the challenged order and the underlying policy. It expressly left open the FCC's ability to create a constitutional policy. It neither overruled Pacifica nor held all broadcast restrictions subject to strict scrutiny, and it did not decide the abandoned profanity finding.
sections.Reasoning:
The networks urged changed media conditions and parental-blocking technology as grounds for abandoning broadcasting's distinctive treatment. The panel discussed that argument favorably but remained bound by Supreme Court precedent. It did not decide Pacifica's outer boundary because the policy was vague regardless. Fair notice and protection against arbitrary enforcement matter especially where ambiguous restrictions chill protected speech, though perfect precision is unnecessary.

Reno did not settle the case for either side. Lower scrutiny for broadcasting did not eliminate broadcasters' right to clarity, and the FCC's additional factors required a fresh evaluation rather than automatic invalidation. Pacifica had not resolved vagueness and had relied on restrained enforcement that had since changed.

The FCC's decisions labeled some expressions indecent and others permissible, often merely repeating the factors without explaining their application, which gave little predictive guidance. The need for flexibility did not justify a standard broadcasters could not anticipate. The exceptions for news and artistic necessity were equally uncertain, as the Saving Private Ryan, Blues, and Early Show rulings showed. Broad discretion also created a risk of subjective content discrimination; the court did not find that the FCC was actually suppressing viewpoints, but the standard did not constrain that possibility.

The record showed chilling beyond the award shows. Fox precleared scripts and used an audio delay, yet Richie's remarks outpaced the bleeping process, and no system could guarantee prevention. Stations curtailed news and withheld programs discussing sexuality even without expletives.

The casebook recounts this stage in a note before turning to the distinct 2012 Supreme Court judgment.

LRS-CLOSURE-026.rule: Due process requires fair notice of what is prohibited, so an agency may not sanction regulated parties under a changed interpretation for conduct that occurred before the change was announced.

sections.Parties: The FCC, the petitioner, sought to reinstate its orders finding broadcasts by Fox Television Stations and ABC actionably indecent. Fox and ABC, the respondents, had obtained Second Circuit judgments setting those orders aside. The case was decided together with FCC v. ABC. The Government defended the orders, arguing among other things that the absence of a sanction against Fox prevented a vagueness claim.
sections.Procedural History: After Fox sought review of the FCC's 2006 omnibus order, a voluntary remand led the FCC to reaffirm its Billboard indecency findings without imposing a forfeiture. The Second Circuit's 2007 judgment rejected the explanation for the policy change; the Court reversed in 2009 and remanded for constitutional review. In 2010 the Second Circuit invalidated the policy in its entirety for vagueness and chilling. Separately, in February 2008 the FCC found ABC's NYPD Blue scene indecent and assessed forfeitures, which the Second Circuit vacated in a 2011 summary order because its Fox judgment controlled. The Court reviewed both judgments and on June 21, 2012 vacated them and remanded.
sections.Material Facts:
Section 1464 prohibited obscene, indecent, and profane broadcast language, and the FCC enforced indecency restrictions between 6 a.m. and 10 p.m. The FCC's 2001 guidance identified explicitness, repetition or dwelling, and pandering, titillation, or shock value as significant considerations, and prior policy treated isolated material differently from repeated material.

Fox's first broadcast was Cher's unscripted expletive during the 2002 Billboard Music Awards; the second was Nicole Richie's unscripted use of the F-word and S-word during the 2003 awards. ABC's case concerned a February 25, 2003 NYPD Blue shower scene in which an adult character's nude buttocks appeared for about seven seconds and the side of her breast for a moment when a child entered the bathroom. All three broadcasts preceded the FCC's 2004 Golden Globes order, which treated the F-word as inherently sexual even when nonliteral and rejected a categorical exemption for isolated use.

The FCC then applied the changed approach to Fox and ABC. It imposed no forfeiture on Fox. It assessed $27,500 against each of 45 ABC-affiliated stations, nearly $1.24 million in total.
sections.Issue: Did the FCC give Fox and ABC fair notice, as due process requires, that their fleeting expletives and momentary nudity, broadcast before the FCC changed its policy, could be found actionably indecent?
sections.Holding: The Court in 2012, in an opinion by Justice Kennedy for seven Justices, joined by Roberts, Scalia, Thomas, Breyer, Alito, and Kagan, with Ginsburg concurring only in the judgment and Sotomayor not participating, held that the FCC had not given Fox and ABC fair notice that their specific broadcasts could be actionably indecent. The agency's standards were vague as applied to these broadcasts, and the orders had to be set aside. The Court vacated both Second Circuit judgments and remanded. It did not adopt the Second Circuit's broad First Amendment invalidation, reconsider Pacifica, or decide the current policy's constitutionality.
sections.Reasoning:
The Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause requires fair notice of prohibited conduct and standards that constrain arbitrary or discriminatory enforcement; when speech is affected, rigorous adherence also keeps ambiguity from chilling protected expression. The Court left facial validity aside. When these broadcasts aired, repetition was a key consideration and prior policy treated fleeting material differently; only afterward did the Golden Globes order change course. Applying the new principle to earlier broadcasts gave no notice that brief incidents could violate the statute as the FCC enforced it.

The Government conceded Fox lacked reasonable notice but argued that the absence of a sanction, and the FCC's promise not to use the findings in license renewals or elsewhere, removed the problem. The Court disagreed: the FCC retained statutory authority to consider prior offenses in future penalties, voluntary assurances could not cure a constitutional violation, and that legal consequence was combined with reputational injury from permanent findings of wrongdoing.

As to ABC, the fine was substantial. A 1960 statement that televising nudes might raise a statutory issue was an isolated, ambiguous warning, and other agency decisions had declined to find brief nudity indecent, including one treating 30 seconds of buttocks as brief in context. The FCC's comparisons of scene length identified no clear preexisting line.

The FCC remained free to modify its policy, and courts remained free to review it. Ginsburg, concurring in the judgment, stated that Pacifica was wrong when decided and deserved reconsideration. There was no dissent.

The casebook's note describes the as-applied ruling and the reservation of general First Amendment validity.

LRS-CLOSURE-027.rule: Mandamus lies to compel an executive officer to perform a ministerial act, but not to direct how a department head exercises judgment in interpreting and administering a statute.

sections.Parties: Susan Decatur, widow of Commodore Stephen Decatur, sought mandamus compelling Secretary of the Navy James Paulding, trustee of the navy pension fund, to pay her an additional pension. She was the plaintiff in error in the Supreme Court. She claimed benefits under both a general statute and a resolution naming her; the government disputed both the availability of judicial coercion and her statutory entitlement.
sections.Procedural History: Decatur asked Secretary Mahlon Dickerson to pay her under both provisions; on Attorney General Butler's advice he offered a choice of one, and she accepted payment under the general statute under protest. In the fall of 1838 she asked Dickerson's successor, Paulding, to reconsider, and he declined. She sought mandamus in the Circuit Court for the District of Columbia, which issued a rule to show cause, considered Paulding's return, and refused the peremptory writ. She brought a writ of error to the Supreme Court, which on March 3, 1840 affirmed the refusal.
sections.Material Facts:
Congress enacted two provisions on March 3, 1837. A general statute allowed the widow of an officer who died in naval service half the officer's monthly pay, calculated under the pay laws in force on January 1, 1835, beginning at the officer's death. A same-day resolution specifically granted Susan Decatur a five-year pension beginning June 30, 1834, together with arrearages of a post captain's half-pay from her husband's death to that date. Both drew on the navy pension fund, whose trustee was the Secretary of the Navy.

Attorney General Butler advised that she could elect either benefit but could not receive both. She accepted payment under the general statute while protesting the denial of the additional benefit and expressly intending to preserve her claim to the balance. She argued that the grants were cumulative and that Congress's specific direction to pay a named beneficiary fixed an enforceable duty. The government argued that the legislation provided alternatives, challenged her inclusion of rations and interest, and warned that applying the same interpretation to other pensioners could exhaust the fund.
sections.Issue: Was the Secretary of the Navy's refusal to pay Decatur under both the general pension statute and the special resolution a ministerial act that a court could compel by mandamus, or an executive duty involving judgment beyond the reach of that writ?
sections.Holding: The Court in 1840, in an opinion by Chief Justice Taney, affirmed the circuit court's refusal to issue a peremptory mandamus. It treated the disputed payment as an executive duty involving judgment rather than a ministerial act enforceable through that writ, and held that the circuit court could not assume jurisdiction over the Secretary's action in this respect through mandamus. It expressly withheld any opinion on whether Decatur's interpretation of the pension legislation was correct. McLean, Baldwin, and Catron gave separate explanations for leaving the refusal undisturbed; the report gives no formal numerical vote.
sections.Reasoning:
Taney began from Kendall: the District of Columbia circuit court could command a federal officer to perform a ministerial act, so Decatur's claim could not be rejected simply because the defendant headed an executive department. The question was whether this duty was ministerial. Heads of departments ordinarily exercise judgment in administering statutes, and their ability to consult the Attorney General confirmed that legal interpretation was part of those responsibilities.

Taney distinguished that from a court's interpretation in a proper lawsuit, where a court would not be bound by the department head's construction and could pronounce it wrong. That did not give the circuit court appellate authority over the Secretary's executive decisions. Paulding had to consider whether to reopen his predecessor's decision, whether the grants were cumulative, what half-pay included, and how the claim affected competing demands on the fund. Those were matters of judgment, and judicial direction could create conflicting rules and impair executive responsibilities. Kendall involved a specifically prescribed credit leaving no comparable judgment.

McLean agreed that mandamus should be refused but considered the duty imperative and ministerial, a view he said Story shared; he concluded Congress did not authorize two pensions. Baldwin also opposed cumulative benefits, disputed Taney's jurisdictional analysis, and maintained that the Supreme Court lacked statutory appellate jurisdiction over this mandamus proceeding. Catron concluded that the circuit court lacked jurisdiction over this subject and stressed the conflict between judicial coercion and executive administration of public funds.

The casebook uses the case in a historical account of deference; the brief cautions that the discussion should be read with the remedial setting and Taney's statement that a court in a proper suit would not be bound by the department's interpretation.

LRS-CLOSURE-028.rule: Courts ordinarily give great weight to an executive department's construction of a statute it administers, but they are not bound by it, and a construction lacking uniformity and consistency has only the force of its valid reasons.

sections.Parties: Burnet, the Commissioner of Internal Revenue, was the petitioner; he had denied Chicago Portrait Company a tax credit and determined a deficiency. Chicago Portrait Company, an Illinois corporation and the respondent, claimed credit for its share of income taxes its foreign subsidiary paid to New South Wales. The Commissioner wanted the credit denied; the company wanted it allowed, as the lower tribunals had held.
sections.Procedural History: The Commissioner allowed credit for taxes paid to the Commonwealth of Australia and New Zealand but denied credit for the tax paid to the State of New South Wales, producing a deficiency. The Board of Tax Appeals rejected that distinction, and the Seventh Circuit affirmed. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to decide the statutory classification and on February 23, 1932 affirmed the Seventh Circuit's judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
Chicago Portrait Company owned 51 percent of the stock of International Art Company, Ltd., of Sydney, Australia. In determining its federal income tax for 1923, it claimed credit corresponding to income taxes the subsidiary had paid abroad.

Section 238(a) of the Revenue Act of 1921 allowed a domestic corporation, within specified limitations, to credit income, war-profits, and excess-profits taxes paid to a foreign country or a possession of the United States. Section 238(e) treated a domestic corporation owning a majority of a foreign corporation's voting stock as having paid a proportionate share of the subsidiary's tax on the accumulated profits from which dividends were distributed. No one alleged that New South Wales lacked authority to impose the tax.

An initial Treasury regulation defined foreign taxation by reference to a government's power to impose the tax. An April 1919 amendment introduced the categories of foreign sovereign states and self-governing colonies. The Commissioner argued that 'foreign country' meant an internationally sovereign state, that New South Wales was only a constituent state, and that congressional reenactment had adopted Treasury's construction.
sections.Issue: Did New South Wales, a constituent state of the Commonwealth of Australia, constitute a 'foreign country' for the credit authorized by § 238(e) of the Revenue Act of 1921, and did Treasury's administrative construction, together with congressional reenactment, require a narrower reading?
sections.Holding: The Court in 1932, in an opinion by Chief Justice Hughes, held that 'foreign country' in the credit provision embraced a foreign government competent to lay the tax for which credit was sought, even though that government was a component of a larger international unit. Because New South Wales's authority to impose this income tax was unquestioned, the Court had no need to determine its constitutional relationship to the Commonwealth or its international status. It affirmed the Seventh Circuit's judgment allowing the credit. No separate writing or numerical vote is recorded.
sections.Reasoning:
Hughes rejected the premise that 'country' had one technical meaning controlling every statute. It could refer to territory, an international state, or a government exercising authority over a particular area or subject, and earlier decisions under tariff and deportation statutes used meanings responsive to those statutes' purposes. The meaning had to emerge from this tax legislation.

The credit's purpose was to mitigate double taxation and facilitate the foreign enterprises of domestic corporations. That burden arose whenever a competent foreign government taxed the income, whether or not it was an international person, so a restriction to internationally sovereign governments had no connection to the statute's practical objective. The legislative history pointed the same way: earlier statutes allowed deductions for taxes imposed by foreign governments or governmental authorities, and the 1918 and 1921 Acts expanded relief without any indication that Congress meant to narrow the covered taxing authorities.

On administrative construction, the Court recognized that courts ordinarily gave great weight to executive construction of statutes entrusted to the executive department. But courts were not bound by it, a construction lacking uniformity and consistency was entitled only to the force of its valid reasons, and an ambiguous regulation offered little help with statutory ambiguity. The Court found no textual or purposive justification for the 1919 restriction; competency to impose the tax, not degrees of self-government, was the useful criterion. Other regulations yielded no coherent sovereign-state test, so the Treasury materials showed uncertainty rather than a clear, consistent construction, and reenactment in 1921 did not establish congressional adoption of a rule excluding New South Wales.

The casebook quotes the case in a paragraph on the history of deference.
