LRS-CLOSURE-029.rule: Under the review statute then in force, a Tax Court determination supported by the record and a reasonable legal basis must stand unless the reviewing court can identify a clear mistake of law.

sections.Parties: In four consolidated tax cases, taxpayers, including Collins's estate and Dobson, contested deficiencies determined by the Commissioner of Internal Revenue on recoveries from stock sellers. The taxpayers argued the recoveries returned capital and that earlier loss deductions had yielded no tax benefit; the Commissioner argued the recoveries were ordinary income. The cases reached the Supreme Court from the Eighth Circuit.
sections.Procedural History: The Commissioner added the settlement proceeds attributable to Collins's sold shares to his 1939 income as ordinary gain. Collins asked the Board of Tax Appeals, since renamed the Tax Court, to redetermine the deficiency, and it accepted his principal position. The Eighth Circuit rejected the Tax Court's tax-benefit reasoning and held the recovery taxable as ordinary income. The Supreme Court granted certiorari. On December 20, 1943 it restored the Tax Court's determinations in each case, affirming the Eighth Circuit in No. 47, Harwick, where that court had upheld the Tax Court, and reversing in Nos. 44 and 45, Dobson, and No. 46, Estate of Collins.
sections.Material Facts:
The opinion used Collins's transactions to explain the shared issue. Collins purchased 300 shares of National City Bank stock in 1929, carrying beneficial interests in National City Company stock. He sold 100 shares in 1930 at a loss of $41,600.80 and another 100 in 1931 at a loss of $28,163.78, kept the last 100, and claimed and received deductions for the losses.

In 1936 he learned that the stock had not been registered under Minnesota's Blue Sky Laws and obtained information indicating fraudulent inducement. He sued the seller for rescission. A 1939 settlement produced a net recovery of $45,150.63, of which $23,296.45 was allocated to the stock sold in 1930 and $6,454.18 to the stock sold in 1931. He reported none of it as 1939 income, and limitations barred adjustment of his 1930 and 1931 liabilities.

Even with the recovery, Collins had not regained his investment in the sold stock, and disallowing the original deductions entirely would still have left him with net losses in the earlier years, so the deductions had not reduced his tax. In two of the other cases, the Tax Court had sustained deficiencies because earlier deductions reduced gross income.
sections.Issue: Could a court of appeals set aside the Tax Court's determination that a recovery on stock sold at an earlier deducted loss was a return of capital rather than taxable income, where no statute or regulation prescribed the answer, merely because it disagreed with the Tax Court's accounting judgment?
sections.Holding: The Court in 1943, in an opinion by Justice Jackson, held that no statute or regulation prohibited the Tax Court's method, and that when a reviewing court cannot separate the elements of a Tax Court determination to identify a clear mistake of law, the determination must stand. No controlling statute, regulation, or legal principle compelled taxable-income treatment where the Tax Court found neither economic gain nor tax benefit. The Court restored the Tax Court's determinations in all four cases, affirming No. 47 and reversing Nos. 44, 45, and 46. It expressly declined to adopt a general tax-benefit rule. No separate opinion or numerical vote is recorded.
sections.Reasoning:
Whether statutes or regulations prohibited the Tax Court's method was a clear legal question for the courts, and the Court found no prohibition. Consulting facts from earlier years did not revise barred liabilities or reopen a closed transaction; it helped identify the character of the present recovery, and the statute expressly authorized considering other years' facts when necessary to redetermine a deficiency correctly.

The harder question was whether an appellate court could replace the Tax Court's judgment merely because it disagreed. Since 1926 Congress had authorized modification or reversal when a decision was not in accordance with law, which Jackson read as a limit on review, not an invitation to decide the controversy afresh. Courts had given tax determinations less finality out of habits formed in earlier refund litigation. Jackson stressed the Tax Court's independent adjudicative role, fair procedures, specialized personnel, and sustained exposure to tax administration; letting appellate courts label accounting disagreements legal questions multiplied inconsistency among circuits. The Tax Court's decision still required support in the record and a reasonable legal basis, and courts could give weight to its judgment on genuine legal questions without treating its decisions as binding precedent.

The annual accounting principle did not say whether connected events should be integrated or divided; absent a controlling statute or regulation, that choice belonged to the Tax Court. The basis-adjustment statute did not automatically reduce Collins's basis to zero. The appellate court's error was treating an accounting question as a fixed legal rule. The same division of functions sustained the Tax Court's determinations against the two taxpayers whose deductions had reduced gross income.

The casebook quotes the case in a historical comparison of Gray, Dobson, and Hearst.

LRS-CLOSURE-030.rule: In extraordinary cases, courts hesitate before reading statutory ambiguity as an implicit delegation to an agency of authority over a significant part of the economy, especially where later, more specific legislation shows Congress withheld it.

sections.Parties: The FDA was the petitioner and defended its 1996 rule regulating cigarettes and smokeless tobacco. Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp. and other tobacco manufacturers, retailers, and advertisers, the respondents, had sued to challenge the rule. They disputed the FDA's jurisdiction over tobacco, argued that the restrictions exceeded its device powers, and raised a First Amendment challenge.
sections.Procedural History: The FDA proposed its new approach in 1995 and issued the final rule in August 1996. The challengers sued in the Middle District of North Carolina. The district court upheld jurisdiction and the access and labeling rules but held the advertising and promotion restrictions outside § 360j(e); it stayed the upheld rules except the ban on sales to minors and certified the order for interlocutory appeal. The Fourth Circuit reversed on jurisdiction and did not decide the alternative device-power and constitutional questions. The Supreme Court granted certiorari on the FDA's authority over tobacco as customarily marketed and on March 21, 2000 affirmed the Fourth Circuit.
sections.Material Facts:
The Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act authorized regulation of drugs and devices, defined to include articles intended to affect the body's structure or functions. The FDA had historically disclaimed authority over tobacco marketed without therapeutic claims.

In the 1996 rule the FDA concluded that nicotine was a drug and that cigarettes and smokeless tobacco were delivery devices. It found nicotine's effects, including addiction, stimulation, tranquilization, and weight control, intended because manufacturers could foresee them, consumers predominantly sought them, and industry research and product design showed deliberate delivery of active doses. The rulemaking record documented more than 400,000 annual tobacco-related deaths and found that most adult smokers had begun before age 18.

The rule prohibited sales to people under 18, required photographic age verification for purchasers under 27, restricted package sizes, free samples, self-service sales, and vending machines, restricted advertising, promotional items, and sponsorships, and required a label. The FDA relied on its restricted-device authority, § 360j(e). Congress had passed six tobacco-and-health enactments since 1965, including warning requirements and broadcast-advertising prohibitions.
sections.Issue: Did the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, read together with Congress's tobacco-specific legislation, give the FDA authority to regulate tobacco products as customarily marketed, that is, without manufacturers' claims of therapeutic benefit?
sections.Holding: The Court in 2000, in an opinion by O'Connor for a five-Justice majority joined by Rehnquist, Scalia, Kennedy, and Thomas, held that the Act, read with Congress's tobacco-specific legislation, did not authorize the FDA to regulate tobacco products as customarily marketed. Applying the then-governing Chevron framework, it found the asserted jurisdiction inconsistent with Congress's clear intent, and it affirmed the Fourth Circuit without deciding the First Amendment challenge. The majority assumed for argument that a product could meet the intended-effects definition without a therapeutic claim. Breyer dissented, joined by Stevens, Souter, and Ginsburg.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority asked first whether Congress had answered the precise question, looking to the whole statute's structure, later and more specific enactments, and the economic and political significance of the authority claimed.

The Act required drugs and devices remaining on the market to be safe and effective for their intended use. Given the FDA's own findings, tobacco would be misbranded and could not receive the required safety determination, so if it fell within the scheme it would have to be removed from the market. Yet Congress's tobacco legislation contemplated continued sales. The FDA's answer, that a ban might cause greater harm, compared regulatory alternatives rather than asking whether the product's therapeutic benefits outweighed its risks to the consumer.

Congress enacted its tobacco laws against repeated FDA disclaimers of authority and created a specific scheme that reserved central tobacco-policy decisions to itself and prohibited additional agency-imposed health-related labeling. The Court denied relying merely on failed bills or inaction, and it did not hold that an agency could never change an interpretation.

Finally, Chevron ordinarily treated ambiguity as implicit delegation, but extraordinary cases could warrant hesitation. The FDA asserted power over a significant part of the economy, including potential power to ban tobacco, and it was unlikely Congress delegated that decision through general definitions and safety provisions. That consideration supported the full statutory analysis rather than standing alone.

Breyer, dissenting, read the text, purpose, and 1938 history as supporting jurisdiction, denied that jurisdiction compelled a ban, found the later laws ambivalent, and attributed the earlier disclaimers mainly to an inability to prove manufacturer intent.

The casebook quotes the passage on extraordinary cases from the final part of the majority's analysis.

LRS-CLOSURE-031.rule: Under the then-governing Chevron framework, a court defers to an agency's permissible interpretation of a statutory ambiguity even when the ambiguity concerns the scope of the agency's own authority.

sections.Parties: Arlington and San Antonio, the petitioners, challenged an FCC declaratory ruling setting presumptive time periods for local action on wireless siting applications; a companion petition came from the New Orleans City Council's telecommunications committee. The FCC was the respondent. They argued that Congress withheld FCC authority to interpret the siting limitations; the FCC defended its ruling, which the Fifth Circuit had upheld.
sections.Procedural History: In July 2008, CTIA-The Wireless Association asked the FCC to clarify the reasonable-time requirement, and in November 2009 the Commission issued a declaratory ruling. Arlington and San Antonio challenged it in the Fifth Circuit, which applied Chevron to the agency-authority question, found the relevant statutory interaction ambiguous, upheld the FCC's construction, and separately upheld the timeframes as reasonable. The Supreme Court granted review limited to whether courts should apply Chevron to an agency's determination of its own jurisdiction. On May 20, 2013 it affirmed the Fifth Circuit.
sections.Material Facts:
Wireless service requires towers and antennas whose placement is ordinarily subject to local zoning. The Telecommunications Act of 1996 limited state and local siting decisions. Section 332(c)(7)(B)(ii) required action on an application within a reasonable period after filing. A nearby saving clause preserved state and local authority except for the limitations in that paragraph, and § 332(c)(7)(B)(v) authorized an affected person to challenge inconsistent action or inaction in court. Separately, § 201(b) gave the FCC general authority to prescribe rules implementing the Communications Act, including its later-added provisions.

CTIA cited lengthy delays in local proceedings. The FCC's 2009 ruling found that unreasonable delays obstructed wireless services and competition, and it set presumptive, rebuttable periods of 90 days for applications to place antennas on existing towers and 150 days for other applications. Arlington and San Antonio argued that the saving clause and the express judicial remedy showed Congress had withheld FCC authority to interpret these siting limitations.
sections.Issue: Should a court apply the Chevron framework to an agency's interpretation of a statutory ambiguity that concerns the scope of the agency's own authority, that is, its jurisdiction?
sections.Holding: The Court in 2013, in an opinion by Scalia joined by Thomas, Ginsburg, Sotomayor, and Kagan, held that the then-governing Chevron framework applied to an agency's interpretation of a statutory ambiguity concerning the scope of its authority, and affirmed the Fifth Circuit. Breyer concurred in part and in the judgment. Roberts dissented, joined by Kennedy and Alito. The judgment was 6 to 3, with five Justices joining Scalia's opinion. The Court did not separately reconsider the substantive reasonableness of the deadlines.
sections.Reasoning:
Scalia began with the two-step approach: a court enforces a clear congressional answer, and where the administered statute is ambiguous it accepts the agency's permissible construction. A distinction between jurisdictional and nonjurisdictional interpretations would undermine that rule because every agency interpretation concerns the limits of the authority Congress supplied. For courts, an erroneous decision within jurisdiction remains a judicial judgment; for an agency, Congress prescribes both whether and how it may act, so an unauthorized application of power and an assertion of power not granted both exceed statutory authority. Hypothetical common-carrier statutes showed that equivalent grants framed differently should not receive different deference, and prior decisions had applied Chevron to questions of agency power, including decisions rejecting expansive assertions. The federalism objection failed because Congress itself imposed the reasonable-time requirement; the question was only whether judges or the FCC would elaborate it.

Mead's prerequisite was satisfied because Congress unambiguously gave the FCC general authority to administer the Communications Act through rulemaking and adjudication, and the interpretation was issued in exercising that authority. The majority rejected a further provision-by-provision inquiry. Agencies still could not disregard a clear statutory boundary or go beyond an ambiguity's permissible range.

Breyer agreed that jurisdictional labels were not useful but emphasized an independent judicial inquiry, using text, structure, history, and the nature of the question, into whether Congress meant the agency's interpretation to carry the force of law; those factors favored delegation here.

Roberts, dissenting, would have courts decide independently whether Congress delegated interpretive authority over the particular ambiguity before deferring. He did not conclude that the FCC lacked authority; he would have vacated and remanded for the Fifth Circuit to decide delegation independently.

The casebook cites the case in a short statement of its holding.

LRS-CLOSURE-032.rule: Under the then-applicable Auer rule, a court defers to an agency's interpretation of its own regulation when that reading is permissible, meaning not plainly erroneous or inconsistent with the regulation, even if it is not the only or best reading.

sections.Parties: Northwest Environmental Defense Center (NEDC) sued Georgia-Pacific West and other timber companies, together with state and local governments and officials including the Oregon state forester, under the Clean Water Act's citizen-suit provision. NEDC claimed they were discharging pollutants without National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System permits. The defendants lost in the Ninth Circuit, and the Supreme Court reviewed that judgment.
sections.Procedural History: NEDC sued in September 2006. The district court dismissed for failure to state a claim, reasoning that the conveyances were not point sources under the Act and the EPA's Silvicultural Rule. The Ninth Circuit reversed: it found jurisdiction over the citizen suit, treated the conveyances as point sources, and held that the Industrial Stormwater Rule's industrial-classification reference unambiguously covered the discharges despite the EPA's contrary interpretation, so permits were required. Three days before argument in the Supreme Court, the EPA issued a final amendment to the rule. On March 20, 2013, the Court reversed the Ninth Circuit and remanded.
sections.Material Facts:
Georgia-Pacific West and other companies harvested timber under contracts with Oregon in the Tillamook State Forest. Rain falling on two logging roads flowed through ditches, culverts and channels into the South Fork Trask and Little South Fork Kilchis Rivers, carrying sediment, including dirt and crushed gravel, with evidence of potential harm to fish and other aquatic organisms.

The Clean Water Act generally requires permits for discharges of pollutants from point sources, defined to include pipes, ditches, channels and other discrete conveyances, into navigable waters. A statutory exemption generally covered discharges composed entirely of stormwater, but not those associated with industrial activity. The EPA's Industrial Stormwater Rule defined that category through conveyances directly related to manufacturing, processing or raw-material storage areas at an industrial plant, and listed industrial classifications including lumber and wood products. The EPA read the rule as not covering this runoff.

The amendment issued three days before argument specified that covered logging operations were rock crushing, gravel washing, log sorting and log storage facilities, and was meant to clarify the rule going forward.
sections.Issue: Whether § 1369(b) barred the district-court citizen suit, whether the EPA's amendment mooted the cases, and whether the preamendment Industrial Stormwater Rule, as the EPA interpreted it, exempted the logging-road runoff from federal discharge-permit requirements.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 2013, in an opinion by Justice Kennedy joined by Roberts, Thomas, Ginsburg, Alito, Sotomayor and Kagan, held that the suit was properly brought, that the amendment did not moot the cases, and that the EPA's permissible interpretation of its preamendment Industrial Stormwater Rule exempted the runoff at issue from permit requirements. Scalia joined the factual and jurisdictional parts but dissented on the merits, making the judgment 7-1; Breyer did not participate. The Court did not decide whether the conveyances were statutory point sources and did not interpret the amended rule.
sections.Reasoning:
Section 1369(b), which channels challenges to specified EPA actions to the courts of appeals, did not bar the suit, because NEDC sued alleged violators to enforce what was at least a permissible construction of the Silvicultural Rule rather than to invalidate a regulation. The amendment did not moot the cases: the earlier rule governed past discharges, and proven violations could support penalties, fees or other relief.

On the merits, the statutory phrase 'associated with industrial activity' did not unambiguously include the runoff; industry could mean economic activity generally or narrower manufacturing and processing, and Congress had not foreclosed a more specific agency definition. The EPA read its rule as addressing traditional industrial facilities, such as sawmills, rather than temporary outdoor harvesting operations, and the rule's references to facilities, establishments, manufacturing, processing, storage and industrial plants supported that reading. Under the then-applicable Auer rule, the interpretation needed only to be permissible, not the only or best reading, and it was not plainly erroneous or inconsistent with the regulation. It was also consistent with prior practice rather than a changed or litigation-driven position, and the EPA could reasonably regard further federal regulation as duplicative given Oregon's detailed practices.

Roberts, joined by Alito, concurred: Scalia's objections to Seminole Rock and Auer were serious, but reconsideration should await a case properly presenting the issue. Scalia would abandon Auer, arguing that letting the rulemaker control its own rule's ambiguities encourages vague drafting and offends separation-of-powers principles, and would affirm the Ninth Circuit on the fairest reading of the regulation. The casebook quotes Scalia's separation-of-powers critique, which is his separate opinion and not the Court's holding.

LRS-CLOSURE-033.rule: A district court cannot compel NLRB officials to prosecute unfair-labor-practice charges, because Congress gave the General Counsel final authority over complaints; possible serious and irreparable harm does not supply jurisdiction absent the prescribed statutory route.

sections.Parties: Maurice and William Dunn, who owned four corporations operating grocery stores in Memphis, were the plaintiff employers and the appellants. The defendants included the Retail Clerks unions and their representatives, NLRB Regional Director Reynolds, and two other Board employees. The employers sought $500,000, protection of their asserted rights, injunctions against the union, or an order requiring Reynolds to perform his duties.
sections.Procedural History: The employers sued in district court, invoking civil-rights jurisdiction and conspiracy provisions, the APA, and federal labor law. The district court dismissed for failure to state a cause of action. The Sixth Circuit expedited the appeal because of the requested emergency relief and, on August 22, 1962, affirmed the dismissal.
sections.Material Facts:
These are complaint allegations accepted for the dismissal motion, not facts established at trial. In an October 4, 1961 representation election, the Retail Clerks union received only 19 of 90 valid votes. The employers alleged that union representatives electioneered inside the stores before and during voting, interfered with employees' work, gathered around the voting area and refused to leave, and that an NLRB agent declined to order them out. The employers hired a commercial photographer to document this; the union then objected that the photographer intimidated employees at one store.

The complaint further alleged that an NLRB employee and a union employee threatened three school-age part-time workers into signing intimidation affidavits. All 24 employees at that store had voted; 21 later signed a statement denying intimidation, and the three workers allegedly told the regional director their affidavits were coerced and inaccurate. Reynolds nonetheless set aside the election on November 16, allegedly knowingly relying on false information. The employers also alleged improper recognition picketing, coercion, threatened violence and obstruction causing irreparable harm. They had not alleged taking the available administrative appeal to the General Counsel.
sections.Issue: Whether the complaint stated a claim within the district court's jurisdiction for damages, for injunctive relief against the union, or for an order compelling the NLRB regional director to act on the election and the alleged unfair labor practices.
sections.Holding: The Sixth Circuit in 1962, in an opinion by Judge Cecil for a unanimous panel of Cecil, Weick and O'Sullivan, held that the complaint did not state a claim within the district court's jurisdiction and affirmed the dismissal. The court could not displace the administrative enforcement arrangements Congress established, however grave the alleged misconduct. It did not determine the underlying unfair-labor-practice charges or restore the election.
sections.Reasoning:
The court agreed that the complaint stated no damages claim under § 1985(3), without extended analysis. It regarded the rest as principally an attempt to compel the regional director to act. Under § 153(d), the NLRB General Counsel had final authority over the investigation, issuance and prosecution of unfair-labor-practice complaints; regulations delegated complaint issuance to regional directors and allowed an administrative appeal of a refusal to the General Counsel, which the employers had not alleged taking. The court described the General Counsel's discretion as comparable to a United States Attorney's decision whether to bring a criminal charge. The statute provided no appeal from that enforcement decision; Congress instead made the Board the administrative adjudicator and allowed appellate review of its final orders. That scheme gave an employer no separate district-court route to compel prosecution. The Norris-LaGuardia Act also restricted injunctions in labor disputes, and the complaint did not allege the circumstances needed for its exception.

As to the election, the regulation gave the regional director discretion to dispose of objections, which the court considered unreviewable in this suit. The employers could have requested a new election but chose to stand on the original result, and no district-court mechanism existed to reinstate it.

The court condemned the alleged behavior if true and expected the General Counsel to correct any demonstrated abuses, but possible serious and irreparable harm from withholding or abusing administrative powers did not supply jurisdiction.

LRS-CLOSURE-034.rule: A court cannot order the NLRB General Counsel to issue a complaint, but it may correct an erroneous legal construction that prevented any consideration of charges; the six-month limitations period does not begin before affected employees exist.

sections.Parties: The Southern California District Council of Laborers and its affiliated Local 1184, labor organizations that had filed unfair-labor-practice charges against Christiana Western Structures, were the plaintiffs. NLRB General Counsel Ordman, who had sustained dismissal of the charges as time-barred, was the defendant. The plaintiffs sought a declaration about when the limitations period began and an order directing consideration of the charges on their merits.
sections.Procedural History: The regional director dismissed the charges on January 27, 1970 as not filed and served within six months of the agreement's signing, and General Counsel Ordman sustained that determination. The labor organizations then sued in the Central District of California and moved for judgment on the pleadings and summary judgment; Ordman moved for summary judgment. The court heard argument on August 24. On September 22, 1970, in an opinion corrected November 9, District Judge Harry Pregerson granted the plaintiffs' summary-judgment motion and denied Ordman's. This is a district-court judgment.
sections.Material Facts: Christiana Western Structures signed a collective-bargaining agreement containing a union-security clause with United Furniture Workers Local 1010, which did not represent the employees covered by the arrangement. At signing, Christiana had no employees who would be subject to the agreement; that was conceded. Employees were hired later. On January 2, 1970, the District Council and Local 1184 filed charges asserting that Christiana violated NLRA §§ 8(a)(1), (2) and (3). The charges were filed within six months of that hiring.
sections.Issue: Whether the six-month limitations period for challenging the collective-bargaining arrangement began at signing or only when employees affected by it were hired, and whether the court had jurisdiction to correct the General Counsel's reading of the limitations provision.
sections.Holding: The Central District of California in 1970, per Judge Pregerson, declared that the limitations period did not begin before employees existed who would be affected by the agreement, so § 10(b) did not bar consideration of these charges and the General Counsel could not refuse to consider them on that ground. The court expressly declined to order issuance of an unfair-labor-practice complaint or to supervise discretionary enforcement decisions, and it did not decide the underlying violations.
sections.Reasoning:
Ordman relied on Local Lodge No. 1424 v. NLRB, where the Supreme Court rejected treating continued maintenance of an agreement signed with a minority union as a continuing violation, because that would expose agreements to challenge throughout their lives. Pregerson distinguished it: there the employer already had covered employees at signing, who could challenge the agreement immediately and enjoy the full six months. Christiana's arrangement initially affected no one, and its existence might not be known outside the contracting parties. Starting the clock at signing would let an employer insulate a handpicked-union arrangement by waiting six months before hiring, and even earlier hiring would cut short the employees' time to complain. To avoid extinguishing statutory rights before anyone could exercise them, the period began when affected employees were hired.

On jurisdiction, the court accepted the ordinary rule that it could not order the General Counsel to issue a complaint or review the daily exercise of enforcement discretion. This case was different because an incorrect legal construction had prevented consideration at all. Interpreting the limitations statute was a legal question, not an administrative-policy judgment requiring enforcement expertise. Pregerson called the undisputed circumstances extreme and invoked precedents, citing Switchmen's Union, allowing limited intervention to prevent the obliteration of congressionally created rights.

The casebook cites the case for this legal-error exception.

LRS-CLOSURE-035.rule: As the D.C. Circuit held before its judgment was vacated as moot, an SEC no-action position that the full Commission itself reviewed and approved is a reviewable order, and prosecutorial discretion does not shield an erroneous legal premise from review.

sections.Parties: The Medical Committee for Human Rights, a Dow Chemical shareholder that wanted its napalm proposal included in Dow's proxy materials, petitioned the D.C. Circuit for review of the Securities and Exchange Commission's approval of a no-action position on Dow's omission of the proposal. The SEC was the respondent and argued against jurisdiction without defending the substantive basis of exclusion. The later Supreme Court stage is captioned SEC v. Medical Committee for Human Rights.
sections.Procedural History: The SEC's Division of Corporation Finance advised that it would recommend no action if Dow omitted the proposal. The Committee requested Commission review, and the full Commission approved the staff recommendation; its minutes recorded a March 24, 1969 decision, with written notification mailed April 2. The Committee petitioned the D.C. Circuit for review on May 29. On July 8, 1970, that court held the determination reviewable and remanded to the Commission for reconsideration and a sufficiently detailed explanation; rehearing was denied August 26. On January 10, 1972, the Supreme Court held the controversy moot, vacated the appellate judgment and remanded to the court of appeals for dismissal.
sections.Material Facts:
The Committee received Dow stock by gift. In March 1968 its chairman proposed a charter amendment prohibiting napalm sales without assurance that it would not be used against people. Dow said the proposal was too late for its 1968 proxy materials. The Committee renewed the request in January 1969, and Dow announced it would omit the proposal. The Committee then revised it into a request that directors consider a charter amendment forbidding manufacture of napalm, subject to federal defense-production requirements.

Dow invoked the then-existing Rule 14a-8 exceptions for proposals primarily promoting general political or social causes and for matters concerning ordinary business operations. The staff's no-action advice relied on Dow's letter and counsel's opinion. The Committee retained counsel and submitted legal arguments, and the full Commission approved the staff recommendation without explanation. Before the Supreme Court decided the case, Dow included the renewed proposal in its 1971 proxy materials; less than three percent of voting shareholders supported it, which allowed exclusion of the same or a substantially similar proposal for three years under another SEC rule. Dow kept its legal position that exclusion was permissible.
sections.Issue: In the D.C. Circuit: whether the petition was timely under Exchange Act § 25(a), and whether a staff no-action position approved by the full Commission is an order reviewable under § 25(a) despite the agency's enforcement discretion. In the Supreme Court: whether the controversy remained live after Dow included the proposal and it drew scant support.
sections.Holding:
The D.C. Circuit in 1970, in an opinion by Judge Tamm for a unanimous panel of McGowan, Tamm and Robinson, held that the petition was timely and that the Commission's determination was reviewable, and remanded for reconsideration within the Commission's proper discretion and a sufficiently detailed explanation. It did not direct that Dow include the proposal, order prosecution, or make every staff letter reviewable.

The Supreme Court in 1972, in an opinion by Justice Marshall for six Justices, held the controversy moot, vacated the appellate judgment and remanded for dismissal. It neither affirmed nor reversed the reviewability theory and did not decide the scope of the proxy exclusions. Douglas dissented; Powell and Rehnquist did not participate.
sections.Reasoning:
On timeliness, the court of appeals refused to start the sixty-day period with an unelaborated telephone call when written information about the decision was unavailable for a substantial interval.

On reviewability, it looked to practical finality, effect on a protected party, and procedural formality. The administrative process had ended for this proposal; shareholders were the statutory beneficiaries of corporate-suffrage protections, and the Committee was aggrieved even though it could sue Dow separately. Rule 14a-8 prescribed an adversarial process placing the burden of justifying exclusion on management, and the Commission accepted the Committee's submissions and made its own final determination. Direct appellate review fit a request to correct the Commission's legal approach.

The court rejected an all-or-nothing view of discretion: prosecutorial discretion remained significant but could not automatically shield an erroneous legal premise. Courts would not supervise resource allocation or require the Commission to consider every staff response; review depended on the Commission's initial choice to review the staff decision. On the proxy rules, read in light of § 14(a)'s corporate-democracy purpose, Dow had not identified controlling Delaware law, which permitted charter amendments changing the nature of the business, and the proposal concerned a product the company itself made.

In the Supreme Court, the majority found a future submission and rejection after three years conjectural, with no reasonable expectation of recurrence. Douglas argued that Dow's reserved right to resume exclusion defeated mootness.

The casebook recounts the case through its comparison with Kixmiller and notes the 1972 vacatur.

LRS-CLOSURE-036.rule: An SEC staff no-action response that the Commission declines to review is not a Commission order reviewable under Exchange Act § 25(a), and a court cannot override the Commission's discretionary refusal to take up the matter.

sections.Parties: Bruce Kixmiller, owner of 1,000 Class B shares of the Washington Post Company, petitioned the D.C. Circuit for direct review after the company planned to omit his three shareholder proposals from its proxy materials and the SEC declined to act. The Securities and Exchange Commission was the respondent and moved to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction.
sections.Procedural History: The company notified the SEC's Division of Corporate Finance that it intended to omit the proposals and sought a staff no-action response. On March 8, 1972, the Division advised that it would not recommend enforcement action. Kixmiller requested Commission reconsideration; the full Commission declined to review the staff's position, hold an oral hearing, or issue its own informal statement. He petitioned the D.C. Circuit for direct review. On January 30, 1974, the court granted the SEC's motion to dismiss the petition.
sections.Material Facts:
On November 19, 1971, Kixmiller advised the company's general counsel that he intended to present three proposals at the 1972 annual meeting and asked that they be included in management's proxy materials. Proposal A sought charter and bylaw changes giving Class B shareholders the rights of Class A shareholders. Proposal B requested a $75,000 ceiling on employee compensation. Proposal C requested a fairness doctrine for the company's newspaper-publishing activities.

Rule 14a-8 required inclusion of qualifying proposals submitted by a security holder entitled to vote at the meeting. The company asserted that Class B holders could vote on thirty percent of directors and certain other matters but not general business matters, so Kixmiller could not submit proposals on which he had no vote. Kixmiller submitted opposing memoranda. The Division reasoned that requiring a proposal in proxy materials when the proponent could not legally present it at the meeting would be inconsistent with preventing misleading solicitations, and that some basis existed for the company's position. The Commission expressly declined to consider the merits.
sections.Issue: Whether a staff no-action response that the Commission declined to review is an order issued by the Commission reviewable under Exchange Act § 25(a), and whether the court could override the Commission's refusal to take up the shareholder's claim.
sections.Holding: The D.C. Circuit in 1974, in a per curiam opinion for a unanimous panel of Tamm, Robinson and Robb, held that the staff response was not a Commission order under § 25(a) and, assuming without deciding that the Commission's refusal to review otherwise fell within § 25(a), that the court could not override that refusal. It granted the motion to dismiss. It did not uphold the exclusion of the proposals on the merits or direct the Commission to reconsider or enforce.
sections.Reasoning:
Section 25(a) required an order issued by the Commission, and staff members, individually or collectively, lacked authority to make Commission orders. The Commission here expressly declined to consider the merits and did not adopt the staff's position. This was a limit on direct review under that statute, not a determination that every form of administrative inaction falls outside the broader APA concept of agency action.

The court distinguished Medical Committee for Human Rights v. SEC, where the Commission had actually examined the controversy and affirmed the staff's recommendation. Medical Committee itself made reviewability depend on the Commission's initial determination to review the staff position, and that prerequisite was absent.

As to the refusal to take up the claim, the Act expressly committed investigations and the institution of enforcement suits to Commission discretion, and decisions to refrain from investigating or enforcing were generally unreviewable. The SEC's regulation left ordinary informal advice to staff and made Commission consideration discretionary, and the court found nothing arbitrary in applying it. Staff had processed 7,023 proxy statements and 141 information statements in fiscal 1973; requiring full Commission review each time would undermine that informal assistance, and priority-setting was for the agency. A dissatisfied shareholder could still litigate proxy-solicitation questions directly.

The casebook reproduces the Medical Committee comparison and the statutory-discretion reasoning.

LRS-CLOSURE-037.rule: A court may overturn the FTC's refusal to postpone enforcement of a cease-and-desist order only for a patent abuse of discretion, asking whether the Commission's evaluation was patently arbitrary and capricious rather than weighing the evidence anew.

sections.Parties: The Federal Trade Commission brought an enforcement proceeding against Universal-Rundle Corp., a manufacturer of china and cast-iron plumbing fixtures sold throughout the United States. Universal-Rundle sought a stay of the resulting cease-and-desist order pending an industry-wide investigation and prevailed in the Seventh Circuit. The Supreme Court reviewed the Seventh Circuit's judgment.
sections.Procedural History: In 1960 the FTC charged Universal-Rundle with violating Clayton Act § 2(a), as amended by the Robinson-Patman Act. After about four years of proceedings, the Commission issued a cease-and-desist order. One month later the company sought a stay; the Commission unanimously denied it. The Seventh Circuit set aside the denial and required an industry investigation, without reaching the merits of the petition challenging the underlying order. On May 29, 1967, the Supreme Court reversed the Seventh Circuit's judgment, set aside the stay, and remanded for further proceedings.
sections.Material Facts:
The Commission found that Universal-Rundle's approximately ten-percent truckload discounts in 1957 favored customers able to buy truckloads over competing customers unable to do so. The company had pleaded cost justification and good-faith meeting of competition but made no effort to sustain those defenses at the hearings. The order required it to cease selling like-quality fixtures to one purchaser at a higher price than that charged to a competing purchaser.

During the proceedings the company had neither supplied competitors' pricing information nor proposed an industry-wide inquiry. Its stay request asked for time for the FTC to investigate industry-wide truckload discounts. Its affidavits suggested competitors offered discounts averaging approximately eighteen percent, and it claimed a 5.75-percent market share excluding Sears sales, with its own losses and larger rivals' profits. Its marketing vice president stated on information and belief that some competitors sold to customers who might not buy truckloads, and predicted that enforcement against Universal-Rundle alone would divert sales and worsen its losses. The Commission answered that a general allegation of truckload discounts did not establish unlawful industry-wide discrimination.
sections.Issue: Whether the court of appeals could set aside the FTC's refusal to stay its cease-and-desist order against one firm, pending investigation of the rest of the industry, on the court's own assessment of the evidence supporting the stay.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 1967, in an opinion by Chief Justice Warren with no separate opinion reported, held that the Commission's refusal to suspend enforcement rested on a reasonable evaluation of the stay petition and was not a patent abuse of discretion, and that the court of appeals erred by making its own findings. The Court reversed and remanded. It did not resolve the petition challenging the underlying order or the legality of competitors' discounts.
sections.Reasoning:
Under Moog Industries, decisions about postponing enforcement lie within the Commission's specialized understanding, and whether apparently widespread illegal practices actually exist calls for administrative judgment. A court may therefore interfere only upon a patent abuse of discretion. The question was whether the Commission's evaluation of the stay petition was patently arbitrary and capricious, not whether the court thought the evidence tended to establish the asserted facts. The Seventh Circuit crossed that line by making its own findings.

Universal-Rundle's evidence did not establish the industry-wide practice found illegal in its own case. Its violation depended on discounted sales to customers who competed with disadvantaged customers unable to buy truckloads, and the stay materials did not show comparable anticompetitive effects from competitors' discounts. The vice president's unsupported speculation did not show the company would be sacrificed or substantially injured.

The Court added that even proof of identical violations by every competitor and substantial injury would not necessarily require a stay: the Commission could weigh the harm of continued violations and decide how to allocate funds and personnel. That discretion was not unbridled; the FTC could not arbitrarily destroy one of many violators through its choice of proceedings. Additional material the company later gave the staff was not properly before the court.

The casebook presents the case as review of remedial discretion and asks, as an editorial question, how patent arbitrariness differs from ordinary arbitrary-and-capricious review.

LRS-CLOSURE-038.rule: As the Third Circuit held, the Secretary of Labor's refusal to sue to set aside a union election under the LMRDA is subject to narrow arbitrary-and-capricious review, and the Secretary must give an adequate statement of reasons for refusing.

sections.Parties: Walter Bachowski, the losing candidate for District Director of District 20 of the United Steelworkers, sued the Secretary of Labor and the union. He asked for the investigative evidence, an agreement extending the period for the Secretary to sue, and an order requiring the Secretary to sue to set aside the election. Bachowski appealed the dismissal of his suit.
sections.Procedural History: After the Secretary investigated and declined to sue, Bachowski sued in district court. The district court dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction; it issued no opinion, but its hearing discussion reflected a conclusion that it could not review the refusal or order litigation. On July 26, 1974, in an opinion amended September 3, the Third Circuit vacated the dismissal and remanded for proceedings consistent with its opinion. This entry covers only the Third Circuit stage, not the later Supreme Court decision in Dunlop v. Bachowski.
sections.Material Facts:
Bachowski lost the February 13, 1973 election by 907 votes out of approximately 24,000 cast. After exhausting internal union remedies, he complained to the Labor Department on June 21, alleging election irregularities and violations of the union constitution and § 401 of the Labor-Management Reporting and Disclosure Act. The Secretary investigated, then advised Bachowski and the union that he would not sue to set aside the election.

Bachowski's complaint alleged that the investigation had substantiated violations affecting the result, yet the Secretary refused to sue or to give his reasons. These were allegations, not appellate findings. Under the Act, only the Secretary could bring a post-election challenge, and the statute called for suit within sixty days after the member's complaint.
sections.Issue: Whether the district court had jurisdiction over a union member's challenge to the Secretary's refusal to bring an LMRDA election suit, and whether that refusal is reviewable under the APA or is precluded from review or committed to agency discretion by law.
sections.Holding: The Third Circuit in 1974, in an opinion by Judge Van Dusen for a unanimous panel of Seitz, Van Dusen and Gibbons, held that 28 U.S.C. § 1337 supplied jurisdiction and that the Secretary's refusal was reviewable under a narrow arbitrary-and-capricious standard. On remand Bachowski was entitled to a sufficiently specific statement of the factors supporting the decision. The court did not set aside the election, award Bachowski the office, or direct immediate prosecution.
sections.Reasoning:
The APA supplied no independent jurisdictional grant and § 402 covered only the Secretary's own suit, but § 1337 supplied jurisdiction because the LMRDA regulated commerce and the asserted right arose under it. APA review remained available unless the statute precluded it or committed the action to discretion by law, and the defendants bore the burden of establishing an exception to the presumption favoring review.

Neither the Secretary's exclusive right to sue nor the sixty-day period showed preclusion. Exclusivity screened out frivolous litigation and centralized challenges in one suit; narrow review of the Secretary would not let a member litigate an independent action against the union, and exclusivity made oversight more important because a wrongful refusal left the individual without a remedy. The sixty-day interest in prompt resolution could yield to an effective remedy.

Discretion was not absolute. The court distinguished a criminal prosecutor's vindication of societal interests from civil enforcement protecting individual rights. There was also law to apply: the Secretary had to determine probable cause that violations occurred and affected the outcome, and if the complaint was meritorious and unsettled the statute directed suit.

At a minimum the Secretary had to explain his refusal adequately. The court went further and rejected complete immunity for the factual determination; applying Overton Park, review should examine relevant factors and clear errors of judgment without substituting the court's judgment. Confidentiality of investigative files was left to the trial court.

The casebook recounts this individual-rights and statutory-standards reasoning within its discussion of the later Dunlop v. Bachowski decision.

LRS-CLOSURE-039.rule: NLRA § 10(l) imposes a qualified mandatory duty: once a Regional Director finds reasonable cause and cannot secure cessation of the unlawful conduct, he must petition for temporary relief and issue a complaint unless the matter is too insubstantial.

sections.Parties: Terminal Freight Handling Co. and Terminal Freight Co-Operative Association, which had charged Teamsters Local 610 with a secondary boycott, sued NLRB Regional Director Joseph Solien. They sought an order compelling an injunction petition and declarations that refusing to petition violated § 10(l)'s mandatory command and that Field Manual § 10230 improperly authorized discretion. Terminal appealed; the Regional Director was the appellee.
sections.Procedural History: Terminal sued on June 19, 1970 and amended on June 26 to add the declaratory claims. After Solien petitioned for a temporary injunction on June 29 and issued a complaint on July 2, Terminal voluntarily dismissed only its request to compel the petition. The district court dismissed the declaratory claims as moot and found the General Counsel indispensable to review of the manual provision. On June 18, 1971, the Eighth Circuit vacated that judgment and remanded with directions to file its opinion as the declaration of the parties' rights. Related settlement and party-status proceedings were separate and not resolved in this appeal.
sections.Material Facts:
On June 12, 1970, Terminal charged Local 610 with a secondary boycott violating NLRA § 8(b)(4)(B). On June 16 Solien found reasonable cause and concluded that a complaint should issue unless the unlawful picketing stopped. He initially sought neither a Board complaint nor a temporary injunction, because on June 18 the union gave written assurance that it had altered its common-situs picketing to meet the Moore Dry Dock standards and tendered an informal settlement. At Terminal's request he deferred the settlement and investigated further. After concluding the picketing remained secondary, he petitioned for a temporary injunction on June 29 and issued the complaint on July 2. The primary dispute had ended June 27, and all picketing ceased June 29.

Section 10(l) provided that, upon reasonable cause to believe the charge true and that a complaint should issue, the officer shall petition for interim relief. Field Manual § 10230 recognized mandatory injunction proceedings but permitted holding them in abeyance where the activity had voluntarily stopped and resumption was not threatened.
sections.Issue: Whether the court had jurisdiction over a live controversy without the General Counsel as a party, and whether § 10(l) requires a Regional Director who has found reasonable cause to petition for interim relief or leaves that decision to his discretion.
sections.Holding: The Eighth Circuit in 1971, in an opinion by Judge Gibson for a unanimous panel of Matthes, Gibson and District Judge Henley sitting by designation, held that 28 U.S.C. § 1337 supplied jurisdiction, the dispute was not moot, and the General Counsel was not indispensable. Section 10(l) imposed a qualified mandatory duty, rejecting both absolute discretion to do nothing and Terminal's wholly mechanical reading, and Field Manual § 10230 was valid under that construction. The court did not order a new petition in the ended dispute.
sections.Reasoning:
The Declaratory Judgment Act created a remedy, not jurisdiction, but § 1337 supplied jurisdiction to decide whether an official exceeded statutory powers; Leedom v. Kyne's rationale applied to disregard of an affirmative statutory command as well as violation of an express prohibition. The dispute was not moot: the parties still disagreed about the Director's duty, recurrence could again affect Terminal, the question was inherently capable of escaping review, and voluntary cessation did not end the controversy. Relief could operate on the Director, so the General Counsel need not be joined.

On the merits, Congress used permissive language in § 10(j) but mandatory language in § 10(l), adopting both in the same 1947 legislation. Legislative history showed concern about the immediate economic harm of secondary boycotts and a compromise rejecting private injunction petitions while requiring prompt agency action; the court acknowledged conflicting floor statements. The Director must investigate forthwith and, after reasonable cause, act promptly. The phrase that a complaint should issue preserved a limited enforcement judgment: he could first demand cessation and negotiate summarily, but if that failed he had to petition for temporary relief and issue a complaint, in either order, unless the matter was too insubstantial. The statute did not require a useless petition where the union had stopped and resumption was unlikely.

Even after petitioning, the Director could settle in lieu of interim relief, subject to the district court's power to reject a settlement that failed to protect the public interest.

The casebook cites the case for this statutory-duty holding and the retained settlement discretion.

LRS-CLOSURE-040.rule: The FTC's choice of pre-complaint consent-negotiation procedure, and its grant or denial of intervention in those negotiations, belong to agency enforcement discretion and are exempt from judicial review under APA § 701(a)(2).

sections.Parties: Action on Safety and Health (ASH), a consumer-protection organization, sued the Federal Trade Commission after the Commission refused to let it intervene in consent negotiations with Volvo. ASH sought review of the intervention denial, a declaration that the consent procedures were constitutionally defective for inadequate public participation, and an injunction against using them until revised. ASH appealed the dismissal of its suit.
sections.Procedural History: The Commission denied ASH's intervention request and a related request to stay negotiations on December 14, 1972. ASH filed its district-court complaint on January 10, 1973. The district court dismissed on January 29, reasoning that intervention in nonadjudicative negotiations was discretionary and unreviewable and that the comment procedure did not establish a constitutional violation; it later denied interim relief. The court of appeals denied a requested stay, and the Commission issued its final order on June 26. On April 17, 1974, the D.C. Circuit affirmed the dismissal of both the intervention challenge and the constitutional claims.
sections.Material Facts:
The FTC's consent-order procedure let staff notify a proposed respondent of an intended complaint and proposed remedy before formal adjudication. If the respondent chose to negotiate within ten days, staff and respondent could attempt settlement. Success could lead to a provisionally accepted agreement placed on the public record for thirty days, during which interested persons could comment and the Commission could withdraw acceptance, modify the proposal, or accept it finally.

On October 12, 1972, the FTC announced an intended complaint alleging that Volvo and others had falsely advertised automobile economy and durability; the proposed order would prohibit those claims without factual substantiation. Volvo elected pre-complaint negotiations. ASH sought intervention during those negotiations on November 6. An agreement was submitted to the Commission on November 17. The FTC provisionally accepted the agreement on March 13, 1973 and opened the comment period, and issued its final order after comments closed.
sections.Issue: Whether the FTC's denial of intervention in pre-complaint consent negotiations is judicially reviewable or is committed to agency discretion under APA § 701(a)(2), and whether the limited public participation violated the Fifth Amendment or the First Amendment right to petition.
sections.Holding: The D.C. Circuit in 1974, in an opinion by Judge Tamm for a panel of Wright, Tamm and Senior District Judge Wyzanski sitting by designation, held that prescribing the consent-negotiation procedure, and granting or denying intervention within it, belonged to agency enforcement discretion and was exempt from review under § 701(a)(2). It also rejected the Fifth and First Amendment claims and affirmed. It did not vacate the Volvo consent order or compel revision of the FTC rules. Judge Wright concurred; there was no dissent.
sections.Reasoning:
ASH invoked the presumption favoring review, but the APA's presumption is subject to § 701(a)(2)'s exception for action committed to agency discretion by law, and the inquiry concerned this particular intervention decision. The FTC Act provided for intervention in adjudication, not in these negotiations, and the Commission's rules excluded consent negotiations from adjudicative proceedings. Relying on Bristol-Myers, the court reasoned that negotiation was a means of avoiding adjudication altogether, and Congress had left agencies room to design informal settlement procedures. The FTC's enforcement authority included judgments about violations, the public interest in proceedings, and allocation of limited resources, and neither the Act nor the rules gave ASH a right to intervene.

The court addressed the constitutional claims separately. Procedural due process required a deprivation of life, liberty or property, and ASH had not identified such an interest with reasonable particularity; a general public desire to participate in enforcement did not qualify, and the FTC Act supplied no private action that this proceeding would determine. The First Amendment claim was inadequately developed; insofar as the right to petition applied, the Commission had not abridged it by failing to expand participation, and the court left the Petition Clause's precise boundaries for a properly briefed case.

Wright concurred, emphasizing that he understood the opinion not to foreclose judicial review of FTC consent orders in all circumstances under § 554(c)(1).

The casebook recounts the Volvo participation dispute and quotes the enforcement-discretion rationale.

LRS-CLOSURE-041.rule: An agency's refusal to invoke a permissive, nonexclusive enforcement power is committed to agency discretion under the APA, and § 1818(i)(1) of the banking statute bars a court from compelling the FDIC to issue what amounts to a cease-and-desist order.

sections.Parties: The Investment Company Institute (ICI) petitioned the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation to declare unlawful, and prevent, Boston Five Cents Savings Bank's plan to sell mutual-fund shares, and then sued the FDIC when it declined to decide the petition. ICI alleged arbitrary agency action under the APA and a Sunshine Act violation. The FDIC appealed the district court's order.
sections.Procedural History: ICI sued in district court and expedited discovery followed. On June 25, 1982, the district court issued an order drafted by ICI, without findings or explanation, requiring the FDIC to hold an open meeting, decide every asserted legal violation, issue a written merits opinion subject to district review, and direct the bank not to implement the plan meanwhile. The FDIC immediately appealed. On February 28, 1984, the D.C. Circuit invalidated the injunction and disposed of ICI's challenge to the refusal to take up the petition, leaving only the Sunshine Act claim on remand.
sections.Material Facts:
In spring 1982, Boston Five Cents Savings Bank planned to sell mutual-fund shares through wholly owned subsidiaries. ICI petitioned the FDIC on April 13. After a May 17 public board meeting, the FDIC declined to decide the petition's merits, explaining that the bank had not yet submitted an application for approval of mutual-fund activities. ICI asserted that the public meeting merely ratified a decision made beforehand in private.

When the FDIC sought dismissal or relief from a discovery order, it offered to reconsider the petition at a new meeting; ICI objected that reconsideration could still end in a discretionary refusal to reach the merits. The district court's order went beyond that offer by mandating merits adjudication. The district court characterized its order as discovery-related and later said the FDIC could escape it by complying with the earlier discovery order, but its text was categorical and it threatened attorney sanctions for noncompliance.
sections.Issue: Whether the district court's order was an appealable injunction, whether the court could direct the FDIC to stop the bank's proposed activity, and whether the FDIC's refusal to decide ICI's petition on the merits was reviewable or committed to agency discretion.
sections.Holding: The D.C. Circuit in 1984, in a per curiam opinion representing Judges Bork and Scalia, held that the order was an injunction appealable under § 1292(a)(1), that the district court lacked authority to command the FDIC to halt the proposed activity, and that the FDIC's refusal to decide the petition was committed to agency discretion under the APA. The court did not decide whether the bank's plan complied with banking law and expressed no view on the Sunshine Act claim. Chief Judge Wright dissented.
sections.Reasoning:
The order's central mandate governed agency action outside the management of the litigation and supplied substantive relief resembling a final injunction, so its discovery label did not control.

Section 1818 protected banks through notice, an adjudicatory hearing and specified review channels, and § 1818(i)(1) barred courts from affecting issuance or enforcement of FDIC notices or orders except through those routes, which presupposed an outstanding agency order. The direction to stop the bank's activities had exactly the effect of compelling a temporary cease-and-desist order, and it bypassed the statutory safeguards: there was no relevant insolvency evidence and no formal proceeding giving the bank notice or a hearing.

The direction to decide the petition also failed. The Sunshine Act alone could not justify setting aside the decision. Applying the circuit's pragmatic framework, the majority considered the need to safeguard the plaintiff, the effect on agency effectiveness, and suitability for judicial resolution. ICI faced no compliance burden and could sue the bank directly; the agency was not the exclusive avenue of protection as in Dunlop. Most importantly, this was a refusal to invoke a permissive, nonexclusive enforcement power: the FDIC had not begun and ended a proceeding, adopted a policy of abandoning statutory duties, or decided a legal question reviewable against substantive standards. Section 1818 supplied no criteria mandating action, and priorities and budgets were poorly suited to judicial reassessment.

Wright would have stayed appellate action pending contempt proceedings and argued that the majority's nonreviewability premise departed from the circuit's Chaney decision. The casebook's account of the case is cut off in the supplied pages.

LRS-CLOSURE-042.rule: An agency's denial of a rulemaking petition is reviewable, but review is extremely limited and highly deferential, with reversal reserved for rare and compelling circumstances such as plain legal errors about delegated authority.

sections.Parties: New York, Connecticut and Massachusetts petitioned the Second Circuit for review of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's denial of rulemaking petitions about spent nuclear fuel stored in pools, invoking the danger that accidents at nearby plants posed to their citizens. The NRC was the respondent. California was an original rulemaking petitioner but not one of the three states seeking judicial review.
sections.Procedural History: Massachusetts in 2006 and California in 2007 petitioned the NRC to revise its treatment of spent fuel stored in pools; New York and Connecticut supported the petitions. The NRC consolidated and denied them in August 2008. New York, Connecticut and Massachusetts sought review in the Second Circuit, which had jurisdiction over final NRC orders under 28 U.S.C. § 2342(4). On December 21, 2009, the court denied the petition for review.
sections.Material Facts:
The NRC's 1996 Generic Environmental Impact Statement treated spent-fuel pool storage as a Category I issue with a small environmental impact. Category I issues were common to nuclear plants, could receive a uniform significance classification, and did not require plant-specific mitigation; Category II issues required individual evaluation. A generic statement combined with a site-specific statement supplied the environmental analysis for a plant's license renewal.

The states argued that newer information showed a greater fire risk and potentially devastating consequences, requiring a higher impact assessment and plant-by-plant consideration. The NRC had studied fuel-pool risks over decades, including fire from terrorist attacks and post-September 2001 information. Most materials submitted with the petitions had already been analyzed, and the Commission examined the one previously unconsidered study and found it less accurate than the studies it relied on. The Commission relied in part on mitigation such as coolant sprays and replacement-water systems, which it required at every operating plant through license amendments and safety evaluations, along with heightened security.
sections.Issue: Whether the NRC's denial of the states' rulemaking petitions was arbitrary, either because the studies showed a risk too significant to classify as small or because reliance on mitigation varying by plant could not sustain a generic Category I classification.
sections.Holding: The Second Circuit in 2009, in a unanimous per curiam opinion by a panel of Chief Judge Jacobs, Judge Kearse and District Judge Gardephe sitting by designation, denied the petition for review. It found the NRC's denial reasoned, supported by relevant studies and factors, and within the agency's broad discretion. The court did not decide whether the NRC must consider terrorism when preparing an environmental impact statement for license renewal.
sections.Reasoning:
The court expressly recognized that denial of a rulemaking petition is reviewable. Under Massachusetts v. EPA and circuit authorities, however, review is extremely limited and highly deferential, at the upper end of the ordinary arbitrary-and-capricious range, with reversal reserved for rare, compelling circumstances, typically plain legal errors about delegated authority. That standard did not deprive the court of power to evaluate whether the decision was reasoned and considered relevant factors, and it considered both of the states' objections.

On the scientific evidence, the states disagreed with the NRC's interpretation of materials the agency had mostly already analyzed. These were technical scientific disputes within agency expertise, and the court would not substitute its own appraisal where the agency's conclusion had a substantial factual basis. The studies supplied that basis for the low-risk conclusion.

On mitigation, the Commission required the mitigation strategies at every operating plant, so the low-impact conclusion did not depend on optional precautions adopted at only some plants. An agency could account for mitigation when judging environmental significance if substantial evidence supported its effectiveness, and the NRC's studies met that requirement.

The court noted a circuit disagreement over whether the NRC had to consider terrorism in a license-renewal environmental impact statement, but did not decide it because the NRC had sufficiently considered terrorist-fire risks here.

The casebook recounts the decision as highly deferential review of a reasoned denial and contrasts it with Flyers Rights.

LRS-CLOSURE-043.rule: Judicial review of an agency's refusal to begin rulemaking is extremely limited and deferential, but the refusal must still reflect reasoned decisionmaking with an adequate explanation and facts supported by the record; deference cannot supply missing evidence.

sections.Parties: Paul Hudson and Flyers Rights Education Fund petitioned the Federal Aviation Administration to regulate minimum commercial-aircraft seat dimensions and spacing, and then petitioned the D.C. Circuit for review when the FAA refused. They sought size standards, a moratorium on further reductions pending a final rule, and an advisory committee or task force. The FAA was the respondent.
sections.Procedural History: The petitioners filed their rulemaking petition with the FAA on August 26, 2015. The FAA denied it on February 1, 2016. The petitioners sought review in the D.C. Circuit. On July 28, 2017, the court granted the petition for review in part and remanded for a properly reasoned disposition of the emergency-egress concerns, otherwise denying review.
sections.Material Facts:
The petition described seat pitch, the distance between corresponding points on successive seats, declining from an average of thirty-five inches to thirty-one and sometimes twenty-eight, and width declining from approximately 18.5 to seventeen inches, while passengers grew in height and girth. It claimed cramped seating could impede evacuation, increase deep-vein-thrombosis risks, and cause soreness and discomfort.

The FAA asserted that existing evacuation demonstrations adequately addressed safety, including tests at twenty-eight- and twenty-nine-inch pitch, and that thinner modern seats could provide more space. It called thrombosis rare and no more prevalent in economy than business class. The denial cited no supporting studies and did not dispute the petition's description of smaller seats and larger passengers. When asked for citations, the agency supplied evacuation reports and medical links, but the evacuation studies did not address how smaller seat dimensions combined with larger passengers affected reaching the exits. The FAA called the claimed successful tests proprietary, did not put them in the record, and declined sealed or redacted submission. FAA regulations required aircraft above forty-four-passenger capacity to be capable of evacuation within ninety seconds.
sections.Issue: Whether the FAA's denial of the rulemaking petition reflected reasoned decisionmaking supported by the record, both as to emergency evacuation and as to passenger health and comfort.
sections.Holding: The D.C. Circuit in 2017, in an opinion by Judge Millett joined by Judge Pillard, with Judge Rogers concurring in part and in the judgment, held that the FAA's evacuation rationale lacked plausible evidentiary support and remanded for an adequately supported response. It rejected the challenge as to routine health and physical comfort. The court expressly declined to compel rulemaking and did not impose the requested seat dimensions or moratorium.
sections.Reasoning:
The FAA had broad statutory authority over aircraft safety standards, and rapid evacuation fell centrally within it. A petition does not automatically require a rule, and review of a refusal is extremely limited and deferential because agencies manage finite resources. The question was whether the refusal reflected reasoned decisionmaking, an adequate explanation, and facts supported by the record.

The petition identified a plausible safety issue, so the agency needed reasonably to address it. Its evidence did not. Studies that failed to measure or control for seat pitch, width and growing passenger size could not show those dimensions were irrelevant; omitting a variable from a test does not prove it harmless. Maximum cabin occupancy was not a sufficient proxy, because larger premium seats could coexist with compressed economy rows. The claimed successful tests at current dimensions were not in the record, and courts cannot assess evidence hidden from judicial view. A refusal-to-rulemake record may be sparse, but not empty of the evidence the agency materially relied on.

The remedy was remand; compelling rulemaking was unwarranted while the agency claimed to possess information that might justify denial.

On health and comfort, § 40101(a)'s public-service factors applied to the Transportation Secretary, not the FAA. The majority recognized that the FAA's safety authority reached at least some passenger-health issues, but the evidence on thrombosis and commonplace temporary discomfort showed no error in declining rulemaking.

Rogers agreed with the evacuation remand but would not reach whether health was inherently part of § 44701(a)'s safety mandate, a theory she understood as first raised in the reply brief.

The casebook contrasts this unsupported denial with the reasoned one in New York v. NRC.

LRS-CLOSURE-044.rule: As the D.C. Circuit held in an opinion later vacated as moot, Heckler v. Chaney does not bar review of a decision to postpone a needed rule, and an agency may not rest that decision on considerations the statute does not permit.

sections.Parties: The Farmworker Justice Fund petitioned the D.C. Circuit to challenge Labor Secretary Brock's October 21, 1985 decision to postpone a federal field-sanitation standard for farmworkers for up to two years to allow state action. The petitioner wanted the standard issued; the Secretary defended the postponement.
sections.Procedural History: In September 1972, El Congreso petitioned the Labor Secretary for field-sanitation requirements covering drinking water, handwashing facilities and toilets, and a December 1973 suit challenged inaction. Earlier appellate decisions recognized the Secretary's discretion over priorities while requiring a timetable, and a 1982 settlement required a good-faith effort to complete the process within thirty-one months. In April 1985 the Secretary decided against a federal standard; Secretary Brock reversed that position on October 21, 1985 but postponed a standard. On February 6, 1987, the D.C. Circuit ordered the Secretary to issue the standard within thirty days of the mandate. After the Secretary issued standards, the same panel on May 7, 1987, before the mandate had issued, vacated the February opinion, judgment and separate writings as moot.
sections.Material Facts:
OSHA proposed a field-sanitation rule in April 1976, acknowledging health hazards from inadequate sanitation, but did not finalize it. It reopened the inquiry in 1983 and in March 1984 proposed a revised standard covering farms employing at least eleven workers in hand labor. Congressional appropriations restrictions barred OSHA spending on farms with ten or fewer employees and no temporary labor camp.

In April 1985 the Secretary decided against a federal standard, invoking priorities and federalism. On October 21, 1985, Secretary Brock found unacceptable health risks and a need for further regulation, but allowed states eighteen months to provide adequate protection; if their response was inadequate, OSHA would issue its standard within another six months. About twenty-five percent of workers within OSHA's relevant jurisdiction remained unprotected, thirty-seven states lacked standards, and only two were developing them. The Secretary issued field-sanitation standards after the February 1987 decision and notified the court by an April 28 letter.
sections.Issue: Whether Heckler v. Chaney foreclosed review of the Secretary's conditional two-year postponement of the field-sanitation standard, and whether that postponement rested on rationales the OSH Act permitted and was adequately supported.
sections.Holding: The D.C. Circuit in February 1987, in an opinion by Chief Judge Wald joined by Senior District Judge Will, with Judge Williams concurring on reviewability and dissenting on the merits and remedy, held that the postponement was reviewable and unlawful and, relying on APA § 706(1), ordered the Secretary to issue the federal standard within thirty days from issuance of the mandate. All three judges agreed that Chaney did not foreclose review. On May 7, 1987, the same panel vacated that opinion and judgment, and both separate writings, as moot; the order did not affirm either side's merits position.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority distinguished the bounds of statutory authority from discretionary judgment within them. Courts must check whether an agency relied on considerations Congress permitted, while review for abuse of discretion stays narrow. Chaney protected many nonenforcement decisions for want of manageable standards; it did not immunize action contrary to law. The majority read the October decision as having already concluded that protection required regulation, leaving only the question of delay.

A general preference for state action was impermissible: Congress had made that institutional choice in the OSH Act, which contemplated federal leadership and a specific § 18 mechanism for state plans. The small-farm exclusion gave no authority to withhold protection from workers OSHA could regulate in order to encourage regulation of workers outside its jurisdiction.
