Existing or genuinely imminent equivalent state protection was a permissible consideration, accepted under then-governing Chevron principles, and could justify a short postponement if virtually all covered workers would soon be protected. The record did not support that expectation, and after more than a decade a further two-year delay lacked support.

Will, concurring, added breach of the 1982 settlement as a further ground, which was his separate position. Williams agreed rulemaking refusals were reviewable but stressed deference on resource allocation; he found one legal error, an erroneous premise that a federal large-farm standard would preempt state small-farm standards, and would have remanded for reconsideration rather than compel promulgation.

The casebook's supplied account begins mid-discussion with the February remedy and Williams's position and then describes promulgation and the vacatur; its earlier pages were not supplied.

LRS-CLOSURE-045.rule: A taxpayer lacks standing unless he challenges an exercise of the congressional taxing and spending power under a specific constitutional limit on that power, and an injury shared in common with the public is a generalized grievance.

sections.Parties: Richardson sued the government as a taxpayer, also describing himself as a citizen and voter, seeking a permanent injunction against publishing Treasury's Combined Statement as fulfillment of the Statement and Account Clause until it actually complied. In practical terms he attacked the CIA Act provision on accounting for expenditures. The government lost in the Third Circuit, and the Supreme Court reviewed that judgment on certiorari.
sections.Procedural History: The District Court dismissed for lack of standing under Flast v. Cohen and because the dispute presented political questions, and initially declined to convene a three-judge court. The Third Circuit, sitting en banc with three judges dissenting, reversed and directed consideration by a three-judge court on remand. The Supreme Court granted certiorari on standing and, on June 25, 1974, reversed the Third Circuit. The Third Circuit's judgment is described only as background.
sections.Material Facts:
Richardson wanted information about the Central Intelligence Agency's expenditures. In 1967 he requested documents published under Article I, § 9, cl. 7, which requires a periodic statement and account of receipts and expenditures of public money. Treasury's Bureau of Accounts supplied its Combined Statement and monthly and daily reports. Richardson then asked how the CIA Act's special accounting provisions could be reconciled with the statement's authenticity and how to obtain the missing CIA figures; the Bureau said it had no further information. Treasury declined his request to seek the Attorney General's opinion on the statute's constitutionality.

His complaint alleged that the government was offering a fraudulent substitute for the required account. The CIA Act provision, 50 U.S.C. § 403j(b), allowed expenditures to be accounted for solely on the Director's certificate. He claimed that his ability to assess government and select candidates depended on expenditure information. His complaint did not state an intention to bring a later challenge to appropriations.
sections.Issue: Whether Richardson had standing, as a federal taxpayer or as a citizen and voter, to challenge the CIA's accounting and reporting arrangements under the Statement and Account Clause.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 1974, in an opinion by Chief Justice Burger joined by White, Blackmun, Powell and Rehnquist, held that Richardson lacked standing and reversed the Third Circuit; the judgment was 5-4. Powell concurred separately; Douglas and Brennan each dissented, and Stewart dissented joined by Marshall. The Court did not decide the validity of the CIA accounting statute or exactly what the Statement and Account Clause requires.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority read Flast as a narrow exception to Frothingham's rejection of federal taxpayer suits based on an indefinite interest in the public treasury. Flast requires a connection between taxpayer status and a challenged congressional exercise of the taxing and spending power, and between that status and a specific constitutional restriction on that power. Richardson failed the test because he challenged the CIA's accounting and reporting arrangements, not an exercise of taxing and spending power alleged to violate a specific limit on it.

His claimed inability to evaluate Congress, the executive and candidates was not a particular concrete injury; the effect was common to the public and so a generalized grievance. Levitt showed that even an asserted violation of an express constitutional prohibition does not excuse the plaintiff from showing an appropriate injury. That perhaps no one could bring the challenge did not change the result; for the majority it supported leaving the matter to congressional oversight and the electoral process.

Powell, concurring, would abandon Flast's two-part nexus test while keeping its result for Establishment Clause taxpayer cases, warning that unrestricted public actions would shift supervision of the elected branches to the judiciary. Douglas would affirm, viewing the clause as protecting the public against fiscal secrecy. Stewart, joined by Marshall, saw a conventional right-and-duty dispute: Richardson alleged a personal entitlement to information and a governmental duty to supply it. Brennan found good-faith allegations of a denied informational right and impaired voting sufficient for standing.

The casebook gives an editorial account of the CIA budget and informed voting that describes the result as dismissal, though the Court's actual action was reversal of the appellate judgment.

LRS-CLOSURE-046.rule: Article III standing requires a concrete personal injury; a citizen's undifferentiated interest in constitutional government is an abstract injury, and neither the provision's supposed precision nor the absence of another plaintiff creates standing.

sections.Parties: The Reservists Committee to Stop the War, a national association of present and former Reserve members opposed to American military involvement in Vietnam, and five of its members, all California residents, citizens and taxpayers, sued the Defense and Service Secretaries. They challenged the Armed Forces Reserve membership of Members of Congress under the Incompatibility Clause. The government lost below and petitioned the Supreme Court.
sections.Procedural History: The District Court rejected standing as antiwar opponents, reservists and taxpayers but accepted citizen standing, rejected a political-question objection, and held a Reserve commission to be an incompatible office. Its partial summary judgment granted declaratory relief but denied the injunction and mandamus requests, which the plaintiffs did not challenge further. The D.C. Circuit affirmed on the district opinion. On June 25, 1974, the Supreme Court reversed the appellate judgment and remanded to the District Court for proceedings consistent with its opinion.
sections.Material Facts:
The suit relied on the Incompatibility Clause, Article I, § 6, cl. 2, which prohibits a person holding an office under the United States from simultaneously serving in Congress. The plaintiffs alleged that reservist status exposed legislators to executive influence and inconsistent obligations, depriving citizens of faithful legislative service; the President's authority to call reservists to duty or discharge commissioned reservists was offered as an example. Actual distortion of a particular legislative act was not established. Four individual plaintiffs were in the Ready Reserve; the fifth's status was unspecified.

They requested removal of congressional reservists from the military rolls, discharge when a reservist entered Congress, efforts to recover Reserve pay received while in Congress, an injunction against future placement on the rolls, and a declaration that Reserve membership was an incompatible office. They proposed to represent antiwar advocates, reservists outside Congress, all federal taxpayers, and all citizens.
sections.Issue: Whether the plaintiffs had standing, as citizens or as taxpayers, to challenge the Reserve membership of Members of Congress under the Incompatibility Clause.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 1974, in an opinion by Chief Justice Burger for Stewart, White, Blackmun, Powell and Rehnquist, held that the plaintiffs had standing neither as citizens nor as taxpayers; the decision was 6-3. It did not decide whether Reserve membership violated the clause or whether the claim presented a political question. Stewart concurred separately; Douglas dissented joined by Marshall, and Brennan and Marshall filed separate dissents.
sections.Reasoning:
Standing and the political-question doctrine are distinct limits, and the Court took standing first here without fixing that order for every case. The injury common to the citizen class was an undifferentiated interest in constitutional government, and it was speculative whether Reserve membership impaired faithful legislative service. Alleged noncompliance with the clause alone was an abstract injury, not actual or threatened personal harm.

The Court read Data Processing's injury-in-fact requirement as part of Article III. Concrete injury gives a dispute specificity, lets the parties explain adverse consequences from actual facts, permits a proportionate remedy, and avoids unnecessary constitutional adjudication. Levitt was a close analogue. Neither the clause's supposed precision nor the plaintiffs' earnestness substituted for injury, and the district court had put merits reasoning before the showing of personal harm. Inability to identify another plaintiff does not create standing. The Court did not hold that a shared injury is always disqualifying; the defect was abstraction, not the number of people affected.

Taxpayer standing failed under Flast because the suit attacked executive conduct permitting legislators to keep Reserve status, not an exercise of the congressional taxing and spending power.

Stewart, concurring, distinguished his Richardson dissent because no plaintiff alleged denial of an affirmative duty to supply requested information. Douglas, joined by Marshall, would affirm, treating the clause as a specific safeguard comparable to the Establishment Clause in Flast. Brennan would accept good-faith taxpayer injury allegations. Marshall saw a concrete First Amendment-related injury to the plaintiffs' antiwar advocacy.

The casebook cites the decision as evidence that injury in fact is rooted in Article III and as the congressional-reservist generalized-grievance case.

LRS-CLOSURE-047.rule: In an equal protection challenge to a set-aside program, the injury in fact is the barrier to competing on equal terms; a plaintiff must show it is able and ready to bid, not that it would have won the contract.

sections.Parties: The Northeastern Florida Chapter of the Associated General Contractors of America, an association of people and firms in construction most of whose members did not qualify for the city's minority set-aside program, sued the City of Jacksonville and its mayor under § 1983. It sought declaratory and injunctive relief on the ground that the program violated equal protection on its face and as applied.
sections.Procedural History: The association sued on April 4, 1989. The District Court restrained and then preliminarily enjoined the program; the Eleventh Circuit reversed the preliminary injunction for failure to show irreparable injury. On May 31, 1990, the District Court entered summary judgment for the association. The Eleventh Circuit vacated that judgment and directed dismissal without prejudice for lack of standing, without deciding the constitutional merits. After certiorari was granted, the city repealed and replaced the ordinance, and the Court denied a motion to dismiss as moot. On June 14, 1993, the Court reversed the Eleventh Circuit and remanded.
sections.Material Facts:
Jacksonville's 1984 ordinance required approximately 10% of annual city-contract expenditures to be reserved for qualifying Minority Business Enterprises, which needed at least 51% qualifying minority or female ownership. Designated projects were reserved exclusively for qualifying firms. The association alleged that many members regularly bid on and performed city construction contracts and would have bid on reserved contracts but for the ordinance. It did not allege that a particular member would have won a contract. These allegations had not been challenged by a factual summary-judgment motion and were assumed true.

On October 27, 1992, after certiorari was granted, the city repealed the ordinance and replaced it effective the next day. The replacement covered black- and female-owned firms, used participation goals from 5% to 16%, and provided five implementation methods chosen project by project. One, the Sheltered Market Plan, retained exclusive competition for qualifying businesses.
sections.Issue: Whether repeal and replacement of the ordinance mooted the case, and whether the association had standing without showing that one of its members would have received a contract absent the preference.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 1993, in an opinion by Justice Thomas for Rehnquist, White, Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy and Souter, held that the case was live and that the pleaded competitive injury was sufficient for standing, and reversed and remanded; the judgment was 7-2. O'Connor, joined by Blackmun, dissented on mootness and would not have reached standing. The Court did not decide whether either version of the preferences violated equal protection.
sections.Reasoning:
On mootness, the majority applied voluntary-cessation principles. The city had already continued the alleged injury through the replacement ordinance: its preferences, especially the Sheltered Market Plan, still disadvantaged the association's members in the same fundamental way, and a lesser degree of disadvantage did not moot the challenge. Mesquite did not require threatened reenactment of an identical statute.

On standing, the Court restated the injury, causation and redressability requirements and rejected the demand for proof that a member would have won a contract. Turner, Quinn and Clements recognized obstacles to being considered for public office without proof of eventual appointment or election, and Bakke treated exclusion from competing for all medical-school places as an injury regardless of whether the applicant would have been admitted. In an equal protection challenge of this kind, the injury is the government's barrier to equal consideration. The challenger must show that it is able and ready to bid and that the policy prevents it from bidding on equal terms. The ordinance causes that disadvantage, and a decree ending the program would redress it. Warth did not require otherwise: the association there complained of inability to obtain variances and permits, not unequal eligibility to apply, and alleged no current project.

O'Connor, dissenting, would have vacated and let the association challenge the replacement ordinance in the District Court, because only prospective relief was sought against a repealed law and the changes were substantial enough to present a different controversy. She did not reject the competitive-injury rule.

The casebook's comparison with Richardson's electoral interests is the editors' question, not the Court's reasoning.

LRS-CLOSURE-048.rule: A citizen's general interest in lawful administration of government and in avoiding wasted public money does not present an Article III case and does not entitle him to a judicial ruling on a constitutional amendment's validity.

sections.Parties: Charles Fairchild sued the Secretary of State and the Attorney General, on behalf of himself and others he purported to represent as citizens, taxpayers and members of the American Constitutional League, which advocated state control of voter qualifications. He sought a declaration that the proposed Nineteenth Amendment was void and injunctions against a proclamation of its ratification and against its enforcement.
sections.Procedural History: Fairchild sued on July 7, 1920 in the Supreme Court of the District of Columbia. That court issued a rule to show cause on interlocutory relief and, after the defendants responded and moved to dismiss, discharged the rule and dismissed the bill on July 14, 1920. The D.C. Court of Appeals affirmed, relying on its earlier Colby decision concerning the Eighteenth Amendment. On February 27, 1922, the Supreme Court affirmed the decree.
sections.Material Facts:
The complaint alleged that thirty-four state legislatures had adopted purported ratification resolutions and another state had supplied a certificate, and it challenged the amendment's susceptibility to legislative ratification and the validity of particular states' actions. It alleged that the Secretary planned to proclaim adoption on receiving one further certificate. Fairchild also attacked a proposed federal enforcement bill, predicting prosecution of officials who excluded women from voting. He alleged that a proclamation would mislead state officials into letting women vote, dilute lawful votes, and nearly double election expenses.

While the appeal was pending, the Secretary received a thirty-sixth ratification certificate and proclaimed adoption on August 26. Fairchild was not an election official. His home state, New York, had already extended suffrage to women through its own constitution and had ratified the federal amendment.
sections.Issue: Whether a citizen and taxpayer with no interest beyond that of the general public may obtain a federal judicial ruling on the validity of a constitutional amendment by suing to enjoin officials from proclaiming and enforcing it.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 1922, in an opinion by Justice Brandeis with no separate opinion reported, affirmed the dismissal on the ground that the plaintiff's asserted interest did not supply an Article III case. The Court found no occasion to examine the court of appeals' rationale about the proclamation and did not decide whether the Nineteenth Amendment was validly ratified.
sections.Reasoning:
The form of a bill in equity could not turn a demand for a declaration that an amendment was void into a constitutional case. Article III judicial power concerns regular proceedings to protect or enforce rights and to prevent or redress wrongs. The threatened proclamation, which Fairchild himself said was legally ineffectual, would supposedly mislead election officials, and the Attorney General's threatened action depended on an enforcement bill not yet enacted and would operate against election officials. Fairchild was not such an official, and his own state had already extended suffrage to women and ratified the amendment. Those circumstances showed the absence of any personal right calling for preventive intervention.

What remained was the citizen's general interest in lawful administration and in avoiding wasted public money. That interest did not authorize an individual to obtain, indirectly through injunctions against officials, a federal judicial ruling on the validity of a prospective statute or of an amendment being adopted. The Court therefore resolved the suit at the threshold. It did not hold that the amendment could never be adjudicated in litigation involving proper parties and an actual affected right.

The casebook gives an editorial account with a condensed quotation from Brandeis before comparing Mellon and Levitt.

LRS-CLOSURE-049.rule: A federal taxpayer's interest in the national treasury is too small, remote and indeterminable to support a suit to enjoin a federal expenditure; a litigant must show a direct injury suffered or immediately threatened by the statute's enforcement.

sections.Parties: In No. 24, Original, Massachusetts sued federal officials administering the Maternity Act, on its own behalf and as representative of its citizens. In the companion case, No. 962, Frothingham, a federal taxpayer, sued the same officials in the Supreme Court of the District of Columbia and appealed after losing. Both plaintiffs sought to restrain enforcement of the act as unconstitutional.
sections.Procedural History: Massachusetts brought its suit as an original action in the Supreme Court. Frothingham's bill was dismissed by the Supreme Court of the District of Columbia, and the D.C. Court of Appeals affirmed. The Court considered the two cases together. On June 4, 1923, it dismissed Massachusetts's original suit and affirmed in Frothingham's appeal, resolving both for want of jurisdiction without considering the constitutional merits.
sections.Material Facts:
The Maternity Act of November 23, 1921 provided an initial appropriation and annual appropriations over five years for cooperating with accepting states to reduce maternal and infant mortality and protect health. Participating state agencies would cooperate with federal administration, submit prescribed reports, and face withholding of payments if funds were improperly spent. A state could accept or reject the offer, and Massachusetts had not accepted.

Massachusetts argued that the appropriations addressed local rather than national concerns and induced states to surrender reserved powers. It alleged that industrial states bore disproportionate burdens and faced an unconstitutional choice between keeping their sovereignty and receiving their share of the money. Frothingham advanced the same general objections and alleged that the appropriations would increase her future federal taxes, taking her property without due process.
sections.Issue: Whether a state, suing for itself or as representative of its citizens, or an individual federal taxpayer, presents a justiciable controversy by challenging a federal appropriation statute as beyond Congress's power.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 1923, in an opinion by Justice Sutherland with no separate opinion reported, held that neither suit presented a case within its jurisdiction. Massachusetts's claim was an abstract political question, the state could not sue as parens patriae against the operation of a federal statute on its citizens, and Frothingham's taxpayer interest was not a sufficiently direct injury. The Court did not decide whether the Maternity Act was within federal spending authority.
sections.Reasoning:
Original jurisdiction requires a dispute of judicial cognizance, and naming a state as a party does not make every assertion of political power one. The statute required Massachusetts neither to do anything nor to surrender a power; it could reject the offer. The tax burden fell on inhabitants, who were subject to federal as well as state taxation, not on the state. An alleged intention to tempt states to yield authority was no invasion where consent could be withheld. The complaint thus reduced to a claim that Congress usurped reserved powers merely by enacting a law, an abstract political question.

The state also could not sue as parens patriae here. Its citizens were also citizens of the United States, and in their relations with the federal government the United States, not the state, was their representative.

Frothingham's alleged future tax increase gave no sufficiently direct interest. The Court distinguished municipal taxpayer suits, which rest on a comparatively direct relationship to the corporate treasury. A federal taxpayer's stake in a national treasury shared with millions was comparatively small and indeterminable, and the effect of any expenditure on future taxes was remote, fluctuating and uncertain. Allowing such suits would invite every taxpayer to contest every appropriation. Courts have no independent power to review and annul legislation; they may disregard an unconstitutional statute only in deciding a concrete controversy, which requires a direct injury suffered or immediately threatened by enforcement.

The casebook cites the case under the name Massachusetts v. Mellon as a short taxpayer-expenditure comparator; the individual taxpayer holding belongs to the jointly reported Frothingham case.

LRS-CLOSURE-050.rule: A private individual who invokes judicial power to test the validity of legislative or executive action must show a direct injury sustained or immediately threatened; a general interest common to the public is not enough.

sections.Parties: Albert Levitt, appearing pro se, moved in the Supreme Court for leave to file an original petition requiring Justice Hugo Black to show cause why he should be permitted to serve as an Associate Justice.
sections.Procedural History: Levitt filed his motion for leave to file an original petition directly in the Supreme Court. On October 11, 1937, the Court denied the motion in an unsigned per curiam order.
sections.Material Facts: Levitt asserted that the President's appointment of Black and the Senate's confirmation were void because Black was ineligible under Article I, § 6, cl. 2, and because there was no vacancy to which he could lawfully be appointed. The Court's order does not recount the factual basis of the objection. The motion papers disclosed no interest other than Levitt's position as a citizen and a member of the Court's bar.
sections.Issue: Whether a person whose only interest is that of a citizen and member of the Court's bar may invoke the Court's power to determine the validity of a Justice's appointment.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 1937, in an unsigned per curiam order with no dissent or separate opinion recorded, denied the motion for leave to file because Levitt's interest as a citizen and member of the bar was insufficient. Black took no part. The Court did not remove Black, issue the requested show-cause order, or uphold the appointment on the constitutional merits.
sections.Reasoning:
The motion papers disclosed no interest beyond Levitt's status as a citizen and a member of the Court's bar, and the Court held that insufficient. An individual who invokes the judicial power to determine the validity of legislative or executive action must show a direct injury already sustained or immediately threatened by that action; a general interest common to the public does not satisfy the requirement. The order cites Tyler, Southern Railway, Newman, Fairchild and Mellon and gives no further constitutional analysis. It thus separates an allegation of structural constitutional invalidity from the moving party's entitlement to have it adjudicated, and it does not say that an appointment objection could never be heard from a properly injured litigant.

The casebook gives a brief account of the Black appointment and the Ineligibility Clause within its structural-constitutional discussion.

LRS-CLOSURE-051.rule: A plaintiff has informational standing under FECA when it identifies information its reading of the statute requires to be disclosed, whose absence harms an interest Congress sought to protect, and that it could obtain if its challenge succeeded.

sections.Parties: Campaign Legal Center, a nonprofit watchdog, and its director Catherine Hinckley Kelley, a registered voter, sued the Federal Election Commission after it dismissed their administrative complaint about Correct the Record and Hillary for America. The FEC lacked the votes to authorize a defense and did not appear; Correct the Record and Hillary for America intervened as defendants. The plaintiffs were the appellants.
sections.Procedural History: The plaintiffs filed an FEC complaint in October 2016. The Commission, then with four members, split 2-2 and dismissed for want of four affirmative votes. The plaintiffs sued in August 2019 under FECA and the APA. The District Court initially accepted standing but at summary judgment changed its conclusion and dismissed the FECA claim for lack of standing; a separate opinion dismissed the APA claim as precluded by FECA. The plaintiffs appealed only the FECA standing dismissal. On April 19, 2022, the D.C. Circuit reversed and remanded for further proceedings.
sections.Material Facts:
The plaintiffs alleged that Correct the Record coordinated millions of dollars in activities with Clinton's presidential campaign, making excessive and impermissibly funded in-kind contributions that neither organization reported as such. Correct the Record openly acknowledged coordination but claimed that an exception for unpaid internet communications covered the associated input costs. It reported $9,617,828.28 in aggregate expenditures without designating any spending as coordinated contributions, and the campaign did not report receiving that assistance. The plaintiffs did not know the coordinated portion.

The FEC General Counsel recommended finding reason to believe violations had occurred, reasoning that activities such as opposition research, message development, staff and office costs, and surrogate work did not become exempt merely because something was later transmitted online. The two controlling commissioners accepted the broad input-cost interpretation. The District Court, relying on Wertheimer, treated identifying coordinated spending within already reported expenditures as only a requested legal determination rather than new facts.
sections.Issue: Whether the plaintiffs suffered an informational injury sufficient for Article III standing when the respondents had reported aggregate expenditures but not how much of that spending was coordinated with the campaign.
sections.Holding: The D.C. Circuit in 2022, in an opinion by Senior Judge Edwards for a unanimous panel of Rogers, Walker and Edwards, held that the plaintiffs had informational standing and reversed and remanded. The unknown breakdown of coordinated and noncoordinated amounts was factual information that FECA, on the plaintiffs' reading, required to be disclosed. The court did not decide the merits of the internet exception or the unappealed APA dismissal.
sections.Reasoning:
Reviewing standing de novo, the court applied Akins and the circuit's informational-injury decisions: the plaintiffs had to identify information that their reading of FECA required to be disclosed, whose absence harmed an interest Congress sought to protect, and that could actually be obtained if their challenge succeeded. An abstract wish to learn whether someone broke the law, information already accessible elsewhere, or a trivial addition would not suffice. A widely shared harm could still be concrete, because election-financing information helps voters assess candidates.

The aggregate disclosures did not tell the plaintiffs how much Correct the Record had contributed in coordination with the campaign. If their theory succeeded, the respondents would have to divide reported overhead and mixed activities into coordinated and noncoordinated amounts. Those unknown numbers were facts about campaign financing, not a legal label attached to an already known transaction. The court illustrated this with a reported biweekly salary payment of $4,521.56 to David Brock: if half were coordinated it would be reported as two $2,260.78 portions, but that fraction was invented for illustration and the true division would be a new fact.

Wertheimer was different because the transactions there had already been disclosed as coordinated by political-party committees, so further reporting would only duplicate the information. The District Court's approach would let ever-broader lump-sum reporting defeat standing even for a meritorious disclosure claim. The FEC's dismissal caused the continuing deprivation, and setting it aside would likely redress it.

The casebook describes the case as a voter-and-watchdog disclosure decision.

LRS-CLOSURE-052.rule: An organization denied campaign information that FECA entitles it to has informational standing even if it cannot vote, and an FEC dismissal is contrary to law if it rests on an impermissible statutory interpretation or is arbitrary, capricious, or an abuse of discretion.

sections.Parties: Campaign Legal Center and Democracy 21, two nonprofit campaign-finance organizations, filed administrative complaints with the Federal Election Commission and then sued to challenge the Commission's dismissal of them. They were the plaintiffs in the district court and the appellants in the D.C. Circuit. The FEC was the defendant and appellee. It contested the organizations' standing and asked the court to affirm either because exercises of prosecutorial discretion are unreviewable or because these particular dismissals were reasonable.
sections.Procedural History: The FEC's General Counsel recommended reason-to-believe findings on four straw-donor complaints but no action on their political-committee allegations, and recommended no reason-to-believe finding on the fifth complaint. In February 2016 the six commissioners divided 3-3 on whether to investigate and then unanimously dismissed all five complaints. The district court dismissed the challenges involving two of the administrative matters for lack of standing and, as to the remaining three, granted summary judgment to the FEC because the dismissals were not contrary to law. Only that summary judgment was appealed. On March 13, 2020, the D.C. Circuit affirmed in a per curiam opinion, with Judge Edwards concurring separately.
sections.Material Facts:
Between August 2011 and April 2015 the two organizations filed five FEC complaints alleging that individuals used closely held corporations and LLCs as straw donors to make Super PAC contributions without accurate disclosure of the true contributors. Four complaints also alleged failures to register and report as political committees. FECA's straw-donor provision prohibits making contributions in another's name and knowingly participating in that arrangement; the political-committee provisions impose separate registration and reporting obligations. These were alleged violations, not judicial findings.

The three commissioners who had opposed investigation supplied the controlling statement of reasons. They invoked prosecutorial discretion and stressed uncertain guidance after Citizens United and SpeechNow changed the legal landscape for corporate political spending. Past agency decisions had treated money in corporate accounts as corporate funds even when an owner could legally convert it to personal funds, and the LLC attribution regulations expressly addressed some but not all corporate forms. The commissioners thought enforcement without adequate notice would be unfair. On the political-committee allegations they relied on the General Counsel's conclusion that the entities were conduits rather than political committees.
sections.Issue: Whether nonprofit organizations that cannot vote, have no voting members and conduct no partisan activity suffer an injury sufficient for standing when campaign information is not disclosed; and whether the FEC's dismissals of the straw-donor and political-committee allegations were contrary to law under FECA.
sections.Holding: The D.C. Circuit in 2020, in a unanimous per curiam opinion of Judges Tatel, Garland and Edwards, held that the organizations had informational standing and affirmed the summary judgment for the FEC because the controlling commissioners' reasons for dismissing both the straw-donor and the political-committee allegations were reasonable. The court agreed that the straw-donor provision, § 30122, applies to closely held corporations and corporate LLCs; it upheld the dismissals rather than declaring such corporations exempt. It did not decide the FEC's claim that dismissals resting on prosecutorial discretion are unreviewable.
sections.Reasoning:
On standing, the organizations' educational, litigation, regulatory and advocacy activities could benefit from contributor and political-committee disclosures. On their reading of FECA they were entitled to information that had not been supplied, and the record gave no reason to doubt its usefulness to their work. The absence of a personal ballot or partisan affiliation did not negate that injury, which was traceable to the dismissals and likely redressable. Standing did not mean they were entitled to prevail.

The court called the reviewability question complicated and nonjurisdictional and went directly to reasonableness. Under FECA's contrary-to-law test a dismissal fails if based on an impermissible statutory interpretation, or if arbitrary, capricious or abusive even under a permissible one. The commissioners' reason for declining to investigate was inadequate notice in an altered legal environment. The court accepted the possible confusion from earlier decisions and regulations, deferred to the agency's understanding of its precedents, and emphasized the undisputed absence of directly applicable post-Citizens United precedent. It declined to judge the intent-to-evade standard the commissioners suggested for future matters, because a statement backed by only three commissioners is not binding; official Commission action requires four votes. The political-committee dismissals stood because the commissioners reasonably relied on the General Counsel's conduit conclusion, and the plaintiffs accepted that an entity could be a conduit or a political committee but not both.

Judge Edwards, concurring, joined the reasons for affirmance but rejected the FEC's contention that labelling a dismissal prosecutorial discretion eliminates judicial review; he viewed FECA's aggrieved-party review provision and Akins as displacing Chaney's nonenforcement presumption, and noted the agency's unexplained change of litigation position.

The casebook quotes the case for its informational-standing rule.

LRS-CLOSURE-053.rule: State senators whose votes would have defeated a ratification resolution have standing to claim those votes were overridden and rendered ineffective, but the effect of a state's prior rejection and of lapse of time on ratifying a constitutional amendment are political questions for Congress.

sections.Parties: Twenty-one Kansas senators, including all twenty who had voted against ratifying the Child Labor Amendment, and three members of the Kansas House were the petitioners in an original mandamus proceeding in the Kansas Supreme Court and the petitioners in the Supreme Court. They sought to have the Senate secretary's endorsement changed to say the ratification resolution had not passed and to stop the legislative officers and the state Secretary of State from authenticating and forwarding it. The State appeared through its Attorney General and was made a defendant.
sections.Procedural History: The legislators brought an original mandamus proceeding in the Kansas Supreme Court. An alternative writ issued. On undisputed facts the Kansas Supreme Court upheld the Lieutenant Governor's vote and the amendment's continuing vitality and denied mandamus. The Court granted certiorari, which was the appropriate route under the then-existing Judicial Code § 237(b) because the legislators did not challenge the validity of a state statute. The Court affirmed the Kansas Supreme Court's denial of mandamus. The official report's prefatory disposition says "reversed," but that contradicts the opinion's express conclusion and judgment, which the brief follows.
sections.Material Facts:
Congress proposed the Child Labor Amendment in June 1924. It would authorize Congress to limit, regulate and prohibit the labor of persons under eighteen. Kansas rejected the proposal in January 1925 and sent its rejection to the Secretary of State. In January 1937 the Kansas Senate considered a resolution ratifying the amendment. The forty senators divided twenty to twenty. The Lieutenant Governor, presiding over the Senate, cast a vote in favor, and the House subsequently adopted the resolution by a majority.

The challenging legislators claimed that the Lieutenant Governor was not entitled to vote in an Article V ratification, that Kansas's previous rejection exhausted its power to act, and that the amendment had expired through widespread rejection and the passage of nearly thirteen years. Congress had set no deadline for ratifying this proposal.
sections.Issue: Whether these legislators could invoke the Court's review; whether Article V permitted the Lieutenant Governor to break the tie; and whether Kansas's prior rejection or the lapse of nearly thirteen years prevented Kansas from ratifying the amendment.
sections.Holding: The Court in 1939, in an opinion by Chief Justice Hughes announced by Justice Stone, sustained jurisdiction on the interest of at least the twenty opposing senators and affirmed the denial of mandamus. It held that the efficacy of a ratification after an earlier rejection, and whether a proposal with no deadline has lost its vitality through lapse of time, are political questions for Congress. The Court stated that it was equally divided on whether the Lieutenant Governor question was justiciable and expressed no opinion on it. Four Justices concurred in the result; Justices Butler and McReynolds dissented.
sections.Reasoning:
Standing rested on the effectiveness of the twenty senators' votes. If their challenge to the Lieutenant Governor's participation was correct, their votes would have defeated the resolution; instead those votes had been overridden and rendered ineffective. Hughes treated that as a direct, adequate interest in vindicating a claimed federal right, not a citizen's undifferentiated interest in constitutional government. Hawke and Leser supported review of state-court decisions on ratification.

On prior rejection, Hughes looked to the political branches' treatment of the Fourteenth Amendment, which Congress declared adopted despite ratifications after rejection and attempted withdrawals. Article V speaks of ratification, not rejection, so the question was for Congress in its control of promulgation. On lapse of time, Dillon v. Gloss upheld Congress's power to set a reasonable deadline but did not mean courts should decide when an undated proposal expired. That judgment turned on changing political, social and economic conditions for which there were no satisfactory judicial criteria.

Justice Black, joined by Justices Roberts, Frankfurter and Douglas, concurred in the result, regarding the entire amending process as exclusively political and controlled by Congress. Justice Frankfurter, for the same four, would have denied standing because legislative effectiveness was not a private injury. Justice Butler, joined by Justice McReynolds, dissented, reading Dillon to require ratification within a reasonable time and finding more than thirteen years excessive.

The casebook cites the case, within its discussion of Raines, for outcome-determinative vote nullification; its reference to the senators' "votes to ratify" is imprecise, since the twenty senators had voted against ratification.

LRS-CLOSURE-054.rule: An intervenor appealing after the primary party declines must show its own standing, and a single legislative chamber lacks standing to appeal invalidation of a redistricting plan when it neither represents the state nor holds the redistricting power alone.

sections.Parties: Voters in twelve Virginia House districts sued state agencies and election officials, alleging unconstitutional racial gerrymandering under the Equal Protection Clause; they prevailed below and were appellees. The Virginia House of Delegates and its Speaker had intervened as defendants and took a substantial role in defending the districts; the House was the appellant and wanted the judgment invalidating the districts reversed. The state defendants, whose Attorney General declined to appeal, moved to dismiss the House's appeal for lack of standing.
sections.Procedural History: The case went through a bench trial, an earlier Supreme Court appeal and a second bench trial. In June 2018 a three-judge district court, divided two to one, held eleven districts unconstitutional, enjoined further elections under the map, and gave the General Assembly about four months to adopt a lawful replacement. Virginia's Attorney General declined to appeal. The House appealed, and the state defendants moved to dismiss. When the General Assembly enacted no replacement, the district court prescribed districts for the 2019 election, and the House noticed an appeal from that remedial order as well. The Court dismissed the House's appeal for lack of jurisdiction without reaching the racial-gerrymandering merits.
sections.Material Facts: Virginia redrew its Senate and House districts in 2011 after the 2010 census. After the district court invalidated eleven House districts, Virginia's Attorney General determined that continuing the litigation would not serve the Commonwealth or its citizens and declined to appeal. Virginia law assigned civil litigation on behalf of the Commonwealth and its institutions to the Attorney General, subject to exceptions that did not apply. Throughout the case the House had claimed to defend its own interests, not to appear as Virginia's agent. Virginia's constitution vested redistricting authority in the General Assembly, not in the House alone, and provided that incumbents continue to represent the districts that elected them for the rest of their terms. The district court's judgment had first allowed the General Assembly to produce a valid plan.
sections.Issue: Whether the Virginia House of Delegates, an intervenor-defendant below, had standing to appeal the judgment invalidating the districts after the state defendants declined to appeal, either as the Commonwealth's representative or on the basis of an injury to the House itself.
sections.Holding: The Court in 2019, in an opinion by Justice Ginsburg for a five-Justice majority (joined by Justices Thomas, Sotomayor, Kagan and Gorsuch), held that the House lacked authority to represent Virginia in the appeal and lacked standing in its own institutional right, and dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction. It did not affirm the district court's constitutional reasoning on the merits. Justice Alito dissented, joined by Chief Justice Roberts and Justices Breyer and Kavanaugh.
sections.Reasoning:
Standing must exist throughout litigation, including on appeal, and cannot be waived or forfeited. An intervenor seeking review when the primary party declines to appeal must show its own standing; the House's earlier roles as intervening defendant and appellee had not required it to invoke the court's jurisdiction.

The House could not represent the Commonwealth. A state may designate an agent to defend its statutes, but Virginia assigned that role to the Attorney General. Vesilind and Karcher did not overcome that statute, and a litigant cannot switch representative capacities for the first time on appeal.

Nor was the House injured itself. Participation in passing a law does not give every governmental component a cognizable injury when a court invalidates it. Redistricting authority belonged to the General Assembly; unlike Arizona State Legislature, a single chamber here sought to litigate an interest assigned to the whole legislature. Coleman did not help: the House did not claim its votes went uncounted, but challenged a judicial ruling on a concededly enacted plan. Changes in membership from new boundaries were not an institutional injury because the electorate, not the House, selects members; Beens, which involved cutting Minnesota's Senate from sixty-seven to thirty-five members, was distinguishable. Greater difficulty in seeking reelection, if cognizable at all, would injure individual legislators, a question left undecided.

Justice Alito, dissenting, reasoned that a districting map determines constituents and the members who produce the legislature's work, so replacing it concretely injured the House's institutional function. He did not reach the claimed authority to represent Virginia.

The casebook uses the case for the mismatch between a single chamber and an interest belonging to the whole legislature, and for the absence of institutional injury from electoral changes in membership.

LRS-CLOSURE-055.rule: A single chamber of Congress has standing to claim that the Executive spent funds without the appropriation the Appropriations Clause requires, because each chamber independently holds the power to withhold consent to spending, but it has no distinct injury from the Executive's violation of an enacted statute.

sections.Parties: The United States House of Representatives sued the executive departments involved and their Secretaries, seeking declaratory and injunctive relief under the Appropriations Clause and the Administrative Procedure Act. The House was the plaintiff and appellant. The executive defendants, appellees, argued that any appropriations injury belonged only to Congress as a whole and that one chamber could not sue independently. In the later Supreme Court stage the case was captioned Yellen v. United States House of Representatives.
sections.Procedural History: The House sued on April 5, 2019. The district court denied a preliminary injunction for want of a cognizable injury and dismissed. It allowed an amended complaint adding a § 9002 transfer claim, again found no standing, and entered final judgment. The House appealed. The appeal was reheard en banc but was returned to the original panel on August 7, 2020, after the en banc McGahn decision rejected a categorical bar against a House suit alleging injury to its own legislative rights. On September 25, 2020, the panel affirmed dismissal of the APA claims, vacated dismissal of the constitutional claims, and remanded. On October 12, 2021, the Court granted certiorari, vacated the judgment, and remanded with instructions to dismiss the case as moot, citing Munsingwear.
sections.Material Facts:
After extended disagreement with President Trump about border-wall funding, Congress appropriated $1.375 billion for specified pedestrian fencing in the Rio Grande Valley, with restrictions on locations and designs. The President signed the legislation but announced he would obtain additional resources through executive action. He identified the Treasury Forfeiture Fund, Defense Department counterdrug funding under 10 U.S.C. § 284, and military-construction resources under § 2808. The House challenged the latter two sources. Its central allegation was that the Executive planned to spend $8.1 billion despite Congress's authorization of only $1.375 billion.

The counterdrug appropriation was $517.171 million. The President transferred $1 billion in March 2019 and another $1.5 billion in May, invoking §§ 8005 and 9002 of the 2019 Defense appropriations legislation; the House alleged the statutory conditions for transfers were not met. He also planned to redirect $3.6 billion under § 2808, having declared a national emergency on February 15, 2019, which Congress did not override. These were pleaded matters, not appellate findings that the transfers were illegal.
sections.Issue: Whether the House of Representatives, suing alone, has Article III standing to challenge executive spending allegedly made without a congressional appropriation, under the Appropriations Clause and under the Administrative Procedure Act.
sections.Holding: The D.C. Circuit in 2020, in a panel opinion by Senior Judge Sentelle joined by Judges Millett and Wilkins, held that the House had standing to bring its constitutional Appropriations Clause claims but not its APA claims. It affirmed dismissal of the APA claims, vacated dismissal of the constitutional claims, and remanded. It did not enjoin the transfers or decide whether the Executive had spending authority. The Court later vacated this judgment and ordered the case dismissed as moot, in a summary order stating no reasons, so the 2020 judgment is not presently operative.
sections.Reasoning:
Because the case was decided at the dismissal stage, the court accepted the House's allegations and assumed the correctness of its legal position on the merits for purposes of standing only.

The Appropriations Clause requires affirmative authorization for expenditure, rather than permitting spending unless Congress prohibits it. Separating the legislative purse from the executive sword checks executive power, and each chamber can refuse the necessary consent without the other's agreement. That differs from a chamber demanding enforcement of a law it could not enact alone.

Reading Coleman, Raines, Arizona State Legislature and Bethune-Hill together, the court asked whether the challenged conduct curtailed a legislative institution's power and whether the plaintiff was the institution possessing that power. Raines involved individual legislators' abstract loss of influence; Bethune-Hill denied a single chamber standing to assert an interest assigned to the whole legislature but did not bar a chamber from protecting its own prerogative. The court also relied on the controlling en banc McGahn decision. On the allegations, the House had withheld additional wall funding, and spending despite that decision nullified its withholding power: the House held one of two keys needed to authorize Treasury expenditure, and the Executive allegedly took that key away. Rejecting the injury would invert the constitutional arrangement, leaving the Executive free to spend until both chambers enacted a veto-proof prohibition.

The APA claims differed. Once legislation is enacted, a legislative body's interest in executive compliance with the statute is not by itself a particularized injury.

The casebook cites the case for the House's specific institutional injury and notes it was later declared moot; the actual order vacated the judgment and remanded with instructions to dismiss as moot.

LRS-CLOSURE-056.rule: Individual members of Congress who do not make up a majority of either chamber lack Article III standing to assert an institutional injury to Congress, however many of them join the suit.

sections.Parties: Two hundred fifteen members of Congress, twenty-nine senators and 186 representatives, sued President Trump in his official capacity, seeking declaratory and injunctive relief under the Foreign Emoluments Clause. They were the plaintiffs and, on appeal, the appellees. The President, defendant and appellant, argued that they lacked standing, lacked a cause of action, failed to state a claim, and could not constitutionally obtain an injunction against him in his official capacity.
sections.Procedural History: The complaint was filed June 14, 2017. The district court separated standing from the other dismissal issues and first found standing; it later held that the members had an implied equitable cause of action and had stated a claim. It denied the President's requests to certify interlocutory review. He sought mandamus in the D.C. Circuit, which denied the petition without prejudice but required immediate reconsideration of certification. The district court then certified both orders and stayed proceedings, and the D.C. Circuit permitted the interlocutory appeal under 28 U.S.C. § 1292(b). On February 7, 2020, the court reversed the standing ruling, remanded with instructions to dismiss the complaint, and vacated as moot the order finding a cause of action and a sufficient claim.
sections.Material Facts: The members alleged that the President's financial interests in businesses dealing with foreign governments caused him to accept, or inevitably to accept, foreign emoluments without congressional consent. The Foreign Emoluments Clause restricts acceptance of foreign presents, emoluments, offices and titles by persons holding an office of profit or trust under the United States without the consent of Congress. The plaintiffs claimed that accepting the benefits first completely nullified their opportunity to vote on granting or withholding consent. They argued the Clause was distinctive because it required prior congressional approval and regulated private conduct, and that Congress's spending power could not effectively reach the President's private businesses. These were allegations taken as true at the dismissal stage, not findings. The plaintiffs conceded that they represented neither the House nor the Senate, and they were not a majority of either chamber.
sections.Issue: Whether individual members of Congress have Article III standing to sue the President for allegedly accepting foreign emoluments without congressional consent, on the theory that he denied them the opportunity to vote on consent.
sections.Holding: The D.C. Circuit in 2020, in a unanimous per curiam opinion of Judges Henderson, Tatel and Griffith, held that the members lacked Article III standing. It reversed the district court's standing ruling and remanded with instructions to dismiss the complaint, and separately vacated as moot the order finding a cause of action and a sufficient claim. It did not decide the meaning of an emolument, whether the Clause covers the President, or whether a proper plaintiff would have an equitable action.
sections.Reasoning:
The court began with Raines, which denied individual members standing to challenge the Line Item Veto Act based on diluted legislative power. These members likewise alleged injury in their official roles, not a private right held personally. They had not been singled out: the alleged loss of power was shared with the other 320 members of Congress who did not join. The number joining did not convert an institutional grievance into a personal injury. Bethune-Hill reinforced that individual members cannot assert institutional interests belonging to a legislative body, just as a single chamber cannot automatically assert interests assigned to the whole legislature.

Because twenty-nine senators and 186 representatives were not a majority of either chamber, they could not themselves approve or deny consent, and the court treated their claim no differently from a single member's. Coleman's narrow vote-nullification example did not apply; as explained in Raines, it concerned legislators whose votes would have sufficed to defeat or enact a specific act but were completely nullified, and these plaintiffs had no such determinative bloc. Circuit precedents Chenoweth and Campbell supported the result. The court did not hold that Congress itself would automatically have standing, and it did not decide the standing of other emoluments plaintiffs with commercial, sovereign or proprietary injuries. The members remained free to press their arguments politically. There were no separate writings.

The casebook mentions the case, between Mnuchin and McGahn, for its 215 plaintiffs and their claim of institutional injury.

LRS-CLOSURE-057.rule: A House committee authorized by the House to sue has Article III standing to seek judicial enforcement of its subpoena against an executive-branch official, because denial of subpoenaed testimony is a concrete informational injury to the body that holds the subpoena power.

sections.Parties: The House Judiciary Committee, authorized by the House to litigate, sued Donald McGahn, former White House Counsel, for declaratory and injunctive relief enforcing its subpoena for his testimony. The Committee was the plaintiff and appellee. McGahn, the defendant and appellant, had been directed by the President not to appear and relied on a claim that close presidential advisers are absolutely immune from compelled congressional testimony; on appeal he argued the Committee lacked standing.
sections.Procedural History: The Committee sued in August 2019. On cross-motions for summary judgment the district court found Article III standing, subject-matter jurisdiction under § 1331 and an implied constitutional cause of action, rejected absolute testimonial immunity, and directed McGahn to appear while preserving his ability to invoke privileges in response to particular questions. McGahn appealed. On February 28, 2020, a D.C. Circuit panel (951 F.3d 510) vacated that judgment and remanded with instructions to dismiss the complaint. The court granted rehearing and vacated the panel opinions. On August 7, 2020, the en banc court (968 F.3d 755) affirmed the district court's judgment in part, on standing, and remanded to the panel to address McGahn's remaining threshold objections and, if reached, the merits.
sections.Material Facts: McGahn had witnessed events investigated by Special Counsel Robert Mueller, including President Trump's efforts concerning that investigation. The House Judiciary Committee sought information to investigate possible obstruction, consider impeachment, evaluate remedial legislation and conduct oversight. In March 2019 it requested documents; on April 22 it issued an authorized subpoena requiring document production and McGahn's testimony on May 21. On May 20 the White House conveyed the President's direction that McGahn not appear, relying on an Office of Legal Counsel opinion asserting absolute immunity of close presidential advisers from compelled congressional testimony. McGahn's private attorney confirmed his refusal while offering to comply with any accommodation reached between the Committee and the White House. The parties ultimately agreed on documents but not on his testimony. The House's later impeachment vote and the Senate's acquittal did not end the Committee's stated legislative, oversight and potential further impeachment interests.
sections.Issue: Whether a House committee's suit to enforce a subpoena for testimony against a former presidential adviser presents an Article III case or controversy, that is, whether the Committee has standing in a direct interbranch dispute over information.
sections.Holding: The D.C. Circuit panel in February 2020, in an opinion by Judge Griffith joined by Judge Henderson with Judge Rogers dissenting, held that the dispute was not an Article III case or controversy. The en banc D.C. Circuit in August 2020, in an opinion by Judge Rogers, held by seven judges that the Committee had Article III standing; Judges Henderson and Griffith dissented, and Judges Katsas and Rao did not participate. The en banc court left subject-matter jurisdiction, the existence of a cause of action, and absolute testimonial immunity undecided, so it did not finally enforce the subpoena.
sections.Reasoning:
The panel reasoned from separation of powers and history: federal courts traditionally resolve the rights of individuals rather than supervise the political branches' relative powers; direct congressional-executive litigation had been absent for nearly two centuries; and political tools such as accommodation, appropriations, appointments and impeachment remained available. Judge Rogers, dissenting, would have affirmed.

The en banc majority applied the usual injury, traceability and redressability requirements with the especially rigorous scrutiny suited to an interbranch case, assuming the Committee's legal entitlement on the merits. Each chamber's subpoena power is an established constitutional means of obtaining information for legislation, oversight and impeachment, so refusal to testify under a concededly valid subpoena was a real informational injury, by analogy to Akins and Public Citizen. The injury was particularized: the House had delegated investigative authority to the Committee and authorized the suit, so, unlike the individual members in Raines or the single chamber in Bethune-Hill, the litigating body matched the body holding the power. McGahn's refusal caused the injury and an order to appear could remedy it.

The majority rejected an automatic structural bar. Judicial enforcement could preserve the accommodation process, since negotiation had occurred against a recognized possibility of litigation, and removing that possibility would reduce the Executive's incentive to negotiate. Civil enforcement did not usurp executive prosecution authority.

Judge Henderson, dissenting, stressed historical cognizability and the judiciary's limited role. Judge Griffith, dissenting, argued that structural concerns should inform injury in fact and that the Committee also lacked a cause of action.

The casebook describes the en banc rejection of a structural standing barrier but prints the citation of the contrary panel decision, 951 F.3d 510; the en banc citation is 968 F.3d 755.

LRS-CLOSURE-058.rule: An organization without formal members has associational standing when its constituents are the functional equivalent of members, and an agency's refusal to begin a rulemaking is reviewed deferentially and requires only a brief statement of grounds that the record supports.

sections.Parties: FlyersRights Education Fund, a nonprofit that educated airline passengers about their rights and advocated on their behalf, and its president, Paul Hudson, petitioned the D.C. Circuit for review of the Department of Transportation's denial of their rulemaking petition. They argued that DOT had disregarded evidence of deception and confusion and had given an inadequate explanation. DOT, the respondent, defended the denial and disputed whether the people FlyersRights served could count as members for standing purposes.
sections.Procedural History: FlyersRights petitioned DOT for a rule. DOT denied the petition in a February 1, 2019 letter. FlyersRights and Hudson sought judicial review in the D.C. Circuit. On May 5, 2020, the court recognized associational standing, rejected the APA challenge on the merits, and denied the petition for review.
sections.Material Facts:
The Montreal Convention, adopted in 1999 and effective in the United States in 2003, imposes liability for damage caused by delay in Article 19. Article 3(4) requires written notice that, when applicable, the Convention governs and may limit an airline's liability for death, injury, baggage damage and delay. FlyersRights asked DOT to require airlines to print summaries of passengers' Montreal Convention rights on every international ticket, including information about obtaining compensation for flight delays.

DOT found insufficient evidence that airlines were violating their existing notice obligations or that consumer confusion justified the rulemaking, and pointed to another pending proceeding on related issues. The resulting April 16, 2019 rule required written summaries on international tickets but not everything FlyersRights had requested.

FlyersRights acknowledged it was not a traditional membership organization. One joined by signing up to receive information. It ran a passenger hotline staffed by member volunteers, frequently polled constituents about policies and actions to pursue, and used member petitions and direct input to guide its work. Members supplied most of its funding but did not elect its leadership. Leopold de Beer declared that he suffered a significant flight delay and that the inadequate notice regime left him uninformed and impeded his ability to obtain compensation.
sections.Issue: Whether an organization that is not a traditional membership organization has associational standing to sue on behalf of the passengers it serves, and whether DOT's denial of the rulemaking petition was adequately explained under the APA.
sections.Holding: The D.C. Circuit in 2020, in an opinion by Judge Randolph for a unanimous panel with Judges Rogers and Millett, held that FlyersRights had associational standing because its constituents were the functional equivalent of members and one of them, de Beer, was injured, and that DOT had adequately explained its denial. The court denied the petition for review. The result was not a standing dismissal, an order compelling rulemaking, or a holding that DOT could never adopt more informative notices.
sections.Reasoning:
Under Hunt an association ordinarily must show that at least one member could sue individually, that the interests are germane to its purpose, and that neither the claim nor the relief requires individual members' participation. For a nontraditional organization the court asked whether its constituents were the functional equivalent of members; Hunt's indicia include selecting leaders, guiding the organization's work and financing its activities. Earlier circuit decisions rejected membership based merely on reading a magazine, watching news, or having worked with an investor group. The court doubted Hunt's list was exhaustive and did not hold that an email signup alone sufficed. Given the hotline, the polling, member petitions and member funding, constituents sufficiently influenced FlyersRights' activities even though they did not elect its leadership. The litigation fit its passenger-rights mission and required no individual participation. DOT did not challenge de Beer's standing, so the court did not resolve the theory of another declarant, Robert Lax, or Hudson's own standing.

On the merits, APA § 555(e) requires notice and a brief statement of grounds for denying a petition. Review is limited and deferential because deciding whether to initiate rulemaking resembles prosecutorial discretion and involves allocating resources, but it is not wholly unreviewable. DOT had reviewed major airlines' contracts of carriage, which contained language that the Convention governed and might limit liability, as the Convention actually requires. FlyersRights' evidence of confusion was meaningful but not overwhelming, and whether it warranted another rulemaking fell within DOT's discretion, strengthened by its parallel proceeding.

The casebook cites the case for functional membership.

LRS-CLOSURE-059.rule: Under Hunt an association suing for its members must identify a member with a concrete injury that is traceable to the defendant and redressable, and it must plead facts making that member's standing plausible under Twombly and Iqbal.

sections.Parties: The Association of American Physicians and Surgeons sued the Food and Drug Administration and other federal health officials, asserting First Amendment, equal-protection and APA claims and seeking broader access to hydroxychloroquine held in the Strategic National Stockpile. The Association was the plaintiff and appellant, relying on appeal on associational standing for its physician members and third-party standing for patients. The federal defendants, appellees, made a facial challenge to standing and also argued the case was moot.
sections.Procedural History: The district court dismissed the complaint for lack of standing. During the litigation the FDA rescinded the emergency use authorization after determining that the available data did not establish effectiveness. On appeal the Association abandoned its own conference-injury theory. The FDA argued that the rescission made the case moot; the Sixth Circuit chose to decide standing first, since Sinochem permits choosing between nonmerits grounds. Reviewing de novo, the court affirmed the dismissal on September 9, 2021.
sections.Material Facts:
The FDA had approved hydroxychloroquine decades earlier for conditions including malaria and lupus, but not to prevent or treat COVID-19. Federal law did not generally prohibit physicians from prescribing an approved drug for an off-label use. During the pandemic the federal government held hydroxychloroquine in the Strategic National Stockpile. A March 2020 emergency use authorization permitted distribution from the stockpile for certain hospitalized COVID-19 patients when a clinical trial was unavailable or participation infeasible. It concerned the federal supply and did not regulate every dose or prohibit off-label prescribing.

The Association alleged that the drug was useful for prophylaxis and early treatment, a position that was not a judicial finding. It alleged injury from a potential conference cancellation, interference with members' desired prescribing, and harm to patients. The complaint referred to a Michigan physician, "Dr. John Doe," and another physician in an unidentified state who wanted to prescribe the drug more broadly, and it suggested state medical boards might discipline doctors. It also described a plentiful, easily manufactured supply, with a million new doses a day feasible.
sections.Issue: Whether the Association had associational standing through its physician members, or third-party standing on behalf of patients, to challenge the limits in the FDA's emergency use authorization for hydroxychloroquine.
sections.Holding: The Sixth Circuit in 2021, in an opinion by Judge Murphy joined throughout by Judge Thapar and by Judge Siler except for Part III.A.1, unanimously affirmed the dismissal for lack of standing. The complaint did not plausibly allege that any identified physician member suffered an injury traceable to the federal defendants, and without an injured member there was no basis for third-party standing for patients. The court did not decide mootness, the drug's efficacy, or the merits, and it applied Hunt as binding rather than abolishing associational standing.
sections.Reasoning:
In Part III.A.1, joined by only two judges, the opinion questioned how Hunt fits recent Article III decisions: whether members' injuries alone give an uninjured association a historical basis to sue; how relief to the association redresses nonparty members' injuries and binds them; and how Hunt's germaneness and individual-participation requirements survive Lexmark's criticism of prudential standing rules. Judge Siler declined to join that discussion as unnecessary. The opinion acknowledged Hunt remained binding.

Applying Hunt, an organization cannot rely on its size or the probability that some unidentified member is injured. The court held that Twombly and Iqbal plausibility applies to standing allegations. The direct theory misread the authorization, which governed distribution from the federal stockpile and left physicians free to prescribe off-label through nongovernmental channels. The claim that federal control made the drug unavailable was defeated by the complaint's own allegations of plentiful supply. The indirect theory failed because the complaint identified no Michigan law, standard, enforcement action or warning creating a credible threat of discipline. Causation independently failed: state boards, not the federal defendants, would make any disciplinary decision, and the chain rested on speculation about independent actors; a Federation of State Medical Boards press release did not cure this.

Third-party standing ordinarily requires the plaintiff's own Article III injury. The court left undecided whether an association may combine associational standing with its members' third-party standing, because no physician member had a sufficiently alleged injury.

The casebook excerpt is a fragment that supports only the existence of the majority's critique of associational standing; it ends mid-quotation and does not give the critique's conclusion, the controlling application, or Judge Siler's qualification.

LRS-CLOSURE-060.rule: A challenge to an announced executive policy is not justiciable when the threatened injury depends on contingent future events that may not occur as predicted, so that the plaintiffs lack standing and the dispute is not ripe.

sections.Parties: States, local governments, organizations and individuals challenged President Trump's memorandum on excluding aliens not in lawful immigration status from the apportionment base; they were plaintiffs below and appellees in the Supreme Court. The Government was the defendant and appellant, seeking to undo the judgment declaring the memorandum unlawful and enjoining the Secretary.
sections.Procedural History: A three-judge court in the Southern District of New York found standing, held that § 141(b) did not authorize the Secretary to submit an additional apportionment count derived from administrative records outside the census and that excluding residents solely by immigration status violated § 2a(a)'s whole-number requirement, declared the memorandum unlawful, and enjoined the Secretary from including information needed to implement it in the statutory report to the President. The Government appealed directly, and the Court postponed consideration of jurisdiction. On December 18, 2020, the Court vacated the district court's judgment and remanded with instructions to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction.
sections.Material Facts:
The decennial census provides the population figures used to apportion House seats and supplies information for federal funding and state redistricting. Under 13 U.S.C. § 141 the Secretary of Commerce conducts the census and reports the state population tabulation; under 2 U.S.C. § 2a(a) the President transmits to Congress a statement showing the whole number of persons in each state and each state's House seats.

In July 2020 President Trump announced a policy to exclude from the apportionment base aliens not in lawful immigration status. His memorandum directed the Secretary to provide additional information so the President could implement that policy, but qualified both collection and implementation by feasibility, practicability and delegated discretion.

The district court found standing because the memorandum discouraged census participation. By the time of Supreme Court review the census response period had ended, and plaintiffs conceded that chilling effect had dissipated. They relied instead on threatened reductions in representation and federal funding. The Secretary's report and the President's statement were still being prepared. Everyone agreed that excluding the entire estimated 10.5 million undocumented population was infeasible, yet the evidence predicting changed apportionment assumed complete exclusion.
sections.Issue: Whether, at the time of the Court's review, the challenge to the President's memorandum presented a live Article III controversy, given that the injuries now claimed were prospective losses of representation and federal funding.
sections.Holding: The Court in 2020, in a per curiam opinion decided 6-3, held that the case was not justiciable because the plaintiffs' claimed injuries were too contingent to establish standing and the dispute was not ripe. It vacated the district court's judgment and remanded with instructions to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction, expressly declining to decide the constitutional or statutory merits. The ruling did not approve exclusion by immigration status or require all census challenges to wait until apportionment is final. Justice Breyer dissented, joined by Justices Sotomayor and Kagan.
sections.Reasoning:
A live controversy must persist throughout litigation; an earlier injury does not establish jurisdiction over a different, prospective injury on appeal. Standing requires a concrete, particularized, imminent injury, and ripeness bars adjudication that depends on contingent future events that may not happen as predicted or at all.

The announced policy did not yet show how many people the administration could or would exclude or what any plaintiff would lose. Any changes had to comply with the actual-enumeration requirement. The record did not establish which aliens had suitable administrative records, whether the Bureau could match them to census responses in time, or which groups the President would ultimately exclude. A substantial risk can support standing, but the record showed nothing about the consequences of partial implementation. Earlier pre-apportionment challenges were different because concrete census procedures predictably altered the count.
