The proposal required each fish, brined to 3.5% water-phase salt, to reach at least 180°F for thirty minutes; the final rule added an alternative of 150°F for thirty minutes with 5% water-phase salt, which the National Fisheries Institute had suggested only as an interim measure while species-specific parameters were developed.

The FDA did not disclose to commenters the scientific material it said it had relied on. Commenters asked for species-specific treatment. The Interior Department's Bureau of Commercial Fisheries questioned the commercial feasibility of uniform requirements and suggested lower temperatures with nitrite and salt, and Nova Scotia and its trade association warned that the temperatures would destroy the commercial whitefish product. The FDA acknowledged that adequate parameters had not been established for every species but said its requirements were the safest then known; it did not meaningfully answer the alternative-preservative proposal or the feasibility objection. No contemporaneous administrative record was made or certified.

FDA inspections established that Nova Scotia was not meeting the requirements. The company did not deny this; it argued that compliance would prevent production of marketable whitefish.
sections.Issue: Did the FDA's authority over food prepared under insanitary conditions extend to processing requirements aimed at organisms present before the food entered the plant? If so, did the FDA's notice-and-comment procedure adequately expose the scientific basis for the rule and address the major objections to it?
sections.Holding: The Second Circuit in 1977, in an opinion by Judge Gurfein for a unanimous panel, held that the FDA had statutory authority under 21 U.S.C. § 342(a)(4) and § 371(a) to regulate processing temperatures and salt levels, but that this regulation was invalid as applied to non-vacuum-packed hot-smoked whitefish. The agency had withheld the scientific material underlying the proposal and had not answered material comments about species differences, alternative controls and commercial feasibility. The court reversed the injunction and ordered the enforcement complaint dismissed. It did not invalidate every sanitation regulation, and the FDA could reconsider the standards through lawful procedures.
sections.Reasoning:
On authority, the court recognized the textual force of the company's argument that the adulteration provision addressed dirty plant conditions, but read it in light of the Act's public-health purpose: inadequate processing could let dangerous spores survive, and a narrow reading could undermine established rules on contaminated raw materials and pasteurization. Authority was fairly inferable from the statute's purpose and language, not from an official's view that initiative was desirable.

On the record, APA § 706 required review of the whole administrative record even under the arbitrary-and-capricious standard, so meaningful review required access to what the agency considered. The district court properly excluded the company's new scientific evidence, because the issues had fairly been presented in the rulemaking; the court reviewed the agency's record and reasoning and did not hold a new scientific trial.

On disclosure, the scientific research was central to the rule, and without it interested parties could not test methodology, data collection or extrapolation. Nothing justified concealing readily available research on precise parameters for which the agency lacked special expertise; trade secrets and national security were possible exceptions that did not apply here.

On explanation, the concise general statement under APA § 553(c) had to answer objections striking at the rule's central justification. The FDA left unanswered whether different species required different treatment and whether the requirements destroyed the commercial whitefish product. Commercial infeasibility was not an absolute veto over public-health regulation, but the agency had to say whether it considered the rule feasible or consciously chose stronger protection despite infeasibility.

LRS-MAX-PETROLEUM.rule: A general statutory grant of power to make rules and regulations to carry out an act can authorize substantive rules defining the statutory standard, where later enforcement still proceeds through the adjudicatory procedures the statute requires.

sections.Parties: Two trade associations and thirty-four gasoline refining companies challenged a Federal Trade Commission rule on octane ratings. They were the challengers in the district court and wanted the rule set aside, disputing the FTC's statutory power to make substantive rules and raising other objections. The FTC, having lost in the district court, appealed and wanted its rulemaking authority recognized.
sections.Procedural History: The challengers disputed the FTC's statutory rulemaking power and also raised constitutional, procedural, evidentiary and arbitrary-and-capricious objections. The district court ruled solely on statutory power, holding that the FTC lacked authority to make such substantive rules. The FTC appealed to the D.C. Circuit, which reviewed only that ground. On June 27, 1973 the court reversed and remanded for consideration of the remaining challenge to the proceedings that produced the rule; rehearing was denied on August 6, 1973. The court did not decide the ultimate validity of the octane rule itself, and the appeal did not involve an adjudicated violation, damages or a civil penalty.
sections.Material Facts:
The FTC adopted a rule treating failure to display octane ratings on covered gasoline pumps as an unfair method of competition and an unfair or deceptive act or practice. It applied to refiners or other distributors selling to retailers when they owned or leased the pumps through which the public bought motor gasoline, and required clear, conspicuous, permanent disclosure of the minimum octane rating. The rule specified an octane-rating methodology, made allowances for existing leases and excluded aviation gasoline.

Section 5 of the Federal Trade Commission Act directed the FTC to prevent specified unfair practices and provided for complaints, hearings, factual findings and cease-and-desist orders. Section 6(g) empowered it to make rules and regulations to carry out the Act's provisions; other parts of § 6 addressed corporate investigations and reports. For decades the FTC had not claimed binding substantive rulemaking authority, and some officials had expressly disclaimed it. Congress had later granted express rulemaking powers in particular product-labeling and consumer-protection statutes.
sections.Issue: Did the Federal Trade Commission Act's general grant of power to make rules and regulations in § 6(g) extend to substantive rules defining unfair methods of competition and unfair or deceptive practices under § 5, or was it confined to procedural and investigatory rules?
sections.Holding: The D.C. Circuit in 1973, in an opinion by Judge J. Skelly Wright joined by Chief Judge Bazelon and Judge Robinson with no separate opinion, held that § 6(g) authorized the FTC to adopt substantive trade regulation rules defining the statutory prohibitions it enforced under § 5. Read together with the statute's purposes and history, §§ 5 and 6(g) let the FTC clarify the statutory standard by rule and then enforce it through the complaint, hearing, findings and cease-and-desist sequence that § 5 required. The court decided authority to make rules, not the validity of the octane rule, and said respondents must have some opportunity to show that unusual circumstances justified waiving a rule.
sections.Reasoning:
The court began from the premise that useful policy alone could not create powers Congress had withheld, but found the words of § 6(g) broad enough to support substantive rulemaking. Section 5 specified how the FTC would obtain an enforceable order; it did not expressly make individualized adjudication the exclusive way to develop the legal standard. The FTC was not bypassing those procedures: a rule would narrow the later inquiry, but a complaint, hearing, findings and order against a particular respondent were still required.

Supreme Court decisions such as Morton Salt instructed courts to read the Act as an integrated whole and not wall off § 6 from § 5. Decisions involving the FCC, the Federal Power Commission and other agencies showed that general rulemaking grants could authorize substantive standards even where statutes contemplated individual hearings. The court rejected the companies' attempt to distinguish the FTC as a prosecutorial agency.

Rulemaking could gather information from a wider group of affected parties, give advance notice, avoid singling out one company and protect complying firms from competitors profiting through delayed enforcement. The court distinguished whether rulemaking was authorized from whether an agency must choose it.

The 1914 legislative history contained evidence cutting both ways and did not unmistakably exclude substantive rulemaking. Long nonuse did not forfeit a granted power, earlier official disclaimers were not controlling, and Congress's later specific grants could reflect caution or a wish to end uncertainty. The court construed the statute itself and did not simply defer to the FTC's former or current position.

LRS-MAX-TEXAS.rule: An agency pronouncement is a substantive rule requiring notice and comment, not a policy statement, if it imposes rights or obligations and does not genuinely leave decisionmakers free to exercise discretion, whether it binds through its text or its practical application.

sections.Parties: Texas and other states sued the United States to stop the Department of Homeland Security's November 2014 memorandum, issued by Secretary Jeh Johnson, which expanded DACA and announced Deferred Action for Parents of Americans and Lawful Permanent Residents (DAPA). The states were the plaintiffs and the movants for a preliminary injunction, which they defended on appeal. The government was the defendant and sought to undo the injunction.
sections.Procedural History: The states alleged a procedural APA violation, a substantive APA violation and a Take Care Clause violation. The district court issued a nationwide preliminary injunction on the procedural claim alone, leaving the other claims unresolved; no evidentiary hearing was held. An earlier Fifth Circuit panel denied a stay, in a separate decision reported at 787 F.3d 733. This panel reviewed the injunction for abuse of discretion, factual findings for clear error and legal conclusions for correctness. On November 9, 2015, in an opinion revised November 25, the Fifth Circuit affirmed the preliminary injunction by a 2-1 vote, adding the substantive APA claim as an alternative ground. Neither court resolved the Take Care claim. This was an appeal from preliminary relief, not a final judgment after trial.
sections.Material Facts:
DHS's 2012 DACA program let qualifying people brought to the United States as children request deferred action. In November 2014 Secretary Johnson's memorandum expanded DACA by removing the age cap, extending deferred action from two to three years and moving the arrival cutoff to January 1, 2010, and announced DAPA; the opinion uses DAPA to cover both. The original 2012 DACA program was not the subject of the injunction.

The parental program potentially covered about 4.3 million people. Applicants needed a citizen or lawful-permanent-resident child, continuous residence since before January 1, 2010, no lawful status, no applicable enforcement priority, and no other factor making deferred action inappropriate in the officer's discretion. The memorandum repeatedly described individual, revocable discretion and denied creating substantive rights, immigration status or a path to citizenship. Deferred action left recipients removable but permitted lawful presence for specified purposes; under existing statutes and regulations recipients could apply for work authorization and, if other conditions were met, obtain Social Security numbers and certain benefits.

Texas's evidence supported at least 500,000 potential beneficiaries and a loss of at least $130.89 per subsidized driver's license. The evidence on how DAPA would be administered included DACA's high approval rate and union president Kenneth Palinkas's declaration; USCIS official Donald Neufeld's declaration described case-specific review and discretionary denials.
sections.Issue: Did Texas have standing, and was DAPA reviewable under the APA? Were the states substantially likely to succeed on their claims that DAPA was a substantive rule requiring notice and comment and, separately, that it exceeded DHS's statutory authority, so that the preliminary injunction should stand?
sections.Holding: The Fifth Circuit in 2015, in an opinion by Judge Jerry E. Smith joined by Judge Elrod over Judge King's dissent, affirmed the nationwide preliminary injunction 2-1. The majority held that Texas had standing, that the program was reviewable, and that the states were substantially likely to prevail both on their notice-and-comment claim and on their separate claim that the program exceeded statutory authority. It found irreparable state losses and held that the balance of harms and the public interest favored preserving the status quo. The court did not order deportations, decide the Take Care claim or invalidate every form of deferred action, and it expressly reserved the validity of individual, genuinely case-specific deferred-action grants.
sections.Reasoning:
Standing rested on Texas's anticipated cost of issuing subsidized driver's licenses to newly eligible applicants; increased tax payments or insurance benefits were distinct transactions and not offsets, and the injury was not manufactured, because Texas adopted its policy before DACA and DAPA. The majority also applied the special solicitude of Massachusetts v. EPA. The states were arguably within the INA's zone of interests, and INA § 1252(g) did not bar a suit in which states asserted their own challenge.

On reviewability under APA § 701(a)(2), the majority distinguished presumptively unreviewable nonenforcement from DAPA's affirmative grant of lawful presence and associated eligibility.

On notice and comment, a policy statement differs from a substantive rule by whether it imposes rights or obligations and genuinely leaves decisionmakers free to exercise discretion; a pronouncement can bind through its text or its practical application. The majority acknowledged that DAPA's text purported to preserve discretion but upheld, under clear-error review, the district court's predictive finding about how it would be administered. It also rejected the procedural-rule and public-benefits exceptions.

On statutory authority, the majority assumed without deciding that Chevron deference applied and found that Congress had directly addressed lawful presence and employment authorization in the INA's detailed scheme; general enforcement grants did not delegate a decision of this economic and political magnitude. Nationwide relief was upheld because immigration administration was intended to be uniform and beneficiaries could move across state lines.

Judge King, dissenting, would have dismissed the case as nonjusticiable, viewing DAPA as a guideline for prosecutorial discretion whose collateral effects came from preexisting law. She would have found a policy statement, criticized the inference from DACA and the conflation of rejections with denials, thought the conflicting declarations required an evidentiary hearing, and rejected the majority's statutory analysis.

LRS-MAX-TIRE.rule: An agency's discretionary safety requirement is arbitrary under APA § 706(2)(A) when the agency does not adequately connect it to safety or support its practicability against concrete record objections, but a court may not reweigh requirements Congress expressly imposed.

sections.Parties: The National Tire Dealers & Retreaders Association petitioned for direct review of a labeling provision in Standard No. 117, adopted by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. The association wanted the permanent-labeling requirement for retreaded tires set aside, taking the position that the information could be supplied on a label affixed at sale. The agency and the Secretary defended the requirement on the strength of available information and agency expertise.
sections.Procedural History: NHTSA adopted Standard No. 117 through informal notice-and-comment rulemaking that included a technical conference and several proposals and reconsideration stages; in denying reconsideration it invoked all available information and agency expertise. The association petitioned the D.C. Circuit for direct review and did not challenge the use of informal procedures. The court applied the review approach of Automotive Parts, under which review of legislative rulemaking is searching for arbitrariness and irrationality but is not formal substantial-evidence review. On January 8, 1974 the court vacated the standard in part: it set aside the permanent-labeling requirement for size, maximum inflation pressure, ply rating, tube type and bias-belted or radial construction, and left in place the requirements Congress had expressly imposed, actual ply number and maximum load.
sections.Material Facts:
Paragraph S6.3.2 of Standard No. 117, adopted under the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act of 1966, required pneumatic passenger tires retreaded on or after February 1, 1974 to have permanently molded into or onto a sidewall the tire's size, maximum permissible inflation pressure, maximum load, actual number of plies or ply rating, tube type, and bias-belted or radial construction designation. Section 201 of the Act itself specified permanent and conspicuous tire labeling, including the actual number of plies and maximum permissible load.

Retreaders reused casings of many sizes and constructions, and removing the old tread could remove markings on the shoulder. About one-third of existing casings bore the information where it would survive buffing. Relabeling the others involved frequently changing information plates in hot molds. Industry comments described large numbers of possible combinations, burn hazards, increased expense and unsuccessful labels; one company's experiment reported only 80% effectiveness and an added cost exceeding $2.50 per retread, approximately 30%. These were industry submissions, not court-certified figures.

NHTSA believed that methods already used for tire identification and recordkeeping could be adapted and that sorting casings into groups could reduce plate changes. It disclaimed any obligation to connect particular records to particular determinations.
sections.Issue: Was NHTSA's requirement that safety information be permanently molded onto retreaded tires arbitrary under APA § 706(2)(A), given § 103's requirement that standards be practicable and meet the need for motor vehicle safety? Could the court also set aside the permanent-labeling items that Congress had expressly specified in § 201?
sections.Holding: The D.C. Circuit in 1974, in an opinion by Judge Wilkey joined by Judge Tamm, with Judge Spottswood W. Robinson III concurring separately in the disposition, held the discretionary permanent-labeling requirements arbitrary on this record. The agency had not adequately connected the extra requirement of permanence to safety or justified its economic practicability. The court vacated the requirement as to size, maximum inflation pressure, ply rating, tube type and bias-belted or radial construction, and preserved the permanent labeling of actual ply number and maximum load that Congress had expressly required. The conclusion concerned the present record and did not establish that no agency could ever support these requirements with further analysis and evidence.
sections.Reasoning:
On safety, the majority accepted that size, load, inflation and construction information helped prevent mismatching, overloading and overinflation. The contested point was permanence: an affixed label could inform the original purchaser, and permanence could matter later, if a tire changed vehicles, was resold or had to be matched with replacements. The Secretary supplied no record illustrations of how frequent or important those later transactions were, and the government acknowledged that an expert could identify many tire characteristics by inspection. The relationship between permanence and safety was too remote on this record to justify the substantial asserted burden.

Congress had nonetheless specified permanent labels for actual ply number and maximum load. APA review of an agency's discretionary choice did not authorize the court to reweigh Congress's express requirement, so those items survived even though the court's policy discussion could logically apply to them too.

On practicability, which the legislative history showed to include economic factors, reasonable cost and feasibility, concrete comments about relabeling burdens required a persuasive explanation, record support or an inherently plausible response. The recordkeeping analogy was incomplete, because retreader identification generally stayed constant across tires while the safety-label characteristics varied among casings, and the sorting suggestion lacked support. The agency's refusal to identify which record materials supported its determinations made the problem more acute; expertise could not overcome contrary record indications by unsupported assertion alone.

Judge Robinson concurred in the partial vacatur because the Secretary had not adequately considered economic practicability; about thirty million tires were retreaded each year and an estimated twenty million lacked suitable labels. He did not share the majority's doubts about safety, regarding the value of permanent information as a matter of common experience.

LRS-MAX-TYSON.rule: On substantial-evidence review, an agency may rest a health standard on cumulative, imperfect scientific evidence and scientifically supported conservative assumptions, but it must explain with evidence why a feasible further protection is unnecessary when significant risk remains.

sections.Parties: Petitioners on both sides sought direct review of OSHA's ethylene oxide (EtO) standard. The Association of Ethylene Oxide Users challenged the evidentiary foundations of the 1 ppm exposure limit and the associated warnings. Public Citizen challenged OSHA's refusal to require a short-term exposure limit and argued that OSHA had unlawfully surrendered its decisional authority to the Office of Management and Budget; members of Congress supported that argument as amici. The Ethylene Oxide Industry Council supported OSHA's decision against a short-term limit.
sections.Procedural History: After litigation over delay, OSHA proposed a new EtO rule in 1983 and held hearings. It prepared an unpublished final rule in June 1984 and submitted the draft for OMB review under Executive Order 12,291. OSHA then published the 1 ppm long-term limit, reopened the record on the short-term limit and, in January 1985, declined to require one. The D.C. Circuit consolidated direct petitions for review of the exposure standard and of the later decision against a short-term limit. On July 25, 1986 the court affirmed the 1 ppm limit, upheld the finding that the record did not establish dose-rate effects, and remanded the short-term limit issue for further proceedings. It declined to decide the constitutional questions concerning OMB's role.
sections.Material Facts:
EtO was widely used in manufacturing and to sterilize hospital instruments; hospital sterilization created particularly serious risks of worker exposure. In 1971 OSHA adopted a consensus limit of 50 parts per million averaged over an eight-hour working day. Later research suggested carcinogenic, genetic and reproductive hazards. OSHA's 1983 rulemaking produced about 1,600 transcript pages and more than 300 exhibits. Its June 1984 draft final rule provided a 1 ppm eight-hour permissible exposure limit (PEL) and a 10 ppm short-term exposure limit (STEL) averaged over fifteen minutes.

OMB challenged the draft's predicted benefits, cost effectiveness and scientific justification, particularly for the STEL. OSHA published the 1 ppm PEL with monitoring, engineering controls, protective equipment, medical surveillance, warnings and recordkeeping requirements, and in January 1985 declined to require a STEL. The draft containing a STEL was never a published, binding rule.

OSHA relied on epidemiological studies of exposed workers together with animal experiments, and extrapolated from the Bushy Run rat study using a linear, no-threshold model. It estimated 634 to 1,093 excess deaths per 10,000 exposed workers at 50 ppm and 12 to 23 at 1 ppm; these were modeled estimates. OSHA chose 1 ppm because it could not demonstrate the feasibility of a lower long-term limit, not because that level eliminated all significant risk.
sections.Issue: Were OSHA's findings about EtO's health hazards and its justification for the 1 ppm PEL supported by substantial evidence in the record as a whole? Did OSHA adequately explain why that long-term limit made a feasible STEL unnecessary despite the significant risk remaining at 1 ppm? The court also faced, but did not decide, the legality of OMB's involvement.
sections.Holding: The D.C. Circuit in 1986, in an opinion by Judge McGowan joined by Chief Judge Robinson and Judge Wright with no separate opinion, upheld OSHA's 1 ppm long-term exposure limit and the warning-sign requirement, and upheld the limited finding that the record did not establish a dose-rate effect. It held that OSHA had not adequately explained its refusal to adopt a STEL and remanded for OSHA either to adopt one or to explain, using empirical or expert evidence on exposure patterns, why one would not further control long-term average exposures. The court did not itself promulgate the 10 ppm limit, and it expressly avoided deciding whether OMB's intervention was lawful.
sections.Reasoning:
The Occupational Safety and Health Act required a threshold finding of significant risk; for toxic substances § 6(b)(5) directed OSHA to select the standard that most adequately protected workers to the extent feasible, using the best available evidence, and § 6(f) required substantial-evidence review. Applying that standard to hybrid rulemaking, the court required the agency to identify its evidence, explain its reasoning, disclose assumptions and answer significant contrary evidence, but would not choose its own scientific conclusion merely because reasonable scientists disagreed. Scientific certainty was not required.

On the PEL, OSHA acknowledged the weaknesses of the worker studies and answered criticisms of the animal studies with expert evidence and reanalysis; read together, the studies supported a reasonable inference of carcinogenicity, reinforced by evidence of genetic changes and reproductive effects. The court rejected the argument that the Benzene case prohibited the no-threshold assumption: Benzene condemned an unsupported assertion of significant risk, while here OSHA developed a dose-response analysis and supported its assumptions with scientific evidence. The court reserved whether an unsupported no-threshold assumption would be valid.

On the STEL, OSHA reasonably found that the record did not establish a dose-rate effect, but that did not answer a different point. Even without such an effect, restricting short bursts could lower a worker's total dose, since a worker with low background exposure could have relatively high brief exposures and still meet the eight-hour average. OSHA assumed the PEL would deliver virtually all the STEL's benefits but made no adequate findings about actual exposure patterns. Because significant risk remained at 1 ppm and STEL feasibility was uncontested at this stage, OSHA had to show why a STEL would not further reduce that risk.

Because statutory review supplied the remand, the court declined to decide the constitutional questions about OMB's role.

LRS-MAX-WV.rule: In extraordinary cases where an agency asserts a power of great economic and political significance, the agency must identify clear congressional authorization for that power; a merely plausible reading of general statutory language is not enough.

sections.Parties: States and private parties defending EPA's 2019 repeal of the Clean Power Plan petitioned the Court after the D.C. Circuit vacated that repeal. The state petitioners wanted reversal of a judgment that purported to restore a rule requiring them to regulate power-plant emissions more stringently. The government, for EPA, continued to defend its authority under Clean Air Act § 111(d) to impose emissions limits based on generation shifting, while saying it did not intend to enforce the Plan as it developed a new rule.
sections.Procedural History: The Court stayed the Clean Power Plan in 2016. After a change in administrations, EPA repealed the Plan in 2019, interpreting § 111 to restrict the best system to measures applicable at individual facilities, and substituted the Affordable Clean Energy rule. States and private parties challenged the repeal and replacement, and other states and companies intervened to defend them. The D.C. Circuit concluded that EPA had misunderstood its statutory authority, vacated the repeal and replacement rule, and remanded. After another change in administrations, EPA obtained a partial stay of the mandate so that the Plan would not return to effect while it developed a new rule. The Court reviewed consolidated petitions by parties defending the repeal, and on June 30, 2022 it reversed the D.C. Circuit and remanded.
sections.Material Facts:
Section 111 of the Clean Air Act addresses categories of stationary sources. EPA identifies the best adequately demonstrated system of emission reduction, taking account of cost, nonair health and environmental effects and energy requirements, and a standard of performance reflects the emissions limitation achievable through that system. For existing sources under § 111(d), EPA establishes the required degree of reduction while states prepare and enforce implementing plans.

The 2015 Clean Power Plan addressed carbon dioxide from existing coal- and gas-fired power plants. Its first building block was heat-rate improvements at coal plants; its second shifted generation from coal to gas; its third shifted generation from coal and gas to renewables. Operators could reduce their own generation, invest in cleaner generation, or acquire allowances or credits through trading. EPA modeled a feasible national shift from coal's 38 percent share of generation in 2014 to 27 percent in 2030, then derived emissions limits that existing coal plants could not meet without generation shifting.

The Plan never took effect, so the compliance costs, plant retirements and employment effects the majority cited were projections. Justice Kagan emphasized projected benefits and later market changes that met the Plan's national emissions target without its implementation.
sections.Issue: Did Congress, in Clean Air Act § 111(d), authorize EPA to set carbon-emissions caps for existing power plants by selecting generation shifting as the best system of emission reduction? The Court also had to decide whether the state petitioners had standing and whether the government's intention not to enforce the Plan mooted the case.
sections.Holding: The Court in 2022, in an opinion by Chief Justice Roberts joined by Justices Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, Kavanaugh and Barrett, held 6-3 that Congress did not authorize EPA under § 111(d) to set carbon-emissions caps using the Clean Power Plan's generation-shifting approach. Because that assertion of power presented a major question, EPA needed clear congressional authorization, and the general authority to select the best system of emission reduction did not suffice. The state petitioners had standing and the case was not moot. The Court declined to decide whether the statutory phrase excludes every measure beyond improving an individual source's pollution performance, and it did not forbid all emissions trading or decide the validity of any replacement rule.
sections.Reasoning:
On justiciability, the judgment below purported to restore a rule requiring the states to regulate more stringently, and reversal would redress that injury. The government bore the burden of showing that its voluntary cessation made recurrence unreasonable to expect; it kept defending its authority to impose generation-shifting limits and did not disclaim their future use.

On the merits, the majority drew on Brown & Williamson, Utility Air, Gonzales and other decisions: in extraordinary cases, the history and breadth of the asserted power and its economic and political significance give reason to hesitate before accepting a merely plausible statutory reading, and separation-of-powers considerations and legislative intent require clear congressional authorization. This claim was extraordinary because EPA invoked a longstanding, rarely used gap-filling provision to restructure the electricity sector's generation mix, a transformative expansion from earlier § 111 standards designed to make sources operate more cleanly. Cost, feasibility and grid-reliability constraints did not sufficiently limit the power, EPA's traditional expertise did not necessarily reach national energy policy, and Congress had repeatedly failed to enact comparable carbon cap-and-trade measures. That the word system can broadly describe generation shifting was not enough for so extraordinary a claim.

Justice Gorsuch, joined by Justice Alito, concurred, explaining the doctrine as a clear-statement rule protecting Article I, democratic accountability, federalism and fair notice.

Justice Kagan, joined by Justices Breyer and Sotomayor, dissented. She read the grant as deliberately broad: system encompassed coordinated market mechanisms, and cost, demonstrated effectiveness and energy constraints supplied meaningful limits. She understood the earlier cases as ordinary contextual interpretation and said the majority confused broad authorization with vague authorization.

LRS-NEXT-009.rule: An appointee who exercises significant authority under federal law is an officer who must be appointed as the Appointments Clause prescribes; Congress and its presiding officers are not permissible appointing authorities for such officers.

sections.Parties: Senator James Buckley, presidential candidate Eugene McCarthy, contributors, political parties and advocacy organizations brought pre-enforcement constitutional challenges to the Federal Election Campaign Act as amended in 1974. They wanted the contribution and expenditure limits, disclosure rules, public financing and the structure of the Federal Election Commission struck down. The Commission and the Act's defenders argued that the Constitution permitted congressional appointment of officials performing appropriate legislative functions.
sections.Procedural History: The litigation used the Act's special procedure: district-court certification of constitutional questions to the D.C. Circuit sitting en banc, followed by direct appeal to the Court. After a remand to develop findings and identify the issues, the Court of Appeals substantially upheld the challenged provisions and treated much of the appointments challenge as premature. A three-judge District Court separately upheld the public-financing provisions of the Internal Revenue Code. Both judgments reached the Court, which found the appointments challenge ripe. In No. 75-436 the Court affirmed in part and reversed in part the D.C. Circuit's judgment; in No. 75-437 it affirmed the District Court. It stayed for up to thirty days the judgment affecting the Commission's powers and accorded de facto validity to the Commission's past actions. The assigned casebook excerpt principally reproduces the appointments issue and omits this remedial treatment.
sections.Material Facts:
The 1974 amendments combined contribution limits, expenditure limits, disclosure, public financing of presidential campaigns and an independent Federal Election Commission. The Commission had eight members. Six voted: two selected by the President pro tempore of the Senate on the majority and minority leaders' recommendations, two similarly selected by the Speaker of the House, and two selected by the President. All six required confirmation by both Houses of Congress. The Secretary of the Senate and the Clerk of the House were nonvoting ex officio members. Commissioners served statutory terms and were not subject to another branch's day-to-day direction.

The Commission did substantially more than collect reports. It could investigate, issue subpoenas, audit, promulgate regulations, formulate policy, issue advisory opinions protecting good-faith reliance, determine eligibility for public campaign funds and seek repayment of overpayments. It had primary civil enforcement responsibility and could bring suits itself, and it had statutory authority, after proceedings, to disqualify a candidate who failed to file a required report. By the time the Court decided the case, the Commission had begun rulemaking.
sections.Issue: Could Congress, consistently with the Appointments Clause, provide for the voting members of the Federal Election Commission, who administered and enforced federal election law, to be selected in part by congressional officers and confirmed by both Houses? Other branches of the case asked whether the Act's contribution limits, expenditure limits, disclosure rules and public financing were constitutional.
sections.Holding: The Court in 1976, in a per curiam opinion with eight Justices participating and Stevens taking no part, held that the Commission's voting members were at least inferior officers and that none of the six had been appointed constitutionally; all eight accepted the appointments defect. The existing Commission could keep functions of gathering, investigating and disseminating information comparable to a legislative committee's work, but civil enforcement litigation, rulemaking, consequential advisory opinions and determinations of eligibility for funds or office could be exercised only by properly appointed officers. In the full decision the Court also upheld the contribution ceilings, the disclosure provisions as construed and public financing, and invalidated the limits on independent expenditures, candidates' personal resources and overall campaign expenditures.
sections.Reasoning:
An appointee who exercises significant authority under federal law is an officer subject to the Appointments Clause. Principal officers require presidential nomination and Senate advice and consent; Congress may permit inferior officers to be appointed by the President alone, a court of law or a department head. The Court did not need to classify the Commissioners more precisely because their selection failed even the methods permitted for inferior officers: the President's two selections were subject to House as well as Senate confirmation, and the other four originated with congressional officers who were neither courts nor department heads. Footnote 162 distinguishes officers from employees, described as subordinate lesser functionaries.

The Court read the Clause within the separation of powers. The branches are interdependent, but Congress cannot enlarge its legislative role by appointing those charged with enforcing its statutes; text, convention history and the danger of congressional aggrandizement supported the same conclusion. Congress's power to regulate federal elections and the Necessary and Proper Clause could not justify a forbidden selection method, and the wish to insulate election enforcement from an incumbent President could not alter the constitutional allocation. Humphrey's Executor and Wiener involved officers selected through constitutionally prescribed appointments, so quasi-legislative and quasi-judicial functions did not place an agency outside the Clause. The Court reserved whether candidate disqualification would itself violate Article I and declined to decide the challenge to congressional disapproval of Commission regulations.

Among the separate opinions, Burger agreed that the appointments were invalid but opposed blanket de facto validation of past Commission acts. White agreed with the appointments defect but would have sustained congressional disapproval of regulations for a properly appointed agency.

LRS-NEXT-011.rule: The power to remove executive officers appointed by the President with Senate consent is constitutionally vested in the President, and Congress may not make its exercise depend on the Senate's consent.

sections.Parties: Frank S. Myers, a first-class postmaster at Portland, Oregon, sued the United States in the Court of Claims for the salary he would have earned during the rest of his four-year term after he was removed without the Senate's consent. His administratrix prosecuted the appeal to the Court. The government answered that Article II gave the President an exclusive removal power. Senator George Wharton Pepper, at the Court's request, presented the arguments against that position as a friend of the Court.
sections.Procedural History: Myers filed his salary action in the Court of Claims on April 21, 1921; a supplemental petition after his term expired on July 21 sought $8,838.71 for the period following removal. The Court of Claims rejected the claim on the ground of laches, reasoning that a dismissed officer had to assert his rights promptly. On the administratrix's appeal, the Court agreed with the general requirement of prompt action but found that Myers had satisfied it, and the Solicitor General conceded orally that laches had not been shown. The constitutional question therefore could not be avoided. On October 25, 1926 the Court affirmed the judgment against the administratrix on the different ground that the statutory Senate-consent condition was unconstitutional.
sections.Material Facts:
Section 6 of the Act of July 12, 1876 provided that postmasters of the first three classes were to be appointed and could be removed by the President with Senate consent, and would hold office for four years unless sooner removed or suspended according to law. Myers was appointed first-class postmaster at Portland, Oregon on July 21, 1917, by the President with the Senate's advice and consent, for a four-year term.

On January 20, 1920 Myers was asked to resign and refused. The majority dates his removal to February 2, 1920, when the Postmaster General acted at the President's direction; Justice McReynolds's recital uses February 3. The Senate did not consent to the removal. On February 10 Myers petitioned the President and the Senate's Post Offices Committee for an opportunity to answer any charges. He kept protesting to the Department through the end of his term, took no other occupation and received no compensation for other service. The President made a recess appointment of Jones in August 1920, and Jones took office on September 19. Neither a notice of removal nor a nomination of a successor was sent to the Senate during the three Senate sessions before Myers's term ended.
sections.Issue: Could Congress require the Senate's consent before the President removed an inferior executive officer whom the President had appointed with the Senate's consent? A threshold question was whether Myers had waited too long to sue.
sections.Holding: The Court in 1926, in an opinion by Chief Justice Taft with Justices Holmes, McReynolds and Brandeis each dissenting, upheld Myers's removal and rejected the salary claim. The power to remove executive officers appointed by the President with Senate consent is constitutionally vested in the President, and Congress could not make its exercise depend on another Senate vote. The Court held the 1867 Tenure of Office Act invalid insofar as it prevented presidential removal of such officers and applied the same conclusion to the postal restriction. It rejected the Court of Claims' laches conclusion. It expressly left undecided whether vesting appointment of an inferior officer in the President alone would permit additional congressional regulation of removal.
sections.Reasoning:
Taft read the Executive Vesting Clause as a grant of authority. A President personally responsible for faithful execution of the laws must work through subordinates, and selecting them and dismissing those who no longer warrant confidence are executive functions; otherwise responsibility would stay with the President while control lay elsewhere.

The Senate's participation in appointment did not imply participation in removal. A rejected nominee can ordinarily be replaced by another suitable candidate, but a Senate veto over removal could force the President to retain an incumbent shown by experience to be unsuitable. Congress could still create an office, define its duties, prescribe reasonable qualifications, establish its duration and set its compensation.

The principal historical support was the 1789 debate on the Department of Foreign Affairs, where the House eliminated an express removal clause in favor of language that Taft read as recognizing an existing constitutional power. He gave that early construction substantial weight, treated Marbury's discussion of irrevocable appointment as unnecessary to the judgment there, and regarded the Reconstruction-era Tenure of Office Act as a departure. Under United States v. Perkins, Congress could restrict removal by a department head in whom it vested appointment, but it could not draw removal participation to itself.

Justice Holmes, dissenting, reasoned that Congress, which could abolish the office and determine its duration and pay, could also protect an incumbent's tenure. Justice McReynolds stressed that this was an inferior officer with a definite term under an explicit restriction, and disputed the majority's reading of 1789 and of Marbury. Justice Brandeis argued that authority to prescribe tenure included authority to specify its ending conditions, and that separation of powers deliberately tolerates friction to restrain arbitrary power.

LRS-NEXT-016.rule: When the Government seeks civil penalties on a statutory claim that is legal in nature, such as securities fraud closely related to common-law fraud, the Seventh Amendment requires a jury trial in an Article III court unless the public-rights exception applies.

sections.Parties: The Securities and Exchange Commission brought an administrative enforcement proceeding against George Jarkesy and his firm, Patriot28, the investment adviser to two funds he launched, alleging securities fraud. Jarkesy and Patriot28, the respondents in the Court, had petitioned the Fifth Circuit for review of the SEC's final order and wanted it set aside. The SEC wanted its order and its use of administrative proceedings to impose civil penalties upheld.
sections.Procedural History: The SEC began administrative enforcement in 2013. An administrative law judge issued an initial decision in 2014, and the Commission reviewed it and entered its final order in 2020. A divided Fifth Circuit panel granted the petition for review and vacated the order on three grounds: the administrative adjudication violated the Seventh Amendment jury right, Congress had insufficiently guided the SEC's choice between agency and court proceedings under the nondelegation doctrine, and two layers of for-cause removal protection for ALJs violated the separation of powers. Judge Davis dissented. After rehearing en banc was denied, the Court granted certiorari. In 2024 the Court affirmed the Fifth Circuit and remanded for further proceedings, resting on the Seventh Amendment ground alone and not reaching nondelegation or ALJ removal protection.
sections.Material Facts:
The antifraud provisions of the Securities Act of 1933, the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 address material misrepresentation or concealment. The SEC can enforce them through litigation in federal court or through administrative proceedings inside the agency, where the Commission or its delegate decides facts and law and later judicial review of supported factual findings is deferential. Before the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act, civil penalties against persons in respondents' position had to be obtained in federal court; Dodd-Frank expanded the SEC's administrative penalty authority to match its court authority.

Between 2007 and 2010 Jarkesy launched two investment funds that raised about $24 million from 120 accredited investors, with Patriot28 as investment adviser. The SEC alleged that they misrepresented investment strategies, the identity of the funds' auditor and prime broker, and the fund values used to calculate management fees. These were the agency's allegations and determinations, not findings from a trial in the Court. The Commission's final order imposed a $300,000 civil penalty, ordered cessation of violations and disgorgement, and barred Jarkesy from certain securities activities; the dissent identifies Patriot28's disgorgement amount as $685,000.
sections.Issue: Did the SEC's claims for civil penalties for securities fraud implicate the Seventh Amendment right to a jury trial? If so, did the public-rights exception nevertheless permit those claims to be resolved administratively without a jury?
sections.Holding: The Court in 2024, in an opinion by Chief Justice Roberts joined by Justices Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, Kavanaugh and Barrett, held 6-3 that respondents were entitled to a jury trial in an Article III court on these securities-fraud civil-penalty claims. The claims implicated the Seventh Amendment, and the public-rights exception did not permit administrative resolution without a jury. The Court affirmed the Fifth Circuit and remanded. It did not reach nondelegation or ALJ removal protection, did not decide whether later cases had effectively overruled Atlas Roofing, did not decide that respondents had committed no fraud, and did not prevent the SEC from pursuing the claims in the constitutionally proper forum. The case concerns civil penalties for securities fraud, not every agency adjudication or every SEC remedy.
sections.Reasoning:
The Seventh Amendment extends to statutory claims that are legal in nature, as opposed to equity or admiralty matters. Under Tull and Granfinanciera a court considers the cause of action's common-law analogue and the nature of the remedy, the remedy being the more important factor. These penalties were punitive and deterrent and not solely restorative: the statutory factors addressed culpability, recidivism and deterrence, and the SEC was not required to distribute the penalty to injured investors. The close relationship between the antifraud claims and common-law fraud reinforced the conclusion; identical elements were not required.

On public rights, Congress can assign some matters, such as revenue collection, aspects of customs and immigration, public lands, tribal relations and public benefits, for initial determination outside Article III, but the presumption favors Article III courts. Granfinanciera supplied the central analogy: designating fraudulent-conveyance actions as core bankruptcy proceedings did not eliminate the jury right, because the substance of the action controlled. Statutory novelty and the Government's participation as enforcer were not sufficient by themselves. The majority distinguished Atlas Roofing because the OSH Act imposed new, detailed safety requirements and did not restate a traditional common-law cause of action.

Justice Gorsuch, joined by Justice Thomas, concurred, emphasizing that Article III and Fifth Amendment due process each independently supported the result alongside the jury guarantee.

Justice Sotomayor, joined by Justices Kagan and Jackson, dissented. She viewed claims belonging to the Government in its sovereign capacity as the central category of the public-rights doctrine, read Atlas Roofing as controlling governmental civil penalties, and stressed precedent, congressional reliance and the potential effects on numerous penalty schemes, some of which agencies could pursue only administratively.

LRS-SUP-0001.rule: Claims that congressional districting is excessively partisan present political questions beyond the reach of the federal courts, because the Constitution provides no judicially discoverable and manageable standards for allocating partisan political power.

sections.Parties: In the North Carolina case, the Democratic Party, Common Cause, individual voters and later the League of Women Voters and additional voters challenged the State's 2016 congressional plan, drawn to favor Republicans; the defendants appealed. In the Maryland case, captioned in the Court as Lamone v. Benisek, three voters challenged a congressional map drawn to favor Democrats, and the state defendants appealed. The plaintiffs wanted the maps held unconstitutional; the state defendants contended that federal courts lacked a manageable constitutional standard.
sections.Procedural History: The North Carolina litigation began in August 2016. A three-judge court found constitutional violations after trial, and the defendants appealed directly under 28 U.S.C. § 1253. The Court remanded for reconsideration after Gill v. Whitford; the district court again found standing and justiciability, invalidated twelve of thirteen districts under equal protection, reaffirmed its other constitutional conclusions and enjoined use of the plan after the November 2018 election. The defendants appealed again. The Maryland voters filed their action in November 2013; the three-judge court granted them summary judgment under the First Amendment, permanently prohibited use of the plan and required a replacement for 2020, and the state defendants appealed directly. On June 27, 2019 the Court vacated both district-court judgments and remanded with instructions to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction.
sections.Material Facts:
Both maps involved admitted partisan objectives. In North Carolina, Republican legislators instructed their mapmaker to produce a delegation of ten Republicans and three Democrats. Representative David Lewis defended that objective because he preferred Republican victories and did not think an eleven-to-two map possible. The legislature adopted the 2016 plan by a party-line vote, and Republicans won ten of thirteen districts in 2016. In 2018 they won nine seats and Democrats three, with a thirteenth seat subject to a new election after fraud allegations. The dissent adds that the 2016 plan followed a judicial finding that two districts in the earlier plan were racial gerrymanders.

In Maryland, Governor Martin O'Malley and Democratic legislators pursued a delegation of seven Democrats and one Republican by converting the Sixth District, then long held by a Republican. Population equality required removing only roughly 10,000 residents, but the plan moved about 360,000 voters out and 350,000 in, reducing registered Republicans by approximately 66,000 and increasing registered Democrats by approximately 24,000. Adopted by a party-line vote, the map flipped the Sixth District in 2012, and a Democrat held it through the period the opinion describes.
sections.Issue: Are claims that congressional districting is excessively partisan justiciable in federal court under the constitutional theories asserted, namely equal protection, the First Amendment, Article I § 2 and the Elections Clause, or do they present political questions?
sections.Holding: The Court in 2019, in an opinion by Roberts for a five-Justice majority with Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch and Kavanaugh, and with Kagan dissenting for four, held that partisan-gerrymandering claims present political questions beyond federal judicial reach because the Constitution provides no judicially discoverable and manageable standards for allocating partisan political power. It vacated both district-court judgments and remanded with instructions to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction. That is a jurisdictional disposition, not a merits determination that the maps were fair. The Court did not deny that the maps were highly partisan, expressly disclaimed approval of excessive partisan gerrymandering, and preserved judicially cognizable racial-gerrymandering and population-equality claims.
sections.Reasoning:
Article III limits federal courts to judicially resolvable cases, and under Baker v. Carr the absence of discoverable and manageable standards can make a claim a political question. The majority traced partisan districting to the founding era and discussed the Elections Clause's assignment of regulation to state legislatures subject to congressional revision, while rejecting the argument that the Clause makes every electoral question exclusively congressional. Gaffney, Bandemer, Vieth, LULAC and Gill had produced no controlling workable standard.

The first obstacle was a legally grounded baseline. Claims about seat outcomes implicitly seek some proper distribution of political influence, but the Constitution does not require proportional representation and does not tell judges how to rank competition, safe seats, traditional criteria or incumbent protection. The second was degree: even with a baseline, nothing told courts how much deviation was unconstitutional. Equal-population cases rest on a mathematical rule and racial-gerrymandering claims target a suspect classification, whereas some political consideration in districting is permissible.

The majority rejected each proposed test. Partisan motivation did not become impermissible solely because it predominated, and predicting durable advantage required uncertain assessments. The First Amendment theories supplied no sufficiently clear measure of burden. Comparison with alternative maps made a federal violation vary with criteria the mapmakers themselves selected. The Article I § 2 argument resembled a nonjusticiable Guarantee Clause objection. The majority identified state constitutional rules, legislation, commissions and Congress as potential responses.

Kagan, joined by Ginsburg, Breyer and Sotomayor, dissented. Her framework required a predominant purpose of entrenchment, substantial vote dilution and no legitimate nonpartisan explanation, measured against what the State would have done given its own geography and nonpartisan priorities, and she relied on expert evidence of thousands of alternative maps showing the North Carolina plan to be an extreme departure.

LRS-SUP-0002.rule: A transaction within the letter of a statute may fall outside the statute where the legislation as a whole, the surrounding circumstances and the consequences show that the legislature did not intend to include it.

sections.Parties: The United States sued the Church of the Holy Trinity, a New York religious corporation, to recover the statutory penalty for arranging the migration of an alien under a preexisting contract for labor or service. The government relied on the enacted prohibition and had won below. The church, the defendant, brought the case to the Court by writ of error and argued that its contract with a rector lay outside the legislative intention and the evil Congress sought to remedy.
sections.Procedural History: The United States brought a penalty action against the church. The federal Circuit Court for the Southern District of New York held that the church's contract violated the Alien Contract Labor Act of February 26, 1885 and entered judgment accordingly. The church obtained review in the Court by writ of error. On February 29, 1892 the Court reversed and remanded for further proceedings consistent with its interpretation that the Act did not apply to the contract. It did not announce that the Act was unconstitutional. The assigned supplement captions the case Rector of Holy Trinity Church v. United States; both captions refer to the same decision.
sections.Material Facts:
The Act prohibited assisting or encouraging the migration of an alien under a contract, made before migration, to perform labor or service of any kind in the United States. It covered persons and corporations, multiple forms of assistance, and express or implied contracts. Congress expressly exempted categories including professional actors, artists, lecturers, singers and domestic servants. Ministers were not named. The Act's title described prohibiting the migration of aliens under contracts to perform labor.

In September 1887 the church contracted with E. Walpole Warren, then an alien residing in England, to move to New York City and serve as its rector and pastor. Warren moved and performed the agreed service.

A Senate committee report said the committee would have preferred to substitute manual labor or manual service but wanted the bill to pass before adjournment and expected the existing language to be construed that way. A House report described imported laborers and the perceived effects on American wages and social conditions. The committee considered the narrower wording but Congress did not enact it.
sections.Issue: Did the Alien Contract Labor Act's prohibition on assisting the migration of an alien under a prior contract to perform labor or service of any kind apply to a church's contract with a foreign clergyman to serve as its rector, when that contract fell within the statute's literal words?
sections.Holding: The Court in 1892, in an opinion by Justice David J. Brewer with no separate writing, held that the Act did not apply to the church's contract for Warren's services. Brewer expressly conceded that the church's act fell within the literal words of the provision. But a transaction within the statute's letter could fall outside the statute where the legislation, the surrounding circumstances and the consequences showed that the legislature did not intend its inclusion. The Court reversed and remanded. The holding concerned the 1885 labor statute; the Court did not hold the Act unconstitutional or award damages to the church.
sections.Reasoning:
Brewer began with an interpretive principle: general language may reach more than the legislature intended, and courts can limit it by considering the whole legislation, its circumstances or absurd consequences. He defended this as fidelity to legislative intention and not a substitution of judicial preference, and used precedents on unreasonable literal applications, including United States v. Kirby, where broadly phrased protection against obstructing the mail did not prevent officers from lawfully arresting a mail carrier for murder.

He then gathered evidence of intention. The title spoke of labor, which he associated with manual labor and not professional intellectual work; he acknowledged that a title cannot add to or subtract from the statutory body but treated it as evidence of design. The mischief Congress addressed was employers importing cheap unskilled labor that depressed wages, and the Court found no comparable concern about foreign clergy. The committee reports, the title and the circumstances converged on a manual-labor purpose.

Brewer added an extensive account of religious language and practices in American history, from colonial charters to state constitutional provisions and Sunday observance, as showing a society in which Congress would not have intended to penalize a church for recruiting a foreign minister. He also imagined Congress considering a bill expressly forbidding recruitment of prominent religious leaders and thought approval inconceivable.

The supplement's editorial notes, which are not the Court's reasoning, criticize the aggregation of legislative intent and report scholarship on floor statements Brewer did not cite. Citing Carol Chomsky's historical scholarship, the editors also describe the prosecution as an effort by an immigration-restriction opponent to discredit the law.

LRS-SUP-0003A.rule: A beneficiary who intentionally murders the testator to prevent revocation and obtain the estate may not take under the will or by intestate succession; statutes are construed in light of their purpose and the maxim that no one may profit from his own crime.

sections.Parties: Mrs. Riggs and Mrs. Preston, daughters of the testator Francis B. Palmer, sued Palmer's grandson Elmer E. Palmer and the administrator of the estate. The daughters were the plaintiffs and, having lost below, the appellants in the Court of Appeals; they sought to prevent Elmer from taking the estate through his crime. Elmer, the residuary beneficiary under the will, was the defendant. The report's formal caption identifies Philo Riggs as guardian ad litem.
sections.Procedural History: The daughters' civil action was tried before a referee, whose findings established the facts. The resulting judgment dismissed the complaint, and the General Term of the Supreme Court in the Third Judicial Department affirmed. The daughters appealed to the New York Court of Appeals. The appeal was submitted on June 21, 1889 and decided on October 8, 1889. The Court of Appeals reversed the General Term's judgment and the judgment entered on the referee's report and, because the findings already supplied the facts necessary for relief, directed entry of a new judgment without a new trial. Elmer had separately been convicted of second-degree murder; the civil court did not have to determine criminal guilt anew.
sections.Material Facts:
Francis B. Palmer executed a will in 1880. He left small legacies to his two daughters, Mrs. Riggs and Mrs. Preston, and the residue of his real and personal property to his grandson Elmer E. Palmer, subject to support for Elmer's mother, Susan. The will also made a conditional gift over to the daughters if Elmer survived Francis but died under age, unmarried and without issue.

Francis later married Mrs. Bresee. Their antenuptial agreement entitled her to support on his farm during her life in place of dower and other claims against his estate, with that support charged upon the farm.

Elmer lived with his grandfather and knew the contents of the will. In 1882, at age sixteen, he poisoned Francis. The findings established that he acted to prevent Francis from changing the will and to obtain immediate enjoyment of the property. Elmer was convicted of second-degree murder and was confined in a reformatory when the civil action was brought. The will had been validly executed and had not been revoked in a manner specified by statute.
sections.Issue: Did the statutes governing wills and descent require the court to recognize Elmer's inheritance because the will was validly executed and had not been revoked in a statutory manner, or could they be construed against the background principle that a person may not obtain property by his own crime? Would excluding Elmer impose an additional punishment or merely prevent a wrongful acquisition?
sections.Holding: The New York Court of Appeals in 1889, in an opinion by Judge Earl with Judge Gray dissenting and Judge Danforth concurring in the dissent, held that a beneficiary who intentionally murders the testator to prevent revocation and obtain the estate may not take the property under the will or through intestate succession. The court directed that Elmer and the administrator be restrained from using estate property for Elmer's benefit, that the devise and bequest to him be declared ineffective to pass title, and that the daughters be declared the true owners, subject to the charges for Susan and for the widow under the antenuptial agreement. Costs in all courts were imposed on Elmer.
sections.Reasoning:
Earl conceded that if the statutes were applied literally and without qualification, the property would pass to Elmer. He asked what the statutes were designed to accomplish: to let owners dispose of property at death and carry out their lawful final wishes, not to create an incentive for a beneficiary to kill the owner. Had lawmakers expressly considered a beneficiary who murdered the testator to prevent revocation, they would not have intended him to take. He illustrated the method with examples of broad statutory language confined by its reason, such as a barber whose bloodletting escapes a street-bloodshed prohibition.

Earl also offered a common-law basis. Legal rules operate against principles forbidding a person to profit from fraud, acquire property by his own wrong or found a claim on his own crime, and those principles govern statutes unless the legislature displaces them; an express slayer exception was unnecessary. He relied on analogies such as the refusal to allow recovery on life insurance after the claimant feloniously caused the insured's death. Excluding Elmer added no penalty, because before the killing he had no vested ownership; the judgment prevented acquisition and did not confiscate existing property. Nor could he obtain the same benefit as an heir instead of a devisee.

Gray, dissenting, accepted the moral repugnance of the killing but disputed the court's legal authority. The legislature had specified how wills were made, altered and revoked, and murder by a beneficiary was not a prescribed mode of revocation; an intention to revoke does not itself revoke a will. Contract and insurance analogies did not fit a testamentary gift, departing from the will risked a judicially created disposition, and depriving Elmer was an additional consequence for the legislature to specify. He would have affirmed with costs.

LRS-SUP-0003B.rule: A nonmechanical bump stock is not a machinegun under the National Firearms Act, because each shot still requires a separate function of the trigger and the shots do not occur automatically through a single trigger function.

sections.Parties: Michael Cargill owned two nonmechanical bump stocks, surrendered them under protest, and challenged under the Administrative Procedure Act a Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives rule classifying such devices as machineguns. The federal defendants were the Attorney General and other officials defending the rule. Cargill wanted the rule held to exceed the agency's statutory authority; the government wanted the classification upheld. The government won at trial and before a Fifth Circuit panel, Cargill won before the en banc Fifth Circuit, and that judgment in his favor was the one the Court reviewed. The dispute concerned statutory authority, not whether the Second Amendment protected a right to possess the devices.
sections.Procedural History: After a bench trial, the Western District of Texas entered judgment for the government, concluding that a bump stock fit the statutory definition of a machinegun. A Fifth Circuit panel affirmed. The en banc Fifth Circuit later reversed: a majority agreed at least that the statute was ambiguous and that lenity required resolving the ambiguity in Cargill's favor, and an eight-judge plurality went further and found the devices unambiguously excluded. The Court granted review to resolve a conflict among the courts of appeals. It affirmed the en banc judgment, but on its own statutory reading that excluded the devices; it did not make lenity the basis of its decision.
sections.Material Facts:
The National Firearms Act defines a machinegun by its ability to fire automatically more than one shot, without manual reloading, through a single function of the trigger, and also reaches a part designed and intended to convert a weapon into a machinegun. A semiautomatic firearm normally fires once for each separate trigger engagement. A bump stock assists rapid repeated firing. The devices here were nonmechanical bump stocks; the majority expressly excluded spring-operated mechanical devices from the question presented.

Before the challenged rule, ATF had repeatedly taken the position that the devices at issue did not fall within the statutory definition. After the 2017 Las Vegas mass shooting the agency reconsidered. Proposed legislation did not become law, and in 2018 ATF issued a final rule that interpreted a single trigger function to include a single pull and analogous motions and treated the devices as self-regulating mechanisms producing continuous fire. Owners were directed to destroy or surrender covered bump stocks within ninety days, with criminal consequences for noncompliance. Cargill owned two, surrendered them under protest, and challenged the rule.
sections.Issue: Whether a semiautomatic rifle equipped with the nonmechanical bump stock at issue fires more than one shot through a single function of the trigger; whether, even assuming it does, it fires those shots automatically through that trigger function; and whether a purpose-based presumption against rendering a statute ineffective can expand the definition to cover the devices.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 2024, in an opinion by Justice Thomas for six Justices, with Justices Sotomayor, Kagan and Jackson dissenting, held that ATF exceeded its statutory authority by classifying the nonmechanical bump stocks at issue as machineguns. It gave two distinct grounds. First, each shot still requires a separate trigger function, so the device does not produce multiple shots through a single function. Second, even assuming the sequence could be attributed to one trigger function, the additional ongoing input required from the shooter prevents it from occurring automatically through that function. The Fifth Circuit's judgment was affirmed. The Court did not decide any constitutional right to the devices or the classification of every rapid-fire accessory.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority started with the statutory words and dictionary definitions of function and trigger, reading the phrase to identify the action by which the trigger activates the firing mechanism. Each reengagement after reset is therefore a distinct trigger function, and the semiautomatic mechanism releases, fires and resets for each shot. A bump stock facilitates the rapid succession of those engagements without turning them into one mechanical function; rate of fire cannot substitute for the elements Congress chose. The statute does not define the relevant event as the beginning of an entire firing sequence, and ATF's own rule treated analogous motions as trigger functions.

Alternatively, the statute requires multiple shots to occur automatically through a single trigger function, and the device still requires ongoing input beyond that function. Justice Thomas distinguished pressure that constitutes the continuing function of the trigger, as in a conventional machinegun, from additional input elsewhere, and used the Ithaca Model 37 shotgun as an analogy. The presumption against ineffectiveness did not apply because the statute still regulates conventional machineguns and Congress may draw a line narrower than every formulation of a law's purpose. An express statutory definition ordinarily controls even if it differs from ordinary usage.

Justice Alito, concurring, thought the enacting Congress likely would not have seen the devices as materially different from machineguns in lethal effect, but considered the text clear and legislation the remedy. Justice Sotomayor, dissenting with Justices Kagan and Jackson, read a single function of the trigger as a single act by the shooter initiating the firing sequence, relied on the 1934 hearings and reports and on Staples, argued that sustained pressure can coexist with automatic fire, and invoked the presumption against ineffectiveness; she would have upheld the classification.

LRS-SUP-0003C.rule: Under the Gun Control Act, at least some weapon-parts kits are weapons that may readily be converted to fire and at least some unfinished frames or receivers are frames or receivers, so ATF's rule is not facially inconsistent with the statute.

sections.Parties: Jennifer VanDerStok and other individual and business challengers brought a pre-enforcement Administrative Procedure Act action, which they described as facial, against a 2022 rule of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. The federal government defended the rule through the Attorney General and other officials. The challengers wanted the rule set aside as exceeding the agency's statutory authority under the Gun Control Act; the government wanted it upheld. The challengers prevailed in the district court and largely in the Fifth Circuit, and the Court reviewed the Fifth Circuit's judgment.
sections.Procedural History: The Northern District of Texas granted summary judgment and vacated the rule. The Fifth Circuit largely affirmed, concluding that weapon-parts kits categorically were not weapons under subsection (A) of the firearm definition and that subsection (B) reached only completed frames or receivers. The Court granted certiorari on both questions. It accepted, for this case, the parties' framing that the challengers had to show the regulatory provisions inconsistent with the statute on their face, treating the government's formulation as unchallenged in the briefing; the dissents disputed that. The Court reversed the Fifth Circuit's judgment and remanded for further proceedings consistent with its opinion, noting in a footnote that the parties could not use the remand to inject arguments they had failed to pursue in the Court.
sections.Material Facts:
The Gun Control Act defines a firearm to include, under 18 U.S.C. 921(a)(3)(A), a weapon that will, is designed to, or may readily be converted to expel a projectile by explosive action, and it expressly includes starter guns. Subsection (B) separately includes the frame or receiver of any such weapon. ATF's 2022 rule applied the Act's existing licensing, recordkeeping, serialization and background-check requirements to weapon-parts kits that are designed to or may readily be completed or assembled into operating firearms, and to partially complete, disassembled or nonfunctional frames and receivers that can be completed or converted to function as those components. The rule did not simply prohibit every kit or every homemade firearm, and the agency excluded objects not yet sufficiently identifiable as unfinished weapon components.

The record included Polymer80 products that the majority regarded as close enough to their intended final form to satisfy the Act, with evidence about the small amount of work needed to complete them.

The assigned class excerpt is limited to the weapon-parts-kit issue; the full brief supplies the frame-and-receiver analysis, the Sotomayor and Kavanaugh concurrences and Justice Alito's dissent from the full opinion.
sections.Issue: Whether a sufficiently complete weapon-parts kit can already count as a weapon that may readily be converted to fire under subsection (A) even though assembly remains, and whether an unfinished but sufficiently developed component can count as a frame or receiver under subsection (B) despite the absence there of subsection (A)'s ready-conversion phrase. A related procedural question, pressed by the dissents, was what suffices to reject the challengers' facial claim.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 2025, in an opinion by Justice Gorsuch for seven Justices, with Justices Thomas and Alito each dissenting, held that the challenged provisions are not facially inconsistent with the Gun Control Act. At least some weapon-parts kits satisfy subsection (A), and at least some unfinished frames or receivers fall within subsection (B), so the Fifth Circuit's categorical exclusions could not stand.
