The judgment was reversed and the case remanded. The Court did not hold that every collection of parts is a weapon or that the agency may regulate raw material, left open questions about particular products and the significance of tools, instructions and similar materials, and did not finally settle the general test for all pre-enforcement APA challenges.
sections.Reasoning:
Subsection (A) requires both a weapon and a specified relationship to firing: present ability, design or ready conversion. Justice Gorsuch described weapon as an artifact noun, a word for a human-made object identified substantially by its intended function; ordinary speakers may call an unfinished manuscript a novel or an unassembled furniture purchase a table. The starter-gun parenthetical confirms that operational completeness is unnecessary and served as a benchmark for conversion effort; on the evidence, the record kit required no greater burden of time, expertise or specialized equipment. That other provisions expressly regulate combinations of parts shows subsection (A) is narrower, not that it reaches no kit at all. The majority acknowledged a continuum of completeness, comparing it to deciding when removing grains means a heap no longer exists, but some products clearly qualified.

On subsection (B), the majority relied on ordinary usage, the serialization provision in section 923(i), the reference to the frame or receiver of any such weapon, and ATF's longstanding treatment of some incomplete components, while maintaining the court's independent responsibility to interpret the statute. It declined to use lenity or constitutional avoidance.

Justice Sotomayor, concurring, said the duties were longstanding and manufacturers could seek agency classifications. Justice Kavanaugh distinguished offenses requiring willfulness from background-check offenses requiring knowledge and identified a possible fair-notice argument. Justice Jackson said courts determine the boundaries of delegated authority rather than second-guess the agency's policy choices. Justice Thomas, dissenting, objected to the facial-challenge framework, read frames and receivers as the actual functional components, treated starter guns as a specified exception, and would apply lenity if ambiguity remained. Justice Alito agreed the rule was consistent with the statute as applied to the majority's examples but would have requested supplemental briefing or vacated and remanded on the proper test.

LRS-SUP-0004.rule: A court may consult legislative history even when statutory words appear clear on first examination; so read, the water statute's reference to radioactive materials excludes source, byproduct and special nuclear materials regulated under the Atomic Energy Act.

sections.Parties: Colorado organizations and residents, claiming potential harm from radioactive effluents discharged by the Fort St. Vrain Nuclear Generating Station and the Rocky Flats nuclear-weapons-components plant, sued the Environmental Protection Agency and its Administrator under the citizen-suit provision of the Federal Water Pollution Control Act. They sought a declaration that all radioactive materials were pollutants and an injunction compelling regulation of their discharge. The EPA defended its exclusion of materials regulated under the Atomic Energy Act from its water-pollution permit program. The plaintiffs lost in the district court and won in the Tenth Circuit, whose judgment the Court reviewed.
sections.Procedural History: The plaintiffs sued under the citizen-suit provision, which permitted an action for failure to perform a nondiscretionary statutory duty. On cross-motions for summary judgment, the District of Colorado held that the Atomic Energy Commission had exclusive authority over discharges of the covered nuclear materials. The Tenth Circuit reversed. It considered the enacted wording plain, because radioactive materials appeared without the exception the EPA wished to recognize while the statute expressly included other exceptions, and it declined to resolve the legislative-history dispute. The Court granted certiorari and reversed the court of appeals.
sections.Material Facts:
The Atomic Energy Act created a comprehensive system governing source, special nuclear and byproduct materials, under which the Atomic Energy Commission regulated permissible releases and required efforts to keep them as low as reasonably achievable. By the time of the decision the AEC's functions had been divided between the Nuclear Regulatory Commission and the Energy Research and Development Administration. The Fort St. Vrain and Rocky Flats facilities operated in conformity with effluent standards imposed under that Act.

The Federal Water Pollution Control Act separately prohibited discharging pollutants into navigable waters without a federal or approved state permit, expressly included radioactive materials in its definition of pollutant, and allowed a substantial state role, including more stringent state limitations. The EPA excluded source material, special nuclear material and byproduct material from its permit program, explaining that the water statute's reference to radioactive materials covered substances beyond the AEC's jurisdiction, such as radium and accelerator-produced isotopes. The plaintiffs wanted the EPA to regulate the plants' radioactive discharges under the water statute as well. Their claim was of prospective harm; there was no judicial finding that either plant had caused an injury or violated its nuclear standards.
sections.Issue: Whether the Federal Water Pollution Control Act's broad reference to radioactive materials in its definition of pollutant encompassed the source, byproduct and special nuclear materials regulated under the Atomic Energy Act, so that the EPA had to regulate their discharge through its permit program, and whether legislative history may be consulted when the statutory words appear plain.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 1976, in an opinion by Justice Marshall for all eight participating Justices, Justice Stevens taking no part, held that the water-pollution permit program did not include source, byproduct and special nuclear materials regulated under the Atomic Energy Act, and that the EPA acted consistently with its statutory mandate in declining to regulate their discharge through that program. The Tenth Circuit was reversed. The holding did not exempt nuclear facilities from the entire water statute or immunize discharges of other pollutants, and the EPA retained authority under a separate reorganization plan to establish generally applicable environmental radiation standards.
sections.Reasoning:
Justice Marshall rejected any rule categorically forbidding available interpretive aids because statutory words appear clear on an initial examination, and examined the legislative history to determine what the words meant within the larger statutory arrangement. A footnote says the Court did not depend on the agency's interpretation in reaching its conclusion.

The House committee report stated explicitly that the radioactive materials covered by the water statute did not include source, byproduct or special nuclear materials regulated under the Atomic Energy Act. The Senate report discussed developing EPA's technical capacity to set controls for nuclear-fuels-processing plants, but the Court distinguished coverage of a plant from coverage of every material it discharged and gave the more specific House explanation greater weight. On the Senate floor, Senator Muskie assured Senator Pastore that the bill did not change the AEC's existing regulatory authority, referring to Northern States Power Co. v. Minnesota; the Court read the assurance as preserving the existing exclusive arrangement. Adding the materials to the water program would also have introduced a state role that the nuclear scheme severely limited. Representative Wolff's amendment to permit states to regulate radioactive waste from nuclear power plants failed by roughly three to one, and because the unamended water statute already gave states a regulatory role over pollutants, the Court read the failure as additional support for exclusion. The conference committee retained the same language, and Representative Harsha explained that it preserved the understanding in the report and the Senate colloquy.

The plaintiffs' argument from the separate absolute ban on discharging radiological warfare agents and high-level radioactive waste had some logical appeal, but a complete ban on one class did not itself establish permit-program jurisdiction over other classes.

LRS-SUP-0005A.rule: A general residual term in a criminal statute takes its meaning from ordinary usage and the specific list it follows, and a criminal law must give fair warning in language ordinary people understand; a motor vehicle statute so read does not reach aircraft.

sections.Parties: The United States prosecuted McBoyle under the National Motor Vehicle Theft Act for transporting a stolen airplane between states knowing it had been stolen. McBoyle was the defendant; he was convicted, lost in the Tenth Circuit, and had his conviction reviewed by the Court on certiorari. The government's necessary position was that the Act's general residual category reached a self-propelled airplane. McBoyle's position was that the statute's language and context confined the covered vehicles to land transportation.
sections.Procedural History: McBoyle was convicted and sentenced to three years in prison and a $2,000 fine. The Tenth Circuit affirmed. The Court granted certiorari specifically to determine whether the National Motor Vehicle Theft Act applied to aircraft. It was reviewing an actual conviction rather than a hypothetical request for guidance about transporting airplanes. The Court reversed the Tenth Circuit's judgment affirming the conviction. No separate opinion appears in the published decision.
sections.Material Facts:
McBoyle transported a stolen airplane from Ottawa, Illinois, to Guymon, Oklahoma, knowing that the airplane had been stolen. The Court's opinion gives no separate narrative of the theft and identifies no additional factual dispute requiring resolution.

The National Motor Vehicle Theft Act of 1919 defined a motor vehicle to include an automobile, automobile truck, automobile wagon, motorcycle, or any other self-propelled vehicle not designed for running on rails. Another section criminalized interstate or foreign transportation of a motor vehicle with knowledge that it had been stolen. Airplanes were already familiar when Congress enacted the statute in 1919, but the enumeration, the reports and the debates contained no reference to aircraft.
sections.Issue: Whether an airplane is a motor vehicle within the National Motor Vehicle Theft Act's residual category of any other self-propelled vehicle not designed for running on rails, so that Congress made interstate transportation of a stolen airplane punishable under this particular statute.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 1931, in an opinion by Justice Holmes with no separate opinion, held that the National Motor Vehicle Theft Act did not cover aircraft, and it reversed the Tenth Circuit's judgment affirming McBoyle's conviction. The Court interpreted the Act and reversed a conviction outside its coverage. It did not invalidate the Act for constitutional vagueness, find that McBoyle did not know the airplane was stolen, or rule that airplane theft was lawful.
sections.Reasoning:
Justice Holmes acknowledged that, etymologically or in an expanded usage, vehicle can describe transportation on land, water or air. But in everyday speech the word evoked something moving on land, and the surrounding enumeration reinforced that understanding: automobile trucks, wagons and motorcycles were all land vehicles, and the phrase about not running on rails continued the same subject. Read as a whole, the definition conveyed a category of land vehicles, and its catchall expanded membership within that category without abandoning it. The full brief notes that this illustrates ejusdem generis, although the opinion does not depend on reciting the Latin label.

Related legal usage corroborated the reading. The general federal statutory definition of vehicle described means of transportation on land, a tariff provision expressly differentiated aircraft, and the Act's language followed several state statutes and District of Columbia traffic regulations that could not reasonably have been understood to regulate transportation through the air. Although airplanes were familiar in 1919, the detailed enumeration, the reports and the debates did not mention them.

The final paragraph adds a criminal-law justification. The law should give the public a reasonably clear warning, in language ordinary people can understand, of the line between permitted and punishable conduct, even though criminals ordinarily do not read statutes before acting. That transporting stolen aircraft raises the same sort of problem as transporting stolen automobiles did not create statutory coverage, and the Court would not assume that Congress would have written broader language had legislators thought about airplanes. The full brief cautions that the case resolves the statutory category through ordinary usage and context and should not be reduced to a rule that every disputed criminal statute is automatically construed for the defendant.

LRS-SUP-0005B.rule: In section 12(2) of the Securities Act of 1933, prospectus is a term of art referring to a document held out to the public in a public offering by an issuer or controlling shareholder, so a privately negotiated stock-purchase agreement is not a prospectus.

sections.Parties: Gustafson, McLean and Butler owned Alloyd, a manufacturer of plastic packaging and heat-sealing equipment, and sold substantially all its stock. The buyer was Wind Point Partners, purchasing through a newly created acquisition corporation, Alloyd Holdings, which later used the name Alloyd Co. The buyers sued the sellers for rescission under section 12(2) of the Securities Act of 1933, contending that the purchase agreement was a prospectus; the sellers contended that prospectus meant a document soliciting the public. The sellers won summary judgment in the district court, the Seventh Circuit vacated, and the Court reviewed the Seventh Circuit's judgment.
sections.Procedural History: The Northern District of Illinois granted summary judgment to the sellers. It considered section 12(2) limited to initial stock offerings and regarded the buyers' access to corporate information and inspection opportunities as distinguishing their negotiated purchase from such an offering. The Seventh Circuit vacated and remanded in light of its intervening Pacific Dunlop decision, which read the statutory definition of prospectus broadly enough to include a stock-purchase agreement. The Court granted certiorari to resolve the conflict with the Third Circuit's narrower approach. For purposes of the statutory issue it assumed that the agreement contained material misstatements and that the sellers could not establish due care; those assumptions were not findings. The Court reversed the Seventh Circuit and remanded for proceedings consistent with its interpretation.
sections.Material Facts:
Alloyd's stock had been issued in 1961. In 1989 its three owners arranged a private, negotiated sale of substantially all that already-issued stock. The buyers conducted an extensive investigation, including review of KPMG's business analysis. Because the parties did not undertake an early inventory, they negotiated using estimates and provided for a later adjustment. The price included $18,709,000 for the stock and an additional $2,122,219 reflecting estimated growth in net worth since the preceding year-end. The sellers represented that the financial statements fairly presented the company's condition and that no material adverse change had occurred, and the agreement required an adjustment if the year-end audit showed a difference between estimated and actual value.

The audit showed lower-than-estimated earnings, entitling the buyers to an $815,000 adjustment, which the sellers paid with interest. The buyers nevertheless sued for rescission under section 12(2), alleging that the contractual representations contained material inaccuracies and that the agreement itself was a prospectus triggering the federal remedy.
sections.Issue: Whether a privately negotiated stock-purchase agreement is a prospectus within section 12(2) of the Securities Act of 1933, which imposed liability on a seller who sold by means of a prospectus or oral communication containing a material misstatement or omission, when section 2(10) defines prospectus to include any prospectus, notice, circular, advertisement, letter, or written, radio, or television communication offering or confirming the sale of a security.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 1995, in an opinion by Justice Kennedy for a five-Justice majority, with four Justices dissenting, held that the contract and its representations were not a prospectus within the meaning of the 1933 Act because they described a private transaction and were not held out to the public. The Court construed prospectus as a term of art referring to a public offering by an issuer or controlling shareholder. It reversed the Seventh Circuit and remanded. The decision removed the asserted section 12(2) rescission theory; it did not adjudicate state-law contract or fraud claims or eliminate other federal securities remedies.
sections.Reasoning:
Justice Kennedy began with section 10, which generally required a prospectus to contain registration-statement information. The parties agreed that this privately negotiated agreement need not contain such information and required no exemption, so it was outside section 10's category. Applying the presumption that identical words in different parts of one Act carry the same meaning, the majority concluded it was not a prospectus under section 12 either, and thought it more natural to link section 12(2) to the Act's public-offering disclosure system than to read it as creating extensive liability for private transactions. Turning to section 2(10), the majority refused to read communication in isolation: the principle against needless redundancy and noscitur a sociis, understanding a word by the company it keeps, pointed to widely disseminated public solicitations, consistent with the ordinary securities usage of prospectus as a document inviting the public to subscribe for securities. It distinguished United States v. Naftalin because section 17(a) lacked the limiting reference to prospectus, and found no basis to attribute to Congress rescission liability for casual secondary-market communications without fraud or reliance. It read the House report as focusing civil liability on information used to solicit the public.

Justice Thomas, dissenting with Justices Scalia, Ginsburg and Breyer, would begin with the provision creating the cause of action and apply the express definition, which is not limited to public offerings. He disputed both canons, noted that definitions apply unless context otherwise requires, and offered a hypothetical Act defining car to include motorcycles, trucks and trailers. Justice Ginsburg, dissenting separately with Justice Breyer, added that the American drafters borrowed the British definition while omitting its public-offering limitation and that early commentators and decisions applying section 12(2) to private transactions supported the broader understanding; she would leave any narrowing to Congress.

LRS-SUP-0005C.rule: Under ejusdem generis, general words that follow specifically named things reach only things of the same kind, so other dangerous weapon after dagger, dirk and stiletto covers stabbing weapons and not a rifle.

sections.Parties: The prosecution charged Smith, a passenger in a van stopped by Detroit police, and three other occupants under Michigan's carrying-concealed-weapons statute, MCLA 750.227, after an M-1 rifle was found in the van. Smith moved to quash the information on two grounds: that an M-1 rifle was not among the dangerous weapons covered by section 227, and that the evidence did not establish probable cause that he knowingly carried the rifle. He lost in the trial court and the Michigan Court of Appeals and then brought an interlocutory appeal to the Michigan Supreme Court.
sections.Procedural History: After a preliminary examination, the defendants were bound over for trial. Smith moved to quash the information, the formal charging document. The trial court denied relief, reasoning that an M-1's military character brought it within the statute. The Michigan Court of Appeals affirmed, noting that the 43-inch rifle was heavy and could also be used as a club. Smith obtained an interlocutory appeal to the Michigan Supreme Court, so the appeal came before any final trial judgment of guilt. The court reversed the lower courts and directed that the information be quashed, without deciding Smith's probable-cause question.
sections.Material Facts:
At the preliminary examination, Detroit police officer Ward testified that he and his partner observed a Ford Econoline van making several erratic U-turns and stopped it. Approaching, Ward saw through the right window what he believed was a rifle stock, opened the door, and removed an M-1 rifle from beneath the second seat. Smith, a passenger, was sitting on the third seat with his feet up. Officers also found a cartridge belt and ammunition clips on the front seat between two other defendants, Gaut and Turner. These were facts presented in preliminary-examination testimony, not jury findings that Smith possessed the rifle or knew it was there.

Section 227's first clause prohibited carrying a dagger, dirk, stiletto, or other dangerous weapon, except hunting knives adapted and carried as such, concealed on the person or concealed or otherwise in an occupied vehicle. A separate clause addressed pistols carried without the required license, and a companion definition treated a pistol as a firearm thirty inches or less in length, or a firearm whose construction and appearance concealed its character as a firearm.
sections.Issue: Whether the residual phrase other dangerous weapon in MCLA 750.227, following dagger, dirk and stiletto, or the statute's separate reference to pistols, made carrying a long M-1 rifle in an occupied vehicle an offense under that section.
sections.Holding: The Michigan Supreme Court in 1975, in an opinion by Chief Justice Thomas Giles Kavanagh joined by four other justices, with two justices not sitting and no dissent, held that section 227 did not cover the M-1 rifle. The general phrase following dagger, dirk and stiletto was limited to weapons of the same class, and the rifle did not fit the separate statutory definition of pistol. The court reversed and directed that the information be quashed, expressly declining to decide the probable-cause and knowledge question. It did not establish that all rifle transportation was lawful or that prosecution under a different applicable law would be impossible.
sections.Reasoning:
The lower courts had focused on the rifle's dangerousness, which the court thought answered the wrong question: whether the rifle was dangerous in ordinary speech did not determine whether the legislature's particular list included it. The court applied ejusdem generis. When general language follows specifically named subjects, courts ordinarily understand it to include other things of the same kind, class, character or nature. Daggers, dirks and stilettos were stabbing weapons, so the residual phrase covered comparable stabbing weapons rather than every object capable of inflicting harm. If dangerousness alone were the common category, the specific list would do little work. Recognizing that limit did not deny the M-1's danger.

The court then tested the pistol clause separately. The rifle was longer than the statutory thirty-inch limit and was not brought into that category merely by being a firearm.

The wider scheme confirmed the narrower reading. Another provision, MCLA 750.226, prohibited going armed with a pistol or other firearm, or listed weapons, with intent to use the weapon unlawfully against another person, and the rifle was unquestionably a firearm within it, so the legislature had addressed long guns. Reading section 227 to cover rifles would permit a serious felony charge without proof of that unlawful intent and could sweep in ordinary hunters transporting rifles. That the chosen reading made some prosecutions harder did not authorize courts to shift conduct into the easier-to-prove offense. A footnote cited a law governing transportation of firearms in vehicles and a provision regulating specified weapons such as machine guns and silencers. Any decision to strengthen long-gun regulation belonged to the legislature.

LRS-SUP-0005D.rule: Where a statute's literal breadth would produce odd results and raise serious constitutional questions, a court may look to purpose and history and adopt a fairly possible narrower construction; so read, FACA's utilized did not cover the Justice Department's use of the ABA committee.

sections.Parties: Washington Legal Foundation sued the Department of Justice in October 1986 after being refused the identities of judicial candidates under consideration and the reports and meeting minutes of the American Bar Association's Standing Committee on Federal Judiciary. Public Citizen intervened in that action. Both organizations sought a declaration that the Federal Advisory Committee Act covered the Department's relationship with the committee and an injunction stopping the Department's use of the committee until compliance. The Department argued that the committee was outside FACA and that applying it would violate separation of powers. The ABA intervened for the appeal and also contested standing.
sections.Procedural History: An earlier suit against the ABA and its committee had been dismissed because the Department was considered the proper defendant. In the action against the Department, the district court for the District of Columbia in 1988 accepted that FACA covered the relationship but dismissed because applying the statute would intrude on the President's Article II nomination authority. The challengers appealed directly to the Court. The ABA intervened for that appeal and contested Article III standing, arguing that the claimed injury was a generalized grievance and that disclosure exemptions meant a favorable ruling would afford no real relief. The Court affirmed the dismissal on statutory grounds, leaving the constitutional questions undecided by the majority.
sections.Material Facts:
Since 1952 the Department of Justice had sought confidential evaluations of prospective federal judges from the ABA's Standing Committee on Federal Judiciary. The ABA was a private professional association; its fourteen-member committee was chosen by the association, received no federal money, and did not independently recommend people for nomination. For most covered lower-court nominations, a prospective nominee completed an ABA questionnaire, a committee representative examined writings and interviewed lawyers, judges and the candidate, and the chair communicated an informal assessment to the Department. If the Department requested a formal evaluation, committee members considered a report and voted; the Department received the rating but not the final report. After nomination the rating became public at the Senate Judiciary Committee's request, while investigations, reports, interviews and deliberations remained confidential.

The Federal Advisory Committee Act, enacted in 1972, defined an advisory committee to include a committee established or utilized by the President or an agency to obtain advice or recommendations. Covered committees generally had to file a charter, announce meetings, keep minutes, allow public access subject to exemptions, and operate with a federal official authorized to attend and adjourn meetings.
sections.Issue: Whether the organizations had standing despite the public character of their concerns and possible disclosure exemptions; whether FACA's reference to committees utilized by the President or an agency covered the Department's solicitation of the ABA committee's evaluations of prospective judges; and, if it did, whether that application would be unconstitutional.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 1989, in an opinion by Justice Brennan for five Justices, with three Justices concurring only in the judgment and Justice Scalia not participating, held that the organizations had standing because they sought specific information and access and had been denied it, but that FACA's definition, construed in light of the statute's purposes, the predecessor regulatory scheme, legislative development and serious constitutional difficulties, did not cover this relationship. The district court's dismissal was affirmed. The majority did not decide whether applying FACA would be unconstitutional, and the holding is not a universal exemption for every private adviser or every committee receiving no federal funds.
sections.Reasoning:
On standing, a refusal of requested information and notice was a sufficiently distinct injury even if many others could make the same request, and possible exemptions did not defeat redressability because FACA could still require a charter and notice.

On coverage, Justice Brennan acknowledged that the Department used the committee in the ordinary sense of utilized. But an unqualified definition could reach nearly any consultation with an outside group, such as an American Legion post, a civil-rights organization or the President's political party. The majority treated those consequences as strong evidence that Congress did not intend the dictionary's full breadth, and, citing Holy Trinity, allowed examination of purpose and history when literal language produced an odd result. It traced FACA to Executive Order 11007, under which several administrations never treated the ABA relationship as covered, and read the House and Senate proposals and the conference report as focused on committees established by or for agencies; it called the question close. A General Services Administration regulation was substantial but not controlling. Constitutional avoidance supplied the deciding consideration: applying management and public-access rules to confidential consultation during judicial nomination raised serious Article II and separation-of-powers questions, and a fairly possible alternative construction was available.

Justice Kennedy, joined by Chief Justice Rehnquist and Justice O'Connor, concurred only in the judgment. He thought the ordinary meaning of utilized plainly covered this recurring institutional arrangement, accepted only a narrow absurdity exception, criticized Holy Trinity, and considered the avoidance construction not fairly possible. Reaching the constitutional question, he concluded that the Appointments Clause assigns nomination to the President and that FACA's interference with his confidential consultation made this application invalid.

LRS-SUP-0006A.rule: The Federal Arbitration Act requires enforcement of agreements for individual arbitration according to their terms; its saving clause does not preserve defenses that attack arbitration's individual character, and the NLRA contains no clear and manifest command displacing the FAA.

sections.Parties: Three cases were consolidated: Epic Systems Corporation v. Jacob Lewis, Ernst & Young LLP v. Stephen Morris and others, and National Labor Relations Board v. Murphy Oil USA, Inc. Employees who had employment agreements requiring individual arbitration sought to pursue Fair Labor Standards Act wage claims and related state-law claims together. The employees argued that the National Labor Relations Act made the waivers of collective proceedings illegal; the employers maintained that the Federal Arbitration Act required enforcement. In the Court, the Solicitor General and the Board submitted opposing interpretations.
sections.Procedural History: In Morris, the district court granted the employer's motion to compel arbitration. The Ninth Circuit reversed in 2016, reasoning that the FAA's saving clause preserved a federal illegality defense because the NLRA protected concerted legal action; Judge Ikuta dissented. The Seventh Circuit likewise accepted the employees' position in Epic in 2016. The Fifth Circuit reached the contrary result in Murphy Oil in 2015. The Board's 2012 D.R. Horton ruling had accepted the labor-law argument, and some circuits agreed or deferred. The Court granted certiorari to resolve the disagreement. It reversed and remanded the Seventh Circuit judgment in Epic and the Ninth Circuit judgment in Ernst & Young, and affirmed the Fifth Circuit judgment in Murphy Oil.
sections.Material Facts:
The employment agreements required disputes to be resolved in individual arbitration rather than class or collective proceedings. The majority used Morris as its principal example. Morris was a junior accountant at Ernst & Young. His agreement permitted him to choose the arbitration provider and authorized the arbitrator to grant relief available in the relevant court, but required different employees' claims to be heard separately. After his employment ended, Morris sued, alleging that the firm had misclassified junior accountants as professional employees and paid salaries without required overtime. He sought a nationwide FLSA collective proceeding under 29 U.S.C. 216(b) and a Rule 23 class proceeding for California claims.

Justice Ginsburg's dissent adds that Epic and Ernst & Young emailed the arbitration terms to employees and treated continued employment as acceptance. The employees did not rely on fraud, duress or unconscionability as contract defenses. The FAA dates from 1925; the NLRA, enacted in 1935, protects organization, collective bargaining and other concerted activities for mutual aid or protection.
sections.Issue: Whether the National Labor Relations Act invalidates agreements requiring individual arbitration of these employment claims, either through the Federal Arbitration Act's saving clause, which preserves grounds for the revocation of any contract, or as a conflicting federal command that displaces the FAA.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 2018, in an opinion by Justice Gorsuch for a five-Justice majority, with four Justices dissenting, held that the NLRA does not invalidate these agreements and that they must be enforced according to their terms. The saving clause preserves generally applicable defenses but not a defense that attacks an arbitration agreement because it requires individual proceedings, even when phrased as federal illegality, and the NLRA does not provide the clear and manifest congressional direction needed to displace the FAA. The holding does not make arbitration agreements immune to ordinary formation defenses, prevent parties from choosing class arbitration, or decide whether the employees were correctly paid.
sections.Reasoning:
Sections 2, 3 and 4 of the FAA require respect for arbitration agreements and the procedures the parties selected, and the majority treated individual arbitration as a fundamental attribute protected by its precedents. Concepcion had rejected a state unconscionability rule conditioning enforcement on class proceedings. The employees did not claim a defect in how the contracts were obtained; they objected to the individual nature of the proceedings, so the defense was incompatible with the FAA whatever its label.

On the NLRA, the majority applied the strong presumption against implied repeal. Section 7 concerns organization and collective bargaining and mentions neither class procedures nor arbitration. Ejusdem generis narrowed the catchall about other concerted activities by reference to the preceding organizational and bargaining activities, and the NLRA's silence on class certification, notice and similar matters confirmed that it created no procedural entitlement. Congress knows how to prescribe litigation procedures or restrict arbitration expressly, and does not hide major changes in ancillary provisions. In the full opinion the Court also refused Chevron deference to the Board, because the Board was construing a statute it did not administer, the Executive spoke with two voices, and traditional tools resolved the question; the full brief presents this as the 2018 analysis, not present law.

Justice Thomas, concurring, read grounds for revocation as concerning formation of the agreement, which public-policy illegality does not address. Justice Ginsburg, dissenting with Justices Breyer, Sotomayor and Kagan, viewed collective litigation as concerted activity for mutual aid, rejected the use of ejusdem generis as too cramped, considered a required prospective waiver unlawful under section 8(a)(1) and illegality a generally applicable defense, argued alternatively that the later and more specific labor statute should prevail, and warned that small wage claims could be uneconomical to pursue individually.

LRS-SUP-0006B.rule: At a preliminary stage, regular forces in 10 U.S.C. 12406(3) likely means the regular military, and the statute likely applies only where the military could lawfully execute federal law but the President is unable to do so with those forces.

sections.Parties: Illinois and other respondents challenged the President's federalization of National Guard members and their deployment around Chicago. The federal government, having been restrained by the district court and only partly relieved by the Seventh Circuit, applied to the Court for a stay of the order restricting deployment. The Government relied on 10 U.S.C. 12406(3) and on inherent presidential constitutional authority to protect federal personnel and property; the respondents wanted the restriction on federalization and deployment maintained.
sections.Procedural History: The Northern District of Illinois entered a temporary restraining order barring both federalization and deployment. The Seventh Circuit allowed Guard members to remain federalized within Illinois but maintained the restriction on deployment. The Government then requested a stay from the Court, and Justice Barrett referred the application to the full Court. The Court requested supplemental letter briefs on the meaning of regular forces, an issue addressed by the district court but absent from the parties' initial briefs in the Court. On December 23, 2025, the Court denied the application, leaving the interim arrangement in place. The ruling is a stay decision at a preliminary stage; it did not finally dispose of the lawsuit, and the full brief does not address the case's later procedural status.
sections.Material Facts:
The federal government asserted that immigration-enforcement operations around Chicago encountered obstruction, threats, assaults, property damage and violent protests, particularly at an Immigration and Customs Enforcement processing facility in Broadview. The Court's account expressly attributes those descriptions to the Government, and the stay decision did not conclusively adjudicate every disputed incident. On October 4, 2025, President Trump called approximately 300 Illinois National Guard members into federal service to protect federal personnel and property. Texas Guard members were federalized and sent to Chicago the next day.

The statute invoked was 10 U.S.C. 12406(3), which permits a call into federal service when the President is unable with the regular forces to execute federal law. In supplemental briefing, the Government argued that regular forces referred to civilian federal law-enforcement officers, while the respondents argued that it meant the regular military. The Government also relied on inherent presidential authority to protect federal personnel and property, while maintaining that such protection did not constitute execution of the laws under the Posse Comitatus Act. The President had not invoked another statute supplying an exception to that Act.
sections.Issue: Whether the Government had shown grounds to stay the order restricting National Guard deployment in Illinois, which turned on what regular forces means in 10 U.S.C. 12406(3) and whether the Government had established the statutory predicate that the President was unable with those forces to execute federal law.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 2025, in an unsigned opinion, denied the application for a stay, with Justice Kavanaugh concurring in the judgment and Justices Alito, Thomas and Gorsuch dissenting, six votes against the stay and three for it. In conclusions expressly framed as likely ones at a preliminary stage, the Court said that regular forces likely means the regular United States military, that section 12406(3) likely presupposes a situation in which the military could legally execute federal law, and that the Government had not identified sufficient authority for that predicate in Illinois. The Court left undecided the reviewability of presidential findings, other deployment authorities, the Insurrection Act and the legality of particular immigration encounters.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court adopted the regular-military reading as the likely meaning after supplemental briefing, without explaining it at length in its short order. Because the statute calls for assessing the military's ability to execute the law, it likely operates where the military could lawfully perform that task. The Posse Comitatus Act generally prohibits military execution of the laws absent express constitutional or congressional authorization, and the President had invoked no other statute supplying an exception. The Government instead relied on a protective power while arguing that protection is not execution of the laws for Posse Comitatus purposes. Citing Azar v. Allina Health Services, the Court applied the presumption that Congress does not silently give the same term different meanings in related statutes; on the Government's own account, the protective task therefore did not show the predicate for this federalization. The Court did not hold every protective military mission unlawful or definitively deny inherent Article II protective authority.

Justice Kavanaugh, concurring in the judgment, agreed that regular forces likely means the military but would have stopped at the narrower ground that the President apparently had not made the required finding that he was unable with the military to ensure execution of federal law. He considered the Court's further analysis difficult and consequential.

Justice Alito, joined by Justice Thomas, would have granted the stay. He objected that the Court reached an argument the respondents had abandoned, would have read unable to mean substantial impairment rather than total incapacity, invoked Martin v. Mott and Luther v. Borden on deference to presidential militia calls, and argued that the same-meaning presumption is defeasible. Justice Gorsuch, dissenting separately, relied on specified parts of Justice Alito's opinion, not including its deference analysis, and reserved the larger questions.

LRS-SUP-0011-SLAUGHTER.rule: Article II requires that the President be able to remove at will the Commissioners of the FTC, principal officers exercising executive power, so their for-cause protection is unconstitutional and Humphrey's Executor is overruled to the extent it permitted otherwise; the Federal Reserve and other entities were reserved.

sections.Parties: Rebecca Slaughter and Alvaro Bedoya, Commissioners of the Federal Trade Commission removed by President Trump without statutory cause, sued the President and other executive officials for declaratory and injunctive relief restoring them to office. They alleged that the removal was ultra vires, violated the Administrative Procedure Act, and violated the Constitution. Bedoya later formally resigned and his claims were dismissed as moot, so only Slaughter's claims reached the Court. The government argued that Article II requires that the President be able to remove FTC leaders at will and sought the rejection or overruling of Humphrey's Executor; Slaughter defended that precedent.
sections.Procedural History: The District Court for the District of Columbia granted Slaughter summary judgment, declared the purported removal ultra vires, and permanently enjoined interference with her performance of lawful duties, considering Humphrey's Executor v. United States controlling. A divided D.C. Circuit panel denied the government's request for a stay pending appeal, with Judge Rao dissenting. The Court stayed the district court's order and granted certiorari before judgment, so the D.C. Circuit had ruled only on interim relief and not on the merits appeal. On June 29, 2026, the Court reversed the judgment of the district court and remanded for further proceedings consistent with its opinion.
sections.Material Facts:
The Federal Trade Commission has five Commissioners appointed by the President with Senate confirmation, serving staggered seven-year terms, with no more than three from the same political party. The Federal Trade Commission Act permits the President to remove a Commissioner only for inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance in office. The Commission administers and enforces approximately eighty statutes, makes substantive rules, investigates regulated businesses, conducts administrative adjudications, and brings civil enforcement suits.

Slaughter, a Democrat, was nominated by President Trump and confirmed in 2018, and was confirmed for a second term in 2024. When Trump began his second term in January 2025, the Commission had two Republicans and three Democrats. He replaced the Chair with Andrew Ferguson, and the former Chair, Lina Khan, resigned her seat shortly afterward. In March, Trump removed Slaughter and Bedoya without alleging any of the statutory causes; his notice stated that their service conflicted with his administration's priorities and invoked Article II. The removals left the two Republican Commissioners.
sections.Issue: Whether the Federal Trade Commission Act's for-cause removal restriction can constitutionally prevent the President from removing Slaughter, a principal officer exercising executive power, without one of the statutory grounds, and whether Humphrey's Executor, which upheld the same provision, should be overruled.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 2026, in an opinion by Chief Justice Roberts for six Justices, with Justice Sotomayor dissenting joined by Justices Kagan and Jackson, held that the removal restriction is contrary to Article II's separation of powers. The FTC's rulemaking, administrative enforcement, adjudication and civil litigation powers place it within the President's general administrative control, so he must be able to remove its Commissioners at will. The Court overruled Humphrey's Executor to the extent it permitted a contrary arrangement, reversed the district court, and remanded. Justice Thomas joined all but Part III-B, which reserved questions about the Federal Reserve and other entities and officials not before the Court. The Court did not abolish the FTC or invalidate its substantive programs.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority began with Article II's vesting of executive power in one President and his duty to take care that the laws are faithfully executed. Those clauses establish a hierarchy in which subordinate officers assist the President and removal makes them accountable to him. On the majority's account, which the dissent contested at length, the Decision of 1789 confirmed a constitutional removal power that Congress cannot diminish. The majority read Ex parte Hennen, Parsons and especially Myers v. United States as supporting presidential control through removal.

Humphrey's Executor had described the FTC as quasi-legislative and quasi-judicial and exercising no part of executive power. The majority considered that classification untenable in light of Buckley, Chadha, Bowsher, Morrison, Free Enterprise Fund and Seila Law. Its stare decisis analysis found the reasoning unsound, the decision inconsistent with later cases and its boundaries uncertain, and rejected reliance on congressional creation of independent agencies. The Commission's binding regulations, administrative enforcement and civil suits are each executive power, and its multimember, bipartisan design did not save the restriction. The majority rejected a general reasonableness test for removal limits. Part III-B cautioned that the opinion does not determine the Federal Reserve's status and reserved tenure protection for judges of non-Article III courts.

Justice Gorsuch, concurring, agreed but warned that removing insulation transfers control of broad delegated rulemaking and adjudicative powers to the President, and urged enforcement of limits such as nondelegation and major questions. Justice Sotomayor, dissenting, would have sustained the protection: Humphrey's Executor addressed the same statute, Congress has power to create offices and enact necessary and proper laws, the Decision of 1789 rejected Senate participation in removals without forbidding for-cause tenure, and reliance on the precedent was unusually strong.

LRS-SUP-MEAD.rule: An agency interpretation qualified for Chevron treatment only when Congress delegated authority to make rules carrying the force of law and the agency issued the interpretation in exercising that authority; otherwise it received Skidmore respect according to its persuasive force.

sections.Parties: Mead Corporation imported day planners and challenged Customs' classification of them as bound diaries subject to a four-percent duty. After unsuccessful administrative protests, Mead sued in the Court of International Trade; the United States defended the classification and argued that Customs classification ruling letters deserved Chevron deference. The government won in the Court of International Trade, Mead won in the Federal Circuit, and the Court reviewed the Federal Circuit's judgment.
sections.Procedural History: After another unsuccessful administrative protest, Mead sued in the Court of International Trade. That court granted the government's summary-judgment motion and adopted Customs' reasoning without addressing deference. While Mead's appeal was pending, the Court decided United States v. Haggar Apparel Co., recognizing Chevron treatment for Customs regulations, and the government argued that classification letters deserved the same. The Federal Circuit rejected the analogy, gave the challenged letter no deference, and rejected Customs' readings of diary and bound. The Court granted review to address the limits of Chevron deference. It vacated the Federal Circuit's judgment and remanded for the Federal Circuit or the Court of International Trade to undertake a Skidmore assessment, without deciding the classification itself.
sections.Material Facts:
Mead's day planners were three-ring binders containing pages for daily schedules, notes, telephone numbers, addresses, calendars and similar information. Under the Harmonized Tariff Schedule, bound diaries, notebooks, address books and specified similar articles carried a four-percent duty at the relevant time, while the residual category was duty free. From 1989 through 1993 Customs repeatedly placed the planners in the duty-free category. In January 1993 it changed position and issued a Headquarters ruling classifying them as bound diaries. The first letter gave little explanation; after Mead protested, Headquarters issued a carefully reasoned but unpublished letter using the broader of two Oxford English Dictionary definitions of diary and reading bound to include metal or plastic fittings.

Ruling letters represented the agency's official position and bound Customs personnel, but they applied to goods identical to the submitted sample or description, could be modified, and ordinarily created no reliance rights for other importers. Forty-six port-of-entry offices as well as Headquarters could issue them, about ten thousand to fifteen thousand a year, ordinarily without notice and comment and often with almost no explanation.
sections.Issue: Whether a Customs classification ruling letter was entitled to Chevron deference, and, if it was not, whether a court should give the letter no deference at all or respect according to its persuasive force under Skidmore v. Swift & Co.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 2001, in an opinion by Justice Souter for eight Justices, with Justice Scalia alone dissenting, held that an agency interpretation qualified for Chevron treatment when Congress had delegated general authority to make rules carrying the force of law and the agency had issued the interpretation in the exercise of that authority. Formal adjudication and notice-and-comment rulemaking could demonstrate that delegation, though other indications of comparable congressional intent remained possible. The Customs letter failed that threshold but remained eligible for respect under Skidmore according to its persuasive force. The Court vacated and remanded without deciding whether the planners were taxable bound diaries.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority distinguished two bases for judicial respect. An agency's experience, consistency, careful reasoning and expertise could make its answer persuasive without making it controlling. Chevron, in the doctrine as of 2001, added a reason to accept a reasonable agency answer: congressional delegation of authority to resolve statutory gaps with legal force. Authorization to act through sufficiently formal procedures was a strong signal of such authority, but the Court refused to make those formats an absolute condition, noting that NationsBank had received Chevron treatment without them.

The question was whether the classification letter invoked authority of that kind. Neither the statute nor Customs' practice indicated that ordinary classification letters should bind beyond their individual transactions. The Court of International Trade could consider new grounds and develop its own record. The letters' limited reliance effects, routine informality, large volume and distribution among many offices did not resemble general lawmaking, and Congress had created no separate category of Headquarters letters with greater authority.

The Federal Circuit's refusal to give any weight went too far. Customs administered an intricate national classification system, and the letter's reasoning, thoroughness, expertise and consistency could matter under Skidmore. The majority rejected an either-or choice between Chevron and no deference.

Justice Scalia, dissenting, would have reversed and sustained Customs' interpretation. He understood Chevron as a background presumption that an agency administering an ambiguous statute has discretion to resolve the ambiguity reasonably, turning on whether the interpretation is the agency's authoritative position rather than on procedural format, and predicted extended litigation and frozen statutory meaning.

The full brief notes that this is a historical account: in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, decided June 28, 2024, the Court overruled Chevron while continuing to recognize that informed agency views can assist through their persuasive force.

LRSR-041.rule: Section 109(b) of the Clean Air Act excludes implementation costs from the setting of national ambient air quality standards, and a delegation is valid if Congress supplies an intelligible principle, which an agency cannot supply by voluntarily limiting its own discretion.

sections.Parties:
Christine Todd Whitman, Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency, and the EPA represented the federal government. The challenged standards were issued in 1997, before Whitman became Administrator. The government sought reversal of the Court of Appeals' nondelegation ruling and defended its interpretation of the provisions governing implementation of the revised ozone standard.

American Trucking Associations and other private companies and organizations, together with Michigan, Ohio, and West Virginia, challenged the standards. They argued that the EPA's interpretation gave it excessive discretion and that the statute should permit consideration of the economic costs of compliance; their cross-petition sought review of the rejection of the cost argument.
sections.Procedural History:
The challengers sought direct review of the rulemaking in the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit under section 307(b)(1) of the Clean Air Act; there was no district-court trial. The panel concluded that the EPA had interpreted section 109 to confer discretion without an intelligible principle, and it remanded so the EPA could adopt a limiting construction constraining its own discretion. Judge Tatel dissented from that conclusion. The court unanimously rejected the argument that the EPA should consider implementation costs, recognized the EPA's authority to revise the ozone standard, and held that Subpart 2 restricted implementation of a revised standard. On rehearing it rejected the EPA's contention that its implementation interpretation was not reviewable final agency action.

The Court granted the EPA's petition and the challengers' cross-petition. It affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded for further proceedings in the Court of Appeals, including disposition of other preserved challenges to the standards.
sections.Material Facts:
Under section 108 of the Clean Air Act the EPA identifies air pollutants and issues air quality criteria describing the scientific knowledge about their effects. Section 109 directs the Administrator to establish national ambient air quality standards. Section 109(b)(1) requires primary standards that, in the Administrator's judgment, based on the criteria and allowing an adequate margin of safety, are requisite to protect public health; secondary standards under section 109(b)(2) protect public welfare. States implement the standards through state implementation plans.

On July 18, 1997, the EPA revised the national standards for ozone and particulate matter, measuring the new ozone standard over eight hours rather than the previous one hour. The EPA maintained that it could set the standards without considering the economic costs of implementing them. The challengers argued that the restrictions could themselves harm public health through their economic effects and that the statute did not specify how much protection was enough.

Part D of Title I contains Subpart 1, with general requirements for areas not meeting a standard, and Subpart 2, added in 1990, with more specific ozone requirements whose classifications and deadlines were built around the older one-hour standard. In the preamble to the revised ozone standard, the EPA announced that it would implement the new standard under Subpart 1 and retain Subpart 2 for the old standard only until an area attained that old standard.
sections.Issue: Does section 109(b) permit the EPA to consider implementation costs when setting a national ambient air quality standard? If not, does the direction to protect public health with an adequate margin of safety supply an intelligible principle, and can an agency cure an unconstitutional delegation by voluntarily restricting its own authority? Was the EPA's ozone implementation interpretation final and ripe for review, and could the EPA implement the revised standard under Subpart 1 so as to displace Subpart 2?
sections.Holding:
The Supreme Court of the United States, 2001, in a principal opinion by Justice Scalia, with a unanimous judgment. All Justices except Justice Breyer joined the part on costs, and all except Justices Stevens and Souter joined the part on nondelegation.

Section 109(b) unambiguously excludes implementation costs from the considerations that determine national ambient air quality standards, primary and secondary; the holding concerns standard-setting under section 109 and does not make costs irrelevant throughout the Act. Section 109(b)(1) supplies an intelligible principle, because the EPA must set standards sufficient, but no more stringent than necessary, to protect public health with an adequate margin of safety. An agency's voluntary self-limitation cannot cure a delegation that lacks an adequate congressional standard. The ozone implementation interpretation was final agency action, ripe for review, and unlawful; the agency was left to formulate a permissible interpretation on remand.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court began with statutory meaning. Section 109(b)(1) tells the Administrator to determine what is requisite to protect public health on the basis of air quality criteria; nothing tells the EPA to trade health effects against the cost of reducing pollution. The Court did not resolve the claim that costly regulation can itself harm health; Congress had not assigned that balancing to the EPA under section 109. Congress expressly referred to costs elsewhere in the Act, and a major alteration of a regulatory program is not hidden in general terms; Congress does not hide elephants in mouseholes. Constitutional avoidance cannot support a reading inconsistent with clear statutory directions.

On nondelegation, the Court applied the intelligible-principle test of J. W. Hampton. An agency cannot repair a missing standard by choosing how much discretion to exercise, because that choice is itself the policy decision reserved to Congress. Section 109 identified the task, the evidence, the protected interest, and the degree of protection, and fell comfortably within delegations previously upheld. Congress need not supply a numerical answer or formula, even for a pollutant with no demonstrable safe threshold.

The implementation interpretation appeared in the final preamble after comment and was a purely legal question whose delay would burden state planning. Applying the then-governing Chevron framework, the Court found real ambiguity in how Subpart 2 fit an eight-hour standard, but the EPA could not reasonably read the Act to make Congress's ozone-specific restrictions largely disappear.

Justice Thomas concurred, expressing willingness to reconsider in a future case whether the intelligible-principle test fully enforces Article I. Justice Stevens, joined by Justice Souter, would have described the power as legislative power permissibly delegated within adequate limits. Justice Breyer would ordinarily hesitate to read a statute to require ignoring a regulation's serious adverse consequences, but found costs excluded here by the Act's structure, history, and technology-forcing purpose.

LRSR-042.rule: A delegation is permissible when Congress supplies an intelligible principle, and its scope must first be fixed by statutory interpretation; a plurality read SORNA to require registration of pre-Act offenders as soon as feasible, leaving the Attorney General only transitional implementation.

sections.Parties: Herman Avery Gundy was the criminal defendant in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York, the appellant in the Second Circuit, and the petitioner in the Supreme Court. The United States prosecuted him for failing to register under the Sex Offender Registration and Notification Act (SORNA) and defended his conviction. Gundy sought relief on the ground that Congress had unconstitutionally delegated legislative power to the Attorney General when it authorized him to specify SORNA's applicability to people convicted before the Act.
sections.Procedural History:
The district court initially dismissed the prosecution on the ground that a necessary trigger for Gundy's registration obligation was absent. In an earlier appeal in 2015, the Second Circuit reversed and reinstated the indictment, holding that he had been required to register no later than August 1, 2008. After reinstatement, the district court rejected Gundy's argument that travel while technically in federal custody could not satisfy the interstate-travel requirement, held a bench trial on stipulated facts, found the elements established beyond a reasonable doubt, and on June 16, 2016, entered judgment imposing time served and five years of supervised release.

The Second Circuit affirmed on June 22, 2017, rejecting his preserved nondelegation argument as foreclosed by circuit precedent. The Court granted review only of the nondelegation question concerning section 20913(d) and affirmed the Second Circuit's judgment, leaving the conviction in place.
sections.Material Facts:
Congress enacted SORNA in 2006 to establish a more comprehensive and uniform national system of sex-offender registration. Section 20913(a) requires a sex offender, defined to include an individual who was convicted of a covered sex offense, to register and keep the registration current where the person resides, works, or studies. Under 18 U.S.C. section 2250(a), a person required to register who travels in interstate commerce and knowingly fails to register faces up to ten years' imprisonment. Section 20913(b) sets initial registration before completion of imprisonment, or within three business days of sentencing when no imprisonment is imposed. Section 20913(d) authorizes the Attorney General to specify the applicability of the requirements to offenders convicted before enactment and to prescribe registration rules for them and others unable to comply with subsection (b).

The Attorney General issued an interim rule in February 2007 specifying that SORNA applied to offenders convicted before its enactment, and a final rule in December 2010 reiterated that coverage.

Gundy pleaded guilty in Maryland in 2005 to a sexual offense involving a minor. During a later federal sentence he was held in Pennsylvania. On July 17, 2012, he traveled unescorted by commercial bus from Pennsylvania to a residential reentry center in the Bronx, and on August 27, 2012, he was released to a private Bronx residence. He did not register in Maryland or New York.
sections.Issue: Does Congress violate Article I's restriction on transferring legislative power when it authorizes the Attorney General to specify the applicability of SORNA's registration requirements to offenders convicted before the statute's enactment? That question turns first on whether section 20913(d) requires application to all pre-Act offenders as soon as feasible, or leaves the Attorney General to decide whether, when, and to what extent those offenders are covered at all.
sections.Holding:
The Supreme Court of the United States, 2019, rejected the nondelegation challenge and affirmed by a 5-3 judgment. Justice Kagan announced the judgment in a plurality opinion joined by Justices Ginsburg, Breyer, and Sotomayor; Justice Alito concurred in the judgment only; Justice Kavanaugh took no part.

The plurality construed SORNA to require the Attorney General to apply the registration requirements to pre-Act offenders as soon as feasible, so that Congress had resolved the coverage policy and left only administrative and transitional problems to him. That limited assignment satisfied the intelligible-principle test. The phrase as soon as feasible is the plurality's construction and is not an express command in section 20913(d). Because Justice Alito did not join that interpretation or reasoning, neither the plurality's analysis nor the dissent's proposed test is a five-Justice holding.
sections.Reasoning:
The plurality reasoned that a court cannot measure the adequacy of Congress's instructions until it identifies what authority the statute confers. Gundy's argument depended on reading the statute to let the Attorney General register all pre-Act offenders, some, or none, for any reason.

The plurality relied on Reynolds v. United States, which held that SORNA did not apply to pre-Act offenders of its own force before the Attorney General acted, and read it as recognizing a limited reason for that step: the practical difficulty of registering a large existing population and the impossibility of meeting a release deadline already passed. It then read the statute as a whole. The declared purpose was a comprehensive national system; the definition of sex offender uses the past tense, was convicted; legislative history showed concern with previously convicted offenders missing from registries; and section 20913(d) addresses offenders unable to comply with subsection (b). The plurality accepted the rule from Whitman that a missing congressional standard cannot be supplied afterward, but said it was identifying a standard the enacted statute already contained. So construed, the delegation was narrower than many previously upheld, and a feasibility judgment is an ordinary administrative function.

Justice Alito, concurring in the judgment, could not say the statute lacked a discernible standard under the Court's existing approach, noted that very broad delegations had been sustained since 1935, and said he would support reconsideration if a majority were willing.

Justice Gorsuch, joined by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas, dissented. He would permit Congress only to let another branch fill in details, to make a rule depend on executive fact-finding, or to assign nonlegislative responsibilities. SORNA fit none of these, because which pre-Act offenders must register was a central coverage choice left to the nation's chief prosecutor. He also rejected the plurality's narrowing construction, since section 20913(d) contains no feasibility command.

LRSR-043.rule: When Congress takes action that is legislative in purpose and effect, altering the legal rights, duties, and relations of persons outside the Legislative Branch, it must comply with bicameral passage and presentment to the President unless the Constitution itself authorizes a different procedure.

sections.Parties: Jagdish Rai Chadha was the person subject to deportation, the petitioner for review in the Ninth Circuit, and an appellee or respondent in the Supreme Court. He challenged the House resolution that overturned the suspension of his deportation and sought to prevent the Immigration and Naturalization Service from deporting him on that basis. The INS, which administered the immigration statute for the Attorney General, was the appellant in the principal Supreme Court case; it agreed that the legislative veto was unconstitutional but would enforce the deportation order unless a court prevented it. The House of Representatives and the Senate defended the veto and separately sought review.
sections.Procedural History:
After the House resolution, the Immigration Judge reopened the proceeding and, concluding that he lacked authority to invalidate an act of Congress, ordered Chadha deported on November 8, 1976. The Board of Immigration Appeals dismissed his appeal on the same ground. Chadha petitioned the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit for review of the final deportation order; there was no district-court merits judgment. The INS agreed that the one-House veto was unconstitutional, and the court invited the House and Senate to submit briefs as amici curiae. In 1980 the Ninth Circuit held that the House lacked constitutional authority to require Chadha's deportation through this mechanism and directed the Attorney General not to deport him on the basis of the resolution.

The INS appealed to the Supreme Court under 28 U.S.C. section 1252, and the House and Senate petitioned for certiorari. The Court granted the petitions, postponed consideration of jurisdiction over the appeal, heard argument and reargument, held the cases properly before it, and affirmed the Ninth Circuit.
sections.Material Facts:
Chadha, of East Indian origin, born in Kenya and holding a British passport, lawfully entered the United States in 1966 on a nonimmigrant student visa. His authorized stay expired on June 30, 1972, but he remained. On October 11, 1973, the INS ordered him to show cause why he should not be deported. At a January 11, 1974, hearing he conceded deportability and sought suspension of deportation under section 244(a)(1) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, which let the Attorney General, in his discretion, suspend deportation of a person with seven years' continuous presence, good moral character, and extreme hardship. On June 25, 1974, an Immigration Judge ordered his deportation suspended. Section 244(c)(1) required the Attorney General to report each suspension to Congress.

Section 244(c)(2) provided that, during the session when a suspension was reported or before the close of the next session, either the House or the Senate could adopt a resolution stating that it did not favor the suspension, in which case the Attorney General had to deport the person or permit voluntary departure.

On December 12, 1975, Representative Eilberg introduced House Resolution 926, opposing permanent residence for six named individuals, including Chadha; the committee had reviewed 340 cases and concluded these six did not satisfy the statutory requirements, particularly hardship. On December 16, 1975, the House adopted it. The resolution had not been printed or made available to other members, the record disclosed no floor debate or recorded vote, and it was not submitted to the Senate or presented to the President.
sections.Issue: May Congress authorize either chamber, acting alone and without presentment to the President, to overturn the Attorney General's suspension of an individual's deportation and thereby require deportation? If the veto is unconstitutional, can it be severed from the suspension authority? Do the parties' alignment and the availability of other possible immigration relief prevent the courts from deciding the constitutional question?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States, 1983, in an opinion by Chief Justice Burger joined by five other Justices, with a 7-2 result, held the one-House veto in section 244(c)(2) unconstitutional. The House's resolution was legislative because it changed the legal rights, duties, and relations of Chadha and executive officials outside the Legislative Branch, so it required bicameral passage and presentment; Congress may alter or revoke delegated authority only through constitutionally prescribed legislative action. The Court severed the veto from the remaining suspension provisions, relying on the Act's severability clause, statutory history, and the workability of the remaining scheme. It also held judicial review available: Chadha faced a concrete, redressable injury, alternative relief was speculative, the INS would enforce the order absent relief, and the question was not a political question.
sections.Reasoning:
On the threshold questions, the Court held that the INS could appeal because the judgment prevented it from carrying out a deportation order it would otherwise execute. Section 406, the severability clause, created a presumption that Congress did not intend the whole scheme to depend on the veto, and the legislative history did not overcome it. Chadha had standing, and his marriage to a United States citizen in August 1980 and the Refugee Act of 1980 offered only speculative relief. Congress's participation supplied an adversarial defense, and Article I supplied judicially manageable standards.

On the merits, the Court began with Article I, sections 1 and 7: bills must pass both chambers and be presented to the President, and section 7, clause 3 extends presentment to orders, resolutions, and votes. Presentment guards against legislative encroachment and improvident measures; bicameralism ensures deliberation by differently constituted bodies. The resolution overruled the Attorney General's decision and imposed an obligation to deport, altering rights and duties outside the Legislative Branch. Without the veto, Congress could have reached that result only by legislation, and the original passage of section 244 did not supply advance compliance for later decisions under it. The Constitution's express one-chamber powers, impeachment, impeachment trial, and advice and consent on appointments and treaties, did not include this veto. Historical use and convenience could not amend the prescribed process.

Justice Powell concurred in the judgment on the narrower ground that the House had assumed an adjudicative function by deciding whether identified individuals met existing legal criteria. Justice White dissented, defending the veto as an accommodation between broad delegation and congressional responsibility and as a condition built into the original, validly enacted grant. Justice Rehnquist, joined by White, dissented on severability; he viewed the veto as an integral limitation on the suspension power and would have reversed.
